For $q\equiv3\pmod4$, even powers have the explicit representation $(q^j)^2+0^2$; if an odd power were represented, repeatedly divide both coordinates by $q$ using the three-mod-four divisibility lemma until an impossible representation of $q$ remained.

items.title: Characterisation of positive integers that are sums of two squares
items.strategy: Use canonical prime factorisation. If every prime congruent to three modulo four has even valuation, represent each prime-power factor by the preceding lemma and multiply the finite list. Conversely, for a represented integer and such a prime $q$, the local divisibility lemma removes $q^2$ from the integer and $q$ from both coordinates. Induction on $v_q(n)$ excludes a final odd exponent and proves that every such valuation is even. Include $n=1$ through the empty factorisation.

items.title: Coprime primitively represented factors have a primitive product representation
items.strategy: Let $P=a^2+b^2$ and $Q=c^2+d^2$ be primitive with $\gcd(P,Q)=1$, and use $(ac-bd,ad+bc)$ for the product. If a prime divided both new coordinates, the two linear combinations with $a,b$ would force it to divide $P$, while the two combinations with $c,d$ would force it to divide $Q$; primitivity rules out the alternative in each case. This contradicts coprimality of $P,Q$.

items.title: Powers of primes congruent to $1$ modulo $4$ have primitive two-square representations
items.strategy: Induct from $(1,0)$ and a primitive representation $p=a^2+b^2$. Given a primitive representation $(u,v)$ of $p^e$, the two sign variants of the identity give candidate representations of $p^{e+1}$. Any prime common to a candidate's coordinates must be $p$. If both candidates had both coordinates divisible by $p$, their sums and differences would force $p\mid u,v$, since $p$ is odd and divides neither $a$ nor $b$. Thus at least one candidate is primitive.

items.title: Characterisation of primitive sums of two squares
items.strategy: If $n=x^2+y^2$ with $\gcd(x,y)=1$, the three-mod-four divisibility lemma excludes every prime congruent to three modulo four, and reduction modulo four shows that $4\nmid n$, equivalently $v_2(n)\le1$. Conversely factor $n$ into a possible single factor $2$ and powers of distinct primes congruent to one modulo four. Represent those prime powers primitively and combine the pairwise-coprime factors using the primitive-product lemma, with the empty factorisation giving $n=1$.

items.title: Primitive sums of two squares are closed under products unless both factors are even
items.strategy: Apply the primitive characterisation to the two positive factors. Neither has a prime divisor congruent to three modulo four. Each has $2$-valuation at most one, and the condition that they are not both even makes the sum of their $2$-valuations at most one. Valuation additivity and the characterisation then give a primitive representation of the product.

items.title: Divisors greater than one of primitively represented integers are primitively represented
items.strategy: Let $d>1$ divide a positive integer $n$ with a primitive two-square representation. Every prime exponent of $d$ is at most the corresponding exponent of $n$. Hence $d$ has no prime divisor congruent to three modulo four and has $2$-valuation at most one. Apply the primitive characterisation.

items.title: Squarefree sums of two squares
items.strategy: For squarefree positive $n$, every prime valuation is zero or one, so the general criterion reduces to the absence of odd prime factors congruent to three modulo four. If a representation had coordinate gcd greater than one, a prime dividing that gcd would have its square divide $n$, contradicting squarefreeness. Thus every representation of an eligible squarefree integer is primitive, including the empty-factor case $n=1$.

pages.title: Sums of Two Squares — Examples

items.title: Thue's collision argument gives $73=3^2+8^2$
items.strategy: Verify $27^2\equiv-1\pmod{73}$ and take $h=8$. The pairs $(0,0)$ and $(3,8)$ collide under $(i,j)\mapsto27i-j\pmod{73}$, so the difference gives $3\cdot27\equiv8$. Multiplying the root congruence gives $73\mid3^2+8^2$, while the small bounds force equality.

items.title: Extended Euclid gives $73=3^2+8^2$ from the root $27$ of $-1$
items.strategy: Verify $27^2\equiv-1\pmod{73}$ and run $73=2\cdot27+19$, $27=19+8$. Back-substitution gives $8=3\cdot27-73$, hence $3\cdot27\equiv8\pmod{73}$. Squaring and using the root congruence shows $73\mid3^2+8^2$, and direct evaluation gives equality. This is the source's Euclidean route, distinct from the preceding collision route.

items.title: Prime factorisation gives two representations of $221$ as a sum of two squares
items.strategy: Use $13=2^2+3^2$ and $17=1^2+4^2$. The two sign variants of the identity give $221=10^2+11^2=14^2+5^2$. Verify both equalities directly and record that composite integers need not inherit prime uniqueness.

items.title: $539=7^2\cdot11$ is not a sum of two squares
items.strategy: Refute the claim that every positive integer is a sum of two squares. If $539=x^2+y^2$, the prime $11\equiv3\pmod4$ would divide both coordinates, so $11^2$ would divide $539$. Its displayed prime factorisation has $11$ to exponent one, a contradiction. Relate this direct obstruction to the general valuation criterion.

items.title: The representations $221=5^2+14^2=11^2+10^2$ recover the factors $13$ and $17$
items.strategy: Normalize the two representations with odd coordinates first and apply the factorisation construction. The half-sums and half-differences yield $e=2,f=3,g=4,h=1$, so the two proper factors are $e^2+f^2=13$ and $g^2+h^2=17$. Check their product and both original representations.

items.title: The primitive two-square criterion distinguishes $289$, $34$, and $833$
items.strategy: Verify the primitive representations $289=15^2+8^2$ and $34=3^2+5^2$. Verify $833=28^2+7^2$, but note that $7\equiv3\pmod4$ divides $833$, so the primitive criterion forbids every primitive representation even though a nonprimitive one exists. Check the displayed coordinate gcds and prime factors.

items.title: $68=8^2+2^2$ is representable but has no primitive two-square representation
items.strategy: Refute the claim that every represented positive integer is primitively represented. Squares modulo four are zero or one, so a representation of a multiple of four must have both coordinates even. Apply this to $68=8^2+2^2$ and compare with the $2$-valuation clause of the primitive criterion.

items.title: Squarefree sums of two squares up to $30$
items.strategy: List the squarefree positive integers at most $30$, discard exactly those with an odd prime factor congruent to three modulo four, and obtain $1,2,5,10,13,17,26,29$. Give an explicit two-square representation of each retained integer and verify that every coordinate gcd is one. This is a bounded, independently checkable construction.

pages.title: Lagrange Four Square Theorem

items.title: Representations as sums of four squares
Euler's four-square product identity
items.strategy: State the identity with Conrad's sign pattern $z_1=x_1y_1+x_2y_2+x_3y_3+x_4y_4$, $z_2=x_1y_2-x_2y_1-x_3y_4+x_4y_3$, $z_3=x_1y_3+x_2y_4-x_3y_1-x_4y_2$, $z_4=x_1y_4-x_2y_3+x_3y_2-x_4y_1$, and prove it by expanding both sides and cancelling cross terms. The sign pattern is load-bearing and must be displayed, not summarised: [[lem-four-square-descent]] uses exactly this pattern to get $m \mid z_i$. The identity is a polynomial identity over $\mathbb{Z}$, so it holds for all integer inputs including zeros and negatives.

items.title: Sums of four squares are closed under products
items.strategy: Take representations of the two factors and substitute into the identity. State the zero case explicitly: $0=0^2+0^2+0^2+0^2$, and the formula still gives a representation of the product when either factor is $0$. No positivity is needed anywhere.

items.title: For every prime $p$ the congruence $x^2+y^2+1\equiv 0\pmod p$ is solvable
items.strategy: Cases on $p$. For $p=2$ take $x=1$, $y=0$: then $1^2+0^2+1=2$ and $2\equiv 0\pmod 2$. For odd $p$ cite the published [[prop-every-nonzero-residue-mod-prime-is-a-sum-of-two-squares]], whose Statement is: let $p$ be an odd prime and let $a\in\mathbb Z$ with $p\nmid a$; then there are integers $x,y$ such that $x^2+y^2\equiv a\pmod p$. Apply it at $a=-1$. Its hypothesis $p\nmid -1$ holds: $p\mid -1$ would give $-1=pq$ for some integer $q$, hence $1=p(-q)$ and $p\mid 1$, so $p=1$ or $p=-1$ because those are the units of $\mathbb Z$, contradicting $p>1$. From $x^2+y^2\equiv -1\pmod p$ and $1\equiv 1\pmod p$, adding congruences gives $x^2+y^2+1\equiv 0\pmod p$. Do not re-run the square-class counting argument here: it is the proof of the cited proposition, which is homed on `sums-of-two-squares`, and running it again is the duplication Alpha finding B1-1 removed. This citation is this page's dependency edge to its declared prerequisite.

items.title: The least absolute remainder modulo a positive integer
items.strategy: For $m\ge 1$ and $a\in\mathbb{Z}$, divide with remainder to get $a=qm+r_0$ with $0\le r_0<m$; set $r=r_0$ when $2r_0\le m$ and $r=r_0-m$ otherwise. Then $a\equiv r\pmod m$ and $-m<2r\le m$, hence $4r^2\le m^2$. Uniqueness: two such remainders differ by a multiple of $m$ of absolute value less than $m$, so by the divisor bound the difference is $0$. State the bound in the integer form $4r^2\le m^2$ so no rational $m/2$ is needed, and record that $2r=m$ occurs exactly for even $m$ with $r=m/2$, the one boundary the four-square descent must exclude by hand.

items.title: Some multiple $pm$ with $1\le m<p$ is a sum of four squares
items.strategy: Take $u,v$ with $u^2+v^2+1\equiv 0\pmod p$ and replace them by their least absolute remainders $x,y$ modulo $p$; congruences are preserved under squaring and addition, so $p\mid x^2+y^2+1$, and $4x^2\le p^2$, $4y^2\le p^2$. The value $x^2+y^2+1$ is positive, so $x^2+y^2+1=pm$ with $m\ge 1$. For the strict bound argue in integers: $4pm=4(x^2+y^2+1)\le 2p^2+4<4p^2$ because $p^2>2$, so $pm<p^2$ and $m<p$. Present the conclusion as $pm=x^2+y^2+1^2+0^2$, a genuine four-square representation.

items.title: The centred residue quadruple of $pm=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2$ has norm $mn$ with $1\le n<m$
items.strategy: This isolates the boundary work of the descent. With $p$ prime, $1<m<p$ and $pm=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2$, let $a',b',c',d'$ be the least absolute remainders modulo $m$. Squares are congruence-stable, so $m\mid a'^2+b'^2+c'^2+d'^2$; write the value as $mn$ with $n\ge 0$. Rule out $n=0$: it forces $m\mid a,b,c,d$, hence $m^2\mid pm$ and $m\mid p$, so $m=p$ by primality, contradicting $m<p$. The bound $4a'^2\le m^2$ on each coordinate gives $4mn\le 4m^2$, so $n\le m$. Rule out $n=m$: equality forces $4a'^2=m^2$ in each coordinate, so $m$ is even and each $a'=m/2$; then $a\equiv m/2\pmod m$ gives $a^2\equiv (m/2)^2\pmod{m^2}$, so $pm\equiv 4(m/2)^2=m^2\equiv 0\pmod{m^2}$ and again $m\mid p$. Hence $1\le n<m$.

items.title: Descent step: a smaller multiple of $p$ is a sum of four squares
items.strategy: Let $p$ be prime, $1<m<p$ and $pm=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2$. Take the centred residue quadruple $a',b',c',d'$ and the preceding lemma's $n$ with $1\le n<m$ and $a'^2+b'^2+c'^2+d'^2=mn$. Multiply the two representations with Euler's identity in the exact sign pattern of [[lem-euler-four-square-product-identity]], taking $x=(a,b,c,d)$ and $y=(a',b',c',d')$, so $pm\cdot mn=A^2+B^2+C^2+D^2$. Reduce each bilinear coordinate modulo $m$ using $a'\equiv a$, $b'\equiv b$, $c'\equiv c$, $d'\equiv d$: $A\equiv a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2=pm\equiv 0$, $B\equiv ab-ba-cd+dc=0$, $C\equiv ac+bd-ca-db=0$, $D\equiv ad-bc+cb-da=0$. Write $A=mA'$ and so on; then $pm^2n=m^2(A'^2+B'^2+C'^2+D'^2)$ and cancelling $m^2\ne 0$ gives $pn=A'^2+B'^2+C'^2+D'^2$.

items.title: Every prime is a sum of four integer squares
items.strategy: Contradiction. Assume the prime $p$ is not a sum of four squares. The set $S=\{m\in\mathbb{Z} : 1\le m<p$ and $pm$ is a sum of four squares$\}$ is nonempty by the small-multiple lemma and is bounded below by $1$, so it has a least element $m_0$. If $m_0=1$ then $p=p\cdot 1$ is a sum of four squares, against the assumption; so $m_0>1$ and the descent lemma supplies $n$ with $1\le n<m_0$ and $pn$ a sum of four squares. Then $n<m_0<p$, so $n\in S$, contradicting the leastness of $m_0$. The least-element principle for integer sets bounded below is what makes the descent terminate; no infinite regress is written.

items.title: Lagrange's four-square theorem: every nonnegative integer is a sum of four integer squares
items.strategy: Contradiction on a least counterexample. Suppose some nonnegative integer is not a sum of four squares; the set of such integers is bounded below by $0$, so it has a least element $n_0$. Now $n_0\ne 0$ because $0=0^2+0^2+0^2+0^2$, and $n_0\ne 1$ because $1=1^2+0^2+0^2+0^2$; hence $n_0>1$ and $n_0$ has a prime divisor $q$. Write $n_0=qk$; then $k\ge 1$ because $n_0>0$, and $k<n_0$ because $q\ge 2$. By leastness $k$ is a sum of four squares, $q$ is one by the prime case, and closure under products makes $n_0$ one. Treat $0$ and $1$ explicitly rather than through a factorisation, since $1$ is the empty product and $0$ is not a product of primes at all.

items.title: Why the descent fixes one sign pattern in the four-square identity
items.strategy: A justifying remark, not a survey. Record that Euler wrote a second choice of signs ($z_2=x_1y_2-x_2y_1+x_3y_4-x_4y_3$, $z_3=x_1y_3-x_2y_4-x_3y_1+x_4y_2$, $z_4=x_1y_4+x_2y_3-x_3y_2-x_4y_1$, with the same $z_1$) and that Hamilton's quaternion identity uses $z_1=x_1y_1-x_2y_2-x_3y_3-x_4y_4$; cite Conrad Remarks 6.3 and 6.7 and Dummit Lemma 1, which states the second Euler pattern. Then give the one-line computation that makes the choice load-bearing: substituting $y\equiv x\pmod m$ into the pattern fixed in [[lem-euler-four-square-product-identity]] sends all four coordinates to $0$ modulo $m$, and does the same for Euler's second pattern, whereas Hamilton's first coordinate becomes $a^2-b^2-c^2-d^2$ modulo $m$, which the hypotheses of [[lem-four-square-descent]] do not force to vanish. Assert only that this proof's divisibility step needs the pattern displayed, never that no proof can use the quaternion pattern.

items.title: A square is congruent to $0$, $1$ or $4$ modulo $8$
items.strategy: Cases on the parity of $x$, obtained from division with remainder by $2$. If $x$ is odd then $x^2$ is odd and the congruence $t^2\equiv x^2\pmod{2^3}$ is solvable (take $t=x$), so the published unit-square criterion modulo powers of two gives $x^2\equiv 1\pmod 8$. If $x=2k$ then $x^2=4k^2$; when $k$ is even $16\mid x^2$ so $x^2\equiv 0\pmod 8$, and when $k$ is odd $k^2$ is odd and $x^2=4(2l+1)=8l+4\equiv 4\pmod 8$. Record the consequence used later: $x^2\equiv 1\pmod 4$ when $x$ is odd and $x^2\equiv 0\pmod 4$ when $x$ is even, since $8\mid t$ implies $4\mid t$.

items.title: No sum of three integer squares is congruent to $7$ modulo $8$
items.strategy: Exhaustive cases on how many of $x,y,z$ are odd, which is $0$, $1$, $2$ or $3$. Each odd square contributes $1$ modulo $8$ and each even square contributes $0$ or $4$. Three odd gives $3$; two odd gives $2$ or $6$; one odd gives $1$ or $5$ (since $1+4+4=9\equiv 1$); none odd gives $0$ or $4$ (since $4+4+4=12\equiv 4$ and $0+4+4=8\equiv 0$). The attainable residues are exactly $0,1,2,3,4,5,6$, and $7$ is not among them. Enumerating by the number of odd coordinates, rather than by the ten multisets of values, keeps the case list to four and makes exhaustiveness visible.

items.title: If $4$ divides $x^2+y^2+z^2$ then $x$, $y$ and $z$ are all even
items.strategy: Modulo $4$ a square is $1$ when its base is odd and $0$ when its base is even, by the last clause of the squares-modulo-eight lemma. So $x^2+y^2+z^2$ is congruent modulo $4$ to the number $t$ of odd coordinates, and $t\in\{0,1,2,3\}$. If $4$ divides the sum then $4\mid t$, which among $0,1,2,3$ forces $t=0$. Halving each coordinate is then legitimate and is what the obstruction's induction step needs.

items.title: Positive integers $4^a m$ with $m\equiv 7\pmod 8$ are not sums of three integer squares
items.strategy: Induction on $a\in\mathbb{N}$, with $4^a$ the power in the commutative monoid $(\mathbb{Z},\cdot,1)$, so that no natural number is written inside an applied embedding. Base $a=0$: $4^0=1$, so the number is $m\equiv 7\pmod 8$, and a three-square representation would give a sum of three squares congruent to $7$ modulo $8$. Step: suppose $4^{a+1}m=x^2+y^2+z^2$. Then $4$ divides the right side, so $x,y,z$ are all even; writing $x=2x'$ and so on and cancelling the nonzero factor $4$ gives $4^{a}m=x'^2+y'^2+z'^2$, contradicting the induction hypothesis. State the hypothesis as $m$ a positive integer with $m\equiv 7\pmod 8$, and note in the item that this is exactly the shape $8b+7$ with $b$ a nonnegative integer.

items.title: Positive integers $4^a m$ with $m\equiv 7\pmod 8$ need four nonzero squares
items.strategy: Contradiction for the second clause. Existence is Lagrange's theorem applied to the nonnegative integer $n=4^a m$. If some four-square representation of $n$ had a zero coordinate, the remaining three coordinates would be integers whose squares sum to $n$, contradicting the three-square obstruction. Hence every four-square representation of such an $n$ has all four coordinates nonzero: four squares are not merely sufficient here, they are necessary.

pages.title: Lagrange Four Square Theorem — Examples

items.title: $7\cdot 15=105$ through all four bilinear coordinates
items.strategy: Take $7=2^2+1^2+1^2+1^2$ and $15=3^2+2^2+1^2+1^2$, so $x=(2,1,1,1)$ and $y=(3,2,1,1)$. The identity gives $z_1=10$, $z_2=1$, $z_3=-2$, $z_4=0$, and $100+1+4+0=105$. Compute every coordinate, including the one that vanishes, so the reader sees that a zero coordinate is a value of the formula and not an omission.

items.title: The two intersecting square sets modulo $11$ give $1^2+3^2+1=11$
items.strategy: Modulo $11$ the square classes including zero are $\{0,1,3,4,5,9\}$, six of them, matching $(p+1)/2=6$. The translate $\{-1-y^2\}$ is $\{10,9,6,1,5,7\}$, also six. The two sets meet in $\{1,5,9\}$; taking the common value $1=1^2$ and $1=-1-3^2$ gives $1^2+3^2+1=11\equiv 0\pmod{11}$. List both sets in full so the count, not an assertion about the count, is what the reader checks. These two sets and their intersection are the argument of [[prop-every-nonzero-residue-mod-prime-is-a-sum-of-two-squares]] at $a=-1$, written out at $p=11$: that proposition supplies a common value for every odd prime, and [[lem-four-square-congruence-for-primes]] cites it instead of re-running it, so this example is where the mechanism behind that citation is displayed.

items.title: Least absolute remainders modulo $7$ and modulo $8$
items.strategy: Tabulate the least absolute remainders of $0,\dots,7$ modulo $7$ (values $0,1,2,3,-3,-2,-1,0$) and modulo $8$ (values $0,1,2,3,4,-3,-2,-1$). Modulo $7$ every remainder satisfies $4r^2<m^2$ strictly; modulo $8$ the class of $4$ attains $2r=m$, and $4$ and $-4$ are congruent, which is why the lemma's normalisation $-m<2r\le m$ selects $4$. This is precisely the boundary that [[lem-least-absolute-residue-quadruple-of-a-multiple]] has to exclude by a separate argument.

items.title: Descending from $13\cdot 11$ to $13$ in two steps
items.strategy: Start from $143=13\cdot 11=11^2+3^2+3^2+2^2$, a nonminimal multiple. Centred residues modulo $11$ are $(0,3,3,2)$ with norm $22=11\cdot 2$, so $n=2$. Euler's identity gives $(A,B,C,D)=(22,33,33,22)$, each divisible by $11$, and dividing by $11$ gives $26=2^2+3^2+3^2+2^2=13\cdot 2$. Repeat with $m=2$: centred residues $(0,1,1,0)$ have norm $2=2\cdot 1$, the identity gives $(6,4,0,0)$, and dividing by $2$ gives $13=3^2+2^2+0^2+0^2$. Verify every displayed product and sum. Both parities of the modulus appear, which is the point of running two steps rather than one.

items.title: Four essentially different four-square representations of $65$
items.strategy: Exhibit $65=1^2+8^2+0^2+0^2=4^2+7^2+0^2+0^2=2^2+5^2+6^2+0^2=2^2+3^2+4^2+6^2$, Conrad's Example 6.1, verifying each sum. The multisets of absolute values are pairwise distinct, so no two are obtained from one another by reordering coordinates or changing signs. Existence is what Lagrange's theorem asserts; the number of representations is a separate question this page does not answer.

items.title: FALSE: a prime has one four-square representation up to order and signs
items.strategy: The claim is the four-square analogue of the two-square uniqueness statement for primes congruent to $1$ modulo $4$, and it fails. Refute it with $31$, which is prime and satisfies $31=5^2+2^2+1^2+1^2=3^2+3^2+3^2+2^2$; the multisets of absolute values $\{5,2,1,1\}$ and $\{3,3,3,2\}$ are different, so neither representation comes from the other by reordering or sign changes. Verify both sums and the primality of $31$ explicitly.

items.title: Building a representation of $105$ from its prime factors
items.strategy: Factor $105=3\cdot 5\cdot 7$ and take $3=1^2+1^2+1^2+0^2$, $5=2^2+1^2+0^2+0^2$, $7=2^2+1^2+1^2+1^2$. The identity applied to the first two gives $15=3^2+(-1)^2+(-2)^2+1^2$, and applied to that result and $7$ gives $105=4^2+8^2+5^2+0^2$. Check both products by expansion. Negative coordinates appear at the intermediate stage and are harmless, since only squares are read off at the end.

items.title: $7$ and $28$ are not sums of three integer squares
items.strategy: For $7$, run the residue obstruction directly: any three squares contribute residues from $\{0,1,4\}$ modulo $8$ and no three of them total $7$. For $28=4\cdot 7$, show the propagation: a three-square representation of $28$ would have all coordinates even, and halving them would represent $7$ by three squares. Give the finite check for $7$ by hand as well, listing the squares at most $7$, so the reader has both the congruence argument and a direct search.

items.title: $3$ and $5$ are sums of three squares and $15$ is not
items.strategy: Dummit's witness. Verify $3=1^2+1^2+1^2$ and $5=2^2+1^2+0^2$, then note $15\equiv 7\pmod 8$, so the obstruction rules out any three-square representation of $15$. This is exactly why the four-square proof may reduce to primes and a three-square treatment may not: the four-square identity has no three-square counterpart.

items.title: $7$ and $28$ have four-square representations with no zero coordinate
items.strategy: Exhibit $7=2^2+1^2+1^2+1^2$ and $28=5^2+1^2+1^2+1^2$, and prove that no representation of either can have a vanishing coordinate: a zero coordinate would leave a sum of three squares, which the obstruction forbids for $4^0\cdot 7$ and $4^1\cdot 7$. The pair shows both the $a=0$ and the $a=1$ case of the corollary.

pages.title: Positive Definite Binary Quadratic Forms and Reduction

items.title: Integral binary quadratic forms
Integers represented, and primitively represented, by a binary quadratic form
Primitive binary quadratic forms
The discriminant of a binary quadratic form
An integer is the discriminant of an integral binary quadratic form exactly when it is congruent to $0$ or $1$ modulo $4$
items.strategy: Necessity is the square-class check modulo $4$. Sufficiency uses the explicit forms $(1,0,-\Delta/4)$ and $(1,1,(1-\Delta)/4)$, matching the two congruence classes.

items.title: The principal binary quadratic form of a discriminant
Proper equivalence of binary quadratic forms
Integral substitution defines a right action of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$ on integral binary quadratic forms
items.strategy: Write $f\mid M$ for substitution by the integer matrix $M$. The identity matrix fixes every form, and associativity of matrix multiplication gives $(f\mid M)\mid N=f\mid(MN)$.

items.title: Properly equivalent binary quadratic forms represent the same integers, with primitive representations in bijection
items.strategy: If $g=f\mid M$ and $g(x,y)=n$, then $f(M(x,y))=n$. The inverse matrix of $M=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}p&q\\r&s\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ is explicit because $ps-qr=1$, so the same argument runs backwards. Primitive vectors stay primitive under unimodular substitution by the Bézout-style formulas for the inverse coordinates.

items.title: Proper equivalence preserves discriminant and primitivity of the form
items.strategy: Compute the transformed coefficients under a general determinant-one substitution. The discriminant changes by the square of the determinant, and the new coefficients generate the same ideal in $\mathbb Z$ as the old ones because the inverse substitution is again integral.

items.title: Some discriminant $\Delta$ form primitively represents $n$ exactly when $\Delta$ is a square modulo $4n$
items.strategy: From a primitive representation $n=f(r,s)$, extend $(r,s)$ to a determinant-one matrix and move the represented integer into the leading coefficient, so the discriminant becomes a square modulo $4n$. Conversely, if $b^2\equiv\Delta\pmod{4n}$, the form $nx^2+bxy+cy^2$ with $c=(b^2-\Delta)/(4n)$ has discriminant $\Delta$ and primitively represents $n$ at $(1,0)$.

items.title: Positive-definite binary quadratic forms
An integral binary quadratic form is positive definite exactly when its leading coefficient is positive and its discriminant is negative
items.strategy: Complete the square in $4af(x,y)=(2ax+by)^2-\Delta y^2$. This gives one direction immediately and the converse by checking positivity on all nonzero real pairs.

items.title: Reduced positive-definite binary quadratic forms
A non-reduced positive-definite form admits an equivalent positive-definite form with smaller reduction measure
items.strategy: Use the two Gauss moves: swap $(a,b,c)\mapsto(c,-b,a)$ when $c<a$, and shear $(a,b,c)\mapsto(a,b+2ka,ak^2+bk+c)$ with $b+2ka\in(-a,a]$ when $|b|>a$. Except for the final boundary normalization $a=c$ and $b<0$, one of these moves strictly improves the integer measure $a+|b|$.

items.title: Every positive-definite integral binary quadratic form is properly equivalent to a reduced form
items.strategy: Iterate the Gauss moves until the reduction measure cannot decrease further, then do the single boundary sign flip when $a=c$ and $b<0$. The measure is a positive integer, so the algorithm terminates.

items.title: The leading coefficient of a reduced positive-definite form is minimal in its proper-equivalence class
items.strategy: If $g=f\mid\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}p&q\\r&s\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, then the new leading coefficient is $f(p,r)$. Because $(p,r)$ is primitive, the reduced-form inequalities force $f(p,r)\ge a$.

items.title: Properly equivalent reduced forms with the same leading coefficient are equal
items.strategy: Equality of the leading coefficient forces the transformation matrix to have first column $(1,0)$ or $(-1,0)$; the reduced-form interval $(-a,a]$ for the middle coefficient and the boundary sign convention then force the shear parameter to vanish, so the coefficients agree term by term.

items.title: Each proper-equivalence class of positive-definite integral binary quadratic forms contains exactly one reduced form
items.strategy: Existence is the reduction theorem. If two reduced forms are properly equivalent, the minimal-leading-coefficient lemma gives equality of their leading coefficients, and the same-leading-coefficient lemma then forces equality of the whole triples.

items.title: A reduced positive-definite form of discriminant $\Delta$ satisfies $a\le\sqrt{|\Delta|/3}$
items.strategy: For a reduced form, $b^2\le a^2\le ac$. Substituting into $|\Delta|=4ac-b^2$ gives $|\Delta|\ge 3a^2$, which is the required bound.

items.title: For each negative discriminant, there are only finitely many proper-equivalence classes of positive-definite integral binary quadratic forms
items.strategy: Every class has one reduced representative, and the reduced inequalities together with the leading-coefficient bound leave only finitely many triples $(a,b,c)$.

items.title: The class number of primitive positive-definite binary quadratic forms of discriminant $\Delta$
Proper equivalence of positive-definite integral binary quadratic forms is decidable
items.strategy: Reduce both forms and compare the unique reduced representatives. Equality of the reduced triples is equivalent to proper equivalence.

pages.title: Positive Definite Binary Quadratic Forms and Reduction — Examples

items.title: Reducing $(458,214,25)$ to $(1,0,1)$
items.strategy: Run the explicit swap-and-shear algorithm, record the intermediate forms, and multiply the corresponding matrices to one determinant-one matrix carrying the original form to $x^2+y^2$.

items.title: The reduced primitive forms of discriminant $-4$
items.strategy: Use the bound on the leading coefficient to force $a=1$, then solve the discriminant equation under the reduced inequalities. Conclude that $(1,0,1)$ is the unique reduced primitive form and that $h(-4)=1$.

items.title: The reduced primitive forms of discriminant $-8$
items.strategy: Enumerate the reduced primitive forms of discriminant $-8$ exactly as for $-4$. The only possibility is $(1,0,2)$, so the unique reduced primitive form is $x^2+2y^2$ and $h(-8)=1$.

items.title: Odd primes congruent to $1$ or $3$ modulo $8$ are represented by $x^2+2y^2$
items.strategy: Show directly that any value of $x^2+2y^2$ at an odd prime is $1$ or $3$ modulo $8$. For the converse, combine the two reciprocity supplements to get $(-2/p)=1$, turn a solution of $t^2\equiv-2\pmod p$ into the discriminant-square condition for $\Delta=-8$, invoke the primitive-representation criterion, and then use the unique reduced form of discriminant $-8$.

items.title: The reduced primitive forms of discriminant $-20$
items.strategy: Enumerate the reduced primitive forms of discriminant $-20$ under the same bound. The two reduced primitive forms give the form class number $h(-20)=2$.

items.title: The reduced primitive forms of discriminant $-23$
items.strategy: Enumerate the reduced primitive forms of discriminant $-23$ and check that the two signs of the middle coefficient can survive as distinct reduced forms. This produces the three reduced primitive classes and $h(-23)=3$.

items.title: Forms of discriminant $-24$ need not be properly equivalent
items.strategy: Compare $(1,0,6)$ and $(2,0,3)$. They share discriminant $-24$, but the first represents $1$ and the second does not, so representation preservation rules out proper equivalence.

items.title: Distinct reduced forms can represent the same integers
items.strategy: Use $(2,1,3)$ and $(2,-1,3)$. Check that each reduced form represents exactly the same integers by the substitution $(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)$, but the uniqueness theorem forbids proper equivalence because the reduced triples are distinct.

items.title: Improper equivalence can merge two distinct proper classes
items.strategy: The determinant $-1$ substitution $(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)$ carries $(2,1,3)$ to $(2,-1,3)$. This shows exactly what forgetting orientation changes: the two forms are improperly equivalent although the reduced-form uniqueness theorem shows they are not properly equivalent.

items.title: An indefinite proper-equivalence class can contain a cycle of reduced forms
items.strategy: Write out Granville's positive-discriminant reduced-form convention and verify two distinct reduced forms in his discriminant-$60$ cycle. This separates the positive-definite uniqueness theorem from the indefinite reduction theory that belongs with Pell equations and continued fractions.

pages.title: Regular Continued Fractions and Diophantine Approximation

items.title: Finite and infinite regular continued fractions
Convergents of a regular continued fraction
Convergents are given by the standard recurrences and tail formula
items.strategy: Induct on the length of a finite continued fraction. The same induction, or the equivalent product of the standard unimodular 2x2 matrices, gives the tail-substitution formula with a final parameter t in place of the last partial quotient.

items.title: Determinant identity for consecutive convergents
items.strategy: Check the identity in the initial case and use the convergent recurrences to pass from n to n+1 by a one-line cancellation, so the determinant alternates sign and consecutive convergents differ by 1 divided by the product of their denominators.

items.title: Convergents are reduced fractions
items.strategy: Any common divisor of p_n and q_n divides the determinant combination p_n q_{n-1} - p_{n-1} q_n, so it must divide 1. The same determinant identity shows that the two consecutive convergent columns form a Z-basis of Z^2.

items.title: Complete quotients in the continued-fraction algorithm
Complete-quotient tail formula
items.strategy: Substitute the next complete quotient alpha_(n+1) for the last tail parameter in the finite-prefix formula and clear the nested reciprocal. This rewrites the original real number as one linear-fractional expression in alpha_(n+1).

items.title: Every infinite regular continued fraction converges to a unique real number
items.strategy: Use the determinant identity to show that even convergents increase, odd convergents decrease, and every even convergent lies below every odd one. Take the supremum of the even convergents in the complete ordered field and use the gap formula together with q_n >= n to force the odd convergents to the same cut.

items.title: The continued-fraction algorithm for real numbers
items.strategy: Iterate the complete-quotient construction. If a complete quotient becomes integral the expansion stops; otherwise the tail formula expresses the original real as a convergent plus a positive tail, and the convergence theorem forces the infinite expansion to have the original real as its value.

items.title: The continued-fraction algorithm terminates exactly on rational numbers
items.strategy: For a rational input, the complete quotients are the successive reciprocal remainder ratios from the Euclidean algorithm, so the positive remainders strictly decrease and termination follows. Conversely, a finite continued fraction is rational by the convergent recurrence.

items.title: Normalized finite regular continued fractions are unique
items.strategy: The Euclidean-algorithm construction gives one finite expansion for each rational. The identity [..., a_n] = [..., a_n - 1, 1] gives the second expansion, and excluding a final 1 or terminal 0 leaves a single normal form with last partial quotient at least 2 unless the number is an integer.

items.title: Convergent error bound
items.strategy: Apply the complete-quotient tail formula to an irrational alpha, then subtract p_n/q_n and simplify with the determinant identity. The sign alternation shows that the convergents alternate around alpha, and positivity of the next denominator gives the 1 over q_n q_(n+1) bound.

items.title: Convergents are best rational approximations of the first kind
items.strategy: Expand an integer pair (s,r) in the unimodular basis formed by two consecutive convergent vectors. The coefficients are integers, their signs are forced by the alternating placement of the convergents around alpha, and comparing signed distances to the line of slope alpha yields the denominator bound s >= q_(n+1).

items.title: Legendre's criterion for convergents
items.strategy: Choose n with q_n <= s < q_(n+1). The best-approximation theorem turns the strict 1/(2 s^2) bound into a comparison with the n-th convergent, and then the integer |r q_n - s p_n| is forced below 1, so the rational must equal p_n/q_n.

items.title: Quadratic irrationals
Eventually periodic regular continued fractions
Eventually periodic regular continued fractions are quadratic irrationals
items.strategy: A purely periodic tail x satisfies x = (a x + b)/(c x + d) for integers a, b, c, d coming from one period, so x solves a quadratic equation. Appending a finite nonrepeating prefix preserves quadratic irrationality, and nontermination rules out rationality.

items.title: Complete quotients of a quadratic irrational lie in a finite state space
items.strategy: Rewrite each complete quotient of a quadratic irrational in the normalized form (P_n + sqrt(D))/Q_n after clearing denominators and rationalizing. The recurrence preserves divisibility Q_n | D - P_n^2, and the inequalities 0 < P_n < sqrt(D), 0 < Q_n < 2 sqrt(D) for large n leave only finitely many integral parameter pairs.

items.title: Lagrange's theorem for regular continued fractions
items.strategy: The forward implication is the previous fixed-point lemma. For the converse, the finite-state lemma shows that some complete quotient repeats; determinism of the continued-fraction algorithm turns repetition of a complete quotient into repetition of the subsequent digits, hence eventual periodicity.

pages.title: Regular Continued Fractions and Diophantine Approximation — Examples

items.title: A rational number has exactly two finite regular continued-fraction expansions
items.strategy: Run the rational continued-fraction algorithm on one explicit fraction, then apply the last-digit replacement [..., a_n] = [..., a_n - 1, 1] and identify which expansion is normalized by the final-digit-at-least-2 rule.

items.title: The continued fraction of 37/11 matches Euclid and Bézout
items.strategy: Compute the Euclidean quotients and remainders for 37 and 11, read off the continued-fraction digits, and compare the convergent determinants with the Bézout coefficients returned by the extended Euclidean calculation.

items.title: The continued fraction [1; overline 2] for sqrt(2)
items.strategy: Apply the real algorithm to sqrt(2), verify the repeating digit 2, tabulate a few convergents, and check both the alternating error bound and the determinant identity on those convergents.

items.title: The continued fraction [3; overline{1,2,1,6}] for sqrt(14)
items.strategy: Run the complete-quotient recurrence for sqrt(14), record the successive (P_n, Q_n) states, and display the return to the initial state that forces the repeating block 1, 2, 1, 6.

items.title: The golden ratio is [1; overline 1]
items.strategy: Set x = [1; overline 1], solve x = 1 + 1/x, keep the positive root, and compare it with the standard quadratic irrational (1 + sqrt(5))/2.

items.title: The convergents 22/7, 333/106, and 355/113 for pi
items.strategy: Tabulate the convergents of pi through 355/113, use the first-kind best-approximation theorem to compare them with nearby competitors, and then apply Legendre's criterion to explain why 355/113 is singled out by its unusually small error.

items.title: A very good rational approximation need not be a convergent once the Legendre constant exceeds 1/2
items.strategy: Choose an irrational with a semiconvergent just beyond the Legendre threshold, verify that its error is less than C/q^2 for some constant C greater than 1/2, and check directly that the fraction is not among the convergents.

items.title: A negative irrational still has positive later partial quotients
items.strategy: Run the complete-quotient algorithm on one negative irrational, show that the integer part absorbs the sign in the first digit, and verify from the recurrence that every later complete quotient is positive and therefore produces a positive partial quotient.

pages.title: Pell Equations and Generalized Pell Orbits

items.title: Pell's equation
Generalized and negative Pell equations
The norm on the explicit order $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{D}]$
The Pell norm is multiplicative
items.strategy: Expand products in the explicit coordinate model $x + y\sqrt{D}$ and compare coefficients. The same expansion gives the star-product formula on coordinate pairs and proves norm multiplicativity without importing abstract field norm machinery.

items.title: Integral Pell solutions form an abelian group
items.strategy: Identify a solution of $x^2 - Dy^2 = 1$ with $x + y\sqrt{D}$. Closure and inverses come from the explicit multiplicative norm law, while commutativity is inherited from the coordinate multiplication formula in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{D}]$.

items.title: The complete quotients of $\sqrt{D}$ satisfy the $P_n,Q_n$ recurrence
items.strategy: Start from a normalized state $\alpha_n = (\sqrt{D} + P_n)/Q_n$ with $Q_n > 0$ and $Q_n \mid D - P_n^2$. Taking $a_n = \lfloor \alpha_n \rfloor$ and rationalizing $1/(\alpha_n-a_n)$ yields the next state $(P_{n+1}, Q_{n+1})$, while the positivity and divisibility conditions make the normalized state unique.

items.title: Convergents to $\sqrt{D}$ satisfy the norm identity
items.strategy: Insert the normalized next complete quotient into the continued-fraction tail formula for $\sqrt{D}$, clear denominators, and compare coefficients. The determinant identity for consecutive convergents then isolates $p_n^2 - Dq_n^2$ as $(-1)^{n+1}Q_{n+1}$.

items.title: The continued fraction of $\sqrt{D}$ has symmetric period ending in $2a_0$
items.strategy: Use the $P_n,Q_n$ recurrence to prove the bounds $0 < P_n < \sqrt{D}$ and $0 < Q_n < 2\sqrt{D}$ for $n \ge 1$, leaving only finitely many normalized states. Determinism forces a first repeated state, which must be $(a_0,1)$, and conjugating the backward recurrence reverses the intervening states and hence the digits.

items.title: Every Pell equation has a positive nontrivial integral solution
items.strategy: Apply the period-structure theorem and the convergent norm identity at the end of one full period. If the period length is even, the terminal convergent already has norm $1$; if it is odd, the terminal convergent has norm $-1$ and squaring it gives a norm-one solution.

items.title: Negative Pell is soluble exactly for odd period length
items.strategy: The symmetric period structure and the convergent norm identity show that an odd period yields a negative-Pell solution at the last convergent before the return state, and identify the least positive norm-one solution in each parity case. For the converse, apply NT-7's strict Legendre criterion to any positive solution of $x^2 - Dy^2 = -1$ so that it must appear among the convergents of $\sqrt{D}$.

items.title: The fundamental Pell solution
All positive Pell solutions are powers of the fundamental solution
items.strategy: Given a positive solution $\alpha$, choose the unique integer $k$ with $\varepsilon_D^k \le \alpha < \varepsilon_D^{k+1}$. The quotient $\alpha\varepsilon_D^{-k}$ is an integral norm-one element between $1$ and $\varepsilon_D$, so minimality of the fundamental solution forces it to equal $1$.

items.title: All integral Pell solutions are $\pm \varepsilon_D^k$
items.strategy: Among $\alpha$, $\alpha^{-1}$, $-\alpha$, and $-\alpha^{-1}$, exactly one lies in the positive cone. Apply the positive-solutions theorem there, then restore the sign and inverse data.

items.title: Pell-equivalence for generalized solutions
Generalized Pell solutions fall into finitely many Pell orbits
items.strategy: For a nonzero solution $\alpha$, choose the unique integer exponent that places the positive real embedding of $\alpha\varepsilon_D^{-k}$ in a fixed half-open logarithmic interval centered at $0$. The conjugate embedding is then $N/\alpha$, which gives explicit bounds on both coefficients and leaves only finitely many possible representatives.

items.title: Generalized Pell solubility is decidable by bounded search
items.strategy: Search the explicit rectangle from the orbit theorem and retain one representative from each orbit under multiplication by powers of $\varepsilon_D$. The search is finite and succeeds exactly when a solution exists.

items.title: One generalized Pell solution generates infinitely many more
items.strategy: Fix one nonzero solution and multiply it by $\varepsilon_D^k$ for all integers $k$. The norm stays fixed by multiplicativity, and the positive real embedding changes strictly with $k$, so the resulting solutions are distinct.

pages.title: Pell Equations and Generalized Pell Orbits — Examples

items.title: The Pell and negative Pell equations for $D=2$
items.strategy: Compute the period $[1;\overline{2}]$, extract the norm $-1$ solution $1 + \sqrt{2}$, square it to obtain the fundamental norm-one solution $3 + 2\sqrt{2}$, and list the first several powers.

items.title: The Pell equation for $D=3$
items.strategy: Compute the even period of $\sqrt{3}$, identify the least norm-one convergent, and use the parity criterion to show that $x^2 - 3y^2 = -1$ has no integral solution.

items.title: The negative Pell equation for $D=5$
items.strategy: Use the odd period of $\sqrt{5}$ to locate the least solution of $x^2 - 5y^2 = -1$, then square it to obtain the least positive solution of $x^2 - 5y^2 = 1$.

items.title: The Pell equation for $D=14$
items.strategy: Reuse the NT-7 complete-quotient states for $\sqrt{14}$, locate the first returned state, and apply the norm identity to identify the first convergent with norm $1$.

items.title: The large fundamental solution for $D=61$
items.strategy: Compute the period data for $\sqrt{61}$, identify the convergent prescribed by the parity criterion, and use it to illustrate that the least solution can be enormous even though the continued-fraction algorithm is finite.

items.title: Generalized Pell orbits for $x^2 - 6y^2 = 3$
items.strategy: Start from the representative $3 + \sqrt{6}$ and the Pell generator $5 + 2\sqrt{6}$, then verify that every solution lies in one of the resulting orbits under multiplication by powers of $5 + 2\sqrt{6}$.

items.title: Bounded representatives for $x^2 - 7y^2 = 57$
items.strategy: Apply the explicit orbit bounds to $x^2 - 7y^2 = 57$, enumerate the finitely many representatives in that box, and regenerate the full solution set from those representatives by powers of the fundamental Pell unit.

items.title: A generalized Pell solution need not be a convergent
items.strategy: Use a sourced solution such as $3 + \sqrt{6}$ or $8 + \sqrt{7}$, check that its rational quotient is not among the convergents of the relevant square root, and explain that the missing hypothesis is the small-norm bound behind the convergent criterion.

items.title: The elementary Pell order can miss units from the larger quadratic order
items.strategy: Use $D = 5$ and compare $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{5}]$ with the larger explicit order $\mathbb{Z}[(1 + \sqrt{5})/2]$. The unit $(1 + \sqrt{5})/2$ has norm $-1$ and lies outside $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{5}]$, which keeps the NT-8 seam visible without using any theorem about maximal orders.

pages.title: Symmetric Polynomials and the Fundamental Theorem of Symmetric Functions

items.title: Symmetric polynomials as the invariants of variable permutations
The symmetric polynomials form a subring
items.strategy: Every variable permutation fixes zero and one and commutes with addition, additive inverses, and multiplication. Thus the common fixed set is a subring. Include the zero-variable ring as the base ring itself.

items.title: The elementary symmetric polynomials $e_0,e_1,\ldots,e_n$
Vieta expansion: $\prod_{i=1}^n(t-x_i)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k e_k t^{n-k}$
items.strategy: Expand the product and group terms by the subset of variables from which the negative term was selected. A subset of size $k$ contributes sign $(-1)^k$, its variable product, and $t^{n-k}$. Check $n=0$ as the empty-product identity.

items.title: Vieta's formulas identify the coefficients of a split monic polynomial with elementary symmetric functions of its roots
items.strategy: Substitute the roots into the universal expansion and compare coefficients to obtain $a_k=(-1)^k e_k(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)$. Retain roots with multiplicity and handle the monic constant polynomial.

items.title: Monomial symmetric polynomials indexed by partitions
Monomial symmetric polynomials form an $R$-basis of the symmetric-polynomial ring
items.strategy: Partition monomials into permutation orbits. Symmetry makes coefficients constant on an orbit, yielding a finite combination of orbit sums. Distinct orbit sums have disjoint monomial supports, giving uniqueness without dividing by orbit sizes.

items.title: Lexicographic order on exponent tuples and the multidegree of a nonzero polynomial
The leading multidegree of a symmetric polynomial is weakly decreasing
items.strategy: If the greatest exponent tuple has $a_i<a_j$ for some $i<j$, swapping variables $i$ and $j$ produces a monomial with the same nonzero coefficient and a lexicographically larger tuple, a contradiction.

items.title: The leading multidegree of $e_1^{b_1}\cdots e_n^{b_n}$ is $(b_1+\cdots+b_n,b_2+\cdots+b_n,\ldots,b_n)$ with coefficient one
items.strategy: The leading monomial of $e_k$ is $x_1\cdots x_k$. Multiply these monic leading terms and record that the cumulative-sum map from $b$ is injective.

items.title: Every symmetric polynomial over a commutative ring is a polynomial in the elementary symmetric polynomials
items.strategy: For leading tuple $a_1\ge\cdots\ge a_n$, subtract the leading coefficient times $e_1^{a_1-a_2}\cdots e_n^{a_n}$. The leading term cancels and the multidegree decreases. Well-founded lexicographic induction terminates; treat zero and $n=0$ separately.

items.title: The elementary symmetric polynomials are algebraically independent over the coefficient ring
items.strategy: In a nonzero formal relation choose the term with maximal cumulative-sum multidegree after $T_k\mapsto e_k$. Those leading multidegrees are distinct and monic, so the selected nonzero coefficient cannot cancel, even over a ring with zero divisors.

items.title: Fundamental theorem of symmetric polynomials: unique expression as a polynomial in $e_1,\ldots,e_n$
items.strategy: Combine lexicographic existence with algebraic independence for uniqueness, and state the resulting $R$-algebra isomorphism.

items.title: A symmetric polynomial in the roots of a monic polynomial is a unique polynomial in its coefficients and lies in the base ring
items.strategy: Write it uniquely as $Q(e_1,\ldots,e_n)$ and replace each elementary value by the signed coefficient from Vieta. This is independent of root ordering.

items.title: Power sums $p_k$ and complete homogeneous symmetric polynomials $h_k$
The generating-series identity $E(-t)H(t)=1$
items.strategy: Compare each coefficient in $\prod_i(1-x_it)\sum_{k\ge0}h_kt^k$. The calculation is finite in each degree and may equivalently be organized by cancellation among monomials.

items.title: The complete homogeneous symmetric polynomials $h_1,\ldots,h_n$ freely generate the symmetric-polynomial ring
items.strategy: Coefficient comparison expresses each $h_k$ as $(-1)^{k-1}e_k$ plus earlier terms and conversely expresses $e_k$ triangularly in the $h_i$. The inverse triangular substitutions transfer generation and algebraic independence.

items.title: Newton's identities: $k e_k=\sum_{i=1}^k(-1)^{i-1}e_{k-i}p_i$
items.strategy: Differentiate the finite product $E(-t)=\prod_j(1-x_jt)$ formally, multiply coefficientwise by $H(t)$, and compare the coefficient of $t^{k-1}$. No logarithms or division are used. Take $e_0=1$ and $e_k=0$ for $k>n$.

items.title: If $n!$ is invertible, then $p_1,\ldots,p_n$ freely generate the symmetric-polynomial ring
items.strategy: Invertibility of $n!$ makes $1,\ldots,n$ units. Newton's identities recursively solve for each $e_k$ in the power sums. The triangular unit-diagonal change of variables also gives algebraic independence. State the field corollary for characteristic zero or greater than $n$.

items.title: The Vandermonde polynomial $\Delta_n=\prod_{i<j}(x_i-x_j)$
The square of the Vandermonde polynomial is symmetric
items.strategy: A permutation reindexes the unordered pairs of variables. In $\Delta_n^2=\prod_{i<j}(x_i-x_j)^2$, reversing the orientation of a pair has no effect, so every permutation fixes the product. This direct square argument includes characteristic two.

items.title: The discriminant of a monic polynomial as the coefficient expression of $\Delta_n^2$
The discriminant is $\prod_{i<j}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2$ and vanishes exactly when a monic polynomial has a repeated root
items.strategy: Evaluate the defining coefficient polynomial in a splitting field. In a field the product vanishes exactly when two roots coincide, in every characteristic. Translate this into the published repeated-root criterion.

items.title: The monic resultant $\operatorname{Res}(f,g)$ from the symmetric coefficient expression of $\prod_i g(x_i)$
For monic $f$, $\operatorname{Res}(f,g)=\prod_i g(\alpha_i)$ and it vanishes exactly when $f$ and $g$ have a common root
items.strategy: The product in formal roots is symmetric, so its elementary expression defines the resultant from coefficients. Vieta evaluation yields the root product. For positive-degree $f$ over a field, it vanishes exactly when some root of $f$ is a root of $g$, including $g=0$.

items.title: For monic $f,g$ of degrees $n,m$ splitting in a common extension, $\operatorname{Res}(f,g)=\prod_{i=1}^n\prod_{j=1}^m(\alpha_i-\beta_j)$
items.strategy: Write $g(x)=\prod_{j=1}^m(x-\beta_j)$ in the common splitting extension and substitute this factorization into $\operatorname{Res}(f,g)=\prod_{i=1}^n g(\alpha_i)$. If either degree is zero, both sides are the same empty product.

items.title: For monic $f,g$ of degrees $n,m$, $\operatorname{Res}(f,g)=(-1)^{mn}\operatorname{Res}(g,f)$
items.strategy: Take a splitting field of $fg$ and apply the double-root product in both orders. Replacing every factor $\alpha_i-\beta_j$ by $-(\beta_j-\alpha_i)$ contributes one minus sign for each of the $mn$ pairs.

items.title: For monic $f$, if $g-g_1=qf$, then $\operatorname{Res}(f,g)=\operatorname{Res}(f,g_1)$
items.strategy: At every root $\alpha_i$ of $f$, evaluation of $g-g_1=qf$ gives $g(\alpha_i)=g_1(\alpha_i)$. The two root-product formulas are therefore equal, including the zero-degree and zero-polynomial boundary cases.

items.title: For monic $f$ of degree $n$, $\operatorname{Res}(f,f')=(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}\operatorname{Disc}(f)$
items.strategy: At each root, differentiate the split product to obtain $f'(\alpha_i)=\prod_{j\ne i}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)$. Multiplication pairs every difference with its negative, one sign per unordered pair, and comparison with the root formulas gives the identity.

pages.title: Symmetric Polynomials: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Reducing a symmetric polynomial in two variables to a polynomial in $e_1$ and $e_2$
items.strategy: Run the leading-term subtraction algorithm on $x^3+y^3+x^2y+xy^2$, recording each lexicographic decrease and verifying the final expression.

items.title: The lexicographic reduction algorithm in three variables
items.strategy: Use a symmetric polynomial with several orbit types, subtract the prescribed elementary monomial at each leading partition, and verify the resulting expression by expansion.

items.title: A fixed unbalanced one-variable substitution need not preserve lexicographic leading terms
items.strategy: Give two exponent tuples for which the lexicographically larger one receives the smaller weighted exponent under a poorly chosen fixed weight list. Explain why degree-dependent separated weights can work but do not replace the lexicographic proof.

items.title: Newton's identities through $p_4$ in three variables
items.strategy: Write the identities for $k=1,2,3,4$, with $e_4=0$, solve for the first four power sums, and over characteristic zero invert $1,2,3$ to recover the elementary generators.

items.title: Power sums need not generate the symmetric ring in characteristic two
items.strategy: In two variables over $\mathbb F_2$, $p_1=e_1$ and $p_2=e_1^2$. Thus polynomials in $p_1,p_2$ lie in $\mathbb F_2[e_1]$ and cannot equal the independent generator $e_2$.

items.title: Complete homogeneous symmetric polynomials and their recurrence in two variables
items.strategy: Compute $h_0,h_1,h_2,h_3$, verify $h_k=e_1h_{k-1}-e_2h_{k-2}$, and express $e_1,e_2$ back in terms of $h_1,h_2$.

items.title: The discriminant of $x^2+bx+c$ and its double-root criterion
items.strategy: Use roots and Vieta to compute $(\alpha-\beta)^2=b^2-4c$. Check vanishing versus a repeated root in every characteristic, while separating the characteristic-two completed-square issue.

items.title: The discriminant of $x^3+px+q$ is $-4p^3-27q^2$
items.strategy: Apply the resultant-with-derivative identity or reduce the Vandermonde square by Vieta. Establish the integer polynomial identity before specializing to any field.

items.title: Computing the monic resultant of two quadratics from roots and coefficients
items.strategy: For $f=x^2+ax+b$ and $g=x^2+cx+d$, reduce $g(\alpha)g(\beta)$ using Vieta, display the coefficient formula, and test cases with and without a common root.

pages.title: Free Groups and Presentations

items.title: Words in an alphabet with formal inverses, elementary cancellation, and reduced words
Free group on a set of generators
Reduced words form the free group on an alphabet
items.strategy: direct

items.title: Group presentation by generators and relations
Free groups on the same set are uniquely isomorphic compatibly with their generators
items.strategy: constructive

items.title: Every group admits a presentation
items.strategy: direct

pages.title: Free Groups and Presentations — Examples

items.title: Reducing the word $xx^{-1}yy^{-1}x$ leaves the reduced word $x$
items.strategy: direct

pages.title: Free Products and Amalgamation

items.title: The free product of an arbitrary family of groups
items.strategy: Define a free product by its coproduct universal property: compatible data are arbitrary homomorphisms from every factor to one target, with one unique mediating homomorphism. Do not assume the structure maps inject until normal form proves it.

items.title: Reduced syllable words in a family of groups
items.strategy: A syllable is a tagged nonidentity element of one factor. Define a reduced word as a finite syllable list whose adjacent tags differ; the empty word is allowed. Specify elementary multiplication by combining adjacent syllables from the same factor and deleting identities.

items.title: Factor elements act by mutually inverse permutations on reduced syllable words
items.strategy: For g in a factor, define left action on a reduced word by prepending g unless the first syllable lies in the same factor, in which case multiply and delete an identity result. Check all seam cases and prove the action for g^{-1} is inverse. Show each factor map into the permutation group is a homomorphism.

items.title: Reduced syllable words form the free product of a family of groups
items.strategy: Use the factor actions to define multiplication as successive action on the empty word and to separate distinct reduced words. Alternatively describe concatenation followed by seam reduction, then prove associativity through the permutation representation. Evaluate syllables in any target to obtain the unique mediating homomorphism, including the empty family.

items.title: Normal form theorem for free products
items.strategy: Identify the constructed free product with its underlying reduced-word set. Prove every element has one reduced syllable expression and that a nonempty reduced word is not the identity by applying its factor action to the empty word.

items.title: Finite-order elements of a free product are conjugate into factors
items.strategy: Represent a nonidentity element by its reduced syllable word and repeatedly conjugate away matching end-factor syllables until a conjugate is either one syllable or has first and last syllables in different factors. In the latter case every positive power is a nonempty reduced concatenation, so normal form gives infinite order. Hence every nonidentity finite-order element is conjugate to a nonidentity finite-order element of one factor. State the identity separately for a nonempty family and note that the empty-family case is vacuous in the nonidentity formulation.

items.title: The center of a free product with at least two nontrivial factors is trivial
items.strategy: Let z be a nonidentity central element with reduced word x_1...x_n. Choose a nonidentity syllable g from a factor different from the factor of x_1. Then gz is reduced of length n+1. If the last syllable of z lies in g's factor, zg reduces to length at most n; otherwise zg is reduced of length n+1 but starts in a different factor from gz. Normal-form uniqueness gives gz not equal to zg, a contradiction. The identity is central, and the hypothesis supplies the required choice of g even when some other factors are trivial.

items.title: Every canonical factor map into a free product is injective
items.strategy: A nonidentity factor element is a one-syllable reduced word, hence is nonidentity by normal form. Apply the trivial-kernel criterion and include the trivial-factor case.

items.title: Free products are unique up to a unique factor-compatible isomorphism
items.strategy: Use the two universal properties to obtain maps in both directions. Uniqueness makes both composites the identity because they agree with every factor map. Handle the empty family, whose free product is trivial.

items.title: Each factor is a retract of a free product when all other factors are sent trivially
items.strategy: Fix one index. Use the identity on that factor and trivial homomorphisms on all other factors in the universal property, then compose with the injective canonical factor map. State the assertion only for an index belonging to the family.

items.title: A free product has the union presentation of presentations of its factors
items.strategy: After replacing generator alphabets by disjoint copies, show that the group presented by the union of all generators and factor relators has the free-product universal property. Use von Dyck to extend each family of factor maps and uniqueness on generators. Cover empty and singleton families.

items.title: Free groups on disjoint bases freely multiply to the free group on their union
items.strategy: For disjoint sets X_i, compare maps from the union to a target with families of maps from each X_i. The universal properties of the free groups and the free product give the same unique extension, so uniqueness identifies the two groups. Include empty bases and an empty family.

items.title: A free product of copies of the infinite cyclic group is a free group
items.strategy: For each tagged infinite cyclic factor C_i=<c_i>, use the description by integer powers, uniqueness of exponents, and the exponent-addition law to prove directly that (C_i,{x_i}->C_i) satisfies the free-group universal property on the singleton {x_i}. Make the singleton bases disjoint and apply the disjoint-basis theorem. Preserve the arbitrary index set and its empty case.

items.title: The free product of two infinite cyclic groups is the free group on two generators
items.strategy: Specialise the preceding arbitrary-family result to two singleton bases and use the finite-rank definition. Record the compatible images of the two standard generators.

items.title: Pushouts of group homomorphisms
items.strategy: For homomorphisms f:K to G and h:K to H, define a group pushout by the commuting-square universal property. Do not build injectivity into the definition and explicitly allow arbitrary, noninjective homomorphisms.

items.title: A group pushout is the quotient of a free product by the amalgamating relations
items.strategy: Form G*H and quotient by the normal closure of f(k)h(k)^{-1} for k in K. The quotient maps agree on K. Given any compatible pair of maps, free-product universality supplies a map that kills those relators, so quotient universality gives the unique mediator. Include K, G, or H trivial and arbitrary kernels.

items.title: Free products with amalgamation along monomorphisms
items.strategy: When f:K to G and h:K to H are injective, call their group pushout the free product with amalgamation G *_K H. Explain that the notation identifies K with its two images only after the embedding theorem is proved.

items.title: A free product with amalgamation has the factor presentations plus the amalgamating relations
items.strategy: Take disjoint presentations of G and H, use their union presentation for G*H, and add relations identifying a chosen generating set of K through the two monomorphisms. Prove the resulting presentation has the pushout universal property and explain why using all k in K gives the same normal closure.

items.title: Transversal normal-form data for an amalgamated free product
items.strategy: After identifying K with subgroups of G and H provisionally, choose left-coset transversals S_G,S_H containing the identity. Define normal words s_1...s_n k with nonidentity representatives alternating between transversals and k in K. Record length zero and the dependence of the written representative on the transversal choices.

items.title: Factor elements act consistently by permutations on amalgamated normal words
items.strategy: Following Schreier's permutation proof, define P_g(w) by multiplying the terminal K coefficient on the right by g^{-1}, rewriting uniquely with the selected left-coset transversal, and merging with the last syllable when it comes from the same factor. Check P_{gh}=P_g composed with P_h under the library's composition convention, prove inverses act inversely, and prove that the two factor actions agree on K.

items.title: Normal form theorem for free products with amalgamation
items.strategy: Use the factor actions to realise the presented amalgamated product as permutations of its normal-word set. Show every element has a unique form s_1...s_n k and that a positive-length normal word is nonidentity. Prove independence of the chosen transversals through the pushout universal property, while retaining the length-zero K case.

items.title: The factor maps into a free product with amalgamation are injective
items.strategy: A nonidentity element of either factor has either a nontrivial K coefficient or a one-syllable normal form, so it cannot map to the identity. Apply the trivial-kernel criterion and keep the trivial factor and K=G boundary cases.

items.title: The two factor images intersect exactly in the amalgamated subgroup
items.strategy: The amalgamated K-image lies in both factors. Conversely, if images of g in G and h in H agree, the normal form of gh^{-1} can be trivial only when both elements represent the same element of K. Include K trivial and K equal to one factor.

items.title: Amalgamation over the trivial group is the ordinary free product
items.strategy: For the two maps from the trivial group, the compatibility condition is automatic, so the pushout and free-product universal properties coincide. Use uniqueness to obtain the canonical isomorphism and check trivial factors.

items.title: The kernels of the amalgamating maps are killed in the opposite canonical maps to a group pushout
items.strategy: If k lies in ker f, commutativity gives i_H(h(k))=i_G(e)=e; symmetrically i_G(f(ker h)) is trivial. Deduce that injectivity of a canonical factor map can fail for arbitrary pushout data and identify the exact kernel containment without claiming equality.

items.title: A pushout along an isomorphism is isomorphic to the other factor
items.strategy: When f:K to G is an isomorphism, use h composed with f^{-1}:G to H and the identity of H as a compatible cocone. Verify the universal property and obtain the unique isomorphism. Treat trivial groups without a separate argument.

items.title: Conventions and proved scope for free products and amalgamation
items.strategy: Record that free products allow arbitrary index sets; group pushouts allow arbitrary homomorphisms; the notation G *_K H and the normal-form, embedding, and intersection theorems require monomorphisms. State that HNN extensions, Kurosh's subgroup theorem, Grushko's theorem, and Bass-Serre theory are not claimed from this page's declared prerequisites.

pages.title: Free Products and Amalgamation — Examples

items.title: C_2 free-product C_2 is the infinite dihedral group, and the product of its generators has infinite order
items.strategy: Use the union presentation to obtain generators s,t with s^2=t^2=e. Normal form shows every positive power of st is a nonempty reduced word, so st has infinite order. Identify this presentation as the standard infinite dihedral group convention.

items.title: C_2 free-product C_3 has presentation with only the two factor relations and is infinite
items.strategy: The presentation theorem gives <s,t | s^2, t^3>. The words (st)^n are distinct reduced normal forms for nonnegative n, proving infinitude without importing the modular-group identification.

items.title: The canonical surjection from a free product to the direct product of its factors
items.strategy: Map G to G times H by g to (g,e) and H by h to (e,h), then use free-product universality. These images generate the direct product, so the induced map is surjective. Show every cross-commutator lies in its kernel and give nontrivial factors for which normal form makes such a commutator nonidentity.

items.title: FALSE: a free product of abelian groups is abelian
items.strategy: In C_2*C_2 the reduced words st and ts are distinct. Thus the two canonical generators do not commute even though both factors are abelian.

items.title: Amalgamating infinite cyclic groups by multiplication by m and n gives the presentation with relation x^m=y^n
items.strategy: For positive m,n, realise each factor as the one-generator word-quotient free group. Its normal form shows that it is infinite cyclic, and the free-group theorem together with the presentation definition and the empty normal closure gives its empty-relator presentation. Apply the amalgamated-presentation theorem to the injective maps taking the edge generator to x^m and y^n. The amalgam normal form embeds both cyclic factors. Specialise to m=2,n=3 without asserting the torus-knot interpretation.

items.title: Amalgamating C_2 inside C_4 and C_6 gives the presentation with a^2=b^3
items.strategy: Embed C_2 as the unique order-two subgroup in each cyclic factor. The presentation is <a,b | a^4, b^6, a^2=b^3>. Apply embedding and intersection corollaries to verify that the factor images remain C_4 and C_6 and meet in precisely C_2.

items.title: FALSE: canonical factor maps into every group pushout are injective
items.strategy: Take the maps from C_2 to the trivial group and to C_2, the first trivial and the second the identity. The pushout is trivial by its universal property, so the canonical map from the second C_2 is not injective. Relate this directly to kernel collapse.

items.title: A pushout along an isomorphism recovers the other group
items.strategy: For an isomorphism K to G and any homomorphism K to H, construct the pushout as H. Work one concrete cyclic case and check both legs and the unique mediator rather than appealing only to the slogan.

pages.title: Conjugacy in $S_n$, Generation, and the Simplicity of $A_n$

items.title: Conjugating a cycle relabels each entry: $g(a_1\,\ldots\,a_k)g^{-1}=(g(a_1)\,\ldots\,g(a_k))$
items.strategy: Evaluate the conjugate at each relabelled cycle point and at every point outside their set. The first calculation advances one position and the second fixes the point, which proves equality as permutations rather than merely agreement on the displayed support.

items.title: Two elements of $S_n$ are conjugate if and only if they have the same cycle type
items.strategy: Conjugate a disjoint-cycle decomposition factor by factor using the relabelling lemma, proving invariance of cycle type. Conversely align equally long cycles, including fixed points, and define one bijection sending their entries positionwise; the same lemma shows it conjugates the first permutation to the second.

items.title: The conjugacy classes of $S_n$ are indexed by the tuples $(c_1,\ldots,c_n)$ with $\sum k c_k=n$
items.strategy: The cycle-type definition gives exactly one such multiplicity tuple for each permutation, and the conjugacy classification says two permutations give the same tuple exactly when they lie in the same conjugacy class. Construct a representative from disjoint cycles for every admissible tuple, including $n=0$.

items.title: If $\sigma\in S_n$ has $c_k$ cycles of length $k$, then $|C_{S_n}(\sigma)|=\prod_{k=1}^n k^{c_k}c_k!$
items.strategy: A commuting permutation must send each $\langle\sigma\rangle$-orbit to another orbit of the same length. For the $c_k$ length-$k$ orbits, choose an arbitrary permutation of those orbits and an independent cyclic offset on each, giving $c_k!k^{c_k}$ choices; prove these choices assemble uniquely and multiply independently across lengths. Check $c_k=0$, the identity, and $n=0$ via empty products.

items.title: The class equation of $S_n$ is $n!=\sum_{\sum k c_k=n} n!/\prod_k k^{c_k}c_k!$
items.strategy: Index the conjugacy classes by cycle-type tuples, combine conjugacy-class cardinality with the centralizer formula, and sum the disjoint class sizes. At $n=0$ the single empty type contributes $1$.

items.title: $Z(S_n)$ is trivial for $n\ge3$
items.strategy: A central permutation has a singleton conjugacy class, hence its cycle type has class-size formula $1$. Show every nonidentity cycle type for $n\ge3$ has more than one relabelling, or directly choose a transposition whose conjugation changes a moved point; conclude only the identity is central. Record the exceptional abelian groups $S_0,S_1,S_2$.

items.title: The adjacent transpositions $(1\,2),(2\,3),\ldots,(n-1\,n)$ generate $S_n$
items.strategy: Express every transposition $(a\,b)$ with $a<b$ as the standard palindromic word in adjacent transpositions, checking the word pointwise. Since all transpositions generate $S_n$, so do the adjacent ones; include $n=0,1$ as empty generating sets for the trivial groups.

items.title: For $n\ge2$, $(1\,2\,\ldots\,n)$ and $(1\,2)$ generate $S_n$
items.strategy: Conjugating $(1\,2)$ by successive powers of the $n$-cycle produces every neighboring transposition around the cycle, in particular the standard adjacent transpositions. Apply adjacent generation; at $n=2$ the two displayed generators coincide and still generate $S_2$.

items.title: $A_n$ is generated by $3$-cycles for every $n\ge3$
items.strategy: Write an even permutation as a product of an even number of transpositions and pair them. Equal pairs cancel, overlapping pairs are one $3$-cycle, and disjoint pairs are a product of two $3$-cycles by explicit identities; hence every even permutation lies in the subgroup generated by $3$-cycles, while every $3$-cycle is even.

items.title: A conjugacy class in an index-two normal subgroup remains one class or splits into two equal classes, with a centralizer criterion
items.strategy: For $H\trianglelefteq G$ of index two and $x\in H$, write $G=H\sqcup tH$. Then $\operatorname{Cl}_G(x)$ is the union of the $H$-class of $x$ and its $t$-conjugate. The two classes agree exactly when some element outside $H$ centralizes $x$; otherwise they are disjoint and conjugation by $t$ bijects them, giving equal size.

items.title: An $S_n$-class of an even permutation splits in $A_n$ exactly when all cycle lengths, including $1$-cycles, are odd and distinct
items.strategy: Use the index-two splitting lemma with $H=A_n$. An even-length cycle is itself an odd centralizer element; two equal odd-length cycles can be swapped by an odd permutation, including two fixed points. Conversely, when the lengths are distinct and odd, every centralizer element preserves each cycle support and restricts there to a power of that odd cycle, hence is even. This proves both directions and the equal-size conclusion.

items.title: All $3$-cycles are conjugate in $A_n$ for $n\ge5$
items.strategy: They have common cycle type $(3,1^{n-3})$. The splitting criterion does not split that type when $n\ge5$ because the fixed-point length $1$ is repeated; equivalently correct an odd $S_n$ conjugator by a transposition on two fixed points.

items.title: Simple groups
A normal subgroup of $A_n$ containing one $3$-cycle equals $A_n$ for $n\ge5$
items.strategy: Normality contains the whole $A_n$-conjugacy class of the given $3$-cycle. All $3$-cycles form that one class for $n\ge5$, and the separate generation theorem says they generate $A_n$.

items.title: Every nontrivial normal subgroup of $A_n$ contains a $3$-cycle for $n\ge5$
items.strategy: Choose a nonidentity element of the normal subgroup with maximal number of fixed points. If it is not a $3$-cycle, split its cycle structure into the two exhaustive regimes: it has a cycle of length at least three with additional moved points, or it is a product of disjoint transpositions. In each regime choose a $3$-cycle $g$ so the nonidentity commutator $g\sigma g^{-1}\sigma^{-1}$ lies in the subgroup but fixes strictly more points, a contradiction. Verify separately the $4$-cycle and two-transposition edge configurations and the availability of a fifth point.

items.title: $A_n$ is simple for every $n\ge5$
items.strategy: Let $N\trianglelefteq A_n$. If $N$ is nontrivial, the preceding support-reduction lemma supplies a $3$-cycle, and the normal-subgroup lemma then gives $N=A_n$. Exhibit two noncommuting $3$-cycles to ensure $A_n$ is nontrivial and nonabelian under the stated convention for simple groups.

items.title: For $n\ge5$, the only proper nontrivial normal subgroup of $S_n$ is $A_n$
items.strategy: For $N\trianglelefteq S_n$, simplicity makes $N\cap A_n$ either trivial or all of $A_n$. The latter gives $N=A_n$ or $S_n$; in the former case sign is injective on $N$, so a nontrivial $N$ has order two and its unique nonidentity element is central in $S_n$, contradicting triviality of the center.

items.title: $[S_n,S_n]=A_n$ for $n\ge2$, and $[A_n,A_n]=A_n$ for $n\ge5$
items.strategy: Because sign has abelian image, the quotient criterion puts $[S_n,S_n]$ inside $A_n$; every $3$-cycle is an explicit commutator of transpositions, so $3$-cycle generation gives the reverse inclusion. For $A_n$, its commutator subgroup is normal; two overlapping $3$-cycles do not commute, so it is nontrivial, and simplicity forces it to be all of $A_n$.

pages.title: Conjugacy in $S_n$, Generation, and the Simplicity of $A_n$ — Examples

items.title: Conjugating $(1\,4)(2\,5\,3)$ by an explicit permutation in $S_5$
items.strategy: Apply the relabelling formula cycle by cycle, then verify the result pointwise and read off that its cycle type is unchanged. Reverse the calculation to demonstrate the constructive direction of the conjugacy classification.

items.title: The five conjugacy classes of $S_4$ and the class equation $24=1+6+3+8+6$
items.strategy: List the five cycle types, compute each centralizer size from $\prod k^{c_k}c_k!$, divide $24$ by it, and sum the resulting class sizes. Include parity and representatives to prepare the $A_4$ examples.

items.title: The seven conjugacy classes of $S_5$ and their centralizer and class sizes
items.strategy: Enumerate the seven cycle types of five, tabulate $z_\lambda=\prod k^{c_k}c_k!$ and $120/z_\lambda$, and check that the class sizes sum to $120$; mark which types are even and which satisfy the alternating split criterion.

items.title: The conjugacy classes of $A_5$: sizes $1,20,15,12,12$ and the split $5$-cycles
items.strategy: Restrict the even $S_5$ cycle types. The identity, $3$-cycles, and double transpositions remain single classes; the distinct odd type $(5)$ splits into two classes of size $12$. Exhibit representatives from the two $5$-cycle classes and verify the total is $60$.

items.title: $V_4=\{1,(12)(34),(13)(24),(14)(23)\}$ is a proper nontrivial normal subgroup of $A_4$
