items.title: The maximal elementary abelian subgroups of the two extraspecial groups of order $2^{1+2n}$ have orders $2^{n+1}$ and $2^{n}$
items.strategy: Counting, not induction on the factors. Every maximal elementary abelian subgroup $E$ contains $Z(P)$, so $\bar E$ is a subgroup of $P/Z(P)$ of order $2^{k}$ on which the square map vanishes, and $|E|=2^{k+1}$; maximality of $E$ says no $\bar v\notin\bar E$ with $\bar v\perp\bar E$ has $q(\bar v)=0$, because $q(\bar e\bar v)=q(\bar e)+q(\bar v)+b(\bar e,\bar v)$ would then vanish on $\bar E\langle\bar v\rangle$. Count the classes with $q=0$ coset by coset of $\bar E$: on $\bar E$ itself there are $2^{k}$; on a coset inside $\bar E^{\perp}$ the correction term $b(\cdot,\bar v)$ vanishes on $\bar E$ so $q$ is constantly $1$ there and the coset contributes none; on a coset outside $\bar E^{\perp}$ the map $\bar u\mapsto b(\bar u,\bar v)$ is a nonzero linear functional on $\bar E$, so $q$ vanishes on exactly half of it. The orthogonal-complement count gives $|\bar E^{\perp}|=2^{2n-k}$, so the total is $2^{k}+(2^{2n-k}-2^{2n-2k})2^{k-1}=2^{2n-1}+2^{k}-2^{2n-k-1}$ classes, hence twice that many elements $x$ with $x^2=1$. The classification of extraspecial $2$-groups counts those elements as $2^{2n}+2^{n}$ for the plus type and $2^{2n}-2^{n}$ for the minus type, so $2^{k}-2^{2n-k-1}=\pm2^{n-1}$; the left side is strictly increasing in $k$, so $k=n$ in the plus case and $k=n-1$ in the minus case, and both are attained. This proves the orders are exactly $2^{n+1}$ and $2^{n}$ for EVERY maximal elementary abelian subgroup, not merely for a largest one, and it separates the two types a second time, independently of the central-product decomposition.

pages.title: Extraspecial P Groups and Central Products — Examples

items.title: The commutator pairings of $\operatorname{Dih}(C_4)$ and $Q_8$ are the same, while the groups are not isomorphic
items.strategy: Compute both pairings on the two-element bases of the central quotients: each is the alternating pairing sending the basis pair to $1$. Then separate the groups by the number of solutions of $x^2=1$, which is six and two.

items.title: The Heisenberg group of order $27$ has exponent $3$ and thirteen subgroups of order $3$
items.strategy: Instantiate the Heisenberg multiplication at $p=3$, verify that every nonidentity element cubes to the identity using the class-two power formula, and count the subgroups of order three as the nonidentity elements divided by two.

items.title: At $p=2$ the Heisenberg construction produces $\operatorname{Dih}(C_4)$, not a group of exponent $2$
items.strategy: Exhibit an element of order four and match the dihedral relations, then note which step of the odd-$p$ exponent argument fails.

items.title: The modular group of order $27$ has exponent $9$ and exactly three cyclic subgroups of order $9$
items.strategy: Instantiate at $p=3$, list the elements as $a^ib^j$, and compute orders from the relation $bab^{-1}=a^4$.

items.title: The two extraspecial groups of order $32$ have $20$ and $12$ solutions of $x^2=1$
items.strategy: Apply the counting formula to $\operatorname{Dih}(C_4)\circ\operatorname{Dih}(C_4)$ and to $Q_8\circ\operatorname{Dih}(C_4)$ using the values six and two for the factors.

items.title: A choice of four generators exhibiting an extraspecial group of order $32$ as an internal central product
items.strategy: Follow the decomposition theorem on a concrete group: pick a noncentral element, solve the pairing equation for a partner, and check that the centraliser of the resulting subgroup of order eight is the second factor.

items.title: The central product of two cyclic groups of order four along their subgroups of order two is abelian of order eight
items.strategy: Apply the external construction, compute the order from the order formula, and identify the quotient group; this shows the construction is not confined to nonabelian factors and does not always produce an extraspecial group.

items.title: The three maximal abelian subgroups of $\operatorname{Dih}(C_4)$ have order four, as the general bound predicts
items.strategy: List the subgroups of order four, check each is abelian and maximal among abelian subgroups, and compare with $p^{1+n}$ at $p=2$ and $n=1$.

items.title: A direct product of two Heisenberg groups is special with centre of order $p^2$, hence not extraspecial
items.strategy: Compute the centre and the derived subgroup of the direct product coordinatewise; both equal the product of the two central lines, which is elementary abelian of order $p^2$, so the group is special while its centre exceeds order $p$.

items.title: An extraspecial group of order $32$ decomposes both as two quaternion factors and as two dihedral factors
items.strategy: Exhibit the two families of generating subgroups inside one group and check both satisfy the internal central-product conditions; the isomorphism type of the factors is therefore not an invariant of the group.

items.title: FALSE: every special $p$-group is extraspecial
items.strategy: Refute with the direct product of two Heisenberg groups, whose centre has order $p^2$.

items.title: FALSE: for each $n\ge1$ there is exactly one extraspecial group of order $p^{1+2n}$ up to isomorphism
items.strategy: Refute with the two types at each order, separated by the count of square roots of the identity when $p=2$ and by the exponent when $p$ is odd.

items.title: FALSE: two extraspecial $p$-groups whose commutator pairings agree are isomorphic
items.strategy: Refute with $\operatorname{Dih}(C_4)$ and $Q_8$: both pairings are the alternating pairing on a two-dimensional space, and the groups differ.

items.title: FALSE: the commutator pairing of an extraspecial $p$-group is defined without choosing a generator of its centre
items.strategy: Refute by replacing the generator $z$ by $z^{c}$ and observing that the pairing is multiplied by $c^{-1}$; only the pairing up to that scaling is choice-free.

items.title: FALSE: the centre of an extraspecial $p$-group has a complement
items.strategy: Refute with the general argument that a complement would be isomorphic to the elementary abelian central quotient and force the group to be abelian.

items.title: FALSE: some extraspecial $p$-group has order $p^{2n}$
items.strategy: Refute from the central-product decomposition, which forces the order to be $p$ times an even power of $p$.

pages.title: Blocks Primitivity and Multiple Transitivity

items.title: Blocks and block systems for a group action
The translates of a block partition its orbit
items.strategy: If B is a block and x belongs to gB∩hB, then h^{-1}gB meets B and therefore equals B; hence gB=hB. The distinct translates are therefore disjoint, and their union is the orbit-union of B.

items.title: Block systems are exactly the invariant equivalence relations
items.strategy: Send a block system to the relation 'lie in the same block' and check invariance. Conversely, the equivalence classes of a G-invariant relation form a partition into blocks because classes are either equal or disjoint after translation.

items.title: Primitive and imprimitive transitive actions
Blocks in a finite transitive action have a common size
items.strategy: In a transitive action every block in a given block system is a translate of every other. Restriction of the acting permutation gives bijections between any two translates, so all blocks have the same finite cardinality.

items.title: Blocks containing a point correspond to intermediate subgroups
items.strategy: Identify a transitive G-set with G/G_alpha. For an intermediate subgroup H, its orbit H·alpha is a block. For a block B containing alpha, its setwise stabiliser lies between G_alpha and G and recovers B as its orbit of alpha.

items.title: A transitive action on more than one point is primitive exactly when a point stabilizer is maximal
items.strategy: By the subgroup-block correspondence, nontrivial blocks through alpha are exactly the orbits of intermediate subgroups strictly between G_alpha and G. Therefore no such block exists exactly when G_alpha is maximal.

items.title: A transitive action of prime degree is primitive
items.strategy: Any nonempty block has size dividing the prime degree, because blocks in its block system all have the same size. Therefore a block has size 1 or the whole degree, so only the trivial blocks occur.

items.title: Normal subgroups of a primitive action are transitive or lie in the kernel
items.strategy: For N normal in G, the N-orbits form a G-invariant equivalence relation. In a primitive action they are therefore either the one-block partition or the singleton partition. The singleton case means every element of N fixes every point.

items.title: Regular actions
Abelian normal subgroups of faithful primitive actions are regular
items.strategy: A nontrivial abelian normal subgroup N is transitive by the previous theorem. If n in N fixes one point, then for every point m·alpha in the N-orbit we have n(m·alpha)=m(n·alpha)=m·alpha, so n fixes all points and faithfulness forces n=e.

items.title: k-transitive and k-homogeneous actions
k-transitivity implies k-homogeneity and lower transitivity
items.strategy: A map sending ordered k-tuples sends the underlying k-element subsets, so k-transitivity implies k-homogeneity. To get j-transitivity for j<k, pad the ordered j-tuples by distinct extra points and apply k-transitivity.

items.title: Every doubly transitive action is primitive
items.strategy: In a doubly transitive action the point stabilizer is transitive on the complement of the chosen point. A block containing that point and one other point must therefore contain every other point as well.

items.title: Rank, suborbits, and subdegrees of a transitive action
Orbits on ordered pairs correspond to suborbits
items.strategy: Fix alpha. Send a G-orbit in Omega×Omega to the G_alpha-orbit of its second coordinate in a pair (alpha,beta). This is well-defined because two such pairs differ by an element fixing alpha, and the inverse sends a suborbit Delta to the G-orbit of (alpha,beta) for beta in Delta.

items.title: A transitive action on more than one point is doubly transitive exactly when it has rank two
items.strategy: Rank counts the point-stabilizer orbits. In a transitive action one orbit is always the fixed point itself, so rank two means the stabilizer is transitive on the complement, which is exactly double transitivity.

items.title: Sharply k-transitive actions
A finite sharply k-transitive action has order n(n-1)...(n-k+1)
items.strategy: Fix one ordered k-tuple of distinct points. Sharp k-transitivity gives a bijection between G and the set of ordered k-tuples of distinct points by sending g to the image of the fixed tuple.

items.title: The imprimitive wreath product of permutation groups
A transitive imprimitive action embeds modulo its kernel in an imprimitive wreath product
items.strategy: Let Sigma be the block system through a chosen nontrivial block B, let K be the induced action on Sigma, and let H be the induced action of the block stabilizer on B. After choosing a transversal of blocks, each g in G is encoded by its permutation of Sigma together with the induced permutation on each chosen copy of B. This gives the wreath-product embedding.

items.title: Iwasawa's simplicity criterion for primitive actions
items.strategy: Let N be a nontrivial normal subgroup. Primitivity makes N transitive, so G=N G_alpha. If A is abelian and normal in G_alpha, then every conjugate of A lies in N A; if the conjugates of A generate G, this forces G/N to be abelian and hence G'<=N. A perfect group satisfying the hypotheses is therefore simple.

items.title: The finite Iwasawa criterion
items.strategy: This is the faithful finite specialization of the previous theorem. Once G is perfect, every nontrivial normal subgroup contains G'=G and so equals G.

pages.title: Blocks Primitivity and Multiple Transitivity — Examples

items.title: Blocks in a regular cyclic action are cosets of subgroups
items.strategy: Let C_n act on itself by translation. For each divisor d of n, the cosets of the unique subgroup of order d form a block system; for composite n these are nontrivial blocks, while for prime n only the trivial systems occur.

items.title: The natural actions of symmetric and alternating groups
items.strategy: Record that S_n is sharply n-transitive on {1,...,n} and that A_n is (n-2)-transitive for n>=4. The example displays the page's transitivity hierarchy on the standard permutation groups.

items.title: Affine general linear groups are doubly transitive
items.strategy: On a finite vector space V over F_q, the affine maps x↦Ax+b send any ordered pair of distinct points to any other by first matching differences linearly and then translating the first point.

items.title: Dihedral actions of prime and composite degree
items.strategy: For D_n on the vertices of a regular n-gon, prime n forces primitivity by the prime-degree corollary, while composite n admits nontrivial blocks given by evenly spaced vertices forming smaller regular polygons.

items.title: Projective linear actions and Iwasawa's hypotheses
items.strategy: For PSL_2(F_q) on P^1(F_q), the action is doubly transitive, the stabilizer of infinity contains the translation subgroup x↦x+b as a normal abelian subgroup, and elementary matrices show its conjugates generate the whole group. This is the model application of Iwasawa's criterion.

items.title: The imprimitive wreath product preserves its fiber blocks
items.strategy: For H wr K on B×Sigma, the subsets B×{sigma} are permuted among themselves. This makes the standard fiber decomposition a nontrivial block system whenever both base sets have size greater than one.

items.title: The square-affine group of F_7 is 2-homogeneous but not 2-transitive
items.strategy: Let G={x↦ax+b : a in {1,2,4}, b in F_7}. Because every nonzero class in F_7 is a square or minus a square, G sends any two-element subset to any other. But ordered pairs detect whether the difference is a square, so (0,1) cannot be sent to (0,3).

items.title: FALSE: every transitive action is primitive
items.strategy: Refute with a regular cyclic action of composite degree, whose subgroup cosets are nontrivial blocks.

items.title: FALSE: every block is an invariant subset
items.strategy: A block may be moved disjointly rather than fixed setwise; the vertex pairs in the dihedral action show this explicitly.

items.title: FALSE: every 2-homogeneous action is 2-transitive
items.strategy: Refute with the square-affine action on F_7, which is two-homogeneous on unordered pairs but splits ordered pairs by square and nonsquare differences.

items.title: FALSE: every nontrivial normal subgroup of a faithful primitive group is regular
items.strategy: The valid general conclusion is transitivity. The natural action of S_n has normal subgroup A_n, which is transitive but not free for n>=4.

items.title: FALSE: Iwasawa's criterion needs only transitivity
items.strategy: The proof of Iwasawa's criterion uses primitivity to force nontrivial normal subgroups to be transitive; without primitivity the block kernel can obstruct the argument.

pages.title: Socles and the Onan Scott Landscape

items.title: Minimal normal subgroups and the socle of a finite group
Distinct minimal normal subgroups centralize one another
items.strategy: For minimal normal subgroups M and N, the commutator subgroup [M,N] is normal in both and lies in M intersect N. Minimality forces [M,N] to be trivial unless M=N, so distinct minimal normal subgroups commute.

items.title: Minimal normal subgroups of finite groups are characteristically simple
items.strategy: If M is minimal normal in G and K is a characteristic subgroup of M, then K is normal in G. Minimality of M forces K to be trivial or all of M, so M has no proper nontrivial characteristic subgroup.

items.title: Finite characteristically simple groups are direct products of isomorphic simple groups
items.strategy: Choose a minimal normal subgroup of a finite characteristically simple group, collect its distinct automorphic images, use characteristic simplicity to show they generate the whole group, and use pairwise commuting minimal normals to obtain an internal direct product of isomorphic simple factors.

items.title: The socle is characteristic and decomposes as a direct product of minimal normal subgroups
items.strategy: Automorphisms permute the minimal normal subgroups, so the subgroup they generate is characteristic. A maximal irredundant family of minimal normal subgroups then centralizes pairwise, and the direct-product theorem shows their product is the whole socle.

items.title: Minimal normal subgroups of faithful primitive groups are transitive
items.strategy: Apply the published primitive-action normal-subgroup theorem to a minimal normal subgroup. Faithfulness rules out containment in the kernel, so the subgroup must be transitive.

items.title: Two distinct minimal normal subgroups of a primitive group are regular
items.strategy: Distinct minimal normal subgroups centralize one another and are transitive. If one element of one subgroup fixes a point, transitivity of the other and commutation force it to fix every point, so faithfulness makes it trivial.

items.title: A finite primitive group has at most two minimal normal subgroups
items.strategy: Any two distinct minimal normal subgroups are regular. A third one would centralize one of them and hence act regularly too, forcing two distinct point stabilizers inside a regular group, which is impossible.

items.title: A unique abelian minimal normal subgroup gives affine type
items.strategy: An abelian minimal normal subgroup in a faithful primitive group is regular. Minimality plus finite abelian-group structure makes it elementary abelian, and the conjugation action of a point stabilizer on this vector space is faithful with no nontrivial invariant subspace.

items.title: Almost simple finite groups
Affine, almost simple, diagonal, product action, and twisted wreath types
Product-action wreath products are primitive under the standard hypotheses
items.strategy: Work with the standard product action of H wr K on Delta^ell. Primitivity of H together with transitivity of K lets one push any nontrivial block across coordinates until it contains a whole fibre, and the hypotheses then force the block to be singleton or all of Delta^ell.

items.title: This page uses the coarse five-type O'Nan-Scott convention
The O'Nan-Scott classification of finite primitive groups
items.strategy: Record the sourced five-type classification in the page's fixed convention map. The local socle lemmas explain the type language, but the classification itself is kept as a bounded survey theorem rather than a new dependency spine.

items.title: CFSG enters later refinements of the O'Nan-Scott reduction
Finite 2-transitive groups have affine or almost simple socle type
items.strategy: Combine the O'Nan-Scott landscape with the extra restriction imposed by two-transitivity. Diagonal, product-action, and twisted-wreath types fail the sourced finite 2-transitivity constraints, leaving only the affine and almost simple cases.

items.title: The O'Nan-Scott theorem reduces finite primitive-group questions to socle types
FALSE: the socle is always a single simple group
items.strategy: Refute with a finite characteristically simple minimal normal subgroup that is a direct product of several isomorphic simple factors, or with a primitive group of product or diagonal type.

items.title: FALSE: every primitive group has a unique minimal normal subgroup
items.strategy: Refute with the primitive groups that have two distinct regular minimal normal subgroups, exactly the exceptional case isolated by the socle analysis.

items.title: FALSE: the O'Nan-Scott theorem is the classification of finite simple groups
items.strategy: The O'Nan-Scott theorem classifies finite primitive permutation actions by socle type. CFSG classifies finite simple groups themselves, and the two theorems serve different purposes.

items.title: FALSE: the O'Nan-Scott theorem requires the classification of finite simple groups
items.strategy: The structural classification of primitive groups by type precedes the CFSG-dependent refinements. What later uses CFSG is the detailed analysis of the almost simple and related families.

pages.title: Socles and the Onan Scott Landscape — Examples

items.title: The natural action of AGL(1,p) is affine type
items.strategy: Identify the translation subgroup of AGL(1,p) with the unique regular elementary abelian minimal normal subgroup and the multiplicative subgroup with the point stabilizer acting irreducibly on it.

items.title: The natural action of A_n is almost simple type
items.strategy: For n at least 5, the socle of S_n or A_n in the natural primitive action is A_n itself, a nonabelian simple group sitting between its inner and full automorphism groups.

items.title: A simple diagonal action
items.strategy: Use T times T acting on the cosets of the diagonal subgroup of T times T. The socle has two simple factors and the diagonal subgroup identifies the standard diagonal type.

items.title: A primitive product-action wreath product
items.strategy: Take a primitive group H on Delta and a transitive group K on ell coordinates, and examine the induced action of H wr K on Delta^ell. The coordinate action displays the product-action type exactly.

items.title: A primitive group with two regular minimal normal subgroups
items.strategy: Use a diagonal-type or holomorph-style primitive action in which left and right regular copies of the socle centralize one another and both act regularly.

items.title: The socle of a finite solvable primitive group is elementary abelian and regular
items.strategy: A minimal normal subgroup of a finite solvable group contains a nontrivial abelian normal subgroup and hence is abelian. The affine-type proposition then forces the socle to be the unique regular elementary abelian minimal normal subgroup.

items.title: A transitive imprimitive action can have a nontransitive minimal normal subgroup
items.strategy: Use an imprimitive wreath-product action where a base-group factor is normal but supported on one block. The action is transitive, but that minimal normal subgroup is not.

pages.title: Subgroups of Free Groups and Schreier Rewriting

items.title: The labeled Schreier coset graph of a subgroup of a free group
The Schreier coset graph is connected and deterministic
items.strategy: Every coset is reached by reading a reduced word from the base coset, and for each generator there is exactly one outgoing and one inverse incoming labeled edge.

items.title: Schreier transversals and Schreier systems
Rooted spanning trees and Schreier systems correspond
items.strategy: Here a rooted spanning tree means a connected acyclic spanning subgraph of the Schreier graph with the base coset as root. It picks the unique reduced label of the tree path from the base coset to each vertex, and the initial-segment closure is exactly the rooted-tree property.

items.title: Schreier generators in the right-coset convention
Every Schreier generator lies in the subgroup
items.strategy: The chosen representative and the generator land in the same right coset as the reduced representative of their product, so their quotient belongs to the subgroup.

items.title: The Schreier rewriting map
Schreier rewriting is invariant under free reduction
items.strategy: Adjacent inverse letters force consecutive Schreier factors to cancel after tracking the same intermediate coset representative.

items.title: The nontrivial Schreier generators generate the subgroup
items.strategy: Track a subgroup word through successive coset representatives and telescope the resulting Schreier factors; the final representative returns to the base coset.

items.title: Tree Schreier generators are freely independent
items.strategy: A nontrivial reduced product of tree generators determines a non-backtracking closed path using an edge outside the spanning tree, contradicting tree normal form.

items.title: Under the stated choice boundary, every subgroup of a free group is free with its nontrivial Schreier generators as a basis
items.strategy: The Schreier generating lemma gives generation, the tree lemma gives free independence, and the statement separates the finite and countable Schreier-system clauses from the arbitrary-rank formulation, which records its Axiom-of-Choice cost explicitly.

items.title: The Schreier index-rank formula
items.strategy: For a finite-index subgroup, count the non-tree edges in a Schreier graph spanning tree and identify that count with the size of an explicit free basis.

items.title: A free group of rank at least two has subgroups of every finite rank
items.strategy: Choose two basis elements to obtain a rank-two free subgroup, then apply the index-rank formula to finite-index subgroups of that rank-two subgroup.

items.title: The Reidemeister-Schreier presentation theorem
items.strategy: Lift the subgroup to the free group on the presentation generators, use a Schreier transversal there, and rewrite conjugates of defining relators into Schreier generators.

items.title: Reidemeister-Schreier relators are independent of word representatives
items.strategy: Replacing a relator by a freely equivalent word changes its rewrite only by cancellations already controlled by Schreier rewriting invariance, and normal closure absorbs the conjugacy choices.

items.title: Finite-index subgroups of finitely presented groups are finitely presented
items.strategy: For a finite-index subgroup, a Schreier transversal and the defining-relator set are both finite, so the Reidemeister-Schreier presentation has finitely many generators and relators.

items.title: Every finitely generated subgroup of a finite-rank free group is a free factor of a finite-index subgroup
items.strategy: Start from the finite core graph of the subgroup, attach a path for a separating word, fold, and complete to a regular finite covering graph; the spanning-tree basis then splits off the original subgroup as a free factor.

items.title: FALSE: every subgroup of a finitely generated free group is finitely generated
items.strategy: Refute with an infinite-index subgroup of a rank-two free group whose Schreier basis is infinite.

items.title: FALSE: the raw Schreier generators are always a free basis
items.strategy: Refute by exhibiting a transversal that is not a Schreier system or that leaves trivial generators in place, so the resulting family is not the reduced basis guaranteed by the theorem.

items.title: FALSE: a finite-index d subgroup of a rank n free group has rank dn
items.strategy: Apply the exact Schreier index-rank formula and compare it with dn on the simplest nontrivial examples.

items.title: FALSE: the Reidemeister-Schreier presentation needs no choice of transversal
items.strategy: Different transversals produce different Schreier generators and rewritten relators even though the resulting presented subgroup is isomorphic.

pages.title: Subgroups of Free Groups and Schreier Rewriting — Examples

items.title: An index-two subgroup of a rank-two free group has rank three
items.strategy: Write the two cosets, choose a Schreier system, list the nontrivial generators, and verify the rank with the Schreier formula.

items.title: The kernel of an exponent-sum map in a free group
items.strategy: Use a Schreier transversal for the kernel of the map to Z, compute the resulting generators, and see directly why the basis is infinite.

items.title: A Schreier coset graph and its spanning-tree basis
items.strategy: Draw the labeled coset graph, choose a rooted spanning tree, and read off the explicit Schreier basis from the non-tree edges.

items.title: A Reidemeister-Schreier presentation for a surface subgroup
items.strategy: Choose a transversal in the ambient presentation, rewrite the conjugated relators, and simplify the resulting presentation to the expected surface form.

items.title: A rank-two free group contains an infinite-rank subgroup
items.strategy: Compute the Schreier basis of a natural infinite-index subgroup and exhibit infinitely many distinct nontrivial Schreier generators.

items.title: Marshall Hall's theorem produces a separating finite-index overgroup
items.strategy: Adjoin a path for a word outside the subgroup, complete the folded graph to a finite covering, and read off the free-factor splitting.

items.title: An arbitrary transversal need not give the reduced Schreier basis
items.strategy: Pick coset representatives that fail the Schreier initial-segment condition and show that the resulting generator list contains redundancy or trivial elements.

pages.title: Hnn Extensions and Brittons Lemma

items.title: An HNN extension with its stable letter
The edge-group presentation is equivalent to the associated-subgroup presentation
items.strategy: Use injectivity to identify the edge group with its two images and transport the relators across the induced isomorphism between the associated subgroups.

items.title: HNN words, pins, and Britton-reduced words
Elementary HNN reductions preserve the represented element
items.strategy: Replace each pin by the conjugate element dictated by the defining relator and observe that this is exactly an equality in the presented group.

items.title: The transversal data used for HNN normal forms
Normal forms in an HNN extension are unique relative to chosen transversals
items.strategy: Model left multiplication followed by reduction on the set of transversal normal forms, reduce the defining relations to the published amalgam normal-form machinery, and read off uniqueness.

items.title: Britton's lemma
items.strategy: Apply the normal-form theorem to the Britton-reduced representative obtained after all elementary pin reductions and observe that a surviving stable letter forces nontriviality.

items.title: The base group embeds in its HNN extension
items.strategy: A nontrivial base-group element is already in normal form of stable-letter length zero, so Britton's lemma forbids it from collapsing to the identity.

items.title: The stable letter has infinite order
items.strategy: Every nonzero power of the stable letter is already Britton-reduced and contains a stable letter, so Britton's lemma rules out finite order.

items.title: The associated homomorphism from an HNN extension to the integers
The universal property of an HNN extension
items.strategy: Use von Dyck's theorem on the defining presentation after checking that the proposed image of the stable letter conjugates the two edge maps exactly as the relators require.

items.title: Ascending HNN extensions of injective endomorphisms
Ascending HNN extensions admit the one-sided normal form
items.strategy: Specialize the two-sided HNN normal form to the case where one associated subgroup is the whole base group and collapse the redundant transversal choice.

items.title: Higman-Neumann-Neumann: every countable group embeds in a two-generator group
items.strategy: Record the exact theorem as a source-backed waypoint only; later use would require a dedicated embedding page and is intentionally not taken here.

items.title: Cyclically Britton-reduced HNN words
Every HNN conjugacy class contains a cyclically Britton-reduced representative
items.strategy: Choose a conjugate with minimal stable-letter length and cyclically reduce one remaining pin at a time; minimality forces the process to terminate.

items.title: Cyclic permutations of a cyclically Britton-reduced HNN word stay in the same conjugacy class
items.strategy: Conjugate successively by the initial base-group and stable-letter segments and use cyclic reduction to keep the permuted word reduced.

items.title: Conjugacy between cyclically Britton-reduced HNN words reduces to base-group conjugacy after cyclic permutation
items.strategy: Compare a cyclically reduced equality after reducing the conjugator; Britton's lemma forces the minimal conjugator into the base group, and conjugating by the initial coefficient converts the result into a cyclic permutation.

items.title: Collins' conjugacy theorem for cyclically reduced HNN words
items.strategy: Pass to cyclically reduced representatives, compare stable-letter lengths by Britton's lemma, rotate one word cyclically, and finish with the base-group conjugacy reduction.

items.title: FALSE: the base group may collapse in an HNN extension
items.strategy: Refute by the embedding corollary: injective associated maps prevent any nontrivial base-group element from becoming trivial.

items.title: FALSE: every word containing a stable letter is nontrivial
items.strategy: Refute with a word containing an explicit pin whose elementary HNN reduction removes the stable letters entirely.

items.title: FALSE: HNN normal form is canonical without choosing transversals
items.strategy: Refute by comparing two different transversal choices that produce different zero-pin representatives of the same element.

items.title: FALSE: every HNN extension is an ascending HNN extension
items.strategy: Refute by choosing proper associated subgroups on both sides, so neither subgroup is the whole base group required in the ascending case.

pages.title: Hnn Extensions and Brittons Lemma — Examples

items.title: The direct product A x Z as an HNN extension
items.strategy: Take both associated subgroups to be the whole base group with the identity isomorphism and identify the resulting presentation with A x Z.

items.title: Baumslag-Solitar groups as HNN extensions
items.strategy: Start from an infinite cyclic base group and use the associated-subgroup maps generated by multiplication by m and n.

items.title: The doubling endomorphism of Z gives an ascending HNN extension
items.strategy: Take the injective endomorphism n |-> 2n on the infinite cyclic group and compute the resulting one-sided normal forms.

items.title: Britton reduction of a word with two pins
items.strategy: Choose a word containing one positive and one negative pin and perform the elementary reductions step by step until the surviving reduced word is clear.

items.title: An HNN extension realising two conjugate subgroups
items.strategy: Adjoin a stable letter that conjugates one chosen subgroup of the base onto another and verify the resulting universal property directly from the presentation.

items.title: A word containing a stable letter need not be Britton-reduced
items.strategy: Exhibit a word with an explicit pin and show that elementary HNN reduction shortens it immediately.

pages.title: Decision Problems for Finitely Presented Groups

items.title: Finite alphabets, encoded inputs, and algorithms
Recursive and recursively enumerable languages
Recursive presentations and finite presentations of groups
The trivial words of a recursively presented group form a recursively enumerable language
items.strategy: Use the normal-closure description of relators as finite products of conjugates and enumerate those products systematically.

items.title: The word problem for a fixed finite presentation
The uniform word problem for finite presentations
Solvability of the word problem does not depend on the chosen finite generating set
items.strategy: Translate words across two finite presentations of the same group and use Tietze equivalence to transport a decision procedure in either direction.

items.title: The word problem for a finitely generated free group is solvable by free reduction
items.strategy: Reduce the input word freely and use the published normal-form theorem to identify the trivial element with the empty reduced word.

items.title: Finitely generated abelian groups admit invariant-factor normal form
items.strategy: Record the exact invariant-factor classification needed for coordinate reduction; the later PID-module page proves the stronger structural theorem, but this page only cites the resulting normal form.

items.title: The word problem for finitely generated abelian groups is solvable
items.strategy: Use the cited invariant-factor normal form to write the group as Z^r plus finite torsion and decide equality by reducing the finite coordinate list modulo the invariant factors.

items.title: Free products and suitable amalgamated free products have solvable word problem
items.strategy: Run the published amalgam normal-form reduction and use the assumed factor word-problem and amalgam-membership procedures to decide each reduction step.

items.title: The conjugacy problem for a finitely generated group
The isomorphism problem for a class of finite presentations
A Markov property of finitely presented groups
Novikov-Boone: some finitely presented group has unsolvable word problem
items.strategy: Record the exact undecidability theorem as a cited scope boundary; no local proof of the Novikov-Boone construction is attempted here.

items.title: Adian-Rabin: every Markov property is undecidable on finite presentations
items.strategy: Record the exact Adian-Rabin theorem with its witness-group hypotheses visible; no local proof of the reduction is attempted on this page.

items.title: Triviality and finiteness are undecidable for finite presentations
items.strategy: Record the exact Adian-Rabin corollaries for the specific Markov properties of being trivial and being finite.

items.title: The isomorphism problem for finitely presented groups is undecidable
items.strategy: Record the classical undecidability theorem exactly as a cited scope boundary and keep it non-load-bearing on the page.

items.title: There exist finitely presented groups with unsolvable conjugacy problem
items.strategy: Record Miller's exact existence theorem as a source-backed boundary result only.

items.title: Algebraic relator area and the Dehn function of a finite presentation
Every null word has a minimal algebraic relator area
items.strategy: Use the existence of at least one relator expression and well-ordering of the natural numbers.

items.title: A recursive Dehn function yields a solution to the word problem
items.strategy: Bound the relator area of a null word by the recursive Dehn function and exhaust the finitely many relator expressions up to that bound, using free-group reduction to test equality in the ambient free group.

items.title: FALSE: every finitely presented group has solvable word problem
items.strategy: Refute with the Novikov-Boone existence theorem.

items.title: FALSE: recursively enumerable trivial words already give a decision algorithm
items.strategy: Refute by distinguishing enumeration of true instances from a halting procedure on both trivial and nontrivial words.

items.title: FALSE: an unsolvable word problem means no individual word can be decided
items.strategy: Refute by separating failure of one uniform algorithm from ad hoc proofs about particular words.

items.title: FALSE: the Novikov-Boone theorem proves only the uniform problem is unsolvable
items.strategy: Refute because the theorem already produces one fixed finitely presented group with unsolvable word problem.

items.title: FALSE: Tietze-equivalent finite presentations can differ on whether their word problem is solvable
items.strategy: Refute by transporting a decision procedure across Tietze-equivalent presentations of the same group.

items.title: Free reduction decides a word in a free group
items.strategy: Reduce an explicit word in a free basis and compare the result with the empty reduced word.

items.title: The word problem in a finite cyclic presentation
items.strategy: Write the presented group as Z modulo n and reduce the input exponent modulo n.

items.title: Conjugacy in a free group by cyclic reduction
items.strategy: Cyclically reduce two explicit words and compare their cyclic permutations using the published free-group conjugacy criterion.

items.title: Todd-Coxeter as a partial coset-enumeration procedure
items.strategy: Run a short finite coset table long enough to show how the procedure can terminate successfully without being a general decision algorithm.

items.title: Computing an algebraic relator area
items.strategy: Express a null word as a short product of conjugates of relators and show that no shorter expression exists.

items.title: Enumerating relator consequences does not decide nontriviality
items.strategy: Use a nontrivial word whose failure to appear in the positive enumeration shows why semi-decision is weaker than decision.

Vector Spaces, Linear Subspaces, Span and Direct Sums

items.title: Vector space over a field: an abelian group together with a scalar multiplication satisfying the four compatibility axioms
items.strategy: THREE THINGS THIS ITEM MUST GET RIGHT. (1) THE FIELD IS THE PUBLISHED ONE: cite [[def-field]] (order 9) and do not restate the field axioms. (2) THE ADDITIVE PART IS AN ABELIAN GROUP in the published sense of [[def-group]]: say so explicitly, so that associativity, commutativity, the uniqueness of $0_V$ ([[lem-identity-unique]]) and the uniqueness of $-v$ ([[lem-inverse-unique]]) are inherited and are never re-derived here. (3) SCALAR MULTIPLICATION IS NOT A BINARY OPERATION ON A SET: it is a map $F \times V \to V$, so [[def-binary-operation]] does not apply to it and must not be cited for it. State the four axioms as $\lambda(u+v) = \lambda u + \lambda v$, $(\lambda + \mu)v = \lambda v + \mu v$, $(\lambda\mu)v = \lambda(\mu v)$ and $1_F v = v$, and note that the last is an axiom and not a consequence.

items.title: In any vector space $0_F v = 0_V$, $\lambda 0_V = 0_V$, $(-\lambda)v = -(\lambda v)$, $(-1_F)v = -v$, and $\lambda v = 0_V$ forces $\lambda = 0_F$ or $v = 0_V$
items.strategy: direct

items.title: The vector space $F^{X}$ of all functions $X \to F$ with pointwise operations, and $F^{n}$ as the case $X = n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$
items.strategy: WELL-DEFINEDNESS: the pointwise rules are genuinely a map $F^{X} \times F^{X} \to F^{X}$ and a map $F \times F^{X} \to F^{X}$, and each axiom is checked pointwise from the field axioms. INDEX DISCIPLINE, and this is the single most likely defect on the page: a natural number here is a von Neumann natural, so $n = \{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]) and the coordinates of an element of $F^{n}$ are $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$, NOT $x_1, \dots, x_n$. Every displayed tuple on this page and its companion must start at index $0$. State the two boundary cases: $F^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function, so it is the zero space; and $F^{1}$ is $F$ up to the obvious identification. DICTIONARY: the same set $F^{X}$ carries the ring structure of [[def-ring-of-functions]] (order 42), with the SAME addition and with pointwise multiplication in place of scalar multiplication; link that item in `## Remarks` and say which operation is which, so the two structures are never conflated.

items.title: The vector space $M_{m \times n}(F) := F^{\,m \times n}$ of $m$ by $n$ matrices over a field, with entrywise operations
items.strategy: This item introduces ONLY the vector-space structure and the notation $a_{ij}$; the matrix product, the ring $M_n(F)$ and the matrix of a linear map belong to order 74 and must NOT be anticipated here, not even in a remark that would need them. Index discipline as in [[def-function-space]]: rows are indexed by $i \in m = \{0,\dots,m-1\}$ and columns by $j \in n$, both starting at $0$.

items.title: A field is a vector space over itself, and over any subfield $K \subseteq F$ every $F$-vector space is a $K$-vector space by restricting the scalars
items.strategy: direct

items.title: Linear subspace of a vector space
items.strategy: NAMING, decided at step 1 and to be honoured: the id says LINEAR subspace and the title says it too, because the library already uses "subspace" for the topological notion ([[def-subspace-topology-top]], order 185) and the two are unrelated. Do not link the topological item and do not remark on it; it is 117 pages later, so a link would be a forward reference needing declaration, and the qualified name is the whole fix. WELL-DEFINEDNESS: state that the restricted operations really are a vector addition and a scalar multiplication on $W$, and that $(W,+,0_V)$ is then a vector space whose zero and whose negatives are those of $V$ (that half is [[lem-linear-subspace-is-a-subgroup]], proved next, and is cited rather than re-argued).

items.title: The additive group of a vector space is an abelian group and every linear subspace is a subgroup of it; conversely a subgroup closed under scalar multiplication is a linear subspace
items.strategy: direct

items.title: One-step subspace test: a nonempty $W \subseteq V$ is a linear subspace if and only if $\lambda u + v \in W$ for all $\lambda \in F$ and $u, v \in W$
items.strategy: direct

items.title: The intersection of a nonempty family of linear subspaces of $V$ is a linear subspace of $V$
items.strategy: direct

items.title: Linear combination of a finite list, and the span $\operatorname{span}(S)$ as the smallest linear subspace containing $S$
items.strategy: WELL-DEFINEDNESS, in the shape the published [[def-generated-subgroup]] already uses and which must be reused rather than invented: the family of linear subspaces containing $S$ is nonempty because $V$ belongs to it, so its intersection is a linear subspace by [[lem-intersection-of-linear-subspaces]], and that intersection is the SMALLEST subspace containing $S$; those two properties determine it, which is what licenses the definite article. A linear combination is $\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$ with $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ and $v : n \to V$, the sum being the finite product of the published [[def-monoid-finite-product]] read additively in the abelian group $(V,+)$: cite it, do NOT define a new finite sum, and note that [[def-finite-sum]] is unavailable because it is stated for sequences into the complete ordered field. Index from $0$, and state that the empty combination ($n = 0$) is $0_V$, so $\operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$ as a consequence and not as a stipulation.

items.title: $\operatorname{span}(S)$ is exactly the set of linear combinations of finite lists of elements of $S$, and $\operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
items.strategy: direct

items.title: The span is monotone and idempotent, $\operatorname{span}(S) = S$ exactly when $S$ is a linear subspace, and $\operatorname{span}(S \cup \{0_V\}) = \operatorname{span}(S)$
items.strategy: direct

items.title: $\operatorname{span}\{v\} = \{\, \lambda v : \lambda \in F \,\}$, which is $\{0_V\}$ when $v = 0_V$ and otherwise meets $\{0_V\}$ only there
items.strategy: direct

items.title: The sum $U + W$ of two linear subspaces and the sum $\sum_{i<n} U_i$ of a finite family
items.strategy: WELL-DEFINEDNESS AND BOUNDARY: the sum is defined as the set of all $\sum_{i<n} u_i$ with $u_i \in U_i$, the finite sum again being [[def-monoid-finite-product]] read additively; the item must PROVE that this set is a linear subspace rather than assert it. Index from $0$, and state the empty case: the sum of the empty family ($n = 0$) is $\{0_V\}$, which is what makes the induction in [[lem-sum-is-span-of-union]] start.

items.title: $\sum_{i<n} U_i = \operatorname{span}\bigl(\bigcup_{i<n} U_i\bigr)$, so the sum is the smallest linear subspace containing every $U_i$
items.strategy: direct

items.title: Internal direct sum $V = \bigoplus_{i<n} U_i$: the sum is everything and each summand meets the sum of the others only in $0_V$
items.strategy: THE TRAP THIS ITEM EXISTS TO AVOID: for three or more summands, PAIRWISE trivial intersections are NOT sufficient, and the condition must be stated as $U_j \cap \sum_{i \ne j} U_i = \{0_V\}$ for every $j < n$. Writing the pairwise condition would make the definition false, and the companion page carries [[cex-pairwise-trivial-intersection-is-not-a-direct-sum]] as the witness. State the two-summand case explicitly as the familiar $V = U + W$ with $U \cap W = \{0_V\}$, and say that for two summands the two conditions do coincide. Index from $0$; the empty direct sum ($n = 0$) is the zero space.

items.title: $V = \bigoplus_{i<n} U_i$ if and only if every $v \in V$ is $\sum_{i<n} u_i$ with $u_i \in U_i$ in exactly one way; equivalently, if and only if the sum is $V$ and $\sum_{i<n} u_i = 0_V$ with $u_i \in U_i$ forces every $u_i = 0_V$
items.strategy: direct

pages.title: Linear Independence, Bases and Dimension

items.title: Linear independence: a finite list $v : n \to V$ is independent when $\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i = 0_V$ forces every $\lambda_i = 0_F$, and a subset $S \subseteq V$ is independent when every injective finite list into $S$ is
items.strategy: TWO NOTIONS, DEFINED TOGETHER AND RELATED, because the page needs both: lists carry ordered bases and coordinates, subsets carry the Zorn argument. (1) The finite sum is the one page 68 already fixed: [[def-monoid-finite-product]] read additively in the abelian group $(V,+,0_V)$, exactly as [[def-linear-combination-and-span]] does. Do not introduce a second finite sum, and do not reach for [[def-finite-sum]], which is stated for sequences into the complete ordered field. (2) THE INJECTIVITY CLAUSE IN THE SUBSET DEFINITION IS LOAD-BEARING AND MUST BE STATED. A linear combination in [[def-linear-combination-and-span]] is indexed by an arbitrary list $v : n \to S$, which need NOT be injective; if repetitions were allowed, $1_F v + (-1_F) v = 0_V$ would make every nonempty $S$ dependent. Quantifying over injective lists is what makes the subset notion the intended one. [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]] then shows the clause is not an extra hypothesis for LISTS -- the vanishing condition forces a list to be injective by itself. (3) BOUNDARY CASES ARE REAL CASES: $n = 0$ makes the empty list independent and $\varnothing \subseteq V$ independent (vacuously), and $\{0_V\}$ is dependent, since $1_F \cdot 0_V = 0_V$ with $1_F \ne 0_F$ ([[def-field]], [[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]). $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, so state both. (4) Dependent means not independent; define the word here so no later item has to.

items.title: An independent finite list is injective and takes no value $0_V$; every sublist of an independent list is independent; and every subset of an independent set is independent
items.strategy: direct, with the witnesses written out. INJECTIVITY: if $v_j = v_k$ with $j \ne k$, take $\lambda_j = 1_F$, $\lambda_k = -1_F$ and $\lambda_i = 0_F$ otherwise; the sum is $0_V$ by (F1) and (F3) of [[def-sum-of-linear-subspaces]] -- CITE THOSE, they are exactly the finite-sum facts page 68 proved so that this page would not rebuild them -- while $1_F \ne 0_F$. NO ZERO VALUE: if $v_j = 0_V$, take $\lambda_j = 1_F$ and the rest $0_F$. SUBLISTS and SUBSETS: extend a witnessing scalar list by zeros and use (F3). Record the consequence used constantly below: an independent list $v : n \to V$ is a bijection onto its range, so its range is a subset with exactly $n$ elements ([[def-equinumerous]], [[lem-pigeonhole]] clause 3), and independence of the list and of its range are the same condition.

items.title: A subset $S \subseteq V$ is linearly dependent if and only if some $s \in S$ lies in $\operatorname{span}(S \setminus \{s\})$
items.strategy: both directions direct. ($\Rightarrow$) A witnessing injective list with some $\lambda_j \ne 0_F$ can be solved for $v_j$, multiplying by $\lambda_j^{-1}$, which exists because $F$ is a field ([[def-field]]); the remaining terms are a linear combination of the other entries, which are distinct from $v_j$ by injectivity, hence lie in $S \setminus \{v_j\}$. Use (F2) and (F3) of [[def-sum-of-linear-subspaces]] for the rearrangement, and [[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]] to land in the span. ($\Leftarrow$) Reverse it. CHECK THE EDGES: $S = \varnothing$ has no $s$ and is independent; $S = \{0_V\}$ is dependent and $0_V \in \operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$ by [[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]], so the equivalence holds there too and must be checked in the proof rather than waved at.

items.title: $S \subseteq V$ is linearly independent if and only if every finite subset of $S$ is; consequently the union of a nonempty chain of independent subsets of $V$, ordered by inclusion, is independent
items.strategy: direct, and this is the lemma that makes Zorn applicable, so it must be proved in full rather than assumed. FINITE CHARACTER: an injective list $v : n \to S$ has finite range, and independence of $S$ is by definition a condition on such lists. CHAINS: let $C$ be a nonempty chain of independent subsets under $\subseteq$ ([[def-chain]], [[def-partial-order]]) and let $v : n \to \bigcup C$ be injective; each $v_i$ lies in some $A_i \in C$, and by induction on $n$ ([[thm-induction-principle]]) using comparability, all $n$ of them lie in a single member $A \in C$ -- WRITE THIS INDUCTION OUT; 'by comparability' is not a proof, and it is the only place the chain hypothesis is spent. Then independence of $A$ gives the conclusion. Note the induction needs $n$ finite, which is why finite character is stated first.

items.title: If $S \subseteq V$ is independent and $w \notin \operatorname{span}(S)$ then $S \cup \{w\}$ is independent and $\operatorname{span}(S) \subsetneq \operatorname{span}(S \cup \{w\})$; and if $w \in \operatorname{span}(S)$ then $\operatorname{span}(S \cup \{w\}) = \operatorname{span}(S)$
items.strategy: contradiction for the first clause. Note $w \notin S$, since $S \subseteq \operatorname{span}(S)$ ([[lem-span-monotone-and-idempotent]] clause 1). Given a dependence on $S \cup \{w\}$, the coefficient of $w$ cannot be $0_F$ (else $S$ would be dependent) and cannot be nonzero (else $w \in \operatorname{span}(S)$ by the solving step of [[lem-dependent-iff-a-vector-lies-in-the-span-of-the-others]]). The second clause is monotonicity and idempotence of the span ([[lem-span-monotone-and-idempotent]]). This lemma is the engine of both [[thm-steinitz-exchange]] and the Zorn argument of [[thm-every-independent-set-extends-to-a-basis]]; state it once, here.

items.title: Basis of a vector space: a linearly independent spanning subset; and ordered basis: an injective finite list whose range is a basis
items.strategy: Definition, with the naming decision recorded. NAMING: the bare id `def-linear-basis` is free, and the library's other basis -- a basis for a topology -- is already namespaced as [[def-topology-basis-subbasis]] with alias `def-basis-top`, so no collision arises; say so in Remarks, in the dictionary style page 68 used for `linear subspace`, and note that the two notions share nothing but the word. CONTENT: $B \subseteq V$ is a basis when $B$ is independent ([[def-linear-independence]]) and $\operatorname{span}(B) = V$ ([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]). $\varnothing$ IS A BASIS OF THE ZERO SPACE, since $\operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$ ([[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]]) -- state this, it is the $n = 0$ case that every later induction on this page starts from. An ORDERED basis is a list $v : n \to V$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$, that is injective and whose range is a basis; by [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]] the injectivity is equivalent to asking only that the list be independent and span. Also fix the word SPANNING SET here if page 68 has not: it has -- [[def-linear-combination-and-span]] defines it -- so cite rather than redefine.

items.title: A finite list $v : n \to V$ is an ordered basis if and only if every $x \in V$ equals $\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$ for exactly one $\lambda : n \to F$; those scalars are the coordinates of $x$ in the ordered basis
items.strategy: both directions direct; this is the well-definedness obligation for coordinates and must be proved, not assumed. EXISTENCE is spanning ([[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]]). UNIQUENESS: subtract two representations using (F2) of [[def-sum-of-linear-subspaces]] to get $\sum_{i<n} (\lambda_i - \mu_i) v_i = 0_V$, then independence. CONVERSE: unique representation gives spanning at once and independence by comparing a vanishing combination with the all-zero one, which represents $0_V$ by (F1). The list is injective by [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]]. State plainly that the coordinates depend on the ORDERED basis and not on the basis as a set -- reordering the list permutes the coordinates -- and leave the map $x \mapsto \lambda$ un-named: it is a linear map, and linear maps are order 72. LANDMARK.

items.title: For $B \subseteq V$ the following are equivalent: $B$ is a basis; $B$ is a maximal linearly independent subset of $V$; $B$ is a minimal spanning subset of $V$ — maximality and minimality being in the inclusion order
items.strategy: three implications, direct. Basis implies maximal independent: any $w \notin B$ lies in $\operatorname{span}(B) = V$, so $B \cup \{w\}$ is dependent by [[lem-dependent-iff-a-vector-lies-in-the-span-of-the-others]]. Maximal independent implies basis: if some $w \notin \operatorname{span}(B)$ existed, [[lem-adjoining-a-vector-outside-the-span]] would contradict maximality. Basis implies minimal spanning, and back, by the same lemma applied to $B \setminus \{b\}$. Use [[def-maximal-element]] and [[def-partial-order]] for the words `maximal` and `minimal`, in the inclusion order on the relevant family of subsets -- name the poset explicitly, because [[thm-every-independent-set-extends-to-a-basis]] feeds Zorn the very same poset.

items.title: The Steinitz exchange lemma: if $L \subseteq V$ is linearly independent and $S \subseteq V$ spans $V$ with $S$ finite of size $n$, then $L$ is finite with $|L| = m \le n$, and there is $T \subseteq S$ with $|T| = n - m$ such that $L \cup T$ spans $V$
items.strategy: induction, on $m$, exchanging one vector at a time. THE EXCHANGE STEP: if $L' \cup T'$ spans $V$ and $w \in L \setminus L'$, then $w$ is a combination of $L' \cup T'$ ([[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]]) with some coefficient on a $t \in T'$ nonzero -- if every coefficient on $T'$ vanished, $w$ would lie in $\operatorname{span}(L')$, contradicting independence of $L$ via [[lem-dependent-iff-a-vector-lies-in-the-span-of-the-others]] -- so solve for that $t$ and replace it by $w$, the new set still spanning by [[lem-adjoining-a-vector-outside-the-span]] and [[lem-span-monotone-and-idempotent]]. THE BOUND $m \le n$ falls out because $T'$ cannot run out before $L$ does. SIZES ARE NATURALS AND ARE HANDLED BY [[lem-pigeonhole]]: a finite set is equinumerous with exactly one natural (clause 3), which is what makes $|L|$ and $|T|$ meaningful; $n - m$ is the unique natural $k$ with $m + k = n$ ([[def-nat-addition]], [[thm-nat-linear-order]]). ALSO PROVE $L$ IS FINITE rather than assuming it: if $L$ were infinite it would contain an independent subset of size $n+1$, which the bound forbids ([[lem-independent-list-is-injective]] for subsets). LANDMARK.

items.title: If $V$ has a spanning set with $n$ elements, then every linearly independent subset of $V$ is finite with at most $n$ elements; in particular $V$ has no independent subset equinumerous with $\mathbb{N}$
items.strategy: direct, from [[thm-steinitz-exchange]]. The last clause is the one later items use to say a space is infinite-dimensional, and it needs [[lem-pigeonhole]] clause 4 ($\mathbb{N} \not\approx n$) plus [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]] to cut a subset of size $n+1$ out of an infinite independent set.

items.title: If $V$ has a basis with $n$ elements and a basis with $m$ elements then $n = m$; and if $V$ has one finite basis then every basis of $V$ is finite
items.strategy: direct, applying [[cor-independent-set-is-no-larger-than-a-finite-spanning-set]] twice, in each direction, then antisymmetry of the order on $\mathbb{N}$. This is well-definedness obligation #12 and it is what licenses [[def-dimension]] to speak of THE dimension. Sizes are compared through [[lem-pigeonhole]] clause 3. THE INFINITE CASE IS NOT CLAIMED: this page does NOT assert that any two infinite bases are equinumerous, and it must not, because the standard proof needs cardinal arithmetic and [[def-cardinal]] is homed on `ordinals-and-transfinite-recursion` at order 183, one hundred and thirteen pages above this one. Say in Remarks that the invariance proved here is the finite one, in the 'not available at this point in the reading order' form -- never 'this library does not develop it'. LANDMARK.

items.title: Finite-dimensional vector space, and its dimension $\dim_F V$; infinite-dimensional means having no finite basis
items.strategy: Definition resting on [[thm-any-two-finite-bases-have-the-same-size]], which is a PREREQUISITE and belongs in `deps`, not in `justified_by`: it does not depend on this item. $V$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ when it has a finite basis, and then $\dim_F V$ is the unique natural $n$ with a basis of $n$ elements. $\dim_F$ IS SUBSCRIPTED BY THE FIELD and the Remarks must say why: page 68's [[lem-restriction-of-scalars]] makes the same set a vector space over a subfield, and the dimension changes when the field does. $\dim_F \{0_V\} = 0$, with basis $\varnothing$. INFINITE-DIMENSIONAL is defined as the negation, with NO cardinal attached -- do not write $\dim V = \infty$ and do not cite [[def-cardinal]] (order 183). Note that the definition is stated relative to a field and a space, so 'the dimension of $V$' is incomplete language, exactly as page 68 says of 'the vector space $V$'. LANDMARK.

items.title: Zorn's lemma gives a basis between any independent set and any spanning set containing it: if $L \subseteq S \subseteq V$ with $L$ independent and $\operatorname{span}(S) = V$, there is a basis $B$ of $V$ with $L \subseteq B \subseteq S$
items.strategy: constructive via Zorn, and the two hypotheses are stated together on purpose so that the two classical statements are corollaries rather than two separate Zorn arguments. THE POSET: $P := \{\, A : L \subseteq A \subseteq S,\ A \text{ independent} \,\}$ ordered by inclusion, a poset by [[def-partial-order]]. NONEMPTY: $L \in P$. EVERY CHAIN HAS AN UPPER BOUND -- and the EMPTY CHAIN MUST BE HANDLED SEPARATELY, its upper bound being $L$, because the union of the empty chain is $\varnothing$, which need not contain $L$; [[thm-zorn]] as published quantifies over every chain, so this case is not optional. For a nonempty chain the union is in $P$: independent by [[lem-independence-has-finite-character]], and between $L$ and $S$ because every member is. [[thm-zorn]] then yields a maximal $B \in P$. FINALLY $\operatorname{span}(B) = V$: if some $s \in S$ had $s \notin \operatorname{span}(B)$ then $B \cup \{s\} \in P$ by [[lem-adjoining-a-vector-outside-the-span]], contradicting maximality; so $S \subseteq \operatorname{span}(B)$ and $\operatorname{span}(B) \supseteq \operatorname{span}(S) = V$ by [[lem-span-monotone-and-idempotent]]. CHOICE IS DECLARED, not hidden: [[thm-zorn]] assumes [[def-axiom-of-choice]], which this library has adopted, and the Statement should say the theorem is proved from Zorn's lemma. LANDMARK.

items.title: Every spanning subset of a vector space contains a basis
items.strategy: direct: apply [[thm-every-independent-set-extends-to-a-basis]] with $L = \varnothing$, which is independent by [[def-linear-independence]]. Note the finite case needs no choice at all -- a minimal spanning subset of a finite spanning set exists by [[lem-pigeonhole]] and downward induction -- and say so, since the library is careful elsewhere about what a proof actually costs.

items.title: Every vector space has a basis
items.strategy: direct: apply [[thm-every-independent-set-extends-to-a-basis]] with $L = \varnothing$ and $S = V$, noting $\operatorname{span}(V) = V$ by [[lem-span-monotone-and-idempotent]] clause 4. The zero space is included, its basis being $\varnothing$. REMARKS, and this is a decision the orchestrator should confirm: the CONVERSE -- that 'every vector space has a basis' implies the Axiom of Choice -- is a theorem of Blass (1984) which this library does not prove. State that in PLAIN PROSE with a real entry in `sources.references` and NO wikilink and NO `external_refs` entry, exactly as the number-theory scaffold orients readers forward without linking; the self-contained-scope rule forbids resting on it, and nothing here does. LANDMARK. See the batch notes: the published [[rem-choice-ledger]] currently says of this statement that 'neither direction is proved here', which THIS ITEM FALSIFIES, and the amendment is recorded in `research/level9-mixed-batch-2.notes.md`.

items.title: The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(j) = 1_F$ for $j = i$ and $0_F$ otherwise is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$
items.strategy: direct, via [[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]: for $x \in F^{n}$ the list $\lambda_i := x(i)$ is the unique one with $x = \sum_{i<n} \lambda_i e_i$, checked by evaluating both sides at each $j < n$, which is legitimate because equality in $F^{X}$ is pointwise ([[def-function-space]]). INDEXING: $F^{n}$ is $F^{X}$ with $X = n = \{0,\dots,n-1\}$ the von Neumann natural, so entries run $x_0,\dots,x_{n-1}$ and the list starts at $0$ ([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]); $n = 0$ gives $F^{0}$, whose single element is the empty function, and the empty list is its ordered basis. Evaluating a finite sum pointwise needs induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]) on the defining clauses of [[def-monoid-finite-product]]; do not assert it.

items.title: If $\dim_F V = n$ and $U$ is a linear subspace of $V$, then $U$ is finite-dimensional, $\dim_F U \le n$, and $\dim_F U = n$ if and only if $U = V$
items.strategy: direct. $U$ is finite-dimensional: an independent subset of $U$ is independent in $V$, hence has at most $n$ elements ([[cor-independent-set-is-no-larger-than-a-finite-spanning-set]]); take one of maximal size, which exists because the sizes form a nonempty set of naturals bounded by $n$ ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]] or the bounded-above form), and it is a basis of $U$ by [[lem-basis-iff-maximal-independent-iff-minimal-spanning]] applied inside $U$ -- note that maximality among independent subsets OF $U$ is what is needed, and that the span in $U$ and in $V$ agree because $U$ is a linear subspace. EQUALITY CASE: if $\dim_F U = n$ and $U \ne V$, pick $w \in V \setminus U$; a basis of $U$ together with $w$ is independent by [[lem-adjoining-a-vector-outside-the-span]] and has $n+1$ elements, contradicting the bound. FINITENESS IS ESSENTIAL and the companion page carries the witness: in infinite dimension a proper subspace can have a basis equinumerous with a basis of the whole space.

items.title: Every linear subspace $U$ of a vector space $V$ has a complement: a linear subspace $W$ with $V = U \oplus W$
items.strategy: constructive, from [[thm-every-independent-set-extends-to-a-basis]]. Take a basis $A$ of $U$ ([[cor-every-vector-space-has-a-basis]] applied to $U$, which is a vector space in its own right by [[def-linear-subspace]]), extend it to a basis $B$ of $V$ with $A \subseteq B \subseteq V$, and put $W := \operatorname{span}(B \setminus A)$. Then $U + W = V$ by [[lem-sum-is-span-of-union]] and [[lem-span-monotone-and-idempotent]], and $U \cap W = \{0_V\}$ because a vector in both has two representations in the basis $B$, contradicting [[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] unless it is $0_V$ -- for an infinite $B$ argue with the finite lists that actually occur, via [[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]], rather than with an ordered basis. Conclude with the two-summand form of [[def-internal-direct-sum]], which that definition states as $U + W = V$ and $U \cap W = \{0_V\}$, and record that the complement is NOT unique -- the companion page of order 69 already exhibits three lines in $F^{2}$ pairwise meeting in $0$.

items.title: The dimension formula: for finite-dimensional linear subspaces $U$ and $W$ of $V$, $\dim_F(U+W) + \dim_F(U \cap W) = \dim_F U + \dim_F W$
items.strategy: constructive. Take a basis $A$ of $U \cap W$ -- which is a linear subspace by [[lem-intersection-of-linear-subspaces]] and finite-dimensional by [[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]] -- extend it to a basis $A \cup A_U$ of $U$ and to a basis $A \cup A_W$ of $W$ ([[thm-every-independent-set-extends-to-a-basis]]). Prove that $A \cup A_U \cup A_W$ is a basis of $U + W$: it spans by [[lem-sum-is-span-of-union]], and independence is the crux -- a vanishing combination puts a vector of $\operatorname{span}(A_U)$ into $W$, hence into $U \cap W = \operatorname{span}(A)$, forcing its $A_U$ coefficients to vanish. Then count, the three pieces being pairwise disjoint (prove that, do not assume it). Arithmetic of naturals: [[def-nat-addition]] and [[lem-pigeonhole]] clause 3 for sizes. CHECK THE EDGES: $U \cap W = \{0_V\}$ gives $A = \varnothing$ and the formula reads $\dim(U \oplus W) = \dim U + \dim W$; $U = W$ gives an identity. LANDMARK.

items.title: If $V = \bigoplus_{i<n} U_i$ with every $U_i$ finite-dimensional, then $V$ is finite-dimensional and $\dim_F V = \sum_{i<n} \dim_F U_i$; in particular $\dim_F(U \oplus W) = \dim_F U + \dim_F W$
items.strategy: induction on $n$, from [[thm-dimension-formula]] and the defining condition of [[def-internal-direct-sum]], which says each $U_j$ meets the sum of the OTHERS only in $0_V$ -- that is what makes the intersection term vanish at each step, and the pairwise condition would not suffice ([[lem-direct-sum-criterion]], and the order-69 counterexample). BASE $n = 0$: the empty direct sum is $\{0_V\}$ and the empty sum of naturals is $0$, so the formula holds; state the base rather than starting at $1$. The sum of naturals is the finite sum of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] read additively in $(\mathbb{N},+,0)$.

pages.title: Bases and Dimension: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The vector $(1,2) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$ has coordinate list $(1,2)$ in the standard ordered basis, $(2,1)$ in its reversal, and $(2,-1)$ in the ordered basis $\bigl((1,1),(1,0)\bigr)$
items.strategy: Compute all three coordinate lists from [[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]], verifying each by expanding the sum. TITLE MUST BE FIXED BY THE AUTHOR: recompute the third list before writing the title -- the scaffold deliberately leaves the arithmetic unverified so it is checked rather than copied, and a title asserting a wrong triple would be a published falsehood. The point of the item, and it should be stated: coordinates are attached to an ORDERED basis, not to a basis, and the same vector has different coordinate lists under different orderings of the same set. This is the concrete half of the distinction that order 74 will formalise as change of basis.

items.title: The standard unit families $e_i \in F^{\mathbb{N}}$ form a basis of the linear subspace of eventually zero families, an explicit infinite basis
items.strategy: B PAGES ARE LEAVES, so this item may NOT depend on page 69's `ex-sequence-space-and-eventually-zero-subspace`, which lives on another examples page; build the eventually zero subspace natively from [[lem-linear-subspace-criterion]] (three lines) and record the agreement with that example in Remarks ONLY, with no `deps` entry. Then prove SPANNING as it does, and add what is new, namely INDEPENDENCE: an injective list $e_{i_0}, \dots, e_{i_{n-1}}$ with $\sum \lambda_k e_{i_k} = 0$ evaluates at $i_k$ to $\lambda_k = 0_F$, the evaluation being legitimate because equality in $F^{X}$ is pointwise ([[def-function-space]]). Then it is a basis by [[def-linear-basis]], and the space is infinite-dimensional by [[cor-independent-set-is-no-larger-than-a-finite-spanning-set]] together with [[lem-pigeonhole]] clause 4. This is the counterweight to [[cor-every-vector-space-has-a-basis]]: here an infinite basis is written down, no choice principle is used, and the contrast with [[ex-hamel-basis-of-r-over-q]] is the item's point.

items.title: $\mathbb{R}$ as a vector space over $\mathbb{Q}$ has a basis, and every such basis is infinite; the existence proof exhibits none
items.strategy: EXISTENCE: [[ex-r-as-a-vector-space-over-q]] (order 69) makes $\mathbb{R}$ a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space by restriction of scalars, and [[cor-every-vector-space-has-a-basis]] supplies a basis. INFINITUDE, primary argument: a basis with $n$ elements would give a unique coordinate list in $\mathbb{Q}^{n}$ for each real ([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]), hence an injection $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{Q}^{n}$; $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable ([[thm-rationals-countable]]) and finite products of countable sets are countable ([[thm-product-of-countable]]), so $\mathbb{R}$ would be countable, contradicting [[thm-r-uncountable]]. SECOND CLAUSE, OPTIONAL AND TO BE CUT IF IT DOES NOT COME OUT CLEANLY: no basis is countably infinite either, because the set of finite $\mathbb{Q}$-combinations from a countable set is a countable union of countable sets ([[thm-countable-union-of-countable]], which costs countable choice and must be flagged as such via [[def-countable-choice]]). SCOPE DISCIPLINE: say that the proof of existence is non-constructive and exhibits no basis; do NOT write that no basis can be exhibited, which is a metamathematical claim this library has not established, and do NOT mention non-measurable sets -- that clause was withdrawn under the self-contained-scope rule. Do not cite [[rem-banach-no-countable-hamel-basis]] or [[rem-hahn-banach-hamel-basis-open]]: both are recorded-not-proved items, the first is still a draft, and depending on either is forbidden.

items.title: The standard unit families $\{e_i : i \in \mathbb{N}\}$ are linearly independent in $F^{\mathbb{N}}$ but do not span it: the constant family $1$ is not a finite linear combination of them
items.strategy: Refutes: an infinite independent set in an infinite-dimensional space must span. Independence is as in [[ex-basis-of-the-eventually-zero-families]]. NON-SPANNING: every element of the span is a FINITE linear combination ([[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]]) and therefore vanishes outside a finite set of indices, while the constant family $1$ vanishes nowhere -- make the finiteness argument explicit, since it is the whole content. Conclude that this set is independent but not a basis ([[def-linear-basis]]), and note that [[thm-every-independent-set-extends-to-a-basis]] says it EXTENDS to one, which does not contradict anything here.

items.title: $\{(1,0), (0,1), (1,1)\}$ spans $F^{2}$ and is linearly dependent, so a spanning set need not be a basis; each of its three two-element subsets is a basis
items.strategy: Refutes: a spanning set of a space of dimension $n$ is a basis. Spanning is immediate from the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]], [[lem-span-monotone-and-idempotent]] monotonicity). Dependence: $(1,0) + (0,1) - (1,1) = 0$, so it is dependent by [[def-linear-independence]], and equally by [[lem-dependent-iff-a-vector-lies-in-the-span-of-the-others]]. Then verify each two-element subset is a basis, which makes [[cor-every-spanning-set-contains-a-basis]] concrete and shows the contained basis is not unique. NOTE THE FIELD: over $F = \mathbb{F}_2$ the identity $-1 = 1$ changes nothing here, but say which field is meant, since page 68 insists the field is part of the data.

items.title: Inside the space of eventually zero families, the subspace spanned by $\{e_i : i \ge 1\}$ is proper and has a basis equinumerous with a basis of the whole space, so "equal dimension forces equality" fails without finite dimension
items.strategy: Refutes: a linear subspace whose basis is equinumerous with a basis of the ambient space equals it. $U := \operatorname{span}\{e_i : i \ge 1\}$ is a proper subspace of the eventually zero families, since $e_0 \notin U$ by the pointwise evaluation argument of [[ex-basis-of-the-eventually-zero-families]]. Both $\{e_i : i \in \mathbb{N}\}$ and $\{e_i : i \ge 1\}$ are bases, of the whole space and of $U$, and they are equinumerous ([[def-equinumerous]]) via $i \mapsto i+1$, which is a bijection $\mathbb{N} \to \{i : i \ge 1\}$. THE POINT: [[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]] states the equality case only for FINITE dimension, and this shows the hypothesis is not decoration. Say explicitly that this item does not compare infinite dimensions as cardinals -- it compares two specific bases through an explicit bijection -- because [[def-cardinal]] is order 183 and no dimension is assigned to either space here.

items.title: Three distinct lines $U_0, U_1, U_2$ in $F^{2}$ have $\dim(U_0+U_1+U_2) = 2$ while the inclusion-exclusion analogue of the dimension formula predicts $3$, so the two-subspace formula does not extend
items.strategy: Refutes: $\dim(U_0+U_1+U_2) = \sum \dim U_i - \sum_{i<j} \dim(U_i \cap U_j) + \dim(U_0 \cap U_1 \cap U_2)$. Take the three lines spanned by $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$ and $(1,1)$ over a field with more than two elements -- CHECK THE FIELD: over $\mathbb{F}_2$ these are still three distinct lines and the computation still works, but say which field is used. Each has dimension $1$ ([[lem-span-of-a-single-vector]], [[def-dimension]]), pairwise intersections are $\{0\}$ ([[lem-span-of-a-single-vector]] clause 3), the triple intersection is $\{0\}$, and the sum is $F^{2}$ of dimension $2$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]); the right-hand side is $3 - 0 + 0 = 3$. Pair this in the prose with the order-69 [[cex-pairwise-trivial-intersection-is-not-a-direct-sum]], which uses the same three lines for the neighbouring failure -- SAME WITNESS, DIFFERENT FAILURE, and saying so is what stops it reading as a duplicate.

items.title: FALSE: the union of two linearly independent subsets of a vector space is linearly independent
items.strategy: Refutation in $F^{2}$: $\{(1,0),(0,1)\}$ and $\{(1,1)\}$ are each independent, and their union is dependent, since $(1,0) + (0,1) - (1,1) = 0$ ([[def-linear-independence]], [[lem-dependent-iff-a-vector-lies-in-the-span-of-the-others]]). Verify independence of each part from the definition. Note the true statements nearby, so the reader knows what survives: a SUBSET of an independent set is independent ([[lem-independent-list-is-injective]]), and adjoining a vector OUTSIDE the span preserves independence ([[lem-adjoining-a-vector-outside-the-span]]) -- the false claim is what you get by dropping the second hypothesis.
