items.strategy: For $a$ algebraic over $K$, take one polynomial over $K$ that it satisfies. Its finitely many coefficients generate a finite extension $M/F$; adjoining $a$ is finite over $M$. The tower law makes $M(a)/F$ finite, hence $a$ algebraic over $F$.

items.title: The relative algebraic closure of $F$ in $K$ has no further algebraic elements inside $K$
items.strategy: If $A$ is the subfield of elements algebraic over $F$ and $b\in K$ is algebraic over $A$, then $A(b)/A$ and $A/F$ are algebraic. Transitivity makes $b$ algebraic over $F$, so $b\in A$.

items.title: For finite subextensions in a common field, $[EE':F]\le [E:F][E':F]$
items.strategy: Products of bases of $E/F$ and $E'/F$ span the generated ring. Algebraicity reduces inverses by minimal polynomials, so this ring is the compositum. Extract a basis from the product spanning set to obtain the bound.

items.title: The prime subfield as the intersection of all subfields
The characteristic of a field is zero or a prime number
items.strategy: The characteristic is not one. If a positive characteristic $n$ were composite, write $n=ab$ with $1<a,b<n$. Minimality makes $a1_F$ and $b1_F$ nonzero, while their product is $n1_F=0$, contradicting the domain property.

items.title: A field's prime subfield is isomorphic to $\mathbb Q$ in characteristic zero and to $\mathbb F_p$ in characteristic $p$
items.strategy: In characteristic $p$, map $[n]$ in $\mathbb Z/p$ to $n1_F$. In characteristic zero, extend the injective integer map by $a/b\mapsto(a1_F)(b1_F)^{-1}$. Each image is a subfield contained in every subfield.

items.title: The binomial theorem over an arbitrary commutative ring
items.strategy: Induct on $n$. Multiply the previous expansion by $x+y$, reindex the two finite sums, and use Pascal's identity. Coefficients are repeated additions, never quotients, so positive characteristic is included.

items.title: A prime $p$ divides $\binom pk$ for $0<k<p$
items.strategy: Use $k\binom pk=p\binom{p-1}{k-1}$. Since $p$ does not divide $k$, Euclid's lemma forces $p$ to divide the binomial coefficient. Keep the endpoint coefficients outside the claim.

items.title: Frobenius $x\mapsto x^p$ is an injective endomorphism in characteristic $p$, and an automorphism for finite fields
items.strategy: The ring binomial theorem gives $(x+y)^p=x^p+y^p$ because the intermediate coefficients vanish. Powers give multiplicativity. The kernel is zero in a field; on a finite field injectivity gives bijectivity. The $n$-fold iterate is $x\mapsto x^{p^n}$.

items.title: Finite fields and their order
Every finite field has order $p^n$ for a unique prime characteristic $p$ and positive integer $n$
items.strategy: The prime subfield has $p$ elements. The finite underlying set spans the field over it and contains a basis of size $n\ge1$. Coordinates identify the field with the functions from an $n$-set to a $p$-set, hence it has $p^n$ elements. Record uniqueness.

items.title: The multiplicative group $\mathbb F_q^\times$ of a finite field is cyclic
items.strategy: A field is an integral domain and its nonzero elements are its units. Apply the published theorem that every finite subgroup of a domain's unit group is cyclic to the whole finite unit group. Its proof already supplies the root-bound and finite-abelian-structure argument.

items.title: In characteristic $p$, the roots of $x^{p^n}-x$ form a subfield and are all simple
items.strategy: Iterated Frobenius proves closure under subtraction and multiplication; zero and one are roots, and inverses follow from $a^q=a$. The derivative is $qx^{q-1}-1=-1$, so the roots are simple. Require $n\ge1$.

items.title: For every prime $p$ and $n\ge1$, a field with $p^n$ elements exists
items.strategy: Take a splitting field of $x^{p^n}-x$ over $\mathbb F_p$. Its roots form a subfield and generate the splitting field, hence are the whole field. Simplicity and the degree show that there are exactly $p^n$ roots.

items.title: A field with $q$ elements is the splitting field of $x^q-x$ over its prime subfield
items.strategy: Cyclicity gives $a^{q-1}=1$ for every nonzero $a$, and zero also satisfies $a^q=a$. Thus all $q$ elements are roots of the degree-$q$ polynomial, and they generate the field.

items.title: Finite fields of the same order are isomorphic
items.strategy: Two fields of order $q=p^n$ have isomorphic prime subfields and are splitting fields of $x^q-x$ over them. Transport the base copy and apply splitting-field uniqueness. Do not claim the isomorphism is unique.

items.title: The subfields of $\mathbb F_{p^n}$ are the unique fields $\mathbb F_{p^d}$ for positive divisors $d$ of $n$
items.strategy: A subfield has order $p^d$ and the tower law forces $d\mid n$. Conversely the roots of $x^{p^d}-x$ inside $\mathbb F_{p^n}$ form a subfield with $p^d$ elements when $d\mid n$. Any subfield of that order has the same root set.

items.title: Over $\mathbb F_q$, $x^{q^n}-x$ is the product of all monic irreducibles whose degrees divide $n$
items.strategy: In the splitting field, an irreducible of degree $d$ contributes roots exactly when their simple extension is the subfield with $q^d$ elements, equivalent to $d\mid n$. The derivative is $-1$, so factors occur once. Normalize them to be monic.

items.title: For every finite field $\mathbb F_q$ and every $n\ge1$, a monic irreducible polynomial of degree $n$ exists
items.strategy: Choose a generator of $\mathbb F_{q^n}^{\times}$. If its minimal polynomial had degree $d<n$, the element would lie in a subfield with at most $q^d-1$ nonzero elements, contradicting its order $q^n-1$.

items.title: Every finite extension of a finite field is simple
items.strategy: Coordinates make the extension finite as a set. A generator of its cyclic multiplicative group, together with zero, lies in and exhausts the subfield it generates.

items.title: Algebraically constructible real numbers as the smallest real subfield closed under positive square roots
A real number is algebraically constructible exactly when it lies in a finite tower of real quadratic adjunctions
items.strategy: The union of all finite towers from $\mathbb Q$ obtained by adjoining positive square roots is a subfield: combine two towers by appending their generators. It is square-root closed, and minimality gives equality with the constructible field.

items.title: An algebraically constructible real algebraic number has degree over $\mathbb Q$ equal to a power of two
items.strategy: Place the number in a finite quadratic tower. The top degree is a power of two by the tower law, and the simple subextension degree divides it. Unique prime factorization makes that divisor a power of two.

items.title: The real cube root of two is algebraic but not algebraically constructible
items.strategy: Eisenstein at $2$ makes $x^3-2$ irreducible, so the simple extension has degree three. Since three is not a power of two, the constructible-degree obstruction applies.

pages.title: Algebraic Extensions and Finite Fields: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)/\mathbb Q$ has degree two
items.strategy: Prove $x^2-2$ irreducible and apply the simple-extension theorem for basis $1,\sqrt2$ and degree two. Display two-coordinate arithmetic.

items.title: $\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]{2})/\mathbb Q$ has degree three
items.strategy: Eisenstein at $2$ proves irreducibility of $x^3-2$. The quotient-and-power-basis theorem gives basis $1,a,a^2$.

items.title: $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$ has degree four and equals $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2+\sqrt3)$
items.strategy: Use the tower law and compare coordinates to get degree four. For $a=\sqrt2+\sqrt3$, compute $a^{-1}=\sqrt3-\sqrt2$ and recover both roots. Verify the four-element product basis.

items.title: The relative algebraic closure of $\mathbb R$ in $\mathbb C$ is all of $\mathbb C$
items.strategy: Every $a+bi$ satisfies the nonzero real polynomial $(x-a)^2+b^2$, so every complex number is algebraic over the reals.

items.title: $\mathbb F_4=\mathbb F_2[t]/(t^2+t+1)$ with complete addition and multiplication tables
items.strategy: Check the quadratic has no root in $\mathbb F_2$, list $0,1,a,a+1$, reduce by $a^2=a+1$, compute both tables, and verify the three nonzero elements form a cyclic group.

items.title: $\mathbb F_8=\mathbb F_2[t]/(t^3+t+1)$ and its power table
items.strategy: Test zero and one to prove the cubic irreducible, list the eight power-basis elements, reduce by $a^3=a+1$, and compute powers through $a^7=1$.

items.title: $\mathbb F_9=\mathbb F_3[t]/(t^2+1)$ and a generator of its multiplicative group
items.strategy: Check that $-1$ is not a square in $\mathbb F_3$, list the nine elements, and find an element of order eight. Contrast it with the residue class of $t$, which has order four.

items.title: Frobenius on $\mathbb F_4$ swaps the two non-prime-field elements
items.strategy: Rebuild $\mathbb F_4$ as $\mathbb F_2[t]/(t^2+t+1)$ and write $a$ for the residue class of $t$. Using $a^2=a+1$, compute the squares of all four elements. Frobenius fixes $\mathbb F_2$, exchanges $a$ and $a+1$, and its square is the identity.

items.title: The subfields of $\mathbb F_{64}$ have orders $2,4,8,64$
items.strategy: Since $64=2^6$, apply the lattice theorem to divisors $1,2,3,6$ and identify each unique subfield as a Frobenius root set.

items.title: The residue class of $t$ generates $\mathbb F_8^\times$
items.strategy: Rebuild $\mathbb F_8$ as $\mathbb F_2[t]/(t^3+t+1)$ and write $a$ for the residue class of $t$. Reduce powers by $a^3=a+1$ to show $1,a,\ldots,a^6$ are the seven distinct nonzero elements and $a^7=1$. No primitive-root definition from the other run batch is used.

items.title: An algebraic extension need not be finite
items.strategy: Inside $\mathbb R$, take the union of $\mathbb Q(2^{1/2^m})$. Every element lies in a finite algebraic stage, but the stage degrees $2^m$ are unbounded; a finite total degree would be divisible by all of them.

items.title: There is no field with six elements
items.strategy: A finite-field order is a prime power, and six is no positive power of any prime. A six-element ring may exist, but not a field.

items.title: FALSE: $\mathbb F_{p^n}$ is the ring $\mathbb Z/p^n\mathbb Z$
items.strategy: For $p=2,n=2$, the finite-field existence theorem supplies a field with four elements, while $\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z$ has the nonzero nilpotent class $[2]$ and is not a field. Equal cardinality does not determine ring structure.

items.title: FALSE: degrees add in a tower of finite field extensions
items.strategy: Use $\mathbb F_2\subset\mathbb F_4\subset\mathbb F_{64}$. The step degrees are two and three, while the total degree is six, not five; the tower law gives the product.

pages.title: Algebraic Closure Embeddings and Separability

items.title: Monomials on an index set as finitely supported exponent families
The polynomial ring $R[x_i:i\in I]$ as finitely supported coefficient families on monomials
Finite convolution makes $R[x_i:i\in I]$ a commutative ring containing $R$
items.strategy: Define multiplication by convolution over pairs of finitely supported exponent families whose pointwise sum is the target monomial. Finite support makes each coefficient sum and the product support finite; reindexing finite sums proves associativity and distributivity, while the zero exponent family gives the unit and constants embed $R$.

items.title: Universal property of a polynomial ring on an arbitrary family of indeterminates
items.strategy: Given a homomorphism $R\to S$ and a family $(s_i)_{i\in I}$ in a commutative ring, evaluate a finite polynomial by sending the exponent family $a$ to the finite product of the $s_i^{a_i}$. Finite-sum reindexing proves multiplicativity, and the monomials force uniqueness.

items.title: A polynomial ring on a finite ordered family agrees canonically with the iterated polynomial-ring construction
items.strategy: Induct on the family length. At the successor step apply the two universal properties to construct mutually inverse homomorphisms fixing $R$ and every indeterminate. Include the empty family, where both constructions are $R$.

items.title: $F$-homomorphisms and $F$-embeddings of field extensions
Conjugate algebraic elements over a field
A base-field embedding carries an algebraic element to a conjugate
items.strategy: An $F$-embedding fixes every coefficient of the minimal polynomial, so evaluation commutes with the embedding and the image is another root. In the splitting-field case this specializes to the published permutation-of-roots proposition.

items.title: $F$-embeddings of $F(\alpha)$ into an algebraically closed field correspond to the distinct roots of $m_{\alpha}$
items.strategy: Send an embedding to the image of $\alpha$. The preceding proposition makes that image a root, and the universal property of adjoining an irreducible root constructs exactly one embedding for each root. Verify the two assignments are inverse and count distinct roots rather than multiplicities.

items.title: Separable algebraic elements and separable extensions
In characteristic $p$, every irreducible polynomial is uniquely $g(x^{p^e})$ with $g$ irreducible and separable
items.strategy: While the derivative vanishes, every exponent is divisible by $p$, so write $f(x)=h(x^p)$ without changing the coefficients and repeat. Irreducibility of $f$ forces irreducibility of each core, and maximality of $e$ makes $g'\ne0$, hence $g$ separable. Uniqueness follows from the least exponent occurring; include $e=0$.

items.title: If $a$ is not a $p$th power in a characteristic-$p$ field, then $x^{p^n}-a$ is irreducible for every $n\ge1$
items.strategy: In an algebraic closure the polynomial is $(x-b)^{p^n}$. Any monic irreducible factor is therefore $(x-b)^{p^r}=x^{p^r}-b^{p^r}$ for some $r$; if $r<n$, its constant coefficient puts $a$ in the image of Frobenius, a contradiction. The hypothesis automatically excludes $a=0$; treat $n=1$ explicitly.

items.title: Perfect fields: every irreducible polynomial is separable
A field is perfect exactly when it has characteristic zero or its Frobenius map is surjective
items.strategy: In characteristic zero a nonzero derivative of an irreducible polynomial cannot share a factor with it. In characteristic $p$, the separable-core theorem shows that failure of separability is exactly the presence of coefficients outside the Frobenius image; conversely a non-$p$th-power element gives an inseparable irreducible polynomial $x^p-a$.

items.title: Fields of characteristic zero, finite fields, and algebraically closed fields are perfect
items.strategy: The characteristic-zero case is one clause of the characterization. In a finite field Frobenius is an automorphism. In an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p$, every $a$ has a root of $x^p-a$. Thus Frobenius is surjective in both positive-characteristic cases.

items.title: Every algebraic extension of a perfect field is separable
items.strategy: Each element of the algebraic extension has an irreducible minimal polynomial over the perfect base, and that polynomial is separable by definition.

items.title: A simple finite extension has only finitely many intermediate fields
items.strategy: For $E=F(\alpha)$ and an intermediate field $M$, let $g_M$ be the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $M$. Its coefficients generate $M$ over $F$, and $g_M$ is a monic divisor in $E[x]$ of the minimal polynomial over $F$. Unique factorization gives only finitely many such divisors and hence fields.

items.title: A finite-dimensional vector space over an infinite field is not a finite union of proper subspaces
items.strategy: Choose a line not contained in any one of the finitely many proper subspaces, after induction on their number and the dimension. Each proper subspace meets a suitable affine line in at most one point, whereas the line has as many points as the infinite base field. Include dimension zero and the empty family.

items.title: A finite extension with only finitely many intermediate fields is simple
items.strategy: If the base is finite, use the published cyclic-multiplicative-group proof that finite-field extensions are simple. If it is infinite, the finitely many proper intermediate fields are proper base-vector subspaces, so their union cannot cover the extension; an element outside that union generates the whole field.

items.title: A finite field extension is simple if and only if it has finitely many intermediate fields
items.strategy: Combine the two preceding implications, retaining the finite-base-field branch in the converse and making both directions explicit.

items.title: A finite extension generated by elements all but possibly one of which are separable is simple
items.strategy: Reduce the generating list to two elements, with the second separable. Over a finite base use the finite-field result. Over an infinite base choose $c$ avoiding the finitely many collisions among conjugate pairs; the gcd of the two translated minimal polynomials recovers one generator from $\alpha+c\beta$, and then the other. Iterate the reduction; a finite separable extension is the special case in which every generator is separable.

items.title: A finite separable extension has only finitely many intermediate fields
items.strategy: The primitive element theorem makes the extension simple, and the forward half of the Steinitz criterion supplies finiteness of its intermediate fields.

items.title: Every finite extension of a perfect field is simple
items.strategy: The extension is algebraic and therefore separable over a perfect base; apply the primitive element theorem.

items.title: An algebraic closure of a field
Artin's ideal generated by $f(x_f)$ for all monic nonconstant $f\in F[x]$ is proper
items.strategy: If $1$ were a finite sum of generators, retain the finitely many polynomials occurring. Put simultaneous roots of those polynomials in a splitting field of their product and use the family-polynomial universal property, sending unused variables to zero. Evaluation turns the alleged identity into $1=0$.

items.title: Assuming Choice, every field has an algebraic extension containing roots of all nonconstant base polynomials
items.strategy: Place Artin's proper ideal inside a maximal ideal and quotient the family polynomial ring. The quotient is a field, each residue class $x_f$ is a root of $f$, and every element uses finitely many such algebraic residues, hence is algebraic over the base. State that the maximal-ideal step uses Zorn's lemma.

items.title: The one-step root condition makes an algebraic extension of a perfect field algebraically closed
items.strategy: For an irreducible $f$ over the perfect base, its splitting field is finite and generated by roots that are separable over $F$; the generalized primitive-element theorem therefore makes it simple, say $F(\alpha)$. A root in the one-step extension of the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ induces an isomorphic copy of the splitting field there, so $f$ splits. Finally, an element algebraic over the one-step extension $L$ is algebraic over $F$ — this step is transitivity of algebraicity applied to $L/F$ algebraic, and is cited, not asserted — and its minimal polynomial over $F$ already splits in $L$; hence $L$ is algebraically closed.

items.title: The elements with a $p^n$th power in the base form a perfect subfield carrying the one-step root condition
items.strategy: For an algebraic root extension $L/F$ of characteristic $p$, let $F'=\{a\in L:a^{p^n}\in F$ for some $n\ge0\}$. Frobenius identities prove it is a subfield. Roots of suitable $p$-power twists show Frobenius is surjective on $F'$, and raising the finitely many coefficients of a polynomial over $F'$ to one common $p^n$th power reduces root existence to the hypothesis over $F$.

items.title: An algebraic extension containing a root of every nonconstant base polynomial is algebraically closed
items.strategy: In characteristic zero the base is perfect, so apply the perfect-case lemma. In positive characteristic pass to the perfect subfield supplied by the preceding lemma; it has the same one-step root property, and the perfect-case lemma then makes the ambient algebraic extension algebraically closed. No iterated tower of root extensions is used.

items.title: Assuming Choice, every field has an algebraic closure
items.strategy: Apply the simultaneous root-extension theorem once. It is algebraic over the base and satisfies the one-step root condition, so the one-step theorem says it is already algebraically closed.

items.title: Assuming Choice, a base-field embedding extends across every algebraic extension
items.strategy: Order partial extensions of the given embedding by domain inclusion. Unions of chains are compatible field embeddings, so Zorn gives a maximal partial extension. If its domain is not the whole algebraic extension, adjoining one algebraic element and sending it to a root of the transported minimal polynomial contradicts maximality. State the use of Zorn explicitly.

items.title: Assuming Choice, any two algebraic closures are base-isomorphic, generally nonuniquely
items.strategy: Extend the identity of the base from one closure into the other. Its image contains every root in the target of every base minimal polynomial because the source is algebraically closed, so the embedding is surjective. Assert existence, not uniqueness; the examples page supplies a nontrivial automorphism witness.

items.title: Assuming Choice, conjugates in an algebraic closure are related by a base automorphism
items.strategy: One direction is preservation of minimal polynomials. Conversely, conjugate roots give an $F$-isomorphism between their simple adjunctions; extend it to the whole algebraic closure and use the closure-isomorphism argument to obtain an automorphism.

items.title: The normal closure of an algebraic extension inside a fixed algebraic closure
The normal closure of a finite extension exists and is finite
items.strategy: Choose finitely many algebraic generators and take in the fixed closure the splitting field of the product of their minimal polynomials. It is finite and normal, contains the original extension, and lies in every normal intermediate extension containing it, so it equals the defined intersection.

items.title: The separable degree $[K:F]_s$ as a count of embeddings into an algebraic closure
The separable degree is independent of the chosen algebraic closure
items.strategy: For a finite extension, put the minimal polynomials of a basis into one product. In each chosen algebraic closure, the field generated by its roots is a splitting field; uniqueness of splitting fields identifies these finite targets, and postcomposition bijects the two embedding sets without invoking Choice.

items.title: Restriction partitions embeddings in a finite tower into extension fibres
items.strategy: For $F\subseteq K\subseteq L$ and an algebraically closed target, restrict each $F$-embedding of $L$ to $K$. Because the tower is finite, extend a restricted embedding by adjoining a finite basis one algebraic generator at a time and choosing roots in the target. Transporting scalars along the restricted embedding identifies each fibre with the corresponding $K$-embedding set, whose size is $[L:K]_s$.

items.title: Separable degree is multiplicative in finite towers: $[L:F]_s=[L:K]_s[K:F]_s$
items.strategy: Count $F$-embeddings of $L$ by the fibres of restriction to $K$. The base has $[K:F]_s$ embeddings and the fibre lemma identifies every fibre cardinality with $[L:K]_s$ after transporting the $K$-structure.

items.title: For a finite extension, $[K:F]_s\le [K:F]$
items.strategy: Induct along a simple generating tower. At each simple step, embeddings correspond to distinct roots of a minimal polynomial and are therefore no more numerous than its degree; multiply the bounds with the two tower laws.

items.title: The separable degree of $F(\alpha)/F$ is the number of distinct roots of $m_{\alpha}$
items.strategy: Apply the simple-extension embedding bijection and the definition of separable degree; independence permits any algebraic closure containing all roots.

items.title: A finite extension is separable if and only if $[K:F]_s=[K:F]$
items.strategy: If the extension is separable, the primitive element theorem writes it as $F(\alpha)$ and the simple-extension root count gives full degree. Conversely, for each $\alpha\in K$, multiplicativity in the tower $F\subseteq F(\alpha)\subseteq K$, the ordinary tower law, and the upper bound on both separable-degree factors show that full degree for $K/F$ forces full degree for $F(\alpha)/F$. The simple-extension root count then makes every minimal polynomial separable.

items.title: Separability is transitive in towers of algebraic extensions
items.strategy: For $L/K/F$ and $a\in L$, place the finitely many coefficients of the minimal polynomial of $a$ over $K$ in a field $E=F(c_1,\ldots,c_r)\subseteq K$. Each successive relative minimal polynomial of the separable $c_i$ divides its separable minimal polynomial over $F$, so a simple tower and multiplicativity give $[E:F]_s=[E:F]$. Stability of polynomial gcd under scalar extension shows that the polynomial of $a$ remains separable over $E$; the same argument gives full separable degree for $E(a)/E$. Multiplicativity now gives full degree for $E(a)/F$, hence $a$ is separable over $F$. Include the trivial steps and arbitrary algebraic towers.

items.title: An algebraic extension generated by separable elements is separable
items.strategy: Every element lies in a subextension generated by finitely many of the given generators. Iteratively adjoining separable elements and using transitivity makes that finite subextension separable, so the chosen element is separable over the base. Include the empty generating set.

items.title: The elements separable over the base form an intermediate field
items.strategy: For separable $a,b$, the finite extension $F(a,b)$ is generated by separable elements and hence separable. Its elements include $a-b$, $ab$, and $a^{-1}$ when $a\ne0$, so the subfield criterion applies; zero and one have linear minimal polynomials.

items.title: The separable closure of the base inside an algebraic extension
Purely inseparable algebraic extensions
Pure inseparability and its conjugate, embedding, and separable-degree criteria
items.strategy: For an algebraic extension inside a fixed algebraic closure, show elementwise that a unique conjugate is equivalent to a minimal polynomial of the form $x^{p^e}-a$, hence to some $p^e$th power lying in the base. These conditions force every base embedding into that closure to be the inclusion. In finite extensions the restriction-fibre lemma supplies the converse and equivalence with separable degree one; for arbitrary extensions, the converse from uniqueness of embeddings requires Choice. Include the trivial and characteristic-zero cases.

items.title: Pure inseparability is transitive in towers and stable under composita
items.strategy: In a tower, raise an element first to a $p^m$th power in the middle field and then to a further $p^n$th power in the base. For two purely inseparable subextensions in a common algebraic extension, every element of their compositum lies in a finitely generated subcompositum; one common $p^e$th power sends all generators and hence that element into the base. Include trivial extensions.

items.title: $p$-bases for finite exponent-one purely inseparable extensions
A minimal generating family in a finite exponent-one purely inseparable extension is a $p$-basis and gives degree $p^r$
items.strategy: Adjoin a minimal generating list one element at a time. Each new generator has $p$th power in the preceding field but is not already there, so its minimal polynomial is $x^p-a$ and the step has power basis of length $p$. Product bases give the displayed $p$-monomials and the tower law gives degree $p^r$; conversely a $p$-basis plainly generates.

items.title: A finite purely inseparable extension in characteristic $p$ has degree a power of $p$
items.strategy: Choose finitely many generators and adjoin them one at a time. The minimal polynomial at each step divides a polynomial $x^{p^e}-a$ and therefore has $p$-power degree; the ordinary tower law makes the total degree a power of $p$. The trivial extension gives exponent zero.

items.title: Every purely inseparable algebraic extension is normal
items.strategy: The minimal polynomial of each element is $x^{p^e}-a=(x-\alpha)^{p^e}$ in the extension, so it splits there. Apply the published definition of normal algebraic extension.

items.title: An algebraic extension is purely inseparable over its separable closure
items.strategy: For $a\in K$, the separable core of its minimal polynomial over $F$ evaluates at a suitable $p^e$th power of $a$, placing that power in $K_s$. Thus every element is purely inseparable over $K_s$; use $e=0$ in the separable case.

items.title: Assuming Choice, separable closures exist and are base-isomorphic
items.strategy: Inside an algebraic closure take the elements separable over the base. They form a separable algebraic field. For a nonconstant separable polynomial over it, first put its finitely many coefficients in a finite subextension; gcd stability preserves separability there, and transitivity shows its roots remain separable over the base, so the polynomial splits in the separable part. Extend base embeddings as for algebraic closures; their images stay in the separable parts, and embeddings between separable closures are surjective. Do not claim uniqueness of the isomorphism.

items.title: For a finite extension, $[K:F]_s=[K_s:F]$
items.strategy: The finite extension $K_s/F$ is separable and therefore has full separable degree. The extension $K/K_s$ is purely inseparable, so its separable degree is one. Multiplicativity in the tower $F\subseteq K_s\subseteq K$ gives the equality, including $K_s=F$.

items.title: The separable degree divides the degree of every finite extension
items.strategy: Use $[K:F]_s=[K_s:F]$ and apply the ordinary tower law to $F\subseteq K_s\subseteq K$. This proof avoids inferring divisibility merely from the inequality.

items.title: The inseparable degree $[K:F]_i=[K:F]/[K:F]_s$ of a finite extension
$[K:F]=[K:F]_s[K:F]_i$, and in positive characteristic the inseparable degree is a power of $p$
items.strategy: The factorization is the definition after divisibility. The two tower laws and $[K:F]_s=[K_s:F]$ identify $[K:F]_i$ with $[K:K_s]$. This is a $p$-power because $K/K_s$ is finite purely inseparable; in characteristic zero it is one.

items.title: An extension that is both separable and purely inseparable is trivial
items.strategy: Every element has a separable minimal polynomial but, by pure inseparability, only one distinct root. An irreducible separable polynomial with one root has degree one, so every element lies in the base.

pages.title: Algebraic Closure Embeddings and Separability — Examples

items.title: Assuming Choice, real algebraic numbers embed properly in an algebraic closure of $\mathbb Q$
items.strategy: Choose an algebraic closure of $\mathbb Q$. The real numbers algebraic over $\mathbb Q$ form a field and embed into it over $\mathbb Q$; they are not algebraically closed because $x^2+1$ has no root in an ordered field. This uses $\mathbb R$ only as an ordered ambient field, not $\mathbb C$.

items.title: $\overline{\mathbb F_p}$ is the union of its finite subfields and is an infinite algebraic extension
items.strategy: Inside an algebraic closure, each element generates a finite extension and hence lies in a finite field. Conversely the unique copies of $\mathbb F_{p^n}$ lie in the closure, and the nested fields $\mathbb F_{p^{n!}}$ exhaust it. Irreducible polynomials of every positive degree force unbounded finite subdegrees and therefore infinitude.

items.title: $\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]{2})$ has three embeddings into $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ but only one $\mathbb Q$-automorphism
items.strategy: Eisenstein makes $x^3-2$ the minimal polynomial, and characteristic zero makes its three closure roots distinct, so the simple-extension theorem gives three embeddings. The chosen positive real root is the only root in the ordered real subfield $\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]{2})$, so an automorphism must fix it and is the identity.

items.title: $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$ has four embeddings into $\overline{\mathbb Q}$
items.strategy: Build the tower here rather than citing the published biquadratic example, which is homed on an examples page (B pages are leaves). Eisenstein at $2$, $3$ and $2$ makes $x^2-2$, $x^2-3$ and $x^2-6$ irreducible over $\mathbb Q$, so none of $\sqrt2,\sqrt3,\sqrt6$ is rational and $[\mathbb Q(\sqrt2):\mathbb Q]=2$ with basis $(1,\sqrt2)$. If $\sqrt3=a+b\sqrt2$ with $a,b\in\mathbb Q$ then squaring forces $ab=0$, and $b=0$ makes $\sqrt3$ rational while $a=0$ makes $\sqrt6=2b$ rational; so $x^2-3$ stays irreducible over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$ and the tower law gives degree $4$. Each square root may then independently be sent to its negative; the simple-extension embedding bijection and the restriction-fibre lemma show that all four sign choices extend and exhaust the embeddings.

items.title: $x^p-t$ is irreducible and inseparable over $\mathbb F_p(t)$
items.strategy: In the UFD $\mathbb F_p[t]$, comparison of exponents in a reduced fraction shows that $t$ is not a $p$th power in $\mathbb F_p(t)$. Apply the pure-power irreducibility lemma. The derivative is zero, and in an extension containing $t^{1/p}$ the polynomial is $(x-t^{1/p})^p$.

items.title: $\mathbb F_p(t)/\mathbb F_p(t^p)$ is purely inseparable of degree $p$ and separable degree one
items.strategy: The element $t$ satisfies $x^p-t^p$ over the base. The same reduced-fraction exponent argument shows $t^p$ is not a $p$th power in $\mathbb F_p(t^p)$, so the polynomial is irreducible and the degree is $p$. Every rational function has a $p$th power in the base, giving pure inseparability and separable degree one.

items.title: $\mathbb F_p(s,t)/\mathbb F_p(s^p,t^p)$ has degree $p^2$, infinitely many intermediate fields, and no primitive element
items.strategy: Adjoin $s$ and then $t$ and apply the preceding one-variable calculation twice to obtain degree $p^2$. For every $c$ in the infinite base field, $s+ct$ generates a degree-$p$ intermediate field; compare coefficients in the basis $s^it^j$ to prove these fields are distinct. The Steinitz criterion then rules out a primitive element.

items.title: $\bigcup_{n\ge0}\mathbb F_p(t^{1/p^n})$ is an infinite perfect field of characteristic $p$
items.strategy: Place compatible $p^n$th roots of $t$ in an algebraic closure. The nested union is a field. Taking coefficientwise $p$th roots in the next stage shows Frobenius is surjective, so the union is perfect; it contains $\mathbb F_p(t)$ and is therefore infinite.

items.title: FALSE: every irreducible polynomial over a field is separable
items.strategy: Use the irreducible polynomial $x^p-t$ over $\mathbb F_p(t)$ from the explicit example. Its derivative is zero and it has one root of multiplicity $p$ in a splitting field.

items.title: FALSE: every finite extension satisfies $[K:F]_s=[K:F]$
items.strategy: The extension $\mathbb F_p(t)/\mathbb F_p(t^p)$ has ordinary degree $p$ and separable degree one, so it directly refutes the equality.

items.title: FALSE: every algebraic extension is simple
items.strategy: Use this page's own algebraic closure of $\mathbb F_p$, which is algebraic over $\mathbb F_p$ and infinite, in place of the published infinite algebraic extension of $\mathbb Q$ (that one is homed on an examples page, and B pages are leaves). Were the closure $\mathbb F_p(\alpha)$, its generator would be algebraic and the extension finite; so it is algebraic and not simple.

items.title: FALSE: an algebraic closure is unique up to a unique base-field isomorphism
items.strategy: In an algebraic closure of $\mathbb Q$, choose a root $a$ of $x^2+1$. The two distinct roots $a$ and $-a$ give a nontrivial $\mathbb Q$-embedding of $\mathbb Q(a)$, which extends by Zorn to an automorphism of the closure. Thus the identity and this automorphism are distinct base-field isomorphisms.

pages.title: The Galois Correspondence

items.title: Relative field automorphisms and $\operatorname{Aut}(K/F)$
$\operatorname{Aut}(K/F)$ is a group and $|\operatorname{Aut}(K/F)|\le [K:F]_s\le [K:F]$
items.strategy: Verify closure, identity, and inverses under composition. For finite $K/F$, choose an $F$-embedding $\tau:K\to\Omega$ into an algebraic closure and inject $\operatorname{Aut}(K/F)$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_F(K,\Omega)$ by $\sigma\mapsto\tau\circ\sigma$; then apply the published separable-degree bound. Treat the trivial extension and degree one explicitly.

items.title: The fixed field $K^G$ of a group of field automorphisms
Dedekind's linear independence theorem for distinct characters
items.strategy: Assume a nontrivial dependence with the fewest nonzero coefficients. Normalize one coefficient, compare the relation at $gx$ with the relation at $x$ multiplied by one selected character value at $g$, and choose $g$ on which two distinct characters differ. The subtraction gives a shorter nonzero dependence, a contradiction. Include the empty and singleton character families.

items.title: Artin's fixed-field lower bound $[K:K^G]\ge |G|$
items.strategy: View the distinct automorphisms in the finite group $G$ as $K$-valued characters of $K^\times$. Dedekind independence gives an invertible evaluation minor on a finite family of field elements. Those elements are linearly independent over $K^G$, because a fixed-field dependence would be annihilated by the same evaluation matrix. Handle the trivial group and the zero element separately.

items.title: Artin's fixed-field upper bound $[K:K^G]\le |G|$
items.strategy: For $|G|+1$ field elements solve the homogeneous system whose rows are their images under the automorphisms in $G$. Choose a nonzero solution with minimal support and scale its first nonzero coefficient to one. Applying any automorphism and reindexing the equations produces another solution; subtracting it from the original lowers the support unless every coefficient is fixed by $G$. The identity row then supplies a nontrivial $K^G$-linear dependence. Check $G=\{1\}$ and repeated or zero input elements.

items.title: Artin's fixed-field theorem: $[K:K^G]=|G|$ and $\operatorname{Aut}(K/K^G)=G$
items.strategy: Combine the two degree bounds to obtain equality and finiteness. The defining fixed-field condition gives $G\subseteq\operatorname{Aut}(K/K^G)$, while the automorphism-degree bound gives the reverse cardinal inequality; equality of finite subsets forces equality of groups. Treat the trivial group without suppressing the degree-one case.

items.title: Distinct finite automorphism groups have distinct fixed fields
items.strategy: If finite groups $G$ and $H$ have the same fixed field, Artin's theorem identifies each with the full automorphism group over that field, so $G=H$. State the contrapositive as the advertised injectivity and include the trivial group.

items.title: For a finite extension, $|\operatorname{Aut}(K/F)|$ divides $[K:F]$
items.strategy: Let $G=\operatorname{Aut}(K/F)$ and $E=K^G$. The automorphism bound makes $G$ finite, Artin gives $|G|=[K:E]$, and the tower law gives $[K:F]=[K:E][E:F]$. Check degree one and the trivial automorphism group.

items.title: Finite Galois extensions and $\operatorname{Gal}(K/F)$
Equivalent characterizations of a finite Galois extension
items.strategy: Prove separately that normal and separable finite extensions are splitting fields of a separable product of distinct minimal polynomials; that a splitting field of a separable polynomial has all of its embeddings as automorphisms and hence the full automorphism count; that the full count forces fixed field $F$ by Artin and the tower law; and that fixed field $F$ makes every orbit polynomial equal the corresponding minimal polynomial, giving distinct roots and normality. Record all four conditions and both directions of every equivalence, including $K=F$.

items.title: A finite Galois extension is Galois over every intermediate field
items.strategy: Normality descends from $K/F$ to $K/E$. The minimal polynomial over $E$ of an element of $K$ divides its separable minimal polynomial over $F$, so it remains separable. Finiteness descends by the tower law, giving that $K/E$ is Galois. Explicitly avoid claiming that $E/F$ is Galois.

items.title: The Galois closure of a finite separable extension
Finite separable extensions have finite minimal Galois closures
items.strategy: Take the published finite normal closure inside an algebraic closure. It is the splitting field of the product of the generators' minimal polynomials; separability of the original extension makes the distinct factors separable, so the closure is finite, normal, and separable. Minimality is the intersection property of the normal closure. Treat the trivial extension and repeated generator polynomials.

items.title: The fundamental theorem of finite Galois theory
items.strategy: For finite Galois $K/F$ with group $G$, send $H$ to $K^H$ and $E$ to $\operatorname{Gal}(K/E)$. Artin proves both inverse identities, not merely injectivity: $\operatorname{Aut}(K/K^H)=H$ and $K^{\operatorname{Gal}(K/E)}=E$. Verify inclusion reversal directly and derive $[K:K^H]=|H|$ and $[K^H:F]=[G:H]$ from Artin and the tower law. Include $H=1,G$ and $E=K,F$.

items.title: Normal subgroups, conjugate fields, and quotient groups in the Galois correspondence
items.strategy: For $E=K^H$, compute $\operatorname{Gal}(K/\sigma(E))=\sigma H\sigma^{-1}$ elementwise. Deduce that $H$ is normal exactly when every $\sigma$ stabilizes $E$, which is equivalent to $E/F$ being normal and, since it is separable, Galois. In the normal case prove restriction $G\to\operatorname{Gal}(E/F)$ is surjective by comparing its fixed field and degrees, identify its kernel as $H$, and apply the first isomorphism theorem. Keep the conjugation formula, biconditional, and quotient conclusion in separate proof blocks.

items.title: A finite Galois extension has finitely many intermediate fields
items.strategy: The finite Galois group has only finitely many subsets and hence finitely many subgroups. The fundamental theorem gives a bijection from those subgroups to intermediate fields. Include the degree-one extension.

items.title: The Galois correspondence exchanges composita with subgroup intersections and field intersections with generated subgroups
items.strategy: For corresponding pairs $E_i=K^{H_i}$, an automorphism fixes the compositum $E_1E_2$ exactly when it fixes both fields, giving $\operatorname{Gal}(K/E_1E_2)=H_1\cap H_2$. The fixed field of $\langle H_1,H_2\rangle$ is exactly $K^{H_1}\cap K^{H_2}$, giving the second identity by the fundamental theorem. Check equal fields, base/top fields, and both binary operations.

items.title: The Galois translation theorem
items.strategy: Let $E/F$ be finite Galois and let $L/F$ lie in a common extension. Show $EL/L$ is the splitting field of the same separable polynomial, so it is Galois. Restriction to $E$ injects $\operatorname{Gal}(EL/L)$ into $\operatorname{Gal}(E/E\cap L)$. The fixed field in $E$ of the restriction image is exactly $E\cap L$, because the fixed field of $\operatorname{Gal}(EL/L)$ in $EL$ is $L$; Artin's theorem then makes the image have order $[E:E\cap L]$, so it is the whole target. Handle $E\subseteq L$, $E\cap L=F$, and $L=F$.

items.title: The Galois group of a compositum is a fibre product of Galois groups
items.strategy: For finite Galois $E_1/F$ and $E_2/F$, restriction embeds $\operatorname{Gal}(E_1E_2/F)$ in the product. Its image consists exactly of pairs with equal restrictions to $E_1\cap E_2$, using the translation theorem to extend compatible pairs. The image is the full product exactly when the intersection is $F$; verify both directions and the case $E_1=E_2$.

items.title: The Galois group of a separable polynomial
A polynomial Galois group acts faithfully on its roots
items.strategy: Every base-field automorphism permutes the finite root set. If it fixes every root, it fixes the splitting field generated by those roots, so the action is faithful and gives an embedding in the symmetric group. Reordering the roots conjugates the embedded subgroup by the corresponding permutation. Include constant separable polynomials and degree one.

items.title: A positive-degree separable polynomial is irreducible exactly when its Galois group is transitive on the roots
items.strategy: If $f$ is irreducible, extend the simple-extension isomorphism sending one root to any other root to an automorphism of the splitting field. Conversely, if the action is transitive, an irreducible factor containing one root contains every orbit root because its coefficients are fixed; separability then forces the factor to be the whole monic polynomial. Require positive degree and prove both directions.

items.title: The Vandermonde product transforms by the sign of the root permutation
items.strategy: For an ordered root list, each Galois automorphism permutes the pair factors in the Vandermonde product. Reordering a product by a transposition reverses exactly one net sign, and the sign homomorphism extends this to every permutation. Squaring gives an invariant discriminant. Treat degree zero and one empty products.

items.title: For a monic separable polynomial in characteristic not two, the Galois group lies in $A_n$ exactly when the discriminant is a square
items.strategy: Let $\delta$ be the Vandermonde product. If the Galois group lies in $A_n$, the sign formula fixes $\delta$, so the fundamental theorem puts $\delta$ in the base field and the discriminant is its square. Conversely, if $\delta^2=d^2$ with $d$ in the base field, the field hypothesis and characteristic not two give $\delta=\pm d$; every automorphism fixes it, and the sign formula forces even permutations. Record why separability makes $\delta$ nonzero and why characteristic two is excluded.

items.title: A monic irreducible separable cubic in characteristic not two has Galois group $A_3$ or $S_3$ according to its discriminant
items.strategy: For a monic separable irreducible cubic over a field of characteristic not two, transitivity leaves only the transitive subgroups $A_3$ and $S_3$. Apply the discriminant criterion to distinguish them. Verify that the separability hypothesis remains explicit in characteristic three and that the square and nonsquare cases are exhaustive.

items.title: The resolvent cubic of a monic quartic
The coefficient formula and discriminant of the quartic resolvent
items.strategy: For $f=x^4+ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$, expand the three pair-product roots of the resolvent. Express their elementary symmetric functions through those of the four roots to obtain $R_f=y^3-by^2+(ac-4d)y-(a^2d+c^2-4bd)$. Factor each difference of two resolvent roots into two differences of quartic roots; multiplying the three squared differences proves $\operatorname{Disc}(R_f)=\operatorname{Disc}(f)$. Check repeated resolvent roots are excluded when $f$ is separable.

items.title: The transitive subgroups of $S_4$ and their action on the three pairings
items.strategy: Classify a transitive subgroup of $S_4$ by its order and intersection with the normal Klein four subgroup acting trivially on the three unordered pairings. The induced quotient is a transitive or intransitive subgroup of $S_3$, leaving $S_4,A_4,D_4,C_4$, and $V_4$. Record the quotient orders and whether the subgroup is contained in $A_4$; prove that the degree-two resolvent case leaves exactly $D_4$ and $C_4$. No classification beyond subgroups of $S_4$ is assumed.

items.title: The five-case resolvent classification of an irreducible quartic Galois group
items.strategy: Let $f$ be separable irreducible of degree four over a field of characteristic not two. Identify the splitting field of the resolvent with the fixed field of the intersection of $G_f$ with the Klein four subgroup. Use resolvent factorization and the discriminant criterion to obtain $S_4$ for irreducible resolvent and nonsquare discriminant, $A_4$ for irreducible resolvent and square discriminant, $V_4$ for a fully split resolvent, and $D_4$ or $C_4$ when the resolvent has one base-field root; distinguish the last two by whether $f$ remains irreducible over the resolvent splitting field. Prove exhaustiveness and all boundary hypotheses.

pages.title: The Galois Correspondence — Examples

items.title: The complete Galois correspondence for $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)/\mathbb Q$
items.strategy: Write the four sign-change automorphisms explicitly and identify the group with $V_4$. Compute the fixed fields of its three order-two subgroups as $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$, $\mathbb Q(\sqrt3)$, and $\mathbb Q(\sqrt6)$, and include the base and top fields. Verify all degrees and reverse inclusions directly.

items.title: The full $S_3$ correspondence for the splitting field of $x^3-2$
items.strategy: In an algebraic closure choose a cube root $a$ of $2$ and a nontrivial cube root of unity $\omega$. Prove the splitting field $L=\mathbb Q(a,\omega)$ has degree six, write generators $r:a\mapsto\omega a$ and $s:a\mapsto a,\omega\mapsto\omega^2$, and identify $S_3$. Match the three order-two subgroups with the three cubic fields and $A_3$ with $\mathbb Q(\omega)$; include base and top fields and label exactly which strict intermediate fields are normal.

items.title: The ten-field $D_4$ correspondence for the splitting field of $x^4-2$
items.strategy: Choose $a$ with $a^4=2$ and $i^2=-1$. Prove $L=\mathbb Q(a,i)$ has degree eight, define $r(a)=ia,r(i)=i$ and $s(a)=a,s(i)=-i$, and obtain the dihedral relations. List every subgroup of $D_4$ and compute its fixed field by solving the coefficient constraints in the basis $1,a,a^2,a^3,i,ia,ia^2,ia^3$. Cross-check subgroup orders with field degrees and identify the normal subextensions.

items.title: $\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]{2})/\mathbb Q$ is separable and nonnormal with trivial automorphism group
items.strategy: Eisenstein gives degree three and characteristic zero gives separability. The other roots of $x^3-2$ are absent from the real root field, so it is not normal. Every base automorphism must send the generator to a root lying in the field, leaving only the generator itself; hence the automorphism group is trivial.

items.title: $\mathbb F_p(t)/\mathbb F_p(t^p)$ is normal and inseparable with trivial automorphism group
items.strategy: Show $x^p-t^p$ is the minimal polynomial of $t$ over $\mathbb F_p(t^p)$ and equals $(x-t)^p$ in the extension. Thus the degree is $p$, the extension is purely inseparable and normal, and $t$ is its only conjugate. Every base automorphism fixes $t$, so the automorphism group is trivial. Keep $p$ prime and include $p=2$.

items.title: $x^3-3x+1$ has discriminant $81$ and Galois group $A_3$ over $\mathbb Q$
items.strategy: The rational-root theorem proves irreducibility. Compute the depressed-cubic discriminant as $-4(-3)^3-27=81=9^2$, verify separability, and apply the cubic discriminant theorem. Record the resulting cyclic degree-three splitting field.

items.title: $x^3-2$ has discriminant $-108$ and Galois group $S_3$ over $\mathbb Q$
items.strategy: Eisenstein proves irreducibility. Compute the discriminant $-27(-2)^2=-108$, which is not a rational square, verify separability, and apply the cubic theorem. Reconcile the result with the explicitly generated group in the earlier lattice example.

items.title: $x^4-x-1$ has Galois group $S_4$ over $\mathbb Q$
items.strategy: Reduction modulo two proves the quartic irreducible. Its resolvent is $y^3+4y-1$, which has no rational root and is irreducible, while the quartic discriminant is $-283$, not a square. Apply the irreducible-resolvent nonsquare row of the five-case theorem.

items.title: $x^4+8x+12$ has Galois group $A_4$ over $\mathbb Q$
items.strategy: The rational-root theorem excludes a linear factor. Modulo five the polynomial factors as one linear irreducible times one cubic irreducible and has only that one root; Gauss's lemma then rules out a product of two rational quadratics, proving irreducibility over $\mathbb Q$. Compute the square discriminant $331776=576^2$ and show the resolvent $y^3-48y-64$ is irreducible modulo five. The square-discriminant irreducible-resolvent row gives $A_4$.

items.title: $x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1$ has Galois group $C_4$ over $\mathbb Q$
items.strategy: Translate by one and apply Eisenstein at five to prove irreducibility. If $\zeta$ is a root, list the four roots $\zeta,\zeta^2,\zeta^3,\zeta^4$ and show $\zeta\mapsto\zeta^2$ extends to an automorphism of order four, so the splitting field has cyclic group $C_4$. Compute the resolvent $(y-2)(y^2+y-1)$ and reconcile this with the one-root cyclic row of the quartic theorem without citing later cyclotomic theory.

items.title: $x^4-10x^2+1$ has Galois group $V_4$ over $\mathbb Q$
items.strategy: Show $\sqrt2+\sqrt3$ has minimal polynomial $x^4-10x^2+1$ and that its four conjugates are $\pm\sqrt2\pm\sqrt3$. Thus its splitting field is the biquadratic field from the earlier lattice example. Compute the resolvent $(y+10)(y-2)(y+2)$ and apply the fully split row of the quartic theorem.

items.title: FALSE: every degree-$n$ extension has exactly $n$ automorphisms
items.strategy: Use the degree-three extension $\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]{2})/\mathbb Q$, whose preceding counterexample proves that its automorphism group is trivial. Contrast the false equality with the valid automorphism bound and divisibility theorem.

items.title: FALSE: every subgroup in the Galois correspondence gives a normal subextension
items.strategy: In the $S_3$ splitting field of $x^3-2$, an order-two subgroup is not normal and its fixed cubic field is not normal over $\mathbb Q$. Identify the missing conjugate root and cite the exact normality clause.

items.title: FALSE: the degree of a polynomial determines its Galois group
items.strategy: Compare the two irreducible cubics already computed: $x^3-3x+1$ has group $A_3$, while $x^3-2$ has group $S_3$. Their common degree and distinct discriminant square classes isolate the missing data.

items.title: FALSE: the Galois correspondence preserves inclusion
items.strategy: In the biquadratic example, the trivial subgroup is contained in every order-two subgroup, but its fixed field is the whole extension and contains, rather than is contained in, each quadratic fixed field. State the general inclusion-reversing implication from the fundamental theorem.

pages.title: Finite Fields and Cyclotomic Extensions

items.title: A finite cyclic group has exactly one subgroup of each order dividing its own
items.strategy: Let $G=\langle g\rangle$ have order $n$. For a positive divisor $d$ of $n$ show $\langle g^{n/d}\rangle$ has order $d$ by computing the order of $g^{n/d}$. For uniqueness, let $H\le G$ with $|H|=d$; every $h\in H$ satisfies $h^d=e$ by Lagrange, and the elements of $G$ with $x^d=e$ are exactly the $n/d$-th powers, of which there are $d$, so $H=\langle g^{n/d}\rangle$. Finally $\langle g^{n/d}\rangle\subseteq\langle g^{n/e}\rangle$ exactly when $d\mid e$. Take $n\ge1$ so the trivial group ($d=1$) is covered.

items.title: A cyclic group of order $n$ has exactly $\varphi(n)$ generators
items.strategy: Transport along an isomorphism with $(\mathbb Z/n,+)$: the class $[a]_n$ generates $\mathbb Z/n$ exactly when $[a]_n$ is a unit, which is the coprimality criterion, and the units are counted by $\varphi(n)$. Check $n=1$, where the single element is a generator and $\varphi(1)=1$.

items.title: The relative Frobenius $x\mapsto x^q$ of an extension of finite fields
The elements of a finite extension fixed by the $q$-power map are exactly the base field
items.strategy: Every $a$ in the base field of order $q$ satisfies $a^q=a$, so the base field is contained in the fixed set. Conversely the fixed set is the root set of $t^q-t$, which has at most $q$ roots in the extension by the root bound, and the base field already supplies $q$ of them.

items.title: For a degree-$n$ extension of a field of order $q$, the $q$-power map has order exactly $n$
items.strategy: The tower law over the prime field gives $|E|=q^n$. Then $x^{q^n}=x$ on $E$, so the $n$-th iterate is the identity. If the $m$-th iterate were the identity for some $1\le m<n$, all $q^n$ elements of $E$ would be roots of $t^{q^m}-t$, contradicting the root bound since $q^m<q^n$. Include $n=1$, where the map is the identity and has order one.

items.title: A finite extension of a finite field of order $q$ is Galois with cyclic Galois group generated by $x\mapsto x^q$
items.strategy: Let $E/\mathbb F_q$ have degree $n$ and let $G=\langle\varphi_q\rangle$, of order $n$. Artin's fixed-field theorem gives $[E:E^{G}]=|G|=n$ and $\operatorname{Aut}(E/E^{G})=G$; the fixed field is $\mathbb F_q$, so $\operatorname{Aut}(E/\mathbb F_q)=G$ has order $n=[E:\mathbb F_q]$, which is the Galois criterion. No separate separability or normality argument is needed once Artin's theorem is applied to $G$.

items.title: The intermediate fields of $\mathbb F_{q^n}/\mathbb F_q$ are the $\mathbb F_{q^d}$, one for each positive divisor $d$ of $n$
items.strategy: Read the correspondence off a cyclic group. The subgroups of $\langle\varphi_q\rangle$ are the $\langle\varphi_q^{d}\rangle$ for $d\mid n$, exactly one of each order $n/d$. The fixed field of $\langle\varphi_q^{d}\rangle$ is $\{x: x^{q^{d}}=x\}$ directly from the definition of a fixed field, and the fundamental theorem gives $[\mathbb F_{q^{n}}:K^{\langle\varphi_q^{d}\rangle}]=n/d$, hence degree $d$ over $\mathbb F_q$ and order $q^{d}$; the fixed-field lemma is the case $d=1$, which is what identifies the bottom of the lattice as $\mathbb F_q$ rather than something larger. Inclusion between two of them corresponds to reverse inclusion of subgroups, which is divisibility of the degrees.

items.title: The Galois description of the subfields of a finite field and the elementary divisibility criterion agree
A monic irreducible of degree $d$ over $\mathbb F_q$ has the $d$ distinct roots $\alpha,\alpha^{q},\dots,\alpha^{q^{d-1}}$
items.strategy: Let $\alpha$ be a root of $\pi$ in an extension. Then $\mathbb F_q(\alpha)$ has degree $d$, so it is $\mathbb F_{q^{d}}$ and is Galois over $\mathbb F_q$ with group generated by $\varphi_q$. Each $\varphi_q^{i}(\alpha)=\alpha^{q^{i}}$ is again a root of $\pi$. If two of $\alpha,\dots,\alpha^{q^{d-1}}$ coincided, $\alpha$ would satisfy $x^{q^{j}}=x$ for some $0<j<d$ and hence lie in a proper subfield, contradicting $\mathbb F_q(\alpha)=\mathbb F_{q^{d}}$. The factor theorem then makes $\prod_{i<d}(t-\alpha^{q^{i}})$ a monic degree-$d$ divisor of $\pi$, so equal to it.

items.title: $\sum_{d\mid n}d\,N_q(d)=q^{n}$ for the counts $N_q(d)$ of monic irreducibles of degree $d$ over $\mathbb F_q$
items.strategy: The published factorisation of $t^{q^{n}}-t$ groups its monic irreducible factors by degree; each degree-$d$ factor contributes $d$ to the total degree and each occurs exactly once. Comparing degrees on the two sides gives the identity. Record that $N_q(d)$ is finite because there are only $q^{d}$ monic polynomials of degree $d$, and check $n=1$, where the identity reads $N_q(1)=q$.

items.title: Normal bases of a finite Galois extension
A polynomial vanishing at every tuple from an infinite subdomain is the zero polynomial
items.strategy: Induct on the number of indeterminates. For one indeterminate a nonzero polynomial of degree $m$ has at most $m$ roots in the ambient domain, while the infinite subdomain supplies more than $m$ elements. For $m>1$ write $f$ as a polynomial in the last indeterminate with coefficients in the polynomial ring on the others; each coefficient then vanishes on every tuple, so is zero by the inductive hypothesis. State it as $R\subseteq S$ with $R$ infinite and $f\in S[x_1,\dots,x_m]$, which is the form the normal basis argument uses with $R=F$ and $S=K$.

items.title: For a finite Galois extension, $(\alpha_j)$ is a base-field basis exactly when the matrix $(\sigma_i\alpha_j)$ is invertible
items.strategy: If the $\alpha_j$ are dependent over $F$, say $\sum_j a_j\alpha_j=0$ with $a_j\in F$ not all zero, then applying each $\sigma_i$ gives $A a=0$ with $a\neq0$, so $A$ is not invertible. Conversely, if the $\alpha_j$ are a basis and $\sum_i c_i\sigma_i(\alpha_j)=0$ for all $j$ with $c_i\in K$, then $F$-linearity of each $\sigma_i$ spreads the relation to all of $K$, so Dedekind independence forces $c=0$; hence $x\mapsto A^{\mathsf T}x$ is injective, so an isomorphism by rank-nullity, so $\det A^{\mathsf T}=\det A$ is a unit and $A$ is invertible.

items.title: Over an infinite base field, no nonzero polynomial vanishes at the conjugate tuple of every element
items.strategy: Fix a base-field basis $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$ of $K$ and let $A=(\sigma_i\alpha_j)$, invertible by the preceding lemma. Writing a general $\alpha=\sum_j c_j\alpha_j$ with $c_j\in F$ gives the conjugate tuple $Ac$. If $f$ vanished at every conjugate tuple, the polynomial $g(x)=f(Ax)$ would vanish at every $c\in F^{n}$, so $g=0$ by the several-variable vanishing lemma; substituting $A^{-1}$ recovers $f=0$.

items.title: Every finite Galois extension of an infinite field has a normal basis
items.strategy: Number the group as $\sigma_1=\mathrm{id},\dots,\sigma_n$ and let $B$ be the matrix of indeterminates with $B_{ij}=x_k$ when $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\sigma_k$. Setting $x_1=1$ and the other indeterminates to $0$ turns $B$ into a permutation matrix, whose transpose is its inverse, so its determinant is a unit; hence $\det B$ is a nonzero polynomial. Algebraic independence supplies $\alpha$ with $\det(\sigma_i\sigma_j\alpha)\neq0$, and the conjugate-matrix criterion applied to $\alpha_j=\sigma_j\alpha$ makes $\{\sigma\alpha\}$ a basis.

items.title: Every finite cyclic extension has a normal basis
items.strategy: View $K$ as an $F$-vector space of dimension $n$ and $\sigma$, a generator of the group, as an $F$-linear endomorphism. Then $\sigma^{n}=\mathrm{id}$, so the minimal polynomial divides $x^{n}-1$; Dedekind independence makes $\mathrm{id},\sigma,\dots,\sigma^{n-1}$ linearly independent over $F$ as maps, so the minimal polynomial has degree at least $n$ and therefore equals $x^{n}-1$. The characteristic polynomial is monic of degree $n$ and is divisible by the minimal polynomial, so the two agree and a cyclic vector $\alpha$ exists; its power basis under $\sigma$ is exactly the conjugate family $\{\sigma^{i}\alpha\}$.

items.title: Every finite Galois extension has a normal basis
items.strategy: Split on the base field. If $F$ is infinite, apply the infinite-base-field theorem. If $F$ is finite, then $K$ is a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space over a finite field and so is itself finite, and the Frobenius theorem makes $K/F$ cyclic, so the cyclic case applies. The two cases are exhaustive, which is the whole content of the split.

items.title: The group $\mu_n(K)$ of $n$-th roots of unity in a field, and primitive $n$-th roots of unity
$\mu_n(K)$ is cyclic of order dividing $n$, and has a primitive $n$-th root of unity exactly when its order is $n$
items.strategy: The set $\mu_n(K)$ is a subgroup of $K^\times$, finite because its elements are roots of $t^{n}-1$ and a field is a domain, hence cyclic by the published subgroup theorem. Its order divides $n$ because every element has order dividing $n$ and the group is cyclic. A generator has order equal to the group order, so a primitive $n$-th root of unity exists exactly when that order is $n$, and there are then $\varphi(n)$ of them.

items.title: $t^{n}-1$ is separable over $K$ exactly when the characteristic does not divide $n$, and then a splitting field carries $n$ distinct $n$-th roots of unity
items.strategy: The derivative of $t^{n}-1$ is $n t^{n-1}$, whose only root is $0$ when $n\neq0$ in $K$ and which is the zero polynomial otherwise; the gcd criterion turns this into separability exactly when the characteristic does not divide $n$. Under that hypothesis a splitting field has $n$ distinct roots, so $\mu_n$ there is cyclic of order $n$ with $\varphi(n)$ generators, and adjoining any one of them gives the whole splitting field since every root is a power of it. Cover $n=1$, where the polynomial is $t-1$.

items.title: In characteristic $p$ the only $p^{k}$-th root of unity is $1$, and $t^{p^{k}}-1=(t-1)^{p^{k}}$
items.strategy: Iterating the freshman's dream in $K[t]$ gives $(t-1)^{p^{k}}=t^{p^{k}}-1$, so the only root is $1$. Deduce that for $n=p^{k}m$ with $p\nmid m$ one has $\mu_n(K)=\mu_m(K)$, which is why every later statement about $\mu_n$ carries the hypothesis that the characteristic does not divide $n$ rather than losing generality.

items.title: The cyclotomic extension $K(\mu_n)$ as a splitting field of $t^{n}-1$
$K(\mu_n)/K$ is Galois and $\sigma\mapsto a_\sigma$ embeds its Galois group into $(\mathbb Z/n)^\times$
items.strategy: Galois because a splitting field of a separable polynomial. An automorphism carries a primitive $n$-th root $\zeta$ to a primitive $n$-th root, hence to $\zeta^{a}$ with $a$ coprime to $n$, and the exponent is well defined modulo $n$ because $\zeta$ has order $n$. Multiplicativity of exponents makes $\sigma\mapsto[a_\sigma]$ a homomorphism, and it is injective because $\zeta$ generates the extension. Check independence of the chosen primitive root by writing any other root of unity as a power of $\zeta$.

items.title: The Galois group of a cyclotomic extension is abelian
items.strategy: A subgroup of an abelian group is abelian, and multiplication on $\mathbb Z/n$ is commutative, so the embedded image and hence the Galois group is abelian.

items.title: For $\gcd(n,q)=1$ the image of $\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb F_q(\mu_n)/\mathbb F_q)$ in $(\mathbb Z/n)^\times$ is generated by $[q]$
items.strategy: The extension $\mathbb F_q(\mu_n)/\mathbb F_q$ is an extension of finite fields, so its Galois group is generated by $\varphi_q$, whose effect on a primitive $n$-th root of unity is $\zeta\mapsto\zeta^{q}$. Hence the embedded image is $\langle[q]\rangle$, and the degree, being the order of the group, is the multiplicative order of $[q]$ modulo $n$. Note the hypothesis $\gcd(n,q)=1$ is what makes $[q]$ a unit.

items.title: The cyclotomic polynomials $\Phi_n\in\mathbb Z[t]$, defined by $\prod_{d\mid n}\Phi_d=t^{n}-1$
The recursion defines a unique monic $\Phi_n\in\mathbb Z[t]$, of degree $\varphi(n)$
items.strategy: Strong induction on $n$. The product of the $\Phi_d$ for proper divisors $d$ is monic with integer coefficients, so dividing $t^{n}-1$ by it is division by a monic polynomial over $\mathbb Z$, which has a unique quotient and remainder there; the remainder is zero because the division is already exact over $\mathbb Q$ and uniqueness transfers. The degree is $n-\sum_{d\mid n,\,d<n}\varphi(d)=\varphi(n)$ by the published divisor-sum identity for the totient. This is the well-definedness obligation of the definition and must be a numbered item, not a parenthesis: the division is over $\mathbb Z$, not over a field.

items.title: $\Phi_1(0)=-1$ and $\Phi_n(0)=1$ for $n\ge2$
items.strategy: Evaluate $\prod_{d\mid n}\Phi_d=t^{n}-1$ at $t=0$: the right side is $-1$ and $\Phi_1(0)=-1$, so the product of $\Phi_d(0)$ over divisors $d>1$ is $1$. Strong induction gives $\Phi_d(0)=1$ for $1<d<n$, leaving $\Phi_n(0)=1$. Handle $n=2$ as the first case beyond the base.

items.title: Over a field whose characteristic does not divide $n$, the roots of $\Phi_n$ are exactly the primitive $n$-th roots of unity
items.strategy: Reduce the integer polynomial into $K$ and work in a splitting field of $t^{n}-1$, where that polynomial is separable. Strong induction on $n$: a root $\alpha$ of $\Phi_n$ has $\alpha^{n}=1$, and if its order were a proper divisor $d$ of $n$ it would be a root of $\Phi_d$ as well, making it a repeated root of $t^{n}-1$. Counting degrees, $\Phi_n$ has $\varphi(n)$ roots and there are $\varphi(n)$ primitive $n$-th roots of unity, so the two sets coincide and $\Phi_n$ is separable.

items.title: $\Phi_n$ is irreducible over $K$ exactly when $[K(\zeta_n):K]=\varphi(n)$, exactly when the embedding into $(\mathbb Z/n)^\times$ is onto
items.strategy: A primitive $n$-th root $\zeta$ is a root of $\Phi_n$, so its minimal polynomial over $K$ divides $\Phi_n$; equality holds exactly when the degrees agree, that is when $[K(\zeta):K]=\varphi(n)$, and since $K(\zeta)=K(\mu_n)$ that is exactly when the injection into a group of order $\varphi(n)$ is surjective.

items.title: $\Phi_{p^{r}}(t)=\sum_{k<p}t^{kp^{r-1}}$, and $\Phi_{p^{r}}(t+1)$ is Eisenstein at $p$
items.strategy: The recursion at $n=p^{r}$ telescopes to $\Phi_{p^{r}}(t)=(t^{p^{r}}-1)/(t^{p^{r-1}}-1)$, which is the displayed sum. Its value at $t=1$ is $p$, giving the constant term of the translate; modulo $p$ the numerator and denominator are $(t-1)^{p^{r}}$ and $(t-1)^{p^{r-1}}$, so the reduction of the translate is $t^{p^{r}-p^{r-1}}$ and every non-leading coefficient is divisible by $p$. Eisenstein then gives irreducibility of the translate, and translation by $1$ is a ring automorphism of $\mathbb Q[t]$, so $\Phi_{p^{r}}$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$. This is a self-contained route for prime powers, independent of the general argument that follows.

items.title: If $p$ is a prime not dividing $n$, a rational minimal polynomial of a primitive $n$-th root of unity also kills its $p$-th power
items.strategy: Write $\Phi_n=fg$ with $f$ the minimal polynomial of $\zeta$; both are monic factors of a monic integer polynomial, so both lie in $\mathbb Z[t]$ by Gauss's lemma. If $g(\zeta^{p})=0$ then $f$ and $g(t^{p})$ share the root $\zeta$, hence a nonconstant common factor over $\mathbb Q$ by gcd stability, hence over $\mathbb Z$. Reducing modulo $p$ and using $\overline g(t^{p})=\overline g(t)^{p}$ gives $\overline f$ and $\overline g$ a common nonconstant factor, so $t^{n}-1$ has a repeated root modulo $p$ — impossible since $p\nmid n$ makes it separable there. Record where $p\nmid n$ is used; without it the last step fails.

items.title: $\Phi_n$ is irreducible in $\mathbb Q[t]$ for every $n\ge1$
items.strategy: Let $f$ be the minimal polynomial over $\mathbb Q$ of one primitive $n$-th root $\zeta$. Every other primitive $n$-th root is $\zeta^{a}$ with $a$ coprime to $n$, and such an $a$ is a product of primes none of which divides $n$; applying the preceding lemma once per prime factor shows $f$ vanishes at every primitive $n$-th root. So $f$ has at least $\varphi(n)$ roots and divides $\Phi_n$, which has degree $\varphi(n)$, forcing $f=\Phi_n$.

items.title: $[\mathbb Q(\zeta_n):\mathbb Q]=\varphi(n)$ and $\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb Q(\mu_n)/\mathbb Q)\cong(\mathbb Z/n)^\times$
items.strategy: Combine irreducibility over $\mathbb Q$ with the general criterion: irreducibility of $\Phi_n$ is exactly surjectivity of the embedding, so the injection is an isomorphism and the degree is the order $\varphi(n)$ of the target.

items.title: For $\gcd(n,q)=1$ the reduction of $\Phi_n$ in $\mathbb F_q[t]$ is a product of distinct monic irreducibles, each of degree the order of $[q]$ modulo $n$
items.strategy: The reduction is separable because it divides $t^{n}-1$, which is separable when $\gcd(n,q)=1$. Every root is a primitive $n$-th root of unity, and adjoining one gives $\mathbb F_q(\mu_n)$, whose degree over $\mathbb F_q$ is the order of $[q]$ modulo $n$; the degree of the irreducible factor with that root is that same degree. So every irreducible factor has the same degree, and distinctness is separability.

items.title: The reduction of $\Phi_n$ is irreducible over $\mathbb F_q$ exactly when $[q]$ generates $(\mathbb Z/n)^\times$
items.strategy: Irreducibility means one factor, so the common factor degree equals $\deg\Phi_n=\varphi(n)$, that is the order of $[q]$ is the order of the whole group. In particular this can happen only when $(\mathbb Z/n)^\times$ is cyclic.

items.title: For $E/F$ finite Galois and $L/F$ finite inside a common field, $[EL:F]=[E:F][L:F]/[E\cap L:F]$
items.strategy: The translation theorem gives $\operatorname{Gal}(EL/L)\cong\operatorname{Gal}(E/E\cap L)$, so $[EL:L]=[E:E\cap L]$, which the tower law rewrites as $[E:F]/[E\cap L:F]$. Multiplying by $[L:F]$ through the tower $F\subseteq L\subseteq EL$ gives the formula. Note the hypothesis that one of the two is Galois is genuinely needed and record it.

items.title: $K(\mu_m)K(\mu_n)=K(\mu_{\operatorname{lcm}(m,n)})$
items.strategy: Both $\mu_m$ and $\mu_n$ sit inside $\mu_{\ell}$ for $\ell=\operatorname{lcm}(m,n)$, so the compositum is contained in $K(\mu_\ell)$. Conversely the subgroup of the cyclic group $\mu_\ell$ generated by a primitive $m$-th and a primitive $n$-th root has order divisible by both $m$ and $n$, hence by $\ell$, so it is all of $\mu_\ell$. Require the characteristic to divide neither $m$ nor $n$ and say so in the statement.

items.title: $\varphi(m)\varphi(n)=\varphi(\gcd(m,n))\,\varphi(\operatorname{lcm}(m,n))$
items.strategy: Compare the two sides prime by prime using the product formula: for each prime $p$, the exponents in $m$ and $n$ are $a$ and $b$, and the exponents in the gcd and lcm are $\min(a,b)$ and $\max(a,b)$, whose multiset is $\{a,b\}$. Treat the case $p\nmid mn$ and the case where exactly one of $a,b$ is zero explicitly.

items.title: $\mathbb Q(\mu_m)\cap\mathbb Q(\mu_n)=\mathbb Q(\mu_{\gcd(m,n)})$
items.strategy: One inclusion is immediate from $\mathbb Q(\mu_d)\subseteq\mathbb Q(\mu_m)$ for $d\mid m$. For equality compare degrees: the compositum is $\mathbb Q(\mu_{\operatorname{lcm}})$, so the compositum degree formula gives $[\mathbb Q(\mu_m)\cap\mathbb Q(\mu_n):\mathbb Q]=\varphi(m)\varphi(n)/\varphi(\operatorname{lcm}(m,n))$, which the totient identity turns into $\varphi(\gcd(m,n))$. State this for $\mathbb Q$ only: the same equality is false over a general base field.

items.title: For an odd prime $p$, $\mathbb Q(\zeta_p)$ has exactly one intermediate field of degree two over $\mathbb Q$
items.strategy: The Galois group is $(\mathbb Z/p)^\times$, the unit group of a field, hence cyclic, of order $p-1$, which is even for odd $p$. A finite cyclic group of even order has exactly one subgroup of index two, and the correspondence turns that into exactly one intermediate field of degree two. A Remark records that identifying that field concretely is a separate computation this proof does not carry out.

items.title: For every $n\ge1$ there are infinitely many primes $p$ with $p\equiv1\pmod n$
items.strategy: Take $n\ge2$ and a finite set $S$ of such primes with product $q$. For large $k$ the integer $N=\Phi_n(knq)$ exceeds $1$; since $\Phi_n(0)=1$, every prime dividing $knq$ leaves $N\equiv1$, so a prime divisor $p$ of $N$ divides neither $k$, nor $n$, nor $q$. As $p\nmid n$, the class of $knq$ in $\mathbb F_p$ is a root of $\Phi_n$, hence a primitive $n$-th root of unity there, so $n$ divides $p-1$ by Lagrange. That produces a prime outside $S$. Handle $n=1$ separately, where the claim is that there are infinitely many primes.

items.title: Every finite abelian group is a quotient of $(\mathbb Z/n)^{k}$ for some $n$ and $k$
items.strategy: Write the group in invariant-factor form as a product of $k$ cyclic groups of orders $d_1\mid\cdots\mid d_k$ and put $n=d_k$. Each $\mathbb Z/n$ surjects onto $\mathbb Z/d_i$ because $d_i\mid n$, and the product of these surjections is a surjection from $(\mathbb Z/n)^{k}$. Cover the trivial group.

items.title: Every finite abelian group is the Galois group of some finite Galois extension of $\mathbb Q$
items.strategy: Reduce to $G=(\mathbb Z/n)^{k}$ by the preceding lemma, since a quotient of a Galois group over $\mathbb Q$ is again one by the normal-subgroup clause. Choose distinct primes $p_1,\dots,p_k$ each congruent to $1$ modulo $n$; each $(\mathbb Z/p_i)^\times$ is cyclic of order $p_i-1$, so it surjects onto $\mathbb Z/n$. The Chinese remainder theorem identifies $(\mathbb Z/p_1\cdots p_k)^\times$ with the product of the $(\mathbb Z/p_i)^\times$, giving a surjection from $\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb Q(\mu_{p_1\cdots p_k})/\mathbb Q)$ onto $G$; its kernel corresponds to an intermediate field with the required group.

items.title: Every intermediate field of $\mathbb Q(\mu_n)/\mathbb Q$ is Galois over $\mathbb Q$ with abelian Galois group
items.strategy: Every subgroup of an abelian group is normal, so every intermediate field is Galois over $\mathbb Q$, and its group is a quotient of an abelian group, hence abelian.

items.title: Recorded, not proved: every finite abelian extension of $\mathbb Q$ lies in a cyclotomic field

pages.title: Finite Fields and Cyclotomic Extensions — Examples

items.title: $\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb F_8/\mathbb F_2)$ is cyclic of order three with no proper intermediate field
items.strategy: Work in the published presentation $\mathbb F_8=\mathbb F_2[t]/(t^{3}+t+1)$ and tabulate the squaring map on all eight elements. Its orbits on the six elements outside $\mathbb F_2$ are two triples, the group is generated by squaring and has order three, and since three is prime the only divisors are one and three, so there is no proper intermediate field.

items.title: The intermediate fields of $\mathbb F_{2^{12}}/\mathbb F_2$ match the divisors of twelve
items.strategy: List the six positive divisors of twelve and the corresponding subfields, drawing the containments and checking them against divisibility; contrast $\mathbb F_{2^{4}}$ and $\mathbb F_{2^{6}}$, neither containing the other, whose intersection is $\mathbb F_{2^{2}}$ and whose compositum is $\mathbb F_{2^{12}}$.

items.title: The divisor-sum identity at $q=2$, $n=3$ finds exactly two monic irreducible cubics
items.strategy: The identity reads $N_2(1)+3N_2(3)=8$ with $N_2(1)=2$, so $N_2(3)=2$; exhibit $t^{3}+t+1$ and $t^{3}+t^{2}+1$ and confirm by the root test that the remaining monic cubics all have a root in $\mathbb F_2$.

items.title: The four roots of $t^{4}+t+1$ over $\mathbb F_2$ are the Frobenius powers of any one of them
items.strategy: Take $\alpha$ with $\alpha^{4}=\alpha+1$ and compute $\alpha^{2},\alpha^{4},\alpha^{8}$ in the basis $1,\alpha,\alpha^{2},\alpha^{3}$, checking each is a root and that $\alpha^{16}=\alpha$ closes the orbit at length four.

items.title: A normal basis of $\mathbb F_8$ over $\mathbb F_2$
items.strategy: With $\mathbb F_8=\mathbb F_2[t]/(t^{3}+t+1)$ and $\alpha$ the class of $t$, compute $\alpha,\alpha^{2},\alpha^{4}$ in the power basis and check the resulting three-by-three matrix over $\mathbb F_2$ is invertible, so the three conjugates form a normal basis.

items.title: $\{1+i,\,1-i\}$ is a normal basis of $\mathbb C/\mathbb R$ while $\{1,i\}$ is not
items.strategy: The nontrivial automorphism is conjugation. The conjugates of $1+i$ are $1+i$ and $1-i$, whose conjugate matrix has determinant $-2i\neq0$. By contrast $\{1,i\}$ is a basis but its two members are not in one orbit, and the orbit $\{i,-i\}$ of $i$ is not a basis; both failures are worth stating because they separate the two conditions in the definition.

items.title: FALSE: every basis of a finite field over a subfield is a normal basis
items.strategy: Refute in $\mathbb F_4=\mathbb F_2[t]/(t^{2}+t+1)$: the pair $\{1,\alpha\}$ is a basis over $\mathbb F_2$, but the only automorphism orbits are $\{1\}$ and $\{\alpha,\alpha+1\}$, and neither orbit is $\{1,\alpha\}$. The normal basis theorem asserts the existence of one such basis, never that every basis is one.

items.title: $\Phi_1$ through $\Phi_{12}$ computed from the divisor recursion
