items.strategy: Run the recursion in order, dividing $t^{n}-1$ by the product of the earlier $\Phi_d$ over $\mathbb Z$, and tabulate the results with their degrees against $\varphi(n)$. Note that every division is exact and stays in $\mathbb Z[t]$, which is the content of the well-definedness theorem.

items.title: $\Phi_7(t+1)$ is Eisenstein at seven
items.strategy: Expand $((t+1)^{7}-1)/t$ by the binomial theorem, exhibit the coefficients $7,21,35,35,21,7$ and the constant term $7$, and check the three Eisenstein conditions at the prime seven, concluding irreducibility of $\Phi_7$ over $\mathbb Q$.

items.title: $\Phi_5$ has four roots in $\mathbb F_{11}$
items.strategy: Since $11\equiv1\pmod 5$, the order of $[11]$ modulo five is one, so every irreducible factor is linear; verify by exhibiting the factorisation of $t^{4}+t^{3}+t^{2}+t+1$ over $\mathbb F_{11}$ and checking each root has multiplicative order five.

items.title: $\Phi_7$ factors over $\mathbb F_2$ into the two monic irreducible cubics
items.strategy: The order of $[2]$ modulo seven is three, so both factors are cubic; multiply out $(t^{3}+t+1)(t^{3}+t^{2}+1)$ over $\mathbb F_2$ to confirm, and identify the two Frobenius orbits $\{\zeta,\zeta^{2},\zeta^{4}\}$ and $\{\zeta^{3},\zeta^{6},\zeta^{5}\}$ of primitive seventh roots of unity.

items.title: $\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb Q(\zeta_{12})/\mathbb Q)\cong(\mathbb Z/12)^\times$ and its three quadratic subfields
items.strategy: List $(\mathbb Z/12)^\times=\{1,5,7,11\}$, check every element squares to the identity, and name its three subgroups of order two. Match each fixed field to $\mathbb Q(i)$, $\mathbb Q(\sqrt3)$ and $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$ by exhibiting an element of $\mathbb Q(\zeta_{12})$ fixed by the corresponding subgroup and squaring to $-1$, $3$ and $-3$ respectively.

items.title: In characteristic three, $t^{3}-1=(t-1)^{3}$ and $\mu_6$ coincides with $\mu_2$
items.strategy: Expand $(t-1)^{3}$ over $\mathbb F_3$ to see the middle coefficients vanish, so the only cube root of unity is one; then $\mu_6=\mu_2=\{1,-1\}$ in every field of characteristic three, and $t^{6}-1$ has two distinct roots rather than six.

items.title: $\mathbb F_3(\mu_5)\cap\mathbb F_3(\mu_7)$ is larger than $\mathbb F_3$ although five and seven are coprime
items.strategy: Compute the order of $[3]$ modulo five as four and modulo seven as six, so the two extensions are $\mathbb F_{3^{4}}$ and $\mathbb F_{3^{6}}$, whose intersection is $\mathbb F_{3^{2}}$ by the subfield lattice. This is the witness that the rational intersection theorem is a statement about $\mathbb Q$ and not a general fact.

items.title: FALSE: every cyclotomic polynomial has all coefficients in $\{-1,0,1\}$
items.strategy: The claim survives every $n$ below $105$, which is exactly what makes it worth stating. Refute it by computing $\Phi_{105}$ from the recursion and exhibiting the coefficient $-2$ that it carries; report the exact monomials at which that coefficient occurs.

items.title: FALSE: $\Phi_n$ is irreducible over every field
items.strategy: Refute with the reduction of $\Phi_5$ over $\mathbb F_{11}$, which is a product of four linear factors. Say precisely what the irreducibility theorem does claim: it is a statement about the base field $\mathbb Q$, and the finite-field factorisation theorem is what governs the general case.

items.title: FALSE: $\mu_n(K)$ has $n$ elements in every field $K$
items.strategy: Two independent refutations: in $\mathbb Q$ the group $\mu_3$ is trivial because $t^{3}-1$ has one rational root, and in characteristic three $\mu_3$ is trivial for a different reason, namely inseparability. State both, since the two failures have different causes and only the second is repaired by passing to a splitting field.

items.title: FALSE: every finite abelian group is $\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb Q(\mu_n)/\mathbb Q)$ for some $n$
items.strategy: For $n\ge3$ the class of $-1$ is a unit of order two, so $\varphi(n)$ is even by Lagrange, and $\varphi(1)=\varphi(2)=1$; hence no cyclotomic field over $\mathbb Q$ has Galois group of order three. Contrast with the theorem actually proved, which produces a subfield of a cyclotomic field, not the cyclotomic field itself.

items.title: A degree-three Galois extension of $\mathbb Q$ inside $\mathbb Q(\zeta_7)$
items.strategy: Since $(\mathbb Z/7)^\times$ is cyclic of order six, it has a unique subgroup of order two, generated by $[-1]$; its fixed field is $\mathbb Q(\zeta_7+\zeta_7^{-1})$, of degree three over $\mathbb Q$ and Galois with cyclic group of order three. Exhibit the minimal polynomial $t^{3}+t^{2}-2t-1$ of that generator and verify it by expanding the power sums of $\zeta_7+\zeta_7^{-1}$.

pages.title: Solvability by Radicals and Kummer Theory

items.title: The norm $N_{K/F}$ and trace $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}$ of a finite field extension
Norm and trace from embeddings, with the inseparable exponent in the norm formula
items.strategy: Let $K_{\mathrm{sep}}/F$ be the maximal separable subextension of $K/F$. For the trace, use the multiplicity-$[K:F]_i$ block decomposition through $K_{\mathrm{sep}}$ to show that inseparability forces $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}=0$ in characteristic $p$ when $[K:F]_i>1$, while in the separable case the trace is the sum over the $F$-embeddings into a normal closure. For the norm, first prove the separable product formula over the distinct $F$-embeddings, then compare multiplication-by-$a$ on $K$ with multiplication-by-$a$ on $K_{\mathrm{sep}}$ repeated $[K:F]_i$ times to get $N_{K/F}(a)=\bigl(\prod_\sigma \sigma(a)\bigr)^{[K:F]_i}$. The exponent is load-bearing and must remain in both the title and the statement.

items.title: Norm is multiplicative, trace is $F$-linear, and both are transitive in towers
items.strategy: Linearity and multiplicativity are immediate from the multiplication operators on the finite-dimensional $F$-vector space $K$. For transitivity in a tower $L/K/F$, either compare the block matrices for multiplication by an element of $L$ after choosing a $K$-basis and an $F$-basis, or use the embedding formulas and count each $F$-embedding through an intermediate $K$-embedding exactly once. Treat purely inseparable subextensions explicitly so the trace-zero case is not silently absorbed into the separable argument.

items.title: Field norm and trace agree with the determinant and trace of multiplication by an element
items.strategy: This is the dictionary item the page owes the earlier determinant and trace pages. Unpack the multiplication map $m_a\colon K\to K$, note that the finite-extension definition of norm and trace was made through $m_a$, and spell out the zero-dimensional convention so the determinant agrees with the already-published linear-algebra definition on the zero field extension.

items.title: The trace form $(x,y)\mapsto \operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(xy)$ of a finite extension
The trace form of a finite extension is nondegenerate exactly when the extension is separable
items.strategy: If $K/F$ is inseparable then the trace theorem makes $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}=0$, so the whole space lies in the radical. If $K/F$ is separable, embed $K$ into a normal closure, write the trace form matrix as $A^{\mathsf T}A$ with $A=(\sigma_i(e_j))$, and use Dedekind independence to show $A$ is invertible for any $F$-basis $(e_j)$. Then the bilinear-form radical vanishes, which is exactly nondegeneracy in the earlier linear-algebra sense.

items.title: The trace map of a finite separable extension is surjective
items.strategy: Regard the trace map as the linear functional $x\mapsto \operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(x\cdot 1)$. If its image were $0$, then $1$ would lie in the radical of the trace form, contradicting nondegeneracy. Since the codomain is the one-dimensional $F$-vector space $F$ over itself, any nonzero linear map onto it is surjective.

items.title: A cyclic extension is a finite Galois extension with cyclic Galois group
Hilbert's theorem 90 for a finite cyclic extension
items.strategy: Let $K/F$ be cyclic with generator $\sigma$. The easy direction is the telescoping product $N_{K/F}(\beta/\sigma(\beta))=1$. For the converse, choose the standard crossed-homomorphism built from an element of norm $1$ and apply Dedekind independence to the linear combination $\sum_i c_i\sigma^i$ acting on a carefully chosen vector, so the vanishing of first cohomology is proved algebraically rather than quoted. Keep the degree-one case visible.

items.title: Additive Hilbert 90: trace zero is the image of $\alpha\mapsto\alpha-\sigma(\alpha)$
items.strategy: One direction is the telescoping trace computation. For the converse, let $K/F$ be cyclic of degree $n$ with generator $\sigma$, choose $c\in K$ with $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}(c)=1$, and for a trace-zero element $b$ use the standard explicit sum $\alpha=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}\sigma^j(b))\sigma^i(c)$ to obtain $\alpha-\sigma(\alpha)=b$. This proof keeps the characteristic-$p$ case honest because it uses only the existence of one element of trace $1$ from the previous corollary.

items.title: The Lagrange resolvent attached to a cyclic action and a root of unity
If $\mu_n\subseteq F$ and $\operatorname{char}F\nmid n$, then a degree-$n$ extension is cyclic exactly when it is $F(\alpha)$ with $\alpha^n\in F$ and $x^n-\alpha^n$ irreducible
items.strategy: For the cyclic-to-radical direction, choose a generator $\sigma$ of the Galois group and a primitive $n$-th root of unity $\zeta\in F$; the Lagrange resolvent gives a nonzero eigenvector $\alpha$ with $\sigma(\alpha)=\zeta\alpha$, so $\alpha^n\in F$ and $K=F(\alpha)$ by primitivity. For the converse, let $K=F(\alpha)$ with $\alpha^n=a\in F$, use the published splitting-field description of $x^n-a$ after adjoining one nonzero root, and conclude that the splitting field already equals $K$ because all roots are $\zeta^i\alpha$ with $\zeta\in F$; the automorphism sending $\alpha$ to $\zeta\alpha$ generates a cyclic group of order $n$. The irreducibility clause is what forces the degree to be exactly $n$.

items.title: In characteristic $p$, a degree-$p$ extension is cyclic exactly when it is generated by a root of $x^p-x-a$ with $a\in F$ and that polynomial irreducible
items.strategy: If $K/F$ is cyclic of degree $p$ with generator $\sigma$, additive Hilbert 90 applied to the trace-zero element $1$ gives $\alpha\in K$ with $\sigma(\alpha)=\alpha+1$, whence $\alpha^p-\alpha\in F$ and $K=F(\alpha)$. Conversely, if $x^p-x-a$ is irreducible, its roots are exactly $\alpha+i$ for $i\in\mathbb F_p$, so the polynomial is separable and its splitting field is $F(\alpha)$ itself; translation by $1$ on the root set defines a cyclic Galois group of order $p$. Record explicitly that this is the characteristic-$p$ replacement for the roots-of-unity Kummer theorem, not a special case of it.

items.title: Kummer extensions from adjoining $n$-th roots over a base field containing $\mu_n$
The Kummer pairing $\operatorname{Gal}(K/F)\times B/(F^\times)^n\to\mu_n$ is perfect
items.strategy: For a finite Kummer extension $K=F(\sqrt[n]{B})$, define the pairing by $\langle\sigma,b(F^\times)^n\rangle=\sigma(\beta)/\beta$ for any chosen $n$-th root $\beta$ of $b$. Prove well-definedness by changing the root by an element of $\mu_n$ and the representative by an $n$-th power. Nondegeneracy on the Galois side uses the earlier cyclic theorem: if $\sigma$ is nontrivial, some one-generator Kummer subextension detects it. Nondegeneracy on the $B/(F^\times)^n$ side uses the same one-generator reduction and the fact that $x^d-b$ cannot split trivially when the class of $b$ has order $d>1$.

items.title: The degree $[F(\sqrt[n]{a}):F]$ is the order of $a(F^\times)^n$ in $F^\times/(F^\times)^n$
items.strategy: Let $d$ be the order of the class of $a$, so $a^d\in(F^\times)^n$ and $d\mid n$. Replace $a$ by the same class viewed modulo $d$-th powers and apply the cyclic Kummer theorem to the irreducible polynomial $x^d-b$ obtained after removing the maximal $d$-th power already present in $F$. The extension degree equals the order of the cyclic subgroup detected by the perfect pairing.

items.title: Kummer theory classifies finite abelian extensions of exponent dividing $n$ by subgroups between $(F^\times)^n$ and $F^\times$
items.strategy: Send such a subgroup $B$ to the field $F(\sqrt[n]{B})$. The previous theorem makes the Galois group a finite abelian group killed by $n$. For the inverse direction, let $K/F$ be a finite abelian extension of exponent dividing $n$ with $\mu_n\subseteq F$, and define $B$ to be the set of elements of $F^\times$ whose chosen $n$-th roots lie in $K$; every cyclic quotient of $\operatorname{Gal}(K/F)$ is Kummer by the cyclic theorem, so the subgroup recovers the whole extension. Inclusion preservation is immediate, and the perfect pairing identifies $\operatorname{Gal}(K/F)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}(B/(F^\times)^n,\mu_n)$.

items.title: A radical extension is a tower obtained by adjoining one $n$-th root at each step
A polynomial is solvable by radicals when its splitting field lies in a radical extension
The normal closure of a radical extension is again radical
items.strategy: Induct up the radical tower. For a single step adjoining an $n$-th root $\alpha$ of $a$, the published splitting-field result for $x^n-a$ shows that after adjoining the relevant roots of unity the normal closure is obtained by adjoining finitely many elements of the form $\zeta\alpha$, which is still radical. At the inductive step, take the normal closure of the previous stage first and then apply the same one-step argument over that normal field. Do not assume roots of unity or Galoisness in the definition; this lemma is exactly what restores them when needed.

items.title: Adjoining roots of unity to a finite Galois extension adds an abelian kernel and preserves solvability
items.strategy: If $K/F$ is finite Galois and $L=K(\mu_n)$, then $L/F$ is again Galois and restriction gives a surjection $\operatorname{Gal}(L/F)\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{Gal}(K/F)$. Its kernel is $\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)$, a subgroup of the cyclotomic Galois group over $K$, hence abelian. Therefore a solvable quotient remains solvable after extending by this abelian kernel, and conversely a quotient of a solvable group is solvable.

items.title: In characteristic $0$, a polynomial solvable by radicals has a solvable Galois group
items.strategy: Let the splitting field sit inside a radical extension. Replace that extension by its normal closure, which stays radical by the previous lemma. Then adjoin all roots of unity needed by the tower; the new Galois group changes only by abelian kernels, so solvability is unaffected. Each successive radical step is cyclic by the cyclic Kummer theorem, hence has solvable Galois group, and repeated use of the extension theorem shows the top Galois group is solvable. Finally pass to the polynomial's splitting field as a quotient.

items.title: In characteristic $0$, a solvable Galois group makes a polynomial solvable by radicals
items.strategy: Let $E/F$ be the splitting field with solvable Galois group. Choose a composition series whose factors are cyclic of prime order. Work upward through the corresponding tower of fixed fields. Before treating a prime-order step, adjoin the relevant roots of unity to the lower field; the preceding lemma keeps the Galois groups solvable and only enlarges the ambient field by radical extensions. The cyclic Kummer theorem then writes the lifted step as adjoining one prime root. Composing these radical steps through the tower puts the full splitting field inside a radical extension of the original base field.

items.title: The symmetric groups $S_n$ are solvable for $nle 4$
items.strategy: Use explicit abelian factor series. $S_1$ and $S_2$ are cyclic. For $S_3$, the alternating subgroup $A_3$ is normal of index $2$ and has order $3$, so $1	riangleleft A_3	riangleleft S_3$ has prime-order abelian factors. For $S_4$, let $V_4={1,(12)(34),(13)(24),(14)(23)}$. Conjugation relabels the double transpositions, so $V_4	riangleleft A_4$; $V_4$ is abelian; $|A_4/V_4|=3$ and $|S_4/A_4|=2$, so $S_4	riangleright A_4	riangleright V_4	riangleright 1$ is an abelian factor series. Apply the published solvable-by-abelian-factor-series criterion.

items.title: Every polynomial of degree at most four is solvable by radicals
items.strategy: For a polynomial of degree $nle 4$, its Galois group is a subgroup of $S_n$ acting on the roots. The preceding lemma makes $S_n$ solvable for $nle 4$, solvability descends to subgroups, and the previous theorem then places the splitting field inside a radical extension.

items.title: For prime $p$, a transitive subgroup of $S_p$ containing a transposition is all of $S_p$
items.strategy: Let $N$ be the subgroup generated by all transpositions lying in the given transitive subgroup $G$. Because conjugates of transpositions are transpositions, $N$ is normal in $G$. The $N$-orbits on a set of size $p$ form a $G$-stable partition, so transitivity of $G$ and primality of $p$ force $N$ to be transitive once $N$ is nontrivial. Now build the graph whose edges are the transpositions in $N$: transitivity means the graph is connected, and the subgroup generated by transpositions along the edges of a connected graph is the full symmetric group.

items.title: The general polynomial of degree $n$ has Galois group $S_n$
items.strategy: Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be algebraically independent over $F$ and let $p_i$ be the elementary symmetric polynomials. The symmetric-functions theorem identifies the fixed field of the natural $S_n$-action on $F(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ as $F(p_1,\dots,p_n)$. Renaming $p_i$ as independent coefficient symbols $t_i$ gives the general polynomial $X^n-t_1X^{n-1}+\cdots+(-1)^nt_n$ with roots $X_1,\dots,X_n$. Its splitting field is exactly $F(X_1,\dots,X_n)$, and the permutation action on the roots embeds the Galois group into $S_n$ while Artin's theorem on invariants makes the extension degree $n!$, forcing equality.

items.title: For $n\ge5$, the general polynomial of degree $n$ is not solvable by radicals
items.strategy: The previous theorem makes the Galois group of the general polynomial equal to $S_n$, and the published solvable-group theorem says $S_n$ is not solvable for $n\ge5$. If the general polynomial were solvable by radicals, the forward solvability theorem would force its Galois group to be solvable, contradiction. State this exactly as a theorem about the general polynomial over the rational-function field, not as a theorem about every quintic over $\mathbb Q$.

pages.title: Solvability by Radicals and Kummer Theory — Examples

items.title: For $\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)/\mathbb Q$, the embedding formulas match the determinant and trace of multiplication
items.strategy: Work in the ordered basis $(1,\sqrt d)$ with $d$ squarefree. For $a+b\sqrt d$, compute the multiplication matrix, its determinant, and its trace. Then compute the two embeddings into an algebraic closure and compare their sum and product with the same formulas. State separately what happens when $d=0$ is excluded by the squarefree hypothesis.

items.title: In $\mathbb F_{q^n}/\mathbb F_q$, norm and trace are the Frobenius product and sum
items.strategy: List the $n$ embeddings of $\mathbb F_{q^n}$ over $\mathbb F_q$ as the powers of Frobenius. Apply the embedding formulas to obtain $N(\alpha)=\alpha^{1+q+\cdots+q^{n-1}}=\alpha^{(q^n-1)/(q-1)}$ and $\operatorname{Tr}(\alpha)=\alpha+\alpha^q+\cdots+\alpha^{q^{n-1}}$. Use the $\alpha=0$ boundary to show the norm formula is understood multiplicatively only on nonzero elements while the polynomial formula still gives $0$.

items.title: For $\mathbb F_p(t)/\mathbb F_p(t^p)$, the trace is identically zero
items.strategy: Take $u=t^p$ so that $t$ is a root of $x^p-u$ and the extension has degree $p$ but only one embedding over the base field. Apply the trace formula from the A page or compute the multiplication matrix in the basis $1,t,\dots,t^{p-1}$ to show every diagonal sum vanishes. This is the reader-facing witness that the trace-form theorem's inseparable direction is not cosmetic.

items.title: Hilbert 90 for $\mathbb Q(i)/\mathbb Q$ recovers the rational parametrization of the unit circle
items.strategy: An element $a+bi\in\mathbb Q(i)$ has norm $1$ exactly when $a^2+b^2=1$. Hilbert 90 writes it as $(m+ni)/(m-ni)$ for rationals $m,n$, and clearing denominators yields the classical formula $(x,y,z)=(m^2-n^2,2mn,m^2+n^2)$ for Pythagorean triples. Keep the degenerate cases $n=0$ and $m=0$ visible so the points $(\pm1,0)$ are not dropped.

items.title: Over $\mathbb Q(\omega)$, the splitting field of $x^3-2$ is a cyclic cubic extension
items.strategy: Because $\omega\in\mathbb Q(\omega)$, the base field already contains $\mu_3$. Show that $x^3-2$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q(\omega)$, for example by the rational-root test through the Eisenstein argument over $\mathbb Z[\omega]$ or by degree comparison with the known cubic subfield, and then apply the cyclic Kummer theorem. The three roots are $\sqrt[3]{2},\omega\sqrt[3]{2},\omega^2\sqrt[3]{2}$.

items.title: Cardano's formula for $x^3-3x-1$ from the Lagrange resolvent
items.strategy: Depress the cubic, form the two nontrivial Lagrange resolvents over a field containing $\omega$, and use the cyclic cubic structure to solve for their cubes in the base field. Then recover one root as the symmetric linear combination of the resolvents and verify directly that it satisfies $x^3-3x-1=0$. The check is load-bearing: without it the example is only a formal manipulation of radicals.

items.title: A quartic solved through its resolvent cubic
items.strategy: Choose a monic irreducible quartic with rational coefficients, write down its resolvent cubic, and solve the cubic first. Use the published resolvent formulas and subgroup classification to reconstruct the quartic roots from one square root and one cubic radical stage. The point is not to reprove the quartic theorem, but to make the passage from the resolvent data to actual radicals explicit once.

items.title: $x^5-2$ over $\mathbb Q$ is solvable by radicals although it is a quintic
items.strategy: Its splitting field is $\mathbb Q(\sqrt[5]{2},\zeta_5)$, so by definition it lies in a radical extension. Compute the Galois group as the semidirect product generated by $\sqrt[5]{2}\mapsto\zeta_5\sqrt[5]{2}$ and $\zeta_5\mapsto\zeta_5^a$ for $a\in(\mathbb Z/5)^\times$, yielding a group of order $20$ isomorphic to $\mathbb Z/5\rtimes\mathbb Z/4$. This is the page's concrete witness that “quintic” and “insoluble by radicals” are not synonymous.

items.title: Over $\mathbb F_p(t)$, the polynomial $x^p-x-t$ gives a cyclic Artin-Schreier extension
items.strategy: Show that $t$ is not of the form $b^p-b$ in $\mathbb F_p(t)$ by comparing pole orders: $b^p-b$ cannot have a single simple pole. The Artin-Schreier theorem then gives irreducibility and a cyclic degree-$p$ Galois group. Write the full root set as $\alpha+i$ for $i\in\mathbb F_p$ so the splitting-field claim is visibly true.

items.title: $\mathbb Q(\zeta_3,\sqrt[3]{2},\sqrt[3]{3})$ is a Kummer extension with quotient $(\mathbb Z/3)^2$
items.strategy: Take $F=\mathbb Q(\zeta_3)$, where $\mu_3\subseteq F$. Show that the classes of $2$ and $3$ in $F^\times/(F^\times)^3$ are independent, so the subgroup they generate has order $9$. The degree formula then gives $[F(\sqrt[3]{2},\sqrt[3]{3}):F]=9$, and the Kummer pairing identifies the Galois group with $\operatorname{Hom}((\mathbb Z/3)^2,\mu_3)\cong(\mathbb Z/3)^2$.

items.title: FALSE: a polynomial solvable by radicals must have abelian Galois group
items.strategy: Use $x^5-2$. The previous example places its splitting field in a radical extension, so it is solvable by radicals. Its Galois group has order $20$ and is the nonabelian semidirect product $\mathbb Z/5\rtimes\mathbb Z/4$, because the order-four automorphism of $\zeta_5$ acts nontrivially on the order-five subgroup generated by adjoining $\sqrt[5]{2}$.

items.title: FALSE: every quintic is insoluble by radicals
items.strategy: Again use $x^5-2$. The point of separating this from the preceding false statement is that the present claim fails already at the level of existence of one radical solution method, while the preceding claim fails at the stronger level of the Galois group's structure.

items.title: FALSE: for every finite extension, the norm is just the product over the embeddings
items.strategy: Refute this with the purely inseparable extension $\mathbb F_p(t)/\mathbb F_p(t^p)$. There is only one embedding over the base field, so the raw embedding product sends $t$ to $t$, while the actual norm is $t^p$ because the inseparable exponent is $p$. This is precisely the omitted factor from the theorem title on the A page.

items.title: FALSE: the trace map of every finite extension is surjective
items.strategy: Use the same purely inseparable extension $\mathbb F_p(t)/\mathbb F_p(t^p)$. The example shows that its trace is identically zero, so its image is the zero subspace of the base field and not the whole field. This is why the surjectivity corollary on the A page is stated with the separability hypothesis in the title, not buried in remarks.

items.title: The direct sum of an indexed family of modules
Universal property of a direct sum of modules
items.strategy: For M=⊕_{i∈I}M_i with coordinate inclusions, send a finitely supported tuple to the finite sum of its prescribed component maps. Prove linearity, uniqueness from the coordinate decomposition, and the empty-family case M=0. No choice is used because each input has finite support.

items.title: The free module on a set and its standard basis
Universal property of the free module on a set
items.strategy: Identify R^(X) with the direct sum of copies of the regular module indexed by X. For a set map f:X→M, apply the direct-sum universal property to the maps r↦rf(x). Give the resulting finite-sum formula, prove uniqueness, and include X=∅ explicitly.

items.title: Every module is a quotient of a free module
items.strategy: Apply the free universal property to the identity set map on the underlying set of M. The induced map R^(M)→M sends e_m to m and is surjective because every m is in its image. This construction is canonical and choice-free.

items.title: Invariant basis number and the rank of a free module
Every nonzero commutative ring has invariant basis number for finite bases
items.strategy: An isomorphism R^m≅R^n and its inverse give rectangular matrices A,B with AB=I_n and BA=I_m. If n>m, expand det(AB) using multilinearity in the n columns: every term selects n columns of A from only m positions, so a column repeats and every term vanishes, contradicting det(I_n)=1≠0. Symmetry excludes m>n. This finite determinant proof is choice-free and does not use maximal ideals.

items.title: Exact sequences and short exact sequences of modules
The endpoints of a short exact sequence encode injectivity and surjectivity
items.strategy: Prove exactness of 0→A→B is equivalent to injectivity of A→B by identifying the kernel with zero; dually prove exactness of B→C→0 is equivalent to surjectivity by identifying the image with C. Combine these into the usual characterization of a short exact sequence.

items.title: Split short exact sequences, sections, and retractions
The splitting lemma for short exact sequences of modules
items.strategy: For 0→A--i→B--p→C→0, show a section s of p gives B=i(A)⊕s(C), construct a retraction r of i by decomposing b-s(p(b)), and obtain an isomorphism A⊕C→B, (a,c)↦i(a)+s(c). Conversely extract section and retraction from a direct-sum isomorphism. Prove every implication and uniqueness of the decomposition.

items.title: The abelian group $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,N)$ and maps induced by pre- and postcomposition
Covariant and contravariant $\operatorname{Hom}$ are left exact
items.strategy: For 0→A→B→C exact, prove 0→Hom(X,A)→Hom(X,B)→Hom(X,C) exact by image/kernel factorization; for A→B→C→0 exact, prove 0→Hom(C,X)→Hom(B,X)→Hom(A,X) exact by factorization through the quotient. Carry out the elementwise well-definedness checks rather than invoking category theory.

items.title: The injective and surjective Four Lemmas
items.strategy: For a commutative diagram with exact rows A→B→C→D and A'→B'→C'→D', chase an element of ker(B→B') using surjectivity on A and injectivity on C to prove the injective version; reverse the chase using surjectivity on B and injectivity on D to prove the surjective version. State hypotheses adjacent to the relevant conclusion.

items.title: The Five Lemma for modules
items.strategy: In a commutative diagram of two exact five-term rows, apply the injective Four Lemma to the middle map using the left outer epimorphism and its neighboring isomorphisms, and the surjective Four Lemma using the right outer monomorphism and neighboring isomorphisms. State the standard weaker outer hypotheses as well as the all-four-isomorphisms corollary.

items.title: The Snake Lemma for modules
items.strategy: For a commutative diagram of short exact rows, define δ:ker(c)→coker(a) by lifting z through the top epimorphism, applying the middle vertical map, and lifting back through the bottom monomorphism. Prove independence of both lifts, linearity, and exactness at each of the six kernel/cokernel terms by a complete element chase; include the initial and terminal zero terms.

items.title: Projective modules and the lifting property
Free modules are projective, with the exact choice boundary
items.strategy: Given a surjection E→M and a map from a free module R^(X) to M, choose one preimage in E for each basis value and extend by the free universal property. For finite X, finite choice (provable in ZF) suffices; for arbitrary X, this is an application of full AC to the family of nonempty fibers. No countable-choice or dependent-choice principle is invoked as a separate hypothesis.

items.title: Equivalent characterizations of projective modules
items.strategy: Assuming AC where arbitrary free modules are used, prove equivalence of: the lifting property; every short exact sequence ending in P splits; P is a direct summand of a free module; and Hom_R(P,-) is exact. The first, second, and Hom-exactness equivalences are choice-free; P projective implies a free summand choice-free via the canonical free cover, while the reverse direction imports the arbitrary-free projectivity choice boundary.

items.title: Direct sums of projectives are projective, and module categories have enough projectives
items.strategy: Under AC, lift each component map from P_i through a fixed epimorphism and combine the lifts by the direct-sum universal property; this proves ⊕P_i projective. The canonical free cover R^(M)→M then gives enough projectives. Note that a finite direct sum needs only finite choice, while arbitrary families and arbitrary bases use full AC.

items.title: Injective modules and the extension property
Equivalent characterizations of injective modules
items.strategy: Prove equivalence of the extension property, splitting of every short exact sequence beginning in I, and exactness of Hom_R(-,I). Extend the identity along an embedding to obtain a retraction; use a split sequence to extend an arbitrary map; combine with contravariant Hom left exactness. These equivalences are choice-free.

items.title: Baer's criterion for injective modules
items.strategy: The forward implication is immediate by extending maps from left ideals R to R. Conversely, assume every map from a left ideal extends to R; partially order extensions of a given map N→I across submodules of M, use Zorn's lemma to obtain a maximal extension, and if its domain is not M use the left ideal {r:rx lies in the domain} to extend across one more generator, contradiction. This converse uses full AC through Zorn, not merely countable or dependent choice.

items.title: Divisible modules over an integral domain
Over a PID, injective modules are exactly divisible modules
items.strategy: For a PID R, injectivity extends the map rR→D sending r to d and produces x with rx=d, so injective implies divisible without choice. Conversely every ideal is rR and a map rR→D is determined by d=f(r); divisibility supplies x with rx=d, so Baer's criterion gives injectivity. Include R=Z as the abelian-group specialization. The converse inherits Baer's full-AC/Zorn boundary.

items.title: Every abelian group embeds in a divisible abelian group
items.strategy: Let F=Z^(A) map canonically onto A with kernel K. Embed F coordinatewise into the divisible group Q^(A), and map F/K into Q^(A)/K. The kernel is (F∩K)/K=0, while a quotient of a divisible group is divisible. Division of a finite-support tuple uses only finitely many explicit rational divisions, so this construction is choice-free; it also corrects Kleshchev's source typo calling the containing group free.

items.title: Products of injective modules are injective, with the exact choice boundary
items.strategy: For an embedding A→B and map A→∏_{i∈I}I_i, extend every coordinate map A→I_i to B→I_i and combine the extensions into a product map. Finite I needs only finite choice; an arbitrary index set uses full AC to choose one extension from each nonempty set of extensions. Conversely each factor is a direct summand of the product and injectivity passes to direct summands.

items.title: Coinduction sends injective abelian groups to injective modules
items.strategy: For a unital ring R and injective abelian group D, give Hom_Z(R,D) the left R-action (r·φ)(s)=φ(sr). Establish the natural bijection Hom_R(M,Hom_Z(R,D))≅Hom_Z(M,D) by evaluation at 1, with inverse g↦(m↦[r↦g(rm)]). Since the right side extends across subgroup inclusions, the left side does too, proving injectivity.

items.title: Module categories have enough injectives
items.strategy: First give the arbitrary-unital-ring coinduction proof: embed the underlying abelian group of M in a divisible (hence, under Baer, injective) group D, then send m to [r↦j(rm)] in Hom_Z(R,D), with evaluation at 1 proving injectivity. For commutative R, also record Stacks' functorial version: character dual (-)^∨=Hom_Z(-,Q/Z) is exact, evaluation M→M^∨∨ is injective, and dualizing the canonical free cover of M^∨ embeds it in J(M)≅∏R^∨; coinduction and the product theorem make J(M) injective. Full AC enters through Baer and arbitrary products, while the divisible-hull embedding itself is choice-free; countable or dependent choice is not separately used.

pages.title: Free Modules and Exact Sequences: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The standard basis and a universal map from $R^3$
items.strategy: Write e_1,e_2,e_3 explicitly and, for chosen m_1,m_2,m_3 in M, compute the unique linear map R^3→M as (r_1,r_2,r_3)↦r_1m_1+r_2m_2+r_3m_3. Verify uniqueness on the three basis vectors.

items.title: $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ is generated but not free as a $\mathbb Z$-module for $n>1$
items.strategy: The residue of 1 generates. Every nonzero free abelian group has a basis element of infinite additive order, whereas every element of Z/nZ is killed by n. Thus generated does not imply free; include the n=1 zero-module boundary separately.

items.title: A regular module with bases of sizes one and two
items.strategy: Let V have countable basis e_0,e_1,… over a field and R=End(V). Define α_0,α_1 by embedding into even and odd coordinates and β_0,β_1 by the inverse projections, so β_iα_j=δ_ij and α_0β_0+α_1β_1=1. The left R-linear maps f↦(fα_0,fα_1) and (g,h)↦gβ_0+hβ_1 are inverse, proving _RR≅_RR^2 and rank failure.

items.title: $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ is projective but not free over $\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$
items.strategy: Use the idempotent 3 in R=Z/6Z: R=3R⊕(1-3)R and 3R≅Z/2Z, so the module is a direct summand of the free module R and hence projective. It is not free because its cardinality 2 is not 6^n for any finite n, while an infinite-rank free module is infinite.

items.title: $0\to\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{\times2}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z\to0$ does not split
items.strategy: Verify exactness directly. If the quotient map had a section, the image of the nonzero residue class would be an integer x with 2x=0 but x odd, impossible. Equivalently, any retraction r of multiplication by 2 would satisfy 2r(1)=1.

items.title: $0\to A\to A\oplus C\to C\to0$ is canonically split
items.strategy: Use inclusion a↦(a,0), projection (a,c)↦c, section c↦(0,c), and retraction (a,c)↦a. Verify exactness and both splitting identities, then identify the splitting-lemma isomorphism with the identity on A⊕C.

items.title: $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(-,\mathbb Z)$ need not preserve surjections on the right
items.strategy: Apply Hom_Z(-,Z) to the nonsplit sequence 0→Z--2→Z→Z/2→0. Since Hom(Z/2,Z)=0 and precomposition by ×2 acts as multiplication by 2 on Hom(Z,Z)≅Z, the resulting map Z→Z is not surjective. This pinpoints why Hom is left exact but not generally exact.

items.title: Every short exact sequence of modules splits
items.strategy: Refute with 0→Z--2→Z→Z/2→0, reproducing the one-line section obstruction inside this item rather than depending on another B-page item. Contrast with the exact projective-ending and injective-beginning criteria.

items.title: Every projective module is free
items.strategy: Reuse the construction—not the B-page item—of the ideal 3R in R=Z/6Z. The idempotent decomposition makes 3R projective, while cardinality rules out every possible free rank. This distinguishes direct summands of free modules from free modules themselves.

items.title: Every injective module is projective
items.strategy: Use Q/Z as a Z-module. It is divisible and hence injective. If it were projective, it would be a direct summand of a free abelian group; free abelian groups are torsion-free, as are their subgroups and direct summands, but Q/Z is nonzero torsion. Thus it is not projective.

pages.title: Tensor Products of Modules
pages.note: frontier-13 D5.1/D5.2 (2026-08-15): added two published pages. dual-spaces-bilinear-forms-and-inertia (order 92) licenses thm-hom-from-a-finite-dimensional-space-as-a-tensor-product and cor-trace-is-tensor-contraction, harvested from Dennis; field-extensions-and-the-complex-numbers (order 54) licenses ex-complex-tensor-square-over-the-reals via def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic, thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field and cor-complex-numbers-are-a-quadratic-real-extension. Both verified published, strictly below order 106, absent from the prior closure (37 -> 39), and seam-free against all 11 run pairs.

items.title: Balanced maps from a right module and a left module, and bilinear maps over a commutative ring
The tensor product $M\otimes_R N$ from the additive group underlying the free $\mathbb Z$-module on $M\times N$, elementary tensors, and finite tensor sums
Universal property of the tensor product for balanced maps into abelian groups
items.strategy: Let $F=\mathbb Z^{(M\times N)}$ be the free $\mathbb Z$-module on $M\times N$, and regard its underlying additive group explicitly as the free abelian group on that set. View the target abelian group as a $\mathbb Z$-module, extend a balanced map uniquely to a $\mathbb Z$-linear map from $F$, check that it kills every generator of the relation subgroup $H$, and factor through $F/H$. Conversely compose a homomorphism out of $F/H$ with the elementary-tensor map. Prove the two assignments inverse and retain the empty and zero-module cases.

items.title: Tensor products are unique up to a unique isomorphism carrying elementary tensors to elementary tensors
items.strategy: Given two representing pairs, apply each universal property to the other's universal balanced map. Each composite fixes every elementary tensor, so uniqueness makes the composites identities. State uniqueness relative to the specified universal maps, which licenses the phrase 'the tensor product'.

items.title: Module homomorphisms induce tensor-product homomorphisms functorially
items.strategy: For a right-linear map $f:M\to M'$ and a left-linear map $g:N\to N'$, verify that $(m,n)\mapsto f(m)\otimes g(n)$ is balanced and invoke the universal property. Check identity and composition on elementary tensors, then use uniqueness; over a commutative ring record that the induced map is linear for the separately constructed module structure.

items.title: A formula on elementary tensors defines a homomorphism exactly when its underlying pairing is balanced
items.strategy: Restate the universal-property bijection as a descent test: a prescription $m\otimes n\mapsto b(m,n)$ extends precisely when $b$ is additive in each variable and balanced. Then give the mandatory failure: on $\mathbb Z\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z$, the prescription $q(m\otimes n)=m$ would send $2\otimes1=1\otimes2$ to both $2$ and $1$, so it is not well defined. Emphasize that checking a formula only on symbols is never enough.

items.title: $(S,R)$-bimodules and commuting left and right scalar actions
A commuting outer scalar action descends to a tensor product
items.strategy: If $M$ is a right $R$-module and $N$ an $(R,S)$-bimodule, use the universal property to define $(m\otimes n)s=m\otimes(ns)$ and check the right $S$-module axioms on elementary tensors. Prove the left-handed analogue and the compatibility needed for iterated tensor products. Each equality is forced by a balanced pairing, not by an unchecked symbol rule.

items.title: Associativity of tensor products for compatible bimodules
items.strategy: For a right $R$-module $M$, an $(R,S)$-bimodule $N$, and a left $S$-module $P$, construct $(M\otimes_RN)\otimes_SP\to M\otimes_R(N\otimes_SP)$ from $(m,n,p)\mapsto m\otimes(n\otimes p)$. Build the reverse map similarly. Prove both maps are defined through successive universal properties and check the composites on elementary tensors.

items.title: Over a commutative ring, $M\otimes_RN$ is an $R$-module with $r(m\otimes n)=(rm)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn)$
items.strategy: Keep this separate from the arbitrary-ring construction. For fixed $r$, descend $(m,n)\mapsto(rm)\otimes n$ through the universal property, use commutativity to verify balance, and check the module axioms on elementary tensors. The defining balance relation proves equality with $m\otimes(rn)$. Note explicitly that no such single $R$-action is asserted for an arbitrary noncommutative ring.

items.title: Symmetry and associativity isomorphisms for tensor products over a commutative ring
items.strategy: Descend $(m,n)\mapsto n\otimes m$ to obtain the symmetry isomorphism and make its square the identity by checking elementary tensors. Specialize balanced associativity to commutative-ring modules, verify $R$-linearity using the constructed module action, and state naturality of both isomorphisms.

items.title: The regular module is a tensor unit: $R\otimes_RN\cong N$ and $M\otimes_RR\cong M$
items.strategy: Send $r\otimes n$ to $rn$ and $m\otimes r$ to $mr$; balance makes both maps well defined. Their inverses send $n$ to $1\otimes n$ and $m$ to $m\otimes1$. Check both composites on elementary tensors and use the unit laws, including the zero ring and zero modules.

items.title: Finite iterated tensor products represent multilinear maps independently of parenthesization
items.strategy: Induct on the number of factors using the binary universal property and associativity. Take the empty tensor product to be $R$ and the one-factor tensor product to be the module itself; verify those two boundaries separately. Use the associativity isomorphisms to transport the representing map between parenthesizations and uniqueness to prove coherence for the comparison used here.

items.title: Tensor products commute with arbitrary direct sums
items.strategy: For an arbitrary family $(M_i)_{i\in I}$ over a commutative ring, construct the map from $(\bigoplus_iM_i)\otimes_RN$ by summing the coordinate tensor maps; finite support makes the sum legitimate. Construct the inverse from the family of maps $M_i\otimes_RN\to(\bigoplus_iM_i)\otimes_RN$. Use the two universal properties and check both composites on summands and elementary tensors. Include $I=\varnothing$.

items.title: The elementary tensors of two bases form the product basis of the tensor product
items.strategy: Identify free modules on basis sets $I$ and $J$ with direct sums of copies of $R$. Apply arbitrary direct-sum distributivity twice and the tensor-unit isomorphism to obtain $R^{(I)}\otimes_RR^{(J)}\cong R^{(I\times J)}$. Track the canonical generators to show that the resulting basis is exactly $(e_i\otimes f_j)_{(i,j)\in I\times J}$, including either empty basis.

items.title: $R^m\otimes_RR^n\cong R^{mn}$ with the product basis, and $\dim_F(V\otimes_FW)=\dim_FV\,\dim_FW$
items.strategy: Apply the product-basis theorem to the standard bases indexed by $m$ and $n$, and identify the product index set with $mn$. Over a field, apply this to finite bases of $V$ and $W$ and the published definition of dimension. Check $m=0$ or $n=0$ explicitly: both sides are the zero module and the product basis is empty.

items.title: The $R$-module $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,N)$ over a commutative ring
For finite-dimensional $V$, the canonical map $V^*\otimes_FW\to\operatorname{Hom}_F(V,W)$ is an isomorphism
items.strategy: Use evaluation to descend $(\phi,w)\mapsto[v\mapsto\phi(v)w]$. Choose a finite basis of $V$ with dual basis and send $T$ to the finite sum of dual-basis tensors with $T$ of the corresponding basis vectors. Check the two composites on basis vectors and elementary tensors; treat $V=0$ by the empty sum.

items.title: Under $\operatorname{End}_F(V)\cong V^*\otimes_FV$, tensor contraction is the trace
items.strategy: For a finite basis and its dual, identify a rank-one tensor $\phi\otimes v$ with the endomorphism $x\mapsto\phi(x)v$. Its matrix has trace $\phi(v)$. Extend linearly and use the finite-dimensional Hom-tensor isomorphism; verify the zero-dimensional case gives the zero map and trace zero.

items.title: Algebras over a commutative ring, central structure maps, and algebra homomorphisms
The tensor product of $R$-algebras has multiplication $(a\otimes b)(a'\otimes b')=aa'\otimes bb'$
items.strategy: For algebras whose commutative base ring acts centrally, use the finite multilinear universal property to descend the four-variable multiplication formula, and separately descend $r\mapsto r(1\otimes1)$ for the structure map. Verify associativity, distributivity, and the identity $1\otimes1$ on elementary tensors; if both factors are commutative, so is the result. The descent guard supplies well-definedness before any ring-law computation.

items.title: Universal mapping property of the tensor product of commutative algebras
items.strategy: For $R$-algebra maps $f:A\to C$ and $g:B\to C$ with $C$ commutative, the pairing $(a,b)\mapsto f(a)g(b)$ is bilinear, so it induces $A\otimes_RB\to C$. Check multiplicativity and the identity on elementary tensors. Conversely any algebra map compatible with $a\mapsto a\otimes1$ and $b\mapsto1\otimes b$ is forced on $a\otimes b=(a\otimes1)(1\otimes b)$, proving uniqueness.

items.title: Hom-tensor adjunction: $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M\otimes_RN,P)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,P))$
items.strategy: Send $F$ to the curried map $m\mapsto[n\mapsto F(m\otimes n)]$ and reverse the construction by uncurrying an $R$-linear map into Hom. Verify additivity, balance, and $R$-linearity explicitly before applying the tensor universal property. Check the two constructions inverse on evaluations and state naturality in all three modules.

items.title: Tensoring is right exact
items.strategy: For an exact sequence $A\to B\to C\to0$ and a module $N$ over a commutative ring, prove surjectivity on elementary tensors by lifting their first factors. Quotient $B\otimes_RN$ by the image from $A\otimes_RN$ and construct the inverse map from $C\otimes_RN$ using a lift of $c$; exactness makes the value independent of the lift. The descent guard and universal property establish the map rigorously. Conclude equality of image and kernel without claiming injectivity at the left.

items.title: The submodule $IM$ generated by products of elements of an ideal $I$ with elements of a module $M$
$M\otimes_RR/I\cong M/IM$ naturally
items.strategy: Tensor the exact sequence $I\to R\to R/I\to0$ with $M$ and use the tensor-unit isomorphism to identify the middle term with $M$. Track $i\otimes m$ to $im$ so that the incoming image is exactly $IM$, then apply the quotient universal property. Record both the $R$-module and induced $R/I$-module interpretations and include $I=0$ and $I=R$.

items.title: Flat and faithfully flat modules and ring homomorphisms
Flatness is equivalent to preserving injections and to the ideal and finitely generated ideal tests
items.strategy: Show exactness implies preservation of injections by adjoining cokernels, and that injection preservation implies both ideal tests. For the finitely generated-ideal converse, reduce a kernel element, represented by a finite tensor sum, to finitely generated submodules and then to an inclusion into a finite free module. Prove injectivity for submodules of $R^n$ by induction on $n$, with the ideal test as the base case. Track $n=0$ and the zero ideal explicitly.

items.title: Every projective module over a commutative ring is flat
items.strategy: First use arbitrary direct-sum distributivity and the tensor-unit isomorphism to show every free module is flat. A projective module is a direct summand of its canonical free cover; tensoring preserves the splitting maps, so its tensor functor is a direct summand of an exact free-module tensor functor and therefore preserves injections. No choice is needed for projective implies flat.

items.title: Under the stated choice boundary, free modules are projective and hence flat
items.strategy: Invoke the published theorem that arbitrary free modules are projective under AC, with finite bases needing only finite choice and the empty basis needing none, then apply projective implies flat. Also note that flatness of a free module follows directly from tensor-unit and arbitrary direct-sum distributivity without AC; keep the two logical routes distinct.

items.title: For flat $M$, one has $IM\cap JM=(I\cap J)M$
items.strategy: Apply flatness to the injection $I\cap J\to R$ inside the exact sequence $0\to I\cap J\to R\to R/I\oplus R/J$. Identify the tensor of $R$ with $M$, use the quotient-tensor isomorphisms to identify the two quotient components, and compute the resulting kernel as $IM\cap JM$. Check $I=R$, $J=R$, and the zero ideal.

items.title: A short exact sequence with flat quotient remains short exact after tensoring
items.strategy: For $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ with $C$ flat, resolve the other tensor factor by a free cover and form the resulting three-by-three diagram. Right exactness supplies the rows and columns, tensoring with the free module gives an exact middle row, and flatness of $C$ gives the required injective outer map. Perform the elementary diagram chase explicitly rather than naming an unbuilt snake lemma.

items.title: Restriction of scalars and extension of scalars $S\otimes_RM$ along a ring homomorphism $R\to S$
Extension of scalars is left adjoint to restriction of scalars
items.strategy: For a ring map $R\to S$, an $R$-module $M$, and an $S$-module $N$, send an $S$-linear map $S\otimes_RM\to N$ to $m\mapsto F(1\otimes m)$. Conversely send an $R$-linear map $f:M\to N$ to $s\otimes m\mapsto sf(m)$, verify balance, and invoke the universal property. Check the two maps inverse and natural in both modules.

items.title: Change of rings: $N\otimes_RM\cong N\otimes_S(S\otimes_RM)$
items.strategy: For $R\to S$, a right $S$-module $N$, and a left $R$-module $M$, specialize bimodule associativity to the $(S,R)$-bimodule $S$ and use $N\otimes_SS\cong N$. Track the isomorphism on elementary tensors as $n\otimes m\mapsto n\otimes(1\otimes m)$ and its inverse $n\otimes(s\otimes m)\mapsto ns\otimes m$.

items.title: Extension of scalars carries flat modules to flat modules
items.strategy: For $R\to S$ and flat $M$ over $R$, rewrite $N\otimes_S(S\otimes_RM)$ as $N\otimes_RM$ by change of rings for every injection of right $S$-modules. Restriction of scalars preserves injectivity, so flatness over $R$ gives injectivity after tensoring; conclude $S\otimes_RM$ is flat over $S$.

items.title: Flatness is transitive under a flat change of rings
items.strategy: Let $R\to S$ be flat and let $N$ be flat over $S$. For an exact sequence of $R$-modules, first tensor with $S$ to retain exactness, then tensor the resulting $S$-sequence with $N$. Use change-of-rings associativity and the tensor-unit map to identify the composite with tensoring directly by the restricted $R$-module $N$. State the corresponding composition result for flat ring maps.

items.title: The character dual of a flat module is injective
items.strategy: Let $R$ be commutative, let $P$ be flat, and let $D$ be an injective abelian group. Give $P^+=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(P,D)$ the action $(r\phi)(p)=\phi(rp)$. Establish the natural bijection $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,P^+)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(M\otimes_RP,D)$. Flatness turns a module injection into an injection after tensoring, and injectivity of $D$ extends the corresponding group homomorphism; transpose back to prove $P^+$ injective.

pages.title: Tensor Products of Modules — Examples

items.title: False: $\mathbb Z/m\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z/n$ is nonzero for all positive $m,n$
items.strategy: Use the quotient-tensor theorem to identify the tensor product with $(\mathbb Z/m)/n(\mathbb Z/m)$, then use Bezout to identify this quotient with $\mathbb Z/\gcd(m,n)$. The concrete choice $(m,n)=(2,3)$ gives the zero group and refutes the claim. Treat the convention $\mathbb Z/1=0$ explicitly.

items.title: $\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z/n=0$ for every positive $n$
items.strategy: Apply the quotient-tensor theorem with $M=\mathbb Q$ and $I=n\mathbb Z$. Multiplication by positive $n$ is surjective on $\mathbb Q$, so $n\mathbb Q=\mathbb Q$ and the quotient is zero. Do not use this statement at $n=0$.

items.title: $(R/I)\otimes_R(R/J)\cong R/(I+J)$ for ideals of a commutative ring
items.strategy: Apply the quotient-tensor theorem to $M=R/I$ and the ideal $J$. Identify $J(R/I)$ with $(I+J)/I$, and use the quotient-of-a-quotient isomorphism to obtain $R/(I+J)$. Include $I=R$, $J=R$, and both zero ideals.

items.title: $S\otimes_RR[x]\cong S[x]$ as $S$-algebras
items.strategy: For a homomorphism of commutative rings $R\to S$, send $s\otimes\sum_i r_ix^i$ to $\sum_i s f(r_i)x^i$. Descend the formula by the tensor universal property and verify multiplication using the tensor-product algebra law. Construct the inverse by sending each monomial coefficient $s x^i$ to $s\otimes x^i$ and use finite coefficient support to prove the composites are identities.

items.title: For a field extension $K/F$, one has $K\otimes_FM_n(F)\cong M_n(K)$ as $K$-algebras
items.strategy: Send $k\otimes(a_{ij})$ to $(k a_{ij})$ entrywise. The matrix units form an $F$-basis, so the tensor-basis theorem proves this is a $K$-module isomorphism; multiplication of matrix units proves it is a $K$-algebra isomorphism. Include $n=0$ under the library's empty-matrix convention and $n=1$ as the tensor-unit case.

items.title: For a field extension $K/F$, one has $K\otimes_FF^n\cong K^n$
items.strategy: Use extension of scalars together with the standard basis of $F^n$: the elements $1\otimes e_j$ form a $K$-basis by the product-basis theorem. Send $k\otimes(a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1})$ to $(ka_0,\ldots,ka_{n-1})$ and verify the inverse on the basis. Include $n=0$.

items.title: $\mathbb C\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C\cong\mathbb C\times\mathbb C$ as $\mathbb R$-algebras
items.strategy: Use the published real embedding and real basis $1,i$ of $\mathbb C$. Descend the bilinear map $z\otimes w\mapsto(zw,\overline z\,w)$, verify multiplicativity from the tensor-product algebra law, and compare the four real basis elements $1\otimes1$, $i\otimes1$, $1\otimes i$, $i\otimes i$ with their images to prove bijectivity. Exhibit the product idempotents as halves of $1\otimes1\mp i\otimes i$.

items.title: Tensoring the injection $k[x]\xrightarrow{\cdot x}k[x]$ with $k[x]/(x)$ gives the zero map
items.strategy: Multiplication by $x$ is injective because $k[x]$ is a domain. Identify each tensor product with $k[x]/(x)$ by the tensor-unit and quotient-tensor results. The induced map is multiplication by the class of $x$, hence zero, while the source is nonzero. This is the polynomial analogue of the integer counterexample.

items.title: False: $m\otimes n=0$ implies $m=0$ or $n=0$
items.strategy: In $\mathbb Z\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z/2$, the nonzero factors $2$ and $\overline1$ satisfy $2\otimes\overline1=1\otimes2\overline1=0$. Use the unit isomorphism to confirm that $\mathbb Z\otimes\mathbb Z/2$ itself is nonzero, so the witness is not caused by a zero tensor-product group.

items.title: False: every element of $M\otimes_RN$ is an elementary tensor
items.strategy: For any field $F$, take bases $e_1,e_2$ of $F^2$ and $f_1,f_2$ of another copy. The tensor $e_1\otimes f_1+e_2\otimes f_2$ has coefficient matrix of rank two. If it were $(ae_1+be_2)\otimes(cf_1+df_2)$, coefficient comparison would give $ac=bd=1$ and $ad=bc=0$, an immediate contradiction in a field.

items.title: False: tensoring preserves injections
items.strategy: Start with the injection $\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{\cdot2}\mathbb Z$. Tensor with $\mathbb Z/2$ and identify both sides with $\mathbb Z/2$ using the unit isomorphism. The induced map is multiplication by $2$, hence zero and not injective. Place it beside right exactness to show precisely why tensoring is not left exact in general.

pages.title: Chain Conditions, Semisimple Modules and the Wedderburn–Artin Theorem

items.title: Noetherian modules: every submodule is finitely generated
Artinian modules by the descending chain condition
Left and right Noetherian rings
Left and right Artinian rings
Composition series and length of a module
The opposite ring $R^{\mathrm{op}}$
The endomorphism ring $\operatorname{End}_R(M)$ under addition and composition
Semisimple modules as direct sums of simple modules
A semisimple ring as a ring whose left regular module is semisimple
The socle as the sum of all simple submodules
Integral elements over a commutative ring and algebraic integers
Second isomorphism theorem for modules
items.strategy: For submodules \(L,N\le M\), map \(L\to(L+N)/N\). Its kernel is \(L\cap N\), and it is surjective by the definition of \(L+N\); the first isomorphism theorem gives \(L/(L\cap N)\cong(L+N)/N\). Include zero and equal submodules.

items.title: Third isomorphism theorem for modules
items.strategy: For \(N\le L\le M\), send \(m+N\) to \(m+L\). Check representative independence, identify kernel \(L/N\), prove surjectivity, and apply the first isomorphism theorem. Include \(N=L\) and \(L=M\).

items.title: Correspondence theorem for submodules of a quotient module
items.strategy: Inverse image and quotient give mutually inverse inclusion-preserving bijections between submodules of \(M/N\) and submodules of \(M\) containing \(N\). Verify both composites and preserve sums, intersections, and simplicity of successive quotients.

items.title: Finite generation, ACC, and maximal-condition characterizations of Noetherian modules
items.strategy: Prove that finite generation of every submodule implies ACC by taking the union of a chain and locating a finite generating set in one stage. Prove that the maximal condition implies finite generation by taking a maximal finitely generated submodule and adjoining one element if it is proper. For ACC implies the maximal condition, use dependent choice to turn the absence of a maximal member into a strict ascending chain. At authoring time state dependent choice in Facts as an adopted foundational axiom; add no dependency, forward reference, or topology prerequisite.

items.title: DCC and minimal-condition characterizations of Artinian modules
items.strategy: DCC gives a minimal member of every nonempty family by contradiction: under dependent choice, absence of a minimal member yields a strict descending chain. Conversely, a nonstabilizing descending chain has no minimal member. Treat repeated terms and the zero module.

items.title: Noetherian and Artinian conditions are each exact in short exact sequences
items.strategy: For \(0\to N\to M\to Q\to0\), submodules and quotients inherit each chain condition. Conversely, intersect a chain in \(M\) with \(N\) and project it to \(Q\); once both chains stabilize, the second isomorphism theorem shows the original chain stabilizes. Prove both Noetherian and Artinian directions and all four converses.

items.title: Finite direct sums preserve and reflect Noetherian and Artinian conditions
items.strategy: Induct on the number of summands using the split short exact sequence for a binary direct sum. Reflection follows because every summand is a submodule and a quotient. Include the empty sum and one summand.

items.title: Finitely generated modules over a left Noetherian ring are Noetherian
items.strategy: A module generated by \(n\) elements is a quotient of \(R^n\). The left regular module is Noetherian, finite direct sums preserve the condition, and quotients inherit it. Include the zero-generated zero module.

items.title: Every surjective endomorphism of a Noetherian module is injective
items.strategy: For a surjective endomorphism \(f\), the ascending chain \(\ker f\subseteq\ker f^2\subseteq\cdots\) stabilizes. Lift an element of \(\ker f\) through a sufficiently high power of \(f\) and use stabilization to force it to zero. Include the zero module.

items.title: A module has a composition series if and only if it is Noetherian and Artinian, the converse using dependent choice
items.strategy: A finite composition series gives both chain conditions by induction through its simple factors. Conversely, under DC choose a maximal proper submodule of each nonzero quotient; Noetherianity prevents an infinite strict ascent while Artinianity guarantees termination in the dual construction. Present a finite construction and include the zero module with length zero.

items.title: Jordan–Hölder theorem for modules
items.strategy: Induct on one series length. Compare its penultimate maximal submodule with the penultimate term of a second series; if unequal, use their intersection and the second isomorphism theorem to identify the two exchanged simple factors, then apply induction below the intersection. Prove equality of lengths and equality of factor multisets up to permutation, including length zero and one.

items.title: Module length is additive in short exact sequences
items.strategy: Lift a composition series of the quotient and splice it above a composition series of the submodule. Correspondence identifies the lifted factors, and Jordan–Hölder makes the resulting length independent of the chosen series. Cover zero endpoints and both directions of finite-length equivalence.

items.title: Module endomorphisms form a ring under pointwise addition and composition
items.strategy: Verify associativity of composition, distributivity over pointwise addition, additive inverses, and the identity endomorphism. For the zero module, identify the one-element zero ring and state the repository's unital convention.

items.title: $\operatorname{End}_R({}_R R)\cong R^{\mathrm{op}}$
items.strategy: Evaluate an endomorphism at \(1\). Left linearity gives \(f(r)=rf(1)\), so endomorphisms are right multiplications; composition reverses the order of their defining elements. Check the inverse map and the zero ring.

items.title: Endomorphisms of a finite direct sum are matrices of Hom-groups
items.strategy: Use inclusions and projections to send \(f\) to entries \(f_{ij}=\pi_i f\iota_j\), and reconstruct \(f\) by finite sums. Verify that composition becomes matrix multiplication with composition in the entries and that the zero- and one-summand cases match.

items.title: Under Choice, every finitely generated nonzero module has a maximal proper submodule
items.strategy: Order the proper submodules by inclusion. The union of a chain is a submodule; if it were all of \(M\), finitely many generators would lie in one chain member, contradicting properness. Zorn supplies a maximal proper submodule. Show why nonzero and finite generation are essential.

items.title: Equivalent characterizations of semisimple modules
items.strategy: Prove equivalence of being a direct sum of simples, being a sum of simple submodules, and every submodule having a complement. For a given submodule, apply Zorn to independent subfamilies of simple summands; for the converse, split off the socle and derive a contradiction by finding a simple quotient of a finitely generated cyclic submodule. Record the full Choice/Zorn cost and include the zero module.

items.title: Choice-free semisimple characterizations for finite-length modules
items.strategy: For a finite-length module, replace Zorn by induction on length: split a simple submodule or a maximal term and recurse on the strictly shorter complement or quotient. Prove the same three characterizations without Choice and include lengths zero and one.

items.title: Under Choice, submodules and quotients of semisimple modules are semisimple
items.strategy: A submodule inherits the complement property by intersecting a complement in the ambient module. For a quotient, complement the kernel and identify the quotient with that semisimple complement. Cover zero and whole submodules.

items.title: Under Choice, the socle is the largest semisimple submodule
items.strategy: The sum of all simple submodules is semisimple by the sum characterization. Every semisimple submodule is itself a sum of simple submodules of the ambient module, hence lies in the socle. Include a module with no simple submodule.

items.title: A finitely generated semisimple module is a finite direct sum of simple modules
items.strategy: In a direct-sum decomposition, each generator has finite support; the union of those finite supports contains every generator and hence the whole module. Remove zero or repeated summands and include the zero-generated case.

items.title: Schur's lemma for simple modules
items.strategy: The kernel and image of a homomorphism between simple modules are each zero or whole. A nonzero homomorphism is therefore injective and surjective. Applied to a nonzero endomorphism, its inverse is linear, so the endomorphism ring is a division ring. Keep the zero homomorphism and nonisomorphic simples explicit.

items.title: Equivalent module-theoretic characterizations of semisimple rings
items.strategy: Under Choice, prove equivalence of the left regular module being semisimple, every left module being semisimple, every short exact sequence splitting, and every left module being projective. Free modules are sums of the regular module and every module is their quotient; the complement and splitting characterizations supply the other implications. State the left-module convention in every clause.

items.title: Matrix rings over division rings are semisimple
items.strategy: Decompose the left regular module of \(M_n(D)\) into the column left ideals \(M_n(D)e_{jj}\). Each is isomorphic to the simple column module \(D^n\), since matrix units carry any nonzero vector to each standard vector. Include \(n=1\); require \(n\ge1\).

items.title: Wedderburn–Artin theorem for semisimple rings
items.strategy: For a semisimple ring, decompose the cyclic left regular module into finitely many isotypic blocks \(S_i^{n_i}\). Schur kills off-diagonal Hom-groups and makes \(\operatorname{End}_R(S_i)\) a division ring. Compute \(\operatorname{End}_R({}_R R)\), then take opposites exactly once to obtain \(R\cong\prod_i M_{n_i}(D_i)\). The converse is the column-ideal theorem. Include the zero ring as the empty product if the repository permits it, otherwise state the nonzero-ring convention explicitly.

items.title: Simple modules over a product of matrix rings over division rings
items.strategy: For \(R=\prod_iM_{n_i}(D_i)\), central coordinate idempotents show a simple left module is supported on exactly one factor. Matrix units then identify it with that factor's column module \(D_i^{n_i}\), and different factors give nonisomorphic modules. Check a one-factor product.

items.title: Uniqueness of the Wedderburn–Artin factors
items.strategy: Recover the factors from the isomorphism classes of simple left modules and their multiplicities in the left regular module. Their endomorphism division rings recover the \(D_i\) with the orientation fixed by the opposite-ring step. Jordan–Hölder makes the multiplicities invariant; conclude uniqueness up to permutation and division-ring isomorphism.

items.title: Left and right semisimplicity of a ring agree
items.strategy: Apply Wedderburn–Artin to the left regular module. Opposites of finite products of matrix rings are matrix rings over opposite division rings, hence are semisimple; translating modules over \(R^{\mathrm{op}}\) gives right semisimplicity. Repeat for the converse.

items.title: Semisimple rings are left and right Noetherian and Artinian
items.strategy: The left regular module is cyclic and semisimple, hence a finite direct sum of simples and therefore has finite length. The chain-condition theorem gives left Noetherian and Artinian. Apply the left/right agreement to the opposite ring for the right-handed statements.

items.title: Integrality and finite-module characterizations for one element
items.strategy: For a commutative ring extension \(A\subseteq B\) with \(A\neq0\) and \(b\in B\), prove equivalence of: \(b\) integral; \(A[b]\) finite as an \(A\)-module; and a faithful \(A[b]\)-module finite over \(A\) exists. A monic relation reduces all high powers. Conversely, write multiplication by \(b\) on finite generators as a matrix and use the adjugate identity; faithfulness turns the annihilating monic determinant into a relation for \(b\). Define faithfulness explicitly, and explain why a zero-generated faithful module is impossible when \(A\neq0\); the nonzero-base hypothesis is required by the repository's monic-polynomial convention.

items.title: Integral elements over a nonzero base ring form a subring
items.strategy: If \(x,y\) are integral, \(A[x,y]\) is finite over \(A\) by adjoining them successively and multiplying finite generating sets. Its elements \(x\pm y\) and \(xy\) therefore generate finite \(A\)-subalgebras and are integral. Include zero, one, negatives, and coincident elements.

items.title: The rational algebraic integers are exactly the integers
items.strategy: Write a rational algebraic integer in lowest terms \(r/s\) with \(s>0\). It is a root of a monic integer polynomial, so the rational-root theorem makes \(s\mid1\), hence \(s=1\). Conversely every integer satisfies the monic polynomial \(X-n\). Include zero and negative integers.

pages.title: Chain Conditions, Semisimple Modules and the Wedderburn–Artin Theorem — Examples

items.title: $\mathbb Z$ is Noetherian but not Artinian as a module over itself
items.strategy: Every subgroup of \(\mathbb Z\) is principal, so every submodule is finitely generated. The descending chain \(2^n\mathbb Z\) is strict from \(n=0\) onward, showing failure of DCC. Check the initial term \(\mathbb Z\).

items.title: The Prüfer $p$-group is Artinian but not Noetherian
items.strategy: Construct \(\mathbb Z(p^\infty)\) as the subgroup of \(\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z\) represented by rationals with \(p\)-power denominator. Its finite subgroups form a strict ascending chain, so it is not Noetherian. Classify its proper subgroups as the unique cyclic groups of order \(p^n\); any descending chain therefore stabilizes. Check the zero subgroup and \(p=2\).

items.title: The ring $(\mathbb Z/2)^{\mathbb N}$ is not Noetherian
items.strategy: Let \(e_i\) be the coordinate idempotents. The ideals generated by \(e_0,\ldots,e_n\) form a strict ascending chain, witnessed by \(e_{n+1}\). Distinguish the full product ring from its finite-support ideal.

items.title: $M_n(F)$ as a direct sum of minimal left ideals
items.strategy: Use the column ideals \(M_n(F)e_{jj}\), exhibit the isomorphism with \(F^n\), and prove minimality with matrix units. Their internal direct sum is the left regular module. Include \(n=1\) and avoid asserting there are only \(n\) minimal left ideals.

items.title: A product of two fields is semisimple with two simple-module types
items.strategy: For \(F\times K\), the central idempotents \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) split the regular module. Identify the two simple left modules and show any module splits into its two coordinate parts. Allow \(F\cong K\) while keeping the factor actions distinct.

items.title: The $\mathbb Z$-module $\mathbb Z/p^k$ has length $k$
items.strategy: Use the chain \(0<p^{k-1}\mathbb Z/p^k\mathbb Z<\cdots<p\mathbb Z/p^k\mathbb Z<\mathbb Z/p^k\mathbb Z\), whose factors are \(\mathbb Z/p\). Check \(k=0\) gives the zero module and \(k=1\) is simple. Note that the ambient ring \(\mathbb Z\) is not Artinian.

items.title: $\sqrt2$ and $(1+\sqrt5)/2$ are algebraic integers, while $1/2$ is not
items.strategy: Give the monic equations \(X^2-2\) and \(X^2-X-1\). The rational corollary excludes \(1/2\); also show directly that a monic integer equation at \(1/2\) has incompatible parity after clearing the exact power of two.

items.title: False statement: every Artinian module is Noetherian
items.strategy: Use the preceding Prüfer \(p\)-group, quoting its complete subgroup classification to establish DCC and its strict ascending chain of finite cyclic subgroups to refute Noetherianity.

items.title: False statement: every module has a composition series
items.strategy: The module \(\mathbb Z\) over itself is Noetherian but not Artinian, so the equivalence theorem rules out a composition series. Also point to the explicit descending chain rather than a scope claim.

items.title: False statement: every semisimple ring is commutative
items.strategy: For any field \(F\), the preceding decomposition makes \(M_2(F)\) semisimple, while two matrix units multiply in opposite orders to different results. Check fields of characteristic two.

items.title: False statement: every subring of a Noetherian ring is Noetherian
items.strategy: Construct the countably generated polynomial domain \(R=F[x_0,x_1,\ldots]\) and its fraction field \(K\). The field \(K\) is Noetherian, while the ideals \((x_0)\subsetneq(x_0,x_1)\subsetneq\cdots\) show that its subring \(R\) is not. Build the polynomial ring natively as finite polynomials so no unavailable multivariable-polynomial definition is cited.

items.title: False statement: every right Noetherian ring is left Noetherian
items.strategy: For \(T=\left\{\begin{psmallmatrix}a&q\\0&r\end{psmallmatrix}:a\in\mathbb Z,\ q,r\in\mathbb Q\right\}\), use the triangular-ring criterion proved inline: right Noetherianity reduces to \(\mathbb Z_{\mathbb Z}\), \(\mathbb Q_{\mathbb Q}\), and the one-generated right \(\mathbb Q\)-module \(\mathbb Q\); left Noetherianity would force \(\mathbb Q\) finitely generated over \(\mathbb Z\), which it is not. Exhibit the corresponding strict ascending chain of left ideals and check the identity and multiplication.

pages.title: Modules over a Principal Ideal Domain and the Canonical Forms

items.title: The $p$-primary component of a module over a domain
Torsion elements and $p$-primary elements form submodules over a domain
items.strategy: For torsion elements killed by nonzero $a$ and $b$, the product $ab$ kills their sum and is nonzero because the ring is a domain; scalar multiples remain torsion. For the $p$-primary component, a common sufficiently large power of $p$ kills a sum. Include the zero element, the zero module, and associate choices of $p$.

items.title: Every principal ideal domain is Noetherian
items.strategy: A submodule of the left regular module is an ideal, and every ideal of a PID has one generator. Thus every submodule is finitely generated, which is the Noetherian condition. Keep the left/right convention explicit and note commutativity makes the two sides agree.

items.title: Every irreducible element of a principal ideal domain is prime
items.strategy: For irreducible $p$, show any ideal strictly containing $(p)$ is the whole ring: if $(p)\subseteq(a)$ then $p=ab$, and irreducibility makes either $a$ a unit or the ideals equal. Thus $(p)$ is maximal, hence prime, and the prime-ideal condition gives divisibility of one factor whenever $p$ divides a product. Exclude zero and units exactly as the irreducible definition does.

items.title: Every principal ideal domain is a unique factorisation domain
items.strategy: For factorization existence, assume that some nonzero nonunit is not a product of irreducibles. PID Noetherianity and the published maximal-condition characterization give a maximal principal ideal $(a)$ among those generated by such bad elements. If $a=bc$ with both factors nonunits, then $(a)$ is strictly contained in both $(b)$ and $(c)$; maximality makes both factors products of irreducibles, a contradiction. For uniqueness, use that every irreducible is prime, cancel an associate factor, and induct on the number of factors. Treat units and the empty product explicitly. The only dependent-choice cost is inherited from the published equivalence between Noetherianity and the maximal condition; no recursive factor selection is made locally.

items.title: A nonzero PID submodule has a maximal coordinate ideal and a primitive pivot
items.strategy: For nonzero $N$ inside a finite free module $M$, consider the ideals $\varphi(N)$ as $\varphi$ ranges over $M^*$. Starting from one nonzero value ideal, UFD factorization gives only finitely many containing principal ideals, so choose a maximal member $(a)=\psi(N)$. If $a=\psi(v)$, combine $\psi$ with any coordinate functional to prove $a$ divides every coordinate of $v$; write $v=ae_1$ with $\psi(e_1)=1$. Then split $M=Re_1\oplus\ker\psi$ and $N=Rae_1\oplus(N\cap\ker\psi)$. Check rank one and $N=0$ separately.

items.title: Simultaneous bases for a submodule of a finite free module over a PID
items.strategy: Induct on the rank of the ambient free module. The maximal-pivot lemma splits off $Re_1$ and $Ra_1e_1$; apply the induction hypothesis to the kernel pair, concatenate bases, and use maximality once more to prove $a_1\mid a_2$. Continue to obtain nonzero $a_1\mid\cdots\mid a_r$, a basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ of the ambient module, and basis $a_1e_1,\ldots,a_re_r$ of the submodule. Include ranks zero and one and the zero submodule.

items.title: A submodule of a free module of finite rank over a PID is free of no larger rank
items.strategy: Read the displayed basis $a_1e_1,\ldots,a_re_r$ from the simultaneous-basis theorem. Its length satisfies $r\le n$, and invariant basis number makes both ranks well defined. The zero submodule has the empty basis.

items.title: Invariant factors and elementary divisors of a finitely generated module over a PID
Invariant-factor decomposition of a finitely generated module over a PID
items.strategy: Choose finitely many generators of $M$ and the induced surjection $R^n\to M$. Its kernel is a submodule of a finite free module, so simultaneous bases put it in the form generated by $a_1e_1,\ldots,a_re_r$ with $a_1\mid\cdots\mid a_r$. Quotienting gives the direct sum of $R/(a_i)$ and a free part; remove unit factors but retain zero and empty cases. This proves existence only; uniqueness is established later.

items.title: Every finitely generated torsion-free module over a PID is free
