items.strategy: In the invariant-factor decomposition, every nonzero cyclic quotient $R/(a_i)$ is torsion. Torsion-freeness forces all such summands to vanish, leaving only the finite free part. Include the zero module and unit invariant factors.

items.title: A finitely generated PID module is its torsion submodule direct-summed with a finite free module
items.strategy: Identify the torsion elements in the invariant-factor decomposition as exactly the cyclic quotient summands; the free summand is torsion-free because the ring is a domain. Thus $M\cong\operatorname{Tor}(M)\oplus R^r$. Explain that the complement need not be canonical and handle $r=0$ and zero torsion.

items.title: Coprime cyclic quotients over a PID split by the Chinese remainder map
items.strategy: For coprime $a,b$, use a Bezout identity $ra+sb=1$ to prove the map $R/(ab)\to R/(a)\oplus R/(b)$ is injective and surjective, giving an explicit inverse. Extend by finite induction to pairwise coprime factors. Check units, zero quotients, and the empty family.

items.title: Primary decomposition and elementary-divisor form for finitely generated PID modules
items.strategy: Factor each nonzero invariant factor into prime powers using the PID-to-UFD theorem. The coprime cyclic-quotient lemma splits each $R/(a_i)$ into prime-power cyclic summands. Group summands by associate prime to obtain the direct sum of $p$-primary components, and reverse the construction by aligning prime powers into divisibility columns. Keep the free part separate and cover the zero torsion module.

items.title: $p$-power torsion dimensions recover the elementary divisors of a PID module
items.strategy: For irreducible $p$, prove $R/(p)$ is a field by the PID Bezout argument. On a cyclic summand $R/(p^e)$, compute the $R/(p)$-dimension of $p^{k-1}M[p^k]$ as one exactly when $e\ge k$ and zero otherwise. Add dimensions over direct sums; the resulting sequence counts elementary divisors of exponent at least $k$ and its successive differences recover each exponent multiplicity. Free summands contribute zero. Check $k=1$ and the zero module.

items.title: Uniqueness of invariant factors and elementary divisors over a PID
items.strategy: An isomorphism preserves the torsion submodule and the free quotient, so invariant basis number recovers the free rank. For every associate prime and every positive $k$, the preceding dimension is intrinsic and recovers the multiplicity of $R/(p^k)$. Hence elementary divisors are unique up to associates and order; aligning their prime-power columns uniquely reconstructs the invariant factors. Prove the converse classification and include torsion-free and zero modules.

items.title: The free rank of a finitely generated module over a PID
Extension to the fraction field recovers the free rank of a finitely generated PID module
items.strategy: Let $Q=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ and apply extension of scalars to the decomposition $M\cong\operatorname{Tor}(M)\oplus R^r$. Every cyclic torsion summand $R/(a)$ vanishes after tensoring with $Q$, since the nonzero $a$ becomes invertible, while $Q\otimes_R R^r\cong Q^r$. Therefore $\dim_Q(Q\otimes_R M)=r$. Include the zero module, zero free rank, and pure free and pure torsion cases.

items.title: Matrix equivalence and Smith normal form over a PID
Determinantal divisors from the minors of a matrix over a PID
Every matrix over a PID has a Smith normal form
items.strategy: View a rectangular matrix as a homomorphism between finite free modules. Its image is finite free; apply the simultaneous-basis theorem to align the image in the codomain. The exact sequence from the domain onto the free image splits, so a basis of the kernel together with chosen lifts of the aligned image basis gives a domain basis in which the matrix is diagonal with divisibility chain. Include zero-sized matrices, the zero map, and rectangular rank deficiency. This is an existence proof over a PID, not a Euclidean algorithm.

items.title: Smith normal form is unique through the gcds of its minors
items.strategy: Use determinant multilinearity to show multiplication on either side by an invertible matrix preserves the ideal generated by all $k$-minors, applying the inverse for the reverse containment. For a Smith diagonal matrix, the $k$th determinantal divisor is associate to the product of the first $k$ nonzero diagonal entries. Successive quotients recover every entry up to a unit and the first zero determinantal divisor recovers the rank. Handle $k=0$, zero matrices, and rectangular endpoints.

items.title: Abelian groups and $\mathbb Z$-modules have the same objects and morphisms
items.strategy: Use the published integer-power construction and exponent laws in additive notation: for an abelian group $G$, $ng$ is repeated addition when $n>0$, is $0$ when $n=0$, and is the additive inverse of the corresponding positive multiple when $n<0$. The exponent laws verify the module axioms over the published integer ring. Prove uniqueness from $1g=g$ and additivity in the integer variable. Additivity shows that a group homomorphism preserves every integer multiple, so group homomorphisms are exactly $\mathbb Z$-linear maps. Subgroups are therefore exactly $\mathbb Z$-submodules; generated subobjects, cyclicity, finite generation, and quotient objects consequently agree. Include the trivial group, the empty generating set, zero and negative scalars, and the zero subgroup.

items.title: The fundamental theorem of finitely generated abelian groups from PID modules
items.strategy: Use the integer ring theorem and multiplicative cancellation to identify $\mathbb Z$ as an integral domain. Every ideal is an additive subgroup, so the subgroup classification makes it principal and hence makes $\mathbb Z$ a PID. Apply the abelian-group/$\mathbb Z$-module dictionary before specializing the invariant-factor and elementary-divisor theorem. Obtain a unique free part $\mathbb Z^r$ and a unique finite torsion part in both canonical forms. Explain why finitely generated torsion abelian groups are finite and include $r=0$ and the trivial group.

items.title: The PID-module and finite-abelian-group classifications have the same canonical data
items.strategy: For a finite abelian group, the free rank in the PID-module theorem is zero. Compare the definitions of its $p$-primary components, elementary divisors, and invariant factors with the published group-theoretic definitions. Uniqueness on both sides forces identical prime powers and identical divisibility chains, in both directions. Include the trivial group.

items.title: The index of a full-rank subgroup of $\mathbb Z^n$ is the absolute determinant of a generating matrix
items.strategy: Put a Smith normal form $PAQ=D$ on the generating matrix, use invertibility over $\mathbb Z$ to replace $L$ by $D\mathbb Z^n$, identify $\mathbb Z^n/D\mathbb Z^n$ with the direct sum of the $\mathbb Z/d_i\mathbb Z$, compare the order with $|\det A|=|\det D|$, and get the converse from the simultaneous basis theorem, which writes any subgroup as a column lattice.

items.title: The companion matrix of a monic polynomial
The $F[x]$-module $V_T$ of an endomorphism
For finite-dimensional $V$, $V_T$ is finitely generated and torsion, with annihilator generated by the minimal polynomial
items.strategy: Any finite $F$-basis of $V$ generates $V_T$ because constants lie in $F[x]$. The minimal polynomial annihilates every vector, so the module is torsion; the annihilator ideal of the whole module is exactly the set of polynomials $p$ with $p(T)=0$, whose monic generator is $\mu_T$. Include the zero vector space, where the generator and characteristic polynomial are $1$.

items.title: Invariant factors and elementary divisors of an endomorphism
Existence and uniqueness of rational canonical form
items.strategy: Apply the invariant-factor theorem to the finitely generated torsion $F[x]$-module $V_T$. Each summand $F[x]/(f_i)$ has the power basis on which multiplication by $x$ is the companion matrix $C(f_i)$, producing a block diagonal matrix with $f_1\mid\cdots\mid f_r$. Module uniqueness makes the monic $f_i$ unique, and change of basis gives similarity. Include dimension zero and constant unit factors.

items.title: On a nonzero finite-dimensional space, the largest invariant factor is the minimal polynomial
items.strategy: A polynomial annihilates the direct sum $\bigoplus F[x]/(f_i)$ exactly when it is divisible by every $f_i$. Since $f_1\mid\cdots\mid f_r$, the annihilator ideal is $(f_r)$; comparison with the module annihilator identifies $f_r=\mu_T$ after monic normalization. State the zero space separately: its invariant-factor list is empty and its minimal polynomial is $1$, so there is no largest factor to name.

items.title: The product of the invariant factors is the characteristic polynomial
items.strategy: The characteristic polynomial of the companion matrix $C(f_i)$ is $f_i$, proved by determinant expansion. The characteristic polynomial of the rational block diagonal form is their product and is similarity-invariant. Include the empty product $1$ in dimension zero.

items.title: Cayley-Hamilton by the PID-module structure theorem
items.strategy: The largest invariant factor is $\mu_T$ and divides the product of all invariant factors, which is $\chi_T$. Write $\chi_T=q\mu_T$ and evaluate at $T$; since $\mu_T(T)=0$, obtain $\chi_T(T)=0$. Treat dimension zero explicitly. Add a Remark linking the published adjugate proof and describing this as a genuinely different module-theoretic route.

items.title: A companion block for $(x-\lambda)^e$ is similar to the Jordan block $J_e(\lambda)$
items.strategy: In $F[x]/((x-\lambda)^e)$ use the ordered basis $1,(x-\lambda),\ldots,(x-\lambda)^{e-1}$, or its reverse according to the library's Jordan convention. Multiplication by $x=\lambda+(x-\lambda)$ has diagonal $\lambda$ and one adjacent string of ones, so it is a Jordan block. Compare with the power basis defining the companion matrix to obtain similarity. Check $e=1$.

items.title: Jordan canonical form from the elementary divisors of $V_T$
items.strategy: Assume $\chi_T$ splits. The elementary divisors of $V_T$ are powers $(x-\lambda)^e$. The elementary-divisor decomposition expresses $V_T$ as their cyclic direct sum, and the preceding lemma turns each multiplication-by-$x$ companion block into $J_e(\lambda)$. Conversely a Jordan block yields the corresponding cyclic primary module. Uniqueness of elementary divisors gives uniqueness of the block multiset. Include the empty space and cross-reference the published generalized-eigenspace proof.

items.title: For split characteristic polynomial, elementary divisors and Jordan strings give the same Jordan blocks
items.strategy: For each eigenvalue $\lambda$ and $k\ge1$, compute $\dim\ker(T-\lambda I)^k$ on a summand $F[x]/((x-\lambda)^e)$ as $\min(k,e)$. Successive differences recover the number of blocks of size at least $k$, exactly the rank/nullity invariant used by the published Jordan-string uniqueness theorem. Thus the two independently proved forms agree, including block multiplicities and the zero space.

items.title: Two matrices are similar exactly when their invariant factors agree
items.strategy: Similarity identifies the two polynomial modules by the same change-of-basis map, so module uniqueness gives equal invariant factors. Conversely equal invariant factors give the same rational canonical block matrix, and each original matrix is similar to it. Prove both directions over an arbitrary field, with no splitting hypothesis, and include zero-sized matrices.

pages.title: Modules over a Principal Ideal Domain and the Canonical Forms — Examples

items.title: Euclidean row and column reduction computes Smith normal form
items.strategy: Over a Euclidean domain, use elementary row and column operations to move a nonzero entry of least Euclidean value into the pivot. Division with remainder strictly lowers the pivot until it divides its row and column; if it fails to divide another entry, combine that entry into the pivot and descend again. Clear the row and column, recurse on the remaining rectangle, and repair adjacent diagonal entries by gcd/lcm operations to obtain the divisibility chain. Prove termination and include zero and empty matrices. Contrast this algorithm with the nonconstructive PID existence proof.

items.title: Smith normal form of an explicit three-by-three integer matrix
items.strategy: For $A=\begin{psmallmatrix}2&1&0\\4&4&6\\2&2&6\end{psmallmatrix}$, carry out integer elementary row and column operations to obtain $\operatorname{diag}(1,2,6)$. Independently check that the gcds of the entries, two-by-two minors, and determinant are $1,2,12$, so the determinantal-divisor uniqueness theorem confirms the result. Interpret the cokernel as $\mathbb Z/2\oplus\mathbb Z/6$.

items.title: The abelian groups of order $360$ in elementary-divisor and invariant-factor form
items.strategy: Use $360=2^3 3^2 5$ and the partitions of the exponents. List the six elementary-divisor combinations and align their prime-power columns to obtain the invariant-factor forms $\mathbb Z/360$, $\mathbb Z/3\oplus\mathbb Z/120$, $\mathbb Z/2\oplus\mathbb Z/180$, $\mathbb Z/6\oplus\mathbb Z/60$, $\mathbb Z/2\oplus\mathbb Z/2\oplus\mathbb Z/90$, and $\mathbb Z/2\oplus\mathbb Z/6\oplus\mathbb Z/30$. Verify every product and divisibility chain.

items.title: $\mathbb Z^2/\langle(2,0),(0,3)\rangle$ is cyclic of order six
items.strategy: The relation matrix is $\operatorname{diag}(2,3)$. Use coprime row and column operations to obtain Smith form $\operatorname{diag}(1,6)$, hence the quotient is $\mathbb Z/6$. Cross-check with $\mathbb Z/2\oplus\mathbb Z/3$ and the explicit generator represented by $(1,1)$.

items.title: Rational canonical form of an explicit four-by-four matrix
items.strategy: Take the block matrix $A=C(x-1)\oplus C((x-1)(x^2+1))$ over $\mathbb Q$ and write it entrywise. Compute the polynomial module as $\mathbb Q[x]/(x-1)\oplus\mathbb Q[x]/((x-1)(x^2+1))$, verify the divisibility chain, and recover characteristic polynomial $(x-1)^2(x^2+1)$ and minimal polynomial $(x-1)(x^2+1)$. The matrix is already in rational canonical form, making every block convention visible.

items.title: One matrix in rational form over $\mathbb Q$ and Jordan form after adjoining its roots
items.strategy: Use the preceding four-by-four matrix. Over $\mathbb Q$ retain its two invariant-factor companion blocks. Over a field containing $i$, factor the elementary divisors into two copies of $x-1$ and one each of $x-i$ and $x+i$, yielding the diagonal Jordan block multiset $1,1,i,-i$. Check that scalar extension changes the elementary divisors but not the characteristic or minimal polynomial identities.

items.title: The real quarter-turn has rational canonical form but no real Jordan form
items.strategy: For $A=\begin{psmallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{psmallmatrix}$ over $\mathbb R$, show $V_A$ is cyclic with invariant factor $x^2+1$, so $A$ is its own companion block in rational canonical form. Since $x^2+1$ does not split over $\mathbb R$, the published criterion forbids a real Jordan form. After adjoining a root, the module proof gives the two one-dimensional Jordan blocks.

items.title: The polynomial module of a two-by-two operator
items.strategy: For $T=\begin{psmallmatrix}0&-2\\1&0\end{psmallmatrix}$ on $\mathbb Q^2$, show $e_1,Te_1$ is a basis and $(T^2+2I)e_1=0$. The vector annihilator is $x^2+2$, so $V_T\cong\mathbb Q[x]/(x^2+2)$, the invariant factor is $x^2+2$, and the displayed matrix is its companion matrix. Verify torsion, finite generation, minimal polynomial, and characteristic polynomial directly.

items.title: FALSE: characteristic and minimal polynomials determine similarity
items.strategy: Compare $J_2(0)\oplus J_2(0)$ with $J_2(0)\oplus J_1(0)\oplus J_1(0)$. Both have characteristic polynomial $x^4$ and minimal polynomial $x^2$, but their invariant factors, equivalently their ranks, differ, so they are not similar. Add a Remark agreeing with the published B-page witness without citing it as a dependency.

items.title: FALSE: every finitely generated module over a domain is a direct sum of cyclic modules
items.strategy: Use the ideal $(2,x)$ as a two-generated torsion-free $\mathbb Z[x]$-module. Every two nonzero elements $a,b$ in this ideal satisfy the nontrivial relation $b a-a b=0$, so it cannot contain a direct sum of two nonzero cyclic torsion-free modules; if it were one cyclic module, the ideal would be principal. Show $(2,x)$ is not principal because a generator would divide both $2$ and $x$, hence be a unit, while $1\notin(2,x)$. This isolates the PID hypothesis.

items.title: FALSE: every torsion-free module over a PID is free
items.strategy: The additive group $\mathbb Q$ is a torsion-free $\mathbb Z$-module. If it had a nonempty basis and $b$ were a basis element, express $b/2$ as a finite integer combination of basis elements; multiplying by two makes the coefficient of $b$ both odd and even, contradicting uniqueness. The zero-basis case cannot span $\mathbb Q$. Thus finite generation is essential.

items.title: FALSE: elementary divisors determine the free rank
items.strategy: The free modules $R$ and $R^2$ over any nonzero PID have no torsion elementary divisors, but invariant basis number gives different free ranks. This shows why the free rank is separate data in the structure theorem. Use $R=\mathbb Z$ as a concrete witness and include rank zero for comparison.

pages.title: Noetherian Rings and Hilbert Basis

items.title: Conventions for this development and where dependent choice and Zorn's lemma are used
items.strategy: Record that every ring here is commutative with identity and that the zero ring is allowed unless a statement excludes it. Cite the Noetherian and Artinian definitions from chain-conditions-and-semisimple-modules rather than restating them as new definitions. State the choice accounting that the rest of the page relies on: the finite-generation definition and every finite-generation argument are ZF; the implication from the ascending chain condition to the maximal condition is the one that uses dependent choice, and it is carried by thm-equivalent-characterizations-of-noetherian-modules; the maximal element among non-finitely-generated ideals used by Cohen's criterion uses Zorn's lemma, hence full choice at this library's granularity. No count, no positional claim, no scope denial about the library.

items.title: The submodule generated by a subset consists of the finite $R$-linear combinations of that subset
items.strategy: Let $M$ be a left $R$-module and $S\subseteq M$. Show the set $L$ of sums $\sum_{i=1}^{k}r_is_i$ with $k\in\mathbb N$, $r_i\in R$, $s_i\in S$ is a submodule by the one-step criterion, contains $S$ because $s=1_Rs$ uses unitality, and is contained in every submodule containing $S$. Conclude $L=\langle S\rangle_R$. Treat $k=0$ explicitly: the empty sum is $0_M$, so $\langle\varnothing\rangle_R=0$. Record that this is the module analogue of thm-generated-ideal-description-in-a-commutative-ring and agrees with it when $M$ is the ring acting on itself, so the two descriptions are not two conventions.

items.title: Every generating set of a finitely generated module contains a finite generating subset
items.strategy: Let $M=\langle T\rangle_R$ with $T$ finite and let $S$ generate $M$. Each $t\in T$ lies in $\langle S\rangle_R$, so by the previous lemma $t$ is a finite $R$-linear combination of elements of $S$; let $S_t\subseteq S$ be the finite set of elements used. Then $S'=\bigcup_{t\in T}S_t$ is finite and $\langle S'\rangle_R\supseteq T$, hence $\langle S'\rangle_R\supseteq\langle T\rangle_R=M$. Boundary: $T=\varnothing$ gives $M=0$ and $S'=\varnothing$ works.

items.title: A commutative ring is Noetherian exactly when every ideal is finitely generated, exactly when its ideals satisfy the ascending chain condition, and exactly when every nonempty set of ideals has a maximal member
items.strategy: First identify the submodules of the regular module ${}_RR$ with the ideals of $R$: a subset is an additive subgroup closed under the scalar action $r\cdot x=rx$ exactly when it is an ideal, so the two collections coincide as sets ordered by inclusion. Then transport thm-equivalent-characterizations-of-noetherian-modules along that identification and unfold def-noetherian-ring. State the choice cost in the Statement exactly as the module theorem does: the implication from the ascending chain condition to the maximal condition uses dependent choice, the others are choice-free. Everything downstream on this page cites this theorem for the ideal-level form, so it must state all three conditions, not only finite generation.

items.title: Noetherian induction: a property that passes to an ideal whenever it holds for every strictly larger ideal holds for every ideal
items.strategy: Let $R$ be Noetherian and $P$ a property of ideals such that $P(I)$ holds whenever $P(J)$ holds for every ideal $J\supsetneq I$. Let $\Sigma$ be the set of ideals for which $P$ fails and suppose $\Sigma\neq\varnothing$. By the maximal condition $\Sigma$ has a maximal member $I$; every ideal strictly containing $I$ lies outside $\Sigma$, so $P$ holds for all of them, so the hypothesis gives $P(I)$, contradicting $I\in\Sigma$. Boundary: the hypothesis applied to $I=R$ is vacuous on the left, which is why the induction starts at the top rather than at $0$. Carry the dependent-choice flag from the maximal condition.

items.title: A subring that admits a module retraction from a Noetherian ring is Noetherian
items.strategy: Let $R\subseteq R'$ be commutative rings with $R'$ Noetherian and let $\rho:R'\to R$ be $R$-linear with $\rho|_R=\mathrm{id}_R$. For an ideal $\mathfrak a\subseteq R$, the ideal $\mathfrak aR'$ is generated by the set $\mathfrak a$, so by lem-finite-generating-subset-of-a-generating-set finitely many $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathfrak a$ generate it. Every element of $\mathfrak aR'$ is a finite sum $\sum a_ir_i'$, so $\rho(\mathfrak aR')\subseteq\mathfrak a$; and $\mathfrak a\subseteq\mathfrak aR'$ with $\rho|_{\mathfrak a}=\mathrm{id}$, so $\rho(\mathfrak aR')=\mathfrak a$. Applying $\rho$ to $\sum a_ir_i'$ gives $\sum a_i\rho(r_i')\in(a_1,\ldots,a_n)R$. Hence $\mathfrak a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$.

items.title: Every ideal of a localisation is generated by the images of any generating set of its contraction
items.strategy: Let $S\subseteq R$ be multiplicative and $J\subseteq S^{-1}R$ an ideal with contraction $\mathfrak a=\lambda_S^{-1}(J)$. By thm-ideal-correspondence-for-localisation the contraction is $S$-saturated and $J=S^{-1}\mathfrak a$. If $\mathfrak a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$ then any $r/s\in S^{-1}\mathfrak a$ has $r=\sum c_ia_i$, so $r/s=\sum(c_i/s)(a_i/1)$; conversely each $a_i/1\in J$. Hence $J$ is generated by $a_1/1,\ldots,a_n/1$. State explicitly that this does not assert that extension and contraction are mutually inverse on all ideals of $R$ — only on the $S$-saturated ones, which is what the cited correspondence gives.

items.title: Every quotient and every localisation of a Noetherian ring is Noetherian
items.strategy: For the quotient: by thm-correspondence-theorem-ideals every ideal of $R/I$ is $J/I$ for an ideal $J\supseteq I$, and the images under the canonical projection of a finite generating set of $J$ generate $J/I$. For the localisation: apply lem-localised-ideal-generated-by-contracted-numerators to a finite generating set of the contraction, which exists because $R$ is Noetherian. Boundary: $I=R$ gives the zero ring, whose only ideal is $0$; $S\ni0$ gives the zero ring likewise, and the argument covers both without special pleading.

items.title: A ring with finitely many ideals of zero intersection whose quotients are Noetherian rings is Noetherian
items.strategy: Let $\mathfrak a_1,\ldots,\mathfrak a_r$ be ideals of $R$ with $\bigcap_i\mathfrak a_i=0$ and every $R/\mathfrak a_i$ a Noetherian ring. Each $R/\mathfrak a_i$ is a Noetherian $R$-module: its $R$-submodules are exactly its ideals by the correspondence theorem, and those are finitely generated over $R/\mathfrak a_i$ hence over $R$. So $\bigoplus_iR/\mathfrak a_i$ is a Noetherian $R$-module by cor-finite-direct-sums-preserve-chain-conditions. The map $r\mapsto(r+\mathfrak a_1,\ldots,r+\mathfrak a_r)$ is $R$-linear with kernel $\bigcap_i\mathfrak a_i=0$, so $R$ embeds as an $R$-submodule and is therefore a Noetherian $R$-module, that is, a Noetherian ring. Boundary: $r=0$ forces the empty intersection convention, so state $r\ge1$.

items.title: A product of two Noetherian rings is Noetherian
items.strategy: In $R\times S$ take $\mathfrak a_1=0\times S$ and $\mathfrak a_2=R\times0$; these are ideals with $\mathfrak a_1\cap\mathfrak a_2=0$, and the coordinate projections identify $(R\times S)/\mathfrak a_1\cong R$ and $(R\times S)/\mathfrak a_2\cong S$ by the first isomorphism theorem. Apply cor-noetherian-from-finitely-many-noetherian-quotients. Note in a Remark that iterating gives every finite product, and that the corresponding statement for infinite products is false, with the witness on the companion examples page.

items.title: The leading coefficients of the degree-$n$ elements of an ideal of $R[x]$ form an ideal of $R$, and these ideals ascend with $n$
items.strategy: For an ideal $\mathfrak a\subseteq R[x]$ and $n\in\mathbb N$ put $\mathfrak a_n=\{\text{leading coefficient of }f:f\in\mathfrak a,\ \deg f=n\}\cup\{0\}$. The adjoined $0$ is not cosmetic: the zero polynomial has no degree by def-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic, so it contributes no leading coefficient. Ideal criterion: for $c\in\mathfrak a_n$ realised by $f$ and $r\in R$, either $rc=0$, which lies in $\mathfrak a_n$, or $rf$ still has degree $n$ with leading coefficient $rc$; for $c,c'\in\mathfrak a_n$ realised by $f,g$, either $c+c'=0$ or $f+g$ has degree $n$ with leading coefficient $c+c'$. Ascent: if $f\in\mathfrak a$ has degree $n$ then $xf\in\mathfrak a$ has degree $n+1$ and the same leading coefficient, so $\mathfrak a_n\subseteq\mathfrak a_{n+1}$. The index runs over $\mathbb N$ and starts at $n=0$, where $\mathfrak a_0$ is the set of constants lying in $\mathfrak a$ together with $0$; do not copy a source that displays the chain from $n=1$.

items.title: A single cancellation step lowers the degree of a polynomial in an ideal once its leading coefficient lies in a realised stage
items.strategy: Fix $n\in\mathbb N$, generators $c_1,\ldots,c_m$ of $\mathfrak a_n$, and $g_1,\ldots,g_m\in\mathfrak a$ with $\deg g_j=n$ and leading coefficient $c_j$. Let $f\in\mathfrak a$ have degree $d\ge n$ and leading coefficient in $\mathfrak a_n$, say $\mathrm{lc}(f)=\sum_jr_jc_j$. Put $h=\sum_jr_jx^{d-n}g_j$, which lies in the ideal of $R[x]$ generated by $g_1,\ldots,g_m$. Each summand has degree at most $d$, and the coefficient of $x^d$ in $h$ is $\sum_jr_jc_j=\mathrm{lc}(f)$. Hence $f-h$ is either the zero polynomial or has degree strictly less than $d$. Boundary: $d=n$ makes $x^{d-n}=1$; and when $d=0$ the alternative 'degree less than $0$' is impossible, so $f=h$ — that is the case the induction below needs and it must be argued, not assumed away.

items.title: Over a Noetherian ring, an ideal of $R[x]$ is generated by finitely many polynomials realising generators of its stages up to the stabilisation degree
items.strategy: Let $R$ be Noetherian and $\mathfrak a\subseteq R[x]$ an ideal. The chain $\mathfrak a_0\subseteq\mathfrak a_1\subseteq\cdots$ stabilises at some $N\in\mathbb N$ by the ascending chain condition. For each $n\le N$ choose a finite generating set of $\mathfrak a_n$ and, for each generator, a polynomial in $\mathfrak a$ of degree $n$ with that leading coefficient; this is a choice from finitely many nonempty sets, so no choice axiom is invoked. Let $\mathfrak b$ be the ideal of $R[x]$ they generate; then $\mathfrak b\subseteq\mathfrak a$. If $\mathfrak b\neq\mathfrak a$, the degrees of the elements of $\mathfrak a\setminus\mathfrak b$ form a nonempty subset of $\mathbb N$ — note $0\notin\mathfrak a\setminus\mathfrak b$ since $0\in\mathfrak b$, so every such element has a degree — so it has a least element $d$; pick $f\in\mathfrak a\setminus\mathfrak b$ of degree $d$. Apply lem-hilbert-basis-degree-cancellation at stage $n=\min(d,N)$, using $\mathfrak a_d=\mathfrak a_N$ when $d>N$. The resulting $f-h$ lies in $\mathfrak a$ and is not in $\mathfrak b$, and is either $0$ or of degree less than $d$; both contradict the choice of $d$. Hence $\mathfrak a=\mathfrak b$.

items.title: Hilbert basis theorem: if $R$ is Noetherian then $R[x]$ is Noetherian
items.strategy: Combine lem-polynomial-ideal-finite-generation with the finite-generation characterisation of a Noetherian ring. The proof is not compressed to a comparison of leading terms: the three preceding lemmas carry the stage-ideal construction, the single cancellation step, and the well-founded induction on degree separately. Mark this item as a landmark.

items.title: If $R$ is Noetherian then $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ is Noetherian for every $n\in\mathbb N$
items.strategy: Induct on $n$ using $R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+1}]=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n][x_{n+1}]$, which is the definition in def-multivariate-polynomial-ring-by-iteration. The base case is $n=0$, where that definition gives $R[x_1,\ldots,x_0]=R$ and the statement is the hypothesis; state it rather than starting the induction at $n=1$.

items.title: $R[x]$ is Noetherian if and only if $R$ is Noetherian
items.strategy: One direction is the Hilbert basis theorem. Conversely, evaluation at $0$ is a surjective ring homomorphism $R[x]\to R$ by the universal property of the polynomial ring, so $R\cong R[x]/\ker$ by the first isomorphism theorem, and a quotient of a Noetherian ring is Noetherian.

items.title: Subalgebra generated by a subset, algebras of finite type, and module-finite algebras
items.strategy: For a commutative ring $R$ and an $R$-algebra $A$, define the $R$-subalgebra $R[a_1,\ldots,a_n]$ generated by finitely many elements as the image of the $R$-algebra map $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\to A$ sending $x_i\mapsto a_i$ supplied by the universal property of the polynomial ring. Call $A$ of finite type over $R$, equivalently a finitely generated $R$-algebra, when $A=R[a_1,\ldots,a_n]$ for some finite list; equivalently when $A$ is a quotient of some $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$. Call $A$ module-finite over $R$, equivalently a finite $R$-algebra, when $A$ is finitely generated as an $R$-module. Record the boundary $n=0$: $R[\,]$ is the image of $R$ in $A$. Record that module-finite implies finite type and that the converse fails, naming the witness on the companion examples page in prose only. Mark as a landmark: the rest of the page and later commutative-algebra pages cite it constantly.

items.title: Every algebra of finite type over a Noetherian ring is a Noetherian ring
items.strategy: An $R$-algebra of finite type is a quotient of $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ by def-finite-type-and-module-finite-algebras and the first isomorphism theorem; that polynomial ring is Noetherian, and quotients of Noetherian rings are Noetherian. Mark as a landmark: this is the form of Hilbert's theorem that later pages actually use.

items.title: Every algebra of finite type over a principal ideal domain is a Noetherian ring
items.strategy: Two lines from results already in hand. cor-principal-ideal-domains-are-noetherian states "Every principal ideal domain is Noetherian", so the base ring is Noetherian; cor-finite-type-algebra-over-noetherian-ring-is-noetherian then applies to any algebra of finite type over it. Do not reprove either input and do not reprove the Hilbert basis theorem here. In the Given line of Facts & Assumptions record the convention that def-principal-ideal-domain admits a field, because a field is an integral domain whose only ideals $(0)$ and $(1)$ are principal, so the field case falls under this Statement rather than outside it. Keep the three sections a corollary takes; add no Remark section. This is Hochster's Corollary 5.9, "A finitely generated algebra over a PID is Noetherian"; def-finite-type-and-module-finite-algebras is where this library says "of finite type" for "finitely generated as an algebra".

items.title: Finitely presented modules and finitely presented algebras
items.strategy: A module $M$ over a commutative ring $R$ is finitely presented when there is an exact sequence $R^m\to R^n\to M\to0$ with $m,n\in\mathbb N$; equivalently, $M\cong R^n/K$ with $K$ a finitely generated submodule. An $R$-algebra is finitely presented when it is isomorphic to $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\mathfrak a$ with $\mathfrak a$ a finitely generated ideal. Record that finitely presented implies finitely generated for both notions, and that $m=0$ or $n=0$ are allowed, so the zero module is finitely presented.

items.title: Over a Noetherian ring a module is Noetherian exactly when it is finitely generated, exactly when it is finitely presented
items.strategy: Noetherian implies finitely generated because $M$ is a submodule of itself. Finitely generated implies Noetherian is thm-finitely-generated-modules-over-noetherian-rings-are-noetherian. For finite presentation: from a finite generating set build a surjection $R^n\to M$; its kernel is a submodule of the Noetherian module $R^n$, hence finitely generated, so a surjection $R^m\to K$ gives the presentation $R^m\to R^n\to M\to0$. Finitely presented implies finitely generated is immediate. Mark as a landmark. State the ring as commutative and Noetherian; the free module $R^n$ is Noetherian by the published finite-direct-sum corollary applied to the regular module.

items.title: Every algebra of finite type over a Noetherian ring is finitely presented
items.strategy: Write the algebra as $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\mathfrak a$; the polynomial ring is Noetherian, so $\mathfrak a$ is finitely generated, which is exactly the definition of a finitely presented algebra.

items.title: Over a commutative ring the homomorphism group $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,N)$ is an $R$-module
items.strategy: The published definition gives $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,N)$ only as an abelian group. For commutative $R$ define $(rf)(m)=r\cdot f(m)$ and check that $rf$ is again $R$-linear — this is exactly where commutativity is used, since $(rf)(sm)=rsf(m)=sr f(m)=s(rf)(m)$ — and that the module axioms hold pointwise. Record the agreement with the published abelian-group structure: the underlying addition is unchanged, so this extends rather than redefines it.

items.title: For a commutative ring, $\operatorname{Hom}_R(R^n,N)\cong N^n$
items.strategy: By the universal property of the free module on the $n$-element standard basis, $f\mapsto(f(e_1),\ldots,f(e_n))$ is a bijection onto $N^n$; check directly that it is additive and commutes with the scalar action of the previous lemma. Boundary: $n=0$ gives $R^0=0$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_R(0,N)=0=N^0$.

items.title: Over a Noetherian ring the homomorphism module between two finitely generated modules is finitely generated
items.strategy: Choose a surjection $\pi:R^n\to M$. Left exactness of the contravariant $\operatorname{Hom}$ makes $\pi^*:\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,N)\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(R^n,N)$ injective, and it is $R$-linear for the module structure above. So $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,N)$ embeds in $\operatorname{Hom}_R(R^n,N)\cong N^n$, which is a finitely generated module over a Noetherian ring, hence Noetherian; a submodule of a Noetherian module is finitely generated. Do not claim the embedding is an isomorphism.

items.title: Module finiteness is transitive along a tower of algebras
items.strategy: Let $A\to B\to C$ be maps of commutative rings with $B$ generated as an $A$-module by $b_1,\ldots,b_m$ and $C$ generated as a $B$-module by $c_1,\ldots,c_n$. Every element of $C$ is $\sum_j\beta_jc_j$ with $\beta_j\in B$, and each $\beta_j$ is $\sum_i\alpha_{ij}b_i$ with $\alpha_{ij}\in A$, so the $mn$ products $b_ic_j$ generate $C$ as an $A$-module. Boundary: $m=0$ or $n=0$ forces the corresponding ring to be zero and the conclusion is the zero module.

items.title: A module-finite algebra over a Noetherian ring is a Noetherian ring, and so is every ring between the two
items.strategy: Let $A$ be Noetherian and $B$ a module-finite commutative $A$-algebra. Then $B$ is a finitely generated $A$-module, hence a Noetherian $A$-module. Every ideal of $B$ is in particular an $A$-submodule of $B$, so it is finitely generated over $A$ and therefore over $B$; thus $B$ is a Noetherian ring. Second clause: if $A\subseteq B$ then every intermediate ring $A\subseteq C\subseteq B$ is an $A$-submodule of the Noetherian $A$-module $B$, hence module-finite over $A$, and its ideals are $A$-submodules of $C$, so $C$ is a Noetherian ring too. Third clause: a finitely generated $B$-module is generated over $A$ by the products of a finite $A$-generating set of $B$ with a finite $B$-generating set of the module, so it is a finitely generated and hence Noetherian $A$-module. Mark as a landmark. The intermediate-ring clause is what makes this theorem, and not only the Artin-Tate lemma, usable downstream, so state it rather than leaving it as an unremarked consequence.

items.title: A subalgebra generated by finitely many integral elements is module-finite
items.strategy: Let $A\subseteq B$ be commutative rings and $b_1,\ldots,b_n\in B$ integral over $A$. If $A$ is the zero ring then $1_B=0$ and $B=0$, so the conclusion is trivial; otherwise thm-integrality-and-finite-module-equivalences applies. Induct: $A[b_1]$ is a finite $A$-module by that theorem; $b_2$ is integral over $A$ hence over $A[b_1]$ because the same monic polynomial works, so $A[b_1][b_2]$ is a finite $A[b_1]$-module; transitivity of module finiteness gives a finite $A$-module. Boundary $n=0$: $A[\,]$ is the image of $A$, generated by $1$.

items.title: The Artin–Tate coefficient subalgebra is a Noetherian algebra of finite type
items.strategy: Let $A\subseteq B\subseteq C$ be commutative rings with $A$ Noetherian, $C=A[x_1,\ldots,x_m]$ of finite type over $A$, and $C=\sum_jBy_j$ module-finite over $B$ with $y_1,\ldots,y_n$ and $y_1=1$ available after enlarging the list. Write $x_i=\sum_jz_{ij}y_j$ and $y_iy_j=\sum_kz_{ijk}y_k$ with all $z_{ij},z_{ijk}\in B$, and let $A'=A[\{z_{ij}\},\{z_{ijk}\}]\subseteq B$. There are finitely many coefficients, so $A'$ is of finite type over $A$ and hence Noetherian by cor-finite-type-algebra-over-noetherian-ring-is-noetherian. State that the coefficients are chosen, not canonical, and that only their finiteness is used.

items.title: In the Artin–Tate setup the intermediate ring is module-finite over the coefficient subalgebra
items.strategy: With $A'$ as above, every element of $C$ is a polynomial in the $x_i$ with coefficients in $A$; substituting $x_i=\sum_jz_{ij}y_j$ and reducing products of the $y$'s by $y_iy_j=\sum_kz_{ijk}y_k$ expresses it as an $A'$-linear combination of $y_1,\ldots,y_n$. Hence $C$ is a finite $A'$-module. Since $A'$ is Noetherian, $C$ is a Noetherian $A'$-module, and $B$ is an $A'$-submodule of $C$, so $B$ is a finite $A'$-module. The reduction is an induction on the total degree of the polynomial; state it as such rather than as a single substitution.

items.title: Artin–Tate lemma: an intermediate ring over which a finite-type algebra is module-finite is itself of finite type
items.strategy: Let $A\subseteq B\subseteq C$ with $A$ Noetherian, $C$ of finite type over $A$, and $C$ module-finite over $B$. The two preceding lemmas give $A'\subseteq B$ of finite type over $A$ with $B$ a finite $A'$-module, say $B=\sum_lA'w_l$. Then $B=A[\{z_{ij}\},\{z_{ijk}\},w_1,\ldots,w_r]$ is of finite type over $A$. Mark as a landmark.

items.title: The Artin–Tate lemma with integrality in place of module finiteness
items.strategy: If $C$ is of finite type over $A$ and integral over $B$, then $C$ is of finite type over $B$ as well, so $C=B[x_1,\ldots,x_m]$ with each $x_i$ integral over $B$; by lem-algebra-generated-by-finitely-many-integral-elements-is-module-finite, $C$ is module-finite over $B$ and thm-artin-tate-lemma applies. Note that finite type over $B$ follows from finite type over $A$ because the same generators work.

items.title: A group acting on a ring by automorphisms and its invariant subring
items.strategy: Let $G$ be a group acting on a commutative ring $C$ so that every $g\in G$ acts as a ring automorphism; when $C$ is an $A$-algebra, an action by $A$-algebra automorphisms is one in which each $g$ fixes the image of $A$ pointwise. Define $C^G=\{c\in C:g\cdot c=c\text{ for all }g\in G\}$ and verify it is a subring containing the image of $A$. Boundary: the trivial group gives $C^G=C$. Record the agreement with the published special case explicitly, in dictionary style: def-symmetric-polynomial already writes $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]^{\operatorname{Sym}_n}$ for the fixed subset of the permutation action on a polynomial ring, and that is exactly $C^G$ for $C=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ and $G=\operatorname{Sym}_n$; the notation and the meaning agree, so this definition extends it and does not compete with it.

items.title: For a finite group of ring automorphisms the orbit polynomial is monic over the invariant subring, so the ring is integral over its invariants
items.strategy: Let $G$ be a finite group acting on a commutative ring $C$ by ring automorphisms and let $x\in C$. Extend the action to $C[T]$ coefficientwise, fixing $T$. Put $P(T)=\prod_{g\in G}(T-g\cdot x)$. For $h\in G$ the map $g\mapsto hg$ is a bijection of $G$, so $h$ permutes the factors and fixes $P$; hence every coefficient of $P$ lies in $C^G$. $P$ is monic of degree $|G|\ge1$ and $P(x)=0$ because the factor at the identity is $T-x$. Therefore every element of $C$ is integral over $C^G$. State the finiteness of $G$ as an explicit hypothesis: the product is over a finite index set and the argument gives nothing for an infinite group.

items.title: Noether's finiteness theorem: the invariants of a finite group acting on a finite-type algebra over a Noetherian ring form an algebra of finite type
items.strategy: Let $A$ be a Noetherian commutative ring, $C$ a commutative $A$-algebra of finite type with $A$ a subring of $C$, and $G$ a finite group acting on $C$ by $A$-algebra automorphisms. Then $A\subseteq C^G\subseteq C$, $C$ is of finite type over $A$, and $C$ is integral over $C^G$ by the orbit-polynomial lemma; cor-artin-tate-integral-form gives that $C^G$ is of finite type over $A$. Mark as a landmark; it is the payoff of the Artin–Tate block and the reason that block is on this page.

items.title: If some ideal is not finitely generated, there is one maximal among the ideals that are not
items.strategy: Order the set $\Sigma$ of non-finitely-generated ideals by inclusion; it is nonempty by hypothesis. For a nonempty chain in $\Sigma$ its union is an ideal, and if that union were generated by finitely many elements then all of them would lie in one member of the chain, forcing that member to equal the union and to be finitely generated — a contradiction. So every nonempty chain has an upper bound in $\Sigma$, and $\Sigma$ is nonempty, so Zorn's lemma gives a maximal member. Flag in the Statement that this uses Zorn's lemma and hence the axiom of choice, and note that no Noetherian hypothesis is available or needed here — Noetherianity is what the criterion below is proving.

items.title: An ideal maximal among the non-finitely-generated ideals is prime
items.strategy: Let $\mathfrak p$ be maximal in $\Sigma$; it is proper because $R=(1)$ is finitely generated. Suppose $ab\in\mathfrak p$ with $a\notin\mathfrak p$ and $b\notin\mathfrak p$. Then $\mathfrak p+(a)\supsetneq\mathfrak p$ is finitely generated, say by $x_1+w_1a,\ldots,x_n+w_na$ with $x_i\in\mathfrak p$. Let $\mathfrak q=(\mathfrak p:a)=\{r\in R:ra\in\mathfrak p\}$, an ideal containing $\mathfrak p+(b)\supsetneq\mathfrak p$, hence finitely generated. Claim $\mathfrak p=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)+a\mathfrak q$: the inclusion $\supseteq$ is clear, and for $z\in\mathfrak p\subseteq\mathfrak p+(a)$ write $z=\sum c_i(x_i+w_ia)=\sum c_ix_i+ya$ with $y=\sum c_iw_i$; then $ya=z-\sum c_ix_i\in\mathfrak p$, so $y\in\mathfrak q$. Both summands are finitely generated, so $\mathfrak p$ is — a contradiction. Hence $\mathfrak p$ is prime.

items.title: Cohen's criterion: a commutative ring in which every prime ideal is finitely generated is Noetherian
items.strategy: If some ideal were not finitely generated, the two preceding lemmas produce a prime ideal that is not finitely generated, contradicting the hypothesis. Emphasise in the proof that the maximal element comes from Zorn's lemma and not from Noetherian induction, since Noetherianity is the conclusion. Mark as a landmark.

items.title: Which constructions preserve the Noetherian condition, and which do not
items.strategy: Collect the stability results proved above — quotients, localisations, polynomial rings in finitely many variables, algebras of finite type, module-finite algebras, products of two Noetherian rings, and subrings admitting a module retraction — and record that none of this extends to an arbitrary subring or to an infinite product; name the companion examples page in plain prose as the place where both witnesses are worked. Cite only items on this page. No count of the listed constructions, no positional claim, and no statement about what the library does or does not develop.

pages.title: Noetherian Rings and Hilbert Basis — Examples

items.title: Fields and $\mathbb Z$ are Noetherian, and so are their polynomial rings in finitely many variables
items.strategy: A field has exactly two ideals, $0=(0)$ and $K=(1)$, each principal. Every ideal of $\mathbb Z$ is an additive subgroup, hence cyclic by lem-subgroups-of-z-are-cyclic, hence principal. Apply cor-finite-variable-polynomial-ring-noetherian to get $K[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ and $\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ Noetherian for every $n\in\mathbb N$, and say explicitly that the conclusion is finite generation of every ideal, not a classification of the ideals.

items.title: $k[x,y]/(xy)$ and $\mathbb Z[x]/(x^2-2)$ are Noetherian without classifying their ideals
items.strategy: Both are quotients of polynomial rings over Noetherian rings, so cor-finite-type-algebra-over-noetherian-ring-is-noetherian settles both at once. Point out that the first has zero divisors and the second is a domain, and that neither fact is used: the argument sees only the finite-type presentation.

items.title: The polynomial ring in countably many variables is not Noetherian
items.strategy: Build $k[x_1,x_2,\ldots]$ as the union of the chain $k\subseteq k[x_1]\subseteq k[x_1,x_2]\subseteq\cdots$ of the iterated polynomial rings of def-multivariate-polynomial-ring-by-iteration, and check that a union of a chain of subrings is a subring so the operations are unambiguous. The ideals $I_n=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ form a strictly ascending chain: setting $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ to $0$ is a ring homomorphism killing $I_n$ but not $x_{n+1}$. By the ascending chain characterisation the ring is not Noetherian. Note that the chain starts at $I_0=0$.

items.title: The subalgebra $k[x,xy,xy^2,\ldots]$ of $k[x,y]$ is not Noetherian
items.strategy: Let $A=k+xk[x,y]=k[x,xy,xy^2,\ldots]\subseteq k[x,y]$ and let $\mathfrak a=(x,xy,xy^2,\ldots)A$. If $f_1,\ldots,f_m\in\mathfrak a$ generated $\mathfrak a$, let $N$ be the largest power of $y$ occurring in any $f_i$; then every element of $(f_1,\ldots,f_m)$ has all its monomials of $y$-degree at most $N$ or divisible by $x^2$, so $xy^{N+1}\notin(f_1,\ldots,f_m)$. Hence $\mathfrak a$ is not finitely generated even though $k[x,y]$ is Noetherian. Record the two consequences: a subring of a Noetherian ring need not be Noetherian, and a subalgebra of an algebra of finite type need not be of finite type. Work the $y$-degree bookkeeping explicitly rather than asserting it.

items.title: The subring $k[x,x/y,x/y^2,\ldots]$ of $k(x,y)$ has a strictly ascending chain of principal ideals
items.strategy: Inside $\operatorname{Frac}(k[x,y])$, which exists because $k[x,y]$ is a domain, let $R=k[x,x/y,x/y^2,\ldots]$. Then $(x)\subseteq(x/y)\subseteq(x/y^2)\subseteq\cdots$ because $x=y\cdot(x/y)$ and generally $x/y^n=y\cdot(x/y^{n+1})$; show each inclusion is strict by a degree-in-$y$ argument on the representations available in $R$. Conclude non-Noetherian from the ascending chain condition. Contrast with the previous example: there the failure is in a finitely generated ideal's generators, here in an unbounded chain of principal ideals.

items.title: Working the Hilbert basis construction on an ideal of $\mathbb Z[x]$ with non-monic stages
items.strategy: Take $\mathfrak a=(2x,3x^2,x^3)\subseteq\mathbb Z[x]$ and compute the stage ideals $\mathfrak a_0,\mathfrak a_1,\mathfrak a_2,\mathfrak a_3,\ldots$ of lem-leading-coefficient-ideals explicitly, including $\mathfrak a_0=0$, identifying where the chain stabilises and why. Then run one cancellation step of lem-hilbert-basis-degree-cancellation on an element of degree above the stabilisation index, and exhibit the finite generating set that lem-polynomial-ideal-finite-generation produces. The point of the example is the non-monic leading coefficients, where the reduction cannot simply divide.

items.title: Identifying the coefficient algebra in a concrete Artin–Tate tower
items.strategy: Take $A=k$, $C=k[t]$, and $B=k[t^2,t^3]$, so that $C$ is of finite type over $k$ and module-finite over $B$ with module generators $1,t$. Write out the relations $t=z_{11}\cdot1+z_{12}t$ and $t\cdot t=z_{111}\cdot1+z_{112}t$ with coefficients in $B$, exhibit the finitely many coefficients that lem-artin-tate-coefficient-subalgebra collects, and check that the resulting $A'$ is of finite type over $k$ and that $B$ is a finite $A'$-module. Conclude with thm-artin-tate-lemma that $B$ is of finite type over $k$, and confirm directly that $B=k[t^2,t^3]$.

items.title: False statement: in a Noetherian ring there is a single bound on the number of generators an ideal needs
items.strategy: Refute in $k[x,y]$, which is Noetherian. The ideal $(x,y)^n$ needs at least $n+1$ generators: if $g_1,\ldots,g_m$ generate it, write each monomial $x^iy^{n-i}$ as $\sum h_jg_j$ and compare homogeneous parts of degree $n$; the degree-$n$ components of the $g_j$ then span the $(n+1)$-dimensional space of degree-$n$ forms over $k$, so $m\ge n+1$. Since $n$ is arbitrary, no uniform bound exists. State that the Noetherian condition bounds each ideal separately and asserts nothing uniform, and set up the graded decomposition of $k[x,y]$ explicitly rather than assuming it.

items.title: An algebra that is finite dimensional as a vector space over a field is a Noetherian ring
items.strategy: Let $A$ be a commutative $k$-algebra whose underlying $k$-vector space is finite dimensional. Every ideal of $A$ is in particular a $k$-subspace, hence finite dimensional by thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace, so a finite $k$-basis of it generates it as an ideal. Note that this gives module finiteness over $k$ and so also follows from thm-module-finite-algebra-over-a-noetherian-ring-is-noetherian; give the direct argument and record the agreement.

items.title: The symmetric polynomials as the invariant ring of the symmetric group, seen through Noether's finiteness theorem
items.strategy: Let $S_n$ act on $k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ by permuting the indeterminates; this is an action by $k$-algebra automorphisms, and its invariant subring is the ring of symmetric polynomials of def-symmetric-polynomial. Noether's finiteness theorem says only that this invariant ring is of finite type over $k$; thm-fundamental-theorem-of-symmetric-polynomials says more, namely that the elementary symmetric polynomials generate it. Check that the two statements agree and say precisely what the extra content of the classical theorem is. Also run the orbit polynomial of lem-orbit-polynomial-has-invariant-coefficients on $x_1$ and identify it with $\prod_{i}(T-x_i)$ raised to the appropriate power, whose coefficients are the elementary symmetric polynomials up to sign.

items.title: When the group order is invertible the Reynolds operator retracts a ring onto its invariants
items.strategy: Let a finite group $G$ of order $n$ act on a commutative ring $S$ by ring automorphisms and suppose the image of $n$ is invertible in $S$. Define $\rho(s)=\frac1n\sum_{g\in G}g(s)$ and check three things: $\rho(s)$ is invariant, because $h\rho(s)=\frac1n\sum_{g}(hg)(s)=\rho(s)$ as $g\mapsto hg$ permutes $G$; $\rho$ is $S^G$-linear, because $g(as)=g(a)g(s)=ag(s)$ for invariant $a$; and $\rho$ fixes $S^G$ pointwise. So $\rho$ is a retraction of the inclusion $S^G\subseteq S$ as a map of $S^G$-modules, and lem-retract-of-a-noetherian-ring-is-noetherian gives that $S^G$ is Noetherian whenever $S$ is. Say what this buys over thm-noether-finiteness-theorem-for-invariants: it drops the finite-type hypothesis on $S$ but adds the hypothesis that $n$ is invertible, so neither statement contains the other. Give the characteristic-$p$ caveat concretely: if the characteristic of a field in $S$ divides $n$, the operator is not defined.

items.title: $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(\mathbb Z/m,\mathbb Z/n)\cong\mathbb Z/\gcd(m,n)$
items.strategy: A homomorphism is determined by the image of $1+m\mathbb Z$, which must be killed by $m$; the elements of $\mathbb Z/n$ killed by $m$ form the subgroup generated by $n/\gcd(m,n)$, of order $\gcd(m,n)$. Check that the resulting bijection is $\mathbb Z$-linear for the module structure of lem-hom-module-over-a-commutative-ring. This is a finitely generated module, as cor-hom-of-finite-modules-is-finite-over-a-noetherian-ring predicts, and here the module is computed outright. Handle $m=0$ or $n=0$ explicitly with the convention $\gcd(m,0)=|m|$.

pages.title: Localisation of Modules and Support

items.title: Localisation of a module at a multiplicative subset
The module-fraction relation is an equivalence relation
items.strategy: Check reflexivity and symmetry directly. For transitivity, combine two annihilating-denominator equations with one common multiplier from the multiplicative set.

items.title: Addition of localised module fractions is independent of representatives
items.strategy: Start from two valid representative changes and clear both denominator changes at once to show the common-denominator sum defines the same class.

items.title: The localised scalar action is independent of representatives
items.strategy: Treat the ring-fraction and module-fraction representative changes separately and then combine them to show ((a/u)(m/s) = am/(us)) is well defined.

items.title: Universal property of localisation for modules
items.strategy: Send m/s to s^{-1}f(m) in the target S^{-1}R-module, prove representative independence from the previous well-definedness lemmas, and force uniqueness by evaluating every class at m/1 and 1/s.

items.title: Localisation of modules is extension of scalars
items.strategy: Construct mutually inverse maps S^{-1}R tensor_R M <-> S^{-1}M by ((a/s) tensor m) mapsto am/s and m/s mapsto (1/s) tensor m, checking balance and the inverse identities explicitly.

items.title: Localisation commutes with quotient modules and arbitrary direct sums
items.strategy: Identify localisation with extension of scalars, then use the published quotient-tensor isomorphism and the direct-sum tensor isomorphism to transport both constructions through localisation.

items.title: A localised module fraction is zero exactly when one denominator kills its numerator
items.strategy: Unpack equality with 0/1 in the localisation relation and rewrite the witness equation as an annihilation statement on the numerator.

items.title: Injective module maps remain injective after localisation
items.strategy: If a localised element maps to zero, apply the zero-fraction criterion in the codomain and then use injectivity of the original map to push the annihilating denominator back to the source.

items.title: Surjective module maps remain surjective after localisation
items.strategy: Lift the numerator of each target fraction along the original surjection and keep the same denominator.

items.title: Localisation of modules is exact
items.strategy: Use the tensor description plus right exactness of tensor products for the cokernel side, and the injectivity-preservation lemma for the left exact side.

items.title: Localisation commutes with kernels images and cokernels
items.strategy: Apply exactness to the standard short exact sequences defining kernel, image, and cokernel.

items.title: Localisation commutes with finite intersections of submodules
items.strategy: Realise a finite intersection as the kernel of the diagonal map to a finite direct sum of quotients, then localise kernels, quotients, and direct sums.

items.title: There is a natural localisation map on Hom
items.strategy: Send a localised homomorphism class f/s to the induced map on localisations, prove the formula respects the localisation relation, and check S^{-1}R-linearity.

items.title: The localised Hom map is an isomorphism for finite free sources
items.strategy: Identify both sides with a finite direct sum of the localised target by evaluating at a chosen finite basis and localising coordinatewise.

items.title: A finite presentation reduces localised Hom to the finite free case
items.strategy: Apply Hom to a finite presentation, localise the resulting kernel diagram, and compare the two rows using exactness and the finite free case on the surrounding free modules.

items.title: Localisation of Hom for finite and finitely presented modules
items.strategy: Prove injectivity from a finite generating set of the source, then use the finite-presentation kernel reduction to obtain surjectivity and hence an isomorphism in the finitely presented case.

items.title: Local criteria for zero modules and for injective, surjective, and bijective maps
items.strategy: Detect a nonzero element by its annihilator and a maximal ideal containing that annihilator, then apply the kernel and cokernel identifications after localisation to translate module tests into map tests.

items.title: A sequence of modules is exact exactly when all prime localisations are exact
items.strategy: Localise the sequence to get necessity, then test the homology module for zero by the previous local criterion.

items.title: Support of a module
A prime lies in the support exactly when some element has annihilator inside it
items.strategy: Translate nonvanishing of m/1 in M_p into the failure of every denominator outside p to annihilate m, and rewrite that condition as Ann(m) subseteq p.

items.title: The support of a cyclic quotient is its vanishing set
items.strategy: Identify (R/I)_p with R_p/I_p and show this quotient is nonzero exactly when the extended ideal I_p is proper, equivalently when p contains I.

items.title: A finite module has the union of its generator-cyclic supports
items.strategy: Localise a finite generating surjection from a finite direct sum of cyclic modules and compare vanishing on both sides.

items.title: For a finite module, support is the set of primes containing the annihilator
items.strategy: Use the annihilator-membership lemma for one direction, and reduce the converse to finitely many cyclic generator quotients whose supports are explicit vanishing sets.

items.title: Support in a short exact sequence is the union of the outer supports
items.strategy: Localise the short exact sequence and read nonvanishing of the middle term directly from exactness of the localised sequence.

items.title: Support of an arbitrary direct sum is the union of the supports
items.strategy: Localise the direct sum termwise and use the zero-module local criterion to see that a direct sum localisation vanishes exactly when every summand localisation vanishes.

items.title: Support under localisation is restriction to primes disjoint from the denominator set
items.strategy: Use the prime-correspondence theorem and iterated localisation to identify the localisations of S^{-1}M with the original localisations of M at primes disjoint from S.

items.title: The Jacobson radical of a ring
An element lies in the Jacobson radical exactly when one minus any multiple is a unit
items.strategy: Intersect over maximal ideals for one direction, and for the converse put a nonunit into a maximal ideal and force the corresponding one-minus-multiple to be a nonunit too.

items.title: Determinant trick for Nakayama
items.strategy: Write chosen generators of M as I-linear combinations of themselves, form the matrix I-A, and apply the adjugate identity to show a determinant in 1+I annihilates M.

items.title: Nakayama's lemma
items.strategy: Apply the determinant trick to obtain an annihilator in 1+I and then use the Jacobson radical unit test to force that annihilator to be a unit.

items.title: Generators modulo an ideal in the Jacobson radical lift to generators
items.strategy: Let N be the submodule generated by the chosen lifts. The quotient M/N is killed modulo I, so Nakayama annihilates it.

items.title: Minimal generators over a local ring are exactly residue-field bases
items.strategy: Use Nakayama for the spanning direction, and if a lifted relation over the residue field is dependent then solve for one generator and remove it.

items.title: Support of a tensor product of finite modules is the intersection of the supports
items.strategy: Localise at a prime. If one factor localises to zero the tensor localises to zero; if both local factors are nonzero and finite over a local ring, pass to the residue field and use Nakayama plus nonzero finite-dimensional tensor products over a field.

items.title: A finite module that vanishes at a prime vanishes on some principal neighbourhood of that prime
items.strategy: Use the support-annihilator theorem to find an annihilating element outside the prime, then invert it so that the localised module is killed by a unit.

pages.title: Localisation of Modules and Support — Examples

items.title: Localising cyclic abelian groups and Q/Z at a prime
items.strategy: Compute Z_(p) tensor_Z Z/n from the quotient-tensor formula by separating the p-primary and prime-to-p parts, then show Q/Z localises to its p-primary summand.

items.title: Localising Z/12Z kills exactly the torsion seen by the denominator set
items.strategy: Work with the multiplicative sets generated by 2 and by 3, compute when a denominator power annihilates each residue class, and read the surviving fractions from the zero criterion.

items.title: The support of Z/12Z is the pair of primes (2) and (3)
items.strategy: Apply the cyclic-support lemma to the quotient Z/(12), then identify the prime ideals of Z containing 12.

items.title: The support of the direct sum over all primes of Z/pZ is the set of all nonzero prime ideals of Z
items.strategy: Localise each summand at a prime q and observe that only the q-summand survives, then apply the direct-sum support theorem.

items.title: Over Z, the ideal (2) acts surjectively on Z/3Z but does not kill it
items.strategy: Show 2 acts as an automorphism of Z/3Z, so (2)M = M, and then note that (2) is not contained in the Jacobson radical of Z.

items.title: The p-primary quotient Q/Z_(p) over Z_(p) shows finite generation is essential in Nakayama
items.strategy: Identify $mathbb Z_{(p)}$ inside $mathbb Q$ via the localisation definition and the field-of-fractions embedding, then show multiplication by $p$ on $mathbb Q/mathbb Z_{(p)}$ is surjective while the module remains nonzero and not finitely generated.

items.title: The ideal (x,y) in k[x,y]_(x,y) has two minimal generators
items.strategy: Pass to the residue field of the local ring k[x,y]_(x,y), compute the classes of x and y in m/m^2, and apply the residue-basis criterion.

items.title: The Chinese-remainder map Z/6Z -> Z/2Z direct-sum Z/3Z is an isomorphism by local tests
items.strategy: Check that localising at primes other than 2 and 3 kills both sides, and that at 2 and 3 the map becomes the obvious identity on the surviving summand.

items.title: Localised Hom can fail without finite presentation of the source
items.strategy: Use Altman-Kleiman's standard non-finitely-presented source module to show the natural localisation-of-Hom map is injective but not surjective, and isolate exactly where the finite-presentation kernel step breaks.

items.title: Localisation need not commute with infinite products
items.strategy: Follow Altman-Kleiman's infinite-product witness and compare the product of the localised factors with the localisation of the product by testing which families admit one common denominator.

pages.title: Prime Spectra and Radicals

items.title: The radical of an ideal
Radical membership via positive powers
items.strategy: Unpack the definition of the radical and record the unit-ideal and zero-ring edge cases explicitly so later uses do not hide them.

items.title: The radical of an ideal is an ideal
items.strategy: Use the binomial theorem for sums, ideal absorption for scalar multiples, and exponent nesting for idempotence and monotonicity.

items.title: The radical of a finite intersection
items.strategy: One inclusion is immediate from monotonicity; for the reverse, raise a common product of witnessing powers into the intersection.

items.title: The radical of a product of ideals
items.strategy: Use IJ subseteq I cap J for one inclusion and multiply witnesses from sqrt(I) and sqrt(J) for the reverse.

items.title: The nilradical and reduced rings
Radicals and quotient correspondence
items.strategy: Translate power-membership in R/I back and forth across the quotient map and use the ideal correspondence theorem.

items.title: Radicals commute with localization
items.strategy: If a fraction has a power in the extended ideal, clear denominators; the forward direction is immediate from functoriality of localization.

items.title: The reduced quotient by the nilradical
items.strategy: Use the quotient-radical identification for reducedness, then factor any map to a reduced ring through the quotient by the nilradical.

items.title: A prime containing an ideal and avoiding a multiplicative set
items.strategy: Take an ideal maximal among those containing I and disjoint from S via Zorn, then prove maximal disjointness forces primality.

items.title: Separating an element from an ideal by a prime
items.strategy: Apply the multiplicative-set lemma to the powers of the chosen element.

items.title: Primes containing an ideal contain its radical
items.strategy: If a power of x lies in a prime containing I, primality removes the power one factor at a time.

items.title: A separating prime for an element outside a radical
items.strategy: If f is not in sqrt(I), no power of f lies in I, so the previous corollary produces a prime over I that omits f.

items.title: The radical of an ideal is the intersection of the prime ideals containing it
items.strategy: Combine the forward inclusion from primality with the separating-prime lemma for elements outside the radical.

items.title: The nilradical is the intersection of all prime ideals
items.strategy: Apply the radical-intersection theorem to the zero ideal.

items.title: A ring is reduced exactly when zero is an intersection of primes
items.strategy: Translate reducedness into vanishing nilradical and invoke the nilradical intersection corollary.

items.title: The prime spectrum and vanishing sets
Krull dimension of a nonzero ring
The height of a prime ideal
Vanishing sets reverse inclusions
items.strategy: A prime containing the larger ideal automatically contains the smaller one.

items.title: Vanishing sets of arbitrary sums
items.strategy: A prime contains the sum of a family exactly when it contains each summand.

items.title: Vanishing sets of finite products
items.strategy: If a prime contains a finite product of ideals, primality forces one factor ideal into the prime.

items.title: Vanishing-set identities
items.strategy: Combine the boundary cases with the arbitrary-sum and finite-product lemmas.

items.title: Vanishing sets detect radicals
items.strategy: Equal vanishing sets mean equal intersections of containing primes, hence equal radicals, and conversely radicals do not change which primes contain an ideal.

items.title: Principal distinguished subsets of the prime spectrum
Distinguished-subset identities
items.strategy: Rewrite D(f) as the complement of V(f) and use primality together with the nilradical criterion for emptiness.

items.title: Distinguished-subset covers detect radicals
items.strategy: Pass to complements and use equality of vanishing sets with equality of radicals.

items.title: The spectrum map respects composition and identities
items.strategy: Contraction of prime ideals is prime, inverse images compose, and the identity map contracts to itself.

items.title: The spectrum map pulls back vanishing sets
items.strategy: A target prime contains the extension IA exactly when its contraction contains I.

items.title: A ring map induces a contraction map on prime spectra
items.strategy: Package the contraction construction and the vanishing-set pullback lemma into the contravariant spectrum map.

items.title: Primes of a quotient lie over the kernel
items.strategy: Apply ideal correspondence and the quotient-domain criterion to transfer primality across R to R/I.

items.title: Prime ideals of a quotient ring are exactly the prime ideals containing the ideal
items.strategy: Read the quotient prime correspondence as the spectrum contraction map onto V(I).

items.title: Primes of a localization avoid the denominator set
items.strategy: Use localization ideal correspondence, checking that extension and contraction are inverse on the primes disjoint from S.

items.title: Primes of a localization at a prime
items.strategy: Specialize the localization-prime correspondence to S = R minus p.

items.title: Primes of a principal localization
items.strategy: Specialize the localization-prime correspondence to the powers of a single element.

items.title: Prime ideals of a localization are exactly the primes disjoint from the denominator set
items.strategy: Promote the localization-prime correspondence to the spectrum-level bijection.

items.title: Passing to the reduced quotient does not change the prime spectrum
items.strategy: Quotient by the nilradical and invoke the quotient-spectrum bijection together with radical detection.

items.title: Minimal primes over a proper ideal exist
items.strategy: First place the ideal inside some prime, then apply Zorn to descending chains of primes over the ideal; intersections of such chains stay prime.

items.title: The Noetherian minimal-prime induction split
items.strategy: If a radical ideal is not prime, choose x and y outside it with xy inside it and split minimal primes according to which element they contain.

items.title: The nilradical of a Noetherian ring is nilpotent
items.strategy: Use finite generation of the nilradical in a Noetherian ring and a common exponent argument for finitely many nilpotent generators.

items.title: A radical ideal in a Noetherian ring is a finite intersection of minimal primes
items.strategy: Reduce to the quotient by the radical ideal, run the Noetherian induction split there, and pull the resulting minimal primes back to R before applying the radical-intersection theorem.

items.title: A Noetherian ring has finitely many minimal prime ideals
items.strategy: Specialize the radical-ideal corollary to the zero ideal.

items.title: Height equals local dimension
items.strategy: Prime chains in R_p correspond exactly to prime chains in R ending at p, so the two suprema agree.

items.title: Dimension of a quotient via chains above an ideal
items.strategy: Translate prime chains in R/I into prime chains of R containing I by the quotient-spectrum correspondence.

pages.title: Prime Spectra and Radicals — Examples

items.title: The prime ideals of a field and of the integers
items.strategy: A field has only the zero ideal. For Z, prove every ideal is nZ by well-ordering, then use quotient criteria to see that nZ is prime exactly for n = 0 or n prime.

items.title: Every prime ideal of a product ring comes from one factor
items.strategy: In R x S the idempotents (1,0) and (0,1) multiply to 0, so a prime contains exactly one of them and therefore comes from one projection.

items.title: Dual numbers and their reduced quotient have the same prime set
items.strategy: Write the dual numbers as k[epsilon]/(epsilon^2); epsilon is nilpotent, so reduction identifies their prime spectra.

items.title: Minimal and maximal primes of the node ring
items.strategy: Work in k[x,y]/(xy): any prime over (xy) contains x or y, so quotient correspondence reduces the computation to the two coordinate-axis quotients and their maximal ideals.

items.title: The distinguished subset D(x) matches the primes of the localization at x
items.strategy: Primes of k[x,y]_x correspond exactly to primes of k[x,y] avoiding x, which is the distinguished subset D(x).

items.title: Computing sqrt((x^2,xy)) from its containing primes
items.strategy: Show every prime over (x^2,xy) contains x, and conversely x^2 already lies in the ideal, so the radical is (x).

items.title: A radical of a product and intersection computation
items.strategy: Compute a monomial example two ways and compare it with the product/intersection radical identities.

items.title: A separating prime for an element outside a radical
items.strategy: Use an explicit polynomial ideal and invoke the separating-prime corollary to exhibit a prime avoiding the chosen element.

items.title: The zero ring has empty prime spectrum
items.strategy: There are no proper ideals in the zero ring, so no prime ideals; then check the displayed V and D boundary cases directly.

items.title: Primes inside a localization at a prime
items.strategy: List primes below (x,y) in k[x,y], then transport them through localization at that prime.

items.title: A common nilpotence exponent in a Noetherian quotient
items.strategy: Generate the nilradical by finitely many monomials and take a common exponent guaranteed by the nilradical-nilpotence theorem.

items.title: A non-Noetherian nilradical need not be nilpotent
items.strategy: Use an infinite-variable quotient whose nilpotent generators have unbounded exponents, so no common power kills them all.

pages.title: Artinian Rings and Length

items.title: An Artinian integral domain is a field
items.strategy: Let $D$ be an Artinian integral domain and take $0 \ne a \in D$. The descending chain $(a) \supseteq (a^2) \supseteq \cdots$ stabilizes, so $(a^n)=(a^{n+1})$ for some $n$. Then $a^n=a^{n+1}b$ for some $b$, and cancellation in the domain gives $1=ab$, so every nonzero element is a unit.

items.title: Every prime ideal of an Artinian ring is maximal
items.strategy: If $\mathfrak p$ is prime in an Artinian ring $R$, then ideals of $R/\mathfrak p$ correspond to ideals of $R$ containing $\mathfrak p$, so $R/\mathfrak p$ is Artinian. The quotient is also a domain because $\mathfrak p$ is prime, and the preceding lemma makes that Artinian domain a field. Therefore $R/\mathfrak p$ is a field and $\mathfrak p$ is maximal.

items.title: An Artinian ring has only finitely many maximal ideals
items.strategy: Among the finite intersections of maximal ideals choose one minimal by inclusion. If some other maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ were missing, then for each listed maximal ideal choose an element in it but not in $\mathfrak m$; their product still avoids $\mathfrak m$ because $\mathfrak m$ is prime, but lies in the chosen minimal intersection, contradiction.

items.title: The nilradical of an Artinian ring is a nilpotent ideal
items.strategy:
Let $N=\operatorname{Nil}(R)$. If $N^n=N^{n+1}$ with $N^n 
e 0$, choose an ideal $\mathfrak a$ minimal among those with $\mathfrak aN^n 
e 0$, then choose $a \in \mathfrak a$ with $aN^n 
e 0$. Minimality forces $\mathfrak a=(a)$ and $aN^n=(a)$, so $a=ax$ for some $x \in N^n$; iterating and using nilpotence of $x$ gives $a=0$, contradiction.

items.title: Chinese remainder theorem for pairwise comaximal ideals
items.strategy: For two comaximal ideals $I,J$, prove $IJ=I \cap J$, identify the kernel of $R \to R/I \times R/J$, and solve simultaneous residues using $u+v=1$ with $u \in I$, $v \in J$. Then show one ideal is comaximal with the product of the rest, so induction on the finite family yields the isomorphism $R/\prod I_i \cong \prod R/I_i$ together with $\bigcap I_i=\prod I_i$.

items.title: Every commutative Artinian ring is Noetherian
items.strategy: Let $N$ be the nilradical. By the preceding results, the maximal ideals are finite in number, $N$ is nilpotent, and $N=\bigcap \mathfrak m_i$; Chinese remainder identifies $R/N$ with a finite product of fields. For each layer $N^i/N^{i+1}$, use the orthogonal idempotents of $R/N$ to split it into field-vector-space components and prove inline that each component is finite-dimensional, since an infinite-dimensional component would yield a strict descending chain of subspaces and hence of ideals. Therefore every layer is Noetherian, and the finite $N$-adic filtration upgrades $R$ itself to Noetherian.

items.title: A commutative ring is Artinian exactly when it has finite length as a module over itself
items.strategy: If $R$ has finite length as an $R$-module, then its ideals satisfy both chain conditions, so $R$ is Artinian. Conversely, if $R$ is Artinian, the previous theorem makes its regular module both Artinian and Noetherian; the published module criterion then yields a composition series, hence finite length.

items.title: An Artinian local ring has nilpotent maximal ideal, and its finite modules have finite length
items.strategy: In a local Artinian ring the unique maximal ideal is the only prime ideal, hence the nilradical, so it is nilpotent. For a finite module $M$, the filtration $M \supseteq \mathfrak mM \supseteq \cdots \supseteq 0$ terminates; each quotient is killed by $\mathfrak m$ and is therefore a vector space over the residue field, and the images of one fixed finite generating set of $M$ generate every quotient, so each quotient is finite-dimensional. Additivity of length along the filtration yields finite length.

items.title: An Artinian ring is canonically the finite product of its localizations at its maximal ideals
items.strategy: Let $\mathfrak m_1,\dots,\mathfrak m_r$ be the maximal ideals and choose $n$ with $N^n=0$ for the nilradical $N$. The powers $\mathfrak m_i^n$ are pairwise comaximal and have zero product, so Chinese remainder gives $R \cong \prod_i R/\mathfrak m_i^n$. Each quotient is local with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_i/\mathfrak m_i^n$, and comparison with localization at $\mathfrak m_i$ identifies these factors with the canonical local rings $R_{\mathfrak m_i}$; the quotient-by-powers presentation depends on the chosen exponent and is not called canonical.

items.title: The prime ideals of an Artinian ring are exactly its finitely many maximal ideals
items.strategy: Combine the theorem that every prime ideal is maximal with the theorem that only finitely many maximal ideals exist. Record just the finite-set identification here; the discrete-topology consequence waits for the later spectrum topology page.

items.title: A Noetherian ring is Artinian exactly when every prime ideal is maximal
items.strategy: The forward direction is the Artinian prime-maximal theorem together with Artinian implies Noetherian. Conversely, if $R$ is Noetherian and every prime is maximal, then the finitely many minimal primes over $(0)$ are all maximal and every prime contains one of them, hence equals one of them.
