The nilradical is nilpotent, the reduced quotient is a finite product of fields by Chinese remainder, and the nilpotent-radical filtration gives finite length for the regular module; therefore $R$ is Artinian.

items.title: Quotients and localizations of an Artinian ring are Artinian
items.strategy: A quotient of an Artinian ring is Artinian because its ideals correspond to ideals above the kernel. For localizations, use the Artinian product decomposition: localizing a finite product acts factorwise, and in a local Artinian factor a denominator in the maximal ideal kills the localization because that ideal is nilpotent, while a denominator outside the maximal ideal is already a unit. Thus a localization keeps exactly the local factors whose maximal ideals avoid the multiplicative set.

pages.title: Artinian Rings and Length — Examples

items.title: The truncated polynomial ring $k[x]/(x^n)$ is local Artinian of length $n$
items.strategy: Let $R=k[x]/(x^n)$ and $\mathfrak m=(x)$. Show $\mathfrak m^n=0$, every ideal is $(x^r)$ for some $0 \le r \le n$, and each quotient $\mathfrak m^r/\mathfrak m^{r+1}$ is one-dimensional over $k=R/\mathfrak m$. The filtration by powers of $\mathfrak m$ then gives the ring length and makes the nilpotent maximal ideal explicit.

items.title: $\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z$ splits as the product of its two local Artinian factors
items.strategy: Use the Chinese remainder theorem to identify $\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z$ with $\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z \times \mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z$. Check that the two factors are local, read off the two prime ideals of the product, and pull them back to the two primes of $\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z$ to see the structure theorem concretely.

items.title: A field has module length one over itself
items.strategy: For a field $K$, the chain $0 \subset K$ is a composition series, so $\ell_K(K)=1$. Hence every field is Artinian and gives the minimal nonzero example for the page's length convention.

items.title: $\mathbb Z$ and $k[x]$ are Noetherian but not Artinian
items.strategy: Use the published Noetherian results for $\mathbb Z$ and for finite-variable polynomial rings. Then exhibit the strict descending ideal chains $(2) \supset (2^2) \supset \cdots$ in $\mathbb Z$ and $(x) \supset (x^2) \supset \cdots$ in $k[x]$ to show that Noetherianity alone does not force Artinianness.

items.title: The module $R/(x^i)$ over $k[x]/(x^n)$ has length $i$
items.strategy: Let $R=k[x]/(x^n)$ and $1 \le i \le n$. Filter $R/(x^i)$ by the images of $(x^j)$, so each subquotient is generated by one class killed by $(x)$ and hence is one-dimensional over the residue field. The short exact sequences $0 \to (x^{i-1})/(x^i) \to R/(x^i) \to R/(x^{i-1}) \to 0$ then verify additivity step by step.

items.title: The ring $(\mathbb Z/2)^{\mathbb N}$ is zero-dimensional but not Noetherian
items.strategy: In $R=(\mathbb Z/2)^{\mathbb N}$ every element is idempotent coordinatewise. Therefore if $\mathfrak p$ is prime then every element of the domain $R/\mathfrak p$ satisfies $x^2=x$, so every nonzero class equals $1$ and the quotient is a field; thus every prime is maximal. On the other hand the ideals generated by the first finitely many coordinate idempotents form a strict ascending chain, so $R$ is not Noetherian and hence not Artinian.

pages.title: Associated Primes and Primary Decomposition

items.title: Associated primes of a module
A cyclic submodule is a residue module by its annihilator
items.strategy: Send the residue class of $r$ to $rm$. The kernel is exactly the annihilator of $m$, so the first isomorphism theorem identifies $Rm$ with $R/\operatorname{Ann}(m)$.

items.title: Associated primes are exactly primes of embedded cyclic residue modules
items.strategy: Use the cyclic-submodule identification to turn an element with annihilator $\mathfrak p$ into an embedded copy of $R/\mathfrak p$, and conversely read the annihilator of the image of $1$ in any embedding $R/\mathfrak p\hookrightarrow M$.

items.title: Associated primes of a cyclic quotient are colon primes
A nonzero module over a Noetherian ring has a maximal element annihilator
items.strategy: The annihilators of nonzero elements form a nonempty set of ideals, and the ascending chain condition on ideals in a Noetherian ring gives a maximal member.

items.title: A maximal element annihilator is prime
items.strategy: If $bc$ annihilates $m$ but $c$ does not, then $cm\neq0$ and maximality forces $\operatorname{Ann}(cm)=\operatorname{Ann}(m)$, so $b$ lies in that annihilator.

items.title: A nonzero module over a Noetherian ring has an associated prime
items.strategy: Choose a nonzero element whose annihilator is maximal among element annihilators, prove that annihilator prime, and then unpack the definition of associated prime.

items.title: A module over a Noetherian ring has no associated primes exactly when it is zero
Associated primes of a submodule lie in those of the ambient module
items.strategy: An embedded copy of $R/\mathfrak p$ inside the submodule remains embedded after composing with the inclusion into the ambient module.

items.title: Associated primes of the middle term lie in those of the ends
items.strategy: Intersect an embedded copy of $R/\mathfrak p$ in the middle term with the submodule. If the intersection is zero it survives in the quotient; otherwise the nonzero intersection already realizes $\mathfrak p$ in the left term.

items.title: Associated primes in a short exact sequence
items.strategy: Combine the left inclusion and the right bound, and record the direct-sum formula as the split special case needed later for primary intersections.

items.title: Associated primes localize forward
items.strategy: Localize an embedding $R/\mathfrak p\hookrightarrow M$ and use the localization prime-spectrum correspondence to identify the source with $(S^{-1}R)/(S^{-1}\mathfrak p)$.

items.title: Associated primes of a localized finite module come from upstairs
items.strategy: Represent an associated prime of $S^{-1}M$ as the annihilator of a localized element, clear finitely many denominators to get a nonzero element of $M$, and use maximality of an annihilator in the contraction ideal.

items.title: Associated primes commute with localization for finite modules
items.strategy: The forward implication localizes an embedded cyclic residue module, and the reverse implication clears denominators from a localized annihilator before contracting the prime.

items.title: Associated primes lie in the support
items.strategy: If $\mathfrak p=\operatorname{Ann}(m)$, then no denominator outside $\mathfrak p$ kills $m$, so $m/1$ is nonzero in $M_{\mathfrak p}$.

items.title: Finite modules over Noetherian rings admit prime filtrations
items.strategy: Because a finite module over a Noetherian ring is Noetherian, the maximal condition on its submodules lets us choose a maximal quotient still lacking a prime filtration. A nonzero quotient has an associated prime, hence a cyclic submodule isomorphic to $R/\mathfrak p$, and adjoining it shortens the induction.

items.title: Minimal support primes of a finite module are associated
items.strategy: Use a prime filtration. Any prime minimal in the support contains one of the filtration primes, and minimality forces equality; the filtration prime is associated by the cyclic quotient.

items.title: The support is the union of the closures of the associated primes
items.strategy: Identify the support with $V(\operatorname{Ann}(M))$, choose a minimal prime below any support prime, and invoke the minimal-support theorem.

items.title: Finite modules over Noetherian rings have finitely many associated primes
items.strategy: Take a prime filtration and iterate the short-exact-sequence inclusions. Every associated prime must occur among the finitely many prime filtration quotients.

items.title: A zero divisor is contained in an associated prime
items.strategy: If $x$ is a zero divisor on $M$, then the annihilator submodule $\{m\in M:xm=0\}$ is nonzero. Apply associated-prime existence to that submodule and then use the short-exact-sequence inclusion.

items.title: Zero divisors on a module over a Noetherian ring are the union of its associated primes
items.strategy: Every element of an associated prime is visibly a zero divisor, and every zero divisor lies in an associated prime by applying existence to its annihilator submodule.

items.title: Primary submodules and primary ideals
The radical of a primary ideal is prime
items.strategy: Pass to the quotient ring by the primary ideal, where every zero divisor is nilpotent. The nilradical of the quotient is therefore prime, and it is the image of the radical of the ideal.

items.title: Primary submodules are exactly quotients with nilpotent zero divisors
items.strategy: Unpack the definition through the quotient module $M/Q$: the condition on products in $M$ is equivalent to saying every zero divisor on $M/Q$ acts nilpotently there.

items.title: Characterizations of primary submodules in the Noetherian finite case
items.strategy: Translate primaryity of $Q$ into structure of $M/Q$. The zero-divisor theorem turns singleton associated-prime support into one prime $\mathfrak p$, and nilpotence of the nilradical on a finite module makes a power of $\mathfrak p$ kill the quotient.

items.title: A finite intersection of primary submodules with one radical is primary
items.strategy: Embed the quotient by the intersection into the direct sum of the quotient modules by each component and use the short-exact-sequence theorem together with the singleton-associated-prime characterization.

items.title: Minimal primary decompositions and isolated components
Irreducible submodules of Noetherian modules are primary
items.strategy: In the quotient by an irreducible submodule, stabilize the colon chain $(0:x)\subseteq(0:x^2)\subseteq\cdots$, intersect the stable colon with a principal submodule, and use irreducibility to force a power of every zero divisor to vanish.

items.title: Redundant components can be deleted from a primary decomposition
items.strategy: Starting from a finite decomposition, remove any component containing the intersection of the others. Finiteness guarantees the deletion process terminates.

items.title: Equal-radical primary components can be combined
items.strategy: Group the components with the same radical and replace each group by its intersection. The previous lemma on intersections preserves primaryity for that common radical.

items.title: Lasker-Noether primary decomposition
items.strategy: Because a finite module over a Noetherian ring is Noetherian, the maximal condition on submodules lets us choose a maximal submodule still lacking a finite primary decomposition. That counterexample is reducible, so it is an intersection of two strictly larger submodules that decompose already; then minimalize by deleting redundancy and combining equal radicals.

items.title: Associated primes are the radicals in a minimal primary decomposition
items.strategy: The quotient by the intersection embeds into the direct sum of the primary quotients, giving one inclusion. For the reverse inclusion, remove one component at a time and use irredundancy to produce a nonzero submodule whose associated prime is exactly that component's radical.

items.title: First uniqueness of primary decomposition
items.strategy: Apply the associated-primes lemma for minimal decompositions. The set of radicals is intrinsic because it equals $\operatorname{Ass}(M/N)$.

items.title: Localisation of a primary submodule either stays primary or becomes the whole module
items.strategy: Localize the quotient $M/Q$. If the denominator set meets the radical, some denominator becomes nilpotent and the localization vanishes; otherwise the localized quotient keeps the same unique associated prime after extension.

items.title: A primary component is recovered by contracting its localization
items.strategy: If $sm\in Q$ with $s$ outside the radical of a primary component, then multiplication by $s$ is injective on $M/Q$, so $m$ already lies in $Q$.

items.title: Isolated primary components are unique
items.strategy: Localize a minimal primary decomposition at a minimal radical among its components. All components with larger radicals disappear, the chosen component stays primary, and contraction recovers it uniquely in the original module.

items.title: Finite prime avoidance
items.strategy: Induct on the number of primes. If an ideal is not contained in one of the first $n-1$ primes or in the last prime, choose elements avoiding those targets and multiply them to build a contradiction.

items.title: Second uniqueness of primary decomposition
items.strategy: Use the associated-primes lemma for minimal decompositions to identify the radicals with $\operatorname{Ass}(M/N)$. For a downward-closed subset of those primes, finite prime avoidance gives a multiplicative set that avoids exactly them. Localize a minimal decomposition, keep precisely the surviving components, and contract back to obtain a canonical intersection.

items.title: Radical ideals are intersections of their minimal primes in Noetherian rings
items.strategy: Apply primary decomposition to the ideal, use the first uniqueness theorem to identify the radicals with the associated primes of the quotient, and note that a radical ideal has only isolated components.

pages.title: Associated Primes and Primary Decomposition — Examples

items.title: Colon ideals in a cyclic quotient recover the associated primes
items.strategy: Compute annihilators of explicit residue classes in a small quotient ring and read off the associated primes as the prime colon ideals that appear.

items.title: Every ideal with maximal radical in an Artinian local quotient is primary
items.strategy: Use the nilpotent maximal ideal in the local Artinian quotient to check directly that every zero divisor modulo the ideal is nilpotent.

items.title: Localization kills the components away from one associated prime
items.strategy: Localize a monomial primary decomposition at each associated prime and track which factors become the whole ring and which survive.

items.title: A redundant primary decomposition can be minimalized explicitly
items.strategy: Start with a deliberately redundant decomposition, delete the dispensable term, and then combine the components with equal radical.

items.title: Embedded components can vary even when the radicals do not
items.strategy: Compare two primary decompositions of the same ideal with the same radical set but different embedded components, and isolate the unique minimal component by localization.

items.title: The zero module has empty support and no associated primes
items.strategy: Check the definitions directly on the zero quotient and note that every primary-submodule statement becomes vacuous only after the proper-submodule hypothesis is enforced.

pages.title: Integral Extensions and Going Up

items.title: Integral ring maps and integral extensions
Integral closure in an extension ring and integrally closed domains
Integral extensions are transitive
items.strategy: Handle the zero base ring first. For an element of the top ring, adjoin the finitely many coefficients of one monic equation over the middle ring, use the published finite-generator integrality lemma to make that coefficient algebra module-finite over the base, then adjoin the element itself and apply the one-element criterion back over the base.

items.title: The integral closure of a domain in a field extension is integrally closed
items.strategy: Use the published subring theorem to see that integral elements over the base form a subring. If an element is integral over that subring, transitivity makes it integral over the original domain, so it was already in the closure.

items.title: Integrality and integral closure commute with localisation
items.strategy: Forwards, divide a monic equation by a suitable power of the chosen denominator. Backwards, clear all coefficient denominators from a monic equation in the localisation so that one multiplier sends the element into the original integral closure. The closure statement is then just a restatement of the two directions.

items.title: For an integral extension of domains, the upper ring is a field if and only if the lower ring is
items.strategy: If the base is a field, take a monic relation of minimal degree for a nonzero element and solve for its inverse. If the upper ring is a field, apply a monic relation to the inverse of a nonzero base element and solve inside the base.

items.title: Under an integral extension, a prime is maximal if and only if its contraction is maximal
items.strategy: Pass to the induced integral extension of quotient domains and apply the field criterion to the two quotient rings.

items.title: Lying over for integral ring maps
items.strategy: Reduce a general map to the injective case by quotienting by the kernel. Then quotient by the chosen prime, localise the resulting domain at its nonzero elements to reach a field, choose a maximal ideal in the nonzero localised upper ring, and contract it back through localisation and quotient correspondences.

items.title: Comparable primes with the same contraction are equal under an integral map
items.strategy: Localise at the common contraction. The two extended primes are then nested primes of the localised upper ring over the maximal ideal of the localised base, so the maximal-ideal contraction corollary makes both maximal and hence equal. Contract back through the localisation bijection.

items.title: Going up for integral ring maps
items.strategy: Quotient by the lower prime of the chain and by the chosen prime upstairs. The induced extension remains integral, so lying over lifts the next base prime and pulling back gives the required over-prime.

items.title: Integral extensions lift finite prime chains from the base
items.strategy: Iterate the one-step going-up theorem along the chain.

items.title: Strict prime chains contract strictly under integral extensions
items.strategy: If two adjacent contractions were equal, incomparability would force the adjacent upper primes to be equal as well.

items.title: Injective integral extensions preserve Krull dimension
items.strategy: Lift every finite chain in the base by going up, and contract every finite chain upstairs strictly by incomparability. The two inequalities give equality of dimensions.

items.title: Minimal polynomials of integral elements over an integrally closed domain have coefficients in the domain
items.strategy: Take a splitting field of the minimal polynomial. Every conjugate satisfies the same monic equation over the domain, so all conjugates are integral; expanding the minimal polynomial as a product of linear factors shows that its coefficients are integral, and integrally closedness pulls them back into the domain.

items.title: A domain is integrally closed if and only if its prime localisations are, equivalently if and only if its maximal localisations are
items.strategy: Forward direction is localisation of integral closure. For the converse, let x be integral over the domain; the finite module A[x]/A vanishes after localising at every maximal ideal by hypothesis, so the local criterion forces it to vanish globally and x already lies in the domain. Prime and maximal localisations are interchanged by iterated localisation.

items.title: Going down holds for integral extensions over integrally closed domains
items.strategy: Localise at the upper prime so the upper ring becomes local and the base stays integrally closed. For an element of the lower extended ideal inside the localised upper ring, build a finite stable module and apply the determinant trick to a multiplication operator; the coefficient lemma then forces the critical denominator into the upper prime, proving the contraction equality needed for a final lying-over step inside the local ring.

items.title: Under going down and incomparability, lying-over primes have the same finite height
items.strategy: Going down lifts every finite chain below the contracted prime, and incomparability shows that every finite chain below the upper prime contracts strictly. The two resulting inequalities force equal finite heights.

pages.title: Integral Extensions and Going Up — Examples

items.title: Every element of k[X] is integral over k[X^2], and k[X] has basis 1, X over k[X^2]
items.strategy: Write f(X) = a(X^2) + X b(X^2). Then f satisfies a quadratic monic equation over k[X^2], and the same decomposition shows that every element lies in the k[X^2]-span of 1 and X.

items.title: Z[square-root of 2, square-root of 3] is finite over Z and contains the sum and product of its generators
items.strategy: Show that 1, square-root of 2, square-root of 3, and square-root of 6 span the ring over Z. This one finite module exhibits both the multi-generator finiteness theorem and the closure of integral elements under addition and multiplication.

items.title: The element 1/p is integral over Z[1/p] but not over Z
items.strategy: After localising Z at the powers of p, the element 1/p already lies in the base ring and is therefore integral. Clearing denominators multiplies it back to 1 in Z, while a direct divisibility argument shows that 1/p itself cannot satisfy a monic equation over Z.

items.title: Lying over in k[t^2, t^3] subset k[t]
items.strategy: Use the cusp subring A = k[t^2, t^3] inside B = k[t]. Track the primes over the zero ideal and the cusp maximal ideal by quotienting and localising exactly as in the proof of lying over.

items.title: In k[Y] subset k[X] with Y = X^2, comparable primes do not share a contraction
items.strategy: Work in the integral extension k[Y] subset k[X] defined by Y = X^2. The upper primes are easy to list, and direct contraction shows that the only comparable chains contract strictly.

items.title: An integral domain extension can fail going down when the base is not normal
items.strategy: Use Hochster's standard example R = K[x(1 - x), y, xy] subset S = K[x, y]. The ring S is integral over R because x satisfies the monic equation z^2 - z + x(1 - x) = 0 with coefficients in R. Let P0 = (x(1 - x), xy)R and Q = (1 - x, y)S. Then Q lies over the maximal ideal P = (x(1 - x), y, xy)R containing P0, but any prime Q0 subset Q lying over P0 would have to avoid x while containing both x(1 - x) and xy, forcing 1 - x and y into Q0 and hence Q0 = Q, whose contraction is P rather than P0. Therefore going down fails if the normality hypothesis on the base is removed.

pages.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra

items.title: Every odd-degree real polynomial has a real root
items.strategy: For a real polynomial of odd degree with nonzero leading coefficient, choose a large positive radius so the leading term dominates the sum of the lower terms in absolute value. This forces opposite signs at a large positive and a large negative argument. The published continuity of real polynomial functions and the intermediate value theorem then give a real root.

items.title: An irreducible polynomial over $\mathbb R$ has degree $1$ or an even degree
items.strategy: If an irreducible real polynomial had odd degree greater than one, the odd-degree theorem would give a real root. The factor theorem would then give a nontrivial linear factor over $\mathbb R$, contradicting irreducibility.

items.title: To prove the fundamental theorem of algebra, it suffices to split every real polynomial over $\mathbb C$
items.strategy: Assume every nonconstant polynomial in $\mathbb R[x]$ splits over $\mathbb C$. For a nonconstant polynomial $g\in\mathbb C[x]$, write $g=u+iv$ with $u,v\in\mathbb R[x]$ and form the conjugate polynomial $\overline g=u-iv$. Then $g\overline g\in\mathbb R[x]$ splits over $\mathbb C$, so it has a complex root $z$. Because $\mathbb C$ is a field, $g(z)\overline{g(z)}=0$ forces $g(z)=0$ or $\overline g(z)=0$, and the second case gives a root of $g$ after conjugating. Therefore every nonconstant polynomial in $\mathbb C[x]$ has a complex root, which is the definition of algebraic closedness.

items.title: A quadratic extension in characteristic not $2$ is obtained by adjoining a square root
items.strategy: Let $E/F$ have degree $2$ and pick $\alpha\in E\setminus F$. Its minimal polynomial over $F$ has degree $2$, so after writing it as $x^2+bx+c$ the quadratic formula expresses $\alpha$ in $F(\sqrt{b^2-4c})$. Because the extension already has degree $2$, this generated subfield is all of $E$.

items.title: A field is algebraically closed exactly when every nonconstant polynomial splits, equivalently when it has no nontrivial finite extension
items.strategy: From algebraic closedness, repeatedly apply the factor theorem to peel off linear factors and show every nonconstant polynomial splits. If every nonconstant polynomial splits, then any finite extension generated by an algebraic element must be trivial because its minimal polynomial already splits into linear factors over the base. Conversely, if the field has no nontrivial finite extension, then adjoining a root of an irreducible polynomial would create a nontrivial finite extension, so every irreducible polynomial already has a root in the field and the field is algebraically closed.

items.title: The complex numbers are algebraically closed
items.strategy: Use the reduction lemma to work with a nonconstant real polynomial $f$. Let $E$ be a splitting field of $f(x)(x^2+1)$ over $\mathbb R$. By characteristic zero, the extension $E/\mathbb R$ is finite Galois, and because $x^2+1$ splits in $E$ one has $\mathbb C\subseteq E$. Let $H$ be a Sylow $2$-subgroup of $\operatorname{Gal}(E/\mathbb R)$ and let $M=E^H$. The fixed-field degree $[M:\mathbb R]=[G:H]$ is odd, so for every $\alpha\in M$ the minimal-polynomial degree $[\mathbb R(\alpha):\mathbb R]$ divides an odd number and is therefore odd; the odd-degree irreducibility corollary forces it to be $1$, hence $M=\mathbb R$ and $G$ is a $2$-group. Then $\operatorname{Gal}(E/\mathbb C)$ is a finite $2$-group. If it were nontrivial, the index-$2$ subgroup theorem would give an intermediate quadratic extension of $\mathbb C$, but the quadratic-extension lemma and the published complex square-root theorem rule those out. Therefore $\operatorname{Gal}(E/\mathbb C)=1$, so $E=\mathbb C$, $f$ splits over $\mathbb C$, and the reduction lemma finishes the proof.

items.title: Every nonconstant polynomial in $\mathbb C[x]$ splits into linear factors
items.strategy: The main theorem says $\mathbb C$ is algebraically closed. Apply the equivalence proposition to convert that root-existence statement into full splitting.

items.title: The complex numbers form an algebraic closure of $\mathbb R$
items.strategy: Combine the main theorem with the published fact that $\mathbb C/\mathbb R$ is a degree-$2$ extension. The definition of algebraic closure then applies immediately.

items.title: The algebraic numbers in $\mathbb C$ form an algebraic closure of $\mathbb Q$
items.strategy: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb C$ be the subfield of elements algebraic over $\mathbb Q$. The published subfield theorem gives that $A$ is a field. For a nonconstant polynomial with coefficients in $A$, the main theorem gives a root $z\in\mathbb C$. Adjoining the finitely many algebraic coefficients and then $z$ produces a finite extension of $\mathbb Q$, so $z$ is algebraic over $\mathbb Q$ and therefore lies in $A$. Thus $A$ is algebraically closed and algebraic over $\mathbb Q$, hence is an algebraic closure.

items.title: A nonreal root of a real polynomial comes with its complex conjugate
items.strategy: If $f\in\mathbb R[x]$ and $f(z)=0$, apply complex conjugation to the coefficient expression. Because conjugation fixes $\mathbb R$ pointwise and is a field automorphism of $\mathbb C$, the conjugated equation is exactly $f(\overline z)=0$.

items.title: An irreducible polynomial in $\mathbb R[x]$ has degree $1$ or $2$
items.strategy: Let $f\in\mathbb R[x]$ be irreducible. By the fundamental theorem of algebra it has a complex root $z$. If $z$ is real, irreducibility forces $f$ to be linear. If $z$ is nonreal, the conjugate-pair lemma gives the quadratic polynomial $(x-z)(x-\overline z)\in\mathbb R[x]$, and the minimal polynomial of $z$ over $\mathbb R$ divides that quadratic. Since the minimal polynomial is $f$ and is not linear, its degree is $2$.

items.title: Every real polynomial factors into linear and irreducible quadratic factors
items.strategy: Factor the polynomial into irreducibles in $\mathbb R[x]$ using the published polynomial-factorization theorem. The preceding corollary says each irreducible factor has degree $1$ or $2$, and every degree-$2$ irreducible factor is already quadratic.

items.title: A complex polynomial of degree $n$ has exactly $n$ roots counted with multiplicity
items.strategy: Use the splitting corollary to write a degree-$n$ polynomial in $\mathbb C[x]$ as a product of $n$ linear factors. Group equal roots together; the exponents are their multiplicities. The UFD property of $\mathbb C[x]$ makes that multiplicity data well defined, and the total multiplicity is exactly the original degree.

pages.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: $x^3-2$ over $\mathbb R$ and over $\mathbb C$
items.strategy: Show that $x^3-2$ has one real root and one irreducible quadratic factor over $\mathbb R$, then split the quadratic over $\mathbb C$ by adjoining the primitive cube roots of unity. The point is the visible difference between the real and complex factorizations of the same polynomial.

items.title: $x^4+1$ factors over $\mathbb R$ into two irreducible quadratics
items.strategy: Start from the complex fourth roots of $-1$, pair conjugates, and multiply each pair to recover the two real quadratic factors. This is the clean witness that irreducible over $\mathbb Q$ and irreducible over $\mathbb R$ are different questions.

items.title: $x^2+1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb R$ and split over $\mathbb C$
items.strategy: Use the published irreducibility item over $\mathbb R$, and then factor $x^2+1=(x-i)(x+i)$ over $\mathbb C$. This is the smallest concrete instance of the theorem.

items.title: $x^5-x-1$ has a real root
items.strategy: Evaluate the polynomial at two explicit real numbers with opposite signs and invoke the odd-degree theorem. The example exists to make the analytic input visible on a nontrivial odd-degree polynomial.

items.title: $x^5-6x+3$ over $\mathbb Q$ is not solvable by radicals
items.strategy: Use Eisenstein at $3$ to prove irreducibility. The derivative $5x^4-6$ has exactly two real zeros, and sign checks plus the intermediate value theorem show the quintic has exactly three real roots, so its splitting field inside $\mathbb C$ has exactly one nontrivial complex-conjugation orbit on roots, giving a transposition in the Galois group. Irreducibility makes the degree-$5$ action transitive, so the published prime-degree transposition theorem gives the full group $S_5$. Since $S_5$ is not solvable, the solvable-by-radicals implication rules the polynomial out.

items.title: FALSE: every polynomial with real coefficients has a real root
items.strategy: Refute the statement with $x^2+1$, whose real irreducibility is already published and whose graph never meets the real axis.

items.title: FALSE: the real numbers are algebraically closed
items.strategy: Use the same polynomial $x^2+1$: it has no root in $\mathbb R$, so $\mathbb R$ fails the defining root-existence property of an algebraically closed field.

items.title: FALSE: every irreducible polynomial in $\mathbb R[x]$ has degree $1$
items.strategy: The irreducible quadratic $x^2+1$ is the smallest counterexample, and the A page explains why degree $2$ is the exact upper bound.

items.title: FALSE: every irreducible quintic over $\mathbb Q$ is insoluble by radicals
items.strategy: Refute the universal claim with the irreducible quintic $x^5-2$. Eisenstein at $2$ shows irreducibility over $\mathbb Q$, while its five roots lie in $\mathbb Q(\zeta_5,\sqrt[5]{2})$, so its splitting field is contained in a radical extension of $\mathbb Q$ and the polynomial is solvable by radicals. This preserves the intended contrast with the neighbouring insoluble irreducible quintic without duplicating the already-published broader false statement that not every quintic is insoluble by radicals.

items.title: The Artin and minimum-modulus proofs of the fundamental theorem of algebra use different machinery
items.strategy: Write this as the design's required agreement record. It compares two proofs of the same theorem, not two pages of the library: this page's proof uses only the intermediate value theorem together with Galois theory and Sylow theory, while the later proof on `the-complex-exponential-and-eulers-formula` uses the minimum-modulus route. At authoring, give the remark `forward_refs: [thm-fundamental-theorem-of-algebra-minimum-modulus-proof]` and no dependency edge to that later theorem.

pages.title: The Spectral Theorem, Positive Operators and Singular Value Decomposition

items.title: Self-adjoint and normal endomorphisms of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space
In an orthonormal basis, self-adjoint means conjugate-transpose symmetry and normal means commuting with the conjugate transpose
items.strategy: Translate the defining adjoint identities through the matrix-of-the-adjoint theorem and read the two operator conditions entrywise.

items.title: If the characteristic polynomial of an endomorphism splits, some orthonormal basis makes its matrix upper triangular
items.strategy: Start from a triangularising basis, read off the invariant flag, and run Gram-Schmidt along that flag so the orthonormalised basis preserves every successive span.

items.title: A normal upper-triangular matrix is diagonal
items.strategy: Compare the norms of each basis vector under the matrix and its conjugate transpose, then peel off the last nonzero superdiagonal row by row.

items.title: Complex spectral theorem: a normal endomorphism of a finite-dimensional complex inner product space has an orthonormal eigenbasis, and conversely
items.strategy: Use the fundamental theorem of algebra to split the characteristic polynomial, apply Schur triangularisation, and then force the triangular matrix to be diagonal by normality.

items.title: A real normal endomorphism is orthogonally block-diagonalisable with 1x1 real blocks and 2x2 rotation-scaling blocks
items.strategy: Represent the operator by a real matrix in an orthonormal basis, apply the complex spectral theorem to that matrix over C, and pair nonreal conjugate eigenvectors by taking real and imaginary parts.

items.title: Real spectral theorem: a self-adjoint endomorphism of a finite-dimensional real inner product space has an orthonormal eigenbasis
items.strategy: Use the real normal classification and observe that self-adjointness forces every 2x2 block to collapse to a real scalar block.

items.title: A normal endomorphism is a sum of its eigenvalues times pairwise orthogonal projections, and each spectral projection is a polynomial in the endomorphism
items.strategy: Group an orthonormal eigenbasis by eigenvalue, write the associated orthogonal projections, and recover each projection from Lagrange interpolation on the distinct eigenvalues.

items.title: The spectral functional calculus f(T) for a normal endomorphism
For normal endomorphisms, the spectral functional calculus respects sums, products, adjoints, and composition of scalar functions
items.strategy: Compute directly on the spectral-resolution formula, using orthogonality and idempotence of the spectral projections.

items.title: Semisimple endomorphisms as endomorphisms diagonalisable over an algebraic closure, and nilpotent endomorphisms
Over a perfect field, every endomorphism has a unique commuting semisimple-plus-nilpotent decomposition, polynomial in the endomorphism
items.strategy: Choose a splitting field inside an algebraic closure, separate the semisimple and nilpotent parts on each primary component by the split Jordan calculation, and descend the resulting operators by using perfect-field separability, uniqueness, and base automorphisms of the algebraic closure to show the polynomial expressions are fixed over the ground field.

items.title: Non-negative and positive operators
Over the reals, non-negative and positive operators correspond exactly to positive semidefinite and positive definite symmetric forms
items.strategy: Apply the bilinear-form correspondence to the form (u,v) -> <Tu,v> and translate the pointwise inequalities through the self-adjoint condition.

items.title: A non-negative operator is equivalently self-adjoint with nonnegative eigenvalues, a positive semidefinite matrix in an orthonormal basis, or an operator of the form S^*S
items.strategy: Use the spectral theorem to diagonalise, read off the quadratic form from the diagonal entries, and reverse the construction by taking square roots of the eigenvalues.

items.title: A non-negative operator has a unique non-negative square root
items.strategy: Diagonalise the operator, take the unique nonnegative square root of each diagonal entry, and compare spectra to force uniqueness inside the non-negative class.

items.title: The non-negative square root of a non-negative operator is a polynomial in the operator
items.strategy: Interpolate the scalar square-root function on the finite spectrum and compare the resulting functional-calculus value with the unique non-negative square root.

items.title: The singular values of an endomorphism as the eigenvalues of the positive square root of T^*T
Singular values are well defined because the positive square root of T^*T is unique
items.strategy: Unpack the definition and appeal only to the uniqueness clause in the square-root theorem.

items.title: Every endomorphism of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space admits a singular value decomposition
items.strategy: Diagonalise T^*T in an orthonormal basis, scale the images of the nonzero right-singular vectors to obtain orthonormal left-singular vectors, and complete both lists to orthonormal bases.

items.title: The rank of an endomorphism is the number of its nonzero singular values
items.strategy: Read the image directly from the singular value decomposition: the nonzero singular directions are exactly the basis vectors that survive.

items.title: An endomorphism and its adjoint have the same singular values
items.strategy: Take the adjoint of the singular value decomposition and observe that the same diagonal entries reappear with the left and right singular vectors swapped.

items.title: Every endomorphism has a polar decomposition T = SU with U non-negative and S an isometry on the orthogonal complement of ker T, and S is unique exactly when T is invertible
items.strategy: Build the isometric factor on the singular-vector bases, identify the positive factor with the square root of T^*T, and compare kernels to isolate the uniqueness boundary.

items.title: The operator norm ||T|| = max_{||v||=1} ||Tv|| in finite dimension
The operator norm equals the largest singular value and is attained at a first right-singular vector
items.strategy: Insert a unit vector into the singular value decomposition, bound the weighted sum by the top singular value, and attain equality on the first right-singular vector.

items.title: The operator norm is submultiplicative and satisfies ||T^*T|| = ||T||^2
items.strategy: Use the max definition for submultiplicativity and the singular-value description for the T^*T identity.

items.title: The best rank-at-most-k approximation in operator norm is the rank-k truncation of a singular value decomposition
items.strategy: Use the singular basis to exhibit the truncation and obtain the lower bound from a dimension-count intersection with the span of the first k+1 right-singular vectors.

items.title: The Rayleigh quotient of a nonzero vector for a self-adjoint endomorphism
Courant-Fischer min-max principle for self-adjoint endomorphisms on finite-dimensional real inner product spaces
items.strategy: Diagonalise orthogonally, compare subspace dimensions against the ordered eigenbasis, and evaluate the Rayleigh quotient on the extremal coordinate subspaces.

items.title: The smallest and largest eigenvalues of a self-adjoint endomorphism are the minimum and maximum Rayleigh quotients
items.strategy: Take the first and last cases of Courant-Fischer.

items.title: The eigenvalues of the orthogonal compression of a self-adjoint endomorphism to a hyperplane interlace those of the original endomorphism
items.strategy: Apply Courant-Fischer on the hyperplane and on the ambient space, comparing the admissible subspaces by one-dimensional codimension counts.

items.title: Weyl inequalities bound the eigenvalues of a sum of self-adjoint endomorphisms
items.strategy: Choose the two subspaces supplied by Courant-Fischer, intersect them, and evaluate the sum on a nonzero vector from that intersection.

items.title: The Gershgorin disks of an endomorphism with respect to an ordered basis
Every eigenvalue lies in some Gershgorin disk
items.strategy: Write an eigenvector in the chosen basis, divide by a coordinate of maximal modulus, and estimate the corresponding row equation.

items.title: An explicit real symmetric 3x3 matrix is orthogonally diagonalised

items.title: An explicit Hermitian 2x2 matrix is unitarily diagonalised

items.title: The real quarter-turn is normal and appears as a single 2x2 block in the real normal classification
items.strategy: Check A^T A = A A^T, compute the complex eigenvalues +/- i, and exhibit the real 2x2 block from the classification theorem.

items.title: A complex symmetric matrix can be nonzero, square to zero, and fail to be normal
