items.title: The non-negative square root of an explicit matrix is exhibited as a polynomial in the matrix
items.strategy: Diagonalise the matrix, take square roots of the diagonal entries, and then interpolate the same operator as a polynomial in the original matrix.

items.title: A worked polar decomposition of an invertible matrix
items.strategy: Compute T^*T, extract its positive square root, and then solve for the isometric factor from T = S sqrt(T^*T).

items.title: A singular matrix has a polar decomposition with visibly nonunique isometric factors
items.strategy: Choose a rank-one matrix, compute the positive factor, and display two distinct isometries that agree on the orthogonal complement of the kernel.

items.title: The singular value decomposition of an explicit 2x3 matrix
items.strategy: Diagonalise T^*T, normalize the image vectors, and write the resulting U Sigma V^* factorisation in full.

items.title: The rank-one truncation of an SVD realises the Eckart-Young minimiser
items.strategy: Truncate the previous SVD after the first singular value, compute the operator-norm error, and match it with the next singular value.

items.title: Courant-Fischer is checked on an explicit 3x3 symmetric matrix
items.strategy: Compute the ordered eigenvalues and then evaluate the min-max expression on the coordinate eigenspaces and their orthogonal complements.

items.title: The eigenvalues of a principal 2x2 submatrix interlace those of a 3x3 symmetric matrix
items.strategy: Compress to a coordinate hyperplane, compute both spectra, and compare the ordered lists entry by entry.

items.title: Gershgorin disks for an explicit 3x3 matrix contain the true spectrum
items.strategy: Compute the row sums, draw the three disks, and check the actual eigenvalues against their union.

items.title: FALSE: Every normal operator is diagonalisable over its base field
items.strategy: Refute the field-free claim with the real quarter-turn, which is normal over R but has no real eigenvalue.

items.title: FALSE: Every complex symmetric matrix is unitarily diagonalisable
items.strategy: Use the worked complex symmetric nilpotent matrix, which is symmetric but not normal and hence cannot satisfy the complex spectral theorem.

items.title: FALSE: If <Tv,v> is nonnegative for every v, then T is automatically self-adjoint
items.strategy: Refute the claim with the real quarter-turn, for which every value <Tv,v> is zero although the operator is not self-adjoint.

items.title: FALSE: A non-negative operator has a unique square root among all operators
items.strategy: Use a diagonal matrix with positive entries and compare its non-negative square root with a distinct diagonal sign choice.

items.title: FALSE: The isometry in the polar decomposition is unique even for singular operators
items.strategy: Appeal to the singular polar-decomposition example, where two distinct isometries agree on the range of the positive factor.

items.title: FALSE: The singular values of an operator are the absolute values of its eigenvalues
items.strategy: Use the nilpotent matrix [[0,2],[0,0]], whose eigenvalues are both zero while its singular values are 2 and 0.

items.title: FALSE: The operator norm is always the largest modulus of an eigenvalue
items.strategy: Use the same nilpotent matrix [[0,2],[0,0]], whose operator norm is 2 although every eigenvalue has modulus 0.

pages.title: The Group Algebra and Representations of Finite Groups

items.title: The group ring $R[G]$ of finitely supported formal $R$-linear combinations of group elements
The group ring $R[G]$ is a unital $R$-algebra with basis $G$, and each $g\in G$ is a unit of $R[G]$
items.strategy: View $R[G]$ as the free $R$-module on the set $G$. Use the universal property of the free module to extend the multiplication table of $G$ uniquely to an $R$-bilinear product on basis sums. Associativity and the identity element are checked on the basis elements and then transported by bilinearity. The basis element indexed by $g^{-1}$ is the inverse of the basis element indexed by $g$.

items.title: The augmentation map $\varepsilon:R[G]\to R$ and the augmentation ideal $I_G=\ker\varepsilon$
If $G$ is finite then $\dim_k k[G]=|G|$
items.strategy: By definition, $k[G]$ is the free $k$-vector space on the set $G$. When $G$ is finite, the basis vectors indexed by the elements of $G$ form a finite basis, so the dimension is exactly the cardinality of that basis.

items.title: For a field $k$, the group algebra $k[G]$ is commutative if and only if $G$ is abelian
items.strategy: If $G$ is abelian then basis elements commute, so every pair of finite $k$-linear combinations commutes by bilinearity. Conversely, if $k[G]$ is commutative, then the basis elements attached to $g$ and $h$ commute inside $k[G]$, so their products are the basis elements attached to $gh$ and $hg$, forcing $gh=hg$ in $G$.

items.title: An $R$-linear action of $G$ on a left $R$-module, and a $G$-module over $R$
A finite-dimensional representation $\rho:G\to \operatorname{GL}(V)$ over a field, and its degree
Subrepresentations, direct sums of representations, and irreducibility
Intertwiners, the spaces $\operatorname{Hom}_G(V,W)$ and $\operatorname{End}_G(V)$, equivalent representations, and faithful representations
For a commutative ring $R$, $R$-linear $G$-actions are exactly the compatible left $R[G]$-module structures
items.strategy: From an $R$-linear action of $G$ on a left $R$-module $M$, extend the action of each basis element $g\in G$ linearly to an action of every element of $R[G]$; the resulting action satisfies $(r[e])m=rm$. Conversely, start from a left $R[G]$-module structure whose restriction along the central map $R\to R[G]$ recovers the given $R$-module structure, and then restrict to the basis elements indexed by $G$. The same formulas show that an $R$-linear map is $G$-equivariant exactly when it is an $R[G]$-module homomorphism.

items.title: Under the dictionary, subrepresentations are exactly submodules and irreducible representations are exactly simple modules
items.strategy: A linear subspace is stable under the group action exactly when it is stable under the basis elements of $k[G]$, hence under every element of $k[G]$ by linearity. Therefore the subobjects on both sides are the same, and the minimality condition defining irreducibility becomes the usual simple-module condition.

items.title: $\operatorname{Hom}_G(V,W)$ is a $k$-vector space and $\operatorname{End}_G(V)$ is a $k$-algebra
items.strategy: Inside the vector space of all linear maps, the intertwiners are exactly the maps fixed by the relation $f\rho(g)=\sigma(g)f$ for every $g\in G$, so they are closed under addition and scalar multiplication. When $V=W$, composition of two intertwiners is again an intertwiner, and the identity map is one too, so the endomorphism space inherits a $k$-algebra structure.

items.title: The trivial representation, the regular representation, and permutation representations from finite $G$-sets
The sign representation of $S_n$ and the restriction $\operatorname{Res}^G_H(V)$ of a representation to a subgroup
The regular representation is faithful
items.strategy: Let $g\ne e$ in $G$. In the regular representation, the basis vector indexed by the identity is sent to the basis vector indexed by $g$, so the action of $g$ is not the identity linear map. Hence only the identity group element acts trivially on every vector.

items.title: Every irreducible representation of a finite group is a quotient of the regular representation
items.strategy: Translate an irreducible representation into a simple $k[G]$-module. Choose any nonzero vector $v$; simplicity makes the submodule generated by $v$ equal to the whole module. The $k[G]$-linear map $k[G]\to V$ sending $a$ to $a\cdot v$ is therefore surjective, so $V$ is a quotient of the left regular module.

items.title: Every irreducible representation of a finite group has degree at most $|G|$
items.strategy: An irreducible representation is a quotient of the regular representation, so its underlying vector space has a spanning set given by the images of the basis vectors of $k[G]$. The published bound comparing a finite spanning set with an independent set then gives the degree estimate together with $\dim_k k[G]=|G|$.

items.title: A splitting field for a finite group: every irreducible representation has scalar endomorphism ring
Brauer's cyclotomic criterion for splitting fields is recorded here only as an external theorem
Schur's lemma for irreducible representations: a nonzero intertwiner is an isomorphism, and $\operatorname{End}_G(V)$ is a division ring
items.strategy: Pass to the corresponding $k[G]$-modules. The module version of Schur's lemma applies to simple modules, and the dictionary theorem translates the conclusion back into representation language.

items.title: Over a splitting field, every $G$-endomorphism of an irreducible representation is scalar
items.strategy: If $k$ is a splitting field for $G$, the definition says that every irreducible representation has endomorphism ring exactly $k$. Combined with Schur's lemma, this restates the division-ring conclusion as the scalar-operator conclusion.

items.title: Over an algebraically closed field, every endomorphism of an irreducible representation is scalar
items.strategy: Triangularize the endomorphism $T\in\operatorname{End}_G(V)$ over the algebraically closed field. One diagonal entry $\lambda$ then makes $T-\lambda I$ singular. Because $T-\lambda I$ is still a $G$-endomorphism, Schur's lemma forces it to be zero, so $T=\lambda I$.

items.title: Every irreducible representation of a finite abelian group over a splitting field is one-dimensional
items.strategy: If $G$ is abelian, each operator $\rho(g)$ commutes with every $\rho(h)$, so each $\rho(g)$ lies in $\operatorname{End}_G(V)$. Over a splitting field that endomorphism ring is just $k$, so every group element acts by a scalar. Any nonzero vector is therefore stable under the whole action and spans a nonzero subrepresentation; irreducibility forces that line to be all of $V$.

items.title: Equivalence classes of degree-one representations are exactly homomorphisms $G\to k^{\times}$; equivalently they factor through $G/G'$, and they form an abelian group
items.strategy: Choosing a basis in a one-dimensional representation identifies it with a normalized representation on $k$ and produces a homomorphism into $k^{\times}$. Two degree-one representations yield the same homomorphism exactly when they are equivalent, so equivalence classes of such representations are classified by characters. Because $k^{\times}$ is abelian, these homomorphisms factor through $G/G'$ and inherit an abelian-group structure under pointwise multiplication.

pages.title: The Group Algebra and Representations of Finite Groups — Examples

items.title: Over $\mathbb{C}$, a cyclic group of order $n$ has exactly $n$ irreducible representations up to equivalence, represented by the characters $g\mapsto \lambda$ with $\lambda^n=1$
items.strategy: Let $G=\langle g\rangle$ with $|G|=n$. Since $G$ is abelian and $\mathbb C$ satisfies the scalar-endomorphism condition, every irreducible representation is one-dimensional and equivalent to a normalized character on $\mathbb C$. Such a character is determined by the scalar assigned to $g$, and the relation $g^n=e$ forces that scalar to be an $n$-th root of unity. The $n$ distinct roots of $x^n-1$ in $\mathbb C$ therefore give the complete list of irreducible classes.

items.title: The regular representation of $C_2$ over a field of characteristic not $2$ is the direct sum of the trivial and sign representations
items.strategy: Write the regular module on the basis $\{e,s\}$ with $s^2=e$. The vectors $e+s$ and $e-s$ are eigenvectors for the action of $s$, with eigenvalues $1$ and $-1$ respectively. In characteristic not $2$ they form a basis, so the representation splits into the trivial line and the sign line.

items.title: The standard $2$-dimensional representation of $S_3$ inside the permutation representation on $\mathbb C^3$ is irreducible
items.strategy: Start from the permutation representation of $S_3$ on the basis vectors of $\mathbb C^3$. The line spanned by $(1,1,1)$ is fixed, and the coordinate-sum-zero plane is its invariant complement. To prove irreducibility of that plane, test invariance under a transposition and a $3$-cycle: any nonzero invariant line would have to be an eigenline for both matrices, and the only common possibilities are the zero space and the whole plane.

items.title: The permutation representation on the left cosets $G/H$
items.strategy: Let $G$ act by left multiplication on the finite set of left cosets $G/H$. The associated permutation representation has basis the cosets themselves, and the action matrix of any $g\in G$ just permutes that basis according to the induced action on cosets.

items.title: Any nontrivial finite group algebra has zero divisors coming from a nonidentity cyclic subgroup
items.strategy: Take a nonidentity element $g$ of finite order $n$. In $k[G]$, the two nonzero elements $e-g$ and $e+g+\cdots+g^{n-1}$ multiply to $e-g^n=0$ after the intermediate terms telescope. This exhibits concrete zero divisors inside every nontrivial finite group algebra.

items.title: The quaternion group $Q_8$ acts on $\mathbb H$ by left multiplication
items.strategy: Use the inclusion $Q_8\subseteq \mathbb H^{\times}$. Left multiplication by each quaternion in $Q_8$ is an invertible real-linear map of the $4$-dimensional real vector space $\mathbb H$, so these operators give a representation of $Q_8$ over $\mathbb R$.

items.title: The real $2$-dimensional irreducible representation of $C_3$ has endomorphism ring $\mathbb C$
items.strategy: Let a generator of $C_3$ act on $\mathbb R^2$ by the companion matrix of $x^2+x+1$. Because that polynomial has no real root, the action preserves no real line, so the representation is irreducible. A real linear map commutes with the action exactly when it is a polynomial in that companion matrix, giving an endomorphism ring isomorphic to $\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+x+1)\cong\mathbb C$.

items.title: FALSE: every representation is faithful
items.strategy: Use the trivial representation. Every group element acts as the identity linear map there, so the kernel is the whole group whenever the group is nontrivial.

items.title: FALSE: if $|G|>1$, then $k[G]$ is a field
items.strategy: Choose a nonidentity element of finite order and use the explicit zero-divisor product from the cyclic subgroup calculation. A field has no zero divisors, so that identity refutes the claim immediately.

items.title: FALSE: every degree-one representation is trivial
items.strategy: On a cyclic group of order $n$, send a generator to a nontrivial complex $n$-th root of unity. This is a degree-one representation, but it is not the trivial homomorphism.

items.title: FALSE: over every field, the endomorphism ring of an irreducible representation is just the base field
items.strategy: Use the real irreducible representation of $C_3$ whose generator acts with minimal polynomial $x^2+x+1$. Its commuting endomorphisms form a copy of $\mathbb C$, which properly contains $\mathbb R$, so the scalar conclusion fails over a nonsplitting field.

pages.title: Maschke's Theorem, Complete Reducibility and the Structure of $k[G]$

items.title: A completely reducible representation as a finite direct sum of irreducible subrepresentations
items.strategy: Define a finite-dimensional representation to be completely reducible when it is an internal direct sum of irreducible subrepresentations, allowing the zero representation as the empty direct sum. Record that under the group-ring dictionary this is the representation-side form of a semisimple $k[G]$-module.

items.title: Maschke's theorem for finite groups over fields whose characteristic does not divide $|G|$
items.strategy: Given a subrepresentation $W\le V$, choose any $k$-linear projection $P:V\to W$. Average it to $$P_G=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\rho(g)P\rho(g)^{-1};$$ the scalar $|G|^{-1}$ is exactly where the characteristic hypothesis is spent. Then $P_G$ is $G$-equivariant, fixes $W$, and has kernel a $G$-invariant complement.

items.title: If $\operatorname{char} k \nmid |G|$, every finite-dimensional representation of $G$ is completely reducible
items.strategy: Induct on $\dim_kV$. A nonzero finite-dimensional representation has a minimal nonzero subrepresentation, hence an irreducible one; Maschke splits it off, and the complementary summand has smaller dimension. The zero representation is the empty direct sum.

items.title: If $\operatorname{char} k \nmid |G|$, then $k[G]$ is a semisimple ring
items.strategy: Apply the previous corollary to the regular representation of $G$ on $k[G]$. Under the published dictionary, a completely reducible regular representation is exactly a semisimple left $k[G]$-module, which is the definition of a semisimple ring.

items.title: If $\operatorname{char} k \mid |G|$, the augmentation ideal of $k[G]$ has no $k[G]$-module complement in the regular representation
items.strategy: Assume $k[G]=I_G\oplus J$ as left $k[G]$-modules. Because $I_G=\ker\varepsilon$, the restriction $\varepsilon|_J:J\to k$ is injective and nonzero, hence an isomorphism of one-dimensional $k$-spaces. Choose $x\in J$ with $\varepsilon(x)=1$. For every $g\in G$, the element $gx\in J$ has the same augmentation, so $gx=x$. Writing $x=\sum a_h[h]$, left translation forces all coefficients $a_h$ to be equal; then $$1=\varepsilon(x)=|G|a_h=0$$ in characteristic dividing $|G|$, a contradiction.

items.title: If $\operatorname{char} k \mid |G|$, then $k[G]$ is not semisimple
items.strategy: If $k[G]$ were semisimple, then every submodule of its left regular module would have a complement. The previous theorem shows that the augmentation ideal does not, so the regular module is not semisimple and neither is the ring.

items.title: The isotypic component of a completely reducible representation
items.strategy: For a completely reducible representation $V$ and an irreducible representation $S$, define $V_{(S)}$ to be the sum of all irreducible subrepresentations of $V$ that are isomorphic to $S$. Record that only the isomorphism class of $S$ matters.

items.title: The isotypic decomposition of a completely reducible representation is unique
items.strategy: Choose a decomposition of $V$ as a direct sum of irreducibles and group the summands by isomorphism class. If two grouped sums for different classes had nonzero intersection, an irreducible subrepresentation of that intersection would admit nonzero maps to two nonisomorphic irreducibles, contradicting Schur. The grouped blocks therefore sum directly to $V$, and each block is exactly the sum of all irreducible subrepresentations of its class, so it is independent of the chosen irreducible splitting.

items.title: A decomposition into irreducible summands need not be unique even when the isotypic decomposition is
items.strategy: Record the contrast the design requires: the isotypic blocks are canonical, but the individual irreducible summands inside one isotypic block need not be. The companion page's two-dimensional trivial representation of $C_2$ is the minimal explicit witness.

items.title: The center $Z(k[G])$ of the group algebra
items.strategy: Define $$Z(k[G])=\{x\in k[G]:xy=yx\text{ for all }y\in k[G]\}.$$ Record it as the central $k$-subalgebra that will be computed both from conjugacy classes and from the Wedderburn factors.

items.title: The class sum $\widehat C$ of a conjugacy class $C$
items.strategy: For a conjugacy class $C\subseteq G$ in a finite group, define its class sum in $k[G]$ by $$\widehat C:=\sum_{g\in C}[g].$$ Fix this hat notation once so the center argument does not drift into ad hoc symbols later.

items.title: If $k$ is algebraically closed and $\operatorname{char} k \nmid |G|$, then $k[G]\cong\prod_{i=1}^r M_{n_i}(k)$
items.strategy: Maschke makes $k[G]$ a semisimple ring. Apply Wedderburn-Artin to write it as a finite product of matrix rings over division rings, one factor for each simple $k[G]$-module. Over an algebraically closed field, the endomorphism ring of each irreducible representation is just $k$, so every division ring factor collapses to the base field.

items.title: If $k$ is algebraically closed and $\operatorname{char} k \nmid |G|$, there are finitely many irreducible representations, and each occurs in the regular representation with multiplicity equal to its degree
items.strategy: Use the product decomposition $$k[G]\cong\prod_iM_{n_i}(k).$$ For each factor there is exactly one simple left module, namely the column module $k^{n_i}$, and the left regular module of $M_{n_i}(k)$ is a direct sum of $n_i$ copies of it. Translating the simple-module statement back across the group-ring dictionary gives finitely many irreducible representations $V_i$, each appearing in the regular representation with multiplicity $n_i=\dim_kV_i$.

items.title: If $k$ is algebraically closed and $\operatorname{char} k \nmid |G|$, then $\sum_i (\dim_k V_i)^2=|G|$
items.strategy: The regular representation has dimension $|G|$ over $k$. Sum the dimensions of the irreducible summands in the previous theorem, counting each $V_i$ with multiplicity $\dim_kV_i$.

items.title: The center of $M_n(k)$ consists of the scalar matrices
items.strategy: Let $E_{ij}$ be the matrix units. If $X$ commutes with every $E_{ij}$, comparing $E_{ij}X$ with $XE_{ij}$ forces every off-diagonal entry of $X$ to vanish and all diagonal entries to agree. Scalar matrices obviously commute with everything.

items.title: For a finite group, the class sums form a basis of $Z(k[G])$
items.strategy: Each class sum is central because left multiplication by $h$ permutes its summands exactly as right multiplication by $h$ does. Conversely, if $$x=\sum_ga_g[g]$$ is central, then comparing coefficients in $hxh^{-1}=x$ shows that $a_g$ is constant on conjugacy classes. The supports of distinct class sums are disjoint, so they are linearly independent.

items.title: The dimension of $Z(k[G])$ is the number of conjugacy classes of $G$
items.strategy: The preceding theorem gives a basis of the center indexed by the conjugacy classes themselves.

items.title: If $k$ is algebraically closed and $\operatorname{char} k \nmid |G|$, the number of irreducible representations of $G$ equals the number of conjugacy classes
items.strategy: Compute $$\dim_k Z(k[G])$$ in two ways. The class-sum theorem makes it the number of conjugacy classes. The Wedderburn product makes it the sum of the center dimensions of the matrix factors, and the scalar-center lemma shows that each factor contributes exactly one dimension. Hence the number of factors, i.e. the number of irreducible representation classes, equals the number of conjugacy classes.

items.title: Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$, every element of finite order acts diagonalisably in a finite-dimensional representation
items.strategy: Let $T$ have finite order $m$ and let the cyclic group $C_m=\langle g\rangle$ act by $g\mapsto T$. Because $m$ is invertible in characteristic $0$, Maschke makes this representation completely reducible. The field is a splitting field for $C_m$, and finite abelian groups have only one-dimensional irreducibles over a splitting field, so the representation has a basis of eigenvectors and $T$ is diagonalizable.

pages.title: Maschke's Theorem, Complete Reducibility and the Structure of $k[G]$ — Examples

items.title: $\mathbb C[\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z]\cong\mathbb C\times\mathbb C\times\mathbb C$
items.strategy: Because $\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$ is abelian, its three elements are three conjugacy classes. The A-page count theorem therefore gives exactly three irreducible complex representations, and the sum-of-squares formula forces all three degrees to be $1$. The Wedderburn decomposition therefore has three $1\times1$ factors and no larger matrix block.

items.title: $\mathbb C[S_3]\cong\mathbb C\times\mathbb C\times M_2(\mathbb C)$
items.strategy: The three conjugacy classes of $S_3$ are $\{e\}$, the three transpositions, and the two $3$-cycles, so the A-page count theorem gives three irreducible complex representations. Their squared degrees sum to $6$, and the only way to write $6$ as a sum of three positive squares is $1+1+4$. The matrix-factor decomposition follows immediately.

items.title: $\mathbb C[Q_8]$ and $\mathbb C[\operatorname{Dih}(C_4)]$ both decompose as $\mathbb C^4\times M_2(\mathbb C)$
items.strategy: For $Q_8$, the five conjugacy classes are $$\{1\},\{-1\},\{\pm i\},\{\pm j\},\{\pm k\};$$ for $D=\operatorname{Dih}(C_4)$, using the standard normal forms and the relation $srs^{-1}=r^{-1}$, they are $$\{1\},\{r^2\},\{r,r^3\},\{s,r^2s\},\{rs,r^3s\}.$$ So both groups have five conjugacy classes. With five irreducibles and squared degrees summing to $8$, the only possible degree multiset is $1,1,1,1,2$ for both groups. The A-page decomposition theorem then yields the identical Wedderburn type.

items.title: The regular representation of $\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z$ over $\mathbb C$ splits into its four characters
items.strategy: Because $\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z$ is abelian, it has four conjugacy classes, so the A-page count theorem gives four irreducible complex representations. Their squared degrees sum to $4$, so all four degrees are $1$. The regular representation contains each irreducible with multiplicity equal to its degree, so each character occurs exactly once.

items.title: The two-dimensional trivial representation of $C_2$ has many irreducible splittings but one isotypic component
items.strategy: In the trivial action every line is invariant and irreducible, so any pair of complementary lines gives a decomposition into irreducible subrepresentations. But every irreducible summand is the trivial representation, so the unique isotypic component is the whole space.

items.title: False statement: Maschke's theorem holds over every field
items.strategy: Take a prime $p$, let $G=\langle g\rangle$ be cyclic of order $p$, let $k=\mathbb F_p$, and let $$\rho(g)=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$ The line spanned by the second basis vector is invariant, but every complementary line is moved by $g$, so no invariant complement exists.

items.title: False statement: every finite-dimensional algebra over a field is semisimple
items.strategy: For a prime $p$, the group algebra $\mathbb F_p[C_p]$ has dimension $p$ over $\mathbb F_p$, but the A-page converse shows it is not semisimple because the characteristic divides the group order.

items.title: False statement: a completely reducible representation has a unique decomposition into irreducible subrepresentations
items.strategy: Reuse the two-dimensional trivial representation of $C_2$: distinct pairs of complementary lines produce different decompositions into irreducible subrepresentations, even though the isotypic component is fixed.

items.title: False statement: the sum of the irreducible degrees equals $|G|$
items.strategy: For $S_3$, the irreducible degrees are $1,1,2$, so their sum is $4$ while $|S_3|=6$. The correct identity is the sum-of-squares formula.

items.title: False statement: a group with $r$ conjugacy classes has an irreducible representation of degree $r$
items.strategy: Both $Q_8$ and $\operatorname{Dih}(C_4)$ have five conjugacy classes, but their irreducible degrees are $1,1,1,1,2$. So neither group has an irreducible representation of degree $5$.

pages.title: Characters and the Orthogonality Relations

items.title: Standing hypotheses for ordinary character theory: $G$ finite, $k=\mathbb C$, and every representation finite-dimensional
The character $\chi_V(g)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_V(g))$ of a finite-dimensional complex representation
Class functions and the complex vector space $\mathrm{cf}(G)$
The standard inner product on $\mathrm{cf}(G)$
An irreducible complex character
The character table of a finite group
The tensor product of two complex representations
The dual or contragredient complex representation
The kernel of a complex character
For a complex character, $\chi(1)=\dim V$, $\chi$ is a class function, and $|\chi(g)|\le\chi(1)$ with equality exactly at scalars
items.strategy: Evaluate at the identity, use finite-order diagonalizability to write $\rho(g)$ with root-of-unity eigenvalues, apply the triangle inequality to their sum, and use trace invariance under similarity for conjugacy invariance.

items.title: The kernel of a complex character agrees with the kernel of any representation affording it
items.strategy: One implication is immediate. For the converse, the equality $\chi(g)=\chi(1)$ and the scalar-equality clause of the basic character proposition force $\rho(g)$ to be the identity.

items.title: Characters add on direct sums, multiply on tensor products, and conjugate on duals
items.strategy: Use block-diagonal trace additivity for direct sums, the trace-of-a-tensor-product identity for tensor products, and the inverse-transpose description of the dual action together with the basic character proposition for duals.

items.title: The character of a permutation representation counts fixed points
items.strategy: In the basis indexed by the underlying $G$-set, each group element acts by a permutation matrix, and the trace of that matrix is the number of diagonal ones, hence the number of fixed basis vectors.

items.title: The fixed subspace $V^G$ of a representation
The averaging operator projects onto the fixed subspace
items.strategy: Average the action operators over the finite group, check that left multiplication permutes the summands, and verify directly that the average fixes exactly the $G$-fixed vectors.

items.title: For finite-dimensional complex $V$, the intertwiners $V\to W$ are exactly the fixed points of $V^*\otimes W$
items.strategy: Use the published isomorphism $V^*\otimes W\cong\operatorname{Hom}(V,W)$ and compare the transported diagonal action with the standard conjugation action on linear maps, where fixed points are exactly the intertwiners.

items.title: The class-function inner product $\langle\chi_V,\chi_W\rangle$ equals $\dim\operatorname{Hom}_G(V,W)$
items.strategy: Identify $\operatorname{Hom}_G(V,W)$ with the fixed subspace of $V^*\otimes W$, apply the averaging projector, and compute its trace using the character formulas for duals and tensor products.

items.title: The first orthogonality relation for irreducible complex characters
items.strategy: Apply the intertwiner-dimension formula to irreducible representations and finish with Schur's lemma.

items.title: The irreducible complex characters form an orthonormal basis of $\mathrm{cf}(G)$
items.strategy: Row orthogonality gives an orthonormal family. The published RT-2 theorem gives the number of irreducibles, while class functions are determined by conjugacy classes, so the family has the full dimension of $\mathrm{cf}(G)$.

items.title: The multiplicity of an irreducible summand is a character inner product
items.strategy: Completely reduce the representation, expand its character as a sum of irreducible characters, and take inner products with the chosen irreducible character.

items.title: Finite-dimensional complex representations of a finite group are determined up to isomorphism by their characters
items.strategy: Completely reduce both representations and compare the multiplicity of every irreducible summand using the character-inner-product formula.

items.title: A complex character is irreducible if and only if its self-inner-product is $1$
items.strategy: Write the representation as a direct sum of irreducibles and sum the squares of the multiplicities furnished by the previous corollary.

items.title: The regular character is $|G|$ at $1$ and $0$ away from $1$
items.strategy: In the basis of group elements, the regular action is the permutation of $G$ by left translation, so the trace counts fixed points of that translation.

items.title: The regular character gives a second proof of the sum-of-squares formula
items.strategy: Take inner products of the regular character with each irreducible character to compute the multiplicities in the regular representation, then evaluate the resulting decomposition at the identity.

items.title: The second orthogonality relation for irreducible complex characters
items.strategy: Normalize the character-table columns by centralizer size so that the irreducible-character basis becomes a unitary matrix; column orthogonality is then the orthonormality of those normalized columns.

items.title: For $g\in G$, the sum of $|\chi_i(g)|^2$ over the irreducible complex characters is $|C_G(g)|$
items.strategy: Apply the second orthogonality relation with the same group element in both column slots.

items.title: The character table is square and invertible
items.strategy: The previous theorem gives mutually orthogonal normalized columns, so there are as many columns as rows and the character table matrix has inverse after the centralizer rescaling.

items.title: A representation with kernel containing a normal subgroup factors through the quotient, and irreducibility is unchanged by inflation
items.strategy: Define $\bar\rho(gN)=\rho(g)$, check well-definedness from $N\subseteq\ker\rho$, and note that the $\rho$-stable subspaces are exactly the $\bar\rho$-stable subspaces because the quotient map is surjective.

items.title: The normal subgroups of a finite group are exactly the intersections of kernels of irreducible complex characters
items.strategy: For a normal subgroup $N$, lift the irreducible representations of $G/N$ to $G$. Their common kernel is exactly $N$ because the regular representation of $G/N$ is faithful and completely reducible. The converse direction is immediate because character kernels are representation kernels.

items.title: A finite group is abelian if and only if all its irreducible complex characters have degree $1$
items.strategy: For abelian groups, use that $\mathbb C$ is a splitting field and every irreducible over a splitting field is one-dimensional. Conversely, combine the regular-character sum-of-squares formula with the published equality between the number of irreducibles and the number of conjugacy classes.

pages.title: Characters and the Orthogonality Relations — Examples

items.title: The irreducible complex characters of a finite cyclic group are the $n$ powers of a primitive $n$th root
items.strategy: Identify irreducible characters of a cyclic group with homomorphisms to $\mathbb C^\times$, send a generator to an $n$th root of unity, and use the finite-abelian splitting-field theorem to see these are all of them.

items.title: The character table of a finite cyclic group over $\mathbb C$
items.strategy: Use the local description of the $n$ degree-one characters and Vieta's formula for $t^n-1$ to obtain the vanishing root sum, then write the table and check both orthogonality relations.

items.title: The standard representation of $S_n$ has character equal to the number of fixed points minus $1$
items.strategy: Subtract the trivial character from the permutation character of the action on $\{1,\ldots,n\}$.

items.title: $S_3$ has three irreducible complex characters of degrees $1$, $1$, and $2$
items.strategy: Use the three cycle-type classes of $S_3$, the trivial and sign characters, the standard character fixed-points-minus-one, and the sum-of-squares formula to see no other irreducible degrees occur.

items.title: The character table of $S_3$
items.strategy: Use the local degree data and the three cycle-type classes to write the table, then verify both orthogonality relations directly.

items.title: The square of the two-dimensional $S_3$ character decomposes as $1+\operatorname{sgn}+\chi_2$
items.strategy: Square the two-dimensional row by the tensor-product character formula and recover the irreducible multiplicities by inner products with the $S_3$ table.

items.title: $A_4$ has a normal Klein four subgroup and four conjugacy classes
items.strategy: Write the Klein four subgroup of double transpositions, use the quotient of order three, and apply the alternating-group class-splitting criterion to separate the two classes of $3$-cycles.

items.title: The character table of $A_4$
items.strategy: Use the normal Klein four subgroup to obtain the three lifted degree-one characters from the quotient of order three, then recover the remaining degree-three row from orthogonality and the sum-of-squares formula.

items.title: $S_4$ has five conjugacy classes of sizes $1$, $6$, $3$, $8$, and $6$
items.strategy: Use the cycle-type classification in $S_4$ and the symmetric-group class equation to read off the five conjugacy classes and their sizes.

items.title: The character table of $S_4$ and the normal subgroups it reveals
items.strategy: Use the conjugacy-class data, the permutation character on four letters, its sign twist, and orthogonality to complete the table; then intersect character kernels to recover the normal subgroups.

items.title: The character table of $Q_8$
items.strategy: Use the unique involution and the abelianization $Q_8/Z(Q_8)\cong C_2\times C_2$ to obtain the four degree-one rows, then determine the remaining degree-two row from orthogonality and the sum-of-squares formula.

items.title: The character table of $\operatorname{Dih}(C_4)$
items.strategy: Use the dihedral presentation and abelianization to obtain the four degree-one rows, then determine the remaining degree-two row from orthogonality and the sum-of-squares formula.

items.title: FALSE: nonisomorphic finite groups always have different character tables
items.strategy: Refute the claim by placing the $Q_8$ and $\operatorname{Dih}(C_4)$ tables side by side: the tables agree even though the groups are distinguished by their involution structure.

items.title: FALSE: a complex character of a finite group is always a group homomorphism
items.strategy: Use the two-dimensional irreducible character of $S_3$: its value $0$ on a transposition cannot lie in a multiplicative image of a homomorphism to $\mathbb C^\times$.

items.title: FALSE: every value of an irreducible complex character is real
items.strategy: The nontrivial one-dimensional rows of the $A_4$ table take the primitive cube roots of unity on the 3-cycles.

items.title: FALSE: distinct irreducible complex characters of a finite group have distinct degrees
items.strategy: The $Q_8$ table already contains four distinct irreducible characters of degree $1$.

items.title: FALSE: every complex class function with self-inner-product $1$ is a character
items.strategy: If $\chi$ is a character, then $-\chi$ has the same self-inner-product but is not a character because its value at the identity is negative.

items.title: Nondecreasing, increasing (strictly increasing), nonincreasing, decreasing, monotone and strictly monotone real functions on a subset of $\mathbb{R}$, with the dictionary to monotone sequences

One-sided limits of a monotone function always exist: for $f$ nondecreasing on an interval $I$ and $c \in I$, $\lim_{x \to c^{-}} f(x) = \sup\{f(x) : x \in I,\ x < c\}$ whenever $I$ has points below $c$, $\lim_{x \to c^{+}} f(x) = \inf\{f(x) : x \in I,\ x > c\}$ whenever it has points above $c$, and these satisfy $\lim_{x \to c^{-}} f(x) \le f(c) \le \lim_{x \to c^{+}} f(x)$

items.title: Discontinuity of $f$ at a point of its domain, and its classification: removable discontinuity, jump discontinuity and essential discontinuity, equivalently Rudin's discontinuities of the first and of the second kind

A monotone function on an interval has no discontinuity of the second kind: at every point both relevant one-sided limits exist, and an interior point $c$ is a discontinuity exactly when $\lim_{x \to c^{-}} f(x) < \lim_{x \to c^{+}} f(x)$

items.title: The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set

Carath\'eodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$

items.title: Higher derivatives and the classes $C^k$ and $C^\infty$
items.strategy: Define $f^{(0)}=f$ and recursively $f^{(j+1)}=(f^{(j)})'$ wherever the latter derivative exists. Define $k$-times differentiability, $C^k$ on an interval (derivatives through order $k$ exist and are continuous, with the published one-sided endpoint convention), and $C^\infty$. State explicitly that $\mathbb N$ contains $0$, so $C^0$ means continuity, and prove the nesting $C^{k+1}\subseteq C^k$. Do not silently identify existence of $f^{(k)}$ with continuity of that derivative.

items.title: The general Leibniz rule for the $n$-th derivative of a product
items.strategy: For $n\in\mathbb N$ and sufficiently differentiable $f,g$, prove $(fg)^{(n)}=\sum_{j\le n}\iota\!\binom{n}{j}f^{(j)}g^{(n-j)}$. Induct on $n$, differentiate the finite sum termwise, shift one index, and combine adjacent coefficients with Pascal's rule. Keep binomial coefficients and factorials in $\mathbb N$ and insert the canonical embedding $\iota$ before multiplying real values.

items.title: Higher-order Rolle theorem
items.strategy: Given an explicitly ordered list $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ of zeros in an interval and an $n$-times differentiable function on the intervening interval, prove that its $n$-th derivative vanishes somewhere between the extreme zeros. Apply Rolle between consecutive listed zeros and iterate; state the exact endpoint continuity and interior differentiability assumptions inherited at each stage. Use induction, with $n=0$ treated separately.

items.title: Darboux's theorem: every derivative has the intermediate-value property
items.strategy: Let $f$ be differentiable on an interval and let $x<y$. For a value $\lambda$ strictly between $f'(x)$ and $f'(y)$, apply the extreme-value theorem to $h(t)=f(t)-\lambda t$. Difference quotients at the endpoints force a minimum or maximum away from both endpoints, and Fermat gives $h'(c)=0$. Handle equality at an endpoint separately and preserve the published one-sided derivative convention.

items.title: A derivative has neither a removable discontinuity nor a jump discontinuity
items.strategy: Combine Darboux's theorem with the published classification of discontinuities. A finite punctured limit different from the value and unequal finite one-sided limits each leave an omitted interval of values near the point, contradicting the intermediate-value property. Do not claim that every discontinuity of a derivative is a jump; discontinuities of the second kind remain possible.

items.title: An injective Darboux function on an interval is strictly monotone
items.strategy: For an injective function with the intermediate-value property, show that any three points $x<y<z$ force $f(y)$ to lie strictly between $f(x)$ and $f(z)$; otherwise the intermediate-value property on one of the two subintervals repeats a value. Deduce a globally consistent order orientation and hence strict monotonicity. Include the nondegenerate-interval and singleton cases.

items.title: An injective or monotone derivative on an interval is continuous
items.strategy: Darboux makes the derivative's image on every subinterval an interval. In the injective case first use the injective-Darboux lemma to obtain strict monotonicity; in either case apply the published theorem that a monotone function with interval image is continuous. This is the valid partial converse. Do not include the false claim that Darboux plus Baire class one implies continuity.

items.title: Cauchy's mean-value theorem in quotient form when the denominator derivative is nonzero
items.strategy: From the published cross-multiplied Cauchy mean-value theorem obtain $(f(x)-f(a))/(g(x)-g(a))=f'(c)/g'(c)$. Prove both denominators are nonzero: $g'(c)\ne0$ is assumed, while $g(x)=g(a)$ would contradict Rolle. State the one-sided endpoint version used by L'Hôpital and do not divide before these facts are established.

items.title: L'Hôpital's rule for the $0/0$ form at finite or infinite, one-sided endpoints
items.strategy: State a single theorem covering a finite one-sided endpoint and $\pm\infty$: $f,g$ tend to $0$, are differentiable in the punctured approach region, $g'$ never vanishes there, and $f'/g'$ tends to $L\in\overline{\mathbb R}$; then $f/g\to L$. At a finite endpoint extend both functions by $0$ and apply the quotient Cauchy theorem. Reduce $+\infty$ and $-\infty$ to the corresponding one-sided limit at $0$ by $t=1/x$; the chain-rule factors $-1/t^2$ cancel in the derivative quotient. Give separate order estimates for finite and infinite $L$.

items.title: L'Hôpital's rule for the $\infty/\infty$ form at finite or infinite, one-sided endpoints
items.strategy: Assume $|g|\to\infty$, the numerator has a signed infinite limit of matching quotient form, $g'$ is nonzero on the punctured approach region, and $f'/g'\to L\in\overline{\mathbb R}$. Apply the quotient Cauchy theorem between a fixed base point and the variable point. Divide by $g(x)$ and use $g(a)/g(x)\to0$ and $f(a)/g(x)\to0$. Spell out sign/order estimates for infinite $L$ rather than performing algebra with $\infty$.

items.title: Taylor polynomials and their remainders
items.strategy: For $f$ with derivatives through order $n$ at $a$, define $T_{n,a}f(x)=\sum_{j\le n}f^{(j)}(a)(x-a)^j/\iota(j!)$ and $R_{n,a}f(x)=f(x)-T_{n,a}f(x)$. The factorial in the plan is a natural finite product; explicitly embed it in $\mathbb R$ before division and prove it is positive. Cover $n=0$ and $x=a$.

items.title: Taylor polynomials match the prescribed derivatives at the centre
items.strategy: Differentiate each finite monomial sum and prove for $0\le r\le n$ that $(T_{n,a}f)^{(r)}(a)=f^{(r)}(a)$. Track falling factorials and cancel their embedded real values, including the cases $r=0$, $j=r$, and $j<r$. Conclude that the Taylor remainder and its first $n$ derivatives vanish at $a$.

items.title: Taylor's Schlömilch–Roche remainder formula
items.strategy: For $a\ne x$, define $\Phi(t)=f(x)-\sum_{j=0}^n f^{(j)}(t)(x-t)^j/\iota(j!)$ and $\Psi(t)=(x-t)^p$. Differentiate the finite sum: all adjacent terms telescope, leaving $\Phi'(t)=-f^{(n+1)}(t)(x-t)^n/\iota(n!)$, while $\Psi'(t)=-\iota(p)(x-t)^{p-1}$. Apply the Cauchy mean-value quotient theorem once on the interval from $a$ to $x$, use the endpoint values, and reflect the argument when $x<a$. Restrict $p$ to naturals with $1\le p\le n+1$; the formula concerns only $x\ne a$ because no point lies strictly between equal endpoints.

items.title: The Lagrange and Cauchy forms of Taylor's remainder
items.strategy: In the Schlömilch–Roche formula set $p=n+1$ to obtain $R=f^{(n+1)}(\xi)(x-a)^{n+1}/\iota((n+1)!)$, and set $p=1$ to obtain the Cauchy form $R=f^{(n+1)}(\xi)(x-\xi)^n(x-a)/\iota(n!)$. Check both substitutions using the factorial recursion and the exponent-zero convention.

items.title: Peano's form: the normalized Taylor remainder tends to zero
items.strategy: If $f$ is $n$ times differentiable on a neighbourhood of $a$, prove $R_{n,a}f(x)/(x-a)^n\to0$ as $x\to a$ for $n\ge1$. Avoid introducing unproved little-$o$ notation: state the quotient limit explicitly. Induct on $n$. Apply Cauchy's mean-value theorem to $R_{n,a}f(t)$ and $(t-a)^n$ between $a$ and $x$; the resulting quotient is the order-$(n-1)$ normalized Taylor remainder of $f'$ at an intermediate point, divided by $n$, and tends to $0$ by the induction hypothesis. This proof does not assume continuity of $f^{(n)}$. State the $n=0$ continuity analogue separately.

items.title: A uniform derivative bound gives a uniform Taylor remainder bound
items.strategy: If $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ between $a$ and $x$, use the Lagrange remainder to prove $|R_{n,a}f(x)|\le M|x-a|^{n+1}/\iota((n+1)!)$. Include $x=a$, the sign of the embedded factorial, and the symmetric case $x<a$.

items.title: The second-derivative test for strict local extrema
items.strategy: Assume $f'(a)=0$ and $f''$ exists and is continuous near $a$. If $f''(a)>0$, continuity gives $f''>0$ nearby, so $f'$ is strictly increasing and changes sign at $a$; the first-derivative monotonicity theorem gives a strict local minimum. Treat $f''(a)<0$ symmetrically and state explicitly that $f''(a)=0$ is inconclusive.

items.title: The first nonzero higher derivative classifies a stationary point
items.strategy: Suppose derivatives through order $r$ exist near $a$, all orders $1$ through $r-1$ vanish at $a$, and $f^{(r)}(a)\ne0$. Peano's formula makes the sign of $f(x)-f(a)$ equal to the sign of $f^{(r)}(a)(x-a)^r$ sufficiently near $a$. Conclude: even $r$ gives a strict minimum or maximum according to the sign, while odd $r$ gives neither. Keep $r\ge2$ and the punctured two-sided neighbourhood explicit.

items.title: If $f'(a)=f''(a)=0$, then the second derivative test still decides whether $a$ is an extremum
items.strategy: Refute the statement by recording that the hypotheses alone allow a strict minimum, a strict maximum, or no extremum. The companion page supplies $x^4$, $-x^4$, and $x^3$. Explain that the valid theorem requires a nonzero first higher derivative; do not label the inconclusive case as a failed theorem.

items.title: Scope, endpoint, factorial, and deferred-remainder conventions
items.strategy: Record the one-sided endpoint convention, the $\mathbb N$-contains-$0$ convention, and the natural-to-real embedding on factorial/binomial coefficients. State that the integral remainder is deferred to the later integration page; Borel's theorem and Dini derivatives are not asserted because their machinery is outside the declared closure. Explicitly reject the false Darboux-plus-Baire-one continuity claim.

pages.title: Darboux, L'Hôpital, and Taylor's Theorem: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: A bounded $C^1$ periodic oscillator made from a quartic Hermite spline
items.strategy: For $t\in\mathbb R$, let $m=\lfloor t\rfloor$, $u=t-m\in[0,1)$, and set $q(t)=u^2(1-u)^2$. Prove the value and first derivative glue at integer endpoints, so $q$ is bounded, nonconstant, $1$-periodic and $C^1$, with $q'(t)=2u(1-u)(1-2u)$ off the integers and the same formula extending there. This replaces trigonometric oscillators and uses the published integer-part theorem.

items.title: A differentiable function whose derivative is discontinuous
items.strategy: Using the periodic polynomial $q$, set $f(0)=0$ and $f(x)=x^2q(1/x)$ for $x\ne0$. Boundedness of $q$ gives $f(x)/x\to0$, so $f'(0)=0$. Away from $0$, compute $f'(x)=2xq(1/x)-q'(1/x)$. Choose two sequences of reciprocal points with different fractional parts to show $f'$ has no limit at $0$, while Darboux's theorem still forces every intermediate derivative value.

items.title: For every $k\ge0$, $x^k|x|$ is $C^k$ but not $C^{k+1}$
items.strategy: Treat the two sides as $x^{k+1}$ and $-x^{k+1}$ with the parity accounted for by $|x|$. Differentiate through order $k$: all one-sided values glue continuously and vanish at $0$. At order $k+1$ the one-sided constants differ, so that derivative does not exist at $0$. This is the corrected family; the source-plan expression $x^{k+1}|x|$ is off by one.

items.title: A function with positive derivative at $0$ that is monotone on no neighbourhood of $0$
items.strategy: Let $F(0)=0$ and $F(x)=x+A x^2q(1/x)$ for $x\ne0$, where $q$ is the periodic polynomial oscillator and choose an explicit natural $A$ large enough (for example $A=10$ after evaluating $q'$ at $u=1/5$). Boundedness gives $F'(0)=1$. Along reciprocal sequences the term $-Aq'(1/x)$ makes $F'$ negative at arbitrarily small points, ruling out nondecreasing behaviour by the MVT; $F'(0)>0$ rules out nonincreasing behaviour directly from the derivative definition.

items.title: L'Hôpital evaluates $\lim_{x\to1}(x^3-x)/(x^2-1)$ as $1$
items.strategy: Verify the $0/0$ hypotheses on a punctured neighbourhood of $1$, differentiate numerator and denominator, and simplify the derivative quotient to $(3x^2-1)/(2x)$, whose limit is $1$. Cross-check by factoring the original quotient to $x$ off $x=1$. The factorization is included to expose every cancellation rather than treating the rule as a black box.

items.title: L'Hôpital's conclusion does not imply convergence of the derivative quotient
items.strategy: Set $f(0)=g(0)=0$, $g(x)=x$, and $f(x)=x+x^2q(1/x)$ for $x\ne0$. Then $f(x)/g(x)=1+xq(1/x)\to1$, but $f'(x)/g'(x)=1+2xq(1/x)-q'(1/x)$ has two different subsequential limits. Verify $g'=1$ and every forward theorem hypothesis except derivative-ratio convergence. This is a log-free, trigonometry-free converse failure.

items.title: The Taylor polynomial of $(1-x)^{-1}$ at $0$ has the exact geometric remainder $x^{n+1}/(1-x)$
items.strategy: For $x\ne1$, use the finite geometric identity $(1-x)\sum_{j\le n}x^j=1-x^{n+1}$. Prove by induction that the $j$-th derivative at $0$ is $\iota(j!)$, so the Taylor polynomial is exactly the finite geometric sum. Deduce the exact remainder and compare it with the Lagrange bound on a fixed interval $|x|\le r<1$.

items.title: The functions $x^4$, $-x^4$, and $x^3$ show that $f''(0)=0$ is inconclusive
items.strategy: Compute the first two derivatives at $0$. Order of powers shows that $x^4$ has a strict minimum, $-x^4$ has a strict maximum, and $x^3$ has neither. Apply the first-nonzero-derivative test at orders $4,4,3$ and explicitly discharge the false statement's common hypotheses.

pages.title: Convexity

items.title: Convex, strictly convex, concave, strictly concave, and midpoint-convex real functions on an interval
For a convex function and $x<y<z$, the three secant slopes satisfy $s(x,y)\le s(x,z)\le s(y,z)$
items.strategy: Rewrite each point as a convex combination of the other two and clear only positive denominators. State all three inequalities, including the middle whole-chord slope, so later one-sided-limit arguments never silently strengthen the lemma.

items.title: A convex real function is Lipschitz on every closed bounded subinterval of the interior of its domain, hence continuous throughout the interior
items.strategy: Trap all secant slopes on a compactly contained interval between two fixed outer secant slopes supplied by the three-slope lemma. Convert the resulting difference-quotient bound into a Lipschitz estimate and then continuity, keeping endpoints outside the claim unless the function is separately continuous there.

items.title: The left and right derivatives of a real function as one-sided limits of its difference quotient
A convex function on an open interval has finite left and right derivatives everywhere, with $f'_-(u)\le f'_+(u)\le (f(v)-f(u))/(v-u)\le f'_-(v)\le f'_+(v)$ for $u<v$
items.strategy: Use monotonicity and local boundedness of the appropriate secant-slope functions to obtain their one-sided limits. Pass the finite three-slope inequalities to those limits and identify the limits with the one-sided derivatives exactly as defined on the preceding item.

items.title: A convex function on an open interval is differentiable except at at most countably many points
items.strategy: Let $g=f'_+$. The ordered one-sided-derivative inequalities make $g$ nondecreasing; identify its left limit at $c$ with $f'_-(c)$. Thus a failure of differentiability is a jump discontinuity of $g$, and Froda's theorem makes the exceptional set at most countable.

items.title: A supporting line of slope $m$ for a real function at an interior point
Every slope between the left and right derivatives of a convex function gives a supporting line
items.strategy: For $x<c$, compare the secant slope from $x$ to $c$ with $f'_-(c)$; for $x>c$, compare $f'_+(c)$ with the secant slope from $c$ to $x$. Insert the chosen slope between the one-sided derivatives and rearrange, treating $x=c$ by equality.

items.title: A differentiable function on an open interval is convex if and only if its derivative is nondecreasing
items.strategy: In the forward direction specialize the ordered one-sided-derivative inequality to ordinary derivatives. In the reverse direction use derivative monotonicity and the derivative-sign theorem on either side of a base point to establish the tangent supporting-line inequality, then recover the convex-combination inequality from the two endpoint supporting inequalities.

items.title: A differentiable convex function on an open interval has a continuous derivative
items.strategy: The preceding equivalence makes the derivative nondecreasing. Darboux's theorem says every derivative has the intermediate-value property, and the published monotone-derivative corollary then gives continuity without assuming a second derivative.

items.title: A twice-differentiable function on an open interval is convex if and only if its second derivative is nonnegative
items.strategy: Apply the differentiable convexity criterion to $f$, then apply the published derivative-sign/monotonicity theorem to $f'$. Preserve both directions and the weak inequality; do not replace nonnegative by positive.

items.title: Midpoint convexity gives the convexity inequality at every dyadic weight $k/2^n$
items.strategy: Induct on $n$, with $0\le k\le 2^n$. Even numerators reduce to the preceding level; odd numerators are the midpoint of the adjacent even dyadic weights. Keep the $n=0$ level and the endpoint weights $0,1$ explicit under the library's zero-based natural-number convention.

items.title: A continuous midpoint-convex function on an interval is convex
items.strategy: For a fixed weight in $[0,1]$, use the Archimedean property to choose dyadic weights converging to it (derive the needed approximation inline because the later dyadic-topology item is unavailable at this order). Apply the dyadic inequality and pass to the limit by continuity. Cover weights $0$ and $1$ directly.

items.title: Finite Jensen inequality for a convex function and nonnegative weights summing to one
items.strategy: Induct on a positive natural number of terms. Split off the final weight. When it equals one, all earlier weights vanish; otherwise normalize the preceding weights by their positive sum, apply induction, and then apply two-point convexity. State the $n=1$ base separately so no empty normalized family is formed.

items.title: Every local minimum of a convex function on an interval is a global minimum
items.strategy: If a point with smaller value existed, convex combinations with weights tending to zero would lie arbitrarily close to the local minimizer and have smaller values. Use the local-neighbourhood radius explicitly and include the one-point-domain case.

items.title: A strictly convex function has at most one global minimizer
items.strategy: Two distinct minimizers would have a midpoint in the interval whose value is strictly below their common minimum. Treat the empty minimizer set and singleton domain as allowed, not as existence claims.

items.title: An inflection point as a point of continuity where convexity changes to concavity or conversely
A continuous function whose second derivative has opposite signs on the two sides of a point has an inflection point there
items.strategy: Use the second-derivative convexity criterion on each one-sided interval, applying it to $-f$ for the concave side, and then invoke the definition's continuity clause. Do not claim that $f''(c)=0$ alone is sufficient.

items.title: Convexity conventions, endpoint scope, dyadic approximation, and the exact use of the Axiom of Choice in the midpoint-convex counterexample

pages.title: Convexity: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The absolute-value function is convex
items.strategy: Apply the triangle inequality to $|\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y|$ and absolute homogeneity for the nonnegative coefficients. Link in a remark, but do not cite as a dependency, the already-published companion-page counterexample showing nondifferentiability at zero.

items.title: Finite Jensen for $x\mapsto x^2$ gives that the square of a weighted mean is at most the weighted mean of the squares
items.strategy: Verify convexity of the square by expanding the Jensen gap as $\lambda(1-\lambda)(x-y)^2\ge0$, then instantiate finite Jensen. Include arbitrary finite positive length, zero weights, and the equality statement only when it is actually proved.

items.title: Assuming Choice, a Hamel coefficient map is midpoint convex but discontinuous and therefore not convex
items.strategy: Choose a Hamel basis vector and its published coefficient map. Additivity and rational homogeneity give midpoint equality. The nontrivial complementary span shows the map is not of the form $x\mapsto cx$; the published Cauchy-equation regularity theorem then makes it discontinuous. Since convex functions are continuous on the interior, it is not convex.

items.title: $x\mapsto x^3$ changes from concave to convex at zero and has an inflection point there
items.strategy: Compute the first and second derivatives from the power rule. The second derivative is negative to the left of zero and positive to the right; continuity at zero and the sign-change corollary finish. Explicitly contrast this with the already-published $x^4$ example, without depending on that B-page item.

pages.title: The Riemann Integral: Definition and Integrability

items.title: Partition of $[a,b]$ as a finite strictly increasing list $a = t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_n = b$, its subintervals and their lengths, its mesh, refinement, and the common refinement of two partitions

For bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ and a partition $P$: the infimum $m_i$ and supremum $M_i$ of $f$ on the $i$-th subinterval, and the lower and upper Darboux sums $L(f,P) = \sum_i m_i \Delta_i$ and $U(f,P) = \sum_i M_i \Delta_i$

Refining a partition raises the lower Darboux sum and lowers the upper one, and every lower sum is at most every upper sum: $L(f,P) \le L(f,P') \le U(f,P') \le U(f,P)$ when $P'$ refines $P$, and $L(f,P) \le U(f,Q)$ for arbitrary partitions $P$ and $Q$
items.strategy: induction

items.title: The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$

If $m \le f \le M$ on $[a,b]$ then $m(b-a) \le L(f,P) \le \underline{\int_a^b} f \le \overline{\int_a^b} f \le U(f,P) \le M(b-a)$ for every partition $P$; in particular every constant function is integrable, with $\int_a^b c = c(b-a)$
items.strategy: direct

items.title: Riemann's criterion: a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ is Darboux integrable if and only if for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a partition $P$ with $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$
items.strategy: direct

items.title: Tagged partitions of $[a,b]$, with a tag $\xi_i$ in each subinterval, and the Riemann sum $S(f,P,\xi) = \sum_i f(\xi_i)\,\Delta_i$

The Darboux and Riemann definitions agree: a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ is Darboux integrable with integral $I$ if and only if for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ such that $|S(f,P,\xi) - I| < \varepsilon$ for every tagged partition of mesh below $\delta$
items.strategy: direct

items.title: A continuous function on $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable, by Heine-Cantor and Riemann's criterion
items.strategy: direct

items.title: A monotone function on $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable: for the uniform partition into $n$ parts the upper minus lower sum telescopes to $|f(b) - f(a)|(b-a)/n$
items.strategy: direct

items.title: A bounded function on $[a,b]$ that is continuous except at finitely many points is Riemann integrable
items.strategy: direct

items.title: Lebesgue's criterion for Riemann integrability: a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable if and only if its set of discontinuities has measure zero
items.strategy: direct

items.title: A bounded function on $[a,b]$ whose set of discontinuities is at most countable is Riemann integrable
items.strategy: direct

items.title: FALSE: every bounded function on $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable
items.strategy: direct

items.title: FALSE: a bounded function on $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable exactly when its set of discontinuities is nowhere dense
items.strategy: direct

items.title: FALSE: a nonnegative Riemann integrable function on $[a,b]$ with $\int_a^b f = 0$ is identically zero
items.strategy: direct

items.title: FALSE: a pointwise limit of a sequence of Riemann integrable functions on $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable
items.strategy: direct

items.title: What this page costs in choice: Riemann's criterion, the Darboux-Riemann equivalence and integrability of a monotone function are theorems of ZF, integrability of a continuous function inherits the single use of countable choice inside Heine-Cantor, and the Lebesgue criterion inherits a second from the countable union of null sets

pages.title: The Riemann Integral: Definition and Integrability: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: $\int_0^1 x^{2} = 1/3$, computed from the Darboux definition with uniform partitions and the closed form $\sum_{k<n} k^{2} = n(n-1)(2n-1)/6$
items.strategy: direct

items.title: One refinement worked out for $f(x) = x^{2}$ on $[0,1]$: adding the point $1/2$ to the trivial partition raises the lower sum from $0$ to $1/8$ and lowers the upper sum from $1$ to $5/8$
items.strategy: direct

items.title: $\int_0^3 \lfloor x \rfloor = 3$: the floor function is nondecreasing, hence integrable, and the integral is computed from the uniform partitions
items.strategy: direct

items.title: The indicator of the Cantor set is discontinuous exactly on the Cantor set, which is null, so it is Riemann integrable with integral $0$ even though it is discontinuous at uncountably many points
items.strategy: direct

items.title: Thomae's function is Riemann integrable on $[0,1]$ with integral $0$: it is continuous at every irrational, so its discontinuity set is countable, and every lower Darboux sum is $0$
items.strategy: direct

items.title: The Dirichlet function on $[0,1]$ has lower Darboux integral $0$ and upper Darboux integral $1$, so it is bounded and not Riemann integrable
items.strategy: direct

items.title: The indicator of the Smith-Volterra-Cantor set is discontinuous exactly on a nowhere dense set, and is not Riemann integrable, because that set does not have measure zero
items.strategy: direct

items.title: For every $F_\sigma$ subset $E$ of $[0,1]$ of measure zero there is a bounded Riemann integrable function on $[0,1]$ whose set of discontinuities is exactly $E$
items.strategy: constructive

items.title: For the Dirichlet function every uniform partition with rational tags gives Riemann sum $1$, so the sums converge along that sequence of tagged partitions although the function is not integrable: the mesh condition of the Riemann definition quantifies over all tagged partitions and cannot be weakened to one sequence
items.strategy: direct

items.title: Thomae's function is nonnegative, Riemann integrable on $[0,1]$ with integral $0$, and nonzero at every rational, so a vanishing integral does not force a nonnegative integrand to vanish
items.strategy: direct

pages.title: Properties of the Integral and the Working FTC

items.title: The integral with oriented limits: $\int_a^a f := 0$ and $\int_b^a f := -\int_a^b f$
items.strategy: MINTED FIRST BECAUSE THE PUBLISHED DEFINITION DOES NOT COVER THE PAGE. Read [[def-darboux-integral]] on disk: it is stated under the standing hypothesis $a < b$ of [[def-partition-and-refinement]], so $\int_a^b f$ is undefined when $a \ge b$, and every additivity statement below would be false as usually written without this item. Extend by the two clauses above, noting there is nothing to prove for consistency because the clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$; the only check is that $\int_a^a f := 0$ agrees with the value the $a<b$ definition would give in a limit, which it does not need to, and should not be claimed. Say what $f$ must be: for $\int_b^a f$ with $b > a$, $f$ is a bounded function on $[a,b]$ that is integrable there. State immediately the two consequences used everywhere below: $\int_a^b f = -\int_b^a f$ for ALL $a,b$ in the domain, and the additivity identity $\int_a^b + \int_b^c = \int_a^c$ holds for every arrangement of $a,b,c$ once [[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]] is proved (record the obligation here, prove it there). Notation and convention only, no new integral: the object is still the Darboux integral of [[def-darboux-integral]].

items.title: A function integrable on $[a,b]$ is integrable on every closed subinterval
items.strategy: direct, through [[thm-riemann-criterion]]. Given $\varepsilon>0$ take a partition $P$ of $[a,b]$ with $U(f,P)-L(f,P)<\varepsilon$; refine it by adjoining $c$ and $d$ (the endpoints of the subinterval), which only decreases the gap by [[lem-refinement-inequalities]] clause 1, and then restrict to the part between $c$ and $d$. THE STEP THAT NEEDS CARE is that the restricted family is a partition of $[c,d]$ in the sense of [[def-partition-and-refinement]] -- that definition packages a partition as a pair $(n,t)$ with a tail convention, so the restriction has to be re-indexed and its tail set to $d$; do this explicitly rather than saying 'restrict'. The dropped subintervals contribute a nonnegative amount to the gap, by [[def-darboux-sums]] ($M_i - m_i \ge 0$) and monotonicity of finite sums ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), which is why the gap on $[c,d]$ is at most the gap on $[a,b]$. Degenerate case $c = d$ is handled by [[def-oriented-integral]].

items.title: Integrable functions on $[a,b]$ form a set closed under sums and scalar multiples, and $\int_a^b(\lambda f+\mu g) = \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g$
items.strategy: direct, in two halves, and the halves are genuinely different. SUMS: $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ and $\inf(f+g)\ge \inf f+\inf g$ on each subinterval, so $U(f+g,P) \le U(f,P)+U(g,P)$ and dually; integrability follows from [[thm-riemann-criterion]] applied to a COMMON refinement of a partition for $f$ and one for $g$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]] supplies the common refinement, [[lem-refinement-inequalities]] the monotonicity), and the value then by squeezing. Note that the inequality between suprema can be STRICT, so linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums -- say so, it is the reason the proof squeezes rather than computes. SCALARS: for $\lambda \ge 0$, $U(\lambda f,P) = \lambda U(f,P)$; for $\lambda < 0$ the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ SWAP, so $U(\lambda f,P) = \lambda L(f,P)$, and the case $\lambda = -1$ must be done explicitly ([[lem-reflection]] on suprema and infima is the published tool). Do not merge the two cases. LANDMARK.

items.title: If $f \le g$ on $[a,b]$ and both are integrable then $\int_a^b f \le \int_a^b g$; and $m(b-a) \le \int_a^b f \le M(b-a)$
items.strategy: direct and short, but state it as its own item because half the page cites it. From $f \le g$ pointwise, $L(f,P) \le L(g,P)$ and $U(f,P)\le U(g,P)$ for every $P$ ([[def-darboux-sums]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so the suprema and infima compare ([[lem-sup-monotone]]). The two-sided bound is [[lem-integral-elementary-bounds]], published -- CITE IT, do not reprove it, and check what it actually says before citing: it bounds both the lower and the upper integral for every partition and includes the value of the integral of a constant. Add the clause used later: if $f \ge 0$ and $f$ is integrable then $\int_a^b f \ge 0$, with equality possible even for $f$ not identically zero (the companion of the previous page carries the false statement; the CONTINUOUS case is a theorem below).

items.title: For $a<c<b$: $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ if and only if it is integrable on $[a,c]$ and on $[c,b]$, and then $\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; with the oriented form for arbitrary $a,b,c$
items.strategy: direct, both directions, then a case analysis for the oriented form. Forward direction is [[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]]. Converse: given partitions of $[a,c]$ and $[c,b]$ with small gaps, splice them into a partition of $[a,b]$ -- again a re-indexing of the pair $(n,t)$ of [[def-partition-and-refinement]], written out -- and add the gaps. The value identity follows because both $L$ and $U$ split additively over a partition point, using the splitting clause of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. THE ORIENTED FORM IS A SEPARATE CLAUSE AND IS WHERE THE PAGE PAYS FOR [[def-oriented-integral]]: for arbitrary $a,b,c$ in an interval on which $f$ is integrable, $\int_a^b f + \int_b^c f = \int_a^c f$; prove it by the six orderings of three points, or by the standard reduction (verify one ordering, then check that both sides change sign consistently under swapping two of the three). Do not assert 'by symmetry'. LANDMARK.

items.title: Changing an integrable function at finitely many points changes neither its integrability nor its integral
items.strategy: direct, by [[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]] plus the one-point case. Reduce to a function $h$ vanishing off a single point $p$: given $\varepsilon>0$, take a partition whose subintervals containing $p$ have total length less than $\varepsilon/(2\lvert h(p)\rvert+1)$; then $U(h,P)-L(h,P)$ is small, so $h$ is integrable with integral $0$ by [[thm-riemann-criterion]] and [[lem-integral-elementary-bounds]]. THE POINT $p$ MAY BE A PARTITION POINT, in which case it lies in TWO subintervals -- handle that, it is the only subtlety. Then a finite set is handled by induction and linearity; 'finite' here is [[def-countable]]'s finite, a set equinumerous with a natural number -- do NOT reach for the counting page's cardinality item, which is not in this page's declared prerequisites. This lemma is what makes the endpoint values of an integrand irrelevant, and the companion page uses it; it is also the honest reason the integral cannot detect a change on a finite set, in contrast with the derivative.

items.title: If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ with values in $[m,M]$ and $\varphi$ is continuous on $[m,M]$, then $\varphi \circ f$ is integrable
items.strategy: direct, the Rudin 6.11 argument, and it is the hardest proof on the page after the FTC; scaffold it in named stages. Fix $\varepsilon>0$. (1) $\varphi$ is uniformly continuous on the compact $[m,M]$ ([[thm-heine-cantor-r]]) and bounded there ([[cor-boundedness-theorem-r]], with $K := \sup\lvert\varphi\rvert$); choose $\delta \in (0,\varepsilon)$ with $\lvert\varphi(s)-\varphi(t)\rvert<\varepsilon$ whenever $\lvert s-t\rvert\le\delta$. (2) By [[thm-riemann-criterion]] pick $P$ with $U(f,P)-L(f,P)<\delta^{2}$. (3) SPLIT THE INDICES into $G = \{i : M_i-m_i<\delta\}$ and $B = \{i : M_i-m_i\ge\delta\}$; on $G$ the oscillation of $\varphi\circ f$ is at most $\varepsilon$, and on $B$ it is at most $2K$ while $\delta\sum_{i\in B}\Delta_i \le \sum_{i\in B}(M_i-m_i)\Delta_i < \delta^{2}$, so the total length of the bad subintervals is less than $\delta$. (4) Add. The splitting is a finite index-set sum ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 3 suffices if the indices are grouped, but stating it as a sum over the subsets $G$ and $B$ of the index range is cleaner and is legitimate). THE ORDER MATTERS AND MUST BE SAID: the hypothesis is CONTINUOUS AFTER INTEGRABLE. Integrable after continuous can fail, and the companion page carries the witness; the remark should point there without stating the false general form. LANDMARK.

items.title: If $f,g$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ then so are $\lvert f\rvert$, $f^{2}$, $fg$, $\max(f,g)$ and $\min(f,g)$, and $\bigl\lvert\int_a^b f\bigr\rvert \le \int_a^b\lvert f\rvert$
items.strategy: direct, all from [[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]] plus [[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]]. Take $\varphi(t)=\lvert t\rvert$ and $\varphi(t)=t^{2}$ (continuous by [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]); then $fg = \tfrac14\big((f+g)^{2}-(f-g)^{2}\big)$ and $\max(f,g) = \tfrac12(f+g+\lvert f-g\rvert)$, $\min(f,g) = \tfrac12(f+g-\lvert f-g\rvert)$. The inequality $\lvert\int f\rvert \le \int\lvert f\rvert$ follows from $\pm f \le \lvert f\rvert$ and [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]]; state it for $a \le b$ ONLY, since with the orientation convention of [[def-oriented-integral]] it is false as written when $b<a$ -- that is a real trap and the item should say so and give the corrected two-sided form $\lvert\int_a^b f\rvert \le \lvert\int_a^b \lvert f\rvert\rvert$. The converse of the first clause fails: $\lvert f\rvert$ integrable does not make $f$ integrable, and the companion page carries the witness.

items.title: If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and $g$ is integrable with $g \ge 0$, there is $\xi \in [a,b]$ with $\int_a^b fg = f(\xi)\int_a^b g$
items.strategy: direct, via the extreme value theorem and the intermediate value theorem. Let $m = \min f$ and $M = \max f$, which exist by [[thm-extreme-value-r]]; then $mg \le fg \le Mg$ pointwise, so $m\int g \le \int fg \le M\int g$ by [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]] ($fg$ is integrable by [[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]]). If $\int g = 0$ then $\int fg = 0$ and ANY $\xi$ works -- handle that case first and separately, it is where the usual proof divides by zero. Otherwise $\int fg / \int g \in [m,M]$ and [[thm-intermediate-value]] with [[cor-continuous-image-of-an-interval-is-an-interval]] supplies $\xi$. THE HYPOTHESIS $g \ge 0$ IS ESSENTIAL and the companion page carries a witness with a sign-changing $g$; the special case $g \equiv 1$ gives the familiar $\int_a^b f = f(\xi)(b-a)$ and should be stated as a clause because the FTC proof below uses exactly that form.

items.title: The integral function $F(x) := \int_a^x f$ of an integrable $f$
items.strategy: definition with its well-definedness discharged inline. For $f$ integrable on $[a,b]$ and $x \in [a,b]$, $f$ is integrable on $[a,x]$ by [[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] when $a<x$, and $\int_a^a f = 0$ by [[def-oriented-integral]] when $x = a$; so $F : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is a genuine function. Record the two identities used constantly below and prove them from [[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]]: $F(y)-F(x) = \int_x^y f$ for ALL $x,y \in [a,b]$, in either order, and $F(a)=0$. Note that $F$ depends on the base point $a$ and that changing it changes $F$ by a constant; that is the observation the primitive corollary below turns into a theorem. Also note, because the companion page needs it, that $F$ is defined for every integrable $f$ whether or not $f$ has a primitive, and that $F$ need not be a primitive of $f$ where $f$ is discontinuous.

items.title: The integral function of a bounded integrable $f$ is Lipschitz, hence uniformly continuous
items.strategy: direct. With $\lvert f\rvert \le K$ on $[a,b]$, [[def-the-integral-function]]'s identity and [[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] give $\lvert F(y)-F(x)\rvert = \lvert\int_x^y f\rvert \le K\lvert y-x\rvert$ -- write the estimate for $x<y$ and then note the symmetric case rather than hiding it in the absolute value. Conclude that $F$ is Lipschitz with constant $K$ in the sense of [[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]] on $(\mathbb{R},d_{\mathbb{R}})$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), hence uniformly continuous by [[thm-metric-regularity-hierarchy]], hence continuous ([[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]] bridges the metric and the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ notions, and citing it is what keeps the library from holding two notions of continuity). NO CONTINUITY OF $f$ IS ASSUMED: this is the strongest statement available before the FTC and it is what makes the FTC's hypotheses visible as hypotheses.
