items.title: The first fundamental theorem: if $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and continuous at $c$, then $F'(c) = f(c)$; in particular a continuous $f$ has $F$ as a primitive
items.strategy: direct, from the definition of the derivative, not from the mean value theorem for integrals (which would need continuity on a whole subinterval and is the weaker route). For $x \ne c$ in $[a,b]$, $\frac{F(x)-F(c)}{x-c} - f(c) = \frac{1}{x-c}\int_c^x\bigl(f(t)-f(c)\bigr)\,dt$ using [[def-the-integral-function]] and [[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]] with $\int_c^x f(c)\,dt = f(c)(x-c)$ ([[lem-integral-elementary-bounds]]); continuity at $c$ bounds the integrand by $\varepsilon$ near $c$, and [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]] with [[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] bounds the whole quotient by $\varepsilon$. WRITE THE ESTIMATE FOR $x<c$ TOO: with [[def-oriented-integral]] the factor $1/(x-c)$ is negative and the naive chain of inequalities reverses; this is the single most common error in this proof. Then $F'(c) = f(c)$ by [[def-derivative]] and [[def-function-limit]]. The one-sided statement at the endpoints $a$ and $b$ is included, since [[def-derivative]] is stated at limit points of the domain and every point of a nondegenerate interval is one. LANDMARK.

items.title: The second fundamental theorem: if $G$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ with $G' = f$ and $f$ is integrable, then $\int_a^b f = G(b)-G(a)$
items.strategy: direct, by the mean value theorem on the subintervals of an arbitrary partition -- the proof that needs NO continuity of $f$, only its integrability, and is therefore the right 'working' form. For a partition $P = (n,t)$, telescoping gives $G(b)-G(a) = \sum_{i<n}\bigl(G(t_{i+1})-G(t_i)\bigr)$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 5), and [[cor-mean-value-theorem]] on each $[t_i,t_{i+1}]$ produces $\xi_i$ with $G(t_{i+1})-G(t_i) = f(\xi_i)\Delta_i$. So $G(b)-G(a)$ is a Riemann sum $S(f,P,\xi)$ ([[def-tagged-partition-and-riemann-sum]]) and therefore lies between $L(f,P)$ and $U(f,P)$ for EVERY $P$; since $f$ is integrable, [[def-darboux-integral]] squeezes it to $\int_a^b f$. THE SELECTION OF THE $\xi_i$ IS FINITE AND NEEDS NO CHOICE PRINCIPLE -- say so, in the style of [[def-tagged-partition-and-riemann-sum]]'s own remark, since a reader who has met [[def-dependent-choice]] will ask. State the hypotheses exactly: $G$ differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ (one-sided at the endpoints), $f = G'$ integrable. Both hypotheses have witnesses on the companion page showing neither is removable. LANDMARK.

items.title: Every continuous function on an interval has a primitive; two primitives differ by a constant; and $\int_a^b f = G(b)-G(a)$ for any primitive $G$
items.strategy: direct, assembling [[thm-ftc-first-part]] (existence) and [[thm-ftc-second-part]] (evaluation) with [[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]] (uniqueness up to a constant). Note the alias [[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]] already carries for exactly this statement, so do not mint a second 'antiderivatives differ by a constant'. Integrability of a continuous $f$ is [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], published. STATE THE SCOPE HONESTLY: existence of a primitive is proved here only for CONTINUOUS $f$; an integrable $f$ need not have one and a function with a primitive need not be integrable, and both witnesses are on the companion page, so this corollary is exactly the intersection of the two failures.

items.title: If $u,v$ are differentiable on $[a,b]$ with $u',v'$ integrable, then $\int_a^b u v' = u(b)v(b)-u(a)v(a) - \int_a^b u'v$
items.strategy: direct, from [[thm-ftc-second-part]] applied to $G = uv$. By [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], $G' = u'v + uv'$; $u$ and $v$ are continuous ([[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]) hence bounded and integrable ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]), so $u'v$ and $uv'$ are integrable by [[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]], hence so is $G'$ by [[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]]; apply the second FTC to $G$ and split the integral by linearity. THE INTEGRABILITY OF THE PRODUCTS IS THE HYPOTHESIS-CHECKING STEP AND IS USUALLY SKIPPED; it is why the theorem is stated with $u',v'$ integrable rather than merely existing. The companion page carries the false statement that drops that hypothesis.

items.title: Substitution: if $\varphi$ is differentiable on $[c,d]$ with $\varphi'$ integrable and $f$ is continuous on an interval containing $\varphi([c,d])$, then $\int_{\varphi(c)}^{\varphi(d)} f = \int_c^d (f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi'$
items.strategy: direct, via a primitive and the chain rule -- the route that needs NO monotonicity of $\varphi$, which is exactly why the theorem is stated with oriented limits. Let $F$ be a primitive of $f$ on the interval $J \supseteq \varphi([c,d])$ ($J$ is an interval containing the compact connected image, by [[cor-continuous-image-of-an-interval-is-an-interval]]), which exists by [[cor-primitives-of-a-continuous-function]]. Then $(F\circ\varphi)' = (f\circ\varphi)\varphi'$ by [[thm-chain-rule]], this is integrable ([[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]] for $f\circ\varphi$, then [[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] for the product), and [[thm-ftc-second-part]] applied to $F\circ\varphi$ on $[c,d]$ gives the right-hand side as $F(\varphi(d))-F(\varphi(c))$, which is the left-hand side by [[thm-ftc-second-part]] again on the oriented interval between $\varphi(c)$ and $\varphi(d)$ ([[def-oriented-integral]] is what makes that step legal when $\varphi(d)<\varphi(c)$). NOTE WHAT IS NOT ASSUMED: $\varphi$ need be neither injective nor monotone. The version with $f$ merely integrable is FALSE without further hypotheses; do not state it, and let the companion page carry the witness.

items.title: Bonnet's second mean value theorem: for $f$ monotone and $g$ integrable on $[a,b]$ there is $\xi\in[a,b]$ with $\int_a^b fg = f(a)\int_a^\xi g + f(b)\int_\xi^b g$
items.strategy: direct, by Abel summation on partitions and a passage to the limit -- the route that does NOT assume $f$ differentiable. Stages. (1) $f$ monotone is integrable ([[thm-monotone-implies-integrable]]) and $fg$ is integrable ([[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]]). (2) Put $G(x) = \int_a^x g$, continuous by [[thm-the-integral-function-is-lipschitz]]. (3) For a partition $P$, apply [[lem-abel-summation-by-parts]] to the finite sums $\sum_i f(t_i)\bigl(G(t_{i+1})-G(t_i)\bigr)$, obtaining $f(b)G(b) - \sum_i G(t_{i+1})\bigl(f(t_{i+1})-f(t_i)\bigr)$; READ THAT PUBLISHED LEMMA ON DISK AND MATCH ITS INDEXING BEFORE USING IT, since a summation-by-parts identity is off by one term under half the conventions in print. (4) The second sum lies between $m\bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)$ and $M\bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)$ where $m,M$ are the extrema of $G$ ([[thm-extreme-value-r]]), because the increments of a monotone $f$ have one sign. (5) Let the mesh go to $0$: the first sums converge to $\int_a^b fg$ by [[thm-darboux-equals-riemann]] and the estimate persists, giving $\int_a^b fg = f(b)G(b) - \lambda(f(b)-f(a))$ with $\lambda \in [m,M]$; [[thm-intermediate-value]] gives $\lambda = G(\xi)$ and rearranging with [[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]] gives the stated form. IF STAGE (5) CANNOT BE MADE CLEAN, state and prove instead the WEAKER form with $f$ monotone AND continuously differentiable (proved in three lines from [[thm-integration-by-parts]] and [[thm-first-mean-value-theorem-for-integrals]] applied to the one-signed weight $-f'$) and record the general case as a scope drop -- a correct weaker theorem is worth more than a shaky general one.

items.title: A continuous $f \ge 0$ on $[a,b]$ with $\int_a^b f = 0$ is identically $0$
items.strategy: contradiction, and it is the TRUE companion of a published false statement: [[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's companion refutes the same claim for merely integrable $f$, so this item is exactly the repair and should say so. If $f(c)>0$ for some $c$, continuity gives a subinterval $[p,q]\subseteq[a,b]$ with $p<q$ on which $f \ge f(c)/2$ ([[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] or directly from [[def-continuity-real]]); then [[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]] and [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]] give $\int_a^b f \ge \int_p^q f \ge \tfrac12 f(c)(q-p)>0$. THE NONNEGATIVITY ON THE OTHER TWO PIECES is what lets the middle piece be isolated -- cite it, do not assume it. Handle $c = a$ or $c = b$ by taking a one-sided subinterval.

items.title: The integral test: for $f \ge 0$ nonincreasing on $[0,\infty)$, $\sum_k f(k)$ converges if and only if the sequence $\bigl(\int_0^N f\bigr)_N$ is bounded, with $\int_0^N f \le \sum_{k<N} f(k) \le f(0) + \int_0^N f$
items.strategy: direct, from a bracketing on each unit interval, then [[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]]. STATED WITH PROPER INTEGRALS ONLY, AND THAT IS A DELIBERATE DESIGN DECISION: improper integrals are homed on a later page and are not available at this point in the reading order, so the conclusion is phrased as boundedness of the increasing sequence $\bigl(\int_0^N f\bigr)_N$ rather than as convergence of $\int_0^\infty f$. Say that in Remarks, and say that the later page will identify the two. On $[k,k+1]$, monotonicity gives $f(k+1)\le f(t)\le f(k)$, so [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]] and [[lem-integral-elementary-bounds]] give $f(k+1)\le\int_k^{k+1} f\le f(k)$; sum with [[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. $f$ is integrable on every $[0,N]$ by [[thm-monotone-implies-integrable]]. Then the equivalence is [[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]] applied to $\sum f(k)$, whose terms are nonnegative. INDEX RANGE: $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, so the sum starts at $k=0$ and the base interval is $[0,N]$; a version starting at $1$ is a tail and is covered by [[lem-series-tail-invariance]] -- do not silently start at $1$ as the classical statement does. LANDMARK.

items.title: Conventions of this page, and which sharpenings of the integral are taken up later in the reading order
items.strategy: the page ledger, in the style of [[rem-riemann-integral-choice-ledger]] and [[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]]. Record: (1) the orientation convention of [[def-oriented-integral]] and the two statements on this page whose form depends on it ([[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]], [[thm-substitution]]); (2) that 'integrable' means Darboux integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], equivalently Riemann integrable by [[thm-darboux-equals-riemann]], and that no other integral is in use; (3) the choice cost: nothing on this page uses a choice principle, and in particular the finitely many tags of [[thm-ftc-second-part]] are chosen by a theorem of ZF, whereas the published [[thm-lebesgue-criterion]] on the previous page does spend countable choice once. WHAT IS TAKEN UP LATER, phrased as reading order and never as a claim about the library: Taylor's integral remainder needs higher derivatives, which are introduced on a later page; bounded variation and the Riemann-Stieltjes integral, improper integrals, and the sharpening of the fundamental theorem all have their own pages later in this track. MENTION, via `external_refs` and not via `deps`, the recorded-not-proved [[rem-ftc-absolutely-continuous]] and [[rem-dominated-convergence-theorem]] on the deferred measure-and-integration page, as the statements a reader will want next and which this library records but does not prove; a mention does not propagate (SCHEMA 3) and nothing here rests on them.

pages.title: Properties of the Integral and the Working FTC: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: $\int_0^1 x^{m} = 1/\iota(m+1)$, computed by the fundamental theorem and checked against the definition
items.strategy: computation, done twice. First by [[cor-primitives-of-a-continuous-function]] with the primitive $x^{m+1}/\iota(m+1)$, whose derivative is $x^{m}$ by [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]] -- read that published lemma's index range before citing it, it is the item the previous page flagged for an index trap. Second, for $m=1$ and $m=2$, from Darboux sums on the uniform partition, which the previous page's companion already does for $x^{2}$; the point of repeating it is the CROSS-CHECK, that the two routes agree. Note the canonical natural: the answer is $1/\iota(m+1)$, not $1/(m+1)$, since $m+1$ is a von Neumann natural ([[def-canonical-natural]]).

items.title: A step function integrated by additivity over subintervals, and the same value from the definition
items.strategy: computation exercising [[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]] and [[lem-changing-a-function-at-finitely-many-points]] together. Take $f = 1$ on $[0,1)$, $f = 3$ on $[1,2]$, and any value at the single point $1$; compute $\int_0^2 f = 1 + 3 = 4$ by splitting at $1$ and using the constant case of [[lem-integral-elementary-bounds]], then observe that the value at $1$ is irrelevant, which is the content of the changing-at-finitely-many-points lemma. This is the smallest example in which the partition point genuinely lies in two subintervals, the case that lemma's proof singles out.

items.title: The integral test applied to $\sum 1/\iota(k+1)^{p}$ for rational $p>0$, cross-checked against the published $p$-series theorem
items.strategy: verification, and the cross-check is the point. Apply [[thm-integral-test-for-series]] to $f(t) = (t+1)^{-p}$ for rational $p>0$ ([[def-rational-power]], positive base, so the power is defined; $p$ MUST BE RATIONAL because real exponents do not exist in this library at this point in the reading order -- [[rem-real-exponents-deferred]]). Compute $\int_0^N f$ by [[cor-primitives-of-a-continuous-function]], separating $p = 1$ (where the primitive is not a power and the integral is not available here, so state only the boundedness question and resolve it by comparison) from $p \ne 1$. Then compare the verdict with the published [[thm-p-series-rational]] and confirm they agree. If the $p=1$ case cannot be settled without the logarithm, say so and settle it by [[thm-cauchy-condensation]] instead, citing the published result rather than inventing a logarithm.

items.title: $H(x) = 2\sqrt{x}$ on $[0,1]$: $H$ is continuous, $H'$ is unbounded on $(0,1]$, and $H'$ is therefore not Riemann integrable
items.strategy: the Bartle and Sherbert motivating example, worked. $H$ is continuous on $[0,1]$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] and the continuity of the square root, which follows from [[thm-continuous-inverse]] applied to $x\mapsto x^{2}$ on $[0,\infty)$ -- cite, do not assume); $H$ is differentiable on $(0,1]$ with $H'(x) = 1/\sqrt{x}$ ([[thm-derivative-of-an-inverse]] or the power rule for rational exponents, whichever is actually published -- CHECK ON DISK), and $H'$ is unbounded, hence not Riemann integrable on $[0,1]$ because [[def-darboux-sums]] is defined only for bounded functions. So the second fundamental theorem does not apply on $[0,1]$ even though $H$ is continuous there and differentiable on the open interval. The honest conclusion available here is exactly that; the improper integral that repairs it belongs to a later page and must not be computed here.

items.title: The sign function is Riemann integrable on $[-1,1]$ and has no primitive there
items.strategy: counterexample with an ELEMENTARY refutation, not by Darboux's theorem on the intermediate value property of derivatives, which lives on a later page and is not available. Integrability: $s$ has one discontinuity, so [[thm-finitely-many-discontinuities-integrable]] applies, and $\int_{-1}^{1} s = 0$ by [[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]]. No primitive: if $G' = s$ on $[-1,1]$ then $G' = 1$ on $(0,1]$ and $G' = -1$ on $[-1,0)$, so by [[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]] applied to $G(x)-x$ and to $G(x)+x$, $G(x) = x + c_1$ on $[0,1]$ and $G(x) = -x + c_2$ on $[-1,0]$, and continuity of $G$ at $0$ ([[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]) forces $c_1 = c_2$; then $G(x) = \lvert x\rvert + c$, whose one-sided difference quotients at $0$ are $1$ and $-1$, so $G'(0)$ does not exist by [[thm-two-sided-limit-iff-both-one-sided]] -- contradicting differentiability at $0$. Note the tension with [[thm-ftc-first-part]] resolved: the integral function of $s$ IS $\lvert x\rvert - 1$, differentiable everywhere except at the one point where $s$ is discontinuous.

items.title: A function differentiable on $[0,1]$ whose derivative is unbounded, hence not Riemann integrable
items.strategy: explicit construction, ENTIRELY POLYNOMIAL, because the classical witness $x^{2}\sin(1/x^{2})$ needs trigonometric functions and this library has none at this point in the reading order -- record that substitution as a deliberate choice. Take $\phi(t) = t^{2}(1-t)^{2}$, which is a polynomial with $\phi(0)=\phi(1)=0$ and $\phi'(0)=\phi'(1)=0$, so translating and scaling it gives bumps that glue to $0$ with matching derivatives. On disjoint intervals $I_n \subseteq (1/\iota(n+2), 1/\iota(n+1))$ of length $h_n$ place the bump $c_n\phi((x-a_n)/h_n)$, and set $G = 0$ elsewhere. Choose $h_n$ and $c_n$ (for instance $c_n$ of order $1/\iota(n)^{3}$ and $h_n$ of order $1/\iota(n)^{5}$) so that (i) $\lvert G(x)\rvert / \lvert x\rvert \to 0$ as $x\to 0$, which gives $G'(0) = 0$ by [[def-derivative]] and [[thm-squeeze-for-function-limits]], and (ii) $\sup\lvert G'\rvert$ on $I_n$, which is of order $c_n/h_n$, tends to infinity. VERIFY BOTH ESTIMATES EXPLICITLY WITH THE CHOSEN EXPONENTS -- the construction is only as good as those two inequalities, and every step is finite algebra plus [[lem-power-monotone]]. Then $G$ is differentiable on $[0,1]$, but $G'$ is unbounded, so $G'$ is not Riemann integrable ([[def-darboux-sums]] requires boundedness). Only ONE bump is nonzero near any point of $(0,1]$, so no series convergence is involved anywhere.

items.title: Integrable $\varphi$ and integrable $f$ with $\varphi\circ f$ not integrable: the order of the hypotheses in the composition theorem cannot be reversed
items.strategy: counterexample, refuting the mirror image of [[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]]. Take $f$ to be Thomae's function on $[0,1]$ ([[def-dirichlet-and-thomae-functions]]), which is integrable with integral $0$ (its discontinuity set is $\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]$, countable hence null, so [[thm-lebesgue-criterion]] applies; or cite the previous page's companion where this is worked), and $\varphi(t) = 1$ for $t>0$, $\varphi(0)=0$, which is integrable on $[0,1]$ by [[thm-monotone-implies-integrable]]. Then $\varphi\circ f$ is the Dirichlet function, not integrable ([[def-dirichlet-and-thomae-functions]], [[thm-lebesgue-criterion]], or the previous page's companion). SAY EXACTLY WHICH HYPOTHESIS OF THE COMPOSITION THEOREM FAILS: $\varphi$ is not continuous. Cross-check the discontinuity sets against [[thm-dirichlet-and-thomae-continuity-sets]], published, rather than restating them.

items.title: A function that is not Riemann integrable although $\lvert f\rvert$ is
items.strategy: counterexample refuting the converse of [[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]]. Take $f = 1$ on the rationals of $[0,1]$ and $f = -1$ on the irrationals; then $\lvert f\rvert \equiv 1$ is integrable with integral $1$, while $f$ has $L(f,P) = -1$ and $U(f,P) = 1$ for every partition, because both the rationals and the irrationals are dense ([[lem-q-and-irrationals-dense-r]]), so $f$ is not integrable by [[def-darboux-integral]]. Note that $f = 2\chi_{\mathbb{Q}} - 1$, so this is the Dirichlet function rescaled, and cross-check with [[thm-lebesgue-criterion]]: the discontinuity set is all of $[0,1]$, which is not null ([[lem-nondegenerate-interval-is-not-null]]).

items.title: Continuous $f_n \to 0$ pointwise on $[0,1]$ with $\int_0^1 f_n = 1$ for every $n$
items.strategy: counterexample: pointwise convergence alone never licenses passing to the limit under the integral. Take $f_n$ to be the piecewise linear tent of height $2\iota(n+1)$ supported on $[0, 1/\iota(n+1)]$, continuous hence integrable ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]) with integral $1$ computed by [[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]] and [[cor-primitives-of-a-continuous-function]] on the two linear pieces. For fixed $x>0$, $f_n(x) = 0$ once $1/\iota(n+1)<x$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]), and $f_n(0)=0$ for all $n$, so $f_n \to 0$ pointwise. THE HEIGHTS ARE UNBOUNDED, and saying so is what makes the example precise: it refutes the interchange for pointwise convergence, and it does NOT refute anything about uniformly bounded sequences, whose interchange theorem is not stated on this page. Do not assert the bounded convergence theorem in any form here.

items.title: Continuous $f$ and integrable sign-changing $g$ with $\int_a^b fg \ne f(\xi)\int_a^b g$ for every $\xi$
items.strategy: counterexample locating the hypothesis $g \ge 0$ of [[thm-first-mean-value-theorem-for-integrals]]. On $[-1,1]$ take $g(t) = t$ and $f(t) = t$; then $\int_{-1}^{1} fg = \int_{-1}^{1} t^{2} = 2/\iota(3) > 0$ while $\int_{-1}^{1} g = 0$, so $f(\xi)\int g = 0$ for every $\xi$ and no $\xi$ works. Compute both integrals by [[cor-primitives-of-a-continuous-function]]. Note the weaker true statement that survives: with $g$ of one sign the theorem holds, and with $g$ integrable of arbitrary sign only the bound $\lvert\int fg\rvert \le \sup\lvert f\rvert\int\lvert g\rvert$ remains ([[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]], [[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]]).

items.title: FALSE: if $u$ and $v$ are differentiable on $[a,b]$ then $\int_a^b uv' = u(b)v(b)-u(a)v(a)-\int_a^b u'v$
items.strategy: refutation: with $u = G$ the everywhere-differentiable function of [[cex-a-function-with-a-primitive-that-is-not-integrable]] and $v(x) = x$, the integrand $uv' = G$ is continuous hence integrable, but $u'v = G'(x)\,x$ is unbounded near the accumulation point and hence not Riemann integrable, so the right-hand side is not even defined. THE FALSITY IS UNDEFINEDNESS, NOT A WRONG NUMBER, and the item should say so in those terms, exactly as the stars-and-bars false statement on the counting page does. State the correct hypothesis of [[thm-integration-by-parts]] ($u',v'$ integrable) and note that it is automatic when $u,v$ are continuously differentiable.

items.title: FALSE: in the substitution theorem the continuity of $f$ may be weakened to integrability, $f\circ\varphi$ still being integrable
items.strategy: refutation, and the cleanest failure is that the right-hand side need not exist: take $f$ to be the Dirichlet function on $[0,1]$, which is not integrable, and $\varphi$ a nonconstant polynomial mapping $[c,d]$ into $[0,1]$ -- but that already fails the hypothesis on $f$, so instead take $f$ integrable and $\varphi$ chosen so that $f\circ\varphi$ is not: with $f$ Thomae's function (integrable) and $\varphi$ a map whose image meets the rationals densely in a controlled way, $f\circ\varphi$ is the Dirichlet-type function of [[cex-a-composition-of-integrable-functions-that-is-not-integrable]]. CONSTRUCT THE WITNESS EXPLICITLY OR WEAKEN THE ITEM: if a clean explicit $\varphi$ cannot be exhibited with the machinery of this page, replace this false statement with the weaker and fully provable one that the substitution identity requires $f\circ\varphi$ to be integrable, and refute the version that omits continuity of $f$ by a two-line undefinedness argument. Do not publish a witness that has not been checked; an honest weaker item is preferred.

items.title: FALSE: for every integrable $f$ on $[a,b]$, the integral function $F(x)=\int_a^x f$ satisfies $F' = f$ on $[a,b]$
items.strategy: refutation by the sign function of [[cex-an-integrable-function-with-no-primitive]]: there $F(x) = \lvert x\rvert - 1$, which is not differentiable at $0$, so $F' = f$ fails at the single point where $f$ is discontinuous. A second, sharper witness: any integrable $f$ that differs from a continuous $g$ at one point has the same $F$ as $g$ ([[lem-changing-a-function-at-finitely-many-points]]), so $F' = g \ne f$ at that point -- this shows the failure is not exotic and cannot be repaired by any hypothesis weaker than continuity at the point. State the true theorem, [[thm-ftc-first-part]], whose hypothesis is continuity AT THE POINT and nowhere else.

pages.title: Bounded Variation and the Riemann–Stieltjes Integral

items.title: Bounded variation and total variation on an interval
items.strategy: For a partition P=(n,t), define V(f,P)=sum_{i<n}|f(t_{i+1})-f(t_i)| and define Var_[a,b](f) as the supremum of these sums when they are bounded. Prove that the set of sums is nonempty and that completeness makes the value well-defined; set singleton variation to zero.

items.title: Total variation bounds increments; bounded-variation functions are bounded; zero variation means constant
items.strategy: Insert x<y into a partition to obtain |f(y)-f(x)|<=Var(f). With x=a, the triangle inequality bounds f. Prove Var(f)=0 iff every increment vanishes, including the constant-function direction and singleton interval.

items.title: Total variation is additive over adjacent subintervals and decreases under restriction
items.strategy: Splice partitions of [a,c] and [c,b] for one inequality. For the other, insert c into an arbitrary partition and split its sum. Take suprema only after both finite-sum estimates; include endpoint cuts and the restriction corollary.

items.title: Variation function and positive and negative variations
items.strategy: For BV f on [a,b], set V_f(a)=0 and V_f(x)=Var_[a,x](f). Define P_f=(V_f+f-f(a))/2 and N_f=(V_f-f+f(a))/2. Leave monotonicity to the next lemma.

items.title: The positive and negative variations are nondecreasing and give the Jordan identities
items.strategy: For x<y, additivity gives V_f(y)-V_f(x)=Var_[x,y](f)>=|f(y)-f(x)|. Remove the absolute value in both directions to show P_f and N_f are nondecreasing, then verify f=f(a)+P_f-N_f and V_f=P_f+N_f algebraically.

items.title: Jordan decomposition for functions of bounded variation
items.strategy: The forward implication uses f=f(a)+P_f-N_f. Conversely, if f=g-h with g,h nondecreasing, bound every variation sum by the endpoint increments of g and h. Prove the minimality of P_f,N_f among normalized decompositions so the canonical construction is characterized, not merely exhibited.

items.title: A bounded-variation function has at most countably many discontinuities, all of the first kind
items.strategy: Apply the published monotone-discontinuity theorem to both functions in a Jordan decomposition. Their one-sided limits subtract, and the discontinuity set lies in the union of two countable sets. Do not claim almost-everywhere differentiability, which belongs to measure theory.

items.title: The jumps of a variation function equal the absolute jumps of the original function
items.strategy: Use additivity and the existence of one-sided limits to identify the right and left increments of V_f with limits of variations on shrinking intervals. Prove the lower bound from the endpoint increment and the reverse bound by fixing a nearly maximizing partition and using convergence of f on the shrinking tail. Conclude that V_f is continuous wherever f is continuous.

items.title: Homogeneity and subadditivity of total variation
items.strategy: Prove Var(cf)=|c|Var(f) and Var(f+g)<=Var(f)+Var(g) first for each partition, then pass to suprema. Include Var(-f)=Var(f) and closure under finite linear combinations.

items.title: Functions of bounded variation form an algebra
items.strategy: Use f(y)g(y)-f(x)g(x)=f(y)(g(y)-g(x))+g(x)(f(y)-f(x)) and boundedness of BV functions to prove Var(fg)<=M_f Var(g)+M_g Var(f). Cite the seminorm laws for sums and scalar multiples.

items.title: Every bounded-variation function on a compact interval is Riemann integrable
items.strategy: Use Jordan decomposition, the published integrability of monotone functions, and linearity of the ordinary integral. Keep this result before Stieltjes notation so the two integrals are not conflated.

items.title: Absolute continuity on a compact interval
items.strategy: Define absolute continuity using every finite family of pairwise nonoverlapping subintervals: small total length must force a small sum of endpoint oscillations. State the empty-family and singleton-interval cases explicitly. Use finite families because that is sufficient for the elementary theory here and avoids importing series into the definition.

items.title: $C^1$ implies Lipschitz, Lipschitz implies absolutely continuous, and absolutely continuous implies continuous and bounded variation
items.strategy: Bound a continuous derivative on the compact interval and apply the mean-value estimate. Sum a Lipschitz estimate over disjoint intervals for absolute continuity. A one-interval family proves continuity; subdivide [a,b] into finitely many intervals shorter than the delta for epsilon=1 and apply the definition on each piece to bound every variation sum.

items.title: Riemann–Stieltjes sums, upper and lower sums, and the Riemann–Stieltjes integral
items.strategy: Define tagged sums S(f,alpha;P,xi)=sum_{i<n}f(xi_i)(alpha(t_{i+1})-alpha(t_i)) and mesh-limit integrability. For nondecreasing alpha and bounded f also define upper and lower Stieltjes sums. Extend by zero on singleton intervals and sign reversal under reversed limits, matching the ordinary oriented integral.

items.title: Darboux criterion for Riemann–Stieltjes integrability with a nondecreasing integrator
items.strategy: Prove that bounded f is integrable with respect to nondecreasing alpha iff for every epsilon there is a partition whose upper-minus-lower Stieltjes sum is below epsilon. Refinement monotonicity and selection of near-extremal tags give both directions. Record the weighted-oscillation form used by composition and finite-discontinuity results.

items.title: The Riemann–Stieltjes integral is unique
items.strategy: If I and J both satisfy the mesh condition, choose one tagged uniform partition below both thresholds and apply the triangle inequality. Arbitrarily fine uniform partitions come from the Archimedean property. Avoid the deprecated notation for canonical naturals.

items.title: Refinement and tag-change estimates for Stieltjes sums
items.strategy: Group refined intervals inside each coarse interval and telescope alpha-increments. If f oscillates by at most omega on each coarse interval, bound the difference between sums by a universal constant times omega Var(alpha). Include the two-tag special case and zero variation.

items.title: A continuous integrand is Riemann–Stieltjes integrable against every bounded-variation integrator
items.strategy: Use uniform continuity and the refinement estimate to make all sufficiently fine tagged sums Cauchy. Obtain their common limit from completeness and compare arbitrary fine sums through a common refinement. Treat zero variation before dividing by a variation bound.

items.title: The total-variation bound for a Riemann–Stieltjes integral
items.strategy: From |f|<=M, bound every tagged sum by M Var(alpha), then pass to the mesh limit using preservation of order. State the bound whenever the integral exists, not only under the continuous-integrand theorem.

items.title: Linearity and interval additivity of the Riemann–Stieltjes integral
items.strategy: Use exact finite-sum identities for linearity in the integrand and integrator. For a cut c, insert c and splice partitions; continuity of the integrand at c controls the one interval changed by insertion. State both restriction and gluing directions with that hypothesis, and do not assert unconditional gluing across a common jump.

items.title: Riemann–Stieltjes integration by parts
items.strategy: Apply finite summation by parts to partition increments. Match the complementary tags and show the endpoint-tag error vanishes with the mesh. Conclude that existence of either integral forces existence of the other and their sum is f(b)alpha(b)-f(a)alpha(a).

items.title: A bounded-variation integrand is Riemann–Stieltjes integrable against every continuous integrator
items.strategy: First integrate the continuous function alpha against the BV function f by the continuous-integrand theorem, then apply Stieltjes integration by parts. This is the symmetric elementary existence rung.

items.title: A bounded function with finitely many discontinuities is Stieltjes integrable against a continuous bounded-variation integrator
items.strategy: Use Jordan decomposition for the integrator. The variation-function jump lemma makes both monotone components continuous. Isolate the finitely many discontinuities in intervals having arbitrarily small component increments; uniform continuity controls oscillation elsewhere. Apply the weighted Darboux criterion to each component and recombine by linearity.

items.title: A continuous function of a Stieltjes-integrable function is Stieltjes integrable for a nondecreasing integrator
items.strategy: For bounded f in R(alpha) with alpha nondecreasing and continuous phi on an interval containing f([a,b]), use uniform continuity of phi. Split partition intervals according to whether f oscillation is below a chosen threshold and charge the remaining alpha-increments to the weighted oscillation sum from the Darboux criterion.

items.title: Every bounded-variation function is uniformly approximable by step functions
items.strategy: Use the existence of finite one-sided limits and compactness to choose a finite partition on whose open subintervals f has small oscillation. A step function sampled on those intervals then approximates f uniformly. Keep all endpoint values explicit because they matter for Stieltjes integration at jumps.

items.title: Two bounded-variation functions with no common discontinuity are Riemann–Stieltjes integrable
items.strategy: Approximate the integrand uniformly by finite step functions whose jump points are continuity points of the integrator, using the regulated lemma and the no-common-discontinuity hypothesis. Prove directly that each such step function is integrable, then use the total-variation bound to show the resulting integrals and arbitrary tagged sums are Cauchy. Record the common-jump hypothesis as sharp via the companion counterexample, not as a dependency.

items.title: The identity integrator recovers the Riemann integral
items.strategy: For alpha(x)=x, every Stieltjes sum is the corresponding Riemann sum term by term. Use Darboux–Riemann agreement in both directions and include the oriented endpoint conventions.

items.title: A continuously differentiable integrator reduces Stieltjes integration to ordinary integration
items.strategy: On each partition interval apply the mean value theorem to alpha and compare the Stieltjes sum with a Riemann sum for f alpha'. Uniform continuity of alpha' and boundedness of integrable f make the error vanish. State alpha continuous on [a,b], differentiable inside, with alpha' extending continuously to the endpoints.

items.title: A countable pure-step integrator evaluates a continuous integrand as the absolutely convergent weighted sum of its values at the jumps
Change of variable for the Riemann–Stieltjes integral
items.strategy: Let phi:[c,d]->[a,b] be a strictly increasing continuous bijection. Map every partition and tag through phi; the Stieltjes sums for f against alpha and for f composed with phi against alpha composed with phi are identical. Uniform continuity of phi and its inverse transfers the mesh condition in both directions.

items.title: Young's partition estimate for rational Hölder exponents
items.strategy: For rational alpha,beta in (0,1] with alpha+beta>1, compare sums on successive dyadic refinements. Pair the inserted-point errors and bound their geometric decay by mesh^(alpha+beta-1). Sum the geometric tail to obtain a uniform Cauchy estimate. Treat zero Hölder constants and singleton intervals separately.

items.title: Young's Riemann–Stieltjes existence theorem for rational Hölder exponents
items.strategy: Apply the partition estimate to show dyadic sums converge and that arbitrary fine tagged sums have the same limit. State the result for rational exponents alpha,beta with alpha+beta>1 because those are the exponents the library currently defines; include integration by parts as a corollary of the general Stieltjes theorem.

items.title: Conventions and proved scope for bounded variation and Stieltjes integration
items.strategy: Collect the singleton and orientation conventions, the distinction between arbitrary BV and nondecreasing integrators in the Darboux criterion, the sharp common-jump obstruction, and the rational restriction on Young exponents. State that no Lebesgue–Stieltjes measure, a.e. differentiability, or real-exponent Hölder theorem is claimed here.

pages.title: Bounded Variation and the Riemann–Stieltjes Integral: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: $|x|$ is Lipschitz and absolutely continuous but not $C^1$ on $[-1,1]$
items.strategy: Use ||x|-|y||<=|x-y| for the Lipschitz claim and the hierarchy theorem for absolute continuity. Compute the unequal one-sided difference quotients at zero to refute differentiability.

items.title: $\sqrt{x}$ is absolutely continuous but not Lipschitz on $[0,1]$
items.strategy: For disjoint intervals, use sqrt(v)-sqrt(u)=(v-u)/(sqrt(v)+sqrt(u)) and split those meeting a short initial segment from those away from zero; choose the cutoff and total length to prove absolute continuity directly. Refute Lipschitz by the ratios sqrt(x)/x=1/sqrt(x) along x=1/n^2.

items.title: The Cantor function is continuous and of bounded variation but not absolutely continuous
items.strategy: Monotonicity gives variation one. At construction stage n, use the finitely many surviving closed intervals: their total length is (2/3)^n while the Cantor-function increment across each is 2^{-n}, so the sum of endpoint increments is one. This directly violates absolute continuity without measure theory.

items.title: A continuous function on $[0,1]$ can have unbounded variation
items.strategy: For x>0 set f(x)=x d(1/x,Z), where distance to the nonempty set Z is 1-Lipschitz, and set f(0)=0. Establish inline that 0<=d(t,Z)<=1/2, that the distance vanishes at integers and equals 1/2 at half-integers. Continuity away from zero follows from the Lipschitz distance map and the algebra of limits, while |f(x)|<=x/2 gives continuity at zero. Alternating zeros and peaks at reciprocals of consecutive integers and half-integers give variation sums dominating a fixed multiple of harmonic partial sums, hence unbounded variation.

items.title: A one-jump integrator evaluates a continuous integrand at the jump
items.strategy: For a<c<b, let alpha=0 left of c and alpha=1 at and right of c. Only the partition interval containing c contributes, and its tag tends to c with the mesh, so the integral is f(c). The same convention captures a jump at b; to capture a jump at a instead set alpha(a)=0 and alpha(x)=1 for x>a. State explicitly that a constant endpoint step has zero integral rather than silently assigning it an atom.

items.title: A finite-step integrator gives a weighted sum over its jumps
items.strategy: Write a finite-step integrator as a constant plus a finite linear combination of one-jump functions. For a continuous f, apply Stieltjes linearity and the one-jump computation to obtain the sum of f(c_j) times the jump at c_j. Check coincident endpoint jumps using the adopted one-sided convention rather than silently counting them twice.

items.title: A Riemann–Stieltjes integrable integrand need not be bounded
items.strategy: On [0,1], let alpha be the unit step at 1/2 and let f(0)=0, f(x)=1/x for x>0. Although f is unbounded near 0, every nonzero Stieltjes contribution comes from the interval containing 1/2, where f is continuous; prove directly from tagged sums that the integral is f(1/2)=2. This also explains why boundedness is an explicit hypothesis in the Darboux formulation but is not forced by a locally constant integrator.

items.title: The Cantor function defines a nonclassical Stieltjes integrator and $\int_0^1 1\,dc=1$
items.strategy: Use continuity and monotonicity of the Cantor function for existence. Every tagged sum of the constant integrand telescopes to c(1)-c(0)=1. Note that the computation uses neither a derivative nor measure theory.

items.title: A common jump can destroy Riemann–Stieltjes integrability
items.strategy: Take f=alpha to be the unit step at an interior c. On arbitrarily fine partitions with c inside one interval, choose its tag on opposite sides of c; the sums are respectively zero and one. Thus no mesh limit exists despite both functions being BV.

items.title: $\int_0^1 x\,d(x^2)=2/3$
items.strategy: Apply the continuously differentiable integrator reduction with alpha(x)=x^2, computing alpha'(x)=2x directly from the difference quotient, and reduce to the ordinary integral of 2x^2. Verify the cubic primitive directly from the difference quotient and evaluate by the working FTC.

items.title: A nonlinear reparametrisation leaves a Stieltjes integral unchanged
items.strategy: Apply Stieltjes change of variable to phi(t)=t^2 on [0,1], f(x)=x, and alpha(x)=x. The identity becomes integral_0^1 x dx = integral_0^1 t^2 d(t^2); compute the needed derivatives directly from difference quotients and verify both sides by the reduction theorem as a concrete check of the reparametrisation formula.

items.title: Young's theorem integrates a Hölder function of unbounded variation against itself
items.strategy: Let gamma=3/4, normalize the convergent widths w_n proportional to n^{-4/3} so their sum is one, and tile (0,1] by adjacent intervals of widths w_n accumulating at zero. On the n-th interval draw a symmetric triangular tent of height w_n^gamma and set f(0)=0. A same-tent/different-tent case split proves a uniform gamma-Hölder bound, while partitions through all peaks and endpoints have variation 2 sum_n w_n^gamma, a constant multiple of the divergent harmonic series. Since 2gamma>1, Young's theorem gives the integral of f against itself although f is not BV.

pages.title: Improper Integrals

items.title: Improper integrals over unbounded intervals
items.strategy: For f properly integrable on every compact truncation, define the integrals over [a,infinity) and (-infinity,b] by the appropriate finite real limits. Define convergence only when that limit is finite, and keep divergence to infinity distinct from convergence.

items.title: Improper integrals at a finite singular endpoint
items.strategy: Define left- and right-endpoint improper integrals by one-sided limits of proper truncations. Require proper Riemann integrability on every closed truncated interval; endpoint values themselves are irrelevant.

items.title: Improper integrals with several singular ends
items.strategy: Choose an interior split point and require every one-ended improper integral to converge separately; define the value as their sum. Cover an interior singularity and the whole real line. Independence of the split point is proved next, never built into the definition.

items.title: Improper convergence is independent of finite truncations and split points
items.strategy: Use additivity of the proper integral before taking limits. Show that moving a finite endpoint changes the value by exactly one proper integral, and compare two interior split points. Include the whole-line and interior-singularity cases.

items.title: Linearity of convergent improper integrals
items.strategy: Apply proper-integral linearity on every truncation and pass through the finite limits. For mixed integrals, apply the one-ended result to every separately convergent piece. State no infinity-minus-infinity convention.

items.title: Cauchy criterion for improper integrals
items.strategy: At infinity, prove convergence iff every sufficiently remote proper tail integral has absolute value below epsilon. Translate between the continuous truncation parameter and an Archimedean sequence, then use completeness. Give explicit left- and right-endpoint forms and check the first permitted truncation.

items.title: Absolute and conditional convergence of improper integrals
items.strategy: Define absolute convergence as convergence of the corresponding improper integral of |f| and conditional convergence as convergence without absolute convergence. For several singular ends, require the property separately at each end.

items.title: A nonnegative improper integral converges iff its truncated integrals are bounded
items.strategy: For f>=0, monotonicity makes the truncation function nondecreasing. It converges exactly when its range is bounded above, by the least-upper-bound property; in that case the improper value is the supremum of the truncated integrals. Give both infinite- and finite-endpoint forms.

items.title: Absolute convergence implies improper convergence
items.strategy: Use |integral_u^v f|<=integral_u^v |f| and the improper Cauchy criterion. Pass the proper triangle inequality to the limit for |integral f|<=integral |f|. Handle mixed integrals piecewise.

items.title: Tails of a convergent improper integral tend to zero
items.strategy: Split a convergent integral at the moving truncation and subtract the initial segment. Give both qualitative and epsilon forms at every type of singular end.

items.title: Comparison tests for improper integrals
items.strategy: If 0<=f<=g eventually and the improper integral of g converges, proper monotonicity and the nonnegative bounded-primitive criterion give convergence of f. Add the absolute form |f|<=g. Tail invariance removes any finite initial interval.

items.title: Limit comparison for positive improper integrals
items.strategy: If f/g tends to a finite positive L, trap it between L/2 and 3L/2 on a tail and apply comparison in both directions. State the corresponding one-sided endpoint form. Keep the L=0 and infinite-limit cases as one-way remarks only.

items.title: Integral test as an equivalence with an improper integral
items.strategy: For nonnegative nonincreasing f, combine the published proper-integral test with monotone convergence of the truncation integrals. Use Archimedean bracketing to show that convergence at integer truncations is equivalent to the full real-parameter limit. Write natural numbers directly in real expressions.

items.title: Truncated integrals of rational powers
items.strategy: For rational p>0, p!=1, choose p=m/q, derive the positive and negative integer power rules by induction, the product rule, and the reciprocal rule, and substitute x=t^q to obtain integral_A^B x^{-p} dx=(B^{1-p}-A^{1-p})/(1-p). For p=1, prove dyadic lower bounds sufficient for divergence without using logarithms.

items.title: The improper $p$-test for rational exponents
items.strategy: Use the truncated formula and rational-power limits to prove integral_1^infinity x^{-p} converges iff p>1 and integral_0^1 x^{-p} converges iff p<1. Treat p=1 by dyadic blocks, p<=0 by direct boundedness near zero and comparison with one at infinity, and preserve the rational-exponent scope.

items.title: Cauchy principal values at a finite singularity and on the real line
items.strategy: At an interior singularity remove symmetric epsilon-neighbourhoods; on the real line use symmetric [-R,R] truncations. Require proper integrability away from the singularity and state visibly that the coupled limit need not give separate improper convergence.

items.title: Separate improper convergence implies convergence of the principal value
items.strategy: Add the two independently convergent one-sided limits at a finite singularity or split the real line at zero. An epsilon estimate shows symmetric truncations approach the same sum. State that the converse fails without depending on the later example.

items.title: Dirichlet's test for improper integrals
items.strategy: Give two source-standard multiplier clauses. If f is locally integrable with bounded truncation primitives and g is nonnegative, nonincreasing, and tends to zero, apply the second mean value theorem on each tail and the improper Cauchy criterion. If f is continuous with bounded primitive, g is differentiable, g tends to zero, and g' is absolutely improperly integrable, apply proper integration by parts on truncations; the boundary term vanishes and the remaining integral converges absolutely by comparison. State both clauses at a finite singular endpoint as well.

items.title: Abel's test for improper integrals
items.strategy: If integral f converges and g is bounded and monotone, prove g has a finite endpoint limit L from completeness. Write g=L+h, orient h so it is nonnegative decreasing to zero, apply Dirichlet to fh, and use linearity for Lf.

items.title: A Dirichlet-type transfer criterion for divergence
items.strategy: Suppose u is continuous with divergent improper integral, v>0 is differentiable and tends to infinity, and v'/v^2 is absolutely improperly integrable. If integral uv converged, its truncation primitive would be bounded. Apply the differentiable-multiplier clause of Dirichlet's test to f=uv and g=1/v; the reciprocal rule gives g'=-v'/v^2 and forces integral u to converge, a contradiction.

items.title: Uniform oscillatory tail mass forces failure of absolute convergence
items.strategy: Let g be nonnegative monotone with divergent improper integral, and suppose an increasing sequence x_j tends to the singular end with bounded gaps and integral_[x_j,x_{j+1}] |f|>=delta. Monotonicity compares each block of |fg| with delta times an endpoint value of g; bounded gaps and divergence of integral g force the resulting block sum to diverge.

items.title: Monotone change of variable for Riemann-integrable functions
items.strategy: Let phi be monotone and differentiable on [c,d], with phi' Riemann integrable, and map [c,d] onto [a,b]. For bounded f on [a,b], prove that f is Riemann integrable iff (f composed with phi)|phi'| is Riemann integrable, and then the integrals agree. Treat the nondecreasing case by transporting partitions, applying the mean value theorem to each phi-increment, and comparing Darboux upper and lower sums; reduce the nonincreasing case by orientation. Include flat subintervals explicitly.

items.title: Change of variable in an improper integral
items.strategy: Let a monotone differentiable map phi carry one half-open or open interval onto another, with phi' locally Riemann integrable and f locally Riemann integrable. Apply the preceding monotone proper change-of-variable theorem on corresponding compact truncations and transfer the endpoint limits through monotonicity and surjectivity. Include decreasing maps through |phi'| and oriented limits; convergence or divergence is preserved, and convergent values agree.

items.title: Frullani's formula with its proper integral factor
items.strategy: For a,b>0 and continuous f on [0,infinity) with limit L, use proper substitutions on [epsilon,R] to rewrite the difference quotient integral as two integrals over the fixed interval between a and b. Uniform estimates send them to f(0) and L times integral_a^b dt/t. Keep this proper factor rather than invoking the later logarithm page.

items.title: Conventions and proved scope for improper integrals
items.strategy: Record separate convergence at every singular end, split-point independence, the difference between an improper integral and a principal value, and the rational restriction in the p-test. State Frullani's value using the proper integral of 1/t and make no Lebesgue-integrability or real-exponent claim.

pages.title: Improper Integrals: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: $1/x$ on $[-1,1]$ has principal value $0$ but no improper integral
items.strategy: Symmetric truncated integrals cancel exactly. Each one-sided integral diverges by the rational p-test at p=1, with opposite signs. This supplies the converse failure to principal-value agreement.

items.title: A step function whose improper integral is the alternating harmonic series
items.strategy: On [k,k+1) give the function value epsilon_k/(k+1), where epsilon_k is the published alternating sign. Integer truncations are alternating-harmonic partial sums; an arbitrary truncation differs from the preceding integer truncation by at most 1/(k+1), so the full real-parameter limit agrees. The absolute integrals are harmonic partial sums. Check local Riemann integrability from finitely many jumps on each compact interval and write natural numbers directly.

items.title: A positive continuous integrand can have finite integral while unbounded on every tail
items.strategy: Add pairwise disjoint triangular spikes to (1+x)^{-2}; the k-th spike has height k and area 2^{-k-2}. Verify a bounded primitive of the baseline directly with the algebra of derivatives. Local finiteness gives continuity, the geometric series bounds total area, and the center values are unbounded. Choose explicit rational supports so no choice principle is hidden.

items.title: $\int_0^1 x^{-1/2}\,dx=2$
items.strategy: Use the finite-endpoint rational p-test for convergence, evaluate the truncation as 2(1-sqrt(c)), and pass to c->0+. Explicitly contrast this with the undefined proper Riemann integral of the unbounded endpoint function.

items.title: The rational $p$-threshold reverses between zero and infinity
items.strategy: Apply both halves of the p-test at p=2 and p=1/2. Compute the two convergent values from the truncation formula and contrast them with divergence at the opposite endpoints.

items.title: A rational-kernel Frullani integral
items.strategy: Apply Frullani to f(t)=1/(1+t), obtaining integral_0^infinity ((1+ax)^{-1}-(1+bx)^{-1}) dx/x = integral_a^b dt/t. Simplify the apparent singularity at zero and compare the tail with x^{-2}; do not replace the proper factor by a logarithm.

items.title: $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(1+x^2)^{-1}\,dx$ converges absolutely
items.strategy: On |x|>=1 compare the nonnegative integrand with x^{-2}; the middle interval is a proper integral. Treat the two tails separately and do not evaluate the integral as pi, since inverse trigonometric functions occur later.

items.title: The substitution $x=1/t$ exchanges the two rational $p$-tests
items.strategy: Apply the improper substitution theorem to integral_1^infinity x^{-p} dx. The transformed integral is integral_0^1 t^{p-2} dt, so the convergence condition p>1 is exactly the finite-endpoint condition for exponent 2-p<1. Check the orientation and absolute derivative explicitly.

items.title: A bounded truncation function need not have an improper limit
items.strategy: Let f(x)=(-1)^k on [k,k+1). The integral from zero to an integer N alternates between zero and one, so its truncations are bounded but have no limit. This shows exactly why the bounded-primitive criterion requires a nonnegative integrand and why a term test has no direct integral analogue.

items.title: $|x-c|^{-1/2}$ has a convergent improper integral across an interior singularity
items.strategy: Split at c and translate each half to a finite-endpoint square-root integral. Apply the rational p-test separately, obtaining 2sqrt(c-a)+2sqrt(b-c) on [a,b]. Keep the two one-sided limits independent as required by the mixed definition.

items.title: $1/x^2$ has no finite Cauchy principal value at zero
items.strategy: Compute the two symmetric truncated integrals on [-1,-epsilon] and [epsilon,1]. Their sum is 2/epsilon-2, which is unbounded as epsilon tends to zero, so symmetry cannot rescue a nonnegative singularity.

items.title: Convergence range of $x^{-p}(1+x)^{-q}$ on $(0,\infty)$ for rational exponents
items.strategy: For rational p,q on the positive domain, compare the kernel with x^{-p} near zero and with x^{-(p+q)} at infinity using limit comparison and rational-power laws. Conclude separate convergence exactly when p<1 and p+q>1; x>0 and 1+x>0 make every displayed rational power well-defined without an extra sign hypothesis on p or q.

pages.title: R^n as a Normed Space; Vector-Valued Functions

items.title: A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
items.strategy: the page's opening definition, and it is where the SEAM with the published metric theory is fixed rather than left to chance. A norm on a vector space $V$ over $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-vector-space]]) is $\lVert\cdot\rVert : V \to \mathbb{R}$ with (N1) $\lVert v\rVert = 0$ iff $v = 0$, (N2) $\lVert\lambda v\rVert = \lvert\lambda\rvert\lVert v\rVert$, (N3) the triangle inequality. NONNEGATIVITY IS NOT AN AXIOM, exactly as in [[def-metric-space]]: derive it from (N2) and (N3) ($0 = \lVert v-v\rVert \le 2\lVert v\rVert$), and say that the verification of a candidate norm therefore has three things to check, mirroring [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]. Then prove the DICTIONARY CLAUSE: $d(u,v) := \lVert u-v\rVert$ is a metric on $V$ in the sense of [[def-metric-space]], and it is translation invariant and absolutely homogeneous, which an arbitrary metric need not be. Say plainly that not every metric on a vector space arises this way and give the reason a reader will need later (an arbitrary metric fails homogeneity); the bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]] is the published example, cite it. Values are real, never $+\infty$, as [[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]] fixed for metrics. LANDMARK.

items.title: The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$
items.strategy: concrete definition with its algebra proved inline; NO abstract inner-product-space theory is developed, and the reason is recorded. $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the function space of [[def-function-space]] on the von Neumann natural $n$, so $x_k := x(k)$ for $k<n$, and $\langle x,y\rangle := \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ is the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. VALID FOR EVERY $n$ INCLUDING $n = 0$, where it is the empty sum $0$ -- unlike the metric $d_\infty$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which needs $n \ge 1$; state that contrast here, because it is the first place on the page where the two index regimes diverge. Prove symmetry, bilinearity and positive definiteness ($\langle x,x\rangle = \sum x_k^{2} \ge 0$ with equality iff $x = 0$, by [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and [[lem-of-square-positive]]) directly from the finite-sum laws. Define $\lVert x\rVert_2 := \sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$ ([[thm-of-square-roots]]) and record that this is exactly the $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] at $y = 0$. SCOPE NOTE, to be stated in Remarks and reported: the general theory of inner product spaces is planned for a page EARLIER in plan order that is not yet built, so this item defines the concrete Euclidean form only and claims nothing about abstract inner product spaces.

items.title: Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation
items.strategy: direct, and the first clause is a CITATION, not a new proof: [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]] is published at order 16 and already gives the root form and the equality case in the symmetric proportionality sense; read it on disk and restate it in the vector notation of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would be the two-notions defect in its purest form. What IS new: (a) $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ satisfies (N1)-(N3) of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]], the triangle inequality following from Cauchy-Schwarz by expanding $\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2}$ -- or by citing [[thm-minkowski-finite]] at $p = 2$, and either route is acceptable provided one is chosen and the other mentioned; (b) the PARALLELOGRAM LAW $\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2}+\lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} = 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2}+2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2}$, by bilinearity; (c) POLARISATION $\langle x,y\rangle = \tfrac14\bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2}-\lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\bigr)$, which says the inner product is recoverable from the norm. Clauses (b) and (c) are what the companion page uses to show that $\lVert\cdot\rVert_1$ on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ comes from no inner product. LANDMARK.

items.title: The $p$-norms $\lVert x\rVert_p$ for rational $p \ge 1$, and $\lVert x\rVert_\infty$
items.strategy: definition, with TWO hypotheses that are not decoration and must both be stated where the object is introduced. (1) THE EXPONENT IS RATIONAL. $\lVert x\rVert_p := \bigl(\sum_{k<n}\lvert x_k\rvert^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}$ uses [[def-rational-power]], which is defined for rational exponents and nonnegative bases only; real exponents do not exist in this library at this point in the reading order ([[rem-real-exponents-deferred]]), and [[thm-minkowski-finite]] is itself stated for rational $p \ge 1$ for exactly that reason -- read it on disk. Do not write 'for $p \in [1,\infty)$'. (2) $\lVert x\rVert_\infty := \max\{\lvert x_k\rvert : k<n\}$ REQUIRES $n \ge 1$, since at $n = 0$ it is a maximum over the empty set; this is the same restriction [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] carries and for the same reason, and it propagates to everything on this page mentioning $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$. Existence of the maximum is [[lem-finite-set-has-max]] with [[def-max-min]]. Record $\lVert x\rVert_1$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2$ as the cases $p = 1, 2$ and note $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ agrees with [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]'s.

items.title: Each $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^n$, and the induced metrics are exactly $d_1$, $d_2$ and $d_\infty$ of the published metric-spaces page
items.strategy: direct, and THIS IS THE DICTIONARY ITEM THAT PREVENTS THE LEVEL-7 TWO-NOTIONS-OF-OPEN DEFECT FROM RECURRING HERE. Clause 1: (N1) and (N2) are computations from [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] and [[lem-rational-power-laws]]; (N3) is [[thm-minkowski-finite]] for rational $p \ge 1$, and the separate elementary argument for $p = \infty$ (a max of sums is at most the sum of maxes), which needs $n \ge 1$. Clause 2, the dictionary: for $p \in \{1,2\}$ and for $\infty$, $\lVert x-y\rVert_p = d_p(x,y)$ where $d_1,d_2,d_\infty$ are the PUBLISHED metrics of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]; the two sides are the same expression, so the proof is a one-line comparison of the definitions -- but the item must exist, because without it the library holds a norm-induced metric and a separately published metric on the same set with no recorded relation, and every later citation would have to guess which is meant. CONSEQUENCE, stated here and used repeatedly below: every published theorem about $(\mathbb{R}^n,d_2)$ -- completeness [[thm-euclidean-space-complete]], Heine-Borel [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], the compactness equivalences [[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] -- applies verbatim to the normed space of this page, WITH THEIR HYPOTHESIS $n \ge 1$ INHERITED UNCHANGED.

items.title: Equivalent norms, and the dictionary with equivalent metrics
items.strategy: definition plus a bridge clause. Two norms on $V$ are EQUIVALENT when there are reals $c, C > 0$ with $c\lVert v\rVert \le \lVert v\rVert' \le C\lVert v\rVert$ for every $v$. Prove that this is an equivalence relation (the reflexive and symmetric clauses are immediate; transitivity multiplies constants) and prove the DICTIONARY CLAUSE against [[def-equivalent-metrics]]: equivalent norms induce STRONGLY equivalent metrics in the sense of the published [[thm-metric-equivalence-hierarchy]], hence the same open sets, the same convergent sequences, the same Cauchy sequences and the same uniformly continuous maps. READ [[thm-metric-equivalence-hierarchy]] ON DISK BEFORE STATING WHICH TIER OF EQUIVALENCE IS MEANT: that item distinguishes topological equivalence, uniform equivalence and Lipschitz/strong equivalence, and the norm condition gives the strongest of them; asserting the wrong tier is a citation defect of exactly the dominant class. Note that the converse fails: a metric equivalent to a norm metric need not come from a norm, [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]] being the published witness.

items.title: The finite and reverse triangle inequalities for a norm; and for $n \ge 1$ every norm $N$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfies $N(x) \le C\lVert x\rVert_1$ and is Lipschitz, hence continuous, for $d_2$
items.strategy: direct, and it is the half of the norm-equivalence theorem that costs no compactness. Expand $x = \sum_{k<n} x_k e_k$ in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]], published, with the coordinate clause giving exactly $x_k = x(k)$ -- read clause 3 before citing) and apply (N2) and (N3) repeatedly: $N(x) \le \sum_{k<n}\lvert x_k\rvert N(e_k) \le C\lVert x\rVert_1$ with $C := \max\{N(e_k) : k<n\}$, a maximum over a nonempty finite set because $n \ge 1$ ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). The repeated triangle inequality is an induction on $n$ -- do it, or cite the finite-sum form if one is available for a general norm, but do not wave. Then $\lvert N(x)-N(y)\rvert \le N(x-y) \le C\lVert x-y\rVert_1 \le C\,\iota(n)^{1/2}\lVert x-y\rVert_2$ (the reverse triangle inequality for a norm, proved from (N3) exactly as [[lem-metric-reverse-triangle]] is for a metric, plus the comparison $\lVert\cdot\rVert_1 \le \iota(n)^{1/2}\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ from [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]] applied with the constant list $1$). So $N$ is Lipschitz for $d_2$ ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]) and continuous ([[thm-metric-regularity-hierarchy]], [[def-metric-continuity]]). STATE THE COMPARISON CHAIN $\lVert x\rVert_\infty \le \lVert x\rVert_2 \le \lVert x\rVert_1 \le \iota(n)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$ as a separate clause, with each inequality proved and each requiring $n \ge 1$ where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ appears.

items.title: For $n \ge 1$ all norms on $\mathbb{R}^n$ are equivalent
items.strategy: direct, by compactness of the unit sphere, and the hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from every step. Let $N$ be a norm; by [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]] it is continuous for $d_2$ and bounded above by $C\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ after rescaling the constant. The sphere $S := \{x : \lVert x\rVert_2 = 1\}$ is closed (preimage of a point under a continuous map, [[thm-metric-continuity-characterisations]]) and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]), hence COMPACT by [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] clause 2, and NONEMPTY because $n \ge 1$ gives $e_0 \in S$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) -- state the nonemptiness, it is exactly where $n \ge 1$ enters a second time and where a proof for $n = 0$ would silently break. By [[thm-extreme-value-metric]] the continuous $N$ attains a minimum $c$ on $S$, and $c > 0$ by (N1) since $0 \notin S$. Homogeneity (N2) transfers the two bounds from $S$ to all of $\mathbb{R}^n$: for $x \ne 0$ apply them to $x/\lVert x\rVert_2$; the case $x = 0$ is separate and trivial. Conclude equivalence with $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, hence with each other by transitivity ([[def-equivalent-norms]]). SAY WHAT FAILS IN INFINITE DIMENSIONS and that the companion page carries a witness; phrase it as a statement about this proof (the sphere is no longer compact), not as a claim about spaces the library has not built. LANDMARK.

items.title: For $n \ge 1$ a sequence in $\mathbb{R}^n$ converges iff each coordinate sequence converges, is Cauchy iff each coordinate sequence is Cauchy, and $\mathbb{R}^n$ is complete in every norm
items.strategy: direct, from the comparison chain and then a citation. Clauses 1 and 2 follow from $\lVert x\rVert_\infty \le \lVert x\rVert_2 \le \iota(n)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$ ([[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]): the $\infty$-norm bounds each coordinate and is bounded by the Euclidean norm, so the two convergence notions squeeze each other. Use [[def-metric-convergence]] and [[def-cauchy-in-metric]] as the definitions, and [[thm-metric-limits-unique]]... check the published id ([[lem-metric-limits-unique]]) before citing. CLAUSE 3 IS A CITATION AND MUST NOT BE REPROVED: [[thm-euclidean-space-complete]] clause 2 is published and states completeness of $(\mathbb{R}^n,d_2)$ FOR $n \ge 1$ ONLY; combine it with [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] and the dictionary of [[def-equivalent-norms]] to get completeness in every norm. DO NOT CITE THE PUBLISHED THEOREM FOR ALL $n$: this is the explicit level-8 instruction carried in the prose scaffold, and $n = 0$ is excluded because $d_\infty$, not the theorem, is what fails there. State the $n = 0$ situation once, correctly and separately: $\mathbb{R}^0$ is the zero vector space with a unique element, the zero norm is its only norm, and everything is trivially true -- but it is NOT covered by the published theorem, so it is asserted here from scratch or not at all. LANDMARK.

items.title: For $n \ge 1$ every bounded sequence in $\mathbb{R}^n$ has a convergent subsequence
items.strategy: direct, assembled from published theorems and NOT reproved by bisection. A bounded sequence lies in a closed bounded set, for instance a closed ball, which is compact by [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] clause 2; a compact metric space is sequentially compact by [[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] -- read that item on disk and cite the exact clause, since it lists several equivalent forms and their choice costs differ. Note the CHOICE LEDGER, in the style of [[rem-compactness-choice-ledger-metric]]: [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] is proved by bisection and uses no choice, while the general implication from compact to sequentially compact may; say which is used here and record it, rather than leaving the reader to guess. The prose scaffold's line 'Heine-Borel in $\mathbb{R}^n$ by bisection' describes work ALREADY PUBLISHED at order 120; this page cites it and adds only the sequential corollary. Also record the relation to the published one-dimensional [[thm-bolzano-weierstrass]], which is the case $n = 1$ under the identification of $\mathbb{R}^1$ with $\mathbb{R}$ -- state that identification explicitly, since $\mathbb{R}^1$ is a set of functions $1 \to \mathbb{R}$ and is not literally $\mathbb{R}$.

items.title: Vector-valued functions $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^m$, their limits and continuity, with the dictionary to the metric notions
items.strategy: definition whose whole job is to AVOID minting a third notion of continuity. For $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ (or $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$) and $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^m$ with $m \ge 1$, define the limit and continuity by the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ conditions with $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ in the codomain, and then PROVE, not assert, that these are exactly [[def-metric-continuity]] and the metric limit for the metrics of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], via [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]. Cite [[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]] as the precedent: the library already bridged the real and metric notions once and this item is the same move one dimension up. Define the components $f_i := \pi_i \circ f$ for $i<m$, where $\pi_i(y) := y_i$; note $\pi_i$ is $1$-Lipschitz since $\lvert y_i\rvert \le \lVert y\rVert_2$. Everything is stated for $m \ge 1$; at $m = 0$ the codomain has one point and every map is continuous, which is true but is not what the page is about -- say so once and move on.

items.title: A vector-valued function has a limit, or is continuous, if and only if each of its components does; with the algebra of continuous vector-valued functions
items.strategy: direct, from [[thm-componentwise-convergence-and-completeness]]'s comparison of norms, or directly from $\lvert y_i\rvert \le \lVert y\rVert_2 \le \sum_{j<m}\lvert y_j\rvert$. Give both directions explicitly: one is a single inequality, the other needs the sum over $m$ components and hence a $\delta$ chosen for $\varepsilon/\iota(m)$ -- and that division requires $m \ge 1$, which is the standing hypothesis. State the immediate consequences that later items use: the algebra of continuous vector-valued functions (sums, scalar multiples, and $\langle f,g\rangle$, using bilinearity of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]] componentwise), and that $x \mapsto \lVert x\rVert$ is continuous for every norm ([[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]). Do not restate the metric algebra results; cite them.

items.title: The derivative and the Riemann integral of a function $[a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^m$, defined componentwise and characterised intrinsically
items.strategy: one definition with two halves, each carrying its own well-definedness. DERIVATIVE: for $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^m$ and $c$ a limit point of $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, $f'(c)$ is the limit of the difference quotient $(f(x)-f(c))/(x-c)$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$ ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]); the limit is unique ([[lem-metric-limits-unique]]), and by [[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] it exists iff each $f_i'(c)$ exists, with $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$. Give the intrinsic form FIRST and the componentwise form as a theorem-clause, not the other way round -- the intrinsic form is the one that survives to the total derivative later. INTEGRAL: for $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^m$ define $f$ to be integrable when each $f_i$ is, and $\int_a^b f := \bigl(\int_a^b f_0,\dots,\int_a^b f_{m-1}\bigr) \in \mathbb{R}^m$, the component integrals being those of [[def-darboux-integral]] with the orientation convention of [[def-oriented-integral]]. Well-definedness is the observation that a tuple of reals is an element of $\mathbb{R}^m$, i.e. a function $m \to \mathbb{R}$ -- write it as such, since $\mathbb{R}^m$ is a function space and not a set of tuples in this library. Record linearity of both operations from [[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]] and [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]] componentwise.

items.title: For $a \le b$ and integrable $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^m$, $\lVert f\rVert_2$ is integrable and $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2$
items.strategy: direct, by the inner-product trick, which is shorter and sharper than any componentwise estimate. Put $v := \int_a^b f \in \mathbb{R}^m$. Then $\lVert v\rVert_2^{2} = \langle v,v\rangle = \sum_{i<m} v_i\int_a^b f_i = \int_a^b \langle v,f\rangle$ by [[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]] applied $m$ times and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; by Cauchy-Schwarz ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]) the integrand is at most $\lVert v\rVert_2\lVert f\rVert_2$ pointwise, so [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]] gives $\lVert v\rVert_2^{2} \le \lVert v\rVert_2\int_a^b\lVert f\rVert_2$; divide by $\lVert v\rVert_2$ WHEN IT IS NONZERO and handle $v = 0$ separately -- that case split is mandatory and is where the usual textbook proof is silently incomplete. INTEGRABILITY OF $\lVert f\rVert_2$ IS A SEPARATE OBLIGATION and must be discharged before the estimate: each $f_i$ is integrable, so $f_i^{2}$ and the sum are ([[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]], [[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]]), and the square root is continuous on $[0,\infty)$, so [[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]] applies. The hypothesis $a \le b$ is needed because the orientation convention flips the inequality; say so, exactly as the scalar case does. LANDMARK.

items.title: The mean value inequality: if $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is continuous and differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\lVert f'\rVert_2 \le M$, then $\lVert f(b)-f(a)\rVert_2 \le M(b-a)$
items.strategy: direct, by reducing to the scalar mean value theorem with a fixed auxiliary vector -- the proof that needs NO integrability hypothesis and therefore no dependence on the integral half of this page. Put $u := f(b)-f(a)$ and $\varphi(t) := \langle u, f(t)\rangle$, a real-valued function on $[a,b]$, continuous by [[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] and differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'(t) = \langle u, f'(t)\rangle$ by [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]] applied to the finite sum defining the inner product. By [[cor-mean-value-theorem]] there is $\xi$ with $\varphi(b)-\varphi(a) = \varphi'(\xi)(b-a)$, that is $\lVert u\rVert_2^{2} = \langle u, f'(\xi)\rangle (b-a) \le \lVert u\rVert_2 M (b-a)$ by [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]. Divide by $\lVert u\rVert_2$ when nonzero and treat $u = 0$ separately. THE EQUALITY FORM IS FALSE FOR $m \ge 2$: there need be NO $\xi$ with $f(b)-f(a) = f'(\xi)(b-a)$, and the companion page carries the witness. Say that here in exactly one sentence, WITHOUT asserting the false statement as though it were a theorem, and note that the $\xi$ produced above depends on $u$ and is therefore not a mean value point for $f$. LANDMARK.

items.title: If $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is differentiable with integrable $f'$ then $\int_a^b f' = f(b)-f(a)$; and a bounded derivative makes $f$ Lipschitz
items.strategy: direct, componentwise from [[thm-ftc-second-part]] together with [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]'s componentwise clause, then the Lipschitz bound from [[thm-mean-value-inequality]] applied on each subinterval $[s,t] \subseteq [a,b]$. State the Lipschitz conclusion in the sense of [[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]] for the metrics of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], not informally. Note the alternative derivation of the mean value inequality from [[thm-norm-inequality-for-the-vector-valued-integral]] when $f'$ is integrable, and say why the theorem above is proved the other way instead: it needs no integrability, so it applies to every differentiable $f$, and the companion page's witness for the failure of the equality form is differentiable but is not assumed integrable. That comparison is the item's real content and should be written out rather than left implicit.

items.title: Series of vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$, absolute convergence, rearrangement, and the set of rearrangement sums
items.strategy: definition, with an explicit agreement clause against the published one-dimensional theory. For a sequence $x : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}^n$ the partial sums are $s_N := \sum_{k<N} x_k$ (the finite sum in the vector space $\mathbb{R}^n$, which is the pointwise finite sum of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 1 -- cite it rather than minting a third finite sum), and $\sum x_k$ CONVERGES to $s$ when $s_N \to s$ in $(\mathbb{R}^n,d_2)$ ([[def-metric-convergence]]); it converges ABSOLUTELY when the real series $\sum\lVert x_k\rVert_2$ converges ([[def-series]]). A REARRANGEMENT is $\sum x_{\sigma(k)}$ for a bijection $\sigma : \mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$, verbatim as in the published [[def-rearrangement-and-unconditional-convergence]]; the SET OF REARRANGEMENT SUMS is $\mathcal{S}(x) := \{\,s : \text{some rearrangement converges to } s\,\}$. AGREEMENT CLAUSE, mandatory: at $n = 1$, under the identification of $\mathbb{R}^1$ with $\mathbb{R}$, these are exactly [[def-series]] and [[def-rearrangement-and-unconditional-convergence]] and $\mathcal{S}$ is exactly the set the published [[rem-rearrangement-in-higher-dimensions]] calls $\mathcal{S}(a)$; state the identification, since $\mathbb{R}^1$ is a function space and not literally $\mathbb{R}$. Everything here needs $n \ge 1$ because $d_2$ does.

items.title: An absolutely convergent series in $\mathbb{R}^n$ converges, and every rearrangement converges to the same sum
items.strategy: direct, in two clauses, both by reduction to the published one-dimensional theory rather than by re-running its proofs. Clause 1: absolute convergence gives a Cauchy sequence of partial sums, by the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]) and the Cauchy criterion for the real series [[thm-series-cauchy-criterion]]; then completeness ([[thm-componentwise-convergence-and-completeness]]) gives convergence.
