pages.title: Set Partitions, Stirling Numbers and Exponential Generating Functions

items.title: This page fixes the Stirling-sign and exponential-generating-function conventions
items.strategy: Record once and for all that $S(n,k)$ denotes the second-kind numbers, $c(n,k)$ the signless first-kind numbers, and $s(n,k)=(-1)^{n-k}c(n,k)$ the signed first-kind numbers used in the inversion theorem. Also record that every exponential generating function on this page lives in a commutative $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra, so the factorial denominators and the formal $\exp$ and $\log$ operations are meaningful.

items.title: Set partitions and blocks
The set partitions of a finite set form a finite set
items.strategy: Encode a partition of a finite set $A$ by the function that sends each element to the least element of its block after transporting the problem to $A=[n]$. This gives an injection from the set of partitions into the finite function set $[n]^{[n]}$, so every level used in the Stirling and Bell definitions is finite.

items.title: The Stirling numbers of the second kind and the Bell numbers
The signed and signless Stirling numbers of the first kind
The rising factorial
Exponential generating functions over a commutative $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra
Labelled classes, labelled product, and the constructions $\operatorname{SEQ}$, $\operatorname{SET}$, $\operatorname{CYC}$, and boxed product
The Stirling numbers of the second kind satisfy $S(n,k)=kS(n-1,k)+S(n-1,k-1)$
items.strategy: Distinguish whether the element $n$ is alone in its block or not. The singleton case strips off the block $\{n\}$ and contributes $S(n-1,k-1)$; otherwise $n$ is inserted into one of the $k$ blocks of a partition of $[n-1]$ into $k$ blocks, giving the factor $kS(n-1,k)$.

items.title: The Bell numbers satisfy $B_{n+1}=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom{n}{k}B_k$
items.strategy: For a partition of $[n+1]$, let $S$ be the block containing $n+1$. Choosing the other elements of $S$ is equivalent to choosing its complement among the first $n$ elements, and the remaining elements may then be partitioned arbitrarily. Summing over the possible complements gives the displayed binomial recurrence.

items.title: The Stirling numbers of the second kind are given by $S(n,k)=\frac{1}{k!}\sum_{i=0}^k(-1)^i\binom{k}{i}(k-i)^n$
items.strategy: Count surjections from $[n]$ onto $[k]$ by inclusion-exclusion and then forget the labels on the codomain blocks. Each set partition into $k$ blocks gives exactly $k!$ surjections after ordering the blocks, so dividing the surjection count by $k!$ yields the formula.

items.title: Ordinary powers expand in the falling-factorial basis by the second-kind Stirling numbers
items.strategy: For a positive integer $x$, the value $x^n$ counts all functions $[n]\to[x]$. Group these functions by the partition of $[n]$ into nonempty fibres of equal value: choosing the partition contributes $S(n,k)$ and assigning distinct values to its $k$ blocks contributes $x^{\underline{k}}$. Since both sides are polynomials in $x$ that agree at all integers $x\ge 0$, the identity holds in the polynomial ring.

items.title: The signless first-kind Stirling numbers satisfy their recurrence and expand the rising factorial
items.strategy: Insert $n$ into a permutation of $[n-1]$ either as a new $1$-cycle or inside one of the existing $n-1$ cycle positions to obtain the recurrence for $c(n,k)$. For the polynomial identity, compare the effect of multiplying $x^{\overline{n-1}}$ by $x+n-1$ with the same cycle-insertion recurrence; the shared initial conditions force the coefficients of $x^k$ to be $c(n,k)$.

items.title: The signed first-kind and second-kind Stirling numbers are inverse transition matrices
items.strategy: Use the second-kind expansion of $x^n$ in the falling-factorial basis and the first-kind expansion of $x^{\underline{n}}$ in the monomial basis. Substitute one into the other and use the fact that a finite linear combination of the falling factorials is uniquely determined by its values at $0,1,\ldots,n$ to read off the Kronecker-delta matrix identity and the corresponding inversion formula for sequences.

items.title: The labelled constructions translate into the usual exponential-generating-function rules
items.strategy: For labelled product, distribute labels by choosing the subset sent to the left factor, producing the binomial convolution that becomes multiplication after division by $n!$. The constructions $\operatorname{SEQ}$, $\operatorname{SET}$, and $\operatorname{CYC}$ are then the iterated labelled-product, unordered labelled-product, and cyclic labelled-product cases, while the boxed product records the unique globally smallest label and therefore integrates the derivative of the left factor against the right factor.

items.title: The two Stirling triangles have the expected vertical exponential generating functions
items.strategy: A partition into exactly $k$ nonempty blocks is a labelled set of $k$ nonempty labelled sets, so the labelled symbolic method gives $(e^x-1)^k/k!$. Likewise a permutation with exactly $k$ cycles is a labelled set of $k$ labelled cycles, giving $\bigl(\log(1/(1-x))\bigr)^k/k!$.

items.title: The exponential formula gives the Bell-number generating function
items.strategy: View a set partition as a labelled set of nonempty labelled sets. The labelled symbolic method therefore translates the specification $\operatorname{SET}(\operatorname{SET}_{\ge1}(\mathcal Z))$ into the formal identity $\sum_{n\ge0}B_nx^n/n!=\exp(e^x-1)$, and the coefficient of $u^k$ in the same argument recovers the block-count refinement.

items.title: Dobinski's formula expresses the Bell numbers as $B_n=e^{-1}\sum_{\ell\ge0}\ell^n/\ell!$
items.strategy: Start from the analytic Bell-number generating function $e^{e^x-1}=e^{-1}e^{e^x}$. Expand $e^{e^x}$ as the absolutely convergent double series $\sum_{\ell\ge0}e^{\ell x}/\ell!$, justify the rearrangement with the library's double-series Fubini theorem, then expand each $e^{\ell x}$ and compare the coefficient of $x^n/n!$.

items.title: Standard labelled specializations give involutions, ordered Bell numbers, and partitions without singletons
items.strategy: Apply the labelled symbolic method to three specifications: involutions are labelled sets of $1$-cycles and $2$-cycles, ordered Bell structures are sequences of nonempty labelled sets, and partitions with no singleton blocks are labelled sets of blocks of size at least $2$. The three resulting EGFs are then immediate symbolic translations.

items.title: The Lah numbers count ordered-block set partitions and expand the rising factorial in the falling basis
items.strategy: Let $L(n,k)$ be the coefficient of $x^{\underline{k}}$ in $x^{\overline{n}}$, so the expansion is a definition by basis coefficients. A combinatorial count chooses a permutation of $[n]$ and then cuts it into $k$ nonempty consecutive lists by placing $k-1$ separators among the $n-1$ gaps, yielding $L(n,k)=n!\binom{n-1}{k-1}/k!$. The same list-of-lists object is exactly a partition of $[n]$ into $k$ linearly ordered blocks.

items.title: Touchard's congruence: for prime $p$, $B_{n+p}\equiv B_n+B_{n+1}\pmod p$
items.strategy: Reduce the Bell recurrence modulo $p$ at the index $n+p-1$. The middle binomial coefficients in the $p$th row are divisible by $p$, so Pascal's rule gives the congruence $\binom{n+p-1}{k}\equiv\binom{n-1}{k}+\binom{n-1}{k-1}\pmod p$; splitting the Bell recurrence with this congruence collapses to the sum of the $n$th and $(n+1)$st Bell recurrences.

pages.title: Set Partitions, Stirling Numbers and Exponential Generating Functions — Examples

items.title: The set partitions of $[4]$ grouped by their number of blocks
items.strategy: List the partitions of $[4]$ explicitly and regroup them by block count. The example gives concrete values of $S(4,k)$ and $B_4$ without hiding the objects behind the notation.

items.title: $S(4,2)$ computed by recurrence, inclusion-exclusion, and direct listing
items.strategy: Evaluate the recurrence and the explicit inclusion-exclusion formula, then compare both answers with the direct list of two-block partitions of $[4]$. The point is to keep the three standard routes visibly synchronized on one concrete value.

items.title: The two Stirling triangles multiply to the identity through size $4$
items.strategy: Write the lower-triangular matrices $(S(n,k))_{0\le k\le n\le4}$ and $(s(n,k))_{0\le k\le n\le4}$ and multiply them explicitly. This makes the signed first-kind convention concrete and visibly shows why the signless first-kind numbers do not invert the second-kind matrix.

items.title: Ordered Bell structures and ordinary Bell partitions differ already on $[3]$
items.strategy: List the ordinary set partitions of $[3]$, then list the ordered partitions obtained by ordering the blocks. The example isolates the precise overcount that turns Bell numbers into ordered Bell numbers.

items.title: The involutions of $S_4$ are exactly the products of disjoint $1$-cycles and $2$-cycles
items.strategy: List the identity, the six transpositions, and the three products of two disjoint transpositions. The example is the finite witness for the symbolic description that leads to the EGF $\exp(x+x^2/2)$.

items.title: The Lah number $L(4,2)$ counts the ordered two-block partitions of $[4]$
items.strategy: Choose the underlying two-block partition shape and then order the elements inside each block, or equivalently cut permutations of $[4]$ into two nonempty consecutive lists. Both counts lead to the same value and make the ordered-block meaning of Lah numbers explicit.

items.title: The partitions of $[4]$ with no singleton blocks
items.strategy: List the partitions of $[4]$ all of whose blocks have size at least $2$. This is the first nontrivial coefficient check for the EGF $\exp(e^x-1-x)$.

items.title: Singleton blocks alone recover the EGF $e^x$
items.strategy: Interpret a partition all of whose blocks have size $1$ as a labelled set of atomic blocks. The example is deliberately trivial: it lets the reader see the labelled $\operatorname{SET}$ rule with no combinatorial noise.

items.title: FALSE: the Bell number counts ordered set partitions
items.strategy: Refute the claim on $[3]$ by counting ordinary partitions and ordered partitions separately. The failure is not small or asymptotic: it is already visible in the first nontrivial case.

items.title: FALSE: $S(n,k)$ counts surjections $[n]\to[k]$
items.strategy: Use a small example such as $n=3$, $k=2$ or the general factor-of-$k!$ comparison. The point is to isolate that $S(n,k)$ counts surjections only after forgetting the labels on the fibres.

items.title: FALSE: exponential generating functions multiply for every informal product of labelled structures
items.strategy: Give two labelled constructions whose decomposition into left and right factors is not unique after the labels are forgotten or reshuffled. The refutation is there to show that the labelled product hypothesis is mathematical content, not presentation.

items.title: Two distinct set partitions can have the same multiset of block sizes
items.strategy: Exhibit two partitions of the same finite set with the same block-size profile but different blocks. This is the local witness that integer partitions forget information that set partitions retain.

items.title: The second-kind inclusion-exclusion formula does not count permutations by cycle number
items.strategy: Compare a small value such as $S(4,2)$ with the number of permutations of $[4]$ having two cycles. The example isolates that the same-looking symbols cannot be interchanged across the first-kind and second-kind settings.

pages.title: Integer Partitions and the Twelvefold Way

items.title: Conventions for integer partitions, Ferrers diagrams, and the twelvefold-way table
items.strategy: Fix once that compositions mean positive parts, weak compositions allow zeros, n counts domain elements and k counts codomain values or boxes, and Ferrers diagrams are read in English convention. Also record that the page cites the published partition definition and Euler-product corollary rather than re-minting them.

items.title: Ferrers and Young diagrams, conjugate partitions, self-conjugacy, and the Durfee square
items.strategy: For a partition of a positive integer, define the Ferrers or Young diagram, the conjugate partition by transposing the diagram, self-conjugacy, the Durfee length, and the Durfee square.

items.title: The functions p(n), p_k(n), and the standard restricted partition families
items.strategy: Define p(n), p_k(n) for partitions into exactly k positive parts, and the families with parts at most m, with largest part m, with distinct parts, and with odd parts.

items.title: Conjugating a partition twice returns the original partition
items.strategy: Transposing a Ferrers diagram twice restores every row length, so conjugation is a well-defined involution on integer partitions.

items.title: Partitions with k parts are equinumerous with partitions whose largest part is k
items.strategy: Conjugation swaps rows and columns of the Ferrers diagram, so the number of rows becomes the number of columns and vice versa.

items.title: Partitions with at most k parts are equinumerous with partitions whose parts are all at most k
items.strategy: Sum the preceding bijection over largest part j at most k, or read both conditions directly from the same conjugation involution.

items.title: Exact-k partition recurrence
items.strategy: Split partitions of n into k parts according to whether a part equal to 1 occurs; remove one 1 in the first case and subtract 1 from every part in the second.

items.title: The direct multiplicity product and the published multiset proof give the same Euler product
items.strategy: Record the page-boundary agreement: the published corollary proves the Euler product through the symbolic multiset construction, while this page also keeps the direct summability proof that builds the infinite product coefficientwise from partition multiplicities.

items.title: Distinct-part product generating function
items.strategy: A distinct-part partition chooses each part size at most once, so specialize the published powerset product formula to one atom of each positive size.

items.title: Odd-part product generating function
items.strategy: Allow unrestricted multiplicity on the odd part sizes and no even part sizes, then specialize the published multiset product formula.

items.title: Euler's theorem by generating functions
items.strategy: Show the two product generating functions coincide by the standard cancellation of even factors, then compare coefficients.

items.title: Glaisher's bijection between odd-part and distinct-part partitions
items.strategy: Group equal odd parts into blocks of size powers of two to merge them into distinct parts, and reverse by splitting each part into its odd core times powers of two. The proof checks the forward and inverse constructions explicitly.

items.title: The generating-function proof and Glaisher's bijection prove the same Euler theorem
items.strategy: Record that the two routes count the same two classes and therefore agree coefficientwise and bijectively; the remark exists so the page does not carry two unrelated equalities.

items.title: Self-conjugate partitions correspond to distinct odd-part partitions
items.strategy: Read the hooks along the main diagonal of a self-conjugate Ferrers diagram; they are distinct odd lengths, and reversing the construction rebuilds the self-conjugate diagram.

items.title: Durfee-square decomposition of the partition series
items.strategy: Partition every Ferrers diagram into its Durfee square plus the cells to the right and below. Conjugation turns the lower piece into another partition with parts bounded by the Durfee length, yielding the standard sum over the Durfee size.

items.title: The unlabelled-to-unlabelled cells of the twelvefold way
items.strategy: A surjective placement is exactly a partition of n into k positive parts; an arbitrary placement is a partition into at most k parts, hence by conjugation into parts at most k; injectivity forces every part to be 1, so there is one class when n is at most k and none otherwise.

items.title: The twelvefold way
items.strategy: State one twelve-clause theorem using the fixed ball-box conventions. The labelled-to-labelled clauses cite the published function and injection counts and the Stirling surjection count; the indistinguishable-domain clauses cite stars-and-bars and compositions; the indistinguishable-codomain clauses use Stirling numbers and the preceding unlabelled-to-unlabelled theorem.

items.title: Euler's pentagonal number theorem by Franklin's involution
items.strategy: Work with partitions into distinct parts and the signed series over their lengths. Franklin's involution pairs all nonexceptional partitions with sign-reversing partners, leaving exactly the generalized pentagonal exponents.

items.title: Euler's pentagonal recurrence for partition numbers
items.strategy: Multiply the pentagonal series by the published Euler product for the reciprocal partition series, compare coefficients, and isolate p(n).

items.title: FALSE: p_k(n) is counted by C(n-1,k-1)
items.strategy: Refute by comparing partitions with compositions: the binomial coefficient counts ordered positive decompositions, and the companion page exhibits the mismatch already at n=5, k=3.

items.title: FALSE: conjugation itself is the distinct-parts to odd-parts bijection
items.strategy: Refute with a distinct-part partition whose conjugate has an even part. Glaisher's map, not ordinary conjugation, is the correct bijection.

pages.title: Integer Partitions and the Twelvefold Way — Examples

items.title: The eleven partitions of 6
items.strategy: List the partitions of 6 by largest part and group them by length to make the later conjugation picture visible.

items.title: Conjugation pairs the partitions of 6 by swapping length and largest part
items.strategy: Draw Ferrers diagrams for the partitions of 6 and transpose them to see the involution and the k-parts/largest-part correspondence.

items.title: A self-conjugate partition produces distinct odd diagonal hooks
items.strategy: Use a concrete self-conjugate Ferrers diagram, read off its diagonal hook lengths, and match them to a partition into distinct odd parts.

items.title: Glaisher's bijection on an odd-part partition
items.strategy: Start with a partition into odd parts with repeated entries, merge equal odd parts in powers of two, and show the image has distinct parts.

items.title: The partition (5,3,3,2,1) decomposes by its Durfee square
items.strategy: Mark the 3 by 3 Durfee square, then identify the right and lower remainders as partitions bounded by the Durfee length.

items.title: Euler's pentagonal recurrence computes p(10)=42
items.strategy: Run the recurrence with the generalized pentagonal offsets 1, 2, 5, and 7 and the alternating signs until every term is known.

items.title: The labelled-to-labelled cells of the twelvefold way at n=3 and k=2
items.strategy: Count all, injective, and surjective maps from a 3-element set to a 2-element set directly and compare with 2^3, 0, and 2!S(3,2).

items.title: The unlabelled-domain to labelled-codomain cells at n=3 and k=2
items.strategy: Interpret the classes as multisets, subsets, and positive compositions for 3 balls and 2 labelled boxes.

items.title: The labelled-domain to unlabelled-codomain cells at n=3 and k=2
items.strategy: Interpret the classes as set partitions with at most two blocks, with singleton blocks only, and with exactly two blocks.

items.title: The unlabelled-to-unlabelled cells at n=3 and k=2
items.strategy: List the partitions of 3 into at most two parts, note that there is no injective class because 3 is greater than 2, and identify the unique surjective class 2+1.

items.title: The recurrence gives p_3(5)=2
items.strategy: Apply p_3(5)=p_2(4)+p_3(2)=2+0 and exhibit the two partitions 3+1+1 and 2+2+1.

items.title: The partitions of 7 into distinct parts and into odd parts match
items.strategy: List both families for n=7 and pair them either by equal count or by Glaisher's map.

items.title: The partition (4,2,1) is not self-conjugate
items.strategy: Transpose its Ferrers diagram and observe that the conjugate is (3,2,1,1), not the original partition.

items.title: Conjugating (4,2,1) does not produce an odd-part partition
items.strategy: The partition (4,2,1) has distinct parts, but its conjugate (3,2,1,1) has an even part, so plain conjugation is not Glaisher's bijection.

items.title: Ignoring summability in the Euler product leads to illegal coefficient manipulations
items.strategy: Exhibit a naive coefficient computation in the infinite Euler product that informally sums infinitely many contributors to one coefficient, and contrast it with the finite-support justification.

pages.title: Incidence Algebras and Möbius Inversion

items.title: Intervals in a poset; locally finite, lower-finite and upper-finite posets
items.strategy: Define $[x,y]=\{z:x\le z\le y\}$. Locally finite means every such interval is finite; lower-finite and upper-finite mean every principal ideal and principal filter is finite. State that either one-sided condition implies local finiteness.

items.title: The incidence functions $I(P,R)$ of a locally finite poset and their convolution
items.strategy: For a locally finite poset $P$ and commutative ring $R$, define functions on comparable pairs and $(f*g)(x,y)=\sum_{x\le z\le y}f(x,z)g(z,y)$. Local finiteness and the general finite-sum definition make the operation well defined.

items.title: The delta and zeta incidence functions
items.strategy: Define $\delta(x,y)=1$ when $x=y$ and $0$ otherwise, and $\zeta(x,y)=1$ on every comparable pair.

items.title: Incidence convolution is associative and distributes over pointwise addition
items.strategy: Expand both bracketings as the same finite sum over pairs $x\le u\le v\le y$, using finite Fubini and bijective reindexing. Prove both distributive laws termwise.

items.title: Pointwise addition and convolution make $I(P,R)$ a ring with identity $\delta$
items.strategy: Obtain the pointwise additive abelian group from the function-ring construction, use the preceding lemma for multiplication and distributivity, and compute $\delta*f=f=f*\delta$.

items.title: If every diagonal value of an incidence function is a unit, recursive interval formulas construct both a left and a right convolution inverse
items.strategy: Use strong induction on the finite cardinality of $[x,y]$. Solve the equations $(f*g)(x,y)=0$ and $(h*f)(x,y)=0$ off the diagonal after isolating the diagonal unit. Then $h=h*(f*g)=(h*f)*g=g$, so the one-sided inverses coincide.

items.title: An incidence function is convolution-invertible if and only if every diagonal value is a unit
items.strategy: Necessity follows by evaluating an inverse equation on $(x,x)$. Sufficiency is the recursive construction. State the criterion for arbitrary locally finite $P$, including infinite $P$.

items.title: The integer-valued Möbius function $\mu_P$ of a locally finite poset
items.strategy: Take the inverse of the zeta function in $I(P,\mathbb Z)$. Existence and uniqueness come from the invertibility criterion because every diagonal value is $1$. This fixes the coefficient ring as $\mathbb Z$ and avoids a characteristic-dependent second notion.

items.title: The Möbius recurrence: $\mu_P(x,x)=1$ and both interval sums of $\mu_P$ vanish when $x<y$
items.strategy: Evaluate $\mu*\zeta=\delta$ and $\zeta*\mu=\delta$. Isolate the endpoint term to obtain the two recursive formulas and uniqueness.

items.title: Möbius inversion on a lower-finite poset, with the dual upper-finite form
items.strategy: For functions $f,g:P\to R$ into a commutative ring, prove $g(y)=\sum_{x\le y}f(x)$ iff $f(y)=\sum_{x\le y}\mu_P(x,y)g(x)$. Interchange the finite double sum and use the recurrence. State and prove the order-dual upper-finite form separately.

items.title: Both forms of Möbius inversion hold on every finite poset
items.strategy: Every principal ideal and filter is a subset of the finite ground set, hence finite; apply both halves of the preceding theorem.

items.title: The Möbius function of a product poset is the product of the Möbius functions
items.strategy: Show intervals in $P\times Q$ are Cartesian products of intervals and hence finite. Verify that the proposed product satisfies the Möbius recurrence using finite Fubini.

items.title: For $A\subseteq B$ in a finite Boolean lattice, $\mu(A,B)=(-1)^{\lvert B\setminus A\rvert}$
items.strategy: Identify the interval $[A,B]$ with a product of two-element chains indexed by $B\setminus A$, then apply the product theorem. Alternatively verify the recurrence by the alternating binomial sum; keep one route as the proof and the other as a Remark.

items.title: The complementary inclusion-exclusion formula is Möbius inversion on the Boolean lattice
items.strategy: Index intersections by subsets of the sieve index set, apply finite-poset Möbius inversion, insert the Boolean-lattice formula, and match every term and sign to the published complementary sieve identity.

items.title: On a finite chain, the Möbius function is $1$ on the diagonal, $-1$ on covers and $0$ on longer intervals
items.strategy: Induct on interval cardinality using the recurrence. The first nontrivial interval gives $-1$ and every longer interval has partial sum $1-1=0$ before the final term.

items.title: The divisibility poset of positive integers
items.strategy: Restrict integer divisibility to positive integers and verify reflexivity, antisymmetry and transitivity. Its interval $[a,b]$ consists of the positive integers $d$ with $a\mid d\mid b$.

items.title: The divisibility poset is lower-finite, and each divisor interval factorises as a product of finite chains of prime exponents
items.strategy: Positive divisors of $n$ lie in a finite initial segment. Use canonical prime factorisation and valuations to biject divisors with exponent tuples $0\le e_i\le v_{p_i}(n)$, preserving and reflecting divisibility.

items.title: The number-theoretic Möbius function $\mu(n)$ from prime factorisation
items.strategy: For $n\ge1$, set $\mu(n)=0$ when some prime square divides $n$, and $\mu(n)=(-1)^r$ when $n$ is a product of $r$ distinct primes. Use uniqueness of prime factorisation to prove $r$ and the value are well defined, including $\mu(1)=1$.

items.title: The number-theoretic Möbius function is the poset Möbius function of divisibility: $\mu(n)=\mu_{\mid}(1,n)$
items.strategy: Use the prime-exponent product decomposition of the divisor interval, the product theorem and the finite-chain formula. A repeated prime exponent contributes zero; otherwise every nontrivial chain contributes $-1$.

items.title: Classical Möbius inversion over positive divisors
items.strategy: Apply lower-finite poset inversion to the divisibility order and substitute the agreement theorem. Give both standard equivalent indexings, with $\mu(d)$ and with $\mu(n/d)$.

items.title: The number-theoretic Möbius function is multiplicative on coprime positive integers
items.strategy: For coprime $m,n$, divisors of $mn$ split uniquely into a divisor of $m$ and a divisor of $n$ by prime factorisation. Apply the product-poset theorem and the agreement theorem.

items.title: False: convolution defines an incidence algebra for every poset
items.strategy: Refute with the companion's poset having an infinite interval: convolution of the constant-one functions asks for an infinite sum not defined by the ring axioms.

items.title: False: $\mu_P(x,y)$ depends only on the cardinality of $[x,y]$
items.strategy: Compare a four-element chain, whose endpoint value is $0$, with the four-element diamond, whose endpoint value is $1$.

items.title: False: classical Möbius inversion and inclusion-exclusion are unrelated inversion principles
items.strategy: Refute by citing their common finite-poset inversion theorem and the two dictionary results for the divisibility and Boolean posets.

items.title: The full Möbius table of the Boolean lattice $2^{[3]}$
items.strategy: List comparable pairs by rank difference and assign $1,-1,1,-1$ according to the Boolean-lattice formula, checking representative recurrence sums.

items.title: The Möbius table of a four-element chain
items.strategy: Compute recursively: diagonal entries are $1$, cover entries are $-1$, and all entries spanning at least two covers are $0$.

items.title: The Möbius function on the divisor poset of $12$ and its agreement with $\mu(1),\mu(2),\mu(3),\mu(4),\mu(6),\mu(12)$
items.strategy: Draw the divisor order, compute from the recurrence, and compare each value with the prime-factor definition.

items.title: The endpoint Möbius value of the four-element diamond is $1$
items.strategy: Compute the two cover values as $-1$, then solve $1-1-1+\mu(\bot,\top)=0$.

items.title: Möbius inversion of $\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)=n$ gives $\varphi(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)(n/d)$
items.strategy: Apply classical Möbius inversion to the totient divisor-sum theorem and verify the formula numerically at $n=12$.

items.title: A poset with a bottom, a top and countably many incomparable middle elements has an infinite interval, so convolution of constant-one functions is not defined
items.strategy: Use the tagged set $\{\bot,\top\}\cup(\mathbb N\times\{m\})$, with every middle element strictly between the endpoints. The endpoint convolution sum has one term for each middle element.

items.title: On a two-element chain, an incidence function with a zero diagonal value is not convolution-invertible
items.strategy: Set $f(0,0)=0$ and evaluate any purported inverse equation on $(0,0)$; the diagonal product remains zero rather than one.

items.title: A four-element chain and a four-element diamond have equal-size endpoint intervals but Möbius values $0$ and $1$
items.strategy: Place the two preceding computations side by side and identify the different internal order structures that change the recurrence.

pages.title: Counting up to Symmetry: Burnside and Pólya

items.title: Naming conventions for Burnside, Cauchy-Frobenius, and Redfield-Pólya
items.strategy: Record that this page cites the published orbit-counting theorem by its on-disk name Cauchy-Frobenius, while noting the alternative names Burnside's lemma and Redfield-Pólya only as terminology.

items.title: The cycle index of a finite permutation group
items.strategy: For a finite group acting by permutations on a finite set, define j_k(g) as the number of k-cycles of g and set the cycle index to be the average of the corresponding monomials in the published multivariate polynomial ring.

items.title: Colourings, weight functions, and the pattern inventory
items.strategy: Define the induced action on colourings X to C, the weight of a colouring from a commutative-ring-valued weight on colours, and the orbit-sum called the pattern inventory.

items.title: The cycle-index series of a graded family of S_n-actions
items.strategy: Take a sequence A=(A_n) of finite sets where each A_n carries an action of S_n. Define its cycle-index series coefficientwise by setting the coefficient of t^n to be the rational polynomial (1/n!) times the sum over sigma in S_n of the number of fixed structures in A_n times the cycle-type monomial of sigma; this keeps every coefficient in Q[s_1,...,s_n].

items.title: Fixed colourings factor by cycle type
items.strategy: A colouring is fixed precisely when it is constant on every cycle of g. For plain colourings each cycle chooses one colour; for weighted inventory the contribution of a k-cycle is the kth power sum of the colour weights.

items.title: Pólya's enumeration theorem
items.strategy: Apply the published Cauchy-Frobenius orbit count to the induced action on colourings and replace each fixed-point count by the cycle-type formula from the preceding lemma.

items.title: The weighted pattern inventory is the cycle index evaluated at the power sums
items.strategy: Combine the weighted fixed-colouring factorization with the weighted orbit average over the acting group, obtaining the cycle index after substitution of the power sums.

items.title: The cycle index of the cyclic group C_n
items.strategy: Classify rotations of an n-gon by gcd(r,n): a rotation by r has gcd(r,n) cycles, and the number of rotations with a given gcd is an Euler-totient count.

items.title: The cycle index of the dihedral group D_{2n}
items.strategy: Average the cyclic rotations with the two reflection types. Odd and even n differ because even-gon reflections split into vertex-axis and edge-axis cases.

items.title: Permutations with a fixed cycle type are counted by the standard factorial denominator
items.strategy: Choose the elements supporting each cycle length, order each k-cycle up to cyclic rotation, and divide again by permutations of the equal-length cycles. The result is the usual n! divided by the product over k of k^{m_k} m_k!.

items.title: The cycle index of S_n is the sum over cycle types
items.strategy: Group permutations by cycle type, insert the same-page cycle-type counting lemma, and divide by n! in the defining average.

items.title: The cycle index of A_n is the parity-filtered symmetric-group sum
items.strategy: Filter the symmetric-group cycle-type sum by the sign condition from disjoint cycles and renormalize by |A_n|=n!/2; equivalently add the parity-twisted symmetric-group sum to the untwisted one and handle the small n cases separately.

items.title: Necklace count from the cyclic-group cycle index
items.strategy: Apply Pólya's theorem to the rotation action of C_n on bead positions and substitute the number of colours for every cycle-index variable.

items.title: The cycle-index necklace count agrees with the published CYC count
items.strategy: Compare the present Pólya derivation with the earlier symbolic-method necklace formula so the library has one necklace sequence with two explained derivations.

items.title: Bracelet count from the dihedral-group cycle index
items.strategy: Apply Pólya's theorem to the full dihedral symmetry group of the n-gon, so reflections and rotations are both counted.

items.title: Pólya enumeration counts edge-set orbits on the 2-subsets of [n]
items.strategy: Let S_n act on the set of 2-element subsets of [n]. A 0-1 colouring of these pairs is an edge-set, and the weighted pattern inventory with the substitution 1 + x^i counts its orbits under relabelling.

items.title: The symmetric-group cycle-index series is coefficientwise exponential
items.strategy: Apply the cycle-index-series definition to the family with one size-n structure fixed by every permutation, so the t^n coefficient is Z(S_n). For fixed n, only the variables s_1 through s_n affect the coefficient of t^n in exp(sum_{k>=1} s_k t^k/k), so truncate to k<=n and expand coefficientwise to recover the same cycle-type denominator sum.

items.title: FALSE: nonisomorphic groups acting on finite sets always have different cycle indices
items.strategy: Refute with two nonisomorphic groups acting through the same quotient permutation action. For example, C_4 and V_4 can both act on four points through a quotient onto C_2, yielding the same multiset of identity and transposition permutations.

items.title: FALSE: the cycle index of a permutation action determines the abstract group
items.strategy: Use the same nonfaithful quotient-action witness as above: equal cycle index need not force isomorphic acting groups.

items.title: FALSE: every weight substitution collapses the pattern inventory to the plain orbit count
items.strategy: Refute with a weight that remembers a colour statistic, so the resulting polynomial distinguishes orbit types instead of collapsing to a single total.

items.title: C_4 and V_4 can share the same cycle index through nonfaithful actions

pages.title: Extremal Graph Theory

items.title: Ordinary-subgraph extremal number $\operatorname{ex}(n,H)$, Turán graph $T_{n,r}$, and balanced blowup $H[s]$
items.strategy: Fix ordinary, not induced, subgraph containment. For a forbidden graph $H$ with at least one edge, define $\operatorname{ex}(n,H)$ as the maximum edge count of an $n$-vertex graph containing no ordinary copy of $H$; the edgeless $n$-vertex graph makes the finite candidate set nonempty. Define $T_{n,r}$ as the complete $r$-partite graph whose part sizes differ by at most one, allowing empty parts when $r>n$. Define $H[s]$ by replacing every vertex of $H$ with an independent $s$-set and every edge with all cross edges. State the induced-free terminology disagreement in a convention remark and never use bare '$H$-free' ambiguously.

items.title: The exact edge count of $T_{n,r}$ and the unique balancing maximum among complete $r$-partite graphs
items.strategy: If $n=qr+a$ with $0\le a<r$, count missing within-part pairs to obtain $e(T_{n,r})=\binom n2-(r-a)\binom q2-a\binom{q+1}2$. Moving one vertex from a part at least two larger than another increases the edge count; iterate to balance. Equality forces all nonempty part sizes to differ by at most one, giving uniqueness up to graph isomorphism. Include $n=0$, $r=1$, and $r>n$.

items.title: Mantel's theorem: $\operatorname{ex}(n,K_3)=\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$, uniquely attained by $T_{n,2}$
items.strategy: Give an independent induction, not a reference to Turán. For a triangle-free graph with an edge $uv$, the two open neighbourhoods are disjoint apart from their opposite endpoints, so $\deg u+\deg v\le n$. Delete $u,v$, apply induction to the remaining $n-2$ vertices, and restore exactly $\deg u+\deg v-1$ incident edges. Verify the floor recurrence. Track equality: the smaller graph is balanced complete bipartite and the degree-sum equality forces $u,v$ into opposite parts with every allowed cross edge, yielding $T_{n,2}$. Handle edgeless graphs and $n=0,1,2$ separately.

items.title: Zykov symmetrisation turns an extremal clique-free graph into a complete multipartite graph without losing edges
items.strategy: For nonadjacent vertices $u,v$, replacing the lower-degree vertex by a twin of the higher-degree vertex preserves $K_{r+1}$-avoidance and does not decrease edges. Apply the operation to degree classes with a termination statistic: first maximise edges, then the sum of squares of twin-class sizes. At termination nonadjacency is an equivalence relation, so the graph is complete multipartite. Record the equality case needed later: an edge-maximiser can be symmetrised without changing its edge count, and reversing an equality-preserving step cannot create a second nonisomorphic maximiser once balanced part sizes are forced.

items.title: Turán's theorem with equality: $\operatorname{ex}(n,K_{r+1})=e(T_{n,r})$, and $T_{n,r}$ is the unique extremal graph
items.strategy: Use Zykov symmetrisation to reduce an extremal $K_{r+1}$-avoiding graph to a complete $k$-partite graph with $k\le r$. The balancing lemma shows the largest such edge count is $e(T_{n,r})$ and identifies the balanced parts. For equality, carry the equality conditions through symmetrisation (or present the standard duplication proof directly) to show the original graph was already complete multipartite and balanced. State the exact quotient-remainder formula from the preceding lemma, not just the asymptotic bound. Cover $r=1$, $n=0$, and $r\ge n$.

items.title: Turán graphs give the Ramsey lower bound $R(s,t)\ge(s-1)(t-1)+1$
items.strategy: On $(s-1)(t-1)$ vertices split into $t-1$ classes of size $s-1$, colour within-class pairs red and cross-class pairs blue. Red cliques have size at most $s-1$, while blue cliques use at most one vertex from each of the $t-1$ classes. Thus there is neither a red $s$-set nor a blue $t$-set. Identify the blue graph as $T_{(s-1)(t-1),t-1}$ and translate the witness through the published arrow and Ramsey-number definitions. Check $s,t\ge2$.

items.title: Edge density and the asymptotic notations $O$, $o$, $\Omega$, and $\Theta$ for extremal functions
items.strategy: For an $n$-vertex graph with $n\ge2$, define edge density as $e(G)/\binom n2$. Define $f=O(g)$ and $f=o(g)$ with explicit constants and quantifiers as $n\to\infty$, and define $\Omega,\Theta$ from $O$. Fix that all forbidden graphs and integer parameters are held constant in asymptotic statements. Avoid defining density for $n<2$, where the denominator vanishes.

items.title: $\operatorname{ex}(n,H)/\binom n2$ is nonincreasing for $n\ge2$
items.strategy: For a fixed forbidden graph $H$ with at least one edge, take an extremal $(n+1)$-vertex graph and double-count pairs $(v,e)$ where edge $e$ remains after deleting vertex $v$. Every $n$-vertex induced subgraph contains no ordinary copy of $H$, so its edges are at most $\operatorname{ex}(n,H)$. Simplify the resulting natural-number inequality before dividing by positive binomial coefficients. State $n\ge2$.

items.title: Every finite graph with an edge has a Turán density $\pi(H)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{ex}(n,H)/\binom n2$
items.strategy: The normalized sequence is nonincreasing and lies in $[0,1]$, hence has an infimum and converges to it. Define that limit to be $\pi(H)$. Give the equivalent epsilon-threshold formulation used by supersaturation. Keep the standing hypothesis that $H$ has at least one edge, so the extremal candidate family is never empty.

items.title: Above Turán density, a graph contains a positive-density family of copies of the forbidden graph
items.strategy: For a fixed graph $H$ with at least one edge and $\varepsilon>0$, choose a fixed sample size $m$ at which the extremal density is below $\pi(H)+\varepsilon/2$. In an $n$-vertex graph of density at least $\pi(H)+\varepsilon$, average edges over all $m$-vertex subsets to show a positive fraction are above threshold and contain $H$. Double-count each unlabelled copy across the $m$-sets containing it to obtain $\delta n^{v(H)}$ copies. Track constants and $n\ge n_0$ explicitly.

items.title: The Zarankiewicz number $z(m,n;s,t)$ for a forbidden $K_{s,t}$ in a bipartite graph
items.strategy: For fixed disjoint sides $A,B$ of sizes $m,n$, define $z(m,n;s,t)$ as the maximum number of cross edges with no ordinary $K_{s,t}$ whose $s$-side lies in $A$ and $t$-side in $B$. Record the transpose symmetry $z(m,n;s,t)=z(n,m;t,s)$ and the relation to $\operatorname{ex}(N,K_{s,t})$. Require positive $s,t$; permit empty host sides.

items.title: The Kővári–Sós–Turán common-neighbour count and the discrete convexity lower bound for degree sums
items.strategy: In a bipartite $K_{s,t}$-avoiding graph with sides $A,B$, count pairs $(S,b)$ with $S\in[A]^s$ and $S\subseteq N(b)$. The upper count is $(t-1)\binom{|A|}{s}$ and the lower expression is $\sum_{b\in B}\binom{\deg b}{s}$. Prove the needed lower bound at a fixed total degree by smoothing integer degrees: moving one unit from a value at least two larger to the smaller value cannot increase the sum. This avoids citing real Jensen and includes average degree below $s-1$.

items.title: Kővári–Sós–Turán: exact bipartite and ordinary-graph upper bounds for excluding $K_{s,t}$
items.strategy: For positive $s\le t$, combine the common-neighbour bound with the discrete convex estimate to prove $z(m,n;s,t)\le (t-1)^{1/s}m n^{1-1/s}+(s-1)n$ in the stated orientation. Apply the symmetric count directly to an $N$-vertex graph to obtain $\operatorname{ex}(N,K_{s,t})\le\tfrac12(t-1)^{1/s}N^{2-1/s}+\tfrac12(s-1)N$, and hence $O_{s,t}(N^{2-1/s})$. Check $s=1$, $N=0$, and the side-orientation convention.

items.title: Every bipartite graph with at least one edge has Turán density zero
items.strategy: If $H$ has bipartition sizes $s,t$, then $H$ is an ordinary subgraph of $K_{s,t}$, so every graph excluding $H$ also excludes $K_{s,t}$. Apply KST and divide by $\binom n2$ to get a quantity tending to $0$. Exclude the edgeless case explicitly and allow isolated vertices by enlarging the two complete parts as needed.

items.title: $r$-uniform hypergraphs and complete balanced $r$-partite $r$-graphs $K^{(r)}_{s,\ldots,s}$
items.strategy: Define an $r$-uniform hypergraph as a finite vertex set with edges in $[V]^r$. Define ordinary subhypergraph containment, the extremal number, and $K^{(r)}_{s,\ldots,s}$ on $r$ disjoint $s$-sets with every transversal an edge. State the graph case $r=2$ as a dictionary, and require $r\ge2$, $s\ge1$ for subsequent use.

items.title: Hypergraph KST: $\operatorname{ex}(n,K^{(r)}_{s,\ldots,s})=O_{r,s}(n^{r-1/s^{r-1}})=o(n^r)$
items.strategy: Induct on $r$. The base $r=2$ is KST. For the inductive step count copies of $K^{(r)}_{s,1,\ldots,1}$ in two ways: fixing the $s$-set leaves an $(r-1)$-uniform link hypergraph excluding $K^{(r-1)}_{s,\ldots,s}$, while fixing an $(r-1)$-tuple contributes a binomial coefficient of its codegree. Use the same smoothing inequality to compare the lower count with the average codegree. Solve the exponent recurrence and state only the little-$o$ consequence where it is used by Erdős–Stone.

items.title: Every finite graph $H$ with $\chi(H)=r$ is an ordinary subgraph of $K_r[s]$ for some $s$
items.strategy: Take a proper $r$-colouring, let $s$ be the largest colour-class size, inject each colour class into one of the $s$-vertex blowup parts, and observe that every edge joins different colours and therefore maps to a cross edge. Handle $H$ null separately, and for nonnull $H$ use the published existence and boundary convention for $\chi(H)$.

items.title: Erdős–Stone for balanced blowups: $\pi(K_r[s])=1-1/(r-1)$ for $r\ge2$
items.strategy: The lower bound is the $(r-1)$-partite Turán graph. For the upper bound, a graph with density above $\pi(K_r)+\varepsilon$ contains $\delta n^r$ copies of $K_r$ by supersaturation. Form the $r$-uniform hypergraph whose edges are those $r$-cliques. Hypergraph KST forces a $K^{(r)}_{s,\ldots,s}$, whose supporting graph is $K_r[s]$. Convert the epsilon statement to the density formula and keep $s=1$ as the Turán theorem boundary.

items.title: Erdős–Stone–Simonovits: $\operatorname{ex}(n,H)=(1-1/(\chi(H)-1)+o(1))\binom n2$ for every graph with an edge
items.strategy: Let $r=\chi(H)\ge2$. The graph $T_{n,r-1}$ contains no $H$, giving the lower bound. Embed $H$ into a balanced blowup $K_r[s]$; excluding $H$ implies excluding that blowup, so Erdős–Stone gives the matching upper bound. State the equivalent epsilon form with an explicit $n_0(H,\varepsilon)$ and treat bipartite $r=2$ consistently as density $0$. The edgeless graph is excluded from the theorem statement.

items.title: The asymptotic extremal density is determined exactly by chromatic number: $\pi(H)=1-1/(\chi(H)-1)$
items.strategy: Divide the Erdős–Stone–Simonovits asymptotic by $\binom n2$ and use existence of Turán density. Spell out the dichotomy: positive density exactly when $\chi(H)\ge3$, while every bipartite graph with an edge has density $0$, agreeing with KST. This is the short citable chromatic-number formulation required downstream.

pages.title: Extremal Graph Theory — Examples

items.title: $T_{10,3}=K_{3,3,4}$ has $33$ edges and is the unique $10$-vertex $K_4$-extremal graph
items.strategy: Use $10=3\cdot3+1$ in the exact edge formula, also count the three cross products $3\cdot3+3\cdot4+3\cdot4=33$, and invoke the equality statement of Turán's theorem. Display a $K_4$ obstruction by the three parts.

items.title: $K_{3,4}$ realises $\operatorname{ex}(7,K_3)=12$
items.strategy: Count $3\cdot4=12=\lfloor49/4\rfloor$, note that a bipartite graph contains no triangle, and apply Mantel's exact equality characterization.

items.title: Deleting one edge from $K_{3,4}$ gives a triangle-free graph one edge below the Mantel threshold
items.strategy: Delete a displayed cross edge, recount $11$ edges, and verify triangle-freeness survives. Compare with the unique $12$-edge equality case to distinguish exact extremality from near-extremality without claiming a stability theorem.

items.title: A Turán-partition colouring witnesses $R(4,3)\ge7$
items.strategy: Partition six vertices into three pairs, colour within pairs blue and cross pairs red. A red clique uses at most one vertex per pair, so has size at most $3$; a blue clique lies within one pair, so has size at most $2$. Translate this explicit colouring to failure of $6\to(4,3)^2$.

items.title: The five-cycle is $K_{2,2}$-avoiding and shows the KST problem is not just a complete-bipartite construction
items.strategy: List the five cycle edges and observe that any two vertices have at most one common neighbour, whereas a $K_{2,2}$ would give two. Record its edge count and compare it with the KST upper bound at $N=5$ without asserting the bound is sharp there.

items.title: Every triangle-free graph is bipartite
items.strategy: Instantiate the published cycle definition at $n=5$ and inspect its five edges to show that $C_5$ has no triangle. The published odd-cycle characterisation of bipartite graphs then shows that $C_5$ is not bipartite. This separates Mantel's equality classification from the much weaker hypothesis of triangle-freeness without depending on the neighbouring AI-generated example.

items.title: The Petersen graph has chromatic number $3$, so its Turán density is $1/2$
items.strategy: Use the published two-subset model to exhibit an odd $5$-cycle, ruling out two colours, and give an explicit three-colouring of all ten vertices. Apply the chromatic-density corollary to obtain $1-1/(3-1)=1/2$.

items.title: Every odd cycle $C_{2k+1}$ has Turán density $1/2$
items.strategy: For $k\ge1$, alternate two colours around the cycle until the closing edge forces a third colour, proving $\chi(C_{2k+1})=3$. Apply the chromatic-density corollary to obtain $1-1/(3-1)=1/2$, and contrast this with the zero density of bipartite graphs without claiming an exact finite extremal number.

items.title: Erdős–Stone–Simonovits determines the extremal number for every graph
items.strategy: Take $H=K_{2,2}$, for which $\chi(H)=2$. Erdős–Stone–Simonovits then gives only $\operatorname{ex}(n,H)=o(n^2)$, while the page's Kővári–Sós–Turán theorem supplies the strictly sharper upper bound $O(n^{3/2})$. Thus the density theorem determines the quadratic leading term but not the finite extremal number or even its order of growth in the bipartite case.

pages.title: Finite Probability Spaces and Random Variables

items.title: Finite probability spaces, outcome weights, events, and event probabilities
Normalization, nonnegativity, monotonicity, complements, and differences in a finite probability space
items.strategy: Expand every probability as a finite sum of outcome weights. Split the ambient finite set into an event and its complement, and split a larger event into a smaller event and its difference. Nonnegativity of every weight gives monotonicity. Explicitly include the empty event and events of probability zero, whose outcomes need not be absent.

items.title: Probability is additive on every finite pairwise-disjoint family of events
items.strategy: Reindex the sum over a disjoint union by the pairs consisting of a family index and an outcome in the corresponding event. Apply the finite Fubini and disjoint-union sum laws. Check the empty family and singleton family rather than silently assuming at least two events.

items.title: Two-event inclusion-exclusion: $\mathbb P(A\cup B)=\mathbb P(A)+\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A\cap B)$
items.strategy: Partition the union into $A$ and $B\setminus A$, and partition $B$ into $A\cap B$ and $B\setminus A$. Apply finite additivity and rearrange in the ordered field of reals.

items.title: The finite union bound
items.strategy: Disjointify $A_1,\ldots,A_n$ by setting $B_i=A_i\setminus\bigcup_{j<i}A_j$. The $B_i$ are disjoint, have the same union as the $A_i$, and satisfy $B_i\subseteq A_i$; finite additivity and monotonicity finish. Treat $n=0$ and $n=1$ explicitly.

items.title: Conditional probability $\mathbb P(A\mid B)$ for $\mathbb P(B)>0$
The multiplication rule and finite chain rule for conditional probability
items.strategy: The two-event identity is the definition after multiplying by the positive denominator. Iterate it for $A_1,\ldots,A_n$, assuming each conditioning prefix has positive probability. State the empty and singleton products and do not write a conditional probability whose conditioning event has probability zero.

items.title: The law of total probability for a finite partition
items.strategy: For a finite partition $B_1,\ldots,B_n$ with every $\mathbb P(B_i)>0$, the events $A\cap B_i$ are disjoint and cover $A$. Apply finite additivity and the multiplication rule. Record separately that zero-probability partition cells may simply be omitted rather than conditioned on.

items.title: Bayes' theorem over a finite partition
items.strategy: Use the multiplication rule to write the numerator $\mathbb P(A\cap B_j)$ as $\mathbb P(A\mid B_j)\mathbb P(B_j)$ and use total probability for $\mathbb P(A)$. Require a positive denominator and check that the asserted posterior is only formed under that hypothesis.

items.title: Independent events, pairwise independence, and mutual independence of a finite family
Two positive-probability events are independent exactly when conditioning on either leaves the other's probability unchanged
items.strategy: Divide the product identity by the appropriate positive probability for each forward implication; multiply the conditional identity back for the reverse implication. State both directions and explain why the positivity hypotheses are needed only to make the conditional probabilities defined.

items.title: Mutual independence is inherited by subfamilies and by replacing events with complements
items.strategy: Subfamilies are immediate from the defining intersection identities. For one complemented event, subtract the intersection with that event from the intersection of the remaining events; then iterate over the finite number of complements. Check the empty subfamily convention, which makes both sides equal to $1$.

items.title: The uniform probability space on a nonempty finite set
The finite product of finite probability spaces
Product weights normalize, and coordinate events are mutually independent
items.strategy: Use finite Fubini repeatedly to factor the sum of product weights as the product of the coordinate sums, hence as $1$. For cylinder events, the same calculation factors their intersection probability into the product of their probabilities. Cover the empty product, empty coordinate subfamily, and coordinates containing probability-zero outcomes.

items.title: Real random variables on finite probability spaces and their finite distributions
Expectation of a real random variable on a finite probability space
Expectation is the sum of each attained value times its probability
items.strategy: Partition the finite outcome space into the fibres of the random variable and reindex the expectation sum by value and fibre. The range is finite; values not attained are omitted. The empty-range case cannot occur because a probability space has total weight $1$.

items.title: Expectation is linear for every finite family of random variables, without any independence hypothesis
items.strategy: Expand the expectation of a pointwise linear combination, interchange the two finite sums, and use distributivity. Prove the finite-family form including the empty sum; explicitly note that no step invokes event or variable independence.

items.title: Expectation preserves pointwise order and lies between the minimum and maximum attained values
items.strategy: A pointwise nonnegative difference has nonnegative expectation because every outcome weight is nonnegative. Apply this to constants equal to the finite minimum and maximum. Deduce the averaging consequences that some outcome has value at least the expectation and some has value at most it, including the constant case.

items.title: The indicator random variable of an event
Indicators turn event probabilities, intersections, and finite counts into expectations and products
items.strategy: Evaluate an indicator on and off its event to obtain $\mathbb E[1_A]=\mathbb P(A)$, verify pointwise that a finite product of indicators is the indicator of the intersection, and verify that the sum of indicators counts how many events occur. Include the empty product and empty sum conventions.

items.title: Pairwise and mutual independence of finite-valued random variables
A finite family of events is mutually independent exactly when its indicators are mutually independent
items.strategy: For the forward direction, every joint value assignment to the indicators is an intersection of chosen events and complements, so use complement-stability. For the reverse direction, specialize the joint-value identity to all values equal to $1$. Treat pairwise independence as the two-variable specialization.

items.title: Expectation factors over a finite product of mutually independent random variables
items.strategy: Group outcomes by the joint values of the variables. Mutual independence factors each joint probability, and finite Fubini factors the resulting multiple sum. Check the empty product, which has expectation $1$, and do not claim the converse.

items.title: Variance, standard deviation, and covariance on a finite probability space
$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-\mathbb E[X]^2$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y]$
items.strategy: Expand the centred products pointwise and apply linearity of expectation, treating expectations as constants. Also record nonnegativity of variance and the zero variance of constants; do not infer that zero variance implies pointwise constancy on zero-weight outcomes.

items.title: Covariance is symmetric and bilinear in finite linear combinations
items.strategy: Use the product-expectation identity for covariance and linearity of expectation to expand each argument. Symmetry follows from commutativity of real multiplication. Include empty linear combinations and constant summands.

items.title: Variance of a finite sum as the sum of all variances and covariances
items.strategy: Write variance as the covariance of the sum with itself and use bilinearity twice. Separate diagonal terms from ordered off-diagonal terms, and give the equivalent $2\sum_{i<j}$ form. Check the empty and singleton sums.

items.title: Variance adds for every finite pairwise-independent family
items.strategy: Pairwise independence factors $\mathbb E[X_iX_j]$, so every off-diagonal covariance is zero. Substitute into the finite-sum variance formula. Emphasize that pairwise independence suffices here even though mutual independence is stronger.

items.title: Bernoulli random variables and binomial random variables as sums of independent Bernoulli trials
A Bernoulli$(p)$ variable has mean $p$ and variance $p(1-p)$; a binomial$(n,p)$ variable has mean $np$ and variance $np(1-p)$
items.strategy: Compute the two-value expectation and second moment directly. For the binomial variable, use linearity for the mean and pairwise-independent variance additivity for the variance. Check $p=0$, $p=1$, and $n=0$.

items.title: Markov's inequality on a finite probability space
items.strategy: For nonnegative $X$ and $a>0$, compare $X$ pointwise with $a1_{\{X\ge a\}}$, take expectations, and divide by $a$. Keep the weak event $X\ge a$ exactly as stated and explain why $a=0$ is excluded.

items.title: Chebyshev's inequality on a finite probability space
items.strategy: Apply Markov to the nonnegative variable $(X-\mathbb E X)^2$ at threshold $t^2$. The two events are equal for $t>0$, and the numerator is the variance by definition. State both the absolute-threshold and standard-deviation forms, with the zero-variance boundary separated.

items.title: Cauchy-Schwarz for finite random variables: $\mathbb E[XY]^2\le\mathbb E[X^2]\mathbb E[Y^2]$
items.strategy: If $\mathbb E[X^2]=0$, nonnegative weighted squares force $X=0$ on every positive-weight outcome and the inequality follows. Otherwise expand the nonnegative expectation of $(Y-tX)^2$ at $t=\mathbb E[XY]/\mathbb E[X^2]$. Do not claim equality characterizations on probability-zero outcomes.

items.title: The finite second-moment bound $\mathbb P(X\ne0)\ge\mathbb E[X]^2/\mathbb E[X^2]$
items.strategy: Apply Cauchy-Schwarz to $X$ and the indicator of $\{X\ne0\}$, using $X=X1_{\{X\ne0\}}$. Divide only when $\mathbb E[X^2]>0$; if it is zero, state separately that $X$ vanishes on every positive-weight outcome.

items.title: $\mathbb P(X=0)\le\operatorname{Var}(X)/\mathbb E[X]^2$ whenever $\mathbb E[X]\ne0$
items.strategy: The event $X=0$ forces $|X-\mathbb E X|\ge|\mathbb E X|$. Apply Chebyshev at this positive threshold. Record the equivalent lower bound on $\mathbb P(X\ne0)$ and do not divide when the expectation is zero.

pages.title: Finite Probability Spaces and Random Variables — Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: A loaded die as a nonuniform finite probability space
items.strategy: Assign six explicit rational weights summing to $1$, compute several event, complement, and conditional probabilities, and verify one instance of the multiplication rule. Include an outcome of weight zero to distinguish possible outcomes from positive-probability outcomes.

items.title: Bayes' theorem for choosing one of two urns and observing a colour
items.strategy: Use a four-branch finite product experiment with unequal prior urn weights and explicit ball-colour probabilities. Compute the posterior by direct event weights and by Bayes' formula, checking that the two rational values agree.

items.title: Three pairwise-independent events that are not mutually independent
items.strategy: On the uniform four-point space of two bits $U,V$, take the events $U=0$, $V=0$, and $U=V$. Compute every pairwise intersection as $1/4$ but the triple intersection as $1/4\ne1/8$; no modular-arithmetic convention is needed.

items.title: Events with the same probability need not be independent
items.strategy: Use two distinct overlapping two-point events in a uniform three- or four-point space. Compute their equal marginal probabilities and an intersection probability unequal to the product, with neither event equal to the other.

items.title: Uncorrelated finite random variables need not be independent
items.strategy: Let $X$ be uniform on $\{-1,0,1\}$ and set $Y=X^2$. Compute $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0$ by symmetry, while $Y$ is determined by $X$ and a joint-value probability fails to factor.

items.title: For dependent variables, $\mathbb E[XY]$ need not equal $\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y]$
items.strategy: Take one fair random sign and set $X=Y$ equal to it. Then both expectations vanish while $XY=1$ identically. Verify dependence directly from a joint-value probability.

items.title: False: linearity of expectation requires independence
items.strategy: Refute the claim by citing the unconditional finite-sum theorem and then computing $\mathbb E[X+X]=2\mathbb E[X]$ for a nonconstant $X$, where the two summands are maximally dependent.

items.title: The union bound can be strict for overlapping events
items.strategy: Choose three explicit events on a small uniform space with a common outcome. Compute the union and the sum of marginal probabilities, then identify the overcount responsible for strictness.

items.title: A symmetric two-point distribution attains equality in Chebyshev's inequality
items.strategy: For every $\varepsilon>0$, take the uniform distribution on $\{-\varepsilon,+\varepsilon\}$. Compute $\mathbb E[X]=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\varepsilon^2$; then $|X-\mathbb E[X]|\ge\varepsilon$ holds everywhere, so both sides of Chebyshev's inequality equal $1$. Keep the weak threshold exactly, and do not include $\varepsilon=0$.

items.title: A two-valued random variable attains equality in Markov's inequality
items.strategy: For $a>0$ and $p\in[0,1]$, take a two-point finite probability space with an event $E$ of probability $p$, and define $X=a$ on $E$ and $X=0$ off $E$. Then $\mathbb E[X]=ap$ and $\mathbb P(X\ge a)=p=\mathbb E[X]/a$. Check $p=0$ and $p=1$, allowing zero-weight outcomes, and keep $a=0$ excluded.

items.title: Markov's conclusion can fail without nonnegativity
items.strategy: On a uniform two-point space, let $X$ take the values $1$ and $-3$, and use threshold $a=1$. Then $\mathbb E[X]=-1$ while $\mathbb P(X\ge1)=1/2$, so the conclusion $\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\mathbb E[X]/a$ would read $1/2\le-1$. State explicitly that this refutes dropping nonnegativity, not Markov's theorem.

pages.title: Finite Probability and the Probabilistic Method

items.title: An event of positive probability in a finite probability space is nonempty
items.strategy: The empty event has probability zero by the basic laws, so take the contrapositive. State clearly that this gives existence of an outcome but does not by itself specify one.

items.title: The first-moment method for avoiding or forcing a finite count of bad events
items.strategy: For a nonnegative integer-valued $X$, Markov gives $\mathbb P(X\ge1)\le\mathbb E X$, so $\mathbb E X<1$ leaves positive probability that $X=0$. Conversely $\mathbb E X>0$ implies a positive-weight outcome with $X>0$. Include the averaging form that some outcome has $X\ge\mathbb E X$ and show by a constant-one example why the strict threshold is necessary.

items.title: The deletion-alteration method converts an expected defect count into a deterministic lower bound
items.strategy: Formalize a finite random object with size $Y$ and $X$ listed defects, together with a deterministic repair that deletes at most one unit for each listed defect. Every repaired outcome has size at least $Y-X$, so averaging gives an admissible repaired object of size at least $\mathbb E[Y-X]$. Allow repeated defects and explain why overcounting only weakens the bound.

items.title: $1+x\le\exp(x)$ for every real $x$, hence $(1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp)$
items.strategy: At $x=0$ there is equality. For $x>0$, the mean value theorem gives $\exp(x)-1=\exp(c)x$ with $0<c<x$, so monotonicity and $\exp(0)=1$ give $\exp(c)>1$. For $x<0$, it gives the same identity with $x<c<0$, so $0<\exp(c)<1$ and multiplication by the negative $x$ reverses the comparison. Thus $1+x\le\exp(x)$ for every real $x$. Apply this at $-p$ and use monotonicity of natural powers on nonnegative bases to obtain $(1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp)$ for $0\le p\le1$, including $m=0$ and $p=1$.

items.title: The Erdős-Rényi finite random graph $G(n,p)$
A prescribed set of present and absent edges in $G(n,p)$ has product probability
items.strategy: Represent each potential edge by its Bernoulli coordinate. Mutual independence of coordinate events gives $p^r(1-p)^s$ for disjoint prescribed present and absent sets of sizes $r$ and $s$. Deduce the weight $p^m(1-p)^{\binom n2-m}$ of a fixed labelled graph, including $p=0,1$ and empty prescriptions.

items.title: The moment generating function $M_X(t)=\mathbb E[e^{tX}]$ on a finite probability space
The moment generating function of a finite sum of independent variables is the product of their moment generating functions
items.strategy: Use the exponential addition law pointwise to turn $e^{t\sum X_i}$ into $\prod e^{tX_i}$. Functions of mutually independent finite variables remain mutually independent by grouping value fibres, so factor the expectation. Include the empty sum/product.

items.title: For a uniform random sign $\varepsilon$, $\mathbb E[e^{t\varepsilon}]\le e^{t^2/2}$
items.strategy: Compute the expectation as $(e^t+e^{-t})/2$. Series linearity cancels the odd powers and yields the nonnegative even-power series. Use $(2j)!\ge2^j j!$ for every $j$, including $j=0$, to compare its finite partial sums with those of $e^{t^2/2}$; the nonnegative-series supremum theorem passes the inequality to the sums. This route is finite-probability throughout and imports no continuous distribution.

items.title: For $n\ge1$ independent random signs, $\mathbb P(|S|\ge t)\le2\exp(-t^2/(2n))$ for $t>0$
items.strategy: For $S=\sum_{i=1}^n\varepsilon_i$, $n\ge1$, and $u>0$, strict monotonicity of the exponential and Markov give $\mathbb P(S\ge t)\le e^{-ut}\mathbb E[e^{uS}]$. Factor the MGF, apply the random-sign bound, and choose $u=t/n$ for $t>0$; handle $t=0$ separately. Use symmetry for the lower tail and the union bound for the two-sided estimate.

items.title: Dependency digraphs for a finite family of bad events
The conditional-probability induction underlying the Lovász Local Lemma
items.strategy: Under the asymmetric local-lemma hypotheses, prove by induction on $|S|$ that $\mathbb P(A_i\mid\bigcap_{j\in S}A_j^c)\le x_i$ whenever the conditioning event is positive. Split $S$ into out-neighbours and non-neighbours of $i$, use dependency for the latter, and lower-bound the denominator by the product of $(1-x_j)$ supplied by smaller induction cases. Separate $S=\varnothing$ and a zero denominator, which means the conditional expression is not formed.

items.title: The asymmetric Lovász Local Lemma for finitely many events
items.strategy: Assume $x_i\in[0,1)$ and $\mathbb P(A_i)\le x_i\prod_{i\to j}(1-x_j)$. Apply the conditional-probability lemma successively to the complements in the probability chain rule to obtain $\mathbb P(\bigcap_iA_i^c)\ge\prod_i(1-x_i)>0$. Check the empty event family and ensure every intermediate conditioning event is positive by the partial product bound.

items.title: The symmetric Lovász Local Lemma under $ep(d+1)\le1$
items.strategy: For $d=0$, set every $x_i=1/e<1$ and apply the asymmetric lemma directly. For $d\ge1$, set every $x_i=1/(d+1)$ and use $1+1/d\le e^{1/d}$ to prove $(1-1/(d+1))^d\ge e^{-1}$; then the asymmetric hypothesis follows from $ep(d+1)\le1$. Preserve the distinction between pairwise independence and independence from a whole non-neighbour collection.

items.title: Every $k$-uniform hypergraph with fewer than $2^{k-1}$ edges is $2$-colourable
items.strategy: Colour each vertex independently and uniformly with two colours. Each fixed $k$-edge is monochromatic with probability $2^{1-k}$, so the expected number of monochromatic edges is $m2^{1-k}<1$. Apply the first-moment method. Include $k=1$, where the hypothesis forces no edges, and the empty hypergraph.

items.title: A $k$-uniform hypergraph is $2$-colourable when every edge meets at most $d$ other edges and $e(d+1)\le2^{k-1}$
items.strategy: Use independent fair vertex colours and take monochromatic-edge events. Each has probability exactly $2^{1-k}$ and is mutually independent of the collection of events for disjoint edges. The edge-intersection graph is a dependency graph of maximum degree $d$, so the symmetric local lemma applies. Treat $k=1$, empty edge sets, and the $d=0$ case explicitly.

items.title: Every finite graph with $m$ edges has a cut containing at least $m/2$ edges
items.strategy: Place each vertex independently on either side with equal probability. An edge crosses with probability $1/2$; express the cut size as the sum of edge indicators and use linearity, not independence of those indicators. Averaging supplies a cut of at least the expectation. Include the edgeless graph.

items.title: Szele's bound: for every $n\ge1$, some $n$-vertex tournament has at least $n!/2^{n-1}$ Hamilton paths
items.strategy: Orient every edge independently and uniformly. For each ordering of the $n$ vertices, the $n-1$ required edges have the prescribed directions with probability $2^{-(n-1)}$. Sum the indicators over all $n!$ orderings and average. Check $n=1$ explicitly; the theorem does not make the source's path-count claim at $n=0$.

items.title: Tournament property $S_k$: every set of at most $k$ vertices is dominated by one vertex
If $k\ge1$ and $n\ge3k^2 2^k$, an $n$-vertex tournament with property $S_k$ exists
items.strategy: Randomly orient every edge. For a fixed $k$-set $S$, the events that distinct outside vertices dominate $S$ are independent and each has probability $2^{-k}$, so failure has probability $(1-2^{-k})^{n-k}$. Union-bound over the $\binom nk$ sets and use the binomial ratio to show this exact upper bound is nonincreasing once $n+1\ge k2^k$. At $n=3k^22^k$, prove $\binom nk\le(en/k)^k$ from $\binom nk k!\le n^k$ and the $k$th nonnegative exponential-series term, then use $\log x\le x-1$ to settle $k\ge3$; check $k=1,2$ by exact finite arithmetic. Extend every smaller set to a $k$-set, justified by $n\ge k$.

items.title: Dominating sets in a finite graph
An $n$-vertex graph of minimum degree $\delta>1$ has a dominating set of size at most $n(\log(\delta+1)+1)/(\delta+1)$
items.strategy: Choose each vertex independently with probability $p=\log(\delta+1)/(\delta+1)$, then add every undominated vertex. The expected size is at most $np+n(1-p)^{\delta+1}\le np+ne^{-p(\delta+1)}$, which equals the claimed bound. Use $1+\log x\le x$ to check $0<p<1$, and then average over the finite product space.

items.title: Sum-free subsets of the integers
There are arbitrarily large primes congruent to $2$ modulo $3$
items.strategy: Given all primes $q\le M$ with $q\equiv2\pmod3$, form $N=3\prod q-1$. A prime divisor of $N$ is not on the list, and at least one prime divisor is $2$ modulo $3$ because their product is. Treat an empty list, $M<2$, repeated prime factors, and the fact that $3$ does not divide $N$.

items.title: Every finite set of $n$ nonzero integers has a sum-free subset of size greater than $n/3$
items.strategy: Choose a prime $p=3r+2$ exceeding twice the maximum absolute value in the set, and let $I=\{r+1,\ldots,2r+1\}\subset\mathbb Z/p$. For uniform nonzero $z$, retain $a$ when $za\in I$. Field multiplication makes each $za$ uniform on the nonzero residues, so the expected retained size is $n(r+1)/(3r+1)>n/3$. Verify that $I$ is sum-free modulo $p$ and that reduction is injective on the original integer set.

items.title: The expected number of cycles of length at most $\ell$ in $G(n,p)$
items.strategy: For each $3\le r\le\ell$, count labelled $r$-cycles as $n^{\underline r}/(2r)$ and give each probability $p^r$. Sum the indicators to obtain the exact expectation and the bound $\sum_{r=3}^{\ell}n^rp^r/(2r)$. Handle $\ell<3$ as an empty sum and $p=0,1$.

items.title: $\mathbb P(\alpha(G(n,p))\ge s)\le\binom ns(1-p)^{\binom s2}\le n^s\exp(-p\binom s2)$ for $s\le n$
items.strategy: If the independence number is at least $s$, some $s$-subset has all its potential edges absent. Compute that probability for a fixed subset and union-bound over the $\binom ns$ choices. Use $\binom ns\le n^s$ and $(1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp)$ for the chained exponential bound needed later. Handle $s=0,1$ and $s>n$ separately rather than applying the second displayed inequality outside its range.

items.title: For all positive $k,\ell$, some finite graph has girth greater than $\ell$ and chromatic number greater than $k$
items.strategy: Choose a sufficiently large $n$ divisible by $2k$ and take $p=n^{-1+1/(2\ell)}$. The short-cycle expectation is $o(n)$, so Markov makes the probability of at least $n/2$ short cycles tend to $0$; the independence-number bound makes $\mathbb P(\alpha(G)\ge n/(2k))$ tend to $0$. The union bound leaves positive probability that both failures are absent. Delete one vertex from every listed short cycle. Fewer than $n/2$ vertices are removed, deletion creates no cycle, and any $k$-colouring of the survivor has a colour class larger than $n/(2k)$, contradicting the independence bound. Spell out $\ell=1,2$ and every strict inequality.

pages.title: Finite Probability and the Probabilistic Method — Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The expected number of triangles in $G(n,p)$ is $\binom n3p^3$
items.strategy: Index triangle indicators by three-element vertex sets. Each requires three prescribed edges and has probability $p^3$; linearity gives the expectation without requiring the triangle indicators to be independent. For variance, identify exactly which pairs have nonzero covariance, without claiming a concentration theorem not scaffolded here.

items.title: First- and second-moment bounds for a nonempty Bernoulli random subset
items.strategy: Let $X$ be the size of a subset of $[n]$ obtained by independent retention with probability $p$. Compute $\mathbb E X$, $\mathbb E X^2$, and the exact probability $1-(1-p)^n$ that $X>0$, then compare the first-moment upper bound and second-moment lower bound at $n=0$, $p=0$, $p=1$, and a nondegenerate case.

items.title: The random-colouring proof of $R(k,k)>2^{k/2}$
items.strategy: View the uniform red-blue edge colouring as $G(n,1/2)$. For each $k$-set, compute the probability of a monochromatic clique, union-bound over all $k$-sets, and reproduce the finite product estimate in the published theorem at $n=\lfloor2^{k/2}\rfloor$. Compare this sharper estimate with the cruder $2^{k/2-1}$ bound in Matoušek–Vondrák, and preserve the strict inequality for every $k\ge3$.

items.title: Checking the symmetric local-lemma condition for a sparse uniform hypergraph
items.strategy: Choose explicit integers $k$ and $d$ satisfying $e(d+1)\le2^{k-1}$, build a small edge-intersection pattern with maximum degree $d$, and verify every bad-event probability and dependency-neighbour count before invoking the hypergraph local-lemma theorem. Contrast the conclusion with what the union bound alone would require as the total edge count grows.

items.title: A parameter ledger for the high-girth, high-chromatic alteration proof
items.strategy: For fixed small $k,\ell$, display the choice of exponent and the two failure bounds as functions of $n$, choose a concrete sufficiently-large multiple of $2k$ by coarse estimates, and track the vertex loss, surviving independence number, girth, and chromatic-number contradiction. The example audits integrality and strict inequalities rather than pretending to construct the graph explicitly.

items.title: Expectation equal to $1$ does not force a nonnegative integer-valued variable to vanish somewhere
items.strategy: Take the constant random variable $X=1$ on a one-outcome probability space. Its expectation is exactly $1$ and $\mathbb P(X=0)=0$, showing why the first-moment avoidance criterion requires $\mathbb E X<1$ rather than $\le1$.

pages.title: Linear Algebra Methods in Combinatorics

items.title: The incidence vector $v_A\in F^{n}$ of a subset $A\subseteq[n]$ over a stated field
items.strategy: For a field $F$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $A\subseteq[n]=\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, define $v_A\in F^{n}$ by $(v_A)_i=1_F$ when $i\in A$ and $0_F$ otherwise. Prove the two facts every later item uses: $A\mapsto v_A$ is injective for every field (compare coordinates), and $v_\varnothing=0$. THE FIELD IS PART OF THE DATA and is written into the notation whenever two fields are in play on the same page; the whole page turns on which field is chosen. Landmark.

items.title: The standard bilinear form $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{i<n}x_iy_i$ on $F^{n}$
items.strategy: Define $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ on $F^n$ over an arbitrary field and prove it is a symmetric bilinear form in the sense of [[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]], and that it is nondegenerate in the sense of [[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]] (its matrix in the standard basis is the identity). SAY EXPLICITLY, IN THE DEFINITION, that this is NOT an inner product unless $F$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ with the published convention: over $\mathbb{F}_2$ there is no order and no positivity, and $\langle x,x\rangle=0$ holds for many nonzero $x$. Record $\langle x,x\rangle=\sum_i x_i$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$, since $t^2=t$ there. Landmark.
