items.title: $\langle v_A,v_B\rangle$ is the image of $\lvert A\cap B\rvert$ in $F$; over $\mathbb{F}_2$ it is $0$ or $1$ according to the parity of $\lvert A\cap B\rvert$
items.strategy: Expand the sum: the term at $i$ is $1_F$ when $i\in A\cap B$ and $0_F$ otherwise, so the value is the sum of $\lvert A\cap B\rvert$ copies of $1_F$, which is the image of that natural number under the unique ring map $\mathbb{Z}\to F$. Write it as $\lvert A\cap B\rvert\cdot 1_F$; do not write the canonical embedding applied to a natural number. State the two specialisations used later: over $\mathbb{R}$ the value IS $\lvert A\cap B\rvert$, and over $\mathbb{F}_2$ it is $1$ exactly when $\lvert A\cap B\rvert$ is odd. Taking $B=A$ gives $\langle v_A,v_A\rangle=\lvert A\rvert\cdot 1_F$. Landmark.

items.title: A finite family of subsets of $[n]$ and its incidence matrix over $F$
items.strategy: A **family** here is a finite list $\mathcal{F}=(A_1,\dots,A_m)$ of pairwise distinct subsets of $[n]$; its **incidence matrix** $N(\mathcal{F})\in F^{m\times n}$ has $v_{A_i}$ as its $i$-th row. Record that the $(i,j)$ entry of $N N^{\mathsf{T}}$ is $\langle v_{A_i},v_{A_j}\rangle$, using the matrix product of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. Distinctness is part of the definition because every bound below counts SETS, and it is the hypothesis a reader drops.

items.title: If the incidence vectors of $A_1,\dots,A_m\subseteq[n]$ are linearly independent over $F$ then $m\le n$
items.strategy: THE MASTER LEMMA OF THE PAGE, and every theorem below is this lemma with a different independence argument in front of it. The incidence vectors lie in $F^{n}$, which has the standard basis of $n$ elements ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), so $\dim_F F^n=n$ and an independent subset has at most $n$ elements by [[cor-independent-set-is-no-larger-than-a-finite-spanning-set]]. Independence of the LIST gives distinctness of the vectors, hence $m$ distinct elements in the set. State it as a lemma about a family, not about vectors: that is the form that makes the citations below faithful. Landmark.

items.title: Diagonal criterion: if $\langle v_i,w_i\rangle\ne0$ and $\langle v_i,w_j\rangle=0$ for $i\ne j$, then $v_1,\dots,v_m$ are linearly independent
items.strategy: Pair a vanishing combination $\sum_i c_iv_i=0$ with $w_j$ and use bilinearity: every term with $i\ne j$ dies and $c_j\langle v_j,w_j\rangle=0$ forces $c_j=0$ since a field has no zero divisors. State it for an arbitrary bilinear form on an arbitrary $F$-vector space, since the page applies it over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and over $\mathbb{R}$ and to polynomial evaluation pairings. NO POSITIVITY AND NO NONDEGENERACY IS USED — only bilinearity and the diagonal, and the Remark says so, because that is exactly what makes the argument legal over $\mathbb{F}_2$. Landmark.

items.title: Triangular criterion: if $\langle v_i,w_i\rangle\ne0$ and $\langle v_i,w_j\rangle=0$ for $j<i$, then $v_1,\dots,v_m$ are linearly independent
items.strategy: Take a vanishing combination with a nonzero coefficient and let $i$ be LEAST with $c_i\ne0$; pairing with $w_i$ kills every term with index $>i$ by the hypothesis and every term with index $<i$ by minimality, leaving $c_i\langle v_i,w_i\rangle=0$. State the index convention once and use it consistently: the hypothesis is one-sided and the direction matters. This is the criterion the intersection bound below uses, where the diagonal criterion is unavailable.

items.title: Determinant criterion: if the matrix $\bigl(\langle v_i,w_j\rangle\bigr)_{i,j}$ is invertible then both $v_1,\dots,v_m$ and $w_1,\dots,w_m$ are linearly independent
items.strategy: If $\sum_ic_iv_i=0$ then $c^{\mathsf{T}}M=0$ for $M=(\langle v_i,w_j\rangle)$, and invertibility gives $c=0$; symmetrically for the $w_j$. Cite the invertible-matrix theorem of [[thm-invertible-matrix-theorem]] for the equivalence with nonzero determinant. The three criteria are stated separately because every later proof names exactly one of them.

items.title: Oddtown: distinct $A_1,\dots,A_m\subseteq[n]$ with every $\lvert A_i\rvert$ odd and every $\lvert A_i\cap A_j\rvert$ ($i\ne j$) even satisfy $m\le n$
items.strategy: Work over $\mathbb{F}_2$. By [[lem-the-standard-form-of-two-incidence-vectors-is-the-intersection-size]] the hypotheses say $\langle v_{A_i},v_{A_i}\rangle=1$ and $\langle v_{A_i},v_{A_j}\rangle=0$ for $i\ne j$, which is the diagonal criterion with $w_i=v_{A_i}$; then apply [[lem-a-family-with-independent-incidence-vectors-has-at-most-n-members]]. Six numbered steps and no rank-of-a-product theorem. Note in a Remark that the form on $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ is not an inner product and that the argument never needs it to be. Statement from Babai–Frankl §1.1 and Matoušek Miniature 3. Landmark.

items.title: The $n$ singletons form an Oddtown family, so the bound $m\le n$ is attained for every $n$
items.strategy: Check the two hypotheses on $\{\{i\}:i<n\}$: each has size $1$, and distinct singletons meet in the empty set. This is what makes the companion page's false statement ("$n-1$ suffices") refutable in two lines, and it is worth an item because the sharpness is used, not merely mentioned.

items.title: A $d$-dimensional vector space over a field with $q$ elements has exactly $q^{d}$ elements
items.strategy: Coordinates with respect to an ordered basis give a bijection onto $F^{d}$ ([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]), and $\lvert F^{d}\rvert=q^{d}$ by [[thm-cardinality-of-a-set-of-functions]]. Check $d=0$: one element, $q^0=1$. The library has this nowhere and the Eventown bound needs it, so it is built here rather than gestured at.

items.title: For a subspace $U\le F^{n}$, $\dim_F U^{\perp}=n-\dim_F U$, where $U^{\perp}=\{x:\langle x,u\rangle=0\text{ for all }u\in U\}$
items.strategy: Choose a basis $u_1,\dots,u_d$ of $U$ ([[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]], which supplies it with NO CHOICE PRINCIPLE in finite dimension) and let $\Phi:F^n\to F^{d}$ send $x$ to $(\langle x,u_1\rangle,\dots,\langle x,u_d\rangle)$. Then $\ker\Phi=U^{\perp}$, and the matrix of $\Phi$ has the $u_i$ as its rows, so its rank is $d$ by [[thm-row-rank-equals-column-rank]] and independence of the rows. Rank–nullity ([[thm-rank-nullity]]) finishes. DO NOT USE THE DOUBLE-ANNIHILATOR THEOREM: it is stated under the axiom of choice, and this page spends none. Valid over every field, degenerate cases $U=0$ and $U=F^n$ included.

items.title: Eventown: distinct $A_1,\dots,A_m\subseteq[n]$ with every $\lvert A_i\rvert$ and every $\lvert A_i\cap A_j\rvert$ even satisfy $m\le 2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$
items.strategy: Let $U\le\mathbb{F}_2^{n}$ be the span of the incidence vectors. By [[lem-the-standard-form-of-two-incidence-vectors-is-the-intersection-size]] all pairwise values AND all diagonal values vanish, so bilinearity gives $\langle u,u'\rangle=0$ for all $u,u'\in U$, i.e. $U\subseteq U^{\perp}$. Then [[lem-the-orthogonal-complement-of-a-subspace-under-the-standard-form]] gives $\dim U\le n-\dim U$, so $\dim U\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$; the $m$ distinct incidence vectors lie in $U$, and $\lvert U\rvert=2^{\dim U}$ by [[lem-cardinality-of-a-finite-dimensional-space-over-a-finite-field]]. The floor appears because $\dim U$ is an integer; treat $n$ even and $n$ odd as separate numbered steps. Statement from Babai–Frankl §2.3. Landmark.

items.title: An Eventown family that no further set can be added to has exactly $2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ members
items.strategy: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be maximal. First show $\mathcal{F}$ is closed under symmetric difference and contains $\varnothing$, by checking the two parity conditions for $A\triangle B$ against $\lvert A\triangle B\rvert=\lvert A\rvert+\lvert B\rvert-2\lvert A\cap B\rvert$ and using maximality; hence $\{v_A:A\in\mathcal{F}\}$ is a subspace $U$ with $U\subseteq U^{\perp}$. Next show maximality forces $U=U^{\perp}\cap H$ where $H=\{x:\langle x,x\rangle=0\}$ is the even-weight subspace, which over $\mathbb{F}_2$ is the hyperplane $\sum_ix_i=0$. Then compute $\dim U=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, treating $n$ even and $n$ odd separately: the odd case is where the floor is earned and is the step most likely to be skipped. Verify the whole statement at $n=3$ by hand inside the proof or on the companion page.

items.title: If $v_1,\dots,v_m\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ satisfy $\langle v_i,v_j\rangle=t\ge0$ for $i\ne j$ and $\langle v_i,v_i\rangle>t$, they are linearly independent
items.strategy: Expand $0=\bigl\langle\sum_ic_iv_i,\sum_jc_jv_j\bigr\rangle=\sum_i c_i^2(d_i-t)+t\bigl(\sum_ic_i\bigr)^2$ where $d_i=\langle v_i,v_i\rangle$. Both summands are $\ge0$ because $t\ge0$ and $d_i>t$, so both vanish, and $c_i^2(d_i-t)=0$ forces $c_i=0$. State the equivalent matrix form as a second clause — the Gram matrix $tJ+D$ with $D$ diagonal positive is positive definite in the sense of [[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]], hence invertible — since that is how the sources phrase it. POSITIVITY OF $\mathbb{R}$ IS USED HERE AND IS INDISPENSABLE, which is exactly why the companion page's $\mathbb{F}_2$ false statement is false. Landmark.

items.title: Fisher's inequality, nonuniform form: distinct nonempty $A_1,\dots,A_m\subseteq[n]$ with $\lvert A_i\cap A_j\rvert=t$ for all $i\ne j$ satisfy $m\le n$
items.strategy: Two cases, and the first is the one that is skipped. CASE A: some $\lvert A_i\rvert=t$. Then $t\ge1$ (the sets are nonempty and distinct), that $A_i$ is contained in every other set, the differences $A_j\setminus A_i$ for $j\ne i$ are nonempty and pairwise disjoint, so there are at most $n-\lvert A_i\rvert\le n-1$ of them and $m\le n$. CASE B: every $\lvert A_i\rvert>t$. Over $\mathbb{R}$, [[lem-the-standard-form-of-two-incidence-vectors-is-the-intersection-size]] puts the incidence vectors in the hypothesis of [[lem-real-vectors-with-equal-pairwise-products-and-larger-norms-are-independent]], and [[lem-a-family-with-independent-incidence-vectors-has-at-most-n-members]] finishes. Also check $t=0$ and $m=1$. Statement from Babai–Frankl §4.1 and Matoušek Miniature 4. Landmark.

items.title: A $k$-uniform family on $[n]$ with all pairwise intersections of size $t<k$ has at most $n$ members
items.strategy: The uniform case falls into Case B of [[thm-nonuniform-fisher-inequality]] outright, since $\lvert A_i\rvert=k>t$. State it separately because it is the form the design-theoretic literature uses and the form the companion page applies to the seven lines of the Fano plane. Say in a Remark that the design-theoretic reading ($b\ge v$ for a $2$-design) is not stated here, because block designs are not among this page's declared prerequisites.

items.title: A decomposition of a graph's edge set into complete bipartite subgraphs
items.strategy: Given a finite simple graph $G$ ([[def-finite-simple-graph]]), a **complete bipartite decomposition** is a list of pairs $(X_1,Y_1),\dots,(X_m,Y_m)$ of disjoint nonempty subsets of $V(G)$ such that every edge of $G$ lies in exactly one of the sets $\{\{x,y\}:x\in X_k,\,y\in Y_k\}$ and every such pair is an edge. Note that the $X_k\cup Y_k$ need not cover $V(G)$, and that "exactly one" is the disjointness hypothesis Graham–Pollak needs. Cite [[def-standard-complete-bipartite-path-and-cycle-graphs]] for the complete bipartite graph itself so the notion is not re-minted.

items.title: Graham–Pollak: a complete bipartite decomposition of $K_n$ has at least $n-1$ parts
items.strategy: Suppose $m\le n-2$. The homogeneous real system $\sum_{i<n}x_i=0$ together with $\sum_{i\in X_k}x_i=0$ for $k=1,\dots,m$ has $m+1\le n-1<n$ equations in $n$ unknowns, so it has a nonzero solution $a$ by [[cor-rank-criterion-for-consistency]] and [[thm-rref-consistency-and-free-variable-parametrisation]]. Substituting into the identity $\sum_{i<j}x_ix_j=\sum_{k}\bigl(\sum_{i\in X_k}x_i\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{j\in Y_k}x_j\bigr)$ — which holds because each edge is covered exactly once and $X_k\cap Y_k=\varnothing$, and which needs its own numbered step — gives $0$ on the right, while the left equals $\tfrac12\bigl[(\sum_ia_i)^2-\sum_ia_i^2\bigr]=-\tfrac12\sum_ia_i^2<0$. Contradiction. Also record that $n-1$ is attained, by the star decomposition. Statement from Babai–Frankl §1.4 and Matoušek Miniature 8. Landmark.

items.title: Shattering and the Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension of a set family
items.strategy: For $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{P}([n])$ and $T\subseteq[n]$, the **trace** of $\mathcal{F}$ on $T$ is $\mathcal{F}\vert_T=\{F\cap T:F\in\mathcal{F}\}$, and $\mathcal{F}$ **shatters** $T$ when $\mathcal{F}\vert_T=\mathcal{P}(T)$. The **VC dimension** is the greatest $d$ such that some $T$ with $\lvert T\rvert=d$ is shattered. WELL-DEFINEDNESS IS AN OBLIGATION, not a remark: the empty set is shattered by any nonempty $\mathcal{F}$, the shattered sets are subsets of the finite $[n]$, so the maximum exists by [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]]; and record the boundary $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal{F})=0$ for a one-element family and the convention for $\mathcal{F}=\varnothing$. Landmark.

items.title: The down-shift $S_j$ of a set family at a point $j$
items.strategy: For $j<n$ define $S_j(\mathcal{F})=\{s_j(F,\mathcal{F}):F\in\mathcal{F}\}$ where $s_j(F,\mathcal{F})=F\setminus\{j\}$ if $j\in F$ and $F\setminus\{j\}\notin\mathcal{F}$, and $s_j(F,\mathcal{F})=F$ otherwise. Prove immediately that $s_j(\cdot,\mathcal{F})$ is injective on $\mathcal{F}$, so $\lvert S_j(\mathcal{F})\rvert=\lvert\mathcal{F}\rvert$; and define the weight $w(\mathcal{F})=\sum_{F\in\mathcal{F}}\lvert F\rvert$, which is what the termination argument decreases.

items.title: $\lvert S_j(\mathcal{F})\rvert=\lvert\mathcal{F}\rvert$, and $w(S_j(\mathcal{F}))\le w(\mathcal{F})$ with equality only when $S_j(\mathcal{F})=\mathcal{F}$
items.strategy: Injectivity of $s_j$: if $s_j(F)=s_j(G)$ with $F\ne G$ then one of them was shifted and the other not, and unwinding the two clauses gives a contradiction — write out the case split rather than asserting it. The weight claim is immediate from the definition. THIS AND THE NEXT LEMMA ARE SEPARATE ITEMS ON PURPOSE: Sauer–Shelah by shifting is unprovable without both, and running them together is how the argument is usually left incomplete.

items.title: Every set shattered by $S_j(\mathcal{F})$ is shattered by $\mathcal{F}$
items.strategy: Let $T$ be shattered by $\mathcal{G}=S_j(\mathcal{F})$. If $j\notin T$ the trace on $T$ only shrinks, and one checks $\mathcal{G}\vert_T\subseteq\mathcal{F}\vert_T$ directly. If $j\in T$, take $A\subseteq T$; both $A$ and $A\cup\{j\}$ are traces of $\mathcal{G}$, and the definition of $s_j$ forces the corresponding pair of members of $\mathcal{F}$ to realise $A$ and $A\cup\{j\}$ as well. Each case is a numbered step, and the case $j\in T$ is where the "and $F\setminus\{j\}\notin\mathcal{F}$" clause of the shift is used.

items.title: Applying down-shifts until none changes the family terminates, and the result is closed under taking subsets
items.strategy: Termination: each effective shift strictly decreases the natural number $w(\mathcal{F})$ of [[def-down-shift-of-a-set-family]], so there is no infinite descending chain. Downward closure of a fixed family: if $S_j(\mathcal{F})=\mathcal{F}$ for every $j$, then $F\in\mathcal{F}$ and $j\in F$ imply $F\setminus\{j\}\in\mathcal{F}$, and induction on $\lvert F\setminus G\rvert$ gives $G\in\mathcal{F}$ for every $G\subseteq F$.

items.title: If $\mathcal{F}$ is closed under taking subsets then $\mathcal{F}$ shatters every $F\in\mathcal{F}$
items.strategy: For $A\subseteq F$ we have $A\in\mathcal{F}$ and $A\cap F=A$, so $\mathcal{F}\vert_F=\mathcal{P}(F)$. Two lines, but it is the step that converts a structural fact into a size bound.

items.title: Sauer–Shelah: a family on $[n]$ of VC dimension at most $d$ has at most $\sum_{i=0}^{d}\binom{n}{i}$ members
items.strategy: Shift $\mathcal{F}$ to a fixed family $\mathcal{G}$ by [[lem-iterated-down-shifting-terminates-in-a-downward-closed-family]]. Then $\lvert\mathcal{G}\rvert=\lvert\mathcal{F}\rvert$ by [[lem-the-down-shift-preserves-the-number-of-sets]] and $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal{G})\le d$ by [[lem-the-down-shift-creates-no-new-shattered-set]]; $\mathcal{G}$ is downward closed, so by [[lem-a-downward-closed-family-shatters-each-of-its-members]] every $G\in\mathcal{G}$ has $\lvert G\rvert\le d$, and the sets of size at most $d$ number $\sum_{i\le d}\binom{n}{i}$ by [[def-binomial-coefficient]] and [[thm-sum-rule]]. Check $d=0$ and $d=n$. Landmark.

items.title: For $d\ge1$ a family on $[n]$ of VC dimension at most $d$ has at most $(n+1)^{d}$ members
items.strategy: Bound $\binom{n}{i}\le n^{i}$ from [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]], then $\sum_{i=0}^{d}n^{i}\le(n+1)^{d}$ by the binomial theorem, since $(n+1)^d=\sum_j\binom{d}{j}n^j$ and $\binom{d}{j}\ge1$ for $0\le j\le d$. STATE THE HYPOTHESIS $d\ge1$ AND CHECK $n=0$ AND $n=1$: the companion page's false statement is the same bound with $n^{d}$ in place of $(n+1)^{d}$, which fails at small $n$, so the two must not be confused.

items.title: The inclusion matrix $W_{t,k}(n)$ of $t$-sets against $k$-sets
items.strategy: For $t\le k\le n$ let $W_{t,k}(n)$ be the matrix over $\mathbb{Q}$ whose rows are indexed by the $t$-element subsets of $[n]$, whose columns are indexed by the $k$-element subsets, and whose $(S,K)$ entry is $1$ when $S\subseteq K$ and $0$ otherwise; fix an ordering of the index sets once so the matrix is well defined up to simultaneous permutation, and say that its rank does not depend on that choice. Record $W_{t,t}(n)=I$ and $W_{0,k}(n)$ = the all-ones row. Also record the composition identity $W_{s,t}(n)\,W_{t,k}(n)=\binom{k-s}{t-s}W_{s,k}(n)$ for $s\le t\le k$, proved by counting the $t$-sets between a fixed $s$-set and a fixed $k$-set; that count is $\binom{k-s}{t-s}$ when $S\subseteq K$ and $0$ otherwise. Landmark.

items.title: $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{Q}}W_{1,k}(n)=n$ for $1\le k\le n-1$
items.strategy: Suppose $\sum_{i<n}c_i[i\in K]=0$ for every $k$-set $K$, that is $\sum_{i\in K}c_i=0$ for every $k$-set $K$. For $i\ne j$ pick a $k$-set $K$ containing $i$ but not $j$ — possible exactly because $1\le k\le n-1$ — and swap $i$ for $j$; subtracting the two equations gives $c_i=c_j$. Hence all $c_i$ are equal to some $c$, and $kc=0$ with $k\ge1$ gives $c=0$ in $\mathbb{Q}$. So the rows are independent and the rank is $n$. STATE THE RANGE AND SHOW BOTH ENDS FAIL: at $k=n$ the single column makes the rank $1$, and at $k=0$ there are no rows to speak of. This is the case the companion page computes; the general rank formula is a separate matter recorded in the next remark.

items.title: What is and is not proved about $\operatorname{rank}W_{t,k}(n)$ on this page
items.strategy: Say exactly what the page establishes — the composition identity and the case $t=1$ — and what it does not: the theorem that $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{Q}}W_{t,k}(n)=\binom{n}{t}$ whenever $t\le k\le n-t$. Give the honest reason, not a gesture: the natural block-triangular induction on $n$ loses one unit of the range at each step and therefore proves nothing new, and the boundary case $k=n-t$ is equivalent to the nonsingularity of the disjointness matrix, whose known proofs go through eigenvalues of the Johnson scheme or Gottlieb's construction. Neither is among this page's declared prerequisites. Say "not built here", never that the library does not develop it, and do not state the unproved theorem as though the page had it.

items.title: Monomials, coefficients, degree in each variable and total degree in $F[x_1,\dots,x_n]$
items.strategy: Using the iterated construction of [[def-multivariate-polynomial-ring-by-iteration]], prove that every $f\in F[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ has a unique expansion $f=\sum_{\mathbf{t}}c_{\mathbf{t}}x^{\mathbf{t}}$ over finitely many multi-indices $\mathbf{t}\in\mathbb{N}^{n}$, where $x^{\mathbf{t}}=x_1^{t_1}\cdots x_n^{t_n}$; define $[x^{\mathbf{t}}]f=c_{\mathbf{t}}$, the **degree in $x_i$** as the largest $t_i$ with $c_{\mathbf{t}}\ne0$, and the **total degree** as the largest $t_1+\cdots+t_n$ with $c_{\mathbf{t}}\ne0$, with the zero polynomial handled separately. THE LIBRARY BUILDS THE MULTIVARIATE RING BY ITERATION AND STOPS THERE, so this expansion is an obligation of this page, proved by induction on $n$ from the univariate coefficient expansion. Also define evaluation at a point of $F^{n}$ by iterating [[thm-universal-property-of-a-polynomial-ring]].

items.title: If $\deg_{x_i}P<\lvert S_i\rvert$ for each $i$ and $P$ vanishes on $S_1\times\cdots\times S_n$, then $P=0$
items.strategy: Induction on $n$. Base $n=1$: a nonzero univariate polynomial of degree $d$ has at most $d$ roots ([[thm-root-bound-for-polynomials-over-a-domain]]), and $d<\lvert S_1\rvert$ roots are supplied, so $P=0$. Step: write $P=\sum_{j\le d}P_j(x_1,\dots,x_{n-1})x_n^{j}$ with $d=\deg_{x_n}P<\lvert S_n\rvert$; for each fixed point of $S_1\times\cdots\times S_{n-1}$ the resulting univariate polynomial in $x_n$ vanishes on $S_n$, hence is zero, hence every $P_j$ vanishes on $S_1\times\cdots\times S_{n-1}$; apply the inductive hypothesis to each $P_j$. Statement is Alon Lemma 2.1. THE HYPOTHESIS IS STRICT INEQUALITY, and the companion page's counterexample is the equality case. Landmark.

items.title: Reducing $f$ modulo $g_i(x_i)=\prod_{s\in S_i}(x_i-s)$ lowers each $\deg_{x_i}$ below $\lvert S_i\rvert$, preserves the values on the grid, and does not change the coefficient of a monomial of top total degree
items.strategy: Replace, repeatedly, an occurrence of $x_i^{\lvert S_i\rvert}$ by $x_i^{\lvert S_i\rvert}-g_i(x_i)$, which has $\deg_{x_i}<\lvert S_i\rvert$; formally, subtract multiples $h_ig_i$ with $\deg h_i\le\deg f-\deg g_i$ and induct on the total degree. Prove three separate claims: the reduction $\tilde f$ has $\deg_{x_i}\tilde f<\lvert S_i\rvert$; $\tilde f$ and $f$ agree at every point of $S_1\times\cdots\times S_n$ because each $g_i$ vanishes there; and if $\deg f=\sum_it_i$ then $[x^{\mathbf{t}}]\tilde f=[x^{\mathbf{t}}]f$, because every subtracted term $h_ig_i$ has total degree at most $\deg f$ and its monomials of that top degree are divisible by $x_i^{\lvert S_i\rvert}$, so with $t_i<\lvert S_i\rvert$ they cannot contribute to $x^{\mathbf{t}}$. THE THIRD CLAIM IS THE ONE THAT DOES THE WORK and it is where a proof is usually waved through.

items.title: Alon's Combinatorial Nullstellensatz: if $\deg f=\sum_it_i$, the coefficient of $x_1^{t_1}\cdots x_n^{t_n}$ in $f$ is nonzero, and $\lvert S_i\rvert>t_i$, then $f(s_1,\dots,s_n)\ne0$ for some $s_i\in S_i$
items.strategy: Suppose $f$ vanishes on the whole grid. Reduce it by [[lem-grid-reduction-of-a-multivariate-polynomial]] to $\tilde f$ with $\deg_{x_i}\tilde f<\lvert S_i\rvert$; $\tilde f$ still vanishes on the grid, so $\tilde f=0$ by [[thm-polynomial-identity-lemma]]. But the third clause of the reduction lemma says $[x^{\mathbf{t}}]\tilde f=[x^{\mathbf{t}}]f\ne0$, a contradiction. Statement is Alon Theorem 1.2, quoted with all three hypotheses; the hypothesis that the coefficient of the TOP monomial is nonzero is load-bearing and the companion page carries the false statement that drops it. Landmark.

items.title: If $p$ is prime and $0\le k\le m<p$ then $p\nmid\binom{m}{k}$
items.strategy: Use the $p$-adic valuation: $\binom{m}{k}k!(m-k)!=m!$ in $\mathbb{N}$ by [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]], and $v_p(m!)=0$ because none of $1,\dots,m$ is divisible by $p$ when $m<p$ ([[lem-p-adic-valuation-basic]], [[lem-p-adic-valuation-additive]]). Additivity of $v_p$ then forces $v_p\binom{m}{k}=0$. Cauchy–Davenport needs exactly this and it is a numbered step there, not an observation.

items.title: Cauchy–Davenport: for $p$ prime and nonempty $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{Z}/p$, $\lvert A+B\rvert\ge\min\{p,\lvert A\rvert+\lvert B\rvert-1\}$
items.strategy: If $\lvert A\rvert+\lvert B\rvert-1>p$ the bound is $p$ and $A+B=\mathbb{Z}/p$ by a pigeonhole argument on $a+b=c$; give that case its own steps. Otherwise suppose $\lvert A+B\rvert\le\lvert A\rvert+\lvert B\rvert-2$, choose $C\supseteq A+B$ with $\lvert C\rvert=\lvert A\rvert+\lvert B\rvert-2$, and set $f(x,y)=\prod_{c\in C}(x+y-c)$ over the field $\mathbb{Z}/p$ ([[thm-z-mod-p-is-a-field]]). Its total degree is $\lvert C\rvert=t_1+t_2$ with $t_1=\lvert A\rvert-1$, $t_2=\lvert B\rvert-1$, and the coefficient of $x^{t_1}y^{t_2}$ is $\binom{\lvert A\rvert+\lvert B\rvert-2}{\lvert A\rvert-1}$, nonzero in $\mathbb{Z}/p$ by [[lem-a-binomial-coefficient-with-top-below-a-prime-is-nonzero-modulo-that-prime]] since $\lvert A\rvert+\lvert B\rvert-2<p$. Apply [[thm-combinatorial-nullstellensatz]] with $S_1=A$, $S_2=B$ to get $a\in A$, $b\in B$ with $f(a,b)\ne0$, contradicting $a+b\in A+B\subseteq C$. Statement is Alon Theorem 3.2. PRIMALITY IS LOAD-BEARING and the companion page's counterexample is a composite modulus. Landmark.

items.title: Covering $\{0,1\}^{n}$ minus the origin by affine hyperplanes avoiding the origin needs at least $n$ of them
items.strategy:
Let $H_1,\dots,H_m$ be given by $\langle a_k,xangle=b_k$ with $b_k
e0$, covering every vertex of $\{0,1\}^n$ except the origin and missing the origin. Suppose $m<n$ and consider $f(x)=(-1)^{n+m}\,b_1\cdots b_m\prod_{i}(x_i-1)\;-\;\prod_{k} igl(\langle a_k,xangle-b_k igr)$ over $\mathbb{R}$. Show $f$ vanishes on all of $\{0,1\}^{n}$: at the origin the two terms cancel by the choice of constant, and at every other vertex both terms vanish. Then $\deg f=n$ with the coefficient of $x_1\cdots x_n$ equal to $\pm b_1\cdots b_m
e0$ (the second product has degree $m<n$ and cannot contribute), so [[thm-combinatorial-nullstellensatz]] with $S_i=\{0,1\}$ gives a vertex where $f
e0$ — a contradiction. VERIFY THE SIGN AND THE CONSTANT BY EVALUATING AT THE ORIGIN as a numbered step; this is the only place a slip can hide. Statement is Alon Theorem 6.3 (Alon–Füredi). Landmark.

items.title: Multilinear polynomials and the reduction $x_i^{2}\mapsto x_i$ on the cube
items.strategy: A polynomial in $F[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ is **multilinear** when $\deg_{x_i}\le1$ for every $i$; equivalently it is an $F$-combination of the monomials $x_T=\prod_{i\in T}x_i$ for $T\subseteq[n]$. Define the **multilinear reduction** $\widetilde{f}$ by repeatedly replacing $x_i^{2}$ by $x_i$, i.e. by reducing modulo the polynomials $x_i^{2}-x_i$ in the sense of [[lem-grid-reduction-of-a-multivariate-polynomial]] with $S_i=\{0,1\}$. Record that $\deg\widetilde f\le\deg f$ and that $x_T$ has total degree $\lvert T\rvert$.

items.title: $\widetilde f$ is multilinear, agrees with $f$ at every point of $\{0,1\}^{n}$, has no larger total degree, and is the unique multilinear polynomial with that agreement
items.strategy: Existence and agreement are [[lem-grid-reduction-of-a-multivariate-polynomial]] with $S_i=\{0,1\}$ (note $t^2=t$ for $t\in\{0,1\}$, so the reduction changes no value there). Uniqueness: a multilinear polynomial vanishing on $\{0,1\}^n$ is zero by [[thm-polynomial-identity-lemma]] with $\lvert S_i\rvert=2>1\ge\deg_{x_i}$. The degree clause needs its own step: reduction never raises total degree.

items.title: The functions $\{0,1\}^{n}\to F$ obtained from $x_T$ with $\lvert T\rvert\le s$ are linearly independent, so they span a space of dimension $\sum_{i=0}^{s}\binom{n}{i}$
items.strategy: A vanishing combination is a multilinear polynomial vanishing on the cube, hence the zero polynomial by [[lem-every-polynomial-agrees-on-the-cube-with-its-multilinear-reduction]], hence has all coefficients zero by the uniqueness of the monomial expansion in [[def-monomials-multidegree-and-total-degree]]. The count of index sets is $\sum_{i\le s}\binom{n}{i}$ by [[def-binomial-coefficient]] and [[thm-sum-rule]]. Boundary $s=0$ and $s=n$ are stated.

items.title: $L$-intersecting families
items.strategy: For a finite set $L\subseteq\mathbb{N}$, a family $\mathcal{F}$ of subsets of $[n]$ is **$L$-intersecting** when $\lvert A\cap B\rvert\in L$ for all distinct $A,B\in\mathcal{F}$. Note that nothing is required of $\lvert A\rvert$ itself — that is the difference from the uniform hypotheses used earlier on the page, and it is exactly what makes the ordering trick in the next theorem necessary. Record that Oddtown and Fisher are the cases $L=\{$even sizes$\}$ (not of this form) and $L=\{t\}$ respectively; state that comparison precisely or not at all.

items.title: An $L$-intersecting family on $[n]$ with $\lvert L\rvert=s$ has at most $\sum_{i=0}^{s}\binom{n}{i}$ members
items.strategy: Order $\mathcal{F}=\{F_1,\dots,F_m\}$ with $\lvert F_1\rvert\le\cdots\le\lvert F_m\rvert$. For each $i$ put $f_i(x)=\prod_{\ell\in L,\ \ell<\lvert F_i\rvert}\bigl(\langle x,v_{F_i}\rangle-\ell\bigr)$ over $\mathbb{R}$, of total degree at most $s$. Then $f_i(v_{F_i})=\prod_{\ell<\lvert F_i\rvert}(\lvert F_i\rvert-\ell)\ne0$, and for $j<i$, $f_i(v_{F_j})=0$: indeed $\lvert F_i\cap F_j\rvert\in L$ and $\lvert F_i\cap F_j\rvert\le\lvert F_j\rvert\le\lvert F_i\rvert$, with equality forcing $F_i\subseteq F_j$ and then $F_i=F_j$, so the intersection size is a member of $L$ strictly below $\lvert F_i\rvert$ and appears in the product. THE STRICT-INEQUALITY TRUNCATION OF THE PRODUCT IS WHAT REMOVES THE USUAL EXTRA HYPOTHESIS; make it a numbered step. Apply [[lem-triangular-independence-criterion]] to the multilinear reductions $\widetilde{f_i}$ paired against evaluation at $v_{F_j}$, then count dimensions with [[lem-the-multilinear-monomials-of-bounded-degree-are-independent-on-the-cube]]. Statement is Babai–Frankl's nonuniform Ray-Chaudhuri–Wilson bound. Landmark.

items.title: If $\mathcal{F}$ does not shatter $T$ then $x_T$ agrees on $\{v_F:F\in\mathcal{F}\}$ with a combination of the $x_S$ for $S\subsetneq T$
items.strategy: Choose $A\subseteq T$ realised by no member of $\mathcal{F}$ as $F\cap T$, and set $g(x)=\prod_{i\in A}x_i\prod_{i\in T\setminus A}(1-x_i)$. At $x=v_F$ the value is $1$ when $F\cap T=A$ and $0$ otherwise, so $g$ vanishes on every $v_F$. Expanding, $g=(-1)^{\lvert T\setminus A\rvert}x_T+\sum_{A\subseteq S\subsetneq T}(\pm1)x_S$, which rearranges to the claim. Each of the three facts — the value of $g$ at a cube point, the expansion, and the rearrangement — is its own step.

items.title: A second proof of Sauer–Shelah, from the multilinear polynomial space
items.strategy: Let $\mathcal{F}$ have VC dimension at most $d$ and let $V$ be the space of all functions $\mathcal{F}\to\mathbb{R}$, of dimension $\lvert\mathcal{F}\rvert$. Every such function is the restriction of a multilinear polynomial by [[lem-every-polynomial-agrees-on-the-cube-with-its-multilinear-reduction]] (interpolate on the cube and reduce). By [[lem-an-unshattered-set-reduces-a-monomial-on-a-family]] and induction on $\lvert T\rvert$, the restriction of $x_T$ for $\lvert T\rvert>d$ lies in the span of the restrictions of $x_S$ with $\lvert S\rvert<\lvert T\rvert$; hence the restrictions of the $x_T$ with $\lvert T\rvert\le d$ span $V$, and $\lvert\mathcal{F}\rvert=\dim V\le\sum_{i\le d}\binom{n}{i}$. A GENUINELY DIFFERENT ROUTE from the shifting proof: a spanning argument in a polynomial space replaces a compression argument, and neither proof is a rearrangement of the other. State the agreement with [[thm-sauer-shelah]] explicitly.

items.title: The shifting proof of Sauer–Shelah uses no field and no vector space
items.strategy: Say precisely which of this page's machinery the shifting proof does and does not use: no incidence vector, no field, no bilinear form and no dimension — only injections, a strictly decreasing natural number and a count of subsets. A reader arriving from Oddtown and Fisher will otherwise assume the theorem inherits a field hypothesis it does not have. Contrast with [[thm-sauer-shelah-by-multilinear-polynomials]], which does use the page's machinery, so the contrast is concrete rather than asserted. Required by the page's design.

items.title: Which field each bound is proved over, and what changes when it is replaced
items.strategy: One short paragraph per theorem, naming the field and the property of it that the proof spends: Oddtown over $\mathbb{F}_2$ using only bilinearity and the diagonal; Eventown over $\mathbb{F}_2$ using the dimension of an orthogonal complement; Fisher over $\mathbb{R}$ using that a sum of squares vanishes only when every term does; Graham–Pollak over $\mathbb{R}$ for the same reason; the Nullstellensatz over an arbitrary field; Cauchy–Davenport over $\mathbb{Z}/p$ with primality used to make it a field and to keep a binomial coefficient invertible. Then say what the companion page's false statements test. A JUSTIFYING REMARK: it explains hypotheses and names only items on this page. Do not count anything and do not rank the results.

pages.title: Linear Algebra Methods in Combinatorics — Examples

items.title: An Oddtown family of four clubs on four citizens, and why a fifth cannot be added
items.strategy: Take the four singletons on $[4]$, check both parities, and then check by hand that no fifth subset of $[4]$ can be adjoined: a candidate must have odd size and meet each singleton evenly, which forces it to be disjoint from every point. Also display the incidence matrix over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and verify $NN^{\mathsf{T}}=I_4$. This makes both [[thm-oddtown]] and [[cor-the-oddtown-bound-is-attained]] concrete.

items.title: The pairing construction gives an Eventown family of size $2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$
items.strategy: Group the points of $[n]$ into the pairs $\{0,1\},\{2,3\},\dots$, leaving one point unpaired when $n$ is odd, and take every union of pairs. Check both parity conditions and count $2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ sets. Write $n=4$ out in full — $\varnothing$, $\{0,1\}$, $\{2,3\}$, $\{0,1,2,3\}$, four sets, matching $2^{2}$ — and then $n=5$, where the same four sets are still maximal and $2^{\lfloor 5/2\rfloor}=4$, so the floor is visible rather than asserted. Check the result against [[thm-eventown]] and [[thm-every-maximal-eventown-family-is-maximum]].

items.title: The seven lines of the Fano plane meet pairwise in one point, and Fisher's bound is tight
items.strategy: Write the seven three-element subsets of $[7]$ explicitly (for instance the translates of $\{0,1,3\}$ modulo $7$), verify that every two of them meet in exactly one point by listing the twenty-one pairs or by a short modular argument, and check $m=7\le n=7$ against [[cor-uniform-fisher-inequality]]. Present the Fano plane as a SET SYSTEM only: block designs and projective planes are not among the page's prerequisites, and no design-theoretic vocabulary is used.

items.title: $K_4$ decomposed into three complete bipartite graphs, and no decomposition into two
items.strategy: Give the star decomposition $(\{0\},\{1,2,3\})$, $(\{1\},\{2,3\})$, $(\{2\},\{3\})$ and check every edge is covered exactly once. Then check the lower bound directly at $m=2$ by running the argument of [[thm-graham-pollak]] on the explicit two-equation system, exhibiting a nonzero solution and the resulting contradiction.

items.title: All subsets of $[4]$ of size at most $2$: VC dimension $2$ and exactly $\sum_{i\le2}\binom{4}{i}=11$ members
items.strategy: List the eleven sets, verify that $\{0,1\}$ is shattered, verify that no three-element set is shattered (the full triple is missing from every trace), and compare with the bound $1+4+6=11$ of [[thm-sauer-shelah]]. Then run one down-shift on a family that is not downward closed and check both compression lemmas on it.

items.title: $W_{1,2}(4)$ written out, and its rank computed
items.strategy: Display the $4\times6$ matrix with rows the points of $[4]$ and columns the six pairs, row reduce it over $\mathbb{Q}$, and confirm the rank is $4$ as [[thm-rank-of-the-point-inclusion-matrix]] predicts. Also check the composition identity $W_{0,1}(4)W_{1,2}(4)=2\,W_{0,2}(4)$ by direct multiplication.

items.title: $A=B=\{0,1,2\}$ in $\mathbb{Z}/7$: the sumset has five elements and the bound is tight
items.strategy: Compute $A+B=\{0,1,2,3,4\}$, so $\lvert A+B\rvert=5=\lvert A\rvert+\lvert B\rvert-1$, matching [[thm-cauchy-davenport]] exactly. Then take $A=\{0,1,2,3\}$, $B=\{0,1,2,3,4\}$ and check the other branch, where the bound is $7$ and the sumset is everything.

items.title: Applying the Nullstellensatz by hand to $f(x,y)=x^{2}y+xy^{2}+x+y$ over $\mathbb{Q}$
items.strategy: Identify $\deg f=3$, the multi-index $(t_1,t_2)=(2,1)$ and the coefficient $1\ne0$; take $S_1$ with three elements and $S_2$ with two and exhibit a point where $f\ne0$, as [[thm-combinatorial-nullstellensatz]] guarantees. Then run [[lem-grid-reduction-of-a-multivariate-polynomial]] on the same $f$ for those grids and check the three claims of that lemma on the reduction. Verify every displayed coefficient before shipping.

items.title: The six $2$-subsets of $[4]$ are $\{0,1\}$-intersecting, and the bound $\sum_{i\le2}\binom{4}{i}=11$ holds
items.strategy: Check that any two distinct pairs meet in zero or one point, so $L=\{0,1\}$ and $s=2$; compare $6\le11$ from [[thm-frankl-wilson-nonuniform-bound]]. Then build the polynomials $f_i$ of that theorem for this family, multilinearise two of them by hand, and verify the triangular pattern of values that the proof uses.

items.title: The $n$ hyperplanes $x_i=1$ cover $\{0,1\}^{n}$ except the origin, so the Alon–Füredi bound is tight
items.strategy: Check that a nonzero vertex has some coordinate equal to $1$ and that the origin lies on none of the hyperplanes, so $n$ hyperplanes suffice; with [[thm-alon-furedi-hyperplane-cover-of-the-cube]] this makes $n$ exact. Then do $n=2$ in full, listing the four vertices and the two lines.

items.title: FALSE: an Oddtown family on $[n]$ has at most $n-1$ members
items.strategy: Refute with the $n$ singletons of [[cor-the-oddtown-bound-is-attained]], written out for $n=4$ and in general. The Refutation should also say where the plausible improvement would have to come from — a strict inequality in the dimension count — and why [[lem-a-family-with-independent-incidence-vectors-has-at-most-n-members]] gives no such thing.

items.title: FALSE: distinct nonempty $A_1,\dots,A_m\subseteq[n]$ whose pairwise intersections all have the same parity satisfy $m\le n$
items.strategy: THE PAGE’S PEDAGOGICAL PAYLOAD, and it must be stated as a PROPOSITION about set systems, not as a claim about a proof. The false statement is the $\mathbb{F}_2$ shadow of [[thm-nonuniform-fisher-inequality]]: over $\mathbb{R}$ the hypothesis is $\lvert A_i\cap A_j\rvert=t$ for all $i\ne j$, and over $\mathbb{F}_2$ all that survives of it is that the intersection sizes share a parity, since [[lem-the-standard-form-of-two-incidence-vectors-is-the-intersection-size]] sees an intersection only through $\lvert A_i\cap A_j\rvert\bmod 2$. Refute with an Eventown family from [[ex-an-eventown-family-of-maximum-size]]: every pairwise intersection is even, so all of them share a parity, and there are $2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ sets by [[thm-eventown]], which exceeds $n$ from $n=6$ on; drop $\varnothing$ if the nonemptiness clause is wanted and the count is still $2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}-1$. Exhibit the family in full for a concrete $n$ and check the two conditions on it. Then name the exact step of [[lem-real-vectors-with-equal-pairwise-products-and-larger-norms-are-independent]] that has no $\mathbb{F}_2$ analogue: the expansion ends in $\sum_ic_i^2(d_i-t)+t(\sum_ic_i)^2=0$ and concludes that each term vanishes, which uses that a sum of nonnegative reals vanishes only when every summand does. $\mathbb{F}_2$ carries no order, so there is nothing to run that step on — and the further clause $\langle v_i,v_i\rangle>t$ has no $\mathbb{F}_2$ analogue at all, which is exactly what the Eventown family exploits.

items.title: FALSE: a family on $[n]$ of VC dimension at most $d$ has at most $n^{d}$ members
items.strategy: CHECK THE WITNESS BEFORE SHIPPING. The true bound is $\sum_{i\le d}\binom{n}{i}$, which exceeds $n^{d}$ for small $n$: at $n=1$, $d=1$ the family $\{\varnothing,\{0\}\}$ has VC dimension $1$ and two members while $n^{d}=1$; verify this instance completely, and give one more, checking the VC dimension of each family by listing its traces. Then state the correct polynomial bound of [[cor-sauer-shelah-polynomial-bound]] and say exactly which inequality the false claim over-tightens.

items.title: FALSE: $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_ix_iy_i$ makes $\mathbb{F}_2^{n}$ an inner product space
items.strategy: State the claim in the form a reader might write it and refute against [[def-inner-product-space]]: an inner product requires $\langle x,x\rangle$ to be a nonnegative real and to vanish only at $0$, and $\mathbb{F}_2$ carries no order at all. Exhibit $x=(1,1)$ with $\langle x,x\rangle=0$ and $x\ne0$. Then say what IS true: the form is a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form, and every use of it on the page needs only bilinearity, so nothing is lost.

items.title: FALSE: if $\deg f=\sum_it_i$ and $\lvert S_i\rvert>t_i$ then $f$ is nonzero somewhere on $S_1\times\cdots\times S_n$
items.strategy: The dropped hypothesis is that the coefficient of $x_1^{t_1}\cdots x_n^{t_n}$ is nonzero. Refute with $f(x,y)=x^{2}-x$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, $t_1=t_2=1$, $S_1=S_2=\{0,1\}$: the total degree is $2=t_1+t_2$, each $\lvert S_i\rvert=2>1$, and yet $f$ vanishes at all four grid points, because the coefficient of $xy$ is $0$. Display the four evaluations. Then cite [[thm-combinatorial-nullstellensatz]] for the correct statement and note that the identity lemma does not apply either, since $\deg_x f=2$ is not below $\lvert S_1\rvert$.

items.title: A set family whose incidence vectors are dependent over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and independent over $\mathbb{R}$
items.strategy: Take $A_1=\{0,1\}$, $A_2=\{1,2\}$, $A_3=\{0,2\}$ in $[3]$, with incidence vectors $(1,1,0)$, $(0,1,1)$, $(1,0,1)$. Over $\mathbb{F}_2$ the three sum to $0$, so they are dependent; over $\mathbb{R}$ the incidence matrix has determinant $2\ne0$, so they are independent. Compute both, showing the determinant expansion. THE ITEM IS ABOUT THE FIELD BEING A HYPOTHESIS, which is why the page states one on every theorem.

items.title: In $\mathbb{Z}/4$ the sets $A=B=\{0,2\}$ have $\lvert A+B\rvert=2$, below the Cauchy–Davenport bound $3$
items.strategy: Compute $A+B=\{0,2\}$ — the four sums $0+0$, $0+2$, $2+0$, $2+2$ give $0,2,2,0$ — so $\lvert A+B\rvert=2<3=\min\{4,\lvert A\rvert+\lvert B\rvert-1\}$. DISPLAY ALL FOUR SUMS: the sumset is $\{0,2\}$ and not $\{0\}$, and a witness whose arithmetic is not shown is where this item would go wrong. Then say exactly which step of [[thm-cauchy-davenport]] fails: $\mathbb{Z}/4$ is not a field, so the polynomial argument has no domain to work in, and $\{0,2\}$ is a proper subgroup, which is the general obstruction — a subgroup $A=B=H$ always has $A+B=H$, so the deficit is as large as the subgroup allows. Cite [[thm-z-mod-p-is-a-field]] for the primality that is being spent.

items.title: $P(x)=x(x-1)$ vanishes on $\{0,1\}$ although $\deg_x P=\lvert\{0,1\}\rvert$
items.strategy: The one-variable instance shows the inequality in [[thm-polynomial-identity-lemma]] must be strict. Give also a two-variable instance, $P(x,y)=x(x-1)$ on $\{0,1\}\times\{0,1\}$, and check that the hypothesis fails only in the first variable. Say which numbered step of the identity lemma consumes the strictness.

pages.title: Block Designs and Finite Projective Planes

items.title: A $2$-$(v,k,\lambda)$ design
The point-block incidence matrix of a $2$-design
Every point of a $2$-design lies in the same number of blocks
items.strategy: Fix a point p and count ordered pairs (q,B) with q != p and {p,q} subseteq B. For each block through p there are k-1 choices of q, while for each q != p there are exactly lambda blocks through {p,q}. The resulting count is independent of p, so the number r_p of blocks through p is constant. State the boundary 2 <= k < v explicitly so k-1 and v-1 are positive.

items.title: A $2$-design satisfies $bk=vr$ and $r(k-1)=\lambda(v-1)$
items.strategy: After the preceding lemma, define r to be the common replication number and b to be the number of blocks. Double-count incident point-block pairs for bk=vr. The second identity is the count used in the constancy proof, now written with the common r. Keep the two counts separate so later items can cite each formula individually.

items.title: The standard divisibility conditions for a $2$-design
items.strategy: From r(k-1)=lambda(v-1) conclude that k-1 divides lambda(v-1), so r=lambda(v-1)/(k-1) is an integer. Substitute that into bk=vr to obtain b=v lambda(v-1)/(k(k-1)). State the conclusion as necessity only, not sufficiency.

items.title: For a $2$-design, $NN^{\mathsf T}=(r-\lambda)I+\lambda J$
items.strategy: Let N be the 0-1 incidence matrix with rows indexed by points and columns by blocks. The diagonal entry of NN^T counts blocks through one point and is r. An off-diagonal entry counts blocks through a pair of distinct points and is lambda. Therefore the whole matrix is (r-lambda)I + lambda J. Keep the matrix-size conventions explicit: N is v by b, so NN^T is v by v.

items.title: Fisher's inequality: every $2$-$(v,k,\lambda)$ design has at least $v$ blocks
items.strategy: Use the incidence identity. Since 2 <= k < v, the counting identity gives r > lambda. If x is orthogonal to the all-ones vector then x^T NN^T x=(r-lambda)||x||^2, and on the all-ones line one gets x^T NN^T x=(r-lambda+lambda v)||x||^2/v. Hence NN^T is positive definite, so rank(NN^T)=v. Since rank(NN^T) <= rank(N) <= b, we obtain v <= b. Keep the proof over R, because positivity is load-bearing and the published false-statement witness over F_2 is on the earlier page.

items.title: A symmetric design
In a symmetric $2$-design, distinct blocks meet in exactly $\lambda$ points
items.strategy: Let N be the square incidence matrix of a symmetric design. By Fisher's inequality and symmetry, N is square and the determinant of NN^T from the previous identity is nonzero because r>lambda, so N is invertible. Use bk=vr with b=v to get r=k, and use the constant row and column sums k to show N^{-1} J N = J. Then N^T N = N^{-1}(NN^T)N = (k-lambda)I + lambda J. The off-diagonal entries of N^T N count block intersections, so every two distinct blocks meet in exactly lambda points.

items.title: Steiner triple systems
A Steiner triple system can exist only when $v\equiv1$ or $3\pmod6$
items.strategy: Specialize the divisibility conditions to k=3 and lambda=1. Then r=(v-1)/2 is integral, so v is odd, and b=v(v-1)/6 is integral, so 3 divides v(v-1)/2. Checking odd residues modulo 6 leaves only 1 and 3.

items.title: Bose's construction gives a Steiner triple system of order $6m+3$ for $m\ge1$
items.strategy: Write v=6m+3=3n with n odd. On Z/n define x circle y = ((n+1)/2)(x+y), which is well defined because 2 is invertible modulo odd n. Form points Z/n x Z/3, add the vertical triples {(x,0),(x,1),(x,2)}, and for each unordered pair x != y add the three triples {(x,i),(y,i),(x circle y,i+1)}. Verify every pair of points lies in exactly one block by splitting into same-layer and adjacent-layer cases. Count the blocks separately to match v(v-1)/6.

items.title: Skolem's construction gives a Steiner triple system of order $6m+1$
items.strategy: Record the exact sourced existence statement for the 1 mod 6 branch and explain that this batch uses the existence consequence but does not rebuild the source's block list locally.

items.title: A Steiner triple system exists exactly for orders $v>3$ with $v\equiv1$ or $3\pmod6$
items.strategy: The forward implication combines the congruence obstruction with the library's own 2-design convention, which forces v>3. For the reverse implication, split by the two odd residue classes: v=6m+3 with v>3 uses Bose, and v=6m+1 with v>3 uses Skolem.

items.title: A finite projective plane
Every line in a finite projective plane has the same number of points
items.strategy: Take two lines l and m. If l=m there is nothing to prove, so assume they are distinct and let p=l intersect m. Use the nondegeneracy axiom to choose a point x off l union m. For each point y on l\{p}, the line through x and y meets m in exactly one point of m\{p}; conversely every point of m\{p} arises this way. This bijection gives |l|-1=|m|-1. Keep the role of the third projective-plane axiom explicit: it is exactly what supplies x.

items.title: The order of a finite projective plane
A finite projective plane of order $n$ has $n^2+n+1$ points and the same number of lines
items.strategy: Fix a line l with n+1 points. Every point off l lies on a unique line through each point of l, and each of the n+1 lines through a fixed point of l contributes n off-line points, so there are n(n+1) off-line points and therefore n^2+n+1 points in total. Fix a point p and a line l not through p to get exactly n+1 lines through p. Double-count incident point-line pairs to obtain equality of the point and line counts.

items.title: A projective plane of order $n$ is a symmetric $2$-$(n^2+n+1,n+1,1)$ design
items.strategy: Read points as the ground set and lines as the blocks. The projective-plane axioms give lambda=1, the count theorem gives v=b=n^2+n+1, and every line has k=n+1 points.

items.title: For every prime power $q$, the space $PG(2,q)$ is a projective plane of order $q$
items.strategy: Take points to be the one-dimensional subspaces of F_q^3 and lines the two-dimensional subspaces. Two distinct points span a unique two-dimensional subspace, and two distinct two-dimensional subspaces intersect in a unique one-dimensional subspace by the dimension formula in a three-dimensional vector space. The coordinate axes provide four points with no three collinear. A line is a two-dimensional F_q-space, so it has q^2-1 nonzero vectors and therefore (q^2-1)/(q-1)=q+1 projective points; the preceding theorem then identifies the order as q.

items.title: A Latin square
Orthogonal Latin squares and complete families of them
The linear Latin squares $L_a(i,j)=ai+j$ over $\mathbb F_q$ are pairwise orthogonal
items.strategy: For each nonzero a in F_q, define L_a(i,j)=ai+j on F_q x F_q. Each fixed row or column is an affine bijection, so L_a is Latin. If a != b and prescribed symbols s,t are given, solving ai+j=s and bi+j=t reduces to (a-b)i=s-t, which has a unique solution because a-b is nonzero in a field. Then j is uniquely determined, so every ordered pair occurs exactly once.

items.title: Every prime power order $q$ admits $q-1$ mutually orthogonal Latin squares
items.strategy: A finite field of order q exists for every prime power q, and the preceding theorem gives one Latin square for each nonzero slope a in F_q. Since there are q-1 nonzero field elements, these form a complete family.

pages.title: Block Designs and Finite Projective Planes — Examples

items.title: The seven translates of $\{0,1,3\}$ form the Fano plane
items.strategy: List the seven translates modulo 7 of {0,1,3}, verify that every pair of points lies in exactly one translate, and then check that the same seven triples satisfy the projective-plane axioms.

items.title: The Fano plane has incidence matrix $N$ with $NN^{\mathsf T}=2I+J$
items.strategy: Choose an explicit ordering of the seven points and seven lines of the Fano plane, write the 7 by 7 incidence matrix, and multiply it out. The diagonal entries should be 3, the off-diagonal ones 1, so this example exhibits both the incidence identity and equality in Fisher's inequality.

items.title: Bose's construction at order $9$ gives a Steiner triple system on nine points
items.strategy: Take n=3, compute x circle y=2(x+y) in Z/3, list the three vertical triples and the nine quasigroup triples, and check that each unordered pair of points appears once. This example is the first nontrivial 3 mod 6 case and is small enough to verify by direct incidence data.

items.title: $PG(2,3)$ has $13$ points and $13$ lines
items.strategy: Count the one-dimensional and two-dimensional subspaces of F_3^3. There are 26 nonzero vectors and each point has 2 nonzero representatives, so there are 13 points; dually there are 13 lines. Display one sample line as the span of two independent vectors and check that it contains 4 projective points.

items.title: The squares $L_1(i,j)=i+j$ and $L_2(i,j)=2i+j$ on $\mathbb F_3$ are orthogonal
items.strategy: Write both 3 by 3 arrays explicitly and list the nine ordered pairs (L_1(i,j),L_2(i,j)). Each pair from F_3^2 should appear once, which is the concrete verification of orthogonality in the first prime-power case beyond q=2.

items.title: The complementary $2$-$(7,4,2)$ design is symmetric but not a projective plane
items.strategy: Take the complements of the seven Fano lines inside the seven-point set. Each complementary block has size 4 and any two meet in 2 points, so the design is symmetric. It is not a projective plane because projective planes have lambda=1: two lines should meet in exactly one point, not two.

items.title: A Latin square need not be orthogonal to an identical copy of itself
items.strategy: Use the addition table of Z/3 twice. The ordered pair (0,0) occurs in every cell of the main diagonal, so the ordered pairs are not all distinct. This is the smallest clean witness that orthogonality is genuinely extra structure.

pages.title: Algebraic and Spectral Graph Theory

items.title: The adjacency matrix of a finite simple graph
Adjacency spectrum, spectral radius, and cospectral graphs
The $(i,j)$ entry of $A(G)^k$ counts walks of length $k$
items.strategy: Induct on the walk length. The case k=1 is the adjacency definition. For the inductive step, the matrix-product formula expands the (i,j) entry of A^(k+1) as a sum over intermediate vertices, and each summand counts the length-k walks ending at that intermediate vertex followed by one final edge.

items.title: The trace of $A(G)^k$ counts closed walks of length $k$
items.strategy: Sum the diagonal entries in the walk-counting theorem. Each diagonal entry counts walks that start and end at the same vertex, so the trace counts all closed walks of the given length.

items.title: The adjacency spectrum is an isomorphism invariant
items.strategy: An isomorphism between finite graphs permutes the vertex basis, so the two adjacency matrices are conjugate by a permutation matrix. Conjugate matrices have the same characteristic polynomial and therefore the same ordered real spectrum.

items.title: A finite simple graph is bipartite if and only if its adjacency spectrum is symmetric about $0$
items.strategy: If the graph is bipartite, conjugate its adjacency matrix by the diagonal sign matrix that is +1 on one part and -1 on the other to obtain -A. Conversely, symmetric spectrum forces every odd power to have trace zero, so there are no closed walks of odd length. The published odd-cycle criterion then gives bipartiteness.

items.title: The adjacency spectral radius lies between the average degree and the maximum degree
items.strategy: For the lower bound, evaluate the Rayleigh quotient on the all-ones vector to obtain the average degree. For the upper bound, each Gershgorin disk is centered at zero with radius equal to a vertex degree, so every eigenvalue has modulus at most the maximum degree.

items.title: An oriented incidence matrix of a finite simple graph
The Laplacian matrix of a finite simple graph
The Laplacian equals $BB^{\mathsf T}$ for every oriented incidence matrix $B$
items.strategy: Compute the diagonal and off-diagonal entries of BB^T directly from the column signs of an oriented incidence matrix. The diagonal entry counts edges incident to a vertex, while an off-diagonal entry is -1 when the vertices are adjacent and 0 otherwise.

items.title: The Laplacian is positive semidefinite and sends the all-ones vector to zero
items.strategy: From L=BB^T, every quadratic form x^TLx is ||B^Tx||^2 and is therefore nonnegative. The column sum of an oriented incidence matrix is zero, so B^T times the all-ones vector vanishes and hence so does L times that vector.

items.title: The multiplicity of the Laplacian eigenvalue $0$ equals the number of connected components
items.strategy: A vector lies in the kernel of the Laplacian exactly when it is constant on every edge, equivalently constant on every connected component. Indicator vectors of the connected components span that kernel and are linearly independent, giving the exact multiplicity count.

items.title: The algebraic connectivity of a finite simple graph
A finite simple graph is connected if and only if its algebraic connectivity is positive
items.strategy: The preceding theorem makes the second-smallest Laplacian eigenvalue positive exactly when the zero eigenspace is one-dimensional, and that happens exactly when the graph has one connected component.

items.title: The Binet-Cauchy formula
items.strategy: Expand the determinant of AB by selecting which m columns of A and corresponding rows of B contribute to a nonzero permutation term. Grouping the terms by that chosen m-set yields the sum of products of m-by-m minors.

items.title: The complete graph $K_n$ has adjacency spectrum $\{n-1,(-1)^{n-1}\}$
items.strategy: Write A(K_n)=J-I. The all-ones vector is an eigenvector of J with eigenvalue n, while every vector orthogonal to it is annihilated by J. Subtracting the identity shifts those eigenvalues to n-1 and -1.

items.title: Kirchhoff's matrix-tree theorem
items.strategy: Delete one row from an oriented incidence matrix B to get B0. Then L0=B0B0^T, so Binet-Cauchy expands det(L0) as a sum over (n-1)-edge subsets. A minor contributes 1 exactly for spanning trees and 0 otherwise, giving the spanning-tree count and simultaneously showing that every principal Laplacian cofactor agrees.

items.title: The matrix-tree theorem becomes an eigenvalue product formula
items.strategy: The deleted Laplacian cofactor is the product of the nonzero Laplacian eigenvalues divided by the number of vertices. For a d-regular graph, L=dI-A, so spectral mapping turns the Laplacian factors into d-lambda_i.

items.title: Cayley's formula follows again from the matrix-tree theorem
items.strategy: Apply the eigenvalue product formula to K_n. Its nontrivial adjacency eigenvalue is -1 with multiplicity n-1, so the regular-graph form gives tau(K_n)=n^(n-2), agreeing with the earlier Prüfer-code proof.

items.title: An $(n,d,\lambda)$-graph and an expander
For an $(n,d,\lambda)$-graph with $\lambda<d$, every nontrivial cut has many crossing edges
items.strategy: Evaluate the second-eigenvalue Rayleigh quotient on the vector that is constant on one side of a vertex partition and constant of opposite sign on the other. Rearranging the resulting inequality yields a lower bound on the cut size, and positivity of that bound gives connectedness.

items.title: The cycle graph $C_n$ has adjacency spectrum $\{2\cos(2\pi j/n):0\le j<n\}$
items.strategy: View C_n as the Cayley graph of Z/nZ with generators ±1. The discrete Fourier basis diagonalizes every circulant matrix, and the corresponding eigenvalue at frequency j is omega^j+omega^{-j}=2 cos(2 pi j/n).

items.title: The complete bipartite graph $K_{m,n}$ has adjacency spectrum $\{\sqrt{mn},0^{m+n-2},-\sqrt{mn}\}$
items.strategy: Write the adjacency matrix in block form with off-diagonal all-ones blocks. Vectors supported on one part and summing to zero, or on the other part and summing to zero, are killed by the matrix. The remaining two-dimensional block has matrix [[0,n],[m,0]], whose eigenvalues are ±sqrt(mn).

items.title: The Petersen graph has adjacency spectrum $\{3,1^5,(-2)^4\}$
items.strategy: Use the two-subset model of the Petersen graph. The adjacency operator is the Kneser operator on two-subsets of a five-element set; the constant vector, the five-dimensional coordinate-sum space modulo constants, and its orthogonal complement are invariant, and the operator acts on them by 3, 1, and -2 respectively.

pages.title: Algebraic and Spectral Graph Theory — Examples

items.title: The cycle $C_4$ has adjacency spectrum $\{2,0,0,-2\}$
A disconnected graph has a Laplacian kernel spanned by its component indicators
Kirchhoff's formula gives $\tau(K_4)=16$
The graph $K_{3,3}$ has adjacency spectrum $\{3,0,0,0,0,-3\}$
The two-subset model reproduces the Petersen spectrum
Two cospectral graphs need not be isomorphic
FALSE: positive second Laplacian eigenvalue characterises 2-connectivity
FALSE: the matrix-tree theorem works only for one distinguished cofactor

pages.title: The Total Derivative in R^m -> R^n

items.title: A linear map $L:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^n$ in Euclidean coordinates
Every Euclidean linear map has a unique matrix and satisfies $\|Lh\|_2\le K\|h\|_2$ for some $K\ge0$
items.strategy: Expand $h$ in the published standard basis, use linearity to obtain $Lh=\sum_j h_jL(e_j)$, and read off the unique matrix columns. Bound the norm by the finite triangle inequality and $|h_j|\le\|h\|_2$, taking $K=\sum_j\|L(e_j)\|_2$. Check $m=0$ is outside the standing hypotheses and zero maps give $K=0$.

items.title: A convex subset of $\mathbb{R}^m$ contains every line segment between two of its points
Directional derivatives and partial derivatives of a map $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^n$
The total (Fréchet) derivative $Df(a)$ as the linear first-order approximation with $o(\|h\|_2)$ remainder
The total derivative at a point is unique
items.strategy: If $L$ and $M$ both satisfy the remainder estimate, test along $h=tv$ inside an open ball about the point. Divide by $|t|$ for $t\ne0$ and use an epsilon contradiction to obtain $(L-M)v=0$ for every $v$, including $v=0$ separately.

items.title: Total differentiability gives a local $O(\|h\|_2)$ increment bound and therefore continuity
items.strategy: Bound $Df(a)h$ by the Euclidean linear-map lemma and make the normalized remainder at most one on a sufficiently small ball. The triangle inequality gives $\|f(a+h)-f(a)\|_2\le(K+1)\|h\|_2$, from which epsilon-delta continuity follows; keep the zero-map and zero-increment cases explicit.

items.title: The Jacobian matrix of partial derivatives and the gradient in the scalar-valued case
A total derivative computes every directional derivative, and its matrix is the Jacobian
items.strategy: Restrict the total remainder estimate to $h=tv$. After division by $t$, homogeneity makes the remainder tend to zero and the derivative of $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ equals $Df(a)v$. Specialize to standard basis vectors and invoke the matrix-column representation to identify the Jacobian, preserving the $v=0$ case.

items.title: For a differentiable scalar field, $D_vf(a)=\langle\nabla f(a),v\rangle$ and the unit direction of steepest ascent is the normalized gradient
items.strategy: Use the Jacobian representation in the scalar case to obtain the inner-product formula. Cauchy-Schwarz bounds unit-direction derivatives by the gradient norm, with equality in the normalized gradient direction when the gradient is nonzero; when it is zero, every directional derivative is zero and there is no unique steepest direction.

items.title: Sums and scalar multiples of totally differentiable maps are totally differentiable with the expected derivatives
items.strategy: Add or scale the two remainder identities and use the norm triangle inequality or absolute homogeneity. Verify that the proposed derivative is linear, and split the scalar-zero case only where division by its absolute value would otherwise occur.

items.title: The chain rule for total derivatives: $D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a)$
items.strategy: Write $f(a+h)-f(a)=Ah+r(h)$ and $g(f(a)+k)-g(f(a))=Bk+s(k)$. The local linear bound makes $k=O(\|h\|)$, so $s(k)=o(\|k\|)=o(\|h\|)$, while boundedness of $B$ gives $B r(h)=o(\|h\|)$. Treat $k=0$ without forming the normalized outer remainder and verify the composite linear map explicitly.

items.title: Small coordinate-by-coordinate increments stay inside a Euclidean ball and telescope the total increment
items.strategy: For $h\in\mathbb{R}^m$, define $p_j=a+\sum_{k<j}h_ke_k$. The norm of each coordinate prefix is at most $\|h\|_2$, so a small increment keeps every $p_j$ in the chosen ball. The finite telescoping identity expresses $f(a+h)-f(a)$ as the sum of the increments $f(p_{j+1})-f(p_j)$.

items.title: If all partial derivatives exist on a neighbourhood and are continuous at a point, then the map is totally differentiable there with Jacobian derivative
items.strategy: Choose a ball where every partial derivative vector is uniformly close to its value at the base point. Telescope along coordinate segments using the preceding lemma; apply the published vector mean-value inequality to each segment after subtracting the fixed linear term. Sum the errors and compare the coordinate $1$-norm with the Euclidean norm. Verify the Jacobian map is linear before invoking the definition.

items.title: On a convex open set, a uniform bound $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ implies $\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2$
items.strategy: Parametrize the segment from $x$ to $y$ by $\gamma(t)=x+t(y-x)$. Convexity keeps the curve in the domain, the chain rule gives $(f\circ\gamma)'(t)=Df(\gamma(t))(y-x)$, and the published vector mean-value inequality supplies the endpoint estimate. Treat $x=y$ directly and use no global operator-norm definition.

items.title: A totally differentiable map with zero derivative on a convex open set is constant
items.strategy: Apply the total-derivative mean-value inequality with $M=0$ to arbitrary points of the domain. Include the empty-domain case (vacuously constant under the library's definition) and singleton/zero-dimensional exclusions explicitly rather than importing the later connected-open-set theorem.

items.title: Dimension, openness, norm, Jacobian, and the native Euclidean linear-map agreement seam

pages.title: The Total Derivative in R^m -> R^n: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The polynomial map $(x,y)\mapsto(1+x+2y+x^2,\,2x+3y+xy)$ and its Jacobian
items.strategy: Compute all four partial derivatives with the one-variable algebra and power rules. Their continuity makes the continuous-partials theorem applicable, and the resulting Jacobian matrix gives the total derivative at an arbitrary point. Verify one increment expansion directly as a check on the matrix.

items.title: $xy/(x^2+y^2)$ has both partial derivatives at the origin but is discontinuous there
items.strategy: Define the value at the origin to be zero. Both coordinate-axis restrictions are identically zero, so both partial derivatives exist and vanish. Along $y=x\ne0$ the function is $1/2$, contradicting continuity at the origin.

items.title: $x^2y/(x^4+y^2)$ tends to zero on every line through the origin but not along $y=x^2$
items.strategy: Define the origin value to be zero. Substitute $(x,y)=(ta,tb)$ and separate $b=0$ from $b\ne0$ to show every straight-line restriction tends to zero. Along $(t,t^2)$ the value is $1/2$, so the map is not continuous at the origin.

items.title: $x^2y/(x^2+y^2)$ has every directional derivative at the origin but is not totally differentiable there
items.strategy: Compute the directional derivative along $v=(a,b)$ as $a^2b/(a^2+b^2)$ for $v\ne0$ and zero for $v=0$. Exhibit a failure of additivity of this direction map. If a total derivative existed, the directional-derivative theorem would make the map linear, a contradiction.

items.title: The map $y(x^2+y^2)/x$ off the line $x=0$, extended by zero on that line, has every directional derivative zero at the origin but is discontinuous there
items.strategy: On every fixed line through the origin the function is quadratic in the line parameter, so the directional difference quotient tends to zero. Along the curved path $x=y^3$ the values tend to one, proving discontinuity and hence failure of total differentiability.

items.title: A locally constant step map on the disconnected open set $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ has zero total derivative but is not globally Lipschitz
items.strategy: In the $\mathbb{R}^1$ identification, take value zero on the negative component and one on the positive component. Each point has a neighbourhood on which the map is constant, so its total derivative is zero. The points $-t$ and $t$ have image distance one and domain distance $2t$, which defeats every proposed global Lipschitz constant for small positive $t$.

pages.title: Mixed Partials, Taylor, and Extrema in Several Variables

items.title: $C^k$ maps and multi-index derivative notation in Euclidean space
The Hessian matrix and critical points of a scalar field
A rectangular second difference equals a mixed partial times the side lengths
items.strategy: Apply the one-variable mean value theorem in one coordinate to the difference across the other coordinate, then apply it again to the resulting one-variable function. State the closed-rectangle and interior differentiability hypotheses exactly.

items.title: Peano's mixed-partial theorem from continuity of one mixed partial
items.strategy: Apply the rectangle formula to shrinking rectangles based at the point. Continuity of one mixed partial controls the quotient, while the assumed existence of the reverse iterated derivative along the coordinate line identifies the other iterated limit.

items.title: Young's theorem: total differentiability of the first partials forces equality of mixed partials
items.strategy: Expand the two first-partial functions at the base point with total-derivative remainders and insert those expansions into a symmetric rectangular difference quotient. Cancellation leaves the two mixed coefficients equal.

items.title: Clairaut–Schwarz theorem for continuous second partial derivatives
items.strategy: Continuity of the relevant second partials gives the hypotheses of Peano's theorem (and, alternatively, Young's differentiability hypothesis); specialize to every coordinate pair.

items.title: The Hessian of a $C^2$ scalar field is symmetric
items.strategy: Apply Clairaut–Schwarz to each pair of coordinate indices and translate the equalities into matrix entries.

items.title: Continuous mixed partials of order $k$ are invariant under permutations
items.strategy: Show invariance under one adjacent transposition by applying Clairaut–Schwarz after freezing the other derivatives; decompose every finite permutation into adjacent transpositions and induct over their number.

items.title: Repeated derivatives along a line expand by the multinomial formula
items.strategy: Apply the total-derivative chain rule once, then induct on the derivative order. Use symmetry of higher mixed partials to collect ordered coordinate choices into multinomial coefficients.

items.title: The multivariable Taylor polynomial in multi-index notation
Multivariable Taylor formula with a Lagrange remainder along a line segment
items.strategy: Restrict the function to the segment, apply the one-variable Lagrange Taylor formula, and substitute the line-derivative multinomial expansion. Convexity keeps the segment inside the domain; separate zero increment.

items.title: Multivariable Taylor formula with $o(\|h\|^k)$ remainder
items.strategy: Apply the one-variable Peano theorem to the line restriction and use the multinomial line-derivative identity; convert the scalar parameter remainder to the Euclidean increment norm.

items.title: Second-order Taylor expansion $f(a+h)=f(a)+\nabla f(a)\cdot h+\tfrac12h^TH_f(a)h+o(\|h\|^2)$
items.strategy: Specialize the Peano formula to order two and collect the first- and second-order multi-index terms as the gradient inner product and Hessian quadratic form.

items.title: Local and strict local extrema for scalar fields on Euclidean open sets
Fermat's theorem: an interior differentiable local extremum has zero gradient
items.strategy: Restrict to each coordinate line through the point, apply the one-variable Fermat theorem, and identify the resulting partial derivatives as the gradient coordinates.

items.title: Positive definite, negative definite, semidefinite, and indefinite quadratic forms
A definite quadratic form has a uniform signed bound on the Euclidean unit sphere
items.strategy: For $n\ge 1$, prove directly that the Euclidean unit sphere is nonempty, closed, and bounded: use $e_0$ for nonemptiness, continuity of the Euclidean norm for closedness, and the norm equation for boundedness. Heine-Borel then makes the sphere compact. Prove continuity of the fixed quadratic form from its finite coordinate formula, apply the extreme value theorem, and use definiteness to make the attained minimum positive or the attained maximum negative.

items.title: The multivariable second-derivative test by definiteness of the Hessian
items.strategy: At a critical point combine the second-order Taylor expansion with the uniform sphere bound. Positive or negative definiteness dominates the little-o remainder and gives a strict extremum; two directions of opposite quadratic sign give saddle behaviour. Make the semidefinite case explicitly inconclusive.

items.title: The two-variable Hessian determinant test
items.strategy: For the symmetric matrix with entries $A,B,C$, complete the square when $A\ne0$. The determinant sign classifies definiteness or indefiniteness; if the determinant is zero, state that the test gives no conclusion.

items.title: A constrained local extremum annihilates every velocity of a differentiable parametrization
items.strategy: Compose the objective with each differentiable curve in the constraint set through the point. One-variable Fermat and the total-derivative chain rule give $Df(a)\gamma'(0)=0$.

items.title: Lagrange multipliers for a regular graph constraint $y=\psi(x)$
items.strategy: Parametrize the graph by $x\mapsto(x,\psi(x))$. The parametrized necessary condition says the objective gradient is orthogonal to all graph tangent vectors; solve the coordinate equations to obtain $\nabla f=\lambda\nabla(y-\psi(x))$, whose last coordinate is nonzero.

pages.title: Mixed Partials, Taylor, and Extrema in Several Variables: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Peano's function has unequal mixed partials at the origin
items.strategy: For $f(x,y)=xy(x^2-y^2)/(x^2+y^2)$ off the origin and zero at the origin, compute the two axis first partials and then their derivatives at zero, obtaining opposite values. Also verify continuity at the origin by a quadratic bound.

items.title: Peano's surface has a strict minimum on every line through the origin but no local extremum
items.strategy: Use $f(x,y)=(y-3x^2)(y-x^2)$. Substitution on an arbitrary line gives a positive leading even power near zero, with vertical lines separate; along the parabola $y=2x^2$ the values are negative.

items.title: A smooth flat refinement has a strict minimum on every line through the origin but no local extremum
items.strategy: Let $\phi(x)=e^{-1/x^2}$ for $x\ne0$ and $\phi(0)=0$, and set $F=(y-3\phi(x))(y-\phi(x))$. Exponential domination proves smooth flatness and linewise positivity; the curve $y=2\phi(x)$ gives negative values approaching the origin.

items.title: $x^2+y^2(1-x)^3$ has a unique critical point, a strict local but nonglobal minimum
items.strategy: Solve the two gradient equations to show the origin is the sole critical point. Its Hessian is positive definite, while values with $x>1$ and sufficiently large $|y|$ are negative, so the local minimum is not global.

items.title: The monkey saddle $x^3-3xy^2$ has an indefinite higher-order critical point
items.strategy: Compute the zero gradient and zero Hessian at the origin, then evaluate along three rays to exhibit alternating signs. Conclude directly that the origin is a saddle although the quadratic test is silent.

items.title: A zero Hessian occurs at a strict minimum, a strict maximum, and a saddle
items.strategy: Compare $x^4+y^4$, $-(x^4+y^4)$, and $x^4-y^4$ at the origin. Compute the common zero gradient and Hessian, then classify by signs.

items.title: A second-order Taylor polynomial computed from gradient and Hessian data
items.strategy: For $f(x,y)=e^x(1+y+y^2)$ at the origin, compute the value, gradient, and Hessian and substitute them into the second-order formula; verify the coefficients by multiplying the one-variable expansions.

items.title: A constrained extremum on an affine graph satisfies the graph Lagrange rule
items.strategy: Minimize $x^2+y^2$ on $y=x+1$ by completing the square in the graph parameter, then compute both gradients and the multiplier at the unique minimizer.

items.title: The degenerate constraint $x^2+y^2=0$ defeats the multiplier conclusion
items.strategy: The constraint set is the singleton origin, so $f(x,y)=x$ has a constrained extremum there. But $\nabla g(0,0)=0$ and $\nabla f(0,0)=(1,0)$, so no scalar multiplier can satisfy the usual equation.
