items.strategy: Extract the construction already used in the published sequence theorem: enumerate the base, replace members by open neighbourhoods, and take running finite intersections.

items.title: Every second countable space is first countable
items.strategy: At a point retain the members of a global countable basis that contain it.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, every second countable space is separable
items.strategy: Choose one point from each nonempty member of a countable basis; the chosen set meets every nonempty basic open set.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, every second countable space is Lindelöf
items.strategy: For each basis member lying inside a member of the cover, choose one such cover member; the selected countable family covers.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, a metrizable space is second countable if and only if it is separable if and only if it is Lindelöf
items.strategy: Use rational-radius balls around a countable dense set for separable implies second countable, the general second-countable implication, and countable subcovers of the radius-$1/n$ ball covers for Lindelöf implies separable.

items.title: Second countability is hereditary
items.strategy: Take traces of a countable ambient basis.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, a countable product of second countable spaces is second countable
items.strategy: Choose a countable basis in each factor and enumerate the finite-support boxes using countable unions of finite products of countable sets.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, a countable product of first countable spaces is first countable
items.strategy: At a point enumerate finite-support products of chosen countable local bases.

items.title: Every separable space satisfies the countable chain condition
items.strategy: Enumerate a countable dense set and assign to each disjoint nonempty open set the least enumerated point it contains; disjointness makes the assignment injective.

items.title: Under choice, $c(X)\le d(X)\le w(X)$ and $\chi(X),L(X)\le w(X)$
items.strategy: Choose a point from each nonempty basis element for density; assign a least dense point to each disjoint open set; obtain local bases by restriction and cover subfamilies by choosing one cover member above each eligible basis element.

items.title: Under choice, for $Y\subseteq X$, $w(Y)\le w(X)$ and $\chi(y,Y)\le\chi(y,X)$
items.strategy: Trace a basis and local bases to the subspace.

items.title: Under choice, a continuous surjection does not increase density or Lindelöf degree
items.strategy: The image of a dense set is dense under a surjection, and an open cover of the codomain pulls back to one of the domain.

items.title: Under choice, every metrizable space has $w(X)=d(X)$
items.strategy: The basic inequality gives $d\le w$; rational-radius balls around a least dense set give $w\le d$ for infinite density, while the finite case is discrete and checked separately.

items.title: Under choice, the uncountable $\Delta$-system lemma for finite sets
items.strategy: Thin to a fixed finite size, induct on that size, and use the uncountable pigeonhole split according to whether one point occurs uncountably often.

items.title: Under choice, every Cantor cube $2^I$ satisfies ccc
items.strategy: An uncountable family of basic cylinders has finite supports; thin the supports to a delta system and then thin again so the finitely many root coordinates carry one common pattern, forcing two cylinders to meet.

items.title: Under choice, if $|I|>2^{\aleph_0}$, then the Cantor cube $2^I$ is not separable
items.strategy: A countable set of points induces at most $2^{\aleph_0}$ coordinate columns; two equal columns leave a two-coordinate basic cylinder disjoint from the alleged dense set.

items.title: Assuming choice, refuted: every ccc space is separable
items.strategy: Take a Cantor cube indexed by a cardinal strictly above $2^{\aleph_0}$.

items.title: Refuted: every first countable space is second countable
items.strategy: Use an uncountable discrete space: singleton local bases give first countability, while every global basis must contain every singleton.

items.title: Refuted: every separable space is second countable
items.strategy: Construct the lower-limit line locally, use the rationals for separability, and inject the reals into any basis by choosing a basis member whose left endpoint is forced at each point.

items.title: Refuted: separability is hereditary
items.strategy: Construct the lower-limit plane locally: its rational grid is dense, while its uncountable discrete antidiagonal has no proper dense subset.

items.title: Refuted: Lindelöfness is hereditary
items.strategy: Take the one-point compactification of an uncountable discrete space; the whole space is compact while the open discrete subspace is not Lindelöf.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, refuted: Lindelöfness is productive
items.strategy: Rebuild the lower-limit line: thin covers by rational intervals to prove it Lindelöf, then use the closed uncountable discrete antidiagonal to show its square is not.

items.title: Assuming choice and countable choice, refuted: arbitrary products of second countable spaces are second countable
items.strategy: A sufficiently large Cantor cube has second countable two-point factors but is not separable, whereas second countability would imply separability under countable choice.

items.title: Implication, preservation, counterexample, and choice ledger for the countability axioms

pages.title: Countability Axioms and Cardinal Functions: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Under choice, for the usual real line, $w=d=\chi=L=c=\aleph_0$ under the raw convention
items.strategy: Use rational intervals and rational points for the upper bounds, then rule out finite bases, dense sets, and local bases and exhibit arbitrarily large finite disjoint open families and covers.

items.title: Under choice, for an infinite discrete space of cardinality $\kappa$, $w=d=L=c=\kappa$ while $\chi=1$
items.strategy: Singletons force the basis, dense set, and cellular family; the singleton at a point is a one-member local base, and the singleton cover forces the Lindelöf degree.

items.title: For the lower-limit line, $\chi=d=L=c=\aleph_0$ and $w=2^{\aleph_0}$ under choice
items.strategy: Reconstruct the half-open basis, use rational density and the Lindelöf thinning argument, force distinct basis members at distinct left endpoints, and bound disjoint open families by density.

items.title: Assuming choice, the lower-limit plane is first countable, separable, and ccc, but not second countable or Lindelöf
items.strategy: Use product local bases and the rational grid, inherit ccc from separability, and use the uncountable closed discrete antidiagonal for the two failures.

items.title: The one-point compactification of an uncountable discrete space is compact and Lindelöf but need not be first countable or separable
items.strategy: Neighbourhoods of infinity have finite complements; a countable local base would make the discrete part countable, and density must contain every isolated point.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, $\omega_1$ is first countable and countably compact but is not separable or Lindelöf
items.strategy: Build countable cofinal local bases below each countable ordinal, then use boundedness of countable subsets and the standard initial-segment cover.

items.title: Under choice, a concrete ccc nonseparable Cantor cube indexed above $2^{\aleph_0}$
items.strategy: Take the index set to be a power set of a set of size $2^{\aleph_0}$ and apply the delta-system ccc theorem and repeated-column nonseparability lemma.

items.title: Assuming choice, a separable space with a nonseparable subspace: the lower-limit plane and its antidiagonal
items.strategy: Expand the rectangle calculation showing the rational grid is dense and every antidiagonal singleton is subspace-open.

items.title: Assuming choice, a Lindelöf space whose square is not Lindelöf: the lower-limit line
items.strategy: Expand the rational-endpoint cover thinning in the factor and the closed-discrete obstruction in the square.

pages.title: Metrization: Urysohn, Nagata–Smirnov, Bing, Smirnov

items.title: Discrete families and $\sigma$-locally-finite and $\sigma$-discrete bases
Every discrete family is locally finite, so every $\sigma$-discrete basis is $\sigma$-locally finite
items.strategy: Unfold the two neighbourhood conditions and then retain the same countable decomposition.

items.title: A locally metrizable space: every point has a metrizable open neighbourhood
Compatible normal sequences of open covers
A $T_1$ space with a compatible normal sequence of open covers is metrizable
items.strategy: Construct dyadic-scale symmetric entourages from successive star refinements, define the chain infimum pseudometric, prove the triangle inequality, and use compatibility plus $T_1$ to obtain point separation and the original topology.

items.title: Under choice, every metric space has a $\sigma$-locally-finite basis
items.strategy: For each positive scale refine the cover by balls of that scale locally finitely using Stone's theorem; the union of these refinements is a basis because the mesh tends to zero.

items.title: Under choice, a regular $T_1$ space with a $\sigma$-locally-finite basis has a compatible normal sequence
items.strategy: Record the source-backed normal-cover construction as an explicitly external fallback after the local pointwise-shrinking route is shown invalid; retain no fictitious local dependency edge.

items.title: Under choice, a space is metrizable if and only if it is regular, $T_1$, and has a $\sigma$-locally-finite basis
items.strategy: Use the metric-basis lemma for necessity. For sufficiency turn the basis into a compatible normal sequence and apply the Alexandroff–Urysohn metrization lemma.

items.title: Under choice, every metric space has a $\sigma$-discrete basis
items.strategy: Record Bing's source-backed necessity construction as an explicitly external fallback after the proposed first-centre cells are shown not to be open; retain no fictitious local dependency edge.

items.title: Under choice, a space is metrizable if and only if it is regular, $T_1$, and has a $\sigma$-discrete basis
items.strategy: Use the sigma-discrete basis lemma for necessity. For sufficiency a discrete family is locally finite and Nagata–Smirnov applies.

items.title: Under choice, every regular $T_1$ second-countable space is metrizable
items.strategy: Enumerate a countable basis as a countable union of singleton, hence locally finite, families and apply Nagata–Smirnov.

items.title: A locally finite open cover by subspaces with $\sigma$-locally-finite bases yields a $\sigma$-locally-finite basis of the whole space
items.strategy: At each countable layer take the union of the corresponding relative bases. Local finiteness of the cover reduces the neighbourhood check to finitely many subspaces, and openness of the cover members makes the union a basis.

items.title: Under choice, a space is metrizable if and only if it is paracompact, Hausdorff, and locally metrizable
items.strategy: For sufficiency refine the cover by metrizable neighbourhoods locally finitely, take sigma-locally-finite bases in the refinements, merge them, and apply Nagata–Smirnov using paracompact Hausdorff regularity. For necessity use Stone's theorem and the space itself as a metrizable neighbourhood.

pages.title: Metrization: Urysohn, Nagata–Smirnov, Bing, Smirnov: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: An uncountable discrete space is metrizable and has a discrete basis, but is not second countable
items.strategy: Use the zero-one discrete metric and the singleton basis; any basis must contain every singleton, so an uncountable underlying set prevents second countability.

items.title: Under choice, the lower-limit line is regular and separable but not second countable and therefore not metrizable
items.strategy: Use the published clopen basis and rational density. A putative countable basis must assign to every real point a distinct basis member whose least point is that real; this contradicts uncountability. The metric countability equivalence then rules out metrizability.

items.title: FALSE: every regular space is metrizable
items.strategy: Use the regular nonmetrizable lower-limit line and identify its missing countability hypothesis.

items.title: Under choice, the Niemytzki plane is Tychonoff and locally metrizable but not normal, paracompact, or metrizable
items.strategy: Build the tangent-disk basis and verify its point-separation and local metrization directly. Prove complete regularity with explicit tangent-disk bump functions. Its countable dense upper-half-plane subset and uncountable closed discrete boundary contradict Jones's normal-space bound; Stone and paracompact-Hausdorff normality then rule out metrizability and paracompactness.

pages.title: Complete Metrizability, Čech-Completeness, and Baire Category

items.title: Nowhere dense, meagre, residual, and comeagre subsets of a topological space
The meagre subsets of a topological space form a sigma-ideal
items.strategy: Subsets of nowhere dense sets are nowhere dense, and a subset of a countable union of nowhere dense sets is covered by the same family. Flatten a countable family of countable covers using the published countability of the natural-number square; include the empty union and empty subset explicitly.

items.title: Equivalent forms of the Baire property
items.strategy: Apply complements and De Morgan's laws to pass between dense intersections of open sets and unions of closed nowhere dense sets. Then localise to a nonempty open set to prove equivalence with no nonempty open subset being meagre; keep the empty-space convention visible.

items.title: Open subspaces and residual subspaces of Baire spaces are Baire
items.strategy: For an open subspace, translate dense-open tests into the ambient open set. For a residual subspace, first note it is dense unless the ambient space is empty, show a relatively nowhere dense set is ambiently nowhere dense, and use the sigma-ideal and nonmeagre-open characterisation.

items.title: Every open subspace of a completely metrizable space is completely metrizable
items.strategy: Choose a compatible complete metric. If the open set is the whole space, restrict that metric. Otherwise add to the restricted metric the absolute difference of reciprocals of the distance to the closed complement. A Cauchy sequence for the new metric cannot approach the complement and therefore converges inside the open set.

items.title: A countable intersection of completely metrizable subspaces is completely metrizable
items.strategy: Assume countable choice to select one bounded compatible complete metric on each subspace. On the intersection, add the ambient bounded metric to a geometrically weighted sum of the selected metrics. A Cauchy sequence is Cauchy in every coordinate metric; the coordinate limits agree in the Hausdorff ambient metric and lie in every subspace.

items.title: Every $G_\delta$ subspace of a complete metric space is completely metrizable
items.strategy: Write the subspace as a countable intersection of open subspaces. Each open subspace is completely metrizable by the reciprocal-distance lemma, and the countable-intersection metric then gives a compatible complete metric on the intersection. State the countable-choice hypothesis used to select the intermediate metrics.

items.title: Every completely metrizable subspace of a metric space is $G_\delta$
items.strategy: For each scale cover the subspace by ambient open sets having small diameter in a chosen compatible complete metric, and let $G_n$ be their ambient union. A point in every $G_n$ yields, using dependent choice, a sequence in the subspace that is Cauchy in the complete metric and converges to the point in the ambient metric. Hausdorff uniqueness puts the point back in the subspace.

items.title: Alexandrov's theorem: a subspace of a complete metric space is completely metrizable exactly when it is $G_\delta$
items.strategy: Apply the two preceding implications to the subspace with its induced topology. In the reverse direction use the given complete ambient metric; in the forward direction use only the existence of a compatible complete metric on the subspace, not completeness of the inherited metric.

items.title: Open, closed, and $G_\delta$ subspaces of completely metrizable spaces are completely metrizable
items.strategy: Use the open-subspace lemma directly. Choose a compatible complete metric for the ambient space; closed subsets are complete for its restriction, while arbitrary $G_\delta$ subsets fall under Alexandrov's theorem. Include the empty subspace.

items.title: Under Dependent Choice, every completely metrizable space is Baire
items.strategy: Choose a compatible complete metric using the definition already established by complete remetrisation. Apply the published complete-metric Baire category theorem to every nonempty open subspace, and translate its dense-open conclusion back to the topology; the empty space is Baire vacuously.

items.title: The standard weighted metric on a countable product of bounded complete metric spaces is complete
items.strategy: Use the sum of $2^{-n}$ times the bounded coordinate metrics. Its balls and finite-coordinate basic neighbourhoods generate the same product topology. A Cauchy sequence is coordinatewise Cauchy; assemble the coordinate limits and use a finite-head plus geometric-tail estimate. Treat the empty product as a singleton.

items.title: Under countable choice, a countable product of completely metrizable spaces is completely metrizable
items.strategy: Use countable choice to select a compatible complete metric in every factor, bound each metric without changing its topology, and invoke the standard weighted product metric. Record the singleton empty product and one-factor product separately from the infinite case.

items.title: Polish spaces are separable completely metrizable spaces
For completely metrizable spaces, the separable and second-countable definitions of Polish space agree under countable choice
items.strategy: A completely metrizable space is metrizable. Apply the published metrizable-space equivalence between separability and second countability under countable choice, without strengthening the choice claim to ZF.

items.title: Every separable metrizable space embeds in the Hilbert cube $[0,1]^{\mathbb N}$
items.strategy: Choose a countable dense sequence and a bounded compatible metric. Map a point to its bounded distances from the dense sequence. The coordinates are continuous and separate points; if coordinate values converge, a coordinate centred close to the proposed point forces metric convergence. Rescale the coordinate range to the unit interval and identify the induced topology with the product topology.

items.title: Under countable choice, a subspace of a Polish space is Polish exactly when it is $G_\delta$
items.strategy: Alexandrov gives the complete-metrizability equivalence. A subspace of a second-countable space is second countable, hence separable under the stated choice hypothesis, while every subspace already inherits metrizability. Combine these facts in both directions.

items.title: A space is Polish exactly when it is homeomorphic to a $G_\delta$ subspace of the Hilbert cube
items.strategy: Embed a Polish space in the Hilbert cube by universality. Since the Hilbert cube is complete for its standard product metric, Alexandrov makes the image $G_\delta$. Conversely, a $G_\delta$ subspace of the compact metrizable Hilbert cube is completely metrizable and second countable, hence Polish.

items.title: Countable products and $G_\delta$ subspaces of Polish spaces are Polish
items.strategy: Use the product theorem for complete metrizability and the published theorem that countable products of second-countable spaces are second countable. For a $G_\delta$ subspace apply the Polish-subspace characterisation. State countable choice once for both countability passages.

items.title: Baire sequence space $\mathbb N^{\mathbb N}$ and its cylinder topology
Baire sequence space is Polish and its standard ultrametric is complete
items.strategy: Give two unequal sequences distance $2^{-k}$ where $k$ is their first differing index. Verify the ultrametric and cylinder topology. A Cauchy sequence eventually stabilises in every coordinate, producing a limit; eventually constant sequences form a countable dense set. Check the zero-index convention at the first coordinate.

items.title: Every nonempty Polish space is a continuous image of Baire sequence space
items.strategy: Choose a compatible complete metric and recursively refine each nonempty open set into a countable cover by open sets whose closures remain inside the parent and whose diameters tend to zero. An infinite branch determines one point by completeness, giving a continuous map from Baire space. For a prescribed target point, dependent choice selects a nested branch containing it, proving surjectivity. Nonemptiness is necessary because the domain is nonempty.

items.title: Simple continued fractions, convergents, and the integer-coordinate coding of $\mathbb N^{\mathbb N}$
Continued-fraction convergents, determinant identities, and nested irrational cylinders
items.strategy: Use recursion on pairs to establish the standard numerator-denominator recurrence from the finite continued fraction, prove the alternating determinant identity by induction in the rational ordered field, and derive the endpoint and diameter formulas for a fixed finite prefix. After the arbitrary integer term, all partial quotients are positive; hence denominators strictly increase and the nested closed-cylinder diameters tend to zero.

items.title: Infinite simple continued fractions parametrise the irrational real numbers
items.strategy: Decode the first natural coordinate by the fixed zigzag bijection with the integers and shift each later coordinate by one. Nested cylinder intervals with vanishing diameter give a unique real value and exclude rational endpoints. Conversely, repeatedly take the integer part and reciprocal of the positive fractional remainder of an irrational; the process never stops, and the cylinder estimates recover the original number. Prefix agreement is exactly the neighbourhood comparison needed for continuity of both maps.

items.title: Baire sequence space is homeomorphic to the irrational real numbers
items.strategy: Decode the zero-th coordinate by the fixed zigzag bijection with the integers and shift every later natural coordinate by one to obtain positive partial quotients. The coordinatewise coding preserves cylinders, and the continued-fraction parametrisation and its inverse therefore give the required homeomorphism.

items.title: Compact metric spaces admit finite refining covers of arbitrarily small diameter
items.strategy: At stage zero use the whole nonempty compact space. Cover each compact piece by finitely many sufficiently small closed subsets obtained from a finite ball cover, retaining only nonempty pieces, and index the children by finite binary words after duplicating terminal choices when necessary. Arrange refinement and diameters tending to zero.

items.title: Every nonempty compact metric space is a continuous image of Cantor space
items.strategy: Use the refining finite small-diameter covers to assign a nested compact set to each finite binary word. Each infinite binary sequence determines one point by the complete compact intersection theorem. The resulting map is continuous by the diameter bound and surjective by recursively choosing a child containing a prescribed point. Keep nonemptiness explicit; no map from nonempty Cantor space can surject onto the empty space.

items.title: Čech-complete spaces as $G_\delta$ subspaces of Hausdorff compactifications
A map of Hausdorff compactifications carries the larger remainder onto the smaller remainder
items.strategy: Let a continuous map between compactifications restrict to the identity on the dense copy of the space. Compactness makes its image closed and density makes it surjective. If a remainder point mapped into the dense copy, Hausdorff separation and density would contradict identity on the copy; conversely compactness of a fibre over a remainder point supplies a preimage outside the copy.

items.title: A Tychonoff space is $G_\delta$ in some Hausdorff compactification exactly when it is $G_\delta$ in every one
items.strategy: Use the Stone–Čech compactification as a common dominating compactification. The remainder-map lemma transfers the compact $F_\sigma$ remainder condition along the canonical maps, and complements convert it back to the $G_\delta$ condition. State the ultrafilter-lemma and dependent-choice assumptions actually used by the compactification machinery.

items.title: Frolík's internal open-cover characterisation of Čech-completeness
items.strategy: From a $G_\delta$ presentation in a compactification, use compact Hausdorff regularity to choose open covers whose ambient closures lie in the successive layers. A centred family subordinate to every cover has centred ambient closures, hence a compactness cluster point; the layer condition puts that point back in the original space and closedness puts it in every family member. Conversely, apply the centred-family condition to neighbourhood traces of each remainder point to construct countably many ambient open sets whose intersection excludes the whole remainder.

items.title: Every completely metrizable space is Čech-complete
items.strategy: Choose a compatible complete metric and locally finite refinements of the covers by balls of radius tending to zero. In a Hausdorff compactification, extend the refined members to ambient open sets and use local finiteness to form open neighbourhoods whose intersection is exactly the original space: a point in every neighbourhood produces a Cauchy filter and hence a limit in the complete space. Invoke compactification independence only after this construction is established.

items.title: Every metrizable Čech-complete space is completely metrizable
items.strategy: Embed the space densely in its metric completion, compactify that completion, and observe that the resulting compact space is also a compactification of the original dense subspace. Compactification independence makes the original space $G_\delta$ there and hence in the completion. Apply the $G_\delta$-subspace theorem to the complete metric completion.

items.title: A metrizable space is Čech-complete exactly when it is completely metrizable
items.strategy: Combine the two preceding implications, retaining metrizability only for the direction from Čech-completeness to complete metrizability.

items.title: Every locally compact Hausdorff space is Čech-complete
items.strategy: The one-point compactification is compact Hausdorff and contains the original space as an open subspace. An open subset is a $G_\delta$ by repeating it in a constant countable intersection, so it witnesses Čech-completeness; handle an already compact space without adding a new point if desired.

items.title: Under Dependent Choice, every Čech-complete space is Baire
items.strategy: Realise the space as the intersection of open sets in a compact Hausdorff space. Starting in a prescribed nonempty relatively open set, use regularity and density to choose nested nonempty ambient open sets with compact closures, each lying in the next $G_\delta$ layer and the next dense open set. Dependent choice produces the chain; compactness gives a point in all closures, hence in the desired intersection.

items.title: Closed subspaces of Čech-complete spaces are Čech-complete
items.strategy: If the space is $G_\delta$ in a compactification and the subspace is closed in the space, take its closure in the compactification. Inside that compact closure, the subspace is the intersection of the inherited $G_\delta$ with an additional closed set, hence is $G_\delta$.

items.title: Topological sums of Čech-complete spaces are Čech-complete
items.strategy: Choose compactification witnesses for the summands and take the one-point compactification of their topological sum after adjoining the compact pieces. Express the original sum by one countable family of open layers, using the same layer number in every clopen summand. Verify the empty sum separately.

items.title: Under countable choice, countable products of Čech-complete spaces are Čech-complete
items.strategy: Choose compactification witnesses and $G_\delta$ presentations for the factors. Their compact product is compact by Tychonoff, and the product of the original spaces is the countable intersection over pairs of a coordinate and a layer of open cylinder sets. Pair the two natural indices and include the empty product.

pages.title: Complete Metrizability, Čech-Completeness, and Baire Category: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Every Baire space is completely metrizable
items.strategy: Refute the claim with the Cantor cube $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb R}$. It is compact Hausdorff and therefore Baire under Dependent Choice, but a countable local base at a point mentions only countably many finite coordinate sets; changing an unmentioned coordinate contradicts that it is a base. Hence it is not first countable, not metrizable, and not completely metrizable.

items.title: The rational numbers form a Baire space
items.strategy: In the subspace topology each rational singleton is closed with empty interior, while the rational numbers are countable. Thus the whole nonempty space is meagre in itself, contradicting the nonmeagre-open form of the Baire property. Cross-check with the published statement that the rationals are meagre and not $G_\delta$ in the real line.

items.title: Cylinder sets and continued fractions exhibit the homeomorphism $\mathbb N^{\mathbb N}\cong\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q$
items.strategy: Work out the first continued-fraction cylinders and show how extending a finite sequence nests the corresponding irrational interval. Use the established parametrisation to identify cylinder convergence with ordinary convergence of irrational values, including the zero-th coordinate convention.

items.title: The Hilbert cube is compact, Polish, and universal for separable metrizable spaces
items.strategy: Give $[0,1]^{\mathbb N}$ the standard weighted complete product metric. Compactness follows from Tychonoff and second countability from the countable finite-coordinate basis; a countable rational grid is dense. Apply the embedding theorem for universality without citing an examples-page item.

items.title: Under Dependent Choice, nowhere differentiable functions form a residual subset of $C([0,1],\mathbb R)$
items.strategy: Use the published closed pointwise-Lipschitz sets and the dense steep-polygonal perturbations to show every such closed set has empty interior. Their countable union contains every function with a finite derivative at some point, so its complement is residual and consists of nowhere differentiable functions, with one-sided endpoint derivatives included.

items.title: Every metrizable space is Čech-complete
items.strategy: The rational line is metrizable but not Baire. Since every Čech-complete space is Baire under the same stated Dependent Choice assumption, the rationals cannot be Čech-complete. Equivalently, Alexandrov and the published non-$G_\delta$ result exclude complete metrizability.

pages.title: Uniform Spaces: the Three Definitions

items.title: Uniform space in the entourage formulation
Every uniformity has a base of symmetric entourages
items.strategy: direct

items.title: The sets containing an entourage ball about each of their points form a topology
items.strategy: direct

items.title: Separated uniformity: the intersection of all entourages is the diagonal
A uniformity is separated if and only if its induced topology is Hausdorff
items.strategy: direct

items.title: Uniformly continuous map between uniform spaces
Every uniformly continuous map is continuous for the induced topologies
items.strategy: direct

items.title: A metric generates an entourage uniformity whose induced topology and uniformly continuous maps are the usual metric notions, and this uniformity is separated
items.strategy: direct

items.title: Uniform space in the uniform-cover formulation
Entourage uniformities and uniform-cover structures determine one another
items.strategy: constructive

items.title: A gauge of pseudometrics and the uniformity it generates
Assuming dependent choice, every entourage begins a decreasing symmetric sequence whose next triple composite lies in the preceding entourage
items.strategy: constructive

items.title: A normal sequence of entourages yields a uniformly continuous pseudometric with controlled dyadic balls
items.strategy: constructive

items.title: Assuming dependent choice, every entourage uniformity is generated by a gauge of uniformly continuous pseudometrics
items.strategy: constructive

items.title: Entourages and uniform covers give equivalent definitions of a uniform space in ZF, and under dependent choice they are also equivalent to gauges of pseudometrics
items.strategy: direct

items.title: Cauchy filter in a uniform space
Every convergent filter on a uniform space is Cauchy
items.strategy: direct

items.title: A Cauchy filter with a cluster point converges to that point
items.strategy: direct

items.title: Complete uniform space: every Cauchy filter converges
Uniform embedding and uniform isomorphism
A Hausdorff completion of a uniform space and its canonical dense map
Every Cauchy filter canonically determines a unique minimal Cauchy filter coarser than it
items.strategy: constructive

items.title: The standard entourages on minimal Cauchy filters form a separated uniformity
items.strategy: constructive

items.title: The uniform space of minimal Cauchy filters is complete
items.strategy: constructive

items.title: The minimal Cauchy filters associated to points define a uniformly continuous dense canonical map
items.strategy: constructive

items.title: Every uniform space has a complete Hausdorff reflection with dense canonical image, and the canonical map is a uniform embedding exactly when the original uniformity is separated
items.strategy: constructive

items.title: Every uniformly continuous map into a complete Hausdorff uniform space extends uniquely across the Hausdorff completion; consequently completions are unique up to a unique uniform isomorphism
items.strategy: constructive

items.title: Totally bounded uniform space
Every ultrafilter on a totally bounded uniform space is Cauchy
items.strategy: direct

items.title: Every compact uniform space is complete
items.strategy: direct

items.title: Every compact uniform space is totally bounded
items.strategy: direct

items.title: Assuming the ultrafilter lemma, every complete and totally bounded uniform space is compact
items.strategy: direct

items.title: Assuming the ultrafilter lemma, a uniform space is compact if and only if it is complete and totally bounded
items.strategy: direct

items.title: Every open cover of a compact Hausdorff space has a finite open star-refinement
items.strategy: constructive

items.title: The covers admitting an open refinement form a compatible uniform-cover structure on a compact Hausdorff space; in particular every open cover is uniform
items.strategy: direct

items.title: A compact Hausdorff space carries exactly one compatible uniformity
items.strategy: direct

items.title: Every continuous map from a compact Hausdorff space to a uniform space is uniformly continuous
items.strategy: direct

pages.title: Uniform Completeness, Completion, and the Samuel Compactification

items.title: The Samuel uniformity generated by bounded uniformly continuous functions
Samuel function pseudometrics generate a uniformity coarser than the original one
items.strategy: For each uniformly continuous f:X-> [0,1], verify that p_f(x,y)=|f(x)-f(y)| is a pseudometric by the real absolute-value laws. Pull every p_f-ball back from the metric uniformity of [0,1]; finite intersections then show that the generated Samuel uniformity is coarser than the original uniformity.

items.title: The Samuel uniformity is totally bounded
items.strategy: Fix a basic entourage involving finitely many [0,1]-valued coordinates. Choose a finite small net in [0,1] for each coordinate, partition X into the finitely many nonempty coordinate cells, and use finite choice to select one representative from each cell. Treat the empty coordinate family and the empty space separately.

items.title: Assuming dependent choice, the Samuel uniformity induces the original topology
items.strategy: Coarsening gives one topological inclusion. For an original neighbourhood O of x, choose U[x] inside O, build a normal entourage sequence and its controlled pseudometric p, and use f(y)=min(1,4p(x,y)). The Samuel f-ball of radius one at x lies in O. Include the empty space explicitly.

items.title: The Samuel completion and, when compactifying, the Samuel compactification
Total boundedness passes to a uniform space with a dense uniformly continuous image
items.strategy: Given a target entourage, choose a symmetric entourage whose square is smaller and pull it back by uniform continuity. Cover the source by finitely many pulled-back balls. Density supplies a source image point near each target point, and a two-entourage composition puts that target point near the image of one of the finite source centres. Separate the empty target case.

items.title: Under the ultrafilter lemma the Samuel completion is compact, and under dependent choice plus the ultrafilter lemma it compactifies every separated uniform space
items.strategy: The Samuel uniformity is totally bounded, and the dense completion remains totally bounded. Completeness plus total boundedness gives compactness under the ultrafilter lemma. Under dependent choice the Samuel and original topologies agree; for a separated original uniformity this makes the completion map a topological embedding with dense image. With both choice principles it is therefore a compactification.

items.title: Under dependent choice and the ultrafilter lemma, uniformly continuous maps to compact Hausdorff spaces extend uniquely over the Samuel compactification
items.strategy: Give a compact Hausdorff target its unique compatible uniformity. Under dependent choice its topology is generated by the gauge of continuous [0,1]-valued functions. Composing those coordinate functions with the given uniformly continuous map shows that the map is uniformly continuous from the Samuel uniformity. Compactness makes the target complete, so the uniform-completion universal property gives the extension and density gives uniqueness.

items.title: Samuel compactifications are unique up to the unique isomorphism fixing the original space
items.strategy: Apply the compact-target extension property in both directions between two Samuel compactifications. The two composites agree with the identity on the dense original image, so uniqueness makes them identities.

items.title: Assuming dependent choice, a totally bounded uniformity equals its Samuel uniformity
items.strategy: For an original entourage U, construct a bounded controlled pseudometric p with a quarter-ball inside U. A finite p-net supplies finitely many distance functions f_z(y)=p(z,y). A sufficiently small simultaneous Samuel entourage for those functions forces p(x,y)<1/4 and hence lies in U. Combine this with the already proved coarsening and treat the empty space.

items.title: Under dependent choice the Samuel completion of a separated totally bounded space is its uniform completion; under the ultrafilter lemma it is compact
items.strategy: The preceding equality identifies the original and Samuel uniformities, so their Hausdorff completions are the same up to the unique uniform isomorphism fixing X. Under the ultrafilter lemma that completion is compact by completeness and total boundedness; keep this compactness clause separate from the DC identification.

items.title: Under dependent choice and the ultrafilter lemma, the Stone-Cech compactification maps continuously onto the Samuel compactification
items.strategy: A separated uniform space is Tychonoff under dependent choice, so use the evaluation-closure Stone-Cech compactification. Its universal property extends the Samuel compactification map. The image of the resulting map is compact and therefore closed in the Hausdorff Samuel compactification, while it contains the dense original image; hence it is onto.

pages.title: Uniform Completeness, Completion, and the Samuel Compactification: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The Samuel compactification of a compact Hausdorff space adds no points
items.strategy: Use the unique compatible uniformity. Compactness gives completeness and total boundedness, so the identity is already a Hausdorff completion; the totally bounded agreement theorem identifies it with the Samuel compactification. Include the empty compact space.

items.title: The Samuel compactification of the open unit interval is the closed unit interval
items.strategy: Give (0,1) and [0,1] their usual metric uniformities. For epsilon>0 choose n>=2 with 1/n<epsilon; the finite grid {j/n:1<=j<n} is an epsilon-net in (0,1), as the integer-part lemma supplies the adjacent grid index. The inclusion has dense image and exactly pulls back the closed interval's uniformity, and compact [0,1] is complete and separated. Thus [0,1] is its Hausdorff uniform completion, and the totally bounded agreement theorem identifies the Samuel compactification.

items.title: The Samuel compactification of the discrete natural numbers is beta N
items.strategy: Define the discrete metric on N directly and verify its metric axioms. Its radius-1/2 entourage is the diagonal, so every map from this discrete uniformity is uniformly continuous. Hence the Samuel extension property and the Stone-Cech extension property quantify over the same maps into compact Hausdorff targets. Apply the two uniqueness arguments to identify the compactifications over N.

items.title: The Samuel compactification map need not be a uniform embedding for the original uniformity
items.strategy: Use the infinite discrete natural numbers and verify the discrete metric directly. Its radius-1/2 entourage balls are singletons, so a finite such ball cover would make N finite, contradicting the pigeonhole theorem. Thus the original uniformity is not totally bounded, while the Samuel uniformity is totally bounded. The completion map pulls back precisely the Samuel uniformity, so it cannot also pull back the strictly finer original discrete uniformity. Distinguish this from its being a topological embedding under dependent choice.

items.title: The Samuel reflection of a nonempty indiscrete uniform space is a singleton
items.strategy: For the indiscrete uniformity {X x X}, uniform continuity into [0,1] forces every Samuel coordinate function to be constant. The generated Samuel uniformity is therefore indiscrete, its separated quotient identifies every pair of points, and its Hausdorff completion is the one-point space.

pages.title: The Ascoli–Arzelà Theorem

items.title: The compact-open topology on $C(X,Y)$ for arbitrary topological spaces
The general compact-open topology agrees with the published metric-domain definition
items.strategy: For a metric space with its metric topology, invoke the exact equivalence between topological and metric compact subsets. The two subbasic families $S(K,V)$ are then literally equal, including $K=\varnothing$ and $V=Y$.

items.title: Equicontinuity on a topological domain and pointwise relative compactness
Topological-domain equicontinuity agrees with metric equicontinuity on a metric domain
items.strategy: Translate a neighbourhood of the point into a contained metric ball for one direction and take the metric ball supplied by the epsilon-delta definition for the other. Preserve the order of quantifiers: the same neighbourhood or radius serves every member of the family.

items.title: Evaluation is continuous for the compact-open topology on a locally compact Hausdorff domain
items.strategy: At $(f,x)$ and an open target neighbourhood $W$ of $f(x)$, shrink the open set $f^{-1}[W]$ to an open $U$ whose compact closure $K$ stays inside it. Then $S(K,W)\times U$ is a product neighbourhood mapped into $W$. Handle the empty domain vacuously; no separation or metric is required on the target.

items.title: Under Choice, pointwise closure is compact exactly when every coordinate set has compact closure
items.strategy: For necessity apply each continuous coordinate projection to the compact pointwise closure. For sufficiency put the family inside the product of the compact coordinate closures, use Tychonoff under the stated Axiom of Choice, and take its closure there. Because the metric target is Hausdorff, the compact coordinate closures are closed in the full target, so this relative closure is exactly the closure in the full product.

items.title: The pointwise closure of an equicontinuous family is equicontinuous and consists of continuous maps
items.strategy: Fix $x$ and an epsilon and take the neighbourhood that works for the original family at epsilon divided into three parts. For a pointwise-limit candidate and $y$ in that neighbourhood, a basic pointwise neighbourhood controlling the two coordinates $x,y$ meets the original family; the triangle inequality transfers the common estimate. The resulting estimate is uniform over the closure and also proves each candidate continuous.

items.title: The compact-open and pointwise topologies agree on an equicontinuous family
items.strategy: Pointwise subbasic conditions are compact-open conditions on singletons. Conversely, around $f$ in a compact-open subbasic set $S(K,V)$, use compactness of $f[K]$ and the metric target to obtain finitely many value tolerances inside $V$; equicontinuity and continuity give a finite cover of $K$. Conditions at the finitely many chosen coordinates then force every member of the family to map $K$ into $V$. Treat $K=\varnothing$ and $V=Y$ before invoking positive tolerances.

items.title: Under Choice, equicontinuity and pointwise relative compactness give compact compact-open closure
items.strategy: Take the pointwise closure $H$. The pointwise compactness criterion makes $H$ compact, and pointwise closure preserves equicontinuity and continuity. On $H$ the pointwise and compact-open subspace topologies agree, so $H$ is compact in the compact-open topology and the original family is dense there; hence $H$ is its compact-open closure. State the Axiom of Choice exactly where Tychonoff is invoked.

items.title: A compact compact-open family is equicontinuous on a locally compact Hausdorff domain
items.strategy: Use joint continuity of evaluation on the compact family times the domain. At a fixed domain point and target tolerance, each function has a product neighbourhood on which two evaluations stay close to its value at that point. Compactness of the family produces finitely many function-neighbourhoods; intersect the corresponding domain-neighbourhoods to obtain one neighbourhood serving the whole family.

items.title: Every compact compact-open family is pointwise relatively compact
items.strategy: Evaluation at a fixed point is continuous because its inverse images are the compact-open subbasic sets on the compact singleton. Its image of the compact family is compact. In the Hausdorff metric target that image is closed, so it already equals the closure of the coordinate-value set.

items.title: General Ascoli theorem for locally compact Hausdorff domains and metric targets
items.strategy: Assume Choice. If the compact-open closure is compact, apply compact-family equicontinuity to that closure and restrict to the original family; apply continuous evaluation to obtain pointwise relative compactness. Conversely apply the general sufficiency theorem, which does not need local compactness. State the result as an iff for compactness of the closure, not merely sequential compactness.

items.title: Ascoli–Arzelà for a compact Hausdorff domain
items.strategy: A compact Hausdorff space is locally compact because the whole space is a compact neighbourhood of every point. Substitute this into the general theorem, retaining the metric target, pointwise relative compactness, the compact-open topology, and the explicit Choice hypothesis.

items.title: On a nonempty compact metric domain, the compact-open topology is the uniform topology
items.strategy: Use the published equality of compact-open and compact convergence. Every compact-convergence basic condition is implied by a uniform ball, while taking the compact set to be the whole domain makes each sufficiently small uniform ball a compact-convergence basic set. Keep the nonempty-domain hypothesis required by the published uniform metric.

items.title: Ascoli–Arzelà in the uniform topology for compact metric domains
items.strategy: Use the metric/topological agreement for equicontinuity and the equality of compact-open and uniform topologies on a compact metric domain. The general theorem then says exactly that the uniform closure is compact iff the family is metric-equicontinuous and pointwise relatively compact.

items.title: For a proper metric target, compact subsets of $C(X,Y)$ are exactly the closed, pointwise bounded, equicontinuous families
items.strategy: Let $X$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let every closed bounded subset of $Y$ be compact. Compactness implies closedness in the uniform metric, equicontinuity, and pointwise boundedness. Conversely, each bounded coordinate set has compact closure inside a closed ball; Ascoli makes the family closure compact, and assumed closedness identifies the family with that closure. Record the Choice hypothesis inherited from Ascoli. This general statement does not postpone the real case: a separate same-page corollary uses the published Heine-Borel theorem for $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb R^n$. Only the complex scalar specialization is blocked; its licensing page is field-extensions-and-the-complex-numbers, outside page 285's declared requires closure.

items.title: A pointwise bounded equicontinuous sequence into a proper metric target has a uniformly convergent subsequence
items.strategy: Follow Shapiro's proof in its natural proper-target generality. Use finite $1/n$-nets to build a countable dense subset of the compact metric domain, successively extract coordinate-convergent subsequences inside compact closed balls, and take the diagonal. Equicontinuity and a finite net make the diagonal subsequence uniformly Cauchy. A proper metric space is complete because a Cauchy sequence is eventually trapped in a compact closed ball; the uniform-limit theorem then gives a continuous uniform limit. Charge Countable Choice and Dependent Choice explicitly; the page's full Choice hypothesis is a valid upper bound.

items.title: Real and finite-dimensional Euclidean Ascoli–Arzelà criteria
items.strategy: Assume Choice, let $X$ be a nonempty compact metric space, and let $n\ge 1$. Do not re-prove the real-valued case: cite the published real $C(K)$ compact-closure theorem and its published subsequence corollary. Heine-Borel makes Euclidean $\mathbb R^n$ a proper metric target, so specialize the proper-target compact-family criterion and subsequence theorem to obtain the corresponding vector-valued statements. State explicitly that in either codomain a family is compact exactly when it is closed in the uniform topology, pointwise bounded, and equicontinuous, and that every pointwise bounded equicontinuous sequence has a uniformly convergent subsequence. For Munkres Corollary 45.5's sup-bounded wording, prove in the vector case that pointwise boundedness plus equicontinuity gives one uniform Euclidean bound by choosing local unit-variation neighbourhoods and taking a finite subcover; the converse is immediate. When Shapiro is cited as scalar corroboration at step 5, do not widen its quantifiers: cite the published compact-domain lemmas that turn pointwise equicontinuity into uniform equicontinuity and pointwise boundedness plus equicontinuity into Shapiro's one uniform bound.

items.title: Under Choice, an equicontinuous family into a compact metric target has compact compact-open closure
items.strategy: Every coordinate-value set lies in the compact target, so its closure is compact as a closed subset. Apply Ascoli sufficiency. This corollary intentionally needs no local compactness of the domain because only the sufficient direction is used.

pages.title: The Ascoli–Arzelà Theorem: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: For finite discrete $X$ and compact metric $Y$, the whole space $C(X,Y)$ is compact
items.strategy: Every map from finite discrete $X$ is continuous and the whole family is equicontinuous because the singleton neighbourhood of a point works for every member. Each coordinate set is $Y$, hence compact; apply Ascoli. Include $X=\varnothing$, where the function space is a singleton.

items.title: A compact set of target values gives a compact family of constant maps
items.strategy: For nonempty locally compact Hausdorff $X$ and compact $K$ in a metric target, the family $c_y(x)=y$ for $y\in K$ is equicontinuous and has coordinate set $K$ at every point, hence is compact by Ascoli. Evaluation at any fixed point is the inverse of $y\mapsto c_y$, so the parameterisation is a homeomorphism onto the family.

items.title: Boundedness does not replace pointwise relative compactness for an arbitrary metric target
items.strategy: Take a one-point domain and an infinite set with the discrete metric of diameter one as target. All constant maps form an equicontinuous and pointwise bounded family, but evaluation identifies its closure with the infinite discrete target, whose singleton open cover has no finite subcover. Thus the family is not compact.

items.title: Translated tent functions on $\mathbb R$ converge to zero in the compact-open topology
items.strategy: Let $b(x)=\max\{1-|x|,0\}$ and $f_n(x)=b(x-n)$. The family has common Lipschitz constant one and coordinate values in $[0,1]$. Every compact subset of $\mathbb R$ is bounded, so it misses the supports for all sufficiently large $n$; hence $f_n$ converges uniformly on each compact set, though not uniformly on all of $\mathbb R$ because $f_n(n)=1$.

items.title: Affine interpolants with endpoints in a compact rectangle form a compact family
items.strategy: For $(a,b)$ in a fixed compact rectangle of $\mathbb R^2$, put $f_{a,b}(t)=(1-t)a+tb$ on $[0,1]$. A common endpoint bound gives a common Lipschitz constant, hence equicontinuity, and each coordinate image is a compact interval as the continuous image of the parameter rectangle. Apply Ascoli and identify the endpoint evaluations as continuous coordinates of the family.

pages.title: Stone–Weierstrass in General

items.title: The two-point duplication property of a function family relative to a target function
Unital point-separating real vector sublattices of $C(X,\mathbb R)$
Unital, point-separating, and nowhere-vanishing real function algebras on a compact Hausdorff space
Self-adjoint complex function algebras, unitality, and point separation
The general real function-algebra definition agrees with the published compact-metric definition
items.strategy: Give the metric space its metric topology. Use the published equivalence between metric and topological compactness, metric Hausdorff separation, and the metric/topological continuity equivalence to identify both ambient spaces of continuous functions. Then compare the algebra, constant, and point-separation clauses one by one. No assertion is made for the empty metric space, which the earlier definition excludes.

items.title: A unital separating real function lattice interpolates arbitrary values at two distinct points
items.strategy: For distinct $x,y$, choose a separator $g$ and apply an affine rescaling so that its values at $x,y$ are the prescribed pair; vector-space and constant closure keep the rescaling in the lattice. When the later sweep encounters $x=y$, use the corresponding constant function rather than invoking this distinct-point lemma.

items.title: A function lattice with the two-point duplication property uniformly approximates its target
items.strategy: Let a sublattice $L\subseteq C(X,\mathbb R)$ have the two-point duplication property relative to $f$. For each $x$, duplicate $f$ at $x$ and every $y$; continuity gives neighbourhoods on which the witnesses lie below $f+\varepsilon$. Compactness leaves finitely many, and their pointwise maximum gives $g_x$ with $g_x>f-\varepsilon$ near $x$ and $g_x<f+\varepsilon$ everywhere. A second finite cover and pointwise minimum gives one member of $L$ within $\varepsilon$ of $f$ everywhere. Define both covering families by their properties and make only the resulting finite choices.

items.title: Lattice Stone–Weierstrass theorem on a compact Hausdorff space
items.strategy: For every target $f\in C(X,\mathbb R)$, the interpolation lemma gives the vector sublattice the two-point duplication property relative to $f$. Apply the general two-sweep lemma at every positive error. This is uniform density. Handle the empty compact space directly, since it has a unique real-valued function, before invoking the nonempty-domain uniform-topology definition.

items.title: The uniform closure of a real function algebra is a vector lattice
items.strategy: First verify that uniform limits preserve the algebra operations. For $f$ in the closure, compactness bounds its image in $[-M,M]$. Approximate $|t|$ there by polynomials, subtract each polynomial's constant term when the algebra is nonunital, and use the available unit when it is unital, to place $|f|$ in the closure. Then use $f\vee g=(f+g+|f-g|)/2$ and $f\wedge g=(f+g-|f-g|)/2$. Treat $M=0$ separately.

items.title: Real Stone–Weierstrass theorem for compact Hausdorff spaces
items.strategy: The uniform closure of the unital separating algebra remains unital and separating and is a real vector lattice by the closure lemma. Apply lattice Stone–Weierstrass to that closure; being both dense and closed, it is all of $C(X,\mathbb R)$. Include the empty-space boundary directly.

items.title: A nowhere-vanishing real function algebra on a compact space approximates the constant one
items.strategy: For every point choose an algebra member nonzero there. Compactness reduces the corresponding nonzero neighbourhoods to finitely many, and the sum of their squares is an algebra member $h$ with positive minimum $m$ and finite maximum $M$. Approximate $1/t$ on $[m,M]$ by a polynomial $p$; then $hp(h)$ lies in the possibly nonunital algebra and uniformly approximates one. Handle the empty domain and the one-point range $m=M$ explicitly.

items.title: A separating real function algebra is dense or its closure consists exactly of the functions vanishing at one point
items.strategy: Let $B$ be the uniform closure. If the algebra has no common zero, the preceding approximate-unit lemma puts the constant one in $B$, and real Stone–Weierstrass gives $B=C(X,\mathbb R)$. If all algebra members vanish at $x_0$, separation makes $x_0$ unique. The algebra obtained by adjoining constants is unital and separating, hence dense; evaluating an approximant $a+c$ at $x_0$ shows that every continuous function vanishing at $x_0$ is approximated by members $a$ of the original algebra. Thus $B$ is exactly that vanishing ideal. Handle the empty space separately.

items.title: A point-separating nowhere-vanishing real function algebra is uniformly dense
items.strategy: Apply the separating-algebra dichotomy. Its proper alternative requires every algebra member to vanish at one fixed point, contradicting nowhere-vanishing there. Hence the closure is all of $C(X,\mathbb R)$.

items.title: The real-valued part of a self-adjoint complex function algebra is separating and has the same common zeros
items.strategy: Self-adjointness puts $(f+\overline f)/2$ and $(f-\overline f)/(2i)$ in the algebra, so the real and imaginary parts of every member lie in its real-valued part. If $f$ separates two points, at least one of those two parts separates them. Verify real-scalar, sum, and product closure pointwise using the published complex field and conjugation laws.

items.title: Complex Stone–Weierstrass dichotomy for separating self-adjoint algebras; the unital case is dense
items.strategy: Apply the real separating-algebra dichotomy to the real-valued part of the self-adjoint algebra. In the dense alternative, approximate the real and imaginary parts of an arbitrary continuous complex function separately and combine them as $u+iv$. In the proper alternative, the same argument identifies the complex closure with all continuous functions vanishing at the unique common zero. A unital algebra has no common zero, so the named unital self-adjoint form is dense. Self-adjointness is indispensable and is not inferred from point separation.

items.title: The unital algebra generated by a separating complex family and its conjugates is dense
items.strategy: The generated algebra contains constants, retains the original separating family, and is closed under conjugation because the generators occur in conjugate pairs and complex conjugation respects pointwise sums and products. Apply complex Stone–Weierstrass.

items.title: The quotient that identifies points indistinguishable by a real function algebra
A closed unital real function algebra is $C(Y,\mathbb R)$ on its indistinguishability quotient
items.strategy: Let $q:X\to Y$ be the quotient by equality of all algebra values. Each algebra member descends uniquely and continuously; the descended algebra separates points. The quotient is compact as a continuous image and Hausdorff because a descended real function separates any two distinct classes. Real Stone–Weierstrass makes the descended algebra dense in $C(Y,\mathbb R)$; pulling uniform approximations back along surjective $q$ and using closedness upgrades density to equality and yields an isometric algebra isomorphism.

pages.title: Stone–Weierstrass in General: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The disc algebra is unital and separating but not self-adjoint or dense
items.strategy: On the closed unit disc let $A$ be the uniform closure of polynomials in the coordinate $z$. The published complex metric identifies the disc with a closed bounded subset of Euclidean $\mathbb R^2$; Heine–Borel and the metric/topological compactness bridge make it compact Hausdorff. If $\overline z\in A$, choose a polynomial $p$ uniformly closer than one to it and set $N=\deg p+2$. De Moivre writes all $N$th roots as powers of $\zeta=\exp(2\pi i/N)$, while the exponential-kernel theorem proves $\zeta^r\ne1$ for $1\le r<N$. Prove $(x-1)\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}x^k=x^N-1$ inline by induction and use it to obtain every shifted-power cancellation not already supplied by the exact root-sum corollary. Averaging $\zeta^k p(\zeta^k)$ then gives zero, while averaging $\zeta^k\overline{\zeta^k}$ gives one, contradicting the uniform error. Hence $A$ is not self-adjoint and, being closed and proper, is not dense.

items.title: Trigonometric polynomials are uniformly dense on the unit circle
items.strategy: Define complex trigonometric polynomials as finite Laurent sums $\sum_{j=-n}^n a_jz^j$, using the published integer-power convention. On the unit circle, $z\overline z=|z|^2=1$, so a numbered algebra step proves $z^{-1}=\overline z$ and converts negative powers into powers of the conjugate coordinate. The published complex metric makes the circle a closed bounded Euclidean subset; Heine–Borel and the metric/topological bridges make it compact Hausdorff. Constants, the coordinate separator, and conjugation closure then satisfy complex Stone–Weierstrass; no Fourier convergence theorem is used.

items.title: The lattice generated by distance functions is dense on every compact metric space
items.strategy: Let $L$ be the smallest real vector sublattice containing constants and all functions $d(a,-)$. Every distance function is continuous by the triangle inequality, and for $x\ne y$ the function $d(x,-)$ takes the distinct values $0$ and $d(x,y)$. Thus $L$ separates points and lattice Stone–Weierstrass applies.

items.title: On a finite compact Hausdorff space a unital separating algebra contains every scalar-valued function
items.strategy: For each point $x$ and every other point $y$, normalize a separator to equal one at $x$ and zero at $y$. Their finite product is the indicator of $x$. Linear combinations of these indicators reproduce every real- or complex-valued function exactly. Treat the empty and one-point spaces separately; on a finite Hausdorff space every scalar-valued function is continuous.

items.title: Endpoint-duplicating functions on $[0,1]$ become all continuous functions on the endpoint quotient
items.strategy: Take the real algebra of continuous functions on $[0,1]$ satisfying $f(0)=f(1)$. It is closed and unital. Explicit piecewise-linear tent functions with equal endpoint values separate every pair except the endpoint pair, so its indistinguishability quotient identifies exactly $0$ and $1$. The quotient representation theorem identifies the algebra isometrically with all continuous real functions on that quotient.

items.title: The polynomial algebra is dense but not closed on a nondegenerate compact interval
items.strategy: For $a<b$, polynomials restricted to $[a,b]$ form a unital separating algebra, so Stone–Weierstrass gives density. Choose $c$ strictly between the endpoints; the continuous function $|x-c|$ cannot agree with a polynomial because its one-sided slopes at $c$ differ. Hence the algebra is proper, and a proper dense subspace is not closed.

items.title: A continuous real function on $[0,1]$ whose every moment $\int_0^1 x^nf$ vanishes is identically zero
items.strategy: Erdman Prop 21.2.9, overturned at step 9 (alpha-step9 F1). Products of continuous functions are continuous hence integrable; linearity carries the hypothesis from monomials to every polynomial. Weierstrass supplies a polynomial within eps/M of f, and f^2 = (f-p)f + pf splits the square integral into a term bounded by eps and a term that vanishes. Letting eps run gives integral of f^2 equal to 0, and the published continuous-nonnegative-zero-integral theorem finishes.

items.title: Every continuous function on $[0,1]$ is uniformly approximated by everywhere-differentiable functions whose derivative vanishes at a prescribed point
items.strategy: Erdman Prop 21.2.10, overturned at step 9 (alpha-step9 F2). Weierstrass gives a polynomial p within eps/3 of f; if a = p_prime(c) is nonzero, subtract (a/lambda)sin(lambda(x-c)), a function with derivative a at c and sup norm at most |a|/lambda. The Archimedean reciprocal chooses lambda so that this correction is below eps/3, leaving the derivative at c zero and the total error below eps.

pages.title: The Inverse Function Theorem Completed

items.title: $C^k$ Euclidean maps and diffeomorphisms
$C^k$ Euclidean maps are closed under componentwise algebra and composition
items.strategy: Use induction on the derivative order. At order zero the assertions are the algebra and composition laws for continuous component functions. For the induction step, differentiate sums and scalar products componentwise and apply the total chain rule to a composition; the resulting first derivatives are finite sums of products of derivatives of lower order, so the induction hypothesis supplies continuity. Treat empty domains and $k=0$ explicitly.

items.title: Matrix inversion preserves $C^k$ regularity where the determinant is nonzero
items.strategy: Write each inverse entry as the corresponding cofactor divided by the determinant. Cofactors and the determinant are polynomials in the matrix entries, hence are $C^k$ by the algebra theorem. Prove by induction from the reciprocal rule that $t\mapsto1/t$ is smooth on each component of $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, then compose it with the nonvanishing determinant. This handles $k=0$, $k=1$, and every finite $k$ without assuming a matrix-valued derivative calculus.

items.title: A local inverse of a $C^k$ regular map is $C^k$
items.strategy: The published inverse function theorem gives a $C^1$ inverse $g$ and $Dg=(Df\circ g)^{-1}$. Induct on $r<k$: if $g$ is $C^r$, then the entries of $Df\circ g$ are $C^r$ by closure under composition, and the matrix-inversion lemma makes the entries of $Dg$ $C^r$; hence $g$ is $C^{r+1}$. The case $k=1$ is the published theorem, and the same finite induction at every order gives the smooth case.

items.title: The regular locus of a square-dimensional $C^1$ map
The regular locus of a $C^1$ Euclidean map is open
items.strategy: At a regular point apply the published Newton-contraction lemma. Its conclusion makes every derivative in a closed ball about that point invertible, so a smaller open ball lies in the regular locus. This proves openness point by point and also covers the empty regular locus.

items.title: A $C^1$ map with everywhere-invertible derivative is open
items.strategy: For an open subset $O$ of the domain and a point $y=f(x)$ in its image, apply the inverse function theorem at $x$ after intersecting its inverse neighbourhood with $O$. The resulting neighbourhood of $y$ lies in $f[O]$. Since every image point is interior, $f[O]$ is open.

items.title: An injective regular $C^1$ map is a diffeomorphism onto its image
items.strategy: Openness makes the image open and makes the inverse of the continuous bijection continuous. At every image point, global injectivity identifies this inverse with the local inverse supplied by the inverse function theorem, so it is $C^1$ locally and therefore on the whole image. Preserve the derivative formula $D(f^{-1})(f(x))=Df(x)^{-1}$.

items.title: An injective regular $C^k$ map is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism onto its image
items.strategy: The $C^1$ theorem supplies the global inverse on the open image. Around each image point it agrees with a local inverse, and the higher-regularity theorem makes that local inverse $C^k$. Regularity is local, so these restrictions give a $C^k$ global inverse. Include $k=1$ as the base case.

items.title: The parametrized implicit function theorem with $C^k$ regularity
items.strategy: Treat the ordinary variables and parameters together as the first coordinate block in the published implicit function theorem. It gives the unique $C^1$ solution and the derivative with respect to the combined block. Apply the higher-regularity inverse argument to the block map $(x,\lambda,y)\mapsto(x,\lambda,F(x,y,\lambda))$ to upgrade the solution to $C^k$, and read the displayed derivative formula by differentiating $F(x,\varphi(x,\lambda),\lambda)=0$.

items.title: Proper maps between Euclidean open sets
A proper Euclidean local diffeomorphism has finite diffeomorphic sheets near every target point
items.strategy: First prove that a proper continuous map between Euclidean open sets is closed by restricting near a target point to a compact closed ball and using compact images. A local diffeomorphism is open, so its nonempty image is clopen and equals the connected target. Each fibre is compact by properness and discrete by local injectivity, hence finite by its singleton cover. Choose disjoint local inverse neighbourhoods around the finitely many fibre points; remove from the common target neighbourhood the closed image of their complement. The remaining neighbourhood has exactly those finitely many disjoint sheets, each mapped diffeomorphically onto it. State the property directly and mention the order-293 covering-map definition only as orientation, never as a proof input.

items.title: A proper Euclidean local diffeomorphism over a connected target has constant finite fibre cardinality
items.strategy: Over each neighbourhood supplied by the finite-sheet theorem, every fibre meets each sheet exactly once, so all fibres there are canonically bijective with the finite sheet index set. The subsets of the connected target on which a fixed finite cardinal occurs are open; two nonempty such subsets would separate the target. Hence every fibre has the same finite cardinality.

items.title: Local orientation of a regular $C^1$ Euclidean map
The Jacobian sign of a regular $C^1$ map is constant on a connected domain
items.strategy: The Jacobian determinant is continuous because it is a polynomial in the continuous derivative-matrix entries. Its image of a connected domain is a connected subset of the real line. Regularity excludes zero, so order-convexity of connected real subsets prevents the image from containing both positive and negative values. Nonemptiness then gives exactly one sign.

items.title: A differentiable map on a connected open Euclidean set has zero derivative exactly when it is constant
items.strategy: The reverse implication follows directly from the total-derivative definition. For the forward implication, polygonal connectedness joins any two domain points by finitely many line segments. Compose each component of the map with each affine segment; the total chain rule gives derivative zero on the parameter interval, so the one-variable zero-derivative theorem makes the composition constant. Concatenate the finitely many equalities.

pages.title: The Inverse Function Theorem Completed: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Polar coordinates are a local diffeomorphism away from zero radius
items.strategy: For $P(r,\theta)=(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)$ compute the derivative determinant as $r$. Thus $P$ is locally orientation-preserving for $r>0$ and locally orientation-reversing for $r<0$. On $(0,\infty)\times(-\pi,\pi)$ give the explicit inverse onto the plane cut along the nonpositive horizontal ray; on $(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ note the periodic failure of global injectivity.

items.title: The map $(x,y)\mapsto(x,xy)$ is a diffeomorphism off the vertical axis
items.strategy: Its derivative matrix has determinant $x$. Restricting to the open set $x\ne0$ gives the explicit inverse $(u,v)\mapsto(u,v/u)$, which is $C^\infty$ on the same set. Verify both composite identities and note that the full-plane image omits every $(0,v)$ with $v\ne0$.

items.title: Two equations implicitly determine two variables near the origin
items.strategy: For the source system $x^2+y^2-(z+1)^3=-1$ and $e^x+e^y+e^z=3$, regard $(y,z)$ as the unknown block and $x$ as the parameter. At the origin the derivative with respect to $(y,z)$ is the invertible matrix with rows $(0,-3)$ and $(1,1)$. Apply the parametrized implicit theorem and record the derivative of the solution pair at zero.

items.title: $x\mapsto x^3$ is a $C^1$ bijection whose inverse is not differentiable at zero
items.strategy: The cube map is a strictly increasing smooth bijection of the line. If its inverse were differentiable at zero, differentiating the identity $g(x^3)=x$ at zero would give $Dg(0)\,0=1$, impossible. Equivalently, the cube-root difference quotient at zero is unbounded.

items.title: Zero derivative need not give constancy on a disconnected open set
items.strategy: On $U=(-2,-1)\cup(1,2)$ let $f$ be $1$ on the first component and $-1$ on the second. Every point has a neighbourhood on which $f$ is constant, so its total derivative is zero everywhere, while the two displayed values show that $f$ is not constant. This is the exact source-backed witness from the Northwestern real-analysis notes.

items.title: FALSE: an invertible derivative at one point gives a local inverse
items.strategy: Use the source-backed function $f(0)=0$ and $f(x)=x+2x^2\sin(1/x)$ for nonzero $x$. Compute $f'(0)=1$, then use the sine and cosine values at reciprocal integer multiples of $\pi$ to obtain derivative values of both signs arbitrarily near zero. A continuous injective function on an interval is strictly monotone, whose derivative cannot have both signs. Thus $f$ is injective on no neighbourhood of zero, and continuity of the derivative near the point is the missing hypothesis.

items.title: FALSE: an everywhere-invertible derivative gives a global inverse
items.strategy: On the punctured plane use $S(x,y)=(x^2-y^2,2xy)$. Compute its derivative and write an explicit inverse linear map at every nonzero point, so the inverse function theorem gives local invertibility everywhere on the domain. The identity $S(x,y)=S(-x,-y)$ gives a fixed antipodal collision and rules out a global inverse. This separates local invertibility from global injectivity without depending on the published companion-page counterexample.

items.title: FALSE: every $C^1$ bijection has a $C^1$ inverse
items.strategy: Use the preceding cube-map counterexample. It is a $C^1$ bijection and an open map, but the vanishing derivative at zero forces the inverse cube root to fail differentiability there.

items.title: FALSE: zero derivative on an open set forces constancy
items.strategy: The two-component locally constant counterexample has derivative zero everywhere and takes two values. Contrast it with the exact connected-open equivalence, isolating connectedness as the omitted hypothesis.

items.title: FALSE: every open $C^1$ map has invertible derivative
items.strategy: The cube map is a $C^1$ open bijection of the line, yet its derivative at zero is the zero linear map. This refutes the converse of the open-map corollary while preserving its forward implication.

pages.title: Constant Rank, Submersions, Immersions and Regular Level Sets

items.title: The rank of a derivative and constant-rank Euclidean maps
Submatrices and minors of a rectangular matrix
A matrix has rank at least $r$ exactly when it has a nonzero $r$-rowed minor
items.strategy: For $1\le r\le\min\{m,n\}$, a nonzero $r$-rowed minor has independent columns, so the ambient matrix has rank at least $r$. Conversely choose $r$ independent columns from a matrix of rank at least $r$; row rank equals column rank for the resulting $m\times r$ matrix, so some $r$ rows form a full-row-rank square submatrix. The invertible-matrix theorem makes it invertible, and its determinant is nonzero. Keep the positive-size restriction explicit so no undeclared empty determinant is used.

items.title: Differential rank is lower semicontinuous
items.strategy: For a $C^1$ map, prove that $\{x:\operatorname{rank}Df(x)\ge r\}$ is open for every positive $r$: when $r$ exceeds either the source or target dimension the locus is empty; otherwise, at a point in the set, the rank-minor lemma selects one nonzero $r$-rowed Jacobian minor, and continuity of the derivative entries and of the determinant keeps that minor nonzero nearby. The $r=0$ locus is the whole open domain. Conclude that every maximal-rank locus is open, including the empty locus.

items.title: Submersions and immersions between Euclidean open sets
Regular and critical points, regular and critical values, and level sets
The tangent space to a regular level set
A nonzero rank minor supplies the source coordinates for the constant-rank theorem
items.strategy: After permuting source and target coordinates, arrange that the leading $r\times r$ minor of $Df(a)$ is nonzero. Form $\Phi(x)=(f_1(x),\ldots,f_r(x),x_{r+1},\ldots,x_m)$. Its derivative at $a$ is block triangular with that minor on the diagonal, so the inverse function theorem and higher-inverse regularity give a local $C^k$ diffeomorphism. Treat $r=0$ by the identity source chart and $r=m$ by the full map.
