items.title: In source rank coordinates, the remaining components depend only on the rank coordinates
items.strategy: Write $g=f\circ\Phi^{-1}$, so its first $r$ components are the first $r$ coordinates. Constant rank $r$ and the rank-minor criterion force every derivative of a remaining component in a remaining source direction to vanish: otherwise adjoining that entry to the identity corner produces a nonzero $(r+1)$-rowed minor. On a small rectangular coordinate neighbourhood, zero derivative on each connected slice makes each tail component depend only on the first $r$ variables. Handle $r=0$, $r=m$, and $r=n$ separately where one coordinate block is empty.

items.title: The Euclidean constant-rank normal form
items.strategy: Use the source-coordinate lemma and write the transformed map as $(u,h(u))$. The target shear $(z,w)\mapsto(z,w-h(z))$ is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism with an explicit inverse, and it changes the map to $(u,v)\mapsto(u,0)$. For rank zero use local constancy on a ball; for full source or target rank keep the empty coordinate block explicit. State both coordinate diffeomorphisms and their domains rather than suppressing the local restrictions.

items.title: A Euclidean submersion is locally a coordinate projection
items.strategy: At a submersion point the derivative has the maximal target rank. Lower semicontinuity therefore makes that rank constant on a neighbourhood, and the constant-rank theorem reduces the map to projection onto the first target-many coordinates. Include the equal-dimensional local-diffeomorphism case.

items.title: A Euclidean immersion is locally the canonical inclusion and is locally an embedding
items.strategy: At an immersion point the derivative has maximal source rank, which persists nearby by lower semicontinuity. The constant-rank normal form becomes $u\mapsto(u,0)$; this is injective with a continuous $C^k$ inverse from its image, so after shrinking the original map is a $C^k$ embedding onto its local image. Treat equal dimensions as the inverse-function case.

items.title: Euclidean submersions are open maps
items.strategy: For a point in the image of an open set, shrink to the local projection coordinates supplied by the submersion normal form. Coordinate diffeomorphisms and the canonical projection are open, so the image contains a neighbourhood of the selected target point. Repeat for every image point; the empty open set is immediate.

items.title: A constant-rank level set is locally a coordinate slice
items.strategy: Apply the constant-rank normal form at a point of $f^{-1}(c)$. In the resulting source coordinates the level-set equation is exactly $u=0$, while the remaining $m-r$ coordinates are free. Pull the slice back by the source diffeomorphism and state the empty level set as a vacuous case. The result is local and does not invoke unbuilt manifold terminology.

items.title: A regular level set is locally a $C^k$ graph of dimension $m-n$
items.strategy: At a point of a regular level set the derivative is surjective, so maximal target rank persists on a neighbourhood. Apply the constant-rank level-set theorem with rank $n$. Use the finite-dimensional orthogonal decomposition $\mathbb R^m=\ker Df(a)\oplus(\ker Df(a))^\perp$; the projection of the pulled-back slice to the kernel has invertible derivative at the point, so the inverse function theorem rewrites it as a graph over the kernel with values in the orthogonal complement. Record the vacuous empty-fibre convention and the zero-dimensional case $m=n$.

items.title: Tangent vectors to a regular level set are exactly its curve velocities
items.strategy: If a differentiable curve stays in the level set, the chain rule sends its velocity into $\ker Df(a)$, which is the defined tangent space. Conversely use the local graph representation: every kernel vector gives a straight curve in graph coordinates, and pulling it back gives a $C^1$ level-set curve with the prescribed velocity. Check the zero vector by the constant curve and both inclusions separately.

items.title: A linear functional annihilating the kernel of a surjection is a unique transpose multiple
items.strategy: Let $A:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ be surjective and choose one preimage of each standard basis vector. If $\ell$ vanishes on $\ker A$, subtract the corresponding finite linear combination of those preimages from an arbitrary vector to show $\ell(v)=\lambda\cdot Av$ for the vector of their $\ell$-values. Surjectivity makes $A^T$ injective, proving uniqueness. The finite coordinate choices use no choice principle, and the cases $m,n\ge1$ match the Euclidean conventions.

items.title: Lagrange multipliers for a regular vector-valued level-set constraint
items.strategy: Let $f$ have a constrained local extremum at $a$ on $G^{-1}(c)$ and assume $DG(a)$ is surjective. Every vector in $\ker DG(a)$ is a level-set curve velocity by the tangent theorem, so the parametrized-extremum theorem makes $Df(a)$ annihilate that kernel. Apply the factorization lemma to obtain the unique $\lambda\in\mathbb R^q$ with $Df(a)v=\lambda\cdot DG(a)v$ for all $v$, equivalently $\nabla f(a)=DG(a)^T\lambda$. Distinguish necessity from sufficiency.

items.title: For one regular constraint, the objective gradient is a scalar multiple of the constraint gradient
items.strategy:
Apply the vector-valued multiplier theorem with a one-dimensional target. The transpose of the one-row Jacobian sends the scalar multiplier to the same scalar multiple of $
abla G(a)$. The regularity hypothesis is exactly $
abla G(a)
e0$, and uniqueness follows from that nonzero vector.

pages.title: Constant Rank, Submersions, Immersions and Regular Level Sets: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: A Euclidean sphere is a regular level set with tangent hyperplanes
items.strategy: For $F(x)=\|x\|_2^2$, compute $DF(x)h=2\langle x,h\rangle$. On $F^{-1}(R^2)$ with $R>0$, the derivative is nonzero and hence surjective to $\mathbb R$. Apply the regular-level-set theorem and identify the tangent space as $x^\perp$. Treat the empty negative level and the singular zero level separately in the discussion.

items.title: A positive-definite quadratic ellipsoid is a regular level set
items.strategy: For a symmetric positive-definite matrix $A$, set $F(x)=\langle Ax,x\rangle$. Compute $DF(x)h=2\langle Ax,h\rangle$. On the positive level $F=1$, one has $x\ne0$ and $Ax\ne0$, since $Ax=0$ would contradict positive definiteness. Thus the derivative is surjective, and the tangent hyperplane is $(Ax)^\perp$.

items.title: The graph of a $C^k$ Euclidean map is a regular level set
items.strategy: For $\psi:U\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$, define $G(x,y)=y-\psi(x)$. Its derivative is $DG=(-D\psi,I_n)$, which is surjective at every graph point. The regular-level-set theorem identifies $G^{-1}(0)$ with the graph, and the tangent space is $\{(v,D\psi(x)v):v\in\mathbb R^m\}$ by solving the kernel equation.

items.title: The one-sheeted hyperboloid is a regular surface of revolution
items.strategy: Use $F(x,y,z)=x^2+y^2-z^2$. On $F^{-1}(1)$ the gradient $(2x,2y,-2z)$ cannot vanish, so the level is regular. Its equation is invariant under rotations in the $xy$-plane, and rotating the profile $x=\sqrt{1+z^2}$ around the $z$-axis gives the whole set. The tangent plane is the kernel of the displayed derivative.

items.title: The orthogonal group is a regular level set of dimension $n(n-1)/2$
items.strategy: Read $A\mapsto A^{\mathsf T}A$ as a polynomial map $\mathbb R^{n^2}\to\mathbb R^{n(n+1)/2}$, compute its derivative $H\mapsto A^{\mathsf T}H+H^{\mathsf T}A$ as a directional derivative, and solve $Df(A)H=S$ by $H=AS/2$ at a point of the fibre to get surjectivity. The graph dimension and the skew-symmetric description of the tangent space follow from the regular level set corollary.

items.title: The cone $x^2+y^2=z^2$ has a rank drop at its apex
items.strategy: Take $F(x,y,z)=x^2+y^2-z^2$. Its zero level is the double cone. Away from the origin the gradient $(2x,2y,-2z)$ is nonzero, so the level is locally regular; at the apex the derivative is zero. Show directly that no neighbourhood of the apex in the cone is a graph over any plane by using the two nappes or the failure of a unique tangent plane.

items.title: The cusp $y^2=x^3$ has a rank drop at the origin
items.strategy: Let $F(x,y)=y^2-x^3$. Its derivative is $(-3x^2,2y)$, nonzero on the zero level except at the origin. The parametrization $t\mapsto(t^2,t^3)$ shows the cusp and gives zero velocity at the origin; the two branches cannot form a $C^1$ graph with a regular parametrization there. This isolates the failure at the critical point.

items.title: The map $(x,y)\mapsto(x,xy)$ has nonconstant rank on every neighbourhood of the origin
items.strategy: Its Jacobian is $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\y&x\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $x$. Hence the rank is two when $x\ne0$ and one when $x=0$. Every neighbourhood of the origin meets both sets, even though the derivative is continuous and the rank-one locus itself is closed rather than open.

items.title: A critical value can have a smooth level set
items.strategy: For $F(x,y)=x^2$, zero is a critical value because every point of $F^{-1}(0)=\{x=0\}$ has nonsurjective derivative. Nevertheless the level set is the vertical line, the graph of the zero function over the $y$-axis. This separates regularity of a defining map from smoothness of the underlying set.

items.title: Lagrange multipliers locate the extrema of a linear functional on a sphere
items.strategy: For nonzero $a\in\mathbb R^m$, optimize $f(x)=\langle a,x\rangle$ subject to $G(x)=\|x\|_2^2-R^2=0$ with $R>0$. The multiplier equation is $a=2\lambda x$, so the constraint gives $x=\pm R a/\|a\|_2$. Evaluate $f$ there and use Cauchy--Schwarz to verify the global maximum and minimum. Treat $a=0$ separately as the constant objective.

items.title: Two constraints on a sphere-plane circle, where one multiplier solution is only a local maximum
items.strategy: Check that $DG$ has rank two everywhere on the circle, substitute $s=x+y$ to reduce the objective to $(s^2+2s-1)/2$ with $-\sqrt2\le s\le\sqrt2$, read off the global extrema by two elementary inequalities, use $\|p-P_4\|_2^2=2+\sqrt2 s$ to turn the $s$-range near the left end into an explicit ball, and show the fourth multiplier solution is a strict local maximum that is not global.

items.title: FALSE: every level set of a smooth map is locally a graph
items.strategy: Inline the source-backed cone witness rather than depending on the AI-generated counterexample item: for $F(x,y,z)=x^2+y^2-z^2$, compute $DF(0)=0$ and identify $F^{-1}(0)$ as the double cone. If it were a $C^1$ graph over any plane near the apex, it would have one tangent plane there, whereas its generating rays supply incompatible tangent directions. Contrast this with the regular-level-set theorem, whose surjectivity hypothesis is exactly what is missing.

items.title: FALSE: a critical value must have a singular level set
items.strategy: Inline the source-backed witness rather than depending on the AI-generated counterexample item. For $F(x,y)=x^2$, compute $DF(x,y)=(2x,0)$, so zero is a critical value because every point of $F^{-1}(0)$ lies on the line $x=0$ and is critical. The same level is the graph of the zero function over the $y$-axis, hence a smooth line. Thus criticality prevents the regular-value theorem from applying but does not make the underlying subset singular.

items.title: FALSE: continuity of the derivative implies constant rank
items.strategy: Use $(x,y)\mapsto(x,xy)$. Its derivative matrix has polynomial entries and is continuous, but its determinant is $x$, so its rank is one on the vertical axis and two off it. This also illustrates the correct lower-semicontinuity theorem: rank can jump upward nearby.

pages.title: Convex and Semicontinuous Functions on R^n

items.title: Convex and strictly convex functions on Euclidean convex sets
The epigraph and hypograph of a real-valued function
A function is convex exactly when its epigraph is convex
items.strategy: If the function is convex, take two epigraph points and compare the function at their convex combination with the same combination of their heights. Conversely apply convexity of the epigraph to the graph points $(x,f(x))$ and $(y,f(y))$ and read the last-coordinate inequality. Check both directions and the empty-domain convention separately.

items.title: Finite Jensen inequality for convex functions on $\mathbb R^n$
items.strategy: Induct on the positive number of weighted points. If the last weight is one, every earlier nonnegative weight is zero. Otherwise normalize the earlier weights by their positive sum, apply the induction hypothesis to their Euclidean convex combination, and then apply two-point convexity with the last point. Verify that every intermediate point remains in the convex domain and that zero weights cause no division.

items.title: Every sublevel set of a convex function is convex
items.strategy: Take two points whose function values are at most the level. Convexity keeps their segment in the domain and bounds the function at every convex combination by the same level. Include empty and singleton sublevel sets under the same definition.

items.title: Nonnegative combinations, affine precomposition, and finite pointwise maxima preserve convexity
items.strategy: For a nonnegative finite combination, multiply each convexity inequality by its coefficient and add. For affine precomposition, an affine map carries a convex combination to the matching combination of its images. For a finite maximum, each constituent at the combined point is bounded by the corresponding weighted values and hence by the same weighted combination of the two maxima; the maximum exists because the family is nonempty and finite.

items.title: A pointwise supremum of convex functions is convex wherever it is finite
items.strategy: Let a nonempty family $(f_i)_{i\in I}$ consist of real-valued convex functions on a common convex set $C$, and let $D=\{x\in C:\sup_{i\in I}f_i(x)<\infty\}$. For $x,y\in D$, $t\in[0,1]$, and every $i$, convexity bounds $f_i((1-t)x+ty)$ by $(1-t)f_i(x)+tf_i(y)$, which is at most $(1-t)\sup_j f_j(x)+t\sup_j f_j(y)$. This common finite upper bound puts the combined point in $D$; taking the supremum over $i$ gives the convexity inequality for $g(x)=\sup_i f_i(x)$. The nonempty-family hypothesis ensures each supremum defining $g$ is of a nonempty bounded-above set, and the empty-domain and singleton-family cases are explicit.

items.title: A convex function is bounded above and below on a smaller interior cube
items.strategy: Choose a closed cube centred at the interior point and contained in the domain. Express every point of the cube as a convex combination of its vertices and apply finite Jensen to bound the function above by the largest vertex value. For a point in the half-sized cube, reflect it through the centre to a point of the full cube; convexity at the midpoint converts the upper bounds at the reflected point and centre into a lower bound. State all constants explicitly and handle dimension one without a separate argument.

items.title: A convex function on an open convex set is locally Lipschitz
items.strategy: Fix a point and choose a full sup-norm cube whose closure lies in the domain. Apply the cube-bound lemma and use its half-sized cube as an outer Lipschitz cube, where a uniform absolute bound $M$ is available; choose a still smaller concentric cube for the two test points. For distinct $x,y$ there, extend the ray from $x$ through $y$ to the boundary of the outer cube. The convexity inequality on that segment bounds the secant slope by a constant depending only on $M$ and the cube radii. Reverse $x,y$ and translate the sup-norm estimate to the Euclidean norm.

items.title: A convex function on an open convex set is continuous
items.strategy: At each point the local Lipschitz theorem supplies a neighbourhood and a Lipschitz constant. Lipschitz maps are continuous on that neighbourhood, so the function is continuous at the point. Since the point is arbitrary, it is continuous on the open domain; the empty domain is vacuous.

items.title: Supporting and strictly separating hyperplanes in Euclidean space
Every point has a unique nearest point in a nonempty closed Euclidean convex set
items.strategy: Choose one point of the set to obtain a finite comparison radius. Any minimizer must lie in the intersection with the corresponding closed ball, which is nonempty and compact by Heine--Borel; the continuous distance function attains its minimum there. If two distinct minimizers existed, their midpoint would lie in the convex set and the parallelogram identity would make it strictly closer. Treat a point already in the set and singleton sets explicitly.

items.title: Metric projection onto a closed convex set satisfies the variational inequality
items.strategy: Let $p$ be the nearest point to $x$ and compare it with $p+t(z-p)$ for $0<t\le1$. Expanding the squared distance and using minimality gives $2\langle x-p,z-p\rangle\le t\|z-p\|^2$. Let $t$ tend to zero to obtain $\langle x-p,z-p\rangle\le0$. Conversely this inequality makes the squared distance to every $z$ at least the squared distance to $p$, so it also characterizes the projection.

items.title: A point outside a nonempty closed convex set is strictly separated from it
items.strategy: Let $p$ be the projection of the exterior point $x$ and use normal $x-p$. The variational inequality gives $\langle x-p,z\rangle\le\langle x-p,p\rangle$ for every $z$ in the set, while evaluating at $x$ raises the value by $\|x-p\|^2>0$. The normal is nonzero because the set is closed and $x$ lies outside it.

items.title: A convex set and its closure have the same interior and boundary
items.strategy: For $n\ge1$ and a nonempty convex $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, first show that $\overline C$ is convex by taking convergent sequences from $C$. Fix $c_0\in C$, put $W=\operatorname{span}(C-c_0)$ and $A=c_0+W$, and define relative interior using Euclidean balls inside $A$. A finite basis of $W$ identifies it with $\mathbb R^d$; the pullback of the Euclidean norm is a norm, so finite-dimensional norm equivalence and Euclidean completeness show that $W$, hence $A$, is closed. Thus $C$ and $\overline C$ have the same affine hull. Basis extraction from $C-c_0$ gives a simplex in $C$ whose positive barycentric core contains a relative ball, so $\operatorname{ri}C$ is nonempty. Prove the line-segment principle directly: if $p\in\operatorname{ri}C$ and $y\in\overline C$, then every point of $[p,y)$ has a relative ball in $C$, using a sequence from $C$ converging to $y$ and the fixed relative ball at $p$. Every point of $\operatorname{ri}(\overline C)$ lies strictly between such a $p$ and a point of $\overline C$ obtained by extending the segment within a relative ball, so $\operatorname{ri}(\overline C)=\operatorname{ri}C$. If $W=\mathbb R^n$, relative and ordinary interiors agree; if $W$ is proper, choose $v\notin W$ and use arbitrarily small nonzero multiples of $v$ to show that every ambient ball about $A$ leaves $A$, so both ordinary interiors are empty. Closure idempotence and $\partial C=\overline C\setminus\operatorname{int}C$ then give equal ordinary interiors and boundaries. Treat $d=0$, $n=1$, singleton sets, and proper affine hulls explicitly.

items.title: Every boundary point belonging to a nonempty Euclidean convex set has a supporting hyperplane
items.strategy: Use the preceding convex-closure lemma to replace the set by its closed convex closure without changing the given boundary point. The boundary definition then supplies points outside that closure tending to the boundary point. Strictly separate each exterior point and normalize its projection normal. Compactness of the unit sphere gives a convergent subsequence of normals. Pass the separation inequalities to the limit to obtain a nonzero unit normal supporting the closure at the boundary point, hence supporting the original set. The same argument includes convex sets with empty interior.

items.title: Disjoint nonempty Euclidean convex sets have a separating hyperplane
items.strategy: For disjoint convex sets $C,D$, the difference set $E=C-D$ is convex and omits zero. If zero lies outside the closure of $E$, strictly separate zero from that closed convex set. If zero lies in the closure of $E$, then it is a boundary point of $E$ because it is not in $E$, so take a supporting hyperplane to $E$ at zero. In either case obtain a nonzero vector $a$ with $\langle a,c-d\rangle\le0$ for all $c\in C,d\in D$, equivalently $\langle a,c\rangle\le\langle a,d\rangle$.

items.title: Subgradients and the subdifferential of a convex function
A convex function has a subgradient at every interior point of its domain
items.strategy: Continuity on the open convex interior makes the epigraph over a small closed ball a closed convex set. Apply the supporting-hyperplane theorem at $(a,f(a))$. Because $a$ is interior, the supporting normal cannot be vertical; normalize its last coordinate to $-1$ to obtain a local subgradient inequality. For an arbitrary domain point $y$, place a small point $a+t(y-a)$ inside the ball, apply the local inequality there, and divide by $t>0$ to extend the same subgradient inequality to $y$.

items.title: Differentiable convex functions are characterized by the gradient inequality
items.strategy: For the forward direction apply convexity to $x+t(y-x)$, divide the chord inequality by $t>0$, and let $t$ decrease to zero; total differentiability identifies the limit with $\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle$. Conversely apply the assumed inequality at the intermediate point $z=(1-t)x+ty$ once toward $x$ and once toward $y$; multiply by $1-t$ and $t$, add, and cancel the gradient terms to obtain convexity. Keep both directions and $t=0,1$ explicit.

items.title: The subdifferential of a differentiable convex function is its gradient singleton
items.strategy: The gradient inequality places $\nabla f(a)$ in the subdifferential. If $v$ is any subgradient, apply its inequality and the differentiability expansion to $a+te_i$ for positive and negative $t$ small enough to remain in the open domain. Dividing by $t$ and taking both one-sided limits gives $v_i=\partial_i f(a)$ for every coordinate.

items.title: Zero is a subgradient exactly at a global minimum
items.strategy: Substituting the zero vector into the subgradient inequality gives $f(y)\ge f(a)$ for every domain point, so $a$ is a global minimizer. Conversely the global-minimum inequality is exactly the subgradient inequality with zero. This is an equivalence and both directions are written separately.

items.title: A $C^2$ function is convex exactly when its Hessian is positive semidefinite
items.strategy: Restrict $f$ to every affine line segment in the open convex domain and differentiate twice by the total chain rule, obtaining $\phi''(t)=\langle H_f(x+tv)v,v\rangle$. If $f$ is convex, every restriction is convex and the one-variable second-derivative criterion makes this quantity nonnegative. Conversely positive semidefiniteness makes every line restriction convex, which is exactly the two-point convexity inequality. Check both directions and nonzero as well as zero directions.

items.title: An everywhere-positive-definite Hessian implies strict convexity
items.strategy: For distinct $x,y$, the direction $v=y-x$ is nonzero. Along the segment the second derivative is $\langle H_f(x+tv)v,v\rangle>0$, so the first derivative is strictly increasing. The one-variable secant-slope argument then makes the chord inequality strict for every $0<t<1$. Endpoints are excluded exactly as strict convexity requires.

items.title: Every local minimum of a convex function on an open Euclidean convex set is global
items.strategy: If $a$ is a local minimum but some $y$ has smaller value, choose a sufficiently small positive $t$ so that $(1-t)a+ty$ lies in the local-minimum neighbourhood. Convexity makes its value strictly below $f(a)$, a contradiction. If $y=a$ or the domain is a singleton the conclusion is immediate.

items.title: A strictly convex function on a Euclidean convex set has at most one global minimizer
items.strategy: If distinct points were both minimizers, their midpoint would be in the domain and strict convexity would give it a value below the minimum. The argument asserts uniqueness only and does not assert existence; empty and singleton domains satisfy it vacuously.

items.title: Upper and lower semicontinuity on subsets of $\mathbb R^n$
Euclidean semicontinuity agrees with the published real-line definition
items.strategy: Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$, a Euclidean ball about $c$ of radius $\delta$ is exactly the real neighbourhood $N_\delta(c)$. Substitute this identity into the upper and lower epsilon--delta clauses. The definitions then agree at every point and hence on every subset, in both directions.

items.title: Semicontinuity on $\mathbb R^n$ is characterized by strict open level sets and weak closed level sets
items.strategy: For upper semicontinuity, prove that every strict sublevel set is relatively open by applying the definition with gap $\alpha-f(c)$; conversely use relative openness of the sublevel at $\alpha=f(c)+\varepsilon$. Take complements to obtain closed superlevel sets. Apply the result to $-f$ to get the lower-semicontinuous strict superlevel and closed sublevel forms. Include both directions of all four equivalences and the empty-domain case.

items.title: Lower semicontinuity is equivalent to a closed epigraph and upper semicontinuity to a closed hypograph
items.strategy: Assume countable choice. If $f$ is lower semicontinuous and $(x,t)$ lies below its epigraph, choose a level strictly between $t$ and $f(x)$; the open strict superlevel neighbourhood in the first coordinates and a short vertical interval form an open product neighbourhood disjoint from the epigraph. Conversely, failure at $x$ puts $x$ in the closure of one fixed bad sublevel set; the metric sequential-closure theorem then supplies a sequence $x_j\to x$ with $f(x_j)\le f(x)-\varepsilon$. The horizontal points $(x_j,f(x)-\varepsilon)$ lie in the epigraph and converge to $(x,f(x)-\varepsilon)$ outside it, contradicting closedness. Apply the argument to $-f$ for the hypograph. State relative closedness in $A\times\mathbb R$ when $A$ is not closed.

items.title: Semicontinuous extreme value theorem on compact Euclidean sets
items.strategy: For lower semicontinuous $f$ on nonempty compact $K$, the open sets $\{f>-N\}$ for positive natural $N$ cover $K$; a finite subcover gives a lower bound. Let $m=\inf f[K]$. The nonempty closed sets $K\cap\{f\le m+1/N\}$ have the finite intersection property, so compactness gives a common point where $f=m$. Apply the result to $-f$ for the upper-semicontinuous maximum. This avoids selecting a minimizing sequence and uses no choice principle.

pages.title: Convex and Semicontinuous Functions on R^n: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The Euclidean norm and its square are convex, with a ball of subgradients at zero for the norm
items.strategy: The triangle inequality and homogeneity prove convexity of $x\mapsto\|x\|_2$. Cauchy--Schwarz shows that its subdifferential at zero is exactly the closed unit ball. For $x\mapsto\|x\|_2^2$, compute gradient $2x$ and Hessian $2I$. The Hessian criterion gives convexity, the positive-definite-Hessian corollary gives strict convexity, and the differentiable-subdifferential theorem gives the singleton $\{2x\}$.

items.title: A finite maximum of affine functions and its active subgradients
items.strategy: For $f(x)=\max_{1\le j\le m}(\langle a_j,x\rangle+b_j)$, the operations proposition proves convexity. Show that every convex combination of the active slopes at $x$ is a subgradient by weighting their affine inequalities. Conversely separate a vector outside those finite convex combinations and move a short distance in the separating direction to contradict the subgradient inequality. Work out $\max\{x_1,-x_1,x_2,-x_2\}$ at the origin explicitly.

items.title: A convex function on $[0,1]$ that is discontinuous at the boundary
items.strategy: Set $f(0)=1$ and $f(x)=0$ for $0<x\le1$. Check the convexity inequality by separating the cases in which a convex combination equals zero; otherwise the left side is zero and the right side is nonnegative. The right-hand limit at zero is zero, not $f(0)=1$. This is the textbook boundary-jump construction and does not contradict interior continuity.

items.title: $x\mapsto-\sqrt{1-\|x\|_2^2}$ has empty subdifferential on the unit-sphere boundary
items.strategy: For $x$ in the closed unit ball put $s_x=\sqrt{1-\|x\|_2^2}$. Given $x,y$ and $0\le t\le1$, the lifted vectors $(x,s_x)$ and $(y,s_y)$ have unit Euclidean norm in one higher dimension. The triangle inequality makes their convex combination have norm at most one, so its nonnegative last coordinate is at most $s_{(1-t)x+ty}$. Negating gives convexity of $x\mapsto-s_x$ on the whole closed ball, including its boundary. Fix a boundary point and suppose a finite vector were a subgradient. Test the subgradient inequality on the radial points $\alpha x$ as $\alpha$ tends to one from below; after division it forces the radial component of the putative subgradient to dominate $\sqrt{(1+\alpha)/(1-\alpha)}$ for every $\alpha<1$, impossible. This shows why the interior hypothesis in subgradient existence is sharp.

items.title: A lower semicontinuous function on $[0,1]$ with no maximum
items.strategy: Put $g(0)=-1$ and $g(x)=-x$ for $0<x\le1$. Verify lower semicontinuity directly from the strict-superlevel or weak-sublevel characterization, treating the exceptional point zero separately. The values have supremum zero but are all negative, so no maximum is attained, while the minimum -1 is attained as the lower-semicontinuous extreme-value theorem requires.

items.title: Characteristic functions of open and closed sets are one-sided semicontinuous
items.strategy: For a subset $E$ of a Euclidean space, use the level-set characterisation on $1_E$. If $E$ is open, every strict superlevel is empty, $E$, or the whole space, so $1_E$ is lower semicontinuous. If $E$ is closed, every strict sublevel is empty, the complement of $E$, or the whole space, so $1_E$ is upper semicontinuous. Taking a set that is closed but not open, such as $E=\{0\}$ in $[0,1]$, shows that one-sided semicontinuity need not give continuity.

items.title: A positive-semidefinite Hessian need not give strict convexity
items.strategy: On $\mathbb R^2$ take $f(x,y)=x^2$. Its Hessian is $\operatorname{diag}(2,0)$, hence positive semidefinite everywhere, and the Hessian criterion makes $f$ convex. Along every vertical line the function is constant, so the strict convexity inequality is an equality for distinct points on that line.

items.title: A strictly convex function can have a singular Hessian
items.strategy: For $f(x)=\sum_{j<n}x_j^4$ on $\mathbb R^n$ with $n\ge1$, the one-variable fourth power is strictly convex, and for distinct vectors at least one coordinate gives a strict inequality while the others give weak inequalities. The Hessian is diagonal with entries $12x_j^2$ and is the zero matrix at the origin, so it is not positive definite there.

items.title: FALSE: a convex function on a convex set is continuous
items.strategy: Use the boundary-jump counterexample on $[0,1]$. It is convex but discontinuous at zero, showing that openness of the domain, or restriction to its interior, is essential in the continuity theorem.

items.title: FALSE: every convex function is differentiable
items.strategy: Use the Euclidean norm at the origin. Its subdifferential is the whole closed unit ball rather than a singleton; direct opposite directional quotients also show that no total derivative exists there.

items.title: FALSE: semicontinuity implies continuity on a compact set
items.strategy: On the compact interval $[0,1]$, the characteristic function of the closed set $\{0\}$ is upper semicontinuous and discontinuous at zero; its negative is lower semicontinuous and also discontinuous there. Thus either one-sided notion fails to imply continuity even under compactness.

items.title: FALSE: a positive-semidefinite Hessian gives strict convexity
items.strategy: Use $f(x,y)=x^2$. Its Hessian is positive semidefinite, but distinct points on one vertical line have equal function values and give equality in the convexity inequality.

items.title: FALSE: strict convexity gives a positive-definite Hessian
items.strategy: Use the strictly convex sum of fourth powers. Its Hessian vanishes at the origin, so strict convexity does not force pointwise positive definiteness. This is the converse actually addressed by the design's proposed fourth-power witness.

pages.title: Areas of Elementary Plane Figures

items.title: Translation of a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$
Jordan inner content, outer content, measurability, and content are translation invariant
items.strategy: Translate every finite rectangular inner packing and outer cover by the same vector. Coordinate side lengths are unchanged, and translation is bijective, so taking the two suprema and infima in both directions gives equality. The empty set and degenerate rectangles remain harmless.

items.title: Riemann area between continuous graphs equals Jordan content
items.strategy: Apply the published Jordan--Fubini theorem for a region between continuous graphs to the constant-one integrand. The inner integral is the graph difference, so its one-variable integral is exactly the published graph-area convention. Include coincident graphs and endpoint sections.

items.title: A closed disc of radius $r\ge0$ has Jordan content $\pi r^2$
items.strategy: For $r>0$, the disc is the region between the two continuous semicircle graphs. Use the agreement proposition to identify its Jordan content with its published Riemann graph area, then substitute $\pi r^2$. At $r=0$, cover the singleton by arbitrarily small squares and obtain content zero directly.

items.title: FALSE: every bounded plane set has Jordan area
items.strategy: Take $E=(\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1])^2$. It is bounded because it lies in the unit square. Density of the rationals and irrationals gives $\partial E=[0,1]^2$. The unit square has inner and outer content $1$ directly from the rectangular definitions, so this boundary is not content zero; the boundary criterion makes $E$ non-Jordan-measurable. Cross-link the published counterexample carrying the same witness in the Remark, not in `deps`, because its home is an examples page and examples pages are dependency leaves.

items.title: Parallelograms and triangles in $\mathbb{R}^2$
Base and perpendicular height for a chosen side of a plane figure
$\lVert v\rVert_2\,d(w,\mathbb{R}v)=|\det[v\ w]|$ for $v\ne0$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$
items.strategy: Project $w$ orthogonally onto the line $\mathbb{R}v$, so the distance is the norm of the residual. The projection formula gives its squared norm. Expanding the two-by-two Leibniz determinant shows that $\det[v\ w]^2=\lVert v\rVert_2^2\lVert w\rVert_2^2-\langle v,w\rangle^2$; compare the two identities and take nonnegative square roots. This also proves attainment.

items.title: A parallelogram has Jordan content $|\det[v\ w]|$, equal to base times height when $v\ne0$
items.strategy: Specialize the published parallelepiped-content theorem to two columns. For a nonzero chosen base vector, apply the determinant--height identity. Retain the singular case, where the determinant and content are zero, without calling the height formula at a zero base.

items.title: A triangle has content $\tfrac12|\det[B-A\ C-A]|$, equal to half base times height when the chosen side is nonzero
items.strategy: First use the graph-area agreement and an elementary antiderivative to compute the standard right triangle's Jordan content as $1/2$. Translate the given triangle so that $A$ is the origin and realize it as the linear image of that standard triangle. Translation invariance and linear content scaling give half the absolute determinant, including the singular case. When $A\ne B$, the determinant--height identity gives the base--height form.

items.title: A triangle has zero Jordan content if and only if its vertices are collinear
items.strategy: Use the triangle formula. Expand the two-by-two determinant directly: if the first displacement is zero the vertices are already collinear; otherwise divide by one of its nonzero coordinates to show determinant zero exactly when the second displacement is a scalar multiple of the first. This is precisely collinearity, including repeated vertices.

items.title: Simple polygonal regions, diagonals, and triangulations
Every simple polygon admits a triangulation
items.strategy: Choose a generic projection direction with distinct vertex coordinates. Between consecutive vertex levels, the polygon is a finite union of bands between noncrossing affine boundary graphs. Close and commonly refine those trapezoidal cells, then split every quadrilateral into two triangles to obtain a finite face-to-face triangulation; subdivision vertices are allowed.

items.title: A simple polygon is Jordan measurable and its content is the sum of the contents of its triangles
items.strategy: Choose a triangulation. Every triangle is Jordan measurable by the triangle formula; distinct triangles meet only along edges and vertices, which have content zero. Repeated finite additivity therefore makes the polygon Jordan measurable and sums the triangle contents. Independence of the triangulation follows because both sums equal the polygon's content.

items.title: The shoelace formula for the area of a counterclockwise simple polygon
items.strategy: For an oriented triangulation, write each triangle's signed determinant area relative to the origin. Contributions from every internal diagonal cancel in opposite orientations, while the boundary edges remain in cyclic order. The resulting signed sum is nonnegative for counterclockwise orientation and equals the polygon's Jordan content.

pages.title: Areas of Elementary Plane Figures: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: One triangle computed by both the determinant and base--height formulas
items.strategy: Use $A=(1,1)$, $B=(5,1)$, and $C=(3,4)$. The determinant has absolute value $12$, while the horizontal base has length $4$ and perpendicular height $3$; both formulas give content $6$.

items.title: The content of a parallelogram from a two-by-two matrix
items.strategy: Take spanning vectors $(3,1)$ and $(1,3)$. Their determinant is $8$, so the parallelogram has content $8$; independently compute the projection height and check that base times height gives the same value.

items.title: Three collinear vertices give a triangle of zero content
items.strategy: Use $A=(0,0)$, $B=(2,1)$, and $C=(6,3)$. The second displacement is three times the first, so the determinant, perpendicular height, and Jordan content are all zero.

items.title: The unit disc has Jordan content $\pi$
items.strategy: Apply the disc reconciliation corollary at radius one and identify the same value through the vertically simple graph description. This records explicitly that the graph-area and Jordan-content conventions agree on the unit disc.

items.title: An irregular pentagon computed by triangulation and the shoelace formula
items.strategy: Use the counterclockwise vertices $(0,0),(4,0),(5,2),(2,4),(0,3)$. Triangulate from the first vertex, sum the three determinant areas, and independently evaluate the cyclic shoelace sum; both give $15$. Check that the chosen diagonals remain inside the polygon.

items.title: A linear bijection need not preserve Jordan content
items.strategy: Map the unit square by $(x,y)\mapsto(2x,y)$. This is a bijective linear map, but the image rectangle has content $2$ while the source has content $1$, exactly as the determinant-scaling theorem predicts.

pages.title: Volumes of Elementary Solids and Solids of Revolution

items.title: A solid between continuous graphs over a compact Jordan base
Solids of revolution about a coordinate axis
The product of a content-zero set and a compact interval has content zero
items.strategy: Given a finite rectangle cover of the bounded content-zero set with total base volume below an assigned tolerance, take products with the interval. Product volumes multiply by the interval length, so choosing the base tolerance relative to that length gives the required cover. Treat the empty set, a degenerate interval, and zero length before dividing by any length.

items.title: The graph of a continuous function on a compact Euclidean set has content zero
items.strategy: Place the compact domain in a fixed bounding cube and use uniform continuity. Partition the cube into small coordinate cells. Above every cell meeting the domain, the graph lies in a vertical stack whose height is the oscillation of the function plus two mesh widths. The number of base cells times their base volume stays bounded by the bounding-cube volume, so the total covering volume tends to zero with the modulus of continuity and the mesh. This extends the published rectangle-domain theorem without assuming that the compact domain is Jordan measurable.

items.title: The boundary of a solid between continuous graphs over a compact Jordan base has content zero
items.strategy: Bound both graph functions on the compact base. Show that the boundary of the solid is contained in the two graphs together with the product of the base boundary and one bounding vertical interval. The two graphs have content zero by the compact-domain graph theorem; the base boundary has content zero by the Jordan boundary criterion, so its product with the interval is null by the product lemma. A finite union and every subset of a null set are null.

items.title: A solid between continuous graphs over a compact Jordan base is Jordan measurable and integrates by vertical sections
items.strategy: The defining inequalities make the solid closed, and compactness of the base plus boundedness of the graph functions makes it bounded; Heine--Borel therefore gives compactness. The boundary lemma and the Jordan boundary criterion give Jordan measurability. A continuous integrand is integrable on that compact Jordan set, every vertical section is the interval between the two graph values, and Jordan--Fubini gives the displayed iterated formula. Explicitly allow coincident graphs, an empty base, and degenerate vertical sections.

items.title: The volume under a nonnegative continuous graph over a compact Jordan base is its integral
items.strategy: In the solid theorem take the lower graph to be zero, the upper graph to be the nonnegative function, and the integrand to be one. The inner integral is the height of the section. Include the empty base and the identically-zero graph.

items.title: The disc formula for the volume of a solid of revolution
items.strategy: For a nonnegative continuous profile on a compact interval, first view the planar region between its positive and negative graphs as a compact Jordan base. The rotated solid is the region between the two continuous square-root graphs over that base, so the general solid theorem makes it compact Jordan. Its section perpendicular to the axis is a closed disc of radius equal to the profile value. Cavalieri and the published Jordan disc-area formula give the sectional area $\pi f(x)^2$ and hence the volume formula.

items.title: The washer formula for a solid of revolution between two nonnegative profiles
items.strategy: For continuous $0\le g\le f$, each axial section is the closed disc of radius $f(x)$ with the open disc of radius $g(x)$ removed. Its Jordan content is $\pi(f(x)^2-g(x)^2)$ because the shared boundary circle has content zero. Establish compact Jordan measurability from the same square-root graph construction as the disc theorem, then apply Cavalieri. Treat $f=g$, $g=0$, and both coordinate-axis orientations.

items.title: A right circular cylinder of radius $R$ and height $h$ has volume $\pi R^2h$
items.strategy: Apply the disc formula to the constant profile $R$ on an interval of length $h$. Separate $R=0$ or $h=0$ before the positive-parameter computation.

items.title: A right circular cone of radius $R$ and height $h$ has volume $\pi R^2h/3$
items.strategy: For $h>0$, apply the disc formula to the linear profile $f(x)=Rx/h$ on $[0,h]$ and evaluate the resulting quadratic integral from its polynomial primitive. Handle $R=0$ separately and do not divide by a zero height.

items.title: A closed three-dimensional ball of radius $r\ge0$ has volume $4\pi r^3/3$
items.strategy: For $r>0$, regard the ball as the solid of revolution with profile $\sqrt{r^2-x^2}$ on $[-r,r]$. The disc formula reduces its volume to $\pi\int_{-r}^r(r^2-x^2)\,dx$, and the fundamental theorem gives $4\pi r^3/3$. At $r=0$ the ball is a singleton and has content zero.

items.title: The volume of a three-ball by Cavalieri's cylinder-minus-cones proof
items.strategy: State the same $4\pi r^3/3$ conclusion as the disc proof but use a genuinely different route. At every height $z\in[-r,r]$, the ball section has area $\pi(r^2-z^2)$ by the Jordan disc formula. The section of a radius-$r$, height-$2r$ cylinder after removing the two cones with common vertex at the centre has the same area. Finite additivity computes the comparison solid from the proved cylinder and cone volumes, and Cavalieri equates it with the ball. Handle $r=0$ and cross-reference the disc proof only in an authored Remark, not as a logical dependency.

items.title: The cylindrical-shell formula for a solid of revolution about the $y$-axis
items.strategy: Let $0\le a\le b$ and let the nonnegative profile be continuous on $[a,b]$. View the rotated solid as the region under the radial height function over the compact annulus; the main solid theorem gives Jordan measurability and volume as an integral over that annulus. Separate $a=b$ before using nondegenerate partitions. For $a<b$, use finite Jordan-cover bounds on radial subannuli, whose contents are differences of disc contents. Uniform continuity makes the upper-minus-lower sum tend to zero, while either tagged sum differs negligibly from the Riemann sum for $2\pi x f(x)$. Include $a=0$ and zeros of $f$.

items.title: Closed Euclidean balls are Jordan measurable and their volumes satisfy the slicing recursion
items.strategy: For $n=1$ the radius-$r$ ball is $[-r,r]$ and has content $2r$. Induct on $n$. The $n$-ball is the solid between the graphs $\pm\sqrt{r^2-\|u\|_2^2}$ over the $(n-1)$-ball, so the main theorem gives compactness and Jordan measurability. Slicing instead by the last coordinate, the section at $t$ is an $(n-1)$-ball of radius $\sqrt{r^2-t^2}$. Apply the published determinant-scaling theorem to the scalar dilation of the unit $(n-1)$-ball, then Cavalieri, to obtain $V_n(r)=V_{n-1}(1)\int_{-r}^{r}(r^2-t^2)^{(n-1)/2}\,dt$. Treat $r=0$, $n=1$, endpoints $t=\pm r$, and the zero-radius sections.

pages.title: Volumes of Elementary Solids and Solids of Revolution: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: A radius-$2$, height-$3$ cylinder and cone have volumes $12\pi$ and $4\pi$
items.strategy: Substitute $R=2$ and $h=3$ into the proved cylinder and cone formulas and check that the cone occupies one third of the corresponding cylinder volume.

items.title: A torus with major radius $R$ and minor radius $r$ has volume $2\pi^2Rr^2$
items.strategy: Assume $R>r>0$ and rotate the disc $(x-R)^2+y^2\le r^2$ about the $y$-axis. At height $y$, the outer and inner radii are $R\pm\sqrt{r^2-y^2}$, so the washer area is $4\pi R\sqrt{r^2-y^2}$. Integrate from $-r$ to $r$ and use the established disc-area integral to obtain $2\pi^2Rr^2$. Verify that $R>r$ prevents the inner radius from changing sign.

items.title: The shell and washer methods both give $8\pi/3$ for a rotated parabolic cap
items.strategy: Use the source region $0\le x\le2$, $(x-1)^2\le y\le1$, revolved about the $y$-axis. The shell formula gives $2\pi\int_0^2x(1-(x-1)^2)\,dx=8\pi/3$. Horizontal washers have radii $1\pm\sqrt y$ and give $\int_0^1 4\pi\sqrt y\,dy=8\pi/3$. Evaluate both proper integrals and compare.

items.title: Gabriel's horn has finite improper volume $\pi$
items.strategy: For each $R>1$, apply the disc formula to the profile $f(x)=1/x$ on $[1,R]$, obtaining $\pi\int_1^R x^{-2}\,dx=\pi(1-1/R)$. Let $R$ tend to infinity using the definition of an improper integral. State only the finite-volume half here; the infinite lateral-surface conclusion belongs to `regular-surfaces-and-surface-integrals`, where the surface-area formula is developed.

items.title: Slicing gives the unit-ball volumes through dimension five
items.strategy: Start from $V_1(1)=2$ and apply the slicing recursion successively. Evaluate the required integrals of $(1-t^2)^{1/2}$, $1-t^2$, $(1-t^2)^{3/2}$, and $(1-t^2)^2$ by the disc-area formula, elementary polynomial primitives, and the Wallis-integral recurrence. Obtain $2,\pi,4\pi/3,\pi^2/2,8\pi^2/15$ without using the later Gamma closed form.

items.title: A compact subset of $\mathbb R^3$ need not be Jordan measurable
items.strategy: Let $S$ be the Smith--Volterra--Cantor set and take $E=S\times[0,1]^2$. It is closed and bounded, hence compact, and has empty interior, so it equals its boundary. For any finite box cover, partition the last two coordinates at every box endpoint. At an interior point of each resulting planar cell, the active boxes project to an interval cover of $S$ and therefore have total first-coordinate width at least $1/2$. Multiply by the cell area and sum to obtain a positive lower bound for the covering volume. Thus the boundary is not content zero and $E$ is not Jordan measurable.

items.title: FALSE: every compact subset of $\mathbb R^3$ has Jordan volume
items.strategy: Invoke the preceding Smith--Volterra--Cantor product. It is a compact subset of three-space and is not Jordan measurable, so Jordan volume is undefined for this set.

items.title: FALSE: solids with equal parallel cross-sectional areas are congruent
items.strategy: Compare the boxes $[0,1]^3$ and $[0,2]\times[0,1/2]\times[0,1]$. Every horizontal section has area one, so Cavalieri gives equal volume. Their diameters are respectively $\sqrt3$ and $\sqrt{21}/2$, which are unequal; Euclidean congruences preserve distances and hence diameter. Thus equal sections determine volume, not shape.

items.title: FALSE: one existing iterated integral guarantees multiple Riemann integrability
items.strategy: Use the published rational-versus-irrational section counterexample. Every integral in the first order exists and equals zero, but the lower and upper section-integral envelopes in the reverse direction have different integrals, so the bounded function is not multiply Riemann integrable.

pages.title: Improper and Parameter-Dependent Multiple Integrals

items.title: Compact Jordan exhaustions of open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$
Every open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ admits a compact Jordan exhaustion
items.strategy: Treat the empty set by the constant empty exhaustion and $\mathbb{R}^n$ by expanding boxes. For a proper nonempty open set, use radius and reciprocal distance-to-the-closed-complement thresholds indexed by $j+1$ to form compact cores. Recursively put the preceding Jordan set together with the next core inside a rational-grid Jordan neighborhood contained in the open set, choosing the least finite code in a fixed enumeration so no countable choice is hidden. Compactness shows every compact subset is eventually contained.

items.title: Improper multiple integrals and absolute convergence on open sets
Every Jordan exhaustion computes a nonnegative improper multiple integral
items.strategy: The compact integrals along an exhaustion increase. Their limit is bounded by the supremum over all compact Jordan subsets. Conversely, compactness places each compact Jordan subset inside one exhaustion member, so its integral is bounded by the exhaustion limit. This proves equality and independence of exhaustion, including infinite value and the empty domain.

items.title: Absolute convergence makes signed improper multiple integrals independent of exhaustion
items.strategy: Apply the nonnegative exhaustion theorem to the positive and negative parts, each bounded by the integral of the absolute value. Their exhaustion limits are finite and their difference is the integral of the signed function on each compact member. Conversely, the adopted signed definition has no conditionally convergent branch: it exists precisely when the absolute integral is finite.

items.title: Comparison and absolute comparison tests for improper multiple integrals
items.strategy: For locally integrable $0\le f\le g$, compare the proper integrals on every compact Jordan subset and take suprema. For signed $f$ with $|f|\le g$, apply the nonnegative comparison to $|f|$ and then the absolute-convergence definition. State the zero dominator and empty domain cases explicitly.

items.title: Parameter-dependent improper multiple integrals
An integrable dominator gives uniform tail control on every compact parameter set
items.strategy: Choose a compact Jordan core on which the nonnegative improper integral of the dominator leaves tail mass below $\varepsilon$. Every dominated slice then has tail integral bounded by the same number, uniformly in the parameter. Use the absolute-value estimate for differences of two slices as well.

items.title: Locally dominated parameter-dependent improper multiple integrals are continuous
items.strategy: Near a fixed parameter, choose one integrable dominator and a compact Jordan core with uniformly small tails. Uniform continuity of the integrand on the product of that core with a compact parameter neighborhood makes the core integrals continuous. Split the total difference into two tails and the compact-core difference.

items.title: Differentiation under an improper multiple integral under an integrable derivative bound
items.strategy: Assume one slice is absolutely integrable and the parameter derivative is continuous and bounded in absolute value by one integrable function on the whole open domain. The mean value theorem first makes every nearby slice absolutely integrable. On a compact core, difference quotients converge uniformly to the parameter derivative; the dominator gives uniform tail control for both the quotients and the derivative. Pass to the limit and use the continuity theorem for the derivative integral.

items.title: Changing a bounded integrand on a content-zero set does not change its Riemann integral
items.strategy: On a bounding rectangle, subtract the two zero extensions. The bounded difference vanishes off the content-zero disagreement set. Cover that set by finitely many cubes of arbitrarily small total volume and use grid control: only cells meeting the cover contribute to the Darboux gap, so the difference is integrable with integral zero. Linearity gives integrability and equality for the modified function, and interchanging the two functions gives the reverse implication. This includes changes made only on a domain seam or boundary.

items.title: The improper integral of $e^{-x^2}$ over $\mathbb{R}$ is finite and positive
items.strategy: On $|x|\ge1$, the inequality $1+x^2\le e^{x^2}$ gives $e^{-x^2}\le x^{-2}$; the rational improper $p$-test gives convergence of both tails. Continuity handles the middle interval, and a positive lower bound on a small interval proves strict positivity.

items.title: The square of the one-dimensional Gaussian integral is the plane Gaussian integral
items.strategy: On every square $[-R,R]^2$, the exponential addition law factors $e^{-(x^2+y^2)}$ into a product, and rectangular Fubini gives the square of the truncated one-dimensional integral. Let the squares exhaust the plane; nonnegative exhaustion convergence and the one-dimensional improper limit give the identity.

items.title: The plane Gaussian integral equals $\pi$ by polar coordinates
items.strategy: For $0<\varepsilon<R$, split the full closed annulus into upper and lower half-annuli. Polar coordinates are injective on the two compact parameter rectangles with angular intervals $[0,\pi]$ and $[-\pi,0]$, so change of variables evaluates both halves. Their overlap is two radial segments of content zero; the content-zero modification lemma therefore recombines the two proper integrals into $\pi(e^{-\varepsilon^2}-e^{-R^2})$ on the full annulus. Circles are finite unions of continuous graphs, so the boundary criterion and Heine--Borel make closed discs compact Jordan sets. Bound the omitted inner disc by its enclosing square and let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Finally let expanding closed discs exhaust $\mathbb{R}^2$ and apply nonnegative exhaustion independence.

items.title: The Gaussian integral $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt{\pi}$
items.strategy: Let $I$ denote the finite positive one-dimensional integral. The product lemma gives $I^2$ as the plane integral, and the polar lemma evaluates that integral as $\pi$. The uniqueness of the positive square root then gives $I=\sqrt{\pi}$.

pages.title: Improper and Parameter-Dependent Multiple Integrals: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Two iterated improper integrals over the unit square are $\pi/4$ and $-\pi/4$
items.strategy: On $(0,1)^2$ use $f(x,y)=(x^2-y^2)/(x^2+y^2)^2$. Recognize it as the $y$-derivative of $y/(x^2+y^2)$ and the negative $x$-derivative of $x/(x^2+y^2)$. The two iterated values are $\pi/4$ and $-\pi/4$. More strongly, evaluate rectangles with lower endpoints $a,b$: choosing $a/b\to0$ or $a/b\to\infty$ gives two compact Jordan exhaustions with those opposite limits, so no exhaustion-independent integral exists.

items.title: A nonnegative function can have both iterated integrals zero and no double Riemann integral
items.strategy: In the unit square let $E$ contain $(k/p,\ell/p)$ for primes $p$ and $1\le k,\ell<p$, and take $1_E$. Each horizontal and vertical section is finite, so both iterated integrals are zero. Arbitrarily fine prime grids make $E$ dense, while its countable complement is also dense; every cell therefore has oscillation one, so the double Riemann integral does not exist.

items.title: Differentiation under an improper integral can fail without uniform domination
items.strategy: Use $f(x,t)=t^3e^{-t^2x}$ on $x\ge0$. Its improper integral is $F(t)=t$, including $t=0$, so $F'(0)=1$. But $\partial_tf(x,0)=0$ for every $x$, whose improper integral is zero. Verify the two calculations directly and show that no integrable parameter-uniform bound for the derivative can hold near zero.

items.title: The scaled Gaussian integral and its parameter derivative
items.strategy: For $a>0$, substitution $u=\sqrt a,x$ and the Gaussian theorem give $F(a)=\sqrt{\pi/a}$. On a compact neighborhood of a fixed positive parameter, dominate the parameter derivative $-x^2e^{-ax^2}$ by an integrable Gaussian-polynomial tail, apply differentiation under the integral sign, and recover $F'(a)=-\sqrt\pi/(2a^{3/2})$.

pages.title: The Real Gamma and Beta Functions

items.title: Log-convex positive functions
The real Gamma function by Euler's integral
Euler's Gamma integral converges exactly for positive real parameters
items.strategy: Split the integral at one. Near zero, real-power primitives handle $s\ne0$, while at the threshold $s=0$ the logarithmic primitive and the unbounded range of $\log$ give divergence; the exponential factor stays between positive constants. At infinity, choose a natural power dominating $t^{s-1}$ and use that the exponential dominates every polynomial. This proves convergence exactly for $s>0$ and discharges the Gamma definition's well-definedness.

items.title: Euler's real Beta integral
Euler's Beta integral converges exactly for two positive parameters
items.strategy: Split at $1/2$. Near zero the factor $(1-t)^{q-1}$ is bounded above and below by positive constants, so convergence is that of $t^{p-1}$; near one use $u=1-t$ and the symmetric comparison. Real-power primitives handle nonzero exponents, while the logarithmic primitive handles the threshold cases $p=0$ and $q=0$. Lower comparisons then give convergence exactly when $p,q>0$ and divergence at either forbidden endpoint.

items.title: The real Gamma functional equation $\Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s)$
items.strategy: For $s>0$, integrate by parts on $[\varepsilon,R]$. The boundary term tends to zero at both ends, using positivity of $s$ at zero and exponential domination at infinity. Pass to the improper limits separately and compute $\Gamma(1)=1$ directly.

items.title: $\Gamma(n+1)=n!$ for every natural number $n$
items.strategy: Use $\Gamma(1)=1$ for $n=0$ and induct with the functional equation. Keep the factorial recursion and zero index explicit.

items.title: The real Gamma function is smooth and its derivatives are logarithmic moments
items.strategy: On a compact parameter interval $[a,b]\subset(0,\infty)$, dominate $|\log t|^kt^{s-1}e^{-t}$ separately near zero and infinity. At zero substitute $u=-\log t$; at infinity combine an integer-power bound with exponential decay. Repeated dominated differentiation gives $\Gamma^{(k)}(s)=\int_0^\infty(\log t)^kt^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$, including $k=0$.

items.title: The real Gamma function is strictly log-convex
items.strategy: For every $c>0$, write $c^s\Gamma(s)$ as an improper integral whose integrand is a positive exponential-affine function of $s$; strict convexity of the exponential and integration make this function strictly convex. Given two parameters, choose $c$ so the endpoint values agree. Convexity at their weighted point rearranges to strict log-convexity of Gamma.

items.title: The real Gamma function has one minimum and diverges at both ends of its domain
items.strategy: The recurrence gives $s\Gamma(s)=\Gamma(s+1)\to1$ as $s\downarrow0$. Strict convexity of $\log\Gamma$ and $\Gamma(1)=\Gamma(2)=1$ make its derivative cross zero exactly once in $(1,2)$, yielding one global minimum. Factorial values plus eventual increase give $\Gamma(s)\to\infty$ and $\Gamma(s)/s\to\infty$ at infinity.

items.title: Gautschi's inequality for the real Gamma function
items.strategy: For $x>0$ and $0\le s\le1$, apply log-convexity to $x+s$ between $x$ and $x+1$, then to $x+1$ between $x+s$ and $x+s+1$. Use the recurrence to obtain $x^{1-s}\le\Gamma(x+1)/\Gamma(x+s)\le(x+1)^{1-s}$. Check $s=0,1$ as equalities.

items.title: Log-convex solutions of the Gamma recurrence obey the Bohr--Mollerup factorial squeeze
items.strategy: For a positive normalized log-convex solution $f$ and $0<x\le1$, compare secant slopes at $n-1,n,n+x,n+1$. The recurrence evaluates integer values and expands $f(n+x)$ as a finite product times $f(x)$. Exponentiating gives factorial-product bounds whose ratio is $(n+x)/n$. Include $x=1$ and the first legal $n$.

items.title: Bohr--Mollerup characterisation of the real Gamma function
items.strategy: Gamma has the required positivity, normalization, recurrence, and log-convexity. Conversely apply the factorial squeeze to a candidate and to Gamma. On $0<x\le1$ both lie between common bounds whose quotient tends to one, so squeezing gives equality; the recurrence extends it to every positive real. Prove both directions.

items.title: Symmetry and the trigonometric form of the real Beta integral
items.strategy: The substitution $u=1-t$ gives symmetry. The substitution $t=\sin^2\theta$, first on compact interior truncations and then at both singular endpoints, gives $B(p,q)=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{2p-1}\theta\cos^{2q-1}\theta\,d\theta$.

items.title: The real Beta--Gamma identity
items.strategy: Rectangular exhaustion and proper Fubini identify $\Gamma(p)\Gamma(q)$ with the nonnegative improper first-quadrant integral. On compact truncations use $x=rt$, $y=r(1-t)$, whose absolute Jacobian is $r$. Exhaustion independence passes to $(0,\infty)\times(0,1)$, where Fubini factors the result as $\Gamma(p+q)B(p,q)$. Positivity permits division.

items.title: The elementary recurrences for the real Beta function
items.strategy: Insert the Gamma recurrence into the Beta--Gamma identity to obtain the two one-step recurrences, then add them to get $B(p,q)=B(p+1,q)+B(p,q+1)$. All denominators are positive.

items.title: $\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi$ from the Gaussian integral
items.strategy: Substitute $t=u^2$ in Euler's integral to obtain $2\int_0^\infty e^{-u^2}\,du$. Evenness makes this the full Gaussian integral, which is $\sqrt\pi$.

items.title: $\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi$ by Wallis's product
items.strategy: The recurrence gives $\Gamma(n+1/2)=((2n)!/(4^nn!))\Gamma(1/2)$. Gautschi shows $\sqrt n\,\Gamma(n+1/2)/n!\to1$, while the published Wallis consequence gives $\sqrt{\pi n}\binom{2n}{n}/4^n\to1$. Comparing the positive limits yields the half-value. Cross-reference the independent Gaussian proof.

items.title: Stirling's factorial asymptotic holds up to a positive constant
items.strategy: Compare $\log r$ with the integral of $\log t$ over $[r-1/2,r+1/2]$. The series for $\log(1+u)$ bounds the symmetric error by a constant multiple of $1/r^2$, so the error series converges. Summing and evaluating the logarithmic integral makes $\log(n!)-((n+1/2)\log n-n)$ converge. Exponentiation gives $n!\sim C\sqrt n(n/e)^n$ for some $C>0$.

items.title: Wallis's product determines the Stirling constant as $\sqrt{2\pi}$
items.strategy: Insert the up-to-constant formula into $(2n)!/(n!)^2$, giving $\binom{2n}{n}\sim(\sqrt2/C)4^n/\sqrt n$. Compare with the Wallis asymptotic $4^n/\sqrt{\pi n}$ to get $C=\sqrt{2\pi}$.

items.title: Stirling's formula for factorials
items.strategy: Combine the undetermined-constant lemma with the Wallis identification. State the ratio form for positive integers and exclude $n=0$ from its square-root denominator.

items.title: The closed form for the volume of the unit $n$-ball
items.strategy: Induct from $V_1(1)=2$. In the slicing recursion substitute $u=t^2$ to identify the integral with $B(1/2,(n+1)/2)$. The Beta--Gamma identity and $\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi$ cancel the induction factor and yield $V_n(1)=\pi^{n/2}/\Gamma(n/2+1)$.

items.title: The volume of a radius-$r$ closed $n$-ball is $\pi^{n/2}r^n/\Gamma(n/2+1)$
items.strategy: Use induction in the slicing recursion and $t=ru$ to prove $V_n(r)=r^nV_n(1)$ for $r>0$, then insert the unit formula. At $r=0$ both sides are zero.

items.title: The volume of the unit $n$-ball tends to zero with dimension
items.strategy: The closed form and Gamma recurrence give $V_{n+2}(1)/V_n(1)=2\pi/(n+2)$. Each parity subsequence is eventually bounded by a geometric sequence with ratio at most $1/2$, so both tend to zero and hence so does their interleaving.

items.title: The unit-ball volume is maximal in dimension five
items.strategy: Use $V_{n+2}/V_n=2\pi/(n+2)$ to locate the maxima of the even and odd subsequences at six and five. The finite-remainder Gregory--Leibniz formula gives $3<\pi<16/5$ from explicit odd and even partial sums. Evaluate $V_5$ and $V_6$; the upper bound gives $V_5>V_6$, so dimension five is the unique global maximum.

pages.title: The Real Gamma and Beta Functions: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Special values of the real Gamma and Beta functions
items.strategy: Use normalization, the Gamma recurrence, the half-value, and the Beta--Gamma identity to compute $\Gamma(1)=1$, $\Gamma(2)=1$, $\Gamma(3)=2$, $\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi$, $\Gamma(3/2)=\sqrt\pi/2$, $B(1,1)=1$, and $B(2,3)=1/12$.

items.title: The unit-ball volumes through dimension eight from the Gamma formula
items.strategy: Substitute $n=1,\ldots,8$ into the closed form and use the Gamma recurrence and half-value to obtain $2,\pi,4\pi/3,\pi^2/2,8\pi^2/15,\pi^3/6,16\pi^3/105,\pi^4/24$.

items.title: A positive convex function need not be log-convex
items.strategy: On $(0,\infty)$ the identity is positive and affine, hence convex. Its logarithm is not convex: at the midpoint of $1$ and $4$, $\log(5/2)>\log2=(\log1+\log4)/2$. This is the possible converse to the design's impossible request for a log-convex function that is not convex.

items.title: A positive non-log-convex solution of the Gamma functional equation
items.strategy: Put $D=	frac12(\log\Gamma(1)+\log\Gamma(3/2))-\log\Gamma(5/4)$ and $A=1+|D|$, and define $F(s)=\Gamma(s)e^{A\sin(2\pi s)}$. Periodicity gives $F(s+1)=sF(s)$ and $F(1)=1$, while $F(5/4)\ne\Gamma(5/4)$. At the midpoint $5/4$ of $1$ and $3/2$, the perturbation adds $A$ and adds zero at both endpoints; since $A>D$, the midpoint log-convexity inequality is reversed.

items.title: FALSE: normalization and the functional equation determine the real Gamma function
items.strategy: Use the preceding periodic perturbation. It has the normalization and recurrence but differs from Gamma; its failure of log-convexity identifies the missing Bohr--Mollerup hypothesis.

items.title: FALSE: Euler's real Gamma integral converges at the nonpositive integers
items.strategy: The convergence theorem says the Euler integral converges precisely for positive real parameters. At every nonpositive integer it diverges at zero. The later complex meromorphic continuation has poles there and is a different construction.

items.title: FALSE: unit-ball volume increases with dimension
items.strategy: The dimension-five maximum gives $V_6(1)<V_5(1)$ and the limit theorem gives $V_n(1)\to0$. Either fact refutes monotone increase; together they show the first failure and eventual behavior.

pages.title: Regular Surfaces and Surface Integrals

items.title: The cross product in $\mathbb R^3$
The cross product is bilinear, alternating, and orthogonal to both factors
items.strategy: Expand the coordinate definition in each argument to prove bilinearity and interchange the factors to prove alternation. A direct dot-product expansion gives the scalar-triple-product determinant identity. Substituting either factor as the third vector makes two determinant columns equal, so both dot products vanish. Keep zero vectors and parallel vectors in the same calculation.

items.title: The squared cross-product norm is the Gram determinant of two vectors
items.strategy: Expand the squared norm of the coordinate cross product and collect terms to obtain $\|u\times v\|_2^2=\|u\|_2^2\|v\|_2^2-\langle u,v\rangle^2$, which is the determinant of the two-vector Gram matrix. The published Gram-determinant criterion then makes this value positive exactly for an independent pair and zero exactly for a dependent pair. Include either vector being zero.

items.title: Regular parametrized surface patches on compact Jordan parameter regions
The tangent plane of a regular surface patch
Surface reparametrizations and their orientation sign
The tangent plane is invariant under regular reparametrization
items.strategy: For $\psi=\varphi\circ h$, the chain rule writes the two tangents of $\psi$ as linear combinations of the two tangents of $\varphi$, so the new tangent plane is contained in the old one. Apply the same argument to the inverse parameter diffeomorphism to obtain the reverse containment. The invertible derivative of $h$ prevents either pair from losing rank, and boundary points are interpreted by the continuous extensions of the tangents.

items.title: A regular reparametrization of a connected parameter region has a constant orientation sign
items.strategy: Restrict the neighbourhood diffeomorphism to the nonempty connected interior of the source parameter region. Its derivative is invertible everywhere, so the published Jacobian-sign theorem makes the determinant everywhere positive or everywhere negative. Continuity and nonvanishing on the compact region extend the same sign to its boundary. Thus every such reparametrization is exactly orientation-preserving or orientation-reversing.

items.title: The first fundamental form, Gram matrix, and area density of a surface patch
The surface area density is the norm of the cross product of the parameter tangents
items.strategy: The first fundamental matrix is the Gram matrix of the two parameter tangent vectors. Apply the two-vector cross-product identity to identify its determinant with the squared cross-product norm, then take the unique nonnegative square root. Regularity makes the common value positive in the parameter-region interior; boundary zeros remain allowed by the patch convention.

items.title: The oriented area vector transforms by the parameter Jacobian determinant
items.strategy: For $\psi=\varphi\circ h$, the total chain rule expresses the two parameter derivatives of $\psi$ as the two corresponding linear combinations of $\varphi_u$ and $\varphi_v$. Bilinearity and alternation of the cross product cancel the diagonal terms and leave $\psi_s\times\psi_t=(\det Dh)(\varphi_u\times\varphi_v)\circ h$. Taking norms gives the absolute-Jacobian transformation law for the area density, including the sign distinction.

items.title: Surface area and scalar surface integrals on a regular patch
Surface area and scalar surface integrals are invariant under regular reparametrization
items.strategy: Substitute the absolute-Jacobian density law into the scalar parameter integral for $\varphi\circ h$. The compact-Jordan change-of-variables theorem for the neighbourhood diffeomorphism $h$ turns that integral into the parameter integral for $\varphi$. This works for either orientation sign; specialize the scalar field to one for surface area. Boundary exceptions contribute nothing under the Jordan convention.

items.title: Unit normal fields, orientations, and flux through a regular surface patch
Flux is invariant under orientation-preserving reparametrization and changes sign under reversal
items.strategy: Write flux as the parameter integral of $F\circ\varphi$ dotted with the oriented area vector. The area-vector transformation supplies $\det Dh$ rather than its absolute value. Apply compact-Jordan change of variables after separating the constant determinant sign: the preserving case gives the same flux and the reversing case its negative. The orientation-sign corollary ensures these exhaust a connected parameter region.

items.title: Content-zero parameter-boundary exceptions do not affect surface integrals
items.strategy: A compact Jordan parameter region has content-zero boundary. Two bounded scalar parameter integrands that agree on the interior therefore differ only on a content-zero set, so the published modification lemma gives equivalent integrability and equal integrals. Apply the same statement to the scalar dot-product integrand for flux. This licenses seam identifications and rank failures confined to the parameter boundary, but no interior failure.

items.title: Finitely patched regular surfaces, their area, scalar integrals, and flux
Regular level surfaces have local regular parametrizations with the same tangent plane
items.strategy: Let $F:U\subseteq\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be $C^k$, let $c$ be regular, and fix $p\in F^{-1}(c)$. The earlier regular-level-set graph theorem gives a $C^k$ graph over the two-dimensional kernel of $DF(p)$. Use equality of dimension to choose a linear isomorphism from $\mathbb R^2$ to that kernel, then restrict the resulting graph chart to a small compact Jordan rectangle about the origin. It is injective and its two derivatives are independent, hence is a regular surface patch. Its tangent span is the graph derivative image, which the level-set theorem identifies with $\ker DF(p)$, exactly the published level-set tangent space. Treat an empty level set vacuously and the nonempty case pointwise.

items.title: A compact regular level surface is covered by finitely many regular surface patches
items.strategy: For every point of the compact level surface, the local-parametrization theorem supplies a patch whose relative interior contains that point. These relative interiors form an open cover in the level-set subspace. Apply the ambient-cover form of intrinsic compactness with the level set itself as the ambient metric space, and select a finite subcover. The empty level uses the empty family and a singleton level cannot occur under a surjective derivative from $\mathbb R^3$ to $\mathbb R$.

items.title: Surface area, scalar integrals, and flux over a $C^1$ graph
items.strategy: For $g$ defined near a compact Jordan region $D$, use $\varphi(x,y)=(x,y,g(x,y))$. Its tangent vectors are $(1,0,g_x)$ and $(0,1,g_y)$, whose cross product is $(-g_x,-g_y,1)$; it is never zero and points upward. Substitute its norm $\sqrt{1+\|\nabla g\|_2^2}$ in the area and scalar-integral definitions, and retain the signed cross product for the upward flux formula. The downward formula is its negative.

items.title: Scalar surface integrals on a surface of revolution
items.strategy: Let $r:[a,b]\to[0,\infty)$ be $C^1$, positive on the open interval, and parametrize the surface by $\varphi(s,t)=(s,r(s)\cos t,r(s)\sin t)$ for $0\le t\le2\pi$. The map is injective and regular in the parameter interior, with only seam identifications and possible endpoint-axis degeneracies on the boundary. Differentiate and use the Pythagorean identity to obtain density $r(s)\sqrt{1+r'(s)^2}$, then substitute it into the scalar surface-integral definition.

items.title: The surface of revolution has area $2\pi\int_a^b r(s)\sqrt{1+r'(s)^2}\,ds$
items.strategy: Set the scalar field equal to one in the surface-of-revolution integral. The density is independent of the angular parameter, so Jordan--Fubini separates the rectangle integral and the integral of the constant one over $[0,2\pi]$ contributes the factor $2\pi$. Endpoint zeros of $r$ lie on a content-zero parameter boundary and do not alter the value.

pages.title: Regular Surfaces and Surface Integrals: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Surface area and flux on a sphere, with scalar integrals on a hemisphere
items.strategy: For radius $R>0$, use spherical parameters on $[0,2\pi]\times[0,\pi]$. The map is injective and regular in the interior; the longitude seam and the two poles lie on the parameter boundary. Compute density $R^2\sin\phi$, integrate to obtain area $4\pi R^2$, and use the outward normal $x/R$ to obtain flux $4\pi R^3$ for the field $F(x)=x$. On the northern hemisphere compute $\iint z\,dS=\pi R^3$ and record the orientation sign in the corresponding flux calculation.

items.title: A closed cylinder as a finitely patched oriented surface
items.strategy: For radius $R>0$ and height $H>0$, present the boundary as its lateral patch and two polar cap patches. Their pairwise intersections are boundary circles, whose parameter preimages have content zero. Direct cross-product calculations give total area $2\pi RH+2\pi R^2$. With outward orientation and $F(x,y,z)=(x,y,0)$, the cap fluxes vanish and the side flux is $2\pi R^2H$.

items.title: The surface area of a torus is $4\pi^2ab$
items.strategy: For $a>b>0$, parametrize by $((a+b\cos\phi)\cos\theta,(a+b\cos\phi)\sin\theta,b\sin\phi)$ on the full angle rectangle. Its interior is injective, the seams lie on the boundary, and the cross-product norm is $b(a+b\cos\phi)>0$. Fubini and the full-period endpoint values make the cosine term integrate to zero, leaving $4\pi^2ab$.

items.title: Downward flux through the graph $z=xy$ over the unit square
items.strategy: Use the downward area vector $(y,x,-1)$ for the graph $z=xy$ over $[0,1]^2$. For $F(x,y,z)=(zx,z^2,xy)$ the pulled-back dot product is $x^2y^2+x^3y^2-xy$. Apply Fubini and the fundamental theorem to the polynomial terms to obtain flux $-1/18$. Reversing upward changes only the sign.

items.title: The lateral area of a right circular cone is $\pi R\sqrt{R^2+H^2}$
