items.strategy: For $R,H>0$, rotate the linear radius $r(s)=Rs/H$ for $0\le s\le H$. It is positive in the open interval and vanishes only at the apex parameter boundary. Substitute its constant derivative into the surface-of-revolution formula and evaluate the remaining linear integral to obtain $\pi R\sqrt{R^2+H^2}$, checking the apex contributes no separate term.

items.title: A degenerate two-parameter map can collapse its image to a curve
items.strategy: On the unit square take $\varphi(u,v)=(u,0,0)$. Its parameter derivatives are $(1,0,0)$ and $(0,0,0)$, so their cross product and Gram determinant vanish everywhere, while the image is a line segment. This checkable witness fails the regularity and nonempty-interior-image conclusions without relying on a picture.

items.title: Opposite parametrizations preserve area and negate flux
items.strategy: Parametrize the unit square in the horizontal plane by $\varphi(u,v)=(u,v,0)$ and compose with the coordinate swap $h(s,t)=(t,s)$. The swap has determinant $-1$. Both parametrizations give area one, while for the constant field $(0,0,1)$ their fluxes are $1$ and $-1$. This computes both reparametrization laws on the same surface.

items.title: Gabriel's horn has unbounded truncated lateral area
items.strategy: Rotate $r(x)=1/x$ on each compact interval $[1,T]$ and apply the surface-of-revolution formula. The density $(1/x)\sqrt{1+1/x^4}$ is at least $1/x$, so monotonicity bounds the truncated lateral area below by $2\pi L(T)$, where the published integral logarithm is $L(T)=\int_1^Tdt/t$. The published unboundedness of $L$ makes the truncated areas unbounded. Keep $T>1$ and never treat the noncompact horn as one compact patch.

items.title: FALSE: finite volume implies finite lateral surface area
items.strategy: Refute the implication with Gabriel's horn, obtained by rotating $r(x)=1/x$ for $x\ge1$. On every compact truncation $[1,T]$, the disc-volume theorem gives $V(T)=\pi\int_1^T x^{-2}\,dx$; the improper rational $p$-test gives the finite limit $\pi$. The surface-of-revolution formula gives $A(T)=2\pi\int_1^T x^{-1}\sqrt{1+x^{-4}}\,dx\ge2\pi\int_1^T x^{-1}\,dx$, and the same $p$-test at $p=1$ makes these lateral areas unbounded. Keep the volume and area claims as limits of compact truncations rather than treating the noncompact horn as one regular compact patch.

items.title: Schwarz lanterns can converge to a cylinder while their polyhedral areas diverge
items.strategy: On a cylinder of radius $r>0$ and height $H>0$, use $m$ horizontal bands and staggered regular $n$-gons to obtain $2mn$ congruent triangles. Compute their total area as $2rn\sin(\pi/n)\sqrt{H^2+m^2r^2(1-\cos(\pi/n))^2}$. Along $m=n^3$, the mesh diameter tends to zero, while the sine-over-angle limit and $1-\cos x=2\sin^2(x/2)$ show the square-root factor grows linearly in $n$; hence the areas diverge. Include positive $n$ and $m$ only and verify every vertex lies on the cylinder.

items.title: FALSE: surface area is the supremum of inscribed polyhedral areas
items.strategy: Apply the proposed definition to the fixed smooth cylinder. Its surface-integral area is finite, whereas the Schwarz lantern counterexample supplies inscribed triangulated polyhedra with arbitrarily small mesh and unbounded area. The supremum is therefore infinite, not the cylinder's surface area. This also shows why the arc-length supremum definition has no direct surface analogue.

items.title: FALSE: continuity alone makes the regular-patch surface-area formula applicable
items.strategy: On a closed disc use the continuous injective cone graph $\varphi(u,v)=(u,v,\sqrt{u^2+v^2})$. Along the horizontal parameter line its third component restricts to $|u|$, whose two one-sided difference quotients at zero are $1$ and $-1$. Thus an interior partial derivative does not exist and the cross-product integrand is unavailable, even though a different polar parametrization treats the cone with its apex confined to the parameter boundary.

items.title: FALSE: flux is independent of the parametrization without an orientation condition
items.strategy: Use the horizontal unit-square patch and the constant field $(0,0,1)$. Its standard parametrization has flux $1$, while swapping the two parameters reverses orientation and gives flux $-1$. The general flux theorem explains the exact distinction: preserving reparametrizations keep the value, reversing ones negate it.

pages.title: The Divergence Theorem and Classical Stokes

items.title: Divergence and curl of a $C^1$ vector field
Divergence and curl are linear and satisfy the scalar product rules
items.strategy: Both operators are finite sums of first partial derivatives of the components, so linearity is the sum and scalar rules for partial derivatives applied coordinate by coordinate. For a $C^1$ scalar $f$ expand $\partial_j(fF_i)=(\partial_jf)F_i+f\partial_jF_i$ and collect: the first group is $\langle\nabla f,F\rangle$ in the divergence and $\nabla f\times F$ in the curl, matching the coordinate formula of the cross product entry by entry, and the second group is $f$ times the operator. Check each of the three curl coordinates separately against the published coordinate definition rather than asserting the pattern.

items.title: The divergence and curl of a cross product
items.strategy: Write out the three coordinates of $F\times G$ from the published coordinate formula and differentiate each with the product rule. Collecting the six terms of $\operatorname{div}(F\times G)$ gives $\langle\operatorname{curl}F,G\rangle-\langle F,\operatorname{curl}G\rangle$. For the curl, collect the twelve terms into $(\operatorname{div}G)F-(\operatorname{div}F)G+DF\,G-DG\,F$, where $DF\,G$ is the derivative matrix applied to $G$, identified with the vector of directional derivatives by the published total-derivative theorem. Do one coordinate in full and obtain the other two by the same computation, not by a symmetry claim.

items.title: A $C^1$ field on an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ is closed exactly when its curl vanishes
items.strategy: Closedness is the system of three independent equations $\partial_jF_i=\partial_iF_j$ for $i\ne j$ in three coordinates, and the three coordinates of the curl are exactly the three differences $\partial_jF_i-\partial_iF_j$ for those index pairs. Match the pairs explicitly, noting that the diagonal equations $i=j$ are trivial and that the pair $(i,j)$ and the pair $(j,i)$ give the same equation, so the three curl coordinates exhaust the system. Both directions are the same matching read in the two directions.

items.title: The curl of the gradient of a $C^2$ function vanishes
items.strategy: For $C^2$ $\phi$ the field $\nabla\phi$ is $C^1$, so its curl is defined. Each coordinate of $\operatorname{curl}\nabla\phi$ is a difference $\partial_j\partial_i\phi-\partial_i\partial_j\phi$ of mixed second partials, which vanishes by the published Clairaut-Schwarz theorem. Do all three coordinates. Record that $C^2$ is used twice: once so that the gradient is $C^1$ and once as the hypothesis of Clairaut-Schwarz.

items.title: The divergence of the curl of a $C^2$ field vanishes
items.strategy: For $C^2$ $F$ the field $\operatorname{curl}F$ is $C^1$, so its divergence is defined. Expanding gives six second partials in three cancelling pairs, each pair equal by the published Clairaut-Schwarz theorem. Write the six terms out rather than appealing to a pattern, and record where each $C^2$ hypothesis is used.

items.title: The Laplacian of a $C^2$ function and of a $C^2$ vector field
The curl of a curl is the gradient of the divergence minus the Laplacian
items.strategy: Expand one coordinate of $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}F$ from the coordinate definition, add and subtract the missing pure second derivative in that coordinate, and use Clairaut-Schwarz to exchange the mixed partials into $\partial$ of the divergence. The remainder is the componentwise Laplacian. Carry out each of the three coordinates; the identity needs $F$ to be $C^2$ for the curl of the curl to be defined and for the exchange to be licensed.

items.title: A $C^1$ field with vanishing curl on a star-shaped open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ is conservative
items.strategy: The curl-free hypothesis is closedness by the preceding corollary, and the published star-shaped equivalence turns closedness into exactness, conservativity, path independence and the vanishing of every closed-loop integral. State all five equivalent conclusions rather than only the potential, and record that the converse direction is the curl of a gradient vanishing, which needs the potential to be $C^2$ as the published equivalence supplies.

items.title: Vector potentials of a $C^1$ field on an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$
A divergence-free $C^1$ field on a star-shaped open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ has a vector potential
items.strategy: Let $U$ be star-shaped about $a$ and set $A(x)=\int_0^1 t\,B(a+t(x-a))\times(x-a)\,dt$, the exact analogue of the published star-shaped potential formula. Differentiating under the integral sign on a compact rectangle is licensed because the integrand and its parameter derivatives are continuous. Apply the cross-product curl identity with the first factor $x\mapsto B(a+t(x-a))$ and the second factor $x\mapsto x-a$: the second has divergence $3$ and derivative the identity, and the first has divergence $t(\operatorname{div}B)(a+t(x-a))=0$, leaving $2B(z_t)+t\,DB(z_t)(x-a)$. Multiplying by $t$ makes the integrand $\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(t^2B(z_t)\bigr)$, so Newton-Leibniz in $t$ gives $\operatorname{curl}A=B(x)$ with the $t=0$ endpoint contributing zero. Check that $A$ has continuous first partials, so it is $C^1$ and its curl is defined.

items.title: The curl measures the antisymmetric part of the total derivative
items.strategy: For a $C^1$ field $F$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ and vectors $u,v$, expand $\langle DF(p)u,v\rangle-\langle DF(p)v,u\rangle$ in coordinates as $\sum_{i,j}(\partial_jF_i-\partial_iF_j)u_jv_i$. Group the three index pairs, identify each coefficient with a coordinate of $\operatorname{curl}F(p)$, and recognise the resulting bilinear expression as $\langle\operatorname{curl}F(p),u\times v\rangle$ using the coordinate formula for the cross product. Verify the identity on the three pairs of standard basis vectors as a check on signs, and note that the diagonal terms $i=j$ contribute nothing.

items.title: A $C^1$ map sends a compact set of content zero to a set of content zero
items.strategy: Let $\psi$ be $C^1$ on an open $W\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ and let $A\subseteq W$ be compact of content zero. Cover $A$ by finitely many closed cubes contained in $W$. On one such cube $Q$ the derivative norm is bounded, and applying the published mean value inequality to $t\mapsto\psi(x+t(y-x))$ along the segment joining two points of the convex set $Q$ makes $\psi$ Lipschitz on $Q$. Compose with the coordinatewise clamping retraction of $\mathbb R^m$ onto $Q$, which is $1$-Lipschitz because $r\mapsto\min\{\max\{r,\alpha\},\beta\}$ is, to obtain a Lipschitz map defined on all of $\mathbb R^m$ agreeing with $\psi$ on $Q$. The published Lipschitz-image theorem sends the null set $A\cap Q$ to a null set; a finite union of null sets is null; and the image is compact, so compactness turns null back into content zero. Treat the empty set separately.

items.title: Additivity of the integral over finitely many Jordan pieces that fill a Jordan set up to content zero
items.strategy: Let $A$ be a bounded Jordan set, let $A_1,\dots,A_N$ with $N\ge1$ be Jordan subsets of $A$ whose pairwise intersections have content zero and with $\operatorname{cont}(A\setminus\bigcup_iA_i)=0$, and let $f$ be bounded on $A$ and integrable on $A$ and on every $A_i$. Work with the zero extensions to one bounding rectangle. The difference between the sum of the extensions and the extension from $A$ is bounded by $(N+1)\sup|f|$ and vanishes off the union of the pairwise intersections with the residual set, a finite union of content-zero sets and therefore itself Jordan of content zero. Linearity and the absolute-value estimate then force that difference to integrate to zero. The case $N=1$ is the residual estimate alone, and the empty index set is excluded by $N\ge1$.

items.title: Change of variables for a $C^1$ map injective and regular only on the interior of a compact Jordan set
items.strategy: Let $\psi$ be $C^1$ on an open $W\supseteq D$ with $D$ compact Jordan, injective on $D^{\circ}$ and with nonvanishing Jacobian determinant there, and put $V=\psi[D^{\circ}]$. The inverse function theorem makes $\psi$ restricted to $D^{\circ}$ a diffeomorphism onto the open set $V$. Since $\partial(D^{\circ})\subseteq\partial D$ and $\psi[\partial D]$ has content zero by the preceding lemma, both $D^{\circ}$ and $V$ are bounded open Jordan sets. Take a compact grid exhaustion $K_1\subseteq K_2\subseteq\cdots$ of $D^{\circ}$ with vanishing content remainder and apply the published compact change-of-variables theorem on each $K_j$ with the open set $D^{\circ}$ as ambient domain. The parameter side converges because the integrand is bounded on the compact $D$ and $\operatorname{cont}(D\setminus K_j)\to0$. For the image side, apply the same exhaustion lemma to $V$ itself: each of its compact pieces lies in some $\psi[K_j]$, so $\operatorname{cont}(V\setminus\psi[K_j])\to0$ and the bounded integrand contributes vanishingly little. Handle an empty interior and a constant sign of the determinant explicitly.

items.title: A cyclic permutation of the coordinates of $\mathbb R^3$ preserves Jordan measurability and integrals
items.strategy: A cyclic permutation of coordinates is a linear bijection of $\mathbb R^3$ whose matrix has determinant $1$, so it is $C^1$ with everywhere invertible derivative and unit absolute Jacobian. The published compact change-of-variables theorem then gives measurability of the image and equality of the integrals with no scale factor. State the transport in the direction that will be used, namely that the integral of $H$ over $E$ equals the integral of $H$ composed with the inverse permutation over the permuted set, and record the determinant computation explicitly rather than asserting that a permutation matrix has determinant $1$.

items.title: Simple solid regions in a coordinate direction and their cyclic coordinate projection
Each coordinate of the oriented area vector is the Jacobian determinant of the matching cyclic projection
items.strategy: For a $C^1$ map $\varphi$ of two variables into $\mathbb R^3$ write out $\varphi_u\times\varphi_v$ from the published coordinate formula. Its $x$ coordinate is the two-by-two determinant of the derivative of $(\varphi_y,\varphi_z)$, its $y$ coordinate that of $(\varphi_z,\varphi_x)$, and its $z$ coordinate that of $(\varphi_x,\varphi_y)$. The cyclic order of the retained coordinates is what makes all three read the same way, and it is exactly the order fixed by the projection in the preceding definition; verify each of the three separately, since the middle one is the case where the naive increasing order gives the opposite sign.

items.title: The outward unit normal at a boundary point of a compact solid
Boundary presentations adapted to a simple solid region in a coordinate direction
The flux of a single-component field through a graph face is a base integral of its trace
items.strategy: Let $(D_j,\varphi_j)$ be a regular patch whose image lies in the graph of a continuous $\gamma$ over a compact Jordan base $D$ in direction $k$, and put $\psi=\pi_k\circ\varphi_j$. Injectivity of $\psi$ on $D_j^{\circ}$ is forced, not assumed: two interior parameter points with the same projection have the same image, because both images lie on the graph of a function, and the patch definition forbids that. By the projected-Jacobian lemma the hypothesis on the sign of the $k$ coordinate of the oriented area vector is exactly a sign hypothesis on $\det D\psi$ in the interior, so the degenerate-boundary change-of-variables lemma applies with $f(w)=R(w,\gamma(w))$ written in the projected coordinates. Replacing $|\det D\psi|$ by $\pm\det D\psi$ changes the integrand only on the content-zero parameter boundary. Both sign cases are stated; the vanishing of the integrand where the determinant vanishes on the boundary is what makes the two agree.

items.title: The single-direction flux identity on a simple solid region
items.strategy: Split the flux over the presentation into its three sublists. A lateral patch contributes zero because its integrand is the product of a continuous function with the $k$ coordinate of the oriented area vector, which vanishes on the parameter interior and hence, by continuity and the density of the interior in a compact Jordan parameter region, everywhere. The upper patches contribute the base integral of $R$ composed with the upper graph and the lower patches its negative, by the graph-face lemma summed with the almost-partition additivity lemma over the disjoint projected images. On the volume side, transport by the cyclic permutation lemma into the coordinate order the published solid-between-graphs Fubini formula uses, then evaluate the inner integral by the second fundamental theorem of calculus, whose integrand is continuous. Where the two graphs agree the inner integral and the increment are both zero, so that degenerate slice needs its own line.

items.title: At interior base points, the graph faces of an adapted presentation induce the outward unit normal
items.strategy: Fix an upper patch and an interior parameter point whose projection lies in the interior of the base. The projected map has invertible derivative there, so the inverse function theorem exhibits the graph function as the composite of the third patch component with the local inverse; hence the graph function is $C^1$ near that projected point and its graph has the patch's tangent plane. The induced normal is therefore a positive multiple of $(-\partial\gamma,1)$ in the projected coordinates, and moving off the surface along it changes the $k$ coordinate faster than the graph function can follow, so the forward points leave the solid. The backward points stay inside because the two graphs are strictly separated on the base interior. The lower case is the same argument with the signs reversed; the hypothesis that the projection lands in the base interior is used and is not removable.

items.title: Elementary solid regions: one boundary presentation adapted in all three coordinate directions
Every patch of an elementary solid region's presentation is a graph face in some direction, and at interior base points its normal is outward
items.strategy: A patch that is lateral for all three directions would have an induced unit normal orthogonal to each of the three standard basis vectors, hence zero, which contradicts its being a unit vector. So each patch is an upper or a lower face in at least one direction, and the preceding proposition gives outwardness at the parameter-interior points whose projection lands in that direction's base interior. State the conclusion with that qualification rather than for every boundary point; the excluded points are exactly the seams and edges.

items.title: The divergence theorem on an elementary solid region
items.strategy: Write $F$ as the sum of its three single-component fields. The same presentation is adapted in each direction, so the coordinate flux identity applies three times to the same boundary integral, and its three right-hand sides are the integrals of the three summands of the divergence. Add them with linearity of the flux sum and of the volume integral. Record that the sum of the three identities is where the requirement of one common presentation is used, and that the outward reading of the normal is the preceding corollary.

items.title: Finite gluings of elementary solid regions and their outward boundary presentation
Internal faces cancel and volume integrals add when elementary solid regions are glued
items.strategy: For the flux clause, the supplied gluing data pairs every internal patch with a patch of another piece that is an orientation-reversing reparametrization of it. The published flux reparametrization theorem negates the flux across such a pair, so each pair contributes zero and the surviving patches are the outer presentation; this is a rearrangement of a finite sum of reals and needs no connectedness. For the volume clause, each piece is a solid between continuous graphs and therefore compact and Jordan measurable, so its boundary has content zero and the pieces have pairwise disjoint interiors; the almost-partition additivity lemma then adds the piece integrals to the integral over the union, with the continuous integrand bounded on the compact union. The single-piece case has no internal pair and is included.

items.title: The divergence theorem for finite gluings of elementary solid regions
items.strategy: Apply the elementary-solid divergence theorem to each piece and sum. Both clauses of the cancellation lemma convert the two sums into the boundary flux over the outer presentation and the volume integral over the union. The field must be $C^1$ on an open set containing the whole union, since the piecewise identities are applied with that same field. State that the supplied decomposition and gluing data are part of the hypothesis and that nothing is asserted for a solid presented without them.

items.title: Vector forms: the boundary integrals of $fn$ and of $n\times F$
items.strategy: For a fixed vector $c$ apply the divergence theorem to $fc$: the product rule makes its divergence $\langle\nabla f,c\rangle$ because $c$ is constant, and the boundary integrand is $f\langle c,n\rangle$. Since the resulting identity holds for every $c$, taking $c$ over the standard basis identifies the two vector integrals coordinate by coordinate. For the second clause apply the theorem to $F\times c$, whose divergence is $\langle\operatorname{curl}F,c\rangle$ by the cross-product identity with a constant second factor, and rewrite $\langle F\times c,n\rangle$ as $\langle c,n\times F\rangle$ with the scalar triple product. Both clauses need the vector integrals to be defined coordinatewise, which is what the basis argument supplies.

items.title: The volume of a glued elementary solid is a third of the outward flux of the position field
items.strategy: The position field $p\mapsto p$ is $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3$ with divergence the constant $3$, so the divergence theorem turns its outward boundary flux into three times the integral of $1$ over the solid, which is the solid's Jordan content by the published indicator characterisation. Record the three one-coordinate variants obtained from the fields $xe_x$, $ye_y$ and $ze_z$, each with divergence $1$, and note that the solid is Jordan measurable because each glued piece is.

items.title: A field with vanishing divergence has zero outward flux through the boundary of a glued elementary solid
items.strategy: The divergence theorem turns the boundary flux into the volume integral of the zero function. State the hypothesis as it is used: the field is $C^1$ and divergence-free on an open set containing the whole solid, not merely on the boundary surface, and the companion page records what fails when only the second holds.

items.title: The flux of a curl through the boundary of a glued elementary solid vanishes
items.strategy: State the hypothesis as $F$ of class $C^2$ on an open set containing the solid, and say where $C^2$ is used: $\operatorname{curl}F$ is built from the first partial derivatives of the components of $F$, so it is $C^1$ exactly when $F$ is $C^2$, and $C^1$ is what the divergence-free corollary requires of the field it is applied to. Then $\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}F)=0$ by the degree-two identity, so $\operatorname{curl}F$ is a $C^1$ divergence-free field on that open set and the preceding corollary gives zero outward flux through the boundary presentation. Do not weaken the hypothesis to $C^1$: with $F$ only $C^1$ the divergence of $\operatorname{curl}F$ need not be defined at all, so neither the identity nor the divergence theorem applies to it.

items.title: The divergence at a point is the limit of outward flux per unit volume
items.strategy: For a sequence of glued elementary solids containing $p$, of positive volume and with diameters tending to zero, the divergence theorem writes the flux as the volume integral of the divergence. Subtract the constant $\operatorname{div}F(p)$ inside the integral and estimate by the supremum of $|\operatorname{div}F-\operatorname{div}F(p)|$ over the solid times its volume; continuity of the divergence at $p$ and the vanishing diameters send that supremum to zero. No lower bound on the volume relative to the diameter is needed because the volume cancels. Record that positive volume is required only so the quotient is defined.

items.title: Green's first identity on a glued elementary solid region
items.strategy:
Apply the divergence theorem to the field $u
abla v$, which is $C^1$ when $u$ is $C^1$ and $v$ is $C^2$. The scalar product rule makes its divergence $\langle
abla u,
abla vangle+u\Delta v$, and its boundary integrand is $u$ times the normal derivative $\langle
abla v,nangle$. State the regularity of $u$ and $v$ exactly as used, and note that no symmetry between them is claimed at this stage.

items.title: Green's second identity on a glued elementary solid region
items.strategy: Write the first identity twice, once as it stands and once with $u$ and $v$ interchanged, which needs both functions to be $C^2$. Subtract: the inner-product terms are equal and cancel, leaving the difference of the two Laplacian terms on the left and the difference of the two normal-derivative terms on the right. Record the symmetry hypothesis explicitly, since it is stronger than the first identity's.

items.title: The induced boundary chain and circulation of a $C^2$ patch over a finite elementary Green region
A vector line integral along an image arc is the parameter line integral of the pulled-back field
items.strategy: Let $\sigma$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ arc in the parameter region and $\varphi$ a $C^1$ map on a neighbourhood of it. On each smooth piece the chain rule gives $(\varphi\circ\sigma)'=\varphi_u\sigma_1'+\varphi_v\sigma_2'$, so the integrand $\langle F(\varphi\circ\sigma),(\varphi\circ\sigma)'\rangle$ equals $P^{*}\sigma_1'+Q^{*}\sigma_2'$ with $P^{*}=\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_u\rangle$ and $Q^{*}=\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_v\rangle$. Summing over the pieces of an admissible partition gives the parameter line integral. Check that $\varphi\circ\sigma$ is piecewise $C^1$ with the composed derivative as its continuous extension on each piece, and treat a degenerate constant piece, whose contribution is zero on both sides.

items.title: The curl flux integrand of a $C^2$ patch is a two-dimensional curl of the pulled-back field
items.strategy: With $P^{*}=\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_u\rangle$ and $Q^{*}=\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_v\rangle$, differentiate each by the product rule. The two terms carrying second derivatives of $\varphi$ are $\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_{uv}\rangle$ and $\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_{vu}\rangle$; they cancel in $\partial_uQ^{*}-\partial_vP^{*}$ by Clairaut-Schwarz applied to each component of $\varphi$, and this is the only place $C^2$ is used. The chain rule turns the remaining terms into $\langle DF(\varphi)\varphi_u,\varphi_v\rangle-\langle DF(\varphi)\varphi_v,\varphi_u\rangle$, which the antisymmetric-part lemma identifies with $\langle\operatorname{curl}F(\varphi),\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\rangle$. Note that no regularity of the patch is used, so the identity holds at parameter points where the cross product vanishes.

items.title: The classical Stokes theorem for a $C^2$ patch over a finite elementary Green region
items.strategy: The pulled-back functions $P^{*}$ and $Q^{*}$ are $C^1$ on an open neighbourhood of the parameter region because $\varphi$ is $C^2$ and $F$ is $C^1$ there. Green's theorem on that finite elementary Green region therefore equates the boundary-chain integral of $P^{*}\,du+Q^{*}\,dv$ with the region integral of $\partial_uQ^{*}-\partial_vP^{*}$. The pullback lemma identifies the left side arc by arc with the circulation around the induced boundary chain, and the integrand lemma identifies the right side with the flux of the curl in the orientation induced by $\varphi$. Shrink the neighbourhood so that its image lies in the domain of $F$, which compactness allows. Record that no regularity of the patch is needed for the identity itself, only for reading the right side as a flux.

items.title: A curl-free field has zero circulation around the induced boundary chain of a $C^2$ patch
items.strategy: Stokes' theorem writes the circulation as the flux of the curl, which is the integral of the zero function. Say exactly which set the curl must vanish on: an open set containing the whole patch image, not merely the boundary curve, and point to the companion page's witness for a closed field on a domain that carries no such patch.

items.title: The normal component of the curl is the limiting circulation per unit area of shrinking discs
items.strategy: Given a unit vector $n$, choose unit $a,b$ orthogonal to each other with $a\times b=n$: an orthonormal basis extension gives an orthonormal pair spanning the orthogonal complement, whose cross product is a unit vector orthogonal to both, hence $\pm n$, and replacing $b$ by $-b$ fixes the sign. Parametrize the disc of radius $r$ about $p$ in that plane by $\varphi(\rho,\theta)=p+\rho\cos\theta\,a+\rho\sin\theta\,b$ on a rectangle, a $C^2$ patch regular in the interior with $\varphi_\rho\times\varphi_\theta=\rho\,n$. Its induced boundary chain has the two radial edges traversed oppositely, so they cancel, and the inner edge is constant, so the circulation is the integral around the boundary circle. Stokes then turns it into $\int\langle\operatorname{curl}F(\varphi),n\rangle\rho$, and Fubini gives area $\pi r^2$. Subtract the constant value at $p$ and estimate by continuity.

items.title: Green's theorem is the curl statement for a planar field lifted to $\mathbb R^3$
items.strategy: Lift a $C^1$ planar field $(P,Q)$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ to the field $(P,Q,0)$ on the open cylinder $U\times\mathbb R$, which is $C^1$ with the same partial derivatives in the first two coordinates and none in the third. Its curl has $x$ and $y$ coordinates zero and $z$ coordinate $\partial_xQ-\partial_yP$, exactly Green's integrand. The identity is therefore the published Green theorem restated, and this dictionary is what makes the planar and spatial statements one development rather than two. Verify each curl coordinate rather than only the third.

items.title: The planar divergence theorem: the flux form of Green's theorem
items.strategy: Apply Green's theorem to the rotated field $(-F_y,F_x)$: its Green integrand is $\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y$, the planar divergence. The boundary integral is $\int_{\partial D}(-F_y)\,dx+F_x\,dy$, and on an arc with nowhere vanishing derivative that integrand is the arc length integral of $\langle F,n\rangle$ with $n$ the unit vector obtained by rotating the tangent a quarter turn clockwise. State the identity in the $dx,dy$ form, which needs no regularity, and record the normal reading as a separate clause under the extra hypothesis, since the published boundary arcs may have vanishing derivative.

items.title: What the classical divergence and Stokes theorems here do and do not cover

pages.title: The Divergence Theorem and Classical Stokes: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The closed unit box, with its six faces, is an elementary solid region
items.strategy: Parametrize each of the six faces of $[0,1]^3$ by the two free coordinates on the unit square, choosing the parameter order in each case so that the oriented area vector points out of the box; compute all six cross products explicitly. For the $z$ direction the base is the unit square with the constant graphs $0$ and $1$, the top face is the upper list, the bottom face the lower list, and the four side faces have vanishing third coordinate of the area vector. The projections of the top and bottom faces are the open unit square, whose complement in the base has content zero. The $x$ and $y$ directions are the same computation with the roles of the faces permuted, and the same six patches serve all three.

items.title: Both sides of the divergence theorem for $F(x,y,z)=(x^2,y^2,z^2)$ on the closed unit box
items.strategy: The divergence is $2(x+y+z)$, and Fubini with the fundamental theorem on the unit cube gives volume integral $3$. On the boundary, the faces $x=0$, $y=0$ and $z=0$ contribute nothing because the matching component of $F$ vanishes there, and each of the faces $x=1$, $y=1$ and $z=1$ contributes $1$. The two sides agree at $3$. Evaluate every one of the six face integrals rather than invoking symmetry.

items.title: The closed ball is an elementary solid region, presented by the eight spherical octants
items.strategy: Cut the spherical parameter rectangle into eight closed rectangles by $\phi=\pi/2$ and $\theta\in\{\pi/2,\pi,3\pi/2\}$ and use $\varphi(\phi,\theta)=R(\sin\phi\cos\theta,\sin\phi\sin\theta,\cos\phi)$ on each; the oriented area vector is $R\sin\phi\,\varphi$, outward, so its coordinates are $R^2\sin\phi$ times $(\sin\phi\cos\theta,\sin\phi\sin\theta,\cos\phi)$. In the $z$ direction the base is the closed disc of radius $R$ with graphs $\mp\sqrt{R^2-x^2-y^2}$, the four octants with $\phi<\pi/2$ are the upper list and the other four the lower list, and the projections are the four open quarter discs. In the $x$ direction the split is by the sign of $\cos\theta$ and in the $y$ direction by the sign of $\sin\theta$, and in each case the vanishing set is a parameter boundary. Show that the same eight patches serve all three directions; this is the point of cutting at both $\phi=\pi/2$ and the four quadrants.

items.title: The volume of a closed ball recovered from the outward flux of the position field
items.strategy: On each octant the integrand $\langle\varphi,\varphi_\phi\times\varphi_\theta\rangle$ is $R^3\sin\phi$, so the eight patch integrals add to $4\pi R^3$. A third of that is $\tfrac43\pi R^3$, which is the published volume of the closed three-ball; state the agreement as a check of the orientation convention, since an inward presentation would give the negative.

items.title: A right circular cylinder is an elementary solid region, presented by two caps and four side quarters
items.strategy: Present the boundary of $\{x^2+y^2\le R^2,\ 0\le z\le H\}$ by two polar cap patches and four quarter side patches $\sigma(\theta,z)=(R\cos\theta,R\sin\theta,z)$ on the quadrant rectangles, with outward oriented area vectors $(0,0,\pm r)$ and $R(\cos\theta,\sin\theta,0)$ respectively. In the $z$ direction the caps are the upper and lower lists over the closed disc with constant graphs and the sides are lateral. In the $x$ direction the base is the rectangle $[-R,R]\times[0,H]$ with graphs $\mp\sqrt{R^2-y^2}$, the two side quarters with $\cos\theta>0$ are the upper list, the other two the lower list, and the caps are lateral; the projections are the two open halves of the base rectangle. The $y$ direction splits by the sign of $\sin\theta$. This is why the side is cut into four quarters rather than taken whole.

items.title: The inverse-square field is divergence free, and its flux through a sphere missing the origin vanishes
items.strategy: For $F(p)=p/\lVert p\rVert_2^3$ on $\mathbb R^3$ without the origin, differentiate each component and collect: the three terms $\lVert p\rVert^{-3}$ sum to $3\lVert p\rVert^{-3}$ and the three terms $-3p_i^2\lVert p\rVert^{-5}$ sum to $-3\lVert p\rVert^{-3}$, so the divergence is zero. Take the ball of radius $1$ about $(0,0,2)$, an elementary solid region by translating the octant presentation, with the origin outside it; the field is $C^1$ on an open set containing it, so the divergence-free corollary gives flux zero. Verify explicitly that the translated graphs are still continuous and that the translated patches are still regular.

items.title: The outward flux of the inverse-square field through a sphere centred at the origin is $4\pi$
items.strategy: Compute directly on the spherical patch of radius $R$: the oriented area vector is $R\sin\phi\,\varphi$ and the field at $\varphi$ is $\varphi/R^3$, so the integrand is $\sin\phi$ and the integral over the parameter rectangle is $4\pi$, independent of $R$. The divergence theorem is not available here and must not be invoked: the field is not defined at the origin, so it is not $C^1$ on an open set containing the ball. Say that in the item.

items.title: FALSE: a field with vanishing divergence has zero outward flux through the boundary of every solid it surrounds
items.strategy: The inverse-square field has vanishing divergence at every point where it is defined, and its outward flux through the unit sphere is $4\pi$. The false claim quietly weakens the hypothesis of the divergence-free corollary from $C^1$ on an open set containing the whole solid to $C^1$ where the field happens to be defined. Name the exact hypothesis that fails and contrast the two computations on the companion items; do not say that the divergence theorem fails, because its hypotheses were never met.

items.title: A U-shaped prism is a finite gluing of three boxes and is not simple in every coordinate direction
items.strategy: Take the union of the three boxes $[0,3]\times[0,1]\times[0,1]$, $[0,1]\times[1,3]\times[0,1]$ and $[2,3]\times[1,3]\times[0,1]$. Their interiors are disjoint and they meet in two rectangular faces. The bar's face on the plane $y=1$ is LARGER than either upright's matching face, so present that face not as one patch but as three, cut at $x=1$ and $x=2$; two of the three are then declared internal and paired with the uprights' faces by an orientation-reversing reparametrization, and the third stays outer. Subdividing a face keeps the presentation adapted in every direction, since the three projections are disjoint and fill it. Without that subdivision the pairing the gluing definition demands does not exist. For $y$ strictly between $1$ and $3$ the section in the $x$ direction is a union of two disjoint intervals, so no description of the solid as simple in the $x$ direction exists and the gluing clause is doing real work. Verify the divergence theorem on the union for the field $(x,0,0)$, where both sides are the volume $7$.

items.title: The planar divergence theorem on a rectangle, checked against a direct boundary computation
items.strategy: On $[0,1]^2$ with the field $F(x,y)=(x^2,xy)$ the planar divergence is $3x$ and the area integral is $3/2$. Traverse the four positively oriented edges, evaluate $\int(-F_y)\,dx+F_x\,dy$ on each, and add: the bottom edge contributes $0$, the right edge $1$, the top edge $1/2$ and the left edge $0$, so the four add to $3/2$. Also record the circulation form on the same field to display both readings of Green's theorem, and check that the outward unit normal on each edge is the rotation the corollary names.

items.title: A function with vanishing Laplacian has zero boundary flux of its gradient on the unit box
items.strategy: Take $v(x,y,z)=x^2-y^2$, whose Laplacian is zero, and $u$ the constant $1$ in Green's first identity: the inner-product term drops and the identity says the boundary flux of $\nabla v$ vanishes. Verify it directly on the six faces of the unit box, where the faces $x=0,1$ contribute $0$ and $2$ and the faces $y=0,1$ contribute $0$ and $-2$, and the two $z$ faces contribute nothing. State the check as a check, not as a proof of the identity.

items.title: Stokes' theorem on a flat disc and on a hemisphere with the same induced boundary circle
items.strategy: For $F(x,y,z)=(-y,x,0)$ the curl is the constant $(0,0,2)$. On the flat disc parametrized in polar coordinates over a rectangle the induced boundary chain reduces to the unit circle once the two radial edges cancel and the degenerate inner edge contributes nothing, and both sides equal $2\pi$. On the upper unit hemisphere parametrized by $(\phi,\theta)$ over $[0,\pi/2]\times[0,2\pi]$ the induced boundary chain reduces to the same circle, and the curl flux is again $2\pi$. Present the shared boundary chain explicitly rather than asserting that the two surfaces span the same curve.

items.title: FALSE: Stokes' theorem requires the surface to be a graph over a coordinate plane
items.strategy: The lateral surface of a cylinder is the image of a $C^2$ patch over a rectangle and is not the graph of a function over any of the three coordinate planes: over the $xy$ plane its projection is a circle carrying a whole interval of heights, and over each of the other two it is two-valued. Verify Stokes on it for the explicit field $F(x,y,z)=(-yz,xz,0)$, whose curl is $(-x,-y,2z)$: the induced boundary chain is the bottom circle traversed with increasing azimuth together with the top circle traversed with decreasing azimuth, the two seam edges cancelling, and both sides equal $-2\pi$. Read the four edges off the published positive boundary of the parameter rectangle rather than assuming which circle is reversed. The hypothesis the theorem actually uses is that the parameter region is a finite elementary Green region, not that the image is a graph.

items.title: A curl-free $C^1$ field on the complement of a line that is not conservative
items.strategy: Take $F(x,y,z)=(-y,x,0)/(x^2+y^2)$ on the complement of the $z$ axis. Differentiate to see that all three coordinates of the curl vanish. Its circulation around the unit circle in the plane $z=0$ is $2\pi$, so by the published zero-circulation property of conservative fields it has no potential. The domain is connected and open but not star-shaped, which is exactly the hypothesis of the star-shaped corollary that fails; the planar restriction of this field is the published vortex counterexample, and the item says so in prose.

items.title: The Mobius band presented by two regular patches, with the induced normals on the two overlap components
items.strategy: Use $\Psi(t,s)=((1+s\cos(t/2))\cos t,(1+s\cos(t/2))\sin t,s\sin(t/2))$ with $|s|\le 1/2$, restricted to two closed parameter rectangles in $t$ that together cover a full turn and overlap in two disjoint closed $t$ intervals. Verify that each restriction is a regular patch, compute the induced normals on the two overlap components, and show that the images agree while the normals agree on one component and are opposite on the other. Give the two normal fields explicitly at a named point of each overlap component, since the whole force of the next item is that this sign pattern is what no reorientation can repair.

items.title: FALSE: the patches of a finite presentation can always be reoriented to make their normals agree on overlaps
items.strategy: Reorienting a patch replaces its induced normal by the opposite one, so a presentation by two patches admits exactly four orientation choices, and only the relative sign of the two matters. On the Mobius presentation of the preceding item the two overlap components force opposite relative signs, so each of the four choices fails on one component. Enumerate all four rather than arguing by parity, and state the conclusion for that presentation: it is what makes the compatibility clause of a finite patch presentation a real restriction and not a normalisation.

pages.title: Picard-Lindelof and First-Order Ordinary Differential Equations

items.title: First-order systems, initial value problems, and solutions on intervals
Local Lipschitz continuity in the state variable, locally uniform in time and parameters
A first-order initial value problem is equivalent to its Volterra integral equation
items.strategy: On an order-convex interval with at least two elements, apply the vector-valued fundamental theorem componentwise to pass from the ODE to the oriented Volterra equation. Conversely, the primitive theorem for a continuous integrand differentiates the integral equation, including the domain-relative endpoints.

items.title: The Picard operator and Picard iterates on a closed ball of continuous curves
Continuous $\mathbb{R}^n$-valued curves on a nonempty compact interval form a complete supremum-metric space
items.strategy: A supremum-metric Cauchy sequence is Cauchy in every coordinate. Completeness of the scalar $C(K,\mathbb R)$ spaces supplies coordinate limits; the finite coordinate list reassembles to a continuous $\mathbb R^n$-valued curve, and equivalence of the Euclidean and maximum norms turns coordinatewise uniform convergence into convergence in the stated supremum metric. Check $n\ge1$ and the one-point interval separately.

items.title: A bounded vector field makes the Picard operator preserve a sufficiently short closed curve ball
items.strategy: A continuous curve gives a continuous composite integrand, so its componentwise integral is again a continuous curve. On a compact time-state cylinder with field bound $M$, the vector integral inequality gives $\|\mathcal T x(t)-x_0\|\le M|t-t_0|\le r$ whenever $hM\le r$. The case $M=0$ is handled without division.

items.title: A state-Lipschitz vector field makes the Picard operator a contraction when $Lh<1$
items.strategy: For two curves in the invariant ball, apply the vector integral inequality and the state-variable Lipschitz bound pointwise. Taking the supremum over $|t-t_0|\le h$ gives $d_\infty(\mathcal T x,\mathcal T y)\le Lh\,d_\infty(x,y)$. The constant-field case $L=0$ and the strict short-time condition are stated explicitly.

items.title: Picard-Lindelöf local existence and uniqueness for first-order systems
items.strategy: Choose a nondegenerate compact cylinder inside the open ODE domain and then choose $h>0$ so that both $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$. The closed curve ball is nonempty and complete, the Picard operator maps it into itself and is a contraction, so Banach gives a unique fixed point. The integral-equation equivalence identifies that fixed point with the unique local solution; interval connectedness propagates local agreement across every common interval.

items.title: Nearby initial values share one Picard–Lindelöf time interval and one state cylinder
items.strategy: Choose nested compact cylinders around the base data. Compactness gives common field and state-Lipschitz bounds, while positive spatial and temporal margins allow one radius and one half-length satisfying the quantitative Picard-Lindelöf hypotheses for every nearby initial point.

items.title: Weissinger's fixed-point criterion for summably contracting iterates
items.strategy: If $\|T^m x-T^m y\|\le a_m\|x-y\|$ and $\sum_{m\ge1}a_m$ converges, telescope the successive iterates to prove they are Cauchy. Completeness gives a limit, continuity follows from the $m=1$ estimate, and the limit is a fixed point. Apply an iterate with $a_m<1$ to prove uniqueness and retain the tail sum as the error bound.

items.title: Picard iteration converges with geometric short-time and factorial cylinder error bounds
items.strategy: On a short interval with $q=Lh<1$, use the short-time contraction lemma before applying the published Banach a priori and a posteriori estimates. On the full invariant cylinder, repeated integration gives $\|\mathcal T^m x-\mathcal T^m y\|_\infty\le (Lh)^m\|x-y\|_\infty/m!$ by induction; Weissinger then yields convergence and the tail bound without requiring $Lh<1$. State the starting iterate at index zero and handle $L=0$ and $h=0$ before division.

items.title: Gronwall's integral inequality with variable and constant coefficients
items.strategy: For forward time, introduce the accumulated integral and multiply it by the integrating factor $exp(-int b)$. Differentiate, integrate the resulting inequality, and divide by the positive factor. State the reflected hypothesis with $int_t^{t_0}$ explicitly and derive the constant-coefficient estimate in both orientations.

items.title: The Grönwall estimate for two solutions of a Lipschitz ODE
items.strategy: Subtract the two Volterra equations, apply the vector integral inequality and the state-Lipschitz estimate, then apply Grönwall to obtain $\|x(t)-y(t)\|\le e^{L|t-t_0|}\|x(t_0)-y(t_0)\|$. Coincident initial values give uniqueness. Check the estimate at $t=t_0$, for $L=0$, and in both time directions.

items.title: Continuous dependence of ODE solutions on initial data and parameters
items.strategy: Choose one compact time-state-parameter cylinder and common field and state-Lipschitz bounds. Apply the quantitative Picard–Lindelöf theorem to each parameter slice with the same radius and time length, then subtract the resulting Volterra equations. Split the integrand into state and parameter discrepancies; compact uniform continuity and Grönwall give the quantitative joint-dependence estimate.

items.title: Extensions, maximal solutions, maximal intervals, and global solutions
Locally unique ODE solutions agree on overlaps and glue across a common endpoint
items.strategy: The set of overlap times on which the two solutions agree is nonempty, closed by continuity, and open by local uniqueness at each agreement point. Since the overlap is an interval it is connected, so the agreement set is the whole overlap. The piecewise union is then well defined; at a common endpoint both derivatives equal the same value of the continuous vector field, so the union is again a solution.

items.title: Every Picard–Lindelöf initial value problem has one maximal solution on an open interval
items.strategy: Take the union of the domains of all local solutions through the initial point. Each domain is an interval containing that point, so their union is an interval; the overlap lemma makes the pointwise union well defined and locally a solution. Its domain is open because local existence extends it around every point, and every other solution is its restriction. No representative is selected from the family.

items.title: A solution whose graph approaches a compact interior region at a finite endpoint extends past that endpoint
items.strategy: A compact subset of the open ODE domain has positive distance from the complement and gives uniform local existence data. If graph points approach a finite endpoint while their states remain in that compact set, extract a convergent state subsequence, use boundedness of the vector field to prove the entire curve has the same endpoint limit, and start a local solution there. The overlap lemma glues it to the old solution.

items.title: At a finite maximal time an ODE solution leaves every compact subset of the domain
items.strategy: If the graph did not eventually leave some compact interior subset, countable choice selects times tending to the finite endpoint with graph points in that compact set, and least later indices give an increasing subsequence. The extension lemma would continue the solution beyond the endpoint, contradicting maximality. State the backward-time version separately and distinguish compact escape from convergence to infinity.

items.title: A globally state-Lipschitz vector field on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ has global solutions
items.strategy: On each finite time slab, continuity bounds $\|F(t,0)\|$ and global state-Lipschitz continuity gives linear growth $\|F(t,x)\|\le M+L\|x\|$. Apply Grönwall to the integral equation to bound the solution on that slab. A finite maximal endpoint would therefore fail the compact-escape criterion, so both maximal endpoints are infinite.

items.title: A scalar first-order linear ODE has a unique solution given by the integrating-factor formula
items.strategy: For continuous $p,q$ on an interval, define $P(x)=\int_{x_0}^x p$ and multiply $y'+py=q$ by $e^P$. The product and chain rules give $(e^P y)'=e^Pq$; integrate and divide by the positive exponential to obtain the formula. Direct differentiation proves existence, while applying the same identity to the difference of two solutions proves uniqueness on the whole interval, including endpoints on either side of $x_0$.

items.title: Euler polygonal approximations for a continuous ODE are uniformly bounded and equicontinuous
items.strategy: For $h>0$ on a cylinder with the given finite field bound $M$, define the Euler polygon recursively at positive-mesh vertices and interpolate linearly. Induction keeps every vertex and segment inside the spatial ball, and every polygon is $M$-Lipschitz, including a shortened final cell.

items.title: A uniformly bounded equicontinuous sequence of $\mathbb R^n$-valued curves on a nonempty compact interval has a uniformly convergent subsequence
items.strategy: Fix an enumeration of the rational points of the compact time interval. At each rational time use deterministic nested-box bisection and least admissible indices to extract a convergent subsequence in $\mathbb R^n$; diagonalize over the fixed enumeration. Equicontinuity and a finite rational net make the diagonal subsequence uniformly Cauchy, and completeness of the vector-valued curve space gives a continuous uniform limit. The construction uses no choice principle.

items.title: Peano local existence for a continuous first-order system
items.strategy: Build forward Euler polygons and repeat the construction after reflecting time. Uniform boundedness and equicontinuity yield a uniformly convergent subsequence on each side; uniform continuity controls the Volterra defects and permits passage under the componentwise integral. Glue the two limiting half-solutions at the initial point to obtain the required two-sided local solution.

items.title: Moduli of continuity and the Osgood divergence condition
Osgood's criterion gives uniqueness without a Lipschitz bound
items.strategy: For two solutions with the same initial value, set $R=|x-y|^2$ and bound $|R'|$ by $2sqrt R,ho(sqrt R)$. Put $q_arepsilon=sqrt{R+arepsilon}$, integrate $q_arepsilon'/ho(q_arepsilon)le1$, and let $arepsilon$ tend to zero. Osgood divergence contradicts any positive separation; reflect time and continue through the agreement set.

pages.title: Picard-Lindelof and First-Order Ordinary Differential Equations: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Picard iteration for $y'=y$, $y(0)=1$, recovers the exponential series
items.strategy: Start from the constant curve one and show inductively that the $m$th iterate is $\sum_{k=0}^m t^k/k!$. Cite the published compact-uniform convergence of these iterates to the exponential, and identify the limit as the unique Picard–Lindelöf solution.

items.title: $y'=y^2$, $y(0)=1$, has maximal solution $y(t)=(1-t)^{-1}$ on $(-\infty,1)$
items.strategy: Differentiate the displayed function and check the initial value. Separation or the reciprocal derivative shows that any solution agreeing at zero equals it wherever defined. Its norm tends to infinity as $t\uparrow1$, so the compact-escape criterion makes $(-\infty,1)$ maximal even though the vector field is defined on all of $\mathbb R^2$.

items.title: $y'=2\sqrt{|y|}$ has a continuum of delayed-start solutions through the origin
items.strategy: For every delay $c\ge0$, put $y_c(t)=0$ on $0\le t\le c$ and $y_c(t)=(t-c)^2$ for $t\ge c$. Verify differentiability at the join and the differential equation on both pieces. Distinct delays give distinct solutions with the same initial value; the right-hand side is continuous but fails every local Lipschitz bound at zero.

items.title: The Dirichlet right-hand side gives a first-order equation with no solution
items.strategy: Let $F(t,y)$ be zero for rational $t$ and one for irrational $t$. Any differentiable solution of $y'=F(t,y)$ would have a derivative lacking the intermediate-value property on every interval, contradicting Darboux's theorem for derivatives. The obstruction is independent of the initial value.

items.title: An almost-Lipschitz vector field has a unique solution through zero but is not locally Lipschitz there
items.strategy: Near zero take $f(x)=x(1+|\log|x||)$ with $f(0)=0$ and extend it continuously outside a small interval. Its quotient $|f(x)-f(0)|/|x|$ is unbounded, so it is not locally Lipschitz. It has the Osgood modulus $\rho(r)=r(1+|\log r|)$ and $\int_{0^+}dr/\rho(r)=\infty$, so Osgood's theorem makes the zero solution unique through the origin.

items.title: False: continuity of the right-hand side guarantees unique ODE solutions
items.strategy: Refute the claim with the earlier delayed-start family for $y'=2\sqrt{|y|}$: the right-hand side is continuous, but every delay gives a distinct solution through zero.

items.title: False: a local ODE solution extends across the whole time-domain of its vector field
items.strategy: The polynomial field $F(t,y)=y^2$ is defined on all of $\mathbb R^2$, while the solution through $(0,1)$ is $(1-t)^{-1}$ and has finite maximal endpoint one. The blowup example and compact-escape criterion refute the asserted extension.

items.title: False: local Lipschitz continuity is necessary for uniqueness of an ODE solution
items.strategy: Use the almost-Lipschitz Osgood example: its vector field admits no finite local Lipschitz constant at zero, yet the Osgood divergence condition proves that the zero solution is the unique solution through zero.

pages.title: The Gauge Integral and Cousin's Lemma

items.title: Gauges and gauge-fine tagged partitions of a compact interval
Cousin's lemma: every gauge on a compact interval admits a fine tagged partition
items.strategy: Assume no fine partition exists and bisect the interval, retaining the left half if it still has no fine partition and the right half otherwise. The nested intervals shrink to one point. Eventually a retained interval lies inside the gauge neighborhood of that point and is itself a one-piece fine partition, a contradiction. Treat the degenerate interval separately and choose the tag at the limiting point.

items.title: The Henstock–Kurzweil integral on a compact interval
The Henstock–Kurzweil integral has at most one value
items.strategy: Given two alleged integral values, choose gauges giving error below one third of their distance and take their pointwise minimum. Cousin's lemma supplies a partition fine for both gauges; the triangle inequality puts the two values closer than their distance. Avoid the circular division when the values are already equal.

items.title: Linearity of the Henstock–Kurzweil integral
items.strategy: For a sum, take the pointwise minimum of gauges for the two integrands and split the Riemann-sum error by the triangle inequality. For scalar multiples, separate the zero scalar and otherwise request error $\varepsilon/|c|$. Cousin's lemma prevents either quantified family of fine partitions from being empty.

items.title: Monotonicity of the Henstock–Kurzweil integral
items.strategy: First prove that a nonnegative integrable function has nonnegative integral: every fine Riemann sum is nonnegative, and an assumed negative integral is contradicted by an error smaller than its absolute value. Apply this to $g-f$ and use linearity. Include equality and the degenerate interval convention.

items.title: The Cauchy criterion for Henstock–Kurzweil integrability
items.strategy: Necessity follows by comparing two fine sums with the same integral. For sufficiency, use countable choice to select, for each $n\in\mathbb N$, a gauge $\gamma_n$ for which all fine sums differ by less than $2^{-n}$. Put $\delta_n=\min_{k\le n}\gamma_k$. The nonempty sets of $\delta_n$-fine sums are nested and have diameter below $2^{-n}$; their closed interval hulls are therefore nested with lengths tending to zero, so the nested interval property gives one common value. Every sufficiently fine sum lies near that value. Cousin's lemma supplies nonemptiness, while no sequence of fine partitions is selected.

items.title: Henstock–Kurzweil integrability on subintervals and additivity over adjacent intervals
items.strategy: For restriction, complete two fine subinterval partitions by one common complementary partition; the whole-interval estimates give the HK Cauchy criterion on each side. Conversely, combine side gauges and shrink them by distance to the cut, so only a cut-tagged cell can cross and it splits validly. Add the side estimates and then orient arbitrary endpoints.

items.title: The Saks–Henstock lemma for fine partial tagged partitions
items.strategy: Fix one whole-interval gauge controlling complete-partition errors before the partial partition is quantified. For a fine partial partition, classify local errors by sign and, on each complementary interval, use a partition fine for the minimum of the fixed gauge and a complement-specific accuracy gauge. Comparing the completed sums with the integral bounds the positive and negative totals separately; combine them to bound the sum of absolute local errors.

items.title: Every Riemann integrable function is Henstock–Kurzweil integrable with the same integral
items.strategy: Use the tagged-partition characterization of the Riemann integral to choose a constant mesh bound. The constant gauge equal to half that bound makes every gauge-fine tagged partition have mesh below the Riemann threshold, so the same Riemann sums converge to the same value. Preserve the universal quantifier over tags and handle the degenerate interval separately.

items.title: Every derivative is Henstock–Kurzweil integrable and satisfies Newton–Leibniz
items.strategy: For each tag, use the least natural reciprocal radius satisfying the derivative estimate, making the gauge canonical without uncountable choice. Split each primitive increment at its tag, sum the two linearization errors, and telescope. This proves the endpoint formula on every nondegenerate compact interval without boundedness of the derivative.

items.title: The indefinite Henstock–Kurzweil integral of a derivative is a primitive
items.strategy: Let $F$ be differentiable on $[a,b]$ with $a<b$, put $f=F'$, and define $G(x)=\int_a^x f$. Apply the derivative form of Newton–Leibniz on each $[a,x]$ to obtain $G(x)=F(x)-F(a)$, with $G(a)=0$ from the degenerate-interval convention. The difference quotient of $G$ at any point of $[a,b]$ is therefore the difference quotient of $F$ there, so $G'=F'=f$, including the one-sided endpoint derivatives used by the library's domain-relative definition.

items.title: Henstock–Kurzweil integration by parts for differentiable factors
items.strategy: For differentiable $F,G$, the product rule makes $(FG)'=F'G+FG'$, and the derivative theorem makes this sum Henstock–Kurzweil integrable with endpoint integral. If either summand is integrable, linearity makes the other integrable and rearrangement gives the integration-by-parts formula. State the symmetric iff and avoid assuming both products integrable at the outset.

items.title: Henstock–Kurzweil substitution for a derivative composed with a differentiable map
items.strategy: If $F'=f$ on an interval containing $\phi([a,b])$, the chain rule gives $(F\circ\phi)'=(f\circ\phi)\phi'$. Apply the derivative theorem to the composite to obtain integrability and the endpoint formula. No monotonicity of $\phi$ and no separate integrability hypothesis on $f$ are needed; check constant $\phi$ and reversed endpoint values.

items.title: Henstock–Kurzweil integrals on half-open and unbounded intervals by compact truncation limits
The Cauchy criterion for a Henstock–Kurzweil integral at a missing endpoint
items.strategy: Apply the ordinary Cauchy criterion for real limits to the truncation primitive $A(c)=\int_a^c f$. Additivity rewrites $A(c'')-A(c')$ as the tail integral. This yields the two-truncation criterion in both finite and infinite endpoint cases; reflect it for a missing left endpoint and treat a finite endpoint already included in the compact domain separately.

items.title: Comparison, absolute-convergence, and limit-comparison tests for noncompact Henstock–Kurzweil integrals
items.strategy: If $|f|\le g$ and $g$ has a convergent noncompact integral, monotonicity bounds every tail integral of $f$ by the corresponding tail integral of $g$; the noncompact Cauchy criterion gives convergence. Taking $g=|f|$ yields absolute convergence. For positive $f,g$ with a finite positive limit of $f/g$, trap the ratio between two positive constants near the missing endpoint and apply comparison in both directions; treat limit zero and infinity as the appropriate one-sided implications.

items.title: Hake's theorem: a finite-endpoint generalized integral is a proper Henstock–Kurzweil integral after assigning the endpoint value
items.strategy: The proper-to-noncompact direction uses Saks-Henstock on an endpoint-tagged tail cell. Conversely, decompose the interval into countably many bands approaching the missing endpoint, choose compatible local gauges with a summable error budget, and shrink them by distances to band boundaries. Every global fine partition then splits into complete bands, one final partial band, and an endpoint-tagged tail cell, whose errors are controlled separately.

pages.title: The Gauge Integral and Cousin's Lemma: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The indicator of the irrationals is Henstock–Kurzweil integrable with integral $1$
items.strategy: Enumerate the rationals in $[0,1]$ and choose the gauge at the $k$th rational so its interval length contributes less than $\varepsilon 2^{-k}$. Give irrational tags an unrestricted small positive radius. In any fine partition the total length of intervals with rational tags is below $\varepsilon$; the Riemann sum of the irrational indicator therefore differs from one by less than $\varepsilon$. Then prove non-Riemann-integrability locally: density of the rationals and irrationals makes every lower Darboux sum zero and every upper Darboux sum one.

items.title: $F(x)=x^2\sin(1/x^2)$ has an unbounded derivative whose Henstock–Kurzweil integral is $\sin 1$
items.strategy: Set $F(0)=0$ and differentiate for $x>0$ to obtain $F'(x)=2x\sin(1/x^2)-2x^{-1}\cos(1/x^2)$, with $F'(0)=0$. Exhibit sequences on which the second term is unbounded. The derivative theorem gives Henstock–Kurzweil integrability on $[0,1]$ and evaluates the integral as $F(1)-F(0)=\sin1$.

items.title: $\sin x/x$ has a Henstock–Kurzweil integral on $[0,\infty)$
items.strategy: Assign the removable value one at zero. Every compact restriction is continuous, hence Riemann and Henstock–Kurzweil integrable. The primitive of $\sin x$ is bounded and $1/x$ is nonnegative, decreasing, and tends to zero, so the published Dirichlet test gives convergence of the compact truncation integrals. The noncompact definition therefore yields an HK integral; do not claim the unproved value $\pi/2$.

items.title: Cousin's lemma yields the Heine–Borel theorem on a compact interval
items.strategy: Given an open cover of $[a,b]$, choose for each point a gauge radius whose centered interval lies in one covering set. A fine tagged partition exists by Cousin's lemma, and the finitely many covering sets selected at its tags cover every partition subinterval and hence all of $[a,b]$. The empty and one-point intervals are handled before choosing tags.

items.title: False: every derivative is Riemann integrable
items.strategy: Use the earlier example $F(x)=x^2\sin(1/x^2)$: its derivative is unbounded near zero, while the definition of the Riemann integral requires boundedness. This directly refutes the universal claim. The Henstock–Kurzweil derivative theorem supplies the correct replacement and evaluates the same derivative by endpoint difference. Mention the stronger published bounded Volterra witness only in a non-load-bearing Remark.

items.title: False: every Henstock–Kurzweil integrable function is bounded
items.strategy: The derivative of $x^2\sin(1/x^2)$ is Henstock–Kurzweil integrable on $[0,1]$ but unbounded near zero, as established in the earlier example.

items.title: Henstock–Kurzweil integrability does not imply integrability of the absolute value
items.strategy: Use the derivative of $x^2sin(1/x^2)$. On compact intervals away from zero, $|f|$ is continuous and hence locally HK integrable. Endpoint increments on alternating sine extrema give a harmonic lower bound for the truncation integrals of $|f|$; Hake then rules out proper HK integrability on $[0,1]$.

items.title: False: Henstock–Kurzweil integrability implies Riemann integrability
items.strategy: Use the preceding example, which establishes both that the irrational indicator has Henstock–Kurzweil integral one and that its lower and upper Darboux integrals are zero and one. The same function is therefore Henstock–Kurzweil integrable but not Riemann integrable, directly refuting the converse of the Riemann-to-HK theorem.

items.title: False: every Henstock–Kurzweil integrable function is a derivative
items.strategy: The indicator of the irrationals is Henstock–Kurzweil integrable but has only the values zero and one on every interval. It therefore fails the intermediate-value property, whereas Darboux's theorem says every derivative has that property.

pages.title: Trigonometric and Oscillatory Examples in One Variable

items.title: Sine and cosine are $1$-Lipschitz on $\mathbb{R}$
items.strategy: The derivative formulas give $|\sin'|=|\cos|\le1$ and $|\cos'|=|\sin|\le1$. Apply the published bounded-derivative Lipschitz corollary on the whole real line, including equal endpoints, to obtain both modulus estimates without introducing a separate mean-value argument.

items.title: The classical Weierstrass function
The classical Weierstrass series converges uniformly to a continuous function
items.strategy: For $0<a<1$, bound the $n$th summand $a^n\cos(b^n\pi x)$ by $a^n$ uniformly in $x$. The geometric majorant and the published M-test give absolute pointwise and uniform convergence from the first index $n=0$. Each partial sum is continuous, so the published uniform-limit theorem makes the sum continuous on $\mathbb{R}$.

items.title: Nearest-integer probe points for the Weierstrass function
items.strategy: Fix $x_0$ and choose an integer $k_m$ nearest to $b^m x_0$, so $z_m=b^m x_0-k_m$ lies in $[-1/2,1/2]$. Put $x_m=(k_m+1)/b^m$. Then $x_0<x_m\le x_0+3/(2b^m)$, hence $x_m\to x_0$. For every $n\ge m$, oddness of $b$ and the shift formulas give $\cos(b^n\pi x_m)=-(-1)^{k_m}$ and $\cos(b^n\pi x_0)=(-1)^{k_m}\cos(b^{n-m}z_m\pi)$.

items.title: Low-frequency bound for the Weierstrass difference quotient
items.strategy: At the probe $x_m$, split the increment of the Weierstrass series before index $m$. Apply the $1$-Lipschitz estimate for cosine to each of the finitely many terms and sum the geometric progression to obtain $|A_m|\le \pi(x_m-x_0)((ab)^m-1)/(ab-1)<\pi(ab)^m(x_m-x_0)/(ab-1)$. Treat $m=0$ as the empty low-frequency sum.

items.title: The Weierstrass tail has one sign and dominates at the probe points
items.strategy: Use the exact tail values from the probe lemma. Every tail increment has the common sign $-(-1)^{k_m}$ because it is a positive multiple of $1+\cos(b^{n-m}z_m\pi)$. Thus no cancellation occurs. Retain the $n=m$ term, use $|z_m|\le1/2$ to get $\cos(z_m\pi)\ge0$, and use $x_m-x_0\le3/(2b^m)$ to conclude $|B_m|\ge(2/3)(ab)^m(x_m-x_0)$.

items.title: Under $ab>1+3\pi/2$, the classical Weierstrass function is continuous everywhere and differentiable nowhere
items.strategy: Assume $0<a<1$, $b>1$ is an odd integer, and $ab>1+3\pi/2$. Continuity is already established. At an arbitrary $x_0$, combine the low-frequency upper bound and tail lower bound with the reverse triangle inequality. The selected right difference quotients have absolute value at least $(ab)^m(2/3-\pi/(ab-1))$, whose coefficient is positive and whose geometric factor tends to infinity. Since the probes tend to $x_0$, no finite derivative exists there.

items.title: A uniform limit of smooth functions need not be differentiable anywhere
items.strategy: The partial sums of the classical Weierstrass series are finite sums of smooth cosine functions and are therefore smooth. They converge uniformly by the convergence theorem, while the limit is nowhere differentiable by the Weierstrass theorem. This supplies the claimed sequence and checks that the failure occurs at every real point, not merely at one exceptional point.

items.title: Riemann–Lebesgue lemma for continuous functions on a compact interval
items.strategy: For continuous $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ with $a<b$, uniformly approximate $f$ by a polynomial $p$. The integral of $(f-p)\sin(nt)$ is controlled by the approximation error. Integrate $p\sin(nt)$ by parts to bound it by $(|p(a)|+|p(b)|+\int_a^b|p'|)/n$. First choose the approximation and then a positive integer $n$ large enough; this proves $\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_a^b f(t)\sin(nt)\,dt=0$. The same proof with cosine is recorded in the Statement.

items.title: Finite sums of the sine harmonics
items.strategy: For a positive integer $N$, sum $e^{inx}$ from $n=1$ to $N$ by the finite geometric identity. When $x\notin2\pi\mathbb{Z}$, rewrite numerator and denominator with Euler's formula and take imaginary parts to obtain $\sum_{n=1}^N\sin(nx)=(\cos(x/2)-\cos((N+1/2)x))/(2\sin(x/2))$. The cosine bound gives absolute value at most $1/|\sin(x/2)|$. At multiples of $2\pi$ the sum is zero and is handled separately so no division by zero occurs.

items.title: Classical counterparts for the trigonometry-free oscillators

pages.title: Trigonometric and Oscillatory Examples in One Variable: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The Weierstrass function with $a=1/2$ and $b=15$
items.strategy: Check that $b=15$ is an odd integer. The published first-zero theorem gives $0<\gamma<2$, and the definition $\pi=2\gamma$ gives $\pi<4$, hence $1+3\pi/2<7<15/2=ab$. The general theorem then proves that $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}2^{-n}\cos(15^n\pi x)$ converges uniformly, is continuous everywhere, and is differentiable nowhere. The construction is a non-load-bearing explicit instance and will be independently rechecked at authoring time.

items.title: FALSE: every continuous real function is differentiable somewhere
items.strategy: Assume the universal claim. The classical Weierstrass function is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$ but the preceding theorem says it is differentiable at no real point. Applying the claim to that function gives an immediate contradiction.

items.title: $x\sin(1/x)$ extended by zero is continuous but not differentiable at zero
items.strategy: The estimate $|x\sin(1/x)|\le|x|$ and the squeeze theorem give continuity of the zero extension. Its difference quotient at zero is exactly $\sin(1/x)$. Two explicit positive sequences tending to zero make the latter constantly $1$ and $-1$, so the sequential criterion rules out a limit and the derivative at zero does not exist.

items.title: $x^2\sin(1/x^2)$ has an unbounded, non-Riemann-integrable derivative
items.strategy: Define $F(0)=0$ and $F(x)=x^2\sin(1/x^2)$ for $x\ne0$. The quotient $F(h)/h=h\sin(1/h^2)$ tends to zero, so $F'(0)=0$; the product and chain rules give $F'(x)=2x\sin(1/x^2)-2\cos(1/x^2)/x$ off zero. At $x_k=(2\pi(k+1))^{-1/2}$ the sine term vanishes and the cosine term makes $|F'(x_k)|=2/x_k\to\infty$. Every extension of $F'|_{(0,1]}$ is therefore unbounded and cannot be Riemann integrable on $[0,1]$ under the published Darboux convention.

items.title: FALSE: every differentiable function has a continuous derivative
items.strategy: Assume the universal claim and apply it to the preceding function $F(0)=0$, $F(x)=x^2\sin(1/x^2)$ for $x\ne0$. That example proves $F$ differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$ and proves that $F'$ is unbounded on every neighbourhood of zero; since $F'(0)=0$, its derivative cannot be continuous at zero, contradicting the claim.

items.title: The sine harmonics are pointwise bounded but have no uniformly convergent subsequence
items.strategy: On $[0,\pi]$ let $f_n(x)=\sin(nx)$ for positive integers $n$. The family is uniformly bounded, but the sequence does not converge pointwise on the whole interval, as the values at $\pi/2$ cycle. It is not equicontinuous at zero because $f_n(\pi/(2n))=1$. If a subsequence converged uniformly, its continuous limit would vanish at zero; continuity near zero and uniform closeness would contradict the same peak values for large subsequence indices. Finally apply the continuous Riemann–Lebesgue theorem to show $\int_0^\pi g(x)\sin(nx)\,dx\to0$ for every fixed continuous $g$.

items.title: FALSE: every pointwise bounded sequence of continuous functions has a uniformly convergent subsequence
items.strategy: Assume the claim and apply it to the sine harmonics on $[0,\pi]$. They are continuous and even uniformly bounded, hence pointwise bounded, but the preceding example proves that none of their subsequences converges uniformly. This contradiction also identifies the missing Arzelà–Ascoli hypothesis: equicontinuity.

items.title: The topologist's sine curve is connected
items.strategy: Let $C=\{(x,\sin(1/x)):0<x\le1\}$ and $S=C\cup(\{0\}\times[-1,1])$. The graph $C$ is a continuous image of the connected interval $(0,1]$. For each height in $[-1,1]$, the full sine range and periodicity give graph points of that height whose first coordinates tend to zero, so the vertical segment lies in $\overline C$. Since $C\subseteq S\subseteq\overline C$, closure preservation makes $S$ connected.

items.title: The topologist's sine curve is connected but not path connected
items.strategy: Use the preceding lemma for connectedness. To rule out path connectedness, assume a path leaves the vertical segment for $C$, take the last parameter at which its first coordinate is zero, and use the intermediate value theorem to force alternating peak and trough values of the second coordinate along parameters tending to that last time. This contradicts continuity of the path.

items.title: The arc length of one sine period is $4\sqrt{2}\,E(1/\sqrt{2})$
items.strategy: Apply the published graph-length formula to $x\mapsto\sin x$ on $[0,2\pi]$ to obtain $\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{1+\cos^2x}\,dx$. Use reflection and period symmetries to reduce to four times the integral over $[0,\pi/2]$, then rewrite $1+\cos^2x=2(1-\tfrac12\sin^2x)$. With $E(k):=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{1-k^2\sin^2t}\,dt$, this gives $4\sqrt2E(1/\sqrt2)$ and checks the nondegenerate modulus $0<1/\sqrt2<1$.

items.title: The sine-period arc-length integrand has no elementary antiderivative
Tangent identifies a bounded incomplete interval with the unbounded complete real line
items.strategy: Use the published principal-branch definition to identify $\tan:(-\pi/2,\pi/2)\to\mathbb{R}$ as a homeomorphism with inverse arctangent. The interval is bounded in the usual metric and $\mathbb{R}$ is unbounded. The real line is complete, while the interval is not closed in it—its points $\pi/2-1/(n+1)$ converge to the missing endpoint—so the complete-subspace criterion makes the interval incomplete. Thus neither boundedness nor completeness is preserved by homeomorphism.

items.title: $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sin(nx)/n$ converges pointwise but not uniformly
items.strategy: At $x\in2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ every term is zero. Elsewhere the finite-sum lemma bounds the partial sums of $\sum\sin(nx)$, and Dirichlet's test with the decreasing weights $1/n$ gives pointwise convergence, with the positive indices implemented as $k+1$ so no $1/0$ term occurs. For nonuniformity on $[0,2]$, given a positive integer $N$ take $x=1/N$ and the tail from $n=N$ through $2N$: each angle lies in $[1,2]$, where the published lower bound gives $\sin(nx)\ge1/3$, while $1/n\ge1/(2N)$. The tail is at least $1/6$, violating the uniform Cauchy criterion for arbitrarily large $N$.
