items.title: FALSE: every continuous function on a compact interval has a rectifiable graph
items.strategy: Assume the universal claim. The published function $f(0)=0$, $f(x)=x\sin(1/x)$ on $(0,1]$ is continuous on the compact interval $[0,1]$, while its graph path is proved nonrectifiable through divergent variation. This is a direct contradiction.

pages.title: Trigonometric and Oscillatory Examples in Several Variables

items.title: Polar-coordinate forms of two Cartesian expressions
items.strategy: For $(x,y)=r(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ with $r>0$, use the Pythagorean and double-angle identities to prove $xy/(x^2+y^2)=\tfrac12\sin(2\theta)$. Where $\cos\theta\ne0$, prove $y(x^2+y^2)/x=r^2\tan\theta$. These are identities only: cross-link the published Cartesian counterexamples in a Remark, not as load-bearing examples-page dependencies.

pages.title: Trigonometric and Oscillatory Examples in Several Variables: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The circular curve defeats the equality form of the vector-valued mean value theorem
items.strategy: Let $f(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$ on $[0,2\pi]$. Its endpoint increment is zero, while $f'(t)=(-\sin t,\cos t)$ has Euclidean norm one for every $t$. Hence no $\xi$ can satisfy $f(2\pi)-f(0)=2\pi f'(\xi)$. Verify continuity and differentiability componentwise and cross-reference the published polynomial witness as a genuinely different route.

items.title: FALSE: the mean value equality holds for vector-valued maps
items.strategy: Apply the universal equality claim to the preceding circular curve. Equal endpoints force the claimed derivative vector to be zero at some interior point, while the Pythagorean identity makes every derivative vector have norm one. State that the mean value inequality remains valid and do not weaken the scalar theorem.

items.title: $\sin(xy)$ and its mixed partial derivatives
items.strategy: For $f(x,y)=\sin(xy)$, apply the chain and product rules to obtain $f_x=y\cos(xy)$ and $f_y=x\cos(xy)$, then compute both mixed partials as $\cos(xy)-xy\sin(xy)$. The explicit equality illustrates the mixed-partial theorem without using that theorem to perform the calculation, and all formulas hold on the whole plane including the coordinate axes.

items.title: $xy\sin(1/(x^2+y^2))$ is differentiable at the origin with unbounded partial derivatives nearby
items.strategy: Extend the function by zero at the origin. The bound $|xy|\le(x^2+y^2)/2$ makes the function $O(\|h\|_2^2)$, so it is totally differentiable there with derivative zero and both partials exist. Off the origin compute the partial derivatives explicitly. Along $y=x$, take $x_k=1/\sqrt{4\pi k}$ for positive $k$, so the cosine factor is one and the term proportional to $1/x_k$ is unbounded. Check both partial derivatives and the first positive index explicitly.

items.title: $r^2\sin(1/r)$ is differentiable at the origin with a discontinuous gradient
items.strategy: Set $F(0)=0$ and $F(x,y)=r^2\sin(1/r)$ for $r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}>0$. Since $|F(h)|/\|h\|_2\le\|h\|_2$, the derivative at the origin is zero. Off the origin the radial chain rule gives $\nabla F=(2r\sin(1/r)-\cos(1/r))(x/r,y/r)$. Along the positive $x$-axis, the radii $1/(2\pi k)$ and $1/((2k+1)\pi)$ for positive $k$ make the radial factor tend respectively to $-1$ and $1$, so the gradient is not continuous at zero.

items.title: The family $\sin(nx)\sin(ny)$ is uniformly bounded but not equicontinuous
items.strategy: On the compact square $[0,\pi]^2$ take positive integers $n$ and $f_n(x,y)=\sin(nx)\sin(ny)$. Closure of $C^1$ Euclidean maps under composition and products, followed by total differentiability implying continuity, puts every $f_n$ in $C(K,\mathbb R)$; the Pythagorean bound makes the family uniformly bounded by one. At the origin $f_n=0$, while at $(\pi/(2n),\pi/(2n))$ it equals one and those points tend to the origin. This violates one common equicontinuity modulus. Use indices $n\ge1$ explicitly so no division by zero occurs.

items.title: The solid generated by rotating $y=\sin x$ on $[0,\pi]$ has volume $\pi^2/2$
items.strategy: The sine profile is continuous and nonnegative on $[0,\pi]$. Apply the RC-5 disc theorem directly: it supplies compact Jordan measurability of the rotated solid and gives $V=\pi\int_0^\pi\sin^2x\,dx$. Power reduction writes $\sin^2x=(1-\cos2x)/2$; use the sine derivative, the chain rule, and the fundamental theorem to evaluate the integral as $\pi/2$. Hence $V=\pi^2/2$. The zero endpoint radii are allowed by the disc theorem and require no separate measurability reconstruction.

items.title: The surface generated by rotating $y=\sin x$ on $[0,\pi]$ has area $2\pi(\sqrt2+\operatorname{arsinh}1)$
items.strategy: The sine profile is $C^1$, positive on $(0,\pi)$, and zero only at the parameter endpoints. Apply the earlier surface-of-revolution corollary to obtain $A=2\pi\int_0^\pi\sin x\sqrt{1+\cos^2x}\,dx$. The inverse-function derivative theorem and the hyperbolic identity give $(\operatorname{arsinh}u)'=1/\sqrt{1+u^2}$. With the real-power derivative and the chain and product rules, verify that $G(x)=-\tfrac12(\operatorname{arsinh}(\cos x)+\cos x\sqrt{1+\cos^2x})$ is a primitive of the integrand. The fundamental theorem, the endpoint cosine values, and oddness of the inverse of the odd bijection $\sinh$ give the integral $\sqrt2+\operatorname{arsinh}1$. Finally use the published logarithm formula $\operatorname{arsinh}1=\log(1+\sqrt2)$ as an equivalent exact form.

items.title: FALSE: spherical coordinates are globally injective
items.strategy: For $S(r,\phi,\theta)=(r\sin\phi\cos\theta,r\sin\phi\sin\theta,r\cos\phi)$ on nonnegative radii, a full polar-angle interval, and a full azimuthal period, periodicity identifies the two seam faces. At $\phi=0$ or $\phi=\pi$, every azimuth gives the same point, and at $r=0$ both angles are lost. Compute $\det DS=r^2\sin\phi$ to show the same loci are singular. Mention the published compact injective box and polar analogue only as cross-references, not dependencies.

A family is a lambda-system exactly when it contains $X$ and is closed under complements and countable disjoint unions

Reverse: $B\setminus A$ is the complement of the disjoint union $A\sqcup(X\setminus B)$, and an increasing union is disjointified.

pages.title: Measures and Their Basic Properties

items.title: Series in the nonnegative extended real line
Limit superior and limit inferior of a nonnegative extended-real sequence
Tonelli's theorem for double series of nonnegative extended real numbers
items.strategy: Define the sum of a nonnegative extended-real series as the supremum of its partial sums. Compare both iterated sums with the supremum of all finite rectangular sums: every rectangle is bounded by either iterated sum, while every finite part of either iterated sum is bounded by a sufficiently large rectangle. Treat an infinite entry and an unbounded family of finite rectangular sums separately so no subtraction or undefined extended-real product is used.

items.title: Measures on sigma-algebras
Measure spaces
Finitely additive nonnegative set functions
Finite, sigma-finite, and semifinite measures
Probability measures and probability spaces
Measure-null sets and almost-everywhere statements relative to a measure
Complete measure spaces
FALSE: every subset of a measure-null set is measurable
items.strategy: On the two-point space use the trivial sigma-algebra and its zero measure. The whole space is measurable and null, but a singleton is a subset of it and is not in the sigma-algebra. This isolates exactly the missing completeness hypothesis without invoking Lebesgue measure or a nonconstructive subset.

items.title: Measures are monotone
items.strategy: For measurable $A\subseteq B$, decompose $B$ as the disjoint union of $A$ and $B\setminus A$ and use nonnegativity; do not subtract when either value may be infinite.

items.title: Measure of a set difference when the smaller set has finite measure
items.strategy: From $B=A\sqcup(B\setminus A)$ and finite $\mu(A)$, cancel the finite term to obtain $\mu(B\setminus A)=\mu(B)-\mu(A)$. State the finiteness hypothesis on the subtracted quantity and separately cover $A=\emptyset$ and $A=B$.

items.title: Finite and countable subadditivity of measures
items.strategy: Disjointize a sequence by $F_k=E_k\setminus\bigcup_{j<k}E_j$. The $F_k$ are pairwise disjoint, have the same union as the $E_k$, and satisfy $F_k\subseteq E_k$; countable additivity and monotonicity give the inequality. Obtain the finite form by padding the list with empty sets, including the empty-list boundary.

items.title: Continuity from below for measures
items.strategy: For $E_0\subseteq E_1\subseteq\cdots$, decompose the union into $E_0$ and the disjoint increments $E_{k+1}\setminus E_k$. Countable additivity identifies the union's measure with the supremum of the measures of finite initial unions, which are exactly the $E_n$. Separate the case in which some $\mu(E_n)$ is infinite before using finite differences.

items.title: Continuity from above when one set has finite measure
items.strategy: Discard finitely many initial terms so the first retained set has finite measure. Apply continuity from below to the increasing complements inside that finite set and use the set-difference formula. This yields the decreasing-intersection limit without ever forming infinity minus infinity.

items.title: Counting measure on an arbitrary set
Counting measure is a measure
items.strategy: For a disjoint sequence, if one member is infinite then both sides are infinite. Otherwise the finite cardinalities add over every finite initial union; if the full union is infinite, the natural-number partial sums cannot remain bounded, while if it is finite only finitely many members are nonempty. This proves countable additivity without a choice principle.

items.title: FALSE: continuity from above needs no finiteness hypothesis
items.strategy: Use counting measure on $\mathbb N$ and the tails $E_k=\{n:k\le n\}$. They decrease to the empty set while every term has infinite measure, so their measures do not converge to zero. Check the $k=0$ tail and the empty intersection explicitly.

items.title: The two-set measure identity $\mu(A\cup B)+\mu(A\cap B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B)$
items.strategy: Partition both sides into the three disjoint pieces $A\setminus B$, $A\cap B$, and $B\setminus A$. The proof uses only addition of nonnegative extended reals and remains valid when one or more terms are infinite.

items.title: Inclusion-exclusion for a nonempty finite family of finite-measure sets
items.strategy: Induct on the number of sets. Apply the two-set identity to the union of the first $n$ sets and the last set, then apply the induction hypothesis both to the first union and to its intersections with the last set. Reindex the resulting nonempty subsets and signs. Check the one-set base case and use the finite-measure hypothesis exactly where signed cancellation occurs.

items.title: Sets whose symmetric difference is null have the same measure
items.strategy: Monotonicity makes both $A\setminus B$ and $B\setminus A$ null. Decompose $A$ and $B$ over their common intersection; adding a null piece changes neither value, including when the common value is infinite.

items.title: Countable additivity and continuity of finitely additive set functions
items.strategy: First prove that a finitely additive nonnegative set function is countably additive exactly when it is continuous from below: one direction is the increment argument, and the reverse applies continuity to partial unions of a disjoint sequence. Then assume the set function is finite and prove equivalence with continuity from above at the empty set by taking complements or disjoint tails. Explicitly explain why the finite hypothesis cannot be deleted from this third clause.

items.title: The first Borel-Cantelli lemma for measures
items.strategy: Write the set limsup as the intersection of the tail unions. For every $N$, monotonicity and countable subadditivity bound its measure by $\sum_{k\ge N}\mu(E_k)$. A convergent nonnegative real series has tails tending to zero, so the limsup has measure zero. The proof does not assume independence or finite total measure.

items.title: The measure of a set liminf is at most the liminf of the measures
items.strategy: Let $F_N=\bigcap_{k\ge N}E_k$. The $F_N$ increase to the set liminf, and $F_N\subseteq E_k$ for every $k\ge N$. Apply continuity from below and monotonicity, then take the supremum over $N$ of the tail infima in the extended real line.

items.title: The limsup of the measures is at most the measure of the set limsup under a finite-union bound
items.strategy: Let $G_N=\bigcup_{k\ge N}E_k$. The $G_N$ decrease to the set limsup, and $E_k\subseteq G_N$ for every $k\ge N$. The hypothesis $\mu(\bigcup_kE_k)<\infty$ licenses continuity from above. Compare each tail supremum with $\mu(G_N)$ and then take the infimum over $N$.

items.title: Measures converge for a convergent sequence of sets contained in one finite-measure set
items.strategy: Pointwise convergence of indicators is exactly equality of the set liminf and set limsup with the limiting set. Apply the two set-Fatou inequalities; the common finite envelope supplies the limsup theorem's finiteness hypothesis, and the two inequalities squeeze the numerical liminf and limsup to $\mu(E)$.

items.title: Null sets are closed under countable unions and, in a complete space, under arbitrary subsets
items.strategy: Countable subadditivity sends a countable union of null measurable sets to zero. Monotonicity makes every measurable subset of a null set null; completeness supplies measurability for arbitrary subsets. Keep these two roles separate so completeness is not incorrectly used for the union clause.

items.title: The completion domain and proposed completed set function of a measure space
Assuming countable choice, the completion domain is a sigma-algebra
items.strategy: Represent a completed set as $A\cup N$ with $A$ measurable and $N$ contained in a measurable null set, first replacing $N$ by $N\setminus A$. Show complements by writing $(A\cup N)^c$ as a measurable complement modified inside the same null set, and show countable unions by taking the union of the measurable parts and using the countable union of their null envelopes.

items.title: The completed measure is independent of the representing measurable set
items.strategy: If one completed set has two representations, each measurable core differs from the other only inside the union of the two measurable null envelopes. Their symmetric difference is therefore null, and the null-symmetric-difference proposition gives equal measures. Check the empty null envelope and infinite common value explicitly.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, every measure space has a unique complete extension to its completion
items.strategy: Use the two completion lemmas to obtain a well-defined set function on a sigma-algebra. For a disjoint sequence choose measurable cores, remove the null overlaps to obtain disjoint measurable representatives, and apply countable additivity; then prove extension and completeness directly. For uniqueness, every added subset lies inside a null measurable set, so any complete extension must give it value zero and hence must assign the prescribed value to every completed set.

items.title: Restriction of a measure to a measurable set
The restriction of a measure to a measurable set is a measure
items.strategy: For fixed measurable $E$, define $\mu_E(A)=\mu(A\cap E)$ on the original sigma-algebra. Intersections with $E$ preserve the empty set, disjointness, and countable unions, so the measure axioms follow directly from those of $\mu$.

items.title: The Dirac set function at a point
A Dirac set function is a probability measure
items.strategy: A point belongs to at most one member of a pairwise disjoint sequence. Split on whether it belongs to none or to the unique successful member; this proves countable additivity, and the whole space has value one. The empty sequence boundary is handled by the empty-set clause.

items.title: Nonnegative scalar multiples and countable weighted sums of measures
items.strategy: For $c\in[0,+\infty]$ and a measure $\mu$, define $c\mu$ by three disjoint branches: $c=0$ gives the zero measure; $0<c<+\infty$ gives $(c\mu)(E)=c\mu(E)$ by the defined extended-real product; and $c=+\infty$ gives value $0$ when $\mu(E)=0$ and $+\infty$ when $\mu(E)>0$. Define a countable weighted sum pointwise by the nonnegative extended series of these already-defined scalar multiples. Thus the notation never forms the library's undefined product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

items.title: Nonnegative scalar multiples and countable weighted sums of measures are measures
items.strategy: Verify the three scalar branches before forming a countable sum. The zero branch is the zero measure. For $0<c<+\infty$, scale finite partial sums and their extended-real supremum to prove countable additivity. For $c=+\infty$, the branch is zero on $\mu$-null sets and infinite otherwise: a disjoint union is null exactly when every member is null, by countable additivity of $\mu$, so this branch is a measure without forming $0\cdot(+\infty)$. Only then apply Tonelli's theorem for nonnegative double series to interchange the measure index with the disjoint-union index in a countable weighted sum.

items.title: A measure on a finite sigma-algebra is a finite weighted sum over its atoms
items.strategy: For each point intersect the finitely many measurable sets containing it; the distinct intersections form a finite measurable partition into atoms. Every measurable set is the union of the atoms it contains, so finite additivity writes its measure as the sum of their weights. Choose one representative from each atom and use the weighted-sum definition for the corresponding Dirac measures. If an atom has weight $+\infty$, its term is zero on measurable sets missing that atom and $+\infty$ on measurable sets containing it, exactly as the explicit infinite-coefficient branch requires. Treat the empty underlying space as the empty sum.

items.title: Every measure on a countable discrete space is its weighted sum of Dirac measures
items.strategy: Separate the empty, finite nonempty, and countably infinite underlying sets. In the finite case use a bijection from one natural number and a finite sum; in the countably infinite case use a bijection from $\mathbb N$, so every point is indexed exactly once and no repeated-point padding is needed. Decompose each subset into its disjoint singletons and apply countable additivity to obtain the weighted Dirac formula. The coefficient at $x$ is forced to be $\mu(\{x\})$ by evaluation on $\{x\}$. When this coefficient is $+\infty$, use the explicit infinite-coefficient branch, which is zero off $x$ and infinite on sets containing $x$.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, an infinite-measure set in a semifinite measure space has arbitrarily large finite-measure subsets
items.strategy: Take the supremum of the finite measures attained by measurable subsets of the given set. If it were finite, countable choice selects subsets approaching it; their union has the supremal finite measure by continuity from below. Semifiniteness then supplies a disjoint positive finite-measure subset of the remaining infinite-measure part, contradicting maximality. Include the case when the supremum is already infinite.

items.title: The semifinite part of a measure
Assuming countable choice, the semifinite part is a semifinite measure and equals the original measure exactly when it is semifinite
items.strategy: For disjoint $E_k$, finite-measure subsets of their union give the easy subadditive bound after intersecting each $E_k$. For the reverse bound, finite choice selects approximating subsets on each fixed finite initial range; finite unions first avoid an unjustified countable union of finite numbers, and a supremum argument closes the inequality. Semifiniteness is immediate from the defining supremum; use the countable-choice-dependent arbitrarily-large-subset lemma for the equality criterion.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, every measure is the sum of its semifinite part and a zero-infinity-valued measure
items.strategy:
Define $
u(E)=0$ when $E$ is sigma-finite for $\mu$ and $
u(E)=\infty$ otherwise. Countable choice and countability of $\mathbb N	imes\mathbb N$ show that a countable union of sigma-finite measurable sets is sigma-finite, while any measurable superset of a non-sigma-finite set remains non-sigma-finite; hence $
u$ is a measure. On sigma-finite $E$, the restriction of $\mu$ is semifinite and the semifinite part agrees with $\mu$; otherwise the $
u$ term is infinite.

items.title: Finite measures agreeing on a generating pi-system and on the whole space are equal
items.strategy: Let $\mathcal D$ be the measurable sets on which the two finite measures agree. Equality of the total masses puts $X$ in $\mathcal D$; finite subtraction gives closure under relative differences, and continuity from below gives closure under increasing unions. Thus $\mathcal D$ is a lambda-system containing the pi-system, so Dynkin's theorem yields the generated sigma-algebra. The convention that a pi-system need not contain $X$ is why total-mass equality is stated separately.

items.title: Measures agreeing on a generating pi-system are equal under an increasing finite-measure exhaustion from that pi-system
items.strategy: Let $P_n$ be the increasing pi-system exhaustion. For fixed $n$, the restricted set functions $A\mapsto\mu(A\cap P_n)$ and $A\mapsto\nu(A\cap P_n)$ are finite measures with equal total mass and agree on the pi-system, so the finite uniqueness lemma makes them equal everywhere. Let $n$ tend upward and use continuity from below on $A\cap P_n$ to recover $\mu(A)=\nu(A)$.

items.title: FALSE: agreement on an arbitrary generating family determines a measure
items.strategy: Use Pollard's four-point probability measures. The north, south, east, and west two-point sets generate the whole power set and receive the same mass under both measures, but the two diagonal pairs of point masses are different. Verify generation by taking intersections and complements, and identify the failed hypothesis: the family is not closed under intersections.

items.title: FALSE: every finitely additive nonnegative set function on a sigma-algebra is a measure
items.strategy: On $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$ assign zero to finite sets and infinity to infinite sets. A finite disjoint union has the required value, but the natural numbers are the countable disjoint union of their singletons, whose assigned values sum to zero. Check the empty set and a union containing an infinite member.

items.title: FALSE: measures are additive on arbitrary countable unions
items.strategy: For a Dirac probability measure repeat the same measurable singleton twice and use empty sets thereafter. The union has measure one while the series of the term measures begins with two ones. This isolates disjointness and also covers the index-zero convention.

items.title: FALSE: a measure on an infinite set that vanishes on every singleton is the zero measure
items.strategy: Assume countable choice, take an uncountable $X$ with the countable-cocountable sigma-algebra, and assign zero to countable sets and one to cocountable sets. Countable choice makes the domain a sigma-algebra and proves countable additivity. Every singleton has value zero while $X$ has value one.

pages.title: Measures and Their Basic Properties — Examples

items.title: Assuming countable choice, counting measure is sigma-finite exactly on countable sets
items.strategy: A countable set is covered by its finite initial segments under a listing, with the finite-set case handled by one set. Conversely, a sigma-finite counting-measure cover is a countable union of finite sets, hence countable under countable choice. Explain why this implication has a genuine choice cost in the library's conventions.

items.title: A Dirac probability measure concentrates all mass at one point
items.strategy: Compute the measure of a set according as it contains the distinguished point, verify the empty and whole-space values, and illustrate restriction to a measurable set both containing and omitting the point.

items.title: The weights $2^{-(k+1)}$ define a probability measure on $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$
items.strategy: Set $\mu(E)=\sum_{k\in E}2^{-(k+1)}$ by the weighted sum of the Dirac measures at $k$. The weighted-sum theorem proves it is a measure and the geometric series gives total mass one. Explicitly contrast the incorrect weights $2^{-k}$, whose total is two because $k=0$ is present.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, zero on countable sets and infinity on cocountable sets is a non-semifinite measure
items.strategy: On an uncountable set with the countable-cocountable sigma-algebra, a disjoint sequence has cocountable union only if one member is uncountable; otherwise countable choice makes the union countable. This proves countable additivity of the zero-infinity set function. The whole space has infinite measure and no measurable subset has positive finite measure, so the measure is not semifinite.

items.title: Assuming choice, the completion of the Borel Dirac measure at zero is defined on every subset of the real line
items.strategy: The Borel set $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$ is $\delta_0$-null, so every subset not containing zero enters the completion, and adjoining $\{0\}$ handles every subset containing zero. Thus the completion domain is $\mathcal P(\mathbb R)$ and the completed value is one exactly on sets containing zero. Use the published Borel-cardinality theorem and Cantor's theorem to verify that the original Borel sigma-algebra is strictly smaller, so this also gives the promised non-complete Borel measure space without a forward reference to Lebesgue measure.

items.title: Borel-Cantelli for the shrinking intervals $(0,2^{-k})$ under a dyadic atomic measure
items.strategy: Let $\mu=\sum_{j\ge0}2^{-(j+1)}\delta_{2^{-j}}$. For $E_k=(0,2^{-k})$, compute $\mu(E_k)=\sum_{j>k}2^{-(j+1)}=2^{-(k+1)}$, so the series of measures equals one. Borel-Cantelli gives null limsup; independently, the geometric sequence tends to zero and the intervals decrease to the empty set, so the limsup is visibly empty.

items.title: Counting-measure tails decrease to the empty set while every term has infinite measure
items.strategy: For $E_k=\{n\in\mathbb N:k\le n\}$, verify $E_{k+1}\subseteq E_k$, every $E_k$ is infinite, and the intersection is empty because $n$ fails membership in $E_{n+1}$. Hence counting measure stays infinite although the intersection has measure zero.

items.title: A free ultrafilter induces a finitely additive zero-one probability that is not countably additive
items.strategy: Assuming the Axiom of Choice, extend the filter generated by the tails of $\mathbb N$ to an ultrafilter and prove it contains no singleton. Define $m(A)=1$ exactly when $A$ belongs to the ultrafilter. The ultrafilter dichotomy proves finite additivity on disjoint pairs, while $m(\mathbb N)=1$ and the countable singleton partition has total assigned mass zero, so countable additivity fails.

items.title: Two four-point probability measures agree on a generating family that is not a pi-system
items.strategy: On the points northwest, northeast, southwest, southeast, put mass one-half on the northwest/southeast diagonal for $\mu$ and on the northeast/southwest diagonal for $\nu$. Both give mass one-half to each row and column, and those rows and columns generate the power set, but the singleton masses differ. Their intersections are singletons absent from the family, pinpointing failure of the pi-system hypothesis.

pages.title: Outer Measure and the Caratheodory Extension Theorem

items.title: Outer measures
Carathéodory measurable sets
Carathéodory measurability is not Carathéodory's differentiability criterion
In the Carathéodory identity, the subadditive inequality is automatic
items.strategy: For arbitrary subsets $A,E\subseteq X$, write $A=(A\cap E)\cup(A\setminus E)$ and apply countable subadditivity with all later terms empty. Thus only the reverse inequality must be proved when checking Carathéodory measurability; include $A=\varnothing$ and infinite outer values without cancellation.

items.title: Carathéodory measurable sets form an algebra
items.strategy: Show that $\varnothing$ is measurable and that measurability is symmetric under complements. For $E,F$ measurable, split a test set into the four cells cut out by $E$ and $F$; regroup three cells into the part inside $E\cup F$, use subadditivity only in the safe direction, and invoke the automatic-inequality lemma for equality. No subtraction is used, so infinite values cause no gap.

items.title: Outer measure splits exactly over finite Carathéodory-measurable partitions
items.strategy: Induct on $n\in\mathbb N$. The empty partition gives zero, and the successor step applies the Carathéodory identity for the new piece to the part of the test set inside the preceding finite union. Pairwise disjointness identifies the new cell and preserves the remainder. State the formula for every test set, including $n=0$ and infinite outer measure.

items.title: Countable disjoint unions of Carathéodory measurable sets are measurable and split every test set
items.strategy: For disjoint measurable $E_k$ and a test set $A$, apply finite splitting to the first $n$ pieces and retain the remainder $A\setminus\bigcup_kE_k$. Let $n$ increase to obtain a lower bound by the nonnegative series, while countable subadditivity bounds $\mu^*(A\cap\bigcup_kE_k)$ by that series. The two inequalities give both measurability and $\mu^*(A\cap\bigcup_kE_k)=\sum_k\mu^*(A\cap E_k)$, including infinite sums.

items.title: Every outer-null set is Carathéodory measurable
items.strategy: If $\mu^*(N)=0$, monotonicity gives $\mu^*(A\cap N)=0$ and $A\setminus N\subseteq A$ gives the reverse inequality needed for the Carathéodory identity. Combine it with the automatic inequality. The argument also proves every subset of $N$ is outer-null and measurable.

items.title: Carathéodory's theorem: measurable sets form a sigma-algebra carrying a complete measure
items.strategy: The algebra proposition and closure under countable disjoint unions make the Carathéodory family a sigma-algebra. Countable splitting with the test set equal to the union gives countable additivity of the restriction. The outer-null proposition shows that every subset of every null measurable set lies in the domain, so the restricted measure is complete.

items.title: FALSE: every subset is Carathéodory measurable for every outer measure
items.strategy: On a two-point set define $\mu^*(\varnothing)=0$ and $\mu^*(A)=1$ for every nonempty $A$. Verify the outer-measure axioms. A singleton fails the Carathéodory test against the whole space because the proposed split reads $1=1+1$.

items.title: FALSE: every outer measure is countably additive on the whole power set
items.strategy: Use the same zero-one outer measure on a two-point set, but verify it independently. The two singleton sets are disjoint, their union has outer measure one, and their individual outer measures sum to two. This isolates failure of additivity from the domain issue.

items.title: Measurable hulls and regular outer measures
Assuming countable choice, regular outer measures are continuous from below on all subsets
items.strategy: For $E_n\uparrow E$, the infinite-value case is immediate. Otherwise use countable choice to select measurable hulls $H_n\supseteq E_n$ with equal outer measure. Put $G_n=\bigcap_{k\ge n}H_k$; then $G_n$ is an increasing measurable hull of $E_n$. Apply continuity from below to the restricted Carathéodory measure on $\bigcup_nG_n$, use $E\subseteq\bigcup_nG_n$, and combine with monotonicity. Tail intersections avoid the false inference that $H_n\setminus E_n$ is null for nonmeasurable $E_n$.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, countable covering costs define an outer measure
items.strategy: Let $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ contain $\varnothing$ and $X$, let $p:\mathcal C\to[0,+\infty]$ satisfy $p(\varnothing)=0$, and define outer cost by the infimum over countable $\mathcal C$-covers. Empty-set and monotonicity are immediate. For countable subadditivity, if every term has finite outer cost, countable choice selects for the $j$th set a cover within $\varepsilon2^{-(j+1)}$; flatten the double cover and use Tonelli. If one term has infinite cost, the inequality is automatic.

items.title: Premeasures on algebras of sets
The outer set function induced by a premeasure
Assuming countable choice, the outer set function induced by a premeasure is an outer measure
items.strategy: Apply the covering-cost theorem with $\mathcal C=\mathcal A_0$ and $p=\mu_0$. An algebra contains $\varnothing$ and $X$, and the premeasure has value zero at the empty set, so every hypothesis is available verbatim.

items.title: A countable algebra cover disjointifies inside the covered algebra set
items.strategy: For $A,A_k\in\mathcal A_0$ with $A\subseteq\bigcup_kA_k$, put $B_k=A\cap(A_k\setminus\bigcup_{j<k}A_j)$. Algebra closure puts every $B_k$ in $\mathcal A_0$; the least index at which a point is covered proves that the $B_k$ are pairwise disjoint with union $A$, and $B_k\subseteq A_k$. Treat $k=0$ with the empty preceding union.

items.title: The induced outer measure agrees with the premeasure on the source algebra
items.strategy: For $A\in\mathcal A_0$, the one-set cover gives $\mu^*(A)\le\mu_0(A)$. For an arbitrary algebra cover of $A$, disjointify it. Countable additivity of the premeasure gives $\mu_0(A)=\sum_k\mu_0(B_k)\le\sum_k\mu_0(A_k)$. Taking the infimum gives the reverse inequality. This is the exact step where premeasure, rather than finite additivity alone, is consumed.

items.title: Every source-algebra set is measurable for the induced outer measure
items.strategy: Fix $E\in\mathcal A_0$ and a test set $A$. If $\mu^*(A)=+\infty$ the reverse inequality is automatic. Otherwise choose an algebra cover of $A$ within $\varepsilon$ of its induced outer measure. Split every covering set by $E$ and $E^c$; finite additivity preserves each cost, and the subfamilies cover the two pieces of $A$. Let $\varepsilon$ tend to zero and use the automatic inequality.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, a premeasure extends through its induced outer measure
items.strategy: The induced set function is an outer measure, its Carathéodory family is a sigma-algebra carrying a complete measure, every source-algebra set is in that family, and agreement holds on the source algebra. Minimality of $\sigma(\mathcal A_0)$ therefore places the generated sigma-algebra inside the Carathéodory domain, and restriction gives an extension on $\sigma(\mathcal A_0)$. Existence is independent of sigma-finiteness.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, a premeasure-induced outer measure is regular with generated measurable hulls
items.strategy: For $E$ of finite outer measure, use countable choice to select for each $n\ge1$ an algebra cover whose cost is below $\mu^*(E)+1/n$. Intersect the countable unions of these covers. The result lies in $\sigma(\mathcal A_0)$, contains $E$, and has the same outer measure. If $\mu^*(E)=+\infty$, take $X$. The extension theorem makes every such hull Carathéodory measurable.

items.title: Among sets of finite outer measure, Carathéodory measurability is equivalent to source-algebra approximation
items.strategy: Assume $E$ has finite outer measure. If $E$ is Carathéodory measurable, choose an algebra cover of $E$ with finite cost within one quarter of a prescribed positive error; its finite partial unions lie in the algebra, its cost tail tends to zero, and measurability makes the part of the full covering union outside $E$ small. A sufficiently large finite union then has symmetric difference from $E$ of outer measure below the prescribed error. Conversely, compare both pieces of an arbitrary test set cut by $E$ with the corresponding pieces cut by a measurable approximant; subadditivity costs at most twice the symmetric-difference error. Let the error tend to zero and use the automatic inequality.

items.title: The Carathéodory extension dominates every other extension and agrees with it on finite-measure sets
items.strategy:
Let $\mu$ be the induced extension on $\sigma(\mathcal A_0)$ and $
u$ any other extension. Every algebra cover of $E$ gives $
u(E)\le\sum_k\mu_0(A_k)$, so $
u(E)\le\mu(E)$. When $\mu(E)<\infty$, choose a covering union $A\supseteq E$ of cost within $\varepsilon$; continuity from below makes $\mu(A)=
u(A)$ because both agree on its finite algebra partial unions. Finite subtraction bounds $\mu(E)$ by $
u(E)+\varepsilon$, and $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ gives equality.

items.title: A sigma-finite premeasure has at most one extension to its generated sigma-algebra
items.strategy: An algebra is a pi-system. From a sigma-finite algebra cover $(A_n)$ form the increasing algebra exhaustion $P_n=\bigcup_{k\le n}A_k$; finite subadditivity gives $\mu_0(P_n)<\infty$. Two extending measures agree on the algebra and hence on this generating pi-system and its finite-measure exhaustion. Apply the published sigma-finite pi-system uniqueness theorem. No choice is spent because the exhaustion is part of the sigma-finiteness witness.

items.title: A finite premeasure has at most one extension to its generated sigma-algebra
items.strategy: A finite premeasure is sigma-finite using the one-term exhaustion $P_n=X$ for every $n$. Apply sigma-finite uniqueness, including the empty ambient set and zero premeasure.

items.title: Under sigma-finiteness, every Carathéodory measurable set differs from a generated measurable hull by a null set
items.strategy: Assume countable choice and take an increasing finite-premeasure exhaustion $P_n\in\mathcal A_0$. For Carathéodory measurable $E$, select generated measurable hulls $H_n\supseteq E\cap P_n$ with equal finite measure. Measurability and finite cancellation give $\mu^*(H_n\setminus(E\cap P_n))=0$. The union $H=\bigcup_nH_n$ belongs to $\sigma(\mathcal A_0)$, contains $E$, and $H\setminus E$ is outer-null by countable subadditivity.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, the Carathéodory domain is the completion of the sigma-finite extension
items.strategy: Completeness of the full Carathéodory restriction includes the completion of the extension on $\sigma(\mathcal A_0)$. Conversely, find $H\in\sigma(\mathcal A_0)$ with $E\subseteq H$ and $H\setminus E$ outer-null. Regularity supplies a generated measurable null hull $Z$ of $H\setminus E$, and $E=(H\setminus Z)\cup(E\cap Z)$ is a completion representation. The measures agree there by uniqueness of the completed measure.

items.title: FALSE: every finitely additive nonnegative function on an algebra extends to a measure
items.strategy: On $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$ assign zero to finite sets and $+\infty$ to infinite sets. Verify finite additivity. Since the algebra is already a sigma-algebra, any extension must equal this function there, but the singleton partition violates countable additivity. This is the obstruction that the premeasure hypothesis removes.

items.title: FALSE: the extension of a premeasure is always unique
items.strategy: On the algebra of finite unions of half-open intervals in $\mathbb R$ with extended endpoints, put $\mu_0(\varnothing)=0$ and $\mu_0(A)=+\infty$ for nonempty $A$. It is a premeasure but not sigma-finite. Both counting measure and the measure assigning $+\infty$ to every nonempty Borel set extend it, and they disagree on singletons. Verify inline that every nonempty source-algebra member contains an infinite sequence obtained by repeated bisection, so counting measure really agrees there; also verify Borel generation and both measure axioms.

items.title: FALSE: the covering construction agrees with every finitely additive source function
items.strategy: On the finite-cofinite algebra of $\mathbb N$, set $\mu_0(A)=0$ for finite $A$ and $\mu_0(A)=+\infty$ for cofinite $A$. Verify finite additivity. The singleton cover has total cost zero, so the induced covering value of $\mathbb N$ is zero although $\mu_0(\mathbb N)=+\infty$. The discrepancy is exactly the failed premeasure clause.

items.title: Metric outer measures
Boundary layers of finite metric outer measure exhaust the complement of a closed set in outer measure
items.strategy: For closed $F$ and $A$ with $\mu^*(A)<\infty$, set $B_n=\{x\in A\setminus F:d(x,F)\ge1/(n+1)\}$ and $C_n=B_{n+1}\setminus B_n$. Closedness gives $B_n\uparrow A\setminus F$. Alternating layers are positively separated, so metric additivity bounds the sums of their outer measures by $\mu^*(A)$. Hence both parity-tail series tend to zero; subadditivity sandwiches $\mu^*(A\setminus F)$ between $\mu^*(B_n)$ and that value plus a vanishing tail. Treat $A\setminus F=\varnothing$ before invoking distance to a nonempty set.

items.title: Closed sets are Carathéodory measurable for metric outer measures
items.strategy: Fix closed $F$ and a test set $A$. If $\mu^*(A)=+\infty$, the reverse inequality is automatic. Otherwise boundary layers $B_n\subseteq A\setminus F$ are positively separated from $A\cap F$, so metric additivity gives $\mu^*(A)\ge\mu^*(A\cap F)+\mu^*(B_n)$. Let $n$ increase and use boundary-layer continuity to replace the last term by $\mu^*(A\setminus F)$; combine with the automatic inequality.

items.title: Every Borel set is Carathéodory measurable for a metric outer measure
items.strategy: The Carathéodory measurable sets form a sigma-algebra and contain every closed set, hence every open set by complements. Minimality of the sigma-algebra generated by the open sets places the Borel sigma-algebra inside the Carathéodory family. Include the empty metric space, where every family involved is the one-element power set.

pages.title: Outer Measure and the Caratheodory Extension Theorem — Examples

items.title: The zero-one outer measure on a two-point set has only the trivial measurable sets
items.strategy: On $X=\{0,1\}$ put $\mu^*(\varnothing)=0$ and $\mu^*(E)=1$ otherwise. Check empty set, monotonicity, and countable subadditivity. The empty set and $X$ satisfy the Carathéodory identity, while either singleton fails it with test set $X$. This computes the entire measurable family.

items.title: Counting measure is an outer measure for which every subset is measurable
items.strategy: Use the published counting measure on $\mathcal P(X)$. Its measure axioms give the outer-measure axioms. For every $A,E\subseteq X$, the disjoint decomposition $A=(A\cap E)\sqcup(A\setminus E)$ gives the Carathéodory identity, so the measurable family is all of $\mathcal P(X)$. Treat finite, infinite, and empty sets through the published definition.

items.title: Counting premeasure on the finite-cofinite algebra induces counting outer measure
items.strategy: On the finite-cofinite algebra of $\mathbb N$, restrict counting measure: finite sets have their cardinality and cofinite sets have value $+\infty$. The restriction is a premeasure. A finite $E$ covers itself at cost $|E|$, while disjointification makes every cover cost at least $|E|$. If $E$ is infinite, any algebra cover either contains a cofinite set or uses finite sets with an unbounded total number of points, so every covering cost is infinite. Thus the induced outer measure is counting outer measure on every subset.

items.title: Counting outer measure is a metric outer measure on the real line
items.strategy: Equip $\mathbb R$ with its usual metric. Positively separated nonempty subsets are disjoint, and counting measure is additive on every disjoint pair; empty-set cases follow from value zero. Hence counting outer measure is metric. Apply the metric Carathéodory criterion to recover Borel measurability, consistently with the stronger direct computation that every subset is measurable.

items.title: A three-point outer measure has nonmeasurable subsets despite passing the whole-space split
items.strategy: On $X=\{1,2,3\}$ put $\mu^*(\varnothing)=0$, $\mu^*(X)=2$, and $\mu^*(E)=1$ for every other nonempty $E$. Verify the outer-measure axioms. Every $E$ passes the equation obtained by testing only against $X$, but if $E$ is nonempty and proper, choose $x\in E$ and $y\notin E$ and test against $\{x,y\}$: the singleton pieces total two while the test set has outer measure one. Thus only $\varnothing$ and $X$ are Carathéodory measurable.

items.title: Zero on finite sets and infinity on cofinite sets is finitely additive but not a premeasure
items.strategy: On the finite-cofinite algebra of $\mathbb N$, put $\mu_0(A)=0$ for finite $A$ and $\mu_0(A)=+\infty$ for cofinite $A$. Check finite additivity by the finite-cofinite dichotomy. The disjoint singleton sequence has union $\mathbb N$ in the algebra, but the term values sum to zero while the union has value infinity. This pinpoints the failed premeasure clause.

items.title: A non-sigma-finite premeasure has distinct Borel extensions
items.strategy: Use the algebra of finite unions of half-open real intervals with extended endpoints and assign infinity to every nonempty member. Verify it is a premeasure and generates $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$. Prove inline by repeated bisection that every nonempty algebra member is infinite, so counting measure and the measure that is zero only at the empty set both extend it; they disagree on every singleton. The premeasure is not sigma-finite because its only finite-measure member is empty.

items.title: An outer measure on two points need not be regular
items.strategy: On the two-point set put outer measure zero on the empty set, one on each singleton, and three-halves on the whole space. Exhaust the finite unions to verify the outer-measure axioms. Neither singleton is Carathéodory measurable, so the only measurable superset available as its hull is the whole space, whose outer measure is strictly larger. Thus no singleton has a measurable hull and the outer measure is not regular.

pages.title: Lebesgue Measure on Euclidean Space

items.title: Half-open boxes in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and their volume
Half-open boxes are closed under intersection, and the complement of a half-open box is a finite disjoint union of half-open boxes
items.strategy: For the intersection, note that $x$ lies in both boxes exactly when $\max(a_i,a_i')<x_i\le\min(b_i,b_i')$ for every $i<n$, the extremes being taken in the extended order, so the intersection is the box with those parameters; the empty case is the one where some coordinate has $\max(a_i,a_i')\ge\min(b_i,b_i')$. For the complement, split coordinate by coordinate: the complement of $(a_i,b_i]$ in $\overline{\mathbb R}$-parameter form is the disjoint union of at most the two boxes $(-\infty,a_i]$ and $(b_i,+\infty]$, so grouping the $n$ coordinates in order writes $\mathbb R^n\setminus B$ as the disjoint union of the boxes obtained by taking, for the first index $i$ at which a point leaves $B$, one of those two pieces in slot $i$, the box's own interval in slots below $i$, and all of $\mathbb R$ above $i$. Check $n=1$ and the degenerate case $B=\varnothing$, whose complement is the single box $\mathbb R^n$.

items.title: Elementary sets: the finite unions of half-open boxes in $\mathbb{R}^n$
The elementary sets form an algebra of subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ containing every half-open box
items.strategy: The empty box gives $\varnothing$ and the box with all parameters $(-\infty,+\infty]$ gives $\mathbb R^n$. Closure under finite unions is immediate from the definition. For complements, write $\mathbb R^n\setminus\bigcup_{j<m}B_j=\bigcap_{j<m}(\mathbb R^n\setminus B_j)$, expand each complement as a finite union of boxes, and distribute the intersection over the unions, using that an intersection of boxes is a box. Verify the empty union $m=0$ separately.

items.title: Every elementary set is a finite disjoint union of half-open boxes, and any finitely many boxes admit a common grid refinement
items.strategy: Given boxes $B_0,\dots,B_{m-1}$, collect for each coordinate $i$ the finite set of parameters $a_{j,i},b_{j,i}$ occurring in them, together with $-\infty$ and $+\infty$, and list it increasingly as $c_{i,0}<\dots<c_{i,N_i}$. The cells $\prod_{i<n}(c_{i,k_i},c_{i,k_i+1}]$ are pairwise disjoint, and each $B_j$ is exactly the union of the cells it contains, because a cell meets $B_j$ only if it lies inside it. Hence $\bigcup_j B_j$ is the disjoint union of the cells meeting it. Cover the cases $m=0$ and boxes with infinite parameters.

items.title: The volume of a half-open box is the sum of the volumes of the cells of any coordinate grid subdividing it
items.strategy: Induct on the number of coordinates that are cut. Cutting a single coordinate at $a_i=c_0<\dots<c_N=b_i$ splits the box into $N$ boxes whose volumes sum to the original by distributivity and the telescoping identity $\sum_{k<N}(c_{k+1}-c_k)=b_i-a_i$; when the cut coordinate has an infinite side, at least one piece is again infinite in that coordinate and both sides are $+\infty$. Iterating over coordinates gives the full grid. Every nonempty half-open box has all sides strictly positive, so no factor is zero and no product of the form $0\cdot(+\infty)$ is ever formed; the empty box is treated by the convention $\operatorname{vol}(\varnothing)=0$.

items.title: The sum of the volumes of a disjoint box decomposition of an elementary set does not depend on the decomposition
items.strategy: Let $A=\bigsqcup_{j<m}B_j=\bigsqcup_{l<p}C_l$ be two disjoint box decompositions. Form the common grid refinement of all $B_j$ and all $C_l$. Each $B_j$ is a disjoint union of grid cells, so $\operatorname{vol}(B_j)$ is the sum of their volumes by the grid lemma, and summing over $j$ gives the total over all cells inside $A$; the same computation applies to the $C_l$. Both sums are nonnegative extended sums of finitely many terms, so the argument uses no subtraction and holds when some volume is $+\infty$. Include the case $A=\varnothing$, where both sums are empty and equal $0$.

items.title: Elementary volume is finitely additive, monotone and finitely subadditive on the elementary algebra
items.strategy: Additivity on a disjoint pair follows by concatenating disjoint box decompositions of the two sets and applying well-definedness to the union. Monotonicity follows from additivity applied to $A\subseteq A'$ through $A'=A\sqcup(A'\setminus A)$, which is legitimate because the elementary sets form an algebra. Subadditivity follows by disjointifying $A_0\cup\dots\cup A_{m-1}$ into $A_j\setminus\bigcup_{l<j}A_l$ and using monotonicity termwise. All three statements hold with the value $+\infty$ allowed, since only addition and comparison are used.

items.title: Every elementary set is squeezed in volume between a compact subset and an elementary set whose interior contains it
items.strategy: For $\delta>0$ define the canonical enlargement $A^{+\delta}:=\bigcup_{s\in[0,\delta]^n}(A+s)$; on a box $(a,b]$ it is the box $(a,b+\delta\mathbf 1]$, so it is elementary for every elementary $A$, contains $A$ in its interior, and its volume tends to that of $A$ as $\delta$ decreases, by finite subadditivity applied to one box decomposition. This enlargement depends on $A$ and $\delta$ alone, so no set is chosen. For the inner approximation fix one disjoint box decomposition of $A$, shrink each bounded box $(a,b]$ to $(a+\delta\mathbf 1,b-\delta\mathbf 1]$ and take closures, obtaining a compact subset of $A$ whose elementary volume tends to that of $A$; when $A$ has infinite volume, intersect first with $(-R,R]^n$ and let $R$ grow.

items.title: Elementary volume is a sigma-finite premeasure on the algebra of elementary sets
items.strategy: Let $A=\bigsqcup_{k\in\mathbb N}A_k$ with all sets elementary. For $\ge$, finite additivity and monotonicity give $\sum_{k<N}\mu_0(A_k)=\mu_0(\bigsqcup_{k<N}A_k)\le\mu_0(A)$ for every $N$, and the nonnegative extended sum is the supremum of these. For $\le$ with $\mu_0(A)<\infty$ and $\varepsilon>0$: choose one compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\mu_0(A)-\varepsilon\le\mu_0(K)$, and for each $k$ set $\delta_k:=2^{-m_k}$ where $m_k$ is the least natural number with $\mu_0(A_k^{+2^{-m}})\le\mu_0(A_k)+\varepsilon 2^{-k}$, so no choice principle is used. The interiors of the $A_k^{+\delta_k}$ cover $K$, Heine-Borel extracts a finite subcover, and finite subadditivity gives $\mu_0(K)\le\sum_{k<N}\mu_0(A_k^{+\delta_k})\le\sum_k\mu_0(A_k)+2\varepsilon$. For $\mu_0(A)=\infty$, apply the finite case to $A\cap(-R,R]^n$ and let $R$ grow. Sigma-finiteness is $\mathbb R^n=\bigcup_k(-k,k]^n$.

items.title: Lebesgue outer measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$
Assuming countable choice, Lebesgue outer measure is an outer measure that restricts to elementary volume
items.strategy: Apply the corollary that a premeasure-induced set function is an outer measure under countable choice, and the choice-free lemma that the induced set function agrees with the premeasure on the source algebra, both to the premeasure of the previous theorem. Record explicitly that only the outer-measure axioms consume countable choice, while the agreement clause does not, and that the covering cost of a single box already bounds the outer measure of that box from above.

items.title: Lebesgue measurable sets, the Lebesgue sigma-algebra $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, and Lebesgue measure $\lambda_n$
Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume
items.strategy: Carathéodory's theorem applied to Lebesgue outer measure gives the sigma-algebra and the complete measure. The extension theorem, applied to elementary volume, gives that every elementary set is Carathéodory measurable and that the restriction agrees with volume there. Note that every set of Lebesgue outer measure zero is measurable, which is the completeness clause, and check the boundary cases $\varnothing$ and $\mathbb R^n$.

items.title: Dyadic cubes of generation $k$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$
For each generation, the dyadic cubes of that generation are pairwise disjoint and cover $\mathbb{R}^n$
items.strategy: For $x\in\mathbb R^n$ and $k\in\mathbb N$ the integers $m_i$ with $m_i2^{-k}<x_i\le(m_i+1)2^{-k}$ exist and are unique, by the integer part applied to $2^kx_i$, so $x$ lies in exactly one generation-$k$ dyadic cube. Record the volume $2^{-kn}$ of each such cube from the box volume, and check $k=0$.

items.title: Two dyadic cubes are either disjoint or one contains the other
items.strategy: Let $Q$ have generation $k$ and $Q'$ generation $k'$ with $k\le k'$. By the partition lemma at generation $k'$, $Q$ is the disjoint union of the generation-$k'$ cubes it contains, so $Q'$ either is one of them, hence contained in $Q$, or is disjoint from all of them, hence from $Q$. Treat $k=k'$ through the same partition statement.

items.title: Every open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the union of a countable pairwise disjoint family of dyadic cubes
items.strategy: For open $U$ let $\mathcal D$ be the family of dyadic cubes contained in $U$ and let $\mathcal M$ be its maximal members under inclusion. Every $x\in U$ lies in some cube of $\mathcal D$, because a small enough generation puts the whole cube containing $x$ inside a ball inside $U$; the generations of the cubes of $\mathcal D$ containing $x$ are bounded below, so $x$ lies in a maximal one. Maximal cubes are pairwise disjoint by the nesting lemma, and the family of all dyadic cubes is countable, so $\mathcal M$ is countable. Check $U=\varnothing$, where the family is empty.

items.title: The sigma-algebra generated by the half-open boxes of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the Borel sigma-algebra
items.strategy: Every half-open box is Borel, being the intersection of the countably many open boxes obtained by pushing each finite lower parameter down by $1/m$ and intersecting with the open box on the upper parameters; hence the generated sigma-algebra is contained in the Borel sigma-algebra. Conversely every open set is a countable union of dyadic cubes, so the open sets lie in the generated sigma-algebra, and minimality of the Borel sigma-algebra over the open sets gives the reverse inclusion. The published generation theorem for rational half-open boxes gives the same conclusion by a second route and fixes the same $(a_i,b_i]$ convention.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable
items.strategy: The Lebesgue measurable sets form a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set, hence every half-open box; minimality of the sigma-algebra generated by the half-open boxes and its identification with the Borel sigma-algebra give the inclusion. State the inclusion as strict nowhere: the strictness is a separate matter settled on the companion page.

items.title: A box in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with parameters $a_i\le b_i$ is Lebesgue measurable of measure $\prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i)$, whichever of its faces are included
items.strategy: The half-open case is the extension clause. For the closed box $[a,b]$, write it as the decreasing intersection of the half-open boxes $(a-1/m\mathbf 1,b]$ and apply continuity from above, legitimate because the first of them has finite measure when the box is bounded; for the open box use the increasing union of $(a,b-1/m\mathbf 1]$ and continuity from below. Boxes with mixed faces sit between the open and closed ones and are squeezed. A box with $a_i=b_i$ for some $i$ has measure zero by the same squeeze, and unbounded boxes are handled by exhaustion with $(-R,R]^n$.

items.title: Lebesgue measure is sigma-finite, and every metrically bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ has finite outer measure
items.strategy: The cubes $(-k,k]^n$ increase to $\mathbb R^n$ and have finite measure, which is sigma-finiteness. A bounded set is contained in one of them by the comparison of the Euclidean and maximum metrics, so monotonicity of the outer measure bounds it. A compact set is bounded, hence of finite measure once it is known to be Borel.

items.title: Every at most countable subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue null; in particular $\lambda_1(\mathbb{Q})=0$
items.strategy: A singleton is the intersection of the boxes $(x-1/m\mathbf 1,x]$, hence Borel of measure at most $m^{-n}$ for every $m$, hence null. Countable subadditivity of the measure over an enumeration gives the general case, and the rationals are countable. State the singleton computation before the countable one so the index $m$ starts at $1$ and no reciprocal of zero appears.

items.title: A box with a degenerate side is Lebesgue null, and so is every coordinate hyperplane in $\mathbb{R}^n$
items.strategy: A box with $a_i=b_i$ has measure zero by the box theorem. The coordinate hyperplane $\{x:x_i=c\}$ is the countable union over $R\in\mathbb N$ of its intersections with $[-R,R]^n$, each contained in a closed box with $i$-th side degenerate, so each is null and the union is null by countable subadditivity. Cover $n=1$, where the hyperplane is a singleton.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, the Lebesgue outer measure of an arbitrary subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the infimum of the measures of the open sets containing it
items.strategy: One inequality is monotonicity. For the other, assume the outer measure finite, fix $\varepsilon>0$ and a countable elementary cover whose volume sum is within $\varepsilon$ of it; replace each cover set $E_k$ by the canonical enlargement $E_k^{+\delta_k}$ with $\delta_k$ the least reciprocal power of two making the volume increase at most $\varepsilon2^{-k}$, and take the union of the interiors. That union is open, contains the set, and countable subadditivity bounds its measure by the volume sum plus $2\varepsilon$. The infinite case is trivial because $\mathbb R^n$ is open.

items.title: Every subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ has a $G_\delta$ measurable hull of the same outer measure
items.strategy: Intersect open supersets whose measures decrease to the outer measure, obtained from outer regularity at the thresholds $\lambda^*(A)+1/m$ when that is finite and from $\mathbb R^n$ otherwise. The intersection is a $G_\delta$, hence Borel, contains the set, and has the same measure. Note that this exhibits Lebesgue outer measure as a regular outer measure in the sense of the measurable-hull definition, which the premeasure regularity theorem also gives.

items.title: For a Lebesgue measurable set and every positive $\varepsilon$ there is an open superset whose difference from it has outer measure below $\varepsilon$
items.strategy: If the set has finite measure, outer regularity supplies an open $U$ with $\lambda(U)\le\lambda(E)+\varepsilon$, and measurability plus finiteness turn this into $\lambda(U\setminus E)\le\varepsilon$ by the difference formula. In general split $E$ along the shells $(-k,k]^n\setminus(-(k-1),k-1]^n$, each piece of finite measure, apply the finite case with $\varepsilon2^{-k}$, and take the union of the open sets. The shell at $k=0$ is empty and must be handled, and the subtraction step is used only where the measure is finite.

items.title: A subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with open supersets of arbitrarily small excess is Lebesgue measurable
items.strategy: Take open $U_m\supseteq E$ with $\lambda^*(U_m\setminus E)<1/(m+1)$ and put $G:=\bigcap_m U_m$. Then $G$ is a $G_\delta$, hence Borel, hence measurable, and $G\setminus E\subseteq U_m\setminus E$ for every $m$, so $\lambda^*(G\setminus E)=0$ and $G\setminus E$ is measurable by completeness. Therefore $E=G\setminus(G\setminus E)$ is measurable. Index the $U_m$ from $m=0$ so the threshold $1/(m+1)$ is defined.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, four equivalent descriptions of a Lebesgue measurable subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$
items.strategy: Prove the cycle: measurable implies small open excess; small open excess implies the $G_\delta$-minus-null form, by the intersection built in the previous lemma; that form implies measurable, by completeness; and complementation converts the open-excess and $G_\delta$ forms into the closed-deficit and $F_\sigma$-plus-null forms. Each implication must be stated for sets of infinite measure as well, which is why the excess is measured by outer measure of the difference rather than by a difference of measures.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, the Lebesgue measure of a measurable set is the supremum of the measures of its compact subsets
items.strategy: The countable choice is inherited from the cited Littlewood theorem and is stated in the Statement rather than dropped, matching the design's ledger row for inner regularity. Littlewood's closed-deficit form gives closed $F\subseteq E$ with $\lambda^*(E\setminus F)$ small when $\lambda(E)$ is finite, and then $\lambda(F)$ is close to $\lambda(E)$. Intersecting $F$ with the closed balls of radius $R$ and using continuity from below replaces $F$ by a compact set, since $\mathbb R^n$ is sigma-compact and closed subsets of compact sets are compact. When $\lambda(E)=\infty$, apply the finite case to $E\cap(-k,k]^n$, whose measures increase to $\infty$ by continuity from below.

items.title: $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is exactly the completion of the restriction of $\lambda_n$ to the Borel sets
items.strategy: Elementary volume is a sigma-finite premeasure and the sigma-algebra generated by the elementary algebra is the Borel sigma-algebra, so the Carathéodory-domain theorem applies verbatim and identifies the Lebesgue sigma-algebra with the completion of the Borel restriction, the measures agreeing there. State the completion in the published sense, sets differing from a Borel set by a subset of a Borel null set.

items.title: Regularity of an outer measure and regularity of a measure with respect to open and compact sets are different conditions, both satisfied here
Countable covers by closed boxes, by open boxes and by closed cubes all compute Lebesgue outer measure
items.strategy: Each closed box is contained in a half-open box of volume as close to it as desired and contains one, and likewise for open boxes, so the three covering infima over boxes coincide with the infimum over half-open covers by an $\varepsilon2^{-k}$ adjustment termwise. For cubes, subdivide each box by a fine dyadic grid and enlarge the finitely many pieces meeting it to cubes of total volume at most the box volume plus $\varepsilon$; the reverse inequality is immediate because a cube is a box. Degenerate boxes have volume zero on both sides and must be included explicitly.

items.title: A subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has Lebesgue outer measure zero if and only if it has measure zero in the sense of countable closed-interval covers
items.strategy: The published definition asks, for every $\varepsilon>0$, for sequences $(a_k),(b_k)$ with $a_k\le b_k$, $A\subseteq\bigcup_k[a_k,b_k]$ and $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(b_k-a_k)$ convergent with sum at most $\varepsilon$; quote it in that form, with the index starting at $0$ and the intervals closed. Given such a cover, the closed-cover lemma bounds the Lebesgue outer measure by $\varepsilon$; conversely a half-open cover of small total volume yields closed intervals with the same endpoints and the same lengths. Handle degenerate intervals $a_k=b_k$, which are permitted on the published side and have length zero.

items.title: A subset of $\mathbb{R}^m$ has Lebesgue outer measure zero if and only if it is null in the sense of countable closed-cube covers
items.strategy: The published definition covers $E$ by a sequence of closed cubes whose volume series has sum at most $\varepsilon$. A cube cover is a box cover, so one direction is the closed-cover lemma; the other replaces each half-open box in a cheap cover by finitely many cubes of total volume within $\varepsilon2^{-k}$ of it, which is the cube clause of the same lemma. Quote the published definition exactly, including that the cubes are closed and that a cube of side length $0$ is permitted.

items.title: A property holding outside a set of elementary measure zero is exactly a property holding $\lambda$-almost everywhere
items.strategy: Combine the two agreement theorems with completeness: a set of elementary measure zero has Lebesgue outer measure zero, hence is measurable with measure zero, and conversely. Then the published almost-everywhere notion relative to $\lambda_n$, whose exceptional set must lie in a measurable null set, coincides with the covering formulation. Name both directions explicitly rather than asserting one.

items.title: A bounded function on a closed bounded interval, or on a closed nondegenerate rectangle, is Riemann integrable exactly when its discontinuity set has Lebesgue measure zero
items.strategy: Substitute the agreement theorems into Lebesgue's criterion and its $\mathbb R^m$ form, whose conclusions are stated with the covering notion of nullity. Repeat the choice ledger of the cited theorems rather than dropping it: the direction from integrability to nullity uses countable choice, the converse does not, and the substitution adds the countable choice already present in the construction of $\lambda$.

items.title: The published refutations separating nullity from nowhere density hold verbatim for Lebesgue measure
Lebesgue outer measure is at most Jordan outer content, and a bounded Jordan measurable set is Lebesgue measurable with Lebesgue measure equal to its Jordan content
items.strategy: A finite rectangle cover is a countable box cover, which gives the first inequality. For a Jordan measurable $E$, its boundary is null by the published boundary criterion, hence Lebesgue null by the agreement theorem, so $E$ differs from its interior by a null set and is measurable. A finite family of almost disjoint rectangles inside $E$ has Lebesgue measure equal to the sum of its volumes, because the pairwise intersections lie in degenerate boxes and are null, so the Jordan inner content is at most $\lambda_n(E)$; squeezing between inner and outer content gives equality. State the inequality direction for every bounded set, not only for Jordan measurable ones.

items.title: The Cantor set is an uncountable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ of Lebesgue measure zero
items.strategy: The published theorem gives that the Cantor set has measure zero in the covering sense and is uncountable; the agreement theorem turns the first clause into $\lambda_1(C)=0$. Say plainly that measure zero is not a countability condition, and cite the published uncountability clause rather than reproving it.

items.title: Lebesgue outer measure, Lebesgue measurability and Lebesgue measure are unchanged by translation
items.strategy: A translate of a half-open box is a half-open box of the same volume, so translation carries elementary sets to elementary sets preserving volume, and therefore carries covers to covers of the same cost; the outer measures of $A$ and $A+h$ are thus equal. Measurability transfers because the Carathéodory identity for $E+h$ tested against $A$ is the identity for $E$ tested against $A-h$. Conclude equality of measures on measurable sets, and record that no choice principle enters beyond that already used to build the outer measure.

items.title: For a nonzero real $c$, dilation by $c$ multiplies Lebesgue outer measure by $|c|^n$, and reflection in the origin preserves it
items.strategy: The image of a half-open box under $x\mapsto cx$ is a half-open box, with the parameters swapped when $c<0$ and with volume $|c|^n$ times the original, by the power laws. Covers therefore correspond with costs scaled by $|c|^n$, giving the identity for outer measures, and the Carathéodory test transports as in the translation theorem. Treat $c<0$ explicitly, so the reflection $c=-1$ is a case and not an afterthought, and note that $c=0$ is excluded because the image is then a single point.

items.title: A translation-invariant Borel measure giving the unit cube measure one gives each generation-$k$ dyadic cube measure $2^{-kn}$
items.strategy: The unit cube $(0,1]^n$ is the disjoint union of the generation-$k$ dyadic cubes it contains, and there are $2^{kn}$ of them, each a translate of $(0,2^{-k}]^n$ by a vector in $2^{-k}\mathbb Z^n$. Finite additivity and translation invariance give $1=2^{kn}\mu((0,2^{-k}]^n)$, and every generation-$k$ dyadic cube is a translate of $(0,2^{-k}]^n$. Verify the count by induction on $k$ and treat $k=0$.

items.title: A translation-invariant measure on the Borel sets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ giving the unit cube measure one is the restriction of Lebesgue measure
items.strategy: By the dyadic lemma such a $\mu$ agrees with $\lambda_n$ on every dyadic cube, and every open set is a countable disjoint union of dyadic cubes, so $\mu$ and $\lambda_n$ agree on the open sets. The open sets form a pi-system generating the Borel sigma-algebra, and the increasing open cubes $(-k,k)^n$ have equal finite measure and exhaust $\mathbb R^n$, so the published uniqueness theorem for a sigma-finite generating pi-system applies. Note that finiteness on bounded sets is a consequence of the normalisation and not an extra hypothesis.

items.title: An invertible linear map of $\mathbb{R}^n$ scales the Lebesgue measure of every Borel set by a positive constant depending only on the map
items.strategy: For invertible linear $T$ the map $E\mapsto\lambda_n(T[E])$ is defined on Borel sets, because $T$ is a homeomorphism and $T[E]$ is the preimage of $E$ under the continuous $T^{-1}$; it is a measure, and it is translation invariant since $T[E+h]=T[E]+T(h)$. Its value $c(T)$ on the unit cube is finite and positive, because $T[(0,1]^n]$ is bounded with nonempty interior. Dividing by $c(T)$ and applying the uniqueness theorem gives $\lambda_n(T[E])=c(T)\lambda_n(E)$, and composing gives $c(ST)=c(S)c(T)$.

items.title: A coordinate scaling and a coordinate transposition send the unit cube to a set of measure equal to the absolute value of the determinant
items.strategy: A coordinate transposition permutes the sides of $(0,1]^n$ and returns the same cube, while its matrix has determinant $-1$. A scaling of one coordinate by $c\ne0$ sends $(0,1]^n$ to a box with that side of length $|c|$ and the others of length $1$, of measure $|c|$, and its matrix has determinant $c$. Both matrices are elementary, and the published table of determinants under elementary row operations supplies the values; treat $c<0$, where the side becomes $[c,0)$ up to a reflection.

items.title: A shear sends the unit cube to a set of Lebesgue measure one
items.strategy: Let $T(x)=x+tx_je_i$ with $i\ne j$. For an integer $k$ put $A_k:=\{x\in(0,1]^n:x_i+tx_j\in(k,k+1]\}$; only finitely many $k$ give a nonempty $A_k$, each $A_k$ is Borel, and $x\mapsto T(x)-ke_i$ on $A_k$ assembles into a bijection of $(0,1]^n$ onto itself, since for each image point exactly one integer $k$ returns the $i$-th coordinate to $(0,1]$. The sets $T[A_k]-ke_i$ are therefore pairwise disjoint with union $(0,1]^n$, and translation invariance plus finite additivity give $\lambda_n(T[(0,1]^n])=1$. The determinant of the shear matrix is $1$.

items.title: A Lipschitz self-map of $\mathbb{R}^n$ carries Lebesgue null sets to Lebesgue null sets
items.strategy: Translate through the agreement theorem: a Lebesgue null set is null in the published cube-cover sense, the published theorem on Lipschitz images preserves that property, and the agreement theorem translates back. Record that the image is then measurable by completeness, which is what later uses need, and that the hypothesis is a Lipschitz map from $\mathbb R^n$ to itself.

items.title: Every affine hyperplane of $\mathbb{R}^n$, and hence every proper linear subspace, is Lebesgue null
items.strategy: Write the hyperplane $\{x:\sum_i u_ix_i=c\}$ with $u_j\ne0$ as the image of the coordinate hyperplane $\{x:x_j=0\}$ under the affine map that replaces the $j$-th coordinate by $(c-\sum_{i\ne j}u_ix_i)/u_j$; that map is Lipschitz, the coordinate hyperplane is null, and the Lipschitz lemma applies. A proper linear subspace is contained in a hyperplane through the origin, and nullity passes to subsets by completeness. The case $n=1$ is a singleton and is covered by the countable-set proposition.

items.title: A linear map $T$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ sends Lebesgue measurable sets to Lebesgue measurable sets, with $\lambda_n(T[E])=|\det T|\,\lambda_n(E)$ when $T$ is invertible and $T[E]$ Lebesgue null when it is not
items.strategy: For invertible $T$ the scaling constant $c$ is multiplicative and matches $|\det|$ on the elementary matrices by the two computation lemmas, so factoring $T$ into elementary matrices and using multiplicativity of the determinant gives $c(T)=|\det T|$. Extend from Borel sets to Lebesgue measurable sets through Littlewood's $F_\sigma$-plus-null form, the Lipschitz lemma handling the null part. When $\det T=0$ the image of $\mathbb R^n$ is a proper subspace, hence null, and the conclusion must be stated as nullity of $T[E]$ rather than as a product, because $|\det T|\lambda_n(E)$ is the undefined product $0\cdot(+\infty)$ when $\lambda_n(E)=\infty$.

items.title: Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is invariant under every orthogonal linear map
items.strategy: An orthogonal operator has determinant of absolute value one, by the published corollary on orthogonal and unitary operators, so the change-of-variables theorem gives $\lambda_n(T[E])=\lambda_n(E)$. Say that rotations are the orientation-preserving case and that reflections are covered too, without asserting anything about which matrices occur.

items.title: How the Lebesgue change-of-variables formula relates to the published formula for Jordan content
A measurable set of positive finite measure occupies more than any prescribed proportion of some dyadic cube
items.strategy: Given $\theta\in(0,1)$, outer regularity supplies an open $U\supseteq E$ with $\lambda_n(U)<\lambda_n(E)/\theta$, and $U$ is a countable disjoint union of dyadic cubes $Q_j$. If $\lambda_n(E\cap Q_j)\le\theta\lambda_n(Q_j)$ for every $j$, summing gives $\lambda_n(E)\le\theta\lambda_n(U)<\lambda_n(E)$, a contradiction. Hence some $j$ has $\lambda_n(E\cap Q_j)>\theta\lambda_n(Q_j)$; the hypothesis $\lambda_n(E)>0$ is what makes the strict inequality available and $\lambda_n(E)<\infty$ is what makes the division legitimate.

items.title: If a Lebesgue measurable subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ has positive measure, its difference set contains an open ball about the origin
items.strategy: Reduce to $0<\lambda_n(E)<\infty$ by intersecting with a large cube and using continuity from below. Apply the density lemma with $\theta=3/4$ to get a dyadic cube $Q$ of side $s$ with $\lambda_n(E\cap Q)>\tfrac34 s^n$, and set $\eta:=\tfrac12((3/2)^{1/n}-1)>0$. For $\|h\|_\infty<\eta s$ both $E\cap Q$ and its translate by $h$ lie in a box of side at most $(1+\eta)s$, whose measure $(1+\eta)^ns^n$ is below $2\cdot\tfrac34 s^n$, so the two sets meet and $h\in E-E$. Conclude with the comparison between the maximum and Euclidean metrics; the $n$-th root is the published rational power.

items.title: A Lebesgue measurable subgroup of $(\mathbb{R}^n,+)$ of positive measure is all of $\mathbb{R}^n$
items.strategy: If $\lambda_n(G)>0$ then some $G\cap(-k,k]^n$ has positive finite measure, so Steinhaus gives a ball $B(0,r)\subseteq (G\cap(-k,k]^n)-(G\cap(-k,k]^n)\subseteq G-G=G$. Every $x\in\mathbb R^n$ lies in $mB(0,r)$ for a large natural $m$, and $G$ is closed under addition, so $x\in G$. Note the contrapositive, that a proper measurable subgroup is null, which is the form the sources state.

pages.title: Lebesgue Measure on Euclidean Space — Examples

items.title: The Lebesgue measure of an interval, of a box, of $\mathbb{Q}$ and of the irrationals in $[0,1]$
items.strategy: Read off $\lambda_1([a,b])=b-a$ and $\lambda_n$ of a box from the box theorem, whichever faces are included. Then $\lambda_1(\mathbb Q)=0$ by countability, and additivity on the disjoint decomposition $[0,1]=(\mathbb Q\cap[0,1])\sqcup([0,1]\setminus\mathbb Q)$ gives the irrationals measure $1$. Include a degenerate interval and the empty box.

items.title: The complement of the Cantor set in $[0,1]$ has Lebesgue measure one, computed from the removed intervals
items.strategy: At stage $n$ the construction removes $2^n$ open intervals of length $3^{-n-1}$; the removed set is their countable disjoint union, so its measure is $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}2^n3^{-n-1}=1$ by the geometric series. Additivity on $[0,1]$ then returns $\lambda_1(C)=0$, agreeing with the corollary proved from the published covering statement. Index the stages from $0$ and check that the first stage removes one interval of length $1/3$.

items.title: The Smith-Volterra-Cantor set has Lebesgue measure exactly $1/2$
items.strategy: The published construction gives $S=\bigcap_nS_n$ with $S_n$ a disjoint union of $2^n$ closed intervals of common length $\lambda_n$, where $\lambda_0=1$ and $\lambda_{n+1}=(\lambda_n-4^{-n-1})/2$. Put $u_n:=2^n\lambda_n$; the recursion becomes $u_{n+1}=u_n-\tfrac14 2^{-n}$, so induction and the geometric series give $u_n=\tfrac12+2^{-n-1}$, and $\lambda_1(S_n)=u_n$ by additivity over the disjoint intervals. The sets $S_n$ decrease and $S_0$ has finite measure, so continuity from above gives $\lambda_1(S)=\tfrac12$. Say explicitly that the published theorem asserts only that $S$ is not null in the covering sense and that the exact value is new here, obtained because $\lambda_1$ is now available.

items.title: For every positive $\varepsilon$ there is a dense open subset of $(0,1)$ of Lebesgue measure below $\varepsilon$
