items.strategy: Enumerate $\mathbb Q\cap(0,1)$ as $(q_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ and take the union of the intervals $(q_k-\varepsilon2^{-k-3},q_k+\varepsilon2^{-k-3})$ intersected with $(0,1)$. The union is open and dense because it contains every rational of $(0,1)$, and countable subadditivity bounds its measure by $\sum_k\varepsilon2^{-k-2}=\varepsilon/2<\varepsilon$.

items.title: A dense $G_\delta$ subset of $\mathbb{R}$ of Lebesgue measure zero containing every rational, and its meager complement of full measure
items.strategy: Intersect the dense open sets of the previous example, taken on each interval $(m,m+1)$ with parameter $2^{-k}$, to get a dense $G_\delta$ containing $\mathbb Q$ whose measure is below every $2^{-k}$, hence zero. Its complement is a countable union of closed sets with empty interior, hence meager, and has full measure on every bounded interval. Relate this to the published counterexamples, which state the same phenomenon in the covering vocabulary.

items.title: The graph of a continuous function $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is Lebesgue null in $\mathbb{R}^2$
items.strategy: On each $[m,m+1]$ the function is uniformly continuous, so for a prescribed tolerance there is a uniform partition fine enough that every point of the graph above one subinterval stays within a narrow vertical strip about the left endpoint value. The resulting closed boxes cover the graph over $[m,m+1]$ with total area bounded by the chosen weight for that integer interval, and the weights are chosen summably over $m\in\mathbb Z$. Countable subadditivity then gives a null closed-box cover. Note that this does not settle the measurable case, which belongs with the product measures.

items.title: The Lebesgue measure of the image of the unit cube under an explicit linear map of the plane and of three-space
items.strategy: Take the plane map with matrix rows $(2,1)$ and $(1,3)$, of determinant $5$, and the three-space map with an explicit triangular matrix; the change-of-variables theorem gives the measures $5$ and the product of the diagonal entries in absolute value. Add a singular example whose determinant is zero and whose image is a line segment, hence null. Verify the determinants by row reduction rather than quoting them.

items.title: Every Lebesgue measurable proper subgroup of $(\mathbb{R},+)$ is null, and $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$ are instances
items.strategy: Contrapose the subgroup corollary: a measurable subgroup of positive measure is the whole line, so a proper measurable subgroup has measure zero. Check the two instances directly, both being countable, and note that the corollary says nothing about non-measurable subgroups.

items.title: $\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]$ is Lebesgue null and has Jordan outer content one
items.strategy: The set is countable, hence Lebesgue null. For the content, a finite family of closed intervals covering it has closed union, and that union contains the closure $[0,1]$ because the rationals are dense there, so the published bound on finite interval covers of an interval makes the total length at least $1$; the single interval $[0,1]$ realises $1$, so the Jordan outer content is exactly $1$. The witness therefore separates the countable-cover notion from the finite-cover notion at a single set, and the inner content is $0$, so the set is not Jordan measurable.

items.title: Lebesgue outer measure agrees with Jordan outer content on every bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$
items.strategy: The inequality holds in one direction, and the theorem on Jordan measurable sets makes the two agree there, which is what makes the false statement tempting. The refutation is $\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]$, of Lebesgue outer measure $0$ and Jordan outer content $1$. State exactly which hypothesis the true theorem carries and which the false statement drops.

items.title: A Lebesgue measurable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ with empty interior has measure zero
items.strategy: The Smith-Volterra-Cantor set is compact, nowhere dense, hence of empty interior, and has measure $1/2$. Present the refutation through the published nowhere-density clause and the exact measure computed on this page, and record that the false statement is true for open sets and for countable sets, which is where the intuition comes from.

items.title: Every translation-invariant measure on the Borel sets of $\mathbb{R}$ is a nonnegative multiple of Lebesgue measure
items.strategy: Counting measure restricted to the Borel sets is translation invariant and is not a multiple of $\lambda_1$, since it gives a singleton the value $1$ and $[0,1]$ the value $+\infty$, while $\lambda_1$ gives $0$ and $1$. The uniqueness theorem is not contradicted, because its hypothesis fixes the value $1$ on the unit cube and thereby forces finiteness on bounded sets. Name the dropped hypothesis explicitly.

items.title: Assuming the Axiom of Choice, every Lebesgue measurable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is a Borel set
items.strategy: The Cantor set is Lebesgue null and is in bijection with the power set of the naturals, so by completeness every one of its $2^{\mathfrak c}$ subsets is Lebesgue measurable, while the Borel sigma-algebra on $\mathbb R$ has cardinality $\mathfrak c$. Cantor's theorem gives $2^{\mathfrak c}>\mathfrak c$, so the two families differ. The refutation is a counting argument and exhibits no particular set; the explicit witness belongs with the non-measurable material.

pages.title: Non Measurable Sets and the Cost of Choice

items.title: Lebesgue inner measure on the real line
For bounded subsets of $\mathbb{R}$, Lebesgue measurability is equivalent to equality of inner and outer measure
items.strategy: For measurable sets, approximate from outside by open supersets and from inside by closed subsets using the published outer-regularity and Littlewood characterisations, then squeeze the two infima. For the converse, choose compact subsets and open supersets whose measures approach the common value and use the small open excess characterisation to recover measurability.

items.title: Vitali set on $[0,1]$
Assuming choice on the cosets of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$, a Vitali set in $[0,1]$ exists
items.strategy: Consider the partition of $[0,1]$ by intersections of the additive cosets of $\mathbb{Q}$ with $[0,1]$. Each class is nonempty, apply the Axiom of Choice to that family, and record explicitly that the family has cardinality continuum, so this is not a countable-choice argument.

items.title: Assuming the Axiom of Choice, a Vitali set is not Lebesgue measurable
items.strategy: Enumerate the rationals in $[-1,1]$, translate the Vitali set by those rationals, and use the selector property to show the translates are pairwise disjoint and cover $[0,1]$ while lying inside $[-1,2]$. Translation invariance and countable additivity then rule out both measure zero and positive measure.

items.title: Assuming the Axiom of Choice, no translation-invariant measure on $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R})$ is both finite and nonzero on $[0,1]$
items.strategy: Run the Vitali argument for an arbitrary measure defined on every subset of $\mathbb{R}$: a selector for the cosets of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $[0,1]$ yields countably many disjoint translates covering $[0,1]$ and contained in a bounded interval, contradicting either nullity or positive finiteness.

items.title: Every subset of $\mathbb{R}$ of positive Lebesgue outer measure contains a nonmeasurable subset
items.strategy: Intersect the given set with the rational translates of a fixed Vitali set. If every such intersection were measurable then each would have measure zero, because its difference set still avoids a neighbourhood of the origin and Steinhaus would fail. Countable subadditivity would then force the original set to have outer measure zero.

items.title: The map $x \mapsto x + c(x)$ is a homeomorphism from $[0,1]$ onto $[0,2]$
items.strategy: Continuity comes from the published continuity of the Cantor function. Strict increase is immediate from the positive contribution of the identity term plus monotonicity of the Cantor function. A continuous bijection from compact $[0,1]$ to Hausdorff $[0,2]$ is then a homeomorphism.

items.title: The homeomorphism $x \mapsto x + c(x)$ sends the Cantor set onto a compact set of Lebesgue measure $1$
items.strategy: Use the gap description of the Cantor function: on every complementary interval of the Cantor set the function is constant, so $x+c(x)$ acts there by translation and preserves interval length. The complement of the Cantor set has measure $1$ inside $[0,1]$, its image therefore has measure $1$ inside $[0,2]$, and the image of the Cantor set is the complementary compact set of measure $1$.

items.title: A continuous image of a Lebesgue measurable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ can be nonmeasurable
items.strategy: Take a nonmeasurable subset of the measure-one image of the Cantor set, pull it back through the homeomorphism to a subset of the Cantor set, and use completeness to make that pullback measurable. The same homeomorphism then sends a measurable set to a nonmeasurable one.

items.title: A continuous preimage of a Lebesgue measurable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ can be nonmeasurable
items.strategy: Use the same witness as in the preceding corollary, but apply the inverse homeomorphism. The measurable subset of the Cantor set stays measurable while its preimage under the inverse map is the chosen nonmeasurable subset of the measure-one image.

items.title: There is a Lebesgue measurable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ that is not Borel
items.strategy: Choose a nonmeasurable subset of the measure-one compact image of the Cantor set, and pull it back through the homeomorphism to a subset of the Cantor set; completeness makes that pullback measurable. If the pullback were Borel in $\mathbb{R}$, the subspace-trace theorem would make it Borel in the Cantor set, continuous-preimage closure applied to the inverse homeomorphism would make the chosen image Borel in the compact image, and the same trace theorem would make it Borel in $\mathbb{R}$, contradicting its nonmeasurability.

items.title: Bernstein subset of $\mathbb{R}$
Every nonempty perfect subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has the cardinality of the continuum
items.strategy: Recursively split a nonempty perfect set into nested rational subintervals, always keeping two disjoint perfect pieces, and thereby inject binary sequences into the set. Since the set is already a subset of $\mathbb{R}$, this gives matching injections with the continuum.

items.title: Assuming the real line can be well ordered, a Bernstein set exists
items.strategy: Well order the family of nonempty perfect subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ and the real line itself, then run a transfinite recursion of length continuum. At stage $\alpha$ pick one fresh point from the $\alpha$-th perfect set for the set itself and one fresh point for its complement; the previous theorem guarantees that fewer than continuum many earlier choices cannot exhaust a perfect set.

items.title: Every compact subset of a Bernstein set is countable
items.strategy: A compact subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is closed. If such a subset inside a Bernstein set were uncountable, the perfect-set theorem for closed sets would give it a nonempty perfect subset, contradicting the Bernstein condition.

items.title: A Bernstein set has inner measure $0$, and in every nondegenerate interval its intersection has full outer measure
items.strategy: Compact subsets of a Bernstein set are countable, hence null, so the inner measure is zero. For an interval $I$, if the outer measure of $B\cap I$ were smaller than $|I|$, outer regularity would produce an open set missing a closed subset of positive measure inside $I\setminus B$; that closed set would be uncountable and therefore contain a perfect subset, contradiction.

items.title: A Bernstein set is not Lebesgue measurable
items.strategy: Apply the bounded inner-versus-outer characterisation on a nondegenerate interval. The preceding theorem gives inner measure zero and outer measure equal to the interval length, so the two cannot agree.

items.title: A Lebesgue measurable subset of $[0,1]$ that is invariant under changing finitely many binary digits has measure $0$ or $1$
items.strategy: Every finite binary digit change is, away from the dyadic rationals, a piecewise translation by a dyadic rational, so it preserves Lebesgue measure. Use dyadic intervals to show that the relative measure of the set inside every generation-$n$ dyadic interval is the same, and then approximate an open superset to force that common density to equal the total measure.

items.title: A free ultrafilter on $\mathbb{N}$, viewed as a subset of $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ and hence of $[0,1]$, is not Lebesgue measurable
items.strategy: A free ultrafilter is invariant under finite modification, so the preceding zero-one lemma forces any measurable representative to have measure $0$ or $1$. Complementing a subset of $\mathbb{N}$ swaps an ultrafilter with its complement and is measure preserving, so a measurable ultrafilter would also have measure $1/2$, contradiction.

items.title: What the Vitali set, Bernstein sets and free ultrafilters cost in choice

pages.title: Non Measurable Sets and the Cost of Choice — Examples

items.title: The cosets of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$ meet $[0,1]$ in pairwise disjoint classes, and rational translates of a Vitali set count them
items.strategy: Work directly with the relation $x-y\in\mathbb Q$. Show that each real of $[0,1]$ differs by a rational in $[-1,1]$ from exactly one point of a Vitali selector, and that distinct rationals give disjoint translates.

items.title: The map $x \mapsto x+c(x)$ carries the Cantor set onto a compact set of Lebesgue measure $1$ inside $[0,2]$
items.strategy: Use the two A-page lemmas and compute the images of a few explicit gaps and Cantor points, so the homeomorphism route behind the measurable-but-not-Borel witness is concrete rather than schematic.

items.title: A Vitali set shows that not every subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is Lebesgue measurable
items.strategy: Use the A-page existence theorem and the nonmeasurability theorem together: the same object exists under choice and contradicts the claim immediately.

items.title: A Bernstein set is dense in every interval, has inner measure $0$, and is not Lebesgue measurable
items.strategy: Combine the Bernstein-existence theorem with the A-page measure theorem. Density comes from meeting every perfect subset of every nondegenerate closed interval, while the inner and outer measure conclusions are already established on the A page.

items.title: Two disjoint nonmeasurable subsets of $[0,1]$ can have the measurable union $[0,1]$
items.strategy: Take a Vitali set $V\subseteq[0,1]$ and its complement. The sets are disjoint, their union is measurable, and the complement cannot be measurable because otherwise the measurable difference $[0,1]\setminus([0,1]\setminus V)=V$ would be measurable.

items.title: Assuming Choice, a proper subgroup of $(\mathbb{R},+)$ can be nonmeasurable
items.strategy: Fix a Hamel basis and one basis vector. The kernel of the corresponding coefficient map is a proper additive subgroup, its rational translates cover $\mathbb{R}$, and measurable-proper-subgroup rigidity rules out both positive measure and measure zero.

items.title: FALSE: assuming the Axiom of Choice, every subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is Lebesgue measurable
items.strategy: Refute the claim with a Vitali set, and state explicitly that the choice assumption is part of the false statement because ZF + DC behaves differently, as the A-page ledger records.

items.title: FALSE: every continuous image of a Lebesgue measurable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is Lebesgue measurable
items.strategy: Use the measurable subset of the Cantor set constructed on the A page whose image under $x+c(x)$ is nonmeasurable.

items.title: FALSE: every continuous preimage of a Lebesgue measurable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is Lebesgue measurable
items.strategy: Use the inverse homeomorphism from the A page: it pulls a measurable subset of the Cantor set back to the chosen nonmeasurable subset of its positive-measure image.

items.title: FALSE: a dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$ of outer measure zero and a dense subset of full inner measure cannot both meet every open interval
items.strategy: Use the published facts that $mathbb Q$ is dense in $mathbb R$ and Lebesgue null. In any bounded nondegenerate interval its complement is also dense, has full Lebesgue measure there, and is measurable, so the bounded inner-versus-outer criterion makes its inner measure equal to the interval length. Thus $mathbb Q$ and its complement witness coexistence.

items.title: FALSE, relative to an inaccessible cardinal: ZF + DC proves that a nonmeasurable subset of $\mathbb{R}$ exists
items.strategy: Refute the claim with the published Solovay and Shelah remarks: relative to an inaccessible cardinal, ZF + DC is compatible with every set of reals being measurable, so DC alone cannot guarantee a nonmeasurable set.

pages.title: Lebesgue Stieltjes Measures and Distribution Functions

items.title: This page uses the nondecreasing, right-continuous, (a,b]-interval convention
A Borel measure on R that is finite on compact sets
The algebra of finite disjoint unions of half-open intervals in R with extended endpoints
The interval set function attached to a nondecreasing right-continuous function
The Stieltjes interval set function is finitely additive on the half-open interval algebra
items.strategy: Order all finite endpoints together with any needed infinite cuts, refine both h-interval decompositions to the common grid they determine, and telescope the interval increments across the adjacent cells. This isolates the representation-independence step from the sigma-additivity step that follows.

items.title: The Stieltjes interval set function is a premeasure
items.strategy: Use the previous proposition for finite additivity. For countable additivity when a disjoint union stays inside the algebra, reduce first to one target h-interval, obtain one inequality from finite additivity and nonnegativity, prove the reverse inequality on bounded intervals by the finite-cover argument, and then recover the ray and whole-line cases by truncation.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, a nondecreasing right-continuous function defines a Borel measure on R
items.strategy: Apply the published Caratheodory extension theorem to the premeasure on the half-open interval algebra, then identify the generated sigma-algebra with the Borel sigma-algebra on R. Keep the statement on intervals explicit: the resulting measure is characterized first on (a,b].

items.title: The interval data on (a,b] determines the Borel measure uniquely
items.strategy: The half-open intervals form a pi-system, and the unit intervals (n,n+1] give a sigma-finite exhaustion. Therefore two Borel measures that agree on every half-open interval agree on every Borel set by the published uniqueness theorem for sigma-finite pi-systems.

items.title: The distribution function of a Borel measure on R, normalized at 0
Assuming countable choice, finite-on-compacts Borel measures on R correspond to nondecreasing right-continuous functions modulo constants
items.strategy: Assuming countable choice, define F_mu by intervals relative to 0, use measure monotonicity and continuity from above to prove that F_mu is nondecreasing and right-continuous, and compare mu with the Stieltjes measure of F_mu on every half-open interval. Uniqueness then gives mu_{F_mu}=mu. Equality mu_F=mu_G is equivalent to equality of interval increments, which is exactly that F-G is constant.

items.title: An atom of a measure on R
Interval formulas and atoms for a Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure
items.strategy: Recover (a,b), [a,b), and [a,b] from (a,b] by countable unions and intersections and use one-sided limits of nondecreasing functions to convert the resulting endpoint terms into F(b-) and F(a-). The singleton formula follows by subtraction. An atom occurs exactly where the left jump F(a)-F(a-) is positive, and the jump set is countable by the published bounded-variation discontinuity theorem applied on compact truncations.

items.title: Lebesgue-Stieltjes measures on R are outer regular and inner regular by compact sets
items.strategy: Use coverings by open intervals to get outer regularity, first on arbitrary sets and then on Borel sets. For inner regularity, localize to bounded pieces E intersect (-n,n], approximate each bounded piece from inside by compact sets, and pass to the whole set by continuity from below. The argument follows the one-dimensional regularity proof for complete Stieltjes measures and keeps the compact truncation visible.

items.title: Lebesgue measure is the Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure of the identity function
items.strategy: The identity function x -> x is increasing and right-continuous, so it defines a Stieltjes measure. Both that measure and the published Lebesgue measure give length b-a to every half-open interval (a,b], hence they agree on Borel sets by the uniqueness theorem.

items.title: The Cantor measure
The Cantor measure is a singular atomless probability measure concentrated on the Cantor set
items.strategy: Use the Cantor function c with c(0)=0 and c(1)=1 to get total mass 1 on [0,1]. The point-mass formula and continuity of c show that every singleton has measure 0. The gap-constancy property of c makes every complementary gap of the Cantor set have measure 0, so the whole complement has measure 0. Because the Cantor set itself has Lebesgue measure 0, the measure is singular with respect to Lebesgue measure.

items.title: Every finite Borel measure on R splits as an atomic part plus an atomless part
items.strategy: Pass from the measure to its normalized distribution function F_mu. The previous jump theorem shows that the atoms are countable and their masses are exactly the positive jumps. Form the atomic part as the weighted Dirac sum over those masses and subtract it from mu. The remainder is still a finite Borel measure and has no atoms by construction.

items.title: FALSE: every nondecreasing function defines a Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure on Borel sets
items.strategy: Refute with the step function that is 0 for x at most 0 and 1 for x above 0. Then the shrinking intervals (0,1/n] all have measure 1, so countable additivity on their decreasing intersection would force 1 to equal 0. This is exactly the failure that right continuity rules out.

items.title: FALSE: a Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure always gives every singleton measure 0
items.strategy: Use the distribution function with one jump at 0. Its associated measure is the Dirac mass at 0, so the singleton {0} has measure 1. The point-mass formula identifies exactly why the claim fails: jumps create atoms.

items.title: FALSE: a Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure determines its distribution function uniquely
items.strategy: If G(x)=F(x)+c for a constant c, then G and F give the same interval increments and hence the same measure. Therefore a measure determines only the right-continuous nondecreasing function modulo constants; the normalization at 0 is what singles out one representative.

items.title: FALSE: every Borel measure on R is finite on compact sets
items.strategy: Counting measure on R is a Borel measure, but every infinite compact set such as [0,1] has infinite counting measure. Thus finiteness on compact sets is a real hypothesis in the correspondence theorem, not a consequence of being Borel.

items.title: FALSE: every atomless Borel measure on R is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure
items.strategy: The Cantor measure is atomless, but it is concentrated on the Cantor set, which has Lebesgue measure 0. Hence it is singular rather than absolutely continuous. This is the standard witness that atomless and absolutely continuous are different notions.

pages.title: Lebesgue Stieltjes Measures and Distribution Functions — Examples

items.title: The identity function generates Lebesgue measure
items.strategy: Compute the half-open interval increment of F(x)=x and appeal to the uniqueness theorem. Then verify the four interval formulas directly to make the convention tangible.

items.title: A single jump generates the Dirac mass at 0
items.strategy: Use the function that is 0 on x less than 0 and 1 on x at least 0. Its interval increments vanish away from 0 and equal 1 exactly when the interval crosses 0 from the left, so the associated measure is the Dirac mass at 0.

items.title: A step function generates a finite atomic measure
items.strategy: Choose a right-continuous step function with three jumps, compute the mass at each jump from the jump sizes, and write the measure as the corresponding weighted sum of Dirac masses.

items.title: Two different normalizations can give the same measure
items.strategy: Take G(x)=F(x)+c with c not equal to 0 and compare the interval increments term by term. The example is the concrete witness for the constant-difference ambiguity in the correspondence theorem.

items.title: The four interval formulas for a function with one jump
items.strategy: Use a function that is linear except for one jump, compute F(b)-F(a), F(b-)-F(a), F(b)-F(a-), and F(b-)-F(a-) where appropriate, and compare the answers for (a,b], (a,b), [a,b], and [a,b).

items.title: The Cantor measure lives on the Cantor set
items.strategy: Use the gap-constancy of the Cantor function to show that each complementary gap has measure 0, sum over the countably many gaps, and then record that the whole mass 1 sits on the Cantor set.

items.title: The arctangent distribution function generates a Borel probability measure
items.strategy: Use F(x)=arctan(x)/pi + 1/2, compute its limiting values at minus and plus infinity, and conclude from the interval formula that the total mass is 1. The example stops before any density calculation, which belongs later in the track.

items.title: Without right continuity the interval formula need not be countably additive
items.strategy: Take the left-continuous jump function at 0. Then the disjoint intervals (0,1/n] all receive mass 1 while their intersection is empty, so continuity from above and hence countable additivity fail. The witness is as concrete as possible because it defends a convention, not a deep theorem.

items.title: The Cantor measure is atomless but not absolutely continuous
items.strategy: Combine the atomless and singular clauses of the Cantor-measure proposition. Since the Cantor set has Lebesgue measure 0 but full Cantor measure, no density with respect to Lebesgue measure can exist.

pages.title: Measurable Functions and Simple Approximation

items.title: Measurability is relative to sigma-algebras on both domain and codomain
The Borel sigma-algebra on the extended real line
A measurable function between measurable spaces
An indicator function is measurable exactly when its set is measurable
items.strategy: Check the inverse image of the singleton {1} and the inverse images of the two Borel rays (-infinity,1/2) and (1/2,infinity). This is the basic dictionary between sets and measurable functions and will be used repeatedly on both pages.

items.title: Borel measurable and Lebesgue measurable functions on R^n
The positive and negative parts of a real-valued function
Simple functions and their canonical representation
The sigma-algebra generated by a measurable function
The convention 0 times infinity equals 0 is used only for pointwise products of measurable functions
To prove measurability it suffices to test a generating family in the codomain
items.strategy: For a fixed function f, the collection of codomain sets whose preimages are measurable is itself a sigma-algebra because inverse image commutes with complements and countable unions. If the generating family sits inside that sigma-algebra, minimality of the generated sigma-algebra finishes the proof.

items.title: Real-valued and extended-real-valued measurability can be checked on threshold sets
items.strategy: Use the generating-family theorem with the right rays (a,infinity], their left-ray complements, and the published generators of the Borel sigma-algebra on R. Then prove the rational-threshold version by approximating every real threshold from above and below with rationals.

items.title: Continuous functions are Borel measurable
items.strategy: A continuous map pulls back open sets to open sets, hence to Borel sets. The definition of Borel measurability is exactly that statement written in sigma-algebra language.

items.title: Monotone real functions are Borel measurable
items.strategy: For a nondecreasing function, each superlevel set {f>a} is an upper ray together with at most one endpoint, and the endpoint behavior is controlled by one-sided limits and jump discontinuities. Therefore every threshold set is Borel, and the threshold criterion gives measurability. The decreasing case reduces by negation.

items.title: A map into R^n is measurable exactly when each coordinate is measurable
items.strategy: The coordinate maps are continuous, so one direction is immediate by composition. For the converse, the rational boxes generate the Borel sigma-algebra on R^n, and the preimage of a box is a finite intersection of coordinate threshold preimages.

items.title: Composing with a Borel function preserves measurability
items.strategy: If g is Borel measurable and f is measurable, then for every Borel set B the preimage (g composed with f)^(-1)(B) equals f^(-1)(g^(-1)(B)). Because g^(-1)(B) is Borel, the right-hand side is measurable. Keep the codomain sigma-algebra explicit so the theorem does not overclaim to merely Lebesgue-measurable outer maps.

items.title: Arithmetic and lattice operations preserve measurability whenever they are defined
items.strategy: Use the rational decomposition {f+g>a} = union over rationals q of {f>q} intersect {g>a-q}; this is the chosen route because it avoids product sigma-algebras. Max, min, absolute value, and positive and negative parts come from threshold identities. For nonnegative products use {fg>a} = union over positive rationals q of {f>q} intersect {g>a/q}, then decompose general products into the four nonnegative pieces with the convention 0 times infinity equals 0.

items.title: Sequential suprema, infima, limsup, liminf, and pointwise limits of measurable functions are measurable
items.strategy: Write the threshold sets of sup_n f_n and inf_n f_n as countable unions and intersections of threshold sets of the individual functions. Then limsup and liminf are built from tail suprema and tail infima, and the set where a pointwise limit exists is exactly where limsup equals liminf. On that set the common value is measurable because it equals either extended-real limit function.

items.title: Every nonnegative measurable function is the increasing pointwise limit of explicit simple functions
items.strategy: Use the dyadic truncations obtained by partitioning the range into intervals [j 2^(-n),(j+1) 2^(-n)) below level n and a final truncation set {f>=n}. The threshold theorem makes each level set measurable, so every approximant is simple. Monotonicity and pointwise convergence are checked directly from the dyadic inequalities, and boundedness of f on a set gives uniform convergence there.

items.title: Every measurable real-valued function has simple approximations dominated by its absolute value
items.strategy: Apply the nonnegative approximation theorem to the positive and negative parts separately and subtract the resulting simple functions. The dominance bound follows because each approximation is monotone from below and the parts sum to the absolute value.

items.title: On a complete measure space, equality almost everywhere preserves measurability
items.strategy: If f=g off a null set N and f is measurable, then each threshold set of g is the union of a measurable piece outside N and a subset of N. Completeness makes every subset of N measurable, so the threshold criterion closes the proof. The same witness shows exactly why completeness is needed.

items.title: A function measurable for a completion is almost everywhere equal to one measurable for the original sigma-algebra
items.strategy: Start with the explicit simple approximants of a nonnegative completion-measurable function. Replace each completion-measurable level set by an original measurable set with null symmetric difference, producing original simple functions that agree almost everywhere with the old ones. Their pointwise limsup is original measurable, and the complete-space almost-everywhere theorem transfers the limit back to the given function. Apply this to positive and negative parts for the general real-valued case.

items.title: Doob-Dynkin factorization through the sigma-algebra generated by a function
items.strategy: First handle countably valued functions g by pulling each fiber back from the generating function f and disjointifying the corresponding codomain sets. For a general extended-real-valued g, approximate it uniformly by simple dyadic truncations, factor each truncation through f, and then define the codomain map h pointwise on the set where the approximants converge. The measurability of h comes from the measurable-limit theorem on the codomain side.

items.title: FALSE: if every level set of a real-valued function is measurable, then the function is measurable
items.strategy: Choose a nonmeasurable Vitali set V in [0,1] and define f(x)=x for x outside V and f(x)=x+2 for x in V. Every level set is empty or a singleton, hence measurable. However f^(-1)([2,3])=V, so f is not measurable.

items.title: FALSE: if the absolute value is measurable, then the function is measurable
items.strategy: Let V be a nonmeasurable Vitali set and define f to be 1 on V and -1 off V. Then |f| is the constant function 1, hence measurable, while f^(-1)((0,infinity))=V is not measurable.

items.title: FALSE: the supremum of an arbitrary family of measurable functions is always measurable
items.strategy: Let V be a nonmeasurable Vitali set and consider the family of measurable indicators {1_{{t}}} indexed by t in V. Their pointwise supremum is 1_V, which is not measurable. The theorem on suprema is therefore genuinely sequential, not arbitrary-family.

items.title: FALSE: equality almost everywhere with a measurable function always implies measurability
items.strategy: Work on the incomplete measure space (R,B(R),lambda restricted to B(R)). Let E be a Lebesgue measurable non-Borel subset of the Cantor set. Then chi_E equals 0 almost everywhere because E lies inside a null set, but chi_E is not Borel measurable. Thus completeness is a real hypothesis in the almost-everywhere theorem.

items.title: FALSE: composing a Lebesgue measurable function with a continuous map always preserves measurability
items.strategy: Use a Lebesgue measurable set E and a continuous map g whose preimage g^(-1)(E) is nonmeasurable. Then the indicator of E is Lebesgue measurable, but composing it with g gives the nonmeasurable indicator of g^(-1)(E). This is exactly why the outer function in the composition theorem must be Borel measurable, not merely Lebesgue measurable.

items.title: FALSE: a pointwise limit of continuous functions is continuous almost everywhere
items.strategy: Let K be a fat Cantor set. The distance-to-set functions x -> max(0,1-n d(x,K)) are continuous and converge pointwise to the indicator of K. That indicator is discontinuous at every boundary point of K, and the fat Cantor set has empty interior and positive measure, so the limit fails to be continuous on a set of positive measure.

pages.title: Measurable Functions and Simple Approximation — Examples

items.title: Indicator functions are the basic measurable functions
items.strategy: Compute the inverse images of the two relevant Borel values 0 and 1 and record exactly which measurable set controls each one.

items.title: A simple function written in canonical form
items.strategy: Start with a function described piecewise on overlapping measurable sets, merge equal values, and then rewrite it using distinct coefficients and disjoint level sets.

items.title: The Dirichlet function is Borel measurable and nowhere continuous
items.strategy: Its value-1 set Q is countable and hence Borel, so the indicator criterion gives Borel measurability. The published continuity-set theorem then supplies nowhere continuity.

items.title: The Cantor function is monotone, continuous, and Borel measurable
items.strategy: Use the published continuity of the Cantor function, then apply the general theorem that continuous maps have Borel preimages of Borel sets.

items.title: The dyadic simple approximants to x^2 on [0,2] for the first two levels
items.strategy: Apply the explicit dyadic formula from the approximation theorem with n=1 and n=2, tabulate the level sets, and compare the resulting step functions with x^2.

items.title: The sigma-algebra generated by an indicator function
items.strategy: For f=1_A, compute all inverse images of Borel subsets of R and show that only the four sets empty, A, A^c, and the whole space appear.

items.title: The sigma-algebra generated by a two-step simple function
items.strategy: Write the function in canonical form, list the preimages of the singleton value sets, and identify the sigma-algebra generated by those level sets.

items.title: A Lebesgue measurable function need not be Borel measurable
items.strategy: Take the indicator of a Lebesgue measurable non-Borel set. The indicator criterion turns the set-theoretic pathology into a function-theoretic one immediately.

items.title: An uncountable supremum of measurable indicators need not be measurable
items.strategy: Take the same family of singleton indicators used in the A-page false statement and compute its supremum as the indicator of the indexing Vitali set.

items.title: A continuous preimage can break Lebesgue measurability
items.strategy: Use the published continuous preimage pathology and rewrite it as an indicator-function composition so the failure is visible as a direct preimage calculation.

items.title: Almost-everywhere equality can fail to preserve measurability on an incomplete space
items.strategy: Use the indicator of the non-Borel measurable subset of the Cantor set and compare it with the zero function on the Borel measure space. The two agree almost everywhere but only one is measurable there.

items.title: A function can have measurable level sets without being measurable
items.strategy: Use the Vitali-set-based injection from the A-page false statement and compute both its singleton fibers and the nonmeasurable interval preimage that defeats measurability.

pages.title: The Lebesgue Integral and the Convergence Theorems

items.title: Extended-real-valued measurable functions
Nonnegative simple measurable functions
Closure properties of measurable functions used by the integral
items.strategy: Preimages of rays control sums and scalar multiples wherever the extended-real pointwise operations are defined. The same ray calculus handles positive and negative parts, products with indicators, countable infima, and monotone pointwise suprema.

items.title: Every nonnegative measurable function is the increasing limit of simple measurable functions
items.strategy: Use the dyadic truncations $2^{-n}\lfloor 2^n(f\wedge n)\rfloor$. They are simple, measurable, increase pointwise, and converge to $f$.

items.title: The integral of a nonnegative simple function
The simple integral is independent of the chosen representation
items.strategy: Refine two simple-function decompositions to a common measurable partition and compare the coefficient sums cell by cell. The $0\cdot\infty=0$ convention is consumed exactly when a zero coefficient multiplies an infinite-measure cell.

items.title: The simple integral is monotone, homogeneous, and additive
items.strategy: After a common refinement, additivity and homogeneity are coefficient algebra, and monotonicity is cellwise comparison of the refined coefficients.

items.title: The nonnegative Lebesgue integral
The nonnegative integral agrees with the simple integral on simple functions
items.strategy: A simple function is one of its own admissible simple minorants, and every competing minorant is bounded above by it coefficientwise.

items.title: Integral over a measurable subset
The indefinite integral of a nonnegative simple function is a measure
items.strategy: If $s=\sum c_j\chi_{E_j}$, then $A\mapsto\int_A s\,d\mu=\sum c_j\mu(A\cap E_j)$ is a finite nonnegative combination of measures.

items.title: Monotonicity and nonnegative homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
items.strategy: Monotonicity is immediate from the set of admissible simple minorants. For scaling, send simple minorants of $f$ to those of $cf$ and conversely.

items.title: Monotone convergence for the integral
items.strategy: The numbers $\int f_n$ increase and are bounded above by $\int f$. For the reverse inequality, fix simple $0\le s\le f$ and $c\in(0,1)$, use the simple-measure theorem on $A_n=\{f_n\ge cs\}$, and then let $c\uparrow1$.

items.title: Additivity of the nonnegative Lebesgue integral
items.strategy: Approximate the two summands from below by increasing simple sequences, add those sequences pointwise, and apply monotone convergence.

items.title: Beppo Levi's theorem for nonnegative series
items.strategy: Apply additivity to the partial sums $S_n=\sum_{k<n}f_k$ and then apply monotone convergence to $S_n\uparrow\sum_k f_k$.

items.title: The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure
items.strategy: For $A_n\uparrow A$, apply monotone convergence to $f\chi_{A_n}$. The simple-case measure statement and additivity then upgrade $A\mapsto\int_A f\,d\mu$ to a measure.

items.title: The measure with density $f$ relative to $\mu$
Integrating against a density agrees with integrating the product
items.strategy: First prove the identity for simple $g$, where it is coefficient bookkeeping against the measure $\nu(A)=\int_A f\,d\mu$. Then pass to general $g\ge0$ by increasing simple approximation and monotone convergence.

items.title: Fatou's lemma
items.strategy: Apply monotone convergence to $g_n=\inf_{k\ge n}f_k$.

items.title: Reverse Fatou's lemma under an integrable majorant
items.strategy: Apply Fatou's lemma to the nonnegative functions $g-f_n$ and rearrange the resulting inequality.

items.title: A nonnegative measurable function has integral $0$ exactly when it vanishes almost everywhere
items.strategy: If $\int f=0$, then for $E_n=\{f\ge 1/n\}$ the inequality $(1/n)\chi_{E_n}\le f$ forces $\mu(E_n)=0$. The converse is immediate because every admissible simple minorant is supported on a null set.

items.title: A nonnegative measurable function with finite integral is finite almost everywhere
items.strategy: The set $\{f=\infty\}$ is contained in $\bigcap_n\{f\ge n\}$, and each of those sets has measure at most $n^{-1}\int f$.

items.title: A nonnegative integral over a null set vanishes
items.strategy: If $\mu(E)=0$, then every simple minorant of $f\chi_E$ integrates to $0$ because every coefficient is multiplied by a null set.

items.title: Almost-everywhere monotone convergence
items.strategy: Modify the sequence on the null exceptional set and use the null-set integral corollary to compare the original and modified integrals.

items.title: Chebyshev-Markov inequality for the integral
items.strategy: For $t>0$, the pointwise inequality $t\chi_{\{f\ge t\}}\le f$ integrates to the desired bound.

items.title: Integrable real and complex functions, and their integrals
The class $L^1(\mu)$ of integrable functions
The Lebesgue integral is linear on $L^1(\mu)$
items.strategy: For real functions, expand positive and negative parts and use nonnegative additivity. For complex functions, apply the real statement to the real and imaginary parts.

items.title: Two integrable functions are equal almost everywhere exactly when all of their indefinite integrals agree
items.strategy: If $f=g$ almost everywhere, then $(f-g)\chi_A$ vanishes almost everywhere for every measurable $A$, so every indefinite integral is $0$. Conversely, if $\int_A(f-g)\,d\mu=0$ for every measurable $A$, apply the nonnegative zero-integral criterion to $(f-g)^+$ and $(f-g)^-$.

items.title: The modulus of an integral is bounded by the integral of the modulus
items.strategy: For real $f$, use $-|f|\le f\le |f|$. For complex $f$, rotate by $\alpha=\overline{\int f}/|\int f|$ and compare $\Re(\alpha f)$ with $|f|$.

items.title: Dominated convergence
items.strategy: Use Fatou on the nonnegative functions $2g-|f_n-f|$ to obtain $L^1$ convergence. Linearity and the integral triangle inequality then give convergence of the integrals, and this route works for complex-valued functions as well as real-valued ones.

items.title: Bounded convergence on a finite measure space
items.strategy: Dominate the sequence by the constant bound times $\chi_X$ and apply dominated convergence.

items.title: Integrable simple functions are dense in $L^1(\mu)$
items.strategy: Approximate the positive and negative parts from below by simple functions and apply dominated convergence to the error terms.

items.title: Absolute continuity of the integral
items.strategy: Truncate $|f|$ by $|f|\wedge n$, use monotone convergence to control the tail, and bound the truncated part by $n\mu(E)$.

items.title: The indefinite integral of an integrable function is countably additive on measurable sets
items.strategy: Write $f=f^+-f^-$ and use the measure property of the two nonnegative indefinite integrals on disjoint unions.

items.title: Continuity under the integral sign
items.strategy: For any sequence $t_n\to t_0$, apply dominated convergence to $x\mapsto f(x,t_n)$ under the fixed dominator.

items.title: Differentiation under the integral sign
items.strategy: Apply dominated convergence to the difference quotients and use the mean value theorem, together with the dominating bound on $\partial_t f$, to control them uniformly on compact parameter intervals.

items.title: Jensen's integral inequality for a probability measure
items.strategy: Take a supporting line to $\varphi$ at $\int f\,d\mu$, integrate its inequality against the probability measure, and use the normalization $\mu(X)=1$.

items.title: FALSE: monotone convergence holds without monotonicity
items.strategy: Use the spike sequence $f_n=n\chi_{(0,1/n)}$ on $(0,1)$: it converges pointwise to $0$ but every integral is $1$.

items.title: FALSE: Fatou's lemma is always an equality
items.strategy: Use the travelling-mass sequence $f_n=\chi_{[n,n+1]}$ on $\mathbb R$: the liminf is $0$, while every integral is $1$.

items.title: FALSE: dominated convergence holds without a dominating function
items.strategy: Again take $f_n=n\chi_{(0,1/n)}$ on $(0,1)$; the pointwise limit is $0$ but the integrals stay equal to $1$.

items.title: FALSE: a nonnegative measurable function with integral $0$ vanishes everywhere
items.strategy: Use the Dirichlet function $\chi_{\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]}$, whose Lebesgue integral is $0$ although it is positive on a dense set.

items.title: FALSE: pointwise limits of integrable functions are integrable
items.strategy: On $(\mathbb N,\mathcal P(\mathbb N),\#)$, let $f_n=\chi_{\{1,\dots,n\}}$; each $f_n$ is integrable but the pointwise limit $1$ is not.

items.title: FALSE: the Lebesgue integral extends linearly to all measurable functions
items.strategy: On $\mathbb R$ with Lebesgue measure, take $f=\chi_{[0,\infty)}$ and $g=-\chi_{[0,\infty)}$; then $f+g=0$ is integrable although neither summand is, so no linear extension can assign values to all three consistently.

items.title: FALSE: Jensen's inequality holds on an infinite measure space without normalization
items.strategy: On $(\mathbb N,\mathcal P(\mathbb N),\#)$, take $f=\chi_{\{1,2\}}$ and $\varphi(x)=x^2$; then $\varphi(\int f)=4>2=\int\varphi(f)$.

pages.title: The Lebesgue Integral and the Convergence Theorems — Examples

items.title: Integrating against counting measure recovers a series
items.strategy: Write the function as the increasing limit of its finite-support truncations and identify each truncated integral with the corresponding finite sum.

items.title: The Dirichlet function is positive on a dense set but has Lebesgue integral $0$
items.strategy: Its support is the countable set $\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]$, so the whole integral lives on a null set even though the function is positive at every rational point.

items.title: The exponential tail function is integrable by monotone truncation and geometric comparison
items.strategy: Approximate by $f_n=e^{-x}\chi_{[0,n]}$. On each interval $[k,k+1]$, one has $e^{-x}\le e^{-k}$, so interval measures and the geometric series bound the tails while monotone convergence identifies the limit.

items.title: The function $x^{-1/2}$ on $(0,1]$ is unbounded and integrable
items.strategy: Use the truncations $f_n(x)=\min\{x^{-1/2},n\}$. On the dyadic interval $(2^{-(k+1)},2^{-k}]$, one has $x^{-1/2}\le 2^{(k+1)/2}$, so the interval measure gives a convergent geometric bound on the total integral.

items.title: Integrating against a Dirac measure is evaluation at the point
items.strategy: Start from simple functions, where only the coefficient of the atom at $x_0$ survives, and then pass to general nonnegative and integrable functions.

items.title: Differentiating $\int_0^{\infty} e^{-tx}\sin x\,dx$ under the integral sign
items.strategy: Use the dominating function $xe^{-ax}$ on any compact parameter interval $[a,b]\subset(0,\infty)$ and differentiate under the integral sign. The resulting parameter integral is the standard starting point for the later closed-form evaluation, but the example's point here is the legal differentiation step itself.

items.title: Jensen's inequality yields the weighted AM-GM inequality
items.strategy: Apply Jensen to the convex function $\varphi(x)=-\log x$ on $(0,\infty)$ over a finite discrete probability space.

items.title: Fatou can be strict and domination can fail simultaneously
items.strategy: Use the spike sequence $f_n=n\chi_{(0,1/n)}$ on $(0,1)$: the pointwise limit is $0$, the liminf integral is $0$, and every integral is $1$.

items.title: A pointwise limit of integrable functions need not be integrable
items.strategy: On counting measure, the indicators of the initial segments $\{1,\dots,n\}$ converge pointwise to the constant function $1$, which has infinite integral.

items.title: Mass can escape to infinity under pointwise convergence
items.strategy: The travelling indicators $\chi_{[n,n+1]}$ converge pointwise to $0$ on $\mathbb R$, but every integral stays equal to $1$.

items.title: Uniform convergence does not force convergence of integrals on an infinite-measure space
items.strategy: The functions $f_n=n^{-1}\chi_{[0,n]}$ converge uniformly to $0$ on $\mathbb R$, but every integral is $1$.

items.title: A decreasing sequence need not satisfy a monotone convergence theorem without an integrable start
items.strategy: The indicators $\chi_{[n,\infty)}$ decrease pointwise to $0$ on $\mathbb R$, but each integral is infinite.

items.title: Linearity can fail without an integrability hypothesis
items.strategy: Take $f=\chi_{[0,\infty)}$ and $g=-\chi_{[0,\infty)}$ on $\mathbb R$; then $f+g=0$ is integrable although neither $f$ nor $g$ is.

items.title: Jensen's inequality can fail on an infinite measure space without normalization
items.strategy: On counting measure over $\mathbb N$, let $f=\chi_{\{1,2\}}$ and $\varphi(x)=x^2$; then $\varphi(\int f)=4$ while $\int\varphi(f)=2$.

pages.title: The Lebesgue and Riemann Integrals Compared

items.title: A bounded Riemann integrable function admits Borel Darboux envelopes with zero integral gap
items.strategy: Choose a nested sequence of partitions whose upper and lower Darboux sums converge to the common Riemann value. The associated lower and upper step functions are Borel, monotone under refinement, and have Lebesgue integrals equal to those Darboux sums. Their pointwise supremum and infimum are therefore Borel envelopes with integral gap zero.

items.title: A bounded Riemann integrable function on a closed bounded interval is Lebesgue measurable and has the same integral
items.strategy: Use the Borel Darboux envelopes from the preceding lemma. Their difference has nonnegative integral zero, so they agree almost everywhere; the bounded function between them is therefore almost everywhere equal to a Borel function and is measurable because Lebesgue measure is complete. Boundedness on a finite interval gives integrability, and almost-everywhere equality identifies the Lebesgue integral with the common Darboux-Riemann value.

items.title: A Riemann integrable function on a closed bounded interval is almost everywhere equal to a Borel function
items.strategy: The envelope lemma already produces Borel lower and upper envelopes whose difference has integral zero. The zero-integral criterion makes the envelopes equal almost everywhere, and the original function lies between them, so it agrees almost everywhere with either Borel envelope.

items.title: Arzela's bounded convergence theorem for Riemann integrals
items.strategy: Convert each Riemann integrable function, and the Riemann integrable pointwise limit, into Lebesgue-integrable functions with the same values on the same interval. The common uniform bound makes the sequence dominated by an integrable constant on a finite-measure space, so bounded convergence gives convergence of the Lebesgue integrals, hence of the Riemann integrals.

items.title: A nonnegative improper Riemann integral on a half-line agrees with the Lebesgue integral
items.strategy: For $R > a$, truncate $f$ to $[a,R]$. Each truncation is Riemann integrable and therefore Lebesgue integrable with the same value on that compact interval. The truncations increase pointwise to $f$, so monotone convergence passes the Lebesgue integrals to the limit, which is exactly the improper Riemann integral when that finite limit exists.

items.title: For a continuous integrand, the Riemann-Stieltjes and Lebesgue-Stieltjes integrals agree
items.strategy: Let $F$ be nondecreasing and right-continuous on $\mathbb{R}$, with Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure $\mu_F$. A continuous integrand on $[a,b]$ is Borel measurable, and the lower and upper Stieltjes sums for a partition are exactly the Lebesgue integrals of the associated lower and upper step functions over $(a,b]$, because $\mu_F((x_{i-1},x_i]) = F(x_i)-F(x_{i-1})$. The Stieltjes Darboux criterion squeezes the Lebesgue-Stieltjes integral between those sums and forces equality with the mesh-limit Riemann-Stieltjes integral.

pages.title: The Lebesgue and Riemann Integrals Compared — Examples

items.title: The indicator of the rationals in $[0,1]$ is Lebesgue integrable with integral $0$ and not Riemann integrable
items.strategy: Use the published continuity-set description of the Dirichlet function together with the nullity of countable sets, the zero-a.e. criterion for the Lebesgue integral, and Lebesgue's criterion for Riemann integrability. This gives the side-by-side comparison without appealing to a separate examples page.

items.title: FALSE: every Riemann integrable function on a closed bounded interval is Borel measurable
items.strategy: Rebuild the MT-5 Hunter witness: choose a nonmeasurable subset $N$ of the positive-measure compact image $\psi[C]$ of the Cantor set and pull it back through $\psi(x)=x+c(x)$ to a Lebesgue measurable non-Borel set $E\subseteq C$. The indicator $\mathbf{1}_E$ on $[0,1]$ is continuous off the closed Cantor set, so its discontinuity set lies in the Lebesgue-null set $C$ and the published Lebesgue criterion makes it Riemann integrable. If $\mathbf{1}_E$ were Borel measurable, then $E=\mathbf{1}_E^{-1}((1/2,\infty))$ would be Borel in $[0,1]$, hence Borel in $\mathbb{R}$ by the subspace-trace theorem since $[0,1]$ is closed, contradiction.

items.title: An open dense set of measure less than $1$ is the monotone $L^1$-limit of Riemann integrable indicators, but its indicator is not Riemann integrable
items.strategy: Enumerate $\mathbb Q\cap(0,1)$ and surround its $k$th term by an open interval of length at most $2^{-k-3}$. Their union $U$ is open and dense, while countable subadditivity and the geometric series give $\lambda(U)<1$. Let $U_n$ be the union of the first $n$ intervals. Each indicator $\mathbf 1_{U_n}$ has only finitely many discontinuities, the sequence increases pointwise to $\mathbf 1_U$, and continuity from below gives $L^1$ convergence. Since $U$ is dense and its positive-measure complement is closed, $\partial U$ has positive measure, so the Lebesgue criterion rules out Riemann integrability of $\mathbf 1_U$.

items.title: The sine integral is improperly Riemann integrable and not Lebesgue integrable
items.strategy: Use Dirichlet's test to obtain convergence of the improper integral of sin x / x, and use the published uniform-tail-mass criterion to show that its absolute integral diverges. Then the Lebesgue integral does not exist although the improper Riemann integral does.

items.title: The indicator of a fat Cantor set is upper semicontinuous and equal almost everywhere to no Riemann integrable function
items.strategy: Take the indicator of the Smith-Volterra-Cantor set. Closed-set indicators are upper semicontinuous, and the set has positive measure. If a function agrees with this indicator almost everywhere, then its disagreement set is null; every neighborhood of every point of the positive-measure set left after removing that null set still contains points outside the Cantor set and outside the null set, so the modified function remains discontinuous on a positive-measure set and cannot be Riemann integrable.

items.title: A null set can fail to be the discontinuity set of any function
items.strategy: Enumerate the rationals as $(q_j)$. For each $k$, let $U_k$ be the union of intervals about $q_j$ whose lengths sum to at most $2^{-k}$. Each $U_k$ is open and dense, and $G=\bigcap_k U_k$ is therefore a dense $G_\delta$ by Baire; monotonicity gives $\lambda(G)\le 2^{-k}$ for every $k$, hence $G$ is null. If $G$ were a function's discontinuity set, the $F_\sigma$ theorem would write it as a countable union of closed null sets. Each has empty interior, making $G$ meager, while its dense $G_\delta$ presentation makes it residual, a contradiction to Baire category.

pages.title: Modes of Convergence Egorov and Lusin

items.title: Convergence almost everywhere relative to a measure
Convergence in measure
Cauchy sequences in measure
Almost uniform convergence
Convergence in L^1(mu)
Convergence in measure determines the limit almost everywhere
items.strategy: If f_n converges in measure to both f and g, then the set {|f-g| > epsilon} sits inside the union of the two bad sets {|f_n-f| > epsilon/2} and {|f_n-g| > epsilon/2}. Let n tend to infinity and then let epsilon descend through 1/m.

items.title: Convergence in L^1(mu) implies convergence in measure
items.strategy: Apply the Chebyshev-Markov inequality to |f_n - f| at threshold epsilon. The measure of the bad set is bounded by epsilon^{-1} times the L^1 error.

items.title: FALSE: convergence in L^1(mu) forces almost-everywhere convergence
items.strategy: Use the typewriter sequence on [0,1]: its L^1 norm tends to zero because the interval lengths go to zero, but each point is hit infinitely often and missed infinitely often.

items.title: Almost uniform convergence implies almost-everywhere convergence and convergence in measure
items.strategy: Intersect the complements of epsilon 2^{-m}-exceptional sets to get a full-measure set of pointwise convergence, and for a fixed threshold split each bad set into a small exceptional set plus the uniform tail.

items.title: On a finite measure space, almost-everywhere convergence implies convergence in measure
items.strategy: For a fixed epsilon, the tail bad sets {|f_n - f| > epsilon} decrease to a null set. Continuity from above turns the finite total measure hypothesis into vanishing measures of those bad sets.

items.title: FALSE: almost-everywhere convergence implies convergence in measure on every measure space
items.strategy: Use the translates of the unit interval on the real line: they converge pointwise almost everywhere to zero, but the bad set at threshold 1/2 always has measure 1.

items.title: On a finite measure space, the truncated L^1 metric metrises convergence in measure
items.strategy: For d(f,g) = integral min{|f-g|,1} dmu, the lower bound epsilon mu(|f-g| > epsilon) <= d gives one direction, while splitting the integral over {|f-g| <= epsilon} and its complement gives the reverse implication on finite total measure.

items.title: Riesz's subsequence theorem for convergence in measure
items.strategy: Choose the least n_k so that mu(|f_n - f| > 2^{-k}) < 2^{-k} for all n >= n_k. The tail unions have summable measures, their limsup is null by continuity from above, and outside it the chosen subsequence is eventually 2^{-k}-close to f.

items.title: Convergence in L^1(mu) has an almost-everywhere convergent subsequence
items.strategy: Compose L^1 convergence implies convergence in measure with Riesz's subsequence theorem.

items.title: FALSE: convergence in measure implies almost-everywhere convergence
items.strategy: Use the typewriter sequence: the interval lengths shrink so the bad-set measures vanish, but no pointwise limit exists at any point of [0,1].

items.title: Cauchy sequences in measure converge in measure
items.strategy: Choose a rapidly Cauchy subsequence, apply the same tail-union argument as in Riesz to get an almost-everywhere limit, and use the Cauchy condition to pull the whole sequence to that limit in measure.

items.title: Egorov's theorem
items.strategy: For each accuracy level 1/m, the tail bad sets E_{k,m} = union_{j >= k} {|f_j - f| > 1/m} decrease to a null set. Continuity from above is the exact place where finite total measure is used, and the least index k(m) with mu(E_{k(m),m}) < epsilon 2^{-m} produces almost uniform convergence without choice.

items.title: FALSE: Egorov's theorem holds on every measure space
items.strategy: The translates chi_[n,n+1] converge pointwise to zero on the real line, but any set whose complement has finite measure still meets infinitely many full translates, so the convergence is never uniform there.

items.title: On a finite measure space, convergence in measure has an almost-uniformly convergent subsequence
items.strategy: Apply Riesz's subsequence theorem to get almost-everywhere convergence and then apply Egorov on the finite measure space.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, simple functions are continuous on a large closed core
items.strategy: Write the simple function in canonical form. Approximate each measurable level set from inside by a closed set with tiny deficit, and on the resulting closed union each level set is clopen in the subspace, so the restriction is continuous.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, simple approximants to a measurable function can be made uniformly convergent on a large closed set
items.strategy: Take dominated simple approximants to f, use Egorov to get uniform convergence off a small measurable set, then take a closed subset of that good set with almost the same measure and intersect with the closed cores on which each simple approximant is continuous.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, Lusin's theorem on finite-measure subsets of R^n
items.strategy: First reduce to bounded measurable functions by truncating on a large-measure set where |f| is bounded. Then apply the uniform simple-approximation lemma and pass continuity of the restriction through the uniform limit on the closed core.

items.title: Assuming countable choice and dependent choice, a measurable function on a finite-measure subset of R^n agrees there, off a small set, with a continuous function on R^n
items.strategy: Take the closed core from Lusin and extend the restriction by Tietze.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, on a bounded measurable set, Lusin's closed core can be chosen compact
items.strategy: The closed core from Lusin sits inside a bounded subset of R^n, hence Heine-Borel makes it compact.

items.title: FALSE: assuming countable choice, Lusin's theorem says measurable functions are continuous off a null set
items.strategy: The Dirichlet indicator of the irrationals is nowhere continuous, but on a large closed set avoiding a small open cover of the rationals its restriction is constant.

items.title: A uniformly integrable family
On a finite measure space, uniform integrability is equivalent to L^1-boundedness plus uniform absolute continuity
items.strategy: Tail control gives a uniform L^1 bound by splitting at one large cutoff, and then small sets are controlled by the bounded part plus the common tail. Conversely, combine the uniform absolute continuity with one large cutoff and the L^1 bound to control the large-value tails.

items.title: Dominated families are uniformly integrable
items.strategy: Use the integrable majorant g. Its tails control the large-value sets {|f| > M}, and absolute continuity of the integral for g gives the small-set bound used later.

items.title: FALSE: uniform integrability implies domination by one integrable function
items.strategy: Use a uniformly integrable family of disjoint spikes whose tail integrals tend to zero but whose pointwise supremum has divergent integral, so no single integrable majorant can dominate them all.

items.title: A tight family of integrable functions
Vitali convergence theorem on finite and sigma-finite measure spaces
items.strategy: For finite measure, combine convergence in measure with uniform integrability by splitting into a small-value part and a small-measure bad set, using a subsequence only to identify the limit. For the sigma-finite form, tightness first traps almost all mass inside one finite-measure set, where the finite version applies.

items.title: Dominated convergence is a corollary of Vitali's theorem
items.strategy: A dominating integrable function makes the sequence uniformly integrable, and on sigma-finite spaces its own tails also supply tightness. Finite-measure convergence in measure on the trapped core plus small tails then feed the general Vitali theorem.

items.title: Implication table for the main modes of convergence on a finite measure space
items.strategy: Record exactly which implications among almost-everywhere, almost uniform, in measure, and L^1 convergence are proved on this page, and point each failed arrow to the specific witness item that refutes it.

pages.title: Modes of Convergence Egorov and Lusin — Examples

items.title: The typewriter sequence converges in measure and in L^1 but nowhere pointwise
items.strategy: Write the n-th term as the indicator of one dyadic interval in generation k, where the interval length is 2^{-k}. The bad-set measures and the L^1 norms are therefore 2^{-k}, while every point of [0,1] is visited infinitely often and omitted infinitely often.

items.title: The leftmost dyadic intervals give an explicit almost-everywhere Riesz subsequence
items.strategy: Take the first interval in each dyadic generation. Its supports shrink to {0}, so the subsequence converges to zero at every x > 0 and therefore almost everywhere; on [delta,1] it is eventually identically zero, so the convergence is even almost uniform.

items.title: The translates of the unit interval converge almost everywhere to zero but not in measure
items.strategy: For each fixed x, only finitely many translates [n,n+1] contain x, so the values eventually vanish. But for every n the bad set {|f_n| > 1/2} is exactly [n,n+1], which has measure 1.

items.title: The translated unit intervals show that Egorov needs finite total measure
items.strategy: Let f_n = chi_[n,n+1] on the real line. If a measurable set F has finite-measure complement, then infinitely many whole intervals [n,n+1] still meet F, so sup_{x in F} |f_n(x)| stays 1 infinitely often and the convergence is never uniform on F.

items.title: The spikes k chi_(0,1/k) converge almost everywhere and in measure to zero but not in L^1
items.strategy: Away from 0 the supports are eventually empty, and the bad set at threshold epsilon is (0,1/k) once k > epsilon. But every L^1 norm is 1, and the same tail computation shows the family is not uniformly integrable.

items.title: Egorov for x^k on the unit interval
items.strategy: Fix epsilon > 0 and remove the interval (1 - epsilon, 1]. On the closed core [0,1-epsilon] one has x^k <= (1-epsilon)^k for every x, so the convergence to zero is uniform there and the exceptional set has the prescribed measure.

items.title: The Dirichlet function satisfies Lusin's conclusion without being continuous anywhere
items.strategy: Enumerate the rationals in [0,1] and cover the j-th rational by an open interval of length less than epsilon 2^{-j-1}. Their union U has measure less than epsilon, its complement F is closed, and the indicator of the rationals restricts to the constant zero function on F.

items.title: A uniformly integrable family need not admit a single integrable majorant
items.strategy: Choose pairwise disjoint intervals I_k inside [0,1] with length 1/k^2 and set f_k = k chi_{I_k}. The tail integrals are at most 1/k above level k, so the family is uniformly integrable, but any pointwise majorant dominates the disjoint sum sum_k k chi_{I_k}, whose integral is the harmonic series.

pages.title: Product Measures and the Fubini Tonelli Theorems

items.title: Measurable rectangles in a product of measurable spaces
The product $\sigma$-algebra and its finite iterates
Finite disjoint unions of measurable rectangles form an algebra generating the product $\sigma$-algebra
items.strategy: Use the rectangle intersection and complement formulas to show that finite unions of measurable rectangles form an algebra. Then disjointify any finite union by the usual refinement into intersection cells, and note that adjoining finite unions does not change the generated $\sigma$-algebra.

items.title: The product measure can also be constructed from the rectangle algebra by Caratheodory extension
Sections $E_x$, $E^y$, $f_x$, and $f^y$ on a product
Every section of a product-measurable set is measurable
items.strategy: Let $\mathcal M$ be the class of subsets of $X \times Y$ whose horizontal and vertical sections are measurable. Rectangle sections are measurable, and the section formulas commute with complements and countable unions. Thus $\mathcal M$ is a $\sigma$-algebra containing the measurable rectangles, so it contains the whole product $\sigma$-algebra.

items.title: Every section of a product-measurable function is measurable
items.strategy: Test measurability against a generating family of Borel subsets of the codomain. The preimage of each such generator under a fixed section is the corresponding section of a product-measurable subset of $X \times Y$, so the previous theorem applies.

items.title: FALSE: if every horizontal and vertical section is measurable, then the set is product-measurable
items.strategy: Use a classical set in $[0,1]^2$ whose horizontal sections are countable and whose vertical sections are cocountable, while the set itself is not measurable in the product $\sigma$-algebra. The witness shows that sectionwise measurability is genuinely weaker than joint measurability.

items.title: For $\sigma$-finite measures, the section-measure functions are measurable
items.strategy: First handle indicator functions of measurable rectangles, then finite disjoint unions of rectangles, and then the monotone class generated by that algebra. Sigma-finiteness is used to exhaust the factors by finite-measure pieces so that the monotone class argument starts from finite values.

items.title: For $\sigma$-finite measures, the two section-measure integrals of a measurable set agree
items.strategy: Verify the equality on measurable rectangles, extend it to finite disjoint unions by additivity, and then pass to the monotone class of measurable sets for which the equality holds. Monotone convergence upgrades the equality from indicators to arbitrary increasing unions inside the exhaustion by finite-measure rectangles.

items.title: The product measure of two $\sigma$-finite measure spaces
For $\sigma$-finite factors, the product measure exists, has the rectangle formula, is $\sigma$-finite, and is unique
items.strategy: Define $(\mu \times \nu)(E)$ by the common value of the two section-measure integrals. Indicator functions on rectangles give the rectangle formula, additivity on measurable unions gives the measure axioms, and exhaustions by finite-measure sets make the product $\sigma$-finite. Uniqueness follows from the published theorem for measures agreeing on a $\sigma$-finite generating $\pi$-system.

items.title: FALSE: the rectangle formula determines a unique product measure without any $\sigma$-finiteness hypothesis
items.strategy: Use Lebesgue measure on one copy of $[0,1]$ and counting measure on the other. The usual primitive product and the locally determined product agree on measurable rectangles but assign different values to the diagonal, so uniqueness fails exactly when the $\sigma$-finite hypothesis is removed.

items.title: Tonelli's theorem for nonnegative measurable functions on a $\sigma$-finite product
items.strategy: Start from indicators of measurable sets, where the statement is the section-measure theorem. Extend to nonnegative simple functions by linearity, and then to arbitrary nonnegative measurable functions by increasing simple approximation and monotone convergence.

items.title: FALSE: Tonelli's theorem still holds without any $\sigma$-finiteness hypothesis
items.strategy: Take Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$ and counting measure on the other factor, and test Tonelli on the indicator of the diagonal. One iterated integral is $1$ while the other is $0$, so the Tonelli equality fails once the counting-measure factor is not $\sigma$-finite.

items.title: Fubini's theorem for $L^1$ functions on a $\sigma$-finite product
items.strategy: Apply Tonelli to $|f|$ to obtain almost-everywhere integrability of the sections and integrability of the section-integral functions. Then decompose $f$ into real and imaginary, or positive and negative, parts and use linearity to recover the signed statement.

items.title: To use Fubini safely, first use Tonelli on $|f|$
The completed product measure
Tonelli and Fubini for the completed product, with only almost-everywhere section measurability
items.strategy: Represent a completed-product measurable function by a base measurable representative that agrees almost everywhere. Apply the uncompleted theorem to that representative, then transport the conclusion back across almost-everywhere equality. The pointwise section statements weaken to almost-everywhere statements because the null exceptional set can meet some sections completely.

items.title: FALSE: every section of a completed-product measurable function is measurable
items.strategy: Take the indicator of a subset of a product-null line whose exceptional section is a nonmeasurable set. The function is measurable for the completion because it is supported on a null set, but the offending section is not measurable for the original factor measure.

items.title: The Borel product of $\mathbb R^m$ and $\mathbb R^n$ is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$
items.strategy: Use the identification $\mathbb R^{m+n} = \mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n$. Rational boxes generate the Euclidean Borel $\sigma$-algebra, so one inclusion is immediate. For the converse, second countability lets every open subset of the product be a countable union of open rectangles, placing every open set in the product $\sigma$-algebra.

items.title: The equality $\mathcal B(X) \otimes \mathcal B(Y) = \mathcal B(X \times Y)$ needs second countability
On Borel subsets of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$, the product $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ agrees with $\lambda_{m+n}$
items.strategy: Transfer the product measure to the Euclidean Borel $\sigma$-algebra through the previous identification. Both measures are Borel, $\sigma$-finite, and translation invariant, and they agree on rational half-open boxes because both compute their value as the product of side lengths. Uniqueness of normalized translation-invariant Borel measure on Euclidean space then forces equality.

items.title: The Euclidean Lebesgue measure is the completion of the product of the factor Lebesgue measures
items.strategy: The product measure agrees with $\lambda_{m+n}$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, while the published Euclidean result identifies the full Lebesgue $\sigma$-algebra as the completion of that Borel measure. Therefore the completion of $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ on the product $\sigma$-algebra is exactly $\lambda_{m+n}$.

items.title: FALSE: the product of two complete measure spaces is complete
items.strategy: Take the Lebesgue $\sigma$-algebra on each factor and place a nonmeasurable subset on a null vertical line. The ambient line is product-null, but the subset itself is not in the product $\sigma$-algebra because one of its sections is nonmeasurable.

items.title: FALSE: $\mathcal L(\mathbb R^m) \otimes \mathcal L(\mathbb R^n)$ already equals $\mathcal L(\mathbb R^{m+n})$
items.strategy: Use the same null-line witness as for incompleteness. It is Lebesgue measurable in the product Euclidean space because it lies inside a null set, but it is not in the product of the one-dimensional Lebesgue $\sigma$-algebras.

items.title: The region under a nonnegative measurable function is product-measurable and has measure equal to the integral
items.strategy: Express the subgraph as the indicator domain of the section lengths $t \mapsto \mathbf 1_{[0,f(x))}(t)$. Measurability of the region is equivalent to measurability of $f$, and Tonelli applied to the indicator function computes the product measure as the integral of the section lengths.

items.title: The graph of a measurable function $\mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R$ is Lebesgue null
items.strategy: The graph is measurable as the intersection of the two subgraphs of $f$ and of $-f$. For each base point its vertical section is a singleton or empty, hence one-dimensional Lebesgue null. Tonelli applied to the graph indicator then gives total measure zero.

items.title: The distribution function $t \mapsto \mu(\{|f| > t\})$ of a measurable function
For $0 < p < \infty$, the layer-cake formula computes $\int |f|^p$ from the distribution function
items.strategy: Apply the region-under-the-graph theorem to the nonnegative measurable function $|f|^p$, then rewrite its subgraph by the change of variable $t = s^p$. One integration-by-parts step in the one-variable parameter yields the formula with the factor $p s^{p-1}$.

items.title: The Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ induced by polar decomposition
Polar coordinates decompose Lebesgue measure into $r^{n-1} \, dr \, d\sigma$
items.strategy: Define the candidate sphere measure by the unit-ball shell formula and verify the product identity first on radial rectangles $(a,b] \times E$. Uniqueness on the product Borel $\sigma$-algebra then identifies the pushed-forward measure under $(r,\omega) \mapsto r\omega$, and Tonelli upgrades the set identity to the integral formula.

items.title: The polar formula recovers the published $n$-ball volumes and Gaussian constants
A $C^1$ diffeomorphism maps Lebesgue null sets to Lebesgue null sets
