items.strategy: Cover the null set by a Borel null superset, decompose that superset into compact pieces, and apply the linearized change-of-variables estimate on each compact set. The image of each null compact is null, and countable subadditivity finishes.

items.title: A $C^1$ diffeomorphism maps Lebesgue measurable sets to Lebesgue measurable sets
items.strategy: Write a Lebesgue measurable set as a Borel set plus a null modification. Continuous images of Borel sets remain Borel, and the previous lemma handles the null correction on both the set and its complement.

items.title: The published Riemann change-of-variables theorem already gives the Lebesgue formula for continuous compactly supported integrands
items.strategy: Choose a compact Jordan neighborhood containing the support and apply the published change-of-variables theorem there. Jordan and Lebesgue integration agree on compact Jordan sets, so the Riemann formula is already the Lebesgue formula for this class of integrands.

items.title: A $C^1$ diffeomorphism satisfies the change-of-variables formula for nonnegative Lebesgue measurable functions
items.strategy: Start from continuous compactly supported functions, extend to open sets by monotone convergence along compact exhaustions, pass from Borel sets to Lebesgue measurable sets by Borel approximation and null-set invariance, and then approximate an arbitrary nonnegative measurable function from below by simple functions.

items.title: A $C^1$ diffeomorphism satisfies the change-of-variables formula for $L^1$ functions
items.strategy: Apply the nonnegative theorem to the positive and negative parts, or equivalently to the real and imaginary parts, and then recombine by linearity once Tonelli has shown that the transformed absolute value is integrable.

items.title: Finite product measures are the base case for later countable-product constructions

pages.title: Product Measures and the Fubini Tonelli Theorems — Examples

items.title: Tonelli and the plane polar formula give $\int_{\mathbb R} e^{-x^2} \, dx = \sqrt{\pi}$
items.strategy: Square the one-dimensional Gaussian integral formally, identify the square with the product integral of $e^{-(x^2+y^2)}$, use Tonelli to justify the product, and then import the published plane polar computation.

items.title: Tonelli and the geometric series compute $\int_0^1 \! \int_0^1 \frac{1}{1-xy} \, dx \, dy = \pi^2/6$
items.strategy: Expand $(1-xy)^{-1}$ into its nonnegative geometric series on the unit square, apply Tonelli termwise, and identify the resulting double series with $\sum_{n \ge 1} n^{-2}$.

items.title: The region under $x \mapsto x^2$ on $[0,1]$ has measure $1/3$
items.strategy: Apply the region-under-the-graph theorem to $f(x)=x^2$, and then evaluate the resulting one-variable integral by the fundamental theorem of calculus.

items.title: Cavalieri computes the area of the unit disc from its sections
items.strategy: Write the disc indicator as a nonnegative measurable function on $[-1,1] \times \mathbb R$, identify each vertical section length as $2\sqrt{1-x^2}$, and use Tonelli to recover the area by a one-variable integral.

items.title: A set can have measurable horizontal and vertical sections and still fail to be product-measurable
items.strategy: Use a classical well-ordered subset of the square whose horizontal sections are countable and whose vertical sections are cocountable. Every section is measurable, but the set itself is not measurable for the product $\sigma$-algebra.

items.title: The diagonal under Lebesgue times counting measure shows that Tonelli needs $\sigma$-finiteness
items.strategy: Take $[0,1]$ with Lebesgue measure on one side and counting measure on the other, and test Tonelli on the indicator of the diagonal. The two iterated integrals are $1$ and $0$.

items.title: The function $(x^2-y^2)/(x^2+y^2)^2$ shows that Fubini's integrability hypothesis is not decorative
items.strategy: Integrate first in $y$ using the antiderivative $y/(x^2+y^2)$ to obtain $1/(1+x^2)$ and hence $\pi/4$, then swap the variables to obtain $-\pi/4$. The absolute value is not integrable near the origin.

items.title: Equal iterated integrals still do not imply product integrability
items.strategy: Place the previous counterexample and its coordinate-swapped copy on two disjoint squares. Their two discrepancies cancel, so the iterated integrals agree, but each square still carries a nonintegrable singularity and the total absolute integral diverges.

items.title: Without $\sigma$-finiteness, the rectangle formula need not determine a unique product measure
items.strategy: For Lebesgue measure on one copy of $[0,1]$ and counting measure on the other, compare the primitive product measure with the locally determined section-sum product. They agree on measurable rectangles but give different values to the diagonal.

items.title: A nonmeasurable subset of a null line shows that the product of complete measures need not be complete
items.strategy: Inside $\mathbb R^2$, place a nonmeasurable subset on a null vertical line. The ambient line is product-null, but the subset fails the section test for membership in the product $\sigma$-algebra.

items.title: A completed-product measurable set can have a nonmeasurable exceptional section
items.strategy: Use the same null-line subset as in the incompleteness example, but view its indicator as a function measurable for the completed product. The exceptional section at the supporting base point is exactly the chosen nonmeasurable set.

pages.title: Covering Spaces and Lifting

items.title: Covering maps, evenly covered neighbourhoods, fibres, sheets, and trivial coverings
Maps and isomorphisms of covering spaces over a fixed base
Lifts of maps, paths, and homotopies through a covering map
Covering maps are surjective local homeomorphisms with discrete fibres
items.strategy: An evenly covered neighbourhood restricts the projection to a homeomorphism on each sheet, which gives the local-homeomorphism property. Intersect a sheet with a fibre to isolate its unique point. Keep surjectivity as part of the covering-map definition rather than infer it from local data.

items.title: The cardinality of a covering fibre is locally constant and is constant on a connected base
items.strategy: Over an evenly covered neighbourhood every fibre meets each sheet in exactly one point, so all fibres there are in bijection with the sheet index set. The subsets on which a fixed fibre cardinal occurs are open; connectedness permits only one nonempty such subset. Do not assert global constancy for a disconnected base.

items.title: Existence and uniqueness of path lifts through a covering map
items.strategy: Pull back evenly covered neighbourhoods along the path to obtain an open cover of the compact interval, choose a Lebesgue subdivision, and lift successively sheet by sheet from the prescribed initial point. Agreement at subdivision endpoints gives a continuous pasted path; sheet uniqueness proves uniqueness, including constant paths.

items.title: Existence and uniqueness of homotopy lifts through a covering map
items.strategy: For a homotopy $H:Y\times I\to X$ and a lift at time zero, use evenly covered neighbourhoods and compactness of the interval to extend the lift over successive time strips locally in $Y$. Pasting gives a global lift, and the set of points where two lifts agree is open and closed on each vertical interval, yielding uniqueness. Record the endpoint-fixed consequence when the original homotopy is relative to endpoints.

items.title: The endpoint of a lifted path depends only on its endpoint-fixed homotopy class
items.strategy: Lift an endpoint-fixed homotopy starting from the chosen lift of one path. Along each endpoint edge the lifted map takes values in a discrete fibre; connectedness of the interval makes it constant, so the terminal endpoints agree.

items.title: A covering map induces an injective homomorphism on fundamental groups
items.strategy: If a loop upstairs maps to a nullhomotopic loop downstairs, lift a nullhomotopy with the given loop as its initial edge. Uniqueness forces the opposite edge to be constant, yielding a nullhomotopy upstairs. Preserve the chosen basepoints and the exact published definition of the induced map.

items.title: Two lifts from a connected space that agree at one point agree everywhere
items.strategy: The equaliser of two lifts is open because a common image point has an evenly covered neighbourhood and both lifts must lie in the same sheet near an agreement point. Its complement is open by choosing disjoint sheets near a disagreement point. Connectedness and the named agreement point force the equaliser to be the whole domain.

items.title: Lifting criterion for maps from path-connected locally path-connected spaces
items.strategy: For a based map $f:(Y,y_0)\to(X,x_0)$ with $Y$ path-connected and locally path-connected, necessity follows by functoriality. For sufficiency, define the candidate lift at $y$ by lifting $f$ along any path from $y_0$; the subgroup inclusion makes the endpoint independent of the chosen path. Local path-connectedness and an evenly covered neighbourhood make the candidate continuous. Uniqueness follows from connectedness.

items.title: The pullback of a covering space along a continuous map
Covering spaces are stable under restriction, finite products, and pullback
items.strategy: Restrict an evenly covered neighbourhood for restriction, take products of evenly covered neighbourhoods for finite products, and identify each pullback sheet with the corresponding open subset of the new base. State surjectivity in every construction and the empty-product convention separately. Do not claim unrestricted closure under composition: an infinite family of intermediate sheets need not admit one common refinement.

items.title: A composite of covering maps is a covering when the outer covering is finite-sheeted
items.strategy: For coverings $p:E\to B$ and $q:B\to X$, evenly cover a neighbourhood of $x$ for $q$. There are only finitely many resulting $q$-sheets. Around the unique point of each such sheet over $x$, choose a smaller neighbourhood evenly covered by $p$; intersect their finitely many images downstairs and restrict all sheets to that common neighbourhood. The resulting two-level sheets evenly cover the composite. Separate the empty base case, and record that the finite-sheet hypothesis is what permits the common intersection.

items.title: The monodromy right action on a covering fibre and its equivalent left-action convention
Monodromy acts by fibre bijections, and its orbits are the intersections of path components with the fibre
items.strategy: Path reversal gives the inverse endpoint permutation and concatenation gives the right-action law under the library's convention that $[\alpha][\beta]$ traverses $\alpha$ first. A lifted loop is a path upstairs joining its starting and endpoint fibre points. Conversely, project any path upstairs between fibre points to a loop downstairs. Thus transitivity is equivalent to path-connectedness of the relevant covering component.

items.title: Deck transformations and the deck-transformation group of a covering
On a connected covering space, a deck transformation is determined by one point and the deck action is free
items.strategy: Two deck transformations are lifts of the same projection. If they agree at one point, uniqueness of lifts from the connected total space makes them equal. Applying this to a deck transformation and the identity shows that a fixed point forces the transformation to be the identity.

items.title: Covering-space actions by disjoint translates of neighbourhoods
The orbit map of a covering-space action is a covering, with the acting group equal to the deck group when the total space is path-connected
items.strategy: For a neighbourhood whose nonidentity translates are disjoint, its orbit image is open in the quotient and its full preimage is the disjoint union of all translates. Each translate maps homeomorphically onto that quotient neighbourhood. The action is free automatically and embeds the acting group in the deck group. If the total space is path-connected, compare any deck transformation at one point with the unique group translate taking that point to its image; one-point determination then proves equality with that translate.

items.title: Local path-connectedness lifts and descends along covering maps
items.strategy: Every point has a sheet homeomorphic to an open neighbourhood of its image. Local path-connectedness passes to open subspaces and across homeomorphisms, which proves both directions using surjectivity to choose a point over each basepoint.

items.title: Semilocally simply connected spaces with explicit basepoint convention
Universal covering spaces
A space admitting a universal covering is semilocally simply connected
items.strategy: At a basepoint choose an evenly covered neighbourhood and a lift of that point. Any loop in the neighbourhood lifts to a loop in its sheet. The induced fundamental-group map of the universal cover is injective and its domain group is trivial, so the inclusion-induced class downstairs is trivial. No local path-connectedness is needed for this necessity direction.

items.title: The based path-class model and basic sets for a universal cover
For a path-connected locally path-connected semilocally simply connected space, the path-class projection is a covering map
items.strategy: Refine each semilocally simply connected neighbourhood to an open path-connected one. For a path class ending at its centre, append paths in that neighbourhood to obtain a basic sheet. Triviality of the inclusion-induced fundamental group makes the endpoint description independent of the appended path, and distinct initial classes give disjoint sheets. Verify that these basic sets form a topology and map homeomorphically onto the chosen neighbourhood.

items.title: Every path-connected locally path-connected semilocally simply connected space has a universal cover
items.strategy: Use the path-class projection, already proved to be a covering. The path-class space is nonempty and path-connected by truncating representatives. A loop upstairs projects to a loop whose path-class endpoint is the starting class, hence to the trivial element downstairs; injectivity of the fundamental-group map then makes every upstairs loop nullhomotopic. Thus the total space is simply connected.

items.title: For a path-connected locally path-connected base, universal covers are uniquely isomorphic over the base and lift to every connected covering
items.strategy: Let the base be path-connected and locally path-connected and fix points over a common basepoint. The lifting criterion applies to a universal cover because its fundamental group is trivial, giving a unique covering map to any connected covering. Applying this in both directions between two universal covers and using uniqueness of lifts makes the composites identities.

items.title: A connected covering of a locally path-connected simply connected space is one-sheeted and trivial
items.strategy: Local path-connectedness lifts to the connected total space, making it path-connected. If two points lie in one fibre, join them upstairs; the projected loop is null-homotopic because the base is simply connected, while endpoint homotopy invariance forces its lift to have the same initial and final point. Thus every fibre is a singleton, and a one-sheeted covering is a homeomorphism by its local sheet descriptions.

items.title: For a nonempty path-connected total space, a covering fibre is in bijection with the cosets of the induced fundamental-group subgroup
items.strategy: Fix a point in the fibre. Send a loop class to the endpoint of its lifted path. Endpoint homotopy invariance makes this well defined; two classes have the same endpoint exactly when their quotient lies in the image of the upstairs fundamental group. Path-connectedness of the total space gives surjectivity onto the fibre. State left-versus-right cosets consistently with the published path-product order, then translate the bijection into the published index convention: the finite cardinalities agree, and one side is infinite exactly when the other is recorded as $\infty$.

items.title: For a finite-sheeted covering, the total space is compact exactly when the base is compact
items.strategy: The forward direction is the continuous image theorem and uses surjectivity. For the reverse direction, over each basepoint choose an evenly covered neighbourhood; because its fibre is finite, shrink once so that every sheet above the smaller neighbourhood lies in a selected member of a given open cover upstairs. Compactness supplies finitely many such base neighbourhoods and hence finitely many cover members upstairs.

items.title: For a path-connected locally path-connected semilocally simply connected base, the deck group of a universal cover is isomorphic to the fundamental group with the inverse-path convention
items.strategy: For a path-connected locally path-connected semilocally simply connected base and a chosen point upstairs, each loop class determines the endpoint of its lift. The universal-cover lifting criterion gives the unique deck transformation taking the chosen point to that endpoint. Because the library multiplies loops in traversal order, insert path reversal in the assignment so composition is a homomorphism rather than an antihomomorphism. Freeness gives injectivity and path-connectedness gives surjectivity.

pages.title: Covering Spaces and Lifting — Examples

items.title: Trivial coverings are products with a discrete fibre
items.strategy: For any space $X$ and discrete set $F$, verify that the projection $X\times F\to X$ is a covering, with every open subset of the base evenly covered. Identify its sheets and fibre, including $F=\varnothing$: the projection then fails surjectivity unless $X=\varnothing$, so state the nonempty-fibre convention explicitly.

items.title: A surjective local homeomorphism need not be a covering map
items.strategy: Let the domain be the disjoint union of $(0,2)$ and $(1,2)$ and map both components by inclusion onto the base $(0,2)$. The first component makes the map surjective and each inclusion is a local homeomorphism. The fibre has one point at $1$ and two immediately to its right, so local constancy of sheet number rules out a covering; equivalently, the second component supplies only a one-sided partial sheet above every neighbourhood of $1$.

items.title: A covering over a disconnected base can have different sheet numbers on different components
items.strategy: Map a three-point discrete space onto a two-point discrete space with one point over the first basepoint and two over the second. Each singleton base neighbourhood is evenly covered, while the fibre cardinal is not globally constant. This isolates exactly why connectedness appears in the sheet-number theorem.

items.title: The quotient $\mathbb R\to\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ is a covering with integer translations as deck transformations
items.strategy: Use the equivalence relation $x\sim y$ iff $x-y$ is an integer and the quotient topology. Intervals of length less than one have pairwise disjoint integer translates whose quotient images are evenly covered. Verify directly that translations are deck transformations and that every deck transformation is the unique integer translation determined by the image of zero, without computing the fundamental group of the quotient.

items.title: The projected unit interval is not nullhomotopic in $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$
items.strategy: The loop $t\mapsto[t]$ lifts from zero to the path $t\mapsto t$, whose endpoint is one. If it had an endpoint-fixed nullhomotopy, homotopy lifting would keep the terminal lift in the discrete fibre while deforming the initial lift to the constant path at zero, forcing endpoints one and zero to agree. This proves essentiality without asserting $\pi_1(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$.

items.title: The maps $[x]\mapsto[mx]$ on $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ are $m$-sheeted coverings for $m\ge1$
items.strategy: Check well-definedness modulo integer translation. Around a class choose an interval short enough that its $m$ inverse branches are disjoint; these branches give the evenly covered neighbourhood and exactly $m$ fibre points. At $m=1$ the map is the identity, so no zero-sheet or division-by-zero case is hidden.

items.title: Pulling a covering back to an evenly covered open set gives a trivial covering
items.strategy: For the inclusion $U\hookrightarrow X$ of an evenly covered open set, identify the pullback with the disjoint union of the sheets over $U$. Write the explicit mutually inverse maps over $U$ and verify their continuity from the pullback subspace topology.

items.title: The Hawaiian earring is locally path-connected but has no universal cover
items.strategy: Model the earring as countably many copies of $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with diameters tending to zero and all zero classes identified, using the standard shrinking-wedge metric. Away from the wedge point, sufficiently short open arcs are path-connected neighbourhoods. At the wedge point, every open neighbourhood contains a smaller metric ball whose intersection with each circle is an arc through the wedge point and which contains every sufficiently small circle, so that ball is path-connected. Retraction to one such small circle and the essential unit loop show its inclusion carries a nontrivial loop, so semilocal simple connectedness fails at the wedge point. The necessity theorem then rules out a universal cover.

pages.title: The Fundamental Group of the Circle

items.title: The circle as $S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with basepoint $[0]$
items.strategy: Put $x\sim y$ exactly when $x-y\in\mathbb Z$, use the canonical copy of the integers in the reals, and verify reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity from the integer ring laws before forming the quotient. Give it the topology induced by $p(x)=[x]$. Author the exact clause: The circle is $S^1:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with the quotient topology induced by $p(x)=[x]$ and basepoint $[0]$; moreover $p^{-1}([0])=\mathbb Z$ and $p(x+n)=p(x)$ for every real $x$ and integer $n$.

items.title: Agreement with the published quotient model of $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$
items.strategy: State that the space defined here is the same quotient $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ already illustrated by the published examples on `subspaces-products-and-quotients-examples` and on `covering-spaces-and-lifting-examples`: the equivalence relation, the quotient topology and the map $p$ agree, so no second notion of the circle is introduced. Name the pages in prose only, because their occurrences are B-page leaves; mint no `deps` edge to a B-leaf item.

items.title: The quotient map is open, and every interval shorter than one embeds in $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$
items.strategy: For open $U\subseteq\mathbb R$, compute $p^{-1}(p[U])=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb Z}(U+n)$, so $p[U]$ is open by the quotient topology. If an interval $J$ has length below one, integer translates cannot identify two of its points. For a relatively open subset of $J$, choose around each of its points a real interval whose radius is smaller than the remaining gap to length one; its quotient image intersects $p[J]$ only in the desired relative neighbourhood. This proves continuity of the inverse of $p|_J$ for open, closed, and half-open intervals alike.

items.title: $p:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ is a covering map with translated interval sheets
items.strategy: For $x\in\mathbb R$, take $J=(x-1/3,x+1/3)$ and $U=p[J]$. Prove the explicit statement $p^{-1}(U)=\coprod_{n\in\mathbb Z}(J+n)$ and that every $p|_{J+n}:J+n\to U$ is a homeomorphism; hence $p$ is a covering map. The openness lemma makes $U$ open, and the sheet calculation verifies every clause of the printed covering-map definition. In Remarks, record that this is the A-spine promotion of the covering clause already illustrated by the B-leaf `ex-real-line-mod-integer-translations-is-a-covering`; do not put that B id in `deps`.

items.title: $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ is compact and path-connected
items.strategy: The restriction $p|_{[0,1]}$ is continuous and surjective: subtract the integer part of any representative to reach $[0,1)$. Heine--Borel and the agreement of metric and topological compactness make $[0,1]$ compact, so its continuous image is compact. For classes $[x]$ and $[y]$, the path $t\mapsto[(1-t)x+ty]$ proves path-connectedness, with continuity obtained from the real continuity algebra and composition with $p$.

items.title: $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ is Hausdorff
items.strategy: Choose the unique representatives $a,b\in[0,1)$ of two distinct classes. The two positive circular gaps are $|a-b|$ and $1-|a-b|$; choose a radius smaller than one third of their minimum. The quotient images of the corresponding real intervals are open by the saturation lemma, and an integer-translation calculation shows that they are disjoint.

items.title: The standard circle loops $\omega_n(t)=[nt]$ for $n\in\mathbb Z$
items.strategy: For every integer $n$, define $\widetilde\omega_n(t)=nt$ and $\omega_n=p\circ\widetilde\omega_n$. Check continuity and the two endpoint values, including $n=0$ and negative $n$.

items.title: The degree of a based circle loop
items.strategy: For a based loop $\alpha$ in $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$, lift it uniquely from $0$. Its terminal point lies in $p^{-1}([0])=\mathbb Z$; define $\deg(\alpha)=\widetilde\alpha(1)$. This is a definition on loops, not yet on homotopy classes.

items.title: Path-homotopic based circle loops have the same degree
items.strategy: Lift an endpoint-fixed homotopy from the lift of the first loop. The lifted terminal edge is constant in the discrete fibre, so the two lifted loops starting at zero have the same endpoint. State explicitly that the covering and common starting lift are the only hypotheses used.

items.title: Degree defines a function $\operatorname{Deg}:\pi_1(S^1,[0])\to\mathbb Z$
items.strategy: Use path-homotopy invariance to show that $\operatorname{Deg}([\alpha])=\deg(\alpha)$ is independent of the representative. This is the well-definedness result required before any homomorphism or isomorphism claim.

items.title: $\deg(\omega_n)=n$ for every integer $n$
items.strategy: The path $t\mapsto nt$ starts at zero and projects to $\omega_n$, so uniqueness identifies it with the defining lift and its endpoint is $n$. Treat $n=0$, positive $n$, and negative $n$ uniformly.

items.title: Lifts of circle-loop concatenations and reversals
items.strategy: If the lifts of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ from zero end at $m$ and $n$, paste the first lift with the integer translate $m+\widetilde\beta$ to lift $\alpha*\beta$ from zero; uniqueness gives endpoint $m+n$. The lift of the reversed loop from zero is $t\mapsto\widetilde\alpha(1-t)-m$, with endpoint $-m$. Check the join and both endpoints before invoking the finite closed-cover pasting lemma.

items.title: Degree sends concatenation to addition, reversal to negation, and the constant loop to zero
items.strategy: Read the concatenation and reversal formulas from their explicitly identified lifts. The constant loop has the constant lift at zero. Preserve the library convention that $\alpha*\beta$ traverses $\alpha$ first and $\beta$ second.

items.title: $\operatorname{Deg}:\pi_1(S^1,[0])\to(\mathbb Z,+)$ is a group homomorphism
items.strategy: The descended map is already well defined. Apply the concatenation law to representatives to obtain $\operatorname{Deg}([\alpha][\beta])=\operatorname{Deg}([\alpha])+\operatorname{Deg}([\beta])$, and cite the integer commutative-ring theorem for the target additive group.

items.title: Based circle loops of equal degree are path-homotopic
items.strategy: Lift both loops from zero. Equal degree gives equal terminal endpoints, so the straight-line homotopy between the two real-valued lifts fixes both endpoints. Postcompose it with $p$ to obtain a path homotopy of the original loops.

items.title: Two based circle loops are path-homotopic if and only if they have equal degree
items.strategy: The forward implication is degree invariance. The reverse implication is the preceding straight-line homotopy of lifts. Keep the two directions as separate numbered steps.

items.title: A based circle loop is nullhomotopic exactly when its degree is zero
items.strategy: Apply the classification theorem to the loop and the constant standard loop $\omega_0$, whose degree is zero. Interpret nullhomotopy here as endpoint-fixed homotopy through based loops.

items.title: $\operatorname{Deg}:\pi_1(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,[0])\to(\mathbb Z,+)$ is an isomorphism
items.strategy: The degree map is a homomorphism. It is injective because equal image degrees make the representing loops path-homotopic, and it is surjective because $\operatorname{Deg}([\omega_n])=n$ for every integer $n$. Its inverse is $n\mapsto[\omega_n]$. No trigonometric fact occurs in this proof.

items.title: $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ is not simply connected
items.strategy: The space is nonempty and path-connected, but $\omega_1$ has degree one and therefore is not nullhomotopic by the degree-zero criterion. This violates the trivial-fundamental-group clause of simple connectedness without relying on an unstated fact that $\mathbb Z$ is nontrivial.

items.title: $[t]\mapsto(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t)$ is a homeomorphism from $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ to the unit circle
items.strategy: The coordinate map on $\mathbb R$ is continuous and is constant exactly on the integer-translation fibres, by common period $2\pi$ and the published half-open parametrisation. The quotient universal property gives a continuous bijection from $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$, and direct evaluation shows that it sends $[0]$ to $(1,0)$. Its source is compact; the unit circle is a subspace of the metrizable plane and hence Hausdorff. Apply the compact-to-Hausdorff continuous-bijection theorem. This is the only proof on the A page that invokes trigonometry.

items.title: The trigonometric loops give $\pi_1(\{(x,y):x^2+y^2=1\},(1,0))\cong\mathbb Z$
items.strategy: The dictionary homeomorphism and its inverse induce mutually inverse fundamental-group homomorphisms by functoriality. Transport the degree isomorphism across them; under this transport $\omega_n$ becomes $t\mapsto(\cos 2\pi nt,\sin 2\pi nt)$. Mint no `aliases` on this item: `items/rem-pi1-circle-is-z.md` still exists as a draft record, so taking its id here would collide, and transferring an id is an owner decision that has not been made.

pages.title: The Fundamental Group of the Circle — Examples

items.title: An interval of length one need not embed under $p:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$
items.strategy: The restriction $p|_{[0,1)}$ is continuous and bijective onto $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$: the integer-part lemma gives surjectivity, and two representatives in $[0,1)$ whose difference is an integer must coincide. The relatively open set $[0,1/2)\subseteq[0,1)$ has image whose full inverse image is $\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb Z}[n,n+1/2)$, which is not open at $0$; hence the restriction is not open and therefore is not a homeomorphism. Also $p|_{[0,1]}$ is not injective because $p(0)=p(1)$. Thus the claim for every open, closed, or half-open interval becomes false if length below one is replaced by length at most one.

items.title: A loop that traverses the circle once and then pauses is homotopic to the standard loop
items.strategy: Let $u(t)=2t$ on $[0,1/2]$ and $u(t)=1$ on $[1/2,1]$, and put $\alpha=p\circ u$. The pasting lemma makes $u$ continuous, it is the lift of $\alpha$ from zero and ends at one, so $\deg(\alpha)=1=\deg(\omega_1)$. Give the explicit projected straight-line homotopy between $u$ and $t\mapsto t$ rather than merely citing the classification theorem.

items.title: A surjective circle loop can have degree zero and be nullhomotopic
items.strategy: Let $u(t)=2t$ on $[0,1/2]$ and $u(t)=2-2t$ on $[1/2,1]$, and put $\alpha=p\circ u$. The two formulas agree at $1/2$, so the finite closed-cover pasting lemma makes $u$ continuous. It begins and ends at zero, is the lift of $\alpha$ from zero, and therefore gives $\deg(\alpha)=0$. Its first half maps onto $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$, so $\alpha$ is surjective; it is nonconstant because $\alpha(0)=[0]$ while $\alpha(1/4)=[1/2]\ne[0]$. Apply the degree-zero criterion to conclude that $\alpha$ is nullhomotopic.

items.title: The geometric loops $t\mapsto(\cos 2\pi nt,\sin 2\pi nt)$ have degree $n$
items.strategy: Under the dictionary homeomorphism the standard quotient loop $\omega_n(t)=[nt]$ becomes the displayed geometric loop. Its degree is $n$, including $n=0$ and negative $n$.

items.title: Based circle loops with the same endpoints need not be path-homotopic
items.strategy: The constant loop and $\omega_1$ both begin and end at $[0]$, but their degrees are zero and one. The degree classification therefore forbids an endpoint-fixed homotopy between them.

items.title: A covering quotient of a simply connected space need not be simply connected
items.strategy: The real line is a nonempty convex subset of $\mathbb R^1$, so the published convex-space theorem makes it simply connected. The map $p:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ is both the defining quotient map and the covering map proved on the companion A page, while $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ is not simply connected. Thus neither passage to a quotient nor passage along a covering map preserves simple connectedness from total space to base.

items.title: FALSE: every continuous self-map of the circle is nullhomotopic
items.strategy: Use the identity as witness. If a homotopy from the identity to a constant map existed, reverse it and lift it from a constant lift; homotopy lifting would produce a section $s:S^1\to\mathbb R$ of $p$. Then $s\circ\omega_1$ would be a closed lift of $\omega_1$, while path-lift uniqueness identifies it with a translate of $t\mapsto t$, whose endpoints differ by one. This contradiction avoids any unbased-homotopy invariance assumption.

pages.title: The Seifert–van Kampen Theorem

items.title: Loops over a two-set path-connected open cover factor through the covering sets
items.strategy: Let $X=U\cup V$, with $U$, $V$, and $U\cap V$ path-connected and containing the basepoint. Pull the cover back along a loop, use a Lebesgue subdivision of $[0,1]$, and insert paths in $U$ or $V$ from subdivision vertices to the basepoint. The connecting paths cancel in adjacent factors, so every loop class is a product of inclusion-images from $\pi_1(U)$ and $\pi_1(V)$. Treat constant loops and a one-piece subdivision explicitly.

items.title: Antipodal complements cover $S^n$ by simply connected sets with path-connected overlap for $n\ge2$
items.strategy: For the north and south poles of $S^n\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}$, use the last coordinate to prove that the two pole complements are open and cover the sphere. Write stereographic projection and its inverse explicitly. Componentwise continuity, continuity of real quotients on nonzero denominators, and direct substitution prove each pole complement homeomorphic to $\mathbb R^n$; deleting both poles corresponds to $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$. Convexity makes $\mathbb R^n$ simply connected. Functoriality applied to each homeomorphism and its inverse transports path-connectedness and the trivial fundamental groups to the pole complements. Polygonal connectedness gives the overlap condition when $n\ge2$.

items.title: $S^n$ is simply connected for every $n\ge2$
items.strategy: Use the antipodal-complement cover. The generation lemma expresses every loop class as a product of classes coming from the two simply connected complements, so every factor and therefore every loop class is trivial. Nonemptiness and path-connectedness follow from the same cover and its nonempty path-connected overlap.

items.title: A path homotopy over a two-set open cover admits a finite subordinate grid
items.strategy: Pull $\{U,V\}$ back along $H:I^2\to X$. Regard $I^2$ as a compact metric subspace of $\mathbb R^2$, take a Lebesgue number, and choose a positive grid mesh smaller than it. Every closed grid rectangle then maps into $U$ or $V$. Refine the bottom and top edges to any prescribed finite subdivisions so the lemma can compare predetermined loop factorizations.

items.title: Homotopic-loop factorizations have the same value in the group pushout
items.strategy: Associate to a subordinate subdivision a word of based loops in $U$ and $V$, using chosen connector paths from grid vertices to the basepoint. Show that subdivision, changing a connector, and moving a grid edge across one rectangle alter the word only by multiplication inside one factor or by identifying the two images of a loop in $U\cap V$. Sweep across the subordinate homotopy grid to prove that any two factorizations of endpoint-homotopic loops define the same pushout element.

items.title: Seifert–van Kampen identifies the fundamental group with a group pushout
items.strategy: For $X=U\cup V$ with $U$, $V$, and $U\cap V$ open and path-connected and with a common basepoint, let $P$ be the pushout of the two inclusion-induced maps from $\pi_1(U\cap V)$. The pushout property gives $P\to\pi_1(X)$. Define the inverse as the unique pushout value shared by every open-cover factorization of a loop class; generation gives existence and factorization invariance gives uniqueness, without selecting factorizations globally. Verify both composites on factor images and on arbitrary loop classes. Do not assume either intersection map is injective.

items.title: A simply connected overlap turns the van Kampen pushout into a free product
items.strategy: When $U\cap V$ is simply connected, both maps from its one-element fundamental group are the unique trivial maps. The van Kampen pushout is therefore the free product $\pi_1(U)*\pi_1(V)$ by the published trivial-amalgamation result.

items.title: If one set in a van Kampen cover is simply connected, the other fundamental group surjects with overlap-generated kernel
items.strategy: If $V$ is simply connected, replace its fundamental group in the van Kampen pushout by the trivial group. The amalgamated-quotient construction identifies the pushout with $\pi_1(U)$ modulo the normal closure of the image of $\pi_1(U\cap V)$. Read the canonical map as the inclusion-induced surjection and identify its kernel exactly, including a trivial overlap and a trivial $U$.

items.title: The wedge of a family of pointed spaces
items.strategy: For a nonempty indexed family, take the tagged disjoint union and quotient by the equivalence relation that identifies all and only the tagged basepoints; the common class is the wedge point. Stipulate the wedge of the empty family to be a one-point space, so it remains pointed and supplies the rank-zero finite wedge. Record binary and finite notation without asserting any neighbourhood property.

items.title: Finite wedges of quotient circles have van Kampen covers at the wedge point
items.strategy: For a finite wedge, use quotient arcs of length less than one around each basepoint. To add one circle, take one open set containing the old wedge and a short arc of the new circle, and another containing the new circle and short arcs in the old wedge. Check openness by saturated preimages under the wedge quotient. Give explicit deformation retractions of the two sets onto the two wedge factors and of their overlap onto the wedge point, and construct paths through the wedge point to verify all three path-connectedness hypotheses, with the zero- and one-circle cases separated.

items.title: The fundamental group of a finite wedge of circles is free of that rank
items.strategy: Induct on the natural number $r$ of quotient-circle summands. The empty wedge is a point and the one-circle case is the published circle calculation. At the successor step use the explicit wedge cover and van Kampen with contractible overlap, then identify the free product of the rank-$r$ free group and one infinite cyclic group as the free group of rank $r+1$. Keep the chosen loop in each summand as the displayed free basis.

items.title: $\pi_1(S^1\vee S^1)$ is the free group on two generators
items.strategy: Specialise the finite-wedge theorem to two summands and name the two standard circle-loop classes as the free basis.

items.title: $\pi_1(X\times Y,(x_0,y_0))\cong\pi_1(X,x_0)\times\pi_1(Y,y_0)$
items.strategy: Send a loop in $X\times Y$ to the pair of its coordinate loop classes. Product continuity and homotopy make this a well-defined homomorphism. Its inverse sends a pair of loop classes to the class of the coordinatewise paired loop. The product universal property verifies continuity and homotopies componentwise, and both composites are identities, including empty or one-point factor spaces whenever the displayed basepoints exist.

items.title: The two-dimensional torus $T^2=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^2$
$\pi_1(T^2)\cong\mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z$
items.strategy: Apply the product theorem to the two quotient-circle factors, then take the product of the two degree isomorphisms. This route uses no surface presentation and no van Kampen computation.

pages.title: The Seifert–van Kampen Theorem — Examples

items.title: Two paths can induce distinct change-of-basepoint isomorphisms on $S^1\vee S^1$
items.strategy: Choose the wedge point and a second point on the first circle. Let one connecting path run along a short arc and let the other first traverse the second circle. Verify inline that conjugating loops by a connecting path gives a basepoint-change isomorphism. After identifying the wedge group with $F(a,b)$, the two maps differ by conjugation by $b$; normal form distinguishes their values on $a$.

items.title: $\pi_1(\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\})\cong\mathbb Z$
items.strategy: Use the published radial deformation retraction onto the Euclidean unit circle. Functoriality and homotopy invariance make the inclusion and retraction induce inverse isomorphisms. Transport the quotient-circle calculation across the published homeomorphism between $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ and the Euclidean unit circle.

items.title: The once-punctured two-sphere has trivial fundamental group and the twice-punctured two-sphere has fundamental group $\mathbb Z$
items.strategy: Use the explicit stereographic homeomorphisms from the antipodal-cover lemma. Removing one pole gives $\mathbb R^2$, whose fundamental group is trivial by convexity. Removing both poles gives $\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}$, whose fundamental group is the preceding example's infinite cyclic group. Verify that the chosen basepoints are carried correctly before applying induced-map functoriality.

items.title: FALSE: every fundamental group is abelian
items.strategy: Use $S^1\vee S^1$. Its fundamental group is free on generators $a,b$, and the free-product normal form makes $ab$ and $ba$ distinct. Thus the two loop classes do not commute.

items.title: FALSE: the two-set van Kampen conclusion needs no path-connectedness hypothesis on the overlap
items.strategy: Cover $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ by two open arcs, each obtained as the image of an interval shorter than one and hence simply connected. Arrange the arcs so their intersection has two components. The pushout of the two trivial fundamental groups over the basepoint component is trivial, while the circle has fundamental group $\mathbb Z$. This witnesses failure of surjectivity when the overlap is disconnected.

pages.title: Classification of Covering Spaces

items.title: Local homeomorphisms
items.strategy: A continuous map $f:X\to Y$ is a local homeomorphism when every $x\in X$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ whose image $f[U]$ is open in $Y$ and whose restriction $f|_U:U\to f[U]$ is a homeomorphism. Do not include surjectivity or the covering condition in the definition.

items.title: A local homeomorphism from a nonempty compact space to a connected Hausdorff space is surjective with finite fibres
items.strategy: A local homeomorphism has open image. Its compact image is closed in the Hausdorff target, so connectedness and nonemptiness give surjectivity. Each fibre is closed in the compact domain and discrete by local injectivity, hence compact; the open cover by its singleton subsets then has a finite subcover, so the fibre is finite.

items.title: A local homeomorphism from a nonempty compact Hausdorff space to a connected Hausdorff space is a finite-sheeted covering
items.strategy: Use the preceding lemma for surjectivity and finite fibres. Around the finitely many points over $y$, use Hausdorff separation and finite choice to select pairwise disjoint local-homeomorphism neighbourhoods. Intersect their target images. The complement of their union is closed and compact; remove its compact closed image from that common target neighbourhood. The remaining open neighbourhood of $y$ is evenly covered by the restricted local sheets.

items.title: A based morphism between connected coverings exists exactly when the induced subgroups are included
items.strategy: For connected coverings $p_i:(E_i,e_i)\to(B,b_0)$ over a path-connected locally path-connected base, apply the lifting criterion to $p_1:E_1\to B$ through $p_2$. This gives existence exactly when $(p_1)_*\pi_1(E_1,e_1)\subseteq(p_2)_*\pi_1(E_2,e_2)$, and uniqueness follows from lift uniqueness. Over a common evenly covered neighbourhood, compare sheets to show that the resulting morphism is itself a covering map; do not import the stronger claim from the earlier universal-cover item, which deliberately did not prove it.

items.title: Based connected coverings are isomorphic exactly when their induced subgroups are equal
items.strategy: Equality gives unique based covering morphisms in both directions. Each composite is a lift of the corresponding projection that fixes the basepoint, so lift uniqueness makes both composites identities. Conversely an isomorphism over the base and its inverse give both subgroup inclusions by functoriality.

items.title: Every subgroup acts on the universal cover with a connected quotient covering that realizes it
items.strategy: Let $G=\pi_1(B,b_0)$ and identify it with the universal deck group using the published traversal-order convention, with no inserted path reversal. A subgroup $H\le G$ acts by deck transformations and inherits the disjoint-translate property. Form $E_H=\widetilde B/H$. On a universal-cover sheet, $H$-orbits of sheets map homeomorphically to the same evenly covered neighbourhood of $B$, giving a connected covering $p_H:E_H\to B$. A loop lifts closed in $E_H$ exactly when its universal lift ends in the $H$-orbit of the chosen point, so $(p_H)_*\pi_1(E_H)=H$.

items.title: Changing the point over a fixed basepoint conjugates the induced covering subgroup
items.strategy: For a path $\widetilde\gamma$ in a connected covering from $e_0$ to $e_1$ over $b_0$, its projection is a loop $\gamma$ at $b_0$. Conjugating an upstairs loop by $\widetilde\gamma$ and projecting gives conjugation of $(p_*)\pi_1(E,e_0)$ by $[\gamma]$, with the direction fixed by traversal-order multiplication. Reverse the path for the opposite inclusion. Conversely path-connectedness supplies such a path between any two fibre points.

items.title: Connected covering spaces are classified by conjugacy classes of fundamental-group subgroups
items.strategy: For a nonempty path-connected locally path-connected semilocally simply connected base, subgroup quotients of the universal cover give a based connected covering for every subgroup, and the based-isomorphism corollary gives uniqueness for a fixed subgroup. Thus based isomorphism classes correspond to subgroups. Forgetting the point over $b_0$ replaces a subgroup by exactly its conjugacy class by the basepoint-change lemma, giving the unbased classification. Prove both surjectivity and injectivity of both correspondences explicitly.

items.title: Regular coverings
items.strategy: For a covering with path-connected total space, define regularity by transitivity of the deck group on every fibre: for points e and e' over the same basepoint, some deck transformation sends e to e'. Record 'normal covering' as a synonym used by Hatcher, but do not build subgroup normality into the definition; that is the following theorem.

items.title: Deck transformations of a connected covering correspond to cosets in the subgroup normalizer
items.strategy: For $H=p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)\le G=\pi_1(B,b_0)$, a loop class $g$ lifts from $e_0$ to a fibre point $e_g$. The basepoint-change lemma says the subgroup at $e_g$ is $g^{-1}Hg$ in the fixed traversal convention. The based-isomorphism criterion gives a unique deck transformation taking $e_0$ to $e_g$ exactly when $H=g^{-1}Hg$, equivalently when $g$ normalizes $H$; the weaker morphism criterion alone would allow noninvertible self-maps of a covering. One-point determination and monodromy show two normalizer elements give the same deck transformation exactly when they lie in the same right coset of $H$, and composition matches coset multiplication.

items.title: $\operatorname{Deck}(E/B)\cong N_G(H)/H$ for a connected covering
items.strategy: Use the normalizer-coset lemma to define the surjective homomorphism $N_G(H)\to\operatorname{Deck}(E/B)$. Its kernel is exactly $H$. The first isomorphism theorem gives the displayed quotient isomorphism, with $G=\pi_1(B,b_0)$ and $H=p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$. Check $H\trianglelefteq N_G(H)$ from the definition of normalizer before forming the quotient.

items.title: A connected covering is regular exactly when its induced subgroup is normal, exactly when deck transformations act transitively on a fibre
items.strategy: The first and third clauses are the definition of regularity and its deck-action formulation. By the basepoint-change formula, fibre points correspond to conjugates of $H$; a deck transformation reaches every fibre point exactly when all those conjugates equal $H$. This is equivalent to $H\trianglelefteq G$. Use monodromy transitivity for the connected total space and prove both directions without assuming a finite fibre.

items.title: A regular connected covering has deck group $\pi_1(B,b_0)/p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$
items.strategy: For a regular covering, the characterization theorem makes $H$ normal in $G$, hence $N_G(H)=G$. Substitute this equality into the normalizer-quotient theorem.

items.title: $\mathbb R\to\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ is a universal covering
items.strategy: The quotient projection is already a covering. The real line is a nonempty convex subset of $\mathbb R$, hence simply connected. Apply the published definition of universal covering space.

items.title: Connected coverings of the circle are classified by the subgroups $n\mathbb Z$ for $n\ge0$
items.strategy: Transport induced subgroups through the degree isomorphism $\pi_1(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,[0])\cong\mathbb Z$. Every subgroup is uniquely $n\mathbb Z$ for a natural $n$. Classification gives one based isomorphism class for each $n$; abelianness makes based and unbased classes agree. For $n\ge1$ the sheet number is $n$, while $n=0$ is the infinite-sheeted universal cover, identified with the real-line cover.

items.title: Every connected covering of the circle is regular
items.strategy: Under the degree isomorphism the induced subgroup lies in the abelian group $(\mathbb Z,+)$, so it is normal. Apply the regular-covering characterization. This includes the universal and one-sheeted cases.

pages.title: Classification of Covering Spaces — Examples

items.title: Maps between connected circle coverings are governed by divisibility
items.strategy: Let $E_m$ and $E_n$ be the based connected covers classified by $m\mathbb Z$ and $n\mathbb Z$, with $m,n\ge1$. The covering-morphism criterion gives a unique based map $E_m\to E_n$ exactly when $m\mathbb Z\subseteq n\mathbb Z$, which is equivalent by a direct multiples argument to $n\mid m$. When $m=nq$, explicit coset representatives show the morphism has $q$ sheets. Include $q=1$ and rule out zero denominators by the stated positive hypotheses.

items.title: Deck groups of connected circle coverings: $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ for $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb Z$ for the universal cover
items.strategy: For $n\ge1$, the classified subgroup is $n\mathbb Z$ and the cover is regular, so the deck group is $(\mathbb Z,+)/n\mathbb Z=(\mathbb Z/n,+)$. For the $n=0$ universal cover, use the universal-cover deck theorem to obtain $(\mathbb Z,+)$. Keep the one-sheeted case, whose quotient group is trivial.

items.title: The two-circle wedge has both regular and nonregular connected three-sheeted coverings
items.strategy: Identify the wedge group with $F(a,b)$. A surjection $F(a,b)\to\mathbb Z/3$ gives a normal kernel of index three and hence a regular three-sheeted cover. A surjection $F(a,b)\to S_3$ taking $a$ to $(12)$ and $b$ to $(123)$ has as the preimage of a point stabilizer a subgroup of index three; conjugating the stabilizer by $(123)$ changes it, so the preimage is not normal and its cover is nonregular. Classification realizes both subgroups, and the index theorem verifies the common sheet number.

pages.title: Applications of the Fundamental Group

items.title: A retract induces an injection on fundamental groups, and a deformation retract induces an isomorphism
items.strategy: Let i:A→X be the inclusion and r:X→A a retraction. Functoriality turns r∘i=id_A into r_*∘i_*=id, so i_* is injective. For a deformation retract, the pointwise-fixed homotopy from id_X to i∘r is based at every point of A, so based-homotopy invariance gives i_*∘r_*=id as well. Keep the basepoint in A explicit in both clauses.

items.title: There is no retraction of the closed disk onto the unit circle
items.strategy: The closed disk is a nonempty convex subset of R^2 and therefore has a one-element fundamental group at the chosen unit-circle basepoint. The unit circle has fundamental group isomorphic to Z and is nontrivial. A retraction would make the inclusion-induced homomorphism injective by the preceding proposition, which is impossible for a homomorphism from a nontrivial group to the one-element group.

items.title: A fixed-point-free self-map of the disk produces a continuous retraction onto the unit circle
items.strategy: For a continuous f:D^2→D^2 with f(x)≠x, put v(x)=x-f(x) and let r(x)=f(x)+λ(x)v(x), where λ(x) is the larger solution of |f(x)+tv(x)|^2=1. Write the quadratic-formula expression explicitly. Its denominator |v(x)|^2 never vanishes, its radicand is nonnegative, and continuity follows componentwise from continuity of inner products, norms, quotients on their cozero sets, and the nonnegative square root. Convexity of the disk shows λ(x)≥1; uniqueness of the outward ray intersection gives r(x)=x on the boundary. Check separately that the formula remains valid when f(x) lies on the boundary and when f(x)=0.

items.title: Brouwer fixed-point theorem for the closed disk
items.strategy: Assume a continuous self-map of D^2 has no fixed point. The preceding formula then gives a continuous retraction D^2→S^1, contradicting the no-retraction theorem. The conclusion is existence only; no uniqueness claim is made.

items.title: A root-free complex polynomial gives nullhomotopic normalized circle loops
items.strategy: Let p be a complex polynomial with no zero. For R≥0, normalize p(Rh([t]))/p(R), where h:R/Z→S^1 is the published circle homeomorphism, and transport the value back to R/Z. The quotient is based at [0] and never vanishes. Varying R continuously down to zero gives a based homotopy to the constant loop. Establish continuity of polynomial evaluation and normalization componentwise from finite real polynomial algebra, and check R=0 explicitly rather than dividing by R.

items.title: The normalized large-radius loop of a monic degree-$n$ polynomial has degree $n$
items.strategy: Write p(z)=z^n+a_1z^{n-1}+...+a_n with n≥1 and choose R>max(1,|a_1|+...+|a_n|). On |z|=R the leading term strictly dominates the lower terms. Scaling all lower coefficients by s∈[0,1] therefore gives a zero-free based homotopy from the normalized p-loop to the standard n-fold circle loop. Degree invariance and the published degree of the standard loop give n. Check a vanishing lower-coefficient sum, n=1, and the strict inequality at every homotopy parameter.

items.title: Fundamental theorem of algebra by the fundamental-group obstruction
items.strategy: Assume a nonconstant complex polynomial has no root and divide by its leading coefficient to make it monic without changing its zero set. The root-free-loop lemma makes every normalized radius-R loop nullhomotopic and hence degree zero. At a radius satisfying the leading-term bound, the large-radius lemma gives degree n, where n≥1, a contradiction. Treat degree one and a zero constant coefficient within the same argument; the zero polynomial is excluded because it is not nonconstant.

items.title: The fundamental-group and minimum-modulus proofs of the fundamental theorem of algebra
An antipodal circle map has odd lift increment and is not nullhomotopic
items.strategy: Use S^1=R/Z and define its antipodal involution by a([u])=[u+1/2]. Let h satisfy h∘a=a∘h, and lift h∘p to a real path. If its value at 1/2 differs from its value at zero by k+1/2, uniqueness of path lifts on the first half interval forces the same relation on the second half. The total increment is 2k+1, so the loop cannot be endpoint-homotopic to a constant loop because homotopic lifts with a common initial value have the same endpoint. Prove a is well defined, and allow k to be negative; oddness, not positivity, is the point.

items.title: Borsuk–Ulam theorem in dimension two
items.strategy: If a continuous f:S^2→R^2 separates every antipodal pair, normalize f(x)-f(-x) to obtain a continuous odd map g:S^2→S^1. Restriction to the equator is non-nullhomotopic by the odd-lift lemma. But the equator loop is nullhomotopic in the simply connected S^2, and postcomposition by g preserves that nullhomotopy, a contradiction. Verify that the normalized difference never vanishes under the contrary hypothesis and that the equator parametrization respects antipodes.

items.title: There is no continuous injection from $S^2$ into $\mathbb R^2$
items.strategy: Borsuk–Ulam supplies x with f(x)=f(-x). On S^2 the equality x=-x would force x=0, contrary to unit norm, so x and -x are distinct and f is not injective.

items.title: One member of every three-set closed cover of $S^2$ contains an antipodal pair
items.strategy: For closed A_1,A_2,A_3 covering S^2, apply Borsuk–Ulam to the two distance functions d(-,A_1),d(-,A_2). Handle an empty A_i by replacing its undefined distance with the constant one function. Equality at an antipodal pair puts both points in A_1 or A_2 when the corresponding distance is zero; if both distances are positive, both points lie in A_3. Use closedness to identify zero distance with membership and treat all empty-set patterns explicitly.

items.title: Pointwise multiplication and concatenation of loops in a topological group agree up to homotopy
items.strategy: For based loops α and β at the identity, form the square (s,t)↦α(s)β(t). Traverse its boundary in the two coordinate orders and use explicit edge-preserving reparametrizations of the square to obtain endpoint-fixed homotopies between the pointwise product loop and each corresponding concatenation product. Continuity comes from the product universal property and continuous group multiplication. Fix the library's first-then-second concatenation convention when stating the order.

items.title: The fundamental group of a topological group is abelian
items.strategy: Loop concatenation and pointwise multiplication descend to two unital operations on loop classes. The preceding homotopies identify them, while the pointwise operation satisfies the interchange law. The Eckmann–Hilton calculation then gives [α][β]=[β][α]. Write the short calculation explicitly and check constant loops supply the common unit.

items.title: The punctured plane has fundamental group $\mathbb Z$, while punctured $\mathbb R^n$ is simply connected for $n\ge3$
items.strategy: At the standard basepoint e_0, radial deformation retraction identifies the punctured R^n fundamental group with that of S^{n-1}. For n=2 the geometric circle calculation gives Z. For n≥3, the sphere S^{n-1} is simply connected, so the group at every sphere basepoint is trivial. Join an arbitrary punctured-space basepoint x to x/|x| by its radial segment and prove inline from the loop laws that conjugation by this path is a basepoint-change isomorphism; this transfers triviality to every basepoint. The same radial paths and sphere paths prove path-connectedness. State the n=2 and n≥3 clauses separately and do not claim anything at n=0 or n=1.

items.title: $\mathbb R^2$ is not homeomorphic to $\mathbb R^n$ for $n\ne2$
items.strategy: Treat every natural n. For n=0, R^0 is a singleton while R^2 has distinct points. For n=1, use the published theorem that R is not homeomorphic to any higher-dimensional Euclidean space and symmetry of homeomorphism. For n≥3, suppose h:R^2→R^n is a homeomorphism. Translate so h(0)=0 and postcompose with an explicit invertible coordinate shear and permutation carrying h(e_0) to e_0. Restriction then gives a pointed homeomorphism of punctured spaces, hence an isomorphism of their fundamental groups, contradicting the preceding Z-versus-trivial calculation. Write the coordinate homeomorphism and its inverse, including the choice of a nonzero coordinate.

items.title: The Hawaiian earring is compact and path-connected
items.strategy: For n≥1 let C_n be the circle of radius 1/n centred at (1/n,0), and let H be their union. The union is bounded. To prove it closed, note that all sufficiently small circles lie in any prescribed ball about the origin, while away from the origin only finitely many circles remain relevant; a point outside their finite closed union has a disjoint neighbourhood. Heine–Borel gives compactness. Every point lies on one C_n and can be joined within that circle to the common origin, so concatenating two such paths gives path-connectedness. Keep the index n≥1 explicit so no radius 1/0 occurs.

pages.title: Applications of the Fundamental Group — Examples

items.title: Radial normalization retracts the punctured disk, but it cannot extend to the disk
items.strategy: Restrict x↦x/|x| to D^2∖{0}; the published radial deformation retraction shows it continuously retracts that punctured disk onto S^1. Any continuous extension agreeing on S^1 would be a retraction D^2→S^1, forbidden by the no-retraction theorem. Show directly that approaching zero along two different rays gives different limiting values.

items.title: The large-circle loop of $z^3-2z+2$ on $|z|=5$ has degree three
items.strategy: The lower-coefficient modulus sum is 4<5. Apply the large-radius polynomial-loop lemma to p(z)=z^3-2z+2 and R=5, and display the coefficient-scaling homotopy to the threefold standard loop. Verify directly that the leading-term bound is strict throughout.

items.title: Orthogonal projection $S^2\to\mathbb R^2$ has exactly one antipodal pair with equal image
items.strategy: For q(x,y,z)=(x,y), equality q(v)=q(-v) forces x=y=0. Unit norm then leaves precisely the north-south antipodal pair. Verify continuity componentwise and distinguish one antipodal pair from two points.

items.title: Four closed sets can cover $S^2$ without any one containing an antipodal pair
items.strategy: Take the four Voronoi regions determined by the vertices of a regular tetrahedron centred at the origin: A_i consists of sphere points whose inner product with v_i is maximal. Finite intersections of closed half-spaces make the regions closed, and a finite maximum makes them cover. If x and -x both lay in A_i, every inner product with x would tie; the three differences v_i-v_j span R^3, forcing x=0, impossible on S^2. Give explicit tetrahedral vertices and verify the spanning calculation.

items.title: The Hawaiian earring retracts onto each of its circles
items.strategy: For fixed n, define r_n to be the identity on C_n and send every other circle to the common origin. Away from the origin, a relative neighbourhood meets only the relevant branch and continuity is immediate. At the origin, preimages of neighbourhoods in C_n contain a sufficiently small planar neighbourhood intersected with the earring; equivalently verify continuity by the subspace closed-set criterion. Thus r_n is continuous and restricts to the identity on C_n.

items.title: FALSE: every compact path-connected subset of $\mathbb R^2$ has a universal cover
items.strategy: Use the Hawaiian earring. The A-page proposition gives compactness and path-connectedness. Every neighbourhood of the origin contains C_n for all sufficiently large n. The preceding retraction r_n makes the inclusion of C_n injective on fundamental groups, so its standard loop remains essential in the earring. Hence no neighbourhood kills all loop classes, semilocal simple connectedness fails, and the universal-cover necessity theorem rules out a universal cover.

pages.title: Cayley Graphs Word Metrics and Quasi Isometry

items.title: Simple graphs on an arbitrary vertex set
Walks, paths, connectedness and components in a simple graph on an arbitrary vertex set
Every walk contains a path between the same endpoints, of no greater length
items.strategy: Among the walks from $u$ to $v$ of length at most that of the given walk, the well-ordering principle selects one of least length. If a vertex occurred twice in it, deleting the segment between the two occurrences would give a shorter such walk. So the chosen walk repeats no vertex and is a path. Finiteness of the vertex set is never used; the walk itself is a finite list.

items.title: The path metric of a connected simple graph
The path metric of a connected simple graph is a metric on its vertex set
items.strategy: Separation holds because the only path of length zero joins a vertex to itself; symmetry because reversing a path preserves its length; the triangle inequality because concatenating two paths gives a walk of the summed length, which the previous lemma replaces by a path no longer than it. Values are natural numbers, so no completeness or archimedean input is needed.

items.title: A bijection of vertex sets is an isometry for the path metrics if and only if it is a graph isomorphism
items.strategy: A graph isomorphism carries paths to paths of the same length in both directions, so it preserves the minima. Conversely an isometry preserves distance one, and distance one is exactly adjacency, so it preserves the edge relation in both directions.

items.title: On a finite vertex set these notions are the published ones, and the path metric is the published graph distance
items.strategy: Compare the definitions clause by clause: a simple graph on a finite vertex set is a finite simple graph, and the walk, path, cycle, connectedness and component notions are literally the published ones. The published graph distance is the least length of a path in the same sense, so the two agree wherever the published one is defined, and the metric axioms proved here specialise to the published component-wise statement. Trees and forests likewise agree.

items.title: Locally finite graphs and vertex degree without a finiteness hypothesis
In a locally finite graph every ball of the path metric is finite
items.strategy: Induct on the radius. The ball of radius zero is a single vertex, and the ball of radius $r+1$ is contained in the union over the ball of radius $r$ of the closed neighbourhoods of its vertices, a finite union of finite sets. Local finiteness is used at every vertex, not only at the centre.

items.title: Cycles, trees and forests in a simple graph on an arbitrary vertex set
A simple graph is a tree if and only if each pair of vertices is joined by exactly one path
items.strategy: If paths are unique the graph is connected, and a cycle would give two distinct paths between two of its vertices, using that a cycle has length at least three. Conversely, in a tree two distinct paths with the same endpoints first diverge at some index and first meet again later, and the two segments between those points form a cycle.

items.title: Labelled directed graphs, their underlying simple graphs, and label-preserving isomorphisms
The directed labelled Cayley graph of a group with respect to a subset
The Cayley graph of a group with respect to a subset
Finitely generated groups
A Cayley graph is connected if and only if the subset generates the group
items.strategy: A walk from the identity to $g$ spells an expression for $g$ as a product of elements of the subset and their inverses, and conversely each such expression is a walk. So the component of the identity is exactly the generated subgroup, and left translation carries it onto the component of any vertex.

items.title: Every vertex of a Cayley graph has the same degree, and the graph is locally finite exactly when the symmetrised generating set is finite
items.strategy: The neighbours of $g$ are the elements $gs$ with $s$ in the symmetrised set minus the identity, and left multiplication by $hg^{-1}$ is a bijection from the neighbours of $g$ onto those of $h$. The common degree is therefore the size of that set, finite exactly when the set is.

items.title: Left translation acts on a Cayley graph by label-preserving automorphisms, freely on vertices
items.strategy: Left multiplication by $h$ sends the arc from $g$ to $gs$ to the arc from $hg$ to $hgs$, which carries the same label; it is bijective on vertices with inverse left multiplication by $h^{-1}$. It fixes a vertex only if $hg=g$, that is only if $h$ is the identity.

items.title: The label-preserving automorphism action on a Cayley graph is the left regular representation of Cayley's theorem
items.strategy: Cayley's theorem embeds a group in the symmetric group on its underlying set by left multiplication. The action just constructed has the same underlying permutations, so it is that embedding followed by the inclusion of the label-preserving automorphism group in the symmetric group; in particular the Cayley graph is a refinement of the regular action, not a second embedding theorem.

items.title: For a finite group the Cayley graph is a finite simple graph in the published sense and the two distances agree
items.strategy: The vertex set is the group, which is finite, and the edges are two-element subsets, so the published definition applies verbatim; the path metric and the published graph distance are then the same minimum over the same set of paths.

items.title: Word length of a group element with respect to a generating set
Word length is defined on every element and satisfies the subadditivity, inversion and vanishing laws
items.strategy: The set of lengths of expressions of $g$ is a nonempty subset of the natural numbers whenever the set generates, so the well-ordering principle supplies a least element. Concatenating expressions gives subadditivity, reversing and inverting each letter gives equality of the lengths of $g$ and $g^{-1}$, and the empty expression gives length zero exactly at the identity.

items.title: The word metric of a group with respect to a generating set
The word metric is a left-invariant metric and coincides with the path metric of the Cayley graph
items.strategy: The metric axioms are the three length laws transported by $d_S(g,h)=|g^{-1}h|_S$, and left invariance is immediate from that formula. For the identification, a walk of length $n$ from $g$ to $h$ in the Cayley graph is the same datum as an expression for $g^{-1}h$ as a product of $n$ symmetrised generators, once identity generators are discarded; taking minima on both sides gives the equality.

items.title: Balls of a word metric are finite if and only if the generating set is finite
items.strategy: If the set is finite, the ball of radius $n$ about the identity is the image of the set of words of length at most $n$ in the symmetrised set, a finite set; left invariance moves this to every centre. If the set is infinite, the ball of radius one about the identity already contains it.

items.title: The word metric is the largest left-invariant metric in which each generator and its inverse lie within distance one of the identity
items.strategy: For any competing left-invariant metric with that property, the triangle inequality along an expression of minimal length bounds the competing distance by the word length. The word metric itself attains the value one at every generator that is not the identity, so it satisfies the constraint and dominates.

items.title: Right translation by a fixed element displaces every point of a word metric space by exactly the word length of that element
items.strategy: Left invariance gives $d_S(h,hg)=|g|_S$ for every $h$, so the displacement is constant. Right translation is therefore an isometry only when it is trivial in the sense that this constant is zero, while it always stays a bounded distance from the identity map.

items.title: The Cayley graph of a free group with respect to a free basis is a tree
items.strategy: The graph is connected because a basis generates. A cycle $g_0,\dots,g_{n-1}$ of length $n\ge3$ makes the successive quotients $g_{j+1}g_j^{-1}$ into basis letters or their inverses whose product around the cycle is the identity, and distinctness of the vertices makes the corresponding word reduced; the normal form theorem says a nonempty reduced word is not the identity.

items.title: With respect to a free basis, the word length of an element is the length of its reduced word
items.strategy: A reduced word of length $n$ is an expression of length $n$, so word length is at most reduced length. Conversely an expression of length shorter than the reduced word would, after free reduction, give a second reduced word for the same element, contradicting uniqueness of normal form.

items.title: If no product of two members of a generating set is the identity and the Cayley graph is a tree, the set is a free basis
items.strategy: The universal property gives a surjection from the free group on the set. A shortest nonempty reduced word in its kernel has length at least two by injectivity on the set, exactly two is excluded by the hypothesis on products of two members, and length at least three produces a cycle in the Cayley graph by taking successive partial products, which are distinct by minimality.

items.title: Geodesics and geodesic metric spaces
Coarse Lipschitz maps and quasi-isometric embeddings
Bounded distance between two maps into a metric space
Bounded distance is an equivalence relation and is preserved by pre-composition and by post-composition with a coarse Lipschitz map
items.strategy: Reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity come from the metric axioms with the bounds added. Pre-composition changes no value. Post-composition with a coarse Lipschitz map multiplies the bound by the multiplicative constant and adds the additive one, which is where the coarse Lipschitz hypothesis is needed and where an arbitrary map would fail.

items.title: Coarsely dense subsets, quasi-inverses and quasi-isometries
Composites of coarse Lipschitz maps and of quasi-isometric embeddings are again such, with explicit constants
items.strategy: Substitute one pair of inequalities into the other and collect terms; the resulting constants are recorded rather than absorbed, since later statements about quasi-geodesics need them.

items.title: A map at bounded distance from a quasi-isometric embedding is one, with the additive constant enlarged
items.strategy: Apply the triangle inequality twice, once on each side, and enlarge the additive constant by twice the bound; the multiplicative constant is unchanged.

items.title: A quasi-isometric embedding with coarsely dense image has a quasi-inverse quasi-isometric embedding
items.strategy: For each target point select a source point whose image is within the density constant; the selection is a use of choice in general, and is choice-free when the source is a group with a fixed finite generating set, where the shortlex-least representative word supplies a definable selection. The selected map is checked to be a quasi-isometric embedding and to be at bounded distance from the identity after composition either way.

items.title: A map is a quasi-isometry exactly when it is a quasi-isometric embedding with coarsely dense image
items.strategy: One direction is the previous theorem. For the other, if a quasi-inverse exists then every target point is within a bounded distance of the image of its quasi-inverse image.

items.title: Being quasi-isometric is reflexive, symmetric and transitive
items.strategy: The identity is a quasi-isometry; a quasi-inverse of a quasi-isometry is a quasi-isometry, which is where the selection of the previous theorem is used again for symmetry; and composites of quasi-isometries are quasi-isometries with the composed constants.

items.title: The quasi-isometry group of a metric space
Quasi-isometries modulo bounded distance form a group, and a quasi-isometry induces an isomorphism of these groups
items.strategy: Composition is well defined on bounded-distance classes by the compatibility lemma, associativity is inherited from composition of maps, the class of the identity is neutral, and the class of a quasi-inverse is an inverse. Conjugation by a fixed quasi-isometry and its quasi-inverse is a homomorphism between the two groups with an explicit two-sided inverse.

items.title: Bilipschitz embeddings and bilipschitz equivalences of metric spaces

Every isometry is a bilipschitz equivalence and every bilipschitz equivalence is a quasi-isometry, and two metrics on one set are Lipschitz equivalent exactly when the identity is a bilipschitz equivalence between them
items.strategy: Each implication is obtained by taking the constants of the stronger notion and weakening them: multiplicative constant one for an isometry, additive constant zero for a bilipschitz equivalence. The last clause is a comparison of two definitions written on the same data, and it is what connects this page to the published notion of Lipschitz equivalent metrics.

items.title: Separated nets in a metric space
Two metric spaces are quasi-isometric if and only if each contains a separated net and the two nets are bilipschitz equivalent
items.strategy: Given a quasi-isometry, choose a separated net in the source whose separation exceeds the additive constant times the multiplicative one; its image is then a separated net in the target and the restricted map is bilipschitz, because on well-separated points the additive error is absorbed into the multiplicative one. Conversely a bilipschitz equivalence of nets extends to the whole spaces by sending each point to the image of a nearby net point, which changes distances by a bounded amount. The extension selects nearby points, so it uses choice in the same place as the quasi-inverse theorem.

items.title: The nonempty metric spaces quasi-isometric to a one-point space are exactly those of finite diameter
items.strategy: A constant map from a space of finite diameter is a quasi-isometric embedding with coarsely dense image. Conversely a quasi-isometry to a point bounds all distances by the additive constant times the multiplicative one.

items.title: The identity map between the word metrics of two finite generating sets is a bilipschitz equivalence
items.strategy: Let $c$ be the largest word length in the second metric of a member of the first symmetrised set, finite because that set is finite.
