Expanding an element of length $n$ in the first metric and applying the triangle inequality along the expression bounds its second length by $cn$; exchanging the two sets gives the other inequality. Finiteness is used exactly to make the maximum exist.

items.title: The quasi-isometry type of a finitely generated group
A finitely generated group is finite if and only if it is quasi-isometric to a point
items.strategy: A finite group has finite diameter in any word metric. Conversely finite diameter with a finite generating set makes the whole group a ball of finite radius, and such balls are finite.

items.title: A subgroup of finite index in a finitely generated group is finitely generated, and its inclusion is a quasi-isometry
items.strategy: Fix a finite transversal containing the identity. Rewriting a product of generators by pushing transversal representatives to the right expresses each subgroup element in the finite set of products falling back into the subgroup, so that set generates. The inclusion is coarse Lipschitz with the resulting constants, is bounded below because ambient length never exceeds subgroup length, and has coarsely dense image because every element lies within the maximum ambient length of a transversal representative.

items.title: The quotient map by a finite normal subgroup is a quasi-isometry of word metric spaces
items.strategy: The image of a generating set generates the quotient, so the quotient map is one-Lipschitz. A shortest expression in the quotient lifts to an expression in the group whose value differs from the chosen lift by an element of the finite kernel, so the lengths differ by at most the largest length in that kernel. Surjectivity gives coarse density for free.

items.title: Quasi-geodesics and quasi-geodesic metric spaces
The vertex set of a connected simple graph with its path metric is a $(1,1)$-quasi-geodesic space
items.strategy: Given two vertices, parametrise a path realising their distance by sending each integer point of an interval to the corresponding vertex and each intermediate real to the nearer of its endpoints. The distances so obtained differ from those of the interval by at most one, which is the additive constant, and the multiplicative constant stays one.

items.title: A group with the word metric of any generating set is a $(1,1)$-quasi-geodesic space
items.strategy: The word metric is the path metric of the Cayley graph, which is connected because the set generates, and the previous proposition applies.

items.title: The composite of a quasi-geodesic with a quasi-isometric embedding is a quasi-geodesic, with computed constants
items.strategy: A quasi-geodesic is by definition a quasi-isometric embedding of an interval, so this is the composition lemma applied to two quasi-isometric embeddings; the constants are those the lemma records.

items.title: A coarse Lipschitz map between word metric spaces of finitely generated groups is Lipschitz
items.strategy: Adjacent points differ by a single generator and so have images at distance at most the sum of the two coarse constants; chaining along a shortest expression turns this into a purely multiplicative bound. The argument uses that the word metric takes integer values and adjacent points are at distance one, so it does not extend to an arbitrary metric source.

items.title: A bijective quasi-isometry between word metric spaces of finitely generated groups is a bilipschitz equivalence
items.strategy: Such a map and its set-theoretic inverse are both quasi-isometries, hence both coarse Lipschitz, hence both Lipschitz by the previous proposition; two mutually inverse Lipschitz bijections are a bilipschitz equivalence. Bijectivity is what makes the set-theoretic inverse available, and the conclusion fails for general metric spaces.

items.title: Quasi-isometry invariants and geometric properties of finitely generated groups
Finiteness is a geometric property of finitely generated groups
items.strategy: Two quasi-isometric finitely generated groups are simultaneously quasi-isometric to a point, and being quasi-isometric to a point characterises finiteness among finitely generated groups.

pages.title: Cayley Graphs Word Metrics and Quasi Isometry — Examples

items.title: The Cayley graph of $\mathbb Z$ for the generating set $\{1\}$ is a line and its word metric is $|m-n|$
items.strategy: Read the edge set off the definition and identify the word length of $n$ as $|n|$ from the length laws; compare with the metric induced from the real line.

items.title: The word metrics of $\mathbb Z$ for $\{1\}$ and for $\{2,3\}$ differ at $1$ and are bilipschitz equivalent
items.strategy: Compute both word lengths at small integers to see the metrics differ, then exhibit the constants the comparison theorem produces.

items.title: The Cayley graph of $\mathbb Z^n$ for the standard basis is the integer lattice, and its word metric is the sum of coordinate differences
items.strategy: Identify the neighbours of a vertex, then compute the word length as the $\ell^1$ norm by exhibiting an expression of that length and bounding below coordinatewise.

items.title: The Cayley graph of the free group on two generators is the tree in which every vertex has four neighbours
items.strategy: Apply the tree theorem to a free basis and compute the degree from the symmetrised set of size four.

items.title: The dihedral group of order eight has Cayley graphs that are a cycle of length eight and a cube
items.strategy: Draw both edge sets from the definition for the generating sets $\{r,s\}$ and $\{s,rs,r^2\}$, and check the degrees.

items.title: The inclusion of $\mathbb Z$ in $\mathbb R$ is a quasi-isometry that is neither surjective nor a bilipschitz equivalence
items.strategy: Verify the quasi-isometric embedding inequalities with constants one and zero, produce the integer-part map as a quasi-inverse, and note that no bijection can exist for cardinality reasons.

items.title: The subgroup $2\mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z$ has index two in $\mathbb Z^2$ and its inclusion is a quasi-isometry
items.strategy: Exhibit a transversal of size two and apply the finite-index proposition, then check the constants directly on the two generators.

items.title: The infinite dihedral group is quasi-isometric to $\mathbb Z$, and to $\mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z/2$
items.strategy: Use the two presentations of the infinite dihedral group to exhibit Cayley graphs isomorphic to that of $\mathbb Z$ and to that of $\mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z/2$, then transport through the comparison theorem.

items.title: Taking $\mathbb Z$ itself as a generating set gives a word metric of diameter one, not bilipschitz equivalent to the standard one
items.strategy: Compute the word length of every nonzero integer as one, so the diameter is one while the standard word metric is unbounded; locate the exact step of the comparison theorem that fails.

items.title: A single map exhibiting a quasi-isometry that is discontinuous, non-injective and non-surjective
items.strategy: Take the integer-part map from the real line to $2\mathbb Z$; verify the quasi-isometry inequalities and then each of the three failures at explicit points.

items.title: FALSE: the Cayley graph of a group is independent of the chosen generating set
items.strategy: Refute with $\mathbb Z$ for $\{1\}$ and for $\{2,3\}$, whose vertex degrees differ.

items.title: FALSE: every word metric is invariant under right translation
items.strategy: Refute in a nonabelian group by exhibiting two points whose right translates move to a different distance.

items.title: FALSE: every quasi-isometry is continuous, or bijective
items.strategy: Refute with the integer-part map, which is neither.

items.title: FALSE: any two infinite finitely generated groups are quasi-isometric
items.strategy: Refute by comparing the sizes of balls in $\mathbb Z$ and in a free group of rank two, which grow linearly and exponentially, and showing that a quasi-isometry would force a linear bound between the two counts.

items.title: FALSE: a nontrivial finitely generated group with a word metric is a geodesic metric space
items.strategy: Refute from the definition: a geodesic between two points at distance one supplies points at every intermediate real distance, while a word metric takes only integer values.

items.title: FALSE: groups with isomorphic Cayley graphs are isomorphic
items.strategy: Refute with the symmetric group on three letters and the cyclic group of order six, each taken with its whole underlying set as generating set: both Cayley graphs are complete on six vertices.

items.title: The Cayley graphs of $\mathbb Z/2$ for $\{1\}$ and of $\mathbb Z$ for $\{-1,1\}$ are trees, and neither generating set is free
items.strategy: Draw both graphs and check they are trees; then note that $\mathbb Z/2$ is not free and that $\{-1,1\}$ has a product of two members equal to the identity, which is exactly the hypothesis the converse theorem needs.

items.title: A nonempty metric space of finite diameter has trivial quasi-isometry group
items.strategy: Every self-map of such a space is at bounded distance from the identity, so there is exactly one bounded-distance class.

items.title: Scaling maps embed the multiplicative group of nonzero reals into the quasi-isometry group of $\mathbb Z$
items.strategy: For nonzero $\alpha$ the map $n\mapsto\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor$ is a quasi-isometry of $\mathbb Z$; composing two of them agrees with scaling by the product up to a bounded error, so the assignment is a homomorphism on classes, and for $\alpha\ne\beta$ the difference $|\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor-\lfloor\beta n\rfloor|$ is unbounded, so it is injective.

pages.title: Geometric Actions Svarc Milnor and Growth

items.title: Isometric, proper, and cobounded actions on metric spaces
Metric properness agrees with proper discontinuity on proper discrete metric spaces
items.strategy: In a proper discrete metric space, bounded subsets are finite and compact subsets are finite. Transporter finiteness for finite subsets is therefore exactly the usual proper-discontinuity condition.

items.title: Geometric actions on metric spaces
Bounded local displacement on a geodesic space implies coarse Lipschitz control
items.strategy: Subdivide a geodesic segment into pieces of length at most r. If the map moves r-close pairs by at most C, summing over the subdivision gives a linear bound in the total geodesic length.

items.title: Orbit maps of isometric actions are coarse Lipschitz
items.strategy: Choose a finite generating set S and basepoint x. The displacement of each generator at x is bounded, so a word of length n moves x by at most n times the maximum generator displacement.

items.title: Cobounded proper geodesic actions produce finite generating sets
items.strategy: Choose a bounded set B whose G-translates cover X. Properness makes the set of g with B∩gB nonempty finite. A geodesic from x to g·x can be followed through successive translates of B, expressing g as a product of those finitely many transporters.

items.title: The Svarc-Milnor lemma
items.strategy: Use the previous lemma to get a finite generating set from a geometric action. The orbit map is coarsely Lipschitz by generator-displacement bounds, coarsely surjective by coboundedness, and has a linear lower bound by tracing a geodesic through the bounded fundamental set.

items.title: Groups acting geometrically on the same space are quasi-isometric
items.strategy: Each group is quasi-isometric to the common space by the Svarc-Milnor lemma, and quasi-isometry is an equivalence relation.

items.title: The growth function of a finitely generated group
Growth comparison and growth type
Growth comparison is a preorder
items.strategy: Reflexivity is immediate from the defining inequality. For transitivity, compose the two comparison inequalities and absorb the resulting constants into one larger constant.

items.title: Growth type is independent of the finite generating set
items.strategy: Bilipschitz equivalence of the two word metrics controls each word ball between two rescaled balls in the other metric. Translating these ball containments into cardinality bounds gives mutual growth comparison.

items.title: Growth type is a quasi-isometry invariant of finitely generated groups
items.strategy: A quasi-isometry between finitely generated groups is coarsely Lipschitz in both directions. Images and quasi-inverse images of word balls sit inside linearly rescaled balls, and finite generating sets ensure those balls are finite, so the two growth functions mutually dominate.

items.title: Polynomial, subexponential, exponential, and intermediate growth
Free groups of rank at least two have exponential growth
items.strategy: With respect to a free basis, reduced words of length n are counted exactly: 2r choices for the first letter and 2r-1 thereafter. The reduced-word length equals the word length, so the growth function dominates an exponential function when r>=2.

items.title: The homogeneous dimension of a finitely generated nilpotent group
Bass-Guivarch growth-degree formula
Finitely generated nilpotent groups have polynomial growth
items.strategy: Apply the Bass-Guivarch formula and keep only the consequence that the growth function is comparable to a polynomial of the homogeneous dimension.

items.title: Gromov's polynomial-growth theorem
Grigorchuk groups of intermediate growth

pages.title: Geometric Actions Svarc Milnor and Growth — Examples

items.title: The integers act geometrically on the real line
items.strategy: Translations n:x↦x+n are isometries. Properness is immediate from bounded interval transporters, coboundedness from the unit interval, and the orbit map identifies Z with the integer lattice in R.

items.title: Z^n acts geometrically on Euclidean n-space
items.strategy: Integer translations on R^n are isometric, proper, and cobounded by the unit cube. The Svarc-Milnor lemma therefore identifies Z^n with Euclidean n-space up to quasi-isometry.

items.title: Free groups act geometrically on regular trees
items.strategy: The Cayley graph of a free group with respect to a free basis is a tree, and left translation acts freely, properly, and cocompactly on it. The orbit map is the inclusion of vertices.

items.title: Horizontal translations of Z on the Euclidean plane are proper but not cobounded
items.strategy: Let n act on R^2 by (x,y)↦(x+n,y). Bounded sets have only finitely many transporting integers, but every orbit stays in one horizontal line, so points with large |y| escape every bounded neighbourhood of a fixed orbit.

items.title: Free abelian groups have polynomial growth of the expected degree
items.strategy: For the standard basis of Z^n, l^1-balls are sandwiched between cubes of side proportional to R, so their cardinalities are bounded above and below by constant multiples of R^n. Comparing n=1 and n>=2 separates linear and higher-degree polynomial growth.

items.title: The discrete Heisenberg group has growth degree four
items.strategy: Present the discrete Heisenberg group on triples $(a,b,c)inmathbb Z^3$, compute directly that its commutator subgroup is central and that the first and second lower-central quotients have free ranks two and one, and then apply the Bass-Guivarch formula $1cdot 2 + 2cdot 1 = 4$.

items.title: Quasi-isometry without bounded geometry need not preserve local ball counts
items.strategy: Attach n leaves by unit edges to the integer vertex n on a bi-infinite line. Collapsing each finite leaf cluster to its spine vertex is a quasi-isometry onto Z, but radius-one balls at the vertices n have size n+3 in the comb space and size 3 in Z.

items.title: FALSE: a proper isometric action has bounded orbits
items.strategy: Refute with the translation action of Z on the real line, whose orbits are unbounded.

items.title: FALSE: cobounded and cocompact are identical without extra hypotheses
items.strategy: Refute with the trivial action on the open interval (0,1): the single orbit is cobounded because the space has finite diameter, but the quotient is not compact.

items.title: FALSE: the growth function is independent of the generating set pointwise
items.strategy: Compare Z with generators {±1} and {±1,±2}: the exact ball counts differ although the growth type is the same.

items.title: FALSE: every subexponential growth group has polynomial growth
items.strategy: Refute with Grigorchuk's groups, whose growth is intermediate.

items.title: FALSE: Gromov's polynomial-growth theorem is proved on this page
items.strategy: The page records Gromov's theorem as an external result and does not supply a local proof.

pages.title: Hyperbolic Spaces and Hyperbolic Groups

items.title: Geodesic segments, geodesic triangles, and geodesic metric spaces
Delta-slim triangles and hyperbolic spaces
Cayley trees are 0-hyperbolic
items.strategy: In a tree each pair of vertices is joined by a unique geodesic, so the three sides of a geodesic triangle meet in a tripod. Every point of one side then lies on one of the other two sides, giving 0-slimness.

items.title: The Gromov product based at a point
Slim triangles, the Gromov product, and the four-point condition are equivalent up to constants
items.strategy: Translate slimness into lower bounds for the Gromov product, compare the three branch lengths in a geodesic triangle, and then rewrite those inequalities into the four-point form. Each implication changes constants explicitly rather than pretending one universal delta survives every reformulation.

items.title: Hyperbolic spaces have thin geodesic quadrilaterals
items.strategy: Cut a geodesic quadrilateral into two triangles along a diagonal and apply slimness to each triangle. The union of the two resulting neighbourhood bounds gives a thin-quadrilateral constant depending only on delta.

items.title: Morse stability of quasi-geodesics
items.strategy: Project a quasi-geodesic to a geodesic with the same endpoints, use thin quadrilaterals to control successive projection jumps, and bootstrap the local control to a global Hausdorff-distance bound depending on delta and the quasi-geodesic constants.

items.title: Hyperbolicity is a quasi-isometry invariant of geodesic spaces
items.strategy: Send geodesic triangles across a quasi-isometry. Their images are quasi-geodesic triangles, Morse stability compares them with honest geodesics, and the four-point or slim-triangle characterisation then transfers hyperbolicity back to the target space.

items.title: Hyperbolic groups
Hyperbolicity of a finitely generated group is independent of the finite generating set
items.strategy: Different finite generating sets give bilipschitz equivalent word metrics and hence quasi-isometric Cayley graphs. Hyperbolicity is therefore unchanged by replacing the generating set.

items.title: Finite groups and free groups are hyperbolic
items.strategy: Finite Cayley graphs have bounded diameter, so every geodesic triangle is diameter-slim. Free groups are hyperbolic because their Cayley graphs are trees, hence 0-hyperbolic.

items.title: Free abelian groups of rank at least two are not hyperbolic
items.strategy: In the standard Cayley graph of Z^2 one finds geodesic rectangles of arbitrarily large width. A fixed slimness constant would force every long side to stay uniformly close to the other two sides, which fails for the midpoints of these rectangles.

items.title: Hyperbolic groups admit finite Dehn presentations
items.strategy: Choose a finite generating set and use the hyperbolic geometry of geodesic bigons and triangles to produce relators with a uniform Dehn-shortening property. The result is stated in the exact finite-presentation form needed for the word-problem corollary.

items.title: Hyperbolic groups have solvable word problem
items.strategy: Run the Dehn reduction procedure attached to the Dehn presentation from the previous theorem. Strict length decrease gives termination, and the Dehn property gives correctness.

items.title: Linear isoperimetric characterisation of hyperbolic groups
items.strategy: Use hyperbolicity to control the area of van Kampen fillings linearly in boundary length, and conversely build slimness from a linear filling inequality by analysing geodesic polygons in the Cayley 2-complex. The area convention is fixed explicitly so the constants are meaningful.

items.title: Finite C'(1/6) presentations define hyperbolic groups
items.strategy: Use the sourced small-cancellation Dehn and linear-isoperimetric consequences to bridge finite C'(1/6) presentations to hyperbolicity. This item is kept as a survey-level agreement theorem and is not allowed to carry later dependencies until GT-8 is on disk.

items.title: Infinite-order elements of hyperbolic groups are undistorted
items.strategy: Powers of an infinite-order element define a uniform quasi-geodesic in the Cayley graph. Morse stability then compares this orbit line with a geodesic axis and yields linear growth of word length in the exponent.

items.title: The centralizer of an infinite-order element in a hyperbolic group is virtually cyclic
items.strategy: Every centralizing element preserves the quasi-axis of the given infinite-order element up to bounded distance. The induced action on the axis gives a homomorphism to the isometry group of a quasi-line with finite kernel, forcing a finite-index cyclic subgroup.

items.title: Abelian subgroups of hyperbolic groups are virtually cyclic
items.strategy: An infinite abelian subgroup contains an infinite-order element, and every element of the subgroup centralizes it. The subgroup therefore lies in a virtually cyclic centralizer.

items.title: Finite subgroups of a hyperbolic group have uniformly bounded order
items.strategy: A finite subgroup orbit has bounded diameter, so one may choose a point minimizing maximal displacement and then compare the finite subgroup action with the uniformly locally finite geometry of the Cayley graph. Hyperbolicity bounds the possible displacement patterns and hence the subgroup order.

items.title: Elementary and non-elementary hyperbolic groups
Non-elementary hyperbolic groups contain a rank-two free subgroup
items.strategy: Choose two independent infinite-order elements with sufficiently separated quasi-axes and apply ping-pong on large translates of their attracting regions. The resulting subgroup is free of rank two.

items.title: The Gromov boundary via asymptotic sequences
Asymptoticity of Gromov sequences is an equivalence relation
items.strategy: Reflexivity and symmetry are immediate from the definition. Transitivity uses the Gromov-product inequality coming from hyperbolicity to keep pairwise products uniformly large after passing through an intermediate sequence.

items.title: The boundary topology defined by Gromov products
The boundary topology is well defined and quasi-isometry invariant
items.strategy: Compare boundary neighbourhoods defined using different basepoints and different representative sequences by the four-point inequalities. A quasi-isometry sends divergent quasi-geodesic rays to divergent quasi-geodesic rays, so Morse stability induces the boundary homeomorphism.

items.title: FALSE: a hyperbolic group is just a group with a hyperbolic-plane subgroup
items.strategy: Finite groups and free groups are hyperbolic, but neither notion is defined by containing a copy of the hyperbolic plane. Hyperbolicity is a Cayley-graph property, not a subgroup test of that form.

items.title: FALSE: the same delta works after every finite change of generating set
items.strategy: Hyperbolicity is invariant under quasi-isometry, but the proof changes constants. Bilipschitz equivalent word metrics need not preserve one universal slimness constant.

items.title: FALSE: every abelian group is hyperbolic
items.strategy: The group Z^2 is finitely generated abelian but not hyperbolic, as witnessed by arbitrarily large geodesic rectangles in its Cayley graph.

items.title: FALSE: all quasi-geodesics in all metric spaces stay uniformly close to geodesics
items.strategy: Morse stability is a hyperbolic-space theorem. Euclidean planes already contain quasi-geodesics that drift arbitrarily far from every geodesic with the same endpoints.

items.title: FALSE: the Gromov boundary definition needs no properness or equivalence check
items.strategy: The boundary construction here depends on asymptoticity being an equivalence relation and on the proper geodesic hypotheses that make the topology behave as stated. Dropping those hypotheses changes the object.

pages.title: Hyperbolic Spaces and Hyperbolic Groups — Examples

items.title: Every tree is 0-hyperbolic
items.strategy: In a tree every geodesic triangle is a tripod, so each side lies in the union of the other two. This is the model zero-hyperbolic example behind free groups.

items.title: The hyperbolic plane is hyperbolic
items.strategy: Use the classical geodesic-triangle comparison in the hyperbolic plane to obtain a uniform slimness constant. The example is geometric rather than combinatorial, but it fits the same definition verbatim.

items.title: Free groups have Cantor-set boundaries
items.strategy: The Cayley graph of a free group is a regular tree, so boundary points are infinite reduced rays. Identifying rays with infinite reduced words gives the usual Cantor-set model of the boundary.

items.title: Closed surface groups are hyperbolic
items.strategy: A cocompact torsion-free lattice in the isometry group of the hyperbolic plane acts geometrically on H^2. Hyperbolicity of the plane and Svarc-Milnor then make the surface group hyperbolic.

items.title: A small-cancellation presentation gives a hyperbolic group
items.strategy: Choose a finite presentation satisfying the strict C'(1/6) overlap condition and apply the sourced agreement theorem. The example is a concrete witness that small cancellation lands inside the hyperbolic world.

items.title: Z^2 is not hyperbolic
items.strategy: Work in the standard square-grid Cayley graph. Midpoints of long sides of geodesic squares move arbitrarily far from the other two sides, so no uniform slimness constant exists.

items.title: A product of two infinite groups need not be hyperbolic
items.strategy: The direct product Z times Z is the simplest witness. It is infinite in both factors and fails hyperbolicity for the same large-rectangle reason as the free abelian rank-two case.

pages.title: Amenable Groups and Folner Criteria

items.title: Means on bounded functions on a group
Left translation on bounded functions
Left-invariant means and amenable groups
Left and right amenability agree by inversion
items.strategy: Precompose bounded functions with inversion to transport a left-invariant mean into a right-invariant one and conversely.

items.title: Finite groups are amenable
items.strategy: Normalized counting on the finite underlying set gives an invariant mean.

items.title: Abelian groups are amenable
items.strategy: Use the directed-union reduction to finitely generated abelian groups and then build an invariant mean from Folner sets, recording the ultrafilter cost explicitly.

items.title: Subgroups and quotients of amenable groups are amenable
items.strategy: Restrict an invariant measure to a subgroup by a transversal argument and push amenability to a quotient through the induced action on cosets.

items.title: Extensions of amenable groups are amenable
items.strategy: Combine invariant means on the normal subgroup and the quotient by averaging first along cosets and then over the quotient.

items.title: Locally finite groups
Directed unions of amenable subgroups are amenable
items.strategy: View the ambient group as the direct limit of the directed system of amenable subgroups and pass invariant finitely additive measures to the limit.

items.title: Solvable groups and locally finite groups are amenable
items.strategy: For solvable groups, induct on derived length using the extension theorem; for locally finite groups, express the group as the directed union of its finite subgroups.

items.title: Folner sets and the Folner condition
Equivalent boundary formulations of the Folner condition
items.strategy: Rewrite symmetric-difference estimates as boundary estimates and compare right and left formulations by inversion.

items.title: The Folner criterion for amenability
items.strategy: Build a mean from Folner sets via an ultrafilter limit, and conversely use finite-dimensional separation to extract almost invariant finite sets from an invariant mean.

items.title: Folner sequences for enumerated groups
Enumerated countable amenable groups admit Folner sequences
items.strategy: Exhaust the group by the finite subsets cut out by the enumeration and choose successive Folner sets with error at most 1/n for the nth finite test set.

items.title: Subexponential growth implies amenability
items.strategy: Use growth balls: if every radius had proportionally large boundary, iterating the boundary growth would force exponential growth.

items.title: Paradoxical decompositions of groups
Paradoxical groups admit no invariant mean
items.strategy: An invariant mean applied to the two translated disjoint decompositions forces 1 to be at least 2.

items.title: A group is amenable if and only if it is not paradoxical
items.strategy: Invoke Tarski's finitely additive measure criterion for paradoxical subsets and specialize it to the left action of the group on itself.

items.title: The free group of rank two is nonamenable
items.strategy: Use either the invariant-mean contradiction from the standard two-piece decomposition or an explicit paradoxical decomposition of reduced words in a free basis.

items.title: Groups containing a rank-two free subgroup are nonamenable
items.strategy: An amenable group has amenable subgroups, so a rank-two free subgroup contradicts the previous theorem.

items.title: Amenability is a quasi-isometry invariant for finitely generated groups
items.strategy: Transfer Folner sets across a quasi-isometry using bounded distortion of boundaries and bounded geometry of Cayley graphs.

items.title: There exist nonamenable groups without nonabelian free subgroups
FALSE: amenable means finite
items.strategy: Refute with infinite abelian groups such as Z.

items.title: FALSE: every nonamenable group contains a rank-two free subgroup
items.strategy: Refute by citing standard nonamenable counterexamples without nonabelian free subgroups.

items.title: FALSE: one finite Folner set proves amenability
items.strategy: The criterion quantifies over every finite test set and every error tolerance, not one accidental almost-invariant finite subset.

items.title: FALSE: every uncountable amenable group has a Folner sequence
items.strategy: The sequence formulation needs a countable indexing of the finite tests; in general one uses Folner nets or the finite-test property itself.

items.title: FALSE: a paradoxical decomposition is just an abstract partition without prescribed translates
items.strategy: The translating group elements are load-bearing: without them the decomposition no longer encodes nonamenability.

pages.title: Amenable Groups and Folner Criteria — Examples

items.title: Intervals in Z are Folner sets
items.strategy: Compute the boundary of symmetric intervals explicitly for a fixed finite generating set and let the interval radius grow.

items.title: Boxes in Z^n are Folner sets
items.strategy: Count the boundary layers of cubes in the standard basis and compare them with the total number of lattice points.

items.title: Finite groups and locally finite groups are amenable
items.strategy: Apply normalized counting in the finite case and the directed-union corollary in the locally finite case.

items.title: The standard lamplighter group is amenable
items.strategy: Describe the lamplighter group as a semidirect product of a locally finite base by Z and apply the extension theorem.

items.title: Boundary expansion in the free group
items.strategy: Show that every finite set of reduced words in a free basis acquires a uniformly positive boundary proportion under multiplication by generators.

items.title: A paradoxical decomposition of a free group of rank two
items.strategy: Partition reduced words by initial letter and write the group as two disjoint translated copies.

items.title: Amenability does not imply subexponential growth
items.strategy: Use the lamplighter group as an amenable group with exponential growth.

pages.title: Simplicial Trees and Group Actions

items.title: An oriented graph with edge reversal
Finite simplicial paths, reduced paths, cycles, and connectedness
A simplicial tree
A simplicial graph is a tree exactly when every two vertices are joined by a unique reduced path
items.strategy: Distinct reduced paths between the same endpoints combine to a reduced cycle, and conversely any reduced cycle splits into two distinct reduced paths with common endpoints.

items.title: The simplicial path metric on the vertices of a tree
The path metric on a simplicial tree is geodesic and integer-valued
items.strategy: The unique reduced path between two vertices realises the metric, and its edge count is an integer that concatenates additively along vertices on that path.

items.title: Finite simplicial trees agree with the published finite-tree notion
items.strategy: Forget orientations to recover a finite simple graph, translate reduced simplicial paths into ordinary graph paths, and compare the two tree characterisations directly.

items.title: Graph automorphisms and group actions on a simplicial graph
Edge inversions and actions without inversions
Barycentric subdivision removes edge inversions while preserving tree actions
items.strategy: Insert a midpoint on every geometric edge, extend the action to the subdivided graph, and note that an inversion can swap the two half-edges but cannot fix either oriented half-edge.

items.title: The quotient graph of an action without inversions
Vertex and edge stabilizers fit together by incidence inclusions
items.strategy: An element stabilizing an oriented edge must stabilize both of its endpoints, so every edge stabilizer sits inside the stabilizers of the incident vertices.

items.title: Fixed subtrees and minimal invariant subtrees
The nonempty fixed-vertex set of a tree automorphism is a subtree
items.strategy: If an automorphism fixes two vertices then uniqueness of the reduced path between them forces every intermediate vertex and edge on that path to be fixed as well.

items.title: The translation length of a tree automorphism without inversions
A tree automorphism without inversions is elliptic or hyperbolic
items.strategy: Show that the integer-valued displacement function attains its infimum; zero displacement yields a fixed vertex, while positive displacement builds a unique embedded axis from successive geodesic segments.

items.title: Translation length is conjugacy-invariant and homogeneous
items.strategy: Conjugation preserves displacement values, and powers act along the same axis by repeated translations whose lengths add.

items.title: Finite groups acting on trees have a global fixed vertex after barycentric subdivision
items.strategy: Take the finite orbit hull of one vertex, reduce to a finite invariant subtree, and use its centre; barycentric subdivision turns a possible fixed edge-midpoint into a genuine fixed vertex.

items.title: Groups acting freely without inversions on trees are torsion-free
items.strategy: A torsion element generates a finite subgroup, and the fixed-point lemma then produces a fixed vertex, contradicting freeness.

items.title: Hyperbolic tree automorphisms satisfy a ping-pong criterion for freeness
items.strategy: Choose disjoint half-trees determined by the attracting directions of the hyperbolic automorphisms and apply the standard ping-pong argument on those domains.

items.title: FALSE: the published finite-tree definition already covers Bass-Serre trees
items.strategy: Refute by an infinite simplicial tree whose reduced-path behaviour is correct but whose vertex set is not finite.

items.title: FALSE: every tree action is without edge inversions
items.strategy: Refute with an action swapping the endpoints of a single edge and then contrast it with the barycentric subdivision repair.

items.title: FALSE: every tree automorphism fixes a vertex
items.strategy: Refute with a translation of the bi-infinite line, which is hyperbolic and has positive translation length.

items.title: FALSE: translation length is always the distance from an arbitrary basepoint
items.strategy: Refute by choosing a basepoint off the axis of a hyperbolic automorphism; its displacement is strictly larger than the minimum translation length.

items.title: FALSE: a quotient of a tree by a group action is always a tree
items.strategy: Refute by a free translation action on the line, whose quotient graph contains a cycle even though the original graph is a tree.

pages.title: Simplicial Trees and Group Actions — Examples

items.title: The bi-infinite line with its translation action
items.strategy: Model the line as a simplicial tree with vertex set Z and compute the axis and translation length of the unit shift explicitly.

items.title: Regular Cayley trees of free groups
items.strategy: View the Cayley graph of a free group with respect to a free basis as a simplicial tree and read off its regular valence directly from the generators.

items.title: An edge inversion and its barycentric subdivision
items.strategy: Swap the endpoints of one edge, observe the inversion, and then subdivide once to produce an equivalent action without inversions.

items.title: A finite group fixes the centre of a finite tree
items.strategy: Take a finite symmetry group of a finite tree, compute its orbit hull, and locate the fixed centre after the possible subdivision step.

items.title: Elliptic and hyperbolic automorphisms of simplicial trees
items.strategy: Contrast a vertex-fixing symmetry with a translation along a line and compute the different translation-length behaviours side by side.

items.title: The quotient of a tree can have cycles
items.strategy: Quotient the bi-infinite line by the translation generated by one step; the quotient graph is a loop.

pages.title: Graphs of Groups and Bass Serre Theory

items.title: A graph of groups
A maximal subtree of a connected graph
The path group of a graph of groups
The fundamental group of a graph of groups relative to a maximal tree
Different maximal trees give isomorphic graph-of-groups fundamental groups
items.strategy: Choose connecting paths between the two tree gauges and conjugate each stable edge generator across those paths to build mutually inverse homomorphisms.

items.title: Reduced words in a graph of groups
Normal form for the fundamental group of a graph of groups
items.strategy: Peel the graph off one geometric edge at a time, reducing to the published amalgam and HNN normal forms at each step.

items.title: Vertex groups embed in the fundamental group of a graph of groups
items.strategy: A nontrivial element of a vertex group is already a reduced graph-of-groups word of length zero, so normal-form uniqueness forbids collapse.

items.title: The Bass-Serre tree of a graph of groups
The Bass-Serre coset graph is a tree
items.strategy: Connectedness comes from reading reduced words as coset paths, and a reduced closed path would contradict graph-of-groups normal form.

items.title: The fundamental group acts without inversions on its Bass-Serre tree
items.strategy: Left multiplication on cosets preserves the incidence maps, and the normal form identifies the quotient graph and the vertex and edge stabilizers up to conjugacy.

items.title: The quotient graph of groups attached to a tree action
The boundary monomorphisms from stabilizers are well-defined
items.strategy: Change of orbit representatives alters the chosen attaching element by conjugation, so the resulting edge-to-vertex maps differ only by the expected inner automorphism.

items.title: Bass-Serre structure theorem
items.strategy: Choose orbit representatives and connecting lifts, map each stabilizer and non-tree edge generator into the acting group, and compare the resulting action with the Bass-Serre tree of the reconstructed graph of groups.

items.title: A one-segment graph of groups gives an amalgamated free product
items.strategy: In the one-edge case, unwind the graph-of-groups presentation and compare it directly with the published amalgam pushout description.

items.title: A one-loop graph of groups gives an HNN extension
items.strategy: Collapse the chosen maximal tree and identify the lone non-tree edge generator with the stable letter of the published HNN presentation.

items.title: A group acting freely without inversions on a tree is free
items.strategy: All stabilizers in the quotient graph of groups are trivial, so the structure theorem identifies the group with the fundamental group of a graph built only from non-tree edge generators.

items.title: The fundamental group of a graph with trivial groups is free
items.strategy: Apply the Bass-Serre action to the trivial-group graph of groups; the action is free, so the previous corollary identifies the fundamental group as free.

items.title: Kurosh subgroup theorem
items.strategy: Restrict the Bass-Serre tree action of a free product to the subgroup, read off the quotient graph of groups, and use trivial edge groups to obtain the free-product decomposition with double-coset indexing.

items.title: Grushko decomposition and rank additivity
items.strategy: Use free splittings with trivial edge groups, derive terminal freely indecomposable factors from maximality, and use Kurosh on two decompositions to compare factor conjugacy classes and the free rank.

items.title: Stallings's theorem on ends and splittings
items.strategy: Record the exact finitely generated theorem only; the ends machinery it needs lies outside this page.

items.title: FALSE: the fundamental group of a graph of groups is a topological fundamental group by definition
items.strategy: Refute because the algebraic graph-of-groups presentation is defined first and only later compared with tree actions.

items.title: FALSE: vertex stabilizers are literally the chosen vertex groups without conjugacy ambiguity
items.strategy: Refute by changing the chosen lift of a quotient vertex, which conjugates the stabilizer inside the acting group.

items.title: FALSE: every tree action is free
items.strategy: Refute with actions having nontrivial vertex stabilizers, such as the Bass-Serre action of a nontrivial amalgam.

items.title: FALSE: the quotient graph determines the acting group without stabilizer data
items.strategy: Refute by comparing nonisomorphic graphs of groups carried by the same underlying quotient graph.

items.title: FALSE: Kurosh says every subgroup of a free product is free
items.strategy: Refute because Kurosh retains conjugates of intersections with factor groups as genuine free-product factors.

pages.title: Graphs of Groups and Bass Serre Theory — Examples

items.title: The Bass-Serre tree of a free product
items.strategy: Take a graph of groups with two vertices and trivial edge group and read the vertices and edges as cosets of the two factors.

items.title: The Bass-Serre tree of an amalgamated free product
items.strategy: Start from the one-segment graph of groups and write down the two vertex-orbit types and the common edge stabilizer.

items.title: The Bass-Serre tree of a Baumslag-Solitar group
items.strategy: Use the one-loop graph of groups description and identify the stable-letter action on the resulting tree of cosets.

items.title: A free action and the quotient-graph basis
items.strategy: Quotient a free action on a tree by a chosen maximal subtree and read the free basis from the non-tree edges.

items.title: A Kurosh decomposition of a subgroup of a free product
items.strategy: Restrict the Bass-Serre action to an explicit subgroup and read off the resulting factor intersections and free part from the quotient tree.

items.title: A graph of finite groups giving a virtually free group
items.strategy: Use finite vertex and edge stabilizers in the Bass-Serre tree and a finite quotient graph to exhibit a virtually free fundamental group.

items.title: The underlying quotient graph does not determine the acting group
items.strategy: Put different vertex or edge groups on the same underlying quotient graph and compare the resulting fundamental groups.

items.title: $\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ as the Euclidean plane and as a normed real algebra: what the identification preserves
items.strategy: Start with the published quotient construction, not an unproved pair model. Under $\Phi(a+bi)=(a,b)$, record that addition and real scalar multiplication are coordinatewise, complex multiplication has the published bilinear coordinate formula, conjugation is reflection in the real axis, and $|z|=\|\Phi(z)\|_2$, so the metric, convergence, continuity, and topology agree with those of $\mathbb R^2$. State equally explicitly what is not being identified: a general real-linear map need not be complex-linear, multiplication is extra structure beyond the real vector space, and the Euclidean identification supplies no compatible field order. Treat the last clause as an inline reminder from $i^2=-1$, not as a second false-statement item.

items.title: A complex domain is a nonempty connected open subset of $\mathbb C$
Complex differentiability at a point, the complex derivative, holomorphic functions, and entire functions
The complex derivative at a point is unique
items.strategy: If two numbers $L$ and $M$ are limits of the same difference quotient, assume $L\ne M$ and apply both limit estimates with tolerance $|L-M|/3$. The triangle inequality then gives $|L-M|<2|L-M|/3$, a contradiction. Keep the punctured-domain quantifier from the derivative definition explicit.

items.title: The Wirtinger derivatives $\partial_z f$ and $\partial_{\bar z}f$, and antiholomorphic functions
Complex differentiability is equivalent to a complex-linear real total derivative, to $\partial_{\bar z}f=0$, and to real differentiability plus the Cauchy–Riemann equations
items.strategy: For $f=u+iv$ on an open set and $a$ in its domain, prove one four-way equivalence in a single item: (i) the complex difference quotient exists; (ii) $f$ is real totally differentiable and $Df(a)$ is multiplication by a complex number; (iii) $f$ is real totally differentiable and $\partial_{\bar z}f(a)=0$; (iv) $f$ is real totally differentiable and $u_x=v_y$, $u_y=-v_x$ at $a$. From (i), subtract $f'(a)h$ to obtain the real total-derivative remainder. Translate a real derivative matrix through the published coordinate model to show that complex-linearity is exactly the CR matrix form, and expand the Wirtinger formula to identify the same two real equations. Record $f'(a)=u_x+iv_x=v_y-iu_y=\partial_z f(a)$.

items.title: Complex differentiability at a point implies continuity there
items.strategy: Use the four-way theorem to obtain real total differentiability under the Euclidean identification, then apply the published local linear bound and continuity theorem. Translate the conclusion back through the metric dictionary.

items.title: Continuous first partial derivatives and the Cauchy–Riemann equations imply complex differentiability pointwise, and holomorphy when they hold throughout an open set
items.strategy: Let $f=u+iv$ on an open set and fix $a$. Assume all four first partials exist on a neighbourhood of $a$, are continuous at $a$, and satisfy CR at $a$. Apply the published continuous-partials theorem componentwise to get real total differentiability at $a$, then use the CR direction of the four-way theorem. Deduce the open-set corollary when the hypotheses hold at every point. State these exact hypotheses; do not replace them by the false assertion that bare existence of partials plus CR is sufficient.

items.title: Cartesian and polar forms of the Cauchy–Riemann equations agree away from the origin
items.strategy: On an open parameter set with $r>0$ and $re^{i\theta}$ in the domain, set $U(r,\theta)=u(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)$ and $V$ similarly. Use the real total-derivative chain rule and the real sine/cosine derivatives to transform the Cartesian equations into $U_r=r^{-1}V_\theta$ and $V_r=-r^{-1}U_\theta$, and reverse the invertible coordinate calculation. Also derive $f'(re^{i\theta})=e^{-i\theta}(U_r+iV_r)$. The statement must exclude $r=0$ and must not presume a global argument branch.

items.title: Linearity, product, reciprocal, and quotient rules for complex derivatives
items.strategy: At a common point of complex differentiability, prove the sum and scalar rules by linearity of limits. For the product insert and subtract $f(a)g(a+h)$ and use continuity of the differentiable factors. For $1/g$, factor the difference quotient and use $g(a)\ne0$ plus continuity to keep the denominator nonzero near $a$; combine with the product rule for the quotient. State the local nonvanishing set precisely and include the constant and identity derivatives as base cases.

items.title: The chain rule for complex derivatives
items.strategy: Regard both complex-differentiable maps as real totally differentiable with derivatives given by complex multiplication. Apply the published total-derivative chain rule; the composite of multiplication by $f'(a)$ and multiplication by $g'(f(a))$ is multiplication by their product. Invoke the four-way equivalence in reverse to recover complex differentiability and the formula $(g\circ f)'(a)=g'(f(a))f'(a)$.

items.title: The Wirtinger chain rule for compositions of real-differentiable complex-valued maps
items.strategy: For real-differentiable $f:U\to V$ and $g:V\to\mathbb C$, write the real differential of each map in the basis $(h,\bar h)$ supplied by its two Wirtinger derivatives. Apply the published real total-derivative chain rule and collect the coefficients of $h$ and $\bar h$. This gives $(g\circ f)_z=(g_w\circ f)f_z+(g_{\bar w}\circ f)\overline{f_{\bar z}}$ and $(g\circ f)_{\bar z}=(g_w\circ f)f_{\bar z}+(g_{\bar w}\circ f)\overline{f_z}$. Check the identity and conjugation maps as sign/conjugation tests, then recover the holomorphic chain rule when both barred derivatives vanish.

items.title: A conjugate difference quotient characterizes antiholomorphic maps
items.strategy: Assume for every $z$ in an open set that the limit $g(z)=\lim_{h\to0}(f(z+h)-f(z))/\bar h$ exists. Replace $h$ by $\bar k$ and conjugate the relevant linear model to prove real differentiability with differential $h\mapsto g(z)\bar h$; equivalently $f_z=0$ and $f_{\bar z}=g$. Conversely, if $f$ is real differentiable and antiholomorphic, its Wirtinger expansion has precisely this form, so division by $\bar h$ gives the limit. Keep the pointwise real-differentiability hypothesis explicit in the converse.

items.title: A holomorphic function with continuous complex derivative has $C^1$ real and imaginary components
items.strategy: For $f=u+iv$, the four-way theorem gives $u_x=\operatorname{Re}f'$, $v_x=\operatorname{Im}f'$, $u_y=-\operatorname{Im}f'$, and $v_y=\operatorname{Re}f'$. The published modulus formula gives $|\operatorname{Re}(w_1-w_2)|,|\operatorname{Im}(w_1-w_2)|\le|w_1-w_2|$, so both coordinate maps are continuous; continuity of $f'$ therefore makes all four first partials continuous. This is a conditional bridge only; do not use it to assume that every holomorphic derivative is continuous before the later regularity theory.

items.title: A continuous local inverse has derivative reciprocal to a nonzero complex derivative
items.strategy: Let $f:U\to V$ be a bijection between open neighbourhoods with inverse $g$ continuous at $b=f(a)$. If $f$ is complex differentiable at $a$ and $f'(a)\ne0$, rewrite the inverse difference quotient as $(z-a)/(f(z)-f(a))$ with $z=g(w)$. Continuity of $g$ sends $w\to b$ to $z\to a$, and the nonzero derivative makes the reciprocal limit legitimate. Conclude $g'(b)=1/f'(a)$. Keep continuity of the inverse as a hypothesis; no inverse-function theorem is available in this page's closure.

items.title: Complex polynomials are entire with the power-rule derivative, and rational functions are holomorphic wherever their denominator is nonzero
items.strategy: Prove the nonnegative integer power rule by induction from the identity and product rules, checking the constant power separately. Finite linear combinations give the displayed formal derivative of a polynomial. Apply the quotient rule to $P/Q$ on the open set where $Q\ne0$, with derivative $(P'Q-PQ')/Q^2$. State the zero polynomial and constant-denominator cases explicitly.

items.title: The complex exponential is entire and its complex derivative is itself
items.strategy: Use the published Cartesian formula $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$. The real exponential, sine, and cosine derivative theorems give continuous first partials, and direct calculation gives CR everywhere. Apply the exact $C^1$ converse and compute $\exp'(z)=u_x+iv_x=\exp(z)$. This proof bridges the already-published definition and Euler formula to complex differentiability without re-proving the power-series construction.

items.title: A holomorphic function with zero derivative on a domain is constant
items.strategy: For arbitrary points of a nonempty domain, use the published equivalence of connectedness and polygonal connectedness for open subsets of $\mathbb R^2$ to choose a finite polygonal path. On each line segment, apply the real total-derivative chain rule to the restriction of $f$; the four-way theorem makes the derivative zero. Apply the one-variable zero-derivative theorem to the real and imaginary components on the closed parameter interval, and concatenate the finitely many constant restrictions. The connectedness hypothesis is essential and is not replaced by mere openness.

items.title: A real-valued holomorphic function on a domain is constant
items.strategy: Write $f=u+iv$ with $v=0$. The CR equations force both first partials of $u$ to vanish and hence $f'=0$ pointwise. Apply the zero-derivative theorem on the domain.

items.title: A holomorphic function of constant modulus on a domain is constant
items.strategy: If the constant modulus is zero, modulus definiteness gives $f=0$. Otherwise differentiate $u^2+v^2=c^2$ in both real coordinates and use CR. The resulting two-by-two homogeneous system for $u_x,u_y$ has determinant $u^2+v^2=c^2>0$, so all four first partials vanish and $f'=0$. Finish with the zero-derivative theorem. This proof deliberately avoids the later maximum-modulus principle.

items.title: If both $f$ and $\bar f$ are holomorphic on a domain, then $f$ is constant
items.strategy: Write $f=u+iv$. CR for $f$ gives $u_x=v_y$ and $u_y=-v_x$, while CR for $\bar f=u-iv$ gives $u_x=-v_y$ and $u_y=v_x$. Combine the pairs to make every first partial zero, hence $f'=0$, and apply the domain theorem.

items.title: Orientation-preserving conformality for a real-differentiable complex map at a point
Plane similarities are complex or conjugate-complex multiplications; the orientation-preserving ones are exactly the nonzero complex multiplications
items.strategy: For a real-linear map with columns $p$ and $q$, the inner-product similarity condition makes the columns orthogonal with the same positive length. A positive signed area factor selects $q=(-p_2,p_1)$ and gives the matrix $[[a,-b],[b,a]]$, multiplication by $a+ib\ne0$; a negative factor selects the conjugate-complex form $h\mapsto\xi\bar h$. Conversely calculate inner products and the signed area factors $|\xi|^2$ and $-|\xi|^2$ directly. This separates angle preservation from orientation instead of silently building orientation into the word similarity.

items.title: A real-differentiable complex map is orientation-preserving conformal at a point exactly when it is complex differentiable there with nonzero derivative
items.strategy: If $f$ is complex differentiable, the four-way theorem identifies $Df(a)$ with multiplication by $f'(a)$; when this number is nonzero the similarity lemma gives oriented conformality. Conversely, the conformal derivative is a nonzero complex multiplication by the lemma, so the real-derivative condition in the four-way equivalence gives complex differentiability and identifies its nonzero derivative. State the pointwise convention, without assuming local or global injectivity.

items.title: The Jacobian determinant of a holomorphic map is $|f'|^2$ and is positive exactly where $f'\ne0$
items.strategy: Use the CR matrix $[[u_x,u_y],[v_x,v_y]]=[[a,-b],[b,a]]$ with $a+ib=f'$. Its two-by-two determinant is $a^2+b^2=|f'|^2$. Modulus definiteness makes this positive exactly for a nonzero derivative and zero exactly when the derivative vanishes; it can never be negative.

items.title: The $C^2$ real and imaginary parts of a holomorphic function satisfy Laplace's equation and form a harmonic-conjugate pair
items.strategy: Let $f=u+iv$ be holomorphic and assume explicitly that $u$ and $v$ are $C^2$. Differentiate $u_x=v_y$ in $x$ and $u_y=-v_x$ in $y$, then use Clairaut–Schwarz to obtain $u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0$. Differentiate the other way for $v_{xx}+v_{yy}=0$. At first use, say that a $C^2$ real function satisfying Laplace's equation is harmonic and that $v$ is a harmonic conjugate of $u$ when $u+iv$ is holomorphic. Do not claim here that every holomorphic function is automatically $C^2$ or that every harmonic function globally has a conjugate; those require later complex-analysis machinery.

items.title: If a holomorphic function has $C^2$ components, then its derivative is holomorphic
items.strategy: Write $f'=u_x+iv_x$. The $C^2$ hypothesis makes these two components $C^1$. Differentiate the CR equations and use equality of mixed partials to verify CR for $f'$. Apply the continuous-partials converse. Emphasize that this is a conditional first step, not the later theorem that arbitrary holomorphic functions possess derivatives of all orders.

items.title: The Hessian determinant of each $C^2$ holomorphic component is nonpositive; a nondegenerate critical point is a saddle
items.strategy: For either component $w$, harmonicity gives $w_{yy}=-w_{xx}$, so $\det H_w=-w_{xx}^2-w_{xy}^2\le0$. If a critical point has nonzero Hessian determinant, it is negative, hence the symmetric Hessian is indefinite and the published multivariable second-derivative test gives neither a local maximum nor a local minimum (a saddle). When the determinant is zero, state that the Hessian test is inconclusive.

pages.title: Complex Differentiability and the Cauchy–Riemann Equations: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: $z\mapsto z^2$ is entire with derivative $2z$, directly from the complex difference quotient
items.strategy: Factor $((z+h)^2-z^2)/h=2z+h$ for $h\ne0$ and take the complex limit. Also display $u=x^2-y^2$, $v=2xy$, verify CR as a consistency check, and verify directly that both satisfy Laplace's equation, so $v$ is a harmonic conjugate of $u$ under the page's $C^2$ convention.

items.title: The complex exponential satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations in Cartesian and polar form
items.strategy: First differentiate from the definition: the addition law gives $(e^{z+h}-e^z)/h=e^z(e^h-1)/h$, and the published power series gives $(e^h-1)/h=1+\sum_{n\ge2}h^{n-1}/n!\to1$ by a uniform bound for $|h|\le1$. Then compute the four Cartesian partials from $e^{x+iy}=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and recover $f'=f$. For $z=re^{i\theta}$, write $e^z=e^{r\cos\theta}(\cos(r\sin\theta)+i\sin(r\sin\theta))$, compute $U_r,U_\theta,V_r,V_\theta$, and verify both polar CR identities for $r>0$. At the origin use the Cartesian calculation, since polar coordinates are singular there.

items.title: $z\mapsto1/z$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ with derivative $-1/z^2$, directly from the difference quotient
items.strategy: For $z\ne0$ and sufficiently small $h$ with $z+h\ne0$, simplify $((z+h)^{-1}-z^{-1})/h=-1/(z(z+h))$ and use continuity of multiplication and reciprocal at the nonzero point. State that zero is excluded from the domain, not merely a point where the derivative formula fails.

items.title: A Möbius map $(az+b)/(cz+d)$ with $ad-bc\ne0$ is conformal wherever $cz+d\ne0$
items.strategy: Use the quotient rule to compute $f'(z)=(ad-bc)/(cz+d)^2$. The determinant hypothesis and domain condition make the derivative nonzero, so the pointwise conformality theorem applies. Treat $c=0$ and the unique pole when $c\ne0$ explicitly; make no global injectivity claim beyond the usual extended-plane setting, which is not yet defined.

items.title: The square map sends a Cartesian grid to two orthogonal families of parabolas away from its critical point
items.strategy: Under $w=z^2$, a vertical line $x=c$ has image $(u,v)=(c^2-y^2,2cy)$ and a horizontal line $y=c$ has image $(u,v)=(x^2-c^2,2cx)$. Eliminate the parameters to identify the parabolic arcs, and use the nonzero derivative $2z$ to prove their tangent directions remain orthogonal at every image of a grid crossing with $z\ne0$. At $z=0$ the derivative vanishes and the conformality conclusion is unavailable.

items.title: FALSE: real differentiability as a map $\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ implies complex differentiability; conjugation is the counterexample
items.strategy: For $f(z)=\bar z$, the real coordinate map $(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)$ is linear and hence totally differentiable everywhere. Its matrix $\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ is not a complex-multiplication matrix, equivalently $u_x=1\ne-1=v_y$, so the four-way theorem makes $f$ nowhere complex differentiable. Optionally confirm directly that real and imaginary increments give quotient limits $1$ and $-1$.

items.title: $z\mapsto|z|^2$ is complex differentiable exactly at $0$, with derivative $0$, but is holomorphic on no neighbourhood of $0$
items.strategy: At the origin the quotient $|h|^2/h=\bar h$ tends to zero. At $z=x+iy\ne0$, the real function has $u=x^2+y^2$ and $v=0$; CR would force $x=y=0$, so differentiability fails. Conclude that differentiability at one point need not extend to any neighbourhood.

items.title: $z\mapsto\operatorname{Re}z$ is real differentiable but nowhere complex differentiable
items.strategy: The real coordinate map is $(x,y)\mapsto(x,0)$, so its total derivative is constant. CR for a real-valued function would require both partials of its real component to vanish, but $u_x=1$. Equivalently, horizontal and vertical difference quotients are $1$ and $0$.

items.title: $z\mapsto|z|$ is nowhere complex differentiable
items.strategy: At zero compare $|t|/t$ along positive and negative real increments. At a nonzero point the modulus is real differentiable with nonzero gradient $(x/|z|,y/|z|)$; CR for a real-valued complex-differentiable function would force that gradient to vanish. Cover the origin and all nonzero points separately.

items.title: $x^3+3xy^2+i(y^3+3x^2y)$ is complex differentiable exactly on the coordinate axes but holomorphic nowhere
items.strategy: The polynomial components have continuous partials. Compute $u_x=v_y=3x^2+3y^2$ and $u_y=v_x=6xy$; CR holds exactly when $xy=0$, so the $C^1$ converse gives complex differentiability exactly on the two axes. Every neighbourhood of every axis point contains a point with $xy\ne0$, so no point has a neighbourhood on which the function is holomorphic.

items.title: FALSE: the Cauchy–Riemann equations at one point imply complex differentiability there
items.strategy: Define $f(0)=0$ and $f(z)=\bar z^2/z$ for $z\ne0$. Since $|f(z)|=|z|$, the function is continuous at zero. Compute the four coordinate partials at zero directly to get $u_x=v_y=1$ and $u_y=-v_x=0$, so CR holds. But $f(z)/z=\bar z^2/z^2$ equals $1$ on the real axis and $-1$ on the line $y=x$, so the complex derivative at zero does not exist.

items.title: FALSE: existence of partial derivatives satisfying Cauchy–Riemann everywhere on an open set implies holomorphy
items.strategy: Set $f(0)=0$ and $f(z)=\exp(-z^{-4})$ for $z\ne0$. Off zero it is holomorphic by the power, reciprocal, exponential, and chain rules, hence satisfies CR. Along both coordinate axes, $e^{-1/t^4}$ decays faster than $|t|$, so all four partials at zero exist and vanish; cite exponential domination for the estimate. Along $z=re^{i\pi/4}$ the value is $e^{1/r^4}$, so $f$ is unbounded in every neighbourhood of zero and therefore discontinuous and not complex differentiable there. Thus CR holds everywhere but holomorphy fails. As a sharper Wirtinger warning, note that $\bar f$ has $(\bar f)_z\equiv0$ continuously although its coordinate partials are discontinuous at zero.

items.title: FALSE: a holomorphic function with zero derivative on an arbitrary open set is constant
items.strategy: Take $U=\{\operatorname{Re}z<0\}\cup\{\operatorname{Re}z>0\}$ and set $f=0$ on the left half-plane and $f=1$ on the right. Each point has a neighbourhood on which $f$ is constant, so $f$ is holomorphic with derivative zero throughout $U$. Values on the two components differ, so $f$ is not constant. Explicitly identify the missing hypothesis as connectedness, hence the use of a domain in the theorem.

pages.title: Complex Power Series and Analytic Functions

items.title: Complex analytic functions as locally representable by convergent power series
Uniform convergence and the uniformly Cauchy condition for complex-valued functions, with the componentwise dictionary
A sequence of complex-valued functions converges uniformly if and only if it is uniformly Cauchy
items.strategy: Uniform convergence implies the uniformly Cauchy condition by the complex triangle inequality. Conversely, pointwise Cauchy sequences converge by completeness of the complex plane; hold one index fixed beyond the uniform Cauchy threshold and pass the other index to its pointwise limit to obtain one uniform error bound. Treat an empty domain vacuously.

items.title: A uniform limit of continuous complex-valued functions is continuous
items.strategy: Use the componentwise dictionary: uniform convergence in complex modulus implies uniform convergence of real and imaginary parts, and complex continuity is componentwise. Apply the published real uniform-limit theorem to both coordinates and recombine. Include an empty domain and arbitrary codomain-open-set points.

items.title: Weierstrass M-test for complex-valued function series
items.strategy: For each tail use the complex triangle inequality and the same convergent real majorant tail. This makes the partial sums uniformly Cauchy; pointwise completeness of the complex plane supplies the sum, and the componentwise dictionary makes the convergence uniform. Check an empty domain and zero majorants explicitly.

items.title: A complex power series converges absolutely and uniformly on every closed subdisc strictly inside its disc of convergence
items.strategy: Fix a closed subdisc of radius r<R. Cauchy–Hadamard gives convergence of the real majorant sum |c_n|r^n. Apply the complex M-test to c_n(z-a)^n, retaining the centre, R=0, and R=+infinity conventions and making no boundary-circle assertion.

items.title: A complex power series, its formal derivative, and its zero-constant-term formal antiderivative have the same radius
items.strategy: The complex radius is the radius of the real modulus-coefficient series. Apply the published real radius lemma to |c_n|; the modulus of the derived coefficient is n|c_n| and the modulus of the integrated coefficient is |c_n|/(n+1). Translate back without writing an applied canonical embedding.

items.title: Inside its disc of convergence a complex power series is holomorphic and may be differentiated term by term
items.strategy: Fix z in the disc and a slightly larger closed subdisc. Prove the finite complex power-difference identity inline by telescoping, then factor each monomial difference quotient. Uniformly dominate the resulting tails on the larger subdisc, pass the finite derivative formula to the limit, and identify the derivative series whose radius is unchanged. Treat the constant term and radius-zero case explicitly.

items.title: A complex power-series sum has complex derivatives of every order, obtained by repeated termwise differentiation
items.strategy: Iterate the termwise theorem because every derived series has the same radius. State the falling-factorial coefficient at order k and check k=0, k>n, and the zero series.

items.title: The coefficients of a complex power series are its derivatives at the centre divided by the corresponding factorials
items.strategy: Evaluate the nth termwise derivative at the centre. Every positive power vanishes, the nth term contributes n!c_n, and terms of lower degree have already disappeared. Include n=0 and use ordinary embedded-number notation only.

items.title: A complex power-series representation about a fixed centre has unique coefficients
items.strategy: If two series agree on a neighbourhood of their common centre, their derivatives of every order agree there. Apply the coefficient formula at the centre to each order, including the constant coefficient.

items.title: Every complex analytic function is holomorphic
items.strategy: At an arbitrary point use the local convergent power-series representation from the analytic definition. The termwise-differentiation theorem gives complex differentiability throughout that representation disc, hence at the chosen point. The empty-open-set case is vacuous.

items.title: The binomial double series for re-expanding a complex power series is absolutely convergent and may be regrouped
items.strategy: For |b-a|+|h|<R, apply the real re-expansion majorant lemma to the nonnegative coefficients |c_n|. The complex binomial theorem expands each term, and absolute convergence licenses regrouping by powers of h. Check h=0 and b=a.

items.title: A complex power-series sum re-expands about every interior point, at least to the distance from that point to the original boundary
items.strategy: Put z=b+h in the absolutely convergent binomial double series and regroup by h. Identify the new kth coefficient with f^(k)(b)/k! using termwise differentiation, and obtain convergence for |h|<R-|b-a|. Do not claim this lower bound is the exact new radius.

items.title: The sum of a complex power series is analytic throughout its open disc of convergence
items.strategy: At each interior point the re-expansion theorem supplies a positive-radius local series representing the same function. This is exactly the analytic definition, including the entire-radius case.

items.title: Sums and scalar multiples of convergent complex power series are represented coefficientwise on the common disc
items.strategy: On any point inside both radii, take finite partial sums and pass their exact linearity identity to the limit. The result converges locally uniformly on every smaller closed subdisc; include zero scalars and unequal radii.

items.title: Products of convergent complex power series are represented by their Cauchy-product coefficients on the common disc
items.strategy: At a point inside both radii, both numerical series converge absolutely. Apply the published complex Cauchy-product theorem and identify the finite convolution coefficient. Local uniform convergence on smaller closed subdiscs follows from the absolute coefficient majorant.

items.title: A composition of convergent complex power series has a convergent local power-series expansion when the inner sum maps the centre to the outer centre
items.strategy: Write the inner displacement as a zero-constant-term series H. Choose a small disc on which the absolute coefficient sum of H is below the outer radius. Expand each outer power by repeated Cauchy products; the scalar majorant is an absolutely convergent composition, so double-series regrouping gives a locally convergent series. Include a constant inner function.

items.title: A convergent complex power series with nonzero constant term has a convergent reciprocal power series locally
items.strategy: For f(a) nonzero write 1/f(z)=f(a)^(-1)/(1-H(z)), where H(a)=0. Continuity of the power-series sum makes |H|<1 on a smaller disc. Prove the finite complex geometric identity inline, compose H with the geometric series, and record the recursive reciprocal coefficients. The nonzero constant term is essential.

items.title: Complex analytic functions are closed under finite linear combinations, products, quotients with nonzero denominator, and composition
items.strategy: Choose compatible local expansions at an arbitrary point. Apply the coefficientwise sum/product results, the local reciprocal lemma when the denominator value is nonzero, and the local composition lemma after recentering the outer expansion at the inner value. State each natural domain exactly.

items.title: Every complex analytic function has a primitive on a neighbourhood of each point
items.strategy: Integrate a local representing power series coefficientwise, using the unchanged radius of the antiderivative series. Termwise differentiation recovers the original function. This is local only and makes no global simply-connectedness claim.

items.title: The exponential definitions of complex sine, cosine, hyperbolic sine, and hyperbolic cosine equal their entire power series
items.strategy: Substitute the entire exponential series at z, -z, iz, and -iz into the published definitions. Separate even and odd indices using absolute convergence and simplify the powers of i. Record all four series and their infinite radii without re-defining the functions.

items.title: Complex sine, cosine, hyperbolic sine, and hyperbolic cosine are entire with their standard derivatives
items.strategy: Differentiate the four entire series term by term and shift indices. Obtain sin'=cos, cos'=-sin, sinh'=cosh, and cosh'=sinh, including the constant terms.

items.title: The addition formulas for complex trigonometric and hyperbolic functions
items.strategy: Insert z+w into the published exponential definitions and use exp(z+w)=exp(z)exp(w). Collect the symmetric and antisymmetric combinations to obtain the sine, cosine, sinh, and cosh formulas for all complex z,w.

items.title: Complex sine and cosine are unbounded on the complex plane
items.strategy: For real y, the published trigonometric-hyperbolic dictionary gives sin(iy)=i sinh(y) and cos(iy)=cosh(y). Expand sinh and cosh by their exponential definitions. Since exp(y) tends to positive infinity while exp(-y) tends to zero, both moduli are unbounded along the imaginary axis. Keep y real and positive and make no boundedness claim on the real axis.

items.title: The zeros of complex sine are the integer multiples of pi, and the zeros of complex cosine are the odd half-integer multiples of pi
items.strategy: Rewrite sin z=0 as exp(2iz)=1 and apply the exact kernel formula. Rewrite cos z=0 as exp(2iz)=exp(i pi), then apply the fibre formula. Prove both converses by substitution and retain the integer quantifier.

items.title: Stolz approach regions at the boundary point 1 of the unit disc
Abel summation by parts for complex coefficients and their partial sums
items.strategy: For s_n=sum_{k=0}^n a_k, substitute a_n=s_n-s_{n-1} into a finite weighted sum and telescope. State both the finite identity and its tail form, checking the initial index and an empty finite range.

items.title: Abel's limit theorem: a convergent complex series is recovered by its power series along every Stolz approach to 1
items.strategy: Subtract the boundary sum so the partial sums tend to zero. Apply complex Abel summation to express the power series through those partial sums. Split at a fixed index; the finite head vanishes as z approaches 1, while the tail is bounded by the small partial-sum supremum times |1-z|/(1-|z|), which is bounded in a Stolz region. Handle the exact boundary point only as a limit and include radial approach as a corollary.

pages.title: Complex Power Series and Analytic Functions — Examples

items.title: The geometric series re-expanded about an arbitrary point of the unit disc
items.strategy: For |b|<1 rewrite 1/(1-z) as (1-b)^(-1) times the geometric series in (z-b)/(1-b). Verify the finite geometric identity directly, obtain coefficients (1-b)^(-k-1), and show the new radius is |1-b|.

items.title: The alternating harmonic power series tends to log 2 at the boundary point 1
items.strategy: Use the published real evaluation of the alternating harmonic series, regard its coefficients as complex, and apply the angular Abel theorem. State the series from its positive first index and make no logarithm-branch claim inside the disc.

items.title: The harmonic complex power series diverges at 1 and converges conditionally at every other point of the unit circle
items.strategy: For |z|=1 with z not equal to 1, the finite geometric identity bounds the partial sums of sum z^n by 2/|1-z|. Apply the complex Abel-summation tail identity with the positive decreasing weights 1/n, using the Archimedean reciprocal estimate to make the boundary term small. At z=1 the series is the divergent p-series with p=1, while at every boundary point the modulus series is the same divergent harmonic series, so all other convergence is conditional. Start at n=1 and never form 1/0.

items.title: A power series with reciprocal-square coefficients converges uniformly on the closed unit disc
items.strategy: For n starting at one, bound |z^n/n^2| by 1/n^2 on |z|<=1 and apply the complex M-test with the convergent real p-series. Contrast the boundary conclusion with what radius alone says, without evaluating the boundary sum.

items.title: The complex geometric series is not uniformly convergent on its open unit disc
items.strategy: Its nth term fails to tend uniformly to zero because the supremum of |z|^n over |z|<1 is one for every n. Nevertheless it converges pointwise by the finite geometric identity. Use no maximum-attainment claim on the open disc.

items.title: Equal radii do not determine convergence on the boundary circle
items.strategy: Compare the geometric series and the reciprocal-square coefficient series. Cauchy–Hadamard gives radius one to both; at z=1 the first has terms that do not tend to zero, whereas the second converges absolutely by the real p-series.

items.title: The lacunary power series with factorial exponents has radius one and diverges at 1
items.strategy: Set the coefficient of z^m to one when m=n! for some positive n and zero otherwise. Its coefficient-root limsup is one because ones occur arbitrarily far out, while all roots are at most one. At z=1 the nonzero terms do not tend to zero. Resolve the repeated exponent 1 by starting the factorial index at two or combining that finite duplication.

items.title: The real function 1/(1+x^2) is smooth on the real line but its Maclaurin series has radius one
items.strategy: Apply the finite geometric identity to 1/(1+x^2) to obtain sum (-1)^n x^(2n) for |x|<1. Cauchy–Hadamard gives radius one, while the quotient rule shows the real rational function is smooth for every real x. This illustrates complex singularities without invoking analytic continuation or the identity theorem.

items.title: Abel convergence of the alternating harmonic power series along a nonradial Stolz approach
items.strategy: Take z_k=1-1/k+i/(2k) for sufficiently large k. Check |z_k|<1 and a uniform bound on |1-z_k|/(1-|z_k|), then apply the angular Abel theorem to the alternating harmonic coefficients and their published sum log 2.

items.title: FALSE: convergence of a complex power series at one point other than its centre forces convergence everywhere
