items.strategy: The geometric power series centered at zero converges at z=1/2 but diverges at z=2. Verify both claims from the finite geometric identity and the nth-term test, then state the correct radius dichotomy.

items.title: FALSE: complex sine and cosine are bounded on the complex plane
items.strategy: The unboundedness theorem gives explicit imaginary-axis witnesses: sin(iy)=i sinh(y) and cos(iy)=cosh(y), whose moduli grow without bound as y tends to positive infinity. Thus neither function admits a global complex-plane bound; distinguish this from their bounded real-axis restrictions.

pages.title: Contour Integration

items.title: Complex contours as planar rectifiable paths: the Euclidean, coordinate-BV, and piecewise-C1 dictionaries
Rectifiable complex contours, reversal, concatenation, closedness, and orientation
The complex line integral over a rectifiable path as a componentwise Riemann–Stieltjes integral
The absolute line integral over a rectifiable path using its arc-length function
Continuous integrands have complex and absolute line integrals along every rectifiable path
items.strategy: Write f=u+iv and gamma=x+iy. Rectifiability makes x and y continuous BV functions, and continuity of f along the compact parameter interval makes u and v continuous. Apply the real continuous-integrand/BV-integrator theorem to all four component integrals. For the absolute integral use the continuous nondecreasing arc-length function. Include singleton and constant paths.

items.title: For piecewise-C1 contours the Riemann–Stieltjes integral agrees with the parametric complex integral and the published real line integrals
items.strategy: On each smooth piece apply the real Stieltjes C1-integrator reduction to the four component integrals. Recombine them into integral f(gamma(t))gamma'(t) dt. Identify its real and imaginary parts with the published vector line integrals of (u,-v) and (v,u), and identify the absolute integral with the published scalar line integral. Sum over pieces and allow corners and zero-speed pieces.

items.title: Complex line integrals are linear in the integrand
items.strategy: Expand the real and imaginary parts of alpha f+beta g and apply real Stieltjes linearity in each component. Recombine the four identities into complex scalar linearity, including zero scalars and singleton paths.

items.title: Complex line integrals change sign under reversal and add under concatenation
items.strategy: For reversal apply the oriented Stieltjes convention after the decreasing affine parameter change, obtaining a minus sign for d gamma while the absolute integral is unchanged. For concatenation split each component Stieltjes integral at the join and use additivity. Check constant pieces and matching endpoints.

items.title: Complex and absolute line integrals are invariant under increasing continuous reparametrization
items.strategy: Let phi be a strictly increasing continuous bijection between nondegenerate compact intervals. Apply the exact real Riemann–Stieltjes change-of-variable theorem to each component and to the arc-length integrator, then recombine. Treat singleton intervals separately and state that decreasing reparametrization changes the complex integral's sign.

items.title: The fundamental inequality |integral f dz| <= integral |f| |dz| for rectifiable contours
items.strategy: Use tagged complex Stieltjes sums for the four component integrals. The complex triangle inequality bounds each sum by the corresponding tagged arc-length sum plus a uniform-continuity error controlled by polygonal length. Pass both limits and then remove the error. This preserves the sharp constant one, unlike separately bounding four real components.

items.title: ML estimate: a contour integral is bounded by a supremum bound times path length
items.strategy: If |f|<=M on the trace, monotonicity of the real Stieltjes integral against the nondecreasing arc-length function bounds the absolute line integral by M times s_gamma(b)-s_gamma(a)=M L(gamma). Combine with the fundamental inequality and include M=0 and L=0.

items.title: The absolute line integral of the constant function 1 is the length of the path
items.strategy: By definition the integral is the Stieltjes integral of one against s_gamma, which is the endpoint increment s_gamma(b)-s_gamma(a). Apply the defining endpoint values, including singleton and constant paths.

items.title: A primitive of a complex function on an open set
The line integral of a function with a continuous primitive is the primitive's endpoint increment along every rectifiable path
items.strategy: For a primitive F with continuous derivative f, uniform differentiability on the compact trace gives F(w)-F(z)=f(z)(w-z)+r with |r|<=epsilon|w-z| for sufficiently close trace points. Sum this identity over a fine partition of the rectifiable path. The main sums converge to the line integral, the endpoint increments telescope, and the total remainder is at most epsilon L(gamma). Let epsilon tend to zero. Include constant paths and avoid assuming the path is differentiable.

items.title: The integral of a continuous complex derivative over every closed rectifiable contour is zero
items.strategy: Apply the contour fundamental theorem to f=F'. Closedness identifies the two endpoint values, so their difference is zero. State continuity of F' explicitly and include constant loops.

items.title: The contour integral of a constant c is c times the endpoint displacement
items.strategy: The entire affine function F(z)=cz is a primitive of the constant c by the published complex derivative algebra. Apply the contour fundamental theorem and simplify. Include c=0 and a constant path.

items.title: For a continuous function on a complex domain, endpoint independence, zero closed-contour integrals, and existence of a primitive are equivalent
items.strategy: A primitive gives endpoint independence by the fundamental theorem, and endpoint independence gives zero on closed contours. Conversely fix a basepoint and define F(z) by integrating along a polygonal path, available because open connected plane sets are polygonally connected. Zero closed integrals makes F well-defined. For a small h use the final straight segment from z to z+h; its difference quotient is an average of f(z+th), which tends to f(z) by continuity. This proves F'=f. Check basepoint choice and both directions separately.

items.title: A uniformly convergent sequence of continuous integrands on a fixed contour permits passage of the limit through the complex line integral
items.strategy: Assume the limit integrand is continuous and state uniform convergence on the trace by its epsilon quantifiers. Apply the ML estimate to f_n-f. Its uniform error times L(gamma) tends to zero, so the integrals converge. Treat zero-length paths without dividing by length and do not cite the separate power-series page's uniform-convergence dictionary.

items.title: On a positively oriented circle about a, the integral of (z-a)^m is zero for every integer m except -1, and is 2 pi i for m=-1
items.strategy: Parametrize the circle by gamma(t)=a+r exp(it), 0<=t<=2 pi, with r>0. The piecewise-C1 agreement formula turns the integrand into i r^(m+1) exp(i(m+1)t). If m=-1 it is the constant i; otherwise integrate its explicit exponential primitive and use exp(2 pi i(m+1))=1. Check negative powers are defined because r>0.

items.title: The normalized integral (2 pi i)^(-1) integral dz/(z-a) around a positively oriented circle centred at a is 1
items.strategy: Specialize the circle monomial theorem to m=-1 and divide the nonzero complex number 2 pi i. The value is independent of the positive radius; no global winding-number theory or Cauchy theorem is invoked.

items.title: FALSE: every continuous complex-valued function on a domain has a primitive
items.strategy: On the punctured plane take f(z)=1/z, which is continuous. The punctured plane is a domain. If f had a primitive, its integral around every circle centred at zero would vanish, but the directly computed circle integral is 2 pi i. State the corrected zero-closed-contour criterion.

pages.title: Contour Integration — Examples

items.title: An exponential contour integral approximated by Riemann sums and evaluated by parametrization and a primitive
items.strategy: On the segment from 0 to 2+i pi/4, display a finite midpoint Riemann sum, then pass to the affine-parametric complex integral. Evaluate it both componentwise and from the primitive exp(z), obtaining exp(2+i pi/4)-1. This compares the Riemann-sum, parametric, and primitive methods without using the power-series page.

items.title: Integrating a complex polynomial along a segment and a parabola by a primitive and by parametrization
items.strategy: Begin with Howell–Mathews's componentwise warm-up integral of (t-i)^3 on a real interval. Then integrate f(z)=z from the same initial to terminal point along both their straight segment and their parabolic path. Compute parametrically and from the primitive z^2/2, verify that the endpoint values agree, and keep both orientations visible.

items.title: The integral of complex conjugation from -1 to 1 differs along a semicircle and a polygonal path
items.strategy: Parametrize Howell–Mathews's upper semicircle and their polygonal path from -1 to 1, compute the integral of conjugate(z) dz on each, and obtain the unequal values -pi i and -4i. This exhibits a continuous integrand without a primitive and checks concatenation signs directly.

items.title: ML bounds for rational integrands on a semicircular arc and a line segment
items.strategy: First choose a semicircle staying a positive distance from a pole, bound the denominator by the reverse triangle inequality, use length pi r, and apply ML. Then reproduce Howell–Mathews's segment from 2 to 2+i for 1/(z^2+1): the distances to i and -i give the stated product bound and the segment has length one.

items.title: Direct computation of the integral of 1/(z-a) around a semicircle and a full circle centred at a
items.strategy: Use gamma(t)=a+r exp(it) and cancel gamma'(t) against gamma(t)-a to obtain the constant i. First integrate from zero to pi to recover the upper-semicircle value i pi, then from zero to 2 pi for the full-circle value 2 pi i, and reverse the orientation to check the sign.

items.title: The unit-circle integral of exp(z)/z is 2 pi i by uniform termwise integration
items.strategy: On |z|=1 the exponential partial sums converge uniformly because the tail is bounded by the convergent numerical series sum 1/n!. Divide the finite sums by z, use finite linearity, and apply the integer-monomial circle formula: the n=0 term contributes 2 pi i and every n>=1 term contributes zero. The uniform-limit interchange theorem passes to exp(z)/z. The unit circle excludes z=0, so division is defined.

items.title: Assembling a keyhole contour from two radial segments and two circular arcs
items.strategy: Specify the four oriented pieces with matching endpoints, compute their lengths, and write the total integral as the signed sum supplied by concatenation. Do not evaluate it by Cauchy's theorem or introduce a logarithm branch; the point is rigorous contour bookkeeping.

items.title: The rectifiable Riemann–Stieltjes definition on an explicit polygonal contour with corners
items.strategy: Use Howell–Mathews's three-segment polygonal path, with its corner parametrization, and an affine integrand. Evaluate the four real Stieltjes components edge by edge, then verify agreement with the piecewise-C1 parametric formula. The corner derivatives need not agree.

items.title: Reversing orientation does not preserve a complex contour integral
items.strategy: Integrate the constant 1 along the segment from 0 to 1 and along its reversal. The values are 1 and -1 by the endpoint formula, while the absolute integrals agree. This separates oriented and unoriented integrals.

items.title: FALSE: the modulus of a contour integral always equals the absolute line integral
items.strategy: For f=1 on a positively oriented circle, the complex integral is zero by the endpoint formula, whereas the absolute line integral is the positive circumference. State the correct fundamental inequality and its equality need not hold.

items.title: FALSE: contour length depends only on the trace and ignores multiplicity
items.strategy: Compare one traversal of a circle with two traversals. They have the same trace but the second path has twice the speed integral and twice the length. Use an explicit parametrization and retain the positive radius hypothesis.

items.title: FALSE: parametrization independence makes orientation reversal leave every contour integral unchanged
items.strategy: Use the segment integral of the constant 1. The orientation-preserving theorem applies only to increasing reparametrizations; reversal is decreasing and changes the sign from 1 to -1. Quote the hypotheses without widening them.

pages.title: Goursat's Theorem and Cauchy's Theorem in a Convex Domain

items.title: Filled complex triangles, their oriented three-edge boundary contours, diameter, and perimeter
Complex star-shaped and convex domains are the published Euclidean notions under the identification $\mathbb C=\mathbb R^2$
Midpoint subdivision of a triangle cancels every interior edge and preserves its outer boundary integral
items.strategy: Name the three side midpoints and write the four oriented three-edge boundaries in full. Add their contour integrals using concatenation additivity; each interior segment occurs once in each direction and cancels by reversal, while each exterior half-edge concatenates to the corresponding outer edge. This is an algebraic contour computation, including repeated or collinear vertices, and does not appeal to the companion-page drawing.

items.title: Goursat bisection selects nested triangles retaining one quarter of the boundary-integral magnitude, with halving diameters and a one-point intersection
items.strategy: At each midpoint subdivision, the cancellation lemma and the complex triangle inequality make one quarter-triangle carry at least one quarter of the parent integral's modulus; choose the least-indexed maximizer to avoid a choice principle. Iterate this selection and prove by induction that diameter and perimeter are multiplied by $2^{-n}$ and the retained lower bound by $4^{-n}$. Realize each filled triangle as the continuous image of the compact barycentric simplex, hence as a nonempty compact and therefore closed bounded subset of the complex plane. Apply the published Cantor intersection theorem in the complete complex plane. If the initial integral is zero the retained estimate is still valid; repeated or collinear vertices are also covered.

items.title: Goursat's triangle theorem: a holomorphic function integrates to zero around every triangle contained in its domain
items.strategy: Use the nested-selection lemma and let $z_*$ be the unique common point. Complex differentiability gives $f(z)=f(z_*)+f'(z_*)(z-z_*)+(z-z_*)\varepsilon(z)$ with $\varepsilon(z)\to0$. The affine part has zero integral around each closed triangle by the published polynomial derivative and closed-derivative theorem. On a sufficiently small selected triangle, the ML estimate bounds the remaining integral by a small constant times diameter times perimeter. Multiplying by the retained factor $4^n$ cancels the two factors $2^{-n}$, leaving an arbitrarily small bound for the original integral. Treat a zero original integral and a zero-perimeter triangle before division or limiting estimates.

items.title: Goursat's theorem for rectangles: a holomorphic function integrates to zero around every rectangle contained in its domain
items.strategy: State first what the objects are: the closed rectangle with vertices $a$, $a+w$, $a+w+ih$, $a+ih$ for real $w,h>0$, and its positively oriented boundary as the closed contour concatenating those four directed sides, in the sense of the published contour definition. Split it along the diagonal from its lower-left to its upper-right vertex. The two resulting filled triangles, in the sense of the page's triangle definition, lie in the rectangle, so Goursat makes both positively oriented boundary integrals zero. Add them: the diagonal occurs once in each orientation and cancels by the published reversal identity, while concatenation identifies the four remaining directed sides with the positively oriented rectangle boundary. No rectangle conclusion is hidden inside the triangle theorem.

items.title: Goursat's triangle theorem remains valid for a continuous function holomorphic away from one point
items.strategy: If the exceptional point is outside the filled triangle, apply Goursat directly. If it is a vertex, cut off a triangle whose two incident sides have arbitrarily small length; Goursat annihilates the remaining triangles, boundary cancellation leaves only the small triangle, and continuity at the exceptional point plus the ML estimate sends its integral to zero. If the point lies on an edge or in the interior, split the triangle into subtriangles having that point as a vertex and cancel the new internal edges. Include coincident vertices and every boundary position.

items.title: Vanishing integrals around triangles construct a primitive for a continuous function on a star-shaped domain
items.strategy: Fix a star centre $a$ and define $F(z)$ as the integral of $f$ along the segment from $a$ to $z$. For small nonzero $h$, the triangle with vertices $a,z,z+h$ lies in the domain: the short edge lies in a ball about $z$, and every segment from $a$ to that edge stays in the star-shaped set. Its zero boundary integral reduces $F(z+h)-F(z)$ to the short-edge integral. Parametrize that edge and use continuity of $f$ to show the difference quotient tends to $f(z)$. Treat $z=a$, constant segments, and $h=0$ only as the excluded difference-quotient value.

items.title: Every holomorphic function on a star-shaped domain has a primitive
items.strategy: Holomorphy supplies continuity, and Goursat makes the integral around every contained triangle zero. Apply the triangle-integral primitive proposition at the specified star centre. The domain is nonempty by the published star-shaped definition, and no path choice is made.

items.title: Cauchy's theorem on a star-shaped domain: every closed rectifiable contour integral of a holomorphic function is zero
items.strategy: Use the star-shaped primitive theorem to obtain $F'=f$. Holomorphy makes $f$ continuous, so the published closed-contour corollary of the complex fundamental theorem applies to every closed rectifiable contour, including a constant contour.

items.title: Cauchy's theorem on a convex complex domain
items.strategy: A nonempty convex open subset of the complex plane is star-shaped with respect to each of its points by the published Euclidean definition and the plane dictionary. Apply Cauchy's theorem on a star-shaped domain to every closed rectifiable contour.

items.title: A continuous function holomorphic away from one point on a star-shaped domain has a primitive and zero closed-contour integrals
items.strategy: The exceptional-point Goursat theorem makes every contained triangle integral zero. Feed that exact conclusion into the triangle-integral primitive proposition, then use the published closed-contour theorem because the constructed primitive has the given continuous function as its derivative. The proof works whether the exceptional point is the star centre or lies elsewhere, and ordinary holomorphy is the special case in which no exception occurs.

items.title: The filled difference quotient is continuous at its exceptional point and holomorphic away from it
items.strategy: For holomorphic $f$ and fixed $z$, set $g(\zeta)=(f(\zeta)-f(z))/(\zeta-z)$ off $z$ and $g(z)=f'(z)$. The derivative definition is exactly continuity of $g$ at $z$. Away from $z$, the derivative algebra makes the quotient holomorphic; at no point is holomorphy of the filled value asserted. Check constant $f$ and every nonzero denominator explicitly.

items.title: Cauchy's integral formula on a circle compactly contained in a disc of holomorphy
items.strategy: Let $f$ be holomorphic on $D(a,R)$, take $0<r<R$, and fix $z$ with $|z-a|<r$. The filled quotient lemma gives a continuous function on the disc that is holomorphic away from $z$. The disc is convex and hence star-shaped, so the one-exception theorem makes its integral around the positively oriented radius-$r$ circle zero. Expand that identity by linearity. To compute the remaining off-centre kernel without winding numbers, use the finite geometric identity for $1/(\zeta-z)$ in powers of $(z-a)/(\zeta-a)$; its remainder is uniformly bounded by a constant times $(|z-a|/r)^{N+1}$ and tends to zero. Interchange this uniform limit with the fixed contour integral, then apply the published centred-circle monomial formula: only the exponent $-1$ term survives and gives $2\pi i$. Do not invoke a keyhole contour.

items.title: Cauchy-kernel contour integrals may be differentiated by a direct difference-quotient estimate
items.strategy: For a fixed rectifiable contour $\gamma$, continuous boundary data $\varphi$, an open set $V$ disjoint from the trace, and $n\ge1$, define $F_n(z)=(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_\gamma \varphi(\zeta)/(\zeta-z)^n\,d\zeta$. At $z_0\in V$, choose a closed ball still in $V$, which supplies a uniform positive lower bound for every denominator. Subtract $nF_{n+1}(z_0)$ from the difference quotient, factor the finite power difference, and bound the remainder uniformly by a constant times $|h|$. The ML estimate sends the integral remainder to zero. This proves $F_n'=nF_{n+1}$ without a general differentiation-under-the-integral theorem; handle $n=1$, a constant contour, and $h=0$ explicitly.

items.title: All higher complex derivatives exist and satisfy Cauchy's integral formula on an interior circle
items.strategy: The case $n=0$ is the circle formula. The Cauchy-integral differentiation lemma makes each kernel integral holomorphic on the circle's interior and gives its derivative, so induction simultaneously proves that $f^{(n)}$ exists and that $f^{(n)}(z)=n!/(2\pi i)\int f(\zeta)/(\zeta-z)^{n+1}\,d\zeta$ for every natural $n$. In the induction step, differentiation multiplies by $n+1$ and raises the kernel power by one. Check $n=0$, $n=1$, the factorial recurrence, and constant functions.

items.title: Cauchy's inequalities bound every derivative by a boundary bound on a compactly contained circle
items.strategy: Assume $|f(\zeta)|\le M$ on the positively oriented circle $|\zeta-a|=r$, where $r>0$ and $M\ge0$. Apply the higher-derivative formula at the centre, take moduli, use the ML estimate, substitute the circle length $2\pi r$, and simplify to $|f^{(n)}(a)|\le n!M/r^n$. Include $n=0$, $M=0$, and constant functions; the positive-radius hypothesis is exactly what licenses the division.

pages.title: Goursat's Theorem and Cauchy's Theorem in a Convex Domain — Examples

items.title: The three edge integrals of $z^2$ around the triangle with vertices $0$, $1$, and $i$ sum to zero
items.strategy: Use the primitive $z^3/3$ on each oriented edge. The three endpoint increments are $1/3$, $(-i-1)/3$, and $i/3$, which sum to zero and agree with Goursat's theorem. Check the edge orientations against the boundary definition rather than treating the triangle as an unoriented trace.

items.title: The four midpoint subtriangles of the $0,1,i$ triangle display all three cancelling interior edges
items.strategy: Label the side midpoints $1/2$, $i/2$, and $(1+i)/2$, draw the four positively oriented subtriangles, and list their twelve directed edges. Pair the six appearances of the three interior segments with opposite orientations, then concatenate the remaining half-edges into the outer boundary. The drawing illustrates the already-proved cancellation identity but the item retains the full computation.

items.title: The circle integral of $e^z/(z-1)$ over $|z|=2$ is $2\pi i e$
items.strategy: The exponential is entire and $1$ lies inside the positively oriented radius-$2$ circle. Apply the circle formula with $f(z)=e^z$ at $z=1$ and multiply by $2\pi i$; verify that the denominator is nonzero on the circle.

items.title: The circle integral of $\cos z/(z-1)^3$ over $|z|=2$ is $-\pi i\cos 1$
items.strategy: Use the higher-derivative formula with $n=2$ and $f(z)=\cos z$. Since $f''(1)=-\cos 1$, the factor $2\pi i/2!$ gives the stated value. Check the natural index $n=2$, the pole lies strictly inside the circle, and the denominator is nonzero on it.

items.title: A holomorphic function on an annulus can have a nonzero closed-contour integral
items.strategy: State explicitly that this refutes the claim that Cauchy's theorem holds for every closed rectifiable contour in every complex domain. Take $A=\{z:1/2<|z|<2\}$, $f(z)=1/z$, and the positively oriented unit circle. The complex triangle inequality gives $||z|-|w||\le|z-w|$; at each $z\in A$, use a radius smaller than both $|z|-1/2$ and $2-|z|$ to prove that $A$ is open. Verify directly that the rational function is holomorphic on $A$ and that the circle integral is $2\pi i$. Use polar form to join each point radially to the unit circle and then along a circular arc, proving path-connectedness. Thus $A$ is a domain and the displayed nonzero integral is the single witness for the stated false claim.

items.title: A connected complex domain need not be star-shaped
items.strategy: Take the punctured plane $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$. The rational-function theorem makes it open and the published punctured-plane lemma makes it polygonally connected, hence connected, so it is a complex domain. If a nonzero point $a$ were a star centre, the point $-a$ would also lie in the domain, but the segment from $a$ to $-a$ passes through $0$ at parameter $1/2$. This excludes every possible centre.

items.title: FALSE: Goursat's triangle conclusion requires a separate continuity hypothesis on $f'$
items.strategy: State the false implication as a claim about the hypotheses needed for the zero triangle integral. The published Goursat theorem derives that conclusion from holomorphy alone and never assumes continuity of $f'$, so the theorem directly refutes the extra-hypothesis claim. Distinguish this from the true sufficient Green-theorem proof under continuous partial derivatives.

items.title: FALSE: every continuous complex-valued function on a convex domain has a primitive
items.strategy: On the convex domain $\mathbb C$, take $f(z)=\overline z$. Along the unit circle, $z\overline z=1$ gives $\overline z=1/z$, so the published circle computation yields integral $2\pi i$. If a primitive existed, the published closed-contour theorem would force the same integral to be zero. Verify continuity of conjugation and convexity of the whole plane directly.

pages.title: Analyticity of Holomorphic Functions; Liouville and Morera

items.title: Locally uniform convergence on an open subset of the complex plane is compact convergence
Real-analytic maps between open subsets of the coordinate plane
The Taylor series of a holomorphic function at a point
The order of a zero of a holomorphic function
A holomorphic function equals its Taylor series throughout the largest centred disc in its domain
items.strategy: For a point a in an open set Omega, let rho be the distance from a to the complement, with rho=+infinity when Omega is the whole plane. Fix z with |z-a|<rho and choose a circle of radius r strictly between |z-a| and rho. Expand the Cauchy kernel on that circle by the finite geometric identity; its remainder tends uniformly to zero because |z-a|/r<1. Pass the uniform limit through the contour integral and use the higher-derivative Cauchy formula at a to identify the coefficient of (z-a)^n as f^(n)(a)/n!. Treat z=a and the whole-plane convention separately, and claim representation only on the largest disc contained in the given domain, not an exact convergence radius beyond it.

items.title: A complex function is holomorphic if and only if it is analytic
items.strategy: For the forward implication, apply the Taylor expansion theorem at every point to obtain a local convergent power-series representation. For the reverse implication, use the published theorem that every complex analytic function is holomorphic. State the equivalence on an arbitrary open set, including the empty set, and retain the same local domains in both directions.

items.title: Holomorphic functions are real analytic and smooth in their two real coordinates
items.strategy: Identify the complex plane with the coordinate plane. Expand the complex Taylor series at a and use the finite complex binomial theorem on h=x+iy. Absolute convergence for |x|+|y| below the complex radius licenses the total-degree real Taylor expansions of the real and imaginary parts, with the coefficients identified by repeated coordinate derivatives. For smoothness, use the real-linear derivative dictionary: repeated x- and y-partials are real and imaginary components of powers of i times the corresponding complex derivative; the higher complex derivatives exist and are holomorphic, hence continuous. Verify every mixed-derivative word, including the word of length zero.

items.title: Agreement of the power-series and Cauchy-integral formulas for Taylor coefficients
The order of a zero is the exponent in its local holomorphic factorization
items.strategy: If the order at a is finite m, the Taylor coefficients below m vanish and the m-th is nonzero. Factor (z-a)^m from the Taylor series and show directly that the shifted coefficient series converges on the same local disc; its sum g is analytic, hence holomorphic, and g(a) is the first nonzero Taylor coefficient, so continuity makes g nonzero nearby. Conversely expand a holomorphic g with g(a) nonzero and multiply by (z-a)^m to identify the first nonzero coefficient. Also prove that infinite order is equivalent to vanishing on a neighbourhood, without invoking the later identity theorem.

items.title: Cauchy's inequalities bound the Taylor coefficients by the circle supremum
items.strategy: On a circle of radius r compactly contained in the domain, write the n-th Taylor coefficient as f^(n)(a)/n!. Apply the published Cauchy inequality |f^(n)(a)|<=n! M/r^n and cancel n!. Include n=0, M=0, and require r>0 before division.

items.title: Liouville's theorem: every bounded entire function is constant
items.strategy: Let |f|<=M on the whole plane. At an arbitrary a, apply Cauchy's inequality with derivative order one on every positive radius r to obtain |f'(a)|<=M/r. If f'(a) were nonzero, choosing r>M/|f'(a)| would contradict the estimate. Thus f' vanishes everywhere, and the published zero-derivative theorem on the complex-plane domain makes f constant. Handle M=0 and the constant functions explicitly.

items.title: An entire function of polynomial growth is a polynomial
items.strategy: Assume |f(z)|<=C(1+|z|)^N with real C,N>=0. For every natural n>N, apply the Taylor-coefficient Cauchy estimate on the radius-R circle. For R>=1, bound (1+R)^N by 2^N R^N and let R grow; the exponential definition of real powers shows R^(N-n) tends to zero, forcing the n-th coefficient to vanish. The entire Taylor expansion therefore truncates after floor N. Treat C=0 and N=0, and use the integer-part inequalities to convert n>N into the exact degree bound.

items.title: Fundamental theorem of algebra by Liouville's theorem
items.strategy: Let p be a nonconstant complex polynomial and suppose it has no complex root. Then g=1/p is entire. Polynomial growth supplies R>=1 such that |g(z)|<=1 for |z|>=R. On the nonempty closed disc |z|<=R, holomorphy makes g continuous, the modulus is continuous, Heine-Borel makes the disc compact, and the extreme value theorem bounds |g| there. Hence g is bounded on the whole plane and Liouville makes it constant; since g never vanishes, p=1/g is constant, contradicting the hypothesis. Treat the boundary |z|=R in both bounds and do not cite the published minimum-modulus FTA theorem in this proof.

items.title: Agreement of the Liouville and minimum-modulus proofs of the fundamental theorem of algebra
The edgewise Riemann integral around a complex triangle for an integrable pullback
Morera's theorem: vanishing triangle integrals characterize holomorphy among continuous functions
items.strategy: For a continuous f on an open set with zero integral around every filled triangle contained in it, fix a point and a small disc with closure in the open set. The triangle-integral primitive construction on that star-shaped disc gives a holomorphic F with F'=f. The published higher-derivative theorem makes F' holomorphic, hence f is holomorphic near the chosen point. The converse is Goursat's triangle theorem. Keep continuity explicit, allow disconnected open sets, and prove both directions including degenerate triangles.

items.title: Cauchy estimates on a smaller concentric disc
items.strategy: Let 0<=r<R and suppose f is holomorphic on an open disc larger than the closed radius-R disc. Apply the higher-derivative Cauchy formula over the radius-R circle at each z with |z-a|<=r. The reverse triangle inequality gives |zeta-z|>=R-r; the ML estimate and circle length 2 pi R then yield |f^(n)(z)|<=n! R M/(R-r)^(n+1). Check n=0, r=0, M=0, and require r<R before every denominator.

items.title: Locally uniform limits of holomorphic functions are holomorphic and their derivatives converge locally uniformly
items.strategy: Use the compact-convergence dictionary to make the convergence uniform on every compact triangle and on a small closed disc around each point. The uniform limit theorem gives continuity, uniform passage through each triangle integral gives zero boundary integral, and Morera gives holomorphy of the limit. For derivative order k, choose nested concentric discs around a point and apply the subdisc Cauchy estimate to f_n-f; the outer-disc uniform error tends to zero, so the k-th derivative error tends uniformly to zero on the inner disc. This proves local uniform convergence for every natural k, including k=0.

items.title: A locally uniformly convergent series of holomorphic functions may be differentiated term by term
items.strategy: Apply the Weierstrass convergence theorem to the sequence of finite partial sums. Finite linearity of complex differentiation identifies the k-th derivative of each partial sum with the finite sum of the k-th derivatives. Passing to the locally uniform limit gives a holomorphic sum and the termwise derivative series for every natural k. Include the empty initial sum and k=0.

items.title: A jointly continuous finite-interval parameter integral of holomorphic functions is holomorphic
items.strategy: Let phi be jointly continuous on [a,b] times an open complex set and holomorphic in z for each parameter. Continuity gives the componentwise Riemann integral F(z). For a triangle compactly contained in the domain, parametrize its three edges and apply the real Riemann-Fubini theorem to the real and imaginary parts on each parameter-edge rectangle; interchange the parameter and contour integrals. Goursat makes every inner contour integral zero, so Morera makes F holomorphic. If the complex z-derivative of phi exists and is jointly continuous, use the complex fundamental theorem along a short z-segment and uniform continuity on a compact parameter-segment box to pass its difference quotient through the parameter integral, obtaining F'=integral of the derivative. Treat a=b separately and do not assert the derivative formula without the stronger joint-continuity hypothesis.

items.title: A holomorphic function equals its average on every circle inside a larger concentric holomorphy disc
items.strategy: Apply Cauchy's circle formula at the centre a of a positive-radius circle contained with its closed disc in the domain. Parametrize zeta=a+r exp(i theta), substitute d zeta=i r exp(i theta)d theta, and cancel the nonzero factors to obtain f(a)=(2 pi)^(-1) integral from 0 to 2 pi of f(a+r exp(i theta)). Check the positive orientation, r>0, and constant functions.

items.title: Every nonconstant entire function has dense image in the complex plane
items.strategy: If the image of an entire f is not dense, choose an open disc D(w,epsilon) disjoint from it. The reciprocal g=1/(f-w) is entire by the derivative algebra and satisfies |g|<=1/epsilon. Liouville makes g constant, hence f constant, a contradiction. Conversely no conclusion is claimed for constant functions. Make the positive missing-disc radius and the nonvanishing denominator explicit.

pages.title: Analyticity of Holomorphic Functions; Liouville and Morera — Examples

items.title: $\sin z-z$ has a zero of order three at the origin
items.strategy: Use the published entire sine series to write sin z-z=-z^3/3!+z^5/5!-... near zero. The coefficient in degrees zero, one, and two vanishes and the degree-three coefficient is nonzero, so the order definition and factorization theorem give order three. Cross-check by differentiating three times at zero, including the signs and the value cos 0=1.

items.title: Morera proves holomorphy of $z\mapsto\int_0^1 t^z\,dt$ on $\operatorname{Re}z>1$
items.strategy: For t>0 use the principal power t^z=exp(z log t), and set 0^z=0 on the half-plane Re z>1. Each z-slice is entire for t>0 and identically zero for t=0. Near any parameter point, |t^z|=t^(Re z)<=t when 0<=t<=1, which proves joint continuity at t=0; continuity elsewhere follows from exponential and logarithm. Apply the parameter-integral theorem. The restriction Re z>1 is chosen so the endpoint extension is justified by the elementary bound t, rather than by an unstated improper-integral argument.

items.title: Uniform convergence on the closed unit disc does not give a holomorphic extension to a larger disc
items.strategy: Set the zeroth coefficient to zero and take F(z)=sum_{n>=1} z^n/n^2. The complex M-test and the p-series show uniform convergence on |z|<=1, while termwise differentiation on |z|<1 gives F'(r)=sum_{n>=1}r^(n-1)/n for real 0<r<1. For each large bound choose a harmonic partial sum above twice that bound, then choose r close enough to one that the corresponding finitely many powers exceed one half; hence F'(r) is unbounded as r approaches one. A holomorphic extension to any disc of radius greater than one would have continuous derivative bounded on the compact interval [0,1], a contradiction.

items.title: $z^n$ tends locally uniformly to zero on the unit disc but not uniformly on the closed disc
items.strategy: For a compact K in the open unit disc, continuity of modulus and compactness give q=max_{z in K}|z|<1. Then |z^n|<=q^n tends uniformly to zero on K. On the closed unit disc, the value at z=1 is one for every n, so uniform convergence to zero fails, indeed pointwise convergence to zero already fails there. Include K empty and n=0 without weakening the eventual estimate.

items.title: Morera's theorem fails without continuity
items.strategy: Read triangle integrals in the page's edgewise Riemann sense, which agrees with the published contour integral for continuous integrands. Let f be one at the origin and zero elsewhere. It is discontinuous at the origin and therefore not holomorphic. On a nonconstant affine triangle edge, the origin has at most one parameter preimage, so changing the zero pullback there leaves the Riemann integral zero; on a constant edge at the origin, the velocity factor is zero. Thus every edgewise triangle boundary integral vanishes, including for degenerate triangles, which isolates continuity as essential without applying the published continuous-integrand contour notation outside its domain.

items.title: FALSE: every smooth map between open subsets of the plane is real analytic
items.strategy: Define phi(x)=exp(-1/x^2) for x nonzero and phi(0)=0, and F(x,y)=(phi(x),0). Repeated product and chain rules show every derivative of phi away from zero is a polynomial in 1/x times exp(-1/x^2); exponential domination makes every such derivative and the next difference quotient tend to zero at the origin. Thus F is smooth and every mixed derivative at (0,0) is zero. Its planar Taylor series there is the zero map, while F(x,0) is nonzero for x nonzero, so the defining local equality for real analyticity fails.

items.title: FALSE: an entire function bounded on the real axis is constant
items.strategy: Use complex sine. Its entire power series and derivative show it is nonconstant, while the real-restriction dictionary and the real trigonometric bound give |sin x|<=1 for every real x. This meets the weakened boundedness hypothesis and refutes the conclusion. Contrast only with Liouville's actual whole-plane boundedness hypothesis.

items.title: FALSE: every entire function with an antiderivative is a polynomial
items.strategy: The complex exponential is entire and is its own antiderivative because exp'=exp. It never vanishes, since exp z exp(-z)=exp 0=1, and it is nonconstant because its derivative is nonzero. If it were a nonconstant polynomial, the published fundamental theorem of algebra would give a zero; if it were constant, its derivative would vanish. Thus it is an entire nonpolynomial with an antiderivative.

pages.title: The Identity Theorem, the Maximum Principle and the Open Mapping Theorem

items.title: Locally injective holomorphic maps
Biholomorphic maps between complex domains
The locally zero locus of a holomorphic function is clopen
items.strategy: For a holomorphic function h on an open set, let L be the set of points having a neighbourhood on which h vanishes. It is open by definition. If a point b is not in L, the published zero-order factorization gives either h(b) nonzero or a finite-order isolated zero; after shrinking, no point near b can belong to L. Thus the complement is open and L is closed. Treat an empty open set and the identically zero function explicitly.

items.title: Identity theorem for holomorphic functions
items.strategy: Apply the argument to h=f-g. At an accumulation point a of the agreement set, finite-order factorization would make a an isolated zero, so h must vanish on a neighbourhood of a. The locally zero locus is therefore nonempty and is clopen by the preceding lemma; connectedness of the domain makes it the whole domain. Keep the hypothesis that the accumulation point belongs to the domain and handle f=g from the outset.

items.title: Zeros of a nonzero holomorphic function are isolated
items.strategy: Let f be holomorphic on a domain and not identically zero. At a zero a, the infinite-order alternative in the published factorization would make f vanish near a and then the identity theorem would make f identically zero. Hence the order is finite, and the nonvanishing factor in the local factorization makes a the only zero in a smaller disc.

items.title: Local degree of a nonconstant holomorphic map
The ring of holomorphic functions on a complex domain is an integral domain
items.strategy: Pointwise addition and multiplication make the holomorphic functions a commutative subring of the full complex function ring. If fg is the zero function and f is not the zero function, choose a point where f is nonzero; continuity makes f nonzero on a neighbourhood, so g vanishes there, and the identity theorem makes g the zero function. Nonemptiness of the domain and 0 not equal to 1 in the complex field separate the zero and unit functions.

items.title: A nonvanishing holomorphic function on a disc has a holomorphic logarithm
items.strategy: For nonvanishing h on a disc, h'/h is holomorphic and has a primitive H because the disc is star-shaped. Normalize H at the centre. The derivative of h exp(-H) is zero, so it is the constant h(a). Choose a scalar logarithm c of h(a); then L=H+c is holomorphic and exp L=h. Check that the disc is nonempty, its radius is positive, and every denominator is nonzero.

items.title: Holomorphic roots of a nonvanishing function on a disc
items.strategy: For a positive natural m, take a holomorphic logarithm L of h and define q=exp(L/m). The complex exponential addition law gives q^m=h. To impose a chosen root value at the centre, normalize the logarithm by a constant whose exponential is that chosen scalar. Treat m=1 and record that m=0 is excluded before division.

items.title: A nonzero complex derivative gives a local biholomorphism
items.strategy: View the holomorphic map as a smooth map between real coordinate planes. Its real Jacobian determinant is |f'(a)|^2, hence is nonzero. Apply the Euclidean inverse function theorem to obtain a local C1 inverse. The real derivative of that inverse is the inverse of multiplication by f', hence is again complex-linear; the real-linearity and Cauchy-Riemann equivalence makes the inverse holomorphic, with derivative 1/f'.

items.title: Local normal form of a nonconstant holomorphic map
items.strategy: Let m be the local degree at a. Factor f(z)-f(a)=(z-a)^m h(z) with h(a) nonzero, shrink to a disc on which h never vanishes, and take a holomorphic mth root q of h. Put phi(z)=(z-a)q(z). Then phi(a)=0 and phi'(a)=q(a) is nonzero, so the preceding lemma makes phi biholomorphic after shrinking once more, while f(z)-f(a)=phi(z)^m on that neighbourhood.

items.title: A local degree-m holomorphic map has m nearby sheets
items.strategy: Given any neighbourhood N of a, intersect it with the source of the local coordinate phi from the normal-form theorem and choose a positive radius r whose disc lies in the resulting open image. Restrict the source to phi^{-1}(D(0,r)), which now lies inside N. The mth-power map carries D(0,r) onto D(0,r^m); the centre has one preimage of multiplicity m, while every noncentral value has exactly m distinct roots and therefore exactly m distinct source preimages. Include m=1 and exclude m=0 through the local-degree definition.

items.title: Open mapping theorem for holomorphic functions
items.strategy: Let f be nonconstant on a complex domain and O an open subset of its domain. At each a in O, the identity theorem rules out local constancy and the local normal form supplies a source neighbourhood whose image contains a disc about f(a). Thus every point of f[O] is interior, so f[O] is open. Handle O empty separately and do not use Rouché's theorem or the argument principle.

items.title: Complex-analytic and Banach-space open mapping theorems
Local maximum modulus principle
items.strategy: If a nonconstant holomorphic f had a local maximum of |f| at a, the open mapping theorem would make the image of a sufficiently small neighbourhood an open set containing f(a). Every complex neighbourhood of f(a) contains a point of modulus strictly larger than |f(a)|, a contradiction. Include f(a)=0 and constant functions explicitly.

items.title: Maximum principle for the real part of a holomorphic function
items.strategy: If Re f has a local maximum at a and f is nonconstant, the open image of a small neighbourhood of a contains f(a)+epsilon for some positive real epsilon, whose real part is larger. This contradiction makes f constant. The Statement keeps only the real-part form.

items.title: Boundary maximum modulus principle on a bounded domain
items.strategy: For a nonempty bounded complex domain Omega and f continuous on its closure and holomorphic inside, Heine-Borel makes the closure compact and the extreme value theorem gives a maximizer of |f|. An interior maximizer makes f constant by the local principle; continuity on the closure then gives the same value on the nonempty boundary. Otherwise a maximizer already lies on the boundary. Check the constant case and boundary nonemptiness.

items.title: Maximum modulus principle with boundary and infinity control
items.strategy: Assume |f| approaches at most M at every finite boundary point and, when the domain is unbounded, outside sufficiently large discs, using an epsilon-neighbourhood formulation. For epsilon>0 the set K={z:|f(z)|>=M+epsilon} is bounded, closed in the plane, and disjoint from the boundary, hence compactly contained in the domain. If K were nonempty, |f| would attain an interior maximum there and the local maximum principle would make f constant, contradicting the boundary or infinity control. Let epsilon decrease to zero and treat the whole-plane domain through the infinity clause.

items.title: Minimum modulus principle for a nowhere-zero holomorphic function
items.strategy: If f is nowhere zero and |f| has a local minimum, then 1/f is holomorphic and its modulus has a local maximum at the same point. The local maximum modulus principle makes 1/f constant, hence f constant. Keep the nonvanishing hypothesis explicit and include constant nonzero functions.

items.title: Constant boundary modulus forces an interior zero or constancy
items.strategy: Let |f| equal M on the boundary of a bounded domain. If M=0, the boundary maximum principle gives f=0. If M>0 and f has no zero, apply the boundary maximum principle to f and to 1/f to get |f|<=M and |f|>=M throughout. Then |f| has an interior local maximum, so f is constant. The only remaining nonconstant case has an interior zero.

items.title: Maximum principle on a closed strip for bounded holomorphic functions
items.strategy: On the strip 0<=Re z<=1, let g be bounded, continuous on the closed strip, holomorphic inside, and have boundary modulus at most one. For epsilon>0 multiply by exp(epsilon(z^2-1)). Its modulus stays at most one on the vertical boundary and decays on high horizontal lines. Choose a large rectangle, apply the bounded-domain boundary maximum theorem, then let the rectangle contain an arbitrary fixed point and send epsilon to zero. Treat g=0 and points on both boundary lines.

items.title: Hadamard three-lines theorem
items.strategy: For bounded f on the closed strip, let M(x)=sup_y |f(x+iy)|. For delta>0 normalize by G_delta(z)=f(z)(M(0)+delta)^(z-1)(M(1)+delta)^(-z), defining positive-base complex powers through exp(z log a). Its modulus is at most one on both vertical boundaries, so the strip lemma bounds it inside. Rearrange and let delta decrease to zero, including a zero boundary supremum. Applying the same estimate after an affine rescaling of any substrip gives log-convexity of M and includes both endpoints.

items.title: Hadamard three-lines and complex interpolation
Holomorphic inverse function theorem and local-degree criterion
items.strategy: For a nonconstant holomorphic f on a domain, prove equivalence of f'(a) nonzero, local degree one, local injectivity, and local biholomorphy. Factorization identifies degree one with a nonzero derivative. The local-biholomorphism lemma proves sufficiency, while local biholomorphy implies local injectivity. If a locally injective map had degree m>1, the local multiplicity theorem would give m distinct nearby preimages, a contradiction. Differentiate the two inverse identities to obtain the reciprocal derivative formula.

items.title: An injective holomorphic map has no critical point and is biholomorphic onto its image
items.strategy: An injective holomorphic map on a complex domain is nonconstant and locally injective at every point, so the inverse theorem makes its derivative nonzero everywhere and gives holomorphic local inverses. The open mapping theorem makes the image open. The global set-theoretic inverse agrees with each local inverse, so it is holomorphic throughout the image and the original map is biholomorphic onto that image.

pages.title: The Identity Theorem, the Maximum Principle and the Open Mapping Theorem — Examples

items.title: The complex Pythagorean identity by the identity theorem
items.strategy: The entire functions h(z)=sin(z)^2+cos(z)^2 and the constant one agree for every real z by the published real trigonometric identity. The real axis has an accumulation point in the complex plane, so the identity theorem gives h=1 on all of C. This is a genuinely different proof from expanding the published complex addition formulas; cross-reference that route without using it in this proof.

items.title: The local mapping of complex squaring at zero and at one
items.strategy: For f(z)=z^2, the order of f(z)-f(0) at zero is two, so the local degree is two and every sufficiently small nonzero value has two local preimages. At one, f(z)-f(1)=(z-1)(z+1) has a nonvanishing factor at one, so the local degree is one and f is biholomorphic on a sufficiently small neighbourhood. Give explicit square-root preimages near zero and an explicit disc around one avoiding the collision z and -z.

items.title: An exact polynomial bound from the boundary maximum principle
items.strategy: For p(z)=z^2-2z+2 on the closed unit disc, the triangle inequality gives |p(z)|<=5. Equality holds at z=-1, a boundary point, where p(-1)=5. The boundary maximum principle shows there is no hidden larger interior value, so the exact maximum is five. Verify the polynomial is holomorphic and the witness belongs to the boundary.

items.title: Agreement accumulating only at the boundary does not force a holomorphic identity
items.strategy: On the punctured plane take f(z)=sin(1/z) and g=0. Both are holomorphic, and f vanishes at 1/(k pi) for every nonzero integer k; these distinct points converge to zero. Yet zero is not in the domain and f is not the zero function, for example at a point whose reciprocal is pi/2. Verify the punctured plane is a complex domain and every displayed point lies in it.

items.title: A flat smooth real function has no holomorphic extension near zero
items.strategy: Define psi(0)=0 and psi(x)=exp(-1/x^2) for nonzero x. Away from zero, induction with the product and chain rules writes every derivative as a polynomial in 1/x times exp(-1/x^2). Exponential domination makes these expressions and the required difference quotients tend to zero at zero, so every derivative extends there with value zero and psi is smooth; exponential positivity gives psi(x)>0 off zero. If a holomorphic function near zero restricted to psi on a real interval, restriction to the real axis would make every complex derivative at zero vanish. The coefficient formula and Taylor expansion would then make the extension zero near zero, contradicting the positive real values. Check both sides of zero explicitly.

items.title: A nonconstant Blaschke factor has constant boundary modulus
items.strategy: Fix a in the open unit disc and use B_a(z)=(z-a)/(1-conjugate(a)z). Its pole lies outside the closed unit disc, it is holomorphic on a neighbourhood of that disc, and direct expansion gives |z-a|=|1-conjugate(a)z| when |z|=1. Thus |B_a|=1 on the boundary while B_a(a)=0, so it is nonconstant and realizes the zero alternative in the constant-boundary-modulus corollary. Include a=0 and general a.

items.title: FALSE: the local maximum modulus principle needs no connectedness
items.strategy: Take the union of two disjoint open discs and define f to be zero on one component and one on the other. The function is holomorphic because it is locally constant. Its modulus has a local maximum at every point of the second component, but f is not constant on the whole open set. This isolates connectedness as the missing hypothesis without weakening the valid theorem on a domain.

items.title: FALSE: every interior local modulus minimum forces constancy
items.strategy: On the unit disc the identity function f(z)=z is holomorphic and nonconstant, while |f| has its global minimum zero at the interior point zero. The valid minimum modulus theorem does not apply because f vanishes there. Verify both the minimum and nonconstancy directly.

items.title: FALSE: every injective real-differentiable planar map has nonzero Jacobian
items.strategy: Use F(x,y)=(x^3,y). The factorization x^3-u^3=(x-u)((x+u/2)^2+3u^2/4) proves injectivity on the whole real plane, and the derivative matrix is diag(3x^2,1), whose determinant is zero on the vertical axis. This contrasts with injective holomorphic maps, whose derivatives cannot vanish, and it does not claim that the real inverse is differentiable at those points.

items.title: FALSE: boundary control alone gives the maximum principle on an unbounded domain
items.strategy: On the upper half-plane take f(z)=exp(-iz). It is holomorphic and continuous on the closed half-plane, and its modulus is one on the real boundary. For z=x+iy with y>0 its modulus is exp(y), which is unbounded. Thus the bounded-domain conclusion fails without the additional control at infinity stated in the preceding theorem.

pages.title: The Winding Number and the Global Cauchy Theorem

items.title: Tagged sums approximate a contour integral within oscillation times length
items.strategy: Subdivide the parameter interval at the partition points; the restrictions of $\gamma$ reassemble to $\gamma$ under an increasing reparametrisation, so the integral is the sum of the subarc integrals. On each subarc replace the integrand by its value at the tag: the difference is the integral of $f-f(\gamma(\xi_i))$, bounded by the oscillation on that subarc times the subarc length by the ML estimate, and the constant integrates to the endpoint increment. Sum and use additivity of arc length. State the bound with the oscillation, not with a limit, so later uses get a modulus of continuity.

items.title: A continuous function holomorphic off a single point is holomorphic
items.strategy: Two steps. Goursat with one exceptional point gives $\int_{\partial T}f=0$ for every filled triangle contained in the open set, the exceptional point being allowed inside, outside or on the boundary. Morera's triangle criterion then upgrades continuity plus vanishing triangle integrals to holomorphy on the whole open set, the exceptional point included.

items.title: A contour integral of a jointly continuous, parameter-holomorphic integrand is holomorphic
items.strategy: Let $\varphi$ be continuous on $\gamma^\ast\times\Omega$ with $\varphi(w,\cdot)$ holomorphic for each $w$. Fix a closed disc $K\subseteq\Omega$. The product $\gamma^\ast\times K$ is closed and bounded in $\mathbb R^4$, hence compact, so $\varphi$ is uniformly continuous there; $\gamma$ is uniformly continuous on its parameter interval. Take the uniform partitions $P_n$ of mesh $(b-a)/n$ with left-endpoint tags: the tagged sums are finite linear combinations of the holomorphic functions $z\mapsto\varphi(\gamma(\xi),z)$, and the previous lemma bounds their distance to $F$ by the common oscillation times $L(\gamma)$, uniformly on $K$. So $F$ is a locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions; Weierstrass convergence finishes.

items.title: A holomorphic logarithm is a primitive of the logarithmic derivative
items.strategy: If $L$ and $h$ are holomorphic on an open $U$ with $\exp\circ L=h$, then $h$ is nowhere zero because $|\exp v|=\exp(\operatorname{Re}v)>0$. Differentiate $\exp(L)=h$ by the chain rule and the derivative of $\exp$: $L'\exp(L)=h'$, so $L'=h'/h$. Apply it to $h(z)=z-p$ on a disc missing $p$ to get $L'(z)=1/(z-p)$.

items.title: A disc missing $p$ carries a holomorphic logarithm of $z-p$
items.strategy: On $D(c,r)$ with $p\notin D(c,r)$ the function $h(z)=z-p$ is holomorphic and nowhere zero, so the published disc lemma supplies a holomorphic $L$ with $\exp\circ L=h$; the preceding corollary gives $L'(z)=1/(z-p)$. Record that any two such $L$ differ by a constant in $2\pi i\mathbb Z$, since their difference is continuous with values in $\ker\exp$ on a connected set.

items.title: A contour missing a point subdivides into arcs lying in discs that miss it
items.strategy: The trace is a continuous image of a compact interval, hence compact, hence closed and bounded; so $d=\inf\{|w-p|:w\in\gamma^\ast\}$ is positive, for otherwise $p$ would lie in the closed set $\gamma^\ast$. Uniform continuity of $\gamma$ gives $\delta>0$ with $|\gamma(t)-\gamma(s)|<d$ whenever $|t-s|<\delta$; take any partition of mesh below $\delta$. Then $\gamma([t_i,t_{i+1}])\subseteq D(\gamma(t_i),d)$ and $p\notin D(\gamma(t_i),d)$ because $|p-\gamma(t_i)|\ge d$. Cover the degenerate case of a constant parameter interval.

items.title: Continuous logarithms and continuous arguments along a contour
items.strategy: Definition only. A continuous logarithm of $\gamma-p$ along $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$ with $p\notin\gamma^\ast$ is a continuous $\lambda:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$ with $\exp(\lambda(t))=\gamma(t)-p$ for every $t$; a continuous argument is $\theta=\operatorname{Im}\lambda$. Distinguish this from a holomorphic logarithm branch on an OPEN set, which is a holomorphic $L$ with $\exp\circ L=\mathrm{id}-p$ there: the first lives on the parameter interval and always exists, the second lives on the plane and need not. Fix the branch ambiguity of each: an additive constant in $2\pi i\mathbb Z$.

items.title: Every contour missing a point admits a continuous logarithm, unique up to a constant in $2\pi i\mathbb{Z}$
items.strategy: Existence: subdivide as in the subdivision lemma, take a holomorphic branch $L_i$ of $\log(z-p)$ on the $i$th disc, and define $\lambda$ on $[t_i,t_{i+1}]$ as the accumulated increment $\lambda(t_{i})+L_i(\gamma(t))-L_i(\gamma(t_i))$, starting from any $\lambda(a)$ with $\exp\lambda(a)=\gamma(a)-p$, which exists by surjectivity of $\exp$ onto the punctured plane. Induct on $i$: the two formulas agree at each $t_i$ by construction, so $\lambda$ is continuous, and $\exp\lambda(t)=\gamma(t)-p$ throughout. Uniqueness: two continuous logarithms differ by a continuous function with values in $\ker\exp=2\pi i\mathbb Z$ on the connected interval, hence by a constant.

items.title: The integral of $dz/(z-p)$ along a contour is the increment of a continuous logarithm
items.strategy: With the subdivision and the branches $L_i$ of the previous two results, the fundamental theorem for contour integrals evaluates $\int_{\gamma|[t_i,t_{i+1}]}dz/(z-p)=L_i(\gamma(t_{i+1}))-L_i(\gamma(t_i))$, since $L_i'(z)=1/(z-p)$ is continuous on the disc. Sum over $i$ using additivity of the contour integral over the subdivision; the sum telescopes to $\lambda(b)-\lambda(a)$ by the definition of $\lambda$. The value is independent of the chosen $\lambda$ because two choices differ by a constant.

items.title: The winding number of a closed contour about a point off its trace
items.strategy: Definition only. For a closed rectifiable contour $\gamma$ and $p\notin\gamma^\ast$, set $n(\gamma,p)=(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_\gamma dz/(z-p)$. The integral exists because $z\mapsto 1/(z-p)$ is continuous on the compact trace and $\gamma$ is rectifiable. Say explicitly that the definition is about the parametrised contour and not about its trace.

items.title: The winding number of a closed contour is an integer
items.strategy: By the logarithm-increment theorem $2\pi i\,n(\gamma,p)=\lambda(b)-\lambda(a)$ for a continuous logarithm $\lambda$ of $\gamma-p$. Since $\gamma$ is closed, $\exp\lambda(b)=\gamma(b)-p=\gamma(a)-p=\exp\lambda(a)$, so $\lambda(b)-\lambda(a)\in\ker\exp=2\pi i\mathbb Z$. Hence $n(\gamma,p)\in\mathbb Z$. No differentiability of $\gamma$ is used anywhere, which is what makes the proof valid for the rectifiable contours this library defines.

items.title: The winding number is the increment of a continuous argument divided by $2\pi$
items.strategy: Write $\lambda=\log|\gamma-p|+i\theta$ with $\theta=\operatorname{Im}\lambda$ a continuous argument. Taking moduli in $\exp\lambda=\gamma-p$ gives $\operatorname{Re}\lambda(t)=\log|\gamma(t)-p|$, which returns to its initial value on a closed contour, so $\lambda(b)-\lambda(a)=i(\theta(b)-\theta(a))$ and $n(\gamma,p)=(\theta(b)-\theta(a))/2\pi$. This is the sense in which the index counts turns.

items.title: The winding number is constant on each connected component of the complement of the trace
items.strategy: Show $p\mapsto n(\gamma,p)$ is continuous on $\mathbb C\setminus\gamma^\ast$. With $d=\operatorname{dist}(p_0,\gamma^\ast)>0$ and $|p-p_0|<d/2$, the identity $1/(z-p)-1/(z-p_0)=(p-p_0)/((z-p)(z-p_0))$ and the ML estimate give $|n(\gamma,p)-n(\gamma,p_0)|\le L(\gamma)|p-p_0|/(\pi d^2)$. A continuous integer-valued function on a connected set is constant, so the index is constant on each component; components of an open subset of the plane are open, so the function is locally constant.

items.title: The exterior of a closed disc in the plane is path-connected
items.strategy: Given $|z-c|>R$ and $|w-c|>R$, put $\rho=\max(|z-c|,|w-c|)$. Move $z$ radially to $c+\rho(z-c)/|z-c|$: the modulus stays between $|z-c|$ and $\rho$, hence above $R$. Do the same for $w$. Join the two resulting points along the circle of radius $\rho$ about $c$, which is path-connected as the image of the unit circle under $x\mapsto c+\rho x$, the unit circle being path-connected in dimension two. Concatenate the three paths.

items.title: The complement of a compact plane set has exactly one unbounded connected component
items.strategy: Let $K\subseteq\mathbb C$ be compact, hence bounded, say $K\subseteq\overline D(0,R)$. The exterior $E=\{|z|>R\}$ is connected by the previous lemma and lies in $\mathbb C\setminus K$, so it lies inside a single component $U_\infty$, which is therefore unbounded. Any other component is disjoint from $U_\infty$, hence from $E$, hence contained in $\overline D(0,R)$ and bounded. Handle $K=\varnothing$ separately: then the complement is the connected plane, and the statement still holds with one component.

items.title: The winding number vanishes on the unbounded component of the complement of the trace
items.strategy: The trace is compact, so by the previous theorem $\mathbb C\setminus\gamma^\ast$ has exactly one unbounded component $U_\infty$. For $p$ there with $\operatorname{dist}(p,\gamma^\ast)$ large, the ML estimate gives $|n(\gamma,p)|\le L(\gamma)/(2\pi\operatorname{dist}(p,\gamma^\ast))<1$; being an integer it is $0$. Points of arbitrarily large distance exist in $U_\infty$ because it is unbounded and $\gamma^\ast$ is bounded. Constancy on the component transfers the value $0$ to all of $U_\infty$.

items.title: Reversal negates and concatenation adds winding numbers
items.strategy: Both identities are the corresponding contour-integral identities applied to $1/(z-p)$: reversal negates the integral and concatenation of composable closed contours adds it. State the hypotheses that keep the results closed contours, namely that the concatenated pieces are composable and the result closed.

items.title: A circle traversed $k$ times has winding number $k$ inside and $0$ outside
items.strategy: For $k\ge1$, $\gamma_k(t)=a+r\exp(ikt)$ on $[0,2\pi]$ is an increasing reparametrisation of the $k$-fold concatenation of the positively oriented circle, so its integral of $1/(z-a)$ is $k$ times the circle's, which is $2\pi i$; hence $n(\gamma_k,a)=k$. For $k=0$ the contour is constant and the integral is $0$; for $k<0$ use reversal. The open disc $D(a,r)$ is connected and misses the trace, so local constancy gives $n(\gamma_k,z)=k$ throughout it. The set $|z-a|>r$ is contained in the unbounded component, so the index is $0$ there.

items.title: Complex chains, their traces, and cycles
items.strategy: Definition only. A complex chain in an open $\Omega$ is a finite list $\Gamma=((m_0,\gamma_0),\dots,(m_{r-1},\gamma_{r-1}))$ of integers $m_k$ and rectifiable contours $\gamma_k$ with trace in $\Omega$, written $\sum_{k<r}m_k\gamma_k$; its trace is the union of the traces of those $\gamma_k$ with $m_k\ne0$. Its boundary is the function on $\mathbb C$ sending $q$ to $\sum\{m_k:\gamma_k \text{ ends at } q\}-\sum\{m_k:\gamma_k\text{ starts at }q\}$, and $\Gamma$ is a CYCLE when that function is identically zero. Define sum and negation of chains by list concatenation and by negating every coefficient. Note that the empty list is a cycle and that a list of closed contours is a cycle, so the definition includes the single closed contour as the case $r=1$, $m_0=1$. Deliberately no free abelian group is invoked: chains are lists, equality of chains is equality of lists, and no theorem below claims that two differently presented chains are equal.

items.title: Integration over a complex chain and the index of a chain
items.strategy: Definition only. For a chain $\Gamma=\sum_{k<r}m_k\gamma_k$ and $f$ continuous on its trace, set $\int_\Gamma f\,dz=\sum_{k<r}m_k\int_{\gamma_k}f\,dz$, and for $p$ off the trace set $n(\Gamma,p)=(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_\Gamma dz/(z-p)$. Both are finite sums of existing integrals. Record that for $r=1$, $m_0=1$ and $\gamma_0$ closed this is the winding number already defined, so the notation is consistent.

items.title: Chain integration and the index are additive in the chain, and reverse with it
items.strategy: Additivity in the chain is the definition together with finite-sum laws: appending lists adds the defining sums, and negating every coefficient negates them. Combine with the reversal and concatenation laws for a single contour to get the sign and sum rules in the form used later: $n(-\Gamma,p)=-n(\Gamma,p)$, $n(\Gamma_1+\Gamma_2,p)=n(\Gamma_1,p)+n(\Gamma_2,p)$, and the same identities for $\int_\Gamma f\,dz$. Include the empty chain, whose integral and index are $0$.

items.title: The index of a cycle about a point off its trace is an integer
items.strategy: For each $k$ choose a continuous logarithm $\lambda_k$ of $\gamma_k-p$ along $\gamma_k$; the logarithm-increment theorem gives $\int_{\gamma_k}dz/(z-p)=\lambda_k(b_k)-\lambda_k(a_k)$. Hence $\exp\bigl(\int_\Gamma dz/(z-p)\bigr)=\prod_k\bigl((\gamma_k(b_k)-p)/(\gamma_k(a_k)-p)\bigr)^{m_k}$ by the addition formula for $\exp$ and the integer-power laws in the multiplicative group of nonzero complex numbers. Group the factors by the point of $\mathbb C$ at which they are evaluated: the exponent of $(q-p)$ is exactly the value of the boundary function at $q$, which vanishes because $\Gamma$ is a cycle. So the exponential is $1$ and the integral lies in $\ker\exp=2\pi i\mathbb Z$. Contours with $m_k=0$ contribute nothing; the empty cycle gives $0$.

items.title: The integral of a continuous derivative over a cycle is zero
items.strategy: If $F$ is a primitive of a continuous $f$ on an open set containing the trace of a cycle $\Gamma$, the fundamental theorem evaluates each $\int_{\gamma_k}f\,dz$ as $F(\gamma_k(b_k))-F(\gamma_k(a_k))$. Summing with the coefficients $m_k$ and grouping by evaluation point, the coefficient of $F(q)$ is the boundary function of $\Gamma$ at $q$, which is zero. This is where boundary-zero, rather than the weaker requirement that every piece be closed, does its work.

items.title: The index of a cycle is locally constant off its trace and vanishes far from it
items.strategy: Apply the corresponding single-contour results termwise: each $p\mapsto n(\gamma_k,p)$ is continuous off $\gamma_k^\ast$, so the finite combination is continuous off the trace of $\Gamma$, and it is integer-valued by the previous theorem, hence locally constant. The ML bound gives $|n(\Gamma,p)|\le\sum_k|m_k|L(\gamma_k)/(2\pi\operatorname{dist}(p,\Gamma^\ast))$, so the index is $0$ once the distance exceeds that finite bound. Conclude that $\{p\notin\Gamma^\ast: n(\Gamma,p)=0\}$ is open and contains the complement of some closed disc.

items.title: Null-homologous cycles and homologous cycles in an open set
items.strategy: Definition only. A cycle $\Gamma$ with trace in an open $\Omega$ is null-homologous in $\Omega$ when $n(\Gamma,p)=0$ for every $p\in\mathbb C\setminus\Omega$; two cycles in $\Omega$ are homologous in $\Omega$ when their difference is null-homologous, equivalently when their indices agree at every point outside $\Omega$. Say explicitly that the notion depends on $\Omega$ and not on $\Gamma$ alone, and that null-homologous does not mean equal to the empty chain.

items.title: Homologically simply connected complex domains
items.strategy: Definition only. A complex domain $\Omega$ is homologically simply connected when every cycle with trace in $\Omega$ is null-homologous in $\Omega$. Keep the qualifier "homologically" in the name and in every use: this page develops no other notion of simple connectivity, and none from its declared prerequisites is invoked.

items.title: Star-shaped plane domains are homologically simply connected
items.strategy: Let $\Omega$ be star-shaped and open, $\Gamma$ a cycle in $\Omega$ and $p\notin\Omega$. Then $z\mapsto 1/(z-p)$ is holomorphic on $\Omega$, so it has a primitive there by the star-shaped primitive theorem, and its derivative is continuous. The cycle integral of a continuous derivative vanishes, so $n(\Gamma,p)=0$. Every convex open set, in particular every disc and the whole plane, is star-shaped.

items.title: On a convex open set the difference quotient is an average of the derivative along the segment
items.strategy: For $z,w$ in a convex open $V$ on which $f$ is holomorphic, the segment from $z$ to $w$ lies in $V$ and $f'$ is continuous there because a holomorphic function is smooth. The fundamental theorem for contour integrals along that segment gives $f(w)-f(z)=\int_{[z,w]}f'(\zeta)\,d\zeta$, and the parametric form of the integral rewrites this as $(w-z)\int_0^1 f'(z+t(w-z))\,dt$. The identity holds for $w=z$ as well, both sides being $0$; and dividing by $w-z$ when $w\ne z$ exhibits the difference quotient as the displayed average.

items.title: The filled difference quotient of a holomorphic function is jointly continuous
items.strategy: Let $g(w,z)$ be $(f(w)-f(z))/(w-z)$ off the diagonal and $f'(z)$ on it. Off the diagonal joint continuity is the algebra of continuous functions. At a diagonal point $(a,a)$ take a disc $D(a,\rho)$ with closure in $\Omega$; for $w,z\in D(a,\rho)$ the segment formula gives $g(w,z)=\int_0^1 f'(z+t(w-z))\,dt$, valid on and off the diagonal, so $|g(w,z)-g(a,a)|\le\sup_{|\zeta-a|<\rho}|f'(\zeta)-f'(a)|$. Uniform continuity of $f'$ on a compact disc makes that supremum small, giving continuity at $(a,a)$.

items.title: The filled difference quotient is holomorphic in each variable separately
items.strategy: The filled quotient is symmetric in its two arguments, so it is enough to treat one of them. With $z$ fixed, the published exceptional-extension lemma says $\zeta\mapsto g(\zeta,z)$ is continuous on $\Omega$ and holomorphic on $\Omega\setminus\{z\}$. The removability lemma of this page upgrades that to holomorphy on all of $\Omega$, the filled point included.

items.title: The Cauchy transform of a cycle is holomorphic off its trace, with the expected derivatives
items.strategy: Apply the published differentiation lemma for Cauchy integrals to each contour of the chain on the open set $V=\mathbb C\setminus\Gamma^\ast$: each $z\mapsto(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_{\gamma_k}\varphi(\zeta)(\zeta-z)^{-n}\,d\zeta$ is holomorphic on $V$ with derivative $n$ times the next one. A finite integer combination of holomorphic functions is holomorphic, and the derivative relation passes through the combination.

items.title: Dixon's glued function is entire and vanishes at infinity
items.strategy: Let $\Gamma$ be a cycle null-homologous in the open $\Omega$ and $f$ holomorphic on $\Omega$. Put $h_0(z)=(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_\Gamma g(\zeta,z)\,d\zeta$ for $z\in\Omega$, which is holomorphic by the parameter theorem of this page applied to the jointly continuous, separately holomorphic filled quotient. Put $\Omega_0=\{z\notin\Gamma^\ast:n(\Gamma,z)=0\}$, open by local constancy, and $h_1(z)=(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_\Gamma f(\zeta)(\zeta-z)^{-1}d\zeta$, holomorphic there. On $\Omega\cap\Omega_0$ linearity splits the integral and the index term is zero, so $h_0=h_1$; null-homology gives $\Omega\cup\Omega_0=\mathbb C$, so the two glue to an entire $h$. Finally $|h(z)|\le ML(\Gamma)/(2\pi\operatorname{dist}(z,\Gamma^\ast))$ on the far part of $\Omega_0$, so $h$ is bounded and $h(z)\to0$ as $|z|\to\infty$.

items.title: Cauchy's integral formula for a null-homologous cycle
items.strategy: The glued function $h$ is entire and bounded, so Liouville makes it constant, and the constant is $0$ because $h(z)\to0$ at infinity. For $z\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma^\ast$ the first expression for $h$ splits by linearity into $(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_\Gamma f(\zeta)(\zeta-z)^{-1}d\zeta - n(\Gamma,z)f(z)$, so that difference is zero, which is the formula. State it for every $z\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma^\ast$ and note that no connectedness of $\Omega$ is required.

items.title: Cauchy's theorem for a null-homologous cycle
items.strategy: Fix $z\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma^\ast$. Such a $z$ EXISTS, and the reason is not that the trace has empty interior: that is a stronger claim about rectifiable curves which this library has not established and which must not be asserted. The trace of a chain is a finite union of continuous images of compact parameter intervals, hence compact, hence closed and bounded; and $\Gamma^\ast\subseteq\Omega$, so $\Omega\setminus\Gamma^\ast=\varnothing$ would force $\Omega=\Gamma^\ast$, making the nonempty open $\Omega$ a bounded clopen subset of $\mathbb C$. Bounded gives $\Omega\ne\mathbb C$, and $\mathbb C$ is connected under the published plane dictionary, so its only clopen subsets are $\varnothing$ and $\mathbb C$ — a contradiction. Then apply the integral formula to $F(\zeta)=(\zeta-z)f(\zeta)$, which is holomorphic on $\Omega$ and vanishes at $z$: the left side is $n(\Gamma,z)F(z)=0$ and the right side simplifies to $(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_\Gamma f$, since $(\zeta-z)$ cancels on the trace, where $\zeta\ne z$. Treat the empty cycle and the empty $\Omega$ separately; both give $0$.

items.title: Holomorphic integrals agree on homologous cycles
items.strategy: If $\Gamma_0$ and $\Gamma_1$ are homologous in $\Omega$ then $\Gamma_0-\Gamma_1$ is a null-homologous cycle in $\Omega$, so Cauchy's theorem gives $\int_{\Gamma_0-\Gamma_1}f=0$; the chain laws split that into $\int_{\Gamma_0}f-\int_{\Gamma_1}f$.

items.title: The higher-derivative form of the global Cauchy formula
items.strategy: On the open set $\Omega\setminus\Gamma^\ast$ the function $z\mapsto n(\Gamma,z)f(z)$ agrees with the Cauchy transform $F_1$ of $f$ over $\Gamma$. The index is locally constant, so on a neighbourhood of any such $z$ it is a constant $k$, and differentiating the identity $kf=F_1$ there $n$ times, using $F_m'=mF_{m+1}$ from the transform lemma and induction, gives $n(\Gamma,z)f^{(n)}(z)=(n!/2\pi i)\int_\Gamma f(\zeta)(\zeta-z)^{-n-1}\,d\zeta$. Include $n=0$ as the formula already proved.

items.title: Every holomorphic function on a homologically simply connected domain has a primitive
items.strategy: Every closed rectifiable contour in $\Omega$ is a cycle, hence null-homologous, so Cauchy's theorem gives $\int_\gamma f=0$ for all of them. The published path-independence criterion, which is stated for a complex domain and a continuous $f$, converts that into the existence of a primitive. Holomorphic functions are continuous, so the criterion applies.

items.title: A nonvanishing holomorphic function on a homologically simply connected domain has a holomorphic logarithm
items.strategy: The logarithmic derivative $f'/f$ is holomorphic on $\Omega$ because $f$ is nowhere zero and holomorphic functions are smooth. Take a primitive $F$ by the previous theorem, adjusted by a constant so that $\exp(F(z_0))=f(z_0)$ at one point, which is possible since $\exp$ is onto the punctured plane. Then $f\exp(-F)$ has zero derivative on the domain, hence is constant, and the constant is $1$; so $\exp\circ F=f$. Uniqueness: two holomorphic logarithms differ by a continuous function into $\ker\exp=2\pi i\mathbb Z$ on a connected set, hence by a constant in $2\pi i\mathbb Z$.

items.title: A nonvanishing holomorphic function on such a domain has holomorphic roots of every positive order
