items.strategy: With $\exp\circ L=f$ from the previous theorem, set $q=\exp(L/m)$ for a positive integer $m$. Then $q$ is holomorphic and $q^m=\exp(L)=f$ by the addition formula and induction on $m$. Note that $q$ is nowhere zero, and that the choice of $L$ shifts $q$ by an $m$th root of unity.

items.title: Equivalent characterisations of a homologically simply connected domain
items.strategy: Prove the cycle $(i)\Rightarrow(ii)\Rightarrow(iii)\Rightarrow(iv)\Rightarrow(vi)\Rightarrow(i)$ and $(ii)\Rightarrow(v)\Rightarrow(vi)$ for a complex domain $U$: (i) every cycle in $U$ is null-homologous; (ii) every holomorphic function on $U$ has a primitive; (iii) every nowhere-zero holomorphic function on $U$ has a holomorphic logarithm; (iv) $1/(z-p)$ has a primitive on $U$ for every $p\notin U$; (v) every holomorphic integral over every cycle in $U$ vanishes; (vi) $\int_\Gamma dz/(z-p)=0$ for every cycle $\Gamma$ in $U$ and every $p\notin U$. Three of the arrows are already proved on this page. For (iii) to (iv), differentiate $\exp(g(z))=z-p$ to get $(z-p)g'(z)=1$. For (iv) to (vi) and (ii) to (v), the cycle integral of a continuous derivative vanishes. (vi) to (i) is the definition of the index restated, and it is where the equivalence closes.

items.title: The principal logarithm is the normalised holomorphic branch on the slit plane
items.strategy: The slit plane $\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$ is open, connected and star-shaped with respect to $1$, hence homologically simply connected, so the identity function on it has a holomorphic logarithm $F$; normalise $F(1)=0$. Then $\operatorname{Re}F(z)=\log|z|$ from $|\exp v|=\exp(\operatorname{Re}v)$. To identify $\operatorname{Im}F(z)$ with the principal argument, run $t\mapsto\operatorname{Im}F(1+t(z-1))$ along the segment, which starts at $0$; if it ever reached $\pm\pi$ the corresponding point would equal $-|w|$, a negative real, which the slit plane excludes, so by the intermediate value theorem the imaginary part stays in $(-\pi,\pi)$. Uniqueness of the principal argument then gives $F=\operatorname{Log}$, and $F'=1/z$ makes $\operatorname{Log}$ holomorphic there with derivative $1/z$.

items.title: Conventions for chains, cycles and the homological adjective on this page
items.strategy: Prose only. Record four conventions and why each is taken: a chain is a finite list, so no free abelian group is imported and no theorem here claims two differently presented chains are equal; a cycle is a chain whose boundary function vanishes, which is what makes the integral of a continuous derivative over it vanish, and it is weaker than requiring each piece to be closed; the adjective is 'homologically simply connected' throughout, because the notion defined here is about indices and this page invokes no other notion of simple connectivity; and the winding number is attached to the parametrised contour, not to its trace, with the false statement on the companion page as the witness. Justify, do not survey.

pages.title: The Winding Number and the Global Cauchy Theorem — Examples

items.title: The unit circle traversed three times has index $3$ at every interior point
items.strategy: Take $\gamma(t)=\exp(3it)$ on $[0,2\pi]$ and apply the circle theorem with $a=0$, $r=1$, $k=3$: the index is $3$ on $|z|<1$ and $0$ on $|z|>1$. Then exhibit the continuous logarithm $\lambda(t)=3it$, verifying $\exp(\lambda(t))=\gamma(t)$ directly rather than by appeal to the existence theorem; its imaginary part is a continuous argument running from $0$ to $6\pi$, and $6\pi/(2\pi)=3$ recovers the same index.

items.title: A figure-eight cycle has indices $+1$ and $-1$ in its two loops
items.strategy: Present the figure eight as the chain $\gamma_1+\gamma_2$ where $\gamma_1$ is the positively oriented circle about $-1$ of radius $1/2$ and $\gamma_2$ the negatively oriented circle about $1$ of the same radius. By chain additivity the index at a point is the sum of the two circle indices, so it is $+1$ near $-1$, $-1$ near $1$, and $0$ outside both discs. Note that the two loops share no point, so the trace is the disjoint union of the two circles.

items.title: The boundary cycle of a round annulus has index $1$ inside the annulus and $0$ on either side
items.strategy: For $0<r_1<r_2$ let $\Gamma$ be the positively oriented circle about $p$ of radius $r_2$ minus the positively oriented circle of radius $r_1$. Chain additivity and the circle theorem give the index $1-1=0$ for $|z-p|<r_1$, $1-0=1$ for $r_1<|z-p|<r_2$, and $0-0=0$ for $|z-p|>r_2$. Draw only the conclusion the computation licenses: $\Gamma$ is null-homologous in the open annulus $r_1<|z-p|<r_2$, because every point of the complement of that annulus has index $0$. Name the open set before naming the homology, since the notion depends on it.

items.title: The winding numbers of a keyhole contour about the origin and about an excluded point
items.strategy: Build the keyhole as a cycle: the large positively oriented circle of radius $R$ about $0$, plus the small negatively oriented circle of radius $\varepsilon$ about $0$, joined by two opposite radial segments that cancel in the boundary count. Compute the index by additivity, at points OFF the trace: $0$ inside the small disc, $1$ in the annulus and off the radial segments, $0$ outside. The two segments have the same trace and both carry coefficient $1$, so that radius belongs to $\Gamma^\ast$ and no index is defined on it. Show the two segments contribute nothing to the index because they cancel as a chain, and check the boundary function is zero so the chain really is a cycle.

items.title: A continuous argument computed along a spiralling contour
items.strategy: Take $\gamma(t)=(1+t)\exp(2\pi i t)$ on $[0,1]$ and $p=0$. The function $\lambda(t)=\log(1+t)+2\pi i t$ is continuous with $\exp\lambda(t)=\gamma(t)$, so it is a continuous logarithm; its imaginary part is a continuous argument increasing by $2\pi$. The contour is not closed, so no winding number is defined, yet the logarithm increment $\log 2+2\pi i$ is exactly $\int_\gamma dz/z$. This separates the logarithm-increment theorem from the integrality theorem.

items.title: Dixon's gluing traced on the boundary cycle of an annulus
items.strategy: Take $\Omega=\{1/2<|z|<3\}$ and let $\Gamma$ be the positively oriented circle of radius $2$ minus the positively oriented circle of radius $1$, both centred at $0$; the preceding example makes $\Gamma$ null-homologous in $\Omega$. For $f(z)=1/z$ on $\Omega$, identify $\Omega_0$ explicitly, write out $h_0$ and $h_1$, check they agree on the overlap, and confirm $n(\Gamma,z)f(z)=(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_\Gamma f(\zeta)(\zeta-z)^{-1}\,d\zeta$ at an explicit $z$ with $1<|z|<2$ by computing both sides from the circle integrals of integer monomials.

items.title: Every cycle in a round annulus has one period, that of the central circle
items.strategy: Let $A=\{r_1<|z|<r_2\}$ and $C$ the positively oriented circle of an intermediate radius. For a cycle $\Gamma$ in $A$ put $k=n(\Gamma,0)$; then $\Gamma$ and $kC$ have the same index at every point of $\mathbb C\setminus A$, since the complement has the two pieces $|z|\le r_1$ and $|z|\ge r_2$ and the index is constant on the components meeting them. So the two cycles are homologous in $A$ and $\int_\Gamma f=k\int_C f$ for every holomorphic $f$ on $A$. Illustrate with $f(z)=1/z$, whose period is $2\pi i$.

items.title: The winding number is the circulation of the planar vortex field
items.strategy: Prose. For a piecewise-$C^1$ closed contour $\gamma$ missing the origin, the parametric form of the contour integral splits $\int_\gamma dz/z$ into the two real line integrals of the vector fields $(x,y)\mapsto(x,y)/(x^2+y^2)$ and $(x,y)\mapsto(-y,x)/(x^2+y^2)$. The second is the published closed-but-not-exact field on the punctured plane, and its circulation is $2\pi n(\gamma,0)$; the first is the gradient of $\tfrac12\log(x^2+y^2)$ and contributes nothing around a closed contour. So the failure of closed to imply exact on the punctured plane and the nonvanishing of the winding number are one fact seen twice. Say which convention is used for the identification.

items.title: A connected plane domain that is not homologically simply connected
items.strategy: Refute: every complex domain is homologically simply connected. Witness: the annulus $A=\{1/2<|z|<2\}$, which is open and connected, together with the positively oriented unit circle $C$ in it. The point $0$ lies outside $A$ and $n(C,0)=1\ne0$, so $C$ is not null-homologous in $A$. Verify connectedness of $A$ and that $C$ has trace in $A$.

items.title: A nonvanishing holomorphic function on a domain with no holomorphic logarithm
items.strategy: Refute: every nonvanishing holomorphic function on a complex domain has a holomorphic logarithm. Witness: the identity function on $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$. A holomorphic logarithm would in particular be a continuous $L$ with $\exp L(z)=z$ on the punctured plane, which the published theorem forbids; the published statement is about continuity alone and so is stronger than what is needed here. Alternatively, integrating $L'=1/z$ around the unit circle would give $0$ while the integral is $2\pi i$. Give both refutations and say which hypothesis of the positive theorem fails.

items.title: The winding number depends only on the trace of the closed contour
items.strategy: The claim is false. The unit circle traversed once and traversed twice have the same trace $\{|z|=1\}$ and indices $1$ and $2$ at the origin. Refute by computing both from the circle theorem. Point out that the same phenomenon already appeared for contour integrals, and that the index is defined from the parametrised contour precisely because of this.

items.title: Every cycle in a connected plane domain is null-homologous in that domain
items.strategy: The claim is false, and it is the claim that would make the homological hypothesis in the global Cauchy theorem vacuous. Refute with the unit circle in the annulus $\{1/2<|z|<2\}$, whose index at $0$ is $1$ while $0$ lies outside the annulus. Add the consequence that the conclusion of Cauchy's theorem also fails there, since $\int_C dz/z=2\pi i\ne0$ with $1/z$ holomorphic on the annulus.

pages.title: Isolated Singularities and Laurent Series

items.title: Annuli in the complex plane
Convergent Laurent series on an annulus
The principal part of a Laurent series
Isolated singularities: removable, poles, and essential singularities
Simple poles
Meromorphic functions on a plane domain
Laurent expansion on an annulus
items.strategy: Use the outer-minus-inner circle cycle in the annulus, apply the global Cauchy formula there, and expand the Cauchy kernels geometrically on the inner and outer regions. The positive and negative powers then assemble into one locally uniformly convergent Laurent series on the annulus.

items.title: Laurent coefficients are given by contour integrals and are unique
items.strategy: Integrate the Laurent expansion term by term on any intermediate circle and use the circle integrals of integer powers to isolate each coefficient. Uniqueness follows because those coefficient integrals are determined by the function, so two Laurent expansions on the same annulus must agree term by term.

items.title: Laurent coefficients are independent of the intermediate radius
items.strategy: Compare the coefficient integrals on two circles inside the same annulus. The difference is the integral over the annular two-circle cycle, which vanishes by the global Cauchy theorem.

items.title: The residue of an isolated singularity
Laurent series split into regular and principal parts
items.strategy: Split the Laurent series into its nonnegative and negative powers, show that each subseries converges on its natural domain, and use coefficient uniqueness to prove that the resulting decomposition is unique.

items.title: Characterizations of removable singularities
items.strategy: Expand the punctured-disc function into a Laurent series and show that boundedness near the center forces the principal part to vanish. The extension, boundedness, and limit conditions are then matched one by one to the absence of negative coefficients.

items.title: Characterizations of poles
items.strategy: Compare the finite principal part with the reciprocal of the holomorphic factor. A finite nonzero principal part gives growth like |z-a|^{-m}; conversely, if |f(z)| tends to infinity then 1/f is bounded and has a removable zero whose order recovers the pole order.

items.title: Every isolated singularity is removable, a pole, or essential
items.strategy: Use the regular-principal decomposition to separate the three Laurent-series possibilities: no negative coefficients, finitely many negative coefficients, or infinitely many negative coefficients. The removable and pole characterizations identify the first two cases, and the remaining case is essential.

items.title: Casorati-Weierstrass theorem
items.strategy: Argue contrapositively. If the image of a punctured neighbourhood misses an open disc about some value w, then 1/(f-w) is bounded there, so the removable-singularity theorem extends it holomorphically; this forces f-w to be removable or a pole, contradicting essentiality.

items.title: The residue is the normalized small-circle integral
items.strategy: Apply the Laurent coefficient formula at n = -1. The residue is exactly the coefficient isolated by the normalized contour integral.

items.title: At a simple pole the residue is the limit of (z-a)f(z)
items.strategy: Write the function as g(z)/(z-a) with g holomorphic and nonzero at a. The Laurent coefficient of (z-a)^{-1} is then g(a), which is also the displayed limit by continuity.

items.title: Residue formula for a pole of order m
items.strategy: Write f(z)=g(z)/(z-a)^m with g holomorphic at a. The residue is the coefficient of (z-a)^{m-1} in the Taylor series of g, which the higher-derivative Cauchy formula identifies with g^{(m-1)}(a)/(m-1)!.

items.title: Residues of p over q at a simple zero of q
items.strategy: Extend q(z)/(z-a) holomorphically across a by the difference quotient, note that its value at a is q'(a), and rewrite p/q as a simple pole with holomorphic numerator p divided by that extension.

items.title: Isolated singularities at infinity
Poles of a meromorphic function form a closed discrete set and are at most countable
items.strategy: Each pole is isolated by definition, so the pole set is discrete. A limit point inside the domain would contradict isolatedness, hence the pole set is closed in the domain. Countability follows by intersecting the discrete set with a countable compact exhaustion, or equivalently by assigning to each pole a rational disc meeting no other pole.

pages.title: Isolated Singularities and Laurent Series — Examples

items.title: The same rational function has different Laurent series on different annuli
items.strategy: Expand 1/(z(z-1)) by geometric series in the regions 0<|z|<1 and 1<|z|<∞, and also expand it about z=1. The example is there to make the annulus dependence of Laurent expansions explicit rather than implicit.

items.title: Polynomials have poles at infinity and reciprocal polynomials have removable singularities there
items.strategy: For f(z)=z^m, rewrite f(1/w)=w^{-m}; for f(z)=1/z^m, rewrite f(1/w)=w^m. The translated classifications at w=0 are exactly the definitions at infinity.

items.title: The residue of e^z/z^3 from the pole-derivative formula
items.strategy: Treat e^z/z^3 as a pole of order three at 0 and apply the derivative formula to the holomorphic factor e^z. The second derivative of e^z at 0 is still 1, so the residue is immediate once the factorial is in place.

items.title: A residue of p over q at a simple zero is p(a)/q'(a)
items.strategy: Pick a concrete quotient with a simple denominator zero and evaluate the residue with the quotient formula. Then differentiate the denominator once at the zero to show the shortcut matches the local-factor computation.

items.title: Zero residue does not imply a removable singularity
items.strategy: Use 1/z^2 at 0. Its Laurent coefficient of (z-a)^{-1} is 0, but the singularity is a pole of order two, so residue zero is weaker than removability.

items.title: e^{1/z} has an essential singularity at 0 and omits the value 0
items.strategy: Its Laurent series has infinitely many negative powers, so the singularity is essential. The exponential never vanishes, so this one omitted value shows why Casorati-Weierstrass gives density rather than surjectivity.

items.title: sin(1/z) has an essential singularity at 0
items.strategy: Expand complex sine through its exponential definition and substitute 1/z. The resulting Laurent series has infinitely many negative powers, so the singularity is essential.

items.title: 1/sin(1/z) has a nonisolated singularity at 0
items.strategy: The real zeros nπ of sine produce poles at z=1/(nπ), which accumulate at 0. So the point 0 is a singularity of the function, but not an isolated one.

items.title: A Laurent series on a punctured disc can have infinitely many negative powers
items.strategy: Use sin(1/z) or e^{1/z} as the witness. The point is not the particular coefficients, but the failure of the 'finite principal part' expectation outside the pole case.

pages.title: The Residue Theorem and the Evaluation of Real Integrals

items.title: This page keeps Cauchy principal values distinct from genuine improper convergence
items.strategy: Point back to the published principal-value and improper-integral definitions, and record that the contour method will sometimes compute only a principal value unless one-sided convergence is separately justified.

items.title: Standard semicircle, rectangle, keyhole, indentation, and sector contours
Admissible cycles for the residue theorem
Only finitely many singularities contribute to the residue sum of an admissible cycle
items.strategy: Use that the cycle trace is compact, the index vanishes far from it and is locally constant off it, so the nonzero-index region is a compact subset of the ambient domain. A closed discrete singular set meets that compact set in only finitely many points.

items.title: The residue theorem for a null-homologous cycle
items.strategy: Around each contributing singularity choose small disjoint circles and subtract the corresponding principal-part integrals. The remaining integrand is holomorphic on the punctured region, homologous-cycle invariance transfers the integral to the small circles, and the local residue formula turns each small-circle integral into 2 pi i times the residue.

items.title: A positively oriented circle integral is the sum of the enclosed residues
items.strategy: Apply the residue theorem to a circle and use the winding-number computation for a positively oriented circle.

items.title: A rational large-semicircle integral vanishes under the zR(z) to 0 condition
items.strategy: Bound the arc integral by arc length times the supremum of |R| on the semicircle. The hypothesis that zR(z) tends to 0 uniformly gives a bound of order o(1/R), which cancels the O(R) arc length.

items.title: Jordan's lemma for rational functions of one complex variable
items.strategy: On the upper semicircle write |e^(i lambda R e^(i theta))| = e^(-lambda R sin theta) and use the convexity-derived bound sin theta >= 2 theta / pi on [0, pi/2] and symmetry on [pi/2, pi]. Combine the exponential decay with the O(1/R) rational bound to dominate the arc integral by an explicitly vanishing integral.

items.title: An indented arc around a simple singularity contributes the expected residue fraction
items.strategy: Expand f into its Laurent series at the indented point. The regular part contributes vanishing length times supremum, while integrating the 1/(z-a) term along a parametrized arc gives i(beta-alpha) times the residue with the correct orientation sign.

items.title: Rational improper integrals without real poles are upper-half-plane residue sums
items.strategy: Integrate the rational function over a real segment closed by a large upper semicircle. The degree gap gives the real-line improper convergence and the large-arc vanishing lemma removes the semicircle, so the limit equals 2 pi i times the residues of the poles in the upper half-plane.

items.title: Indented real-axis contours compute principal values with half-residue corrections
items.strategy: Replace each real pole by a declared upper or lower indentation. The large arc still vanishes, the straight pieces converge to the principal value, and the indentation lemma contributes the signed half-residue terms.

items.title: Rational Fourier integrals are evaluated by residues and Jordan's lemma
items.strategy: Apply the residue theorem to e^(i lambda z) R(z) in the upper half-plane when lambda > 0 and in the lower half-plane when lambda < 0. Jordan's lemma kills the large arc, and the real-pole case is handled by the same indentation bookkeeping as for principal values.

items.title: Trigonometric integrals become contour integrals by the unit-circle substitution
items.strategy: Use z = e^(i theta), Euler's formula, and the identities cos theta = (z + z^(-1)) / 2, sin theta = (z - z^(-1)) / (2i), d theta = dz / (i z) on the positively oriented unit circle. This converts an integral of a rational expression in sine and cosine into a residue computation, provided the transformed integrand has no unit-circle poles.

items.title: A keyhole contour sees the two boundary values of z^(alpha-1)
items.strategy: Define the branch by z^(alpha-1) = exp((alpha-1) Log z) with Arg z in (0, 2 pi). On the upper and lower lips of the positive axis the arguments differ by 2 pi, so the boundary values differ by the factor e^(2 pi i (alpha-1)).

items.title: Keyhole contours evaluate Mellin-type rational integrals
items.strategy: Integrate z^(alpha-1) R(z) over a keyhole contour with the declared logarithm branch. The large and small circular arcs vanish under the endpoint-decay hypotheses, the two radial edges differ by the branch factor from the previous lemma, and the residue theorem yields the contour identity from which the real integral is solved.

items.title: Cotangent residues sum a rational function over the integers
items.strategy: Apply the residue theorem to pi cot(pi z) f(z) on expanding rectangles. The poles at the integers are simple with residue f(n), the boundary integrals vanish from the O(z^-2) decay and periodic cotangent bounds, and the remaining residues occur exactly at the nonintegral poles of f.

items.title: Cosecant residues sum an alternating rational series over the integers
items.strategy: Replace pi cot(pi z) by pi csc(pi z). The pole at n now has residue (-1)^n f(n), and the same rectangle estimate turns the bilateral alternating sum into the negative sum of the nonintegral residues.

items.title: The Basel sum is pi squared over six by a residue computation
items.strategy: Integrate pi cot(pi z) / z^2 over an expanding rectangle. The nonzero integer poles contribute the bilateral sum of 1 / n^2, the origin contributes the constant term from the Laurent expansion, and comparison of residues yields the classical value while recording that the page's cotangent-summation theorem itself does not apply to 1 / z^2.

items.title: FALSE: the residue theorem applies to every cycle in the ambient domain
items.strategy: Refute by taking a cycle that winds around a singularity but is not null-homologous in the punctured ambient domain. The point of the counterexample is that null-homology in the ambient region is a real hypothesis, not cosmetic language.

items.title: FALSE: existence of a Cauchy principal value forces improper convergence
items.strategy: Use the odd integrand x / (1 + x^2), whose symmetric truncations cancel but whose two one-sided improper integrals diverge logarithmically. This isolates the principal-value dictionary remark as a real distinction, not a notation change.

items.title: FALSE: denominator degree one more than numerator degree already forces convergence
items.strategy: Use a rational function asymptotic to c / x with nonzero c, so the real-line tails grow like log R. The correct degree hypothesis for unconditional improper convergence is the two-degree gap used in the rational-integral theorem.

items.title: FALSE: pointwise decay alone makes every large semicircle integral vanish
items.strategy: Use 1 / z on upper semicircles: the function tends to 0 pointwise but z f(z) does not, and the arc integral tends to i pi rather than 0. This shows why the large-arc lemma uses the stronger z f(z) to 0 control.

pages.title: The Residue Theorem and the Evaluation of Real Integrals — Examples

items.title: The integral of 1 / (1 + x^2) over the real line is pi
items.strategy: Close the contour in the upper half-plane, note the unique enclosed pole at i, and apply the rational real-integral theorem.

items.title: The integral of 1 / (1 + x^4) over the real line is pi over sqrt(2)
items.strategy: Use the two poles of z^4 + 1 in the upper half-plane and sum their residues before invoking the rational real-integral theorem.

items.title: The integral of cos x / (1 + x^2) over the real line is pi / e
items.strategy: Evaluate the integral of e^(i x) / (1 + x^2) by the Fourier-integral theorem and take real parts.

items.title: The principal value of the sine integral is pi / 2
items.strategy: Apply the Fourier-integral theorem to e^(i z) / z with an upper indentation at the origin and then take imaginary parts.

items.title: The integral of 1 / (a + cos theta) over [0, 2 pi]
items.strategy: Use the unit-circle substitution, reduce to a rational function of z, and compute the enclosed residue when |a| > 1.

items.title: The integral of x^(alpha-1) / (1 + x) over (0, infinity) is pi / sin(pi alpha)
items.strategy: Apply the keyhole theorem to R(z) = 1 / (1 + z), compute the residue at z = -1, and solve the resulting branch-factor identity.

items.title: A rectangle contour evaluates the Gaussian cosine integral
items.strategy: Integrate e^(-z^2) e^(2 i b z) on a rectangle, translate by i b to complete the square, and compare opposite sides to recover the real cosine integral.

items.title: The residue theorem gives the Basel sum
items.strategy: Unpack the rectangle computation behind the Basel corollary and then divide the bilateral sum by two.

items.title: The sine integral converges conditionally but not absolutely
items.strategy: Use Dirichlet's test for convergence of integral_1^infinity sin x / x dx and the uniform-tail-mass criterion to show that the absolute-value integral diverges.

items.title: The function 1 / z makes the large-semicircle shortcut fail
items.strategy: Parametrize the upper semicircle directly to see that the arc integral tends to i pi, so the weakened hypothesis in the false statement is genuinely wrong.

items.title: Treating a double pole as simple gives the wrong answer
items.strategy: Compare the correct derivative formula for the residue of e^z / (z-a)^2 with the incorrect simple-pole limit rule to show the numerical mismatch.

pages.title: The Argument Principle and Rouché's Theorem

items.title: The logarithmic derivative of a meromorphic function
Zero and pole counts weighted by multiplicity and winding number
The logarithmic derivative has residue equal to local order
items.strategy: Factor a holomorphic zero as (z-a)^m h(z) with h(a) nonzero, and write a pole by the reciprocal form. Differentiating the logarithm of the factorization isolates the simple principal part m/(z-a) or -m/(z-a).

items.title: The argument principle for an admissible null-homologous cycle
items.strategy: The logarithmic derivative is meromorphic with simple residues given by local orders at the zeros and poles. Summing those residues over the finitely many singularities inside the cycle and applying the residue theorem gives the weighted count formula.

items.title: The argument-principle integral is the winding number of the image cycle
items.strategy: Compose the cycle with f and use the contour-change identity for the logarithmic derivative to rewrite the integral as the normalized argument increment of the image curve. The winding-number formula from the global Cauchy page then identifies the result.

items.title: The argument principle counts preimages of a target value
items.strategy: Apply the argument principle to f-w. Its zeros are exactly the preimages of w, with the same local multiplicities, and its poles are the poles of f.

items.title: The weighted argument principle
items.strategy: Multiply the logarithmic derivative by a holomorphic test function g. The only singularities are still the zeros and poles of f, and each residue is scaled by the value of g at that point, so the residue theorem yields the displayed weighted sum.

items.title: Rouche's theorem in the classical strict-inequality form
items.strategy: Join g to f by the nonvanishing boundary homotopy g+t(f-g). The image winding number about 0 is constant along the homotopy, so the argument principle gives the same interior zero count for the endpoints.

items.title: Rouche gives the standard leading-term proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra
items.strategy: On a sufficiently large circle, the lower-degree tail of a polynomial is strictly smaller than its leading term. Rouche then gives the degree count and the remark records the agreement with the library's canonical fundamental-theorem page.

items.title: Small perturbations preserve the total local zero multiplicity
items.strategy: Choose a small disc containing exactly the chosen zero cluster and no boundary zero of the reference function. Rouche on the boundary transfers the total multiplicity inside the disc to every sufficiently small perturbation.

items.title: Locally uniform convergence preserves the total multiplicity near an isolated zero
items.strategy: Use the Weierstrass convergence theorem to place the approximating functions uniformly close on a small boundary circle around the isolated zero. The local Rouche corollary then fixes the interior zero count for all sufficiently late functions.

items.title: Hurwitz's zero-free limit theorem
items.strategy: If the nonzero limit had a zero, the continuity-of-zeros theorem would force nearby zeros of the approximating zero-free functions. Therefore a locally uniform limit of zero-free holomorphic functions is either zero-free or identically zero.

items.title: A locally uniform limit of injective holomorphic functions is injective or constant
items.strategy: Assume the limit is nonconstant and takes the same value at two distinct points. On disjoint discs around those points, Hurwitz applied to f_n-w forces two equal-value preimages for large n, contradicting injectivity of f_n.

items.title: The argument principle recovers the open mapping theorem
items.strategy: If f is nonconstant and w is near f(a), the argument principle applied on a small boundary circle around a gives a preimage count that stays positive. The remark records that this reproduces the earlier open-mapping theorem without changing the reading order.

items.title: Argument-principle multiplicity agrees with the earlier local degree
items.strategy: Compare the zero count of f-w on a small disc with the local multiplicity count already extracted from the holomorphic normal form. Both procedures count the same local sheets and therefore define the same integer.

items.title: A contour formula for a locally single-valued holomorphic inverse
items.strategy: Apply the weighted argument principle with g(z)=z to f(z)-w on a cycle that encloses exactly one simple preimage and no boundary preimage. The weighted zero sum then returns the enclosed inverse value.

pages.title: The Argument Principle and Rouché's Theorem — Examples

items.title: The polynomial z^5 + 3z + 1 has one zero in the unit disc
items.strategy: Compare z^5+3z+1 with 3z on the unit circle. The linear term dominates there, so Rouche gives the single interior zero count.

items.title: The same polynomial has four zeros in the annulus 1 < |z| < 2
items.strategy: Count zeros in |z|<2 by comparing with z^5, subtract the unit-disc count, and interpret the difference as the number of zeros in the annulus.

items.title: The equation e^z = 3z has exactly one solution in the unit disc
items.strategy: Apply Rouche to e^z-3z and -3z on the unit circle, using the elementary bound |e^z| < 3 when |z|=1. The dominating linear term forces exactly one interior zero.

items.title: A cubic image curve winds three times around the origin
items.strategy: Evaluate the argument-principle integral for a cubic on a circle containing all three zeros. The integral equals the total zero count and therefore the winding number of the image curve about 0.

items.title: Hurwitz preserves a simple zero under local uniform convergence
items.strategy: Use the sequence f_n(z)=z+z^2/n converging to z and isolate the zero at 0 on a small disc. The continuity-of-zeros theorem shows that each large n contributes one zero there.

items.title: The inverse contour formula recovers a local inverse value
items.strategy: Apply the contour formula to f(z)=z+z^2 on a small circle around 0 and evaluate at a nearby target value w. The integral returns the unique nearby preimage branch.

items.title: The sequence z/n shows why the injective-limit theorem needs the constant escape clause
items.strategy: Each map z/n is injective, but the locally uniform limit is the constant 0. This shows that injectivity alone does not survive the limit without the stated exception.

items.title: The function e^(1/z) shows that essential singularities lie outside the argument principle
items.strategy: Inside a small circle around 0 the function has an essential singularity and infinitely many zeros of e^(1/z)-1, so there is no finite zero-minus-pole count to match the argument-principle formula.

items.title: The weak inequality |f-g| <= |g| does not suffice in Rouche
items.strategy: Take g(z)=z and f(z)=z+1 on the unit circle. Equality holds at one boundary point, but the boundary zero obstructs the usual zero-count conclusion.

items.title: FALSE: a locally uniform limit of injective holomorphic functions is always injective
items.strategy: The sequence z/n converges to a constant map, so the theorem must say injective or constant. The false statement omits exactly the required escape clause.

items.title: FALSE: the argument principle ignores multiplicity
items.strategy: Apply the formula to f(z)=z^m on a small circle. The integral returns m, so multiplicity is built into the statement and cannot be dropped.

pages.title: The Riemann Sphere and Möbius Transformations

items.title: The Riemann sphere is the published one-point compactification of the complex plane
items.strategy: Cite the existing one-point compactification item and fix the notation \(\widehat{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}\) for the rest of the page.

items.title: The standard holomorphic charts on the Riemann sphere, with holomorphy and poles at infinity
Stereographic projection identifies the Riemann sphere with the unit two-sphere
items.strategy: Write the projection and its inverse explicitly, check continuity in coordinates, and then use compact-to-Hausdorff homeomorphism to finish.

items.title: The chordal metric on the Riemann sphere
The chordal metric induces the standard topology of the Riemann sphere
items.strategy: Transport the Euclidean metric of the unit sphere through stereographic projection and compare the resulting neighborhoods with the one-point-compactification topology.

items.title: Meromorphic functions on the Riemann sphere
Möbius transformations of the Riemann sphere
The cross-ratio of an ordered quadruple of sphere points
Circlines and their reflections on the Riemann sphere
Möbius transformations form a group and identify with the projective linear quotient of GL_2(C)
items.strategy: Compose fractional linear maps by matrix multiplication, identify scalar matrices as the kernel, and use the quotient vocabulary already developed earlier in the library.

items.title: Every Möbius transformation is a biholomorphism of the Riemann sphere
items.strategy: Check the chart formulas away from the pole and at infinity, then write the inverse map by the inverse matrix.

items.title: A unique Möbius transformation carries any ordered triple of distinct sphere points to any other
items.strategy: Write the normalizing map to \(0,1,\infty\) by a cross-ratio formula and compose the two normalizations.

items.title: The cross-ratio is invariant under Möbius transformations
items.strategy: Reduce to the unique normalizing map that sends three of the points to \(0,1,\infty\), then compute the fourth coordinate there.

items.title: Four distinct sphere points lie on one circline exactly when their cross-ratio is real
items.strategy: Move three points to \(0,1,\infty\), where circlines become the real line or a circle through infinity, and read the condition off directly.

items.title: Möbius transformations preserve circlines and conjugate their reflections
items.strategy: Transport a circline to the real line by three-point transitivity, compute the standard reflection there, and conjugate back.

items.title: Meromorphic functions on the Riemann sphere are exactly the rational functions
items.strategy: Compactness gives finitely many poles, subtract their principal parts, and apply Liouville to the resulting entire function on the finite chart.

items.title: The degree of a rational self-map of the Riemann sphere
A nonconstant rational map has total fibre multiplicity equal to its degree
items.strategy: Apply the argument principle to \(R(z)-w\) after sending infinity to a regular chart and read the total zero multiplicity from the pole order at infinity.

items.title: Every biholomorphic self-map of the Riemann sphere is Möbius
items.strategy: A sphere automorphism is meromorphic, hence rational; bijectivity forces degree one, and degree-one rational maps are exactly Möbius transformations.

items.title: Every biholomorphic self-map of the complex plane is affine
items.strategy: Extend the map across infinity as a sphere automorphism and then read off the condition that infinity stays fixed.

items.title: Every biholomorphic self-map of the punctured plane is of the form az or a/z
items.strategy: Extend across the missing points as a sphere automorphism and observe that a punctured-plane automorphism preserves the set \(\{0,\infty\}\).

items.title: Nonidentity Möbius transformations are parabolic or conjugate to a dilation, with the projective trace invariant
items.strategy: Classify by the number of fixed points, normalize those fixed points to \(\infty\) or \(0,\infty\), and record the projectively well-defined trace-squared-over-determinant invariant.

pages.title: The Riemann Sphere and Möbius Transformations — Examples

items.title: The Cayley transform carries the upper half-plane biholomorphically onto the unit disc
items.strategy: Check directly that \((z-i)/(z+i)\) sends the real axis to the unit circle and the upper half-plane to its interior, then invert the formula.

items.title: A Möbius transformation is recovered from three point correspondences
items.strategy: Normalize both triples to \(0,1,\infty\) and compose the two normalizing maps.

items.title: The maps z+1, 2z, and 1/z realize the parabolic, hyperbolic, and elliptic branches of the classification
items.strategy: Compute fixed points and conjugacy normal forms directly from the defining formulas.

items.title: Stereographic projection and its inverse are explicit in coordinates
items.strategy: Evaluate the formulas in both directions and check the north-pole and infinity conventions directly.

items.title: The chordal distance has the standard coordinate formula on the finite plane
items.strategy: Transport two finite points to the sphere, compute the Euclidean distance there, and simplify the expression algebraically.

items.title: The exponential function is meromorphic on C but not meromorphic on the Riemann sphere
items.strategy: Its singularity at infinity is essential, so the rational-function theorem excludes it from sphere-meromorphicity.

items.title: The exponential map is a holomorphic surjection C to C^× that is not an automorphism
items.strategy: Use periodicity to show noninjectivity while the punctured-plane automorphism theorem records the genuine automorphisms.

items.title: Complex conjugation is a homeomorphism of the Riemann sphere that is not holomorphic
items.strategy: It preserves the underlying sphere topology but reverses orientation and cannot be a Möbius transformation.

items.title: FALSE: every Möbius self-map of the Riemann sphere restricts to an entire biholomorphism of the complex plane
items.strategy: A genuine pole on the finite plane blocks restriction to an entire bijection, so only the affine branch survives.

items.title: FALSE: a Möbius transformation with three fixed points can be nonidentity
items.strategy: Uniqueness on ordered triples forces any Möbius map fixing three distinct sphere points to be the identity.

items.title: FALSE: every self-homeomorphism of the Riemann sphere preserves the cross-ratio
items.strategy: Complex conjugation preserves the sphere topologically but changes nonreal cross-ratios by conjugation.

items.title: FALSE: the Riemann sphere is homeomorphic to the complex plane
items.strategy: The sphere is compact while the complex plane is not, so no homeomorphism can exist.

pages.title: Conformal Mapping, Branches, and the Schwarz Lemma

items.title: Dictionary for holomorphic logarithm branches, the principal logarithm, and principal powers
Complex powers defined from a holomorphic logarithm branch
Branch-defined complex powers agree with integer powers
items.strategy: Use the defining identity $\exp(L(z)) = z$ together with the complex exponential addition formula to collapse repeated branch powers to the already-published integer powers.

items.title: On positive reals, the principal branch power agrees with the published real power
items.strategy: For $x > 0$, the principal logarithm equals the real logarithm. Substituting that identity into the branch-power definition recovers the published real-power definition word for word.

items.title: Different branches shift logarithms by $2\pi i k$ and complex powers by roots of unity
items.strategy: Subtract two logarithm branches, exponentiate the difference, and use the kernel description of the exponential map. The power discrepancy then follows by applying the exponential addition formula to $\alpha(L_1-L_2)$.

items.title: Conformal equivalence and the automorphism group of a domain
The unit disc, the upper half-plane, and Blaschke factors
Blaschke factors are automorphisms of the disc
items.strategy: Check the boundary-modulus identity for $\varphi_a(z) = (a-z)/(1-\overline{a}z)$ on $|z|=1$, use the maximum principle to keep the image inside the disc, and compute the inverse directly.

items.title: Schwarz lemma with the equality cases
items.strategy: Apply the maximum principle to $f(z)/z$ after removing the removable singularity at the origin. The equality cases are exactly the interior-maximizer cases for the maximum principle.

items.title: Schwarz-Pick lemma on the unit disc
items.strategy: Conjugate an arbitrary disc self-map by the Blaschke automorphisms that move one chosen point and its image to the origin, apply Schwarz's lemma there, and rewrite the conclusion in pseudohyperbolic and derivative form.

items.title: Every automorphism of the disc is a rotated Blaschke factor
items.strategy: Move the zero of the automorphism to the origin with a Blaschke factor, apply the rigid equality case in the Schwarz lemma, and move back.

items.title: Automorphisms of the upper half-plane are real Mobius maps
items.strategy: Conjugate by the Cayley transform to transfer the disc-automorphism classification to the upper half-plane, then simplify the resulting formula to the $PSL_2(\mathbb R)$ form and verify the converse directly from the imaginary-part formula.

items.title: The Poincare metric and distance on the unit disc
The Poincare distance has the formula $2\operatorname{artanh}|\varphi_z(w)|$ and is disc-automorphism invariant
items.strategy: Move one point to the origin with a Blaschke factor, integrate the metric along radial segments to identify the distance there, and then use the disc-automorphism classification to transport the formula to all pairs of points.

items.title: Biholomorphisms are conformal and have holomorphic inverse
Conformal equivalence is an equivalence relation
items.strategy: Identity maps, inverse maps, and compositions of biholomorphisms give the three clauses directly from the definition.

items.title: Power maps are biholomorphisms on sectors of width less than $2\pi/n$
items.strategy: Choose a logarithm branch on the sector, write $z^n$ as $\exp(nL(z))$, and use the branch width to show injectivity and to identify the inverse sector by division of the argument interval.

items.title: A slit-plane root branch biholomorphically parametrizes a sector
items.strategy: Write the root branch as $\exp(\operatorname{Log}(z)/n)$ on the slit plane and read its image from the principal-argument interval. The inverse is the appropriate power map on the target sector.

items.title: The principal logarithm is a biholomorphism from the slit plane to the principal strip
items.strategy: Use the published holomorphy of the principal logarithm on the slit plane, identify its image from the principal-argument normalization, and check injectivity by the classification of complex logarithms.

items.title: The exponential is the inverse biholomorphism from the principal strip to the slit plane
items.strategy: Compose the principal logarithm with the exponential in both orders, using the strip bound on the imaginary part to force the principal branch and recover exact inversion.

items.title: The Joukowski map is a biholomorphism from the exterior disc onto $\mathbb{C}\setminus[-1,1]$
items.strategy: Differentiate $J(z) = (z + z^{-1})/2$ to locate the critical points, check that they stay off the exterior domain, and build the inverse from the holomorphic square root branch of $w^2-1$ on the complement of the segment.

items.title: The sine map biholomorphically sends an upper half-strip onto the upper half-plane
items.strategy: Rewrite sine as a Mobius transform of $e^{2iz}$, identify the exponential image of the half-strip, and compute the final Mobius image explicitly.

items.title: The sphere, the plane, and the disc are pairwise non-biholomorphic
items.strategy: Use compactness and open mapping to separate the sphere from the noncompact models, and use Liouville's theorem to rule out a biholomorphism between the plane and the bounded disc.

pages.title: Conformal Mapping, Branches, and the Schwarz Lemma — Examples

items.title: The principal logarithm fails to turn multiplication into addition at $(-1,-1)$
items.strategy: Compute the two principal logarithms and compare $\operatorname{Log}((-1)(-1))$ with $\operatorname{Log}(-1) + \operatorname{Log}(-1)$ directly.

items.title: The principal square root fails to respect products at $(-1,-1)$
items.strategy: Evaluate the principal square roots of $-1$, of $(-1)(-1)$, and compare the two sides explicitly on the declared principal branch.

items.title: A horizontal strip is mapped biholomorphically to the disc by an exponential and a Cayley transform
items.strategy: Map the strip to the upper half-plane by the exponential and then to the disc by the Cayley transform, checking the boundary correspondence on both steps.

items.title: A disc automorphism carrying one prescribed point to another
items.strategy: Compose the two Blaschke factors that move the source point to the origin and the origin to the target point, and simplify the resulting formula.

items.title: A power map sends a sector to a half-plane
items.strategy: Choose a sector whose doubled angle interval is exactly $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ and apply the sector-power theorem with that normalization.

items.title: The Joukowski map sends circles centered at the origin to ellipses
items.strategy: Parameterize the source circle, apply the Joukowski formula, and isolate the resulting real and imaginary parts to read off the ellipse equation.

items.title: Boundary tracking for the sine biholomorphism of the upper half-strip
items.strategy: Follow the vertical sides and the real boundary of the half-strip under the sine map and compare them with the real-axis boundary of the upper half-plane.

items.title: Complex conjugation preserves angle magnitudes but is not conformal
items.strategy: Compare the action of $z \mapsto \overline{z}$ on tangent directions. The map preserves the absolute angle but reverses orientation, so it fails the page's conformal convention.

items.title: FALSE: conformal maps preserve Euclidean lengths
items.strategy: Use a nontrivial rotation-scaled linear map or a simple disc automorphism to preserve angles while changing the length of a tangent vector.

items.title: FALSE: Schwarz's lemma remains true without the hypothesis $f(0)=0$
items.strategy: Use a disc automorphism that moves the origin. It is still a holomorphic self-map of the disc, but it violates the modulus and derivative conclusions centered at zero.

pages.title: Harmonic Functions and the Poisson Integral

items.title: Plane harmonic functions
Agreement with the earlier C^2 holomorphic-components theorem
items.strategy: Record that the published C^2 holomorphic-components theorem proves the same Laplace-equation conclusion starting from a holomorphic function. This page keeps that convention and develops the converse direction from harmonic data.

items.title: Every plane harmonic function is locally the real part of a holomorphic function
items.strategy: For harmonic u, the combination u_x-iu_y satisfies the Cauchy-Riemann equations by the mixed-partial theorem, hence is holomorphic. On a small disc it has a primitive, and the real part of that primitive has the same first partials as u, so the two differ by a constant.

items.title: Harmonic conjugates
Harmonic conjugates exist on homologically simply connected plane domains
items.strategy: Apply the local construction globally to g=u_x-iu_y. On a homologically simply connected domain g has a primitive G; the real part of G has the same gradient as u, so u-Re(G) is constant and the imaginary part of G is the desired harmonic conjugate.

items.title: Two harmonic conjugates differ by a real constant
items.strategy: If u+iv_1 and u+iv_2 are holomorphic, then i(v_1-v_2) is holomorphic and real-valued. A real-valued holomorphic function on a domain is constant, so v_1-v_2 is constant as well.

items.title: Plane harmonic functions are smooth and real analytic
items.strategy: Near each point, a harmonic function is the real part of a holomorphic function. The published analyticity theorem for holomorphic functions then transfers smoothness and real analyticity to the harmonic function.

items.title: The circle and disc mean-value properties
Plane harmonic functions satisfy the mean-value property
items.strategy: Write the harmonic function locally as the real part of a holomorphic function. Apply the holomorphic mean-value property to that holomorphic potential, then integrate the circle averages radially to obtain the disc average formula.

items.title: Maximum and minimum principles for plane harmonic functions
items.strategy: On a disc, represent the harmonic function as the real part of a holomorphic function and apply the maximum principle for real parts. The bounded-domain boundary form follows by applying the local statement to u and to -u.

items.title: The bounded plane Dirichlet problem has at most one continuous harmonic solution
items.strategy: Take the difference of two harmonic solutions with the same boundary data and apply the maximum and minimum principles to the difference.

items.title: A plane harmonic function bounded above or below is constant
items.strategy: On the plane, choose a global harmonic conjugate and form an entire holomorphic potential F. If the harmonic function is bounded above, then exp(F) is bounded entire; if it is bounded below, then exp(-F) is. Liouville then makes F constant.

items.title: A plane harmonic function that vanishes on a nonempty open set vanishes everywhere on the domain
items.strategy: Let S be the union of open subsets on which u vanishes. It is open by definition. If a point lies in the closure of S, a local holomorphic potential has real part zero on a nonempty open subset of a disc, so the maximum principle for real parts forces that potential to be constant on the disc; hence the point lies in S. Thus S is nonempty, open, and closed in the connected domain.

items.title: Plane harmonicity is preserved by holomorphic and antiholomorphic changes of coordinate
items.strategy: For a holomorphic change of variable, precompose a local holomorphic potential with the map and take real parts. For an antiholomorphic change of variable, compose once more with complex conjugation to reduce to the holomorphic case.

items.title: The Poisson kernel on the unit disc
The Poisson kernel is positive, has total mass one, and concentrates at a boundary point
items.strategy: Positivity is immediate from the formula. The unit-mass statement comes from the corresponding holomorphic circle average, and the concentration estimate is proved by bounding the kernel uniformly on the complement of a short arc.

items.title: The Poisson integral on the unit disc
Poisson integrals are harmonic on the unit disc
items.strategy: Differentiate under the integral sign with respect to the real coordinates on compactly smaller discs. The explicit kernel satisfies Laplace's equation in the disc variable, so its convolution with continuous boundary data is harmonic.

items.title: The Poisson kernel is a boundary approximate identity
items.strategy: Split the boundary integral into a short arc around the target point and its complement. Continuity of the datum controls the nearby arc, while the concentration estimate from the kernel-properties lemma drives the far arc to zero uniformly.

items.title: The Poisson integral gives the unique continuous harmonic extension on the closed unit disc
items.strategy: Combine harmonicity of Poisson integrals with the boundary approximate-identity lemma to get existence, and use the maximum/minimum principle on the difference of two candidates for uniqueness.

items.title: A harmonic function is recovered from its values on any containing circle by the Poisson formula
items.strategy: Fix a smaller concentric disc, apply the Poisson integral theorem to the boundary values of the harmonic function on the larger circle, and identify the resulting extension with the given function by Dirichlet uniqueness.

items.title: A continuous plane function with the local mean-value property is harmonic
items.strategy: On a compactly contained disc, solve the Dirichlet problem for the boundary values of u by the Poisson integral. The difference between that harmonic solution and u still has the local mean-value property and vanishes on the boundary, so the mean-value maximum principle forces the difference to vanish.

items.title: A bounded harmonic function near an isolated puncture extends harmonically
items.strategy: On the punctured disc, the complex gradient u_x-iu_y is holomorphic. Local boundedness of u and a local harmonic conjugate on small circles give the estimate |u_x-iu_y|<=C/|z-a|, so (z-a)(u_x-iu_y) is bounded and the removable-singularity theorem extends it holomorphically across the puncture. The remaining residue obstruction vanishes, so the extended derivative has a primitive whose real part differs from u by a constant, giving the harmonic extension.

items.title: Positive harmonic functions on a disc satisfy Harnack's inequality
items.strategy: Represent the function by the Poisson formula on a containing circle and compare the Poisson kernel at two interior points by its explicit extremal bounds. The resulting ratio estimate is the Harnack inequality.

items.title: An increasing harmonic sequence converges locally uniformly to a harmonic limit or diverges to +infinity
items.strategy: Either the sequence diverges to +infinity at every point, or it is bounded at one point and Harnack's inequality makes it locally uniformly bounded on smaller discs. Poisson representation on those discs then turns monotone pointwise convergence into local uniform convergence to a harmonic limit.

items.title: Harmonic and holomorphic Schwarz reflection across the real axis
items.strategy: For the harmonic statement on an upper half-disc, reflect the boundary values oddly on the circle and compare the Poisson solution with the given function by Dirichlet uniqueness. For the holomorphic statement, apply harmonic reflection to the imaginary part and recover the reflected holomorphic function by the harmonic-conjugate construction; the explicit lower-half formula is F(z)=overline{f(conj z)}.

pages.title: Harmonic Functions and the Poisson Integral — Examples

items.title: log|z| is harmonic on the punctured plane
items.strategy: Write log|z| as (1/2)log(x^2+y^2) and differentiate twice directly on C\{0}. The Laplacian cancels exactly, so this standard witness really is harmonic away from the origin.

items.title: The real parts of z^n are harmonic polynomials
items.strategy: The polynomial z^n is entire, so its real part is harmonic by the earlier holomorphic-components theorem. Expand a few low-degree cases explicitly to connect the abstract statement with concrete harmonic polynomials.

items.title: 2xy is a harmonic conjugate of x^2-y^2
items.strategy: Use z^2=(x^2-y^2)+2ixy. The example is the fastest concrete instance of the local-potential theorem and gives an explicit conjugate pair to cite later.

items.title: The Poisson integral of cos(theta) is r cos(theta)
items.strategy: Insert the boundary datum cos(theta) into the Poisson integral and identify the resulting function with the harmonic real part of z by uniqueness of the disc Dirichlet problem.

items.title: The Poisson kernel realizes the sharp Harnack bounds on concentric discs
items.strategy: Evaluate the Poisson kernel at the extremal boundary angle and compare its values at the center and an interior radial point. The computation shows exactly where the disc Harnack constants come from.

items.title: log|z| has no global harmonic conjugate on C\{0}
items.strategy: If log|z| had a harmonic conjugate v on C\{0}, then log|z|+iv would be a continuous logarithm of the identity function on the punctured plane. The published no-continuous-logarithm theorem rules that out.

items.title: A harmonic function can vanish on a line without being zero everywhere
items.strategy: Take u(x,y)=x. It is harmonic on the whole plane, vanishes on the y-axis, and is not the zero function, so vanishing on a curve is weaker than vanishing on a nonempty open set.

items.title: The product of two harmonic functions need not be harmonic
items.strategy: Take u(x,y)=x and v(x,y)=x. Each is harmonic, but uv=x^2 has Laplacian 2, so the product leaves the harmonic class.

items.title: Re(1/z) is harmonic on a punctured disc and does not extend harmonically across 0
items.strategy: The rational function 1/z is holomorphic on the punctured disc, so its real part is harmonic there. Its values are unbounded near 0 along the real axis, so the bounded removable-singularity theorem does not apply and no harmonic extension across 0 exists.

pages.title: Subharmonic Functions and the Dirichlet Problem

items.title: This page uses the standard upper-semicontinuous subharmonic convention
items.strategy: Record that plane subharmonic functions here take values in [-infinity, infinity), are upper semicontinuous, and are not allowed to be identically -infinity on a connected component. Explain that this is the convention needed for log|f| and for Perron's method, while the continuous real-valued convention in older potential-theory sources is treated as a special case rather than as a competing definition.

items.title: Subharmonic functions on plane domains
Superharmonic functions on plane domains
Upper semicontinuous functions are Borel and their circle averages are defined
items.strategy: For an upper semicontinuous u, the sets {u < a} are open and the sets {u >= a} are closed, so u is Borel-measurable. On a compact circle the upper semicontinuity gives a finite upper bound, so the only possible improper value in the average is -infinity, which is allowed by the page convention.

items.title: Subharmonicity is equivalent to harmonic comparison on compactly contained discs
items.strategy: Use the Poisson solution of the disc Dirichlet problem to convert the circle submean inequality into comparison with the harmonic extension of the boundary values. For the converse, compare u(z0) with the harmonic majorant solving the disc boundary problem for u|partial D and read off the center value from the Poisson formula.

items.title: A C^2 function is subharmonic exactly when its Laplacian is nonnegative
items.strategy: For the forward direction, apply the submean inequality to a Taylor expansion of the circle average. For the reverse direction, solve the disc Dirichlet problem for the boundary values of u and apply the harmonic-comparison characterization to the difference between u and that harmonic extension.

items.title: Plane subharmonic functions are locally integrable
items.strategy: On a compactly contained disc, compare the function with the harmonic majorant of its boundary values and use the submean inequality to bound its positive part by a finite boundary average. Upper semicontinuity on compact circles supplies the remaining local bound needed to conclude integrability on smaller discs.

items.title: The logarithm of the modulus of a holomorphic function is subharmonic
items.strategy: Away from the zeros of f, write log|f| as the real part of a holomorphic logarithm and use the C^2 criterion. Near a zero, factor f(z)=(z-a)^m g(z) with g(a) nonzero and combine the harmonicity of log|g| with the standard logarithmic singularity of m log|z-a|.

items.title: Positive powers of the modulus of a holomorphic function are subharmonic
items.strategy: Use the harmonic-majorant form of subharmonicity. If h majorizes log|f| on a disc, then exp(ph) majorizes |f|^p there, and the convexity of the exponential preserves the boundary comparison.

items.title: Positive linear combinations and finite maxima preserve subharmonicity
items.strategy: For positive linear combinations, add the submean inequalities termwise. For a finite maximum, solve the harmonic comparison problem on a small disc and observe that the maximum of functions dominated by the same harmonic majorant is still dominated by it.

items.title: A decreasing limit of plane subharmonic functions is subharmonic or identically -infinity
items.strategy: A decreasing limit of upper semicontinuous functions is upper semicontinuous. On a fixed circle, add one constant large enough to make the sequence nonnegative there and apply monotone convergence to the submean inequalities; if every interior value diverges to -infinity then the limit is the excluded trivial case.

items.title: Upper-semicontinuous regularization
The upper-semicontinuous regularization of a locally bounded-above subharmonic supremum is subharmonic
items.strategy: Take finite maxima of the family to obtain an increasing net of subharmonic minorants, regularize the pointwise supremum, and use the harmonic-comparison characterization on each compactly contained disc. Local boundedness above is the hypothesis that keeps the envelope finite and prevents the raw supremum from leaving the class.

items.title: A plane subharmonic function with an interior maximum is constant on its component
items.strategy: Apply the submean inequality on discs centered at a maximum point. Equality of the center value with the boundary average forces equality almost everywhere on each circle, and upper semicontinuity then propagates the constant value across the connected component.

items.title: Poisson modification on a compactly contained disc
Subharmonic pieces glue across a boundary under the limsup inequality
items.strategy: Use the harmonic-comparison form of subharmonicity on discs lying wholly inside one side or the other. On discs meeting the seam, the limsup boundary condition prevents the harmonic majorant from being violated when the two pieces are compared through shrinking circles.

items.title: Poisson modification is subharmonic and majorizes the original function
items.strategy: Inside the modified disc the function is harmonic by construction; outside it is the original subharmonic function. The gluing lemma handles the seam, and the harmonic boundary-value solution majorizes the original function by the harmonic-comparison characterization.

items.title: The Perron lower family for continuous boundary data
The Perron envelope and its regularization
The Perron family is nonempty and uniformly bounded by the boundary data
items.strategy: Constant functions below min(phi) and above max(phi) show nonemptiness and provide trivial barriers for the lower family. The subharmonic maximum principle then keeps every lower function between the global minimum and maximum of the boundary datum.

items.title: The regularized Perron envelope is harmonic
items.strategy: At a chosen interior point, approximate the envelope from below by lower functions, replace each on a small disc by its Poisson modification, and take finite maxima to keep them in the lower family. Harnack convergence of the harmonic lifts produces a harmonic function on the disc that agrees with the envelope at the center; varying the center gives harmonicity everywhere.

items.title: Barriers and regular boundary points
A boundary point is regular exactly when it admits a barrier
items.strategy: A barrier squeezes every Perron lower function below the boundary datum at the marked point, forcing the Perron solution to attain the correct limit there. Conversely, solve the Perron problem for a carefully chosen bump datum that vanishes only at the point and turn the resulting harmonic solution into a negative subharmonic barrier.

items.title: On a regular bounded plane domain, Perron's method solves the Dirichlet problem
items.strategy: The Perron envelope is harmonic by the previous theorem. If every boundary point is regular, the barrier characterization forces the harmonic envelope to approach the boundary datum pointwise on the whole boundary, and published Dirichlet uniqueness supplies the uniqueness clause.

items.title: Exterior disc points and exterior cone points are regular
items.strategy: For an exterior disc point, use a translated logarithmic potential as an explicit barrier. For an exterior cone point, straighten the cone, apply a power map that turns it into a half-plane, and take the negative real part there to obtain a barrier after pulling back.

items.title: A local strict subharmonic peak function globalizes
items.strategy: Follow Boas §7.6.3. Shrink the local neighborhood, scale the local peak function so it stays below -1 on the seam circle, and define the global candidate by taking the maximum of that scaled local function with the constant -1. The maximum construction preserves subharmonicity and keeps the required boundary upper limits, so the result is a global peak function.

items.title: A weak local subharmonic peak function implies regularity
items.strategy: Use the Bouligand refinement quoted in Boas §7.6.4: a weak local subharmonic peak function upgrades to a strict local one. Then apply the locality lemma to globalize the peak function and invoke the barrier characterization to conclude regularity.

items.title: A boundary point whose complementary component contains another point is regular
items.strategy: Follow the peak-function construction in Boas §7.7. Send the boundary point to 0 and a second point of the same complementary component to infinity by a linear fractional map. On the transformed slit complement choose a holomorphic branch of log and use Re(1/log z) as a weak local harmonic peak function. The previous lemma then upgrades that local weak peak data to regularity at the boundary point.

items.title: A point on a nonsingleton boundary component is regular
items.strategy: Use the same logarithmic peak-function route as in the complementary-component lemma, now in the boundary-component setting recorded by Khoruzhenko's Theorem 53. Once the corresponding local weak peak function is in hand, the previously declared weak-local-to-regularity bridge yields the conclusion.

items.title: Every bounded simply connected proper plane domain is regular
items.strategy: Keep the current source-backed complementary-component route explicit as a scoped pushback against the still-live CA-14 design route until a separate sourced no-singleton-boundary-component bridge exists. In Boas's planar working definition, a simply connected domain is one whose complement in the extended plane is connected. For a bounded proper domain that connected complementary component contains both the chosen boundary point and infinity, so the previous lemma applies at every boundary point. Khoruzhenko's Theorem 52 confirms this same endpoint directly, while thm-nonsingleton-boundary-component-is-regular remains a separately scaffolded theorem rather than the load-bearing route for this corollary on current bytes.

items.title: A conformal homeomorphism of closures transports continuous Dirichlet solutions
items.strategy: Compose the boundary datum on the target with the inverse boundary homeomorphism, solve the regular-domain Dirichlet problem on the source, and then compose the harmonic solution with the inverse conformal map. Conformal invariance preserves harmonicity in the interior, the closure homeomorphism gives the right boundary limits, and uniqueness identifies the transported solution.

pages.title: Subharmonic Functions and the Dirichlet Problem — Examples

items.title: The functions |z|^2 and log|z| are subharmonic
items.strategy: Compute the Laplacian of |z|^2 directly and invoke the C^2 criterion. For log|z|, use the dedicated logarithmic-modulus theorem with the holomorphic function f(z)=z.

items.title: Poisson modification of |z|^2 on a concentric disc is constant there
items.strategy: On the circle |z|=r the boundary values of |z|^2 are the constant r^2. The Poisson solution with constant boundary data is constant, so the modification replaces the inner disc by the harmonic function r^2 and leaves the outer annulus unchanged.

items.title: The Perron solution on an annulus with radial boundary data is affine in log|z|
items.strategy: Write the candidate harmonic function as A log|z| + B, determine A and B from the two boundary circles, and then appeal to bounded-domain Dirichlet uniqueness. The example exhibits Perron's solution explicitly on a non-disc regular domain.

items.title: A corner of a square has an explicit barrier
items.strategy: Translate and rotate the corner to the first quadrant and use the standard power-map barrier coming from an exterior cone. This computes the abstract geometric regularity criterion in a concrete polygonal case.

items.title: The punctured disc has an irregular boundary point and a continuous datum with no harmonic solution
items.strategy: Take boundary data equal to 0 on the unit circle and 1 at the puncture. Any bounded harmonic solution on the punctured disc would extend harmonically across the puncture by the published removable-singularity theorem, forcing the center value to agree with the circle limit and contradicting the prescribed datum.

items.title: FALSE: every bounded plane domain admits a continuous harmonic solution for every continuous boundary datum
items.strategy: Refute the universal claim by the punctured-disc datum from the previous counterexample. The failure is not a matter of smoothness or explicit formulas: the domain is bounded, yet one boundary point is irregular.

items.title: FALSE: the Perron envelope always attains the boundary values
items.strategy: Use the same punctured-disc datum. Perron's construction still produces a harmonic envelope on the interior, but regularity fails at the puncture, so the boundary limit there does not match the prescribed value.

items.title: FALSE: every subharmonic function attains a maximum somewhere in the interior
items.strategy: The function |z|^2 on the unit disc is subharmonic and attains its maximum only on the boundary. This single witness refutes the universal claim and matches the maximum-principle theorem on the A page.

items.title: FALSE: the raw pointwise supremum of an arbitrary family of subharmonic functions is subharmonic
items.strategy: On the unit disc, each function u_n(z)=max(n Re z,-1) is subharmonic, but the pointwise supremum is -1 on the left half-disc, 0 on the imaginary axis, and +infinity on the right half-disc. The example shows exactly why local boundedness above and upper-semicontinuous regularization are load-bearing in the upper-envelope theorem.

pages.title: Normal Families and Montel's Theorem

items.title: Every plane domain has the canonical nested compact exhaustion by distance and radius cutoffs
items.strategy: Use Euclidean closedness and boundedness for each stage, then check interior nesting and exhaustion directly from the distance-to-boundary definition.

items.title: Locally uniform convergence on a plane domain is the already-published compact-convergence notion
items.strategy: Cite the published dictionary and fix the local notation for this page's function spaces.

items.title: The exhaustion metric on a function space over a plane domain
The exhaustion metric induces exactly the topology of locally uniform convergence
items.strategy: Compare metric tails with sup bounds on finitely many exhaustion members and use the local-uniform dictionary in both directions.

items.title: The compact-open topology on C(Ω,C) is independent of the chosen compact exhaustion
items.strategy: Different exhaustion metrics induce the same locally uniform topology, and that topology is the compact-open topology on a metric domain.

items.title: Continuous complex-valued functions on a plane domain are complete for an exhaustion metric
items.strategy: A Cauchy sequence is uniformly Cauchy on each exhaustion member, so the local limits glue to a continuous function and the weighted metric forces convergence back to it.

items.title: Holomorphic functions form a closed subspace for locally uniform convergence
items.strategy: Apply the Weierstrass convergence theorem inside the complete continuous-function space.

items.title: Normal families of holomorphic functions on a plane domain
Locally bounded families of functions on a plane domain
Locally equicontinuous families of functions on a plane domain
Locally bounded holomorphic families are locally equicontinuous
items.strategy: Use a slightly larger disc and Cauchy's formula to convert one common bound into a uniform Lipschitz estimate on the smaller disc.

items.title: Montel's theorem: every locally bounded holomorphic family is normal
items.strategy: On each exhaustion member, local boundedness gives equicontinuity; then compact-domain Ascoli provides successive compact convergence, and a diagonal extraction gives the global subsequence.

items.title: Normal holomorphic families are locally bounded
items.strategy: If one compact neighborhood carried arbitrarily large values, choose a sequence and evaluation points there; compactness of the neighborhood and local uniform convergence of a normal subsequence contradict boundedness of its limit.

items.title: Vitali-Porter convergence theorem for holomorphic functions
items.strategy: Montel gives a locally uniformly convergent subsequence, and the identity theorem forces any two subsequential limits agreeing on a set with an interior limit point to coincide.

items.title: Every derivative operator is continuous for locally uniform convergence on holomorphic functions
items.strategy: Apply the already-published Weierstrass convergence theorem and restate its derivative conclusion as continuity of the derivative maps.

items.title: Chordal local uniform convergence and meromorphic normality
A chordally locally uniform meromorphic limit is meromorphic or identically infinity
items.strategy: Work in a sphere chart away from the limiting poles, use local compact convergence there, and invoke Hurwitz to control the branch where the limit takes the value infinity.

items.title: Local chordal equicontinuity is equivalent to meromorphic normality on compact exhaustions
items.strategy: Apply compact-metric Ascoli on each exhaustion member with the chordal sphere as target, then combine the compact convergence theorem with a diagonal extraction.

pages.title: Normal Families and Montel's Theorem — Examples

items.title: The family z^n is normal on the unit disc and not normal on the complex plane
items.strategy: Bound the family on compacta of the disc and apply Montel there, then use local boundedness failure on large circles in the plane.

items.title: The family of holomorphic functions bounded by one is normal on every plane domain
items.strategy: Uniform bound one on every compact subset is exactly the hypothesis of Montel.

items.title: Montel's diagonal extraction can be written out concretely on a disc
items.strategy: Take successive subsequences on the compact discs of radius 1-1/n and follow the diagonal subsequence.

items.title: The exhaustion metric is explicit on the unit disc
items.strategy: Use the canonical compact exhaustion of the disc and write the first few weighted sup terms directly.

items.title: The family nz is not normal on any domain containing zero
items.strategy: The family is not locally bounded near the origin, so the converse-to-Montel theorem excludes normality.

items.title: The family e^(nz) converges chordally to infinity on the right half-plane without being holomorphically normal there
items.strategy: Real parts tend to plus infinity on compacta of the right half-plane, so the reciprocal tends uniformly to zero while the finite-valued holomorphic limit does not exist.

items.title: FALSE: a normal family contains every locally uniform sequential limit of its own sequences
items.strategy: Normality guarantees subsequential convergence, not closure of the family under limits.

items.title: FALSE: Arzelà-Ascoli alone proves Montel's theorem
items.strategy: The real work is the holomorphic equicontinuity step; without it the compactness theorem has no hypothesis to apply.

items.title: FALSE: a chordally locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions can never be identically infinity
items.strategy: The right-half-plane exponential family gives the standard contrary witness.

pages.title: The Riemann Mapping Theorem
The Riemann Mapping Theorem — Examples
Simply Connected Plane Domains: the Grand Equivalence
Simply Connected Plane Domains: the Grand Equivalence — Examples
Infinite Products and the Weierstrass Factorisation Theorem

items.title: Dictionary for using the published infinite-product definition over $\mathbb{C}$
Absolute convergence criterion for complex infinite products
items.strategy: Translate the product to the deviations from $1$, compare the convergence problem with the published real criterion for $\prod (1 + |a_n|)$, and use the same tail estimates pointwise in $\mathbb{C}$.

items.title: Normal convergence of holomorphic products
