Normally convergent products define holomorphic functions with the expected zeros
items.strategy: Take logarithmic deviations from $1$, use the compact-uniform absolute control to apply the Weierstrass convergence theorem to the partial products, and then isolate the finite set of factors that can vanish on a given compact set.

items.title: The logarithmic derivative of a normally convergent product
items.strategy: Differentiate the partial products, divide by the nonvanishing limit away from the zero set, and pass to the locally uniform limit on compacta disjoint from the zeros.

items.title: Weierstrass elementary factors
The unit-disc estimate for Weierstrass elementary factors
items.strategy: Differentiate $1 - E_p(w)$ explicitly, identify its zero of order $p+1$ at the origin, and bound the normalized quotient on the closed unit disc.

items.title: Weierstrass products, canonical products, and genus
The exponent of convergence of a zero sequence
A canonical product converges when the $(p+1)$-power reciprocal sum converges
items.strategy: Apply the elementary-factor estimate to each compact set and compare the resulting majorant with the convergent reciprocal power series that defines the genus threshold.

items.title: Weierstrass product theorem on the complex plane
items.strategy: Choose the elementary-factor orders so that the reciprocal-power convergence criterion applies to the repeated nonzero zero-sequence, and multiply by the correct power of $z$ for the zero at the origin.

items.title: Weierstrass factorization for entire functions
items.strategy: Build an entire product with exactly the zeros of $f$, divide $f$ by it, and use the zero-free quotient to define the residual entire exponential factor.

items.title: Every meromorphic function on $\mathbb{C}$ is a quotient of entire functions
items.strategy: Cancel the pole divisor of the meromorphic function with an entire denominator provided by the Weierstrass product theorem, leaving an entire numerator.

items.title: The Weierstrass product for sine
items.strategy: Apply the factorization theorem to $\sin(\pi z)$, use its zero set and multiplicities, and determine the zero-free factor by comparing growth and the derivative at the origin.

items.title: Jensen's formula on a disc
items.strategy: Factor the zeros inside the disc, apply the harmonic mean-value relation to the zero-free quotient, and then remove the generic-radius restriction by a radial limiting argument.

items.title: Jensen's formula bounds the number of zeros in a smaller disc
items.strategy: Estimate each logarithmic zero term in Jensen's formula from below by the common smaller-radius contribution and solve for the zero count.

items.title: The order of an entire function
The zero-sequence exponent is at most the entire order
items.strategy: Insert the finite-order growth bound into Jensen's formula, derive a zero-count estimate, and convert that bound into convergence of reciprocal powers above the order.

items.title: Hadamard factorization for finite-order entire functions
items.strategy: Choose the canonical genus allowed by the zero-exponent bound, divide the entire function by the resulting canonical product, and prove the remaining entire logarithm has vanishing derivative above degree $\lfloor \rho \rfloor$.

items.title: A nonintegral order bounds the canonical genus by its floor
items.strategy: Read the polynomial degree and canonical genus bound off Hadamard's factorization and simplify when the order is not an integer.

pages.title: Infinite Products and the Weierstrass Factorisation Theorem — Examples

items.title: The product $\prod_{n \ge 1}(1 + z/2^n)$ defines an entire zero-free function
items.strategy: Use the geometric-series bound on compacta to verify normal convergence of the deviations from $1$, and track the zero set factor by factor.

items.title: The sine product recovers the Basel sum
items.strategy: Compare the quadratic term in the Taylor expansion of $\sin(\pi z)/(\pi z)$ with the quadratic term in its Weierstrass product expansion.

items.title: Jensen's formula for a polynomial
items.strategy: Factor the polynomial into linear terms and substitute the factorization directly into Jensen's formula to read off the finite zero sum.

items.title: A genus-zero canonical product for zeros at the squares
items.strategy: Check the convergence of $\sum 1/n^2$ for the reciprocal-square zero sequence and apply the canonical-product convergence theorem with genus $0$.

items.title: A conditionally convergent linear term does not force a nonzero product limit
items.strategy: Apply the published signed infinite-product criterion to $a_n = (-1)^n/\sqrt{n+2}$, using the conditional convergence of the linear series and the divergence of the square series.

items.title: FALSE: Weierstrass factorization is unique
items.strategy: Multiply any valid factorization by $e^{g(z)}$ for a nonconstant entire function $g$ and compare the zero divisor with the unchanged function after adjusting the nonzero factor.

items.title: FALSE: every discrete zero sequence admits a genus-zero canonical product
items.strategy: Use the zero sequence at the positive integers, whose reciprocal first powers diverge, so the genus-zero product fails while the genus-one sine product succeeds.

items.title: FALSE: the order of an entire function always equals the canonical genus in its factorization
items.strategy: Compare a finite-order entire function such as $e^z$ or a polynomial with its trivial zero divisor: the function has positive or zero order while the canonical product has genus $0$.

items.title: Complex $m$-space and its real coordinate dictionary
items.strategy: Prose. Fix $m\ge1$ and let $\mathbb C^m$ be the set of functions $m\to\mathbb C$, so coordinates are $z_k$ for $k<m$, matching the library's indexing of $\mathbb R^n$ from $0$. Writing $z_k=x_k+iy_k$ identifies $\mathbb C^m$ with $\mathbb R^{2m}$ by $z\mapsto(x_0,y_0,\dots,x_{m-1},y_{m-1})$; record that this is the chosen ordering and that the alternative grouping is a different bijection. Check the Euclidean norm $\lVert z\rVert=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|z_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$ agrees with the $\mathbb R^{2m}$ Euclidean norm under it, so open sets, convergence, compactness and completeness transfer verbatim, and note the $m=1$ case reduces to the published plane dictionary. Also record the $\mathbb C$-vector-space structure and that a subset is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded.

items.title: Balls, polydiscs and the distinguished boundary in $\mathbb{C}^m$
items.strategy: Definition only. For $a\in\mathbb C^m$ and a polyradius $r$ with $r_k>0$ for $k<m$, define the open polydisc $\Delta_r(a)=\{z:|z_k-a_k|<r_k\text{ for all }k<m\}$, its closure, and its distinguished boundary $\Gamma_r(a)=\{z:|z_k-a_k|=r_k\text{ for all }k<m\}$, presented as the product of the $m$ circles. Define the ball by the Euclidean norm. Say explicitly that for $m\ge2$ the distinguished boundary is a proper subset of the topological boundary, and that a scalar $r$ abbreviates the constant polyradius. Note that a polydisc is convex, hence star-shaped, and that each of its one-variable slices is a disc.

items.title: Holomorphic functions on an open subset of $\mathbb{C}^m$
items.strategy: Definition only. $f:U\to\mathbb C$ with $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ open is complex differentiable at $a$ when there is a $\mathbb C$-linear $L:\mathbb C^m\to\mathbb C$ with $f(a+h)=f(a)+L(h)+r(h)$ and $\lVert h\rVert^{-1}|r(h)|\to0$; $L$ is then unique and written $Df(a)$. Holomorphic on $U$ means complex differentiable at every point. State that $\mathbb C$-linear means additive and homogeneous over $\mathbb C$, not merely over $\mathbb R$, and that at $m=1$ this is the published notion because a $\mathbb C$-linear functional on $\mathbb C$ is multiplication by a scalar. Do NOT put continuity or local boundedness into the definition: the point of this page is that they are consequences or, in the separate case, theorems.

items.title: Separately holomorphic functions
items.strategy: Definition only. $f:U\to\mathbb C$ is separately holomorphic when, for every $a\in U$ and every $k<m$, the slice $\zeta\mapsto f(a_0,\dots,a_{k-1},\zeta,a_{k+1},\dots,a_{m-1})$ is holomorphic in the published one-variable sense on the open set of $\zeta$ for which the point lies in $U$. Record that no continuity in the remaining variables is asked, and that the slice domains are open because $U$ is.

items.title: Wirtinger operators in $\mathbb{C}^m$
items.strategy: Definition only. At a point where the $2m$ real partial derivatives of $f$ exist, set $\partial_{z_k}f=\tfrac12(\partial_{x_k}f-i\partial_{y_k}f)$ and $\partial_{\bar z_k}f=\tfrac12(\partial_{x_k}f+i\partial_{y_k}f)$ for $k<m$, the partial derivatives being those of the published real definition under the coordinate dictionary. Record the differential identity $Df(h)=\sum_{k<m}(\partial_{z_k}f)h_k+\sum_{k<m}(\partial_{\bar z_k}f)\overline{h_k}$ at a point of real total differentiability, and that at $m=1$ these are the published Wirtinger derivatives.

items.title: A real-linear functional on $\mathbb{C}^m$ is complex linear exactly when its antiholomorphic part vanishes
items.strategy: Every $\mathbb R$-linear $T:\mathbb C^m\to\mathbb C$ is uniquely $T(h)=\sum_{k<m}c_kh_k+\sum_{k<m}d_k\overline{h_k}$: get $c_k,d_k$ from the values of $T$ at $e_k$ and $ie_k$ by solving the two-by-two system, and check uniqueness by evaluating at those same vectors. Then $T$ is $\mathbb C$-linear iff $T(ih)=iT(h)$ for all $h$, and substituting the representation gives $-2i\sum_kd_k\overline{h_k}=0$ for all $h$, hence every $d_k=0$; conversely a sum of $c_kh_k$ is $\mathbb C$-linear. Include $m=1$ and the zero functional.

items.title: A holomorphic function of several variables is continuous and separately holomorphic
items.strategy: Continuity at $a$: the defining expansion gives $|f(a+h)-f(a)|\le|L(h)|+|r(h)|$, and $|L(h)|\le C\lVert h\rVert$ since a linear functional on $\mathbb C^m$ is bounded on the unit sphere by the standard-basis expansion. Separate holomorphy: restrict the expansion to $h=\xi e_k$, so $f(a+\xi e_k)-f(a)=L(e_k)\xi+r(\xi e_k)$ with $|r|/|\xi|\to0$; hence the slice is complex differentiable at $a_k$ with derivative $L(e_k)$, and that derivative equals $\partial_{z_k}f(a)$.

items.title: Multi-indexed power series in $\mathbb{C}^m$ and their absolute convergence
items.strategy: Definition only. Reuse the published multi-index conventions for $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ with $\alpha\in\mathbb N^m$ indexed from $0$, and add the complex monomial $z^\alpha=\prod_{k<m}z_k^{\alpha_k}$. Say that $\sum_{\alpha}c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ converges absolutely at $z$ when for one, equivalently every, bijection $\mathbb N\to\mathbb N^m$ the resulting complex series converges absolutely; the set $\mathbb N^m$ is countable, and absolute convergence and the sum are independent of the bijection by the published complex rearrangement theorem, so the sum is well defined and written $\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$. Define uniform absolute convergence on a set by a summable majorant, so the Weierstrass test applies. Do not introduce a second notion of unordered sum.

items.title: The Cauchy kernel expands as an absolutely and uniformly convergent multi-indexed geometric series
items.strategy: Fix $a$, a polyradius $r$ and $z$ with $|z_k-a_k|\le\theta r_k$ for a single $\theta<1$. For $\zeta$ on the distinguished boundary $\Gamma_r(a)$, each factor $1/(\zeta_k-z_k)$ is $\sum_{j}(z_k-a_k)^j/(\zeta_k-a_k)^{j+1}$ by the one-variable geometric series, converging absolutely since the ratio has modulus at most $\theta$. Multiplying the $m$ series and using the Cauchy-product/rearrangement theorem gives $\prod_{k<m}(\zeta_k-z_k)^{-1}=\sum_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha\prod_{k<m}(\zeta_k-a_k)^{-\alpha_k-1}$, with the majorant $\prod_k\theta^{\alpha_k}/r_k$ summing to $\prod_k(r_k(1-\theta))^{-1}$. Conclude absolute convergence uniform in $\zeta\in\Gamma_r(a)$ and in $z$ on the closed subpolydisc.

items.title: The iterated Cauchy integral formula on a polydisc
items.strategy: Let $f$ be continuous on the open polydisc $\Delta_\rho(a)$ and separately holomorphic there, and let $r_k<\rho_k$ for $k<m$. Induct on $m$. At each step apply the published one-variable circle formula in the variable $\zeta_k$, whose slice is holomorphic on the disc of radius $\rho_k$; the remaining variables are held fixed, so no interchange of integrals is performed anywhere and Fubini is not invoked. Joint continuity is what makes each successive integrand continuous on the circle, so each contour integral exists and the next application is legitimate. The result is the iterated integral over the $m$ circles of $f(\zeta)\prod_{k<m}(\zeta_k-z_k)^{-1}$, divided by $(2\pi i)^m$, valid for every $z\in\Delta_r(a)$. State it as an iterated integral, not as an integral over the distinguished boundary.

items.title: A continuous separately holomorphic function is the sum of an absolutely convergent power series with Cauchy-integral coefficients on every smaller polydisc
items.strategy: Substitute the kernel expansion into the iterated Cauchy formula. The expansion converges uniformly in $\zeta$ on each circle of integration and absolutely, so the sum may be taken through each of the $m$ contour integrals in turn by the published uniform-limit interchange, applied to the partial sums of a fixed enumeration of $\mathbb N^m$; uniformity of the remaining integrand in the outer variables is what licenses the next interchange, and the majorant of the kernel lemma supplies it. The result is $f(z)=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ with $c_\alpha$ the iterated integral of $f(\zeta)\prod_k(\zeta_k-a_k)^{-\alpha_k-1}$ over $(2\pi i)^m$, converging absolutely and uniformly on every closed subpolydisc. The identification $c_\alpha=\partial^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$ is NOT available here — it needs termwise differentiation, which is the next theorem — so neither the title nor the Statement of this item may claim it; it is recorded in cor-holomorphic-functions-in-several-variables-are-smooth.

items.title: An absolutely convergent multi-indexed power series is holomorphic and differentiates termwise
items.strategy: Suppose $\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ converges absolutely at some point of every polyradius direction, so that on a closed subpolydisc $\sum_\alpha|c_\alpha|\theta^{|\alpha|}\prod r_k^{\alpha_k}<\infty$. Show the sum $g$ is complex differentiable at each interior point with $\mathbb C$-linear differential $h\mapsto\sum_{k<m}\bigl(\sum_\alpha\alpha_kc_\alpha(z-a)^{\alpha-e_k}\bigr)h_k$: expand $((z-a)+h)^\alpha$ by the multinomial expansion, isolate the constant and first-order terms, and bound the remainder by the majorant series with a factor $\lVert h\rVert^2$, using that $\sum_\alpha|c_\alpha||\alpha|^2\theta^{|\alpha|}\prod r_k^{\alpha_k}$ converges. Conclude that each derived series has the same convergence polydisc and that the coefficients are $\partial^\alpha g(a)/\alpha!$ by induction.

items.title: Osgood's lemma: continuous and separately holomorphic implies holomorphic
items.strategy: Let $f$ be continuous on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ and separately holomorphic. Around each $a\in U$ choose a polydisc with closure in $U$; the expansion theorem writes $f$ as an absolutely convergent power series on a smaller polydisc, and the previous theorem makes that sum holomorphic there. Holomorphy is a local property, so $f$ is holomorphic on $U$. Together with the earlier proposition this makes the three conditions equivalent for continuous functions: complex differentiability, local power-series representability, and separate holomorphy.

items.title: Holomorphic functions of several variables are smooth and their complex derivatives are holomorphic
items.strategy: By Osgood's lemma and the expansion theorem a holomorphic $f$ is locally a convergent power series; termwise differentiation gives every $\partial_{z_k}f$ as a convergent power series on the same polydisc, hence holomorphic, and the real partial derivatives of every order exist and are continuous by the same expansion in the real coordinates. Iterate to obtain $C^\infty$ and $\partial^\alpha f$ holomorphic for every multi-index, together with $c_\alpha=\partial^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$.

items.title: The coefficients of a convergent multi-indexed power series are its derivative coefficients, hence unique
items.strategy: If $\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha=\sum_\alpha c'_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ on a polydisc about $a$, both sums are holomorphic there and termwise differentiation gives $\alpha!c_\alpha=\partial^\alpha f(a)=\alpha!c'_\alpha$ for every $\alpha$; since $\alpha!\ne0$ the coefficients agree. Record the consequence that a function has at most one power-series representation about a given centre.

items.title: Cauchy estimates for mixed derivatives on a polydisc
items.strategy: From the coefficient formula, $c_\alpha$ is an iterated integral of $f(\zeta)\prod_k(\zeta_k-a_k)^{-\alpha_k-1}$ over $(2\pi i)^m$; bound each of the $m$ integrals by the ML estimate, with circle length $2\pi r_k$ and kernel modulus $r_k^{-\alpha_k-1}$. This gives $|c_\alpha|\le M\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k}$ with $M$ the supremum of $|f|$ on the distinguished boundary, hence $|\partial^\alpha f(a)|\le\alpha!\,M\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k}$. Note the estimate uses only the distinguished boundary, not the whole topological boundary.

items.title: A bounded separately holomorphic function on a polydisc is Lipschitz on every smaller polydisc
items.strategy: Let $|f|\le M$ on $\Delta_\rho(a)$ with $f$ separately holomorphic, and let $\theta<1$. For $z,w$ in the closed polydisc of polyradius $\theta\rho$, telescope in one coordinate at a time: the difference $f(w)-f(z)$ is the sum over $k<m$ of the increments obtained by changing the $k$th coordinate from $z_k$ to $w_k$ with the earlier coordinates already changed. Each increment is a difference of one-variable holomorphic function values, bounded by $|w_k-z_k|$ times the supremum of the slice derivative on a segment in the disc of radius $\theta\rho_k$; that supremum is at most $M/((1-\theta)\rho_k)$ by the published Cauchy inequality, UNIFORMLY in the other coordinates because $M$ bounds $f$ everywhere. Summing gives a Lipschitz bound. This uses no continuity of $f$ in the remaining variables at any point.

items.title: Locally bounded and separately holomorphic implies holomorphic
items.strategy: Local boundedness gives, around each point, a polydisc on which $f$ is bounded; the Lipschitz lemma then makes $f$ continuous on a smaller polydisc, hence continuous on the whole open set since continuity is local. Osgood's lemma upgrades continuity plus separate holomorphy to holomorphy. State plainly that the local-boundedness hypothesis is what is removed by the Hartogs theorem, which is not available at this point in the reading order, and do not use that later theorem here.

items.title: For $C^1$ functions, holomorphy, complex linearity of the real derivative, and the Cauchy–Riemann system agree
items.strategy: For $f:U\to\mathbb C$ of class $C^1$ in the real coordinates, prove three equivalences. Holomorphy gives real total differentiability with the same differential, so the real derivative is $\mathbb C$-linear by uniqueness of the total derivative. Complex linearity of the real derivative is equivalent to the vanishing of every $\partial_{\bar z_k}f$ by the criterion lemma applied to the Wirtinger representation of the differential. Conversely, $C^1$ gives real total differentiability by the published continuous-partials theorem, and a $\mathbb C$-linear total derivative turns the real expansion into the complex one. Say explicitly that the $C^1$ hypothesis is used only in the last implication.

items.title: Sums, products and nonvanishing quotients of holomorphic functions are holomorphic
items.strategy: Work from the defining expansion. Additivity and scalar multiples are immediate. For a product, expand $f(a+h)g(a+h)$ using both expansions and collect: the first-order part is $f(a)Dg(a)+g(a)Df(a)$, a $\mathbb C$-linear functional, and the remainder is $o(\lVert h\rVert)$ using continuity of $f$ and the linear bound on $Dg(a)$. For a quotient with $g(a)\ne0$, use continuity of $g$ to keep it away from zero near $a$ and expand $1/g$ as in one variable. Record the resulting product and quotient rules for $\partial_{z_k}$.

items.title: Locally uniform limits of holomorphic functions are holomorphic, with locally uniform convergence of all derivatives
items.strategy: A locally uniform limit $f$ of continuous $f_n$ is continuous. Each slice of $f$ is a locally uniform limit of the corresponding holomorphic slices, so it is holomorphic by the published one-variable Weierstrass convergence theorem; hence $f$ is continuous and separately holomorphic, and Osgood's lemma makes it holomorphic. For the derivatives, apply the Cauchy estimates on a polydisc to $f_n-f$: the bound is $\alpha!\sup_{\Gamma}|f_n-f|\prod_kr_k^{-\alpha_k}$, which tends to $0$ uniformly on the smaller polydisc.

items.title: The modulus of a holomorphic function on a closed polydisc is bounded by its supremum on the distinguished boundary
items.strategy: Let $f$ be continuous on the closed polydisc and holomorphic on its interior. Apply the one-variable boundary maximum-modulus principle in the first variable with the others fixed on their closed discs, then in the second, and so on; after $m$ steps every coordinate has been pushed to its circle. Each step is legitimate because the slice is continuous on the closed disc and holomorphic inside. Conclude $\sup_{\overline\Delta}|f|=\sup_{\Gamma}|f|$, and note this is stronger than the one-variable statement only in that the bounding set is far smaller than the topological boundary.

items.title: Holomorphic maps $\mathbb{C}^m \to \mathbb{C}^n$ and the complex Jacobian matrix
items.strategy: Definition only. $F:U\to\mathbb C^n$ with $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ open is holomorphic at $a$ when there is a $\mathbb C$-linear $L:\mathbb C^m\to\mathbb C^n$ with $F(a+h)=F(a)+L(h)+r(h)$ and $\lVert r(h)\rVert/\lVert h\rVert\to0$; $L$ is unique. Define the complex Jacobian $J_{\mathbb C}F(a)$ as the matrix of $L$ in the standard bases, whose $(j,k)$ entry is $\partial_{z_k}F_j(a)$ for $j<n$, $k<m$, using the published matrix of a linear map over the field $\mathbb C$. Record that $n=1$ recovers the scalar definition.

items.title: A map into $\mathbb{C}^n$ is holomorphic exactly when each of its components is
items.strategy: If $F$ is holomorphic with differential $L$, then $F_j=\pi_j\circ F$ has differential $\pi_j\circ L$, which is $\mathbb C$-linear, and the remainder estimate passes to a component because $|r_j(h)|\le\lVert r(h)\rVert$. Conversely, if every $F_j$ is holomorphic with differential $L_j$, assemble $L(h)=(L_0(h),\dots,L_{n-1}(h))$, which is $\mathbb C$-linear, and bound $\lVert r(h)\rVert$ by the sum of the $|r_j(h)|$ using the norm comparison in $\mathbb C^n$; each term is $o(\lVert h\rVert)$ and there are finitely many. Cover $n=0$, where the statement is vacuous, and $n=1$.

items.title: The composite of holomorphic maps is holomorphic and its complex Jacobian is the product
items.strategy: Let $F:U\to V$ and $G:V\to\mathbb C^p$ be holomorphic at $a$ and $F(a)$. Substitute the expansion of $F$ into that of $G$: the first-order term is $DG(F(a))\circ DF(a)$, a composite of $\mathbb C$-linear maps, hence $\mathbb C$-linear. Bound the remainder by splitting it into $DG(F(a))$ applied to the remainder of $F$ and the remainder of $G$ evaluated at $DF(a)h+r_F(h)$, using the linear bound and continuity of $F$; both are $o(\lVert h\rVert)$. The Jacobian identity is the published matrix-of-a-composite theorem applied to the two differentials.

items.title: The complex Jacobian determinant of a composite of equidimensional holomorphic maps is the product
items.strategy: When $m=n=p$, the Jacobians are square matrices over $\mathbb C$, which is a commutative ring, so the published multiplicativity of the determinant applies to the chain-rule identity: $\det J_{\mathbb C}(G\circ F)(a)=\det J_{\mathbb C}G(F(a))\cdot\det J_{\mathbb C}F(a)$. Record the consequence that a biholomorphic map has nowhere-vanishing Jacobian determinant, obtained by applying this to a two-sided inverse.

items.title: A holomorphic function vanishing on a nonempty open subset of a domain vanishes identically
items.strategy: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be a domain and $f$ holomorphic with $f=0$ on a nonempty open $W\subseteq U$. Put $A=\{z\in U:\partial^\alpha f(z)=0\text{ for every }\alpha\}$. It is closed in $U$ as an intersection of zero sets of continuous functions, nonempty since $W\subseteq A$, and open because at $a\in A$ the power-series expansion has all coefficients $\partial^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$ equal to zero, so $f$ vanishes on a whole polydisc about $a$ and with it all its derivatives. Connectedness gives $A=U$, hence $f\equiv0$. State the theorem in the form the several-variable setting actually supports and say in the Statement itself that vanishing on a set with an accumulation point is NOT assumed and would not suffice.

items.title: The holomorphic functions on a domain in $\mathbb{C}^m$ have no zero divisors
items.strategy: The holomorphic functions on $U$ form a commutative ring under pointwise operations by the algebra proposition. If $fg\equiv0$ and $f\not\equiv0$, then $\{f\ne0\}$ is a nonempty open subset of $U$ on which $g$ vanishes, so $g\equiv0$ by the identity theorem. Record that connectedness of $U$ is essential and that the ring is nonzero because constants are holomorphic.

items.title: An interior local maximum of the modulus forces a scalar holomorphic function to be constant
items.strategy: Let $f$ be holomorphic on a domain $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ with $|f(z)|\le|f(a)|$ on a ball $B$ about $a$. For each $v$ with $\lVert v\rVert=1$ the slice $g_v(\xi)=f(a+\xi v)$ is holomorphic on a disc about $0$ by the chain rule, and $|g_v|$ has a local maximum at $0$, so $g_v$ is constant near $0$ by the published one-variable local maximum-modulus principle. Every point of a smaller ball has the form $a+\xi v$, so $f$ is constant on that ball; the identity theorem applied to $f-f(a)$ makes $f$ constant on $U$.

items.title: A bounded holomorphic function on all of $\mathbb{C}^m$ is constant
items.strategy: For fixed $z\in\mathbb C^m$ the slice $\xi\mapsto f(\xi z)$ is entire in one variable by the chain rule and bounded by the same bound, hence constant by the published Liouville theorem; evaluating at $\xi=0$ and $\xi=1$ gives $f(z)=f(0)$. Since $z$ was arbitrary, $f$ is constant. Note that no connectedness argument is needed and that $m=0$ is degenerate.

items.title: A nonconstant scalar holomorphic function on a domain in $\mathbb{C}^m$ is an open map
items.strategy: Let $f$ be holomorphic and nonconstant on a domain $U$, let $O\subseteq U$ be open and $a\in O$. Choose a polydisc $\Delta\subseteq O$ about $a$; the identity theorem forbids $f$ from being constant on $\Delta$, so there is $b\in\Delta$ with $f(b)\ne f(a)$. The set $W=\{\xi\in\mathbb C:a+\xi(b-a)\in\Delta\}$ is open and convex, hence a domain, and contains $0$ and $1$; $g(\xi)=f(a+\xi(b-a))$ is holomorphic on $W$ by the chain rule and nonconstant since $g(0)\ne g(1)$. The published one-variable open mapping theorem makes $g(W)$ open, and $f(a)=g(0)\in g(W)\subseteq f(\Delta)\subseteq f(O)$, so $f(a)$ is interior to $f(O)$. State that the theorem is about scalar targets and asserts nothing for maps into $\mathbb C^n$ with $n\ge2$.

items.title: Conventions on this page, and what the several-variable identity theorem does not say
items.strategy: Prose that justifies rather than surveys. Record: coordinates and multi-indices are indexed from $0$, matching the library's $\mathbb R^n$; holomorphic means complex differentiable, and local boundedness or continuity is never built into the definition, so Osgood's lemma and the locally bounded theorem are theorems rather than tautologies; the distinguished boundary, not the topological boundary, is what the Cauchy formula and the estimates use. Then state precisely why the identity theorem here is weaker than its one-variable ancestor: the hypothesis is a nonempty OPEN set of zeros, and an accumulation point of the zero set does not suffice, with the companion page's false statement carrying the witness. Do not describe what other pages contain.

pages.title: Holomorphic Functions of Several Complex Variables — Examples

items.title: The power series of $z_0z_1$ on a bidisc centred away from the origin
items.strategy: Expand $f(z)=z_0z_1$ about $a=(1,1)$: writing $z_k=1+(z_k-1)$ gives $f(z)=1+(z_0-1)+(z_1-1)+(z_0-1)(z_1-1)$, a finite multi-indexed series with coefficients $c_{(0,0)}=c_{(1,0)}=c_{(0,1)}=c_{(1,1)}=1$ and all others $0$. Check the coefficients against $\partial^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$ and note that a finite series converges absolutely everywhere.

items.title: The power series of $\exp(z_0+z_1)$ on every bidisc
items.strategy: Multiply the two one-variable exponential series and use the Cauchy-product theorem for absolutely convergent complex series to get $\exp(z_0+z_1)=\sum_{\alpha}z^\alpha/\alpha!$ over $\alpha\in\mathbb N^2$, absolutely convergent on every bidisc. Verify the coefficient identity $\partial^\alpha f(0)/\alpha!=1/\alpha!$ and confirm the majorant bound of the definition on a closed bidisc of polyradius $(R,R)$.

items.title: The power series of $z_0/(1-z_1)$ and the shape of its domain of convergence
items.strategy: On $\{|z_1|<1\}$ expand the geometric series to get $z_0/(1-z_1)=\sum_{j}z_0z_1^{\,j}$, that is $c_\alpha=1$ when $\alpha_0=1$ and $c_\alpha=0$ otherwise. Verify absolute convergence exactly when $|z_1|<1$, with no constraint on $z_0$, so the set of absolute convergence is an unbounded product region rather than a bounded polydisc. Note that this is a legitimate reading of the definition and that the function is holomorphic on the whole region by the termwise theorem.

items.title: The iterated Cauchy formula computed for $z_0z_1$ on a bidisc
items.strategy: Take $f(z)=z_0z_1$ on the unit bidisc and $r=(1/2,1/2)$. Compute the iterated integral $(2\pi i)^{-2}\oint\oint\zeta_0\zeta_1(\zeta_0-z_0)^{-1}(\zeta_1-z_1)^{-1}d\zeta_1\,d\zeta_0$ by evaluating the inner circle integral with the one-variable formula and then the outer one, and confirm the value is $z_0z_1$. Do the two integrals in the stated order and do not interchange them.

items.title: Cauchy estimates on a bidisc, computed and compared with the exact derivatives
items.strategy: For $f(z)=\exp(z_0+z_1)$, $a=0$ and polyradius $(r,r)$, the supremum of $|f|$ on the distinguished boundary is $\exp(2r)$, so the estimate gives $|\partial^\alpha f(0)|\le\alpha!\exp(2r)r^{-|\alpha|}$. The exact value is $1$; minimise the bound over $r$ to see how close the estimate comes for $\alpha=(1,1)$, and record that the bound is finite for every $r>0$ while the exact value does not depend on $r$.

items.title: Componentwise holomorphy checked for an explicit map $\mathbb{C}^2\to\mathbb{C}^3$
items.strategy: Take $F(z)=(z_0z_1, z_0+z_1, \exp(z_0))$. Verify each component is holomorphic directly from the definition or the algebra proposition, hence $F$ is holomorphic by the componentwise theorem, and write out the $3\times2$ complex Jacobian $\bigl(\partial_{z_k}F_j\bigr)$ explicitly at a general point and at $0$. Confirm the differential is $\mathbb C$-linear by exhibiting it as a matrix product.

items.title: The complex Jacobian and its determinant for $(z_0z_1, z_0+z_1)$
items.strategy: For $F(z)=(z_0z_1,z_0+z_1)$ compute $J_{\mathbb C}F(z)$ and $\det J_{\mathbb C}F(z)=z_1-z_0$. Identify the set where it vanishes, the diagonal, and check the multiplicativity corollary on the composite of $F$ with the linear swap $(w_0,w_1)\mapsto(w_1,w_0)$, whose Jacobian determinant is $-1$.

items.title: A function whose modulus attains its maximum only on the distinguished boundary of a bidisc
items.strategy: Take $f(z)=z_0z_1$ on the closed unit bidisc. Then $|f|\le1$ with equality exactly when $|z_0|=|z_1|=1$, that is exactly on the distinguished boundary. Exhibit a point of the topological boundary, say $(1,0)$, where $|f|=0$, so the topological boundary carries no information about the maximum. This is the concrete content of the distinguished-boundary corollary.

items.title: A nonzero holomorphic function on $\mathbb{C}^2$ whose zero set is an unbounded hyperplane
items.strategy: Refute: a holomorphic function on a domain in $\mathbb C^m$ that is not identically zero has isolated zeros. Witness: $f(z)=z_0$ on $\mathbb C^2$, holomorphic and not identically zero, with zero set $\{0\}\times\mathbb C$. Verify the zero set is unbounded and that no point of it is isolated in it, by exhibiting nearby zeros. Record that in one variable the corresponding claim is a published theorem, so the failure is a genuine several-variable phenomenon and not an oversight.

items.title: A holomorphic function on a domain in $\mathbb{C}^2$ vanishing on a set with an accumulation point vanishes identically
items.strategy: The claim is false, and it is exactly the one-variable identity theorem carried over without change. Refute with $f(z)=z_0$ on $\mathbb C^2$: its zero set is the hyperplane $z_0=0$, every point of which is an accumulation point of the zero set, and $f$ is not identically zero. Explain in the refutation which step of a one-variable proof breaks, namely that a zero of a nonzero holomorphic function of one variable has a finite order and an isolated zero, and that no such local factorisation is available here.

items.title: A bounded function of two real variables whose every coordinate slice is real analytic is continuous
items.strategy:
The claim is FALSE, and it is the real-variable analogue of thm-locally-bounded-separate-holomorphy — which is exactly why the several-variable holomorphic theorem is not a formality. Refute with the witness $f(x,y)=xy/(x^2+y^2)$ off the origin, $f(0,0)=0$, and prove ALL THREE of its properties here; this item is self-contained and cites no counterexample from another page. Bounded: $2|xy|\le x^2+y^2$ gives $|f|\le 1/2$ everywhere, and at the origin $f=0$. Every slice is real analytic on all of $\mathbb R$: for fixed $b
e0$ the slice $x\mapsto bx/(x^2+b^2)$ is a quotient of polynomials whose denominator never vanishes, and polynomials are real analytic as finite sums of products of constants and the identity, so the published closure theorem applies; for $b=0$ the slice is identically $0$, since $f(x,0)=0$ for $x
e0$ and $f(0,0)=0$. The same holds in the other variable by the symmetry $f(x,y)=f(y,x)$. Discontinuity at the origin is proved HERE in one line and not imported: along $y=x$ with $x
e0$ the value is $1/2$, which does not tend to $f(0,0)=0$, so $f$ is not continuous at the origin by def-metric-continuity. The published `cex-partial-derivatives-without-continuity` on `the-total-derivative-examples` states the discontinuity for the same function; name it in prose WITHOUT a wikilink and WITHOUT a deps edge — it lives on a B page, B pages are leaves, and validate-plan rejects the citation outright (error `b-leaf`). Say in the refutation which hypothesis of the holomorphic theorem has no real analogue: a one-variable bound on $f$ gives no bound on the slice derivative in the real case, whereas the Cauchy inequality supplies exactly that bound in the complex case, uniformly in the remaining coordinates.

items.title: Why local boundedness gives joint continuity here and nothing like it holds in the real case
items.strategy: Prose, justifying the hypotheses of the locally bounded theorem. State the real contrast concretely: the function that is $x_0x_1/(x_0^2+x_1^2)$ off the origin and $0$ at it is bounded and has a real-analytic slice in each coordinate through every point — the slice through the origin being identically zero — yet is not jointly continuous. Cite the false statement on this page, which carries the whole refutation including the discontinuity; do NOT cite the published `cex-partial-derivatives-without-continuity`, which is homed on the B page `the-total-derivative-examples` and is therefore not a legal deps target (validate-plan `b-leaf`). It may be named in prose without a wikilink. Then explain what makes the holomorphic case different: the one-variable Cauchy inequality converts a bound on the function into a bound on each slice derivative that is uniform in the remaining coordinates, and no real-variable hypothesis supplies such a bound.

pages.title: The Hartogs Phenomena

items.title: Holomorphic extension and domains of holomorphy in several variables
The Hartogs figure H(r,s) and its bidisc hull
Laurent coefficients on Hartogs slices depend holomorphically on the remaining variables
items.strategy: Fix an annular circle in the distinguished variable. Cauchy's coefficient formula expresses each Laurent coefficient as a contour integral whose integrand is jointly continuous and holomorphic in the parameter variables, so the parameter-integral theorem makes the coefficient holomorphic in the remaining coordinates.

items.title: Negative Laurent coefficients vanish on a Hartogs figure
items.strategy: On the thin cylinder of the Hartogs figure each slice is actually holomorphic through the inner disc, so its negative Laurent coefficients vanish there. The previous lemma makes those coefficients holomorphic in the other variable, and the identity theorem propagates the vanishing across the whole parameter domain.

items.title: A holomorphic function on a Hartogs figure extends to the full bidisc
items.strategy: Expand on the annular slices in the distinguished variable. The negative coefficients vanish by the previous lemma, so the remaining nonnegative series defines a holomorphic function on the whole bidisc; equivalently one may write the same extension by a fixed-circle Cauchy integral and use the identity theorem on the overlap.

items.title: A domain containing a Hartogs figure but not its hull is not a domain of holomorphy
items.strategy: If a domain contains the Hartogs figure and omits a point of its bidisc hull, then every holomorphic function on the smaller domain extends across that omitted point inside a neighborhood. This contradicts the page's fixed simultaneous-extension definition of domain of holomorphy.

items.title: An isolated puncture is removable in complex dimension at least two
items.strategy: Work in a polydisc around the puncture and fix all but one variable. Cauchy's formula on a circle in the remaining variable defines a candidate extension that is holomorphic in the parameter variables, agrees with the original function on a punctured overlap, and therefore extends uniquely across the point by the identity theorem.

items.title: Holomorphic functions of several variables have no isolated singularities
items.strategy: A singularity at an isolated deleted point would contradict the puncture-removability theorem.

items.title: A locally bounded punctured slice has a holomorphic parameter extension
items.strategy: For fixed parameter values, the one-variable slice across the missing coordinate point is bounded and hence removable. Use a Cauchy integral on a fixed circle to represent the extended value and the parameter-integral theorem to show that the extension varies holomorphically with the remaining coordinates.

items.title: A locally bounded holomorphic function extends across a coordinate hyperplane
items.strategy: Apply the preceding slicewise extension lemma near each point of the missing hyperplane. The local extensions agree with the original function off the hyperplane, so the identity theorem glues them into a unique holomorphic extension.

items.title: Separate holomorphy forces local boundedness on smaller polydiscs
items.strategy: On a closed polydisc, use Baire category in the real parameter cube to find a nontrivial subpolydisc on which the function is bounded in one variable uniformly over the others. Expand in the remaining variables by Cauchy's formula; the logarithms of the coefficient moduli are subharmonic in the last variable, and a Hartogs-lemma/Fatou argument upgrades the subpolydisc bound to a bound on every smaller polydisc.

items.title: Separate holomorphy implies joint holomorphy in finite dimensions
items.strategy: Combine the local-boundedness lemma with the already established theorem that a locally bounded separately holomorphic function is jointly holomorphic.

items.title: Hartogs figures give local extension across polydisc shells
items.strategy: Near a boundary point of a compact hole, choose product coordinates so that a small neighborhood outside the hole contains a Hartogs figure while the local hull reaches farther inward. Apply the Hartogs-figure extension theorem in these coordinates and transport the extension back.

items.title: Local Hartogs extensions propagate along chains and glue uniquely
items.strategy: Extend across one shell at a time along a finite chain of overlapping neighborhoods. Uniqueness on nonempty overlaps follows from the identity theorem, so the local extensions are independent of the chosen chain and glue to a single holomorphic continuation.

items.title: Hartogs extension across a connected compact hole
items.strategy: Cover the compact hole by finitely many local shell neighborhoods. Starting from the given function on the connected exterior, use propagation across the finite chain and gluing uniqueness to extend holomorphically across every shell and hence across the whole compact set.

items.title: FALSE: every holomorphic function on a punctured several-variable domain is unbounded near the puncture
items.strategy: Refute by the puncture-removability theorem: bounded holomorphic functions near the deleted point extend, and even the coordinate functions restricted to a punctured polydisc stay bounded and extend.

items.title: FALSE: isolated singularities in several variables can be poles or essential
items.strategy: The several-variable puncture theorem collapses the one-variable trichotomy at a deleted point: an isolated deleted point is always removable.

items.title: FALSE: every domain in C^2 is a domain of holomorphy
items.strategy: Use a domain that contains a Hartogs figure but not its hull, or equivalently the bidisc minus the origin. The Hartogs figure corollary shows that such a domain admits extension across the missing point.

items.title: FALSE: separate holomorphy can fail to imply local boundedness
items.strategy: The local-boundedness lemma is exactly the contrary statement. A false claim here would collapse Hartogs's theorem back to the weaker continuous or bounded Osgood setting.

pages.title: The Hartogs Phenomena — Examples

items.title: The Hartogs figure in (|z1|, |z2|) coordinates
items.strategy: Describe the thin cylinder and thick shell pieces explicitly and identify the missing bidisc core that the extension theorem fills.

items.title: The function 1 / (1 - z1 z2) extends holomorphically from a Hartogs figure
items.strategy: The function is holomorphic on the whole bidisc because |z1 z2| < 1 there, so restricting it to a Hartogs figure gives a concrete example whose extension theorem recovers the obvious global formula.

items.title: A holomorphic function on the punctured bidisc extends across the origin
items.strategy: Use f(z1,z2) = z1 / (1 - z1 z2) on the punctured bidisc. The extension across the origin is manifest, illustrating the puncture theorem with a nonconstant example.

items.title: The bidisc minus the origin is not a domain of holomorphy
items.strategy: Every holomorphic function on the punctured bidisc extends to the full bidisc, so the missing origin cannot support the nonextendability demanded by the definition of domain of holomorphy.

items.title: The one-variable function 1 / z does not extend across the origin
items.strategy: Its Laurent series has a nonzero principal part and the singularity is a simple pole, so the several-variable puncture theorem genuinely needs complex dimension at least two.

items.title: C^2 minus a complex line is a domain of holomorphy
items.strategy: On Omega = {z1 != 0}, the holomorphic function 1 / z1 has no extension across the missing hyperplane. This shows that hypersurface holes behave differently from point or compact holes.

pages.title: The Holomorphic Inverse Function Theorem and Weierstrass Preparation

items.title: Biholomorphic maps between open sets in $\mathbb{C}^m$
The real Jacobian determinant of a complex-linear automorphism is the squared modulus of its complex determinant
items.strategy: Write the complex matrix as $A=B+iC$, so the underlying real matrix is the block matrix $\begin{psmallmatrix}B&-C\\ C&B\end{psmallmatrix}$. Conjugate it over $\mathbb C$ by the fixed change-of-basis matrix that sends $(x,y)$ to $(z,\bar z)$, obtain the block-triangular matrix $\operatorname{diag}(A,\overline A)$, and compare determinants.

items.title: The holomorphic inverse function theorem in several complex variables
items.strategy: View the holomorphic map as a $C^1$ map on $\mathbb R^{2m}$. The determinant lemma turns an invertible complex Jacobian into an invertible real Jacobian, so the real inverse function theorem gives a local $C^1$ inverse. Differentiate the inverse identities and use the complex chain rule to show that the inverse differential is complex-linear, hence the inverse is holomorphic.

items.title: The holomorphic implicit function theorem
items.strategy: Apply the holomorphic inverse theorem to the block map $H(z,w)=(z,f(z,w))$. Its complex Jacobian is block upper triangular with the dependent-variable Jacobian on the diagonal, so it is invertible at the base point. The inverse has the form $(z,\psi(z,\eta))$, and restricting to $\eta=0$ gives the holomorphic graph of the zero set.

items.title: The holomorphic constant-rank theorem
items.strategy: Apply the real constant-rank normal form to the underlying $C^1$ map to obtain smooth source and target coordinates in which the map is $(u,v)\mapsto(u,0)$. Then express those coordinate changes as the inverse and graph maps singled out by the holomorphic inverse and implicit function theorems for the chosen nonzero minor, upgrading the smooth normal form to a holomorphic one without assuming an unproved smooth-to-holomorphic result.

items.title: The ring of holomorphic germs at $0$ and its maximal ideal
A germ is a unit exactly when its value at $0$ is nonzero, so $\mathcal O_{m,0}$ is local
items.strategy: If a germ has nonzero value at $0$, continuity gives a smaller neighborhood on which a representative never vanishes, and the holomorphic-algebra proposition makes its reciprocal holomorphic there. If the germ vanishes at $0$, every representative does too, so no product with another germ can equal $1$ at the base point.

items.title: Regular holomorphic germs in the last variable
Weierstrass polynomials in the last variable
After a linear coordinate change, every nonzero germ is regular in the last variable
items.strategy: Expand the germ as a power series and take its first nonzero homogeneous part. Choose a vector on which that homogeneous polynomial does not vanish, then send the last coordinate axis to that vector by an invertible complex-linear change of coordinates.

items.title: Nearby slices of a regular germ have the same zero count
items.strategy: Choose a small circle on the last axis containing exactly the order-$d$ zero of the central slice and no boundary zero. Uniform continuity of the germ on the product torus makes the nearby slices uniformly close on that circle, and Rouché preserves the zero count inside the circle.

items.title: The power sums of the slice zeros vary holomorphically
items.strategy: On the fixed circle from the zero-count lemma, the integrand $\zeta^k\partial_{z_m}f/f$ is jointly continuous and holomorphic in the parameter variables. The contour-parameter integral theorem therefore makes the power sums holomorphic, and the argument principle identifies the integral with the sum of the slice zeros counted with multiplicity.

items.title: Finite Newton recurrences for the slice zeros
items.strategy: Write the monic polynomial with roots $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_d$, differentiate its logarithm, and compare coefficients. The resulting triangular system expresses each elementary symmetric coefficient in terms of the earlier power sums.

items.title: Weierstrass preparation theorem
items.strategy: Use the slice-zero count to keep exactly $d$ zeros inside a fixed circle for nearby parameters. The power sums of those zeros are holomorphic, Newton recurrences turn them into holomorphic coefficients, and the resulting monic polynomial with those roots differs from the original germ by a nowhere-vanishing holomorphic factor.

items.title: Uniqueness in Weierstrass preparation
items.strategy: If $f=uW=vP$ with both $W$ and $P$ monic Weierstrass polynomials of the same degree, then $W/P=v/u$ is holomorphic and nonvanishing. Restrict to the last coordinate axis to see that the quotient is $1$ there, and compare coefficients in the monic identity to force $W=P$ and then $u=v$.

items.title: Weierstrass division theorem
items.strategy: Choose a polydisc on which the Weierstrass polynomial is holomorphic and monic in the last variable. Cauchy's formula on a circle surrounding the slice zeros gives explicit integral formulas for the quotient and the remainder coefficients, and uniqueness reduces slice by slice to one-variable monic division.

items.title: Noetherian commutative rings and modules
Finite modules over Noetherian rings are Noetherian
items.strategy: Present a finitely generated module as a quotient of a finite free module. A finite direct sum of copies of a Noetherian ring is Noetherian by the submodule definition, and quotients preserve the condition.

items.title: A quotient by a Weierstrass polynomial is a finite module over the smaller germ ring
items.strategy: Use the division theorem to represent each class modulo $(W)$ by a unique remainder $a_0+a_1z_m+\cdots+a_{d-1}z_m^{d-1}$. Those remainders identify the quotient with a free module of rank $d$ over the smaller germ ring.

items.title: The ring of holomorphic germs is Noetherian
items.strategy: Induct on the dimension. For a nonzero proper ideal, choose a nonzero element, change coordinates to make it regular, and replace it by its Weierstrass polynomial in the ideal. Remainders modulo that polynomial form a submodule of a finite module over the smaller germ ring, so finitely many remainders together with the polynomial generate the ideal.

items.title: Noetherian domains are atomic
items.strategy: A Noetherian domain satisfies the ascending chain condition on principal ideals. If a nonzero nonunit failed to factor into irreducibles, repeatedly splitting off a nonunit nonirreducible factor would create a strictly increasing chain of principal ideals, contradiction.

items.title: Gauss lemma over a UFD
items.strategy: Factor out the content of each polynomial using unique factorization in the coefficient ring. Reduce primitive products modulo an irreducible divisor to prove they stay primitive, then clear denominators in a factorization over the fraction field to recover a factorization by primitive polynomials over the original ring.

items.title: Prepared factorizations correspond to germ factorizations
items.strategy: If a prepared polynomial factors in the polynomial subring, multiplying by the preparation unit gives a factorization of the germ. Conversely, prepare each factor of a germ factorization; uniqueness of preparation forces the prepared polynomial of the product to equal the product of the prepared factors, so irreducibility is detected in the polynomial subring.

items.title: The ring of holomorphic germs is a UFD
items.strategy: Use the Noetherian-domain lemma to obtain factorization once irreducibility can be promoted to primality. After a coordinate change and preparation, factor the prepared polynomial in the smaller polynomial ring, apply the UFD form of Gauss's lemma there, and transfer irreducibility and uniqueness back to the germ ring by the prepared-factorization correspondence.

items.title: A nonzero holomorphic hypersurface in complex dimension at least two has no isolated points
items.strategy: Near any zero of a nonzero germ, either the germ vanishes identically on a neighborhood or a coordinate change makes it regular in the last variable of positive order. Nearby parameter values then produce slice zeros inside the fixed circle, so every neighborhood contains zeros other than the original one.

items.title: Riemann extension across a holomorphic hypersurface zero set
items.strategy: Near a point of $Z(g)$, use preparation to write $g=uW$ with $W$ Weierstrass. For each nearby parameter value the complement of the finite slice zero set $W(z',\cdot)=0$ is a one-variable punctured domain on which the bounded holomorphic function extends across each missing point. The slice extensions are separately holomorphic and locally bounded, hence jointly holomorphic, and the zero-set theorem gives uniqueness on overlaps.

items.title: A locally bounded meromorphic quotient has no genuine pole
items.strategy: Off the zero set of the denominator, the several-variable holomorphic algebra rules make the quotient holomorphic. Local boundedness near that zero set therefore brings the hypersurface extension theorem into play and produces a holomorphic continuation.

pages.title: The Holomorphic Inverse Function Theorem and Weierstrass Preparation — Examples

items.title: $z_1^2-z_2$ prepares to the Weierstrass polynomial $z_2-z_1^2$
items.strategy: Apply the preparation theorem directly to $f(z_1,z_2)=z_1^2-z_2$. The unit is the constant $-1$, so the prepared factor is exactly the monic polynomial in $z_2$ with the same zero set.

items.title: $z_1z_2$ is not regular in $z_2$ at the origin
items.strategy: Fix $z_1=0$. Every slice value $f(0,z_2)$ vanishes identically, so the last-variable restriction has no finite order of vanishing and the germ is not regular in $z_2$.

items.title: A linear shear makes $z_1z_2$ regular in $z_2$
items.strategy: Replace $z_1$ by $z_1+z_2$. Then $z_1z_2$ becomes $(z_1+z_2)z_2=z_1z_2+z_2^2$, whose last-variable restriction at $z_1=0$ is $z_2^2$, so the transformed germ is regular of order $2$ in $z_2$.

items.title: Dividing $z_1$ by the Weierstrass polynomial $z_2^2-z_1$
items.strategy: Take $W(z_1,z_2)=z_2^2-z_1$. Then $z_1=(-1)W+z_2^2$, so the quotient is $-1$ and the remainder is the unique degree-$<2$ remainder.

items.title: Near $(0,1)$, the equation $z_1^2+z_2^2=1$ is a holomorphic graph
items.strategy: Apply the holomorphic implicit function theorem to $f(z_1,z_2)=z_1^2+z_2^2-1$ at $(0,1)$. The derivative in $z_2$ is $2\neq0$, so near that point the zero set is the graph of a unique holomorphic function $z_2=\varphi(z_1)$.

items.title: The map $(z_1,z_2)\mapsto(e^{z_1},z_2)$ has invertible complex Jacobian everywhere and is not injective
items.strategy: The complex Jacobian is $\operatorname{diag}(e^{z_1},1)$, and the complex exponential is never zero. But $e^{z_1+2\pi i}=e^{z_1}$, so $(z_1,z_2)$ and $(z_1+2\pi i,z_2)$ have the same image.

items.title: FALSE: an everywhere-invertible complex Jacobian forces global injectivity
items.strategy: Use the exponential counterexample immediately above. Its complex Jacobian is invertible at every point, but the map identifies $(z_1,z_2)$ with $(z_1+2\pi i,z_2)$.

items.title: FALSE: the holomorphic inverse function theorem is global
items.strategy: The theorem is irreducibly local. The exponential counterexample has invertible complex Jacobian everywhere, so each point has a biholomorphic neighborhood, but the whole map is still not globally one-to-one.

items.title: FALSE: every nonzero germ is regular in the last variable without a coordinate change
items.strategy: Use $f(z_1,z_2)=z_1z_2$. The last-variable restriction at $z_1=0$ is identically zero, so the germ is not regular in $z_2$ even though an arbitrarily small shear makes it regular.

items.title: FALSE: Weierstrass preparation is unique without requiring the nonpolynomial factor to be a unit
items.strategy: Take $f(z_1,z_2)=z_2^2$. Then $f=1\cdot z_2^2$ is a genuine preparation, but also $f=z_2\cdot z_2$ if one drops the unit condition on the first factor. Both polynomial factors are Weierstrass, so uniqueness fails without the unit normalization.

items.title: FALSE: a nonconstant scalar holomorphic function in dimension at least two can have an isolated zero
items.strategy: The A-page zero-set theorem rules this out completely: every zero of a nonzero scalar holomorphic function in complex dimension at least two is a limit point of other zeros.

pages.title: Domains of Holomorphy, Plurisubharmonicity and Pseudoconvexity

items.title: Holomorphic hulls and holomorphic convexity
Basic properties of the holomorphic hull
items.strategy: Check directly from the defining inequality that K sits inside its hull, that the hull is closed, and that taking the hull twice does not enlarge it. Coordinate projections show boundedness when the set is compact.

items.title: The equal-radius polydisc boundary function
Cauchy estimates propagate from a compact set to its hull
items.strategy: Fix a polydisc radius valid over the compact set, apply the several-variable Cauchy estimates there, and then view each derivative as a holomorphic function bounded on the hull by its bound on the original compact set.

items.title: Cartan-Thullen boundary-radius theorem
items.strategy: If a hull point were closer to the boundary than the original compact set, a polydisc centered there would leave the domain while the Cauchy estimates from the smaller radius neighborhood of K would still force holomorphic extension across that boundary point. That contradicts the domain-of-holomorphy hypothesis.

items.title: Cartan-Thullen theorem
items.strategy: The boundary-radius theorem gives the domain-of-holomorphy to holomorphic-convexity direction once compact hulls are known to stay away from the boundary. For the converse, use the standard compact exhaustion and diagonal separation argument that manufactures a function blowing up along any chosen boundary approach.

items.title: A compact convex set and an exterior point admit a complex-linear separator
items.strategy: Apply strict separation in the underlying real Euclidean space and then rewrite the resulting real-linear functional as the real part of a complex-linear functional on C^n.

items.title: Convex domains are holomorphically convex
items.strategy: Separate an exterior point from the convex hull of K by a complex-linear functional and exponentiate that separator. The resulting holomorphic function is larger at the exterior point than on K, so the point cannot lie in the holomorphic hull.

items.title: Convex domains are domains of holomorphy
items.strategy: Combine convexity of the domain with holomorphic convexity of compact hulls, then apply Cartan-Thullen.

items.title: Plurisubharmonic functions
Affine reparametrization does not change the line-test definition
items.strategy: Compose the candidate function with a nonconstant affine map of one complex variable. The subharmonic line condition is preserved because such reparametrizations are holomorphic and locally biholomorphic away from degenerate cases.

items.title: The Levi form and strict plurisubharmonicity
The C^2 Levi criterion for plurisubharmonicity
items.strategy: Restrict a C^2 function to each affine complex line and compare its one-variable Laplacian with the Hermitian form built from the complex Hessian. The plane C^2 criterion for subharmonicity then becomes exactly semipositivity of the Levi form.

items.title: Decreasing limits of plurisubharmonic functions
items.strategy: Apply the line test pointwise to the decreasing sequence. On each complex line, the limit is subharmonic or identically minus infinity by the one-variable decreasing-limit theorem.

items.title: Holomorphic pullbacks of C^2 plurisubharmonic functions are plurisubharmonic
items.strategy: Approximate the target plurisubharmonic function from above by smooth plurisubharmonic functions on slightly smaller neighborhoods, pull each approximation back by the holomorphic map using the chain rule and the C^2 Levi criterion, and then pass to the limit with the decreasing-limit theorem.

items.title: Basic stability operations for plurisubharmonic functions
items.strategy: Check the line test after applying a nonnegative sum, a finite maximum, or a convex increasing scalar function. Each operation reduces to the corresponding one-variable closure property for subharmonic functions.

items.title: Upper envelopes of locally upper-bounded plurisubharmonic families
items.strategy: Take the upper-semicontinuous regularization of the pointwise supremum and test on each affine complex line. The one-variable upper-envelope theorem then supplies subharmonicity line by line.

items.title: Maximum principle for plurisubharmonic functions
items.strategy: Restrict to every affine complex line through a finite local maximum point. Each restriction is a one-variable subharmonic function with a local maximum, so it is constant near the center; this makes the original function locally constant, and connectedness propagates that constancy across the whole component.

items.title: The logarithm of the modulus of a holomorphic function is plurisubharmonic
items.strategy: Restrict to any affine complex line. The restriction becomes the one-variable function log|f|, which is subharmonic, so the line test gives plurisubharmonicity with the standard minus-infinity convention on the zero set.

items.title: Plurisubharmonic exhaustions and Hartogs pseudoconvexity
Hartogs pseudoconvexity yields a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion
items.strategy: Use the boundary-distance function to build a continuous exhaustion in one direction, and in the other direction combine the exhaustion with standard convex blow-up functions so that the domain carries the same plurisubharmonic boundary barrier data.

items.title: Levi pseudoconvex domains
Levi pseudoconvexity does not depend on the defining function
items.strategy: Replace a defining function rho by h rho with h positive. On complex tangent vectors the extra first-derivative terms vanish on the boundary, so the Levi form is scaled by h and keeps the same sign.

items.title: Continuous families of analytic discs
Continuity principle for domains of holomorphy
items.strategy: Assume a first analytic disc in the family leaves the domain while the boundary curves stay in one compact subset. A small Hartogs figure built from the first escaping disc would then force holomorphic extension past the domain, contradicting the domain-of-holomorphy hypothesis.

items.title: Domains of holomorphy are Hartogs pseudoconvex
items.strategy: Use the continuity principle to rule out analytic-disc families that would violate plurisubharmonicity of the negative logarithmic boundary-radius function. Hartogs figures then convert that disc-control statement into Hartogs pseudoconvexity.

items.title: Hartogs pseudoconvexity implies Levi pseudoconvexity for C^2 domains
items.strategy: One direction differentiates the boundary-distance model and applies the C^2 Levi criterion. The converse builds a local plurisubharmonic defining model from the boundary Levi condition and compares it with the negative logarithmic boundary-distance function.

pages.title: Domains of Holomorphy, Plurisubharmonicity and Pseudoconvexity — Examples

items.title: The bidisc is holomorphically convex
items.strategy: The bidisc is a convex domain, so the convex-domain theorem already gives holomorphic convexity. This example records the conclusion in the standard model domain.

items.title: The unit ball is Levi pseudoconvex
items.strategy: Take the defining function |z|^2-1 and compute its Levi form. The complex Hessian is the identity Hermitian form, so the tangential Levi form is nonnegative everywhere on the boundary.

items.title: A convex domain is a domain of holomorphy
items.strategy: Apply the convex-domain corollary to a concrete half-space or ball. The example exists to make the geometric route tangible before the later nonconvex counterexamples.

items.title: The holomorphic hull of a circle in C is the filled disc
items.strategy: Identify the hull of the unit circle inside C by the maximum principle: a holomorphic function on the disc is bounded on the interior by its boundary supremum. Hence every interior point lies in the hull and no exterior point does.

items.title: The holomorphic hull of a product torus in the bidisc is the closed polydisc it bounds
items.strategy: Apply the one-variable maximum principle in each coordinate and use the product structure of the distinguished boundary. The torus forces bounds on every coordinate disc and therefore on the whole polydisc.

items.title: Minus log boundary distance is plurisubharmonic on a half-space
items.strategy: For a half-space the equal-radius boundary-distance function is an affine multiple of the real part of one coordinate, so its negative logarithm is a convex increasing function of a harmonic coordinate and hence plurisubharmonic.

items.title: The bidisc minus the origin is not holomorphically convex
items.strategy: A small product torus around the origin has hull reaching the missing point, and every holomorphic function extends across that puncture by Hartogs. This one domain witnesses failure of domain of holomorphy and of holomorphic convexity.

items.title: A domain of holomorphy need not be convex
items.strategy: Take the hypersurface complement U = C^2 \ {z_1 z_2 = 1}. The function 1/(z_1 z_2-1) is holomorphic on U and singular along the removed hypersurface, while the midpoint of (2,0) and (0,2) lies on the missing set, so U is not convex.

items.title: FALSE: every domain in C^n is a domain of holomorphy
items.strategy: The punctured bidisc in dimension two is the standard counterexample: Hartogs extension fills in the missing point. This records the several-variable failure point while the one-variable contrast has been rescoped to the later Weierstrass and Mittag-Leffler supplier pages.

items.title: FALSE: the union of two domains of holomorphy is always a domain of holomorphy
items.strategy: Two overlapping domains can fill in a Hartogs-type obstruction even when each piece separately carries nonextendable holomorphic functions. The statement is therefore too optimistic without extra hypotheses.
