items.title: Under the ultrafilter lemma, an ultrafilter algebra maps each ultrafilter to its unique limit
items.strategy: The defining open-set condition makes $\xi(\mathcal U)$ a limit of $\mathcal U$. If $x$ is another limit, the closure formula places $x$ in $\xi[\widehat A]$ for every $A\in\mathcal U$. Extend the resulting finite-intersection family on $\beta X$ to an ultrafilter of ultrafilters; the two algebra laws force $x=\xi(\mathcal U)$. Include principal ultrafilters and the empty underlying set.

items.title: Under the ultrafilter lemma, every ultrafilter algebra determines a compact Hausdorff topology
items.strategy: Use the preceding topology and unique-limit lemmas. Every ultrafilter converges, so the published ultrafilter compactness characterization gives compactness under the stated ultrafilter-lemma assumption. If two distinct points could not be separated, their two neighbourhood filters would have the finite-intersection property; an ultrafilter extension would converge to both, contradicting uniqueness. Thus the topology is Hausdorff.

items.title: Under the ultrafilter lemma, compact Hausdorff spaces and ultrafilter algebras are recovered by the two limit constructions
items.strategy: Starting with an algebra, the unique-limit lemma says the limit map of its induced topology is exactly its structure map. Starting with a compact Hausdorff space, characterize closed sets by stability under limits of ultrafilters containing them; this recovers the original topology. The continuous-map lemma gives one morphism direction, and the open-set definition plus preservation of algebra limits gives the converse. These object and morphism identities make the two functors inverse.

items.title: Under the ultrafilter lemma, compact Hausdorff spaces are monadic over sets
items.strategy: The inverse-constructions theorem identifies $\mathbf{CompHaus}$ over $\mathbf{Set}$ with the Eilenberg–Moore category of the ultrafilter monad. Transport the free–forgetful Eilenberg–Moore adjunction across this identification. The induced monad is the published ultrafilter monad, and the comparison is an equivalence; no separate Stone–Čech construction or dependent-choice hypothesis is imported.

items.title: A continuous bijection of compact Hausdorff spaces is a homeomorphism, by conservativity
items.strategy: Under the compact-Hausdorff monadicity hypothesis, the underlying-set functor is conservative. A continuous bijection has an isomorphism as its underlying function, so it is an isomorphism in $\mathbf{CompHaus}$; its inverse is continuous and it is a homeomorphism. The authored Remark cross-links the existing direct compact-to-Hausdorff proof.

items.title: Torsion-free abelian groups give a conservative right adjoint that is not monadic
items.strategy: Compose the free-abelian-group adjunction from sets with the inclusion of torsion-free abelian groups. Free abelian groups are torsion-free, so the induced monad is canonically isomorphic to the usual free-abelian-group monad, but its comparison misses every abelian group with nonzero torsion, such as $\mathbb Z/2$. The underlying-set functor is conservative because a bijective group homomorphism is an isomorphism.

items.title: FALSE: ordinary Beck creation characterizes strict monadicity
items.strategy: Build the category whose objects are tagged sets $(X,i)$ with $i\in\{0,1\}$ and whose morphisms are all functions of underlying sets. The forgetful functor to $\mathbf{Set}$ has a left adjoint choosing tag zero and induces the identity monad. Its comparison is an equivalence but not an isomorphism, because two distinct tagged objects have the same image. Thus ordinary creation yields monadicity, while strict creation is the extra hypothesis for strict monadicity.

items.title: FALSE: every conservative right adjoint is monadic
items.strategy: Use the preceding torsion-free-abelian-group counterexample. It has a left adjoint and reflects isomorphisms, but its comparison with algebras for the induced free-abelian-group monad is not essentially surjective.

items.title: FALSE: every $U$-split pair is split in the domain
items.strategy: Use the canonical presentation of an algebra. Its underlying fork is split by the unit components, so the parallel pair is $U^T$-split. For the free-monoid monad on a nontrivial monoid, the canonical unit section is not an algebra homomorphism, so that base splitting is not a splitting in the algebra category.

items.title: FALSE: the underlying-set functor from topological spaces is monadic
items.strategy: A monadic functor is conservative. The identity from a two-point discrete space to the same set with the Sierpiński topology is a continuous bijection and hence an underlying-set isomorphism, but it is not a homeomorphism and therefore not an isomorphism in $\mathbf{Top}$. Thus the underlying-set functor is not conservative and cannot be monadic.

pages.title: Monadicity and Becks Theorem — Examples

items.title: A split coequalizer on a two-element set
items.strategy: Take $X=Y=\{0,1\}$, let $g=t=1_Y$, let $f$ be constant at $0$, and let $h:Y\to\{*\}$ be the unique map with section $s(*)=0$. Verify all four splitting equations and then check the coequalizer universal property directly. This is a finite exhaustive witness.

items.title: The canonical free-algebra presentation of a two-element idempotent monoid
items.strategy: For $M=\{1,e\}$ with $e^2=e$, write the two maps from words of words in $M$ to words in $M$: evaluation of each inner word and concatenation. Their coequalizer evaluates a word in $M$ to its product. Verify on arbitrary finite words, including the empty word, and identify the unit splittings on underlying sets.

items.title: The comparison functor for the free-group adjunction
items.strategy: For a group $G$, compute the comparison object as the underlying set $UG$ with structure map evaluating a reduced word in $UG$ to its product in $G$. Check that group homomorphisms are exactly the algebra homomorphisms and illustrate the formula on the cyclic group of order two.

items.title: The Kleisli adjunction for the maybe monad is monadic but not strictly monadic
items.strategy: For the maybe monad $T(X)=X\amalg\{\bot\}$, identify its Kleisli category with sets and partial functions and its Eilenberg–Moore category with pointed sets. Adjoining and deleting a basepoint give quasi-inverse comparison functors, but the comparison is not bijective on objects under the fixed concrete encodings. Thus it is an equivalence and not an isomorphism.

items.title: A reflexive coequalizer of sets not preserved by $\mathbf{Set}(\mathbb N,-)$
items.strategy: Let $f=[\sigma,1]$ and $g=[1,1]:\mathbb N\amalg\mathbb N\rightrightarrows\mathbb N$, with common section the second coproduct injection; the unique map $\mathbb N\to1$ is their coequalizer. After applying $\mathbf{Set}(\mathbb N,-)$, each generating relation changes every coordinate by at most one, so any finite zigzag has a uniform coordinatewise bound. The zero sequence and identity sequence have unbounded difference and are not identified, although both map to the sole sequence in $1^{\mathbb N}$.

items.title: The ultrafilter algebra on a finite discrete space
items.strategy: For a finite set $X$, use the ultrafilter decision property to prove every ultrafilter is principal at a unique point. The limit map is therefore inverse to the principal-unit bijection and satisfies the algebra laws. Verify the empty set separately, where both $X$ and $\beta X$ are empty, and compute the two-point case explicitly.

items.title: $\beta\mathbb N$ as the free ultrafilter algebra
items.strategy: The free algebra on $\mathbb N$ for the ultrafilter monad has carrier $\beta\mathbb N$ and structure map $\mu_{\mathbb N}:\beta\beta\mathbb N\to\beta\mathbb N$. Expand the membership formula for flattening, check both algebra laws from the monad laws, and distinguish principal from free ultrafilters only under the explicitly stated ultrafilter-lemma hypothesis.

pages.title: Ends Coends and Weighted Limits

items.title: Dinatural transformation between functors on $\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal C$
Composing a dinatural transformation with a natural transformation on either side gives a dinatural transformation
items.strategy: Let $\sigma:P'\Rightarrow P$ and $\tau:Q\Rightarrow Q'$ be natural and $\alpha:P\to Q$ dinatural. For $\gamma_c:=\alpha_c\sigma_{c,c}$ rewrite each side of the hexagon at $f:c\to c'$ using naturality of $\sigma$ at the two product-category morphisms $(f,1_c):(c',c)\to(c,c)$ and $(1_{c'},f):(c',c)\to(c',c')$; both sides then reduce to the two sides of $\alpha$'s hexagon precomposed with $\sigma_{c',c}$. The post-composition case uses naturality of $\tau$ at $(1_c,f)$ and $(f,1_{c'})$ in the same way.

items.title: Dinatural transformations do not compose in general
items.strategy: Constructive. Take $\mathcal C$ to be the walking arrow $0\xrightarrow{u}1$ and $\mathcal D=\mathbf{Set}$. A functor $\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal C\to\mathbf{Set}$ is four sets and four functions subject to one square. Choose $P$ with all four sets singletons; $Q$ with $Q(1,0)=\varnothing$, $Q(0,0)$, $Q(1,1)$ and $Q(0,1)$ singletons; and $R$ with $R(1,0)=\varnothing$, $R(0,0)=\{c\}$, $R(1,1)=\{d\}$ and $R(0,1)=\{y_1,y_2\}$ two-element, $R(1_0,u)(c)=y_1$, $R(u,1_1)(d)=y_2$. The empty set in the $(1,0)$ slot makes the required functor square vacuous for $Q$ and $R$, and makes every family $Q\to R$ dinatural; the singleton $Q(0,1)$ makes the chosen family $P\to Q$ dinatural; and the composite fails the hexagon at $u$ because its two legs land on $y_1\ne y_2$. Record explicitly that the empty and singleton slots are what make each check finite.

items.title: Wedges and cowedges, and the categories they form
The end and the coend of a functor $\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$
An end and a coend are unique up to a unique isomorphism compatible with every component
items.strategy: Direct. An end is a terminal object of the category of wedges and a coend an initial object of the category of cowedges, so the published uniqueness of terminal and initial objects applies verbatim; the compatibility clause is exactly the statement that the connecting isomorphism is a morphism of wedges, that is, commutes with every component.

items.title: A natural transformation of functors induces a unique morphism of their ends and of their coends
items.strategy: Direct. For $\eta:P\Rightarrow P'$ show that the family $\eta_{c,c}\circ\omega_c$ is a wedge from $\int_c P(c,c)$ to $P'$, using naturality of $\eta$ at $(1,f)$ and at $(f,1)$ together with the wedge condition for $\omega$; terminality then gives the unique induced arrow. Record functoriality (identity and composite) as separate numbered steps, since both follow only from uniqueness of the induced arrow.

items.title: The twisted arrow category and its projection to $\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal C$
The twisted arrow category is the category of elements of the hom-bifunctor
items.strategy: Direct. For locally small $\mathcal C$ the hom-bifunctor is a covariant functor $\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal C\to\mathbf{Set}$, so its category of elements has objects $((c,c'),f)$ with $f\in\mathcal C(c,c')$ and a morphism to $((d,d'),g)$ given by $(a,b)$ in the product category with $\mathcal C(a,b)(f)=g$, that is $bfa=g$. Match this against the twisted arrow definition object for object and morphism for morphism, and check that the projection functor is the category-of-elements projection. This is the item that keeps the page from silently re-minting a published construction.

items.title: An end is a limit over the twisted arrow category, and a coend is a colimit over its opposite
items.strategy: Direct, by matching universal properties. From a wedge $\omega$ build the cone with component at $f:c\to c'$ equal to $T(1_c,f)\omega_c=T(f,1_{c'})\omega_{c'}$, and check naturality against a twisted arrow morphism $(a,b)$; conversely restrict a cone to the identity arrows. Show the two constructions are mutually inverse and carry morphisms of wedges to morphisms of cones, so terminal objects correspond. For the coend clause state the reindexing explicitly: the colimit is over $\mathrm{Tw}(\mathcal C)^{\mathrm{op}}$ of the functor sending $f:c\to c'$ to $T(c',c)$, with the domain and codomain SWAPPED. Getting that swap backwards is the page's designated fatal error.

items.title: The end of a functor made mute in its contravariant variable is the ordinary limit of that functor
items.strategy: Direct. For $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ let $F'(c_1,c_2):=F(c_2)$ and check that $F'$ is a functor on $\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal C$. The wedge condition on a family $X\to F'(c,c)=F(c)$ then reads $F(f)\alpha_c=\alpha_{c'}$, which is exactly the published cone condition, and morphisms of wedges are morphisms of cones. Hence the two universal properties coincide. State the dual clause for coends and colimits. This is the item that says ends generalise limits rather than sitting beside them, so it cites the published cone and limit definitions and restates neither.

items.title: Ends exist over a small index category in a complete target, and coends in a cocomplete one
items.strategy: Direct. The objects of $\mathrm{Tw}(\mathcal C)$ are the morphisms of $\mathcal C$ and its morphisms form a subset of a product of two morphism sets, so $\mathrm{Tw}(\mathcal C)$ is small when $\mathcal C$ is; completeness then supplies the limit. Carry out the smallness count inline rather than asserting it.

items.title: An end is the equalizer of two products, and a coend the coequalizer of two coproducts
items.strategy: Direct from the wedge universal property, NOT by instantiating the published products-and-equalizers construction of a limit: the two index sets here are the objects of $\mathcal C$ and the morphisms of $\mathcal C$, which is not the indexing that construction uses on $\mathrm{Tw}(\mathcal C)$. Show that a morphism $X\to\prod_cT(c,c)$ equalises the two displayed maps exactly when its components form a wedge, then transport the universal property. State the existence hypothesis as: the two products and the equalizer exist (which small $\mathcal C$ plus completeness supplies), so no proper-class product is formed.

items.title: A set-valued coend is the disjoint union of the diagonal values modulo the dinaturality relation
items.strategy: Direct. Combine the coequalizer description with the published construction of colimits in $\mathbf{Set}$: the coend is $\coprod_cT(c,c)$ modulo the least equivalence relation identifying $T(f,1_{c'})(x)$ with $T(1_c,f)(x)$ for every $f:c\to c'$ and every $x\in T(c',c)$. Write the relation with its variance displayed and check the generating pairs lie in the two summands named, since this is where an index swap hides.

items.title: A module-valued coend is the direct sum of the diagonal values modulo the dinaturality submodule
items.strategy: Constructive, direct from the universal property rather than through a general cocompleteness theorem, because the published $R$-module cocompleteness asserts existence without exhibiting the coequalizer. Build $Q=\bigl(\bigoplus_cT(c,c)\bigr)/S$ with $S$ the submodule generated by $T(f,1_{c'})(x)-T(1_c,f)(x)$; verify the canonical family is a cowedge, then use the direct-sum and quotient universal properties to factor an arbitrary cowedge uniquely through $Q$. The $I=\varnothing$ case of the published direct sum makes the empty-index case explicit.

items.title: A functor preserving twisted-arrow limits preserves ends, and dually for coends
items.strategy: Direct. State the hypothesis at the exact strength the proof uses: $F$ preserves $\mathrm{Tw}(\mathcal C)$-limits. Then add the corollary form for small $\mathcal C$ and continuous $F$, since 'continuous' in this library means preservation of SMALL limits and $\mathrm{Tw}(\mathcal C)$ is small only when $\mathcal C$ is. Do not state a blanket 'continuous functors preserve all ends'.

items.title: A right adjoint preserves ends and a left adjoint preserves coends
items.strategy: Direct. The published theorem that a right adjoint preserves every limit that exists applies at the indexing category $\mathrm{Tw}(\mathcal C)$ with no size hypothesis, so this corollary carries none either.

items.title: The hom-functor turns a coend into an end and carries an end to an end
items.strategy: Direct. Apply the published statement that $\mathcal D(-,X)$ sends a colimit to a limit over the opposite index, at index $\mathrm{Tw}(\mathcal C)^{\mathrm{op}}$, and read the resulting limit back as an end through the twisted-arrow description. Quote the published corollary exactly: it gives $\mathcal D(\operatorname*{colim}D,X)\cong\lim_{\mathcal J^{\mathrm{op}}}\mathcal D(D(j),X)$, which is the direction needed, and separately gives continuity of $\mathcal D(X,-)$ for the second clause.

items.title: Ends and coends with parameters
A chosen family of ends is the object part of exactly one functor making the counit natural in the parameters
items.strategy: Direct, and stated in the data-supplied form the library uses for chosen limits: GIVEN a choice of end for each value of the parameter, there is exactly one functor structure on those chosen objects making every counit component natural in the parameter. Prove existence and uniqueness of the arrow map from terminality, then the two functor laws as separate steps. Do not state an unconditional 'the end is a functor', which would select an end for a proper class of parameters.

items.title: A family into a parametrised end is natural in the parameter exactly when its composite with the counit is
items.strategy: Direct, both directions separately. One direction is composition of a natural family with a natural counit; the other uses the uniqueness half of the end's universal property applied to the two candidate factorisations of the same wedge. This is the step Fubini spends.

items.title: A wedge on a product index category is exactly a family dinatural in each variable separately
items.strategy: Direct, both implications. Forwards, specialise the hexagon at $(f,1_d)$ and at $(1_c,g)$. Backwards, factor $T(1_c,f,1_d,g)$ as a composite of the two one-variable actions in either order and substitute the two separate hexagons; the four-variable functor's independent action in each slot is the only fact used and must be cited as such. Check the identity cases $f=1$, $g=1$ so the reader sees the reduction is not circular. The statement is about WEDGES, whose source is constant, and it must not be generalised in the text to arbitrary dinatural transformations between two varying functors: separate dinaturality does not give joint dinaturality there, and the constancy of the source is what the backward direction spends. Item 3 on this page is the standing evidence that dinaturality is fragile under exactly this kind of extension.

items.title: Fubini: an end over a product index category and the two iterated ends exist together and agree
items.strategy: Universal property, NOT the copower-and-adjoint route of Loregian's proof, which needs the target to have copowers that this statement does not assume. Hypotheses: a chosen family of inner ends in each of the two orders. Establish a bijection, natural in the test object, between wedges into the product-index functor and wedges into the parametrised inner end, by composing the separate-dinaturality lemma with the unique factorisation through each inner end. Terminal objects then correspond, so any one of the three ends exists iff the others do, with canonical isomorphisms. State the reindexing $\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal C\times\mathcal D^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal D\cong(\mathcal C\times\mathcal D)^{\mathrm{op}}\times(\mathcal C\times\mathcal D)$ explicitly as part of the setup. Dualise for coends. NO smallness hypothesis is used or claimed.

items.title: Iterated ends may be taken in either order
items.strategy: Direct. Both iterated ends are canonically isomorphic to the end over the product index category, so they are canonically isomorphic to each other; the hypotheses are exactly Fubini's two chosen families.

items.title: For a small source category, the set of natural transformations is an end of the hom-bifunctor of the values
items.strategy: Direct. For SMALL $\mathcal C$ and locally small $\mathcal D$ the set of natural transformations is a hom-set of the functor category by the published size proposition, so the claim is about a genuine set. Unwind the wedge condition on a family $Y\to\mathcal D(Fc,Gc)$: it says precisely that each element of $Y$ names a natural transformation. Then exhibit evaluation as the terminal wedge. Say explicitly which size hypothesis is used where, since this theorem is what makes the functor category's size hypothesis visible again.

items.title: The end of the hom-bifunctor is the commutative monoid of natural endomorphisms of the identity functor
items.strategy: Direct. Take $F=G=1_{\mathcal C}$ in the previous theorem for small $\mathcal C$. For the monoid clause, note that vertical and horizontal composition of natural endomorphisms of an identity functor share the identity transformation as unit and satisfy the interchange law, so the published Eckmann-Hilton theorem applies verbatim and gives one commutative operation. Keep the two operations named separately until Eckmann-Hilton identifies them.

items.title: The end of the function-set functor on a representable is evaluation
items.strategy: Direct. Both isomorphisms are the previous theorem taken at $\mathcal D=\mathbf{Set}$ with one argument a representable, followed by the published Yoneda bijection. Check the variance of the integrand in each of the two cases before writing the display: the first slot of the integrand carries the representable and is contravariant precisely because $\mathbf{Set}(-,X)$ reverses it.

items.title: The co-Yoneda isomorphisms: a set-valued functor is a coend against a representable
items.strategy: Direct, by a chain of natural bijections in a test set $Y$: the hom-functor turns the coend into an end; currying in $\mathbf{Set}$ moves the product across; the end is then a set of natural transformations; and the published Yoneda bijection evaluates it. Conclude with the published statement that representables detect isomorphism of objects, which is what upgrades a natural bijection of representables into an isomorphism of the represented objects. State all four isomorphisms, covariant and contravariant, and derive the two end-form ones from the previous item rather than repeating its proof. The library publishes ONLY the contravariant detection statement, $\mathcal C(-,a)\cong\mathcal C(-,b)\iff a\cong b$; the chain of bijections here is natural in a test object and so exhibits an isomorphism of COVARIANT representables. Apply the published corollary in $\mathbf{Set}^{\mathrm{op}}$ and say so in a numbered step. Do not cite it as though it read $\mathcal C(a,-)\cong\mathcal C(b,-)$.

items.title: The tensor product of a presheaf and a covariant set-valued functor
Set-weighted limits and colimits
A weighted limit and a weighted colimit are unique up to a unique compatible isomorphism
items.strategy: Direct. A weighted limit IS a representation, so the published uniqueness of representing objects applies once the counit cylinder is identified with the universal element. Make that identification a numbered step rather than an aside; it is the whole content.

items.title: A weighted limit of a set-valued diagram is the set of natural transformations from the weight
items.strategy: Direct. Take the test object to be a one-element set in the defining representation and use that a function out of a singleton is an element of the codomain; naturality in the test object is what makes this an equality of functors and not just of underlying sets.

items.title: The power and the copower of an object by a set
A power by a set is the product of that many copies and a copower is the coproduct
items.strategy: Direct, and it is the seam item: it says that the power minted here is the published product of a constant family, not a second notion. Compare the two universal properties, noting that a function $S\to\mathcal M(m,c)$ is exactly an $S$-indexed family of morphisms $m\to c$. Handle $S=\varnothing$ explicitly: the power is then terminal and the copower initial, which is the published convention for empty products and coproducts.

items.title: A weighted limit is an end of powers and a weighted colimit a coend of copowers
items.strategy: Direct, by a chain of bijections natural in the test object: natural transformations from the weight into $\mathcal M(m,F-)$ form an end of function sets; the power's defining bijection moves each function set inside the hom; and the hom-functor's preservation of ends pulls the end out. State the hypotheses as existence of the displayed powers or copowers and of the displayed end or coend, not as completeness of the target.

items.title: A weighted limit is an ordinary limit over the category of elements of the weight, and a weighted colimit an ordinary colimit over it
items.strategy: Direct, by an identity of data rather than by Kelly's density route: a cone with apex $m$ over the composite of the category-of-elements projection with the diagram is literally the same family as a natural transformation from the weight into $\mathcal M(m,F-)$, once a component at $(c,x)$ is read as the value at $x$ of the component at $c$. Write both compatibility conditions out and observe they are the same equation. State the weighted-colimit clause as a separate numbered part and prove it, do not leave it to the reader: for a weight $W:\mathcal J^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathbf{Set}$ the same identification reads a cocone under the composite of the category-of-elements projection with the diagram as a natural transformation from $W$ into $\mathcal M(F-,m)$, so $W\star F$ is the ordinary colimit over $\int W$. Riehl CHT (7.1.8) and (7.2.4) are the two clauses and the harvest rows for both name this item. No smallness and no choice are used; record that the category of elements of a $\mathbf{Set}$-valued weight on a small index category is small, since its objects are the disjoint union of the weight's values, because the existence corollary spends exactly that.

items.title: A limit weighted by a $\mathbf{Set}$-valued weight on a small index category exists in a complete target, and the weighted colimit in a cocomplete one
items.strategy: Direct, and it is the weighted half of the existence corollary the ends half already carries. For small $\mathcal J$ and $W:\mathcal J\to\mathbf{Set}$ the category of elements $\int W$ has as objects the disjoint union of the sets $W(j)$ and as morphisms a subset of a disjoint union of morphism sets of $\mathcal J$, so it is small; the previous theorem exhibits $\{W,F\}$ as an ordinary limit over it, and completeness of the target supplies that limit. Dually for $W\star F$ over $\int W$ with a cocomplete target. Carry out the smallness count inline rather than asserting it, exactly as the corresponding corollary for ends does. Say explicitly that this is sufficiency and not necessity: the definitions apply whenever the representing object exists, and an individual weighted limit over a large index category may exist.

items.title: A colimit of a set-valued functor is the set of connected components of its category of elements
items.strategy: Direct. The published construction of colimits in $\mathbf{Set}$ presents the colimit as the tagged union of the values modulo the least equivalence relation generated by the transition maps; the objects of the category of elements are exactly that tagged union and its morphisms are exactly the generating pairs, so the quotient is the set of connected components in the published finite-zigzag sense. Handle the empty index category: both sides are empty.

items.title: Weighting by the constant singleton gives exactly the ordinary limit
items.strategy: Direct. A natural transformation from the constant singleton weight into $\mathcal M(m,F-)$ is exactly a cone over $F$ with apex $m$, so the two representations represent the same functor. This is a comparison theorem: it does not redefine the ordinary limit, and the proof cites the published cone definition rather than restating it. Record the alternative one-line route through the category of elements of the constant singleton weight.

items.title: Weighting by a representable evaluates the diagram
items.strategy: Direct. The published Yoneda bijection identifies natural transformations out of a representable with an evaluation, so the defining representation of the weighted limit is satisfied by the value of the diagram at that object. Do both variances: the covariant representable weights the limit, the contravariant one the colimit, and the naturality clause of the published Yoneda statement is what makes the identification compatible.

items.title: A representable functor carries a weighted limit to the weighted limit of the composed diagram
items.strategy: Direct. Read the defining representation together with the identification of a weighted limit in $\mathbf{Set}$ with the set of natural transformations out of the weight; the statement then says that the hom-set of the weighted limit is the weighted limit of the hom-sets. State the weighted-colimit clause separately, since there the representable is contravariant and the result is again a weighted LIMIT in $\mathbf{Set}$, not a colimit.

items.title: A set-valued coend is a colimit weighted by the hom-bifunctor, and a set-valued end a limit weighted by it
items.strategy: Direct, for a set-valued functor: expand the hom-weighted colimit by the coend formula, apply Fubini in the pair variable, and evaluate the inner coend by co-Yoneda. Fix the variance of the weight on the product index category in the setup before any computation, because the hom-bifunctor has to be read on the OPPOSITE of the index category, and record the copower generalisation as a remark rather than proving it. Together with the twisted-arrow item this closes the loop between the two descriptions of a coend.

items.title: Why weights are needed once the base of enrichment is not $\mathbf{Set}$
Orientation and notation conventions in force on this page
Dinatural transformations compose
items.strategy: Refute by the witness of the composition theorem, restated in full so the item stands alone, and then say exactly which weaker composition statement IS true: a dinatural transformation composed with a natural one on either side.

items.title: Every functor on $\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal C$ has an end
items.strategy: Refute with a SMALL index category, so the reader sees that smallness of the index alone is not the issue. Take $\mathcal C$ discrete on a countably infinite set, so a wedge is an unconstrained family and an end is the product of the diagonal values; take the target to be the full subcategory of $\mathbf{Set}$ on the finite sets and every diagonal value a two-element set. A finite object representing that product would have to have infinitely many elements, so no end exists. Add a second sentence recording the separate size failure for a large index category, without making the refutation depend on it.

items.title: Under this page's convention a coend is the colimit of the same twisted-arrow diagram whose limit is the end
items.strategy: Refute by computing both sides on the walking arrow $0\to1$ with the hom-bifunctor as integrand. The twisted arrow category is then a cospan, whose colimit is the value at the non-identity arrow, a one-element set; while the coend is the two-element quotient computed from the coproduct description, because the slot indexed by the reverse direction is empty. State the CORRECT description in the refutation: the colimit is over the opposite category and of the functor with domain and codomain swapped.

items.title: Every functor preserves the ends that exist in its domain
items.strategy: Refute with two finite poset witnesses, both bounded and both checkable by hand. Regard a preorder as a category and a monotone map as a functor, using the published dictionary; in such a category a binary product is a meet, and by the mute-functor proposition that product is the end of the corresponding two-variable functor. First witness: the four-element diamond collapsed onto the two-chain, where the meet of the two incomparable elements is the bottom but the meet of their images is the top. Second witness: a full subposet from which the ambient meet has been removed, so the full inclusion carries a meet to a different element. State the true statement beside it: preservation of the twisted-arrow limits is what is needed, and a right adjoint has it.

items.title: Every weighted limit is the ordinary limit of the diagram it weights
items.strategy: Refute with the kernel-pair weight: index category the walking arrow, weight the two-element set mapping onto a one-element set, diagram a map of finite sets from a two-element set to a one-element set. The ordinary limit is the domain, with two elements; the weighted limit is the pullback of the map along itself, with four. Count both by hand. Then state the true comparison: the ordinary limit is the case of the constant singleton weight, and there is only a canonical comparison map in general.

items.title: The integral notation of Yoneda's original paper means the same as the modern one
items.strategy: Refute documentarily from the recorded convention: Yoneda's 1960 paper calls integration what is now the coend and writes it with the subscripted integral sign now reserved for the end, writing cointegration with a starred superscript for what is now the end. Cite the exact source clause and give the modern reading of each symbol so the reader can convert. Keep the refutation about the two notations and make no claim about the mathematics changing.

pages.title: Ends Coends and Weighted Limits — Examples

items.title: The end formula checked by hand against natural transformations on the walking arrow
items.strategy: Take the index category to be the walking arrow and two set-valued functors on it. Compute the equalizer of the two displayed products directly, list the elements, and match them one for one against the natural transformations, which are pairs of functions making one square commute.

items.title: Evaluation of functions is dinatural in its argument set
items.strategy: Verify the hexagon for the family $\mathrm{ev}_{(B)}:Y^B\times B\to Y$ regarded as a dinatural transformation from $(B_1,B_2)\mapsto Y^{B_1}\times B_2$ to the constant functor at $Y$. Chase a single pair through both legs at an arbitrary $f:B\to B'$; this is the family whose failure to be natural motivates the whole notion.

items.title: The twisted arrow category of the walking arrow is a cospan
items.strategy: Enumerate the three objects and every morphism, checking in each direction whether the required factorisation exists, and note that no morphism runs out of the non-identity arrow. Then read off that the end of a functor on the walking arrow is the pullback of its two non-diagonal legs.

items.title: The tensor product of monoid sets as a coend
items.strategy: Regard a monoid as a one-object category, a presheaf on it as a right action and a covariant functor as a left action, and compute the coend from the quotient description: it is the product of the two underlying sets modulo the relation identifying $(xm,y)$ with $(x,my)$. Check the relation is exactly the generating dinaturality relation for this index category, where the coproducts have one summand.

items.title: The coend of the hom-bifunctor
items.strategy: Compute $\int^c\mathcal C(c,c)$ from the quotient description: the endomorphisms of all objects modulo the relation identifying $gf$ with $fg$ whenever both composites are defined. Evaluate it on the walking arrow, where nothing is identified, and on a one-object category, where it is the set of conjugacy-type classes of the monoid under this relation.

items.title: Fubini checked by hand on a product of two walking arrows
items.strategy: Take both index categories to be the walking arrow and a small set-valued functor in four variables. Compute the end over the product index directly from the equalizer description, then compute both iterated ends, and exhibit the isomorphisms elementwise.

items.title: A weighted limit computing a kernel pair
items.strategy: With the index category the walking arrow and the weight the map from a two-element set to a one-element set, unwind the defining representation into a pair of morphisms with a common composite, and identify the representing object as the pullback of the diagram's arrow along itself. Confirm by computing the category of elements of the weight and recognising the pullback shape.

items.title: Powers and copowers of a set by a set
items.strategy: Identify the power of a set by a set as the function set and the copower as the product with that set, verify both defining bijections, and count both on finite examples including the empty exponent and the empty copower.

items.title: A module-valued coend computed as a quotient of a direct sum
items.strategy: Take the index category to be the walking arrow and a functor into modules over a fixed ring, write down the generating elements of the dinaturality submodule, and identify the quotient explicitly. Check the answer against the general cowedge universal property on one nontrivial test module.

pages.title: Kan Extensions Density and the Free Cocompletion

items.title: Left and right Kan extensions
items.strategy: State the local universal properties on the nose. A left Kan extension of F along K is a functor L with a natural transformation eta: F => LK universal among such pairs; dually a right Kan extension is a functor R with epsilon: RK => F terminal among such pairs. Keep the direction of eta and epsilon explicit, because the page later compares modern and older naming conventions.

items.title: Mac Lane's warning about left and right Kan extensions
items.strategy: Record the convention disagreement reader-facingly. Mac Lane warns that some authors reverse the left/right naming, but this library follows the modern convention fixed in item 1: left Kan extensions come with eta: F => LK and right Kan extensions with epsilon: RK => F. Keep the remark about notation and orientation only; it is not a second definition.

items.title: Kan extensions are unique up to unique isomorphism
items.strategy: For two left Kan extensions of the same F along K, factor each unit through the other universal pair and obtain natural transformations in both directions. The two composites are forced to be identities by uniqueness, yielding a unique natural isomorphism compatible with the units. Repeat dually for right Kan extensions and state both compatibilities explicitly.

items.title: Global Kan extensions as adjoints to restriction
items.strategy: For a small source C and locally small target E, define restriction K^*: [D,E] -> [C,E] by precomposition. A global left Kan extension along K is a left adjoint Lan_K to K^*, and dually a global right Kan extension is a right adjoint Ran_K. Distinguish this functor-level notion from the local extension of a single F, and say once that a class-sized family of local extensions is supplied data rather than silently chosen.

items.title: Lan is left adjoint to restriction, and restriction is left adjoint to Ran
items.strategy: Assume that for each F: C -> E a local left Kan extension along K is supplied, and similarly a local right Kan extension. These local universal pairs are exactly the objectwise universal arrows to and from the restriction functor K^*, so the published assembly theorem turns them into adjunctions Lan_K ⊣ K^* and K^* ⊣ Ran_K on the legitimate functor categories. Keep the family supplied rather than selected.

items.title: Comma-category limit and colimit formulae compute Kan extensions
items.strategy: For fixed d in D, a colimit of the diagram (K ↓ d) -> C -> E gives an object with the left Kan universal property at d, and a limit of the diagram (d ↓ K) -> C -> E gives the right Kan universal property at d. In each direction, the natural transformation component at c is the leg indexed by the identity on Kc. When such cones are supplied for every d, the action on arrows is forced by the local universal properties and is unique.

items.title: Pointwise Kan extensions by the comma-category formula
items.strategy: Define a pointwise left Kan extension to be a local left Kan extension whose value at each d is computed by the colimit cone of item 6, and dually for a pointwise right Kan extension by the limit cone. State explicitly that eta_c is the colimit leg at id_{Kc} and epsilon_c the limit leg at id_{Kc}; that clause is what later fully faithful and density arguments use.

items.title: Pointwise Kan extensions exist under smallness and completeness hypotheses
items.strategy: If C is small and D locally small, then each comma category K ↓ d and d ↓ K is small. Hence cocompleteness of E supplies the objectwise colimits and completeness of E the objectwise limits of item 6. State the result in the owner's required split form: objectwise existence is automatic from the hypotheses, while the global functors Lan_K F and Ran_K F arise only from supplied chosen colimits or limits for every d.

items.title: Pointwise Kan extensions as those preserved by representables
items.strategy: When D and E are locally small, define a right Kan extension to be pointwise when every covariant representable E(e,-) preserves it. Define a left Kan extension to be pointwise after passage to opposite categories, so that each contravariant representable E(-,e) sends it to the corresponding pointwise right Kan extension. Spell the variance out; 'preserved by representables' alone is ambiguous.

items.title: The comma-category and representable-preservation notions of pointwise Kan extension agree
items.strategy: One direction is immediate because representables preserve the small limits and colimits used in item 7. For the converse, identify cones over d ↓ K and cocones under K ↓ d with natural families from the appropriate representable weights, then apply Yoneda. Keep the locally-small hypotheses on both D and E explicit: this is the corrected second-edition statement, and the first edition omitted them.

items.title: Absolute Kan extension
items.strategy: Define a left or right Kan extension to be absolute when it is preserved by every functor out of its codomain. Keep it separate from pointwise: pointwise asks only for preservation by representables, while absolute is strictly stronger.

items.title: Left adjoints preserve left Kan extensions
items.strategy: Whisker a left Kan extension through a left adjoint L ⊣ R and use the adjunction between L and R to convert a factorization problem out of LLan_K F into one out of Lan_K F. Uniqueness transfers back through the adjunction, so the whiskered pair is again a left Kan extension. The right-handed dual is recorded in the proof but not used as a separate deps target on this page.

items.title: A pointwise Kan extension along a fully faithful functor genuinely extends the original functor
items.strategy: If K is fully faithful, then the relevant slice or coslice category at Kc has the identity on c as a terminal or initial object. The pointwise formula therefore computes the value at Kc by evaluation at that identity, making the unit or counit component invertible. This is the precise theorem behind 'restriction recovers the original functor', and the pointwise hypothesis is essential.

items.title: Kan extensions as coends and ends
items.strategy: Use the hom-weighted coend and end formulas from the previous page. For small C and locally small D, the left Kan extension value at d represents the hom-weighted colimit ∫^c D(Kc,d) · Fc, and the right Kan extension value at d the weighted limit ∫_c F(c)^{D(d,Kc)} when the required copowers, powers, coends and ends exist. The proof identifies these objects with the universal objects of item 6.

items.title: Limits and colimits are Kan extensions along the functor to the terminal category
items.strategy: Let !: C -> 1 be the unique functor. Then K ↓ * and * ↓ K identify with C itself, so item 6 specializes to the ordinary colimit and limit universal properties. State both sides explicitly: a colimit is a left Kan extension along ! and a limit is a right Kan extension along !.

items.title: Adjunctions as absolute Kan extensions, with the preserved converse
items.strategy: If F ⊣ G with unit eta and counit epsilon, then G is the left Kan extension of 1_C along F and F the right Kan extension of 1_D along G; absoluteness follows from item 12. Conversely, a left Kan extension of 1_C along F yields a right adjoint only when it is preserved by F, and dually on the other side. State the preservation clause in the Statement, because dropping it is a genuine falsehood in the literature.

items.title: Evaluation is the limit over the coslice category
items.strategy: Apply the right Kan formula of item 6 to K = id_C. The comma category c ↓ id_C is the coslice c / C, and its initial object id_c computes the limit directly. Record separately the equalizer calculation that appears when C is small and the target has products and equalizers; that calculation is not the universal-property proof itself.

items.title: Evaluation is the colimit over the slice category
items.strategy: Dualize item 17. For K = id_C, the comma category id_C ↓ c is the slice C / c, and the terminal object id_c computes the colimit directly. Keep this as the dual evaluation formula, not as a second definition of co-Yoneda.

items.title: Density theorem for a small category
items.strategy: For small C and a covariant Set-valued functor F, build the canonical diagram of covariant representables indexed by the opposite of the category of elements of F. Show that giving a cocone from this diagram to any G is exactly giving a natural transformation F => G, so F is their colimit. Keep the smallness restriction explicit, even though some sources formulate a larger locally-small version.

items.title: The Yoneda embedding is its own pointwise left Kan extension
items.strategy: Apply item 19 inside the presheaf category Set^{C^op}. For a presheaf X, the canonical colimit of representables indexed by its category of elements is exactly the comma-category colimit of the Yoneda embedding over X, so the identity functor with the identity natural transformation is the pointwise left Kan extension of y along itself.

items.title: Dense functor and dense subcategory
items.strategy: Define a functor F: D -> C with D small to be dense when the identity on C is the pointwise left Kan extension of F along itself, equivalently when every object of C is the canonical colimit of the comma diagram F ↓ C. A small full subcategory is dense when its inclusion is dense.

items.title: The presheaf category on a small category is the free cocompletion
items.strategy: For small C and locally small cocomplete E, define Lan_y F objectwise by the density colimit over the category of elements of a presheaf X. Item 20 gives the pointwise left Kan extension of y along itself, item 13 makes Lan_y F a genuine extension of F along y, and Yoneda identifies the right adjoint with the presheaf e |-> E(F-,e). Conversely, any adjunction out of the presheaf category is recovered by restricting its left adjoint along y. Keep the chosen colimits supplied rather than selected.

items.title: Codensity monad
items.strategy: For a functor G: D -> C, define its codensity monad to be the right Kan extension Ran_G G when it exists. The counit is the Kan-extension counit, the unit is induced from the identity on G, and the multiplication is induced by pasting the counit with itself. Record that a codense functor is one whose codensity monad is the identity.

items.title: The codensity construction satisfies the monad axioms
items.strategy: Using the universal property of the right Kan extension, show that the unit induced in item 23 and the multiplication induced by the twice-pasted counit are the unique natural transformations making the two unit triangles and the associativity square commute after whiskering with G. Uniqueness then forces the monad laws in C, so item 23 is genuinely a monad and not only an endofunctor formula.

items.title: The codensity monad of the small skeleton of finite sets is the ultrafilter monad
items.strategy: Use the explicit small skeleton FinOrd of Set on the standard finite ordinals [n] = {0, ..., n-1}. Apply the pointwise right Kan formula to the inclusion FinOrd -> Set and identify a cone from X into a finite set J with a natural choice of a value in J for every finite-valued function X -> J. Leinster's characterization turns these natural choice operators into ultrafilters, and the formulas for the induced unit and multiplication agree with the published principal-ultrafilter and flattening maps. This keeps the source small and avoids any appeal to an unchosen large skeleton of FinSet.

items.title: Every Kan extension is pointwise
items.strategy: Refute with the standard fully faithful inclusion 1+1 -> (ell <- m -> r) into a five-object target category having no initial object. The universal left extension exists vacuously, but the comma category at m is empty, so the pointwise colimit formula would need an initial object that the target does not have. State the positive correction beside it: item 13 needs pointwise, and item 10 explains why.

items.title: Along a fully faithful functor every left Kan extension restricts back to the original functor
items.strategy: Use the same witness as the previous false statement: the unit components at the two source objects are non-invertible even though the inclusion is fully faithful. The correct theorem is item 13, which needs the pointwise hypothesis and then computes the restriction by the identity object in the relevant slice category.

items.title: The free cocompletion theorem holds for a large source category
items.strategy: Refute by the house size policy, not by a fake counterexample. For a large source category C, the functor collection Set^{C^op} is not one of the legitimate functor categories recognized by the library's small-source rule, and the category of elements or presheaf colimits used in item 22 no longer live in an accepted functor category. State the positive replacement: item 22 is for small C, deliberately.

items.title: The Yoneda embedding preserves colimits
items.strategy: Take a small category with an initial object 0 and at least one object. The colimit of the empty diagram is 0, but the initial presheaf in Set^{C^op} is pointwise empty, while y(0)(0) = C(0,0) is a singleton. Hence y does not preserve this colimit. Record the true statement beside it: the published corollary says Yoneda preserves and reflects small limits.

pages.title: Kan Extensions Density and the Free Cocompletion — Examples

items.title: A left Kan extension along a full inclusion
items.strategy: Take the full inclusion of the two-point chain {0 < 2} into the three-point chain {0 < 1 < 2}, regarded as categories. A Set-valued functor on the smaller chain is just a map X -> Z. Compute the pointwise left Kan extension by the comma-category colimits: the new middle value is X, the top value remains Z, and item 13 explains why restriction along the full inclusion recovers the original diagram.

items.title: The free group functor as a Kan extension
items.strategy: Let 1 be the terminal category, let F: 1 -> Grp pick out the infinite cyclic group Z, and extend F along the Yoneda embedding y: 1 -> Set. Item 22 identifies Lan_y F(X) with the colimit of X copies of Z, hence with the free group on X. Compare the resulting adjunction with the published free-group adjunction to show the Kan extension really recovers the familiar free functor.

items.title: Induction and coinduction as Kan extensions along a subgroup inclusion
items.strategy: Regard groups as one-object categories. For a subgroup H ⊂ G and a representation X: BH -> C, item 6 turns the left Kan extension along BH -> BG into the usual induced object and the right Kan extension into the coinduced object. Unwind the comma categories as G/H-cosets to recover the standard coequalizer and equalizer descriptions. When H has finite index, both formulas collapse to the same finite coproduct or product of copies.

items.title: The orbit-category right Kan extension is the fixed-point functor
items.strategy: Embed B(G^op) into the orbit category O_G by the object G/e. For a left G-set X, compute the right Kan extension to O_G^op at a subgroup H by identifying the relevant comma category with the action groupoid of G/H. Its limit is the subset of H-fixed points of X, so the Kan extension is the fixed-point functor H |-> X^H. This example is the category-theoretic shadow of the fixed-point constructions used in equivariant homotopy theory.

items.title: A two-object presheaf rebuilt as a colimit of representables
items.strategy: Take the walking arrow category 0 -> 1 and a presheaf X with two elements over 0 mapping to one element over 1. Write down its category of elements explicitly, list the two representables that occur, and compute the colimit diagram in Set^{C^op}. The colimit reproduces X exactly, making the density theorem concrete on the smallest nontrivial presheaf category.

items.title: A fully faithful left Kan extension that is not pointwise
items.strategy: Work the standard witness from the A-page false statements in full detail. Take the fully faithful inclusion 1+1 -> (ell <- m -> r) and the five-object target category whose middle comma category has no initial object. Show the local universal pair exists uniquely, then compute K ↓ m and see that the pointwise colimit would need an initial object that is absent. This is the concrete witness behind items 28 and 29.

items.title: The real exponential is the Kan extension of the rational exponential
items.strategy: View Q and R as poset categories. The monotone functor q |-> 2^q from Q to the positive reals has a pointwise left Kan extension along Q -> R obtained by taking suprema over q <= x, and the density of Q in R identifies that supremum with 2^x. The same density argument makes it the right Kan extension by infima over x <= q, so the left and right pointwise extensions coincide in this case.

pages.title: Preadditive and Additive Categories and Biproducts

items.title: Preadditive category
A one-object preadditive category is the same thing as a ring
items.strategy: Identify the unique hom-group with the ring's additive group, take composition as multiplication, and use functoriality plus additivity to recover exactly the unital ring-homomorphism laws.

items.title: Additive functors from a ring to abelian groups are left modules
items.strategy: Unpack an additive functor on the one-object category attached to a ring as an action by endomorphisms, and read naturality of a transformation as module-linearity.

items.title: Additive functor
An additive functor preserves zero morphisms
items.strategy: An additive functor carries the zero element of each hom-group to the zero element of the target hom-group.

items.title: The opposite of a preadditive category is preadditive
items.strategy: The opposite category has the same hom-groups, and reversing composition preserves bilinearity because the original composition is bilinear in both variables.

items.title: A small product of preadditive categories is preadditive
items.strategy: Use componentwise abelian-group operations on each hom-set and check bilinearity coordinatewise.

items.title: Additive functors and natural transformations form a preadditive category
items.strategy: Add natural transformations pointwise, use the codomain hom-group laws objectwise, and cite the small-source size theorem to keep the hom-collections sets.

items.title: In a preadditive category, an object is initial exactly when it is terminal
items.strategy: Either universal property makes the endomorphism group trivial, so the identity equals zero and every map to or from the object is forced to be the unique zero arrow.

items.title: In a preadditive category with a zero object, the zero morphism is the neutral element of each hom-group
items.strategy: Compare the published zero morphism A -> 0 -> B with the additive identity by composing with arbitrary arrows and using uniqueness through the zero object.

items.title: A preadditive category with a zero object has zero morphisms in the published sense
items.strategy: Combine the published zero-object construction with the identification of those arrows with the hom-group zero elements.

items.title: Canonical morphism from a finite coproduct to a finite product
Biproduct
Biproduct data characterisation without addition
items.strategy: From a biproduct, read off the product and coproduct cones and the four zero equations; conversely, the same equations plus the universal properties identify one object as both.

items.title: The empty biproduct is a zero object
items.strategy: The empty coproduct is initial and the empty product is terminal, so an isomorphism between them makes the same object both.

items.title: Biproducts are associative, commutative, and unital up to canonical isomorphism
items.strategy: Transport the standard product and coproduct uniqueness isomorphisms across the canonical comparison that identifies each product with the corresponding coproduct.

items.title: A category with finite biproducts is enriched in commutative monoids
items.strategy: Define f + g using the diagonal into A + A and codiagonal out of B + B, then verify commutativity, associativity, zero, and bilinearity from the biproduct identities.

items.title: The commutative-monoid enrichment of a category with finite biproducts is unique
items.strategy: Any bilinear commutative-monoid law compatible with the same biproduct structure must reproduce the diagonal-codiagonal formula that defines addition.

items.title: The uniqueness of the enrichment is an Eckmann-Hilton phenomenon
items.strategy: Apply Eckmann-Hilton to two candidate bilinear monoid laws with the same unit and interchange supplied by composition.

items.title: Semiadditive category
On a biproduct, the injections and projections satisfy the identity-sum relation
items.strategy: Expand the diagonal-codiagonal formula on A + B to show i_A p_A + i_B p_B = 1, and use the same equality together with the zero equations to recover the universal properties.

items.title: A semiadditive category is preadditive exactly when every morphism has an additive inverse
items.strategy: The semiadditive hom-sets are already commutative monoids with bilinear composition, so preadditivity is exactly the extra existence of negatives.

items.title: Additive category
In a preadditive category, a finite product is automatically a biproduct
items.strategy: Use zero morphisms to define the coproduct injections from a product cone, and use the nullary case to identify the terminal object with an initial one.

items.title: Additive categories are closed under passage to the opposite
items.strategy: The opposite stays preadditive, and finite products in the opposite are finite coproducts in the original, hence again biproducts.

items.title: Morphisms between finite biproducts correspond to matrices
items.strategy: Recover a map from its projection-component-injection entries by summing injection-component-projection composites, and prove bijectivity by decomposing the identities of the source and target biproducts.

items.title: Composition between finite biproducts is matrix multiplication
items.strategy: Insert the identity decomposition of the middle biproduct and read off the resulting entrywise sum using the matrix representation theorem.

items.title: The biproduct of morphisms is the diagonal matrix
items.strategy: Apply the matrix-entry formula to the block map obtained by taking a biproduct of the given morphisms.

items.title: An infinite coproduct need not agree with the infinite product
items.strategy: In Ab, compare the finite-support subgroup direct sum_n Z with the full product of all sequences and use the constant 1-sequence as a non-image of the canonical map.

items.title: The additive category of matrices over a ring
The matrix category over a ring is additive
items.strategy: Use block injections and projections to exhibit m + n as the biproduct of m and n, with matrix addition on hom-sets inherited entrywise from the ring.

items.title: The matrix category is equivalent to the finitely generated free modules
items.strategy: Send n to R^n and a matrix to the corresponding linear map on column vectors; full faithfulness is matrix arithmetic and the essential image is exactly the finitely generated free modules.

items.title: The matrix category is the finite-biproduct completion of a ring
In a preadditive category, the equalizer of a parallel pair is the kernel of their difference
items.strategy: Equalizing f and g is equivalent to forcing their difference f - g to vanish, so the universal properties coincide.

items.title: In a preadditive category, the coequalizer of a parallel pair is the cokernel of their difference
items.strategy: Pass to the opposite category and apply the equalizer-as-kernel theorem there.

items.title: An additive category with all kernels and cokernels has all finite limits and colimits
items.strategy: Finite limits reduce to products and equalizers, with products coming from preadditivity and equalizers from kernels; dualize for colimits.

items.title: In a preadditive category with a zero object, a morphism is monic exactly when its kernel is zero
items.strategy: If a kernel is zero, any equality fu = fv gives f(u - v) = 0 and forces u - v to factor through zero; conversely, a monic map makes its kernel arrow factor through the zero object.

items.title: In a preadditive category with a zero object, a morphism is epic exactly when its cokernel is zero
items.strategy: Apply the monic-kernel criterion in the opposite preadditive category.

items.title: A zero kernel does not force monicity in a merely semiadditive category
items.strategy: In CMon, the quotient q: N -> {0,a} with a+a=a has trivial kernel but identifies the maps sending 1 to 1 and 1 to 2, so q is not monic.

items.title: An additive functor preserves finite biproducts
items.strategy: Apply the functor to the biproduct equations and use additivity plus preservation of zero morphisms to keep the identities and zero entries intact.

items.title: A functor between additive categories is additive exactly when it preserves finite biproducts
items.strategy: One direction is biproduct preservation by additivity; conversely, recover F(f + g) from preservation of the diagonal, codiagonal, and the binary biproducts.

items.title: A functor between additive categories preserving finite products is additive
items.strategy: Finite products are finite biproducts in an additive category, so the biproduct criterion applies.

items.title: Any adjoint between additive categories is additive
items.strategy: Right adjoints preserve finite limits and left adjoints preserve finite colimits; in an additive category either side is enough to recover biproduct preservation.

items.title: An additive functor is left exact exactly when it preserves kernels
items.strategy: Finite limits are products plus equalizers; additive functors preserve finite products, and equalizers are kernels of differences in a preadditive setting.

items.title: An additive functor preserves split biproduct diagrams
items.strategy: Apply the functor to the chosen injection, projection, section, and retraction maps and reuse the preserved biproduct identities.

items.title: The Hom bifunctor of a preadditive category takes values in abelian groups
items.strategy: Each hom-set already carries an abelian-group structure, and pre- and post-composition are homomorphisms by biadditivity.

items.title: Hom functors on a preadditive category are left exact
items.strategy: View Hom(A,-) as covariantly representable and Hom(-,B) as representable on the opposite category, then invoke the published theorem that representables preserve limits.

items.title: The published module statement is the instance of this corollary
A covariant hom functor on an additive category need not preserve cokernels
items.strategy: Apply Hom(Z/2,-) to Z --2--> Z -> Z/2 and compute that the induced map on hom-groups is not surjective onto the cokernel.

items.title: Idempotent and split idempotent
A splitting of an idempotent is simultaneously an equalizer and a coequalizer and is unique up to unique isomorphism
items.strategy: Use the relations ip = e and pi = 1 to show i equalizes e and 1 while p coequalizes them, then identify any two splittings by the corresponding universal properties.

items.title: Idempotent-complete category
An additive category with kernels is idempotent complete
items.strategy: For an idempotent e, take the kernel of 1 - e and use the additive splitting identities to show that this kernel object is exactly the image summand of e.

items.title: The idempotent completion of a preadditive category
The idempotent completion is idempotent complete, and its inclusion is fully faithful and universal
items.strategy: Build Kar(C) explicitly from pairs (A,e), prove split idempotents inside it, show the inclusion A -> (A,1_A) is fully faithful, and extend functors by sending (A,e) to a chosen splitting image of F(e).

items.title: The addition on an additive category is extra structure that must be chosen
items.strategy: Refute the claim by citing the uniqueness theorem showing that the biproduct structure forces a single possible addition law on every hom-set.

items.title: A category with finite products and finite coproducts has biproducts
items.strategy: Refute the claim in pointed sets, where the zero object and both finite constructions exist but the canonical map from wedge to product need not be an isomorphism.

items.title: A functor preserving zero morphisms is additive
items.strategy: Use the reduced free-abelian-group functor on underlying pointed sets: it preserves zero morphisms but does not preserve sums of homomorphisms.

items.title: A preadditive category with a zero object has binary biproducts
items.strategy: Refute the claim with the full subcategory of Ab on 0 and Z, where hom-groups and a zero object exist but Z x Z is not an object.

items.title: Every idempotent splits
items.strategy: Refute the claim by exhibiting a preadditive category whose formal idempotent completion strictly enlarges it, so some idempotent is unsplit before completion.

pages.title: Preadditive and Additive Categories and Biproducts — Examples

items.title: The biproduct of two abelian groups computed as a matrix calculus
items.strategy: Write the injections, projections, diagonal, and codiagonal in Ab and compute a sample composite entrywise as an ordinary matrix product.

items.title: Abelian groups, modules, and vector spaces are additive
items.strategy: Use the familiar pointwise hom-group structures and products, then invoke the additive-category criterion to package the standard examples together.

items.title: A ring viewed as a one-object preadditive category with its matrices
items.strategy: Start from the single-object ring category and then display its finite-biproduct completion as block matrices of all finite sizes.

items.title: The idempotent completion of a ring is the finitely generated projective modules
items.strategy: Identify an object (R^n,e) with the retract of the free module R^n cut out by the idempotent matrix e, and recognize those retracts as the finitely generated projectives.

items.title: Pointed sets are not additive
items.strategy: Compute the wedge and product of two nontrivial pointed sets and show that the canonical map from the wedge to the product is not an isomorphism.

items.title: Commutative monoids are semiadditive and not additive
items.strategy: Use the standard finite product-coproduct coincidence in CMon, then note that additive inverses fail and the zero-kernel witness already records the obstruction.

items.title: Additive functors out of the matrix category
items.strategy: Translate an additive functor out of Mat_R through the finite-free-module equivalence and read it as a finite-biproduct-preserving module construction.

items.title: A preadditive category with two objects and a nonzero hom-group
items.strategy: Specify two objects, choose abelian groups for all four hom-sets, and define a bilinear composition law directly.

pages.title: Abelian Categories

items.title: Normal monomorphisms and conormal epimorphisms
The kernel of a monomorphism is zero and the cokernel of an epimorphism is zero
items.strategy: Use the universal properties of kernel and cokernel against the unique maps to and from a zero object. Monicity or epicity forces every candidate factorization through the zero map.

items.title: The cokernel of the zero map out of the zero object is the target, and dually for kernels
items.strategy: Check that the identity of the target satisfies the cokernel universal property of the zero map out of the zero object, and dualize for kernels into the zero object.

items.title: Image and coimage in a category with kernels and cokernels
A morphism factors uniquely through its coimage
items.strategy: Apply the cokernel universal property to the kernel of the morphism, since the composite with that kernel is zero.

items.title: A morphism factors uniquely through its image
items.strategy: Apply the kernel universal property to the cokernel of the morphism, since the composite with that cokernel is zero.

items.title: The canonical morphism from the coimage to the image exists and is unique
items.strategy: Compose the two universal factorizations of the same morphism. Uniqueness on one side identifies the mediating arrow uniquely.

items.title: The coimage projection is epic and the image inclusion is monic
items.strategy: The coimage map is a cokernel and the image map is a kernel, so the standard equalizer and coequalizer calculus applies directly.

items.title: Abelian category
This page uses Grothendieck's AB1 and AB2 labels, and records the competing conventions
An abelian category is balanced
items.strategy: For a bimorphism, compute the coimage and image using the zero kernel and zero cokernel, identify both endpoint objects, and use the AB2 isomorphism between coimage and image.

items.title: The opposite of an abelian category is abelian
items.strategy: Passing to the opposite preserves additivity, swaps kernels with cokernels and swaps image with coimage, so the same AB2 clause is carried to itself.

items.title: Every monomorphism is the kernel of its cokernel, and dually every epimorphism is the cokernel of its kernel
items.strategy: For a monomorphism, the kernel is zero, so the coimage is the source. AB2 identifies that source with the image, which by definition is the kernel of the cokernel.

items.title: Every morphism factors as an epimorphism followed by a monomorphism, uniquely up to unique isomorphism
items.strategy: Take the canonical coimage to image map, use AB2 to make it an isomorphism, and compose it with the epic coimage projection and monic image inclusion. Uniqueness follows from balancedness applied to the comparison map between two epi-mono factorizations.

items.title: The image is the least subobject through which a morphism factors
items.strategy: Use the epi-mono factorization and compare any other factorization through a subobject to the image factorization by the universal property of the kernel of the cokernel.

items.title: In an abelian category, monic means zero kernel and epic means zero cokernel
items.strategy: An abelian category is preadditive with a zero object, so the published kernel and cokernel characterizations apply immediately.

items.title: Freyd's axioms A0, A1, A1*, A2, A2*, A3, and A3* for abelian categories
Freyd's axioms force the additive structure and recover the AB2 definition
items.strategy: First prove balancedness directly from normality and conormality, then show the canonical map from coproduct to product is an isomorphism, recover the unique commutative-monoid enrichment from biproducts, and use the shear automorphism on a biproduct to build additive inverses.

items.title: Freyd and Mitchell's characterisation of abelian categories
items.strategy: Compare the working AB2 formulation with the Freyd normal-conormal axiomatisation. The equivalence runs by recovering additivity from Freyd's axioms, using the published finite-limit and finite-colimit theorem for the pullback and pushout clause, and recovering products, coproducts, kernels, and cokernels from pullbacks and pushouts against the zero object.

items.title: Additivity can be derived rather than postulated, depending on the axiomatisation
An abelian category has all finite limits and all finite colimits
items.strategy: The ambient category is additive and has kernels and cokernels, so the published finite-limit and finite-colimit theorem for additive categories applies directly.

items.title: A pullback is the kernel of the difference of the two legs, and dually for pushouts
items.strategy: On a biproduct, package the two legs into a single map to the codomain. Equalizing the two composites is equivalent to killing their difference, so the pullback is realized as that kernel.

items.title: The pullback of an epimorphism is an epimorphism
items.strategy: Write the pullback as a kernel inside a biproduct and use exactness of the resulting short sequence to identify the pullback projection as a cokernel-zero map.

items.title: The pushout of a monomorphism is a monomorphism
items.strategy: Dualize the pullback-of-epimorphisms theorem through the opposite abelian category.

items.title: In a pullback square, the induced map on the kernels of the two parallel arrows is an isomorphism
items.strategy: Use the pullback-as-kernel description together with the universal property of kernels to build inverse comparison maps between the two kernels.

items.title: A square with monic legs is a pullback exactly when it identifies the source with the intersection subobject
items.strategy: Interpret the two monics as subobjects of the common codomain, identify their pullback with the greatest lower bound, and compare the induced map from the source to that intersection.

items.title: Pullback pasting in an abelian category
items.strategy: Cite the published pullback-and-pushout pasting theorem and record that it applies verbatim in abelian categories.

items.title: Kernel and cokernel are mutually inverse order-reversing correspondences between subobjects and quotient objects
items.strategy: Send a subobject to the cokernel of a monic representative and a quotient to the kernel of an epic representative. Normality and conormality show the two constructions undo one another, and factorization reverses the order.

items.title: The quotient of an object by a subobject
The quotient by a subobject is independent of the chosen representing monomorphism
items.strategy: Mutually factoring monic representatives have canonically isomorphic cokernels, so the quotient depends only on the subobject class.

items.title: First isomorphism theorem in an abelian category
items.strategy: The quotient by the kernel is the coimage, the image is the kernel of the cokernel, and AB2 identifies the two through the canonical coimage-to-image morphism.

items.title: Third isomorphism theorem in an abelian category
items.strategy: Apply the first isomorphism theorem to the canonical quotient map between successive quotients and identify its kernel with the intermediate quotient subobject.

items.title: The quotient by the kernel followed by the image inclusion is the canonical epi-mono factorization
items.strategy: Compare the quotient-by-kernel factorization from the first isomorphism theorem with the canonical image factorization and use uniqueness of epi-mono factorizations.

items.title: Exact functor between abelian categories
A left or right exact functor between abelian categories is automatically additive
items.strategy: One-sided exactness preserves the relevant finite limits or colimits, hence zero objects and biproducts. The published biproduct-preservation criterion then forces additivity.

items.title: Left exactness, right exactness, and exactness are characterized by short exact sequences
items.strategy: Once one-sided exactness is known to imply additivity, the short exact sequence tests are equivalent to preserving finite limits or finite colimits in the abelian setting.

items.title: An additive functor is exact exactly when it preserves kernels and cokernels
items.strategy: Use the published kernel criterion for left exactness and its opposite-category dual for cokernels, then combine both halves with the definition of exactness.

items.title: A left exact functor preserves monomorphisms and a right exact functor preserves epimorphisms
items.strategy: Translate monicity and epicity into zero-kernel and zero-cokernel conditions, then apply the short-exact-sequence characterization of one-sided exactness.

items.title: An exact functor need not be faithful
items.strategy: Take the product of two nonzero abelian categories and verify its abelian structure componentwise: preadditivity, zero objects, kernels, cokernels, biproducts, and the coimage-image comparison all reduce to the factors. Projection to the first factor therefore preserves kernels and cokernels and is exact, but it sends every morphism supported in the second factor to zero, so it is not faithful.

items.title: An equivalence between abelian categories is exact
items.strategy: Equivalences preserve and reflect all limits and colimits that exist, so they preserve finite biproducts, kernels, and cokernels. The published biproduct-preservation criterion then gives additivity, and the left- and right-exact clauses follow from the preserved finite limits and colimits.

items.title: Abelian subcategory and exact embedding
Abelian groups form an abelian category
items.strategy: Identify abelian groups with $\mathbb Z$-modules. Ordinary subgroup kernels and quotient cokernels give the categorical kernel and cokernel constructions, biproducts are direct sums, and the first isomorphism theorem identifies coimage with image, verifying the abelian-category axioms directly.

items.title: Modules over a ring form an abelian category
items.strategy: Use the ordinary module kernel and cokernel constructions, note that the category is additive and complete enough, and recognize AB2 as the first isomorphism theorem for modules.

items.title: Additive functors from a small preadditive category to an abelian category form an abelian category
items.strategy: The additive-functor category is already preadditive. Kernels, cokernels, biproducts, and the coimage-image map are computed pointwise in the ambient functor category, so the abelian structure descends pointwise as well.

items.title: A small product of abelian categories is abelian
items.strategy: All structure is computed componentwise: preadditivity, zero objects, kernels, cokernels, biproducts, and the AB2 map all reduce to the corresponding statements in each factor.

items.title: Filtered vector spaces can be additive with kernels and cokernels without being abelian
