items.strategy: Use the standard one-dimensional filtered-vector-space witness in which the identity map has trivial kernel and cokernel but is not an isomorphism because the filtrations differ.

items.title: Torsion-free abelian groups do not form an abelian category
items.strategy: In the torsion-free full subcategory of abelian groups, multiplication by 2 on Z is monic and epic by cancellation but not invertible. That shows balancedness fails, so the subcategory cannot be abelian.

items.title: An abelian category that is a preorder is trivial
items.strategy: In a preorder every morphism is both monic and epic, so balancedness forces every morphism to be an isomorphism. A preorder with a zero object and only isomorphisms collapses to the trivial case.

items.title: Freyd-Mitchell gives a fully faithful exact embedding of every small abelian category into a module category
The library does not use Freyd-Mitchell to prove the diagram lemmas
FALSE: every additive category with all kernels and cokernels is abelian
items.strategy: Refute with the filtered-vector-space example, where kernels and cokernels exist but the canonical coimage-to-image morphism can fail to be an isomorphism.

items.title: FALSE: if coimage and image happen to be isomorphic as objects, then the canonical map is automatically an isomorphism
items.strategy: Refute with multiplication by 2 on Z inside torsion-free abelian groups: coimage and image are both Z, but the canonical map is multiplication by 2 rather than an isomorphism.

items.title: FALSE: in an abelian category a morphism can be monic and epic without being an isomorphism
items.strategy: Balancedness is precisely the theorem that rules this out.

items.title: FALSE: every abelian category is equivalent to a module category
items.strategy: Refute with finite-dimensional vector spaces over a field: they form an abelian category, but they do not have the countable coproducts that every module category has.

items.title: FALSE: pullbacks preserve epimorphisms in every category with pullbacks
items.strategy: Refute in the category of Hausdorff spaces: the dense inclusion \(\mathbb Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb R\) is epic because continuous maps into Hausdorff codomains are determined on dense subsets, but its pullback along the inclusion of an irrational singleton is the empty map to a point, which is not epic.

pages.title: Abelian Categories — Examples

items.title: Kernels, cokernels, images, and coimages in abelian groups are the familiar subgroup and quotient constructions
items.strategy: Compute everything for a homomorphism of abelian groups exactly as in elementary algebra and compare the canonical coimage-to-image map with the usual first isomorphism theorem map.

items.title: A module homomorphism factors as quotient by its kernel followed by inclusion of its image
items.strategy: Use the ordinary module quotient M/ker f and the image submodule im f, then identify their comparison map with the published first isomorphism theorem for modules.

items.title: A pullback of module maps is computed as a kernel of a difference map
items.strategy: For module maps to a common codomain, realize the fibre product as the submodule of pairs whose images agree, then identify that submodule with the kernel of (f,-g).

items.title: Vector spaces over a field form an abelian category
items.strategy: Treat vector spaces as modules over a field and inherit the entire abelian-category structure from the module theorem.

items.title: Representations of the quiver 1 -> 2 in abelian groups form an abelian category
items.strategy: Identify a representation with a homomorphism A -> B in abelian groups and a morphism of representations with a commuting square. Kernels and cokernels are then computed pointwise.

items.title: Topological abelian groups are additive but not abelian
items.strategy: Use continuous homomorphisms as morphisms, note that products, coproducts, and hom-set addition are available, and then exhibit a continuous bijection whose image/coimage comparison fails because the inverse is not continuous in the ambient topological category.

items.title: The third isomorphism theorem in abelian groups matches the categorical statement
items.strategy: Compute (A/C)/(B/C) and A/B explicitly for nested subgroups C <= B <= A and compare them through the ordinary quotient-group map.

items.title: Localization of modules gives an exact functor between module categories
items.strategy: View localization as a functor from R-Mod to S^{-1}R-Mod and use the published exactness of localization to show that it preserves short exact sequences.

items.title: Filtered vector spaces can have zero kernel and zero cokernel without satisfying AB2
items.strategy: Unpack the standard one-dimensional filtered-vector-space witness and compute its coimage, image, and comparison map explicitly.

pages.title: Subobject Lattices Generators and the Grothendieck Axioms

items.title: Modular lattice
The join of two subobjects in an abelian category
The join of two subobjects is their least upper bound
items.strategy: Represent the two subobjects by monomorphisms into a common object A, form the induced map from their biproduct to A, and use the image factorization. The image contains both representatives, and the least-subobject characterization of images shows that any common upper bound factors through it.

items.title: The meet of two subobjects is their pullback
items.strategy: Pull back the two monomorphisms into A. The pullback leg is monic, so it represents a subobject of A. Its universal property makes it a lower bound, and any other lower bound factors uniquely through the pullback, making it the greatest one.

items.title: The subobjects of an object in an abelian category form a lattice
items.strategy: Use items 3 and 4 to supply binary joins and meets in the subobject poset. The zero monomorphism into A gives the bottom element and the identity of A gives the top element.

items.title: The subobject lattice of an abelian category is modular
items.strategy: Identify each interval [B1, B2] in Sub(C) with the subobject lattice of the quotient B2/B1 via the third isomorphism theorem, then use the interval-complement criterion for modularity recorded in the source notes. The point of the proof is that modularity is derived from abelian-category quotient calculus, not assumed as a lattice axiom.

items.title: The published subgroup modular law is the group instance
items.strategy: Record that the library already proves Dedekind's modular law for subgroups and that item 6 is the categorical statement of which the group theorem is an instance. Do not restate the group proof.

items.title: A subobject lattice of an abelian category need not be distributive
items.strategy: Work in Ab with $A=(\mathbb Z/2)\oplus(\mathbb Z/2)$ and let $L_1,L_2,L_3$ be its three nonzero proper subobjects. Then $L_i\wedge L_j=0$ and $L_i\vee L_j=A$ for $i\neq j$, so $$L_1\wedge(L_2\vee L_3)=L_1\neq 0=(L_1\wedge L_2)\vee(L_1\wedge L_3).$$ Thus the subobject lattice is the diamond $M_3$ and is not distributive.

items.title: Second isomorphism theorem in an abelian category
items.strategy: Let B and C be subobjects of A. Compare the quotient map B -> A/C with its image in A/C. Its kernel is B ∧ C, its image is the image of B in the quotient, and that image is represented by (B ∨ C)/C. The first isomorphism theorem then yields the canonical isomorphism.

items.title: Direct and inverse image of a subobject
Direct and inverse image of subobjects form a Galois connection
items.strategy: Unpack the definitions. A factorization of the direct image f_*B through C is equivalent, by the image universal property, to a factorization of B through the pullback f^*C; conversely the pullback factorization composes to give the direct-image factorization. This is exactly the adjunction inequality f_*B <= C iff B <= f^*C.

items.title: Inverse image preserves meets and direct image preserves joins
items.strategy: Apply the general order-theoretic fact that right adjoints preserve limits and left adjoints preserve colimits in posets to the Galois connection of item 11. Keep the proof at the level of lattice operations rather than repeating a pullback or image computation.

items.title: Kernel and image are inverse and direct images along a morphism
items.strategy: The pullback of the zero subobject along f is exactly the kernel of f, while the image of the identity subobject of the source along f is exactly the ordinary image of f. This lets later pages move between image-kernel language and subobject-language without a second argument.

items.title: Simple object
Composition series and composition factors of an object
Zassenhaus butterfly lemma in an abelian category
items.strategy: Form the usual butterfly from pairs of subobjects in a common ambient object. Use modular-lattice interval comparisons for the refinement pattern, then identify the relevant interval factors as quotient objects via item 9 and the third isomorphism theorem. This keeps the proof honestly split between lattice structure and quotient identification.

items.title: Schreier refinement theorem in an abelian category
items.strategy: Run the standard modular-lattice refinement argument for two finite subobject chains, using item 16 to identify the corresponding refined factors up to isomorphism. The theorem is stated for arbitrary finite subobject chains, not only composition series.

items.title: Jordan-Hölder theorem in an abelian category
items.strategy: Apply Schreier refinement to two composition series. Because each factor is simple, an equivalent refinement can only repeat the original factors up to permutation and isomorphism, so both length and factor multiset are determined.

items.title: Object of finite length
Length is additive along a subobject
items.strategy: Given B <= A, concatenate a composition series for B with the pullback of a composition series for A/B along the quotient map A -> A/B. Items 9 and 18 identify the factors and show that the resulting chain in A is a composition series, so the lengths add.

items.title: Objects of finite length form an abelian subcategory
items.strategy: Show first that subobjects and quotients of a finite-length object inherit finite composition series by restriction and quotienting. Then use item 19a to prove the extension clause: if B and A/B have finite length, the concatenated chain in A has finite length as well. The result is stated as closure under kernels, cokernels, and biproducts inside the ambient abelian category.

items.title: The published group composition-series development is the instance
items.strategy: Record that the group page already contains the subgroup versions of the butterfly, Schreier, and Jordan-Hölder theorems together with the group definition of composition length. The categorical page cites them as instances and does not reopen the group proofs.

items.title: Generator and cogenerator of a category
The axioms AB3 and AB3*
The cancellation and epimorphism descriptions of a generator agree
items.strategy: Assume AB3 so that the coproduct over Hom(G, A) exists. If G is a generator, form the canonical map from that coproduct to A and show its cokernel must vanish, since any nonzero quotient would admit a map from G contradicting the construction. Conversely, if every such canonical map is epic, then unequal morphisms are separated after precomposition by a map from G.

items.title: A locally small abelian category with a generator is well-powered
items.strategy: For a subobject A' -> A, identify Hom(G, A') with its image inside Hom(G, A). If two subobjects induce the same subset, the generator property forces them to coincide. Since Hom(G, A) is a set, the set of its subsets bounds the subobjects of A.

items.title: Generator, separator, and the three inequivalent-looking definitions
items.strategy: Record that the library's definition is the separating one from the adjoint-functor page, while Grothendieck and the Stacks Project use the subobject form and Freyd the faithfulness of Hom(G,-). Item 23 is exactly the theorem that reconciles them under the stated cocompleteness hypothesis, so the remark is convention bookkeeping rather than a second proof.

items.title: A cocomplete locally small abelian category with a generator satisfies the SAFT hypotheses dually, once representatives are supplied
items.strategy: Item 24 gives well-poweredness, while the kernel-cokernel anti-isomorphism between subobjects and quotient objects transfers this to co-well-poweredness. The generator supplies the separating side through item 22. The only extra datum named explicitly is a chosen representative family for each set of subobject classes when intersections are invoked.

items.title: A generator detects equality of subobjects
items.strategy: If B <= C then factorization through B obviously implies factorization through C. Conversely, if B is not below C, then B ∧ C is a proper subobject of B. Applying the generator property inside B yields a map from G to B that does not factor through B ∧ C, hence after composing into A it factors through B but not through C.

items.title: The axioms AB4 and AB4*
The axioms AB5 and AB5*
AB5 implies AB4
items.strategy: Apply AB5 to the directed family of finite partial coproduct images inside a coproduct of monomorphisms. Intersecting that directed join with any summand reduces to the same summand, forcing the coproduct map itself to remain monic.

items.title: Grothendieck category
Module categories are Grothendieck categories
items.strategy: Use the ring R as generator and item 23's canonical-epimorphism characterization. AB3 holds because R-Mod is cocomplete, and AB5 holds because filtered colimits of modules are computed on underlying sets and preserve exactness. Package these into the definition of a Grothendieck category.

items.title: Abelian groups satisfy AB4*
items.strategy: A product of monomorphisms of abelian groups is coordinatewise injective. Therefore products preserve kernels of quotient maps in Ab, which is exactly the AB4* condition in this primitive formulation.

items.title: Abelian groups do not satisfy AB5*
items.strategy: Take A = product_{n>=1} Z, let T_n be the subgroup of sequences whose first n coordinates vanish, and let B be the direct sum of countably many copies of Z inside A. Then intersection_n T_n = 0, but T_n + B = A for every n, so (intersection_n T_n) + B = B while intersection_n(T_n + B) = A. This violates the AB5* lattice identity.

items.title: A nonzero abelian category cannot satisfy both AB5 and AB5*
items.strategy: Follow Weibel's Exercise A.4.7 route: use a countable family built from a nonzero object and compare the two exactness behaviors forced by AB5 and AB5*. If the direct proof does not close cleanly at authoring time, this item is the designated conversion point to a sourced recorded-not-proved remark naming the exercise.

items.title: The opposite of abelian groups does not satisfy AB5
items.strategy: By item 34, Ab fails AB5*. Passing to the opposite category exchanges AB5 and AB5*, so Ab^op fails AB5. State the example explicitly to make the dual failure concrete.

items.title: Projective object
Characterisations of projective objects
items.strategy: Show that exactness of Hom(P,-) is equivalent to the lifting property against epimorphisms by unpacking surjectivity on Hom sets. Then apply the lifting property to the identity on P to characterize projectives by splitting every epimorphism onto P.

items.title: Injective object
Characterisations of injective objects
items.strategy: Pass item 37 to the opposite abelian category. The extension property against monomorphisms, exactness of Hom(-,I), and splitting of every monomorphism out of I are exactly the dual statements.

items.title: A coproduct of projectives is projective, and a product of injectives is injective
items.strategy: For a family of projectives, a map from the coproduct is the same as a family of maps from each summand; choose lifts componentwise across the target epimorphism and assemble them. Dualize in the opposite category for injectives and record that the arbitrary-family case uses one chosen lift or extension per index.

items.title: A direct summand of a projective is projective
items.strategy: If P = Q ⊕ Q' is projective and an epimorphism targets Q, precompose with the split inclusion Q -> P, lift across the epimorphism using projectivity of P, and postcompose with the split retraction P -> Q. The composite is the required lift for Q.

items.title: A category with enough projectives and enough injectives
Module categories have enough projectives
items.strategy: Every module is a quotient of a free module, and free modules are projective. Combine the published quotient theorem with the projective-module characterisation to package the result at the level of the ambient category R-Mod.

items.title: Module categories have enough injectives is already published
items.strategy: Cite the published enough-injectives and Baer-criterion theorems for modules, and record explicitly that this page does not claim the deeper theorem that every Grothendieck category has enough injectives.

items.title: A projective generator detects isomorphisms
items.strategy: Because P is a generator, Hom(P,-) is faithful; because P is projective, Hom(P,-) is exact. If Hom(P,f) is an isomorphism, exactness forces Hom(P,ker f) = 0 = Hom(P,coker f), and faithfulness forces ker f = 0 = coker f. Hence f is both monic and epic and therefore an isomorphism in an abelian category.

items.title: FALSE: the subobject lattice of an abelian category is distributive
items.strategy: Refute the statement with item 8's diamond subobject lattice in (Z/2) ⊕ (Z/2). The refutation should also say explicitly that modularity from item 6 is weaker than distributivity.

items.title: FALSE: every abelian category has a generator
items.strategy: Refute the statement with the abelian category of finite abelian groups. Any single finite abelian group has bounded exponent and only finitely many prime divisors, so it cannot separate all morphisms involving cyclic groups of unrelated prime-power order. The point is that the generator hypothesis in item 31 is a genuine size condition.

items.title: FALSE: every object of an abelian category has a composition series
items.strategy: Use Z in Ab. Its only nonzero subobjects are nZ, none of whose quotients yield a finite composition series beginning at 0, so the statement fails even in the basic module example.

items.title: FALSE: AB4 implies AB5
items.strategy: The positive implication on this page is AB5 => AB4, not the converse. Refute the converse with a verified witness at authoring time; the scaffold keeps the statement present so that the proof must either supply the witness or convert this row into a sourced remark naming the failure.

items.title: FALSE: a generator is the same thing as a projective generator
items.strategy: Refute the statement in Ab by taking Z ⊕ Z/p. It is a generator because it contains Z as a summand, but it is not projective because the Z/p summand is not. This separates the generator and projective hypotheses used together in item 44.

items.title: FALSE: Jordan-Hölder needs only a finiteness hypothesis on the category
items.strategy: Refute the statement by contrasting a finite-length object with Z in the same abelian category Ab. The hypothesis that matters is on the object having a composition series, exactly as items 18 and 19 state.

pages.title: Subobject Lattices Generators and the Grothendieck Axioms — Examples

items.title: The subobject lattice of a cyclic group of order twelve
items.strategy: Identify subgroups of C12 with divisors of 12. The example exhibits explicitly how meet, join, and modularity reduce to gcd and lcm in a familiar lattice that is distributive, unlike the diamond example on the A page.

items.title: The subobject lattice of a two-dimensional vector space
items.strategy: Work with a two-dimensional vector space over a field and list its zero subspace, its one-dimensional lines, and the whole space. This gives a second concrete modular-not-necessarily-distributive picture and shows how the diamond appears already in linear algebra over F2.

items.title: The Galois connection of images and preimages for a module homomorphism
items.strategy: Choose a concrete module homomorphism, compute direct images and pullback submodules on a short list of subobjects, and verify the adjunction inequality f_*B <= C iff B <= f^*C on each pair. Keep the example finite enough that the lattice operations are visible by hand.

items.title: Two composition series of a module refined
items.strategy: Pick a finite-length module with two visible composition chains, refine them explicitly, and match the simple factors. The goal is to show the Schreier and Jordan-Hölder statements as calculations rather than as abstract lattice theorems alone.

items.title: The ring as a generator of its module category
items.strategy: Show directly that maps from R into a left R-module M are in bijection with elements of M, so the canonical coproduct map from copies of R indexed by M onto M is the obvious surjection. This is the concrete content behind item 32.

items.title: The category of finite abelian groups has no nonzero projective object
items.strategy: Substitute the denied sheaf example with the abelian category of finite abelian groups. Any nonzero projective there would have a nonzero simple quotient Z/p; splitting that quotient would make Z/p projective, but the epimorphism Z/p^2 -> Z/p does not split. Hence no nonzero projective object exists.

items.title: A directed union of subgroups meeting a fixed subgroup
items.strategy: Take an increasing chain of subgroups in an abelian group and compute both sides of the AB5 lattice identity with a fixed subgroup. The example shows the directed-union form of AB5 in the concrete module case that item 32 packages abstractly.

items.title: Length computed for a finite abelian group
items.strategy: Choose a finite abelian group in invariant-factor or primary decomposition form, write a composition series explicitly, and compute its length as the total multiplicity of simple p-primary factors. Then verify item 19a on a visible subobject.

pages.title: Exactness and the Member Calculus

items.title: The subobject inequalities underlying exactness
items.strategy: Factor f as an epimorphism followed by a monomorphism m. The implication gf = 0 forces m to factor through ker g, while the converse is immediate from the kernel universal property; the dual inequality is then exactly the universal factorization condition through m.

items.title: Exactness at a node
The arrow-theoretic criterion for exactness
items.strategy: Translate im(f) = ker(g) into the statement that gf = 0 and that the kernel inclusion of g is also the cokernel kernel comparison for f. The reverse direction packages the two arrow equalities back into the image-kernel comparison from item 1.

items.title: Exact sequence and short exact sequence in an abelian category
A short exact sequence is a kernel-cokernel pair
items.strategy: Apply item 3 to the sequence 0 -> A -> B -> C -> 0. The endpoint zeros identify the left arrow as the kernel of the right arrow and, by the dual criterion, the right arrow as the cokernel of the left arrow.

items.title: Degenerate exactness criteria
items.strategy: Specialize item 5 and its one-sided halves to the cases where one or both endpoints are zero. The bridge from exactness to monic or epic uses the published zero-kernel and zero-cokernel characterizations in abelian categories.

items.title: Exactness is self-dual
items.strategy: Pass the defining equality im(f) = ker(g) to the opposite category, where image and coimage as well as kernel and cokernel are interchanged. The opposite of an abelian category is abelian, so the same definition applies on both sides.

items.title: Split short exact sequence in an abelian category
Splitting lemma in an abelian category
items.strategy: Starting from a section or retraction, use the kernel-cokernel description of a short exact sequence to construct the missing projection or section. The biproduct equations then show the five-tuple is a direct sum, and uniqueness follows by composing with the defining injections and projections.

items.title: FALSE: a short exact sequence splits whenever its middle object is isomorphic to the biproduct of the outer two
items.strategy: Refute the statement with the stabilized nonsplit extension over k[eps]/(eps^2) described in the design notes. The point of the witness is that an abstract isomorphism of objects does not supply the compatible section or retraction demanded by item 9.

items.title: Member of an object
Equivalence of members
Member equivalence is reflexive and symmetric
items.strategy: Reflexivity uses the identity epimorphism on the member domain, and symmetry just swaps the two comparison maps. The point of separating this from item 14 is to isolate the sole nonformal use of abelian exactness there.

items.title: Member equivalence is transitive
items.strategy: Given xu = yv and yw = zr with u, v, w, r epic, form the pullback of v and w. The induced legs remain epic by the pullback-of-an-epi theorem, and the two comparison equations then exhibit x and z as equivalent over the pullback object.

items.title: Members modulo equivalence correspond to subobjects
items.strategy: Factor each member through its epi-mono factorization and assign to it the represented subobject. Equivalent members have mutually factoring monic parts, while every subobject is represented by its own monomorphism viewed as a member.

items.title: Each object has a zero member and each member has a negative
items.strategy: The zero arrow into an object is a member, and the additive inverse of any arrow gives the negative member. If x is equivalent to zero, then cancel the witnessing epimorphism to conclude that x itself is the zero arrow.

items.title: A morphism carries members to members and preserves equivalence
items.strategy: Postcompose the representative arrows with the morphism. Any witnessing pair of epimorphisms for x equiv y still witnesses fx equiv fy because the defining square remains commutative after composition.

items.title: Monicity is detected by members
items.strategy: If f is monic and fx is equivalent to zero, cancel the common comparison to show x is zero. Conversely, test the stated property on the member given by the equalizer of a parallel pair to recover left cancellability.

items.title: Monicity by member cancellation
items.strategy: Apply item 18 to the difference of two members after transporting them to a common domain. The reverse implication is immediate by setting one member to zero.

items.title: Epimorphy is detected by members
items.strategy: Translate the existence of a preimage member for every member of the codomain into the statement that every member-subobject of the codomain lies in im(g). By item 15, that means the image subobject is the whole codomain, hence g is epic.

items.title: A zero arrow is detected by members
items.strategy: One direction is immediate from preservation of equivalence. For the converse, apply the hypothesis to the identity member 1_r : r -> r and use item 16 to convert equivalence to the zero member into literal equality of arrows.

items.title: Exactness is detected by members
items.strategy: Use item 15 to identify a member y of b with the subobject represented by its image. The condition gy equiv 0 means that subobject lies in ker g, and the existence of x with fx equiv y says the same subobject lies in im f; item 1 then converts this to exactness.

items.title: The subtraction surrogate
items.strategy: Choose a common epic comparison domain with gxu = gyv, and define z = yv - xu on that domain. Then gz = 0 by additivity, and the two moreover clauses come from substituting z into any morphism that already kills x or y.

items.title: What the subtraction rule does not say
items.strategy: Record the three failure modes the designer called out: z is not unique, members have no ambient subtraction law, and the rule constrains z only through morphisms already killing x or y. The remark exists to stop later pages from silently reintroducing element arithmetic.

items.title: The members of an object do not form a group
items.strategy: Work in Ab and use the identity member of Z. Item 16 shows every member is equivalent to its negative, but 2 * 1_Z is not equivalent to zero, so no group law on equivalence classes can be inferred from the ambient additive structure on arrows.

items.title: Two morphisms agreeing on every member need not be equal
items.strategy: Again in Ab, compare 1_Z and -1_Z. Every member x : X -> Z is equivalent to -x after precomposition with -1_X, but the two endomorphisms of Z are distinct, so memberwise agreement is weaker than equality.

items.title: The cost of the member calculus
items.strategy: State the exact proof inputs honestly: finite limits and colimits together with the pullback-of-an-epi theorem from MA-8. The remark also records what is not used and avoids the unsupported stronger claim that the method is constructive.

items.title: A square is cartesian exactly when a short sequence is exact
items.strategy: Encode a commutative square over f and g as the kernel diagram of (f, -g) on the biproduct X oplus Y. The pullback universal property and the kernel universal property are then the same statement, with the sign needed to express commutativity as vanishing.

items.title: A cartesian square induces an isomorphism on the kernels of its parallel legs
items.strategy: Apply the published kernel-isomorphism theorem to a pullback square, or rederive it from item 28 by comparing the two short exact sequences attached to the square. This is the exact-sequence form later diagram chases quote.

items.title: A cartesian square over an epimorphism is also cocartesian
items.strategy: Use item 28 to identify the square with a short exact sequence on the left, then use epicity of the parallel leg to make the right-hand comparison map a cokernel as well. This recovers the pushout statement without leaving the exact-sequence language.

items.title: Epimorphisms in an abelian category are universal
items.strategy: This is the pullback stability of epimorphisms from MA-8, restated as a named property because items 28, 30, 32, and the next page cite it as such.

items.title: The covering criterion for exactness
items.strategy: Translate the covering condition into the exactness of the pullback sequence supplied by item 28, and use item 31 to transport the needed epimorphism through the pullback. The reverse implication is just the pullback construction attached to a kernel comparison.

items.title: The covering criterion and the member calculus are the same tool
items.strategy: Record explicitly that a member is an arrow into the object and that equivalence of members is agreement after precomposition by epimorphisms. This identifies item 32 with item 22 stripped of notation and licenses both idioms on the next page.

items.title: The kernel row and cokernel row of a morphism of short exact sequences are exact at two nodes each
items.strategy: Build the relevant pullback squares from the morphism of short exact sequences and use items 28 and 29 to read off the first two exact nodes in the kernel row. The cokernel row follows by duality through item 7.

items.title: The kernel row of a morphism of short exact sequences need not be short exact
items.strategy: Compute the kernel row for the vertical morphism (2, 2, 0) on two copies of 0 -> Z -> Z -> Z/2 -> 0. The first two exactness nodes survive as item 34 predicts, but the last arrow is not epic and the snake connecting morphism is the missing Z/2 -> Z/2 isomorphism.

items.title: Exactness of kernel and cokernel sequences under endpoint hypotheses
items.strategy: Apply the covering criterion to the kernel sequence in the presence of a monic left endpoint, and dualize for the cokernel sequence when the right endpoint is epic. The statement is kept with all letters displayed because later diagram-lemma proofs cite it by shape.

items.title: The kernel-cokernel sequence of a composite
items.strategy: Apply item 36 to the natural morphism between the two short exact sequences attached to f and gf, and then to gf and g. Splicing the resulting exact rows produces the six-term exact sequence for the composite.

items.title: Comember and the dual calculus
Two routes to every dual statement
items.strategy: Record that one may either dualize a member argument through item 7 or run the comember calculus directly. The remark exists so the next page can cite a deliberate choice rather than silently swap methods mid-proof.

items.title: Hom is left exact in each variable
items.strategy: Representable functors preserve all existing small limits, hence kernels. Therefore a short left exact sequence stays left exact after applying Hom(x, -); the contravariant variable follows by passing to the opposite abelian category.

items.title: Hom is not exact
items.strategy: Reuse the standard sequence 0 -> Z -> Z -> Z/2 -> 0 as a concrete short exact sequence in Ab and apply Hom_Z(-, Z) inside the abelian-category setting. The example keeps the same witness as the published module counterexample, but does not depend on a B-page item from another page.

items.title: An object is projective exactly when Hom out of it is exact
items.strategy: Combine the lifting characterization of projective objects with item 40 to upgrade left exactness to exactness precisely when epimorphisms are sent to surjections. The injective half is the dual statement in the opposite category.

items.title: AB5 is equivalent to exactness of filtered colimits
items.strategy: Use the AB5 lattice law to show filtered colimits preserve kernels and hence exact sequences, and conversely apply exactness of filtered colimits to the filtered system of finite partial joins of a directed family of subobjects. The statement keeps all small filtered index categories explicit and does not replace them by directed posets without proof.

items.title: FALSE: two morphisms that agree on every member are equal
items.strategy: Item 26 is the direct refutation. Item 21 remains the only legitimate member-based equality test, and only against zero.

items.title: FALSE: the members of an object form an abelian group
items.strategy: Item 25 supplies the witness in Ab. The failure is structural: the subtraction surrogate of item 23 is weaker than a binary operation on member classes.

items.title: FALSE: member equivalence is transitive in any pointed category with pullbacks
items.strategy: Refute the statement by pointing back to item 14: the proof spends the pullback stability of epimorphisms, not just the existence of pullbacks. The false statement exists so later authoring cannot quietly weaken that hypothesis.

items.title: FALSE: the kernel row of a morphism of short exact sequences is short exact
items.strategy: Item 35 gives the explicit multiplication-by-two witness. The positive theorem is only the two-node exactness of item 34, and the missing third exactness is exactly what the snake lemma repairs on the next page.

items.title: FALSE: the subtraction rule produces a unique member
items.strategy: Refute the statement with item 24's nonuniqueness warning. The surrogate only guarantees existence of a suitable z, not a canonical difference object.

items.title: FALSE: exactness can be defined without first producing a canonical monomorphism
items.strategy: Item 1 is the refutation: the comparison im(f) -> ker(g) is not ambient data but must be constructed from gf = 0. Without that arrow there is no well-typed equality of subobjects to call exactness.

pages.title: Exactness and the Member Calculus — Examples

items.title: Members of an abelian group correspond to its subgroups
items.strategy: Identify a member x : X -> A with its image subgroup im(x) in the ordinary sense, and compare member equivalence with equality of image subgroups. This is the concrete Ab instance of item 15.

items.title: An ordinary element as the member from the integers
items.strategy: For an abelian group A and element a in A, view a as the morphism Z -> A sending 1 to a. The example shows how ordinary elements embed into the member formalism without exhausting it.

items.title: A general member of an abelian group need not come from an element
items.strategy: Use the identity morphism of Z^2 as a member of Z^2. Its image is noncyclic, so it cannot factor through Z and therefore cannot arise from a single ordinary element.

items.title: A member chase verifying monicity

items.title: The kernel-cokernel sequence of a composite of module maps

items.title: A non-split short exact sequence of abelian groups

pages.title: The Erdős–Hajnal Property and Homogeneous Sets

items.title: Homogeneous vertex sets and the homogeneous number $\operatorname{hom}(G)=\max{\omega(G),\alpha(G)}$
The Erdős–Hajnal property and an Erdős–Hajnal constant for a hereditary graph class
Every smaller positive exponent is again an Erdős–Hajnal constant
items.strategy: Let $0<\delta\le\epsilon$ and let $G$ be a nonempty graph in the class, with $n=|V(G)|\ge1$. From $\log n\ge0$ and monotonicity of the exponential, deduce $n^\delta\le n^\epsilon$, then apply the defining bound. Treat $n=1$ explicitly so no zero-base real power is invoked.

items.title: Every nonempty $n$-vertex graph satisfies $\operatorname{hom}(G)\ge \tfrac12\log_2 n$
items.strategy: Put $k=\lfloor\tfrac12\log_2 n\rfloor+1$. The published Ramsey bound gives a clique or stable set of size $k$ once $n\ge\binom{2k-2}{k-1}$. Bound the middle binomial coefficient by the total number $2^{2k-2}$ of subsets of a $(2k-2)$-set, and use $2k-2\le\log_2 n$. Conclude $\operatorname{hom}(G)\ge k>\tfrac12\log_2 n$, including $n=1$.

items.title: For every $t\ge1$, the class of $K_t$-free graphs has the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: For $t=1$ the class has no nonempty member, and for $t=2$ every member is empty. Let $t\ge3$. For all sufficiently large $n$, choose $s=\lfloor\tfrac12 n^{1/(t-1)}\rfloor$ with $s\ge t-2$. Apply the published Ramsey theorem with parameters $t,s$: since $\binom{t+s-2}{t-1}\le(t+s-2)^{t-1}\le(2s)^{t-1}\le n$, every $K_t$-free $n$-vertex graph has a stable set of size at least $s$. For large $n$, $s\ge n^{1/t}$. Reduce the positive exponent if necessary so that the finite initial range is covered by the elementary bound $\operatorname{hom}(G)\ge2$ for $n\ge2$, and treat $n=1$ separately.

items.title: Every $P_3$-free graph $G$ satisfies $\operatorname{hom}(G)\ge\sqrt{|V(G)|}$
items.strategy: If two nonadjacent vertices lie in one connected component, take a shortest path between them. Its first three vertices induce $P_3$: consecutive vertices are adjacent, while an edge joining the first and third would shorten the path. Hence every component is a clique. If the component orders are $c_1,\ldots,c_r$, then $\omega(G)\ge\max_i c_i$, while one vertex from each component is a stable set and gives $\alpha(G)\ge r$. Therefore $|V(G)|=\sum_i c_i\le r\max_i c_i\le\alpha(G)\omega(G)\le\operatorname{hom}(G)^2$. Take nonnegative square roots and identify $\sqrt n=n^{1/2}$; thus the $P_3$-free class has Erdős–Hajnal constant $1/2$.

items.title: For every $n\ge16$ there is an $n$-vertex graph with $\operatorname{hom}(G)<3\log_2 n$
items.strategy: Take $G\sim G(n,1/2)$ and $k=\lceil3\log_2 n\rceil$. Let $X$ count $k$-subsets inducing either a clique or a stable set. For each subset the probability is $2\cdot2^{-\binom{k}{2}}$, so linearity gives $\mathbb E X=2\binom nk2^{-\binom{k}{2}}\le2n^k2^{-k(k-1)/2}<1$; verify the last exponent inequality from $\log_2 n\ge4$. The first-moment method gives $X=0$, and every larger homogeneous set would contain a homogeneous $k$-subset, so $\operatorname{hom}(G)\le k-1<3\log_2n$.

items.title: The hereditary class of all finite graphs does not have the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Assume an exponent $\epsilon>0$ works for every graph. The logarithm-versus-power limit makes $3\log_2n<n^\epsilon$ for all sufficiently large $n$; choose such an $n\ge16$ and contradict the random-graph upper-bound theorem. Spell out the harmless change from natural to base-two logarithm.

items.title: A hereditary class has the Erdős–Hajnal property exactly when its complementary class does, with the same constants
items.strategy: Complementation bijects the two classes and swaps cliques with stable sets, hence preserves $\operatorname{hom}$. Apply the defining inequality in each direction, using that complementation is an involution. Record the fixed-pattern consequence: $H$ and $\overline H$ have the same Erdős–Hajnal constants.

items.title: Every graph on at most three vertices has the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Up to isomorphism and complementation, a graph on at most three vertices is one of $K_1,K_2,K_3$, or $P_3$. The complete cases have the property by the $K_t$-free theorem, the path case has exponent $1/2$, and complement invariance supplies their complements. Check the null pattern separately if graphs of order zero are admitted by the final Statement.

items.title: The Erdős–Hajnal property and each of its constants pass to hereditary subclasses
items.strategy: If $\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal C$, every nonempty graph tested for $\mathcal D$ is already tested for $\mathcal C$. Restrict the same inequality and keep the exponent unchanged.

items.title: If $H$ is an induced subgraph of $H'$ and $H'$ has the Erdős–Hajnal property, then $H$ has it with every constant of $H'$
items.strategy: Composition of induced embeddings shows that every $H$-free graph is $H'$-free when $H$ embeds inducedly in $H'$. Thus the $H$-free class is a hereditary subclass of the $H'$-free class; apply subclass monotonicity. State the direction carefully, since reversing this inclusion is a common error.

items.title: The single-forbidden-graph and finite-nonempty-family formulations of the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture are equivalent
items.strategy: For the forward direction, given a finite nonempty family $\mathcal F$, choose $H\in\mathcal F$; every $\mathcal F$-free graph is $H$-free, so the single-pattern assertion and subclass monotonicity supply an exponent. For the reverse direction apply the family assertion to the singleton family ${H}$. Make clear that this is an equivalence between two universally quantified conjectures, not an equivalence for one fixed family and each of its members.

items.title: The Erdős–Hajnal conjecture: every fixed forbidden induced graph admits a positive exponent

pages.title: The Erdős–Hajnal Property and Homogeneous Sets — Examples

items.title: $K_n$ and $\overline K_n$ both have homogeneous number $n$
items.strategy: Compute $\omega$ and $\alpha$ directly in the two graphs, including $n=0$, and take their maximum.

items.title: For positive $a,b$, $\operatorname{hom}(K_{a,b})=\max{2,a,b}$
items.strategy: A clique contains at most one vertex from each side and an edge supplies a 2-clique, while a stable set lies in one side and either whole side works. Take the larger of the clique and stability numbers; keep both sides nonempty as stated.

items.title: The self-complementary five-cycle satisfies $\operatorname{hom}(C_5)=2$
items.strategy: Exhibit an edge and a nonedge, then show every three vertices in a five-cycle contain both an edge and a nonedge. Give an explicit isomorphism from $C_5$ to its complement to illustrate complement invariance.

items.title: The classes of complete graphs and of empty graphs have Erdős–Hajnal constant $1$
items.strategy: Each nonempty graph in either class has homogeneous number equal to its order, so the defining inequality holds with exponent $1$. Check heredity under induced subgraphs and use complementation to relate the two examples.

items.title: Every hereditary graph class of bounded order has the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Let $\mathcal C$ be hereditary, and suppose every graph in $\mathcal C$ has at most $N$ vertices. Choose a positive exponent $\epsilon$ with $N^\epsilon\le2$ when $N\ge2$. Every nonempty graph has a homogeneous set of size at least one, and every graph with at least two vertices has one of size at least two. Handle $N\le1$ separately.

items.title: Forbidding $P_3$ and forbidding $\overline{P_3}$ have the same Erdős–Hajnal constants
items.strategy: Identify $\overline{P_3}$ as an edge plus an isolated vertex, apply the forbidden-pattern complement dictionary, and then apply complement invariance of homogeneous number and EH constants.

items.title: The universal logarithmic Ramsey guarantee cannot be replaced by any universal positive power
items.strategy: Fix $\epsilon>0$, choose $n$ large enough that $3\log_2n<n^\epsilon$, and invoke the constructed $n$-vertex graph with homogeneous number below $3\log_2n$. This supplies a counterexample for every proposed universal exponent.

items.title: Every hereditary graph class has the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Refute the statement with the hereditary class of all finite graphs and the published corollary showing that this class has no positive EH exponent.

pages.title: Modules, Substitution and Prime Graphs

items.title: Modules of a graph, and the trivial modules
Three equivalent descriptions of a module: purity of every outside vertex, equality of outside neighbourhoods, and indistinguishability of the members
items.strategy: Prove (i) implies (ii) implies (iii) implies (i) in a cycle. (i) says every $v\notin M$ is complete or anticomplete to $M$; (ii) says $N(x)\setminus M=N(y)\setminus M$ for all $x,y\in M$; (iii) says $vx\in E$ iff $vy\in E$ for all $x,y\in M$ and $v\notin M$. Each implication is a direct rewriting of the quantifiers; the empty module and the singletons satisfy all three vacuously.

items.title: A vertex set is a module of $G$ exactly when it is a module of $\overline G$
items.strategy: For $v\notin M$ the pair $(\{v\},M)$ is disjoint, so complementation exchanges complete with anticomplete and preserves purity. Apply the criterion of the module lemma in both directions, using $\overline{\overline G}=G$.

items.title: Every union of connected components is a module, and so is every union of anticonnected components
items.strategy: Let $M$ be a union of components and $v\notin M$. The component of $v$ is disjoint from every component inside $M$, and distinct components are anticomplete, so $v$ is anticomplete to $M$. For anticomponents, distinct anticomponents are complete, so $v$ is complete to $M$; alternatively read the first statement in $\overline G$ and apply complement invariance.

items.title: Two disjoint nonempty modules form a complete or an anticomplete pair
items.strategy: Let $M,N$ be disjoint nonempty modules. Every $x\in M$ lies outside $N$, so $x$ is complete or anticomplete to $N$. If some $x$ were complete and some $x'$ anticomplete, pick $y\in N$: then $yx\in E$ and $yx'\notin E$, contradicting that $y\notin M$ is pure to $M$. So all vertices of $M$ agree, giving $(M,N)$ complete or anticomplete.

items.title: The intersection of two modules is a module
items.strategy: Take $v\notin M\cap N$. Either $v\notin M$, and then $v$ is pure to $M\supseteq M\cap N$, or $v\in M\setminus N$, and then $v$ is pure to $N\supseteq M\cap N$. Purity to a set passes to its subsets. No overlap hypothesis is needed, and the empty intersection is a module.

items.title: The union of two modules with a common vertex is a module
items.strategy: Let $u\in M\cap N$ and $v\notin M\cup N$. Then $v$ is pure to $M$ and pure to $N$, and both sides are decided by whether $vu\in E$: if $vu\in E$ then $v$ is complete to $M$ and to $N$, otherwise anticomplete to both. Hence $v$ is pure to $M\cup N$.

items.title: If two modules overlap, then each difference and their symmetric difference are modules
items.strategy: Overlap means $M\cap N$, $M\setminus N$ and $N\setminus M$ are all nonempty. For $M\setminus N$: a vertex outside $M$ is pure to $M$, hence to $M\setminus N$; a vertex $v\in M\cap N$ is handled by picking $w\in N\setminus M$ and chaining $x\sim v\iff x\sim w\iff x'\sim w\iff x'\sim v$ for $x,x'\in M\setminus N$, where the outer equivalences use purity of $x,x'$ to $N$ and the middle one purity of $w$ to $M$. The symmetric difference uses the same chain to show a vertex of $M\cap N$ treats $M\setminus N$ and $N\setminus M$ the same way. The overlap hypothesis is necessary: it fails for nested modules.

items.title: If $M$ is a module of $G$ and $W\subseteq V(G)$, then $M\cap W$ is a module of $G[W]$
items.strategy: A vertex $v\in W\setminus M$ lies outside $M$, so it is complete or anticomplete to $M$ in $G$; adjacency in $G[W]$ is the restriction of adjacency in $G$, so the same holds towards $M\cap W$ inside $G[W]$.

items.title: A module of $G[M]$ is a module of $G$ whenever $M$ is a module of $G$
items.strategy: Let $X\subseteq M$ be a module of $G[M]$ and $v\notin X$. If $v\in M\setminus X$ then purity comes from $X$ being a module of $G[M]$; if $v\notin M$ then $v$ is pure to $M$, hence to the subset $X$.

items.title: In a connected graph, some vertex outside a nonempty proper module is complete to it
items.strategy:
Let $\varnothing
e M\subsetneq V(G)$ be a module of a connected $G$. Take $u\in M$ and $w
otin M$; a path from $u$ to $w$ leaves $M$ at some edge, giving $x\in M$ and $v
otin M$ adjacent. Then $v$ is not anticomplete to $M$, so it is complete to $M$.

items.title: Prime graphs: those whose only modules are the trivial ones
No graph on exactly three vertices is prime
items.strategy: On three vertices a nontrivial module is a two-element set. Count edges: with $0$ or $3$ edges every pair is a module; with exactly one edge the two ends of that edge form a module; with exactly two edges the two vertices of degree one form a module. These four cases are exhaustive up to isomorphism, and the conclusion is invariant under isomorphism.

items.title: Substituting one graph for a vertex of another
In $G_1$ with $G_2$ substituted for $a$, the vertex set of $G_2$ is a module, the two factors are recovered as induced subgraphs, and substituting a one-vertex graph changes nothing
items.strategy: Write $G=G_1[a\to G_2]$. A vertex $u\in V(G_1)\setminus\{a\}$ is adjacent in $G$ to every vertex of $V(G_2)$ if $ua\in E(G_1)$ and to none otherwise, which is exactly the module condition. The restriction of $G$ to $V(G_1)\setminus\{a\}$ is $G_1-a$ by the second clause of the definition, the restriction to $V(G_2)$ is $G_2$ by the third, and for any $w\in V(G_2)$ sending $a\mapsto w$ and fixing the rest is an isomorphism $G_1\to G[(V(G_1)\setminus\{a\})\cup\{w\}]$. Taking $|V(G_2)|=1$ gives $G\cong G_1$.

items.title: The complement of $G_1[a\to G_2]$ is $\overline{G_1}[a\to\overline{G_2}]$
items.strategy: Both graphs have the same vertex set. Compare the three kinds of pair separately: two vertices of $V(G_1)\setminus\{a\}$, two vertices of $V(G_2)$, and one of each. In each case adjacency in the complement of the substitution and adjacency in the substitution of the complements are the negations of the same condition.

items.title: A graph with at least two vertices is prime exactly when it is not obtained by substituting one graph on at least two vertices for a vertex of another graph on at least two vertices
items.strategy: If $G\cong G_1[a\to G_2]$ with $|V(G_1)|,|V(G_2)|\ge2$, then $V(G_2)$ is a module of size between $2$ and $|V(G)|-1$, so $G$ is not prime. Conversely, given a module $M$ with $2\le|M|\le|V(G)|-1$, fix $x\in M$, put $G_2=G[M]$ and $G_1=G[(V(G)\setminus M)\cup\{x\}]$, and check the four clauses of the substitution definition using purity of each outside vertex to $M$. Both factors then have at least two vertices.

items.title: Modular partitions and the quotient graph they define
For a modular partition, a set of parts is a module of the quotient exactly when the union of those parts is a module of the graph
items.strategy: Write $\mathcal P=\{M_1,\dots,M_k\}$ and $X\subseteq[k]$, and let $U=\bigcup_{i\in X}M_i$. A vertex outside $U$ lies in some $M_j$ with $j\notin X$, and by disjoint purity its adjacency to each $M_i$ is constant on $M_i$; so $v$ is pure to $U$ exactly when $j$ is complete or anticomplete to $X$ in the quotient. Quantifying over all $j\notin X$ gives the equivalence in both directions.

items.title: A graph is recovered from any modular partition by the induced subgraphs on the parts together with the quotient graph
items.strategy: For $x\in M_i$ and $y\in M_j$ with $i\ne j$, disjoint purity makes $xy\in E(G)$ equivalent to $v_iv_j\in E(G/\mathcal P)$; for $i=j$ it is equivalent to $xy\in E(G[M_i])$. That adjacency rule determines $E(G)$, and for $k=2$ it says exactly that $G$ is $ (G/\mathcal P)$ with $G[M_1]$ and $G[M_2]$ substituted for its two vertices.

items.title: The quotient by a modular partition is isomorphic to the subgraph induced by any set meeting each part exactly once
items.strategy: Let $\mathcal P=\{M_1,\dots,M_k\}$ be a modular partition of $G$, pick $t_i\in M_i$ for each $i$ and put $T=\{t_1,\dots,t_k\}$; the $M_i$ are nonempty and finite in number, so the selection is a choice from finitely many nonempty sets and needs no further principle. Send the quotient vertex $v_i$ to $t_i$; this is a bijection onto $T$ because the parts are disjoint. For $i\ne j$ the pair $(M_i,M_j)$ is complete or anticomplete, and $v_iv_j\in E(G/\mathcal P)$ is defined to record which; since $t_i\in M_i$ and $t_j\in M_j$, that is exactly the condition $t_it_j\in E(G)$, so the bijection both preserves and reflects adjacency. Hence $G[T]\cong G/\mathcal P$, and the quotient is isomorphic to an induced subgraph of $G$. For $k=1$ both sides are the one-vertex graph.

items.title: In a connected and anticonnected graph, the union of two proper modules that meet is again a proper module
items.strategy: The union is a module. Suppose $M\cup N=V(G)$ with $M,N$ proper and $M\cap N\ne\varnothing$; then $A=M\setminus N$, $B=N\setminus M$ and $C=M\cap N$ are all nonempty. Purity of each $a\in A$ to $N$ and of each $b\in B$ to $M$, combined as in the disjoint-purity argument, forces $(A,N)$ and $(B,M)$ each to be complete or anticomplete; the mixed choices contradict each other on the pair $(A,B)$. If both are complete then no edge of $\overline G$ joins $A$, $B$ and $C$, so $\overline G$ is disconnected; if both are anticomplete then $G$ is disconnected. Either way a hypothesis fails.

items.title: In a connected and anticonnected graph with at least two vertices, each vertex lies in a largest proper module, and two such modules are equal or disjoint
items.strategy: The singleton $\{v\}$ is a proper module, so the family of proper modules containing $v$ is nonempty and finite. Any two of its members meet at $v$, so their union is again a proper module containing $v$; iterating over the finite family gives that the union $M(v)$ of all of them is a proper module, necessarily the largest one. If $M(u)$ and $M(v)$ meet, their union is a proper module containing both, so maximality forces $M(u)=M(u)\cup M(v)=M(v)$.

items.title: Gallai's modular decomposition theorem: a graph on at least two vertices is disconnected, or has a disconnected complement, or has a modular partition into its maximal proper modules whose quotient is prime
items.strategy: The first two cases exclude each other because a graph on at least two vertices is connected or anticonnected. In the third case the maximal proper modules are pairwise disjoint and cover $V(G)$, so they form a modular partition with $k\ge2$ parts; a nontrivial module of the quotient would pull back to a proper module strictly containing a maximal one, so the quotient is prime. In the first case the components are modules and the quotient by them is edgeless; in the second the anticomponents are modules and that quotient is complete.

items.title: The prime quotient produced by the modular decomposition of a connected and anticonnected graph has at least four vertices
items.strategy: The quotient has $k\ge2$ vertices. If $k=2$ the two parts are complete or anticomplete to each other, making $G$ or $\overline G$ disconnected. If $k=3$ the quotient is a three-vertex graph, which is never prime. So $k\ge4$.

items.title: In a connected and anticonnected graph, a modular partition with at least two parts whose quotient is prime consists of the maximal proper modules
items.strategy: Let $G$ be connected and anticonnected with at least two vertices and let $\mathcal P=\{M_1,\dots,M_k\}$ be a modular partition with $k\ge2$ whose quotient is prime. Each part is then a proper module. If $k=2$ the two parts are disjoint modules, so they are complete or anticomplete to each other and $G$ or $\overline G$ is disconnected, against the hypothesis; and $k=3$ is impossible because no three-vertex graph is prime, so $k\ge4$. Fix $i$ and $x\in M_i$, and let $M(x)$ be the largest proper module containing $x$; then $M_i\subseteq M(x)$. If a part $M_j$ meets $M(x)$, then $M(x)\cup M_j$ is a module, and it is proper because two meeting proper modules of a connected and anticonnected graph have a proper union, so maximality gives $M_j\subseteq M(x)$: that is, $M(x)$ is a union of parts. Its index set is therefore a module of the quotient, hence trivial; it is nonempty and cannot be every part, since $M(x)$ is proper, so it is a single part and $M(x)=M_i$. Every part is thus a maximal proper module, and those partition the vertex set, so $\mathcal P$ is the partition into maximal proper modules and is the only modular partition with at least two parts and a prime quotient. Both hypotheses are used: the edgeless graph on three vertices carries two different two-part modular partitions whose quotients are prime.

items.title: $\operatorname{hom}(G[W])\le\operatorname{hom}(G)$ for every vertex subset $W$
items.strategy: A clique of $G[W]$ is a clique of $G$ and a stable set of $G[W]$ is a stable set of $G$, because $G[W]$ has the induced adjacency. So $\omega(G[W])\le\omega(G)$ and $\alpha(G[W])\le\alpha(G)$, and the maximum of the two is monotone.

items.title: If $\epsilon$ is an Erdős–Hajnal constant for $H$ and $W$ is a nonempty vertex set with $|W|^{\epsilon}>\operatorname{hom}(G)$, then $G[W]$ has an induced copy of $H$
items.strategy: Contrapositive. If $G[W]$ had no induced copy of $H$ it would be a nonempty member of the hereditary class of $H$-free graphs, so $\operatorname{hom}(G[W])\ge|W|^{\epsilon}$; monotonicity of $\operatorname{hom}$ then gives $\operatorname{hom}(G)\ge|W|^{\epsilon}$, contradicting the hypothesis.

items.title: If every $m$-element vertex set contains an induced copy of $H$, then at least $\prod_{i<h}(n-i)/\prod_{i<h}(m-i)$ of the $h$-element vertex sets induce a copy of $H$
items.strategy: Let $h=|V(H)|\ge1$ and $h\le m\le n=|V(G)|$. Double count the pairs $(W,S)$ with $|W|=m$, $S\subseteq W$, $|S|=h$ and $G[S]\cong H$. Every $W$ contributes at least one pair, so the count is at least $\binom nm$; every good $S$ lies in exactly $\binom{n-h}{m-h}$ such $W$, so the count is at most (number of good $S$) times $\binom{n-h}{m-h}$. Dividing and cancelling factorials leaves the stated ratio of falling factorials, which is at least $((n-h+1)/m)^h$.

items.title: The induced copies of $H_1$ in $G$ are counted by summing, over the induced embeddings of $H_1-v$, the number of vertices that extend them at $v$
items.strategy: Restricting an induced embedding of $H_1$ to $V(H_1)\setminus\{v\}$ is an induced embedding of $H_1-v$, and the fibre over a given $\varphi$ is exactly the set of admissible images of $v$. So the relation pairing $\varphi$ with its extensions has row fibres the extension sets and total size $\operatorname{ind}_{H_1}(G)$; double counting gives the identity. The number of induced embeddings of $H_1-v$ is at most the number of injections $V(H_1)\setminus\{v\}\to V(G)$, hence at most $n^{h_1-1}$.

items.title: An induced copy of $H_2$ inside the extension set of an induced embedding of $H_1-v$ yields an induced copy of $H_1$ with $H_2$ substituted for $v$
items.strategy: Combine $\varphi$ on $V(H_1)\setminus\{v\}$ with the embedding $\psi$ of $H_2$ into the extension set. The map is injective because the extension set avoids the image of $\varphi$. Check the three kinds of pair: inside $V(H_1)\setminus\{v\}$ use that $\varphi$ is induced; inside $V(H_2)$ use that $\psi$ is induced; across, use that each vertex of the extension set has, towards the image of $\varphi$, exactly the adjacencies $v$ has in $H_1$, which is the substitution rule.

items.title: Alon–Pach–Solymosi: if $H_1$ and $H_2$ have the Erdős–Hajnal property, so does the graph obtained from $H_1$ by substituting $H_2$ for a vertex
items.strategy: Let $h_1=|V(H_1)|$, let $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2$ be Erdős–Hajnal constants for $H_1,H_2$, put $\beta=1/(2(h_1+1))$ and $\epsilon=\beta\min\{\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2\}$. Suppose $G$ is $H$-free on $n$ vertices with $\operatorname{hom}(G)<n^{\epsilon}$, and let $m$ be the least natural number with $m\ge n^{\beta}$, so $m<n^{\beta}+1$. Since $\beta\epsilon_1\ge\epsilon$, every $m$-set contains an induced $H_1$; supersaturation then gives at least $((n-h_1+1)/m)^{h_1}$ good $h_1$-sets, hence at least that many induced copies of $H_1$. Averaging over the at most $n^{h_1-1}$ induced embeddings of $H_1-v$ produces one whose extension set has size at least $4^{-h_1}n^{1-\beta h_1}$, which exceeds $m$ once $n\ge n_0(h_1)$ because $1-\beta(h_1+1)=1/2$. That extension set is then large enough to contain an induced $H_2$, and the previous lemma builds an induced $H$ inside $G$ — a contradiction. Finally shrink $\epsilon$ to $\min\{\epsilon,1/\log_2 n_0\}$, which handles $n<n_0$ because $\operatorname{hom}(G)\ge2$ for $n\ge2$ and $\operatorname{hom}(G)=1$ for $n=1$.

items.title: Every graph has the Erdős–Hajnal property if and only if every prime graph does
items.strategy: One direction is trivial. For the other, induct on the number of vertices. A graph on at most one vertex is prime, and a graph on at least two vertices is either prime or a substitution $G_1[a\to G_2]$ with $|V(G_1)|,|V(G_2)|\ge2$; both factors then have strictly fewer vertices, so the induction hypothesis and the substitution theorem apply.

items.title: Substituting a complete or an edgeless graph for a vertex preserves the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: The class of $K_t$-free graphs has the Erdős–Hajnal property for every $t\ge1$. A graph is $\overline{K_t}$-free exactly when its complement is $K_t$-free, so the class of $\overline{K_t}$-free graphs is the complementary class of the $K_t$-free graphs and has the property with the same constants. Now apply the substitution theorem with $H_2=K_t$ or $H_2=\overline{K_t}$.

items.title: Why this page says module where its sources say homogeneous set
Which small graphs count as prime, and why the convention matters

pages.title: Modules, Substitution and Prime Graphs — Examples

items.title: Every vertex set is a module of a complete graph and of an edgeless graph
items.strategy: In $K_n$ every outside vertex is adjacent to everything, so every $M$ is a module; in $\overline{K_n}$ every outside vertex is adjacent to nothing. Hence neither is prime once $n\ge3$, while $K_1$ and $K_2$ are prime because they have no set of size between $2$ and $n-1$.

items.title: The four-vertex path has only trivial modules
items.strategy: Write $P_4$ as $0$-$1$-$2$-$3$ and check the six pairs and four triples. Each time exhibit one outside vertex adjacent to one member and not the other, for instance $2$ separates $\{0,1\}$ and $1$ separates $\{0,2\}$. So $P_4$ is prime.

items.title: Up to isomorphism the four-vertex path is the only prime graph on four vertices
items.strategy: A prime graph on four vertices is connected and anticonnected, since a union of components or of anticomponents is a module. List the connected graphs on four vertices: $P_4$, the star, $C_4$, the paw, the diamond and $K_4$. The complement of each of the last five is disconnected, and $P_4$ is prime by the previous example.

items.title: $P_n$ is prime for every $n\ge4$
items.strategy: Let $M$ be a module of $P_n$ with $2\le|M|\le n-1$. Since $P_n$ is connected some vertex $v\notin M$ is complete to $M$, so $M\subseteq N(v)$ and $|N(v)|\ge2$ forces $v$ to be an interior vertex and $M=N(v)=\{v-1,v+1\}$. A vertex two steps from $v$ then exists because $n\ge4$, and it is adjacent to exactly one member of $M$.

items.title: The five-cycle is prime
items.strategy: A nontrivial module $M$ of $C_5$ has a vertex $v\notin M$ complete to it, so $M\subseteq N(v)$, which has two nonadjacent elements; the remaining two vertices each see exactly one of them.

items.title: Substituting into $K_2$ gives the join and substituting into $\overline{K_2}$ gives the disjoint union
items.strategy: Substitute $G_1$ for one vertex of $K_2$ and then $G_2$ for the other: the two parts become complete to each other, which is the join. The same construction inside $\overline{K_2}$ leaves them anticomplete, which is the disjoint union. Read off that a disconnected graph and a graph with disconnected complement are both substitutions.

items.title: The modular decomposition of a five-cycle with each vertex blown up into an edgeless graph
items.strategy: Take $C_5$ and substitute $\overline{K_t}$ for each vertex in turn, with $t\ge2$. The graph is connected and anticonnected, each of the five blown-up sets is a module, and no larger proper module exists because the quotient $C_5$ is prime. So the maximal proper modules are exactly those five sets and the quotient is $C_5$.

items.title: Counting the induced copies of $P_3$ in $P_4$ by extension sets
items.strategy: In $P_4$ exactly the vertex sets $\{0,1,2\}$ and $\{1,2,3\}$ induce $P_3$, and $P_3$ has two automorphisms, so $\operatorname{ind}_{P_3}(P_4)=4$. Deleting an endpoint $v$ of $P_3$ leaves $K_2$, whose induced embeddings into $P_4$ number six; summing the extension sizes over those six embeddings recovers $4$.

items.title: Substituting an edge for an endpoint of $P_3$ gives a four-vertex graph with the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: $P_3$ and $K_2$ both have the Erdős–Hajnal property, the first because every graph on at most three vertices does. Substituting $K_2$ for an endpoint of $P_3$ produces the paw, so the paw has the property. The same recipe covers every four-vertex graph except $P_4$ itself.

items.title: Two disjoint modules whose union is not a module
items.strategy: In $P_4$ written $0$-$1$-$2$-$3$, the singletons $\{0\}$ and $\{2\}$ are modules, but $3$ is adjacent to $2$ and not to $0$, so $\{0,2\}$ is not. This shows the hypothesis that the two modules meet cannot be dropped from the union lemma.

items.title: A difference of two nested modules that is not a module
items.strategy: On $\{a,b,c,d\}$ take the two edges $ca$ and $cb$. Then $N=\{a,b\}$ is a module and $M=\{a,b,c,d\}$ is the whole vertex set, but $M\setminus N=\{c,d\}$ is not, because $a$ is adjacent to $c$ and not to $d$. Here $N\subseteq M$, so the two do not overlap.

items.title: Maximal proper modules need not be disjoint when the graph or its complement is disconnected
items.strategy: In the edgeless graph on $\{a,b,c\}$ every vertex subset is a module, so $\{a,b\}$ and $\{a,c\}$ are proper modules, and each is maximal because the only module properly containing it is the whole vertex set. They meet in $a$, and their union is the whole vertex set rather than a proper module. So without connectivity of the graph the maximal proper modules need neither be pairwise disjoint nor have proper unions. Reading the same three vertices in the complement, the triangle is connected and its complement is disconnected, and the two sets are still overlapping maximal proper modules there because a set is a module of a graph exactly when it is a module of the complement. The same example gives two different modular partitions, $\{\{a\},\{b,c\}\}$ and $\{\{a,b\},\{c\}\}$, whose quotients are the edgeless graph on two vertices and so are prime.

items.title: An induced subgraph of a prime graph need not be prime
items.strategy: $P_5$ is prime, but deleting its middle vertex leaves two disjoint edges, in which each edge is a module of size two. So primality is not a hereditary property, unlike $H$-freeness.

items.title: Every graph with at least four vertices has a nontrivial module
items.strategy: True for one, two and three vertices in the sense that no nontrivial module can exist or one always does, but false from four onwards: $P_4$ is prime. Refute by exhibiting $P_4$ and checking all six two-element and four three-element subsets.

pages.title: Regular Pairs and Induced Counting

items.title: Edge counts and densities between nonempty vertex sets
$\epsilon$-regular pairs and self-regular vertex sets
Complementation sends a disjoint $\epsilon$-regular pair of density $d$ to one of density $1-d$
items.strategy: For disjoint $X,Y$, every ordered cross-pair is an edge in exactly one of $G$ and $\overline G$, so all relevant densities add to $1$ and their differences change sign. Explicitly note the diagonal correction when $X$ and $Y$ overlap; the exact $1-d$ formula is claimed only in the disjoint case.

items.title: All but fewer than $\epsilon|X|$ vertices have typical degree into every large subset of a regular pair
items.strategy: If at least $\epsilon|X|$ vertices have degree into $Y'\subseteq Y$ below $(d-\epsilon)|Y'|$, take them as $X'$ and contradict regularity of $(X,Y)$; repeat for degrees above $(d+\epsilon)|Y'|$. State the strict bad-set bound and the hypothesis $|Y'|\ge\epsilon|Y|$.

items.title: Slicing lemma: large subpairs remain regular and their density shifts by at most $\epsilon$
items.strategy: For an $\epsilon$-regular pair $(X,Y)$ and subsets $X',Y'$ of relative sizes at least $\alpha,\beta\ge\epsilon$, first apply regularity to get $|d(X',Y')-d(X,Y)|\le\epsilon$. If $A\subseteq X'$ and $B\subseteq Y'$ have relative sizes at least $\epsilon'=\max{\epsilon/\alpha,\epsilon/\beta,2\epsilon}$, then they meet the original thresholds; compare both $d(A,B)$ and $d(X',Y')$ with $d(X,Y)$.

items.title: Regularity survives sufficiently small changes of vertices and cross-edges
items.strategy: Given $\epsilon'>\epsilon$, choose an explicit $\delta$ small compared with $\epsilon'-\epsilon$ and $\epsilon$. Compare the old and new densities after adding or deleting at most a $\delta$-fraction of each vertex set and changing at most $\delta|X||Y|$ cross-edges; transfer any hypothetical $\epsilon'$-irregular witness back to large old subsets and contradict $\epsilon$-regularity.

items.title: $\epsilon$-regular vertex partitions, equitable partitions, and refinement
The mean-square density, or energy, of a vertex partition
Energy lies in $[0,1]$ and cannot decrease under refinement
items.strategy: For each old ordered pair of parts, regard the densities between its refined subparts as a finite random variable weighted by relative product sizes. Its expectation is the old density, so Cauchy–Schwarz gives mean square at least square of the mean. Sum with the global weights. The bounds $0\le q\le1$ follow from $0\le d\le1$ and the weights summing to one.

items.title: An irregularity witness raises the pair energy by more than $\epsilon^4|X||Y|/n^2$
items.strategy: Split $X$ and $Y$ by witness sets $A,B$. Express the refined-minus-coarse pair energy as the variance of the subpair-density random variable. The event $A\times B$ has weight at least $\epsilon^2$, and its density differs from the old one by more than $\epsilon$, giving the stated strict boost.

items.title: Every nonregular $k$-part partition has a refinement with energy gain greater than $\epsilon^5$ and at most $k2^{k+1}$ parts
items.strategy: Choose witnesses for every irregular ordered pair. Inside each part take the common refinement generated by all witness subsets incident with it; this makes at most $2^{k+1}$ cells per old part. Sum the irregular-pair boosts, using the weighted definition of a nonregular partition to obtain a total gain above $\epsilon^5$, while monotonicity makes every unselected contribution nonnegative.

items.title: Szemerédi regularity lemma with an equitable partition and an explicit tower-type upper bound for graphs of order at least $m_0$
items.strategy: For a graph with $n\ge m_0$, start with an equitable partition into exactly $m_0$ nonempty parts. When it is not $\epsilon$-regular, apply the energy increment and then re-equitabilise with energy loss at most half the gain by cutting parts and distributing leftovers. Energy stays at most $1$, so fewer than $2\epsilon^{-5}$ iterations occur. Track part counts by $m_{r+1}=\lceil\epsilon^{-5}m_r2^{m_r+2}\rceil$; thus $M=m_{\lceil2\epsilon^{-5}\rceil}$ is a proved tower-type bound, not a polynomial or single exponential. Handle $n<m_0$ only in corollaries that allow singleton partitions; do not claim the impossible lower bound $k\ge m_0$ there.

items.title: A prescribed finite vertex partition has a bounded $\epsilon$-regular refinement, equitable when the initial partition is equitable
items.strategy: Run the same witness-refinement iteration starting from the prescribed partition. Without an equitability requirement, the recurrence $k_{r+1}\le k_r2^{k_r+1}$ applies directly. When the initial partition is equitable, split every old cell into the same controlled number of nearly equal subcells and distribute each cell's own leftovers internally; this never crosses an old cell, yields a globally equitable refinement, and costs at most half the $\epsilon^5$ gain after enlarging the recurrence by the same $\epsilon^{-5}$ factor used in the equitable theorem. In both forms the number of rounds is bounded by energy.

items.title: Every finite graph has a linearly large $\epsilon$-self-regular vertex subset
items.strategy: Apply the regularity lemma at a sufficiently smaller parameter to a large enough equitable partition. Use the weighted irregular-pair bound to find a sizeable union of parts whose internal density is stable, and verify self-regularity by decomposing two large test subsets across the partition. Record a constant $\delta(\epsilon)>0$ independent of the graph order and handle graphs below the partition threshold by shrinking $\delta$.

items.title: Every finite graph has a bounded partition into self-regular vertex sets
items.strategy: Repeatedly extract a linearly large set that is regular at a parameter smaller than the target until only a small remainder remains. There are boundedly many extracted sets. Distribute the remainder among them and apply robustness under small vertex edits; handle bounded small graphs with singleton parts.

items.title: Triangle counting lemma for three pairwise regular vertex sets
items.strategy: Discard the fewer than $2\epsilon|X|$ vertices of $X$ that are atypical into $Y$ or $Z$. For every remaining $x$, its two neighbourhoods are large enough to invoke regularity of $(Y,Z)$; multiply the resulting lower bounds to obtain the stated product estimate, keeping the exact density-minus-$\epsilon$ factors and their positivity hypotheses.

items.title: Counting lemma: regular dense pairs contain many part-respecting copies of every fixed graph
items.strategy: Order the vertices of the fixed graph $H$ and embed them greedily. Maintain for each unembedded vertex a candidate set of the expected product size. The typical-degree lemma shows that all but a controlled fraction of choices preserve every future candidate set; multiply the choice bounds. State both a quantitative homomorphism count and the injective-copy consequence when all host sets are sufficiently large, subtracting collision choices explicitly.

items.title: Induced counting lemma: regular edge and nonedge pairs force many induced copies
items.strategy: For a labelled $h$-vertex graph $H$, assume every required edge pair has density at least $\eta$, every required nonedge pair has density at most $1-\eta$, and every relevant pair is $\gamma$-regular with $\gamma\le\eta^h/(4h)$. Complement the disjoint nonedge pairs and apply the greedy counting proof, while treating repeated host sets through self-regularity and excluding collisions. Derive an explicit positive lower bound such as $(\eta/4)^{\binom h2}\prod_i|W_i|$ under the stated minimum-size condition.

items.title: Graph edit distance and being $\epsilon$-far from an induced-hereditary property
Graph removal lemma for a fixed ordinary subgraph
items.strategy: Apply equitable regularity at a parameter chosen for the counting lemma. Delete all edges inside parts, across irregular pairs, and across regular pairs below a small density threshold; bound these three edit contributions by $\epsilon n^2$. If the cleaned graph still contains $H$, its part assignment consists of regular dense pairs, so the counting lemma produces at least $\delta n^{|V(H)|}$ labelled copies in the original graph. Contraposition gives removal.

items.title: Equitable strong regularity lemma: a very regular refinement that changes energy only slightly
items.strategy: First obtain an equitable $\epsilon_0$-regular partition $P_0$. Recursively use the equitable prescribed-refinement clause to choose an equitable $\epsilon_{|P_i|}$-regular refinement $P_{i+1}$. Energy is nondecreasing and at most $1$, so among at most $\lceil\epsilon_0^{-1}\rceil+1$ successive pairs one satisfies $q(P_{i+1})\le q(P_i)+\epsilon_0$. Set $P=P_i$, $Q=P_{i+1}$ and track the iterated tower recurrence; with the sequence used for induced removal this is a wowzer-type bound. For graphs below the first lower-part threshold, use the common equitable singleton partition for both $P$ and $Q$.

items.title: A small energy increment makes fine-pair densities close to their coarse densities almost everywhere
items.strategy: For uniformly random ordered vertices $x,y$, let $Z_P$ and $Z_Q$ be the densities of their coarse and fine part pairs. Refinement gives the conditional-expectation identity $\mathbb E(Z_Q-Z_P)^2=q(Q)-q(P)$. If this is at most $\epsilon^3$, Markov's inequality shows $|Z_Q-Z_P|>\epsilon$ on at most an $\epsilon$-fraction of ordered pairs.

items.title: Strong regularity with linearly large representative subsets and no irregular representative pair
items.strategy: Use strong regularity with much smaller parameters and equitable coarse and fine partitions. Inside every fine atom choose a linearly large self-regular subset; slicing preserves regularity and controls density shifts on good cross-pairs. Independently choose one refined atom inside each coarse part. The expected number of irregular selected pairs and of coarse-to-selected density failures is below one after the parameter choices, so the first-moment principle gives a simultaneous choice. The resulting $W_i\subseteq V_i$ have size at least $\delta n$, every pair including $i=j$ is $f(k)$-regular, and all but $\epsilon_0k^2$ coarse densities are $\epsilon_0$-approximated.

items.title: Ordinary regularity gives tower upper bounds; the strong-regularity proof used here gives wowzer upper bounds
Induced graph removal lemma for a fixed graph
items.strategy: Fix $H$ and $\epsilon>0$, choose a density threshold $\eta\ll\epsilon$, and apply the representative-subset theorem with regularity small enough for induced counting.
