For every coarse pair, delete all edges when its representative density is below $\eta$ and add all edges when it is above $1-\eta$; density approximation, the exceptional-pair count, and within-part edits keep the total below $\epsilon n^2$. If the cleaned graph contains an induced $H$, its possibly repeated part map makes every required representative density bounded away from the forbidden extreme. Self-regularity handles repeated parts, and induced counting yields $\delta n^{|V(H)|}$ induced embeddings in the original graph, contradicting the few-copy hypothesis.

pages.title: Regular Pairs and Induced Counting — Examples

items.title: Complete and anticomplete disjoint pairs are $0$-regular
items.strategy: Every nonempty subpair of a complete pair has density $1$, and every nonempty subpair of an anticomplete pair has density $0$. Thus every density difference vanishes; explain the conventional reading of $0$-regularity despite the definition being stated for positive parameters.

items.title: The half graph has no regularity across its natural bipartition at a fixed small parameter
items.strategy: For the bipartite half graph with $a_ib_j$ present exactly when $i\le j$, compute the full cross-density and compare it with the densities on the first and last quarter blocks. For all sufficiently large orders these blocks witness failure of $\epsilon$-regularity for one explicit absolute $\epsilon$; keep rounding errors visible.

items.title: A $0.01$-regular pair restricted to two half-sized subsets is $0.02$-regular
items.strategy: Substitute $\epsilon=0.01$ and $\alpha=\beta=1/2$ into the slicing constant $\max{\epsilon/\alpha,\epsilon/\beta,2\epsilon}$, and retain the density-shift bound $0.01$.

items.title: The trivial partition has energy $d(G)^2$, while the singleton partition records every adjacency
items.strategy: Evaluate the energy definition for one part and for singleton parts. Under the ordered-pair density convention, the singleton partition has energy $2|E(G)|/n^2$; compare it with $d(V,V)^2$ and verify monotonicity directly, including the null-graph convention separately.

items.title: The triangle counting lemma is exact for three complete cross-pairs
items.strategy: Take three disjoint nonempty vertex sets with every cross-edge present. All three pairs are $0$-regular of density $1$, and every ordered triple, one vertex from each set, is a triangle, giving exactly $|X||Y||Z|$.

items.title: Two complete pairs and one anticomplete pair produce exactly $|X_1||X_2||X_3|$ induced copies of $P_3$
items.strategy: Make $(X_1,X_2)$ and $(X_2,X_3)$ complete and $(X_1,X_3)$ anticomplete. Every transversal triple induces the labelled path $1-2-3$, and every pair is $0$-regular, so this is the zero-error model of the induced counting lemma.

items.title: Three pair densities equal to $1/2$ need not produce a single transversal triangle
items.strategy: Split each of $X,Y,Z$ into equal halves labelled by bits. Join $X$ to $Y$ and $Y$ to $Z$ when the bits agree, and join $X$ to $Z$ when the bits differ. Each cross-density is $1/2$, but a triangle would require simultaneously $x=y$, $y=z$, and $x\ne z$. This isolates the regularity hypothesis in counting.

items.title: Induced removal must permit adding edges as well as deleting them
items.strategy: Let $G$ be $K_n$ with exactly the three edges on one chosen triple deleted, and let $H$ be the empty three-vertex graph. That triple is the unique induced copy of $H$. Deleting further edges can never destroy its three nonedges, whereas adding any one missing edge does; hence a deletion-only induced-removal statement is false.

pages.title: Sparse Restricted Subgraphs and the Rödl–Nikiforov Theorems

items.title: $c$-sparse, $c$-dense and $c$-restricted vertex sets
Sparsity of one vertex set to another, and weak sparsity of a pair
For disjoint nonempty vertex sets, weak $c$-sparsity says exactly that the edge density is at most $c$
items.strategy: For disjoint $X,Y$ each edge between them contributes exactly one ordered pair to $e_G(X,Y)$, so $|E(X,Y)|=e_G(X,Y)$ and dividing by $|X||Y|$ turns the inequality $|E(X,Y)|\le c|X||Y|$ into $d(X,Y)\le c$. The two notions are therefore the same, which is why this page never introduces a second density.

items.title: A set is $c$-sparse exactly when the maximum degree of the graph it induces is at most $c$ times its size
items.strategy: For $x\in X$ the set $N_G(x)\cap X$ is the neighbourhood of $x$ in $G[X]$, so the defining inequality is $\deg_{G[X]}(x)\le c|X|$ for every $x$. Consequently $c$-sparsity of $X$ in $G$ and in any induced subgraph of $G$ containing $X$ are the same condition.

items.title: A $c$-sparse set has self-density at most $c$, and a $c$-dense set has self-density at least $1-c-1/|X|$
items.strategy: Sum the degrees: $e_G(X,X)=\sum_{x\in X}|N(x)\cap X|$, which is at most $c|X|^2$ in the sparse case, so $d(X,X)\le c$. In the dense case each $x$ has at most $c|X|$ non-neighbours inside $X\setminus\{x\}$, hence at least $|X|-1-c|X|$ neighbours, and the same sum gives $d(X,X)\ge1-c-1/|X|$. The extra $1/|X|$ is forced by the convention that diagonal pairs never contribute.

items.title: A set of self-density at most $c$ has a subset of at least half its size that is $4c$-sparse
items.strategy: Sum the degrees inside $X$: $\sum_{x\in X}|N(x)\cap X|=e(X,X)\le c|X|^2$. By the averaging bound, fewer than half the vertices of $X$ have $|N(x)\cap X|>2c|X|$, so the remaining set $X'$ has $|X'|\ge|X|/2$ and every $x\in X'$ satisfies $|N(x)\cap X'|\le2c|X|\le4c|X'|$. Reading the same computation in the complement gives the dense form. Some loss is unavoidable: a star has tiny self-density and no large sparse subset containing its centre.

items.title: A set is $c$-sparse in $G$ exactly when it is $c$-dense in $\overline G$, so $c$-restrictedness is complement-invariant
items.strategy: For $x\in X$ the neighbours of $x$ in $\overline G$ inside $X$ are exactly its non-neighbours in $G$ inside $X\setminus\{x\}$, so the two counting conditions are literally the same inequality read in the two graphs. Restrictedness is the disjunction of the two, hence unchanged.

items.title: A subset occupying at least a $\lambda$ fraction of a $c$-sparse set is $(c/\lambda)$-sparse
items.strategy: For $x\in X'$ we have $|N(x)\cap X'|\le|N(x)\cap X|\le c|X|\le (c/\lambda)|X'|$, using $|X'|\ge\lambda|X|$. The same computation in the complement gives the dense version. The loss is real: without the size hypothesis a subset of a sparse set need not be sparse.

items.title: Sparsity is preserved when the parameter grows, and every set of at most two vertices is $0$-restricted
items.strategy: The defining inequality $|N(x)\cap X|\le c|X|$ only weakens as $c$ grows. A single vertex has no neighbour and no non-neighbour inside its own singleton. A two-element set is $0$-sparse when its two vertices are nonadjacent and $0$-dense when they are adjacent, so either way it is $0$-restricted. This is what makes the conclusion of the theorems below trivially available for small graphs, and it is also why a partition into restricted sets may need singleton and two-element parts.

items.title: A $c$-sparse set $X$ satisfies $\alpha(G[X])\ge|X|/(c|X|+1)$, and a $c$-dense set satisfies $\omega(G[X])\ge|X|/(c|X|+1)$
items.strategy: The maximum degree of $G[X]$ is at most $c\lvert X\rvert$, so [[lem-greedy-colouring-bound]] gives $\chi(G[X])\le c\lvert X\rvert+1$, and $\lvert X\rvert\le\chi(G[X])\alpha(G[X])$ from [[thm-clique-independence-chromatic-bounds]] finishes the sparse case. Reading that case in the complement, where a $c$-dense set is $c$-sparse by [[lem-restrictedness-is-complement-invariant]] and stable sets become cliques by [[lem-complement-swaps-cliques-and-stable-sets]], gives the dense case. THE PAGE MEETS $\alpha$ AND $\omega$ UNDER TWO PUBLISHED DEFINITIONS AND MUST SAY ONCE, IN A NUMBERED STEP, THAT THEY AGREE: [[def-clique-and-independence-numbers]] (order 215) and [[def-clique-stable-set-and-numbers]] (order 393) define the same two invariants under the same symbols, and this item is the only place both are cited — [[lem-greedy-colouring-bound]] and [[thm-clique-independence-chromatic-bounds]] are stated against the first, [[lem-complement-swaps-cliques-and-stable-sets]] against the second. Verify the agreement from the two Definitions rather than assuming it from the notation. The bound tends to $1/c$ rather than to a fraction of $\lvert X\rvert$, and a disjoint union of cliques of order $c\lvert X\rvert$ shows it cannot be improved to a linear one.

items.title: An $\epsilon$-regular pair is $\epsilon'$-regular for every $\epsilon'\ge\epsilon$ with $\epsilon'>0$
items.strategy: Subsets qualifying at level $\epsilon'$ already qualify at level $\epsilon$ because $\epsilon'|X|\ge\epsilon|X|$, and the density deviation they inherit is at most $\epsilon\le\epsilon'$.

items.title: Deleting the high-degree vertices of a $\gamma$-self-regular set of density $d$ leaves more than $(1-\gamma)$ of it, and that remainder is $((d+\gamma)/(1-\gamma))$-sparse
items.strategy: Apply the typical-degree lemma to the pair $(W,W)$ with $Y'=W$: fewer than $\gamma|W|$ vertices have more than $(d+\gamma)|W|$ neighbours in $W$. Let $W'$ be the rest, so $|W'|>(1-\gamma)|W|$ and $W'$ is nonempty. Each $x\in W'$ has $|N(x)\cap W'|\le|N(x)\cap W|\le(d+\gamma)|W|<((d+\gamma)/(1-\gamma))|W'|$.

items.title: Deleting the low-degree vertices of a $\gamma$-self-regular set of density $d$ leaves more than $(1-\gamma)$ of it, and that remainder is $((1-d+2\gamma)/(1-\gamma))$-dense
items.strategy: The other half of the typical-degree lemma bounds by $\gamma|W|$ the number of vertices with fewer than $(d-\gamma)|W|$ neighbours in $W$. For $x$ in the remainder $W'$, at most $\gamma|W|$ of its neighbours were deleted, so $|N(x)\cap W'|\ge(d-2\gamma)|W|$ and the number of non-neighbours of $x$ inside $W'$ is at most $|W|-(d-2\gamma)|W|$, which is less than $((1-d+2\gamma)/(1-\gamma))|W'|$.

items.title: A large $\gamma$-self-regular set whose density lies between $\eta$ and $1-\eta$ forces at least $c|W|^{|V(H)|}$ induced copies of $H$
items.strategy: Feed the induced counting lemma the $h$ sets $W_1=\cdots=W_h=W$, which is permitted because it allows repetitions and pairs with $W_i=W_j$. Its density hypotheses read $d(W,W)\ge\eta$ on edges of $H$ and $d(W,W)\le1-\eta$ on non-edges, both supplied by $\eta\le d(W,W)\le1-\eta$; its regularity hypothesis follows from $\gamma\le\gamma(H,\eta)$ and monotonicity. The maps it produces are injective and induce $H$, so they are counted by $\operatorname{ind}_H(G)$.

items.title: If $G$ has fewer than $(\delta n)^{h}$ induced copies of $H$ and $|W|\ge\lambda n$, then $G[W]$ has fewer than $((\delta/\lambda)|W|)^{h}$
items.strategy: An induced embedding of $H$ into $G[W]$ is one into $G$, so $\operatorname{ind}_H(G[W])\le\operatorname{ind}_H(G)<(\delta n)^h\le((\delta/\lambda)|W|)^h$, the last step because $n\le|W|/\lambda$.

items.title: Nikiforov: for every $H$ and every $\epsilon\in(0,\tfrac12)$ there is $\delta>0$ such that every graph $G$ with $\operatorname{ind}_H(G)<(\delta|V(G)|)^{|V(H)|}$ has an $\epsilon$-restricted vertex set of size at least $\delta|V(G)|$
items.strategy: Set $\eta=\epsilon/4$ and choose $\gamma\le\min\{\epsilon/8,\gamma(H,\eta)\}$, so that both trimming constants $(\eta+\gamma)/(1-\gamma)$ and $(\eta+2\gamma)/(1-\gamma)$ are at most $\epsilon$. Let $\delta_1=\delta(\gamma)$ come from the linearly large self-regular subset theorem and let $c,N$ come from the induced counting lemma, then put $\delta=\min\{\delta_1/N,\ \delta_1c^{1/h},\ (1-\gamma)\delta_1\}$. Given $G$ nonempty, take a $\gamma$-self-regular $W$ with $|W|\ge\delta_1n$. If $|W|<N$ then $n<N/\delta_1$, so $\delta n\le1$ and a single vertex is the required set. Otherwise the middling-density lemma would give $\operatorname{ind}_H(G)\ge c|W|^h\ge(\delta n)^h$, so $d(W,W)<\eta$ or $d(W,W)>1-\eta$, and the matching trimming lemma returns an $\epsilon$-restricted subset of size more than $(1-\gamma)\delta_1 n\ge\delta n$.

items.title: Rödl: for every $H$ and every $\epsilon\in(0,\tfrac12)$ there is $\delta>0$ such that every $H$-free graph has an $\epsilon$-restricted vertex set of size at least $\delta|V(G)|$
items.strategy: An $H$-free graph has $\operatorname{ind}_H(G)=0$, and for a nonempty $G$ the bound $(\delta|V(G)|)^{|V(H)|}$ is strictly positive, so Nikiforov's hypothesis holds with the same $\delta$.

items.title: Rödl's theorem for a nonempty family of forbidden induced subgraphs
items.strategy: Fix any $H\in\mathcal F$. An $\mathcal F$-free graph is $H$-free, so the single-graph statement applies with $\delta=\delta(H,\epsilon)$; taking the largest such $\delta$ over $H\in\mathcal F$ gives the best constant this argument yields.

items.title: The edge-density form of Rödl's theorem: a linearly large set of self-density at most $\epsilon$ or at least $1-\epsilon$
items.strategy: Apply the theorem with parameter $\epsilon/2$ and pass to densities. In the sparse case $d(X,X)\le\epsilon/2\le\epsilon$; in the dense case $d(X,X)\ge1-\epsilon/2-1/|X|$, which is at least $1-\epsilon$ once $|X|\ge2/\epsilon$, and that holds for $n\ge n_0=2/(\epsilon\delta)$. The threshold on $n$ is not removable, because the self-density of a clique of size $s$ is $1-1/s$.

items.title: The edge-density form of Rödl's theorem implies the maximum-degree form, with $\epsilon$ and $\delta$ each shrunk by a constant factor
items.strategy: Given a linearly large $X$ with $d(X,X)\le\epsilon/4$ or $d(X,X)\ge1-\epsilon/4-1/\lvert X\rvert$, apply [[lem-a-weakly-sparse-set-has-a-large-sparse-subset]] to get $X′\subseteq X$ with $\lvert X′\rvert\ge\lvert X\rvert/2$ that is $\epsilon$-restricted, taking $c=\epsilon/4$ so that $4c=\epsilon$. THE DENSE BRANCH IS NOT THE SAME COMPUTATION AND NEEDS ITS OWN NUMBERED STEP: the trimming lemma is stated for a set of small self-density, so the dense case is run inside $\overline G$, where $d_{\overline G}(X,X)=1-1/\lvert X\rvert-d_G(X,X)\le\epsilon/4$ by the diagonal convention of [[def-edge-density-between-vertex-sets]]; the lemma returns an $\epsilon$-sparse $X′$ of $\overline G$, and [[lem-restrictedness-is-complement-invariant]] carries it back as an $\epsilon$-dense set of $G$. Do not write that the trimming lemma “gives the dense version too”: its Statement is one-sided, and the complement passage is the step that supplies the other side. So the two statements of Rödl’s theorem differ only in the constants, which is why the density form quoted in the literature and the maximum-degree form proved here are the same theorem.

items.title: A linearly large induced subgraph of a graph with few induced copies again has a linearly large restricted set
items.strategy: Combine the inheritance lemma with the theorem applied inside $G[W]$: the hypothesis transfers with $\delta$ replaced by $\delta/\lambda$, and a set that is $\epsilon$-restricted in $G[W]$ is $\epsilon$-restricted in $G$ because sparsity depends only on the induced subgraph.

items.title: For every $\lambda>0$ a bounded number of disjoint $\epsilon$-restricted sets covers all but $\lambda|V(G)|$ vertices of an $H$-free graph
items.strategy: Repeatedly apply Rödl inside the graph induced on what is left. Every induced subgraph of an $H$-free graph is $H$-free, and each step removes at least a $\delta$ fraction of the current remainder, so after $t$ steps the remainder has at most $(1-\delta)^t n$ vertices; $t$ may therefore be taken proportional to $\log(1/\lambda)/\delta$, a bound depending only on $H$, $\epsilon$ and $\lambda$. Sparsity is internal to the induced subgraph, so each extracted set is $\epsilon$-restricted in $G$ as well. The leftover $\lambda n$ vertices are not covered by this argument.

items.title: Every $H$-free graph partitions into boundedly many vertex sets of self-density at most $\epsilon$ or at least $1-\epsilon$
items.strategy: Run [[cor-boundedly-many-restricted-sets-cover-all-but-a-small-fraction]] with parameter $\epsilon/2$ and a leftover fraction $\lambda$ still to be chosen, obtaining disjoint sets $X_1,\dots,X_t$ with $t\le C\log(1/\lambda)/\delta$ and a remainder $R$ of at most $\lambda n$ vertices. Add $R$ to a largest $X_i$, whose size is at least $(1-\lambda)n/t$. The added vertices contribute at most $\lambda n\,\lvert X_i\cup R\rvert$ to the edge count on either side, so $X_i\cup R$ still has self-density at most $\epsilon$ or at least $1-\epsilon$ provided $\lambda t^2$ is small enough; since $t$ grows only logarithmically in $1/\lambda$, such a $\lambda$ exists. TWO THRESHOLDS ARE HIDDEN HERE AND EACH IS ITS OWN NUMBERED STEP. First, passing from the maximum-degree form to self-density in the dense case costs the $1/\lvert X_i\rvert$ slack of [[lem-a-sparse-set-has-small-self-density]], so it needs $\lvert X_i\rvert\ge2/\epsilon$, which holds for every extracted set because the last extraction still runs inside a remainder of at least $\lambda n$ vertices and so returns a set of at least $\delta\lambda n$ of them. Second, that forces $n\ge n_0(H,\epsilon)$. STATE THE SMALL CASE RATHER THAN LEAVING IT: for $n<n_0$ partition $V(G)$ into singletons, each of self-density $0$, giving at most $n_0(H,\epsilon)$ parts, so the bound on the number of parts is $\max\{t+1,n_0\}$ and depends only on $H$ and $\epsilon$. Without that case the theorem is stated for all $H$-free graphs and proved only for large ones. The corresponding statement for the maximum-degree form is not obtainable this way: a large star shows that a set containing a high-degree vertex may have no restricted extension, as [[cex-weak-sparsity-does-not-imply-sparsity]] records.

items.title: Bounded degree against bounded density: the two statements of Rödl's theorem, and which one is stronger
Why the dense alternative carries a $1/|X|$ slack
What this proof gives for $\delta$, and why the regularity route is expensive

pages.title: Sparse Restricted Subgraphs and the Rödl–Nikiforov Theorems — Examples

items.title: The $0$-sparse sets are exactly the stable sets and the $0$-dense sets exactly the cliques
items.strategy: With $c=0$ the condition reads $|N(x)\cap X|\le0$ for every $x\in X$, which says $G[X]$ has no edges. Complementing gives the clique statement.

items.title: A clique of size $s$ has self-density $1-1/s$
items.strategy: Count ordered pairs: $e(X,X)=s(s-1)$ because every ordered pair of distinct vertices is an edge and diagonal pairs never contribute, so $d(X,X)=s(s-1)/s^2$. In particular self-density never reaches $1$, which is exactly the slack recorded in the dense half of the sparse-density lemma.

items.title: In a disjoint union of cliques of order $k$ the whole vertex set is $(k/n)$-sparse
items.strategy: Every vertex has exactly $k-1$ neighbours, and $k-1\le(k/n)\cdot n$. So the sparsity parameter one can claim for the whole vertex set is governed by the largest component, not by the number of edges.

items.title: For $P_3$-free graphs Rödl's theorem holds with $\delta=\epsilon$, by an explicit argument
items.strategy: In a $P_3$-free graph adjacency is transitive inside a component, so every component is a clique. If some component has more than $\epsilon n$ vertices it is a clique of that size and is $0$-dense; otherwise every vertex has fewer than $\epsilon n$ neighbours and the whole vertex set is $\epsilon$-sparse. Either way an $\epsilon$-restricted set of size at least $\epsilon n$ exists, with no appeal to regularity.

items.title: In a union of two equal cliques the restricted sets are the ones concentrated on a single side
items.strategy: Write $a$ and $b$ for the sizes of the two traces. A set inside one clique is $0$-dense. A set meeting both has a vertex with $\max\{a,b\}-1$ neighbours and one with $\max\{a,b\}$ non-neighbours, so being $\epsilon$-restricted with $\epsilon<1/2$ forces $\max\{a,b\}\le1/(1-2\epsilon)$; the set is then bounded independently of $n$.

items.title: In a balanced complete bipartite graph the two sides are the restricted sets of linear size
items.strategy: Each side is stable, hence $0$-sparse of size $n/2$. A set taking $a$ vertices from each side gives every vertex $a$ neighbours and $a-1$ non-neighbours inside a set of size $2a$, so it is neither $\epsilon$-sparse nor $\epsilon$-dense once $a$ is large and $\epsilon<1/2$.

items.title: A star has tiny self-density, yet no restricted subset containing its centre has more than two vertices
items.strategy: Let $X$ be the vertex set of a star $K_{1,m}$, of size $m+1$; its self-density is $2m/(m+1)^2$, which tends to $0$. Now let $Y\subseteq X$ contain the centre and $k$ leaves. The centre has $k$ neighbours in $Y$, so $\epsilon$-sparsity forces $k\le\epsilon(k+1)$, and each leaf has $k-1$ non-neighbours in $Y$, so $\epsilon$-density forces $k-1\le\epsilon(k+1)$. For $\epsilon<1/3$ both fail as soon as $k\ge2$, so $|Y|\le2$. The converse of the sparse-density lemma therefore fails, and the loss of a factor in the weakly-sparse trimming lemma is real.

items.title: A subset of a $c$-sparse set that is not $c$-sparse
items.strategy: Let $G$ be a perfect matching on $2m$ vertices and $X=V(G)$, which is $(1/(2m))$-sparse since every vertex has one neighbour. The two ends of a single edge form a subset of size $2$ in which each vertex still has one neighbour, so that subset is not $c$-sparse for $c<1/2$. This is why the transfer lemma charges a factor $1/\lambda$.

items.title: $X$ can be $c$-sparse to $Y$ while $Y$ is not $c$-sparse to $X$
items.strategy: Let $X=\{x\}$ and let $Y$ have $m\ge3$ vertices, with $x$ adjacent to exactly one $y_0\in Y$. Then $x$ has $1\le\tfrac12m$ neighbours in $Y$, so $X$ is $\tfrac12$-sparse to $Y$; but $y_0$ has $1$ neighbour in $X$ and $\tfrac12|X|=\tfrac12$, so $Y$ is not. Weak sparsity, being an edge count, is symmetric.

items.title: The dense alternative in Rödl's theorem cannot be dropped
items.strategy: $K_n$ is $\overline{K_2}$-free, so Rödl's theorem applies to it. Any $X\subseteq V(K_n)$ with $|X|\ge2$ has every vertex adjacent to the other $|X|-1$, so $\epsilon$-sparsity would force $|X|-1\le\epsilon|X|$, impossible for $\epsilon<\tfrac12$ and $|X|\ge2$. The linearly large set the theorem produces is therefore dense, never sparse.

items.title: Every $c$-sparse set of size $m$ contains a stable set of size at least $m/2$
items.strategy: Refute with a disjoint union of $1/c$ cliques of order $cn$: every vertex has $cn-1$ neighbours, so the whole vertex set is $c$-sparse, while a stable set meets each clique at most once and therefore has at most $1/c$ vertices — a constant, not a fraction of $n$. The witness is exhibited and both claims are checked directly from the definitions, so the refutation does not rest on the general lower bound the page records elsewhere.

pages.title: Classical and Log-Log Erdős–Hajnal Bounds

items.title: Fox–Sudakov: a quantitative density form of Rödl's theorem
items.strategy: Record the exact H-free specialization of Fox and Sudakov's quantitative density theorem, with the source's base-2 logarithm convention stated explicitly. This item is source-cited and proved_here=false: later proofs on the page depend on its statement, not on a local derivation of the theorem itself.

items.title: Every $H$-free graph has a homogeneous set of size at least $2^{c\sqrt{\log_2 n}}$
items.strategy: Fix the constant from the Fox-Sudakov remark and let L=log_2 n. Choose x=2^{-sqrt(L/(2c_H))}. The remark gives a vertex set S of size at least sqrt(n) whose induced subgraph, or its complement, has density at most x. Use the published weak-density trimming lemma to pass to a subset of S with maximum degree at most 4x|S|, then apply the greedy colouring bound and |V|<=chi alpha to obtain a stable set of size at least |S|/(4x|S|+1); in the complement branch that becomes a clique in G. Convert the denominator to a constant multiple of 1/x and absorb the small-n boundary into the final constant c.

items.title: Bucić–Nguyen–Scott–Seymour: a log-log quantitative density theorem
items.strategy: Record the H-free specialization of theorem 1.8 from the 2024 paper, again keeping the source's base-2 logarithm convention explicit. This is the second source-cited proved_here=false input: the page proves the announced Erdős-Hajnal consequence from it, not the density theorem itself.

items.title: Every $H$-free graph has a homogeneous set of size at least $2^{c\sqrt{\log_2 n\,\log_2\log_2 n}}$
items.strategy: Let L=log_2 n and choose x=2^{-beta sqrt(L log_2 L)} with beta depending only on the constant in the log-log density remark, so that the theorem's delta satisfies delta n >= sqrt(n) for all large enough L. Apply the remark to get a dense-or-sparse set S of that size, trim it as in the classical proof, and use greedy colouring plus the clique/stable-set bounds to obtain a homogeneous set of order at least a constant multiple of 1/x. The resulting lower bound is 2^{Omega(sqrt(L log_2 L))}; absorb the finitely many small n cases into the constant c.

items.title: For fixed $H$, the log-log scale eventually exceeds every classical scale $2^{c\sqrt{\log_2 n}}$
items.strategy: Compare the exponents. For large n, sqrt(log_2 n log_2 log_2 n) is sqrt(log_2 log_2 n) times larger than sqrt(log_2 n), so any positive log-log constant eventually beats any fixed classical constant. State the conclusion with an eventual threshold, not as a uniform inequality for all n >= 2.

pages.title: Classical and Log-Log Erdős–Hajnal Bounds — Examples

items.title: For large $n$, the Fox–Sudakov choice of $x$ leaves a dense-or-sparse set of order at least $\sqrt n$
items.strategy: Let L=log_2 n and x=2^{-sqrt(L/(2c_H))}. Compute delta=2^{-c_H(log_2(1/x))^2}=2^{-L/2}, so delta n=sqrt(n). This is the one-line algebra the main theorem uses before the trimming argument begins.

items.title: For large $n$, the log-log choice of $x$ still leaves a dense-or-sparse set of order at least $\sqrt n$
items.strategy: Let L=log_2 n and choose x=2^{-beta sqrt(L log_2 L)} with beta=1/(4 sqrt(c_H)). For large L, bound log_2 log_2(1/x) from below by (1/2) log_2 L and deduce delta n >= sqrt(n).

items.title: A lower bound of size $2^{c\sqrt{\log_2 n}}$ is still subpolynomial in $n$
items.strategy: Fix epsilon>0 and write n=2^L. Then 2^{c sqrt(L)} / n^epsilon = 2^{c sqrt(L)-epsilon L}, and the exponent tends to -infinity because sqrt(L)=o(L). This example is the honest reason the classical bound does not by itself prove the Erdős-Hajnal conjecture.

items.title: A lower bound of size $2^{c\sqrt{\log_2 n\,\log_2\log_2 n}}$ is still subpolynomial in $n$
items.strategy: Again write n=2^L. Then 2^{c sqrt(L log_2 L)} / n^epsilon = 2^{c sqrt(L log_2 L)-epsilon L}, and sqrt(L log_2 L)=o(L). This example shows that the log-log improvement is genuine but still falls short of the conjectured power law.

items.title: The $P_3$-free case is much stronger than the general lower bounds
items.strategy: Use the published theorem that every P_3-free graph has a homogeneous set of order at least |G|^{1/2}. Compare n^{1/2}=2^{(1/2)log_2 n} with the general scales 2^{c sqrt(log_2 n)} and 2^{c sqrt(log_2 n log_2 log_2 n)}: for large n the square-root exponent is much larger. This example keeps the reader from confusing a universal lower bound with the best possible bound for a specific class.

pages.title: Polynomial Rödl, Virality and Erdős–Hajnal Equivalence

items.title: The polynomial Rödl property for a finite forbidden family
The viral property for a finite forbidden family
The $(t,k)$-homogeneous property
Many good $2t$-vertex subsets force many homogeneous $k$-sets
items.strategy: Use the Bucić–Fox–Pham / Nguyen double-counting step. Count incidences between homogeneous $k$-sets and $2t$-vertex subsets; every good $2t$-set contributes at least one homogeneous $k$-set because it contains a $t$-vertex induced subgraph in the hereditary class, and every graph in that class has the $(t,k)$-homogeneous property.

items.title: Small total induced-copy expectation forces many homogeneous $k$-sets
items.strategy: Package the family version of the sampling lemma. If a random $2t$-vertex subset has expected total forbidden-copy count at most $t/2$, Markov makes at least half of those subsets good; deleting one vertex from each forbidden copy leaves a $t$-vertex family-free induced subgraph, so the previous lemma yields many homogeneous $k$-sets.

items.title: Without a large $\epsilon$-sparse induced subgraph, the number of $k$-vertex stable sets is bounded
items.strategy: Follow Nguyen's Kleitman–Winston style induction. A stable $k$-set either contains a chosen high-degree vertex or avoids it; recurse on the non-neighbour set in the first case and on the deleted graph in the second, using the no-large-sparse-set hypothesis to keep the parameters admissible.

items.title: Every finite family with the Erdős–Hajnal property is viral
items.strategy: Handle the vacuous $K_0$ and $K_1$ cases first. Otherwise take an Erdős–Hajnal exponent $c$, choose an integer $m$ with $mc\ge1$, set $t=k^m$, and use the family-free class to guarantee that every good $t$-vertex induced subgraph contains a homogeneous $k$-set. Bound the expected forbidden-copy count in a random $2t$-vertex subset by linearity of expectation, get many homogeneous $k$-sets from the sampling lemma, and then apply the stable-set counting lemma to $G$ and to $\overline G$ to contradict the absence of an $\epsilon$-restricted linear subset.

items.title: The viral property implies the polynomial Rödl property
items.strategy: If a graph is $\mathcal H$-free, then every forbidden induced-copy count is zero, so the viral hypothesis applies with no extra work.

items.title: The polynomial Rödl property implies the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Let $d$ witness the polynomial Rödl property. For large $n$, choose $\epsilon=n^{-1/(d+1)}$ and take the restricted set $X$ of size at least $n^{1/(d+1)}$; if $X$ is sparse, greedy colouring of $G[X]$ gives a stable set of size at least $1/(2\epsilon)$, and if $X$ is dense the same bound in the complement gives a clique. A finite small-order check closes the remaining values of $n$.

items.title: For a finite family, the Erdős–Hajnal property, the polynomial Rödl property, and virality are equivalent
items.strategy: Combine the previous theorem and corollaries to close the cycle Erdős–Hajnal $\Rightarrow$ viral $\Rightarrow$ polynomial Rödl $\Rightarrow$ Erdős–Hajnal.

items.title: For a single graph, the Erdős–Hajnal property, the polynomial Rödl property, and virality are equivalent
items.strategy: Apply the finite-family theorem to the singleton family $\{H\}$, using that $\{H\}$-free means $H$-free.

pages.title: Polynomial Rödl, Virality and Erdős–Hajnal Equivalence — Examples

items.title: The singleton family $\{P_3\}$ is viral
items.strategy: The published three-vertex classification gives the Erdős–Hajnal property for $P_3$, and the new singleton equivalence turns that immediately into the viral property.

items.title: A family containing $K_1$ is viral for vacuous reasons
items.strategy: For every nonempty graph $G$, the labelled induced-copy count of $K_1$ is exactly $|V(G)|$, so for every $\epsilon<1$ the inequality $\operatorname{ind}_{K_1}(G)<(\epsilon^d|V(G)|)^1$ never holds. The viral implication therefore has no instances to check.

items.title: The polynomial Rödl witness need not be the whole graph
items.strategy: Use the disjoint union of two equal cliques, which is $P_3$-free and therefore lies in a polynomial Rödl family by the singleton equivalence. The whole graph has about half the vertices adjacent to each vertex and about half nonadjacent, so for every fixed $\epsilon<1/2$ it is neither $\epsilon$-sparse nor $\epsilon$-dense, even though one clique side is a $0$-dense restricted set.

items.title: The empty forbidden family is not Erdős–Hajnal
items.strategy: For the empty family, every graph is vacuously family-free, so its free class is the class of all finite graphs. The published random-graph corollary shows that class is not Erdős–Hajnal, so the empty family cannot satisfy any of the equivalent properties.

pages.title: Blockades, Combs and Pattern Graphs

items.title: Blockades are ordered sequences, and directional sparsity follows that order
items.strategy: Record the two conventions the later Erdős-Hajnal pages depend on: a blockade is an ordered list of blocks, and the phrase '$x$-sparse blockade' is directional rather than symmetric. This prevents later pages from silently dropping the order or replacing directional sparsity by weak density.

items.title: A blockade, its length, and its width
Complete, anticomplete, pure, weakly sparse, and $x$-sparse blockades
Combs built on a blockade
The pattern graph of a pure blockade
The sparse orientation attached to an ordered blockade
$P_4$-free pattern graphs have homogeneous sets of square-root size
items.strategy: Argue by induction on the order of the pattern graph. A nontrivial $P_4$-free graph is disconnected or its complement is disconnected, so one of the two complementary decompositions splits the graph into two smaller pieces; applying the inductive hypothesis to the larger homogeneous side of each piece and then combining across a complete or anticomplete cut gives the square-root bound.

items.title: A pure blockade whose pattern graph is $P_4$-free contains a large complete or anticomplete subblockade
items.strategy: Take the pattern graph of the pure blockade and apply the square-root homogeneous-set lemma to it. A clique in the pattern graph yields a complete subblockade and a stable set yields an anticomplete one, with the same block width because only blocks are discarded, never thinned.

items.title: The maximal-pattern argument forces a long pure blockade before theorem 2.3 can fail
items.strategy: Assume a maximal pure blockade whose pattern graph is $P_4$-free and whose block sizes satisfy the weighted sum invariant used in the source proof. If it has too few blocks, apply the hypothesis of theorem 2.3 inside the largest block, replace that block by the complete or anticomplete blockade found there, and enlarge the pattern by substituting a clique or an independent set at the corresponding vertex, contradicting maximality.

items.title: Polynomially large complete or anticomplete blockades force polynomially large restricted induced subgraphs
items.strategy: Follow the maximal pure-blockade route of Nguyen--Scott--Seymour. Build a maximal pure blockade whose pattern graph is $P_4$-free and whose block sizes satisfy the source's $1/a$-power sum invariant, use the previous lemma to show that the pattern has many vertices, extract a complete or anticomplete subblockade of length at least $\varepsilon^{-1}$, and then compress along the source's cograph-pattern argument to obtain an $\varepsilon$-restricted induced subgraph of size at least $\varepsilon^{3a}|G|$.

items.title: Repeated large sparse pairs produce a long $x$-sparse blockade
items.strategy: Iteratively apply the sparse-pair hypothesis inside the current large remainder. At stage $i$, record the sparse side as the next block and continue inside the almost-all remainder; the size inequality $|Y|\ge(1-by)|F|$ guarantees that enough vertices survive for $\lceil y^{-1}\rceil$ stages, and the directional sparse-to relation is preserved by taking later blocks from later remainders. The resulting ordered sequence is an $x$-sparse blockade of the required length and width.

pages.title: Blockades, Combs and Pattern Graphs — Examples

items.title: A three-block blockade and its width
items.strategy: Specify three pairwise disjoint vertex sets in a small graph and compute the blockade width as the minimum block size. The example exists purely to make the ordered-sequence viewpoint concrete.

items.title: A pure blockade need not be complete or anticomplete
items.strategy: Give a three-block blockade in which one pair of blocks is complete and another is anticomplete. This is the smallest explicit witness that purity is a pattern condition, not a uniform adjacency condition.

items.title: A three-tooth comb built on a blockade
items.strategy: Exhibit three attachment vertices and three blocks satisfying the definition of a comb. The verification checks exactly which adjacencies are required and which are forbidden.

items.title: The pattern graph of a four-block pure blockade
items.strategy: Start from a pure blockade and write down the graph on block indices whose edges record complete pairs. The example is there so later pages can cite a finite witness when they use pattern language.

items.title: An ordered blockade determines a sparse orientation
items.strategy: Choose four blocks so that later blocks are sparse to earlier ones in a specified order. The example shows that the order of extraction is part of the data, not a cosmetic choice.

items.title: FALSE: every pure blockade is complete or anticomplete
items.strategy: Reuse the smallest mixed complete/anticomplete pattern from the earlier pure-but-not-complete example. A single finite blockade refutes the claim because purity only asks for each pair of blocks to be pure, not for all pairs to behave the same way.

items.title: FALSE: reordering a blockade never changes whether it is $x$-sparse
items.strategy: Construct two blocks $A,B$ with $B$ sparse to $A$ but not conversely. The same unordered pair therefore yields one ordered blockade that is $x$-sparse and one that is not.

items.title: Weak sparsity does not force directional sparsity
items.strategy: Give a pair of vertex sets with small average edge density but one high-degree witness in one direction. This separates the weak edge-count notion from the directional maximum-degree notion used in sparse blockades.

items.title: A would-be comb fails if one attachment vertex sees a foreign block
items.strategy: Modify a valid comb by adding a single forbidden adjacency from one tooth to another block. The point of the counterexample is to show that the anti-complete-away-from-own-block clause is genuinely load-bearing.

pages.title: Pure Pairs, Forests and Path–Antipath Classes

items.title: The strong Erdős–Hajnal property for a hereditary graph class
Every nontrivial $P_4$-free graph is disconnected or has disconnected complement
items.strategy: Record the Seinsche cograph characterization in the form used by Bousquet-Lagoutte-Thomasse: a nontrivial graph with no induced $P_4$ cannot be both connected and anticonnected. This is the structural input behind the strong-to-weak Erdős-Hajnal implication.

items.title: Every $P_4$-free graph has a clique or stable set of size at least the square root of its order
items.strategy: Induct on the number of vertices using the previous disconnected-or-antidisconnected dichotomy. In the disconnected case combine maxima across components; in the complement-disconnected case apply the same argument to stable sets.

items.title: The strong Erdős–Hajnal property implies the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Follow Bousquet-Lagoutte-Thomasse's induction: the strong property recursively builds a large induced cograph by splitting along a complete or anticomplete pair, and the square-root bound for $P_4$-free graphs then yields the required polynomial clique-or-stable-set bound.

items.title: Every $H$-free graph has a polynomial-size pure pair
items.strategy: Record the Erdős-Hajnal-Pach bipartite analogue as the general pure-pair baseline: the source's candidate-set embedding argument forces a large complete or anticomplete pair whenever the forbidden induced pattern is fixed.

items.title: For every $k$, the class forbidding $P_k$ and $\overline{P_k}$ has the strong Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Use the Bousquet-Lagoutte-Thomasse route: the earlier Rödl/Fox-Sudakov family corollary supplies a large restricted induced subgraph, and the source's connected-case lemma then forces a linear biclique in the graph or its complement.

items.title: For every $k$, the class forbidding $P_k$ and $\overline{P_k}$ has the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Apply the strong-to-weak implication to the hereditary class from the previous theorem.

items.title: Every forest-free graph has a linear anticomplete pair or a linear-degree vertex
items.strategy: Record the main sparse theorem from Pure pairs I: in an $H$-free graph for a fixed forest $H$, either some vertex has linear degree or there are two large anticomplete sets. This is the source endpoint that the forest pure-pair theorem is derived from.

items.title: For every forest $H$, graphs excluding $H$ and $\overline{H}$ have a linear pure pair
items.strategy: Use the source's derivation from the preceding sparse theorem together with complement symmetry to package a linear complete or anticomplete pair for graphs excluding a forest and its complement.

items.title: For every forest $H$, graphs excluding $H$ and $\overline{H}$ have the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Apply the strong-to-weak implication to the previous forest pure-pair theorem.

items.title: Co-leaves of a finite graph
Deleting a leaf from each of two forbidden graphs preserves virality
items.strategy: Use Nguyen-Scott-Seymour's unordered leaf-deletion theorem: if the two smaller families obtained by deleting the chosen leaves are viral, then the original family is viral.

items.title: Deleting a leaf and a co-leaf preserves virality of a finite forbidden family
items.strategy: Translate the co-leaf side into a leaf in the complement and then use the earlier leaf-deletion theorem, with Huang-Ju-Zhou's Theorem 1.7 fixing the exact family notation that later E-graph deductions use.

items.title: Deleting a leaf and a co-leaf preserves the Erdős–Hajnal property of a finite forbidden family
items.strategy: Combine the virality preservation theorem with the finite-family equivalence between the Erdős-Hajnal property and virality.

pages.title: Pure Pairs, Forests and Path–Antipath Classes — Examples

items.title: The path-antipath theorem specialized to $P_5$ and $\overline{P_5}$
items.strategy: Instantiate the path-antipath Erdős-Hajnal theorem at $k=5$ and identify the two forbidden graphs using the library's standard path notation.

items.title: The forest pure-pair theorem specialized to $P_4$
items.strategy: Note that $P_4$ is a forest and is isomorphic to its complement, so the forest-complement theorem applies to the cograph case without changing the forbidden graph.

items.title: A co-leaf of $\overline{P_5}$ is exactly a leaf of $P_5$
items.strategy: Label the five-vertex path in order, compute the degrees in its complement, and check that the two degree-three vertices of $\overline{P_5}$ are precisely the images of the two leaves of $P_5$.

items.title: The leaf/co-leaf corollary recovers the $P_5$ case from the $P_4$ case
items.strategy: Apply the leaf/co-leaf Erdős-Hajnal corollary to the family $\{P_5,\overline{P_5}\}$: deleting a leaf on each side leaves $\{P_4,\overline{P_4}\}$, and the previous example identifies that smaller family with the cograph case.

pages.title: Bull-Free Graphs and the Erdős–Hajnal Property

items.title: The bull graph
A bull-free graph
A graph is bull-free if and only if its complement is bull-free
items.strategy: The bull is self-complementary, so taking complements preserves the forbidden induced configuration. Apply the published complement construction to transport induced copies in both directions.

items.title: Holes, antiholes, and odd holes
A perfect graph
Weak Perfect Graph Theorem
Strong Perfect Graph Theorem
A good function on a graph
An $\alpha$-narrow graph
Every perfect graph is 1-narrow
items.strategy: If G is perfect, then G itself is one of the perfect induced subgraphs tested in the definition of a good function. Therefore every good function has total weight at most 1 on all of V(G), which is exactly 1-narrowness.

items.title: An $\alpha$-narrow graph contains a perfect induced subgraph of order at least $|V(G)|^{1/\alpha}$
items.strategy: Let K be the maximum order of a perfect induced subgraph and test the narrowness inequality on the constant function 1/K. This function is good by definition of K, so the alpha-power bound forces |V(G)|/K^alpha <= 1.

items.title: An $\alpha$-narrow graph has a clique or stable set of size at least $|V(G)|^{1/(2\alpha)}$
items.strategy: Take a largest perfect induced subgraph from the preceding theorem. On that subgraph, the perfect-graph inequality alpha times omega at least the order yields a clique or stable set of square-root size, which becomes |V(G)|^(1/(2 alpha)) after substitution of the lower bound on the perfect subgraph order.

items.title: Basic and composite bull-free graphs
A split set in a bull-free graph
A split set with both a complete and an anticomplete outside vertex yields a nontrivial module
items.strategy: Follow the source's two-case bull obstruction for a mixed outside vertex, then grow the anticomplete side by paths through anticomplete vertices until its union with the split set becomes homogeneous to the rest of the graph. Translate the source's homogeneous-set conclusion into the library's module terminology.

items.title: Every composite bull-free graph has a nontrivial module
items.strategy: A composite bull-free graph contains an odd hole or odd antihole with one outside vertex complete to it and another anticomplete to it. Check that the vertex set of the hole is a split set, then apply the previous theorem.

items.title: Every prime bull-free graph is basic
items.strategy: If a prime bull-free graph were composite, the composite theorem would give a nontrivial module, contradicting primality.

items.title: In a basic bull-free graph, a hole with a complete outside vertex has tightly constrained neighbors
items.strategy: Assume a vertex outside the hole misses some hole vertex. The source's repeated bull obstructions force either complete adjacency to the hole or the exceptional five-hole configuration with at least three neighbors.

items.title: In a basic bull-free graph, a hole with an anticomplete outside vertex forbids consecutive neighbors
items.strategy: If a vertex adjacent to the outside anticomplete vertex had two consecutive neighbors on the hole, then the source's minimal non-neighbor argument produces a bull. The resulting spacing also gives the lower bound on the number of hole non-neighbors.

items.title: Substituting perfect graphs preserves perfection
For a vertex in a basic bull-free graph, either its neighborhood or its antineighborhood is perfect
items.strategy: Argue by contradiction: if both induced sides were imperfect, the strong perfect graph theorem would force odd holes or odd antiholes on each side. The two structural lemmas then overcount cross adjacencies and non-adjacencies between those witness cycles, producing the source contradiction.

items.title: Every basic bull-free graph is 2-narrow
items.strategy: Choose a vertex of maximum weight under a good function. One side of its neighborhood partition is perfect by the preceding theorem, and the other is smaller and still basic after complementing if needed. Rescale the good function on the imperfect side exactly as in the source and combine the two quadratic bounds.

items.title: Substituting two $\alpha$-narrow graphs yields another $\alpha$-narrow graph
items.strategy: Follow the source's two-graph substitution proof: compress the substituted block to one vertex whose weight is the maximum perfect-subgraph weight on that block, invoke preservation of perfection under substitution to verify the resulting good-function constraints, and combine the two alpha-power bounds.

items.title: Every bull-free graph is 2-narrow
items.strategy: Induct on the number of vertices. If the graph is prime, the prime-implies-basic corollary and the basic theorem apply. Otherwise the prime-graph theorem and the quotient-as-induced-subgraph lemma realize the graph as a substitution of two smaller bull-free graphs, and alpha-narrowness is preserved under substitution.

items.title: Every bull-free graph has a clique or stable set of size at least $|V(G)|^{1/4}$
items.strategy: Combine two-narrowness with the general alpha-narrow clique-or-stable-set corollary at alpha=2, and restate the conclusion in the Erdős-Hajnal language already fixed earlier in the track.

items.title: The bull graph is self-complementary
The five-cycle is bull-free but not perfect
$K_4$ is bull-free and has a nontrivial module
The five-cycle is 2-narrow but not 1-narrow
FALSE: every bull-free graph is perfect

pages.title: Cographs, Perfect Patterns and Pure Pairs

items.title: The complete connection of two disjoint graphs
Cographs by the singleton, disjoint-union, and complete-connection recursion
Every induced subgraph of a cograph is a cograph
items.strategy: Let $\mathcal F$ be the class of graphs all of whose induced subgraphs are cographs. A one-vertex graph lies in $\mathcal F$, and taking an induced subgraph of a disjoint union or of a complete connection splits into the same operation on the traces on the two sides. Since cographs are the smallest class closed under those operations, every cograph belongs to $\mathcal F$.

items.title: Every nontrivial cograph is disconnected or has disconnected complement
items.strategy: Use the recursive definition. A nontrivial cograph is built from two smaller cographs either by disjoint union, which is visibly disconnected, or by complete connection, whose complement is the disjoint union of the complements of the two parts and is therefore disconnected.

items.title: The cographs are exactly the $P_4$-free graphs
items.strategy: For the forward direction, induced subgraphs of cographs are cographs and every nontrivial cograph satisfies the previous disconnected-or-complement-disconnected dichotomy, while the standard path P4 has edges 12, 23, 34 and complement edges 13, 14, 24, so it is connected and its complement is connected. For the reverse direction, induct on the order of a $P_4$-free graph and use the published Seinsche theorem to split it into a disjoint union or a complete connection of smaller $P_4$-free induced subgraphs.

items.title: Every prime graph on at least four vertices contains an induced $P_4$
items.strategy: Harju's small-primitive-subgraph theorem gives a primitive induced subgraph on three or four vertices. The published three-vertex lemma rules out size three. If the primitive subgraph has four vertices, then unions of components or anticomponents would be modules, so primeness forces the graph to be connected and anticonnected; a four-vertex connected anticonnected graph has no degree 0 or 3 vertices, so a short degree count forces a degree-1 vertex and hence the path P4.

items.title: Perfect graphs
The parameter $\kappa(G)=\alpha(G)\omega(G)$
A disjoint union of two perfect graphs is perfect
items.strategy: Every induced subgraph of a disjoint union is the disjoint union of the induced subgraphs on the two sides. For such a union, the clique number and chromatic number are both the maximum of the corresponding two side values, so equality on both sides passes to the union.

items.title: A complete connection of two perfect graphs is perfect
items.strategy: An induced subgraph of a complete connection is the complete connection of the traces on the two sides. In a complete connection, every clique is the union of a clique from each side and every proper colouring uses disjoint colour sets on the two sides, so both $\omega$ and $\chi$ add across the construction. Equality therefore passes from the two perfect factors to the whole graph and to all its induced subgraphs.

items.title: Every cograph is perfect
items.strategy: Let $\mathcal P$ be the class of perfect graphs. One-vertex graphs are perfect, the previous two lemmas show that $\mathcal P$ is closed under disjoint unions and complete connections, and the cographs are the smallest class with those closure properties.

items.title: Every perfect graph satisfies $|V(G)|\leq\kappa(G)$
items.strategy: For a perfect graph, the defining equality gives $\chi(G)=\omega(G)$. Combine this with the published bound $|V(G)|\leq\chi(G)\alpha(G)$ and the definition of $\kappa(G)$.

items.title: Every perfect graph has a clique or stable set of size at least the square root of its order
items.strategy: If $h=\max\{\omega(G),\alpha(G)\}$, then $\kappa(G)=\alpha(G)\omega(G)\leq h^2$. Combine this with the previous theorem and take square roots.

items.title: The perfect-induced-subgraph formulation of the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture
The Erdős–Hajnal property is equivalent to the large-cograph, large-perfect, and $\kappa$ formulations
items.strategy: Work with existence of some positive exponent, not a fixed one. A homogeneous set is itself an induced cograph and an induced perfect graph; every cograph is perfect by the previous theorem; a perfect induced subgraph of size $m$ contains a homogeneous set of size at least $m^{1/2}$ by the previous corollary; and $\operatorname{hom}(G)^2\geq\kappa(G)\geq\operatorname{hom}(G)$ for every nonempty graph, so the homogeneous and $\kappa$ formulations differ only by rescaling the exponent.

items.title: A pure blockade with a perfect pattern has a large complete or anticomplete subblockade
items.strategy: Apply the perfect-graph square-root corollary to the pattern graph. A clique of pattern vertices gives a complete subblockade, a stable set gives an anticomplete subblockade, and the width is unchanged because only whole blocks are discarded.

items.title: A $\tau$-critical graph
A minimal counterexample to a $\kappa$-bound is $\tau$-critical
items.strategy: Fix $\tau>0$ and a forbidden family, and choose a counterexample $G$ with the fewest vertices among those with $\kappa(G)<|G|^\tau$. Every proper induced subgraph of $G$ is smaller and therefore satisfies the bound, which is exactly the second clause of the $\tau$-critical definition.

items.title: A pure blockade with a cograph pattern has additive $\kappa$
items.strategy: Induct on the number of blocks. A nontrivial cograph pattern splits into two nonempty parts that are either complete or anticomplete across. Read the complete case in the complement, apply the induction hypothesis to the two unions, and combine the two bounds across an anticomplete split by adding stable sets and comparing clique numbers.

items.title: A $\tau$-critical graph has no wide pure blockade with cograph pattern
items.strategy: If such a blockade had length $t$ and width at least $|G|t^{-1/\tau}$, then every block would satisfy $\kappa(B_i)\geq |B_i|^\tau\geq |G|^\tau/t$ by $\tau$-criticality, and the previous theorem would force $\kappa(G)\geq |G|^\tau$, contradicting the definition.

items.title: A blockade-rainbow induced copy

pages.title: Cographs, Perfect Patterns and Pure Pairs — Examples

items.title: The four-cycle is a cograph
items.strategy: Build $C_4$ as the complete connection of two disjoint edges. This witnesses the recursive cograph definition directly and keeps the example small enough that the decomposition can be checked from the adjacency list alone.

items.title: The five-vertex path is perfect but not a cograph
items.strategy: The induced subgraphs of $P_5$ are smaller forests, so each has clique number and chromatic number both equal to $1$ or $2$; verify this directly by finite case checking. It is not a cograph because its first four vertices induce a $P_4$.

items.title: A two-block pure blockade can realize equality in the additive $\kappa$ theorem
items.strategy: Take two disjoint cliques that are complete to each other. Each block contributes its order to $\kappa$, and the union is again a clique whose size is the sum of the two block sizes.

items.title: A pure blockade can have a perfect pattern that is not a cograph
items.strategy: Use five singleton blocks whose pattern graph is $P_5$. The previous example supplies that $P_5$ is perfect and not a cograph, and the singleton blocks make the blockade and its pattern transparent.

items.title: A four-block blockade-rainbow copy of $P_4$
items.strategy: Take one vertex from each of four singleton blocks whose induced graph is a path. Then each block meets the copy in exactly one vertex, so the copy is rainbow by definition.

Quotient Blockades and Mixing Relations

items.title: The mixed-block reachability relation on a blockade
Mixed-block reachability is an equivalence relation
items.strategy: The relation is reflexive by definition, symmetric because mixedness is symmetric for unordered pairs of disjoint sets, and transitive by concatenating mixed block chains.

items.title: The quotient blockade obtained from mixed-block reachability
A quotient block of connected or anticonnected blocks is again connected or anticonnected
items.strategy: Induct along a mixed block chain. Mixedness gives at least one edge between consecutive connected blocks and at least one nonedge between consecutive anticonnected blocks, so connectivity in the graph or its complement survives each union.

items.title: Blocks from distinct mixed-block classes are pure to each other
items.strategy: If two blocks in different classes were mixed, that mixed edge would itself be a length-one witness putting them in the same reachability class.

items.title: A vertex mixed on a quotient block but pure on each member block yields two mixed member blocks with opposite adjacency
items.strategy: Choose member blocks on which the external vertex is complete and anticomplete, then walk along a mixed chain inside the quotient class until the adjacency switches for the first time.

items.title: A quotient-level mixed-block witness descends to two mixed member blocks
items.strategy: Apply the previous two lemmas inside the first mixed quotient block: the no-mixing hypothesis on the other quotient block forces the needed mixed vertex to come from that side, and its two opposite adjacencies descend to member blocks.

pages.title: Quotient Blockades and Mixing Relations — Examples

items.title: Mixedness of block pairs is not transitive
items.strategy: Exhibit three disjoint blocks $A,B,C$ with $(A,B)$ and $(B,C)$ mixed but $(A,C)$ anticomplete. This shows why the quotient page uses the reachability closure of mixedness rather than mixedness itself.

items.title: A mixed chain of blocks collapses to one quotient block
items.strategy: Take a four-block blockade in which consecutive pairs are mixed and the end pair is pure; compute the reachability classes explicitly and verify that the quotient merges exactly the chain component.

items.title: A vertex may be mixed on a quotient block while pure on each member block
items.strategy: Choose two mixed member blocks inside one quotient class and an external vertex complete to one but anticomplete to the other. Their union is then mixed to that vertex although each member block is still pure to it.

items.title: The quotient-witness reduction in a four-block configuration
items.strategy: Write down a four-block example with two quotient classes and vertices $x,y,u$ satisfying the quotient-level hypotheses, then track the reduction to concrete member blocks $A_1,A_2$ as in Lemma 6.2.

Smooth Manifolds and Smooth Maps

items.title: Topological manifolds without boundary
Manifold charts, coordinate domains, and coordinate functions
The coordinate representation of a map
Smoothly compatible charts
Smooth chart compatibility is symmetric and reflexive
items.strategy: Reflexivity is immediate from the identity transition map. Symmetry is not hidden in bijectivity: it uses the two-sided clause in the compatibility definition exactly as stated.

items.title: Smooth atlases
The union of two compatible smooth atlases is a smooth atlas
items.strategy: Check that cross-chart compatibility is the only extra condition beyond the two given atlas conditions. Once every chart in one atlas is compatible with every chart in the other, pairwise compatibility for the union follows immediately.

items.title: Compatibility of smooth atlases is an equivalence relation
items.strategy: Use the previous lemma to package transitivity at the atlas level. The proof avoids pretending that chartwise compatibility is transitive without a covering argument.

items.title: All charts compatible with a smooth atlas form a smooth atlas
items.strategy: At a point of overlap between two new charts, choose a chart from the reference atlas and factor the new transition through that chart. Smoothness is local, so the chain rule turns compatibility with the atlas into compatibility with each other.

items.title: The smooth structure generated by an atlas
Each smooth atlas is contained in a unique maximal smooth atlas
items.strategy: The previous lemma gives existence of the atlas of all compatible charts. Uniqueness comes from maximality, and the same argument shows that two atlases determine the same smooth structure exactly when their union is again a smooth atlas.

items.title: Smooth manifolds
An open subset of a smooth manifold has a canonical restricted smooth structure
items.strategy: Restrict each chart to the open trace. These restricted charts still cover the subspace, their transition maps are inherited from the ambient ones, and the maximal-atlas theorem removes dependence on the presenting atlas.

items.title: Open subsets of Euclidean space have the standard smooth structure
items.strategy: Use the identity chart on the Euclidean open set. Every compatible chart has smooth transitions with that identity chart, so the resulting maximal atlas is exactly the standard one.

items.title: Products of smooth manifolds have a canonical product smooth structure
items.strategy: Take products of charts and write the transition maps blockwise. The product universal property and the Euclidean product topology identify the local models, while the transition maps are smooth componentwise.

items.title: Countable disjoint unions of fixed-dimensional smooth manifolds are smooth manifolds
items.strategy: Use the disjoint-union topology and the component charts from each summand. Countability is the point: it lets the union of the countable chart bases remain countable, so second countability is preserved.

items.title: $C^r$ and smooth maps between smooth manifolds
Chart independence of $C^r$ smoothness
items.strategy: Change source and target charts by composing with transition diffeomorphisms on the left and right. The Euclidean chain rule shows that if one coordinate representative is $C^r$, then every other one is too.

items.title: Smooth maps are continuous
items.strategy: A smooth coordinate representative is in particular $C^1$, hence continuous. Compose with the chart homeomorphisms and use locality on the source to lift continuity to the manifold map.

items.title: Identity maps and composites of smooth maps are smooth
items.strategy: The coordinate formula for a composite is the composite of coordinate formulas on the correct overlap restriction. The Euclidean chain rule gives smoothness once the domains are written out honestly.

items.title: Diffeomorphisms and local diffeomorphisms of manifolds
Chart maps are diffeomorphisms onto Euclidean open sets
items.strategy: A smooth chart belongs to the maximal atlas, so every transition between that chart and itself or another smooth chart is smooth in both directions. The chart map and its inverse are therefore smooth by the very definition of smooth structure.

items.title: Smoothness is local on the source
items.strategy: If a map is smooth on an open cover, then around each point one of those open sets supplies the needed chart pair. The chart-independence lemma then turns that local witness into a chart-independent smoothness statement.

items.title: Smooth maps paste over an open cover
items.strategy: First use the topological pasting lemma to get a well-defined continuous map. Then apply smoothness locality on the source to each open set of the cover.

items.title: A map into a product is smooth iff its components are smooth
items.strategy: Write product charts componentwise and identify the coordinate representative with the product of the component representatives. The product universal property turns the manifold statement into the Euclidean componentwise one.

items.title: A map from a disjoint union is smooth iff each restriction is smooth
items.strategy: On a disjoint union, every point lies in exactly one summand, so smoothness is checked there. The coproduct universal property packages the converse statement about maps assembled from the restrictions.

items.title: Restrictions, corestrictions, and products of smooth maps are smooth
items.strategy: Each construction is a direct application of the earlier locality, composition, and product criteria once the openness hypotheses are stated explicitly.

items.title: A smooth map with everywhere smooth local inverses is a local diffeomorphism
items.strategy: By hypothesis each point has neighborhoods on which the map has a smooth inverse. The local inverses agree where both are defined, because both are inverse to the same map on the overlap, so the local-diffeomorphism condition follows directly.

items.title: Coordinate balls form a basis of a topological manifold
items.strategy: Inside a chart image, choose an ordinary Euclidean ball around the coordinate point with compact closure still inside the image. Pulling such balls back through the chart produces a neighborhood basis in the manifold.

items.title: Topological manifolds are locally compact and locally path connected
items.strategy: Transport the Euclidean local compactness and polygonal connectedness of open balls through coordinate charts. The coordinate-ball basis keeps both properties local at every point.

items.title: Components of a topological manifold are open and at most countable
items.strategy: Local path connectedness makes components of open sets open, hence manifold components open. A countable basis then injects the family of components into the basis by sending each component to its first basis element.

items.title: Topological manifolds are sigma-compact
items.strategy: Start from a fixed countable basis of coordinate balls whose closures are compact. Local compactness and the chart-basis lemma show that those compact-closure basis elements cover the manifold, so enumerating their closures gives a countable compact cover with no pointwise choice.

items.title: Topological manifolds are metrizable and paracompact
items.strategy: Use the published topology route recorded in the design: locally compact Hausdorff implies regularity, second countability implies Lindelof, regular Lindelof implies paracompact, and second-countable regular spaces are metrizable by the Urysohn theorem. This avoids the stronger Stone-first route the design explicitly rejected.

items.title: Manifold conventions and the role of second countability
Hausdorff and locally Euclidean do not by themselves make a manifold
items.strategy: Use the long line. It is Hausdorff and locally homeomorphic to an interval, but it fails second countability, so it is excluded by the library convention.

items.title: A chart domain need not be a Euclidean open set
items.strategy: The domain of a chart is open in the manifold, while the Euclidean open set is its image. Confusing the two swaps the ambient spaces and breaks the coordinate language at the outset.

items.title: Two atlases on the same topological manifold need not have a union atlas
items.strategy: A union is an atlas only when all cross-transition maps are smooth. The cubic coordinate atlas on the line gives a direct counterexample to unconditional union.

items.title: A bijective smooth map need not be a diffeomorphism
items.strategy: The map $x \mapsto x^3$ is smooth and bijective on $\mathbb R$, but its inverse has derivative blowing up at the origin, so smoothness of the inverse is genuinely extra data.

items.title: One smooth transition direction does not guarantee chart compatibility
items.strategy: The same cubic-coordinate example shows that smoothness of one transition map does not force smoothness of its inverse. Both directions must be stated.

items.title: An arbitrary disjoint union of second-countable manifolds need not be second-countable
items.strategy: An uncountable discrete union of one-point manifolds is locally Euclidean and Hausdorff, but every singleton is open, so no countable basis can cover distinct points separately.

pages.title: Smooth Manifolds and Smooth Maps — Examples

items.title: Euclidean spaces and Euclidean open subsets as smooth manifolds
items.strategy: Use the identity chart on $\mathbb R^n$ and its restrictions to open subsets. The A-page standard-structure proposition then supplies the smooth structure immediately.

items.title: The circle from two stereographic charts
items.strategy: Write the north- and south-pole stereographic charts explicitly and compute both transition maps on the overlap. The example witnesses the chart-compatibility definition without importing later regular-level-set machinery.

items.title: The $n$-sphere with its standard smooth atlas
items.strategy: Generalize the two-chart circle construction to the standard stereographic atlas on $S^n$. The transition maps are rational coordinate formulas on $\mathbb R^n \setminus \{0\}$.

items.title: Real projective space from affine charts
items.strategy: Cover projective space by the standard affine patches $x_i \neq 0$ and use the affine coordinate ratios on each patch. The overlap maps are rational and smooth on their domains.

items.title: The torus as a product smooth manifold
items.strategy: Take the product of two circle atlases. The resulting product charts exhibit the torus as a smooth manifold by the A-page product construction.

items.title: A countable disjoint union of lines is a smooth manifold
items.strategy: Apply the countable disjoint-union proposition to a countable family of copies of $\mathbb R$. Each summand contributes its standard chart, and the countability hypothesis is visibly used.

items.title: The long line is locally Euclidean and Hausdorff but not a manifold under the library convention
items.strategy: Invoke the long-line construction and check the only missing axiom: second countability. This is the companion witness for the adopted manifold convention.

items.title: Two noncompatible atlases on the real line
items.strategy: Use the identity chart and the cubic chart on $\mathbb R$. One transition map is $x^3$, while the inverse cube-root map fails to be smooth at $0$.

items.title: A bijective smooth map with nonsmooth inverse
items.strategy: The smooth bijection $x \mapsto x^3$ on $\mathbb R$ has inverse $x \mapsto x^{1/3}$, whose first derivative is unbounded at the origin. So bijectivity plus smoothness does not force a diffeomorphism.

items.title: An uncountable disjoint union of points is not second-countable
items.strategy: Every singleton is open in the disjoint-union topology, so a basis must already distinguish uncountably many points. This is the direct witness behind the countability restriction in the A-page disjoint-union theorem.

Euclidean Ordinary Differential Equations with Smooth Dependence

items.title: Autonomous ordinary differential equations
The variational equation along an ODE solution
Linear matrix ODEs have unique global solutions on a fixed interval
items.strategy: View an $n \times n$ matrix as a vector in $\mathbb R^{n^2}$ and apply the published Picard-Lindelof theorem on small subintervals. The compact-interval coefficient bound and the continuation theorem then prevent finite-endpoint breakdown inside the interval.

items.title: A fundamental matrix is invertible
items.strategy: Solve the inverse linear equation and differentiate the product of a candidate inverse with the fundamental matrix. Uniqueness for the identity-valued solution forces the product to stay equal to the identity.

items.title: $C^1$ dependence of solutions on initial data
items.strategy: Difference quotients satisfy a linearized integral equation. The linear comparison estimate and continuous dependence from the published Picard-Lindelof page drive those difference quotients to the solution of the variational equation.

items.title: Smooth dependence of solutions on initial data
items.strategy: Differentiate the Volterra integral equation inductively. At each order the new highest derivative solves an inhomogeneous linear ODE with coefficients built from lower-order derivatives already known to be smooth.

items.title: Smooth dependence of ODE solutions on parameters
items.strategy: Adjoin the parameter as a constant extra variable and reduce the parameter-dependent system to the autonomous initial-data theorem. The common local interval is carried through the augmented system rather than assumed silently.

items.title: A bounded vector field on all of Euclidean space is complete
items.strategy: The integral equation bounds the displacement by the bound on the speed times the elapsed time. A finite maximal endpoint therefore cannot force escape from every compact subset of $\mathbb R^n$, contradicting the published continuation criterion.

items.title: A compactly supported smooth Euclidean vector field is complete
items.strategy: A smooth vector field that vanishes outside a compact subset is bounded on that compact set and zero elsewhere. The previous corollary then gives global existence.

items.title: The fundamental theorem for autonomous smooth ODEs
items.strategy: Combine the published Picard-Lindelof existence and uniqueness theorem with the smooth dependence theorem on a common local interval. The result is stated on the honest open domain of triples where the maximal solution exists.

items.title: The fundamental theorem for nonautonomous smooth ODEs
items.strategy: Adjoin the time variable with $\dot s = 1$ and rewrite the nonautonomous system as an autonomous one in one higher dimension. Apply the autonomous theorem and project back to the original variables.

items.title: The maximal solution domain is open
items.strategy: Take a point where a maximal solution exists, move to the corresponding point on its graph, and apply the local fundamental theorem around that point. The resulting common existence neighborhood propagates existence and smoothness to a whole open set of triples.

items.title: Solutions compose under a change of initial time
items.strategy: Both sides solve the same initial value problem at the intermediate time, so uniqueness on the common domain identifies them. The open-domain proposition ensures the equality is stated exactly where both expressions make sense.

items.title: A smooth Euclidean vector field need not be complete
items.strategy: The scalar equation $\dot x = x^2$ has a smooth right-hand side but the solution from $x(0)=1$ blows up at time $1$. Smoothness does not control growth at infinity.

items.title: Pointwise local existence does not force one global uniform time interval
items.strategy: Uniform time intervals are local in the initial data, not global over all of $\mathbb R^n$. A family of initial conditions moving toward faster and faster blow-up witnesses the failure.

items.title: A maximal ODE solution need not have a closed interval domain
items.strategy: Maximal domains are open intervals because local existence always extends a solution a little away from an interior point. Finite-time blow-up produces a maximal domain of the form $(-\infty,1)$ or $(a,b)$ rather than a closed interval.

items.title: Continuous dependence does not by itself imply differentiable dependence
items.strategy: Differentiable dependence uses derivatives of the vector field and the variational equation. Continuous dependence from Picard-Lindelof is strictly weaker than the smooth-dependence block built on this page.

pages.title: Euclidean Ordinary Differential Equations with Smooth Dependence — Examples

items.title: A constant vector field has translation solutions
items.strategy: Solve $\dot x = v$ explicitly to get $x(t)=x_0+tv$. This is the easiest model of the autonomous fundamental theorem and of completeness.

items.title: A linear system and its fundamental matrix
items.strategy: For $\dot x = Ax$ with constant matrix $A$, the matrix exponential gives the solution operator. This example makes the variational equation and fundamental-matrix language concrete.

items.title: The harmonic oscillator as a first-order system
items.strategy: Rewrite $\ddot q + q = 0$ as a planar linear system and solve it by sine and cosine. The example shows how a classical second-order equation fits the first-order framework used later for geodesics.

items.title: A compactly supported vector field with global solutions
items.strategy: Choose a smooth bump multiple of a constant vector field. Outside the compact support the solution becomes constant, so the completeness corollary is visible directly from the phase portrait.

items.title: Smooth dependence in an ODE with a parameter
items.strategy: Solve $\dot x = \lambda x$ as $x(t)=e^{\lambda t}x_0$ and differentiate the explicit formula in both $x_0$ and $\lambda$. The variational equation matches the derivative formulas exactly.

items.title: A nonautonomous equation made autonomous by adjoining time
items.strategy: Rewrite $\dot x = t x$ as the autonomous system $\dot s = 1$, $\dot x = sx$. The reduction illustrates exactly how the nonautonomous fundamental theorem is proved.
