Complexification, Realification and Real Structures

items.title: Realification of a complex vector space by restriction of scalars
Complexification as $\mathbb C\otimes_{\mathbb R}V$ with its canonical real-linear embedding
The direct-sum model $V\oplus iV$ of a complexification
Complexification of a real-linear map
Conjugations and real structures on a complex vector space
The fixed real form of a conjugation
The tensor and direct-sum models of complexification are canonically complex-linearly isomorphic
items.strategy: Send $z\otimes v$ to the formal vector $zv$ in $V\oplus iV$, verify well-definedness from the tensor universal property, and recover the inverse from the canonical embedding of $V$ and the complex scalar action.

items.title: Complexification is initial for real-linear maps into complex vector spaces, and is unique up to unique isomorphism
items.strategy: For a real-linear map $f:V\to W$, define the factor on $\mathbb C\otimes_{\mathbb R}V$ by $(a+bi)\otimes v\mapsto af(v)+ibf(v)$ and use the tensor universal property. Uniqueness up to unique isomorphism is the standard representing-object argument.

items.title: Complexification is a functor on real vector spaces and real-linear maps
items.strategy: Define $T_{\mathbb C}=1\otimes T$ on elementary tensors, and check the identity and composition laws on generators using tensor functoriality.

items.title: Complexification preserves kernels, images, finite rank, nullity, and short exact sequences
items.strategy: Pass to the direct-sum model, where $T_{\mathbb C}(v+iw)=Tv+iTw$ acts componentwise. Kernels, images, dimensions, and exactness then reduce to the corresponding real statements on each coordinate.

items.title: A real basis becomes a complex basis after complexification, so $\dim_{\mathbb C}(\mathbb C\otimes_{\mathbb R}V)=\dim_{\mathbb R}V$
items.strategy: Apply the tensor-product basis theorem to the real basis of $V$ and the basis $1,i$ of $\mathbb C$, then use the direct-sum model to show that the embedded real basis vectors alone already form a complex basis.

items.title: Realification doubles finite dimension
items.strategy: If $(e_j)$ is a complex basis, prove over $\mathbb R$ that $e_1,ie_1,\dots,e_n,ie_n$ span the realification and remain independent by separating real and imaginary coefficients.

items.title: The fixed points of a conjugation form a real vector space whose complexification recovers the ambient complex space
items.strategy: Show the fixed set is closed under real scalars. For $v$, split it as $(v+\sigma v)/2+i\,(v-\sigma v)/(2i)$ to obtain fixed vectors giving surjectivity from the fixed-point complexification, and use the standard embedding argument for injectivity.

items.title: Real forms of a complex vector space correspond exactly to conjugations
items.strategy: From a real form take the canonical conjugation on its complexification; from a conjugation take the fixed real form and use the reconstruction theorem to identify the original complex space with its complexification.

items.title: A complex-linear operator comes from a real operator exactly when it commutes with the chosen conjugation
items.strategy: A complexified real operator obviously commutes with canonical conjugation on elementary tensors. Conversely, restriction to the fixed real form is well defined for a commuting operator, and the reconstruction theorem shows that its complexification recovers the original map.

items.title: Complexification preserves the characteristic and minimal polynomials of a finite-dimensional real operator
items.strategy: Use a real basis and its complexified basis to see that $T$ and $T_{\mathbb C}$ have the same matrix, hence the same characteristic polynomial. The minimal polynomial is then unchanged by the published field-extension lemma.

items.title: For a real operator, nonreal generalised eigenspaces of the complexification occur in conjugate pairs
items.strategy: If $\sigma$ is canonical conjugation, then $\sigma\,(T_{\mathbb C}-\lambda I)^e=(T_{\mathbb C}-\overline\lambda I)^e\sigma$. Therefore $\sigma$ carries $\ker(T_{\mathbb C}-\lambda I)^e$ anti-linearly onto $\ker(T_{\mathbb C}-\overline\lambda I)^e$.

items.title: A nonreal eigenvector yields an invariant real two-plane and the standard rotation-scaling block
items.strategy: Write a nonreal eigenvector as $u+iv$ with $u,v$ in the fixed real form. Comparing real and imaginary parts of $(T-a-bi)(u+iv)=0$ gives the invariant plane and its matrix $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}a&-b\\ b&a\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ with $b\ne0$.

pages.title: Complexification, Realification and Real Structures: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The standard embedding $\mathbb R^n\hookrightarrow\mathbb C^n$ is the canonical complexification map
items.strategy: Identify $\mathbb C\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb R^n$ with $\mathbb C^n$ by sending $z\otimes e_j$ to the $j$th standard vector scaled by $z$, and track the real basis vectors under the canonical embedding.

items.title: Complexifying a real polynomial space gives the same degree bound with complex coefficients
items.strategy: Write a complexified polynomial as $p+iq$ with $p,q$ real and check directly that the universal map identifies $\mathbb C\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb R[x]_{\le d}$ with $\mathbb C[x]_{\le d}$.

items.title: Realifying $\mathbb C^n$ gives $\mathbb R^{2n}$ with basis $e_1,ie_1,\dots,e_n,ie_n$
items.strategy: Start from the standard complex basis of $\mathbb C^n$, rewrite every vector in real and imaginary parts, and verify real linear independence of the doubled basis.

items.title: The real quarter-turn diagonalises after complexification but has no real eigenvector
items.strategy: For the matrix $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, compute the eigenvalues $\pm i$ over $\mathbb C$, diagonalise there, and compare with the absence of real roots of $x^2+1$.

items.title: One nonreal eigenvector reconstructs the invariant real plane of a rotation-scaling block
items.strategy: Take an eigenvector $u+iv$ for $a+bi$ with $b\ne0$, pass to real and imaginary parts, and display the real $2\times2$ block on $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{u,v\}$.

items.title: Different conjugations on $\mathbb C^2$ can have different fixed real forms
items.strategy: Compare coordinatewise complex conjugation with a conjugation twisted by a complex-linear involution, and compute the two fixed real subspaces explicitly.

items.title: A complex-linear map need not preserve a chosen real form
items.strategy: Choose a fixed conjugation on $\mathbb C^2$ and a complex-linear operator that does not commute with it; the descent criterion then shows that the map does not come from the fixed real form.

items.title: FALSE: complexification doubles finite dimension
items.strategy: Refute the claim with $\mathbb R^n$, whose complexification is $\mathbb C^n$ and therefore has the same numerical dimension over its new scalar field.

items.title: FALSE: every complex vector space has a preferred real form
items.strategy: Use one complex vector space with two distinct conjugations and compare their fixed subspaces. The difference shows that a real form is extra structure, not canonical data.

items.title: FALSE: every complex-linear operator descends to every chosen real form
items.strategy: Use a chosen conjugation and an operator that fails to commute with it. The descent criterion isolates the missing hypothesis exactly.

items.title: FALSE: complexification creates a real eigenvector whenever it creates a complex one
items.strategy: The quarter-turn on $\mathbb R^2$ gains the eigenvalues $\pm i$ after complexification but still has no real eigenvector, so the real and complex eigenvalue questions are different.

pages.title: Exterior Powers, Orientation and Hodge Duality

items.title: Alternating $k$-linear maps
The $k$th exterior power as the tensor-power quotient by repeated-vector relations
Decomposable $k$-vectors and the basic wedge product
The graded exterior algebra $\Lambda V$
The induced map $\Lambda^kT$ on exterior powers
Orientation of a finite-dimensional real vector space
Exterior powers represent alternating multilinear maps and are unique up to unique isomorphism
items.strategy: Factor an alternating $k$-linear map through the tensor power, note that the repeated-vector relations lie in its kernel, and pass to the quotient. Uniqueness is the usual representing-object argument.

items.title: The basic wedge map $(v_1,\dots,v_k)\mapsto v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_k$ is multilinear and alternating
items.strategy: Because the wedge is the image of the universal tensor map under a quotient, multilinearity is inherited from tensors and alternation is forced by the repeated-vector relations.

items.title: Increasing-index wedges of a basis form a basis of $\Lambda^kV$
items.strategy: Start from the tensor-product basis, use alternation to rewrite every wedge into increasing order, and prove independence by evaluating against alternating coordinate forms.

items.title: If $\dim V=n$, then $\dim\Lambda^kV=\binom{n}{k}$
items.strategy: The basis theorem indexes a basis of $\Lambda^kV$ by the $k$-element subsets of an ordered basis of $V$, so the dimension is the resulting count.

items.title: If $k>\dim V$, then $\Lambda^kV=0$
items.strategy: When $k$ exceeds the basis size, there are no increasing $k$-tuples, so the basis theorem leaves no nonzero basis wedges.

items.title: A decomposable wedge is nonzero exactly when its vectors are linearly independent
items.strategy: Dependent vectors give a repeated direction after solving one vector in terms of the others, so alternation kills the wedge. For independent vectors, extend to a basis and observe that the wedge is one of the basis vectors from the preceding theorem.

items.title: Exterior multiplication is well defined, graded, associative, unital, and graded-commutative
items.strategy: Define products on decomposable wedges by concatenation, descend from the tensor algebra, and compute the sign of block swaps. In characteristic two, formulate the law through alternation rather than a sign cancellation that becomes vacuous.

items.title: Exterior powers are functorial
items.strategy: Use the induced tensor map on the quotient, then check the identity and composition laws on decomposable wedges and lift them to the whole exterior power.

items.title: In basis-wedge coordinates, the matrix of $\Lambda^kT$ is the signed matrix of $k$-minors
items.strategy: Expand $T(e_{j_1})\wedge\cdots\wedge T(e_{j_k})$ in the wedge basis and collect coefficients. Multilinearity and alternation leave exactly the determinant of each $k\times k$ submatrix.

items.title: On $\Lambda^{n}V$, the induced map $\Lambda^{n}T$ is multiplication by $\det T$
items.strategy: When $k=n$, the exterior power is one-dimensional with basis the wedge of an ordered basis, and the signed-minor matrix has the single entry $\det T$.

items.title: Determinant multiplicativity follows from the top exterior power
items.strategy: Compare $\Lambda^n(S\circ T)$ with $\Lambda^nS\circ\Lambda^nT$ on the one-dimensional space $\Lambda^nV$ and read off the two resulting scalars.

items.title: A real linear isomorphism preserves or reverses orientation according to the sign of its determinant
items.strategy: Track one positively oriented basis through the map. The top exterior action multiplies its oriented volume element by $\det T$, so the sign decides whether the transported basis remains in the chosen orientation class.

items.title: The Gram inner product on $\Lambda^kV$
The Gram formula gives a well-defined positive-definite inner product on exterior powers, and $\|v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_k\|^2$ is the Gram determinant
items.strategy: Define the pairing on decomposable wedges by the determinant of the Gram matrix, descend it through the quotient, and use the Gram-determinant criterion together with the basis theorem to prove positivity and the independence test.

items.title: The oriented unit volume form
The Hodge star on an oriented finite-dimensional real inner-product space
The Hodge star exists uniquely and is given by the complementary-basis formula in an oriented orthonormal basis
items.strategy: For fixed degree $k$, represent the functional $\beta\mapsto \alpha\wedge\beta$ against the one-dimensional top exterior power using the Gram inner product and the chosen unit volume form. In an oriented orthonormal basis, compute the image of each basis wedge by the complementary index set and its permutation sign.

items.title: The Hodge star is an isometry and satisfies $\star^2=(-1)^{k(n-k)}$ on $\Lambda^kV$
items.strategy: Apply the orthonormal-basis formula twice. The same basis calculation shows that $\star$ permutes an orthonormal basis up to sign, so it preserves the Gram inner product.

items.title: Interior product on the exterior algebra
Interior product is the adjoint of exterior multiplication by a vector
items.strategy: For each $v$, exterior multiplication by $v$ is a linear map $\Lambda^kV\to\Lambda^{k+1}V$ between finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, so it has a unique adjoint. Compute that adjoint on decomposable basis wedges and identify it with contraction by $v$.

items.title: Exterior multiplication and interior product satisfy the graded anticommutation identity
items.strategy: Verify the identity on decomposable wedges by separating whether the contracted vector already appears. Extend by linearity and use the adjoint characterization to keep the sign bookkeeping honest.

items.title: In oriented Euclidean three-space, the cross product is $\star(u\wedge v)$
items.strategy: Using the standard coordinate cross-product formula in an oriented orthonormal basis, verify directly that both constructions are bilinear, alternating, orthogonal to the input vectors, and have the same oriented unit-basis values. The uniqueness forced by those properties identifies them.

pages.title: Exterior Powers, Orientation and Hodge Duality: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Bases and dimensions of exterior powers of $\mathbb R^2$, $\mathbb R^3$, and $\mathbb R^4$
items.strategy: List the increasing-index wedge bases explicitly and count them degree by degree to match the dimension formula and the vanishing above top degree.

items.title: A wedge product detects linear dependence in concrete coordinates
items.strategy: Compute a few sample wedges in low dimension and compare the zero and nonzero cases with the linear-independence criterion.

items.title: All exterior powers of a diagonal operator are diagonal
items.strategy: Apply the functoriality and minor-matrix theorem to a diagonal matrix and read the diagonal entries as the products of the chosen eigenvalues.

items.title: A concrete second exterior-power matrix matches the signed $2\times2$ minors
items.strategy: Choose one non-diagonal matrix, compute $\Lambda^2T$ on the wedge basis directly, and compare each coefficient with the corresponding signed minor.

items.title: Oriented area and volume are recovered from wedges and Gram determinants
items.strategy: Compute the norm squares of sample wedges from their Gram matrices and compare them with the familiar squared area or volume formulas.

items.title: The Hodge star in dimensions two, three, and four
items.strategy: Write the star of each basis wedge in oriented orthonormal coordinates and check the square and norm formulas degree by degree.

items.title: The cross product is recovered from $\star(u\wedge v)$ in $\mathbb R^3$
items.strategy: Compute $u\wedge v$, apply the Hodge star, and compare with the coordinate cross-product formula on a few sample pairs.

items.title: Reversing orientation negates the Hodge star while keeping the metric fixed
items.strategy: Compare the oriented unit volume form and Hodge star for two opposite orientations on the same Euclidean space and compute the sign change on basis wedges.

items.title: A bivector in $\mathbb R^4$ need not be decomposable
items.strategy: Use a sum such as $e_1\wedge e_2+e_3\wedge e_4$, wedge it with itself, and show the result cannot vanish as it would for a decomposable bivector.

items.title: FALSE: $\Lambda^kV$ is canonically a subspace of $V^{\otimes k}$ over every field
items.strategy: The exterior power is defined as a quotient of the tensor power. Show that the quotient map need not admit a canonical splitting, so without extra structure there is no preferred subspace realizing $\Lambda^kV$ inside $V^{\otimes k}$.

items.title: FALSE: an inner product determines an orientation
items.strategy: On one Euclidean space, exhibit the two opposite orientations with the same metric. The Hodge-star example makes the difference visible while the inner product stays fixed.

items.title: FALSE: an orientation determines an inner product
items.strategy: Keep one orientation on $\mathbb R^n$ and compare two distinct positive-definite inner products. Their Gram norms and Hodge stars differ, so orientation alone is insufficient.

items.title: FALSE: Hodge star needs only the vector-space structure
items.strategy: Compare the stars arising from different orientations or different inner products on the same underlying vector space. The operator changes, so it is not purely linear-algebraic without metric and orientation data.

pages.title: Matrix Norms, Condition Numbers and Numerical Stability

items.title: Absolute and relative forward error for an approximate value of a problem map
Absolute and relative local condition numbers of a problem map
The matrix norm induced by a published vector p-norm
Induced matrix norms are compatible with multiplication, submultiplicative, and satisfy ||I|| = 1
items.strategy: Use the defining supremum over nonzero vectors. Compatibility is immediate from the ratio definition, submultiplicativity follows by inserting Bx into the estimate for A, and the identity has norm one because every nonzero vector attains ratio one.

items.title: The induced 1-norm is the maximum column sum and the induced infinity-norm is the maximum row sum
items.strategy: For the 1-norm, expand Ax by columns and use the triangle inequality to bound ||Ax||_1 by the maximum column sum times ||x||_1, then attain equality on a basis vector at a maximizing column. The infinity-norm is the rowwise analogue, with equality on a sign choice that saturates a maximizing row.

items.title: The Frobenius norm $||A||_F=(\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^2)^{1/2}$ on real or complex matrices
Spectral and Frobenius norms are unitarily invariant, are given by singular values, and satisfy the sharp rank comparison
items.strategy: Write A = U Sigma V^* by the singular value decomposition. The spectral norm is the largest singular value by the published operator-norm theorem, the Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the singular-value vector, and left or right multiplication by orthogonal or unitary matrices leaves those singular values unchanged. The rank comparison is the max-versus-Euclidean bound on the singular-value vector, with equality when all nonzero singular values coincide.

items.title: The condition number kappa_p(A) = ||A||_p ||A^{-1}||_p of a nonsingular linear system
Right-hand-side perturbations in Ax = b are amplified by the condition number
items.strategy: If A(x + dx) = b + db, then A dx = db and hence dx = A^{-1} db. Bound dx by ||A^{-1}|| ||db|| and bound ||x|| below by ||b|| / ||A|| to obtain the relative estimate with kappa_p(A).

items.title: Matrix perturbations in Ax = b obey a first-order condition-number bound
items.strategy: Subtract (A + dA)(x + dx) = b from Ax = b to get A dx = -dA(x + dx). Rearranging gives an exact bound with denominator 1 - ||A^{-1}|| ||dA|| whenever that quantity is positive, and the first-order estimate is the small-perturbation expansion of the exact inequality.

items.title: The reciprocal spectral condition number is the relative distance to singularity
items.strategy: Use the smallest singular value to prove that every perturbation smaller than sigma_min(A) leaves A invertible, then attain that distance by subtracting sigma_min(A) times the outer product of a left and right singular vector for the smallest singular value. Divide by ||A||_2 = sigma_max(A).

items.title: Residual bounds on forward error for a nonsingular linear system
items.strategy: For r = b - A x_hat and e = x - x_hat, the identity r = A e gives both r = A e and e = A^{-1} r. Apply the induced-norm inequalities in the two directions and normalize by ||b|| and ||x|| to show that a small residual controls the forward error only up to the condition number.

items.title: Normwise and componentwise backward error for an approximate linear-system solution
Residual formulas for normwise and componentwise backward error
items.strategy: Write the residual as r = d b - d A x_hat. Any admissible perturbation must therefore dominate r, which gives the lower bounds. Equality is attained by choosing perturbations aligned with the residual in the normwise case and entrywise saturated in the componentwise case, with the usual 0/0 = 0 convention.

items.title: The standard relative floating-point model and unit roundoff
Forward and backward stability for a problem family under an arithmetic model
If |delta_i| <= u and nu < 1, then (1 + delta_1) ... (1 + delta_n) = 1 + theta_n with |theta_n| <= gamma_n
items.strategy: Expand the product only through its extremal estimates: it lies between (1 - u)^n and (1 + u)^n. Geometric-series algebra turns the upper deviation into gamma_n = nu / (1 - nu), and theta_n is defined as the product minus one.

items.title: The computed floating-point dot product obeys componentwise and normwise error bounds
items.strategy: Model each product and each addition by the relative floating-point rule. Absorb the resulting factors with the theta_n lemma to rewrite the computed dot product as the exact dot product of slightly perturbed summands, then take absolute values to obtain the normwise bound.

items.title: Local conditioning times backward error controls forward error to first order
items.strategy: Interpret a backward error as the size of the smallest nearby data perturbation for which the computed answer is exact. Apply the local condition-number inequality at that nearby input and then normalize by the definition of relative forward error; the first-order form is exactly the local linearization built into the condition-number definition.

items.title: For full-column-rank A, the normal equations square the spectral condition number
items.strategy: The normal-equation matrix is A^* A. Its eigenvalues are the squared singular values of A, so its 2-norm condition number is sigma_max(A)^2 / sigma_min(A)^2 = kappa_2(A)^2. The full-column-rank hypothesis is exactly what makes sigma_min(A) positive.

items.title: Exact rank is locally constant at full-rank matrices and discontinuous at nonmaximal-rank matrices
items.strategy: If A has full rank, its smallest singular value is positive, so every sufficiently small spectral perturbation leaves all singular values positive and preserves rank. If A has nonmaximal rank, add an arbitrarily small singular-vector outer product in a zero singular direction to raise the rank, proving discontinuity there.

items.title: Numerical rank relative to a declared norm, scale, and tolerance
In the spectral norm, numerical rank counts the singular values above the declared threshold
items.strategy: Use Eckart-Young to identify the least spectral-norm distance from A to the set of matrices of rank at most k with the next singular value. Comparing that distance with the declared threshold gives the smallest admissible exact rank, hence the numerical rank. Changing the threshold changes the count whenever a singular value lies between the two thresholds.

pages.title: Matrix Norms, Condition Numbers and Numerical Stability: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Two 2x2 systems can have dramatically different condition numbers
items.strategy: Compute kappa_1 and kappa_infinity for one diagonal matrix and one nearly singular matrix with the same shape. The comparison makes the geometry of well-conditioning versus ill-conditioning visible without any asymptotics.

items.title: Low-order Hilbert matrices already have large condition numbers
items.strategy: Compute the inverse of H_2 and H_3 explicitly and evaluate one induced condition number. The point is not asymptotic growth but that severe ill-conditioning appears at very small orders.

items.title: Vandermonde conditioning improves after centering and scaling the nodes
items.strategy: Compare two small Vandermonde systems representing the same interpolation problem before and after an affine change of variable. The rescaled system has a visibly smaller condition number, so conditioning depends on the chosen coordinates even when the underlying polynomial task is the same.

items.title: A tiny residual does not force a small forward error
items.strategy: Use a diagonal system with one very small singular value. An approximate solution can miss the small component badly while leaving the residual tiny in norm, exactly because the inverse amplifies that residual by the condition number.

items.title: A backward-stable computed solution of an ill-conditioned system can still have large forward error
items.strategy: Choose an ill-conditioned diagonal system and an approximate solution whose residual gives a backward error of the same order as the small diagonal entry. The backward error is tiny, but the forward error is order one, showing both that ill-conditioning is not the same as instability and that backward stability does not remove ill-conditioning.

items.title: A cancellation-prone formula can be replaced by a stable reformulation
items.strategy: Evaluate 1 - sqrt(1-z) for small z both directly and after rationalization. The direct form loses relative accuracy through cancellation, while the algebraically equivalent reformulation z / (1 + sqrt(1-z)) avoids subtracting nearby quantities.

items.title: A short floating-point dot product obeys the gamma_n error bound
items.strategy: Choose short vectors whose exact dot product and absolute summand total are easy to compute. Apply the theorem directly to verify the componentwise perturbation form and the resulting normwise bound on the computed value.

items.title: Normal equations square the conditioning compared with QR on a nearly dependent least-squares problem
items.strategy: Take a full-column-rank matrix with one small singular value and compare kappa_2(A) with kappa_2(A^T A). The normal equations magnify the ill-conditioning by a square, while a QR solve keeps the original least-squares conditioning visible instead.

items.title: Condition number depends on the chosen norm and on diagonal rescaling
items.strategy: Use one explicit matrix, compute condition numbers in at least two induced norms, and then compare it with a diagonally rescaled equivalent system. The numbers change, so condition number is not an invariant of a bare linear relation without declared norms and scaling.

items.title: The same matrix can have two different numerical ranks under two declared tolerances
items.strategy: Pick a diagonal matrix with one singular value sitting between two tolerances. The spectral numerical-rank formula then gives two different counts from the same exact matrix, so numerical rank is not an exact invariant.

items.title: The relative floating-point model excludes overflow, underflow, and invalid operations
items.strategy: Use one operation that overflows, one that underflows into a subnormal regime, and one invalid expression such as 0/0. These cases produce infinity, subnormal behavior, or NaN rather than a result of the form x(1 + delta), so the standard model needs its exclusions stated explicitly.

Formal Languages, Encodings, and Decision Problems

items.title: Computation alphabets, words, the empty word, and $\Sigma^*$
The computation-word convention agrees with the published finite-word definition
items.strategy: Let $\Sigma$ be finite. Unpack the local definition of a word of length $n$ as a function $n\to\Sigma$ and compare it term-for-term with [[def-finite-words-factor-avoidance-and-prefix-states]]. The only real work is to note that both pages use the same empty word and the same offset concatenation, so the underlying set $\Sigma^*$ is literally the same set and not merely a canonically isomorphic copy.

items.title: Languages over an alphabet
Boolean operations on languages over a fixed alphabet
Language concatenation, powers, and Kleene star
Language concatenation is associative
items.strategy: For $w\in (L_1L_2)L_3$, choose witnesses $u\in L_1$, $v\in L_2$, and $x\in L_3$ with $w=(uv)x$. The offset definition of word concatenation makes $((uv)x)(i)$ and $(u(vx))(i)$ equal for every position $i$, so $(uv)x=u(vx)$. This gives $w\in L_1(L_2L_3)$, and the reverse inclusion is symmetric.

items.title: Kleene star is the least concatenation-closed language containing $L$ and $\varepsilon$
items.strategy: First show directly from the recursive definition of powers that $\varepsilon\in L^*$ and $LL^*\subseteq L^*$. For minimality, let $K$ be any language with $\varepsilon\in K$ and $LK\subseteq K$. Prove by induction on $n$ that $L^n\subseteq K$: the base case is $L^0=\{\varepsilon\}$, and the step uses $L^{n+1}=L^nL$ together with the induction hypothesis and the closure assumption. Taking the union over all $n$ gives $L^*\subseteq K$.

items.title: Word reversal and language reversal
Reversal is an involution and reverses concatenation
items.strategy: Prove the word identities first. Induct on the length of the second factor to show $(uv)^R=v^Ru^R$, using the defining clause $(wa)^R=aw^R$. A second induction on length gives $(w^R)^R=w$. The language statements then follow pointwise from the definition $L^R=\{w^R:w\in L\}$.

items.title: Alphabet maps into $\Delta^*$ and their induced maps on words
The induced word map is the unique concatenation-preserving extension
items.strategy: Let $h:\Sigma\to\Delta^*$ be the alphabet map of the definition and let $\widehat h:\Sigma^*\to\Delta^*$ be its induced map. Prove $\widehat h(uv)=\widehat h(u)\widehat h(v)$ by induction on the length of $v$ and the explicit block-concatenation definition of $\widehat h$. For uniqueness, let $g:\Sigma^*\to\Delta^*$ preserve concatenation and agree with $h$ on one-letter words. Induct on word length: the empty word must map to $\varepsilon$, and a nonempty word splits as $ua$, so $g(ua)=g(u)g(a)=\widehat h(u)h(a)=\widehat h(ua)$.

items.title: Effective binary encodings and total decoders
Finite tuples admit effective prefix-free binary encodings
items.strategy: Use an explicit self-delimiting code for a single binary word, for example $c(w)=1^{|w|}0w$. Then encode a tuple $(w_1,\dots,w_k)$ as $1^k0\,c(w_1)\cdots c(w_k)$. Decode by first reading the initial unary block to recover $k$, then parse exactly $k$ self-delimiting word blocks. Prefix-freeness comes from the first block determining the tuple length and each subsequent block determining its own endpoint.

items.title: Decision problems, search problems, and function problems
Instance size and polynomially related encodings
Polynomially related encodings preserve polynomial size bounds
items.strategy: Let $\sigma$ and $\tau$ be polynomially related encodings of the same instance family, and suppose some quantity $m(x)$ satisfies $m(x)\le p(|\sigma(x)|)$ for a polynomial $p$. If $|\sigma(x)|\le q(|\tau(x)|)$ for a polynomial $q$, then $m(x)\le p(q(|\tau(x)|))$, still a polynomial bound. The reverse implication is identical with the roles of $\sigma$ and $\tau$ exchanged.

items.title: FALSE: a language is a set of symbols
items.strategy: Refute the claim on the binary alphabet $\Sigma=\{0,1\}$ with the language $L=\{01\}$. The element $01$ is a word of length two, so $L\subseteq\Sigma^*$ is a language, but $01\notin\Sigma$. The falsehood is exactly the design's syntax-versus-denotation warning: a language is a set of words over an alphabet, not a subset of the alphabet itself.

items.title: FALSE: every effective encoding is prefix-free
items.strategy: Refute the claim with the binary encoding $e(w)=1w$. It is injective, and the total decoder that strips the first bit on inputs beginning with $1$ and returns a fixed malformed-code token otherwise decodes it effectively. But the image is not prefix-free: $e(\varepsilon)=1$ is a prefix of $e(0)=10$.

pages.title: Formal Languages, Encodings, and Decision Problems: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: A concrete calculation of $(L_1L_2)L_3=L_1(L_2L_3)$
items.strategy: Take $L_1=\{a\}$, $L_2=\{\varepsilon,b\}$, and $L_3=\{a,bb\}$ over $\{a,b\}$. Compute $L_1L_2=\{a,ab\}$ and then $(L_1L_2)L_3=\{aa,abb,aba,abbb\}$. Compute $L_2L_3=\{a,bb,ba,bbb\}$ and then $L_1(L_2L_3)=\{aa,abb,aba,abbb\}$. The example should exhibit the same four words on both sides rather than only appealing to the general lemma.

items.title: Ordinary binary numerals and doubled-bit numerals are polynomially related
items.strategy: Encode a natural number $n$ first by its standard binary numeral $\sigma(n)$ and second by the doubled-bit code $\tau(n)$ obtained by replacing each bit by two copies. Then $|\tau(n)|=2|\sigma(n)|$ for every $n$, so the two encodings are polynomially related in the strongest possible way. Check a concrete instance such as $13$, where $\sigma(13)=1101$ and $\tau(13)=11110011$, and then show how a bound like $|\tau(n)|^3$ translates back to $8|\sigma(n)|^3$.

items.title: The language $\{01\}$ is not a set of alphabet symbols
items.strategy: Use the binary alphabet $\Sigma=\{0,1\}$. The one-element set $L=\{01\}$ is a language because $01\in\Sigma^*$, but it is not a subset of $\Sigma$ because $01$ is a word of length two rather than a single symbol. Write both containments explicitly: $01\in\Sigma^*$ and $01\notin\Sigma$.

items.title: The encoding $w\mapsto 1w$ is effective but not prefix-free
items.strategy: Take the encoding $e(w)=1w$ on binary strings. The decoder reads the first bit: if it is $1$, remove it and output the remainder; if it is $0$ or the string is empty, return the fixed malformed-code output. This shows effectiveness directly. Prefix-freeness fails because $1=e(\varepsilon)$ is a proper prefix of $10=e(0)$.
